column1: How do INFJs grieve the loss of a family member?
column3: Right.. This is critical to keep in mind as you read the following. I am speaking only for myself. I am obviously not one of those warm and fluffy infj. Disclosure out of the way, onto the actual answer. Going to answer with the assumption that you mean direct blood relation, like sibling, parent, very close grandparents or perhaps aunts and uncles. The last time I had a remotely typical reaction to death was for my father when I was ten. Ignoring surrounding circumstances and repercussions. I think it was a fairly normal emotional response to a parent passing. My life went to hell after that though, so I’d say that's when things really began to change for me. At least when it came to the subsequent passing of the rest of my family over the years. My family and I.. Let's just say we weren't what the other wanted. The fact we shared blood didn't bring us closer together. For a long time, I actually “strongly disliked” that connection. I viewed it as a taint of sorts. I really couldn't stand being of these people. In my head, it often felt to me like no matter what I did or who I became, I’d still be basically unclean because of my blood. Who I came from. I know everything I took to heart, the lessons I learned, was to spite them, to be different, better than them. So no.. As they passed, I wished them well, thanked them for whatever little good I felt they provided, and pretty much didn’t even blink. In some cases, it was a relief. They were free from their suffering. It's not like I wished them ill or anything. I just didn't feel a sense of loss or anything. Listed as an exception, my mother was the latest to pass. That was rough. She wasn't perfect. Hell, she barely kept me alive, but she was mom. She had her own problems. Some of which I hadn't yet come to really understand till after she passed. In her case, the biggest thing I feel is regret that I didn't understand her better. She probably did the best she could, considering. So I of course find myself feeling like I could of done more or tried a little harder. So, to begin wrapping up this part of the answer.. Aside from general “I wish things could've been different” sentiments.. I didn't grieve my family, as there was nothing emotional there to be hurt. Now.. Was one of my chosen to pass? I might try to lie down and die with them, or go john wick on whoever took ’em from me. I’d erect a shrine in their memory, where I'd visit every time I had something to share with them that we used to talk about. I’d do all I could to keep their memory, their spirit alive. I’d do my best to honor them, their memory, I'd make their mission part of my own. I'd have moments where I'd literally break down cursing them and the gods for separating us.. It would always hurt. I would always remember, and fondly recall all the good, the bad, and the ugly. For me.. Family made me what I am. While I am proud of that person, I do wonder what might've been had we actually cared for each other, been better people. For my closing thought.. Just because you're related to someone doesn't mean you need to care. Nobody can help the genetic lottery. Some get lucky, others not so much. Personally, I feel “infj, how do you grieve for someone you cared about/loved?” Is a somewhat better question.

column1: Is it wrong to date someone who is still grieving the loss of a family member?
column3: Depends on what you mean by “Date.” In some dialects, “Date” means “hook up.” In some, it means “courtship.” Others use it to mean prostitution. A person who is grieving may be feeling raw and vulnerable and fragile. Or, they may be adjusting to a loss, and further along in their healing (at least, at the moment. Grief is not linear.) Ask yourself this: Is my intention for this person’s highest good? Am I interested in their healing, growth, and happiness? Or am I motivated MUCH MORE by my own wants and desires? As long as you’re not exploiting the person’s vulnerability, or ignoring any indications they are giving you that they DON’T WANT to date you, then you should be fine. Ask the questions you fear the answers to. Do you want to date me? Do you want to date now? What do you need in this moment?

column1: How do I reply to “How are you?” when I’m grieving the loss of a family member?
column3: I am sorry for your loss and the grief you are going through. I am going through some very heavy grieving right now so I will answer your question with my personal experience. If it’s someone who doesn’t know me well and/or doesn’t know that I am grieving I stick with the “I’m fine and you?” standard reply. If it’s someone who knows me and my situation, I still keep it brief but answer honestly. Things like, “I’m hanging in there.” “Doing okay. Every day can be a bit of a roller coaster but I’m handling it.” “I’m good. It’s a terrible situation but I’m doing my best.” I hope those examples are of some help to you.

column1: How long does it take for a cat to grieve the loss of a friend or family member?
column3: I had three cats once years ago. Two of them were brother & sister from the same litter that I got as kittens and the other was a male 10 years older than them. When the sister kitty was only 4 yrs old she suddenly became sick with acute kidney failure and I ended up having to have her euthanized. I brought her body home and layed her on the floor so her brother and the other male cat could take a look and sniff if they wanted, etc. My 10 yr old cat sort of sniffed and was like “whatever” and walked away. Her brother, however, was scared and seemed shocked and I wasn’t sure if he knew what was going on. I would assume instinct would kick in and he’d realize that his sister was dead but he seemed too scared to go to the body. He mourned her for a couple of weeks. We had a 1500sqft completely finished basement where I put the kittens at night and that’s where their food/water bowls, beds, and their litter boxes were. I’d feed them in the morning then keep the door to the basement open so that when they were finished with breakfast they could come upstairs and have access to the rest of the house for the entire day, then I’d put them back down at bedtime. After sister kitty died, her brother would go to the top of the basement stairs and wait for her to run around the corner and run up the stairs and when she didn’t he’d jump up on the couch next to me and had the saddest look on his face. Then he’d go back and peek around the corner to see if he could see her and when he didn’t, again he’d walk up to me and lay next to me and look so sad. He did this off and on for a couple of weeks until he realized she wasn’t coming back. He seemed to finally accept it and although he didn’t really hang out with my other cat I would catch them laying on my bed together so I think he found comfort in that.

column1: Adult What are some things that a person grieving the loss of a family member should avoid saying? What are some things that they can say that will help them move on from grief?
column3: Topics or sayings to avoid. They’re better off now…. we don’t know that. They're with Jesus, angels, up in heaven, with grandma. They wouldn't want to see you like this so cheer up. Get over it. You should be over it by now. Don’t cry You're young enough to have more children. Avoid the griever altogether. What to do. Just listening. Being there. Offer a pitch should they want to talk. Give a thinking of you phone call. Give them a heads-up that associates may avoid them, This is because of fear they will say something wrong and hurt the griever. They don’t know what to say, so they avoid. Get the booklet: Good Grief by Granger Westberg. It’s easy to understand and inexpensive.

column1: How has having a close family member suffer from mental illness affected you and do you grieve the loss of a relationship?
column3: Growing up with mentally ill parents is an uphill task. So growing up is basically swimming against the current all the time. How this affects you? If you are born with resilient genes you can escape with severe PTSD but otherwise good mental health. But most people don’t survive this well. As for the loss of these relationships, yes it’s a huge loss. You never had them in the first place because these people are not fit to parent. Looking at the larger picture, it’s mentally ill grand parents who raise traumatized children and the cycle goes on. So it can be the loss of not just parents, but aunts uncles grandparents. Not to mention toxic siblings because dysfunctional families often destroy sibling relationships. It’s a huge loss that you can grieve and let go. The good news is that you can escape, recover, build your own wonderful family and be a wonderful parent. You can love. And enjoy life. Grieve all you want, but get away and Live your life. I did.

column1: Should I wait on an INTJ who is grieving the loss of a close family member? He enjoys me and wants to explore what the future can hold for us, but doesn't feel he's capable of a committed relationship right now.
column3: I’m surprised by some of the INTJ answers on here from what seems to be the guys saying its a line. Look I don’t think you should wait for anyone. However INTJ is pretty big on grieving and processing the big life stuff very privately and would also be very reluctant to put this on someone new in their life and push the boundary of too much too soon. While there seems to be a lot of criticism about INTJ being introverted and this being misinterpreted to INTJ having some apparent major emotional malfunction all it really means is we just process things quietly, recharge by taking time out alone and are selective of who we open up to rather than spew every single emotion over everyone unfiltered without a second thought. I think our ability to control our emotions and check in with the brain before we speak and often choose not to is what makes people uncomfortable. The contradiction to this, and often from the very same people who judge INTJs different way of processing emotions so harshly, is within moments of a new connection we get finite detail of all their problems, tears, wanting advice and pretty big favours usually trying to force a relationship to a level that should take time to develop naturally. INTJ also often learn that the expectations of those people are always a one way street. We are cautious of avoiding that uncomfortable situation in the first place but even more so to not do that to other people especially if we are genuinely interested in them. I can also tell you as an INTJ that I would be very reluctant to go into a new relationship if I didn’t think I could truly make time for it and didn’t have control over that with something like grieving or supporting family with a significant death. A true connection for INTJ doesn’t happen very often and we would be very careful with that. If you were well down the track of an established relationship with INTJ it would be a very different story and possibly the only person they are talking to. INTJ are a slow burn and big on authenticity. If they have told you this is going on, would like to explore it but just can’t handle that right now its likely true. Again don’t wait for them. However you can keep the door open. I would suggest the best thing you could say is ‘hey I know you like to keep to yourself right now with everything going on but just saying hi and seeing how your doing’.

column1: Do pets understand when their owner is grieving the loss of a human family member?
column3: Animals have the IQ generally of a two year old at the most. They definitely know something is making their human very sad. But the complexity of knowing what exactly is the problem they may not comprehend. But they know if it is because of a family member in the house is no longer there. They won’t understand as much when its a loved one who never lived in the house with them per say. My Jack Russel was very distraught over hearing me cry out loud when I lost my 18 year old son. A year latter I was laughing out loud like for the first time in a long time and I had tears from laughing. My boy looked at me very distraught over the sound of me like it was happening all over again. I literally had to go over and console him that every thing was ok and we went outside to toss the ball. It wasn’t until that moment how my state of being affected him. My poor boy!

column1: Do dogs really grieve the loss of family members and fellow pets, or are they just mirroring the owners' behaviors without feeling emotions? I thought it was grief, but someone said they don't feel emotions, and they just feel the energy from humans.
column3: Do dogs really grieve the loss of family members and fellow pets, or are they just mirroring the owners' behaviors without feeling emotions? I thought it was grief, but someone said they don't feel emotions, and they just feel the energy from humans. I firmly believe that pets grieve when a family member dies or a fellow pet dies. I had three dogs. One was about eight years old when I got my other two dogs. The older of the two new dogs was six months old when I got another puppy. So, the girl is six months older than the boy and they are inseparable. The older one died and there was not a lot of reaction from the other two who had each other while the older dog just kind of hung out with me. Fast forward …… the younger of the two by six months, dies. He has just turned eleven and the other one is 11.5 years old. At first she did not seem to notice that the other dog was not there but after a couple of days she began to look for him. She would wander all over the house looking into rooms. When I would take her for a walk she never wanted to go any farther than a block and kept looking back at our house. Often, she would turn around and want to go back home. She did not want us to leave her. If we tried to leave her alone in the house she would bolt out the door as if to make sure she came with us. We did not leave her alone for about two months. She stopped eating regularly. She was lethargic and just wanted to lay around. She also followed me around the house and did not want me out of her sight. This was something new for her but something the dog who had died always did. She was losing her independence. On walks if we saw someone in the distance walking a large dog her head would perk up as if she was wishing it was our dog. This went on for about three months until we noticed that she was starting to enjoy her walks again. She started eating regularly again. So, yes. She grieved for her boy.Freddy, the Ridgeback in the rear is the one who died. Kaede, the husky mix in front, is still with us and is almost 14.Here they are as puppies. Kaede, in the rear, was six months old when I got Freddy, the Ridgeback in the forefront. They were best friends for 11 years. EDIT. On 17th December 2018 our beautiful girl, Kaede, left us.
column9: Absolutely they grieve…my furbaby and I lost my husband this last June. He hardly ate anything for three to four weeks and kept looking around for my husband…anytime my dog was inside he would lay on my husband's side of the bed and on his pillows. He still on occasion will look for my husband after he smells something of his.

column1: How does one comfort a friend who just lost a loved one?
column3: When someone is in pain, chances are they need to talk. They need to talk and talk, because every time they talk they process, because every time they talk they untangle, because every time they talk they forgive themselves a tiny bit more for the role they believe they played in this horrible thing that has happened to them. You don’t need to do anything. You don’t need to fix or help or adjust or clarify. You don’t need to console. What you need is to clear your calendar. What you need is to push everything else aside. What you need is to listen, just listen, and either intently, soundlessly think or even say out loud — there is no limit. There is no limit to the amount of time I am willing to sit here and listen to you.

column1: How can I eliminate the urge to consume alcohol or drugs as a coping mechanism? I've been grieving over the loss of family members, and now my wife and family. It's been years. Still I ask, how?
column3: For some reason, Quora won’t approve my losing my daughter in a tragic accident as a credential. But that’s what happened, and she was only 21, and beautiful inside and out. When you use alcohol or drugs to cope, the situation never changes - you wake up the next day, your family members are still dead, and now you have a drug or alcohol problem as well. There are many support groups for people who have lost the ones that they love. Sometimes you have to try several until you find the right fit. A good therapist can also help you, but again, sometimes you have to try more than one before you find one that you like. Also think of a way that you can memorialize your loved ones, perhaps by supporting a group that is connected to the illness or crime that took their life. And, of course, you will find others in your situation in drug and alcohol support groups.

Animals grieve when they lose loved ones whether human or animal. It takes time for the grieving process to complete its stages, and we need to be patient and kind while they go through this process. Also what is your definition of grieves too much. I would allow them to go through the process of grieving and love them. Hold them thereby giving them sanctuary. Just like humans, they will come out it.

column1: What advice would you give to someone who is supporting a family member through the grieving process after a pregnancy loss?
column3: Thank you for reaching out and supporting this person. I’m so sorry your friend or relative has had a death of such magnitude. If I were the one to support my relative or friend I would let her talk about whatever she wants to talk about as often she wants to talk. You can just be there with her and in the moment with her. You can offer her some light fruit or a light meal of some sort. I say this, because usually people really don’t have an appetite while grieving. Or they could over eat too. Give her a approximate a month or two and suggest that she go to her local hospital or hospice. Please call and get that information for her. They have professional counselors who specialize in grief counseling. It’s free and they have individual sessions and group therapy as well. You could go with her to support her and any family members too. If she says she doesn’t want to go to any type of grief counseling. You can call or stop by your local hospice and get some information and/or pamphlets. Don’t hand them to her directly leave them in a place in her home somewhere. One day she might decide to go for counseling. Let her know that you are there for her anytime she needs you. Thank you for being a good friend. I hope this helps you and your friend or family members. May God send her peace of mind and love.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: When you say loss, I’m taking it you mean a loved one who is deceased. The harsh truth is no you don’t ever get over it. You learn to find some sense of acceptance of it. Until the day you leave this world there will only be learning to live with and through that loss that forever has an open wound in your heart that will never fully heal along with the void of their absence. I can assure you there will come a day you will smile before you cry whenever thinking of them. It doesn’t mean you are not still carrying around some sadness, but it will be much less compared to the rawness right after their passing. There will still be those days down the road you still will shed a tear and it will catch you off guard, but it’s normal. Any and all emotions you go through is ok to feel how you feel. If anyone tells you its been long enough and is time to move on, tell them to take a hike. They can’t possibly understand the deep loss you feel from your loved one(s) death if they haven’t experienced it themselves. When the day comes they too will experience and begin to understand what you have been experiencing this whole time. I can tell you as a 42 year old woman today who lost my mother when I was 19 I still have moments when I still cry. In fact, it just happened to me the other day hearing a song that reminded me of her. Give yourself the time and space to grieve. It is part of the healing process. Be good to yourself and don’t allow anyone to tell you how to feel or say to get over it, you never will completely be over it. I wish you many beautiful moments of happiness when thinking of your loved one to help you through the sad times.🦋
column9: So on point and a true description of grief. I lost my parents 12 years ago and still shed tears, especially when I heard that I have a progressive decrease in kidney function. I wanted them so badly. I would have more hope. They were my best friends and my support. They were always there for me and had my back. I don't have that now.

column1: What are the most interesting shows of respect by one culture to another?
column3: Three examples: One: Indonesia gave President Bush (Sr) a Komodo dragon back in 1990.Two: The president of Azerbaijan gave the Clintons a custom, hand-woven rug in 1997.There are strict government rules in the US on gifts. They can’t accept presents that have a value of over $400. (My dad is a government official and gets presents like this periodically from leaders. He received a set of swords from Mongol leaders but couldn’t keep them.) Three: Oddly enough the sweetest gift I’ve heard of was from a Maasai tribe. It was in the aftermath of 9/11, and a lot of people in my country were grieving and reeling from the loss of life. Many people, even today, know someone who lost a family member. Extending their condolences, a Maasai tribeoffered the United States ambassador 14 holy cows that they had put a blessing on. It was the highest expression of sympathy in Maasai culture as the cows were their livelihood. Those cows are everything to them. Initially the Maasai were upset that the ambassador couldn’t send the cows back to the United States as there were logistical/legal constraints. As an alternative, the U.S. created a special farm for the cows to feed/reproduce and used the proceeds to offer scholarships to the tribe’s young people, which they greatly appreciated.
column9: As a Kenyan I am proud of them

column1: What lessons have you learnt from grieving the loss of a parent?
column3: The lessons that I have learnt are that the sadness and emptiness never go away. My mother was staying with me from the last 16 years after my father passed away. She had 2 falls after that and though there were no fractures, she couldn't sit for more than 15 to 30 minutes without getting a bad back pain. So she was partially bed ridden. I was taking care of her. Whenever I was sick or needed a small holiday, my sister would take care of her. Whenever I fell sick and told her I would most probably die, she would say that as long as she was alive nothing would happen to us. She was right because even if any of us fell sick, we always recovered after a few days. Also inspite of us going out for purchases or my husband going to office during the Corona pandemic none of us caught it. Of course we were taking great precautions because of my aged mother. My mother passed away in August 2021 due to age related problems. From the last 4 months, I have been facing some health issue or the other. Last month, inspite of still taking adequate precautions all of us including all members of my sisters family were down with cold, cough and fever. My sisters family has recovered now, but my son and husband continue to have cough and I have still not recovered fully. All these years, I was under the misconception that we were taking care of my mother. I was very wrong. To all outward appearances I was taking care of her. But in actual fact, it was she who was taking care of us by keeping her hand of blessing and protection on our heads. As long as she was alive we were safe. Now we are like the tree swaying in the breeze. We don't know which gust of wind will knock us down. So to all children who are staying with, and taking care of their parents, don't be under the misconception that you are the one taking care of them. In actual, they are protecting and taking care of you with their prayers and blessings. These are the things which I have realised whilst grieving the loss of a parent.

column1: Is it necessary for someone to fully overcome their grief before adopting another animal? If so, how long does it typically take to grieve the loss of a pet?

People differ in how they deal with mourning. Nothing is right or wrong. Whatever eases your spirit, go with it. Yesterday I took a coat out of the closet and found a long cat hair on it; both my longhair cats left for the Rainbow Bridge a year ago. I cried They never leave your heart, but you learn to deal with it.

column1: How do cats cope with the loss of another cat?
column3: They grieve just as much, if not more, as humans do, the loss of their Feline, Canine and Human family members. They also comfort their humans and each other. MINI, now 10 years, was only 6 months old when his brother, ONYX was killed. When my husband dug a grave we had MINI see his brother for the last time. column1: As someone who works in an emergency room, what is your best story?
column3: One evening a young man in his 20′s was brought into the E.R. He had sustained a head injury in an accident. It turned out that he was brain dead, and was only alive due to the aid of machines. He had a very large family, who all showed up. It was a huge family. And, it seemed that they were a relatively poor family. I would also hazard a guess that they were not highly educated, either formally or informally. When confronted with the news, his family was understandably distraught. In their grief, they lashed out at the doctor, saying that all hope wasn’t lost, and their son could be saved. One of the family members put forth the idea that if they had money and good insurance, things would be different, and the young man would be saved. Hospital staff tried to reason with them, telling them that his brain was damaged beyond repair, and nothing could be done. But the family wouldn’t hear it, and kept insisting that if they had money things would be different. One hospital staff pointed out that nothing could be done, even with all the money in the world. To which, the brother of the young man responded, “You could do a brain transplant.” (I kid you not.) The parents immediately grasped at this, and a rally cry went up among the family. “Brain transplant! You could do a brain transplant! If we were rich, you would do it!” No matter what was said, the family would not be consoled, and was convinced that the hospital was holding out providing a brain transplant for their son because they were poor. The ER staff left the family to themselves and discussed the matter.There was no comforting this family. No reasoning. It was suggested that Doctor H. agree to do a brain transplant, and that the doctor explain to the family that for a brain transplant to succeed, there had to be a 100 percent match with the donor brain. And the only way there would be a 100 percent match is if the donor brain was the brain of an immediate family member. Either a Father, Mother, Brother or Sister. Doctor H. said that it was a risky move, but he agreed to it. Doctor H. presented his case to the family. Family members were nodding their heads around the room, commenting under their breath, “I told you so.” There was a moment of silence, and then the dad asked, “Doc, what’s gonna’ happen to the person who gives their brain? What will they do? How will it affect their life?” (Again, I’m not making up this stuff.) Doctor H. looked at them for awhile. How he kept his composure, I don’t know. Finally, he said, “Well, sir, they will die. People can’t live without a brain.” This hit the Dad hard. “Doc,” he said, “Can you give us a moment to discuss this? In private?” Doctor H. told them to take the time that they needed and he would be back in a half hour. Before the half hour was up, the Dad sought out Doctor H. and told him that after much discussion, the family had decided that they sure were gonna’ miss their son. There would be no brain transplant. And then, the family settled into grieving the loss of their son. P.S. Thank you for the edit, Diana Cretu. Peace.
column9: Given the circumstances, it was an elegant and kind way to help the family accept the death of their son. Empathy is understanding a situation from someone else’s perspective, which is especially difficult when it’s vastly different from your own.

column1: What is the rudest/meanest thing a family member has said to you?
column3: It probably wasn’t meant to be rude or mean, but it shot out of my stepmother’s mouth anyway. My brother and I were both in our fifties when our mother died. My father remarried a woman who was rather spoiled. She had been an only child, did not work and still lived off her retired parents. My brother had a family and four children. I was divorced, did not remarry and had a career. Unexpectedly my brother became ill, was diagnosed with cancer and died within a few weeks. It was a shock for everybody. Several months later this family tragedy came up in a telephone conversation with my stepmother. She said for a family with four children the loss of a father is the worst thing that could have happened, and it would have been so much easier if I had died instead of my brother. There would be no grieving children left behind. I must admit it actually took time for me to get over the guilt complex of not dying instead of my brother.

column1: Why do some people grieve more when their dog dies than when a close family member dies?
column3: Your dog gives you unconditional love and loyalty every day. You can be a grouch, lay around the house in your underwear, do crimes, even bring other dogs home to share your life, and your dog will still love you and look up to you. It’s no wonder you might grieve the loss of that kind of friend even more than the death of a family member who lived on the other side of the country, fought you unceasingly over money, and never had a kind word for anyone else in the family. If you want a friend, get a dog. It’s a true saying.
column9: Bingo. Well said.

column1: If a psychopath loses family members such as a father, a mother, a spouse or their children, how would they feel?
column3: We don’t have the brain pathways to feel sadness. We notice loss. It is something that affects us quite differently that neurotypicals. When someone dies, be it a family member, inner circle member, a pet, we are disappointed that they are no longer present. We notice the missing person. We don’t prefer their absence.That’s the extent of it. We don’t mourn, or grieve. It’s just not in our wiring to do so.
column9: I think this is one area where I would wish to be like you. I fear that if I lost any one of my family I would go mad with grief. I fear that I would no longer be functioning, having lost my mind to an abyss of loss. And I know it is inevitable.

column1: My dog passed away and I can't stop thinking about stuff I never did or should have done with him. How do I cope with the loss of my dog?
column3: The passing of our beloved pets brings on emotions so strong and are completely in alignment with the grieving process. I think for some of us, the loss of a pet can be more intense then the loss of a family member. Sounds crazy, but if you are animal passionate, you completely understand that statement. When it comes to dealing with the loss, especially grief, you must forgive yourself. In truth, your dog had no idea you had plans to other things with him that didn’t happen. He was likely just as happy spending the day in bed with you on sick days, watching the football game on the couch on Sunday and cleaning up the mess you made on the kitchen floor while making a big dinner. He simply wanted you! Not what you could do for him. The magic we enjoy with our animals is something we will never (or very rarely) experience with any human being on the planet. That magic is even something we struggle to give back regardless of how hard we may try. This magic is a one of a kind and is something I personally strive to give and receive by those that matter the most to me. The magic I speak of is nothing other than 100% unconditional love. Your dog had it for you. The sorrow you feel with your loss is so incredible that it physically hurts your heart beating in your chest. You feel so much sadness all at once you think you will never be ok again. I have been there in many occasions and I will tell you what makes it better for me. Don’t get me wrong, the pain from the loss will always be there. It will change over time but you will always have memories of your dog that may bring tears to your eyes 10 years from now. My way of dealing with the loss is to get another furry friend. Not to replace my lost one, but to allow myself to love another that needs me as much as I need him. He will keep me distracted, maybe do some things that remind me of my last friend or even make me laugh when I thought I never could again. I know not everyone is one to get another pet right away, but I am usually left with an open void to fill and I know how many animals are literately dying in the shelters waiting for a home like mine to be a part of. It is a win win for me and my new friend. I am sorry for your loss, and pray the sweet memories of the times you shared will soon fill your heavy heart with joy.
column9: Just had to put my best buddy down (Blanco- 3/3/20) after 14 years and 5 months together so I’m heartbroken. But I’ve decided to get another dog in memory of him so I can do something with all this love I would have given my boy that is no longer here.

column1: How would the act be interpreted by attending military members if a family member didn't take the offered flag at a military funeral?
column3: It’s generally understood, during a casualty event, that 1) the family is grieving the loss of their servicemember, and 2) YOU might be interpreted as having taken their servicemember away from them. “I never wanted him to join, and now he’s dead, and it’s YOUR FAULT!” In the extremely large majority of cases, when the government car pulls up to a house, and some servicemembers walk up to the house in their pressed uniforms, and they deliver the horrible news, the family is devastated, but accepts it. After delivering the news, telling them that there will be more work to be done (insurance, burial, etc), and leaving a business card, they leave, and let them begin unpacking their grief. But in a few exceptional cases, something else might happen. There are worst-case stories of a father who loses his shit (I mean, his son just died, do you really blame him?), screams, punches a wall, grabs a baseball bat, and goes outside the trashes the shit out of the government car. (What’s the best response? Do nothing. Not only because he has a bat and could turn on you, but because it would be bad form to have him arrested in the hour that he learned his son died. It’s just a car. Let him do his thing, and report it later. It can be fixed/replaced, and his insurance can be billed. Just let him do it.) Or the wife who threatens bodily harm to herself. Or the mother who drives to the unit and begins picketing. The abnormal cases are rare, but they happen. It’s best to let them happen. They’re grieving. Let them. So my immediate take about a military burial, followed by the next of kin refusing to accept the folded flag, is to simply nod, and not make an issue of it. “He’s dead, and the military did it, and I hate them, and I hate YOU!” I’m not going to fight that emotion. They are going through one of the worst periods of their life, obviously. Refuse the flag? No problem. I am NOT going to make an issue here. If it was offered to the mother, perhaps turn subtly to the father and gesture to him, as though to ask, “Sir, would you like it?” If he indicates yes, hand it to him and say the same words of condolence. (If the parents are divorced, protocol says that each gets their own flag.) I might make a minor, unobtrusive attempt to leave the flag with some member of the family who will accept it, but if the circumstances don’t warrant, then I’m not going to make a big show of it. I’ll hold on to it, and try again in a few days. Same goes for refusing to shake hands, or saying something very unkind under their breath. This is THEIR horrible day to suffer through, not mine. This isn’t about me, or the funeral party. The military members are going to be as crisp, military, professional, and solemn as possible. It’s the uniformed members’ job to be transparent, part of the background, not the stars. Whatever the grieving family is going through is okay. Nothing they do is going to be wrong on this day. When they leave this spot, they’re leaving one of their own behind, at the bottom of a hole. What’s the interpretation by attending military members if the family doesn’t accept the flag? To feel horrible for them, and to carry on.
column9: Your answer embodies professionalism.

column1: Is it okay to reach out to an ex when you learn they’ve lost a close family member that passed away, even if we broke up on bad terms?
column3: Your ex is human too. Said human is grieving the loss of a family member. Reaching out to give them condolences, and be there for them is the best way to be human.

column1: How can I cope with the death of my spouse?
column3: My husband died 3 months ago (Nov of 2015) and I'm still working through my grief. Here's the thing. Everyone deals with grief and pain differently. Some people face it directly while others (like me) find ways to escape. One thing to remember is that while it may seem like people are just over it, that can be deceiving. Many of my friends and family members have told me how well I am handling everything. How they would not handle things as well if they were in the same situation and that I seem to be doing just fine. They don't see me when I go home by myself. My public persona has me laughing, occasionally going out with friends, going to work and pretending I'm fine. When my work day is finished I drive home and park in my garage and then I sit there for one to two hours before I work up the motivation to go upstairs into my house. I'm reading a book a day because when I immerse myself in a fantasy world I'm not having to face how alone I am all the time. I don't allow people to come over because while I'm escaping from the real world, I haven't been cleaning or taking care of my house. If you were to see me on the street I seem like I have my stuff together, but I don't. My friends and family would be there in a heartbeat if I was to ask for help, but I can't do that. I don't ask for help, not even when I was younger. Asking for help makes me feel like a burden and I hate that feeling. Maybe the people you know that seem like they are just over everything are just like me. Hell, maybe you know me and are asking because you think I'm over it. Just know that as humans, we each handle situations differently. There could be a lot more going on there then you are aware of.
column9: I am in the same situation although it’s only been one month. Everyone says how brave and strong I am. I try to keep my self busy in my work, but a moment alone, even in the shower, and I am crying. Every little thing reminds me of him. I feel lost. It seems to be getting worse with time, as the reality of the situation is dawning on me. I don’t know if it will ever get easy. Anyone who hasn’t been in a similar situation will never understand, it is different to lose a parent, friend than to lose your partner. It’s good to read your feelings as it makes me feel someone understands….Thanks for sharing

column1: How long did your grieving process last after ending relationship with narcissist? I’m asking because I haven’t done much. No focus, energy, agoraphobia, and wondering if I should see a Dr for depression. It’s been since Dec 14th.
column3: The grieving and acceptance after ending it with a Narcissist is so different from anything I’ve experienced. Typically, the stages of grief look something like this:You can see that while these stages are not at all linear, there is a progression to acceptance and a return to normal. I had experienced grief before, of course, with the loss of family members, friends, and my husband. I don’t believe that acceptance means forgetting or not missing a loved one. I think often of them. With the end of the entanglement with the Narcissist, all these phases were overshadowed by trauma-bonding, cognitive dissonance, emotional shock, and self-deprecation. As much as I hated what was done, for the first several months I hated more that I had somehow permitted the abuse. There were times I did not recognize myself. There was a lot of anger. I decided to process my anger by writing, daily yoga, meditation, and committing to self care. This process lasted about a year. At the end of one year, I just moved on. I threw myself into my work, my volunteering, my family. I do not miss the Narcissist. Each experience with grief will vary from one individual to another. I recently met someone who lost a child to suicide. You just don’t ever get over the loss of a child. If you feel you would benefit from therapy, by all means, do so. Depression often accompanies loss and grief and sometimes masks anger.
column9: Thank you for sharing that. My feelings have been all over the place. Anger, sadness, feeling like I want to be heard, but under no circumstances do I want to live on that merry go round again. I think in the past I would tell myself I’m done to only to go back. I learned the hard way. This past discard I found myself counting my pills to see if I had enough to make me sleep for good. Thank goodness I snapped out of it. The discards get worse and that was the universe telling me to get away and heal. 💜 I’m just trying to make sense of all the emotions and hear everyone else’s stories. Btw you are a awesome! I love hearing that you got yourself back! Hopefully one day I will be able to do the same for someone starting their journey.

column1: Why is it often harder to cope with the loss of a beloved animal than the loss of a human family member or friend?
column3: I lost a cat who was like a best friend to me about five years ago. It was incredibly painful and difficult. He was extremely old (20+ years old), no longer had very many teeth, much fur or whiskers left (he was not too attractive by the end there) and when he had a stroke paralyzing his hind half I consulted with two separate vets before we decided to put him out of his misery. The reason it was so hard to lose this cat was because he was completely dependent on me for everything: food, love, attention. He was my constant companion in a way that no person has ever been for me. Furthermore he was dependent upon me even to release him from his suffering since I do not know how long he would have lasted if I hadn't had him put to sleep. When a creature is 100% vulnerable and dependent it is different from losing a family member or friend. It's more like losing a child. Thankfully this has never happened to me and I can't imagine how it would feel if one of my kids died. But it was much worse than losing older friends who have never lived with me and lived a separate life, independent of mine. A loved pet truly is family, truly is a baby as Janet says in her answer, and when you consider it that way it is not hard to see why it is so incredibly painful and difficult and I offer you my deepest condolences if you are grieving the loss of your pet.

column1: Is it possible to seek legal action against a physician who put in a DNR order for a patient, but it was not authorized by the patient or the family? The patient died because of this.
column3: It’s very complicated. There is something called HIPAA that restricts communication with others, even family members and spouses who are not listed on the communication form. For example, I took care of a patient with metastatic breast cancer who listed no one, deliberately, on her HIPAA form. I couldn’t get permission from her to speak to her spouse or her daughter because she wanted to control the information. She never permitted either of them to accompany her to her visits with me. They might drive her but she made them wait in the car. That was fine and okay by me until she became very ill. I discussed and documented a DNR status on her and insisted that I be able to speak with her family in order to help her get the help that she would be needing at home. She agreed, added them to her HIPAA list, and we contacted her husband and asked him to come with their daughter to her upcoming vitas. On that appointment, we met and reviewed her situation in detail. Her family suspected that she was in declining health, but clearly needed explanation and offers to get additional help for her and them at home. To directly answer the question. Physicians in the US are not required to provide futile care. There are ethics panels that can step in and make those tough hard decisions when patients are no longer capable. Patients don’t die from a DNR order. They die because they have intractable progressive illness that is medically untreatable. Putting and keeping a patient on a ventilator in those situations only prolongs the time of death, and undoubtedly prolongs the suffering. In those patients, the success of resuscitation and intubation in restoring health or quality of life are zero. Reasonable people, including family members, understand that. Of course physicians try to work with family members and even close friends to keep a patient alive until family member can arrive from out of state. But sometimes even that is not possible. And physicians are not expected to do crazy on a dying terminal patient. They are responsible for providing standard of care. That includes allowing end of life patients, death with dignity and limited suffering. One can always consult a malpractice attorney to review the medical records to help decide if what happened was egregious or standard of care in the community. Grieving the loss of a loved one is very very hard. Bereavement groups can be very helpful in facilitating some kind of emotional healing. This answer is not a substitute for professional medical advice. This answer is for general informational purposes only and is not a substitute for professional medical advice. I am an oncologist but I am not your oncologist.
