column1: What do you say when someone is grieving the loss of a pet?
column3: I say something like "I'm so sorry 'Josh' died! He was such a good dog and so cute!" If they say they don't want you to say anything, I stop talking. If I'm close enough, I might give them a hug. I would also tell stories of memorable times. It is pretty much the same as what I'd say if a person died. A lot of us see our pets as family members.
column9: http://www.deathofapet.com Rachel, thanks for your thoughtful and insightful answer. With your permission I will quote you in an article that we are preparing at Animal Human Connection. Blessings, Judy Helm Wright

column1: How do people deal with their grief over the loss of a pet?
column3: The hardest Thing for a person, especially if you loved the dog. Just cry. Once I lost my pekingese and I was so distraught, I called my 8th grade teacher (I was in my 20s at the time)to ask what I could do for the dog. I just cried, it was and is always a horrible feeling. Mourn him and eventually when you are reading and sometimes that is for a while, Get another dog. They will always find you. They always do. One day, you’ll see a dog and say, “that's the new one.” Happens all the time. I just got a bordercollie Mutt from the Crow Indian Reservation in Montana. I was playing with him and when I left to go and take some pictures, coming back on the same road, there he was, looking for me, out by the freeway. I put him in my car and took him home with me. He had over 250 ticks on him and it took me three hours to watch and pick them off at the dog wash, but it was so worth it. Never thought or wanted a border collie and now I have one. Your friend or family member should be ashamed for leaving him out there, but perhaps they did not know his behavior and that he would try to find them. don’t worry, it will all work out. bury him somewhere and remember.
column9: Thanks :( They knew. That’s why they tied him up, they said that he kept trying to escape. They have a dog of their own who they allow to play leash-free in the yard. They were just …careless. I guess I wanted closure more than a question answered. You gave me that. I come from a family of people who don’t really like dogs and didn’t grow up around them like I did. They don’t understand my hurt.

column1: Is it appropriate to take the day off work if a pet dies?
column3: Absolutely. It is a known fact that losing an animal can be as difficult and as heartbreaking as losing a two-legged member of your family. But sometimes losing a pet can be more heartbreaking and more debilitating than losing a two-legged family member. Grief is grief no matter how you dissect it. There should be NO shame, judgement, or condemnation when a person grieves the loss of a precious four-legged companion, especially if that companion was the person’s only and closest living “kin”.
column9: Anyone more upset about losing a pet compared to an actual human needs serious help.

column1: Where were you and how did you feel when Princess Diana died?
column3: I was on duty on a busy surgical ward looking after sick and dying people, and grieving the loss of my daughter’s teacher who had passed away in the ward overnight. She was 26, a beautiful kind young woman. Diana had a pretty good life compared to most people who die at aged 36, . A few months later a beautiful 36yo nurse I worked with died suddenly from an asthma attack. Her four children were home at the time. Sadly a lot of people die and much as Diana’s passing was a sad loss, especially for her family, it was a long time ago, and grieving over one famous icon’s death for 25 years is unnatural. Different for the family, but none of us knew the ladly, so it’s not healthy to keep talking about it. Seven years is the standard grieviing period when you deal with losing a close family member, but for losing a child, that loss must take a lifetime to deal with, but surely not for the loss of someone you only ever fawned over in tabloid magazines.
column9: I was in bed and my husband came in off the night shift In the morning and told me I was shocked we were flying out to Florida on the day of her funeral so it was a bitter/ sweet moment at the time , Very sad but I do wish they would give it a rest now ! Enough is enough ,,

column1: How did you deal with the death of your parents?
column3: My father had nausea and diarrhea on 12 April 2021, which we thought is not so common symptoms of COVID and gotta be coz of mango juice (Aamras) he had last night. 13 April - Things started escalating… Father developed fever and cough and we decide to take him to the doctor. 14 April - At dawn, I developed fever and my sister started coughing badly at night. At least mom was doing fine, I was relieved. This was the time I took all three of them to the family doctor. The Family doctor suggested us to ‘get tested'. As soon as father heard those words that he didn't want doctor to say, his blood pressure dropped. After making him calm and giving an injection shot doctor asked me to take him to get an HRCT scan done. 15 April - We got the report, the score was 7/25 and was quite manageable. Both got tested and were both positive. We both didn't go home from there and started searching for an oxygen bed for him as he was aged 54. We couldn't find any bed on that day until we went to the government hospital. I was happy that he got the oxygen bed and I went home to take both of ours clothes.We got admitted on same day to different buildings. 16 April - Medication started hitting us both hard. We lost taste, smell, and a little bit of control on our walks. My father's oxygen level started dropping to 89–90. We all started worrying but the doctor said that he is in good condition and will recover. 17 April - We were both trying to recover but father was losing patience. He was calling all the doctors and friends he knew to soothe himself. 18 April - My uncle went to give him dinner at 9:00 PM and found he was doing fine mentally. All members at home decided to move him to a private hospital the next day on 19th. But God had another plan, the patient besides my father died in front of my father and my father's chest starts paining and he had a heart attack. And we lost him… 19 April - Me sitting in the next building still didn't know what happened last night apparently for some reason my family chose not to tell me. I opened colony's what's app group and saw last thing that I ever wanted to see with my father's photo. I couldn't believe it, so I called my mom to verify. My mom was playing cool till she got to know that I know. She immediately asks her brother to take me home. At that point, I was restless, feeling-believing nothing at all. All I wanted was, someone to wake me up and tell me u had a nightmare. I couldn't shed a tear coz I couldn't believe it. I came home, I can see all people crying but still didn't feel like crying. I started searching on quora why I am not feeling anything. I never cried in front of my family as I had to support my mother and sister during their mourning as they were nearly uncontrollable. Every heartbeat was crushing my heart. Everyone was blaming themselves that they should have moved him to a private hospital way before. Even some people around us were blaming at this time of grieving. My father was great father, great husband and great teacher, great person altogether. He was smart, had best warm-magnetic personality. He had rough childhood since he lost his father at the age of 18. Since then he left his dream way behind for his family by working in the Xerox center and then as a clerk and then finally a teacher. No one has ever met a person that has talked ill about him. My heart breaks every time remember that he had 4-years left for retirement and to start enjoying his life with his life partner and children. Now mother has lost her support and she always gonna be lonely even she has us. I was always the most logical person in the room 30 days before and now I keep asking God if there is any way I can meet him for five minutes. Every stupid or tech-illiterate things that he did, now feels cute. Now every day, I wake up and look for him in the prayer room to get scolded for waking up late, but he's not there anymore. I have never felt this many emotions before as we always had everything. I never put a story on social media regarding this incident. I have written RIP many times before but this time I almost used to pass out even trying it. My hand used to shiver every time I wrote Kai (late) before my father's name on every government document. I hated it, every bit of it. This incident has made me more mature, awake and has taught me what life is at the age of 20. Now, I don't even need big things to be happy, even a poor father holding his kids hand at a construction site is enough. Having parents with you is a privilege, not a burden!As all billionaire like to preach, but now a fatherless kid - Please don't put anything on priority than your family. Coz every time you achieve something, you would wanna have your family for feeling proud of you, not the jealous neighbors. Start having more stupid, goofy photos with your parents. We are reluctant to take photos with photos with our parents especially with the father.Everyone's got their problems but you can tolerate them when you've your family members healthy. This is my first long and emotional post. Had to share my feelings.
column9: You would not believe me when I say this but while reading this, it feltlike I am reading my own story except my father passed away in an instant, just before my eyes. It has been almost 9 months and I am still in the state of shock and numbness that only people who have suffered this know. I know for sure, it never ever gets better. In fact, each day since the first day has been worse to a point that none of us remaining in the family have even clue what we’re doing here. Still feels like something that didn’t happen and we’re still waiting for this nightmare to end. My father was 52. He was also a teacher, a self-made man from a small town and the person with the kindest and greatest heart in the world. He was my soulmate, he has been for my entire life and will always be the reason and purpose for my life.

column1: What's the best way to support a friend after the loss of their pet?
column3: The biggest thing is to be there for her. Listen to her when she wants to talk and reach out to her if you don't hear from her. Let her talk about her sorrow and remember she has just lost a part of her family. Many many people just do not understand how close we get to our pets. They downplay our relationship with them and say “they were only a dog” (or cat) or say “get over it already”. The pain and sorrow one feels with the loss of a pet is REAL. It is a genuine loss. An emotional pain inside your body. Treat your friend like she has lost a family member. There is Grief counseling for people with pets out there. Send her a Sympathy card and/ or flowers.

column1: How would you feel about a co-worker taking a few days off short notice when their dog dies? Is it appropriate as it would be for other family bereavements?
column3: Unless you have walked in the shoes of a grieving pet owner or unless you have been a grieving pet owner, you will never understand the magnitude of their loss. Studies have shown that for some the loss of a pet can be equal to or greater than a loss of a two-legged family member. In fact, people who have lost a beloved companion experience the same feelings (shock, denial, bargaining, anger, acceptance) as if they had lost a human family member. Losing a pet is and can be extremely devastating for a person. I’ve lost numerous dogs and I know how debilitating it is and can be. How would you feel about a co-worker taking a few days off short notice when their dog dies? Is it appropriate as it would be for other family bereavements? I don’t have any issue about a co-worker taking a few days off after the loss of their dog and I feel it would be totally appropriate if they used family bereavement leave if allowed to.

column1: Why does the loss of my cat hurt more than the loss of any human?
column3: As a child - when are you able to be who you are in the moment - do what you want, in the way you want, say or not say what you want - or fail miserably - and never cause as much as a raised eyebrow from siblings, parents and peers? We throw the term “unconditional love” around often, but we seldom consider what it entails. If you dig into it, you realize there is no such thing as unconditional love among humans. There are ALWAYS conditions… and consequences. Now enter your cat. How can you not become deeply invested and head over heals in love with a family member (and our pets ARE family members) who daily confirms - without waiver - that there is no one as important and wonderful as you! Regardless of your behavior. With the death of your cat, you probably feel a part of you has died as well. It will take time to grieve your cat’s absence, but it will also take time to grieve the loss of who you were when you were together. And it will take time before you realize that, while your cat is no longer physically present, your relationship is still alive. To remind you of this, frame 2–3 of your favorite pictures of your cat. Eventually, I hope the value of your continuing bond with your deceased cat will propel you to develop a new bond with another furry friend. Until then, expect a roller-coaster of emotions. Try to eat well, force yourself to exercise and be sure to get adequate rest. Wishing you the best, Vicki
column9: I noted your qualifications as I began reading your reply, but even so, didn't expect such a soul-touching reply. You are truly just what someone needs when they've lost someone. My mother never understood why she couldn't grieve for her cold, cruel mother, but was distraught over the loss of her Sabrina, who slept on her pillow each night and followed her around the house. And just loved her.

column1: My friend’s dog just died 1 hour ago at 25 years old. Should I insist he get the dog buried or cremated?
column3: If you are a true friend you will keep your thoughts to yourself and be supportive while he grieves the major loss of his loving friend of 25 years . Losing a loved pet can be as traumatic as losing a human family member . Just be there for your friend…they will let you know if they need anything further !
column9: U could gently suggest He might want to think of cremation... that way His old friend can come back home and always be with Him. My Dear Old Best Friend is only feet from me on what I call a “Memorial” Table. A decision HAS to be made SOON.... and some people Don't even Know IF Cremation is Available in their area... IF.. their aware of the option at all. Sometimes u need someone with a level unemotionally mixed up head. If He's your friend, let Him know your there if He needs u. 25 YEARS! That's a looonngg attachment... and THAT'S... FAMILY!! I DON'T AGREE with “keeping your nose to yourself “…..to Me... it tell me, my “friend” doesn't really care. There IS a way to gently bring up... “what are u going to do? “ “do u have a plan? “

column1: What happens to adults with Down syndrome when their parents can't look after them any more?
column3: Just a short back story here. I am the 3rd child of 6 kids. My mom had a stillbirth of her 5th child and my sister Kathy, is her 6th. Kathy was born with Downs Syndrome. They attempted to talk mom into placing her into a home (this was in the 60’s) telling her my sister would be a vegetable never walking or talking. My mom refused to believe them and brought her home to us 4 remaining kids. As a family we raised Kathy teaching her how to talk. Our German Shepherd always wore a harness rather than a collar and he would sit in our backyard with Kathy for hours. He’d sit next to her and she would grab hold of his harness and he wouldn’t move til she was standing and steady. He then would walk around the yard with her holding onto him. If she fell, he sat til she was ready to go round again. They did this for months til eventually Kathy began walking on her own. She attended the special school here in town, graduating at 26 yrs old. VERY proud moment for all of our family-both immediate and extended as everyone has grown to love her. Fast forward…Kathy is 49 yrs old and my mom is dying of cancer. My sibs have all moved out of state except my brother and I. Needless to say, my brother isn’t really equipped to handle caring for my sister. I’m a retired nurse so for me it’s not a problem. My sister that lives in NC and I need to decide what is in Kathy’s best interest. She has ALWAYS been with my mom. An adult foster care or extended living would confuse her and slowly depress her and we felt would be the beginning of the end for her. That would not be the correct thing for her. I live 5 min from my moms house. Even on the same road. As my mom's health began to rapidly deteriorate we decided that Kathy should not be in the house watching my mom slowly pass away. The decision was easily made that Kathy would come live with me and my family. We had the extra bedroom and she would not have to leave the only town she has ever lived in. Originally, my mother’s wishes, were to have her move to NC to be with my oldest sister. After lengthy discussions with my mom and my sister we felt uprooting her ESP while grieving the loss of our mom may be too much for her at once so staying with me was the best option. This was September 30, 2018. My mom passed away on December 14, 2018. Kathy has adjusted extremely well living here with me and has handled my moms passing prob the best out of all us kids. Before mom got sick, they attended church regularly and Kathy has become extremely religious so explaining my moms passing to her wasn’t as difficult as we thought it was going to be. Now that moms gone, she refuses to go to church now, but her bedroom looks like a religious shrine..lol. Occasionally she will ask why mommy had to die, and I’ll remind her of the cancer my mom had and then she will be ok again. When going to court to obtain guardianship for her, due to the fact that my sister and I are sharing guardianship of her, the judge was extremely impressed that there were 2 of us “stepping up to the plate” he said. He said normally they have probs finding ppl to take guardianship over special needs adults and here he has 2 siblings that are coming forward WANTING to share guardianship. This made me sooo heartbroken and sad to hear that even here in our little town in Michigan, there are ppl that turn their backs on family members with special needs cuz they don’t want to deal with them! We absolutely LOVE having my sister here!! She is fun, funny, helpful, and has the biggest heart of anyone Ive EVER met!! I wouldn’t change ANYTHING we’ve done!! I just have a hard time thinking of what it would be like without her here or in a home somewhere… I could NEVER turn my back on her! She’s my blood and my baby sister-how can ppl do that??? Is that how selfish ppl have become?? How disgusting!!! 😱😱😱This is our Kitty Kat as we all call her. It was taken at her 50th birthday party we had for her last year. We figured since she will never be married and have that big reception we all love to have, we threw her a HUGE party with over 100 people in attendance. Rented a hall, hired a DJ, caterer, dancing, cake the whole 9 yards…she had a blast!!! ♥️♥️ Edit: I want to thank EVERYONE for the number of views, upvotes and comments that I have received on my post!!! NEVER did I even dream of these many people reading this!! I was shocked when I saw this today and it’s not even 3 days old!!! LOL. I was only trying to top my last 2 and this did by almost 100k!! Again, TYSM and Kitty Kat was sooo excited when I showed her her pic on here!! Then I showed her all your comments and she rubbed her hands together so fast (her way of showing excitement..lol) I thought she would start a fire!! LMAO!!! God Bless everyone!!! Stay safe!! With love, Jodie and Kathy..♥️ Edit #2: I think I need to set something straight here. When I said that people disgust me when they turn their backs on love ones with special needs I don’t mean everyone. I totally agree with those who aren’t equipped emotionally, financially, physically to deal with it. I also understand that some special needs cant be cared for in the private home setting. What I was referring to was the families that DO HAVE these means that are selfishly turning their backs on these people and walking away when their help is needed the most. THOSE people disgust me!!! Hope this clears the air for those who were thinking I was against everyone who didn’t stand up and take their family member in…♥️
column9: I have known three people with Down syndrome, and you are correct, it is a challenge to do the right thing for the person with special needs. She is so fortunate to have you guys as her sisters. Love her smile! ❤️

column1: Do cats miss their owner if the owner gives them away?
column3: Yes, they absolutely do. I run a cat rescue group. We primarily rescue cats off death row at one specific shelter to give them a second chance at life. Occasionally we are also contacted by people seeking to find new placements for their cats as an alternative to dumping them at the shelter where they stand a good chance of being killed if not adopted or rescued. We’ve heard just about every reason under the sun for why people opt not to follow through on the lifelong commitment they made to the cat when they took them into their care. People want to explain and justify their choices. I don’t care to know details. The bottom line is the same - the cat is being abandoned by the original owner. Occasionally the owner dies and, in those cases when family members didn’t sign on to commit to caring for the cat, abandonment can’t be helped. Most kittens under 4 months are resilient and rebound quickly from abandonment simply because they’re often too young to have formed a depth of attachment to the people caring for them. However, cats older than 4 months who have been cared for by a person or family can and do give indication that they grieve the loss of their people if given away or admitted to a shelter. They often don’t adjust well and are frequently traumatized while enduring the shelter environment experience and, if rescued or adopted, often exhibit behavioral issues in the foster or adoptive home until they re-stabilize and form new bonds with the new people. With dogs we have rescued, on average it takes about 6 months before they start to calm down, feel secure, trust again and allow their true and unique personality and nature to emerge. It’s no different with cats. A big part of our work in rescue is rehabilitation work - both physical/medical as well as emotional/behavioral. Yes, I get there are those who will argue animals don’t have feelings. I know it’s been studied and, so far, it’s concluded it’s not so much a question of whether they do or not but more of degree in accordance with measuring scales set by humans in accordance with human understanding of thoughts and emotions. The thought and feeling process for animals is different than that of human beings but that doesn’t negate the reality that they do experience thought, feeling, happiness, sadness, pain, etc. . In a couple situations, we’ve taken in older cats whose owners had died. In both cases, the cats went on hunger strikes. It’s like they just gave up the will to live. We had one of them at our vet for nearly a month, trying to get her to eat. We had to have a tube surgically inserted into her neck so we could syringe food into her body because nothing we tried could entice her to feed herself. Eventually, we had to take the tube out. She continued to refuse to eat, her organs began to shut down and eventually we had to make the choice to euthanize her. Having direct experience with animals daily, I believe strongly based on my own observation and experience that yes, cats do miss their people when the people give them away, abandon them or die. They absolutely do.
column9: Bless you, Renée. Great answer and thank you so much for caring for abandoned felines (also known as, in my house at least, fla's—Furry Little Assholes). I have 16 rescues of my own and have found homes for hundreds of others. Ten years ago i moved from the city to a deadend country road. I quickly found out this was THE road to abandon your cats. The first week I “found" two almost starving cats people threw away and it went from there. One guy I rescued I found a home for almost 50 miles away. 4 days later he showed back up at my door. I called the people and asked how the cat was and they said he was fine. Okay then…I wasn't returning him to them and since he obviously wanted to be with me he still lives here.

column1: Were Brian may and Freddie Mercury friends?
column3: Yes. Here are some things I put together to give you an idea of Brian and Freddie's friendship. Freddie Mercury had a plethora of ideas about what he wanted to do with their songs. But that didn’t mean their musical masterpieces weren’t the products of a collaborative effort. From Bohemian Rhapsody to We Are The Champions, Queen worked on them together. From their formation to their rise in rock ‘n roll and up to Freddie’s death, the band members were together in the studio, on the road, and performing in festivals and large events for two decades. They had their share of arguments and misunderstandings, but at the end of the day, they were family. When his health was already starting to deteriorate, he continued to make music – finding strength and solace in his craft. He wanted to keep doing something and making songs has always been his outlet. When they lost Freddie, they didn’t just lose their frontman. They lost a brother. Brian struggled with the loss of Freddie so deeply, he had to seek out mental therapy. He was in a deep emotional depression. “We all handled it in different ways. For a time, I really wanted to escape from Queen; I didn’t want to know about it. I think that was my grieving process. But I’m very proud of what we did together.” – Brian May Brian has gotten through the grieving process and now accepts the grief as something that will never truly go away. He compares losing a bandmate to losing a family member. The fact is, when you spend 20 years together with the same person, or in this case people..you become family. Brian is honored to be an ambassador for the Mercury Phoenix Trust, set up in memory of Freddie Mercury to support AIDS projects. Over 700 projects and millions of people have benefitted from the Trust as the global battle against HIV/AIDS continues.
column9: Well said, Ann Marie. Just wanted to add that in early days of touring as Queen Brian shared hotel rooms with Freddie and Roger with Deaky! I also don’t think they were just friends, more like family.

column1: Can losing a pet or seeing a pet die cause PTSD?
column3: Yes. First of all, PTSD is not something that need be set in motion by having bombs explode, or being a war refugee or escaping a serial killer. You can most certainly suffer PTSD from the loss of a pet. Losing a pet is a unique experience to the owner. It’s inherently hard to grieve because nobody knows the subject animal the way you do personally. Others may empathize or have experienced a loss of a pet themselves but their lack of intimately knowing your pet makes it harder to relate or feel as though anyone understands your grief. Because of this it’s often traumatic for one person which makes resolving it hard because you feel in it alone. Added with this the fact that many in our society view pets as simply “a dog” or “a cat” while others (including me) view them as family members. I can honestly tell you I have grieved the loss of a cat more than my own grandmother. It may sound foolish but I’m being honest. I have lost a few pets in my lifetime. What I have come to find out is that my level of grief and the trauma I experienced was worse when the loss was very sudden or unexpected (losing a pet before it’s full life) In 2014 in the span of 30 days I had a relationship of 3 years end, my dad had a heart attack and was in a coma afterwards and I woke up for work on a Friday morning and found my 8 year old cat dead on the kitchen floor. He had been in my room 100% normal a few hours before. Come to find out he had an incurable heart condition called HCM that often shows it’s first symptom as your pet collapsing and instantly dying when the heart finally stops. I remember being hit with this 1–2–3 punch back to back and not even crying. Not even feeling anything. I was numb. It’s like if you hit someone enough times they don’t even defend themselves anymore they just sit there dazed absorbing more blows. I was short circuited with grief, stress and guilt. I blamed myself for him dying. I would wake up in the middle of the night with horrible nightmares in cold sweats reliving the moment I found him. I would see the spot on the kitchen floor where I found him and not be able to look at it. I would walk around it. I stayed in bed for 2 days staring at a wall. No expression. Dead inside. Numb. Not even watching tv. I could not eat, I didn’t answer my phone. All of this is in retrospect. I’m good now but for a year afterward I could not see his picture without my heart racing, tears building and my stomach turning in knots. I couldn’t talk to anyone about it because they didn’t know him I lived alone with him. I was dealing with my father’s health and I felt guilty even mentioning the grief I felt about my pet, the blame I had for myself which grew to hatred of myself. It wasn’t until about a year after that I was in the shower one day and I guess because the water was loud and I felt alone that I simply lost it. I cried for an hour in there. I silently prayed and talked with him letting out how sorry I was for failing him and how much I missed him. It was not until I finally allowed myself to emotionally grieve, to talk about it that I felt the weight lift off of me. I slept for the first time for a full night shortly after and learned a valuable lesson about being a tough guy vs. being authentic. Authentic is better and I was hurting very bad. I’m positive that the experience I had was a form of PTSD. I was caught in a negative loop that affected my health, my sleep, that triggered a depression that lasted a year. I avoided pictures, my own kitchen, I had anxiety attacks for something as simple as when I would see an email in my sent folder that had the date on it that he died. You aren’t weak because you are in pain over the loss of your pet. It’s quite the opposite. It means you have a big and loving heart. You aren’t weird if you “can’t get over it” and it’s not just a cat or a dog. Having a pet is an exercise in bravery. You fall in love with them the day you get them and because of their life span you voluntarily sign up to one day have your heart ripped out. But you do it anyway. That is commendable and courageous. It’s ok to grieve as long as it takes. It does get better. And I can unequivocally say that the 8 years I had my buddy there with me through all the ups and downs of life to begin and end each day was well worth the pain of eventually losing him. Nobody should ever avoid loving hard, it makes life more enjoyable. The key is being authentic. The answer is to understand that the grief you feel for as long as it takes is perfectly ok and the pathway to healing. When we don’t allow ourselves to grieve as hard as we need to or for as long as we need to, that is when the problem happens. You can’t escape those feelings of sorrow and when you try to ignore them or bury them they never go away, they just come to the surface and if it was traumatic enough those symptoms can in every way be classified as Post Traumatic Stress.
column9: Thank you for sharing your experience. I lost my rabbit today. She was like a daughter to me. She was five and died of an illness that my husband and I tried three times to cure. She didn’t get better and died in my arms last night. I was feeling so low, scared and angry that I was losing my mind. Your comment helped me greatly.

column1: What should one say to a friend when someone from his family has died?
column3: Whatever you do, don't use the phrase "I know how you feel" and don't compare their loss to a loss you might have endured. When I lost my parents and sister it was a very frustrating to hear from other people that they "had lost someone too" even though it was their 86 year old grandfather and I just lost my 18 year old sister. Those things should just never be compared, in my mind. Also, please don't say things like "It was God's plan" because even as a Christian, I don't know how that can be comforting. I'm also touchy about when people tell those that have lost someone that they're praying for them. It's best to try and learn what religion the family is before making such comments, if you can help it. I think the best thing that you can do is to say any of the following: You and your family will be in my thoughts.I'm so sorry.I cannot imagine what you're going through.I'm here for you and please let me know if you ever need anything.Just give them a hug and let them cry on you, or heck, cry with them.Yep, it all sounds cheesy but those things turned out to be the most comforting things to hear for me. The folks that tried to give advice or be positive at a time like that just felt insincere. Sometimes the best thing you can do is just be sad with someone and grieve with them without saying anything at all.
column9: Excellent advice, Ashley. Thanks for sharing this.

column1: How do I help my dog deal with the death of another dog?
column3: Just like you do when grieving the loss of a person close to you. You just have to go through the entire grieving process. You may consider getting another pet, which may make it easier, but you still would mourn the loss. I’ve had to have several dogs put down, and have had one die in my lap from old age. We had him for almost 14 years before he died. He was a member of the family, and was like a child to us. He slept in bed with us, under the blankets and was just… the best dog ever.

column1: Our 7 year old dog doesn’t seem to understand that her mother died. What can I do to help her?
column3: Understand how? She would only “know" if she saw the Mother's dead body. If not, her Mom is just away… and she will forever be waiting for her to return. If she saw the body, and still acting aloof that means she knew ahead of time and was prepared for it. Pets need closure as much as humans do because they grieve and mourn their loss of human, canine and feline family members as much as we do. For all our deceased pets, we had their surviving canine/feline siblings see them before we took the body to the Pet Crematorium.

column1: What are the best and worst times in prison?
column3: For me, the best times in prison are visits with my family and loved ones. For the majority of my incarceration I’ve been in prisons that are far away from my family so I haven’t had as many opportunities as I’d like to see them. However, the visits I’ve been blessed to have are moments I will cherish for the rest of my life. My most recent, and perhaps most significant visit was last June (2011) when I graduated from Patten University here at San Quentin. My mom, my aunt, and a friend drove up from San Diego to attend. It was a special day on many levels, but what stood out most for me was how happy my mom was. She was beaming with joy. I remember being in the staging area with all of the other graduates and someone saying, “Hey, there’s my mom.” When I turned to look out of the window I could see all of the families going into the chapel and waving as they walked by. I immediately spotted my mom and I could see her searching the crowd trying to find me. I waved and when she saw me, her eyes lit up and she made her way to where I was at. My mother has the most beautiful smile in the world and the way she smiled at me right then was one of the greatest moments of my life either in or out of prison. Without a doubt, the worst times in prison are when a family member passes away. I’ve been through race riots where people lost their lives; I’ve endured lock-downs that have lasted for months; I’ve done time in the hole; I’ve been punched, kicked, sliced, and jumped, but none of what I’ve described compares to the pain of losing a family member while in prison. Over the years, I’ve lost my grandmother, my grandfathers on both sides, and just last week, my uncle passed away. Learning how to grieve the loss of a loved one from a prison cell has been one of the most difficult things I’ve ever had to do. But it was been necessary. When I first heard of my uncle’s death, I went numb. I couldn’t even begin to think about it. As I write this, I’m wrestling with feelings of sadness and helplessness because I can’t be there to support my family. I’ve been through all of this before, but despite my experience, I’m still struggling. I have no doubt that just beyond all of this pain I’m feeling lays the acceptance that has always helped me move forward. That said I can’t ignore the reality that having a death in the family is indeed the worst experience I’ve had while incarcerated. All communications between inmates and external channels are facilitated by approved volunteers since inmates do not have access to the internet. column1: Are there family members you've chosen to not talk to anymore?
column3: Okay, this answer is going to sound kind of weird, but hear me out on the whole thing, if you don’t mind. My parents got divorced before my 2nd birthday, which ended up resulting in my being raised by my maternal grandmother. There’s a lot more to that story as well, but I digress for now. A couple of years ago, I got into a text fight with my dad’s brother. After the death of my father, and seeing that side of the family for the first time in a long time, we did the usual thing that happens with anyone in your life, friend or family, after long periods apart: promises were made to try harder to maintain relationships this time, we would make time to see each other, and so forth. Not long after my father’s funeral, my sister discovered that our family had been staging annual reunions, frequently occurring in the town in which they grew up, which was only about 30 miles away from us on Long Island!! As if to add insult to injury, our father was a frequent attendee!! The fight came about after I wrote a eulogy on my Facebook page about my dad. While I didn’t hold anything back, I felt that it had been a respectful representation of my time with my dad - which, to put it kindly, was truncated, at best. The response that I received in return was fascinating in its revisionist history: “Don’t you dare speak about my brother like that!! He was a great uncle to my kids!!”; and so on, in that vein. Needless to say, this led to a blowout between myself and him, in which I wrote a lengthy response. Interestingly enough, however, I never hit “send”, for some reason. Then, shortly before the election of Trump, I got a message from the same uncle, which boiled down to, “I can’t love you because you’re not a Republican”. That’s not an actual quote, but it summarizes his words pretty succinctly. It was only then - and this was a couple of years after I had written my previously mentioned response - that I finally sent my uncle the message that I hadn’t hit send on before. But wait: this story gets weirder. A couple years back, my brother dies of an overdose. Literally no member of my father’s side of the family shows up for the funeral. This same uncle does send flowers, however, so my (step)mom - who has done an incredible job, along with the rest of her family, of being my family for the last thirty years - asks me for my uncle’s address. I can’t remember it at the time, so I text him to ask him for it, on my mom’s behalf. His response? “Since it has been over a year since I responded to your acidic rant and didn’t get the courtesy of a response, I think I will be as timely in my response to you now.” That is the verbatim quote of a roughly 60 year old man to his grieving nephew, shortly after the death of my brother. But wait, this gets even better: A few months back, my other uncle passes away. His son, my cousin, is told not to attend the funeral of his father, ostensibly out of some sort of concern about his younger brother’s “precarious” health. (I’m not going to go into it, out of respect to my cousin’s privacy). And my aunt, who’s a mental health professional, not only supported all this, she’s the one who made the call to my cousin. My response was to fly to my cousin on the day of the funeral, so that he knew that, should he choose to attend, I would stand next to him, between him and the rest of my family, whatever was needed to give him the time he needed to grieve the loss of his father. TL;DR: At this point in time, I’ve completely written off my father’s side of my family. Due to an amazing stroke of good luck, I have an incredible Italian family, with aunts, uncles, grandparents, a mom, and cousins who love me. They’re not blood, they’re something better: my “all volunteer family”; and to them, I’m not a step- or a half-anything, I’m just Rob: their nephew, son, grandson, and cousin. I’m the luckiest man in the world.

We were talking about having a child and moving in together. She maskeraded as codependent. A hopeless romantic. Someone who had been treated badly by everyone she'd every been with. A helpless victim, exploited by predators. She had so many friends and was so well liked and loved by everyone. A real pillar of the community. I was caught completely off guard. I never suspected that this sweet innocent, girl next door was in fact a predator. A manipulator and an abuser. That all the people she claimed had mistreated her, were in fact victims and she was the villain. The mask came off when a family member of mine passed away. I was devastated and completely heartbroken. I needed time to sort my head out and asked for space. She switched over night. Became agressive and vindictive. She would manipulate me with pity plays. Bully me and attempt to black mail me. All because I wasn't giving her “what she needed”. She smeared me to everyone we knew, even trying to turn my own friends against me. Told everyone that I was neglecting her. Told everyone that I was unstable and implied I had a drink problem. All for committing the crime of grieving the loss of a loved one. She told me that she wasn't getting what she needed anymore and so the relationship wasn't enough. She abandoned me in my grief and within a week and a bit was with someone else. column1: How much is a small ivory carving worth?
column3: I usually include a warning for those who may be sensitive to graphic photos. This post won't include a warning. I don't want you to turn away. I want you to look at it, see it and recognize what we've done..They say elephants never forget. How could they ever forget the images— the terror of genocide burned into their gentle and empathetic complex minds?Photo: Brent Stirton, National Geographic/Getty ImagesHow could they ever forget the vicious images of being stalked by bands of poachers for days, weeks, months and years— pursued on foot, or by vehicle as they pad silently across the dusty savanna? Sleep—interrupted by the sudden blinding spotlights and flashbulb terror, capturing a momentary glimpse of the panicked gray elephant faces surrounding them, moments after the guns roared to life like thunder, and the dusty stampede panicked out into the greasy darkness. It is only by the breaking dawn's light that some of the herd will first discover their missing loved ones. And boy, will they be missed. Family bonds run strong among elephants. And elephants have a long memory. Especially for those Forever Gone. (An elephant never forgets). By daybreak, the plains come to life with the twitter of birds in the frolick of the bush—sounds of morning— sounds of mourning (a symphony of frantic trumpets) and the rumbles of low-frequency calls sung entirely by an infrasonic opera which rumbles across the plains searching for non-existent survivors. Calls which are rarely answered. They sing sorrowful melodies—songs which may be passed on as language, songs which include “words” such as blood, and death, and hunt, man, face and danger, and speak of the loss of their loved ones.Photo credit: Edwin SabuhoroThey speak of the bones. Bones abandoned where the slaughter took place. Bones bleached white in the sun, pecked over and cleaned by the scavengers of the plains. Bones of family which the herd will frequently trek back to visit. An elephant graveyard. They will lift the bones in their gentle trunks, turning them over, smelling them, remembering the creature it once used to be. Remembering their mother or father, cousin or daughter. (An elephant never forgets). How could these elephants ever forget the scene of horror unfolding before them as they watched from the perimeter of the bush the night before? —Swarms of Bloodthirsty Humans butchering their beloved family members and completely annihilating their gentle faces with sharpened machetes in order to pull out their tusks? Those faceless elephants who will no longer frolick or play. The tuskless, who will no longer splash-fight in the cooling mud baths, or share gentle caresses— loving hugs from a friend. Dismembered and desecrated in such a way that it will change the very DNA which sullies the breed.Photo credit: Mashudu Netsianda and Temba Dube Senior ReportersThe big tuskers have been poached. Their trophy tusks, which once proudly graced Africa's continent, hung nearly low enough to scrape the very ground the majestic animals walked upon, have been taken—their hosts killed off in a fit of human greed. Fine breeding stock with Eons of powerful genetic destiny wiped out with a single bullet. They will bear no future stock, and big-tuskers are fast becoming extinct with the breed. (But it's okay. You have a tiny piece of them proudly displayed on your mantelpiece). The poachers carve out their faces in order to get to the tusks. They will amputate the trunk and carelessly discarded it in the dirt for the scavengers and carion to dispose of; the hyenas and vultures descend upon the carcass—the bones will be visited by the grieving herd for years to come. Imagine the terror of the infant having to witness the brutal murder of its mother. Imagine how it will slowly wither and succumb, even as its herd tries to urge it along, and stuffs the young mouth with dry prairie grasses—food its infant milk-tongue simply hasn't matured enough to absorb. Imagine how easy it will be for the lions to take down and eviscerate the lonely and weakened baby, dragging the wailing infant off so they may feast, bloody-fanged in the high grasses.Photo: Greg Du Toit / Barcroft ImagesImagine the piercing screams as the light fades from the fearful infant's eyes. Eyes which once beheld wonders in dust storms and rainbows after a drenching rainstorm. Eyes which once shared the imagination of dreams as the tribe peacefully slumbered under a full golden moon, or shared in laughter at the tickle of its mother's trunk, or the splendor of silently padding along night trails startling the crickets along the way. Eyes—filmed over by the white cloud of death— a life erased by the simple need for a few tchotkes displayed on a heartless human's mantelpiece.Photo credit: Geoffrey EinonImagine the death of happiness. The entire parade will suffer in grief at having witnessed their sisters, daughters, aunts, cousins, fathers, friends and mothers staggering and fighting to stay upright even as the last of their life drains from them and bleeds out into the dry African soil. How could they ever forget? It costs the life of a beautiful sentient being.Satao was killed by poachers and his face was hacked off in Tsavo East National Park in May 2014. Photo by Mark Deeble and Victoria StoneHow much would it cost you to obtain an African elephant tusk on the black market? According to an article from NPR*, approximately $1,000 per pound. How much is happiness worth to you? I guess as long as you're happy with your irrelevant tchotchke, knickknack, doodad, gewgaw, or carved whatnot which you display on your pathetic mantle or shelf, then it is all worth it. It cost the well-being of a family unit. It cost the lives of an endangered species. It cost the safety of the poachers who gathered the sample. It cost the reputation of the owner. (Surely, you don't think that ivory doo-dad is going to garner the admiration of people who are social media-friendly, do you?) It cost the respect of millions of people who are against the ivory trade. It cost the taxpayer who pay for the National Parks which honor the conservation of elephants. It costs the government for judicial proceedings against poachers who illegally stalk endangered animals. It costs the families of those who are prosecuted for the crimes. It costs the world for the loss of a truly wondrous species. It costs the world a beautiful species, as a rapid decline in population (100,000 elephants poached in merely three years in Central Africa or, 64% of its total elephant population in a decade) erases their existence. It costs the delicate balance of an entire ecosystem when an animal such as an elephant becomes extinct. Congratulations! —Your small ivory carving is priceless! *Slaughtering Of Elephants Is Soaring Because Of China'sper Demand For Ivory

column1: Widows and widowers: what are some things you weren't prepared for after your spouse died?
column3: It will be 7 years in May since my husband Steve killed himself in our home and I found him. We met each other late in life and were only together for 15 years, married for 13. If I had known then what I know now, I would have seen that he was having suicidal ideations when we were dating. I dealt with his drinking problem(which I know now was to quiet the voices in his head), his depression, his paranoia, his overspending, etc. When I found him, probably the third emotion to wash over me was relief. The relief didn't last long because every member of his family turned on me. I understand now that it was because of their enormous guilt and their grief but they made sure that my life was a living hell. These were all well off, educated people too. It took me years to get over their betrayal. What I didn't expect was that my brain would stop working, I lost my identity, I lost my footing because the bottom fell out of my world and I felt so profoundly insecure in a world that I didn't recognize without him. I actually starting to feel like myself again the beginning of 2020, and then the the pandemic hit and I had to isolate. Shit got very real then. Therapy, and a lot of it, helped me get back on my feet. The thing that terrified me the most was living on my own but I began to enjoy being alone. I learn to be independent and to enjoy my own company. I was 62 when he died and I'm going to be 69 in a few months. As I age, I'm liking being alone a little less and I'm wishing for a male companion. At the same time, I went through one of the worst things that a spouse can go through and I'm actually leery of letting someone into my life who could also possibly die, because I think worse than being alone is having to grieve the loss of someone else because I remember the hell I went through with losing Steve.

column1: Why do people not show empathy after a family pet dies?
column3: Loss of a family pet, or even a wild animal one has cared for is just as valid of a reason for grief as loss of a human friend of family member, and the amount of grief experienced is dependent on the depth of the relationship between the deceased or otherwise lost person or animal, and the person left behind, not the type of relationship. As to why some people do not show empathy for people who are grieving following the loss of a pet, I would say these people either have no idea what kind of bond can develop between an animal and a person, or they lack the sensitivity and skill to handle these situations appropriately. A lot of people look at animals as disposable and replaceable. Many see them strictly as a commodity. Many believe animals don't have souls. But, there are also many who know the depth of a relationship with an animal, and I'd rather be one of these people than one of those who never knew what it was like to love an animal and be loved by one.

column1: What is the most outrageous thing you can remember your parents doing?
column3: My parents were both in their late 70’s when my youngest brother disappeared. It happened during the first 3 days of a trip out west. My parents and my brother and his wife set off on what was meant to be 3 weeks of traveling in the motor home to see some of the National Parks. It was in Mesa Verde, CO, that my brother went on a short hike, alone, and never returned. If you’ve never had a beloved family member go missing, then you probably can’t imagine the kind of torture it brings. Of course there was a week long search, which proved fruitless. My family ended up having to leave Colorado and come back to Texas without my brother. Unthinkable. Unheard of. But it’s been nearly seven years, and no sign of him has ever been found. Nothing. Not a button, not a hair, nothing except for one ping on a cell phone tower and then silence from his cell phone. So there was and is grief untold for this family. My mother grieved the hardest. My father was also devastated, but he made himself go through the motions of life. My poor heartbroken Mom, however, just couldn’t cope with the loss of her youngest child, and she could barely speak for nearly a year. And that is the backstory that leads me to the outrageous thing my parents did. They live in the country, in south Texas. Town is about 30 minutes away. One morning not long after they came home from Colorado, they decided they needed to get some food in the house, so they set off for town. They came upon a vehicle parked a little bit off the road, close to the stop sign at the end of the Farm to Market road they live on. My dad, for some reason, decided to pull over and see if they needed help. It turned out to be a young man that they didn’t know, who had run out of gas, and needed a lift into town. Now, you have to understand that I was taught to be cautious when approaching strangers, especially in a situation like that. It was just common sense; we live in a strange world. Normally my dad might have cracked his window and asked if he could call someone for the young man. But that is not what he did. My dad offered the guy a ride into town. I never in my life would have thought my father would pick some stranger up and take him anywhere. Don’t get me wrong, my dad is a kind-hearted and generous man. Just cautious. So the guy thanked my dad, and got in the back seat of the car, and proceeded to tell Dad that he didn’t have any money for gas, nor a gas can to put gas in. So my dad drove the guy to WalMart, bought him a gas can, then went down the street and filled the can up, then drove the guy all the way back to the boonies so he could gas up his car and go. When my parents told me of this adventure, well, you can only imagine some of the scenarios that played in my mind. Anything could have happened. They could have been robbed, car jacked, even murdered. They knew nothing about the person they took under their wing and rescued. They both expressed to me that if their son had been stranded and out of gas, they would have hope that some kind soul would come along and help him out. I have always felt that losing their son so recently is what made their hearts so soft that day. They were missing him so much and were longing for the universe to send them a distraction. What better way to be distracted from our own troubles than to help someone else with theirs. I appreciate that my parents have suffered a great loss. There can be no closure to a situation like we are in, other than to finally accept that most likely, no answers will be forthcoming regarding the whereabouts of my brother. I appreciate that they are kind and good people. I also appreciate that God was with them the day they gave a stranger a ride and a can full of gas. But I have asked them not to pick anyone else up like that in the future. And they have agreed that if they encounter a similar situation down the road, they will be more cautious, and maybe just offer to call for help for a person in need. Maybe I’m overprotective. But I want to keep my parents, who are now 82 and 83 years old, with me for as long as possible. I just don’t think I can handle another mysterious disappearance, or worse, again. EDIT 9/22/2020: A few days ago, the family got word that my missing brother had been found. He was found deceased deep in the wilderness, by a hiker who went off trail. We are all so relieved to have our answer and to have some closure. He will be brought home and will be buried beneath a big oak tree on his property, the place where he always said he wanted to be buried.
column9: Your parents' actions remind me of a true book I read recently by my former landlady in Israel. Her entire nuclear family survived the Nazi occupation of Holland during World War II. They were sheltered for two and a half years by a family in Rotterdam who did not know them previously. This was at great risk to them, since the Nazis might have executed them for the crime of sheltering Jews. Their motivation was that their son was serving in the Dutch army in Indonesia when it fell under Japanese occupation. They hoped that their act of kindness would somehow be reciprocated by someone in Indonesia protecting their son.

column1: What year of grief is the hardest?
column3: Each type of loss and stage of grief has its own difficulty. I lost two family members a week apart. The loss where you have to take the wheel, the first year is painful for a lot of different reasons. The pain of their stark absence, getting paper work taken care of, having to repeat too many times that they are deceased to extended acquaintances, and professionals, closing accounts, settling debts, their clothes and personal affects, surrounding you. This kind of loss is very hard to bear. I would seek support to endure that kind of loss, which usually means the death of an immediate family member residing in your home. The other was a sibling, whom I was close to, whom I loved, but had no responsibilities in laying him to rest. We lived in different states. The phenomenon with his passing was that my mind (or heart), delayed in grieving him until 2 years later. Meaning after the dust had settled it was as if something inside of me said you can carry this now. So then the tears came and the reality that he was really gone finally was able to settle in. The first year I was in a stage of grief that may have been what they call denial, although I knew he was gone. The human heart and mind was beautifully designed by God, as a minister I have to say prayerful meditation and trust in Jesus Christ was my anchor through it all. Even now while I am grieving the loss of my elderly father, I know where to draw my strength.

column1: Doctors or nurses, what is the strangest experience with a patient's family you have had?
column3: One of our Hospice patients died and we supported his wife and family as funeral arrangements were made. His Hospice nurse social worker went to the funeral and the family introduced them to other extended family and friends. But after the cremation there was a small group of people standing apart from the other mourners grieving openly and clearly distraught. The thing was no one seemed to know who they were. Our Chaplain went over to introduce himself, offer his condolences and thereby attempt to find out who they were, former workmates perhaps? Oh dear me no! These people were ALSO his wife and family! They lived in a relatively distant State and had found out about the death from someone who had seen the obit and photograph in the paper. For almost 20 years our patient, loving Father, husband and church member had two wives and two families simultaneously. Neither suspected the existence of the other . I won't go into details obviously but to be brief there was some anger and sense of betrayal expressed by both families as they grieved the loss of their Father and husband. An episode no one involved ever forgot.

column1: What happens to adults with Down syndrome when their parents can't look after them any more?
column3: Just a short back story here. I am the 3rd child of 6 kids. My mom had a stillbirth of her 5th child and my sister Kathy, is her 6th. Kathy was born with Downs Syndrome. They attempted to talk mom into placing her into a home (this was in the 60’s) telling her my sister would be a vegetable never walking or talking. My mom refused to believe them and brought her home to us 4 remaining kids. As a family we raised Kathy teaching her how to talk. Our German Shepherd always wore a harness rather than a collar and he would sit in our backyard with Kathy for hours. He’d sit next to her and she would grab hold of his harness and he wouldn’t move til she was standing and steady. He then would walk around the yard with her holding onto him. If she fell, he sat til she was ready to go round again. They did this for months til eventually Kathy began walking on her own. She attended the special school here in town, graduating at 26 yrs old. VERY proud moment for all of our family-both immediate and extended as everyone has grown to love her. Fast forward…Kathy is 49 yrs old and my mom is dying of cancer. My sibs have all moved out of state except my brother and I. Needless to say, my brother isn’t really equipped to handle caring for my sister. I’m a retired nurse so for me it’s not a problem. My sister that lives in NC and I need to decide what is in Kathy’s best interest. She has ALWAYS been with my mom. An adult foster care or extended living would confuse her and slowly depress her and we felt would be the beginning of the end for her. That would not be the correct thing for her. I live 5 min from my moms house. Even on the same road. As my mom's health began to rapidly deteriorate we decided that Kathy should not be in the house watching my mom slowly pass away. The decision was easily made that Kathy would come live with me and my family. We had the extra bedroom and she would not have to leave the only town she has ever lived in. Originally, my mother’s wishes, were to have her move to NC to be with my oldest sister. After lengthy discussions with my mom and my sister we felt uprooting her ESP while grieving the loss of our mom may be too much for her at once so staying with me was the best option. This was September 30, 2018. My mom passed away on December 14, 2018. Kathy has adjusted extremely well living here with me and has handled my moms passing prob the best out of all us kids. Before mom got sick, they attended church regularly and Kathy has become extremely religious so explaining my moms passing to her wasn’t as difficult as we thought it was going to be. Now that moms gone, she refuses to go to church now, but her bedroom looks like a religious shrine..lol. Occasionally she will ask why mommy had to die, and I’ll remind her of the cancer my mom had and then she will be ok again. When going to court to obtain guardianship for her, due to the fact that my sister and I are sharing guardianship of her, the judge was extremely impressed that there were 2 of us “stepping up to the plate” he said. He said normally they have probs finding ppl to take guardianship over special needs adults and here he has 2 siblings that are coming forward WANTING to share guardianship. This made me sooo heartbroken and sad to hear that even here in our little town in Michigan, there are ppl that turn their backs on family members with special needs cuz they don’t want to deal with them! We absolutely LOVE having my sister here!! She is fun, funny, helpful, and has the biggest heart of anyone Ive EVER met!! I wouldn’t change ANYTHING we’ve done!! I just have a hard time thinking of what it would be like without her here or in a home somewhere… I could NEVER turn my back on her! She’s my blood and my baby sister-how can ppl do that??? Is that how selfish ppl have become?? How disgusting!!! 😱😱😱This is our Kitty Kat as we all call her. It was taken at her 50th birthday party we had for her last year. We figured since she will never be married and have that big reception we all love to have, we threw her a HUGE party with over 100 people in attendance. Rented a hall, hired a DJ, caterer, dancing, cake the whole 9 yards…she had a blast!!! ♥️♥️ Edit: I want to thank EVERYONE for the number of views, upvotes and comments that I have received on my post!!! NEVER did I even dream of these many people reading this!! I was shocked when I saw this today and it’s not even 3 days old!!! LOL. I was only trying to top my last 2 and this did by almost 100k!! Again, TYSM and Kitty Kat was sooo excited when I showed her her pic on here!! Then I showed her all your comments and she rubbed her hands together so fast (her way of showing excitement..lol) I thought she would start a fire!! LMAO!!! God Bless everyone!!! Stay safe!! With love, Jodie and Kathy..♥️ Edit #2: I think I need to set something straight here. When I said that people disgust me when they turn their backs on love ones with special needs I don’t mean everyone. I totally agree with those who aren’t equipped emotionally, financially, physically to deal with it. I also understand that some special needs cant be cared for in the private home setting. What I was referring to was the families that DO HAVE these means that are selfishly turning their backs on these people and walking away when their help is needed the most. THOSE people disgust me!!! Hope this clears the air for those who were thinking I was against everyone who didn’t stand up and take their family member in…♥️ credit : jodie bishop

column1: How do you deal with losing your best friend when you had to cut it off due to having a toxic friendship?
column3: Sadly, as Lana has shown, some friendships turn bad, shocking the caring one to the core. You have to cope with the loss pretty much as a loss of a family member. Best friendships are often closer than that of sisters (or brothers) and when this collapses, it is heartbreaking. Do what you would in any other circumstance - keep busy, seek the support of family and friends and allow yourself to grieve. You will get over this, but you will never forget. Sending a granny hug to help out.

column1: What is the most back stabbing thing a friend or family member has done to you?
column3: I’m the FT caregiver to my mother, who is bedridden and has dementia. My sister used to help me with respite but for many reasons has now walked away from me, my family, and our mother. We haven’t seen her since mid-April and we don’t expect to see her again. In the last four months, I’ve gone through a lot of emotions and have actually grieved the loss of a sister, upset that I’d never see her again. And then a mutual friend comes over a few days ago, and mentions that my sister (who is 50) used to snoop through my husband’s medicine cabinet, then talk about everything she found to her kids and they would all laugh and make fun of him. Then she tells this story to the friend, bragging about what a good time they had talking about my husband. “Oh yeah” she says to our friend, “my son thought it was hilarious!” All this went on behind our backs, while my husband and I spent our days caring for their mother and grandmother. She was nice to his face but made fun of him when we weren’t around and he’s never done anything but be nice to her. I wish I had known what back-stabbing, horrible people they were before I let them into my house, but it’s too late for that. It’s onward and upward, without those nasty assholes.

column1: Adult How long does it take to get over losing your mother?
column3: I'm reluctant to answer this since everyone grieves differently, and because it took a while. Losing a parent is very hard. I lost my mother over 34 years ago. The first two years were bad, and although the shock wears off and acceptance sets in, you never get over it. You learn to get on with it, but there's always been the sense of loss for me. It got worse with each new death of a close family member. You will get through it, but you could be changed.

column1: What can I do to help the pain of my pet passing away?
column3: It is really not easy to answer this because I feel there is absolutely nothing we can do to get over it. It was a part of your life, a family member and you will never forget it! I have faced the same thing a couple of years ago, as I had a female dobermann named Sheena. Sheena was a very lively, playful, energetic and childish girl. We had to leave her at a boarding facility on account of us going out of station.The boarding facility was well researched by us and infact the concerned person wanted to keep Sheena at his house itself so that she will be comfortable enough. After a few days this man informed us that Sheena has expired ; it was so sudden and so blunt that we were totally shocked, devastated and taken aback.. there are no words to describe the feeling. It was negligence on his part that he never informed us at the right time and he didn’t seek medical help in time. We just could NOT move on, Sheena was a family member to us. But as they say, life goes on. What I really suggest is that you first of all let go off all his/her belongings . You may want to lock it up in the cupboard or give it away. You may keep the photos, one or two favourite toys but remove everything else from sight or you will always feel miserable. The only thing which heals is TIME. When Sheena expired we sweared to never get a pet again. Fast forward 10–12 years and here we are: Tiger - the 1 year old gsd boy and scooby : 1 year old spitz. my current pets: Tiger the gsd and Scooby Many a times, I feel that it is Sheena residing inside Scooby because all his mannerisms and behaviours closely match that of my deceased pet!! Just, give it time and try to get busy in your work and if you happen to be free at home - maybe plan a trip to some place with your friends/family(it really helps). Just keep yourself busy with just about ANYTHING (even Quora) Your pet lived well, you gave it all the love it ever wanted , this is what you have to content yourself with.

column1: Do "hardened criminals" cry in prison?
column3: Sure they do. Losing a family member will usually do it. Being locked up when you lose a family member and you can’t be there to grieve with your loved ones is very difficult. I’ve seen convicts who were just sentenced with decades or a life sentence cry. Who wouldn’t feel deep loss knowing you’ll never see the outside again? I’ve never seen anyone balling like a baby, that doesn’t happen. But I’ve seen plenty of times close friends consoling some convict who was grieving for the loss of their Mother who just passed. In the privacy of your cell… I don’t doubt every convict had shed a tear or two.

column1: What is the hardest thing to accept about a loved one’s addiction?
column3: When a person is deep into active addiction, all aspects of what you consider a “Normal Life” cease to exist. Family members basically grieve the loss of the person they once new. They miss the person an addict used to be buried deep inside their addiction. The hardest thing to accept is to watch the person:. this person so close to your heart, you do not know them anymore. It is difficult to accept: The person rarely attends family functions. The only time you see the person is when they need money etc. The person has physically changed dramatically in a negative way. The person seems as though they could care less about you or your life. The worst thing to accept, is not knowing if the person will die tomorrow!

column1: How do I continue living after my husband has died?
column3: I am so sorry. The overwhelming grief is what it is. For me there was no way to cope with it. I just had to go through it, give in to it, let it sweep through me like a wave. I had to live through days when I didn't even want to be on earth anymore, days when I had to imagine that my husband was just at work, days when I panicked about all the empty days to come. But at the same time, I struggled to put one foot in front of the other, do the tasks that had to be done, learn to manage life on my own. The most valuable thing I ever heard in therapy was to “feel the fear and do it anyway.” I had to repeatedly say to myself, “I can't do this. I don't want to do this. I can do this. I will do this.” It was important to me to force myself to get out, to expose myself to the rhythm of everyday life even when I was unable to really participate. It was important to me to clarify my spiritual beliefs about death and what happens after. Crying helped me, because after crying, I would come to a place of calm. The book that was most helpful to me was “It's Okay That You're Not Okay”, by Megan Devine. In it, I read that our society has starkly unrealistic beliefs about grief, and what helps grief. What we need most are people to listen and sit with us in our grief, to hear our feelings, and to not try to fix it or minimize them. Deep grief is not something we leave behind; it is something we learn to carry with us.

column1: How did Batman cope with the death of Jason Todd?
column3: In a word: badly. Okay, fine, expanding. He dealt in several ways, as Bruce, as Batman, and in both identities. As Bruce, he compartmentalized hard. He didn’t tell Dick Grayson, the first Robin and Jason’s adopted brother (admittedly, where the official adoption status was and what their relationship was varies from Crisis to Crisis, but they had a relationship) about his death. Dick had to learn from the ever-tactful Danny Chase.“Danny: C’mon, they gotta find out sometime. It isn’t a big deal, anyhow. Happens all the time. Dick: C’mon, already, what is it? Danny: I’m not positive, but I’m pretty sure. I think Jason Todd was killed. -New Titans #55“Dick: Bruce never called to tell me what happened to Jason…he didn’t even leave a message on my phone.” -New Titans #55 Dick returned to the manor to find that (almost) all of the signs and reminders of Jason are gone.“Dick: Alfred was right…the trophies end with my last case with Bruce. There’s nothing of Jason’s. Nothing to remind one he fought alongside Batman as Robin.” -Batman #436 Bruce and Dick had a somewhat tumultuous relationship in the early Nightwing era. The reasons for it vary (similarly to Dick and Jason’s relationship), but suffice to say that it was not pretty. Bruce’s neglecting to inform Dick of Jason’s death and later criticism of him for missing the funeral didn’t help matters and served to reignite old tensions. Falling back on his oldest coping mechanism, Bruce dealt as Batman. As Batman, he made the iconic Memorial Case, which he spends a lot of time symbolically staring at while he broods to this day across mediums. Jason’s death threw a wrench in his designated coping mechanism. He was more pushed to prevent or punish crime than ever, both to avenge Jason/prevent similar events, and to cope as he always does. But that particular coping mechanism led directly into Jason’s death as Robin. Jason’s death is arguably as much of a source of brooding and a driving force for Bruce as the deaths of the Waynes. If the Waynes are Batman’s Uncle Ben, Jason is Gwen Stacy: someone close to him once he was an established superhero who he should have been able to save, whose death is less well known outside of comics but overwhelmingly present within them. After Jason died, Batman grew more brutal. As Dhanush Abeyratne pointed out in another answer, this era of Batman is similar to Affleck’s portrayal in BvS and JL—exceedingly violent (movie version skipped into murder, as movie versions of Batman are wont to do. As far as I know, comic!Bruce in his grief did not cross the line into direct and intentional murder). In his introductory storyline, A Lonely Place of Dying, Tim Drake (soon-to-be Robin III) points out Batman’s noticeable difference to Dick Grayson and notes to himself that even the newspapers are picking up on it.“Tim: You know as well as I do that he hasn’t been acting right since Jason died…He needs a Robin. He needs him to remember what he used to be. Before his parents died.” -New Titans #60 (Note: The order in which Tim reveals what he knows is a bit confusing, as is the line “he needs to remember what he used to be. Before his parents died,” because Bruce’s parents died when he was eight and were the motivation for him to become Batman, but that’s irrelevant to this discussion.)“Tim: Bruce hasn’t been the same since he died. The newspapers don’t know about Jason’s death, but even they’ve had stories about Batman acting…well, acting differently. He seemed happier with Dick. Now, I guess it’s like he just doesn’t care. But I want him to care again. I want him to be the Batman I remember.” —Batman #440(Another parallel to Batffleck, although the Bat Brand was a movie invention that probably wouldn’t have flown even in the later days of the Comics Code Authority) Tl;dr Batman struggled and arguably failed to cope with Jason’s death by compartmentalizing it, growing more brutal as Batman, and isolating himself (or rather, failing to maintain relationships or move to heal existing issues between him and other members of the Batfamily like Dick). His struggle to deal with it led directly to Tim Drake confronting him and eventually becoming Robin, the creation of one of the strongest and longest-lasting symbols in Batman comics, and Bruce’s secondary push to his crusade.

column1: Atheism: How do atheists deal with the death of a loved one?
column3: Death comes to all living things. It is simply the end of the journey of life. When death takes a loved one, the loss is ours. We mourn. We grieve. We do our best, and slowly the pain subsides. This is exactly the same thing that happens to theists who hope for an afterlife. They may take some comfort in the hope of being reunited with their loved ones. Nevertheless, their loss is now, and it hurts now. Those who are accustomed to finding solace in their belief, their religion, and their religious community will do so. Those who are accustomed to finding solace through close friends, family, and loved ones will do that. It's really not that different. Just a certain amount of wishful thinking eliminated for atheists. And it does make us value our time with our loved ones now.
