column1: How do people deal with their grief over the loss of a pet?
column3: Our pets can mean so much to us. Because of their uncanny ability to connect they begin to feel like our natural offspring, as if they carry our very DNA in their floppy, little ears or waggy tails. How many of us have said that our pet is family? Such could be said about Mario. I referred to Mario daily as “son.” “Come here, son.” “How’s it going, son?” Oh, sure, I called him “bud” plenty of times but only in the lighthearted way I refer to my human sons. We shared life together with Mario for nine, wonderful years. Less than a year before we put him down last weekend, we noticed a bump on the side of his hind leg. It was soft and didn’t appear to hurt him. I assumed it was some sort of boil or infection that would subside in a week or two. At worst, I expected that we might need to get it lanced or simply put him on an antibiotic. But, it continued to grow. The tumor began to be of sufficient size that it soon developed its own identity. My kids playfully called it Luigi. As Luigi continued to power-up, Mario also began hacking more and he started to develop smaller tumors all over his body. We waited as long as we could but he started to go downhill rapidly. My wife texted me late last week letting me know that his appointment would be that Saturday. My son was coming home from college so it was the best time for everyone to say their goodbyes. When Saturday morning came we all gave our final hugs and half of us drove him to the clinic while the others stayed home. It was a quiet drive with tear-swelled eyes. My son let his window down and Mario eagerly climbed out the window and took the blast of air head-on. It seemed like such a courageous moment for him. But, I couldn’t help but feel even deeper sadness because I could not remember ever letting him do that before. What kind of father doesn’t let their doggy-son stick their head out the window? Gulp. As we arrived, I went to the front counter to let them know we were there. My wife pulled around the back of the building and waited for me. The clinic had offered us the option to euthanize him right in our car. I had never heard of such a thing but it seemed to us to be a good alternative. It wouldn’t be so sterile and empty feeling and we could simply drive him home from there. But, I couldn’t help but notice the back-alley feel to the place. The clinic shared a building with a hardware store. There was chain link fence and pallets and things lying about. Cars were driving by and life was going on while we prepared to do our “deal.” A gowned woman appeared from behind a battered, metal door beaming from ear-to-ear. She fumbled around in a small caddy as she gaily explained the process. Never slowing with words, she shaved Mario’s front leg and inserted a small catheter. She produced a needle already loaded with it’s dope. It willingly slid in and she loosed the tourniquet. The whole thing seemed way too easy. Her thumb pushed the hit into his veins and, in what amounted to only three to five seconds later—way sooner that I was prepared for—his head dropped quickly to the seat. In only a manner of a few more seconds… he was gone. We dug his grave right next to Beatrice. A gentle Washington rain weeped down on us as we lowered his body to his final resting place. He deserved so much more than to lay there in that cold, hard pit. I lunged my shovel into the stockpile— it gave an eerie sound like the thrust of a blade sealing someone’s fate. With every shovel load he slowly disappeared behind dirt and tears. At every step of the process I felt as though I gave him less than he deserved. He should be sprawled carefree on the blankets on my bed, not wrapped in a thick blanket of soil; he should be inside and warm, not locked outside my home, cold and neglected.That day came and went. He wasn’t there at his food bowl Sunday morning and he didn’t greet me at the door when I got home from work Monday night. It’s a little quieter around the house now. Every time I think of him it stirs up a deep well of sadness. But, at the same time, it is a reminder to me of the brevity of life. I use it as a reminder to live life a little better, to enjoy it a little more, to make better memories, and to leave a better legacy. How do you cope with the loss of a pet? I choose to remember the best and to believe that Mario had a far better life with us than he would have anywhere else. Whether he was our dog or someone else’s he still would have passed. He was bound to his fate regardless and there was nothing I could do to save him from death. I take comfort in at least knowing that we got to share life together, that he wasn’t someone else’s son, that we even knew each other. The real tragedy would have been to miss that opportunity.“Dogs are not our whole life, but they make our lives whole.” Roger Caras

column1: How do you deal with the death of your pet dog?
column3: He came to us via a Craigslist ad. "Free to good home. Black Schipperke dog. 5 years old." I'd always wanted a schipperke. I heard they were smart, willful and intelligent. I love a challenge. Smile. I left a phone message to a couple who lived nearby. The woman called me shortly after, and sounded fairly hysterical. "If you fall in love with him, you can take him right away! Tonight! RIGHT AWAY!" I drove the short distance to their apartment, met the dog and he rose on his hind legs on his back legs doing the little "begging dance". I took him for a walk and immediately guessed the urgent reason for rehoming. He had to pee. Desperately and fiercely. My guess is the 9 year old boy, supposed to take the dog for walks wasn't doing that and dog had yet another accident in the house. I thanked them, gave them $20 "for your baby", as the woman had a newborn child in her arms. He was playful, sassy, disobedient in an extreme but he did it with such charm that I accepted it. He wasn't really a "bad" dog, he was just his own man. Example. Time to leave the dog park. I say: "Let's go home!". Two dogs run to the car and sit at the door. Dog takes the indirect way. Walks around every single tree. Some of them twice. Does a deep analysis of a random weed and having concluded his study, pees on it. Stops to look at a bird in the tree. I say, “COME HERE." He wagged his tail and walked in the other direction. Finally, oh and just when he was good and ready, he joined us at the car and smiled up at me. Sigh. My little Problem Child. He was amusing, fun and exasperating at the same time and I'm glad we had eight years together. He forced his way under the covers with the velocity of a heat-seeking missile. He was a ridiculous bed hog. He loved to body slam me in bed. And just when I'd finally gotten to sleep, he needed to stretch with a 4 legged kick that left me breathless and checking my kidney. He danced, he pranced, he wiggled. His joy was infectious. It just all happened too fast. About 2 months ago his eyes were very glazed over. Time for his bi-annual allergy shot. He never really recovered fully and he spent increasing amounts of time under a blanket. He lost a distressing amount of weight. Two days ago we went to the dog park and he was his usual disobedient self, refusing commands to COME HERE. Sigh. Yesterday I picked him up and placed him on the grass to urinate and he staggered and wobbled as if he were drunk. It was clear he was in bad shape. I stayed up that night, fed him a half-portion of his favorite wet dog food that he later threw up. and kept him hydrated by dabbing water on his mouth. Early this morning, he was almost completely limp. I can't let my friend, my Problem Child, suffer. My neighbor drove us to the veterinarian's office we use. I'm grateful my neighbor was there. I was shaking too hard to drive. He is the 6th dog to leave me and go over the Rainbow Bridge ... as the vet waited, I picked him up, looked in his eyes, held him to me, and said, "Goodbye. I love you. And I'll see you again." Then I left the room. He's fine. I'm going to be fine. RIP my bad, spirited, funny and sassy little man. His name was THUNDER.

column1: How do atheist parents cope with the death of their child?
column3: Unfortunately I have experience with this question. I have lost 3 if my children. I lost son 14 years ago in infancy (sids). He was perfectly healthy and we woke up to our month old child gone. We were treated like criminals and until the autopsy proved we did nothing wrong we still had to work a Cps plan to get our older children back. The system is broke but we made it through that part of it. Bear in mind that we were never able to grieve for our son as a family. It was the worst feeling in the world. I just knew that I could not survive another death of a child. I was borderline suicidal as a result of my son. I focused on helping the mother through it which took some of the focus from my sorrow. As an atheist I hated when people told me he was in a better place or that he is with his creator now because I know that he is not with his creator as we are still alive. And if you believe death is a better place then why are you here. You should kill yourself immediately. Believing in an afterlife that does not exist whether you believe it or not, devalues this short life you were lucky enough to get. Well fast forward 13 years 6 months I wake up to a phone call from my oldest daughter telling me my oldest child Mark Jr., 26, killed himself. He was the kindest, most non aggressive beautiful man who did the most aggressive act. He had just gotten married and bought a house. I'll leave the details out as they are too hard to type.. Well now I have all these unanswered questions and what if's that I will never be able to get rid of. I'm mad at him for not reaching out to me or his mom beforehand but I miss him too much to hang on to any real anger. I just love and miss him. And I get to see firsthand what suicide does to the people who love you after your gone. It's torture. So now what I thought I could never survive I have no choice but to deal with it. Suicide is no longer an option as I could not put those questions on my loved ones again.. fast forward 4 months (a little over a month ago) we are woken up at 130am from knocks at the door. It was the state police informing us of our youngest daughter dying in a solo car accident. She was 21, had a 2 year old daughter and still lived with us at home.. I have not dealt with her death emotionally as I currently am not able to. I am still dealing with my oldest son's passing. So coming from a religious upbringing and having many religious friends and family who want to try to say the right thing to help it usually ends up with me telling them thank you but nothing can be said to help. Just know i understand you want to help. But don't do it with words as your beliefs are not the same as mine. When they eventually try anyways and I tell them that I aM comfortable knowing I will never get to see them in an afterlife. it's the fact that I didn't get to tell them I loved them or hug and kiss them one last time or tell them I'm sorry for all the mistakes I made as a father that hurt the most. They knew I loved them as they saw what I went through with losing the infant son. But all the Bible heads think I'm mad at God for taking my children. It is the most ludicrous thing to hear someone say about me. How can I be mad at something that does not exist? So now I try to live my life one day at a time doing whatever I can to attempt to take my mind off of the recent deaths. It doesnt help much at times..I am a very manly 47 year old who cries a few times a day and it happen at anytime and anywhere.. I don't care what people think about that. Fuck em, I don't owe anyone an explanation on why I am crying. I know that we are made of the same stuff as every living thing on this planet and I know what happens when anything dies. It ceases to exist. We are no different. We are a very new species compared to most species on earth as a product of evolution. Anyways I don't know if I answered your question. The short answer is everyone regardless of religion or lack there of handles grief differently. Coping with the loss is just something you got to do and it is not easy. Factor in losing 3 very close friends whom each I've known 25+ years passing away in the middle of the 4 months between my older children passing and I'm just numb. I'm not writing this looking for pity. I'm just giving my perspective to answering the question. Take care

column1: How do you deal with the death of a friend?
column3: It might be tough at first but it will get better after a while. Things ALWAYS get better. Hold on for yourself.Using the friend’s family’s agony as a comfort might seem inhumane but it’s the inevitable truth that in most cases of death, family members suffer from a larger hole in their heart than the friends. Many “someone else” is having a harder time dealing with the loss than you are so it’s okay for you to feel devastated or overwhelmed or constantly distracted by the event.Friends eventually go away; in one way or another. It’s just life and life goes on and on. You deal with it.Talk to other friends of yours about any depression or upset you’re experiencing. You lost one, okay, but you still have other friends right? Release your emotions to them so you don’t smother your inner self with negativity but also remember, don’t be a dick to your other friends just because you are feeling down. Look at them: I’m not saying they can be dead at any sec or anything, but you CAN LOSE THEM!Friends are hard to find, harder to keep and the hardest to forget. I lost a childhood friend to cancer while in middle school (which was like 8,9 yrs ago). We were friends but we weren’t exactly close. Yet the death of him, the scenes at the funeral still haunts me. When you witness someone die at such a young age, it struck you with some kind of disbelief and forced you to reflect on your own life, especially when you’re about the same age.This period of your life dealing with the death of a friend, the memory of this, it won’t go away easily and thoroughly; it might not go away at all. You might have to live with it. It’s normal and you don’t have to feel like you have to deal with it intentionally or anything. Keep living up your life. Go outdoors. Go to bars. Dive into your work. Make more new friends or even just chat up with strangers on subway or in line. There’s so much to lose but there’s also so much more to embrace.[If you’re planning on visiting the friend’s family to offer condolences at some point, try to arrange the meeting at an open and public place like an outdoor restaurant on a sunny day. Bring some positivity to all of you ON PURPOSE because when sad people meet up, the atmosphere just becomes extra bitter and I don’t want you to drown in that. Don’t ask how they’re doing but instead, bring up hilarious moments or awkward moments you and your friend share. If you have to visit his/her family in their house, bring a bouquet of multiple colors, by “multiple” I mean as many colors as the florist can arrange. Colors flood away the brain’s sadness and I would say this is a good distraction.]I’m not going to say I can understand what you’re going through blahblahblah because every friendship is unique and I’m not knowing enough to judge how much you are trying to let go. But hope your friend rest in peace and hope you will get through it.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of my sister?
column3: My sympathies for your loss. My situation was not the same as yours. I had 2 sisters and 2 brothers. I was very close to my oldest sister, who passed away when I was 29. The last photo we have of her was her holding one of my daughters shortly after my daughter was born. My sister’s passing was also sudden. I was supposed to have lunch with her the day she passed away. There is not a set pattern for mourning. I observed what my family wanted during my visits with them, but in my home, I followed the jewish traditions. I found that the structure and the traditions actually gave me a way to focus and remember and mourn, and I believe it made it much easier for me to deal with her passing than it did others in my family. I covered the mirrors in my home. I said the prayers for the loss of a loved one. I lit candles, and I spent the time thinking about her. At first it was more painful than I could handle with sobbing. Then I began to think of her laughter. My family and I began telling stories, and we cried and we laughed. People will tell you that with time you’ll get over it. That is not exactly true. With time you will smile, and you will find a calm. My sister passed away 25 years ago. To this day there are still times that I want to pick up the phone and call her to tell her something going on. I felt much the same when one of my brothers passed away as well. The only advice I can give you is to live a life that honors both you and your sister. Remember her, love her, and share your life with her, and her memories with those that will come into your life. My prayers are with you.
column9: It's very hard. This does. by no means, can compare. When you love someone, it never stops hurting, it just gets easier over time. I wasn't blessed with children, but my cat Lucy, when she abandoned, at 5, became my love. She's been gone 4 years, and still I cry for her. We gave her 12 years, she might never had. She was my child, and I was her mom. I'm sorry for your loses, everyone has felt the pain of losing someone, but unfortunately, its part of life. Animals lives are short, and the best thing we can do, is remember, the good memories. Evelyn Lennon

column1: How do I cope with the death of a 25-year-old son?
column3: Shocking is a word that would be justified in thinking about the loss of a young man whom you have brought into the world. Especially this loss would be felt if your son is your only son. My sister lost her son, her only son and he was about the same age as your son. He was a wonderful young man in that he was so considerate and thoughtful of others around him, and I am proud to be his uncle. I see my sister coping with the loss by keeping good memories close to her heart. The hurt lasts a life-time easily and that is justified. Remember that Mary, the mother of Jesus, lost her only son, and the Bible said it was like a sword piercing through her very heart, but really when you think about it, I think the Bible really said it was a ‘sword’ and it did pierce her heart, so it was more than just ‘like a sword.’ Your heart is bleeding and no one around you truly understands or they can’t relate even though they are emphathetic. I don’t know how you stop the bleeding from this loss, whatever the cause was, it still is a great loss. You respect the life your son brought into the world. If he contributed to the welfare of others and respected them as people with needs, he leaves behind a kind of legacy that will not be forgotten by those he touched with his demeanor, cheerfulness or encouragement. These kind of characteristics have nothing to do with money or the lack thereof. What would your son want? He would want that those positive and uplifting characteristics that he employed in his interactions and relationships with others be carried out by those who are left behind in this world to deal with their unique problems and situations. Observing this kind of respect towards his memory would benefit you greatly and of course all who knew him. God bless you. May God comfort you always as you pray to do His will in your life. You are not alone.
column9: Thank you so much.

column1: How are Germans coping with the death of Helmut Kohl?
column3: Quite well, generally. While he may have been an efficient, or even truly great, statesman (the final decision on that will rest with generations yet to come), he wasn't actually liked by many, even at the top of his career. Others have rightly pointed out his not-so-stellar private life, and, more importantly, his obvious corruption. CDU donations scandal - Wikipedia The thing that got most people really worked up about that wasn't so much the CDU on his watch’s accepting bribes—excuse me: ‘irregular donations’ from corporations, arms dealers and the like and partly diverting them to party leaders’ private coffers—we were pretty much expecting that by then. They'd apperently been doing it more or less sneakily since the mid Fifties at least. It was that a person (and I'm using that in the loosest sense) would use ‘I promised not to tell’ as a reason not to divulge relevant knowledge in court procedings, get away with it (anybody else would have been detained for quite a while for being in contempt of court under similar circumstances), and had the gall to claim his actions were honourable afterwards. Especially since he was officially a hardliner as far as law enforcement and curtailing individual's rights to privacy etc. were concerned. He basically told the world that he considered (and always had considered) himself and those he considered his equals above the law. Which didn't exactly come as a surprise to many either. His blatant and public display of that attitude and obvious pride in being bent and staying bent is what taints his memory most in many Germans’ perception. Almost. What led me and my peers to vote Schröder back in 1998 was that anything was better than yet another four years of Kohl’s policy of ‘sitting things out’. Yes, we were aware of Schröder being a pro-big-business reactionary (like Kohl), of his abysmal track record at reigning in overreaching police etc. forces, of his disregard for human and civil rights coupled with a tendency to appoint borderline or outright corrupt cronies to key positions. We'd been living in Lower Saxony with him as head of government for years. He still looked like a less bad idea than Kohl. Not least of all because we were pretty sure his personal ‘style’ would be kept in check by the compromise cabinet he was almost certain to have to come up with… and we were somewhat vindicated. While it might not be appreciated by many, Schröder’s government did get some long overdue societal changes started. Not as much as some hoped for, and arguably not always for the better, but there was change, at last. What everyone answering up to now has missed is that dreary, leaden sense of nothing ever changing, that complete and utter sense of being left behind in a changing world with a Dinosaur in charge many Germans of my generation grew up with. Kohl may have handled the whole collapse of the USSR/German reunification thing quite well—but by the time he was voted out roughly a decade later, his administration had squandered away most of the political capital gained by that. Alright. Back to the question: Germany dealt with it like with any other former high-ranking politician’s death: flags at half-mast at most official buildings for a day or three, condolence books being laid out in many town halls, lying through gritted teeth ‘of the dead, only speak well’-type eulogies and lots of media coverage. There's a State Funeral in the making, probably. This German dug out Kranz’ 1992 ‘Helmut Kohl ist tot’ for good old times sake:As others have mentioned: Kohl hadn't been in the public’s eye much after his declaration that he considered staying bought more important than his sworn duty to the state. And, yes, by the time that one came up, he wasn't Chancellor anymore. There were ‘scandals’ about his private life and whatnot after, sure. They didn't reach a broad audience, though. Many Germans simply weren't sure whether he was still alive or had already passed away over the last couple of years, right up until his death made the news…

column1: Psychology of Everyday Life: How can I cope with the death of my dog?
column3: Aww. It sounds as if you really, really loved your dog. I wish everyone loved their animals as much as you clearly loved your dog... Here are my tips on how to deal with the grief that follows the death of your dog: 1. Read the book "Your Older Dog" by Jean Callahan. Even if your dog wasn't old, you may still find some helpful tips and advice in the chapters "facing death" and "the future". Yes, I know the chapter is called "facing death", but it does contain advice and/or tips about how to cope after your dog has already died, including a section entitled "The Grieving Process" and another one entitled "Talking to Children about a Pet's Death". Even if you do not have your own children, this section may be helpful for if other children who really liked/loved your dog need help with dealing with her death. It may be better for their parent and/or guardian to talk to them about as they are their parent/guardian. Also, if you were to take them out to a room alone to talk to them about the death of your dog, a parent/guardian of theirs may get angry at you about it. 2. Talk calmly to a person whom you know and trust about your dog's death. Pick the person whom you talk to wisely; pick someone whom you know will understand and will not say unhelpful things like "Get over it. It was just a dog." 3. Take a walk. It has been clinically proven that exercise can be as good for treating mild to moderate depression as any anti-depressant. 4. Do not expect to just be able to bounce back to your normal self tomorrow. You clearly loved your dog a lot, and now she has died. You will grieve. You may grieve for weeks, months or even years. Things will (hopefully) get better for you, but it will take time. 5. Do something you enjoy. Go out with a friend (I would suggest that you keep this as a friendly, happy outing and do not turn it into a date. I am not against dating, but you do not want any more heartache at this point). Read your favourite book or magazine. Watch your favourite happy movie, or your favourite happy TV programme. Go to a place that makes you feel happy (it may be best not to go to a place that will remind you of your dog. You have to decide on that one). Listen to your favourite song. 6. Eat healthily. A good diet can contribute to a good mood. Try to eat proper meals at proper times (say, breakfast at 9:00 am, dinner at 1:30 pm, and tea at 6:30 pm), and try to eat your five-a-day, and limit yourself to only four (or less) sweet things (such as chocolate, sweets and desserts). If you are not already a vegetarian or vegan, why not give vegetarianism or veganism a try? A good, healthy vegan diet, with all the right nutrients, can actually drastically improve your health. Also, if you are an animal lover (or just a very good, conscientious person), you may feel better about yourself for not contributing to the abuses and killings in the dairy, egg and meat industries... 7. Try drawing. It doesn't have to be a good drawing; you don't have to be an artistically talented person. Art can be great therapy. As long as it helps you, is totally ethical and isn't offensive, and as long as it does promote violence or hate, it is a good thing as far as I am concerned. 8. Try reading. Even if you aren't a big reader, reading may take your mind off of this situation temporarily. 9. I don't want to sound unsympathetic or anything here (I am a dog lover myself. I love you and your dog...), but you could, as a matter of fact, get another dog when and if you ever feel that the time is right. Why not adopt a rescue dog? That way some good will be coming out of this situation... Rescue dogs are not always badly behaved or scarred by past mistreatment; in fact, many rescue dogs are very friendly dogs who can go on to become very loving, loyal and well-behaved companions. Besides, wouldn't your dog like you to give a loving new home to one of her fellow canines? 10. If you really are struggling with this, I would advise that you talk to a pet bereavement counsellor about your dog's death. Here are some links to pages with information about pet bereavement counsellors: UK: https://www.bluecross.org.uk/pet-bereavement-support http://www.allyforall.co.uk/ USA: http://www.aplb.org/support/support_groups/ (this is a link to a page in which, if you are in the USA, you can select your state to (hopefully) find a suitable support group in your area). https://berkeleyhumane.org/Pet_Loss Australia: http://www.petloss.com/phones.htm New Zealand: http://thepetnetwork.co.nz/petbereavement.php?region_id=2 Here is another website that you might find helpful (I might add that I love the music to their home page:)). http://www.petloss.com/

column1: How do I help my dog deal with the death of another dog?
column3: Part 1 of 2:Alleviating Your Dog's Grief Many people believe that letting the surviving dog see the body of his deceased companion helps him come to terms with the death. The theory is that the dog forms an understanding that his companion is dead and therefore copes better with the loss; however, there is no scientific proof one way or the other that this is the case, so do what you feel is best for you and your pup. It's difficult to pinpoint why some dogs do better than others and if viewing the body has anything to do with that. However, it's unlikely that seeing his old friend would do him any harm, so, ultimately, the choice is up to you. Often times, the grief or depression that a dog exhibits after the death of another dog stems from an evident change in "pack order." This can then lead to a lost sense of security or routine. 2. Keep a regular routine to help them adjust.The survival instinct of dogs in the wild means that they don't take time out to grieve, and tend to keep going with the daily pattern of hunting and grooming. Keeping to your normal routine decreases the dog's feeling of stress – the last thing he needs after the loss of a companion is for his world to be turned upside down. Thus, hard as it is when one of the dogs has gone, stick to your usual habits: feed him at the same time as usual, take him for walks, and visit places you normally go. This reassures the dog that life goes on, which in turn helps him to cope. 3. Be careful not to enable your dog. It is human nature to want to comfort a pet after a loss; however, this may not be the best way to alleviate his grief. Take the example of a dog that stops eating. The owner's reaction is then to hand-feed the pet, and praise him when he accepts morsels from the hand. In effect the owner is rewarding the dog for eating from his hand, rather than from a bowl. Thus, when you want the dog to eat from the bowl he refuses, preferring the one-to-one attention of hand-feeding. This becomes a habit that is unhealthy for him and unsustainable for you. A much better option is to act normally around food and feeding time, thus reinforcing the impression that although the other dog has gone, all is still right with his world. Thus, put the food down as usual, and if the dog doesn't eat, after ten minutes throw the food away and don't offer anything else until the next mealtime. This sounds harsh, but in dog language it is enforcing a sense of routine and security, which is what he needs during this time. 4. Give him time to find his place.Dogs need to know their place in "the pack" in order to feel secure, and when a member of their pack passes away, it can leave the survivor feeling confused and anxious. The key to this period of adjustment, be it for the leader or subordinate, is keeping to a regular routine and spending time training or playing with the dog, continuing as normal. If the deceased dog was the leader, the survivor may feel insecure since his understanding of who is in charge has changed. This can show itself as barking excessively at other dogs, either to assert his new found freedom, or more likely because he feels threatened and barks to warn other dogs off. If the deceased was the subordinate dog, the surviving pack leader may experience a loss of purpose, in that his guidance and support is no longer needed. He may seem restless and aimless as he patrols around, without a pack member to follow his lead. Two dogs that live together are constantly interacting with each together in subtle ways. When one of the dogs dies, his companion may well feel under-stimulated and even bored. It helps the dog to adjust if you can fill the gap with mental stimulation such as games, extra walks, and even teaching him a new trick or two. This excellent one-on-one interaction will divert his attention and strengthen the bond between you. It may even help alleviate your grief, too. 6. Carefully consider getting a new dog.The best time to get another dog is when you feel ready, rather than immediately so as to comfort another dog. Dogs are individuals and if the survivor had a strong bond to the deceased, it is unlikely you will replicate this purely by adding another dog into the household – think of it in terms of "buying" a new best friend – as nice as it sounds, it just doesn't work like that. There is also a possibility of making the situation worse by stressing the survivor with a strange dog intruding on his territory. Only get another dog if you're confident the two of you are ready. 7. Test out a friend's dog before adding a new dog to your family.If you feel strongly that a new dog is the answer, test it out by borrowing a friend's dog and letting them play together. See how your dog reacts and whether it helps or not. If he takes to the other dog, he may be ready. If he doesn't, it's best to wait. If you're dead set on another dog and your current one doesn't take to your friend's, consider another of a different sex or size. Your dog may be likely to take to a dog that's less (or more) intimidating or one of another disposition. Part 2 of 2:Treating Canine Depression Dogs usually show their depression through their body language. Seeing your dog show symptoms of depression might be alarming, but it's normal for them to show these symptoms after a loss. However, if your dog continues to show signs of depression for longer than a month or your dog is behaving out of character, talk to your vet to discuss potential treatment options. Here are the common signs of canine depression: Refusing to eat Refusing to engage in activities he once enjoyed A change in sleeping patterns (either sleeping more than usual or being unable to settle) A change in habits (for example, he no longer gets up to greet you upon your return home) 2. Talk to your vet about dog appeasing pheromones.Grief is a natural process that needs to be worked through, and numbing those feelings with medication is not the way ahead unless the depression goes on for several weeks. If, however, you have done everything right and three or four weeks down the line your dog still seems depressed, then it is worth getting him assessed by a veterinarian. One option he or she may suggest is a dog appeasing pheromone. This is marketed as Adaptil, and is available as a plug-in diffuser that infuses the pheromone into the air, or on a collar worn close to the dog's skin. Adaptil contains a synthetic analogue of the chemical messenger (pheromone) given off by a nursing doggy mom that makes her pups feel safe and content. The dog breathes the pheromone in and it activates feelings of safety and wellbeing. While this is not a quick fix, it can help to decrease anxiety levels in a stressed dog, which can help him turn a new corner and become more well-adjusted. 3. Talk to your vet about prescription anti-depressants.Another option your vet may suggest is a prescription anti-depressant, usually reserved for when all else fails and the symptoms have lasted over a month. The anti-depressant medication that is licensed for use in dogs is called clomipramine, which is a tricyclic antidepressant. This works by blocking the reuptake of certain neurotransmitters (serotonin and norepinephrine) in the brain, which has an anti-anxiety effect. The dose is 1-2mg/kg twice a day by mouth. Thus a 30kg Labrador requires half an 80mg tablet, twice a day. This drug does have side effects such as a dry mouth and constipation, and can increase the plasma levels of certain anti-epileptic drugs and so should be used with caution in these cases.

column1: How do unreligious people cope with the death of a pet?
column3: Compassion, empathy, sympathy, sorrow, love, loss…those are human emotions, not religious ones. So any kind person (the only type that should own pets) would react with those emotions, regardless of whether they practice any religion or not.

column1: How have you been coping with the death of Kobe Bryant?
column3: Pretty well. I didn’t know Kobe Bryant or his daughter so I don’t feel like it’s appropriate to “mourn” someone I didn’t know personally. I feel like to have someone’s death that I didn’t know effect me in such a way that it would prevent me from living life normally would be an insult to his wife who now has to raise their other kids without him, their kids who no longer have a dad, his friends who no longer have a great friend, and all the other people who actually knew Kobe. I’m definitely sad he’s gone because he was a really good basketball player but that’s it to my knowledge.

column1: How do I cope with the death of a friend?
column3: I'm deeply sorry for your loss. Losing someone you care for is incredibly difficult. Grieving is an important part of the healing process. It's different for everyone, but we all go through sadness, bargaining, denial, and depression before reaching acceptance. You might want to see if there is a grief support group in your area. It's fundamentally essential to find someone you feel safe with to express your feelings while grieving. If you are a person of faith, clergy can also provide assistance. However, counseling is available if you are having difficulty moving forward.

column1: How are the people of London truly coping with the death of Prince Phillip?
column3: The people of London? The ‘people of London’ are a melting pot of cultures, languages and religions. There are NOT representative of the heart of England. We in the shires are all a little sad to find he’s died although of course many were expecting it. ‘Phil the Greek’ was in my eyes, almost a caricature of ‘English’, Kind, thoughtful, always up for a bit of banter and happy to take the piss at every opportunity. Good bloke, sorely missed.
column9: Far from ‘kind, thoughtful…’, over at least 60 years I have tended to find those English people who set the tone in a school or workplace to be constantly alert for reasons to exclude a new person from their ranks, and indeed from the ranks of those they deign to treat as if they were almost human. You have to ‘get’ and share that ‘sense of humour’, for instance. If your background is very foreign, don’t swap anecdotes about it—pretend that your parents might have been Yorkshire, or Lancashire, or wherever (‘oop North’ is definitely better), and definitely don’t let it be known that they were middle-class people who went to university in their ‘old country’ (remember that they certainly consider that place ‘some foreign sh*thole’). Remember they consider speaking a foreign language an almost impossible but absolutely useless accomplishment, and the fact that even a French toddler speaks French just shows them how unnatural and dishonest their closest neighbours actually are. (And I’ve actually twice experienced English people close to tears giving their account of visiting central Wales in the expectation of finding an especially ‘unspoiled’ part of ‘their’ country, and encountering obviously local people speaking a completely impenetrable foreign language.) In no other country would it be normal unselfconsciously to say that your own nation is ‘kind and thoughtful’, as if it were a simple fact. It isn’t.

column1: How did you cope with the death of your best friend?
column3: Personally, I don’t know if there is such a thing as coping. This is a word that is used to say we are getting by with what he have. I lost my lifelong best friend/ cousin three years ago, this year. I can tell you that the hurt, pain, and tears never cease to go away. I have learned that you just simply have to live with the cards you have been dealt. I now appreciate every moment I had with him, here on earth. For me to feel peace, I have to believe that he is in a much better place than I am. Also, that one day soon or far away I will get to see him again. All you can do is live a life they would be proud of.

column1: Can you ever get over the death of your baby?
column3: I am so sorry you've been through this, and offer you my heartfelt condolences on the loss of your little boy. I know what it's like to hold an angel in my arms and I struggle to understand the reasons behind life or death when they are so innocent. I cannot hope to understand all of the feelings you are going through, but I will attempt with what limited ability I have to try to help. In your life, you will never stop missing your baby, so don't try. Allow yourself time to grieve. It's okay- just let it out, and don't worry about what anyone else thinks. Trying to hold it in won't benefit you or anyone else. I know, beyond just a belief... I know that God lives, loves you, and has received your little one into heaven as a valiant and loved child in glory and honor. I know that God is a loving and a just God and that you will see and hold your child again. I know that God has prepared a way for us to be together as families forever, and that through Jesus Christ, we can overcome our sins and death, and that mothers and fathers who have tried to live as best as they know how will be given the opportunity to live with their family members and grow together. I know that by accepting Jesus Christ and living righteously, you will be given the opportunity to raise your son as a mother raises a child here on this earth. See Can a husband and wife be together forever? Will families will live together in heaven?

column1: How do you deal with the death of your husband?
column3: The death of any spouse is a terrible thing to cope with, and of course that is assuming that deep down you did still love them. Don’t look so surprised, I have known any number of people who, when a spouse died and all the burial and everything was over and they could sort of relax a bit tell me. “Just between us, I’m so glad he/she is gone. I swear I was not looking forward to divorcing them.” Or, my personal favorite,, day after the funeral I drop by to see if he’s ok and see if he needs anything or some help with something and he, takes me in for coffee and he looks about and says, “THANK GOD! That bitch is finally dead!” Then he sort of relaxed. “Ken, just between us, if she hadn’t come down with cancer like she did we would have been in divorce court in no time at all.”

column1: How do I overcome the death of my girlfriend?
column3: I’m so sorry for your loss. Everyone processes and copes with loss in their own way. Know that it takes time and you won’t feel better right away. Counselors, therapists or grief groups may help you understand your feelings but only you can work through the sadness and figure out how to move forward. Love for your girlfriend will most likely never leave you and you will learn to live with her loss rather than “get over it.” People who want to support you and help you feel better, may not know what to say at all, act like nothing has happened, or even pressure you to let it go. But trust your gut and when you feel sad, let out the tears. Don’t hold your feelings in as that can prolong your grief. Let your body feel the gr...

column1: How can I cope with the death of my father (I'm a teenager and an atheist)?
column3: I am going to assume that this is genuine. Nothing will ever assuage the pain, no matter what anyone says, you just have to bear it as best you can in whatever manner seems to be best for you. After I had watched my father take his last breath and had howled at the moon to the wee small hours, I wrote the following. (Part of a blog/diary detailing a year in the life of an emperor penguin in Antarctica). I have nothing more to offer as condolence. Day 203 - 22nd October 2007 - Tread lightly, for you know not that which lies beneath your feet I cannot delay writing this any longer, although it is a terrible hardship for me; much more terrible and terrifying than a mere Sisyphus and his rock, doomed for all eternity. I do not wish to do this, and yet still I must; I am driven by forces unknowable and unfathomable to me! Were it to be possible, I would have you let this cup pass from me! However, I know that this is truly impossible, just as he did. Perhaps I was always meant to do this. Perhaps this journal had only one purpose from the outset? Perhaps it is all but fickle fate! Havelock has made his decision, a decision which he has deferred making for so long; perhaps for me, perhaps for Fricka, perhaps for little Fricka and for all those like her? Perhaps, for the one chick which he tries to save each year? Perhaps it was only ever for himself? Who can know? Who will ever now know? He has decided that life without Myfanwy, finally, is no life. Whatever small compensations he could conjure for himself to assuage his pain, they will no longer suffice and he has chosen. Rather than a life without her, he will have unlife with her; who now remains to dare challenge his choice? It is his, and was only ever his, to make; it was always so. I found him that morning out by the rig, dozing in the early morning sunshine; perhaps he was dreaming of flying, somersaulting penguins. I did not want to wake him but I needed him to keep an eye on 'little’ Fricka while I wrote my journal. Laying my wing across his back, I felt him, cold and stiff; there was no warmth left in him, no charity, no love and no life. Wherever Havelock may be, he is no longer here. He is no longer in the rookery, no longer by my side. What remained of my father was no more than cold, dead flesh. Solid bone left rigid, but lifeless, throughout the night. Those stiff feathers are now useless for protection, for insulation; there is no longer warmth to retain. The life has gone from that which was once so alive; the penguin that once was Havelock has departed and all that remains now is food for the bonxies. There is a switch inside each and every penguin. At certain times, you can press the button and the penguin in front of you, in spite of all of your probing, prodding and poking, finally becomes a non-penguin. It is as simple as that! At every chick’s death, its parents flip the switch and there is no longer a chick, no to-be-penguin; no beloved, no heart's dearest, no tender fruit of your union. It is merely a husk, empty now, barren; a shell that once contained a penguin but contains one no more. If the penguin is no longer a penguin, in what way is it different from the snow; from the rocks; from the concrete around the station; from the remains of half digested fish left by over-stuffed chicks, intent on mayhem? It is in no way different. So we leave it, wherever it may lie; a stiff and frozen reminder of the price that we will all be asked to pay. For life exacts its own price for this existence. A price for this joy, this excitement, this suffering, this contentment, which we all, penguin or human or orca, must pay, whether we will or no. Only by paying the true cost, do we come to appreciate the value of what we have bought. When? Tomorrow? Next month? Next year? When is not important; only the inevitability of the final settlement remains. We ignore them, these empty, lifeless urns; full now only of ashes. We cast them not a glance as we waddle from one side of the rookery to the other. After a few days, they are little more than feathers on skin, discarded remnants from an alien and incomprehensible haberdasher; mere rags in scarlet drenched snow. Even the husk, now empty of the penguin that once was, becomes truly empty; a meal of guts and lights for a hungry petrel. Such is the life and the death here. You would, I think, consider us heartless, cold, callous, to so treat those we loved; those we reared. Those we spent the long winter protecting to the very limits of our endurance and sometimes beyond. Why else would we suffer, as we do, through the harsh winds, the freezing air, the hunger, if not for love? And, if for love, then do we not debase, besmirch and demean our love in acting so? Is love so easily switched off? Like a table lamp? Is our love no more than a meal for the bonxies? However, we do not love the husk, the empty shell, the ash-filled urn. We do not love the feathers, the bones, the guts. We love the penguin and, if the penguin has gone, what is there left to love; except the memory? And memory has no shell. We buried him, Fricka and I, beneath the rig. All through the day, we shovelled snow and ice with our wings, our feet. It was neither easy nor deep, but deep enough, we hope, to preserve him from the bonxies. That much, at least, is owed. Never before; the rookery has been keening long into the night for three days now. Little Fricka will not eat. Little Charlie will not speak. But tomorrow is a new dawn and, with each new sun, there is always new hope.Bonxie - the penguin’s epithet for the predatory skuas and petrels which loiter around the rookery in search of an easy meal.

column1: How do you cope with the death of a narcissistic parent? Is it normal to not feel guilty?
column3: guilty? i wont feel guilty. i will feel some relief. and i will grieve the fact that i didnt get a better mother, one who wasn’t a self centred narc. you know, one of my exes once heard me on the phone with my mom, and when the call ended, he said to me “i cant believe how you speak to her.” of course he had never met her. because previous boyfriends who had met her didn’t have a high opinion of her and the way she treated me. and i thought to myself “you dont have a fucking clue”. he was lucky enough to have had a good, loving mother, so he couldnt understand how some moms could be awful. if i sounded hostile towards her in the phone call, maybe it was from decades of mistreatment by her and pent up resentment, something he’d never understand but the way he looked at me after that phone call, as if i was evil. i will never forget that. no, i won’t feel guilty. just bad i didn’t get better.

column1: How does a parent cope with the death of a child? Does the family that remains work through the loss collaboratively or largely as individuals? Is a new family constituted along different lines?
column3: I lost my 16 year old son to a sudden brain hemmorhage (2007). My experience of grief was so consuming that I didn't ever feel I could cope. For a long time I didn't; days blurred and merged and 6 months passed without knowing what i was doing. I was taking anti depressants and my health deteriorated fast. After receiving a diagnosis of ME/CFS followed quickly by Crohn's disease, I had to give up my teaching job. There were mental health and emotional issues attached to my resignation also, and I resigned myself to the fact that life was different now. Family and acquaintances were telling me to get over it, move on and go back to work...this incensed me to the point of despair. How dare they say that, they have absolutely no understanding of my grief and you can't compare one persons experiences with another's. It is coming up for 5 years since Kyle passed away, and not a single day goes by that he isn't in my thoughts. In 2008 my husband and I founded a charity in Kyle's memory. It very quickly became successful and has developed into something Kyle would have loved, and been immensely proud of. We work longer hours than ever before, and on a purely voluntary basis but the rewards are many. We put our all into the development of others and have created a 'family' of young people and volunteers who are all striving to keep Kyle's memory alive. It is my rock and my sanity. Without (Red Dreams), I would be just a shell of a person. Life in no way resembles what it was, and I too am a different person. My grief is still apparent, and time does not heal. What it does do is allow you to manage the thoughts, memories and feelings so that they become a driving force rather than reducing you to a quivering wreck. Having said that, there are still moments when the door opens and I have to succumb to it, it's natural and cathartic and whether it is 5 years or 15 years, this will never go away. Losing a child is the single most devastating experience one can have. The journey that follows is unique and individual and nobody, even others who have lost children, can say they know how you feel. Having a focus, a determination and drive is the only thing that has kept me going. For some that is faith, or other children/family but for me it is the pride and achievement of other young people, knowing that even though my own son has gone, I can still have a positive and influential effect on others, as I would have with Kyle. I still battle through the stages of grief, and some months are worse than others due to anniversaries, Christmas etc. but I know I can get through it and come out the other side with more determination. I will never get over it, or fully accept my new life (I struggle mentally with the fact that Red Dreams only exists because Kyle doesn't), but I know that I can cope with whatever comes next, as nothing can ever be as bad as losing my son; and if I have survived that, I can survive anything.
column9: I lost my 20 year old son in 2007. He was my only child. I know what you are talking about. I wish I had the strength as yours. I am living life but no one knows, no one.

column1: Has a teacher of yours died? How did that feel?
column3: Yes. Dave Sanders. He was killed on April 20, 1999 at Columbine High School, along with a good bit of my childhood. And it feels … weird. Let me amend that. It feels extremely weird, just like everything else about Columbine. Edit: When I initially wrote this I indicated that the shooting happened in August, not April. This is a symptom of a learning disability I have. I substitute words that start with the same first letter. I certainly know it happened in April, and I proofread this maybe six times before I posted it, and I STILL didn’t see it! Arg. I fixed it now - apologies. When the shooting happened I was 15 years past high school and living in another state. On that gorgeous day in April I was giving a tour of the Garden District in New Orleans. I had just wrapped up the morning tour and I had about an hour until the afternoon group showed up. After I had lunch I decided to call my mom. I don’t remember the reason - maybe I just wanted to say hi. She was still in Littleton, so I checked my watch, calculated the time change and dialed. I remember her voice like it was yesterday. I didn’t even finish saying hello before she said “Are you calling about the shooting?” “What shooting? “ “THE Shooting! Columbine! They’re shooting everything!” A part of my brain locked up at that point. By the sound of her voice, Mom was pegged at a full maxed out level 11 panic, even though both of her kids graduated long ago. “They’re shooting up your school!” Her words didn’t make sense to me. So I said the first thing that came into my head. “… not MY Columbine…” I still think that, actually. Not my Columbine. Not my school. They did NOT walk down the halls of my memory and attempt to blow it up inch by inch.I don’t remember how I got home. I found out later that I called my boss and told him to cover for me - I had an emergency. I don’t remember making that call. Or getting on the streetcar. Or walking home, walking up my stairs or turning on my television. My next memory is of my roommates and me. We’re seated on the sofa, holding hands. I was crying, but I don’t think I was blinking. It was like my eyes sort of froze. But I could hear everything. And I kept thinking, over and over, that I didn’t know where my class ring was. I desperately wanted it, my tangible part of that school that only a day before I held in mild contempt. I still can’t find it, so I’m guessing it’s gone forever. As that day spun out, and the days to follow, I discovered a few things. Like Columbine had been remodeled a few years before the shooting. SWAT’s weirdly delayed response was due to the fact that the guy leading the party was familiar with my school. Or, he thought he was. Like me, he knew where the cafeteria had been, and headed to the old location - the opposite end of the building from where he needed to be. I would have made the same mistake.I found out too that the worst of it all had happened in the library. That’s where so many of the kids were executed. Would you like to know where my first job was? I was an assistant librarian. At Columbine. For school credit no less! I was crazy about books and spent many happy hours there. Like the cafeteria, the library had been moved from where I remember it being. Even so… that was where two killers blew their brains out in a last act of senseless mayhem. The National Enquirer published the uncensored photos of them, crumpled up, blood everywhere, blood on the books. My books. In my library. I do not recommend that you click this link. It’s graphic as hell and you don’t need to have triggers to be freaked out by this. Did you know there’s a video game you can play? Someone built a version of Doom (very popular with the killers) so you can run through the halls of my school and kill people too. And the reason I include this detail is because you asked what it feels like for a teacher of yours to die. Keep in mind that I hadn’t been inside Columbine for 15 years before the shooting. As I type we’re nearing the 20th anniversary of the incident. And it’s still this raw. It still hurts this much. I wasn’t even in the same state on the day of the shooting. Just imagine what it was like to actually BE there. When I attended Columbine things were a bit different. It was the early 80’s. One of the newer hires was teaching AP History - a guy named Frank DeAngeles, but we all called him Mr. D. And we LOVED him. I know. It’s easy to idolize someone who is now, like it or not, famous. But this isn’t a rose colored glasses thing. Mr. D loved his job. He loved working with kids. He was seriously good at what he did. In fact I’d rank him as one of the top 3 best teachers I ever had. When I heard the name of the principal at the time of the shooting… Oh holy Christ. Not Mr. D. Not him, not there, not happening. Just… no. Of all people… I found out too that Cassie Bernall had died. It was another shock, because I met her. Her father knew my father. He had been looking for some reliable transportation for his daughter and as luck would have it my dad was selling our old Bronco. I went with him to close the deal - someone had to drive him back home! Which is where I met Cassie. We were both bored stupid, it wasn’t a memorable meeting. I just took away the impression that she was bright and pretty. I didn’t think of her again until I saw her picture. Even so… of all people… Which leads me to Dave Saunders, and why I feel as weird as I do. At the time of the shooting, 15 years after I graduated, there were only three people left that I knew. Mr. D, Sue Carruthers (aka “Mrs. C”, our drama teacher, who will forever hold a dear place in my heart) and Dave Saunders. The one teacher who, without fail, drove me crazy. I was taking typing lessons (yes, in the days before the PC they taught teenagers how to type - electric typewriters no less). I didn’t know much about Mr. Saunders, but it was obvious he didn’t want to be there. It turns out his passion was for sports - he just picked up the typing class because no one else wanted it. Back then I had a thing about loud noises. I didn’t like to be all that close to them. This was 30+ years before I was diagnosed as autistic. Had I known then I’m sure I could have gotten some help. But as it was, I just knew that being in an enclosed room with 30 electric typewriters was like someone wearing cleats jumping on my last nerve. I told Mr. Saunders I was having serious trouble concentrating on the lessons. Then I asked him if it would be possible to move into the hallway, just to give me a chance to think. I’d be happy to move the typewriter myself… It wasn’t just that he wouldn’t hear of it. I swear, I nearly got a Malfoy-style sneer from him. Absolutely not, out of the question, and if I didn’t sit down and get to work I was probably going to fail. I think he thought I was acting like an entitled brat. I thought he was an intolerant jerk. Needless to say, we didn’t think much of each other. And then I saw this.That sign was in the window. A man inside the classroom had been shot from behind. He had been shot in his torso, head and neck after trying to clear the cafeteria of students. He crawled into an upstairs classroom and waited for help to arrive. They put the sign in the window to direct first responders where to go. 911 assured the kids that help was on the way. But no one came. Instead, Dave Saunders bled to death. So how does it feel? Extremely strange. It was the year of our 15th anniversary / class reunion. I had already decided I wasn’t going to go. I had a few good memories, as most people do of High School. But at the time of my graduation all I really took away from Columbine were a lot of bad memories combined with relief that I’d never have to go back. It wasn’t Columbine itself. It was the High School experience I objected to. Nothing about it is suited for someone who’s bipolar, much less autistic. I was so glad to be gone that I didn’t even know where my class ring was - that same class ring I spent hours looking for on 4/20/99. Mr. Saunders and I didn’t get along. But that doesn’t change the fact that he saved so many lives that day, at the cost of his own. I’m sorry I didn’t know him better. The emotions surrounding his death are very complicated, wrapped in a lot of anger and regret. One thing is certain, I’m very sorry he died in that place, in that way.

column1: How do parents cope with the death of adult children?
column3: How parents “get through” the death of an adult child depends on many things. First, their understanding of life, or their religion. If the parent has come to understand that the soul chooses the length of time it will be on earth prior to being born, it is easier to accept the death, even though the parent will miss their child. If the parent doesn’t realize this, it is harder to accept death. If the parent believes that life continues after death of the body and believes they will see their child again, it also makes the death of their child easier to bear as they are hopeful that they will see their child again when they cross over. Another factor for consideration is how their adult child died. Was it in a car crash, overseas in a war, doing drugs, or suicide? There are more ways than just those four, yet how the death occurred matters, whether it was what is considered ‘natural’ or not. I’m not sure anyone gets “through” any death of a loved one. We miss the person. I think of my dad daily and he’s been gone nine years now. Granted he wasn’t my child, but he was treasured and much loved. I am grateful for the time we had together.
column9: I disagree with you on the following statement. “The death of a child is easier to bear, if the parent believes that life continues after death of the body and believes they will see their child again.” My 18 year old son passed away this year on June 7th. I believe that life continues after death and one day I will see my son again. However, this gives me no comfort at all. Absolutely none. The pain in my heart is the worst feeling ever. I will miss him everyday, until the day I die and see him again.

column1: How did you cope with the death of your child?
column3: I swear, I was so busy trying to comfort my despondent wife I’m not really sure I did. I was comforted by my atheism, to a degree. I know it sounds weird, but NOT believing in an afterlife made it so much easier for me. I really wanted to know it was over, once and for all. One thing I learned was to forgive people for saying clumsy things before they even finished saying them. People mean well, they just have no words for their sorrow.

column3: You never really get over it… you just kinda learn to live with it. The pain will ease a bit over time, but depending on how deep your love for them, determines how long you’ll grieve.

column1: How do you cope with the death of your husband in the first few weeks?
column3: My ex wife hadn't yet bought any new mourning clothes for my demise, but she maintained a healthy noire in her wardrobe. She would have done all the things she was supposed to do, with the appropriate amount of sorrow and depression showing, and stayed home from work for two weeks. She would have already researched if there are any “red flags" to watch out for in regards to timing where the life insurance policies were concerned. If a “red flag" would be raised for her attempting to claim the policies within 7 days which would have garnered a deeper investigation into the manner of my death, then she would have waited 8. She would have cashed the checks, then gone back to work. She would have sainted me upon my death, rather than slander me to her workmates as she has done since she abandoned me instead. She would have seemed aptly forlorn and despondent, probably needing to go home early out of distress every now and again, and any curious detective may well have been thrown off the scent at her obvious grief. The toxicology report would have been clean. Then she would have relaxed. She wouldn't have been as kind to my parents as she should have, after she got her money. My mom would have mentioned this to my brother in law, if my brother in law didn't ask of his own accord what her behaviour was like (He would have). A new toxicology request would have been generated by his office and this one would not be clean. When on trial for first degree murder, the paper trail she left behind would have convicted her. But that's down the line….. How would she have coped? With joy and peace in her heart that her adoring husband was dead, that he finally provided enough money in his demise to put a smile on her face, if in private, and happiness that she could find a new target to go after who would give her real, real money. It would be the happiest and most content she had ever been. And she would have thrown away the liquid phenobarbitol, in this scenario, that she left behind when she disappeared.

column1: How does a grieving mother cope with the death of a child?
column3: For parents who have lost a child, it makes no sense for life to end at such a young age—particularly when the death is sudden and without warning. The loss cuts so deep, it can be suffocating. If you are dealing with this type of loss in your family, here are some ways to help you and your family cope. Live Together Live together as a family and lean on each other for help. While everyone in the family will need to have their private time, you also can find comfort in each other. Being together can help you remember that you are not alone in your grief. Use the strength of your family's sense of belonging to help you manage your sorrow. Be there to consistently support one another. Approach a Grief Counselor However, since everyone grieves differently, facing the loss of a child can certainly put strain on a marriage and on each parent's relationship with surviving children. Seek professional help when coming to terms with your loss. Don't try to get through this situation on your own. Family counseling can give you and your family the skills you need to get through the tremendously difficult loss. Accept Help Be open and willing to accept help from extended family members, friends, or neighbors. Allow them to help you with meals, watching your other children, helping around the house, running errands, and most importantly, being there to listen when you need to talk.

column1: How do you help someone cope with the death of a spouse?
column3: I have been through this a number of times. And not just with friends and family. Since I sell life insurance for a living, I am often called upon to expedite claims. I have been the one to deliver checks to the grieving widows and widowers, and their very distraught children. For me, it’s really a question of “follow the leader.” The person in mourning has to run the show. You are there for him or her. He may want to talk. So you listen. He may want to yell and scream and cry for a long time. So you weather the storm. He may want to sit silently and sullenly, deep in thought and feeling very sad. So you keep him company. In any case, the mere fact that you are there is a source of comfort. It definitely helps him cope. And you know what? Sometimes you shouldn’t be there. People in grief often like to be left alone. They need the time and space to process what they are going through. The emotions are overwhelming. Their brains are flooded with all kinds of thoughts. Regrets. Resentments. If only... If only... If only... Let them alone. That is also how you help people cope with the death of a spouse.

column1: How do you cope with the sudden death of your child?
column3: Everyone processes grief differently and unfortunately you won’t know how you will do this until it happens to you. As for me after losing my only son I went through many different phases and levels of misery. For a long time my brain would not allow me to truly believe my son was never coming home. Which is also known as denial in the grief process. As far as the stages I felt like I cycle through each stage several times a day. Several times I felt like I just wanted to give up. I can’t count the times I literally wanted to die. If I could’ve died from a broken heart I would have. As a Christian I had a lot of anger towards God mostly due to unrealistic expectations of my own. As If this doesn’t happen to good people. The truth is this can happen to anyone. I grieved for the life my son never got to live and the life I never got to live with him in it. There is no end to that. I will forever miss him and wish he would’ve gotten to live his life out. I literally had to just tell myself every day to hold on one more day and fake it until you get to a better place. I wish I had done more counseling and handle things better or more healthy manner. The grief and my inability to deal with it destroyed everything I had worked so hard for in my life to that point. I tried so hard to run from the pain but it finally became impossible to run any longer. Once I finally made peace with God and prayed for his help. I began to heal. I know he loves me as much as I loved my son. If this could’ve been avoided by live alone it would’ve been. This is the way things had to be and one day I will know the reason why. Until then I have to find a way to continue living my life until I can be with my son again in Heaven. So I continue to pick up all the pieces and strive to find happiness in my life one day at a time.

column1: How do I cope with the death of a friend?
column3: You’re gonna have to seek the support of other friends and family to help you get through this. It’s very hard to deal with the loss of a friend as it makes you question your own mortality and you feel like it’s just not fair. You will cope with it and you will be OK. You have to reach out to God and also have him help you through it.
column9: One breath at a time. Stay in the moment. Be cautious and take good care. Find solitude. Practice mindfulness techniques. Keep your surroundings tidy. Nourish your body well. Don’t listen to other peoples’advice- find your own path. Trust your ability to survive this pain. Don’t get into drama with other people, avoid dramatic or toxic people right now. Find yourself vulnerable yet strong enough. Be assertive in your needs and wants. Don’t avoid the pain of missing - you can only cry a tear once, and there is an end to the flow of tears. Enjoy beauty and good things consciously. Meet Nature. You will always miss this person, but keep in mind it is possible to heal from this wound if you grieve well, and healthy. Keep the relationship with their memory vivid and clean of pain. Accept that there will be fallbacks, but every step will make you stronger, and every fallback will show you how far you already came.

column1: How do I deal with the death of a loved one? How do I cope with the anxiety of losing one?
column3: I recently lost my JROTC Army Instructor. He was everything to me! He was the father that I never had as a child. I loved him. He supported me always. Then one day he just didn’t show up. I thought maybe he had a trip somewhere which was common for him. Then we got the news he passed away on the way to the hospital. didn’t even make it. The day before though, he laughed with me and told me so many amazing things. It hurt so much to know he would never again talk to me. Not even get on to me for not having my hair up in a good bun. It felt like I was dying too, but that same Friday he passed away, I started writing the things he would tell us on the expo board. Everyone kept adding things and I realized that he didn’t leave pain. He left me amazing moments, goals, love. These things keep me going. They keep me doing the things we loved to do together. They keep me going to accomplish the goals he helped me to set. I loved him with all of my heart and honestly (Don’t tell anyone lol) I still talk to him like I when I would storm into his office. He always listened to me and my dumb problems. Just think of all of the great moments you two had together and know that they would want you to smile and laugh and live your life! (to my sgt) Love you so much Sgt. “Big Will!” I’m still smiling and running that lake! Also about the anxiety, well we never know when another loved one will leave us. I think so much about how I don’t want to loose my only living Grandpa. I call him everyday even if it’s just to tell him I love him. Just seeing his smile when I say that, makes me so happy. I think just letting him know that I love him and that I miss him will make him happy. Losing someone hurts, but they’re gone and there’s nothing we can do but to remember that they loved us back and that they made us in some way. Like they built our character. My grandpa and Sgt built my strong character. Thanks to them, I want to help others. I want to pursue a career that gives back. Losing someone is painful once again, but they left you something great. Take it and change someone else’s life like they did to you. I guess that’s all. Good luck!
column9: Thank you so much for sharing with me such personal story! I really appreciate it and I wish you the best life.♥️

column1: How do doctors cope with the death of a child?
column3: When my son died I saw two doctors cry, tears coming out of their eyes. One of the Drs gave my son a tree planting service. My son had such a bright personality, he just was witty and funny as hell. I felt sorry for the Dr and his teachers, they were so sad.

column1: How did the Virgin Mary spend the rest of her days after the death of Jesus Christ? Does history tell us anything about it? How did she cope with the loss of her son?
column3: Among the mystics of the Catholic Church at least two have received visions of the life of Mary before and after the death of Her Son. Blessed Mary of Agreda, Spain, and Blessed Anne Catherine Emmerich of Germany recorded the Life of Mary. While the visions have been recognized as authentic, they remain private revelations and faithful Catholics are not required to believe them. column1: How do you cope with death and the nothingness that comes after it?
column3: I don’t love it, but telling myself a fairytale isn’t going to make the inevitable sadness I feel that life must end any easier to deal with. My parents never told me any of those fairytales commonly known as religion, and I had to come to terms with the reality of death at an early age. My best friend was diagnosed with leukemia when we were four, and though she ultimately survived, death came close enough that I had frequent discussions on the subject, both with my parents and my friend, during those play dates spent wearing masks on opposite sides of the room. When Eva was sick I was still too young to fully grasp the meaning of death, but when I was 8 my aunt who was like a second mom to us had a cold that wouldn’t go away. After a few weeks the doctors decided the cold was pneumonia, and after a few more weeks they realized it was cancer, and three months later she was gone. I still hadn’t understood everything as a grownup would have, but fate is a real dick, because a year later we had to cancel our summer vacation when my mom’s doctor found “something” on her ovary. “Something” was removed, but like “something” often does, it returned when I was 11. I was old enough now to understand that this “something” was of the same variety as what almost killed my friend, and what did kill my aunt. I was also old enough to comprehend the entire terrifying truth when my parents told me that this terrifying something could no longer be stopped. We talked a lot, and my mom told my sisters and I that she’d always be a part of us, and that whatever energy made her wouldn’t disappear. She would be gone, but what used to be her would be part of nature. It was terrifying and most definitely not okay, but somehow I got used to living with the knowing that my mom had seen her last Christmas. My dad took a long leave from work, and we went on vacation. Once you accept that this life is all there is, you make the most of it. We traveled for weeks and had a blast, while she was still well enough to enjoy life. We returned home briefly for my sister’s finals, when my mom still had an estimated six months to live. One morning she tickled me awake as always, she made coffee and were preparing to go out, and suddenly her body stopped working. I wasn’t mad that we’d been robbed of those months, just relieved that she never had to get as sick as my aunt, and grateful that my sister and I had been building a sandcastle around her five days earlier in Spain. It was not okay, but I could live with it.
