column1: How does it feel when someone you care about walks out of your life?
column3: From Wikipedia: “The Kübler-Ross model, or the five stages of grief, postulates a series of emotions experienced by survivors of an intimate’s death, wherein the five stages are denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance.” The loss of someone you care about is like a death, and you go through those five stages—not necessarily in that order. And sometimes there are additional components to the model, such as betrayal. The denial is the feeling of disbelief you experience right after it happens; it’s like the person you care about suddenly turned around and clocked you in the jaw when you least expected it. You can’t make sense of it. You keep telling yourself, “That didn’t just happen.” The other emotions follow—the anger that they would just turn their back on you. The bargaining and pleading. Sometimes you beg them to give you another chance, but it falls on deaf ears, sometimes routing you right back to denial, because you can’t believe that anyone would be that irrational. Or cold. Or unkind. This is someone you thought cared about you deeply. Depression is where I feel a lot of people get stuck. It’s the mid-way point between the initial event and acceptance, and it takes a lot of work to muddle through it. But acceptance, when it finally comes, is such a relief. One morning, you wake up, and you feel lighter. And then you realize that you haven’t dwelled on the past at all—in fact, it’s been a long time since you’ve thought of your former friend/other. It might not seem like it, but that ambivalence is a gift. Ambivalence has made you whole again.

column1: I feel like im dying after a breakup with the man I thought I was gonna spend my whole life with. How do I survive this?
column3: Break ups can feel like the death of someone you are close to in that they are permanently removed from your life. You can expect to go through the five stages of grief which include denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. I find these stages do not alway progress in a straight line or predictably. Because the person you are grieving actually exists still I find people have the most trouble when they express that anger directly to the person or try to bargain with them to get back together. My recommendation is to be gentle with yourself and let yourself grieve. Eat some ice cream, watch sappy movies, stay in your pajamas all day and read … If you need to express your anger, throw some darts at his picture or write him a heartfelt letter and then burn it. If it feels good to be with friends, reach out to them. If it feels good to be alone, that is fine too. Don’t rush the process. I know it feels like the world is over now but trust that some day the pain will be gone.
column9: Then sometimes you through the 5 stages of grief and they are still there so you grieve more while there is no resolve so your heart remains forever broken

column1: Is it normal for someone who has been a part of an abortion to act as though nothing happened afterwards?
column3: Part of an abortion? You may need to explain this. The overwhelming majority of women who have an abortion simply get on with their lives. Many of those who get on with their lives go through all the stages of grief that women who have had miscarriages and stillbirths do, but ultimately carry on. Only a tiny fraction of women who have had abortions go through more extreme reactions. It is not possible to know in advance which reaction is more likely: perhaps it's the women who were coerced, either literally or by circumstance, or those with pre-existing tendencies to, for example, depression. But most will ‘act normally’, in the same way that everyone does, eventually, after a death.
column9: In my case, it was the father. Everytime I would see him he would talk and act as though nothing had happen. He once told me that “I always wanted to talk about the abortion.” I felt like it was an elephant in the room.

column1: What is distinct in the loss of a spouse that isn't generally experienced in another type of loss by death?
column3: My beloved husband of 35 fantastic years was feeling under the weather. His breathing became somewhat laboured and we both thought he had a ‘bug’. After a week he was getting worse . Even though he was being stubborn, as most men are, I insisted we go to the emerg dept at our local hospital. After some tests and a CT scan, the doctor came in and shut the door behind her. Oh-oh I thought, something’s up. We were told he was in 4th stage cancer which had spread into his brain, lungs, thyroid and elsewhere. He didn’t have long….maybe a month or two at the most. The very first thing he did was turn to look at me. I was weeping quietly but my heart was breaking. There was tears in his eyes as he looked at me and said “I love you deeply”. His words tore through me and I couldn’t speak. We loved each other so much. He spoke for us both. The suddenness of the deadly diagnoses was an arrow piercing every part of me. “This can’t be true I thought! “They’ve got him mixed up with someone else!!” He’s hardly ever been sick in all the years we’d been together and now he’s dying??? He was so lovingly caring for me more than I him. I couldn’t understand what was happening. Later at home alone, I received a call from the doctor who reiterated that my husband had possibly a few months remaining. Ten days later he died. I wasn’t there. My strong, beautiful and gentle husband was dead. I wanted to die. He had forgotten to take me with him! How will I carry on without the dearest love of my life near me. We did everything together and were seldom apart. We were told often that we were joined at the hip, that you would rarely see one without the other. We were the very best of friends. Is it possible to love someone too much? The first few days, then weeks, then months, now a year of grief were horrible. The pain is too hard to describe. The loneliness without him was unbearable. They say the deeper the love, the greater the grief. People have said “ it’s been a year, you should be getting over it by now” WHAT?!!! How do you ‘get over’ suddenly losing your life partner, your soul mate, the one who’s heart was a part of your own heart. A year is just a flash in the pan. I know the pain will never go but will become easier to bear eventually. The tears will be less and less but the memory of him and our wonderful life together will always be foremost in my mind. He was 75. ”Tis better to have loved and lost than to never have loved at all” Alfred Lord Tennyson
column9: I hope you find peace in your heart. I also lost my dear best friend, my husband. There were days I could barely breathe. If I counted through ten minutes without feeling I was falling apart I gave myself a pat on the back. It has been two and a half years. I miss him terribly, however now I manage a silly smirk when I recall sailing mishaps and our fantastic life together. My heart goes out to you. My request is you be kind and patient with yourself and your feelings. Do not allow anyone to tell you how to deal with your grief.

column1: Is it normal to still grieve 5 months after a death?
column3: Absolutely normal. We never really get completely over the death of a loved one. There are stages of grief also and we go through over again at times. The death of a loved one is a devastating experience. It leaves a hole. The edges grow closer so we don’t fall head first every time it comes up in our minds and hearts. But it is always there. My niece died 4 years ago and yesterday I was feeling very sad about her being gone for the holidays. Sometimes I see someone who reminds me of her and my heart feels a stab of pain. It is good to acknowledge our pain and work through it. There are times when we need to stop and feel. We have to learn not to live in it. No one who loves you wants you to be devastated forever. I also say that “normal” is just a setting on the dryer.. We can set ourselves up when we compare ourselves to others or think that how we feel isn’t normal. Your loved ones and your relationships are unique to you. No one should tell you time’s up or get over it. It doesn’t work that way. If you feel you need help.. and we often do.. with your grief, there are counselors and support groups available in many venues. Be gentle with yourself. I am sorry for your pain.

column1: Are there grief stages in leaving a narc? If so, how many stages are there? So far I’ve felt anger, pain, guilt, bargaining, depression. Now I’m just lonely, thinking I’m never gonna feel or get the good times we had with someone new.
column3: Coming to the realization that you have been in or are in a relationship with someone who is narcissistic can tear apart your understanding of the world. Whether it’s your parent or partner, you probably feel unsettled after this discovery; maybe even feel like you are an emotional wreck. You can also find yourself crying all the time, feeling exhausted mentally, emotionally and physically beyond all understanding, feeling your world is falling apart. Many NPD victims will say, “I don’t know who I am now,” “I’m having a identity crisis,” or “I can’t seem to pull myself together.” This is often revered to the “The Realization” as a significant moment in their life. So how do you process this new information? One way to understand the process is by looking at the stages of grief. Because after all, you are experiencing grief and loss. Loss of what you thought was reality; of a future you thought you had; of the love you thought you had; of a past that is no longer what you thought it was, and most likely the loss of a relationship. Stages of Grief Realizing a Narcissistic Relationship Much like the stages of grief, this discovery is the beginning of a long journey. Swiss-American psychiatrist, Elisabeth Kubler Ross defined grief in five stages: Denial, Anger, Doubt (Bargaining), Depression, and Acceptance. Similar to grieving death, these stages are not experienced in a linear fashion. You will bounce back and forth between stages and much of the time it will feel unpredictable. Just when you think you are done with one stage, something happens to bring you back to that place again. Below is a description of what the stages can look like when discovering you have been in a narcissistic relationship.DenialMaybe you were reading something and came across a definition of narcissistic abuse or narcissism and it sounded just a little too familiar. Or maybe a family member or friend mentioned that this might apply to your relationship. However the discovery happened, most people will ignore this new information, regardless how true it may feel. It can take several years for this information to sink in. I have had clients come to therapy and say that they knew in the back of their mind their parent or partner was narcissistic but could just not face the truth. It took several years before they were able to acknowledge and process what they had experienced. For some the denial may be shorter. Either way, recognizing that you have been in a narcissistic relationship is painful and opens up old wounds that you may not be ready to deal with. 2. Anger Yes, you get angry! Once you realize the abuse for what it is, you get angry! Many people finally recognize what they have suffered through and cannot believe the abuse they have been enduring. Finally acknowledging that you have been manipulated, lied to, gaslighted, and made to feel you will never be good enough causes the anger to surface. Recognize that under the anger is trauma and a deep sense of hurt. It is okay and understandable that you are angry, it’s a necessary part of healing process. 3. Bargaining (Doubt) Another label for the bargaining phase is Doubt. People bounce to this stage often. The questions of doubt surface regularly. Doubt makes you ask yourself, “Maybe it’s me,” or “Am I right, are they really narcissistic?” Bargaining makes you rationalize, “Maybe it’s not as bad as I think.” Due to the nature of narcissistic abuse, it is normal for someone to question their reality and wonder if they are the one with the problem or if they are the narcissist. This is what you have been trained to do by your abuser. 4. Depression Once you have allowed yourself to truly identify with being in a narcissistic relationship, depression can surround you like a fog. The emotional abuse you experience is deep, painful and attacks the core of who you are. It messes with your sense of self. The pain and sadness can be overwhelming and many people fear never moving past this stage. They begin to feel stuck, they lack motivation to do the emotional work, they wish they could go back to not knowing, they worry about never having healthy relationships, and they fear they will never heal. 5. Acceptance This can look different for everyone. Acceptance happens after someone has done the emotional work of really understanding their experience and healing from the trauma. At that point, some people choose to cut off all contact with the narcissistic person and some learn how to set strong boundaries and choose to stay in relationship. There is no right or wrong answer. Acceptance is understanding the abuse was not your fault, but being able to take ownership of any unhealthy patterns you may have adopted and learn to let those go. It is being able to learn to set boundaries that allow you to be in healthy relationships and to regain a strong sense of who you are. Acceptance is not about placing blame but recognizing the abuse you experienced and taking responsibility for your healing and future growth. Healing Is Possible Just like the stages of grief, people will bounce back and forth between these stages, even revisiting them after years of healing. It’s a journey. There is no calculated time you have to work through them, everyone’s experience is different. Let that be okay. Allowing yourself the time and space to work through these stages is part of the healing process. If you find yourself in one of these stages, please be kind to yourself. Pay attention to your self-talk. Adopt a hopeful mantra and continue to repeat it over and over. Post it where you can see it. Something like, ‘healing is possible’ or ‘I know that I will be okay.’ Because it is true, you can find healing and go on to live a vibrant life! I wanted to add… I’ve communicated with thousands of NPD survivors on these prideful and mentally disordered men & women who believe that they have the right to destroy someone mentally, emotionally, verbally, financially, socially, spiritually, sexually and some physically with their insidious manipulations and abuse. These survivors have endure and overcome unbelievable torture only to find their incredible strength to get out. After healing they become exceptional people who have survived something the public has no understanding that exists in our world. They turn out to be smart, loving, caring, kind, supportive, loyal and beautiful people that I am honored to be a part of their healing. This is what drives my passion to educate people on the truth of a Narcissist. Take Care, ❤️Marlene Matlock

column1: Throughout the series, has Gon shown signs of being psychotic?
column3: DISCLAMER: SPOILERS> A LOT OF THEM> READ AT YOUR OWN RISK Thank you Yes. Gon has shown multiple signs of being an unhinged person growing up. Gon being the person he is, he grew up off of his curiosity. His caretakers, Aunt Mito and his great grandmother, both allowed him very much freedom when he was younger. He was younger than 4 years old when he was hanging out all over his home island with no super vision what so ever. Therefore, Gon did not generally grown up off of what was right or wrong, but what was simply “good or bad”. Gon grew up with no childhood trauma unlike many of the people he knows like Killua, who grew up being tortured by his family, or Kurapika and Leorio, who lost people that were important to them. Gon has always identified someone as good or bad based off of how the benefit him. If you have anything of good use to him, he considers you as good. On the other hand, if you are absolutely no use to him, then you could drop dead for all he cares. With this, we come to one of our first examples of Gon being mentally unstable. In season 3, when Gon and Killua had been captured by the phantom troupe for the second time, Gon asked Chrollo a question: “How can you kill people that have nothing to do with you?” However, in season 5, Gon allowed his emotions to take over, as he had gone through the 5 stages of grief for the first time in his life, and he threatened to kill Komugi, an innocent girl who had nothing to do with the situation, but because she was considered a weak spot to both Meruem and Nefer Pitou, Gon decided to use her life as a threat. The next bit of my reasoning is lying. Gon has lied to others or not kept his promise before. So when it comes to punishments' for breaking those promises or lying, he does whatever the other person wants. And he’s serious about it too. He will voluntarily stick thousands of needles in his eye, and be okay with it. So this just says how serious he is about lying and other people lying to him. Not only that but Gon will let you lie to him, just so he can feel justified about jacking you up with no remorse what so ever. I have 2 primary examples for this. The first one is when Gon is fighting Genthru on Greed Island in season 4. Genthru tells Gon that he surrenders, but is just lying to Gon so he can lure him over and strike him. However, Gon knew from the very moment Genthru’s mouth moved, that it was a lie. So Gon let Genthru hit him, because that was the all clear signal for Gon to absolutely screw Genthru up without a second thought. My second example is when Gon first meets Meleoron in season 5. Gon saw promise and great benefit in Meleoron, which is why Gon gave him a warning. Knowing that Meleoron was going to be turning traitor to his own kind, he told Meleoron that if he was just lying to Gon so that the Chimera Ants could get the advantage, then Gon would kill him without thinking twice. When Gon did this, he allowed his bloodlust to leak so Meleoron would not only see, but feel how serious Gon was. These two images above are both images of the scene in which Gon threatens Meleoron. The first one is from the 2011 anime. The second one is from the manga. I have now come to my next reasoning of Gon being psychotic. I probably should’ve put this one first since not only is it all from the first season, but definitely relates with my first paragraph. Season 1, the hunter exam. During that exam, Gon watched almost 400 people die, and didn’t even give a FIRST thought about them. Now I say it like this, because out of everyone in the hunter exam, Gon is the only examinee who has NEVER experienced or seen anything like that. All of the other examinees are either adults who have gone through horrible things, adults who have already been properly educated as to what is happening around them, or it’s Killua, who has been dealing with death, killing, and torture since he was a baby. Gon out of a good 400 something people, was the only one who had never even SEEN a dead body up close before, and when he had seen people getting killed right before him, he didn’t even bat an eyelash. This is all because, THEY HAD NO BENEFIT TO HIM. Therefore, Gon didn’t care whether they lived or died, because to him, they were useless. And this is again because of Gon’s perspective on what is Good and bad. Anything that helps and benefits him is good, and anything that does the opposite is bad. If Gon had actually been taught properly, he probably wouldn’t have become a hunter, because he would hate his dad from child neglect. This is my FINAL reasoning to Gon being crazy. This is the part when he actually went crazy. Season 5, Kite’s death. Now generally, we could understand why Gon was so angry. Kite wasn’t just another person or mentor to Gon. He was like a big brother. Gon originally met Kite when he was 4 years old. Kite is the reason Gon was able to find out his dad was still alive, and might not have become a hunter and met all his friends if it weren’t for Kite. So Kite is a very important person to Gon… and then spoiler alert- Pitou kills him- BUT HE COMES BACK ALIVE DON”T WORRY! When Kite dies, Gon goes through the 5 stages of grief for the first time in his life, as he had never lost anyone important to him. I mean, Gon literally said that he couldn’t care less who his mom was or if she was alive or not, all because he had never met her. So when Kite dies, Gon goes through the first stage- denial. Gon still believes, or wants to believe, that Kite is still alive. Then Kite gets turned into a puppet but isn’t actually alive, but Gon, Killua, Morel, Knov, Shoot, and Knuckle don’t know that, which is why when they save Kite’s body from the Chimera Ant nest, Gon doesn’t know that Kite is just a walking corpse. However, Kite’s appearance now looks as if he has been tortured, and this is what unlocks the second stage of grief for Gon- anger. At this point, Gon is ready to let his bloodlust take over whenever, so when he gets tested by Morel, and Morel says something related to Kite’s death and what happened to him, Gon nearly kills Morel unconsciously, without realizing that it was Morel he was up against, and not Pitou. Our next stage of grief is of course- the bargaining. Gon wants Pitou to heal Kite, still not knowing that he’s actually dead, and then he’ll make the decision as to whether he still wants to kill Pitou or not. However, because Pitou was in the middle of healing Komugi when Gon found them, Pitou manageably ( with the help of Killua) was able to get Gon to agree and wait for one hour. After that hour is over, Gon and Pitou go to see Kite, in which once they get there, Gon tells Pitou to heal him. Pitou tells Gon that because he was able to respect their whishes to heal Komugi, Pitou agrees to tell Gon the truth, that Kite is already dead. This brings us on to the 4th stage of grief- depression, however, it’s not only depression for Gon, it’s also a large sense of anger and rage (the second stage). Basically when I say this, I mean that Gon went through the depression and that depression turned into anger and hate. Gon then used that anger and hate, to kill Pitou. And even had Pitou was defeated, Gon kept going. It wasn’t til the very end of that battle, in which Killua found Gon, turned into his adult form. We finally move onto out final stage- acceptance. At this point, Gon has accepted everything that’s happened. Kite’s death, Pitou’s lying, and the consequences Gon will suffer from his transformation. He’s accepted it all. So generally, this was by far, the most traumatic thing Gon had ever gone through so far. You could only imagine what would happened if somebody super duper close to him like Killua, Aunt Mito, Ging, or great grandmother were to be killed. And even if it wasn’t one of them, I think Gon would definitely go in rage mode again, DESPITE all of the risks Killua and Alluka took to save him. So there you have it. All of my reasons that I believe Gon is unhinged. Have a good day.(✿◕‿◕✿)
column9: > Gon out of a good 400 something people, was the only one who had never even SEEN a dead body up close before, and when he had seen people getting killed right before him, he didn’t even bat an eyelash. column1: Why do I feel I'm dying without my narcissist?
column3: You feel you are dying because you miss someone you loved so much. It is such an overwhelming feeling of loss. You may not be dying, but you are grieving, and that grief is profound, and very real. Although it may appear insurmountable to you at this time, it will get better. These words hold little meaning for you right now, as they are undoubtedly overshadowed by cutting shards of glass pain…but it will change, and mellow into a bittersweet memory, and a hard learned lesson as well. You miss all the beautiful feelings, you miss the closeness, the connection and the deep emotions that can only be experienced when you are in love. THE STAGES OF GRIEF were originally intended for coming to terms with the death of a loved one. It is also helpful when mourning the death of a relationship. THE FIVE STAGES OF GRIEF:DENIAL -it helps us survive the loss. In this stage, the world becomes meaningless and overwhelming. Life makes no sense.ANGER - it is a necessary part of the healing process. Be willing to feel your anger, even though it may seem endless.BARGAINING: After the loss (breakup) your head is filled with “and only” and “what if’s” because we wish we could go back in time and have everything the way it was before.DEPRESSION - the empty feelings present themselves, and grief enters our lives on a deeper level. You come to realize you are not getting back together. If grief is a process of healing. Then depression is one of the many necessary steps along the way.ACCEPTANCE- Acceptance is often confused with everything being okay with what has happened. You will not likely ever feel this way. This stage is ACCEPTING the reality that the other person is gone from your life, and that this new reality is a permanent reality.These feelings are natural, and although they are incredibly uncomfortable, they are part of the process of recovering from your extreme loss. The list of stages can be useful when addressing the often abrupt and bewildering end of a relationship with a Narcissist. But for this post, I wanted to keep it simple. I am not really addressing the “narcissistic “ element to your question. You are certain to receive many insightful responses from others on this site. My thoughts today are about dealing with the loss of the person who made your life so intensely exhilarating , if only for a short while. Because when you love someone, you just love them. I am right in there with you on this. I currently share your pain. I am so sorry you have to endure it. Sending love your way. Grace
column9: In addition to the answer given, I’d like to add research everything you can about trauma bonding. You feel like you’re dying because you are going through very real withdrawals. It does get better, I promise.

column1: I rejected a guy for arranged marriage because although I liked him, I thought he wasn't interested in me. He did not pursue further either. I'm still not over him and its been 2 years. What should I do?
column3: Feel the feelings. Allow yourself to experience them. Don’t try to hide from them or push them away. Let them come. Feel them. Let them out. You may worry they will never stop, but remind yourself it will get better. No matter how hard we cry, at some point we stop.Understand you will go through the stages of grief. The loss of a relationship is like a death. Feelings of disbelief, shock, anger, hurt, bargaining, sadness, fear, and depression are normal.Think of your pain like a wave. There will be times where, for a brief period, you may “forget” about it—and then it will hit you all over again. If you fight the feeling and try to push it away, it will grip you harder. Imagine yourself diving into the emotional wave.Stop the self-blame. It’s natural to turn the blame on yourself and ask what you did wrong, why you weren’t good enough. Remember it is not your fault.Find a therapist who can help. The journey of recovery after a partner leaves takes time, support, and patience.I hope it helps 🙏 Salaam

column1: Adult Who came up with the 5 stages of grief?
column3: Dr. Elizabeth Kubler-Ross. After many years of working with those who were dying and with their families after the death, she came up with the 5 stages of grief. She used an inverted bell-curve to identify these stages, however, in reality, you pass through the stages at different time. They do not go through each stage one by one. If you want to know the reality of the stages of grief, then this should explain it very well.The, “My Experience,” if equal to dropping a superball into an enclosed room and the ball goes bat-shit crazy. The stages can repeat themselves many times over, can come at the oddest time, even years later. The most important thing is to remember to be kind to yourself. Lastly, when it comes to dealing with grief, on Amazon there is a fantastic book I recommend highly, “The Grief Recovery Handbook.” The book is invaluable. Blessed Be.

column1: What is it like to have a classmate die in high school?
column3: On April 26th, 2017, the loudest, most vibrant, lively boy that I have ever known died in a classroom, unexpectedly and spontaneously, with no underlying conditions. His heart stopped. No one knew what happened. Rumors flew that afternoon. Drug overdose. Seizure. Suicide. None of it was true; he was a drummer, incredibly happy, very religious, surrounded by great friends. The school called all the parents. The day was a blur. Nothing was real. His closest friends went silent for weeks. No one heard from them. Other students reached out however they could to comfort his friends and family, but everyone was affected. The day after he passed, the halls were silent. Grief counselors abundant, but nobody wanted to talk; we just wanted this to not be happening. We’re a close-knit school. It was like this huge shadow was cast over us. As someone who had been close to him, I (along with others) was called in by investigators trying to rule out homicide. That’s how completely out of left field this was. We were sixteen. A few weeks passed. At the funeral, they still hadn’t figured out the cause of his death. Inconclusive autopsy. It was devastating. As time passed, we all came to terms with it, moving through various stages of grief. Eventually, we found out that his death was caused by an unintentional caffeine overdose; supposedly, he’d had a coffee, a soda, and an energy drink within maybe six hours. His body couldn’t handle it. A year later, on the anniversary of his passing, my school put on an event to honor and celebrate him. I swear, there was this huge hole where he should have been. Losing him still hurts, but things heal with time. It seems so incredibly unfair that the world has lost such a powerful spirit so soon, but our best efforts are put toward living our lives to our greatest ability. As a school, we came together through this hardship, and I share a close bond with those that felt his loss the way I did. So what’s it like? Shocking, frame-shifting, heartbreaking. Crazy existential. You never see it coming. It’s hard for me to answer this question because after losing a classmate, so much has changed. Maybe if the student had been a stranger to me, this wouldn’t keep me up at night. But he wasn’t, and I will never be the same knowing that he is not here. In his memory, all I know to do is live life loud.
column9: So sad. Such a tragedy. My heart goes out to his friends and family.

column1: Adult Do the five stages of grief follow a specific and definitive kind of order or can they be varied and change from moment to the next?
column3: Elizabeth Kubler-Ross who is famous for her book ‘On Death and Dying’ coined the 5 stages of grief: Denial Anger Bargaining Depression Acceptance Now, if you take into account that each one of us is different, and we all grieve in different ways, you will see that this ‘recipe’ just cannot apply to everybody in all circumstances. There are many variants. Some people do not grieve at all when somebody they love dies. Perhaps they have been taught to repress their emotions in childhood. They might even be completely out of touch with their emotions altogether. Other people will be able to pass through the stages without interruption then get stuck somewhere and find it hard to move on. This often applies to the stage of depression. In fact, for many people depression lasts so long and is so severe that they have to go to the doctor and get treatment. For other people, it is quite normal for grief to come and go in spurts - feel sad one day, then fine the next and so on. Which ever way we look at it, it is not a continuum. These feelings come and go and do not keep to any order at all. Just when you have got to the depression stage, for example, you might suddenly find yourself feeling angry again because there is still something not resolved. Many people get angry with themselves, or doctors or even God. For some this can be a test of their faith and a very dark time indeed. The only way you can know that you are done with grieving, and have completed your journey, is that you will have arrived at the peace of acceptance. Acceptance is not pleasant, there will always be recriminations, but it marks a time when the person can move on with their life. There will always be the memories to cling to even long after the person has died. Grieving is like going out on a long journey. There are many bumps in the road, but eventually you get to your destination.

column1: My 44 year old husband passed away unexpectedly 9 months ago. Just now it is really starting to hit me that this is permanent. Nobody understands that I'm still grieving deeply. Is this normal?
column3: That’s because society puts a time limit on grief. They say there are 5 stages of grief, and that after the first year, you’ll “feel better” or you should be “over it”. These are words from people who have obviously never experienced the loss of someone close to them. Unfortunately, I have, twice in my life, and I’m only 43 years old. First, my husband passed away when he was only 34 years old, the day before my 32nd birthday. He was perfectly healthy and came down with flu like symptoms that shut down every organ in his body, he passed away within 2 weeks of getting sick. I was never given the exact reason he passed. I thought that was the worst thing I would ever go through, but sadly, I was wrong. 10 months ago, my only son, and my oldest child, Alex, passed away from an accidental fentanyl overdose at our house. He was 25 years old, and had battled addiction for 10 years, following the death of his Dad. I can tell you from experience, you will never “get over” your loss. Your grief will always be with you, it’s just something that you learn to live with. I can tell you that although it never goes away, it does change with time. You will always miss them, you will always wonder what life would be like if they were still here, you will never be the same person you were when they were alive, but you will survive, and you will not always feel so sad, so hopeless, so alone. I don’t ever like to say things will get better, but they will change, as will you. I am sorry for you loss, I truly am. Just know that you’re not alone, there are actually quite a few young widows. Forums like this are a great help, so are support groups, and getting with a counselor you really click with. I like to read and do workbooks based on my specific losses, I find that helpful too. Hang in there, and don’t give up!
column9: I am so sorry for your loss! When you have a spouse pass on, no matter what anyone say’s you don’t have to get over them passing. There is no time limit on grief. My wife passed on Sept. of 2024 from cancer, I will never get over her passing and the grief will always be with me. She was the most true blessing I have ever received in my life! I miss everything about her and how special she is! Anyone that has not lost a spouse has no idea how that feels, the emptyness, loss of the loved one you care about and Love with all your heart! My wife and I have always been blessed with a spiritual connection all of our married life and we still are spiritually connected. That helps a lot but it is still not the same as having those physical moments to be able to hug, hold hands, go for beautiful walks together! Those of you that have had a spouse pass on don’t let anyone tell you that you should be over it, you don’t have to be. I miss my wife a lot and Love her with all my heart always will! She knows that from heaven and is waiting for me, your spouse knows the love you feel for them and will be waiting for you as well. Peace be with you all 🙏

column1: How did you forgive who wronged you?
column3: You work through the five stages of grief - even if the way they wronged you didn’t result in a death, you suffered a loss and you need to mourn that loss. Do NOT let anyone rush you through the five stages - shock, denial, bargaining, anger and acceptance. You need to work through them at your own pace. Once you have reached acceptance - and only you can decide what acceptance looks like - then you can start to think about forgiveness. But understand that forgiveness does NOT mean forgetting what happened; it does NOT mean letting the person off without repercussions or allowing yourself to be injured again. You can forgive and still modify your behavior to prevent the person who hurt you from hurting you again. Expect that the other person will object to you modifying your behavior, but that isn’t their decision to make. You may even decide to cut off all contact with the person who hurt you so that they can not hurt you again - and, yes, that can be part of forgiveness, too. You don’t give forgiveness to benefit the person who hurt you - no matter what they may claim. You give forgiveness to benefit yourself. Forgiveness means letting go of the anger and the hurt so that you can move forward without the burdens of the past. So forgiveness can be part of letting go of the person who hurt you, or letting go of your expectations of how that person should behave. Forgiveness is freedom and the acceptance that you were hurt but the injury has healed - this is why you can not rush to forgiveness until after you have worked through the five stages of grief, and maybe even longer. Don’t rush it, it will come with time.

column1: Has anyone or knows anyone that has lost their baby to SIDS? I am heartbroken and trying to find a desire to live.
column3: My wife and I lost our first born at 33 days old almost 20 years ago. When the autopsy results came back with a SIDS death ruling, it felt more like “we have no clue why he died so we are just going to say it was this”. Confusion came over now amongst the stages of grief from shock, denial, anger, etc. After the funeral ended, the family and friends left, I remember my wife and I standing on the balcony to the apartment with all of the flowers from the funeral. In that quiet moment of where do we go from here, she told me that just at least holding a child would help right now, as she has love to give, yet no child to give it to. When he passed away, he was rushed to Texas Children's Hospital in Houston. I looked into what volunteer options they had available there, and were in fact looking for weekday day hour and weekend night people to help in the baby nursery section. We talked it over, decided to go ahead and try it, and disclosed that we had recently lost ours in their long background check/application volunteer process (took about a month and a half) The first night was kind of heartbreaking, if for the simple fact that many in that section were within the same week of age as our son would be. But it definitely helped my wife immensely as she got to spread that love she felt that was “non-giveable” or forever traped in the days after our son's death. Because we could not make a difference in the world now with our firstborn, we tried to make as much of a difference as we could every weekend there for a couple of hours walking amongst 30 infants in the hospital. It became comforting and soothing on both ends, for both holder and baby involved. And parents showing up were always thankful when they came and saw us volunteering caring for their babies while they had to do work or other errands. In the end, my wife volunteered about 200 hours worth there, until she became pregnant with our daughter. The hospital wanted volunteer people to go through medical tests that fall and, seeing as our firstborn was a SIDS death, was cautious and did not want to do all of these tests while pregnant with our daughter. I stayed and volunteered an extra 50 hours or so, right up until the week before she was born, and left my volunteer position when she was born. It was a nervous start, not knowing how it would go even a month and a half after his death, but I am thankful for it because of the care we provided for others that was stopped short with our own son.

column1: Can someone ever fully recover from deep loss and sadness?
column3: People do recover from deep loss and sadness, but it can take a long time for some people. Any loss is sad, especially losses like divorce, losing a job and losing your health. But many people will have to face losses and go on with life. The older you get, the more losses you will have to suffer. It is also known that a person can suffer more with each loss as they think of all the losses gone before. Losing a pet is a very difficult thing to get over for many people. After all, your pet has been your faithful companion. It is sad to lose them. Every loss will have to be grieved, even the small ones. If you have had a divorce, it is not a small loss, and you will likely grieve the loss of what might have been if you had had a successful marriage. Grief comes in stages. Some stages will overlap, and others will be experienced at different times. It is not unusual for people to miss out on various stages altogether. This shows that we are very different in our grief. Here is a note of the stages of grief as written by Elizabeth Kubler-Ross in her book “Death and Dying.” SHOCK AND DENIAL It doesn’t matter if the death is sudden or expected, a person may initially be in shock and denial. How could this have happened to me? ANGER Many people experience anger after death. It is quite normal. People find themselves angry with everybody: the nurses, the doctors, themselves, and even God. This anger can last a very long time. BARGAINING If it were possible to bargain with God, the person would do so as they would give anything to have their loved one back. But bargaining never works because the person is dead. DEPRESSION Many people go through a phase of depression and this is quite normal. It is not clinical depression, unless it goes on for a long time. It is a reaction to the events that have taken place. However, some people find themselves stuck in the depressive phase so would be advised to seek help from their doctor. ACCEPTANCE This is the final stage of grief. It is when the person finally accepts that the death has occurred and there is nothing left to do. It is very hard to get to this phase because it means the loss of all hope. But if you can get there sooner rather than later, you will be able to be free of the loss. Of course, many people never recover from a loss. In this case, therapy might provide the answer.

column1: Why can't I even cry even if I'm in pain after a break up?
column3: When you break up, you go through the same stages of grief as you do when you mourn the death of a loved one. So, there will be stages when you cry and stages when you don’t. But, this does not necessarily follow a pattern. It doesn’t mean that just because you’re not crying now, that you’ve moved past that grief stage. As, grief has a funny way of turning up when you least expect it (triggered by a whole variety of things including people, places, celebrations, even taste (food) and smell. A good way to move through the pain of the break up is to start a journal. That way, you can get some of your thoughts out of your head and some of your feelings out of your body. Eventually, the thoughts and feelings will diminish.

column1: How does an INTJ behave in the presence of someone he loves?
column3: It's uncannily similiar to the five stages of Death, if you know anything about psychology. If you know an INTJ going through these stages, have fun watching the mask of aloof boredness fade off their faces and be replaced with complete emotional vulnerability. They'll snap if you touch them. They'll go from the confident smart-aleck who thinks the world is beneath them to bumbling idiots. Watch the perspiration collect on their faces, their fidgety and sweaty hands that they are trying not to wring together in case their secret admirer noticed (note, they probably don't have one), and endless and endless pacing, and quiet muttering of “stupid, stupid, stupid.” Here is where their ESFP dual shows up: the face of true insecurity. Be warned, if you're documenting this surreal phenomenon. In case you haven't figured it out yet, here are the five stages of dea — I mean, of an infatuated INTJ:Awareness (or lack of it): Hell, they probably don't realize that they're really uncomfortable only around you. They laugh nervously and give you a very awkward compliment (which is strange because they never compliment anyone else) that your eyebrow raises in inquiry, because how the hell is “you burn like molten lava” a compliment, anyway. But you shrug and smile politely. Then they go home and wonder, “What was that all about? Did I make a fool of myself? But she’s so different than other people — I bet she accepts me even if I am really stupid. What am I saying? She probably knows I'm really smart. But why do I care so much, anyway?” Then they freeze, and their eyes widen in horror. “Oh, crap, maybe I care too much! What are these strange stirrings? I can't possibly be in love! Love is for the weak, and INTJ is never weak!”Avoidance: Remember their last compliment? Well, sorry to tell you, but . . . Forget that. What compliment? He never meant to compliment you. In fact, take that, silly person that thinks he likes you. He doesn't even care that you exist anymore. Look, he's not even looking at you right now! He’s too cool to talk to a silly person like you. Oh, he's leaving without a goodbye? Good heavens, did you think you were actually friends with him — much less, acquaintances? Hah! He doesn't need you. You're not useful. Take your frivolous ideas of love and shove it up your a—Denial: After some intense staring at the girl who is complaining to a friend about you, unaware that your head chanting is onpar with a Nazi regime, you shake your head and move to your work — Calm, but too calm. “I don't actually like her,” you wonder to yourself. “She's just looks nice and smells nice and is very intelligent and can keep up with me like no else has done before.” Then you grow silent — and stare and stare. “Okay, maybe my heart likes her, but my mind doesn't,” then it dawns on you, and your eyes widen. “Oh, crap!”Grief: In his room drowning his sorrows in a pillow: “My ambitions! My plans — Gone! Gone because of a silly crush that I’m not certain I'll keep. Damn! Who knows if I'll marry her, and we'll have kids together? But I can't have kids because I've got to go to Medical School! I have no time for a silly infatuation! And what if we grow old, and she dies first, oh God, that would kill me. I'll probably have to arrange our funeral soon! What was it that Shakespeare suggested, die together? I guess we'll live together in heaven, then!”Acceptance: Suddenly, the INTJ gets up in the morning with a strange, beaming smile that unnerves their parents and their friends. Their dog snarls at them, then whimpers when their smile widens in response. Even the birds flutter away in fright. For the INTJ is happy now after arranging a meet-up with said person, and they sit contently at the dinner table, their head filled with strange fancies because they've been planning this moment for years, and even had the whole conversation played out in an approximation of what the discussion might sound like. They are confident in what they want to share and what they don't, and they're eager to start challenging the person. Because . . . they might have found the one! But alas, a hypothesis must always be verified!Now that we have discussed the five stages of Death — pardon, love, I hope this will give you an insight on the absurdity of an INTJ falling in love.

column1: Adult How do you know when you've reached the acceptance stage of grief?
column3: You don’t know. You have to go through all of it. Maybe more than once. Grieving is very personal and individual. You may go through different stages at different times, not in the order as is usually given. You may return to one stage or another throughout your life or for a long time. My grief is about a year and a half old. The first year was a fog of grief. When the first year passed it was sort of like a relief that we had experienced all the firsts:First Christmas,first Easter,First Mother’s and Father’s Day,then his first birthday without him,Thanksgiving,then the awful day of his death.And ten days later Christmas again.He was 18 years old when he was killed in a car accident. He and his friend had left high school and were on the way to work. It was pouring rain and their car hydroplaned into a truck, both boys were killed instantly. He was my grandson. Grief strikes without warning, at the oddest times. Last December (2017) my 10 year old granddaughter was in the Nutcracker ballet as she had been the year before, the night after he was killed. Every year we go and usually my grandson and I sat together. He would tell me about the ballerinas he knew and once introduced me to the lead after the dance. But last December he wasn’t there and it hit me like a hurricane. I was sitting next to my 8 year old Grandson (his little brother) and I just started crying uncontrollably. I wanted to leave and go cry in the restroom but we were in the middle of a packed row of people so I sat there and weathered it. We all grieve differently. We seem to be unable to stop thinking about all the coulda shoulda woulda and what ifs that constantly niggle at us. So if you are grieving or if you know someone who is, the grieving really never ends, it just softens gradually but still hits hard sometimes. Be patient with yourself or your friend.
column9: Give yourself grace—every day. Grief for me is like a room in a house with a door that's never locked, and emotions that never really fade away. You can walk past that room mostly unaffected for days or even weeks, knowing what's inside; but the moment you open it up and look in, that grief comes pouring out as though it happened yesterday. It's been more than four years since my mom passed away, but I'm still learning about the process of grief.

column1: Have you lost a child to death? I lost my 18 year old son, it's going on 7 years since his accident, I still can't conceive that he is really gone.
column3: Yes, I have. My son died at the age of 27 ten years ago. Since then, I have been lost in time and space, desperately hoping for the whirlwind of confusion as to "why", along with the ever evasive comprehension of his death, to slow down so I can grab hold of some type of understanding. I crave some semblance of hope of regaining, if just one percent, my bearings in this lifetime so I can move forward in spite of this waking nightmare. Instead, I find myself paralyzed with grief, frozen as if both legs are stuck in the thickest of mud, unable to move in any direction except in my mind. There, I can see his face as if in a slideshow, from birth until his death, with each slide depicting and tearing open the moments of his precious life...from when I first held him, along with the other countless memories he left me and the rest of his family with. Now, with his death, the last memory of him being buried is just too much to ask of a mother to bear. When he died, he took half of me with him and it's gone forever. I feel empty inside, yet full of pain. I wouldn't wish this on anyone, and I mean anyone. It was a Sunday morning, a beautiful fall day, when I woke with an indescribable overbearing sense of sadness. I called my son to see if he had begun the hour-long drive to the lake to spend the day with his dad. No answer. I left a voicemail. No reply. I had no idea the police were listening to the message as I left it. He had been found dead after sleeping overnight at a couple's home, friends from college. He had been battling several illnesses for months, and had come home so that his family could help him with doctors appointments and heal. He had only been home for one week. When the detectives came to tell me he was dead, I immediately lost all concept of the present. Their words began to make no sense as they appeared to sound far away and jumbled. The environment seemed to swirl around my grief stricken body as I stood there paralyzed. All of the sudden, in an instant, all color had drained from the world. Everything would now be seen by me in shades of browns and grays. The life drained out of my eyes... …a mother's soul half dead. Chaos erupted upon our household like a thick blanket of smoldering lava, searing our skin with the sadness that only someone who has lost a child and sibling would know. From that moment on, we were each violently thrown into another dimension of life. The whole family fell apart as we each went into our own corners to grieve. I was heartbroken that we lost him, but was equally heartbroken for my other two children that were losing me in a deep well of grief I had fallen into because of the loss of my firstborn. Research states that 75-90% of marriages in which a child has died ends in divorce. My husband and I barely made it. However, we are different people now than we were before this. We have to be. If we had stayed the same, we would have lost our minds from the sadness. I must end this with telling you the truth. Your grief will never end. The intensity will lessen as time goes on, but it ebbs and flows. The five stages of grief, as identified by Elizabeth Kublar-Ross, were never meant to be linear. She never meant them to be. They all rotate, and pop back up, when you least expect it. You will always feel as if something is missing. Grief will strike you at the most inopportune time, and also enable you when you least expect it. 'Life and time' is actually the process of moving forward. I know I am moving forward though I have a hard time realizing it. You will also. Please allow me this opportunity to say how sorry I am for what you're going through. I truly do understand.

column1: Would Bill Murray’s character in Groundhog Day have gone insane after repeating so many days?
column3: Phil Connors (Bill Murray) goes through the 7 stages of grief/death as theorized by Katherine Kubler-Ross: anger, denial, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. First, he is pissed that he has to do Groundhog Day again. He spends a lot of time denying this has happened to him…going for so far as to take advantage of this time-space hiccup. He tries very hard to rework everything for a long time in the film. He goes to great lengths to fix his day and make it better as an escape. And we see him try several attempts to kill himself. The final day before he successfully transitions to February 3, he goes about the day, doing good stuff (albeit not completely happily), recognizing what he cannot do, and by and large being less cynical, less sarcastic, and more accepting of life’s ups and downs.

column1: How do you prepare for winter where you are?
column3: Classic stages of grief.In the last, humid days of summer, I start hating on summer.On the first crisp day of fall, I’m like a perky nipple. Lovin’ it. Lovin’ the sensation. More, please.Then fall starts to get dark and gloomy. I get anxious and depressed and wondering what insane, random decision provoked me ever to move to where I live. God help me. Save Our Ship. Get me the fuckouttaheah.Red leaves hit. Sheer beauty. Spectacular stuff. I’m loving it again. But it’s the last goodbye. Death strikes. “Shock and denial.”Around November 1, a big, walloping windstorm hits — and blows every beautiful leaf into the gutter. “Pain and guilt.”By November 15, you’re staring at a grey wall. Depression. You. notice more spit on sidewalks and public transit, you sleep longer, and the heart throbs with angst. Cabin fever is really setting in. Life is grinding to a standstill. It feels like nothing interesting is happening.Your winter clothes come out. I actually like the feel of winter clothes. You can’t take your skin off in the summer. But there’s a lot of things you can do to stay warm in the winter. Long underwear feel really good.You’re struggling, but then a bright sunny winter day happens. Still snowless, but… “this isn’t so bad.”By December 1, the world is STILL getting darker. It’s basically dark by about 4:30, and if you don’t stay busy around other people — smell the smells, talk, get exercise, go shopping, keep your mind focused on some sort of interesting activity, go out around people some more, maximize your time in brightly lit places even if it’s a restaurant — you can get impossibly gloomy.Advent hits, my favorite season in the Catholic year. LIttle bits of liturgical beauty help you keep “Chin up, buttercup.” Mystery and subtle magic.If you’re lucky, it starts to snow. Only morons want winters without snow. It’s the opposite. Pity the people who live in places that are still cold but where it rarely snows. Snow makes things brighter if it sticks around, and as long as the sun stays out, life is a lot more cheerful.Maybe a walloping, roaring blizzard hits. Now you’re in for some real excitement and fun. Get a book and a dram of scotch and listen to the old bitch howl. Drama and action. I’d take a blizzard over some sad-sack grey drizzle down South any day. Blizzards put me in a great mood. Embrace the blizzard.Go out hiking in the snow. On a sunny day after a snowstorm, this is one of the best things in life.Take up a winter sport. You can’t cross-country ski in the summer. Deal with that fact, and do what you can do now.I drink more scotch, something I almost never drink in summer. And I’m lucky to have two gas fireplaces in my house. Scotch + great book next to a fireplace (or hey… scotch + naked woman next to a fireplace): drink responsibly, and this is a winter mood lifter.Speaking of which: my sex life has usually been terrible in the summer, but it gets busier in the winter. Most women hate winter with an absolute undying passion and don’t know how to stay warm. Sex is one way to relieve the boredom and stay warm.But by January — February at the latest — I’m frazzled again. Is this the “anger and bargaining” stage of grief on the road to acceptance? By mid-January, I’ve usually got a trip booked to somewhere tropical. I get down there and exhale an enormous sigh of relief and shock, discovering that warmth, color and happiness still exist. “Jesus! Look at that green. Green has not been scoured and exterminated from the face of the earth.” I take a shower outdoors. I plunge into a pool. And then when I fly back, I suffer reverse culture shock for a week or two. Hint: if you’ve adjusted to winter in a cold place, try to avoid taking a tropical vacation in February. Instead, go somewhere even colder, where winter is even more dramatic — go to Iceland or Alaska — so you don’t screw your body and brain into thinking winter is over. The end is not even close. Not in January.Then acceptance: as hard as winter can be, sometimes at the very beginning of spring, as things start to pick up again — after March makes a serious attempt to kill you — you realize that you’ve actually enjoyed some of the quiet. In April or May, things can start to seem too busy even when they’re just getting going again. You feel a little sorry for winter, that it has to go. It’s a friend you hated at first, but who just wanted to tell you something you didn’t want to hear — and needed to, because it was important. To be a full human being, you need a range of emotions. Winter gives you some, for sure.There are bad days and good days in winter, just like any season. Awful, horrible, gloomy, lonesome, crack-ass ugly days when you wonder where you’re going and what you’re doing. I’ve had the same days in July. But this one’s definitely true: if you’re not prepared for winter, winter is still prepared for you. People who suffer the most from winter are the ones who don’t do a damned thing to make it better or even try to enjoy a little bit of it, see what beauty it might contain, and try to appreciate at least some of the same experience that billions of people have already survived before you and will survive again. Is it hard? Yes. Yes, it’s hard.

column1: What does it feel like to be betrayed?
column3: You can only be betrayed by somebody you trust, and said betrayal marks the irrevocable death of said trust. I hate to make it seem all clean and straightforward, because you go through a dizzying array of thoughts and emotions, but since it is a death, you go through the stages of grief (your mileage may vary on the order, although denial probably comes first and acceptance always comes last). Denial - there's no way they could have done that! I know them! They would never have pulled that crap! Betrayal is shocking; this is how you'll probably initially respond to that shock.Anger - self explanatory. This one is obviously pretty intense, and has led me to do things I am not at all proud of.Bargaining - because you KNOW and TRUST this person. Doing what they've done to you just isn't in their character, right? It could have been circumstantial, a brief lapse in judgement, arm-twisting, something else you weren't privy to. This is the worst one, I think. Most people don't give their trust to others very easily, so the first instinct is to repair the trust you've spent so much time building so carefully. It's very dangerous since it does have a certain charm, and giving into it just puts you in the position to be betrayed by this person again, and again, and again.Depression - again, self-explanatory. This part sucks. Losing something you've trusted leaves a hole in your life and routine, whether this was a business relationship or a personal one. It's difficult to see what could possibly go where something previously simply was and was going to be.Acceptance - you'll get here eventually. I promise.

column1: Why is it so hard to cut the emotional ties to a narcissist, even after your brain knows what a horrible person they are?
column3: It isn’t cutting the emotional ties that’s hard - I’ve found that this actually happens very naturally - it’s reigning in your mind and forcing yourself to face and accept the truth that is hard. It’s perfectly acceptable and healthy to allow yourself to mourn the person you thought existed for the first several weeks to months after the discard/replacement. You have to let yourself feel the shock, the disbelief, the pain, the anger, the grief… the loss. It is a death. Mourn him/her. But, the same way we have no choice but to return to work after even the death of one most beloved to us, you have to get back to work too. You’re not going to feel ready. You’re going to want to sink into your grief forever. But you have to work, to get to the acceptance stage and be able to surpass so many of the thoughts and feelings that you’re being bombarded with in your grief. How do you get to the acceptance stage? You read. You learn. You spend hours on Quora learning about other peoples’ experiences with narcs. You focus entirely on narcissism and what it means, instead of focusing on the phony “happy” memories you have with the narc. And suddenly, without you even consciously realizing it had happened… your brain accepts the truth. The narc is an actor. Your partner didn’t exist. Poof. The illusion disappears. I don’t feel any emotional tie anymore to the person who never existed. I don’t feel the undying love I had for him, the dreams I had for us, the care, the empathy, the addiction… nothing. It all went away once I accepted the truth. It sounds almost too easy. But it’s just logic. It makes sense. You can’t be tied to someone that has never existed (your fake “ex”). You can’t love someone who never existed. The illusion gets shattered with your acceptance of the truth, and with that, so many complications just get swept away and forgotten. Then you can begin to think clearer and realize how free you really are. I think maybe anyone who feels emotionally chained to the narc has not yet done the work they need to do on acceptance, or is too early into the process to do that work yet… which is okay. Like I said, you HAVE to grieve, and feel all the unpleasant feelings, before you can even focus your mind on acceptance. This is death. It’s a process. I was down for the count for weeks, cried myself to sleep so many nights feeling like I couldn’t live without my ex. Couldn’t bear the thought of him never coming back. Couldn’t even live with knowing he had replaced me with a new supply. Picturing him in my mind made me ache and yearn for him and sometimes howl in pain. I wanted the pain to be over, but it just kept going and going. Be patient with yourself…. It’s traumatic. You do have work to do to cut that emotional tie, but just know that it is absolutely possible to do, when you’re fully ready to accept the truth about the “person” you loved. It’s not something you can rush.

column1: What did you do after the death of your service dog?
column3: The day I had to put Bach down was a very difficult one. I knew that morning Bach was ready. I had been sleeping downstairs with him for the last several nights because he was unable to climb the stairs to the upper level, and he didn't want to use the ramp I built for him anymore. When I woke up I discovered he had lost control of his bladder in the night, and as I tried to pick him up he lost control of his bowels too. He was listless, had no appetite, and I could tell by the look in his eyes he was ready to let go. I asked him. "Is today the day, buddy?" There was no doubt in my mind that his eyes said yes. They were sad, and so were mine. I called a friend on the police department, and he came right over to help me put Bach in the back of a squad car. The veterinarian was ready for us. We carried Bach into one of the examination rooms. I sat on the floor next to him. I am certain he knew what was going to happen and he was very comfortable with it. The vet, who had seen Bach since the day I was assigned to K9, told me he had to shave part of Bach's front leg, and that he would give him an injection. He said Bach wouldn't feel any pain, but that he might briefly struggle to take a breath. I held Bach as the vet gave him the injection. My wife and my friend waited outside the room. Bach never struggled at all. He closed his eyes and relaxed. It was very peaceful for him. After he was gone, I sat there with him for about 20 minutes. I remembered all the times we had, first in our initial training, our years on the street, some of the high-profile incidents we were involved in, his retirement and his home life. I composed myself, and went out to where the others were waiting. Bach stayed in the examination room. The staff were outstanding. Most of them had known Bach for over 10 years, and they assured me he would be looked after. They would call me when his ashes were ready to be picked up. So we went home, and I grieved. I had lost a close friend, one who only wanted to please me, who only wanted to be around me, who would have protected me with his life if he needed to. He was my best friend. An hour later I went for a 10 mile run. That helped. So did time. Pet owners know this kind of grief to an extent, but not as well as other police K9 handlers. I lost a friend and a partner, and a relative. I found myself going through many of the same stages every person in mourning goes through. In the following days I got condolence cards from the mayor, from the schools and other organisations we had done demonstrations for, from other K9 handlers and instructors, from kids, and from the senior citizen homes. They were wonderful. I still have many of them. The guys on the department got together and had a stone made for Bach. The chief told me it would be incorporated into the wall of the police station when it is extended. That was pretty cool, and I appreciated it. Bach's ashes are in a container less than 4 feet from me as I write this. His police star and his "dog tags" are next to him. My ashes will be mingled with his some day, and I think that will be pretty cool too.

column1: Adult What is the top stage of grief and why?
column3: There is no top stage of grief because there are no stages of grief. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross was a psychiatrist whose work with the dying led her to formulate the theory that there are five stages of grief people go through when they are faced with their own death. These five stages—denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance—have since been used to describe the grief process after the death of a loved one, but this one-size-fits-all model of grief is fundamentally wrong. This five stages model makes people think that grief is a checklist. You are in shock, then you deny, then you get angry and depressed, and finally you accept. But grief is not so clinical. It is a wildly chaotic state that encompasses dozens of different feeling as well as all facets of a person — emotional, psychological, spiritual, physical. Even worse, all these things happen at once, so you can never quite get a grip on where you are in relation to your loss. If there is one attribute of grief that stands out among all this horror, it is change. Grief changes us, changes our values, changes the way we see ourselves and the world, changes us into someone who can both be sad and happy at the same time, changes our awareness of death and yet still allows us to maintain an interest in living. Mostly, grief changes us into someone who can survive the loss of a loved one. But this change doesn’t take place over night, and it doesn’t take place when you try to fit your grief into various stages. It’s an ongoing process.

column1: Is it possible that I still grief 10 years since losing my dad? Could this cause depression or borderline?
column3: What you need to know about grief: Grief is the natural emotional response resulting from a significant loss—especially the death of a loved one. Everyone deals with grief differently. People cry, laugh, busy themselves with work, throw up, or even feel numb. Some recover quickly, while others take their time. Grief is a natural healing process, and there’s no “right” way to do it. For some people, grief can become too painful. It can grow into something totally different, like depression or anxiety. Other times, grief might last far too long, and take over a person’s life for years on end. This is called complicated grief. Acute Grief Immediately after a loss, and for months afterward, it’s normal to have intense symptoms of shock, distress, sadness, poor appetite, sleep trouble, and poor concentration. These symptoms will slowly diminish with the passage of time. Complicated Grief Sometimes, the symptoms of acute grief never seem to go away. They can last for years. The loss of a loved one continues to feel unreal and unmanageable. You might constantly yearn for the deceased, or experience guilt about the idea of “moving on” and accepting the loss. Integrated Grief After resolving the most intense symptoms of acute or complicated grief, you will enter the lifelong stage of integrated grief. At this point, you have come to accept the reality of the loss, and you’ve resumed daily life activities. This doesn’t mean that you miss your loved one any less, or that you don’t feel pain in their memory—you’ve just learned how to cope. Acute grief may show itself again, especially around holidays, anniversaries, and other reminders. If you are concerned and this low mood is affecting your personal, social and work/school life, you should consider talking to a grieving counselor or a therapist. A mental health professional can give you the tool and the coping skills in order to overcome this hardness.If you found this answer helpful, please leave an upvote.

column1: What is it like to lose a child?
column3: My deepest sympathy to all of you who have lost a child. Somebody once told me that losing a child is wholly contrary to nature, since usually the older people go first. When I was a lot younger, our 6 weeks old baby daughter had an ear infection, after consulting our friend the pediatrician we together decided not to do anything about it, especially since in a very recent paper it had been demonstrated that with or without antibiotics the otitis (ear infection) would heal in about the same time, so no need to prescribe antibiotics for that. Pus was coming out of the ear, so we though the drainage was OK. After two more days when coming home from the hospital (where I among other things was supervising the adult intensive care unit) I noticed her to be quite ill, lying in classical opistotonus with her back arched back, so the diagnosis of a meningitis was made. Our friend saw her in our hospital where I took her to, a lumbar puncture confirmed the diagnosis, the next day she was transferred to an academic children's intensive care unit, where she went into full blown septic shock, needing fluids, pressor-amines and mechanical ventilation. The staff and child intensivist were great, giving us all the information and leeway we needed, unfortunately I had to keep on working, since my partner on the job was on vacation, so in the morning I did, and in the afternoon went to the academic center to see our daughter. When after about 10 days nothing good happened, I asked her intensivist how to proceed further, so he stopped the sedatives (at that time we still believed in keeping the critically ill in a coma to spare the brain) and after a day made an EEG, and another one the next day, both of them were flat, so it was clear she was brain dead. I already knew beforehand that we were most likely to lose her. In the midst of all the emotions I felt we shouldn't prolong everyone's agony, so instead of accepting her intensivist's offer to wait another night, we decided to stop the treatment the moment we knew she was beyond hope, I disconnected the breathing tube myself, took her on our lap, and we waited many, many hours until everything stopped. It was terrible, after that we all were in a daze. During her illness her brother who at that time was 2,5 years old was present most of the time, since I sincerely believe that he as a part of our family should be present too. He now still remembers some fragments from that time. Afterwards we asked for a postmortem, which showed nothing new. Her intensivist told us he couldn't bring himself to ask us for permission to do a postmortem, and was rather surprised by my request. I on the other hand wanted to know everything we could learn about her illness, in the spirit of my normal line of work, so of course I would like to know so wanted to have it done. Like everybody else I was looking if we had done something wrong. After that I took a day off to arrange for her cremation and such practical matters, but started working two days after her death, I think that kept me sane, and the flow of work going, since my partner hadn't returned from her vacation. We kept it very much to ourselves, but when the day of her cremation came (that was the second day I was absent from work), a lot of colleagues and co-workers were there for us, which moved us deeply. After some weeks we had to do something about all her things, which we did while in tears most of the time, but it gave us some closure. During her illness and afterwards, I often took a step back from myself and looked at which stage of grief I was in, very weird. We don't forget her, but time makes it possible to live with the loss, speak about her loss without choking up or getting tears in our eyes. We have a photograph of her in our living room. Each year on her birthday, and the day she died, my wife goes to a small chapel to pray, I come with her although no believer myself. After that if possible I avoided treating (very sick) children, especially since our intensive care unit is not for children. I do what is needed, when somebody comes to take over I withdraw and feel unwell for some time. After all, we docs are human too. On the other hand, one must remain practical, so I kept treating our very asthmatic son myself since both the pediatricians and family doctor were not comfortable with treating the asthma according to the latest insights, and I was, since I treated a lot of grown-ups with asthma. No doubting myself if I would make a mistake and cause big harm to our children. They are both quite well now, although I did initially miss a broken but not dislocated wrist after a fall in both of them when they were still young. In the aftermath I felt I needed some practical advice, so talked a lot with a colleague who's 7 year old son was killed in a car accident right in front of his eyes some years before, I noticed he too worked very hard, maybe also as a way to cope with his loss, and with a good friend, a respected family doctor of my age, who told me if we wanted a family with two children, not to wait too long since they needed to be not so far apart in years or else wouldn't connect, so contrary to our first thoughts after a bit less than a year our second daughter was born. We took great care not to let her become the surrogate for our first daughter. Our son promised himself and us that he would raise his new little sister and teach her all he knew, which he indeed did. A very special relationship. I think this experience has made me a better doctor, at least that is what I hope, since I empathize better with my patients and their family, while still retaining my very practical and business like way of doing things. Did the fact that I as a physician was doing intensive care at that moment help? It did, since I better understood what the situation was and what we could or could not achieve, so could make sound decisions uncluttered by emotions which at times can make it worse. EDIT: April 17, 2017: almost 34 years after all this took place last week we again had dinner together with our friend, the pediatrician, who saw and admitted our daughter on that fateful first night, and his wife. When we discussed how life had treated us, and I said in spite of all I felt we had had quite a good life, having two healthy children, being in reasonable health etc., he got emotional, and after excusing himself, him not knowing whether it was an opportune moment to discuss it, told us that during all those past years he felt so guilty not having been able to save our little baby girl, even to the point of willing to accept and understand should we not want to know him anymore, while we only felt gratitude for all he had done for our baby girl. I told him that I as a (former intensive care) doc knew that we couldn’t win them all, my wife and I assured him of our positive feelings, our gratitude, about his involvement, and hoped he could leave this all behind him, like we for the most part had done.
