column1: How did you deal with the death of your parents?
column3: I rarely use the word “cope” to describe what I’ve tried to do since my mom died almost four years ago. Coping is about surviving and I see surviving as only the first stage of what I want to do with my grief. Yes, do with my grief. I want to do something with it. I want to activate it in a way that makes me and the world around me better. I can’t possibly imagine any other reason to go through this kind of pain. And so to answer your question simply that’s what I’ve done: I’ve tried to activate this grief. That gives me a feeling of purpose. It makes me feel like my life has meaning. That said, no loss is the same. No grief is the same. There is objectively no right way to go through grief, just as there is no objectively right way to live your life. There is no straight line to being okay again. There is no timeline you need to try and follow. The “5 Stages of Grief” only matter in hindsight (or from the therapist’s seat). You do what you need to do. And I do what I must do. Losing a parent is a powerful, earth-shattering experience. One that we can never be fully prepared for. One that we can’t quite understand the potential impact of. My grandfather said to me, just hours after my mom passed: “Well this a huge day in your life, isn’t it Katie?” My first thought was an expletive. I won’t lie. But over time, I’ve come to see what he was trying to get at. That her death was a turning point. Everything in my life is colored by her life and her death. My choices. My beliefs. My purpose. My work. My relationships. Every. Single. Thing. If there’s a goal in grief, especially in the loss of our parents, it’s to figure out how to make that work for us rather than against us. That’s a lifelong process. One we can never escape. One we are blessed, somehow, oh somehow, to be burdened with. Here are a few of the things I’ve done to keep moving on this path:I did what I needed to do to survive. I moved three times in three years. I got the heck out of any situation that caused deep suffering.I listened. To myself. To the universe. To the stories people wanted to tell.I tried to forget. Oddly enough, my brain was ahead of me on this. I couldn’t remember anything about her for awhile. Because everything — every smell, feeling, and dream — associated with the loss hurt (bad).I resisted “getting over it.” I put myself through pain. I woke up every day with the words “my mom died” trailing across my mind.I faked it. I told everyone I was okay. Because theoretically, I was. I understood why this loss might be a good thing, though I couldn’t quite feel it.I exercised. I started running every day—5 or 6 miles—to get closer to my mom. And to find some space to process the pain.I wrote. In journals. In my phone notes. On a blog. In random word documents that I saved. I did anything I could to get the thoughts out of my head and on paper.I read. Anything I could get my hands on. Any book that I thought would help me find a new perspective. Any idea that might make me feel a bit better.I found distractions. Specifically, jobs that took up 60+ hours per week. New career paths. New cities. New people. Things that would zap up all my energy so I couldn’t even focus on the loss.I compartmentalized. The thing about losing a parent is that a lot of other crap is going to be uncovered with it. What psychologists call “secondary losses.” You have to figure out what those other losses are—friendships, family relationships, feelings, beliefs, etc.—and approach them separately. Address each one on its own and you will begin to heal.I reprioritized. I used this as an excuse to figure out what was important in my life. What was essential. People, places, things, ideas, activities.I built. Chuck Palahniuk writes in Fight Club (yes I’m quoting Fight Club): “It’s only after we’ve lost everything that we’re free to do anything.” With your parents come your beliefs, assumptions, and purpose for being in the world. When they are gone, you decide these things for yourself.I connected. As I found the courage, I started connecting with other people that had lost parents. I found other people who had experienced trauma. I found people who could understand life with this new level of depth I’d just stumbled upon.I forgave. My mom for things she said. My dad for cheating on her. The doctors for messing up so royally. Myself for being so closed off.I honored. I found little moments to celebrate my mom. I got a tattoo on my wrist (which I never thought I’d do). I put her initials on my running shoes. I celebrated her on days we’d have celebrated together if she was alive.I allowed myself to feel. It’s so easy to numb the pain. To try and escape the moments. But sometimes, you just have to feel them. You just have to go in and feel the range of human emotion.I integrated. I made this experience a part of who I am. I share the story when I have the courage. I talk about her to people on the street. I activated my purpose for being in the world, using this earth-shattering loss as the foundation.I’ve written this all in the past tense as if it’s something that’s somehow “over.” That’s false. Grief is never over. Not until life is over, at least. My mom’s mom (my grandmother) also died when my mom was in her early twenties. What’s true for me so far was true for her. The grief never goes away. It dulls, but it never disappears. My relationship with my mom was changed for the better because she had lost her mom young. It was because she was hyper-aware of her own mortality, she didn’t want to waste a minute with me. Our relationship blossomed from that one ideal. My only hope is that if I ever have a daughter, I have the courage to do the same—to be there and love her, not in spite of my loss, but because of it. And so in, wherever this message meets you, in however you choose to walk this path, in whatever you choose to do, I hope you find ways to activate your pain. I hope you make space for the range of emotions and do what you need to survive. I wish you way more than luck, my friend.

column1: Why did they kill Kite so fast in HXH? I thought he was a really cool character.
column3: For Gon´s epic development. For the core themes of the arc. For an intricate duality to be created Gon and Meruem. There are many reasons Kite was killed, and I think that his death, while shocking was the best possible route for the series to take.You see, its the fact that his death was so sudden and abrupt that makes it so great and so important. If HxH were a normal, generic shonen series, then Kite would´ve somehow survived and returned in order to help Gon and Killua train and get stronger. But here, he was killed. And things only spiral downward from there. Gon goes through multiple stages of grief provoked by Kite´s death, which he believes to be impossible. Which he refuses to accept until Pitou straight up tells him Kite isn´ coming back. Kite was there for a brief period of time, but his impact on Gon was profound. Kite was a father figure of sorts to Gon. He saved his life on multiple occasions and was a guiding source of light for Gon. Him and Gon became attached to one another, and when Gon was unable to do nothing to help his friend, he felt regret and guilt. And to cling on to his sanity and cope with the fact that he had lost someone close to his heart, hope blossomed in his mind. Hope which was quick to mutate into dark and twisted obsession.His childish mentality is fixed in a state of denial and refusal to accept Kite´s fate.When Gon sees Kite in this state after he´s recovered. After he says the man who inspired him so much turned into this his denial twists into hatred and anger. When Gon encounters Pitou again, and Pitou tries to make him compromise and wait. Wait for someone else when he has been waiting for so long. Gon starts making almost inhuman and cruel bargains. He holds Komugi hostage, sets a time limit, and refuses to budge in his single minded determination.When Pitou tells Gon the truth he crumbles down into a state of depression. Which is quick to transform into acceptance of the fact that Kite is gone. But not normal acceptance. The hope he held onto, the obsession, contorting into hatred and murderous intent. Gon become a monster. And the very creature that killed Kite brutally is so viciously slaughtered that she is almsot redeemed. And the core theme of this arc… Or one of the core themes I should say. Is the cruelty of humanity and how monstrous they are. Unlike many shonen arcs which paint things in black and white, the Chimera Ant arc creates gray. While the ants, the original antagonists, become more humanized, the humans become more twisted. And there are two catalysts for both of these progressions. Kite for the devolution of humanity to monster, and Komugi for the evolution of Chimera Ant to human. So while Kite was a likable character, his death was essential to furthering the plot and driving the core ideas and themes of the arc forward.

column1: What is the best way to heal after a serious loss?
column3: It is different for every person. It is important to work through the process and NOT ignore it and try to be fine. Talk with someone (if you have a good friend or family member or if you do not, go to a counselor) to get perspective, write in a journal to get your feelings out, be patient with yourself as you work through the stages of loss. Get a good book on grieving (even if it isn’t a death, these stages of grief are the same) and find a hobby or expression of yourself that makes you feel better (art, singing, etc) to give you an outlet.

column1: When do the horrible waves of gut wrenching grief leave you after losing a grown child?
column3: Three months and six days ago I lost my daughter to Metastatic Melanoma Cancer. She lived only nine months from her diagnosis day and was initially given two months to live. We embraced the hope of remission as she qualified for the newest treatments available, the BRACH 1 Gene Targeted and Immunotherapy drugs that were less than two years available. Her doctor, the top Melanoma specialist at Seattle Cancer Care Alliance was directly overseeing her treatment. Since I lost my husband to Glioblastoma (Stage IV Brain Cancer) less than a year previously, I refused to believe that she would die. Surely God would not let me lose my husband, the love of my life, and my oldest daughter, who had five small children under the age of ten who desperately needed her. But sadly, it did not matter what I wanted. I held out hope until the last week of her life and then in a blink of an eye, she was gone. Since my grief now intertwines with losing my husband and child, I get lost in the overall anguish of missing both of my best friends who I will never stop loving or missing. There is no fix to the pain, but the grief morphs into different entities as time slowly moves on. For me, the soul crushing sadness was debilitating in the first few months. Thoughts of suicide, apathy, lack of interest in usual activities, loss of appetite and being unmotivated or excited about anything in general were my initial responses. But leaning heavily on spiritual beliefs, brought on by my many tangible signs of afterlife from my husband, and visiting mediums to help me connect to their spirits, helped me tremendously. The comfort of knowing they are not dead, dust or nothing gave me the serenity to continue my life through the absolute suffering of their loss. Finding that truth, whether it be positive knowledge in afterlife, religion or lifes purpose will help the healing. After a few months, the grief seems to morph in waves. Instead of ...

column1: What can I say to my girlfriend who suddenly lost her father to console her?
column3: It’s so hard to believe, when you hear that your father has passed away. My brother called me one evening. I missed the call, then called him back and started joking around. He said, “Are you sitting down?” I thought he was going to tell me my older brother had been injured in kung fu. I never thought it would be something so much worse. I teased him about being over dramatic. He said, “Sad’s dead.” I didn’t believe him. I thought it was a cruel joke, even after I forced him to put mum on the phone and she confirmed. Even when I travelled to Brisbane and saw his body in a coffin. That man with so much white hair, and so many lines on his face, that wasn’t my dad. It couldn’t be. Denial is one of the stages of grief. The best you can do for your girlfriend is to sit with her. Let her cry on your shoulder. Make sure she eats and drinks (this is important, tears really dehydrate you). Hold her while she pretends to sleep. Listen to her when she shares memories. Laugh when she laughs. Cry when she cries. Remind her that she is strong, and while the pain will never go away, each day, it will get easier to bear. Mark the date in your calendar and make sure you’re there with her on the anniversaries - his birthday, Father’s Day, the anniversary of his death. Don’t ever say, “It’s been ___ months/ years, you should be over it by now.” You’re never over grief. It just becomes less raw.

column1: What is a disturbing fact most people are unaware of?
column3: Death by Fashion: How Victorian Mourning Veils Could Kill You Who knew that grieving for a loved one could lead to one’s own demise. In 19th-century America, mourning the death of a family member or friend was a highly structured ritual. Following strict rules of mourning dress and etiquette supposedly demonstrated one’s sincerity and Christian piety, and middle-class Victorians latched onto these customs as a way to prove their gentility and solidify their class position. Mourning rituals reached their peak in the 19th century as fashion became aligned with mourning and the resulting elaborate mourning codes became widespread in society. A number of factors contributed to this; first, high mortality rates were still prevalent during this period, the expansion of the middle class and finally the development of the retail sector and advances in technology meant that the use and production of black fabric became much more widespread than in the past.[1] Though there were certain expectations for men, such as wearing a black band on their arm or hat[2] , these small gestures paled in comparison to the expected duties of women in mourning. Unsurprisingly, women bore the brunt of the emotional labor that this culture of mourning demanded, and no woman was so constrained by cultural expectations as the widow. To demonstrate their bereavement, widows were to spend two and a half years proceeding through three stages of mourning — deep mourning, full or second mourning, and half mourning — each with its own fashion requirements and restrictions on behavior.[3]Victorian mourners (Widow’s Weeds & Victorian Funerals) A lady’s clothes would become progressively less dour as her loss receded into the past, and the length of time she wore mourning clothes would depend on how close of a relation she was mourning: a widow wore mourning clothes for two years, while a woman who lost a parent or child would wear them for a year.[4] To change the costume earlier was considered disrespectful to the deceased and, if the widow was still young and attractive, suggestive of potential sexual promiscuity. Those subject to the rules were slowly allowed to re-introduce conventional clothing at specific time periods; such stages were known by such terms as “full mourning”, “half mourning”, and similar descriptions.[5] For half mourning, muted colours such as lilac, grey and lavender could be introduced.[6] Dresses also progressed from more to less modest as mourning progressed, with high collars replaced by square necklines and long sleeves giving way to show more of the arm.[7]During the first stage of mourning which lasted for a year and a day (‘deepest’ or ‘first mourning’), a woman must wear a paramatta or bombazine dress and mantle with crape applied to the skirt. Cuffs and collars were made out of lawn and the rest of the dress (the bodice) was made out of crape. The bonnet should be made entirely out of crape; inside should be a widow’s cap with a crape veil.[8]Victorian half mourning dress (https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/80097085?img=0) By the second stage which lasted nine months, duller black silk fabrics were permitted and widows were allowed to divest their dress of some of their crape, although not all, in order not to appear to have recovered too quickly. Crape could be restricted to trimming into dresses, capes and bonnets; then after six months widows could lessen the crape still further and the cloth could be recycled through other means particularly as trimmings for hats or dresses.[9] Mourning also extended into underwear and accessories such as parasols, shawls, gloves and handbags. Underwear and handkerchiefs were trimmed with black ribbon or black border.[10] Hats were also in black with a veil and a widow’s cap underneath trimmed with black crape. Deep mourning lasted a year and a day and required a widow to wear simple black dresses and don a full-length black veil anytime she left the house.[11] Called a “weeping veil,” this shroud was made of a crimped silk fabric called crape, and wearing it allowed one to “weep with propriety,”.[12] Unfortunately, due to the dyes and chemicals used to the process the fabric, these veils could also cause skin irritation, respiratory illness, blindness, and even death.[13] Beginning around 1830, middle-class American culture became dominated by sentimentalism, an emphasis on feelings and sincerity that included a romantic obsession with death.[14] Advances in textile manufacturing combined with a new consumer appetite for mourning apparel led to the establishment of stores — like Besson & Son in Philadelphia[15] and Messrs. Jay of Regent Stree. In England[16] , that sold ready-made mourning clothes, while department stores like Lord & Taylor added mourning departments.[17] Fashion magazines advertised the latest in mourning attire, while etiquette manuals instructed people how to dress to grieve properly for different family members.The inventory advertised by Besson & Son, includef“Black Crape Grenadines / Black Balzerines / Black Baryadere Bareges / Black Bareges”.[18]Queen Victoria in mourning attire 1873 (Queen Victoria's dress is sold) On the death of her husband Prince Albert in 1861, Queen Victoria began a prolonged mourning and wore black in his memory until her own death in 1901.[19] The standards and etiquette of mourning, which originated from the observation of court mourning in previous centuries, had already been established, but Queen Victoria’s own mourning for her husband was echoed by the widespread observation of mourning etiquette by almost every sector of the population. These social and market forces helped standardize what women wore to express bereavement, and the dominant fabric used to do so was crape.[20] Spelled with an “a” when referring to mourning clothing, crape was a matte silk gauze that had been crimped with heated rollers; dyed black; and stiffened with gum, starch, or glue.[21] Custom forbade fabrics that reflected light during deep mourning, so lusterless crape was the perfect solution. Manufacturers also heavily promoted crape as the ideal mourning fabric, because it could be made from waste silk and was thus cheap to produce, but could be sold at a high markup.Example of dress fabric for mourning by Peter Robinson’s Mourning Warehouse (ca. 1890) (Layers of Sorrow – the Fabrics of Mourning) The world’s chief manufacturer of mourning crape was a British company called Courtaulds, which mechanized the production process for massive output and established a veritable monopoly on its creation.[22] The company exported the material internationally, with particular success in the United States and France. Courtaulds raked in the cash from making mourning crape, earning a 30 percent return on capital during the fabric’s boom years of 1850 to 1885. It manufactured mass quantities of black crape — 90,000 pounds’ ($126,684) worth in 1865.[23] Crape was “a most costly and disagreeable material, easily ruined by the dampness and dust — a sort of penitential and self-mortifying dress, and very ugly and very expensive,” wrote Mrs. John Sherwood in her 1884 etiquette guide, Manners and Social Usages.[24] Known for shedding its dye anytime it got wet, crape would spot in the rain and stain the skin anytime the wearer would sweat. Women’s etiquette and fashion manuals included recipes for removing crape’s black dye from skin, as it “often resists successfully the most lavish use of soap and water.”[25] Hartley Florence’s 1876 book The Ladies's Book of Etiquette and Manual of Politeness, recommended using a mix of oxalic acid and cream of tartar to banish these stubborn stains, but caution that the former ingredient is poisonous.[26] The scratchy fabric would also rub against the face, causing irritations and abrasions to the skin. In 1894, Dr. Prince A. Morrow stated “I have frequently been consulted for an eczemaform eruption of the face occasioned by wearing mourning veils of crèpe.[27](Wearing a 19th-Century Mourning Veil Could Result in — Twist — Death) Crape was unpleasant to wear for other reasons, too. The traditional widow’s veil was six feet long and made of two layers of black crape, fastened onto a bonnet placed at the back of the head. “Is it feared that the bereaved one may grow too soon consoled unless she is weighed down by this literal load of mourning?” quipped an 1878 editorial in The Canadian Monthly and National Review.[28] The thick fabric made it hard to breathe and hard to see; the widow’s veil was “blinding and stifling.”[29] The veil served a purpose:“it would protect a woman while in deepest grief against the untimely gayety of a passing stranger. But yet, the black veil […] is most unhealthy: it harms the eyes and it injures the skin.”[30]By the 1880s, medical journals had begun to address the health effects of heavy crape veils. The New York Medical Journal stated “the irritation to the respiratory tract caused by minute particles of poisonous crape,” [31] while a syndicated column from the North-Western Lancet declared the mourning veil “a veritable instrument of torture” in hot weather, staining the face and filling the lungs with toxic particles.[32] Doctors speaking of poisonous fabric were not being hyperbolic: Many of the substances used to color and treat crape were seriously toxic, and as the 19th century progressed, the dyes in use only became more dangerous.[33] In the early part of the 19th century, mourning crape was colored with plant dyes, usually made from valonia, oak galls, or logwood.Acorn cups from the valonia oak are high in tannins, as are oak galls (spherical growths on oak trees caused by parasitic insects, bacteria, or fungi), and both could be used to make vivid black dye.[34] Neither is toxic unless ingested in high quantities. Logwood dye, on the other hand, made from the heartwood of a flowering Central American tree, contains haematoxylin, a chemical compound that can cause eye or skin irritation, as well as respiratory problems.[35]Hands damaged by arsenic dyes, lithography from an 1859 medical journal (Fatal Victorian Fashion and the Allure of the Poison Garment) Even if the dye itself was nontoxic, the mordant (a substance used to set the dye) could present problems. While some were innocuous, chromium, frequently used mordant, is highly toxic, and can cause pulmonary irritation or disease if inhaled as dust.[36] Bichromate of potash, as potassium dichromate was called in the 19th century, is even more dangerous. An 1870 manual on dyes, warned that bichromate of potash, while “extensively used, both in dying and printing,” is “an intense poison,” and that “The hands of dyers who work much with this salt, become swollen and ulcerated, and in time the mischief extends to the toes, palate, jaw-bones, etc.” [37] The U.S. National Library of Medicine notes that potassium dichromate is “Highly corrosive to skin and mucous membranes,” can cause serious eye damage, and is fatal if inhaled in its pure form.[38]Mourning Dress During the Early Victorian Era In the 1850s, scientists began synthesizing aniline dyes, which are produced from coal tar. To create aniline black, the coal-derivative benzene — itself highly toxic — was often mixed with potassium dichromate, as well as copper chloride, another corrosive chemical that can irritate the skin and eyes and harm mucous membranes.[39] Aniline dyes were also processed using arsenic, which resulted in a 2 to 3 percent of arsenic left behind in the finished product.[40] Though aniline black was more popular for dying cotton than silk, some mourning crape was likely still colored with the dye. In 1879, British surgeon Jabez Hogg documented a female patient who suffered “arsenical poisoning” from a black crape dress.[41] The British Medical Journal proclaimed that “The risk incurred by wearing aniline or arsenic next to an absorptive skin […] overbalances any ornamental effects which these pigments can afford.”[42] Even voices from beyond the grave were concerned: according to the American medium Carrie E.S. Twing, a spirit named Samuel Bowles commented to her that “the coloring matter that enters into black crape is a blood poison, and would be deadly were it to come more in contact with the body.”[43] One physician wrote “many a woman has been laid in her coffin by the wearing of crape,” in an 1898 issue of The Dietetic and Hygienic Gazette.[44] The medical community was particularly concerned about harm to the respiratory tract caused by toxic particles emanating from the gauze. The stiff fabric’s folds would rub against each other and emit particles of chromium, arsenic, or some other toxic substance into the air, which then would enter the eyes and the lungs.[45] “The eyes that survive the bitterness of tears succumb to the poisonous rasping of crape,” lamented the fashion magazine The Delineator in 1895.[46] The harsh black fabric was also used as trimming for mourning dresses and bonnets, and even covered some deep mourning outfits entirely, but the crape veil caused the most health problems, as the orifices of the face gave its toxic emissions access to the body’s mucous membranes.[47] Additionally, as crape was expensive, many women who put on mourning were unable to afford an entire ensemble. Most middle class women splurged on the bonnet and veil, the two most deadly components of mourning attire.[48] The rising middle class at the time used mourning customs as means to try to keep up with the gentry by mimicking their customs and trying to keep up with the quality and extent of the mourning wardrobe. What made this “ritual” even more expensive was the idea that keeping the set of mourning items that were purchased for a specific event of death was an act that was seen as a cause for bad luck, making them a bad thing to keep. Families had to purchase a new set of mourning wardrobe for every member of the family with every loss – and with death being such an everyday phenomenon in Victorian England, every loss was also connected with big expenses and many had to go into debt to keep up with the expensive mourning customs.[49]Edwardian period mourning dress (Fripperies and Fobs) Cultural expectations for respectable middle- and upper-class Victorian mourners, obligated them to wear an uncomfortable, unhealthy piece of clothing, such that the death of a loved one could cause a woman to risk her own health. But by the 1890s, mourning conventions had shifted. Many fashion magazines and etiquette manuals were now urging readers to wear just a light net veil, or stick with the crape veil but let it hang down one’s back.[50] Sales of mourning crape plummeted. Between 1883 and 1894, Courtaulds’ sales figures decreased in value by 62 percent, and in 1896, it began to shift its production emphasis, introducing new lines of colored silks.[51] Stiff, dull mourning crape would never return to popularity; even the mass casualties of World War I did not improve sales figures for the fabric. As the 20th century dawned, mourning customs became laxer and laxer, freeing women from the discomfort — and health risks — of heavy weeping veils. The nail in the coffin of mourning clothes was the coming of World War I. With so many young men dead, customs changed. Mourning clothes seemed indulgent and behind the times.As an article in American Vogue put it in 1918: “…the whole feeling with regard to the wearing of mourning has undergone a change. In former days the custom of wearing mourning had a double significance; it was considered to be a sign of respect for the dead, and at the same time it announced the seclusion of the mourner. …The war has done still more towards moderating the old customs in regard to mourning… woman’s part in war means, not only giving herself and her time and her work, but her loved ones as well. Women felt, and rightly, that the indulgence of personal grief, even to the extent of wearing mourning, was incompatible with their duty to themselves, to their country, and to the men who cheerfully laid down their lives.”[52]Footnotes[1] Women’s Expressions of Grief, from Mourning Clothes to Memory Books | JSTOR Daily[2] Victorian Men's Fashion History[3] The Stages of Victorian Mourning[4] Women’s Expressions of Grief, from Mourning Clothes to Memory Books | JSTOR Daily[5] A Guide to the Stages of Mourning[6] http://To change the costume earlier was considered disrespectful to the deceased and, if the widow was still young and attractive, suggestive of potential sexual promiscuity. column1: Why do I feel sad after a car accident?
column3: You feel sad because there is a loss. Whether of a favorite car, a financial impact, maybe some injuries or even a death. All of those are causes for grief. There is a process that has been described for grieving. It begins with denial, includes anger, bartering, if only thoughts, and finally gets to acceptance that this is the reality. When we can recognize these feelings that come up we can handle them and move closer to the acceptance stage.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: You don’t. You can’t. Loss is forever. But life will continue, and the constant grief will fade into “less constant” grief. You will go on, and you will spend more time thinking about other things most of the time. But then you will want to remember but you will also NOT want to remember. You will have trouble driving past the cemetery, for example. Certain days will be bad pretty much long term. I wish I could say that grief ends, but I really don’t believe it does.
column9: I agree. You eventually just get used to them not being around. You get on with your life and then- unexpectedly- something triggers your memory and it feels like a stab to your heart. The stabs become less frequent but they persist.

column1: How does one comfort a friend who just lost a loved one?
column3: I became a widow on January 27, 2007. That day I learned that those "If you need anything let me knows" and the "I'm here for yous" are all pretty much lies. When you're really really hurt people don't know what to do to comfort you so they hope someone else does the job. And usually that's the same thing the someone elses are thinking, too. Also, in late 2007 I became an administrator of a Young Widow group on facebook. I've listened to hundreds upon hundreds of widows share their grief and stories. I've compiled a list of things either they or myself NEEDED. So. Keep your word. Don't tell them you'll be there if you really won't. "We'll get through this together" would have worked miracles on me if I knew the person saying it was sincere. DO NOT tell them to get over it or that they aren't grieving right. LISTEN to them. Let them talk about how bad they're hurting and don't say, "I know exactly what you're going through. I had a cat die when I was 12." You could replace cat with grandparent and it's going to do the same thing to the bereaved. You don't know how it is. Only they do. If they've watched a loved one suffer, tell them that you're relieved X isn't in pain anymore. They are no longer suffering. DON'T tell them that god takes the good ones while they're young. That is NOT comforting. Call them frequently and let them know you're thinking of them. INITIATE a conversation. It's easy to feel forgotten when someone you love dies. If they've lost someone through suicide DO NOT tell them their loved one is in hell. Really. Don't. If you feel overwhelmed by dealing with them, LET THEM KNOW you're uncomfortable because you just don't know what to do or how to help. No one let me know. They just abandoned me. Make sure they're taking care of themselves, too. Don't assume someone else is checking up on them. See if they've eaten or if they've even left the house for groceries. Don't tell them they look like shit. A better thing would be for you to say, "Let's get you in the shower and go have some coffee while we talk." Don't ask them what you can do for them if you're unwilling to do much. Offer to help with some chores. Those seem really difficult to accomplish when you're hurting. If it's a woman who's lost her husband, offer to do the things her husband might have done for his chores. *Take the garbage out. Reach some things that are high up or lift some things that may be too heavy for her. Take her car for an oil change. Help with her lawn.* Those things were terribly neglected when my husband died. If it's a parent that lost their spouse, offer to take their kids off their hands for a bit. Help their kid with homework if you can. That's probably where I see my most overwhelmed widows... they need a break from their kids to work on LIFE. Gently motivate them to get back to living. Take them to dinner. Take them to the grocery store. Take them for coffee. The things that comfort them won't just be words. Actually, there aren't any words that they've not already heard and they're all overused. Show them you care by your actions. They'll be forever grateful.
column9: Thank you. This is a good reminder. I never have a father daughter relationship with my dad...I never have an intimate meaningful conversation with him about life. He seems to think only about himself....Then I read this writing and it hit me where you said "offer to do all the chores which the departed partner used to do". My dad used to clean up my car every morning before I go to work, he always puts money in the car so I can pay highway and parking tickets easily. My dad is still very much alive at the moment ... you remind me that it's not late yet for me to start appreciating what my dad has done and realize nobody's perfect, if I can mention two to three good sides of him then I consider myself being very lucky

column1: How do I get over a parent's death?
column3: To begin with it’s a shock, the shock so big that we feel devastated. Gradually we realize that it had to happen some day as it happens to everyone. When it happens all of a sudden, while in normal health, we consider that they suffered no prolonged illness and escaped agony of hospitalization, pain and suffering. If it happens after protracted illness and on path of no return, it is the end of their misery. When my mother died at the age of 78, I passed through all these stages. The thought that with death, she is relieved from chromic knee pain, from recurrent cough, from repeated episodes of abdominal pain and ever present toothache. She will now be born with brand new body and all new healthy organs and will lead next life as a healthy individuals for many decades. Although we will miss her for ever but she may get even better family members and better life than this one because of her good karmas. At least Hindu mythology allows us to think of re-birth and of carrying forward of karma. More so, I consider that she is surviving through me. Half of my genes are from my mother. Every cell of my body has a stamp of my mother. My gestures, my etiquettes and my behavior are to big extent the copy of my mother. So where has she gone; she is surviving in me, she is surviving through me and will survive through many generations to come. This all makes my pain less and less. Time heals me and heals every one in my position, dear Virali.
column9: Thank you. My mother passed away from cancer, and I know that she’s gotten a new and healthy body, and I know that she isn’t suffering anymore, but I miss her - every single moment.

column1: My cat died today. I have felt like crying since then. What should I do?
column3: Original question: How do you cope with the loss of a pet cat It's hard. I lost this baby, Gandalf, 6 years ago.He was only a year and a half. He and his sister were bonded to me moreso than the rest of my family. I first noticed his sickness and after documenting his weightloss for a few days, convinced my mom to take him to the vet. Long story short, a month later his conditioned had worsened enough that we put him down. My parents were in the room, and I was the one who held him and comforted him in his last moments. It's 6 years later. It still hurts. Remember your good moments, mourn them. Cry. I had a lot of one-on-one time with his sister, Tabitha afterEven though she wasn't as affectionate as Gandalf. Cats don't have the reputation of bonding with humans as much as dogs, but they do. Just like dogs, they're a part of your family. Especially if you have them from the time that they were kittens, they become your babies, your children. You may never get over the loss. But over time it does get easier. If you have another pet, take comfort in them. If not, family members. Maybe look into adopting another kitten who needs your help. There are millions of cats who would love to be accepted into your home and loved. We're in the middle of kitten season right now, so go by a local shelter and there are going to be countless kittens needing homes. Older cats too! It's painful right now. But it does get easier.
column9: I lost my beloved cat Xarli 2.5 months ago. I was devastated until I decided to adopted 2 kittens. I am still extremely sad, but having the kittens with me gives me so much comfort. I recommend you to adopt one or two kittens. You will feel better and you will be saving and helping other cats. I am so sorry for your lost.

column1: Adult How can you deal with the sudden death of a friend?
column3: “Death is absolute truth, Our lives are just lies we are living” Not a long time ago a was in a situation similar to this, wondering about the same question. I would stick only to loosing a friend and not family member even though I consider friends to be my family. I came as shock to me when my friends girlfriend called me saying that he is admitted at hospital, in a state of coma with serious head injury. Knowing the person I was clear that he was not the rash driving types and neither would break any traffic rules. But a sane Gujjar Bhai in his SUV jumped signal and hit his bike and my friend had a massive head injury despite wearing helmet. If he was not wearing one I am sure he would have died on spot. The SUV fled from place like all Indian scenario. He struggled there for many days and finally passed away. I did not know what to do. First came sadness, for having lost an honest friend and an innocent one too. I had not known him for long, but I knew it was worth. Dealing with sadness was something that I was learning but a little part of me blamed myself for it as I was not able to convince his parents to not move him from hospital to home. The cost was too much for them to bear and I was not earning that time to have helped them out. It was same for a long time and then finally I talked to our common friends. It was reassuring that it was just not me who missed him, sharing our feelings helped all of us get it out and knowing that there were so many of us for each other was even better. Acceptance: It was not easy, but being in denial was not at all helpful. I used to visit his Facebook page. For couple of years I posted Birthday wishes, Miss You messages. It made me go through the process of grief all over again. I decided that I will not repeat it and stopped doing the Facebook thing. If I have to remember him I would, but not on a social networking site. I deleted his number from my phone book next. Not for being rude but as part of acceptance that he won’t be coming back and I would not be taking to him again. Moving on: After 2 years I saw his girlfriend getting married to someone, I was happy. I was happy that she could find courage to take that step. Its not easy to fix oneself after you have loved someone so much and move on. That gave me courage too. I got busy, made new friends, every now and then I remember him. I promise myself to be extra careful when I will ride a bike, and drive carefully when I learn to drive a car. It was a difficult journey, but I was not all alone, I had support. Talk, express yourself, share what you feel. It helps more than you can imagine.
column9: My friend is also in coma. He is not dead yet but doctors say that they had given up and if you can bear the expenses then keep him or take him.he will die the moment we remove ventilation. I just can't accept the fact that I might have to live without him. It's unimaginable.

column1: People: How do you deal with rude family members?
column3: If you can not be around them, don’t. That’s not always possible. Perhaps you are financially dependent on them. If that’s the case deals oth to the best you can until you can further distance yourself. Or possibly they depend on you. If that is the case I have other ideas that might help you. First off, walk away when you need a break. One thing being in a toxic family environment taught me was to stay and fight. Something maturity and experience taught me was that staying and fighting often makes it worse. Make your point and walk away. Give them time to think. Give yourself time to think. Get some fresh air or hide in your locked room with a good book or social media and process. Don’t stand around and let the fight get so ugly that you demean your point by calling them names or letting it get physical. Do your best to be rational and analytical of the situation. Toxic family will often put blame where it doesn’t belong or be unreasonable in other ways. Think it through. Get to the actual root and consider all the variables. Don’t let guilt or shame enter into the equaltion. Guilt and shame are feelings that help no one if pondered over for too long. Acknowledge the problems and look for solutions. Don’t allow yourself to get dragged into their toxic habits. If you do, own up to them and apologize. Don’t hate yourself for it, as that will only make things worse. Consciously try to do better and forgive yourself for using their tactics against them because sadly sometimes that will be the only thing that works and you will hate it. Seriously though, forgive yourself. Especially if these people are older than you they likely have a lasting impact on your behavioral patterns. Forgive yourself for doing the best you can to cope and sometimes acting other Han the way you would like to. It’s better to use sarcasm than rage out and hit them. It’s better to begrudgingly apologize when it wasn’t your fault than for them to lose their temper and hit you. Know that things will get better one day even if it’s frok you leaving and never talking to them again. You are capable of healthy relationships even if this person in your life is refusing to build one with you.

column1: How does a person cope with losing contact with her children by parental alienation?
column3: How does a person copes with parental alienation? I am sorry, really sorry, that you have to live this hell on earth. I find the project “cope” to be a long and winding road. I will list what has help me the most and what I have been trying to do below, in no particular order:Accept the fact that you did not do anything wrong.Learn about parental alienation. Join support groups in order to exchange notes. Realizing that this was not a personal issue but a pattern than many, many people have to go through helps. You are not alone.Join more support groups. Facebook is a great source to find support groups about Parental Alienation and Pathogenic Parenting. Meetup.com is also a great source to meet face to face with your peers.I found a great source of information that makes sense in Dr. Childress logs at Dr. Craig A. Childress.Learn about narcissism. Quora.com seems to be a great place to find survivors of narcissism abuse as well as culprits that may be sharing some of their inner thoughts (?).Rebuild your life in a healthier environment. Meet new people, build new friendships, try to smile more often.Understand that at this point nothing, but i mean nothing, that comes from the other parent is truth. If (s)he tells you that today is a beautiful sunny day with not a cloud in the horizon, get your umbrella and your raincoat.Therapy, lots of it. EMDR really helped me deal with C-PTSD. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) - Treatment.Do not stop trying to contact your children. Whatever they tell you, keep trying any way you can (within legal parameters). They need to know that you are there for them.Moving away and getting married helped a bit. I have built a great relationship with my step-children. I think I was lucky enough to meet two great ones in the same age range as my own children, so i believe I will have parameters to be able to understand my own kids when they come back.It has been a long and winding road. Six years have gone by, I am still working on it.Don’t expect people that have not experience this to understand. Mourning a live child is not within the realm of the living.Move away. Moving from Texas to California helped a lot. When we were in the same town I expected every day to hear the right knock at the door. With the distance a surprise visit is not possible, so that anxiety is repressed.It gets better with time, never right, but better. Take care of yourself.
column9: I wanted to let you know that your answer really helps me. Especially your point about other people and their understanding.Don’t expect people that have not experience this to understand. Mourning a live child is not within the realm of the living.I think most often people look at it like you are some kind of absentee parent and can’t comprehend the idea that your children are separated from you due to parental alienation and not something you must have chosen or done.

column1: How do I cope with losing a school leadership election to an undeserving person? What should I do?
column3: In life you will be going through many situations like that and what you should always be doing with it? Nothing you just need to accept it, you can't do anything else. This is part of our lives. In addition to that if you didn't succeed in anything, then it means one thing, there is a missing step or experience which you need to get in order to succeed. Which ultimately means there is a lesson to be learnt. Search for that lesson, learn it, move on and never ever complain about anything, do not let yourself to fall in that trap in life. Complaining means you feel helpless , not planning to take action to succeed and worse just staying where you are right now. On the other hand, judging him whether he deserves it or not, I don't think or believe that it is something which you need to consume your time and energy focusing on. Your right direction is to focus on yourself and not others. The ideal way to look at it in my opinion starts with accepting the result, accepting what it means to you (a lesson to be learnt) then set with yourself and begin you search for the lesson through analyzing the result : Why has that happened? What has gone wrong from your side? What was the missing factor or factors which led to this result? Then set with your team and take from them their feed back as well taking in consideration their answers to the same questions. If you want to succeed on the next one start your preparntation for it from the day you lost the current one (this way you don't lose you right focus). Do not let your frustration or disappointment lead you in those moments. Leaders are leaders because they can control their emotions and lead and control themselves before leading and controlling others. This is your real battle, start with yourself and everything else will follow. Do not bother about other things, just do your part and with patience and time things will fall into place before you even know it or realize it.

column1: How do you cope with losing the only person who cared about you?
column3: The most important thing is to realize that your value was never dependent on what other people think of you - good or bad. We cherish the time we have and the feelings that we get from being cared about, but when it stops, we are still the same person. It is at that time you need to learn to care about yourself. On a more spiritual level - yes, learning about and accepting Jesus Christ as a savior can be helpful, but I think the timing is wrong. I think it would create a shallow spiritual experience at this exact moment. First you have to accept that your value was not dependent on the other person. Then, after some time of thinking about that and reflecting on all the good times you had, you realize that the memories are a priceless treasure. Embrace the time that you did have and then after some healing time - a month or two perhaps, then you may want to visit a Bible believing church. You have to be careful not to fall into a trap by going to a cult. They can suck you in like a vacuum and never let you go. This is why you have to really be ok with yourself before you go out looking. That will keep you from falling from anyone with a smile that is trying to fill their quota by pulling you in. After losing my best friend - my dad - in a couple of days I started thinking through the thousands of things that made our relationship special. The things we loved doing together. Then I started being thankful that I had those experiences and I let them live in me. I did not dwell on the fact i would not have them any more - I was thankful that I had them in the first place. Work on that and you will be just fine.

column1: How do you cope with losing all your friends because of one person?
column3: When things have settled down (that you're over what sounds like parting ways with this one person) take the time to reflect on exactly what it is that caused you to lose your friends. Then, establish what you need to say/do to resolve it. Reach out and fix it. You might have your tail inbetween your legs as you go to seek forgiveness but if the friends are worth it then try and fix it. Take responsibility for what you've done (if anything) and be mindful of how you come across. It's why I started off with “when things settle down between you and the other” because it's important you don't go running back the second things fall apart with the person who is to blame. Your old friends will see it that you're only coming back because you have no one else. You don't want that, you want to go back with a clear understanding of why they're not your friends at the moment so that the apology is well thought out and acceptable. And that there it doesn't come with a side dish of “ive got no one right now and suddenly I'm back because Im desperate”. If you can acknowledge why your friends departed, they will feel like you truly understand and take accountability. And that your not just running back because someone else didn't work out. Then they can respect you and forgive you. And thus, that is how i would deal with “losing all my friends”…that is…. I wouldn't lose all my friends. I'd be of the mind frame “they're not here just now, but it's probably fixable…just not today”.

column1: How can a person cope with losing faith in God and relying solely on science for answers?
column3: Understand that nearly everyone has questioned or abandoned their faith at one time or another. You aren't the first person to do it, that's ridiculous to even think so. The problem is that science doesn't have all the answers either. Life will do that you know? Pull the rug out from under your feet, have your faith tested, and if you aren't steadfast in them, you're probably going to find yourself falling away from the faith. I can't tell nobody what to think or what to believe, but one thing I've learned, if you're going to do something, the only way it works is if you do it with all your heart. No book, no research, no nothing will ever have all the answers. All the answers you need are in here (pointing at my heart). Don't let external circumstances sway internal feelings..

column1: How do I cope with losing all my friends? They all told me I’m toxic and a horrible person.
column3: A family of three lived long ago – a Papa pigeon and two Baby pigeons. The Papa pigeon used to drink a lot of Bird alcohol (human polluted water). The alcohol inhibited senses and hampered his thinking. As a result, he turned into a ‘Bad’ pigeon. The baby pigeons hadn't learnt yet to fly. The Papa pigeon was short-tempered. Every morning, he would scold them and peck at them consistently for being scared of heights and not even trying to fly. He would call them names and peck at them over and over which would make them cry. At the sight of tears, the Papa pigeon would lower their morale by calling them a *cat* and a toxic pigeon. He would peck at them and fly away only to come back at the nest before sunset. During his absence, the Baby pigeons would be disheartened. One Baby pigeon would cry himself to sleep thinking that he had no place in this world and he is worthless. His sibling would swallow whatever he heard and would say to himself that he would not let the opinions of others affect him. He made a resolution to work harder and show the world his worth. Day after day, the Papa pigeon would take their classes. They would fail each day and the Papa pigeon would peck them and fly away. One Baby pigeon would cry at his failure, the other would compliment his efforts. Slowly and slowly, the second Baby pigeon showed remarkable improvement. He could fly from branch to branch while his sibling would cower in the nest. One day, while the Papa l pigeon was away, a snake slithered up the tree and spotted the Baby pigeons. The second Baby pigeons' determination and hard work paid off. He dived out of the nest and flew away. What happened to the first Baby pigeon is still unknown.The moral of the story is:- Papa and Mama birds are becoming Dipsomaniacs and, more and more Baby birds are unable to fly. So, Stop water pollution!!! Else…… . . . .You will be named!!™Hey!!! If you really need someone to talk to, feel free to chat with me. Don't give up. I would love to help you out. A lot of people go through this phase. It takes a lot of strength to snap out of it and when you do, and when you look back, a sense of achievement lights up your face!!Nisarg Kudgunti · 4yWhat made you sigh this morning?It was getting late already. I had to reach home in time. My parents must be getting worried. It was a dismal weather that paralleled my mood. The sun had set across the cityscapes long ago. The last light sieved through the annihilated remnants of the distant skyscrapers. The roads were void of life. The air was still and there was an ominous silence that sent a chill down my spine. I quickened my pace. I reached for my left pocket to ensure that the pills I had bought were safe. They cost me my entire savings. Most of the houses and the few people within, had already shut every door and windows, for it was time for the dawn of the night. I made out a few faces peeking at me behind the curtains. They must've thought I was mad. My ears picked up a faint cacophony and no sooner than I realized what that sound was, I made a run for it. It was the Siren. I dashed towards my home. The Siren kept getting louder. It seemed as if it was coming to get me. I took a turn, reached my home and found my parents already waiting outside. We scuttled inside and shut the door, only to hear the Siren pass in front of our house. What took you so long? Asked my father impatiently but his tone suggested that he was worried. I took out the pills and handed it to him. You shouldn't have risked your life. You were only seconds away from the Siren. I replied, We are already running low on the resources and the pantry won't keep us lasting forever. He nodded. Did you find anything else? I put my hand in my back pocket and took out a AAA battery and a few toffees. That ain't much. He lowered his head after hearing that. I'll try the bungalow next to the station tomorrow. I assured him. We carefully treaded to the living room amidst the dark house. My sister had lit a candle that drew us to the living room like a moth is to a flame. We all sat down in a circle, or rather a square, considering it was only the four of us. A long silence ensued which would occasionally be broken by the pressure cooker in the kitchen. We gazed at the candlelight. The food was ready as the final whistle blew. We ate it in silence and again started gazing at the candlelight, waiting for it to burn out completely, before we are left in the dark again. My sister put her hand in front of her and said Give me the AAA battery that you found. I looked at my father who handed it to her. She took out our radio and started it. The battery was working. At least today's endeavor of mine was worth something. I joked. I received faint smiles. My sister turned on the radio. She kept changing the frequency and all she got was white noise. I lied down with my leg on top of the other and my hands folded beneath my head. It's a waste of time. I muttered. But, she didn't give up. I closed my eyes in vain. No thoughts came across my mind. This has been ever since the arrival of the Siren. That was two months ago. Entire world had been brought to a standstill thereafter. Each day seems as long as eternity. Several people couldn’t find a reason to live. Depressed and lonely with no purpose to live for, they committed suicide. Several died due to hunger, or being exposed to the radiation. While a few unlucky were taken by the Siren never to return again. Our city was one of the few places that managed not to get nuked by one of the several countries. Although, the Siren hit us too, just like every other place. Most of the buildings of our city were reduced to rubble by enemy airships. It was a nuclear world war. How did it begin? No one knows, but we all do on how it ended. The war lasted for six days and six billion people lost their lives according to the Radio. One by one every nuclear state joined in and started dropping bombs on each other to fuel their animosity. The governments and the diplomats ruined relationships with each other. As a result, they brought an end to the world as we know it. Nobody cared about us, the common people. They hid in their luxurious bunkers while we struggled to peel of our burning clothes melted to our skin. Still, most cities were still quite habitable — if you forget the Siren. What was the Siren? No one has seen it, but only heard it. Those who tried to see it didn't live to tell the rest. We all were afraid of it. Suddenly, the Radio gave out a high pitched ringing noise. My sister threw it and covered her ears. The Radio knocked the candle down and they both went off. It was pitch black and pin drop silence. I gulped, for I knew the end was near. We tried to find and hold each other's hands. My mom started crying. I wanted to console her but the Siren drew my attention. It was getting louder and louder as every second passed by. Within no time our front door broke and the Siren came into the living room. My sister was pulled and I lost my grip on her, thereafter my mom and my father slipped from my hands. They shrieked at the top of their lungs. I cried loudly unable to see anything. Slowly, the wailing and the crying faded away. I heard the birds chirping. I could hear the faint voice of the Azaan and the Pooja Bell ringing. I closed my eyes and opened them. I saw light. I saw my pillow. I got up on my bed. It was a cold morning but my body was sweating profusely. I was scared and discombobulated (confused). What kind of a dream it was? I asked myself. Suddenly I heard the Siren outside my window, I gave out a shriek. My mom came into my room and said , Don't worry, it's an Ambulance. I sighed. We are safe from the Siren. She said wistfully looking in my eyes. I was relieved. Wait what?? . . . Well, do you wanna know what made me happy this morning after the horrific encounter with the Siren ( just kidding)? This question was requested by none other than Gopalkrishna Vishwanath . Thank you so much Gopalkrishna ji. I hope you guys liked my answer. If not, then…… . . . . You will be named!!™ Nisarg Kudgunti's answer to How do you respond to someone who has a crush on you? Nisarg Kudgunti's answer to What song would you like to hear in the last 5 minutes of your life? column1: How can someone cope with losing a person who no longer wants to be in a relationship due to their own unhappiness?
column3: Coping with a breakup involves self-care, seeking support from friends or family, and allowing time for emotional healing. Focus on personal growth, engage in activities you enjoy, and prioritize your well-being. Acceptance of the situation is crucial, and seeking professional help, such as counseling, can provide additional support. It's important to remember that healing takes time, and building a strong support system can assist in navigating the emotional challenges of losing a relationship.

column1: How do you cope with losing so many friends because of a bad friendship with one person?
column3: Jeez thank you for asking. Isn’t it amazing how one person is able to totally destroy your life? All the kindnesses performed for years after years made to seem like intentional acts of manipulation. Your quiet, withdrawn personality made to be seen as the personality of a psychopath, rather than a person who has been hurt by years of bullying and emotional abuse. column1: What are the effects of early onset dementia on a person's relationships and career? How do people with early onset dementia cope with losing their memory?
column3: Receiving the diagnosis of early onset Dementia is tragic and people generally enter deep depression. We are able to get so much information about the condition that no one can ignore the future and its distress. Many people remain in a denial mode until the issues become so impairing they cannot avoid facing the reality and the facts. Each individual will respond differently, of course, to the news, but personal stamina, love of life, optimism are short lived as the patient enters in mood swings phase, sadness, fatigue, and more and more difficult times with daily life. Family has to demonstrate patience and treat the patient as close as possible to what used to be, avoid speaking about serious decisions which have to be made when the loved one is in a more depressed mood, and maintain family routines, while preparing for inevitable changes as calmly as possible.

column1: What if you lose a relationship because you didn't know better and the other person doesn't want to associate with you anymore? How do you cope with it?
column3: You just have to cope with what happens. My ex-wife and I were best friends —12 years—in love. I screwed it up. And even when she warned me that she wouldn’t talk to me afterwards, that she couldn’t continue talking to me, I didn’t realize the severity of that statement. But she doesn’t even acknowledge I exist anymore. It’s hard to deal with. Basically, you “killed” your spouse. Yes, I will say that again. I killed my wife. I also killed myself. The people we were with each other are no more. The people we were as individuals in our relationship are no more. Yes, I’m still the same person. She is still the same person. But part of her personality is gone, the part that loved me. The part of me that loved her — that’s still within me— its holding on for dear life to her. Unfortunately, she’s moved on and is with someone new now. So I’m holding on to a dead woman. Even as I hold on to this person who is still very much alive, she is sleeping with another man. Is she thinking about me while she is sleeping with him? Probably not. Yet here I am still thinking about her? So how do I cope? It’s not easy. I did this. I caused my own divorce. The coping part is realizing that I can hold on to this woman for the next 10 years of my life. But she’s dead. She’s gone. She doesn’t exist anymore. I’m holding on to the memory of her.

column1: My social worker of 15 years is retiring. How do I cope with losing such a valuable support person?
column3: I would encourage you to talk with your current worker about the transition and your perfectly normal anxieties around this major change. I would assume you will be getting a new social worker so perhaps you could meet her while you are still working with your current friend. Maybe the three of you can meet in whatever way you normally connect and just have a friendly talk. Get to know her a little bit and share some important things about yourself. Especially express your concerns about the future and whether you will be able to build the same kind of relationship that you have had with your old worker. Change is never easy. We humans like to fight it but, of course that never helps. If possible I would encourage you to try reassuring yourself that you aren't going to be alone in the world. That you have all the internal resources your have learned and built over the years, especially with the help of your old worker. She had helped you strengthen your inner resources so you can be strong in the world. And you aren't alone.
column9: A most humble thank you. I was afraid to tell him how I felt. … I know he doesn't think of me when we're not working together, but that's not the case for me. I don't have any romantic feelings or anything like that, it's just been a long time and it's EASY. He knows me, knows where, how and with what I struggle, he knows how I'm likely to react. I TRUST him. Trust is hard for me. Thank you for your kindness.

column1: Adult Everyone in your life will have a last day with you and you don't even know when it will be. How do you cope with losing the most important person in your life?
column3: We grieve because we have lovedNo love, no grief. Deep love, deep and complicated griefWhen we choose to love someone, we also accept that one of us will die before the other.The person we loved dies, our love for them doesn’tGrief is the final responsibility for loving someone.If we can understand these ideas, we will love differently. Our love will be more open and honest, but also have more urgency because we acknowledge that life is a time limited passage and that all of us will die. The greatest challenges in grief at regrets. “I wish I had”, “If I had known”, “I should have never said”. “I should have said”. If we love openly, we share our fears, we express that we might be the survivor that must grieve our loss, and we can openly discuss how we would want our loved one to grieve our loss. These are not morbid discussions, they are open and honest, and they should always include planning the tings we both want to do while we ate still both alive. Love like today is your last day on Earth, love like you and your lover will live to be 120. The fleeting joys of today are important, but so is the caring and planning for a lone life of loving someone. Never leave an argument unfinished, never let your last word to someone be an angry one, never leave a hurt you have caused unresolved. You will live with fewer regrets, especially when a loved one dies. Be well, seek peace, and build love openly and honestly and with a sense of urgency. You will be ready for anything, and your life will be richer and fuller.

column1: How does a person go on after losing their only child?
column3: You donʻt really have a choice, so you just wake up every day and keep going, because there are other people who need you. I lost my son in 2016. He was 18, and he is the third of my four children. Every day I miss him; some days it the missing of him is unbearable, and some days, the missing is a bit more bearable - at least after these 2.5 years. You change. You are not the same person who you were before your child died. I think that is a universal feeling of child loss - the pieces of your life get picked up and assembled back together, but itʻs like gluing a broken glass together, always a little more fragile. I, at least, find that things that would have seemed terrible obstacles before seem kind of unimportant, but little things can feel completely overwhelming. Having an occupation that is just hard enough to be distracting, that has skill levels that you can strive for, that is creative, can help. For me, it was quilting. I wanted my sonʻs t-shirts to be made into quilts, but when it came down to having to give the tshirts to someone to actually made the quilt, I couldnʻt do it. So I learned to sew so I could do them myself. It is not a natural skill; it challenged me, and there is always something to learn. It helps on the medium days. The really bad days - well, those days you just sit and ride it out. Allowing yourself to feel all the feelings is important. Some of them are less than attractive, but theyʻre yours and denying them only means they come back later with a vengeance. I write them down, and I completely hope no one but me ever reads them. It helps me acknowledge them and the time it takes to write creates space for new ideas to flow in. Allow the people around you - your spouse, your other children, extended family - to have their feelings, too. Their feelings arenʻt always admirable or attractive either, but, just like yours, they are theirs and they need to feel them. Itʻs a hard thing, grieving separately, but together - parallel grief tracks. Be open to offers of help. If someone offers, take them up on it. This is a hard thing for me, but I remind myself that when I offer to help people, I really mean it, and it makes me feel better to help. When people say stupid things as their own way of coping - just realize they have zero idea about child loss (and thank goodness for that! Itʻs the worst thing in the world). Sometimes I tell them itʻs not helpful (one of the ways I have changed) and why; and sometimes I just acknowledge their comment. I found grief counseling helpful. My husband found a clergyman he could speak to. Sharing it can help.
column9: Thank you, I know that this was written quite some time ago but I just found it now. I’m 8 months in and found what you wrote both helpful and comforting. My emotions bounce around so wildly, one moment I’m almost ‘myself’ the next I’m a mess. Your story has made me feel less alone.

column1: How do you cope with the fact that the person you love is never coming back?
column3: The process of getting over from a break up is very crucial and it depends from relationship to relationship, person to person, time to time. Every relationship comes with its own levels of seriousness. so is the breakup. some breakups take time to heal others take ages to heal but one heals in the end. everyone does. there is nothing that can not be done. If you know that your partner is not going to come back then you must try to live with this fact for sometime by doing certain things :-Erase all the pictures , messages, call records, history of chats, mails to not see the Ex on anything that you use daily like cellphones, facebook, instagram, google chats, yahoo messenger etc etc.Stop doing whatever you were doing with that person. like going to the same place where you used to go on dates. stop eating food items that you used to eat as a favourite food.Stop meeting common friends who will ask you about how you are doing and start giving you updates about your Ex if he/she is doing great in life. you need to stay away from negative people.Do not take stupid drugs or do anything stupid to prove nothing but create drama for no reason.Change your daily routine and build new hobbies to keep your self busy. work hard at office, work on yourself, go out for vacations with friends and family.Stay strong, believe me you can overcome anything in life even a breakup.If a breakup is hard to digest just think of the most loving person in your and think how will he/she feel if he/she would have had seen you in a bad condition. In my case i think of my mother and i overcome most of my problems in life even a breakup.It is a breakup not AIDS that cannot be cured…. anything is curable but you need to live positively so start following positive motivational speakers online. start listening to speech’s that preach good thinking. start meeting new people who are going to give you positive thinking support.Try to write down all the negative and positive thoughts about your Ex that you wanted to say to him/her post your breakup and after the letter is completed, burn it to burn your bridge.Rest if you are still confused message me , will guide you few more steps to get over with the Ex.

column1: How do people cope with losing their personal identity when joining the military?
column3: I'm not sure what you think, but you don't become a mindlessness robot when you join the military. The military helped to develop the person I've become, they showed me the wider world through travel to places I may never have gone on my own. I met people from many countries that I would never have met without being in the service. They made me feel grateful for what I have and where I'm from. I'm proud of my service and looking back I wouldn't change it. I didn't lose my personal identity when I joined the military, I found it.

column1: How do you cope with losing your personal style and identity in a relationship where your partner has strong preferences?
column3: The best answer would be to “negotiate” so you can keep both: You could ask your partner if you could use some space where you can decorate it with your style. If your partner won't budge : Then, you are FREE to choose: The answer depends on you: What are your priorities ? A) To keep your relationship with your partner “but” lose your identity and style? B) To keep your identity and style “but” lose the relationship with your partner and look for another place to live alone or look for another partner ?
column9: If someone wants to keep you from being You then You leave if they won’t budge to allow you some of your things you prefer to have as well. It’s called compromise with one another if it’s not going to work

column1: How could I cope with losing my beauty in an accident and feeling like a different person afterwards?
column3: I think we all need to work on our inner beauty which is not ephemeral as is our outward appearance. It would be very hard indeed to lose good looks. But if you have been cultivating your inner beauty, that can compensate enormously. We all know that outward appearance is superficial. A beautiful woman can be vicious and hard-hearted. She can take someone's husband away. She can wrap her boss around her little finger. She can make you feel ugly. We know the type. Audrey Hepburn was a stunningly beautiful woman. Google what she had to say about looks. She valued the inner beauty of people and expressed her perspective really well. Invest in being beautiful. That starts with showing a proper interest in others. Give them your time and your ear and your heart. Cultivate a caring spirit and a genuine interest in the other person. People will respond to the inner you and not worry at all what you look like.

column1: Adult How does an old man cope with losing his wife?
column3: Slowly, for most. If you are an old man you are already in the latter part of your life and for many it seems to be a holding waiting period for the end. My late wife and I had been sexual players for some years, each seeing others for sex and fun. After a morning period I continued on with other women as before. Sexually it has not been much different than before her death.

column1: What do I do if I lose a personal pet and feel like I'm all alone? How would I cope?
column3: What do I do if I lose a personal pet and feel like I'm all alone? How would I cope? Our cats have never been a substitute for human family and friends, but they are a wonderful addition to our lives. They are creatures of pure spirit, unburdened by the curse of reason. They give affection without envy. They have needs without wanting. They are pedagogs without dogma. ..and they take up real estate in your heart bigger than you realize while you watch them play, sleep, eat, live... Unlike our little furry persons, we humans have a great deal of choice in how we face the world and ordeal. I have 10 pictures up on our kitty memorial wall. Every single one of them owned a large plot of real estate in my heart.We have grieved for them. We have then used that grief as fuel to give another furry person a home. The mostly white kitty in the leftmost picture is the semi-famous Miss Teia, who received the Final Kindness on 23 NOV 18 due to kidney failure. Teia was a few weeks under 21 1/2. Her brothers, Cooper (greybie) and Buff missed her, as did we.An opportunity came up in January to adopt a 12 1/2 year old kitty who needed a new home. Miss Blue joined the family on 14 JAN 19.That is how we cope, turning the grief into action, by adopting a new furry person who needs a home.
column9: That is a nice way of thinking about your deceased kitty. I have had had 2 cats and 2 dogs that I have had to be put to sleep due to serious issues that seemed to happen overnight. Oh how I cried each and every time. My pets take a place in my home so of course I cried. I believe that if you think you can handle a new pet quickly/slowly that you should find another one. In my mind they all take a piece of my heart. I usually wait until I stop thinking I can see my previous pet roaming my house. I'm not saying that I believe in voodoo, but I guess from them being part of the family for so many years it causes me to think I see their tail going into another room, etc. When I lost my dachshund my son and his girlfriend (who breeds dachshunds) they picked the perfect puppy for me. He is perfect in every way and I couldn't imagine my life without him. Good luck with your new cat, Im not saying that it will be easy but you'll get there soon
