If she can talk to her parents and tell them she wants happiness for all of them by accepting her choice,it is a win -win situation. When you truly love someone , it is impossible to let go that person. In the end of nothing works, she can leave the house or if she is independent you both can stay together and get married .

column1: How do I deal with handling my insecurities? I have no idea what they are or why I’m so worried about losing the person I love, I’ve been cheated on dozens of times and I know that won’t help but I just don’t know how to cope with this.
column3: Let’s unpack this one. You’ve been cheated on dozens of times. It sounds like you have a horrible track record picking potential mates for a life-long commitment. You’ve become a magnet for the wrong type of lover. You also stated you have no idea what your insecurities are but you are certain you have them. Time to get a professional opinion on this. Because, as Dr. Phil is fond of saying “You can’t change what you don’t acknowledge.” But for you, you don’t even know what you should be acknowledging. So, you’re starting at a great disadvantage that requires a more gifted therapist to unlock and explore. How do you cope? You take a deep breath. You inform the partner that you are with right now that you are coming from a terrible place of chronic insecurity. Then, you gauge their response to your confession. If they appear to be compassionate, you stick with them and lean on them for further support as you begin the healing process. And, if not, you leave them and DO NOT begin another relationship until such time as you’ve had the opportunity to experience some badly needed ‘quiet time’ alone with your thoughts and your insecurities, so that you can better assess what they are and face them head on, focusing on the future rather than your disastrous past. Again, a therapist will help you work through these issues. Best of luck as you begin your healing process.

column1: What are some effective ways to cope with job loss? How does it impact a person to lose their only source of income and means of living?
column3: Here are my suggestions:Cut your expenses and sign up for temp work or a restaurant job. (Even if you just volunteer it still gives you something to fill in a gap on your resume.)Work out and get in really good shape. It matters.Put yourself in situations where you can get a lucky break - networking, job fairs, charity projects. Investigate where the jobs are and what skills are required. Retrain if needed, even if it’s self-study.Be strategic and remember that success is the best revenge.I’ve been there several times - it was tough but my situation always eventually ended up a lot better than it was prior to the job loss. Good luck. Gary

column1: How can you move beyond always thinking about someone who has died?
column3: It is not necessary to forget the memories of those who have passed away. Forgetting is a natural process, we automatically forget as time passes if we make no deliberate attempt to remember. The trouble is we deliberately remember. We consciously throw our mind back into the days gone by and get onto the journey of reliving the moments. We should stop such perverse contemplation. If we were to make no special attempt to talk about the one who has passed, then we will naturally forget him and her, that’s how God wishes us to be. God wants us to live in the present. The person is not here, that’s our present. But the person is present somewhere else, he or she is present elsewhere, that’s his or her present, and we must respect that. We can’t let our heart sink into the stupidity of thinking the person is ACTUALLY ceased. The person is living elsewhere, we can’t insist that the person should be here with us. Remembering those who have passed comes from a tendency to revisit our sorrow. The loss is great indeed; it’s a terrible blow, a part of us is gone and we want to acknowledge that through our sorrow. When a foreign body like a bacteria enters our body, the body naturally responds with fever or a swelling. That’s the body’s way of p[protecting us. Similarly, death of a near one brings reaction like sorrow. That’s a signal that we must let go. Sorrow is a sign of the fact we not well mentally and spiritually well. First of all, we must understand that there’s nothing wrong that has happened to the one who has gone. He or she has just dropped the body and would have assumed another body already as we sit here and grieve. Our crying here is not good for the passing soul. In the Bhagavad Gita Krishna tells Arjuna Ma Shuch, do not grieve. We should follow God’s command and stop grieving over the dead. Don’t keep belongings, clothes etc of those who have passed. These unnecessarily bring the memories alive. It’s not advisable to re-live. Every time you feel sad over the one who has passed, tell yourself that you are committing an offence against him or her by grieving. It’s a negative energy that the one who has gone does not need. Firmly believe that one who has passed has really moved on and is living his or her new life with a new body, it’s all good out there. You alone are stuck in the past. You too must move on. By thinking it was not good for the passing soul, you are not wishing well, you are wishing ill. How do you know that the person isn’t happier now than when he or she was alive to you? Think that grieving over someone is not a proof of love, it’s just weakness. If you truly loved the person, then you won’t be cast in sorrow. If you truly loved the person, you would let him or her go fully, even from your memories. You won’t bind them. You must think from his or her point of view and not yours. Your memories and thoughts are subtle chains that bind the soul freed from one body. Why force him or her to hang on here? Get real. Think hard as to where that person is. Do you even care? Or are you just lost in your own emotion? Think which action of yours can actually help him or her. Sorrow definitely doesn't. Think that your grieving is a double offence. Offence against one who has passed who will sense your vibrations astrally and offence against your present life, the people and situations around you, which need your cheer and enthusiasm. Your happiness will be sensed by the one who has passed. He or she is concerned about you and can actually feel you. Why complicate his or her journey with your emotional nonsense? You can do greatest good to those who have passed by letting go. If you love your life and be happy, you help the kith an kin who is not here. When you recognise these facts and train your heart accordingly and not be foolish, the sorrow will disappear. Understanding abolishes sorrow. Death is not bad at all, grieving over dead is worse, it kills the fact of our immortality. Everyone is deathless, our grieving over physical death trivialises and insults our immortality which is the divine truth. We have to grow up. We have to get the emotional maturity about death and that will help us forget the smaller things like passing of the body. After understanding this, if we remember, we will not plunge into melancholy or grief. We will just smile and say, it’s alright. Things are meant to be the they are. That’s the best!

column1: How much should a therapist disclose if a personal change impacts therapy? Revoking email support between session & client hurt by losing way of coping. Reducing workload so declining client requests for extra sessions to help with the change.
column3: That probably depends on the situation, don’t you think? But if things change, a client is entitled to an explanation that makes sense of the situation. I’ve had to do that twice, that I can think of; once when I landed in the hospital after an accident, and the other when my late husband died. In both cases, I explained the situation to my clients but did not dwell on the impact to me, because that was both unnecessary and irrelevant. Instead, I presented a full explanation of the circumstances, what I thought might come next, and their options if my absence did not work for them. I think that my situations were relatively easy to explain, however, and I don’t know if that would be true for everyone, although I do believe there is a way to explain almost everything, and if there is a change in policies, procedures, availability or things like that, then it is incumbent upon the therapist to produce a cogent explanation. Now admittedly, saying “hi, I’m having an episode of major depression and can’t handle my normal workload” or “you know, my cocaine addiction seems to be getting in the way of my work,” “my child is in rehab” or “I have to begin weekly chemo and will be sick as a dog,” or even “my husband has walked out in me and I’m crushed,” are all rather tricky things to explain without creating all kinds of boundary issues, but not explaining and leaving people to speculate, or feel abandoned is worse, so some kind of neutral explanation is called for. You disclose as much as is necessary to explain the changes while trying to avoid burdening the client or creating any unnecessary alarm. Sometimes that is not going to be possible, because the reality IS alarming, but then you work through it the best you can. And sometimes a therapist may not be able to fully explain because it is too much for them to do so. Again, reality can intrude on the most perfect plans and intentions. People need to own up and do the best they can to be there for their clients, as part of the job, but I suspect that sometimes, that may not be possible, although I do not know. On the other hand, I suspect sometimes therapists don’t handle this well, or as well as they could, and that is truly unfortunate. But it is up to each client to determine what they can tolerate and what they cannot. If it doesn’t work for them, they should explore other options.

column1: How do I control my neurotic tendencies?
column3: A neurosis is caused by the repression of one or more experiences that were seen as traumatic at the time. Speaking in psycho-analytic terms, your conscious mind, which watches out for you, analyses and determines the world around you and filters it to suit your world view doesn't begin forming until the age of 7 or so. Before this time, children take things literally and have no mechanism to filter the information and experiences entering the mind. Once the conscious mind begins to form, it looks at any information deemed irrelevant or threatening to it/you and tucks it away deep down in the subconscious, hidden away safely from your conscious thinking. The problem with this is that the trauma or emotional experiences that have been hidden away in this manner produce a mental and emotional energy within your mind that must be released in some way (through motor action). This is why neuroses begin to show themselves. The cause has been hidden from your conscious recollection therefore you do not remember exactly what the traumatic or emotional event was, or even, in many cases, that it happened at all. You may occasionally release a partial memory during a dream in a literal or usually, more symbolic sense that you may be unable to decipher. The energy may release itself in the form of a stutter, a tic, a spasm, panic attacks or any number of irrational fears or phobias. If the cause isn't found and dealt with (through Hypno-analysis in my opinion - obviously!) then it will continue to produce symptoms until it is. Should your particular neurotic symptoms fade and you notice a symptom is no longer there, think and see if you now have another neurotic symptom in its place. This is known as 'symptom substitution' and will likely continue to occur until the cause is dealt with. Yes, drugs can help, masking the problem by distracting yourself with something else can help. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy & traditional psychotherapy can help. But none of them work at a subconscious level to determine the actual root cause as realized by the subconscious mind. Once the cause is released back into conscious awareness and you are then able to assess it as an adult and to deal with it rationally, the symptoms will all disappear one by one. These traumatic memories or repressions can vary from extremely bad experiences to simply being scared by a bee you thought might sting you so please, don't think neurosis = severe trauma. It can, but it is usually because of more innocent things that as an adult, you may think were silly. But as a child, they were obviously traumatic enough to be hidden away, as the mind's self-defence mechanism kicked in and 'protected' you from it. Analysis takes a number of sessions, it is not a quick fix and requires determination on your part to explore and face the causes of your neurotic issues. Then, yes, you can live without them in a much happier and more fulfilling life. I will always advocate my therapies when I know they can help. But please, take some time, do some research and listen to what all the other wise Quora members have to say. There are many other great therapies out there and some experts right here on this site. You are obviously not prepared to accept your neurosis and that is an excellent and brave first step towards overcoming your issues. I hope my answer has helped in some way and I wish you all the best with your research and improvement.

column1: How do I overcome a lisp?
column3: There are actually quite a few different kinds of lisps and quite a few different causes. If you’re an adult, I recommend you bite the bullet and find a certified Speech Language Pathologist in your area. They are trained to help you with your individual needs. If you are hesitant to incur fees and want to do it yourself, at the very least I would invest in at least 1–2 therapy sessions and have them tell you what they are seeing. I would talk to the SLP first about what your needs are and what you would like from them. See if they are willing to do an assessment and then create an intensive at-home plan for you. This would need some serious commitment and self-motivation on your end. You may have to interview a few on the phone to see if that is something they would be willing to do. Some lisps are very tricky and you might need some additional feedback through individual therapy to help you. Some lisps are much easier than others though! I think its worth finding a professional, especially at first. If you live in a remote area, online therapy is becoming much more common and if the therapist is good, it’s very effective! If you are someone who just can’t see themselves going to a professional or are broke, broke, broke, there are quite a few videos that teach what to do. I can’t speak to the quality of these, but they’re worth a look and you can see what the therapist is doing with their tongue and teeth position. In addition, watch a video of yourself saying some words and sentences with s and z and do this often as you progress. Watch your mouth and tongue. Maybe make a video of a friend (who has speech you like) and have them say the same words and sentences. Compare them. Watch what the differences are. If you have a frontal lisp (you make a “th” sound instead of an “s”or “z” and your tongue protrudes), for the “s” and “z” sounds, try to focus on keeping your tongue behind your teeth either on the top or sometimes the bottom teeth. Teeth are together. The air should be forward. Practice saying the individual sound (s or z), then words (with s, z)and then get more complex with sentences (with s,z). Once again, there are LOTS of different variations of what people consider a lisp and some you really need a professional to learn techniques for your individual needs or see if there is an anatomical difference that needs to be addressed. If what you are doing at home doesn’t work, then please see a certified Speech Language Pathologist. Go to ASHA (American Speech and Hearing Association ASHA.org) or a University in your area that has a Speech and Language program. I think most, if not all, SLP graduate programs have a clinic they use to help graduate students learn how to be therapists and they can provide therapy at greatly reduced cost. Most SLPs really want to help people and would do their best to find a way to support you. Sadly, oftentimes schools or hospitals are governed by strict guidelines who they consider “severe” enough to receive therapy. Good Luck!

column1: Adult How can you deal with the sudden death of a friend?
column3: The really important thing about friendship — and all personal relationships, for that matter — is the manner in which your identity incorporates the other person. My father is my father because I’m his son; part of my identity is “so-and-so’s son.” I think of myself as being some particular person’s son; one thinks of oneself as some particular person’s wife, or husband, or friend, or whatever. Your identity is, in part, constituted by your relationship to a particular person, which is what creates that relationship in the first place. You are who you are, in some sense, because of who you have relationships with. This relationship deepens the more your identity incorporates the other person. This is one reason, among others, that going through things with another person helps cement your relationship with them. “I lived with this person for three years; we went on a roadtrip together; in college we joined the same club; we graduated together.” The more intense the experiences you have with a person, the more deeply they cement your relationship with them. When a loved one dies, what you’re experiencing is a blow to your identity. I cannot be my father’s son if my father is dead. You cannot be your spouse’s husband or wife if they are dead. If it feels as if a piece of you is missing, that’s why. A part of your identity is no longer valid, and you’ve lost part of yourself. The obvious shift here is from “I have this relationship to this person” to “I once had this relationship to this person.” It’s a process of letting go of that part of yourself, not so that it vanishes but so that it changes. The person you knew passes into memory, and the part of you that knows them becomes the part of you that knew them. This process is painful, but it’s a part of grief. If you are a person who responds to things by grieving, then it’s necessary. With the sole exception of romantic partners, I, personally, do not grieve. This is a result of my peculiar psychological makeup, in which isolation and independence are the rule, not the exception.

column1: How can I get over the sudden death of my dad?
column3: Hi, Coping father's death is not impossible. I think of my dad all the time. There is not a moment I would not be reminded of him. Somehow, it gives me tears, but it also gives me strength. To be the kind of person, he wanted me to be. To do the kind of things he wanted me to do. I didn't cry a lot over his death. It was sudden. It was painful. But, being the first child, with a younger sibling and a widowed mother, I really had to pull myself together. I keep thinking of the things my dad tells me all the time. The fact is, he is not completely gone. He lives in your blood, in your genetic system. All our ancestors live in us. You are his image on this world. So, pull yourself together and do things that he would want you to do. The first few months, I didn't laugh, I was without emotions. I thought it was better that way. But, after a few months, when a joke happened, and involuntarily when I laughed. I used to feel guilty. I used to think. What kind of a daughter am I? My dad is dead and am laughing at a stupid joke. It took time, to realize, (of course with the help of friends and family), that he wouldn't want me to be unhappy. He will want me to laugh, be happy and move on with my life. Moving on, doesn't mean you will forget him. It can't happen. You ll never forget him. He will be the guiding star. An angel who would pull you out of misery. When you can handle yourself. He will be at peace. Understand that what's happened has happened! Don't think and rethink how things should have been! I know exactly how our brains work. What if I could have spent some more days when he was sick! What if this didn't happen.! What if that didn't happen! Please don't take a road down on the guilt trip. That sucks! It's a phase! It truly is! Live your life full and wholeheartedly. He is there with you and wishes you Happiness. Always! Remember that! That will give you inner strength! Even now, when there is a door bell ring! I somehow wish it is him. I truly can't believe that he is gone. May be he is not! His reflection is there everywhere, governing every part of our lives. Parents are the examples of true Unconditional Love. Living a life that he would be proud of and doing that happily, is your responsibility. Having said all this, if you wish to cry, cry! Grieve as much as you want! Talk to people! Talk to your family! Support each other! Be there for them, and let them be there for you. Wish you Happiness! :) keep smiling.

column1: What are some advice for someone who is depressed?
column3: After years of being a psychiatrist and dealing with depression and other mental health issues, this is what I’ve learned: When someone is depressed, there are things you should say and things you shouldn’t say. You should say the following 5 things:“I see that you’re having a hard time.” People feel better when they’re understood and not judged or analyzed.“I’m here for you.” Depression is very isolating and alienating. Depressed people feel a sense of relief when they don’t feel so alone in their pain.“You don’t have to figure this out on your own.” Depressed people often believe that they have to figure out on their own how to fix themselves. Then they feel guilty when inevitably, they can’t. They feel a lot less guilty and a lot less overwhelmed when they’re reassured that they don’t have to fix things all by themselves.“Are you thinking of hurting yourself?” You should always ask a depressed person if they’re having suicidal thought or plans, because you could prevent a tragedy by getting them immediate help.“Let’s get you some professional help.” Depression is a mental illness and it needs to be treated by qualified mental health professionals. Just like any illness, it won’t go away by thinking different thoughts or going for a brisk walk.You shouldn’t say the following:“Snap out of it.” This is an illness. They can’t just snap out of it. They need mental health help in the form of psychotherapy and often they’ll need medication as well to alleviate their symptoms and their suffering.“You brought this on yourself.” People don’t make themselves depressed with a bad attitude. They become depressed because of a profound loss they’ve experienced and/or because they’re genetically prone to depression. This type of statement only makes them feel bad about themselves and more depressed.“It’s not so bad.” To the depressed person who feels helpless, hopeless and unable to see the light at the end of the tunnel, it really is that bad. When you minimize their experience you only make them feel worse.“It’s going to be okay.” You have no idea how it’s going to be. Telling a depressed person something like this will only make them lose their trust in you, because they’re not sure if it’s going to be okay at all. They don’t need your cheer-leading; they need your empathy right now.

column1: How do you spot a fake INFJ?
column3: The same way you spot a fake INTJ: observe how he or she behaves under stress. INFJ has the same stress reaction as INTJ - namely extroverted sensing (Se). While I am an INTJ, pretty much the same applies to INFJ as well. The stress reaction is important as you cannot fake the stress reaction - it either is the genuine INFJ reaction or it isn’t, in which case the person in question isn’t an INFJ. When the INFJ is first faced with a stressful situation, they may attempt to find solitude. They will want to recharge and will first attempt to use the things that comfort them to do so. They may attempt to continue as if nothing is wrong and take the stress upon themselves. INFJs are very good at viewing the long-term solutions and will attempt to solve them. They will attempt to rely on their intuition to figure out how to cope with the stress. Isolating themselves and attempting to regain their energy is just how the INFJ attempts to cope with stress. When the INFJ is under extreme amounts of stress, they will begin to act like a very different person than the INFJ you may be used to. They may begin to act very impulsively and only focus on the present moment. They may start to make decisions without thinking through the long term ramifications. They will become more aware of their physical presence, and indulge in things like eating, drinking or any kind of physical activities. They may appear more materialistic or self-preserving than their usual caring and complex selves. The INFJ may begin to focus on unimportant details and lose sight of the deeper meaning that they so normally value. They will be withdrawn from loved ones and will not have the energy to give them the general care that they the INFJ provides.

column1: Why do parents whose children pass away keep their bedrooms untouched? Is that even a healthy way to cope?

I don't know how long it will take me. I have people who tell me to snap out of my grief and get on with my life. They think I'm overdoing it. So now I smile I laugh when I meet people and keep my grief tucked away in my heart so that people outside my close family don't see it. If I as a child miss my mother so much, then how much more gut wrenching it must be for parents to lose their children. I can't even begin to imagine their grief. How difficult it must be for them to get rid of their child's stuff. It may seem like a sacrilege to their childs memory to some. Only a person who has lost a child knows what it feels like. Nobody else can even understand or imagine what they are feeling or going through. I don't know whether keeping their deceased children's room untouched is a healthy way to cope. But I feel every person has the right to grieve and cope in the way they choose. In my own family I have an aunt and a cousin who lost their children. It took them more than a year to come out of their grief and even interact with people leave alone getting rid of their child's things. For some people it doesn't take long to cope up with the loss and for some it may take years. So let's not judge people for the ways they chose to cope up with grief of losing a child.

column1: What are some good ways to cope with anxiety and depression without using medication?
column3: Here are 11 natural anxiety remedies that have completely changed my life.Stop watching the news. I get it. The world is ending. I don’t want to think about it. I don’t want to watch it. I check for updates on worldly events through Twitter sometimes, but I never sit down to “watch the news”. I don’t think too much about the world’s problems because I haven’t mastered my own yet.Meditation. I meditate almost every day. It’s just good to decompress. It’s good to sit and think every once and a while because eventually, you run out of things to think about. When you do that, you actually start meditating. 10–30 minutes per day, every day possible.Start cutting out people that suck. I’ve alienated so many people in the past year. So many people. My inner circle is smaller, but also it’s stronger than it’s ever been. I have people in my life who actually look out for me. I have friends that love me. These people have helped me realize that I should never settle for less.Intense physical exercise. “Being active” is great for my physical health, but it doesn't actually make my anxiety go away. However, going to the gym and pushing myself as hard as I can (while not breaking my body) makes me completely free from anxiety—at least for a while.Reading. None of these “remedies” are secrets. There are no secrets here. If there was a magical remedy that got rid of anxiety and had no negative consequences, everyone would do it. Reading made me realize that I’m not alone in having anxiety. Studying other people’s thoughts makes me realize that my thoughts are not as weird as I thought.Doing scary shit. I’m not saying that you should start jumping out of airplanes, but seriously, stop holding back in your life because you have anxiety. Anxiety compounds over time. The longer you think about stuff, the scarier it gets. Sometimes, you just have to jump off the deep and end and see if you can swim.Talking to your friends. People have “friends”, but most of their friends don’t really know them. One of my friends and I sit in the sauna 3 days a week after Jiu-Jitsu training and talk about life. We’ve shared some pretty personal stuff during those talks. Frequent, unfiltered conversations will change your life.Writing. The main reason that I write so damn much is that writing makes my brain feel physically lighter. The act of putting my words onto a page helps me stop having to think so much. I publish them because sometimes they help people. However, private journaling can have the same mental benefits for people struggling with depression/anxiety.Eating healthier. When you eat like shit, you feel like shit. When you eat better, you feel better. While there is certainly more to taking care of your mental health than eating vegetables, eating better does help. I only drink alcohol a couple of times per year and I try to limit caffeine intake after my morning cup of coffee. I don’t smoke or do drugs. If you read my answer on derealization, you know why.Sleeping enough. Most people do not sleep enough. I don’t understand it. When I sleep less than 7 hours per night for more than a few days, I feel like I’m on a slippery slope to burnout, depression, anxiety, and losing my bloody mind. All these other remedies are great, but if you don’t sleep, you’re fighting a losing battle.Giving my all in everything I do. This seems like a cop-out, but how many people do you know who actually give their all? Putting everything I have into everything I deem worthy of my effort makes me feel like I have fewer regrets. It also makes me less anxious about outcomes, because I know I have done everything I can to influence said outcomes.These are just a few of my “non-medication” remedies for anxiety and depression. I’ve also worked with a therapist for my mental health, but not everyone has access to a therapist, so I left that out of this list. These are 11 solo habits that will help you become less anxious, less depressed, and more peaceful. Hope this helps :)

column1: How can a person with anxious preoccupied attachment break free from their relationship with a dismissive avoidant?
column3: Go or stay, the route is the same, in my opinion, speaking as a person who has been in this situation many times. The best possible way you can leave is to invest deeply in strengthening you. You bring your locus of control inside yourself. You challenge your need for approval and external validation. You discover and accept and value the gifts that are uniquely yours. You commit to treating yourself with gentleness and compassion. You find a hobby that absorbs and fulfills you (especially a creative outlet) and pursue it with passion. You build your confidence by trying and succeeding (and failing!) at hard, scary things. You increase your self-awareness and determination to be brutally honest with yourself. You learn how to tune in to your mental/emotional states and regulate them. You figure out how to get your needs met through many different avenues, rather than trying to pull everything from that one source. You give up the fantasy and idealism, and you face the reality that this person cannot give you what you most crave - in fact, no one can, except for you. Being in relationship with a person who has attachment adaptations so diametrically opposed to yours can be pure hell. It can also be the most phenomenal growth opportunity, if you have the right resources to support you in understanding and coping with the ways that your styles trigger the deepest wounds inside each of you. The speed and intensity of the fire burning up old patterns can be very, very difficult to cope with. What it asks may be beyond your tolerance level. But if you dedicate yourself to doing the things I outlined above, you may be shocked when things shift significantly. Occasionally the other feels the freedom to step forward into the vacuum created when you fully relinquish relating from a place of need. Either way, go or stay, you have gained something that you can never lose - yourself.

column1: What does it feel like to have your sibling die?
column3: I lost my only sibling a little more than 2 1/2 years ago. My little brother (five years younger than me) died of an overdose when he was 27 years old. He was (and in some ways, still is) my best friend. Losing a sibling is a strange thing. I have friends who have lost parents, so they understand the grief of losing a loved one ... but it's still different. Losing a sibling is more "out of order" than losing a parent. There is a deep loneliness and isolation, both from having to deal with this horrific loss and, also, from not really having anyone who can relate to the experience (not that I would wish it on anyone--no one should have to deal with this). As awful as the thought of losing a parent is, deep down we all know that at some point--hopefully as far down the road as possible--our parents will pass on. Siblings are different, though. They are the only people who really understand everything about us and where we come from. They are supposed to be around for the long haul. Losing that is tragic and terrifying. Since Nick died, I try to live in the moment and to live life to the fullest. It's hard to stop those late night/panic-attack-inducing thoughts, though: What happens when I am all alone? What happens when I am the last person standing in my family? This is especially troubling to me because I am single. I always expected that it would be my brother and I, making our way through the world together. That is no longer in the cards. I still have a difficult time adjusting to that. It's mind-bending because I often find myself wanting to talk to him about this. He is the only person who would understand. But then I realize, all over again, that he's not here to talk to about it. Two and a half years after the fact, that realization seems to hit me over and over and over again. I often find myself thinking strange thoughts that then make me feel guilty. For example, my cousins lost a brother. There were originally four children in the family. Right after Nick died I found myself feeling jealous of them--as in, "Well, at least there are three of them in it together. I wish I had that." Similarly, about a week ago, my uncle had a heart attack. My dad told me that his two children (my cousins) were in the hospital together, getting one another through it. I was jealous because I know that when my parents pass, I won't have my brother to lean on. These are nonsensical thoughts that you hate yourself for having … but you also can't stop them from coming. The death of a sibling colors your world in some bizarre shades. My family dynamic has changed. My parents and I are like a car that's lost one wheel. We just don't run right without our fourth part. Even in happier moments, something is always missing. We are incomplete. I admire them more than I can say, though. For as awful as this is for me, I know it has to be worse for them. I am unspeakably proud of and in awe of them for continuing on. I can't imagine what they go through on a daily basis. No one should have to lose a child. Losing Nick didn't feel like I would have imagined losing a sibling would feel. I didn't cry a lot. What I mostly felt was empty and suffocated. As though I was suddenly walking around a world that was unfamiliar and gray and menacing. Death is a difficult thing to wrap your mind around--how can someone be here one moment and then gone the next? I learned that grief does not move in a straight line. I don't think that the full impact of the loss and Nick's total and complete "gone-ness" hit me until a year after he died, when all of the anniversaries started rolling around. To be honest, I didn't give myself time to think that first year: I kept myself busy in a psychotic sort of way and immersed myself in bad, distracting relationships. Anything to distract myself. I can definitely see how people drown themselves in alcohol, drugs, or pills to avoid reality when coping with the death of a loved one. I didn't do that, in large part because of the circumstances of Nick's death. But I can see why people would. That's another thing, too: the circumstances of his death. People who are lucky enough to have not had to deal with addiction don't understand that it's a disease. A therapist once explained it to me as being much like cancer: Addiction is progressive and, ultimately, fatal if not cured. That certainly was my family's experience. Nick fought and fought and fought--NO ONE wanted to beat the addiction more than he did. It was horrible to watch such a sweet, kind-hearted, intelligent, talented, creative, hilarious, loving person fight and fight and fight against a losing battle. If there is any solace in his death, it is the fact that at least he is out of pain and doesn't have to fight this horribly evil disease that dictated his life and robbed him of so many things he should have had--most of all, peace of mind. Another thing I didn't understand before losing my brother is that "broken heart" is a LITERAL term, rather than a figurative one. For well over a year (and still in certain moments), the pain of losing Nick is so intense that it feels as though someone took a bat to my heart and smashed it over and over again. It obviously hurts emotionally--but to the extent that it feels physical at times. Everything is different now. As many others have mentioned, it affected a lot of my friendships and social interactions in general. It's getting better as time goes on, but I do feel somehow separate from everyone else. It can be difficult to interact with others at times. For a while, it feels like you have a blinking neon sign on your forehead, like you are defined by the death of your sibling. Not a moment goes by when you're not thinking about that loss. Particularly during that first year, it's as though you're defined by it. My brother is still a big part of my daily life. I talk to him all the time. Sometimes it feels like he is there, other times it doesn't. I've learned that love is the one thing that is truly eternal--I love him just as much now that he's gone as I did when he was alive. As others here have mentioned, I live my own life differently: I want to make him proud, and it sometimes feels as if I'm living for both of us. I don't think that I will ever recover from the loss, and while I know that life is unfair, I can't help but feel like my family got a horribly short end of the stick. However, I also know that if I had the ability to choose the brother I have versus some sort of "alterna-brother" who would have lived a longer life, I would still choose Nick every time. I would rather have him as my brother for 27 years than any other brother for a longer period of time. Those of you here who have lost a sibling, you have my deepest and most sincere empathy and condolences. For those of you who still have your siblings, try your hardest to appreciate them--even during the difficult times. They understand and love you in a way that no one else will ever be able to. Though I loved my brother immensely, I'm not sure that I appreciated him as much as I should have until it was too late. But I suppose that's life. In retrospect, the ability to take someone for granted is sort of a beautiful thing. EDIT: I just want to thank every person who took the time to share their experience on this page. As some others have also said, I have never once posted an answer to anything on this site (or any others like it, for that matter), but this question happened to pop up in the Quora digest in my email, and it hit too close to home to not speak up. It's sort of funny because I think I've said more and been more honest here about the experience of losing my brother than I ever have to anyone in "real life." Losing a sibling is an extremely difficult experience that (thankfully) not everyone can relate to--particularly for those of us in the younger set. As many here have mentioned, the death of a sibling is often difficult/tricky to talk about, and something that you have to wade through alone. Reading everyone's posts here has--for the first times since my brother died--offered me the feeling of a bit of solidarity. I didn't actually realize how much I needed that until right now. For as much as all of our experiences are unique, I think I've literally read something in every last one of these posts that's made me nod my head and think, "Me too!" … and in some cases, these are things that I've never been able to articulate on my own. There's a lot of strength and (sometimes painful) honesty on this page, and I just want to thank everyone, both for sharing and for "listening." Okay, kumbaya moment over ...

column3: I recently saw Taemin come back… And before that; the rest of SHINee, most of EXO, all of BtoB and Pentagon's hyung line. I also have a bunch of other faves enlisted right now - like Onewe's Yonghoon and Kanghyun. Astro's MJ, Monsta X's Shownu and Minhyuk and Victon's Seungwoo. These enlistments affected me differently. 1. MJ etc. Astro was the first group I got into and the one I know the best, but I didn't even flinch when MJ enlisted. MJ will survive a zombie apocalypse. I would say that goes for most of the idols I've mentioned. I don't worry - I just wait while I focus on everyone else. But a few felt very different.2. Baekhyun and Sungjae I missed them a lot. I rarely worried about them, but the groups felt different without them. Being into EXO and BtoB was a lot less fun because they're important mood-makers. So I counted the days until their return. I got really frustrated when I heard that Baekhyun might be going through a rough time due to people wanting to see him shower. But I heard that he was offered a private shower to fix the situation, so I didn't stay angry for too long. Sungjae unexpectedly showed up in my feed a few times because he got to perform as a member of the military band. That was really great. But as I said, I mostly just missed them. I spent some time watching old content when missing them became hard. But that was it. 3. Hui and Yonghoon I'm in love with their voices and I had a minor freakout before their enlistments because I felt like I would loose the sound of their groups as well. It turned out to be untrue in case of Hui. Pentagon was still amazing and I began noticing other members more without Hui there. I'm grateful for that - and even more grateful to have him back (although he's not with the group yet). I can't even imagine how a comeback without Yonghoon's gonna be like. But hopefully, I'll get into the other members more. I'm just slightly pessimistic about it. Yonghoon is such a vital part of their sound and as their main composer, I don't think they'll sound like Onewe without him. I listen to their music when I miss them. Time went fast with Hui. I also didn't worry too much because I knew he'd be enlisted as a social service worker. 4. Minhyuk This one was a bit rough. I'd been so excited about Taemin returning that I didn't even notice that Minhyuk was about to go - until I saw the shaved head selfie. I think, it's the shock of having to get used to this news a little too fast that has me rattled. I'm not really worried about him. But he's another mood-maker so I'll probably end up missing him when watching Monsta X content.5. Taemin I hated it. Even before he enlisted, I felt dread. Really, I was a twisted bundle of nerves and I didn't know why. I got emotional when I watched any reminder of him - even IG pictures of his cat. When the news about him not doing well as an active duty soldier broke, I mostly just took my emotional reaction as me having a hunch or something. I really thought, he'd be safe in the military band. I don't cry easily, but I had to remind myself to breathe a lot around the time the news broke. I'm still angry that the military wasn't able to protect him and that he wasn't offered some privacy while showering like Baekhyun. I also hated that the other soldiers treated him like this. I just… I still get angry just thinking about it. But I calmed down a lot after Minho reassured the fandom that Taemin was home and they took care of him after he was moved to social services. I never really got emotional after that. But a part of me was desperate to see him again - to see him smile and be Taemin. I shrieked when seeing his first live update. He looked happy and healthy - like he'd been eating and sleeping well.So, to sum up:Time goes faster than you think.It becomes easier when you focus on other members or other groups (or other interests).When you miss them, watch old content. There're always a few social media accounts dedicated to count down the days until your fave returns. Most of them will warm your heart greatly.Remember that others have done this before. BTS members will most likely be the most famous Korean men to enlist in this decade, but the military and the government must have learned from the Taemin situation as well as a lot of other situations that blew up and prepared to step in and help faster without getting accused of special treatment.Your faves will get a chance to reflect on them themselves. This is great because they've been way too busy since before debut to really do that. But they won't change. They will mature - just like they would anyway. Just like they're already doing. But as far as I can see, they won't let go of their playfulness unless they want to. All my faves are still hilarious and entertaining.When they return, they'll feel awkward and nervous the first few times they talk to fans again. And it will be adorable. Another upside is that the immature fans who mostly sound like haters will have matured as well - or disappeared entirely. You can look forward to that.BTW, don't worry about them loosing popularity. The real fans won't forget…

column1: If you grew up dissociating to cope with trauma, how did that play out in your adult life? (not referring to very severe cases of DID, just dissociative issues).
column3: I didn’t lose all connection to my emotions, I’ve always been sensitive to feelings, but it feels like I didn’t develop emotional connection to the more ‘normal’ social aspects of life, and a sense of completeness or matching between my life out in the world and my inner-self. Taking action and making choices doesn’t come easily for me, it’s always an effort to focus and not feel discouraged. My life’s ‘structure’ is fragile, easily broken or ghostly in places, and in other places, I embody a rigid discipline to maintain my grasp on security. Then there is my sacred, free time, where I repair the damages done to my self-connection. It’s like being forever separated from a sense of belonging, invisibly isolated, with the surreal anxiety that others might notice my alienness and have a ‘bad reaction’ - so I hide who I am. That feels like rejection. But it also feels safe. Being a ‘person’ in the world gives people identity, love, meaning to hardships, a full life. But it also seems to come at the cost of your freedom of mind and spirit.. A lot of my ‘self repair’ is on the physical level of emotions, my body and energy levels. If I don’t do this, or get time alone, I get very tired, have no energy, become numb and more disconnected.. emotions can feel physically painful and I can get more neurotic. Going numb isn’t a relief, because I can still feel the stress reactions, if not more so. My therapy has been focused on how to connect to my life more, have stronger emotional boundaries so I’m not triggered by others so much, to have more ‘emotional agency’ and use up less energy in my reactions/defenses, especially ones that happen deep within myself on an unconscious level.
column9: Poppy, your explanation here is so vivid, and I relate to it so much. As in, profoundly. I like how you write about learning to have stronger emotional boundaries so you are less triggered by others and so that you use less energy in your defenses. I am constantly triggered by others even when they don’t mean to be triggering and don’t know that they are triggering me. I am just a raw nerve, and I need copious amounts of alone time and dissociation to recover. So my therapy focus now is on understanding the triggers and challenging them. But I really like how you frame it here—that it also needs to be about strengthening our boundaries—our own inner resources—so that the impact of the triggers is dulled. That is a very useful reframing for me. Thank you so much for writing this!

column1: Will I ever get over the loss of my dog?
column3: I lost a dog to cancer last February. He was just like a son to me. He was my constant companion and best friend. He helped me through some of the roughest times of my life and he knew my emotions better than any person. Then, at seven years old, he got sick. He grew a malignant tumor that enveloped his entire abdomen. We tried to save his life, but as the surgeon put in the very last stitch to close him up, his heart stopped and he died. A bit of me died too and life will never be exactly the same. I thought I’d never overcome Sammy’s death. As a matter of fact I’m tearing up just writing this and thinking about him. Honestly, if you truly loved the dog, I don’t think you ever really totally get over their death. You learn to live with the void. Allow yourself to grieve. It’s totally natural. Don’t give a damn in the world about what other people might think. It is cliche, but time slowly eases the pain. You come to realize that death is an inescapable part of life. Remember the good times that you had together and that he/she had a good life. I had him cremated and I keep his ashes near my bedside. Although they may be physically gone, the memories and love you had for each other will always remain.** The author and Sam Adams on his last day.

column1: How does one recover from failure?
column3: Ankit did his engineering from a tier-3 college. Couldn't get a good job. He was passionate about the UPSC-CSE exam, decided to pursue it with dedication instead of running here and there for a below average placement. His general knowledge and IQ were above average. He was confident of selection. He cleared the prelims in his first attempt itself and surprised everyone by clearing mains also. His parents were too anxious, excited and hopeful until the results were out. He was rejected. He didn't lose hope and tried harder the next time, but couldn't even clear the prelims. He was shocked seeing the prelims papers, his focussed studies couldn't help while people with general awareness got hold of the paper with quite ease. In his third try, he couldn't clear the mains. It had been years of trying and failing now, he was still a burden on his lower middle class parents, and there was almost no hope for future. He went into deep depression. His mind kept thinking about just one thing 'career' in a never ending loop. He couldn't sleep at nights, stopped talking to friends and lost interest in everything. Seeing his condition, his mother took him to a great saint, staying a 100 kilometres away from their home. The place was beautiful, surrounded by forests, on the footsteps of hill. Ankit, otherwise disturbed felt quite better there. Finally the saint met them and Ankit's mother explained everything. He smiled and looked at Ankit. 'Son, are all your attempts exhausted?’ ‘No, I have three more attempts' he replied. 'And then there would be other similar papers for government jobs' 'Yes Guruji, there are many other papers as well, like SSC, PCS and many others' 'Then why are you sad? You haven't even lost all hopes of selections and you are giving up in between? You have assumed a certain failure in future without even trying? My son, you should be happy and excited that despite three failures you still have some chances left, also you must have learnt many essential lessons from your failures which books can't teach' Saint’s words touched Ankit like a magic pill. He went back and started preparing with a fresh zeal and enthusiasm. Next time, Ankit failed again, and slowly, he exhausted all the remaining three options as well. He couldn't be selected in any other reputed exam as well. His passion was over, there was no hope now, he would never be an IAS officer in this life, he went into depression once again. In agony and frustration, he went to that saint again. He greeted the saint and said 'Guruji, you asked me to keep trying, but all attempts are exhausted now. What should I do with my life? My dreams have shattered' Guruji smiled and said 'That’s great son' He looked at Guruji in surprise and anger. ‘Since all scope is over, a chapter of your life has ended with this, and you passed in it with flying colours' continued the saint. ‘But I failed' said Ankit in a firm tone. ‘But you succeeded in giving your best till there was any hope left, this is the best a human can do for his/her life' said the saint. ‘But what now?’ said anxious Ankit. ‘Now what? Turn the next chapter, see what you can do best, create new goals. I don't think you have any time to waste on regretting? Also why cry for something which doesn't have any relevance in your life now?’ said Guruji with all the calmness one could have. ‘But Guruji it was my dream?’ cried Ankit. ‘But it was not your life son, you still have a big life to live, a long journey to cover. You wanted to get out at a beautiful station, but it is gone now, don't jump out of the moving train in regret and waste your life, keep going with the flow and look out of the window with hope, you will definitely find something more exciting, sooner or later.’ Guruji's words brought peace to Ankit, and he went back relieved and motivated to pursue new goals. Finally he wasted his Parent's some more money and did an MBA from a relatively better college. This time he got a good job, and the stats of his life improved remarkably. He could fulfill some of his most beautiful dreams now, like getting a car, taking parents to Goa via flight, decorating his home etc. He went to Guruji once again, but only to thank him.Till you have hope you don't fail, after you lose all hope, you can't fail and a new chapter of life unveils itself. You fail in life only when you stop trying in fear of failure.

column1: How do you heal a broken heart?
column3: If We were in 2015 right now, I would definitely be like “ I Wish I was a little girl again, Because skinned knees are easier to fix than a broken heart” I can still remember the day at my college when we had our OOPs exam (yeah engineering :p). My friend recently broke up with her Bf and when she told me her story, I got emotional too and we both Left the exam unattended. ( though the situation was sad at that point of time, now it feels silly. Still lucky enough as we didn't have to face that paper, I bet it would have made us cry even more) But today, the case is not the same. I have grown up to become a better as well as a stronger person too :) I will share how me as well as my friends dealt with our broken hearts :Start taking care of yourself. Go out to the nearest restaurant and treat yourself. Eat lots and lots of icecreams/chocolates of your choice and pani puris too ( my mouth literally watered when I typed pani puri). Think Food=Bae.Bae=Food. Forver and always.Now That we have consumed so many calories, it's time to hit the gym. Play hard, Run fast.Drain out all your negative energy on the Physical activities. This will not only tire your body but also your mind and won't let any hurtful thoughts resonate your mind.Shop a lot. Oh shopping is so satisfying. Buy yourself a good pair of jeans, shirt, googles, shoes, belt, purses , antique items etc. Devote all your energy to Groom yourself.Listen to music that is soothing to the ears. I personally love Bryan Adams,James Blunt, Train etc, my favorite being Travie McCoy's Billionaire. In hindi, I love Lucky Ali songs, Euphoria, Bombay Vikings. Evergreen they are!Read a lot. Gain knowledge and try to learn about a new topic every day. Read good books, avoid love stories for some time, instead go for thrillers,Fiction, science, history. I really loved R. L Stine Fear Street series. Quite interesting and engaging as well.Cry yourself out. Let those tears wet your pillow at night. Yes! you read it correct! If anytime you feel Low, share /show your emotions ,never keep them Inside you or else it will eat you up. Always share what you are feeling to your closest friend/family member etc. Keeping yourself company will help you a lot.Meditate. Meditation will not only help you focus on good things around you, it will calm your mind as well as keep your body healthy too. Peace in, peace out.Spend time with your parents, your siblings ,friends and all those who love you and embrace their love :)Life's too short to just deal with our broken hearts. Always remember, it's not the end of the world. There's so much to see and learn out there. So always focus on good things. Live it, Laugh it out and travel as much as Possible!
