column1: How much time off should I approve for an employee mourning the loss of a child?
column3: PJ - I don’t know if you are the owner of the company, or part of corporate management, if you have few employees or many (therefore, there are others who can pitch in to relieve the grieving employee’s workload), or if the business culture is one of concern for employees’ welfare or only for the bottom line. Other than what the law mandates, you clearly have a choice as to how much support you will offer your employee moving forward. The gracious answer would be as much as the person needs. I have unfortunately stalled in the final draft of a book about death in the workplace. That said, I thought it might help if I cut/pasted some of the book below. It also might help your other employees as well. No one, no matter how trained, can comfort an individual who is experiencing fresh grief. · Accept that you can only support them – which means listening · Approach the person from a “not-knowing” perspective, rather than “knowing” based upon your own experience or your awareness of another’s experience. Just don’t bail. People spend most of their lives focused on how they can find happiness, experience pleasure and minimize discomfort. Therefore, it is not surprising that they don’t like to be around grieving individuals. We would all like the bereaved to get on with their lives. Therefore, it’s quite common for us to be supportive of a friend or coworker in the first few weeks, and then disappear when most needed. Stop doing what makes you feel comfortable if you want to make a difference. Grieving is isolating and a lonely struggle. Remember, it will happen to you. If the bereaved don’t want to talk or join you for lunch, keep asking in the 12 months post loss. In asking, you are showing your support and concern. Communicating with employees during difficult times. We tend to shy away from what causes discomfort · Being willing to feel uncomfortable while talking to a bereaved employee may be the deciding factor in your employee’s ultimate recovery. If they can count on spending 10-15 minutes with you to talk about their loved one, and you listen without expecting the conversation expecting a result is a luxury in business. If it is obvious that there isn’t much to say today – let the person know there is always tomorrow · When we aren’t willing to be uncomfortable, we miss being valuable. · When we turn away from being present for another who needs to be heard, we pass up an opportunity to emotionally mature. The negative aspect to the “voice of authority” Authoritarian managers generally: · aren’t comfortable with appearing vulnerable · confuse being vulnerable with being weak · feel that a stiff upper lip solves most everything · create more staff tension/stress · and don’t have the strongest team How to express yourself effectively · Volume, tone and pitch are important, so go slow, low and steady. · Vary your speech pace to keep the people’s attention. · Pause at times so people can comprehend what you are saying. · Drop any bravado or cheerleading. · Be honest: “This is tough, but we will get through it together.” · Be part of the group, as well a leader, and share how the death affects you, if it does. Body language · Body language, facial expressions and eye movement reveal your feelings. (Go back to your childhood to recall how much information was transferred with just a glance from a parent.) · People give more credibility to body language than the words being spoken. · We continually search and often unconsciously pick up on another person’s body language for meaning, but we rarely think about what we are telegraphing with our own body language. Listening The most valuable communication skill we have is the ability to listen. We don’t come out of the womb a listener. It is a learned skill, and it takes practice. It is in our nature to: · talk, not listen · judge/size up the person/situation before he or she is finished speaking · attempt to offer advice so we can “fix them” · take control of the conversation so it ends sooner rather than later The next time you are required to listen, ask yourself: · are you “pretending” to listen? (The speaker will intuitively know.) · are you judging the speaker from your cultural background rather than theirs? Or from your “station” in life or from theirs? Have the wisdom to: · expect to be uncomfortable · create rapport by being honest, yet brief, about your feelings · pause and allow silence after speaker finishes, so you can gather your thoughts · notice the speaker’s word pacing and voice volume · ask questions to better understand the speaker · not offer advice/problem-solve; you can’t comfort a grieving person but you can support them by listening · admit you don’t have the answers, but reinforce your willingness to listen when the employee feels a need to share · and acknowledge to employees that everyone occasionally just needs a day off. Don’t assume a person is resistant because they aren’t talking. It is important for them to find their way without your advice. There are many reasons why an employee may not speak up. · They are naturally introverted. · They fear what they say won’t remain confidential. · They are on emotional overload. · They weren’t raised in an environment where they were safe to express themselves. · They need time to consider what you have said and will get back to you. · Their cultural norms dictate a different way of responding than your own. If you offer them options, understand they might make a choice you wouldn’t. · They have never experiences a death, first hand, and are practically and emotionally lost. This isn’t a teaching moment for you, it is a learning moment for them. Therefore, your role is to simply support them and allow them to feel safe. · Remember, it is up to you to meet the person where they are, so ask them what they need. Open door vs. closed door: preventing trouble down the road Employees want to feel they are important to management. They will stick by and trust management that is available and genuinely listens, even if they know their leadership doesn’t always agree with them. “Holding space” for another The goal in “holding space” is for the other to feel safe speaking about their circumstance. It is essential for the listener to mentally walk alongside the other. · Create a container to hold for another · Give a person space to share their thoughts and emotions without judgment. · Understand that if the employee shows emotion, you have not upset them. They are already upset and you have given them permission to show the emotion they feel. Also, when listening, allow the other person to make their own choices and don’t try to “fix,” problem solve or give advice. · A newly bereaved employee is not emotionally able to absorb “good advice,” even if it is appropriate. · Fixing people takes away the other person’s power and can shame them or imply that if they were stronger, smarter, etc., they would know what you know. Assisting with a Bereaved’s Return to Work Determine paid and unpaid leave · This is uncharted territory for an employee. They won’t know how much time they need. Some employees will function better than others. No two people handle loss in the same way. · If the deceased is an immediate family member, the employee may need more than the allotted few days to plan and attend the funeral, especially if it is out of state. Employees often fear they will lose their job if they take extended leave. It is common for workers to worry about losing their jobs if they appear unreliable or ask management for added leave. Make all employees aware of your extended leave policy, so they know they will be treated in the same manner as the employee currently on extended leave. Offer a flexible conversion plan. Workers convert their vacation time and personal time to cash, used to offset income for coworkers to take time off to deal with crises. Develop a plan to share responsibility · Arrange workloads so the employee doesn’t return to a backlog of work and an overflowing inbox. · When it seems appropriate, calendar a time to talk to the employee about his or her taking back more responsibility. · Urge the employee to be proactive and provide feedback if he or she isn’t doing well, rather than leaving it to employees to comment to management When people return to work too soon, they may be: · moody, disorganized, disoriented, and tardy · unable to concentrate/read; have memory issues · emotionally and physical exhausted from insomnia · depressed and lack patience · quick to anger · prone to panic attacks · and even taking work to an extreme One ineffective way to cope with loss is to become a compulsive workaholic. Some employees may welcome returning to work right away, as it can serve as a valuable distraction. Regardless of when the employee comes back to work, respect his/her need for privacy. If an employee leaves a meeting or the office or doesn’t accept an invitation, don’t expect him or her to explain. The grieving employee and addiction/substance abuse Whatever unhealthy “strategy” a person may have used pre-loss to cope with stress will likely increase and can become destructive. It’s not uncommon for an employee to abuse alcohol, recreational/prescription drugs after the loss of a loved one. · An individual may drink alone initially. With time their abuse leads them to drop old friendships and seek people who also abuse alcohol and drugs. · Drinking and doing drugs mask a person’s emotions—but don’t eliminate the emotional chaos that is underneath. The longer they bury their emotions the more likely alcohol or drug addiction will occur. Understand they are struggling for a new identity. If they are no longer a child’s father, a wife’s husband, who are they? Finding out takes time. · Provide counseling support so they can come to realize that, with help and time, they can take control of their life—rather than letting a behavior or a substance do that. Work as relief from grief or an addiction? For some, work can provide the bereaved with a needed respite. The office or job site may be the only place where a bereaved employee knows who they are (since they are no longer someone’s husband/wife, father/mother, brother/sister, son/daughter). For others, working excessively long hours is an unhealthy crutch that prevents the employee from accepting their loss and rebuilding a life without the deceased. Signs a grieving employee isn’t doing well Heads up when there is: · continuing absenteeism · significant change in behavior, such as socially withdrawing · significant change in performance · and a lack of personal hygiene Provide employee with contact info for professional help. Make sure to pre-qualify any provider. Fresh grief is not a time for psychotherapy. It is a time for professional grief support and a counselor who: · understands the grief process · provides the employee with tools for coping · and can reinforce/remind the employee of the resources they already possess to survive the loss. What to say to a returning employee after a bereavement leave Here are a few things you can say to an employee coming back from bereavement leave to break the ice: · “It’s nice to have you back.” · “You were missed.” · “We all will try to have your back.” · “I am sorry you have to go through this.” · “I am available if you want to talk.” · “I am willing to help in any way I can. Is there anything I can do right now?” · “Would it be OK if I call again next week?” · “I know there is nothing I can say to make things better, but let’s talk regularly, ok? I would really like to do that. And don’t hesitate to call me.” (Follow through when you are offering this much.) Be brief · Don’t get involved in talking about your losses. Remember no two family dynamics are the same i.e, cultural/ethnic/religious background is likely to be different. Don’t suggest they concentrate on the “good times, and don’t chatter nervously about office news Later, ask: · How has the past week been for you? · Is there something we could do to help? Note: the returning employee may not show signs of grief or talk about the loss for several months. Fellow employees may assume all is going well and then be surprised when the employee starts to struggle. Don’t assume the behavior signals a “new” problem but rather offer them stress management counseling when grief counseling is called for. Reach out to an employee if you share his/her experience If you’ve suffered a similar loss, invite the newly bereaved out for lunch. It is usually helpful to share time with someone who has had a similar experience. If an employee’s child has died, have someone take the bereaved aside and acknowledge that fellow employees are going to continue to talk about their children, and that everyone will understand if the bereaved excuses him- or herself during those times without explanation. Providing Support to the Deceased’s Family The best way to honor your employee’s family is with your presence—immediately after the death and before/during and after the service. Here are just a few of the things you can do: · Call and touch base with the family members. · Help with landscaping, house repair, child care. · Invite the family to office picnics for the first couple of years after the death. · If you were close to the decreased, occasionally include the children of the bereaved when taking your children to the movie/dinner · Help the family to develop the legacy of their loved one. Put together a book ofinspirational and funny stories about the deceasedwhat you learned from the deceased and what you will miss the mostinclude previous company picnic and holiday party photos, etc.· If the deceased was Hispanic, participate in a Family of Dead celebration on November 2nd. Also, send flowers to the family to take to the celebration, help care for gravel, and share stories about the person. · If the deceased had a history of emotional problems, the death could be a result of a suicide. However, the family may announce that it was a natural death or accident. A good rule of thumb is to never assume suicide wasn’t the cause, and to be thoughtful about how you express yourself to the bereaved family. · If an employee’s child has died, don’t try to convince them to come to a picnic full of playing children. Lastly, remember to send a card on the anniversary of the employee’s death The sad truth: spending time with a bereaved family is the last thing we “tend” to do. · Typically, fellow employees stop asking how the bereaved are doing, because they don’t want to hear the answer. · If a spouse has died, it is common for workplace friends to cease inviting the surviving spouse to social events. Connecting a grieving employee to outside resources While EAP providers and professional counselors are helpful, grief support groups offer the grieving employee a setting where 1) they don’t have to pretend they are fine, and 2) they aren’t alone in thinking they are going crazy. Most hospices offer grief support groups and one-on-one counseling; and many hospitals, churches, and community-based agencies offer grief support groups. Supporting the children of the deceased Those supporting the children should be aware of their second loss: the parents or remaining parent will not be the same parent the child knew before the death of their parent. Therefore, they are facing not just one, but two losses. When supporting a grieving child, the goal is to help the child feel safe. This is difficult when: · “normal” family patterns are interrupted, · schedules aren’t met, · expectations regarding behavior/rules become slack, · the children feel abandoned by the deceased, as well as by the surviving parent, who is barely able to function. Children say they are fine when they aren’t. There are many reasons why a child won’t express themselves, but the primary reason is their desire to keep the surviving parent stable. When a remaining parent becomes emotional, the child senses the remaining parent is incapable of keeping them safe. If you are around the child and the opportunity presents itself, introduce yourself and talk to the child about his or her deceased parent. Tell them a story and/or relate what was special about the deceased family member. Find out what IS stable in the child’s environment Is your employee divorced? If so, do they have custody of children. Who will step in and stabilize the home environment so the children feel they have some control over their lives? Are there aunts/uncles/grandparents/in-laws geographically close by? If so, are they available to pick up the slack and help with the children? Is the oldest child taking having to assume too much responsibility since the family death? This is common. The child may seem to be doing well, but in reality, he or she are being forced to grow up too soon too fast and can be anxious, resentful, jealous and afraid. Therefore, the child is desperate to connect to a dependable adult who doesn’t expect something of them. if you’re functioning in a major support role: · Learn about how the child’s developmental stage will relate to what he/she can and can’t understand about death. · Don’t slack regarding rules and expectations: a death in the family does not mean it is OK for the child to act irresponsibly. Maintaining expectations allows the child to connect to something that remains constant—before and after the death of their parent. · Don’t expect the child to speak up at school about their loss; children hate to be different. · Don’t be surprised when they are teased by other kids (this is a bizarre but normal response—kids don’t know how to act around another child after they are told a parent or sibling has died). · Expect the child to blame themselves—often beyond what is reasonable; have headaches, stomach problems, etc.; not want to go to school; and swing from acting as they did prior to the death to withdrawing completely; shifting from being pleasant to becoming angry and aggressive What the parent and you need to know. In general: · Tell children the truth—their grandparent, parent or sibling died and he/she is not coming back. · If the family is religious, find out what the child has been told about an afterlife. If you do talk to the child about an afterlife, explain that there are many religious faiths and many of their school friends’ families will not necessarily believe as their family does. · Don’t use euphemisms, such as your father is “asleep.” Children are very literal and can become afraid to go to sleep. · Answer their questions but don’t offer more than they have asked for. · Know that it’s a myth that the child is doing well if he/she doesn’t talk about a deceased parent. Kara’s (a grief support agency in Palo Altos, CA which focuses on a child’s grief) research showed that the opposite is true. Parents incorrectly concluded that if their children weren’t talking about the death, they were doing well; and if they were speaking up, they weren’t doing well.
column9: When my son was murdered 12 years ago, I was working as a high school teacher. I only took one week off and came back to all my regular workload. I needed to be around the people that I felt close to and who understood that I had just experienced a terrible loss. It also gave me a reason to get out of bed and leave my house everyday. I also mentioned at one point that regardless of how bad I felt, the students were so funny I couldn't help but laugh at them. They were therapeutic. It wasn't until I lost my son that I became aware of other people who had also lost children. Most people don't talk a lot about it unless it happens to someone else. There is a silent “club” of parents who have lost children that you don't realize exists until you become a member.

column1: Is there a psychological reason why a person would lose their rich fantasy world, especially if that was their best coping strategy for anxiety/depression and now they can't cope?
column3: A ‘rich’ fantasy world is not usually a ‘best coping strategy’ for anxiety/depression, both of which tend to limit the imagination, while they are in operation. Anxiety (over) and depression (chronic/clinical), tend to seek relief through ‘Pleasure Principle’ outlets, which do not include ‘richness’ as a rule, but ‘repetition’. While it is very true that we can lose our capacities for creative imagining, that creativity was not the ‘coping strategy’ you describe, but rather the positive results of being previously able to cope.

column1: What's an efficient way to overcome procrastination?
column3: I think it helps to understand the cause of your procrastination. I’ve given a lot of thought to this (probably when I should have been doing other things!) and have come up with 9 causes of procrastination (there are surely more, but these 9 should cover most of the cases). Each of these causes requires its own solution or set of solutions. . Nine Causes of Procrastination: Fuzzy GoalsSketchy PlansOverwhelmUnexpected ComplicationsInterruptionsBoredomAnxietyImpatienceExhaustion Let’s look at each of these, and consider what thoughts they provoke (so you can diagnose them), and lay out some rough strategies for dealing with them: 1. Fuzzy goals When you have fuzzy goals, you are likely to think things like this: “Why am I doing this project?”“What should the final product look like?”“How will people actually benefit from this?”“Should I work on this now, or is something else more important?” And here are some strategies for dealing with fuzzy goals: Ask yourself why you're doing the project. When you do this, you will come up with some purpose.Then ask yourself why you’re pursuing that purpose. And keep doing that until your project is set within the context of your whole life.After all this, it might turn out you don’t have a good reason to work on this project, and that you need to work on another project.Work out the relative importance of all your projects, so you can make sure you’re working on your most important project. 2. Sketchy Plans When you have sketchy plans, you are likely to think things like this: “I have to keep my place in my head too much as I work”“I’m not sure this plan will work”“I’m a bit concerned that it’s more complicated than it looks” And here are some strategies for dealing with sketchy plans: Break your project down further to expose hidden detail.Consider whether there are any conflicts within the project, or between this project and other projects.If you find conflicts, resolve them and create a plan that works. 3. Overwhelm When you’re suffering from overwhelm, you’re likely to think thoughts like this: “I can’t get it all done”“I need to work, but I can’t stop thinking about [some unrelated issue]”“I don’t know if I should work on X or Y or Z” And here is a sure-fire strategy for dealing with overwhelm: Follow the clear mind procedure outlined here: Jim Stone's answer to What can I learn/know right now in 10 minutes that will be useful for the rest of my life? 4. Unexpected Complications When you encounter unexpected complications, you’re likely to think things like: “Why can’t things just work as planned?” And here are some strategies for dealing with unexpected complications: Work in shorter sprints – you should work on only 1-2 week projects that get you feedback regularly. There is less chance of running into unexpected complications when you break projects into smaller deliverable modules.Get the complication out of your head and into your plan. That way you’ll see it sooner, and be able to resolve complication before you start working. 5. Interruptions When you encounter interruptions, you’re likely to think things like: “Why can’t I stay on task?” And here are some strategies for dealing with interruptions. Try to have periods in your work day where you can’t be interrupted, and train the people you work with to respect this.When you get interrupted, write down exactly where you are in your plan, and the next step, so you can get back to work right away when the interruption passes. 6. Boredom When you’re bored, you’re likely to think things like: “This work is repetitive and beneath me.” When you’re bored, you can try: Playing games within the game (setting mini-goals for yourself, and such)Looking for opportunities to outsource the work, if possible.Organizing your job/business so you can do more challenging projects. 7. Anxiety When you have anxiety about your work, you’re likely to think thoughts like: “I don’t know if I’m doing this right”“I don’t know how to do this.” And when you’re feeling anxiety, you can do the following: Take some time to plan the project in more detail and identify the areas you don’t understand well enoughGet expert advice if needed. 8. Impatience When you’re impatient, you ‘re likely to think thoughts like: “Are We There Yet?”“Why does this have to take so long?”“The finish line seems so far away” And here are some strategies for dealing with impatience: Break your work into 1-2 week modules so you don’t ever find yourself 3 months into a project with 3 months to go before getting meaningful feedback.Zoom your focus in on TODAY’s work and make up a story about why today’s work is important. 9. Exhaustion. When you’re exhausted, you’re likely to think thoughts like: “I can’t think”“I can’t keep my eyes open”“I need a break” And here are some strategies for dealing with exhaustion. Set up work-rest rhythms at hourly, daily, weekly, and bigger scales.Take care to get enough sleep, exercise, sunshine and nutrition to keep your energy high.Take a break! For an expanded discussion, see 12 Things That Take You Out of Flow.
column9: I found that my main source of procrastination was fear. I simply feared failure, and rejection. I was stuck on doing preliminary and preparatory work forever, causing anxiety. I think the root of anxiety is mostly fear, thus I do not fully agree with "Take some time to plan the project in more detail and identify the areas you don’t understand well enough" because we already know that and are stuck on always projecting and preparing. I had to face it and start actually working. My new motto is "stop trying to do it and do it".

column1: What is a less severe form of narcissism?
column3: There are two basic forms that narcissism can take: Narcissistic Personality Disorder (serious) and Narcissistic traits (much less serious). When I talk about narcissism or say that someone is a Narcissist, I am almost always using those terms as shorthand for Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD). What are narcissistic traits? These are ways of thinking and behaving that are similar to those that are also seen in people who have a Narcissistic Personality Disorder. However, if you only have narcissistic traits, you do not qualify for a personality disorder diagnosis. Some common narcissistic traits are:Self-centeredness.Being very concerned with status.Lacking emotional empathy.Being controlling.Not taking responsibility for your own mistakes.Blaming other people when things go wrong.Devaluing other people.Needing constant validation.Dominating conversations.Being uninterested in other people except when it serves your needs.Narcissistic traits exist on a spectrum. Some people have lots of narcissistic traits, while other people have very few. What is a Personality Disorder? In brief, a personality disorder is a maladaptive and rather rigid set of beliefs, behaviors, deficits, and coping strategies that are believed to have their start in early childhood, before the age of five, when the personality is forming. In order to qualify for being a personality disorder, this pattern of being in the world must be pervasive, relatively stable across time, occur in almost all situations, and be used with most people. in addition, from an Object Relations (OR) theoretical point of view, all people who qualify for a personality disorder must lack Whole Object Relations (WOR) and Object Constancy (OC). What are whole object relations? This is the ability to see yourself and other people in a realistic, integrated, and stable way that simultaneously includes both good and bad qualities. Without WOR, you can only see yourself and other people as all-good or all-bad with nothing in between. What is object constancy? This is the ability to stay emotionally connected to someone you like while you are hurt, frustrated, angry, disappointed, or physically distant from them. Without OC, during a fight, love can quickly turn to hatred and your loved one can seem like your enemy. The lack of OC is one of the main reasons that people abuse people they claim to love. During a fight, they “forget” the love and lose touch with all the positive past history. What is Narcissistic Personality Disorder? This is a personality disorder that is characterized by narcissistic traits, deficits, and coping mechanisms. In essence, people with NPD have all the issues of a personality disorder and they express these issues in distinctly narcissistic ways. Punchline: Many people have narcissistic traits who do not qualify for a full diagnosis of Narcissistic Personality Disorder. Narcissistic traits are a less severe form of narcissism. Having a few narcissistic traits is the mildest form of narcissism. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com
column9: This is a very balanced view of what narcissism actually is. A lot of different articles about narcissism but this gives the clearest explanation of all. Thank you.

column1: Mental health practicioners, why do you label hypersensitive (emotionally vulnerable) people as narcissists?
column3: Let’s start with the idea of “Emotionally Vulnerable.” All humans are emotionally vulnerable. That is a given. We all can be hurt by other people’s reactions to us—even when the other people do not mean to hurt our feelings. There are only a handful of ways that humans typically react when they have been hurt:Attack: We attack the person who is hurting us.Flee: We leave and go to a safer place.Pretend: We stay, but pretend that nothing happened and we are not hurt.Assume: We create theories to explain why this person hurt us—He hates me, I am unlovable, She is a mean person, etc.Defences: After being hurt a few times, we find ways to protect the emotionally vulnerable parts of ourselves—we keep our distance from other people, we attack them first, we learn to be hyper vigilant, we make fun of ourselves before the other person does, we hide our real self and wear a “public mask,” and so on.So why do psychotherapists diagnose? There is a dark side to many of our coping mechanisms. Many of the strategies that humans develop to protect themselves from emotional pain lead to new problems. Instead of making people happier, people end up angry, disappointed, anxious, and depressed. In addition, some of these strategies make it very hard to have satisfying relationships with other people.People Need Help Understanding the Connection between their Coping Strategies and their Current ProblemsJust taking the brief list above: Attack: Attacking people leads to fights. Even if we win the fight, we still lose because the other person no longer feels safe with us. We also end up outraged and angry a lot—not the most pleasant feelings. The more we use “attack” as a coping mechanism, the less likely we are to be able to form stable and satisfying intimate relationships. Flee: If we mainly leave to protect our feelings from getting hurt, we never learn to negotiate differences. We also spend a lot of time scared of other people. This too makes it hard to sustain satisfying relationships. Pretend: The more we pretend and hide our real feelings when we are with other people, the less real we feel. It is also hard for other people to get to know us. This method also prevents us from learning how to communicate our real feelings and desires to other people. We become stuck playing the narrow role that we have created. Our hurt does not go away just because we are pretending that nothing bad is happening. Assume: Many of our assumptions about why the other person caused us emotional pain are wrong or overly broad. For example: This person may not have loved you, but that does not mean you are unlovable. Defences: “Defenses” can be thought of as “The Fences.” Like all fences, they (1) Do not discriminate very well between potential friends and enemies, and (2) They keep us in and limit our experiences.We Diagnose Patterns, not PeopleMost people never see the pattern—how this coping strategy leads to that problem. Or, how certain coping strategies tend to occur together. Our coping mechanisms that were initially invented by us to protect us, are now automatic, habitual, and mostly done without awareness. They have become “Ego Syntonic.” Ego Syntonic: We misidentify our ingrained ways of protecting our emotional vulnerability as simply “us,” instead of something that we are choosing to do. When something is ego syntonic, we do not think we have a choice about whether we do it or not, so we do not try to improve it. Ego-Alien: One of our jobs as psychotherapists is to recognize these patterns of coping strategies, name them (the diagnosis), and start to bring them into the person’s awareness. Our goal is to give people back the ability to choose the best course of action, instead of just automaically reacting. From this point of view, Narcissistic Personality Disorder is just another name for a pattern of coping strategies to protect one’s vulnerabilities. People with NPD are mostly focused on protecting and stabilizing their shaky self-esteem. When people with Narcissistic adaptations come for therapy, it is important for the therapist to recognize that they are using typically Narcissistic coping strategies—idealization, grandiosity, and devaluation—in order to choose the best interventions. Narcissistic disorders (or patterns) require psychotherapists to alter how they talk with the client. Narcissists are easily offended because one of their emotional coping strategies is to be hyper vigilant about noticing things that they interpret as disagreement or disrespect. The therapist needs to find ways to move the therapy work forward without overly distressing the client. Punchline: Diagnoses, whether of Narcissistic Personality Disorder or some other pattern of outmoded and destructive coping strategies, are given to clients to help them get the appropriate treatment—not to insult or stigmatize them. Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com

column1: How are you feeling about the recent changes in Quora?
column3: (These are not artisan breads. They are industrial and are trimmed by bread designers to seem artisan and even given appropriate names. It depends on you to look more closely.) There is one development that I don't like at all. There are now entire profiles that are created almost entirely with AI/artificial intelligence , that is, with chat GTP. There are therapists, coaches and others who create profiles to advertise their products and write mass responses. These answers are completely sterile. Meanwhile, they post a picture and color a part of the written black or write a personal sentence to it, so that it somehow seems authentic. But it isn't. Chat GTP is always the same. I will not use it directly now to show it to you. So there is the question asked (let's say: how to cope with depression?) and the chat always answers stereotypically. First he says something like: Depression is a mental disorder that many people have. (after that some more gobbledygook , which is completely general). Then something like: There are various coping strategies for depression (another little paragraph of general gobbledygook). Then comes: The ways to cope with depression are as follows. Then: numbered bullet points like: 1. you can go to a therapist (general gobbledygook about therapists) 2. one can take medication (two to three generalities about medication). And. so . Further. About 5-6 stiuch points. Now follows a small concluding paragraph: Overall, it can be said that there are some ways to deal with depression. However, it should be noted that this could be different for each depressed person That's kind of what a response looks like. And these people write them en masse and post them as comments as well. I can't understand that this is considered good and most quorans don't even notice it. column1: How many people in the UK don’t have healthcare?
column3: I was an assistant at a weekend residential workshop in the UK, which was being facilitated by an American couple who had been flown over for the event. Everyone arrived on the Friday, but one of our facilitators fell ill, and had a bad night. At the team meeting next morning, the remaining facilitator bravely undertook to do the two-pronged job single handed. Yes, he was that good - full on running a large participative workshop for about forty punters, with no partner. I was asked to look after the invalid, so that our remaining facilitator didn't have to worry unduly on that score. I sat with the invalid, listened to what was wrong, and called our national health service helpline for advice. Having asked a few questions, they despatched an ambulance, which was going to take a while because we were in a very rural location. I went back down to the group room, and the facilitator asked me for an update. I told him not to worry, an ambulance was on its way, and his wife would be whisked in for rehydration and a battery of tests. Sadly, I had not thought about the implications of that news under the health system he was used to, and the poor guy went white, every emotion passed across his face, and he looked unsteady on his feet. My fault! It took several people to convince him he was not going to be hit with a huge bill, lose his house, or anything else. His wife and I were at the hospital much of the day, the care was superb, and eventually we arrived back with a diagnosis, some coping strategies and enough medication to cover the rest of the trip. That is what we take for granted as our right as UK citizens, to the extent that we think it is wrong for treatment to be a bit slow at busy periods. Nobody expressed anything but pride that our National Health Service extended that courtesy to a visitor from another country who had a real need for it. If you really want to, you can buy private health care in the UK, but I personally have never felt the need. Edit, to save some comments: It seems that A&E is never chargeable in the UK NHS - a combination of ethics and practicality, I suspect. "Treatment in A&E departments and at GP surgeries remains free for all" . https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidance-on-overseas-visitors-hospital-charging-regulations/summary-of-changes-made-to-the-way-the-nhs-charges-overseas-visitors-for-nhs-hospital-care

column1: When a person gaslights a victim to deny perceivable reality, initiates a smear campaign, recruits third parties to fight her for him, and then refuses to talk to her once called out as a narcissist, does that confirm he's diagnosable NPD?
column3: The Short Answer: Lots of people besides those with NPD do all manner of nasty things in service of their aims. In the object relations diagnostic system that I use, people can have typically narcissistic traits (such as self-centeredness, a need to be right, etc.) and use some narcissistic coping strategies, (such as gaslighting , devaluing, triangulation, initiating a smear campaign) without qualifying for a diagnosis of Narcissistic Personality Disorder. So what else is necessary to qualify for a diagnosis of NPD? In addition to narcissistic traits and coping mechanisms, I need to see evidence that the person lacks:Whole Object RelationsThis is the capacity to see people (including themselves) in a stable, integrated, and realistic manner. This translates to the ability to simultaneously see both the things you like about a person and the things you dislike. If you lack whole object relations, you cannot see the big picture in a wholistic way. You either see people as all-good or all-bad. The NPD version of this involves dividing people into special vs. worthless. People with NPD may switch from idealizing someone as special, perfect, and flawless to devaluing the very same person as worthless, defective garbage when they are displeased. This leads to very unstable relationships.Object ConstancyThis is the ability to stay in touch with your good feelings about someone, while you are angry, disappointed, or frustrated by this person. If you do not have object constancy, during a fight this person that you claimed to love 10 minutes ago is now perceived as the enemy. This greatly increases the likelihood that you will act abusively towards this person while you are feeling hurt or enraged.Emotional EmpathyPeople with NPD lack emotional empathy for other people. They do not feel bad when they hurt you. They also cannot share in your joy, unless they can take credit for it in some way. They may have cognitive empathy. This involves the ability to figure out what someone else might be feeling. You can think of emotional empathy as an automatic felt response, whereas cognitive empathy only occurs when the person makes an effort. During a fight, when Narcissists lose whatever small bit of object constancy they might have, they are not likely to press “pause” and stop to consider how they are hurting the other person. Punchline: While a person’s actions may conform to your idea of how someone with Narcissistic Personality Disorder would act, that is not sufficient to determine if this person qualifies for the disgnosis. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com

column1: What is your personal way to get over shyness?
column3: I am a shy extrovert. Not only am I a shy extrovert, I am a shy extrovert who does a lot of public speaking. I don’t believe it’s possible to “get rid of your shyness forever.” Being shy is something I battle daily. I don’t act like people think a shy person acts. In fact, most people who know me would never know I’m shy. You have to know me very well indeed to recognize the shyness. But make no mistake: it’s there. I have learned coping strategies. I have made conscious choices not to let my shyness stop me. But it has never gone away, and possibly never will. I still feel it. I simply choose not to allow it to stop me from doing the things I want to do. I think a lot of shy people believe that they will start making the choices they want to make as soon as they can figure out how to make the shyness go away. That isn’t how it works, at least in my experience. Instead, it’s a lot like courage. Being courageous doesn’t mean making fear go away, it means doing the thing even though you’re afraid. Conquering shyness doesn’t mean making the shyness go away, it means choosing to interact with people even though you’re shy.⁸

column1: Can a person become a sociopath later in life?
column3: Not necessarily. If you don’t have the genetic predisposition, nor a history of conduct disorder, you likely won’t. My main diagnosis is Schizoid Personality Disorder. However, I would say that I do not suffer from that anymore. I have no issues with boundaries, no dissociation, I am not passive or docile, and don’t create elaborate and unrealistic fantasies in my head as much. This took several years to change. However, I was also assessed as having Antisocial features. The difference between Schizoid and Antisocial is Schizoid is very typically debilitating. ASPD itself is not. So, it’s possible to have someone who has the temperament of a sociopath, but developed coping strategies that mask it or push it more towards being subclinical. Once those coping strategies cease, they revert to their naturally irritable and calloused state. Personally, 3–4 years ago, I was a mess. Simping for women who had issues, being lead on, walked all over, sexually harassed, accused of pedophila and sexual predation by coworkers, losing my hair (right when I started valuing my attractiveness), being purposefully sleep deprived by my parents whilst working manual labour, poverty, and told by my mother that my shitty life was all my fault. I figured, “Hm, it seems what I’m doing isn’t working. My life was better when I was younger and actually expressed how I felt.”. So, with very little outside help, I worked on fixing that. I was naturally quite unempathetic and angry, but I just kind of hid that and tried to be nice; I knew that wasn’t going to last. So, I reverted back to what worked as a child, which was saying exactly how you felt, and being honest. I had a variety of coping habits that just weren’t working. Being too kind, too compassionate, too patient, putting up with too much bullshit, wanting people to like me, that I flipped a switch. I have no regrets. I would do it again. Anyway, no. You can’t, but you can pick up other destructive coping strategies, which you can treat later and revert back to what is more primitive and natural. I know I would never tolerate be used, degraded, and mistreated like that again. Being firm, straightforward, and an asshole when necessary has always worked better than being shy and weak.

column1: Does the character of Ranbir Kapoor (Ved) in movie Tamasha have symptoms of bipolar disorder?
column3: This movie is very close to my heart because perhaps I could relate to it in multiple ways. To answer your question, No, he's not suffering from any disorder, syndrome, or anything else that one would like to use labels for. What he's really suffering with is a confusion of self-identity. He spends his entire life pleasing people around him, curbing his own soul, his own needs in the process. When I say needs, it's not something that has to present itself in an overbearing way over others, but something that's subtle, especially, something that's shaped through of his own personal experiences. Ved as a kid is shown to be someone who takes interest in stories, fantasies. This does not mean he's a crackpot, but has his own interests as an individual. These interests are something that captivate most of his thoughts. There has been a lot of research done in this area but the one that comes first to my mind is the concept of Flow (psychology) It's a mental state which makes you the most happy / engaged without a sense of fleeting time, something that you won't do for money or fame, but just because it interests you so much so that you even forget what money or fame is. An example that comes to mind is of Einstein. He never set out to win a Nobel Prize but to understand why one can never exceed the speed of light. When Ved's needs are thwarted away by pressure to conform to a mold defined by his parents, he loses his identity. And it's really hard to curb feelings; they find their own unhealthy ways to manifest. In fact, some of the best materials I've read on psychology explains that behaviors are nothing but coping strategies. The experience one undergoes shapes your psyche subconsciously to build coping strategies. Playing Don was Ved's coping strategy to vent out his build up. Once his life hits bottom, he gets in touch with his feelings that were subdued deep within him, and that transforms him. All of his 'perceived disorders' go away because he no longer has to cope up with his own subdued feelings. He discovers the new "I" that is assertive about his needs and likes what it does, and that helps him find his truest happiness. And it has been truly shown that one cannot be happy in any relationship if the 'self' is unhappy, because in all relationships, 'self' is always present. A lot about self-identity, self-respect and self-love has been championed by Nathaniel Branden in his books.

column1: How did you get over your avoidant attachment style?
column3: As a person with an Avoidant attachment style I can tell you most of us won’t be that motivated to change our attachment style unlike other attachment styles i.e. anxious attachment and fearful Avoidant attachment style. This is because people with this attachment style don’t experience any subjective distress (subconscious distress is experienced by them) and they use coping strategies such as repression, denial and disassociation. So there is no incentive to change. Even though I am fully aware about attachment theory and have a lot of knowledge about it I still didn’t want to change it for a long time but now I am working towards changing it to secure attachment style. If a person wants to change their Avoidant attachment style some tips are-Gain as much knowledge about your attachment style if you have insight about your attachment style it is easier to identify when you engage in typical behaviours of your attachment style and try things differently for example if you use deactivating strategies with your partner try not using it in certain situations. Start with few incidents and then move up.Individualisation- this is an important process in the recovery of Avoidant attachment style and the reason for that is because Avoidant attachment style people have a fear of engulfment which means that they believe that if they get too close to someone they will lose themselves or their identity. So an individualisation is a process wherein a person needs to do self introspection and maybe stay away from people for sometime and find your identity and do self reflection. Maybe taking a solo trip would help.Somatic experiencing therapy- this can be beneficial for Avoidant attachment style people as it helps them connect with their bodies and link it to how triggers make them react. There is a book called Why can’t I change? By Dr Shirley Impellizzeri which is very good for healing any attachment style and change it to secure attachment. She herself had an Avoidant attachment style and has now changed it used somatic experiencing therapy.Cognitive behavioural therapy can also be helpful as people not only with Avoidant attachment style but also with other unhealthy attachment styles hold unhealthy core beliefs like they can’t trust people to meet their needs or the world is not a safe place etc. Identify the unhealthy core beliefs you have about yourself and try and replace it with realistic thought patterns it and find evidences contrary to the beliefs you hold.People with Avoidant attachment style can be uncomfortable with physical contact with people so you can start slow and maybe go for massages first to get comfortable with physical contact gradually.Recognise what caused you to generate your fear of intimacy mostly people with Avoidant attachment style associated intimacy with distress or suffering at some point in their life which could range from all the way upto infancy to anytime in adulthood. It might be difficult if you were very young to remember all the details that are now stored in your implicit memory (memory where all our subconscious beliefs and fears are stored which we may not be aware about now) but if you can recall events in a situation which caused you a fear of intimacy you can change the way you look at the situation and realise that past doesn’t equal to the present moment.Ask for help- this is very difficult for the person with Avoidant attachment style as they fear being dependent on others and don’t like relying on others. You need to realise that it’s ok to ask for help and it is not a weakness. Remember we as people are wired for interdependence and it’s ok to not be self sufficient as no one is completely.

column1: Can a person have both borderline personality disorder and schizotypical or schizoid personality disorder?
column3: Short Answer: No, you cannot have Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), Schizotypal Personality Disorder (STPD) and Schizoid Personality Disorder (SPD) at the same time. They are entirely separate disorders with very different characteristics. Schizotypal Disorder is a more severe type of disorder than either BPD or SPD. It can be thought of as existing in the gray area between the personality disorders and the psychotic disorders. It usually involves distinctly odd or eccentric behaviors, paranoid and superstitious beliefs, and may include transient psychoses. I am not going to include Schizotypal Disorder in my comparison of BPD and SPD because:Schizotypal belongs in a different category of disorders than BPD and SPD.I do not consider myself an expert on Schizotypal Personality Disorder.I have only seen a couple of people with that diagnosis in therapy during my over 40 years of practice.Let’s compare BPD and SPD: The following comparisons are broad generalities based on looking at groups of individuals with these diagnoses. This means that this will not necessarily apply to each and every person with BPD or SPD.Common SymptomsBPD—Severe abandonment fears, difficulty meeting adult responsibilities, starts many projects that they do not finish, feels like a child in an adult body, difficulty being alone, feelings of rage, panic, emptiness, helplessness, and hopelessness. Inability to function when stressed or feeling abandoned. SPD—Mistrust of other people. Fear of intimacy, difficulty connecting with other people, social anxiety, dissociates from their body and their life when stressed, retreats into a rich fantasy life, feelings of unreality, loss of meaning in life, and existential dread. Usually can continue to function and meet everyday responsibilities even when has to dissociate to do so.Main Solution to Life ProblemsBPD—Look for someone to love who is nurturing and will love you back. SPD—Become independent and maintain a safe distance from other people.Reaction When StressedBPD—Reach out to other people for help. SPD—Avoid other people.Primary Relationship NeedBPD—Unconditional Love. SPD—Interpersonal Safety.Main Interpersonal FearsBPD—Abandonment or Engulfment by the other person’s emotional needs. SPD—Losing one’s independence, being intruded upon, being treated as an object to be used.Main DefensesBPD—Clinging to destructive personal relationships to avoid old, underlying abandonment issues and negative emotions. Destructive coping strategies, such as: substance abuse, cutting and other self-harming behaviors, over spending, gambling, reckless sexual activity, picking fights, and constantly seeking reassurance that they are loved and lovable. Finding people who will take care of them. SPD—Keeping their physical and emotional distance from other people, retreating into fantasy, dissociating, finding ways to have enough contact with other people, so that they do not feel completely isolated, and becoming self-sufficient and financially independent so that they never have to depend on other people to take care of them.TreatmentBPD—Involves helping clients to learn to structure their lives, identify and work towards meaningful goals, teaching them methods of tolerating negative emotions and how to self-sooth, curbing impulsive destructive acting out, work on self-care issues, work on abandonment issues and childhood traumas. SPD—Teach negotiating skills, work on lack of basic trust, explore tendency to use distancing and isolating to solve interpersonal problems, work on teaching how to verbalize their interpersonal discomfort instead of dissociating or distancing, work on discriminating safe from unsafe people. Work on trauma and other issues related to their childhood abuse and neglect. Punchline: The reason we call two personality disorders by different names is that they are significantly different from each other. People with BPD and SPD have different issues, coping strategies, and need very different types of therapy. In the diagnostic system that I use, a client could not be diagnosed with both of these disorders. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com
column9: All you’ve done is written about how they’re different, not why they can’t coincide with one another. It seems perfectly plausible that a person could deal with symptoms of their SPD by indulging in the extreme habits formed by their BPD. Or that someone with BPD could exhibit SPD-related behaviours. Your comment also makes no mention of the covert symptoms of SPD, which can look very similar to those of BPD and other personality disorders. It also takes a very reductive look at BPD; like everything else this disorder is complex. It affects everybody differently. Small bullet points really aren’t enough to summarise the symptoms. Lastly, some form of study to back up such a claim would be very welcome. I will concede that SPD and BPD may not be common bedfellows but it’s pretty unscientific to dismiss the possibility completely.

column1: Why is disassociating from your emotions so dangerous?
column3: Good question. The state of dissociation as i understand it is a state of being disconnected from the self or one's own experiences, emotions included, and the danger to dissociation as i understand it from my limited perspective of having dissociation as a woman who has been terrorized and dissociated as a survival reflex… the danger to dissociation from your feelings is that you don't get to process trauma. Your dissociation prevents clear examinations of traumatic events, may lead to compartmentalizing or “showing a different face to appease people or situations where you were unable to behave naturally.” In extreme cases, you will develop trauma coping strategies such as the formation of a new personality or so your friends will believe, you dissociated your feelings and compartmentalize them, making your behavior appear erratic and potentially forming trauma response to normal overwhelming situations. Dissociation from your feelings is dangerous because all people have uncomfortable, unpretty, really intense, unpleasant, even maladaptive emotions. If you dissociated, you lose control of your processing. You become a blank doll, waiting for the trauma to end. Unresolved feelings may lead to fights with friends, not knowing who to trust, who to be to be most pleasing, you may even… cultivate coldness. Not everybody is emotional tho. Some people will dissociate from emotions that are too difficult to deal with and come out with level heads. To kitties like me, dissociation from stress and intense negativity is a survival issue. You dissociated because your true feelings were unacceptable to your caregiver and peers. And some people don't care about me, and want to harm me, in those cases, operating on automatic is dangerous because you need the connection to your feelings to sense threats. Not everybody is equally able to deal with the intense emotional pain of traumatic stress and anxiety. And to survive we have to step outside ourselves. Yet it is dangerous because you're not going to feel natural warning signs. In extreme cases your separated feelings may become disabled and you will appear robotic to others. Unresolved feelings often cause health problems. Thanks so much. Xoxo
column9: What you are describing is alexithymia, the inability for being able to differentiate, identify, and express emotion. Expression of emotions are modeled by parents and encouraged expression in healthy families. In alexithymic families, parents don’t express their emotions, and don’t encourage and even discourage their children’s verbal expression of emotion. Based on neuroimaging findings I believe the alexithymic mental trait is also an example of dissociation. Alexithymic families can show love and sensitivity without verbally expressing emotions; however, many alexithymic families tend not to address the social motivational needs for showing love, validation, patience with early child learning, show insensitivity to their children’s needs for well being and control over outcomes. And due to these insensitivities to the social emotional motivational needs of their children, many discipline in the same manner as their parents (that is, by physical punishment, verbal degradation, verbal devaluation, social rejection, etc). When children are raised in an environment with such adversity, they experience stress, which is trapped in the body, without words and trusting relationships to facilitate their expression. And when said child develops into adulthood, these deficits are expressed in the manner described in your post. And I should add, various degrees of alexithymia are present in our culture. Therapists note, that the alexithymic trait serves to interfere in therapeutic attempts, in processing previous traumatic experiences and relationship interactions in one’s life. So in therapy, it is really important to help an awareness individual to differentiate, identify, and express one’s emotions before and during trauma processing.

column1: If a person is diagnosed young, at what age does a person "grow" out of needing medicine for ADD/ADHD? If ever?
column3: There's a small percentage of children that will grow out of ADHD. Usually they become less hyperactive but it becomes internalized. People can develop a certain number of coping strategies that the symptoms become less bothersome. I would suggest to you to keep both views in mind: he may or may not grow out of it. His hyperactivity may decrease but he may not completely grow out of ADHD. The most important thing is for him to get control of the symptoms with a combination of medication, therapy and developing coping strategies. A simple to-do list can make a world of difference for someone with ADHD. It will be difficult at first to get into any sort of routine but with persistence it might just turn into a regular part of his day. If he does have hyperactivity I would also suggest to keep him active. On my worst focusing days hyperactivity can at least keep me moving, which means exercise and other active tasks. I'm an adult and have severe ADHD. I don't have boundless childhood hyperactivity but I have enough hyperactivity for it to be impairing and rather damaging to personal relationships. I'll have to be on this medication for life if I want to have a life. I didn't take any medication today and I have forgotten to write that very simple to-do list so I haven't really done anything today. I did clean my room because it is a part of a routine. Some of us can't just stop taking our medication and expect to handle our problems ourselves. I have two days off and that's long enough to work on my problems on my own. However I was not diagnosed as a child. It could go either way for your son. The best thing to do is work on him developing skills and overcoming his symptoms to the degree they become less burdensome. Just don't wait for him to outgrow ADHD with little intervention. ADHD can be a lifelong disorder and I don't believe it can be completely cured. You can reduce your symptoms to lose a diagnosis but the brain is still ADHD. Or perhaps I can't even comprehend what a life without ADHD would be like.

column1: If a person keeps losing their jobs due to mental illness and depression, what should they do if working is the only means they have to support themselves?
column3: I am not sure if the question relates to you or you are merely generalising. If you are talking about yourself, I salute you for the zeal you exhibit in wanting to beat the odds presented by mental illness including depression. I am amazed by your eagerness to sail on in work. If I was an employer myself, I would give you all the support there is to ensure you can still contribute within the limitations of your challenges and not leave you as victim of mental illness. Sometimes it helps to discuss these issues 1 : 1 because the only person who understands affliction of mental health is one who suffers from it. But I will give you my advice which I am not necessarily imposing on you. There are lots of questions I would have asked but I do not feel that is going to help things at this point. Let me start by giving these examples. A ball that is deflated cannot bounce. A tyre that is flat will not go far. Do not be offended. I am not calling you any of this. What I am saying is that, despite your good intention to sail on against the presenting odds, I do not feel you are helping the problem. Addressing the mental health challenges, to the point of knowing all your coping strategies as well as relapse indicators, is very important. Relapse indicators can be referred to as “warning signs” pointing to the fact that things are getting worse than better. I am not in the least nullifying all that you know about your coping strategies, because I believe through all the challenges presented by your mental health problems, which you have overcome time and time again, you have, to a very large extend become an expert with a good understanding of your problems. But even experts sometimes do not see what sits in their blind - spot. And that includes you and me. There is no point in rushing back to work before you are able to effectively manage your symptoms. It becomes more detrimental to your existing mental health challenges if you repeatedly have to deal with the frustration of losing jobs. That reinforces rather than challenge the mental illness. You also need to look for jobs with employers that embrace mental health as a reality of modern life and have systems in place to provide support when warranted. Do not just look at the need to earn a living. It is difficult for me to underplay this, considering the financial implications involved, but remember that prioritising your wellness is crucial when making all decisions about the challenges of mental illness. What is the point rushing to work when unresolved challenges will send you back home? I know your heart sinks to think of surrendering to mental challenges by not working but that is not the point. You are faced with a delicate gamble between a job and looking after yourself, and for me personally, the latter has to take precedence. I am sorry to hear your predicament. I send you my support. I am willing to answer any of your other questions. Be strong. You are a lot more special in any work environment because you are dealing with more than just work. For that, you deserve credit and more support than staff who seek help just about work. Best of luck. Sharing on Quora is caring. Don’t forget to follow or upvote or share. Your feedback is giving back

column1: Do autism symptoms come and go?
column3: I would like to use a different word than “ symptom”. I really think we need to distance ourselves from a medical/ pathological association with autism. It is doing our community more harm than good because most people associate autism as a defect or sickness instead understanding it from the perspective of someone who just has different neurological needs. People think it needs to be “cured” instead of understanding it is a state of being. It shifts the burden to the autistic person to change instead of society to change and accommodate our needs. The better words to describe a person’s neurology, be that NT or ND, is that their neurology expresses itself through a person in different traits characteristic of how that neurological system was formed and other factors unique to each individual. Autistic symptoms don’t just come and go as in, it is there one moment and gone the next. These traits are hard wired into the mind and body. But, YES traits do evolve or change with stages of development, coping strategies learned, with age, fatigue, physical/ emotional/ environmental circumstances, other influences such as co-morbid disorders that coexist and so on. We do change neurologically as we mature. As we learn how to cope with our growing minds and bodies, we develop needed skills and behaviors. Traits we had as young children may stay the same, evolve to more effective behaviors. Some, like myself learned to “mask” or hind our traits to cope and “fit into” societies expected ways to behave “normally”. I’ve learned from personal experience that even after a lifetime of suppression and denial of my traits, the fundamental autistic neurology has not changed.. If we had a tendency to stim we will still stim in some manner. If we rely on repetitive behaviors they are still there in some form.. and so on.. It may be possible to suppress a trait to extinction.. I don’t know… But I’m amazed at the person I’m becoming as I let my traits express themselves again. It as if you are letting the real system relax and more subtle traits are able to find expression too. Another important consideration that affects the daily changes in autistic traits is stress and fatigue.. The more stress there is neurologically, the more sensitive the person is to other stressful situations. It all about keeping the mind and body in balance or homeostasis. Some autistic people react differently to stress than others. Some can physically/ psychologically manage that stress more efficiently than others. I believe AGE is the reason I finally discovered my ASD. It becomes harder to cognitively over power our instinctual side as we get older. You get tired of “faking it” and eventually you just don’t have the will, desire, or energy to maintain the facade called masking. I think there is an element of realizing that it is an unnecessary expenditure of energy and ultimately it is harmful to suppress your natural tendencies. LOL- in short: You get tired of the B.S.! This is one reason I strongly encourage and support all autistic people to be themselves and not try to be or even act neurotypical unless it is by choice and done without sacrificing personal dignity, self-respect, self-worth etc. We cannot be our best if we are denying our real selves the recognition and development we need to be our best. It not only hurts us as individuals, but casts a grave misunderstanding that autistic people should conform to NT standards even at such a terrible personal cost. We ALL lose ( NT +ND) when we are not true to ourselves and become our best.

column1: What motivates extremely angry people? When someone lashes out and escalates arguments quickly, what is their motivation?
column3: The triad of anger: It's quite possible that a perpetually angry person suffers from a personality disorder, but diagnosis doesn't explain motivation. From the trenches, anger is usually generated by some mix of three different things: pain, power or fear. Pain-Anger (Confused Anger) What it is: Pain anger is mechanical. Sometimes it's simple physical pain that's making the person short tempered. Sensitivity can also push a person to the edge, for example, someone may have extremely sensitive hearing; what the rest of us perceive as normal sends their system into high alert. Another person may suffer from a chemical imbalance, or a brain tumor - prior to my mother's diagnosis with glial cell cancer she suffered bouts of uncontrollable rage which disappeared once the tumor was removed. What it looks like: If the angry is coming from pain, there will usually be an element of disorganization detectable in the rage. It's subtle, but you can sometimes see that even they are confused by their reaction. They don't seem to be enjoying the anger, and when it's over they often seem puzzled at everyone else's reaction. It is like they're striking out from a painful grey fog. How to respond: The most rational and compassionate way to respond to pain anger is to try and remove the painful stimuli. They are often unable to articulate what the actual problem is. You can sometimes reduce their level of arousal by subtly dimming lights (for example, adjusting the window shades), turning down background noise (a television or radio) or speaking softly. Sometimes anything you do triggers more rage, if this is the case position yourself so you are not facing them directly and very slowly put more distance between you and them. Like a dog that has been hit by a car, people in pain/confusion anger can be quite dangerous. When (if) the rage subsides consider getting them medical treatment. Power (Red Anger) What it is: When I used to get angry my motivation was power. I was a potent, traumatized child and I learned to channel my psychic pain into anger and heat. My ability to create fear in others made me feel strong. It felt good and special. Anger energized me, it allowed me to control my frequently uncontrollable environment The more I used anger the more it replaced other coping strategies. What it looks like: If the angry person is suffering from power, there will usually be a sense of smugness to their anger. They tend to bully or rant. They will seek out eye contact and use it to intimidate. They may be angry on "behalf" of an ideal or another person. On some level they are enjoying themselves. They may seem "evil" or "cruel." While it is possible for a power anger person to amplify so intensely that they lose control, more often there is a strategic end game they have in mind. This is "red" hot anger. How to respond: This is the only type of anger that can be successfully met with anger. Like putting out an oil well fire with explosives, power anger can often be interrupted by a strong unexpected response. That said, it is important that your response be more strategic, controlled and powerful than the person you are facing. In the presence of power-anger you might experience your own ego or anger being triggered. This can show up in a personal desire to fight back, "win", or even destroy them. Power-anger is anticipating this response and will push to make you lose control if engage in this way. Unless you are confident and calm, it is wise to engage back up (someone with authority, such as a supervisor or law enforcement). On the other hand, attempts to reason will often cause a power-angry person to press their attack. Placating should only be done to buy time to come up with a plan for escape or assistance. Fear (White Anger) What it is: Fear-anger is developed to stop something or push it away. Fear anger can range from protectiveness (fear that you will hurt my valuables) to defensiveness (afraid that you will hurt me). It can have the manipulative elements of power-anger (I'm afraid you will reveal me so I will attack you to create a diversion) or it can be blended with physical/pain problems, as when a psychotic or schizophrenic perceives their life to be in danger. What it looks like: Fear-angry people watch, but usually don't stare. Their bodies are tense. From the outside, their anger usually seems understandable but out of proportion. They will tend to withdraw into passive-aggressiveness if possible, but if they feel the threat is acute they can also attack with sudden intensity. If this sort of anger turns to violence, the sufferer is often in a "white out" and unreachable until the emotion passes. How to respond: People who are in white anger want you to disengage. At first they may charge to hasten your retreat, but if you continue back off they will let you go. State your intention to retreat and then back off as rapidly as possible. When the situation is calm, you might want to reassess your behaviour with the goal of being more strategic and less threatening before you re-engage.
