column1: Has someone ever just disappeared from your life without warning? How did you cope with it?
column3: Yes, one of my childhood besties ghosted me. We were thick as thieves as little girls, always over at each other’s houses, sleepovers, family dinners with each other’s families, always together on the playground at school. When we got a little older, she realized that she was pretty and blonde and could be popular if she wanted to be. I, on the other hand, was little, mousy, quiet and shy, dark-haired, and the brainy girl. You don’t become popular hanging around with the likes of me. So one day, she just started pretending that I didn’t exist. She wouldn’t look at me, she wouldn’t speak to me, she wouldn’t respond if I spoke to her, she wouldn’t talk to me on the telephone, she wouldn’t stand anywhere near me if she could avoid me. She never spoke to me again after that day, despite the fact that we were in school together for another 8 years. It was a uniquely painful way to lose a friendship. She was right in front of me the whole time and never acknowledged me again. I was even friends with several of the girls in whose circle she was firmly entrenched, but whenever I had reason to speak to any of them, she acted like I wasn’t there. We went our separate ways after High School, and even though I’ve now re-connected with that whole crowd on social media, she has not acknowledged any friend request I’ve sent her. She still won’t speak to me, even 20+ years after any of this mattered to anyone. I don’t know what her motivation was in ghosting me. Maybe she wanted to be popular. Maybe she never really liked me at all. The whole experience made me wary of trusting people who say they are my friends and worried that I’m not really as good a person as I try to be. I can count on two fingers the number of people I’ve let get that close to me since 9-year-old me got ghosted by her best friend in the world. I coped by withdrawing from people and refusing to make myself vulnerable to anyone. I wouldn’t recommend it as a coping strategy unless you are willing to accept the loneliness that is the price of safety.
column9: Erin, I had several good friends in elementary school who totally dropped me once we hit middle school. They became cheerleaders and the popular girls, and I, being the only Asian girl, and less pretty and less out-going, became an outcast. It really hurt. And, like you, to this day, I have a hard time trusting people enough to become close to them. Thanks for sharing your experience, - belle

column1: Did James Potter truly change?
column3: Warning: Ctrl + f “answer finished” to get to the bottom of the answer, without having to read it. This may be an unpopular opinion. It may be unpopular with James fans. It may be unpopular with Snape fans. Warning continued: If you don’t like my opinion that James’ change isn’t believable to me; or you don’t like my opinion that James being raised in a healthy loving home environment isn’t believable to me either. If you don’t like my opinion that James wasn’t truly arrogant, and instead suffered from insecurity. Use the Ctrl+ f function to search up “answer finished” so you can avoid having to see even bits and pieces of this answer by accident. However, if you’re in a good state of mind, and you think you can handle reading an alternative view point without being too emotionally affected by it. I hope you find the answer interesting, even if you disagree. Answer started What evidence is there that he didn’t change? Great question Letasha! A better question would be: Was James’ change believable? What was James? James was either a bully/abuser, a sadist, or a maladaptive person. Or he can be a mix of two or three of those. Choose your poison. Personally, my poison is James was a maladaptive person. James a bully/abuser? Person A is a bully/abuser because person A hurts person B to get person B to do what they want. Now, I know that sometimes getting someone to do what you want is necessary, like say if there are innocent lives involved, and you need an enemy to give up their location. In exceptions like that a person isn’t a bully/abuser. But, a bully/abuser wants someone to do what they want, even when it’s detrimental to that someone’s well-being. For example, a boyfriend might not allow his girlfriend to speak to her male friends. If James is a bully/abuser, he’s bad at it, because he never tells Snape what to do. He never tells Snape to stop hanging out with Lily. He just expects Snape to read his mind. ================================================================= Was James a maladaptive person? A maladaptive person is someone who deals with emotional upset in maladaptive ways. When James gets annoyed he hexes people. That’s why Lily said “hexing people just because they ANNOY you.” Where did people get the idea that he hexed random people for fun? When James got angry enough he may have stripped Snape to cope with his hurt feelings, over Lily’s harsh rejection. ================================================================= Where was James’ therapy - Was James a maladaptive person, continued? Maladaptive people in real life don’t just lose their maladaptive coping strategies with maturity. They need therapy. If maturity was all that James needed, then there would be no maladaptive adults. Because they would just lose their maladaptive coping strategies with maturity. Yet, in real life, we do have maladaptive adults, who are much older and much more mentally mature than James was. If James matured is your proof, it’s not good enough. Maladaptive people don’t magically lose their maladaptive coping strategies just because they WANT to change. They actually have to do things to bring that change about. And in many cases they need help to bring those changes about. James’ can’t just snap his fingers and say “I want to change for Lily!” and then magically rewire all of his coping strategies just like that, coping strategies that are hardwired into his brain. Maladaptive people go to therapy, because they can’t magic a change in themselves, and it may be affecting their life in a bad way. I.e James not being able to respond in healthy ways to annoyance and anger, makes Lily not want to date him. WHERE WAS JAMES’ THERAPY? ================================================================= Was James a non-sexual sadist? We don’t know. James never says he’s hurting Snape, because it gives him pleasure. He doesn’t say “because it makes me feel good.” He says “it’s because he exists.” ================================================================= The author’s word But, if the author told you, that James really did change. Would you believe her? Yes and no. No, if she tells me: “James changed.” on her twitter. Yes, if she writes an article on how James went from point A to point B. Who helped him learn healthier coping strategies? How did he learn to get through moments of anger and hurt without lashing out in a violent way? Or without making Snape the scapegoat for when Lily has hurt his feelings? Without hexing people just because they’re slightly critical of him? If she writes an article like that, I’d believe the change. If Rowling told you that James sexually desired Snape, would you take her word for it? Or would you demand proof? It’s the same situation here. ================================================================= Headcanon that could explain James’ change. Mindfulness meditation, over a short period of time, physically changes the brain. James’ ends up with generalized anxiety, because he keeps thinking about Lily being killed for being muggleborn, He thinks about Remus accidentally killing an innocent person and being executed. These thoughts are becoming a lot more prominent with the war taking better footing, and the fact that Remus came close to accidentally killing Snape. James copes with it by making calming draughts for himself. Calming draughts have the same effect on the brain that fourty minutes of meditation does. Over a short period of time, physical changes happen in James’ brain, because he takes a calming drought everyday. A calming draught that has the same effect on the brain as a fourty minute session of meditation does.MRI scans show that after an eight-week course of mindfulness practice, the brain’s “fight or flight” center, the amygdala, appears to shrink. This primal region of the brain, associated with fear and emotion, is involved in the initiation of the body’s response to stress.^ If James doesn’t feel his negative emotions as strongly, he’d be able to cope with them better.As the amygdala shrinks, the pre-frontal cortex – associated with higher order brain functions such as awareness, concentration and decision-making – becomes thicker.^ James would be better able to think through the consequences of his decisions, and act accordingly. He knows the consequence will be, Lily won’t like him, if he keeps up his behaviour. 20 Scientific Reasons to Start Meditating TodayIncreases volume in areas related to emotion regulation, positive emotions & self-controlEmotional regulation is the ability to stop negative thoughts and feelings from driving our behaviour. A calming draught that works the same as meditation, having positive physical changes on James’ brain, over a short period of time; is the only headcanon I can think of that would make James’ change believable. ================================================================= Did James’ change vs do I believe it? Yes he did, but I don’t believe it. If the author said that “James was sexually attracted to Snape, but he hated that about himself, and decided to hurt Snape for it.” Then it’s true. Because author’s story, author’s character, author’s rules. But, it’s not believable. The question we need to be asking is NOT “Did James change?” The question we need to be asking is “Was James’ change believable?” If you take off your “James lover glasses” it’s not believable. In fact it’s not believable to me that James was raised in a loving home environment. ================================================================= What was James’ home life like? - According to the author it was loving and healthy. That’s true, because, author’s story and author’s rules. But imho, it’s not believable. As far as I am concerned, James has insecurity issues, he can end up losing it over even the slightest bit of criticism. Look at how he handles Lily telling him: I’m surprised your broomstick can get off the ground with that fat head on it. You make me SICK.’ …. ‘Reading between the lines, I’d say she thinks you’re a bit conceited, mate,’ said Sirius. ‘Right,’ said James, who looked furious now, ‘right –’ This may be an indicator of a child raised in a home where their parents only love them when they’re perfect. Then abuse them emotionally and maybe physically when the child doesn’t reach their standards. When anyone criticizes them, it can trigger the shame and trauma from the abuse of their parents. They may deal with that triggered shame and trauma by lashing out in emotionally/physically hurtful ways. There is a pro-con thing to me not taking Rowling’s word for it. The con is that I don’t believe Rowling when she says James changed. The pro is, I don’t believe Rowling when she says James was raised in an entirely healthy and loving home. Which is why although I find James’ actions inexcusable, I find it understandable, based on my own analysis of the text. Because I believe James was raised in a home that looks loving on the surface, but is poisonous deep down. The parent loves the child, as long as they’re great, until the child isn’t great. Where other Snape fans see a sadistic bully. I see someone who didn’t have healthy coping strategies to any shame triggered over criticism. Who was arrogant on the outside, but insecure on the inside. To conclude: There is a difference between what is truthful and what is believable. What is truthful is anything the author says. What is believable depends on you. Answer finished Edit: I forgot to add this bit. Some people might think “James had the air of looking well cared for” is proof against my belief that his home life isn’t as loving as Joanne paints it to be. I don’t think it contradicts my belief. Abusive parents who care about their reputation, and see their child(ren) as part of their reputation, aren’t going to send their child(ren) out looking neglected. Because it will make themselves as parents look bad. I wonder if Joanne only knows James’ parents on a surface level? It is possible to create a character, and only know them on a surface level, because you haven’t explored the character you’ve created enough. What would she find if she investigated into James’ parents?
column9: You may be right about James being maladaptive, but the idea that he hexes people for fun comes from this: ‘She started going out with him in seventh year,’ said Lupin. ‘Once James had deflated his head a bit,’ said Sirius. ‘And stopped hexing people just for the fun of it,’ said Lupin. Nor do I see any reason to think his parents were abusive. It’s been shown that children whose parents praise them all the time can become very insecure because they never know whether they have truly done well or not. Also he may have been teased a lot because although his family were Purebloods they weren’t in the Sacred 28, and his father had a very silly name and made his fortune by selling hair-oil, which makes James only lower middle to middle middle class. Lucius probably looked at him and then smirked.

column1: Do psychotic people know they are psychotic? Or would thinking they themselves are psychotic, make them sane?
column3: Yes and no! It depends on the individual and the sum of their experiences. Some people may develop insight into their mental state and others may not. Some people may develop limited insight into their mental state and lose it shortly afterwards. Would you agree that when a person develops insight into their symptoms (i.e. psychotic symptoms) they are considered to be more sane than insane! However, most people that have been diagnosed with a psychotic illness tend to have insight into some areas of their thinking and behaviours and lack insight in other areas. Moreover, some people with psychotic disorders are able to learn to identify the early warning signs of psychotic symptoms. The client works with the therapist to implement coping strategies that can reduce the intensity and frequency of the symptoms. However, the fact that a person has been diagnosed with a psychotic disorder means that they are not in complete control. There will always be times when they suffer from florid psychotic symptoms like hallucinations and delusions. When a person is floridly psychotic, they lose whatever insight they may have gained into their mental health condition. They are literally controlled by and persecuted by their symptoms. Imagine having to contend with or cope with ongoing, underlying psychotic ideation during your waking hours! The psychotic symptoms are directly related to the individual’s rigid belief system and level of anxiety. Some people that experience a psychotic episode are 100% certain that their experiences are real. They cannot challenge their belief system or even contemplate an alternative explanation for the phenomena that they are experiencing.Example of Psychotic Episode Experienced by a Person Diagnosed with Paranoid Schizophrenia A former client of mind told me about a psychotic episode that he had when he went to the local shopping centre. He told me that he believed that he was being followed by multiple individuals whose intent was to harm him. He tried everything he could to avoid the people that were following him, including reckless driving, parking his car in a car park and running across a highway (almost getting run over by a car) and jumping on the back of a tram while it was moving (he fell off it and injuring himself). He felt that his life was being threatened and that if he did not act the way that he did, he would have been hurt by his pursuers. During the heat of the moment, he believed (100%) that his life was at risk. However, after a few days, his psychotic episode resolved to an extent (reduced intensity and frequency of psychotic symptoms) and he was able to reflect on his behaviour and on some of the events that transpired during his outing. He told me that upon reflection, he felt embarrassed and scared that he had no insight into what was happening and he feared another psychotic episode.People Diagnosed with a Psychotic Illness Have Unique and Individual Experiences I think that it is important to note that not everyone diagnosed with schizophrenia or a psychotic illness experience florid psychotic episodes. Many people experience ongoing, underlying psychotic ideation. Many people tend to always feel on edge, anxious, fearful, persecuted and other distressing emotions. Moreover, they don’t know why they are feeling the way they do. In fact, if you challenge the psychotic beliefs of a person with paranoid schizophrenia you will not have any success. In fact, the person may start to feel agitated and resent you. I have always respected people that suffer from severe mental illness. In particular, I admire their strength and resilience. I know that I couldn’t cope with the ongoing stress and anxiety that people with severe mental illness have to cope with on a daily basis. In fact, I’m quite certain that being on edge all the time and unsure about what to believe would significantly impair my functioning and ability to lead my life as per normal.
column9: The psychotic symptoms are directly related to the individual’s rigid belief system and level of anxiety this comment is very interesting. Rigid belief system? I feel like there is something here and that if that rigid belief system can be solved, would psychosis relieve itself? Along with calming the anxiety.

column1: Can individuals with borderline personality disorder change their ways of thinking, or will they always exhibit unstable and abusive behavior towards others, including outside of romantic relationships?
column3: I’m a quiet BPD woman and now 43 years old. My behaviour in some ways has changed quite drastically since my 20s, but some of that is going to be down to general maturity. I will probably always have intense emotional swings, some issues with jealousy, and abandonment. When I’m pushed significantly by anything that could mean abandonment (a partner splitting up with me), however, I can go from 0 to 100 rather quickly - not enough time to enforce my coping strategies. I generally have very good control of my external behaviour now, and better control of my internal emotional world, though it’s still bumpy as hell. Unfortunately,I noticed a transition from expressing outwards to more inwards, which means I have ended up struggling with a lot of physical neglect issues for the latter part of my life. I do not consider myself abusive. When I was in my 20s and 30s, I was quite guilt trippy, however, and its only with hindsight that I can see this was manipulative and not driven from conscious intention. The manipulation was driven by the need to avoid perceived abandonment, rather than a personal benefit such as money, sex, etc. or to hurt the other. With that said, my behaviour became verbally abusive in my last relationship but that was with an NPD who took pleasure in setting off my abandonment trauma for control of me. column1: If someone has been diagnosed with PD, would they have developed a personality considering there may be a false self? Could they for example be typed in the Myers-Briggs test?
column3: I know it can be confusing when therapists talk about a personality disorder and a “false self.” One way to think about this is to first consider the larger picture. Here are some things to consider: What is personality? Most definitions of personality describe it as a combination of inborn traits, patterns of cognition (thinking), emotional style, and learned coping mechanisms that are relatively stable over time. There have been multiple attempts by research psychologists to find and quantify personality traits that are inborn and endure unbroken to adulthood. This turned out to be a difficult endeavor because the personality often changes over time. For example, some research has shown that when we look at small children who are shy and then re-evaluate them as adults, many are no longer shy. When people say: “Oh, you will grow out of that,” this is in recognition that not everything that is part of our personality or approach to life is fixed at birth. We react to our social situation, our parents, cultural expectations, and so on. Many shy children learn new strategies that compensate for their early social timidity and allows them to be more relaxed and outgoing when they are around new people. Theorists do not agree on how much of out personality is inborn and how much is “created” by the social context we find ourselves in. They also do not agree on how many personality traits there are and how we should group traits. There are 4-Trait, 5-Trait, 8-Trait systems and more. What is there general agreement about?Babies are born with different temperaments and traits.They are not empty vessels that are totally formed by environmental influences. This is in contrast to the influential English philosopher, John Locke’s (1692–1704) tabula rasa theory of personality development that popularized the concept that infant’s minds were literally blank slates (without inborn temperament and traits). In Locke’s theory, the entire responsibility for how the child’s personality is formed is attributed to the influence of parents, caregivers, and teachers. Modern infant research has demonstrates over and over again that children’s personalities are a combination of inborn traits and temperament and also how children with those characteristics adapt to their external circumstances and such things as their physical abilities and limitations.Everyone has a personality.In the case of people who go on to develop personality disorders, it is believed that the interaction of their inborn characteristics with their parents or early caretakers expectations and style of parenting negatively impacted the development of the child’s personality. They then entered adulthood with fixed, maladaptive patterns that interfere with their ability to form normal, stable, and mutually satisfying relationships with other people. This means that people with personality disorders have a personality—just one with more than the usual amount of maladaptive coping mechanisms, specific psychological defense patterns that relate to the type of personality disorder the person “has,” and certain limitations and underdeveloped capacities, such as a lack of whole object relations or low emotional empathy.People are capable of learning.It used to be thought that once the brain was formed in adulthood, that was it. It was believed to be unalterable and best accepted. This concept was encapsulated in the expression, “You can’t teach an old dog new tricks.” That turned out to be false. Modern brain research includes many new tools that allow us to actually view people’s brains in action. This led to the startling realization that our brains are “plastic.” Plastic in this context means capable of being remodeled by further learning. We grow new neuronal connections throughout our life, this does not stop at the end of childhood as previously thought. This fact is what allows us to change with appropriate psychotherapy. Brain studies have shown that our brains actually rewire themselves in new ways as a result of good psychotherapy. Physical changes can occur through talk therapy alone without medication. I believe that in the future, therapists will have their clients get brain scans before therapy begins and then compare them with the scans at the end of therapy. Perhaps this will become so easily available and inexpensive that clients can be rescanned every few months to judge progress. This will allow us to really know what works for our clients and what does not. What is a false self? All children want to please their caregivers. Within the limits of our temperament, we all tried to win our parents’ approval and maximize the amount of love and positive attention we received from them. When our natural personality and our strengths are not a good fit for our parents expectations, some children will stop focusing on what they actually are interested in and switch to doing things that their parents find pleasing. A “false self” develops when the gap between the child’s authentic self and parental expectations is too large. The child then has to make a hard choice: Do I please my parents or do I please myself? When there is a very large gap between who the child authentically is and what the parents want, this adaptation results in the child eventually losing touch with his or her authentic developing self, and a “false self” designed to please the parents is constructed. The real self is still there, but it is pushed out of awareness. It is like a plant that goes dormant until it receives appropriate nurturing and water. Most of the process of developing a false self is unconscious. During this process, children lose touch with many of their authentic feelings and likes and dislikes. By the time the person reaches adulthood, the false self feels real. The real self is forgotten and deeply buried. It can re-emerge and restart its development with the help of appropriate therapeutic encouragement. Stella Chase and Alexander Thomas are infant researchers who looked at the interaction between children’s inborn temperament and their parents expectations and abilities to adjust to their children's needs. They viewed many adult psychological problems as having their roots in a bad mismatch between what the child needed and what the parents could supply. (See their book: Temperament and Behavior Disorders in Children, 1968.) How does having a personality disorder affect taking personality tests? If you have a personality disorder and you want to get a fairly accurate picture of your personality, you need to take psychological tests that were designed to recognize dysfunctional psychological patterns. The personality tests designed to be used by trained mental health professionals are designed to give both a picture of the person’s overall personality and the person’s psychopathology. These tests require specialized training to assess and administer. For example, I took a year long course in psychological testing in graduate school that taught me how to properly administer and score the WAIS and WISC multipart intelligence tests, the Rorschach Test (inkblots), the Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), and Draw a Person Test, among others. I added the MMPI on my own which then had 567 true/false questions and was good at catching attempts to influence the results in different ways through lying. Compared to the above tests, the results from the Myers-Brigg test are not considered valid enough to base anything serious on. It is a fun test to take, but if you take the same test multiple times, its results can differ widely. Experienced testers are very aware of the Myers-Briggs test’s limitations. As its results are not consistent for normal people, it is hard to say how personality disorders affect it. It is not designed to pick up personality disorders. Trained testers are more likely to give a battery of tests that, when taken collectively, give a fairly accurate picture of the client’s personality and psychological issues. If I only have time for one professional test, I choose the older and longer form of the MMPI and send it out for computer scoring because it is so complicated. Punchline: People with personality disorders have personalities that can be tested. Their “false self” will influence the results. If the appropriate tests are administered, a fairly accurate and well-rounded picture of the person’s personality and psychological issues will emerge. Myers-Briggs is not considered an appropriate or highly useful test. Its main virtues are it is fun to take and encourages self-reflection. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com
column9: Thanks Elinor Greenberg. Your answer has been super insightful and it’s helped me to better understand how personalities develop. I personally believe it’s a mixture of being born with certain traits and adapting to environments/experiences. I used to be really shy when I was a child and forced myself out of it. Can still get shy at times but nothing like how I used to be. The conversation that prompted this question was actually a debate about MB types, PDs, and criminality. Some people were arguing that certain PDs and MB types were more prone to becoming criminals but I didn’t understand the relationship between the three. I didn’t feel it would be possible to get a picture of an MB type as their false self would influence the results and I didn’t really see the relationship between this and criminality. It sounds like from what you’re saying the MB test don’t really give us the bigger picture about personality types regardless of one having a PD or not.

column1: Will psychotherapy make a narcissist happier? If not, and if there is no cure, what is the point of it?
column3: Asking whether psychotherapy will make a person happier is a bit like asking if physical therapy will make a person happier. Happiness is subjective. Therapy, whether psychotherapy or physical therapy, deals with restoring as much normal functioning as is possible for a specific individual. This is not a full list, but it will begin to give you an idea of what people with NPD can gain through psychotherapy. In the case of Narcissistic Disorder, the main therapeutic goals are:Achieve Whole Object RelationsWhole Object Relations (WOR) involves the ability to see oneself and other people in a realistic, integrated, and stable way. This capacity is normally developed in childhood. Almost everyone starts off with the capacity to develop WOR, but if your parents lack WOR, they cannot model it for you and are not focused on teaching you about it. Small children normally start to develop WOR AT ages 2–4 years and refine it in their teen years. People with NPD do not have WOR, but can learn it as an adult in therapy. Without WOR, people with NPD can only see themselves and other people as either all-good (special and perfect) or all-bad (defective and worthless).Achieve Object ConstancyObject Constancy grows out of WOR. It is the ability to maintain a sense of your positive feelings for someone you love, and the ability to access your memories of good times together, while you are hurt, angry, frustrated, or disappointed with the person. Without OC, in a fight the person with NPD goes from loving you to hating you. Then you become the enemy. Most of the abuse between people who live together—lovers, married couples, parents and children—is the result of the abuser losing (or never having attained) OC.Stabilize Self-EsteemStep 1—Develop WOR & OC In order to have self-esteem, you first need to develop WOR and OC. Without them, the person with NPD can quickly go from feeling great about themselves to feeling shame and self-hatred. Step 2—Encourage Authenticity People with NPD have developed a false self persona. Some time during childhood, they adapted to their family situation by adopting a set of behaviors and view points that were designed to maximize the amount of attention, support, and approval they could get from their parents. Step 3—Increase Awareness Most people with NPD are so used to faking high self-esteem, that they often fail to notice or value their real strengths. As a therapist, I notice what my Narcissistic clients do well and bring what I see into their awareness. Eventually, pride in their real accomplishments replaces fake grandiosity. Or, in worse cases where no support was forthcoming and only criticism was received, they failed to develop any self-confidence. Now as adults, they cannot see their own strengths. One of the therapeutic goals for people with NPD involves helping them get reacquainted with themselves. This involves detaching from their need to impress other people and get validation, Instead, the focus is on finding what they really like and why, and what they do not like.Curb ImpulsivityAnyone who has been around many people with NPD has had the opportunity to notice that many Narcissists insist on expressing themselves and venting their negative feelings, even when that behavior is highly inappropriate and even detrimental to their own goals. It is a novel idea to most people with NPD that they can have a thought or judgement or complaint without immediately expressing it. If you follow the stories of people who get escorted off planes for devaluing the stewardess or upsetting other passengers, the ones who are not drunk or mentally disabled are often Narcissists.Stop Devaluing and Insulting PeopleStep 1—Increase Awareness Most people with NPD devalue other people so often that they no longer are even aware that they are doing so. Insults just flow like a river from their mouth on a daily basis. In therapy, clients with NPD are brought back to awareness by calm questions, such as: Was it your intention just now to insult me? Are you aware that comment was devaluing? What are you hoping to accomplish by that comment? Step 2—Look at Consequences Once clients with NPD start to be aware of how often they devalue and insult other people, they can be helped to explore the consequences of their behaviors. How does saying that to your wife affect your marriage? Do you think calling your boss an idiot in front of the staff will help or hinder your career? How did you feel after you stormed out of the restaurant cursing your waiter? Step 3—Develop Different Coping Strategies This involves finding new, more adaptive ways of handling the situations that previously were managed by being grandiose or devaluing. The person now has to think before they speak, handle their negative emotions without shifting blame, gaslighting, or yelling, and face reality head on. Facing reality for people with NPD can be painful. They are not really more special than everyone else and they are not automatically entitled to get their way. Punchline: People with Narcissistic Personality Disorder can gain a lot by appropriate psychotherapy. Their life becomes calmer and more stable, their relationships improve, and they can step off the never ending treadmill of trying to convince everyone that they are perfect. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com

column1: Why and how do people go mad?
column3: I think that madness is marked by a complete loss of one's centre. Whatever organizing principle that holds all the different threads of your personality together no longer coheres. Because your centre collapses, you have no way to make your experience cohere and everything stops making sense. The person's sense of self literally fragments. This leads to a huge sense of uncertainty and an inability to function. It's also completely horrifying. The world loses its proportionality, it's directionality. When I deal with severe schizophrenics, it is like watching homeless people stranded in the hostile streets of their own minds. Shelter would be as simple as walking back into their house, but they can't find their way there. Their mind has become a hostile place that doesn't welcome them in any way. They lose the ability to stay at the helm of their experience, and as a result, they get tossed and shoved around in their own experience. The clinical term for this would be dissolution of self, but sometimes delusional schizophrenics emerge and talk about their experiences, so there often is a core there, no matter how fragile. But then their madness devours them all over again and they disappear. It becomes impossible to relate to them as they get absorbed into the very fabric of their delusions. As we see with severely delusional people, "there is no there, there." They can't respond to you directly as a personality because there is no centre available to respond to you. Say that you walk into a dentist's office. You notice the decor, you feel comfortable or uncomfortable, you might or might not like the music. You might be preoccupied or have a memory. Every single one of these sensations relates back to a sense of 'you', you're lived experience in your body. But a schizophrenic often feels that they don't have a body. They could feel they are made entirely of glass, or that they are dead. They can't relate their experience back to a coherent centre they think of as themselves. So they might get devoured by the color, or become completely engulfed by an expression on the secretary's face, or experience a sudden horrible dissociation because someone coughs and that terrifies them. Nothing has a fixed quality or size. Everything is dissociated. It could be as simple as the texture on a chair. Everything is nothing is everything. column1: In the disability service like the autistic program and special ed, have other autistic people been allowed to lose their tempers if they want to?
column3: In my son’s rehabilitation program, some specialists patiently wait while he’s going through meltdowns, screams and rips things into pieces. (Thankfully, mostly paper and pencils.) Others just stop the session (e. g. the masseur). Different specialists and rehabilitation centers have different approaches. In the end of the day, even a meltdown in the therapist’s presence is just another opportunity to reflect on it, to find coping strategies, to discuss the experience, to improve communication skills, and to find ways of avoiding it next time. Which is what therapy and education are for. However, I wouldn’t say that the word “want” applies to autistic people losing their tempers. I think no autist wants to lose their temper. It’s a difficult, exhausting event, it’s a stressful conflict. The meltdowns that happen signal a total momentary crash of the system. A person should dread going through that. For your sake, I hope that, instead of “allowed to lose their tempers if they want to”, you were trying to describe “allowed to go through a meltdown should it happen”.

column1: Can borderline personality disorder be cured?
column3: People with Borderline Personality Disorder can recover if they get appropriate treatment and stick with their psychotherapy long enough to do the necessary work. The good news is that there are a number of effective treatments available.Borderline Personality Disorders Exist on a SpectrumIt is important to remember that no two people with BPD are alike. Borderline Personality Adaptations exist on a spectrum: High Functioning BPD: At the high functioning end of the spectrum are people who marry, hold down jobs, and manage their emotions fairly well (while secretly suffering from the same typical issues as other people with BPD). They are likely to marry someone who also has a personality disorder and is about their equal in functioning. They usually choose a career that allows them to be creative and not constrained by a 9–5pm job. Moderate Functioning BPD: They usually work, have spouses or lovers, and friends. They tend to be poorly organized and have trouble finishing projects that they start and meeting commitments. They are likely to procrastinate about anything that they wish that they did not have to do— such as save for the future, do routine medical tests, get their teeth cleaned, or pay bills. They are likely to be working at a job or profession that is below their intellectual capacities. They may have started a graduate degree program and dropped out because the stress of doing a dissertation brought out all their self doubt. They have tumultuous relationships and lots of drama and crises in their lives. Low Functioning BPD: At the lowest end of the spectrum are the extremely volitile and vulnerable people who cannot manage the normal responsibilities of adult life—they get evicted because they do not pay their rent on time, they lose jobs because they stay up all night and sleep through their alarm, they are freezing because they never got around to buying a winter coat or warm boots. They may still be living at home with their parents or depending on them for financial and psychological support. These are the people with the Borderline diagnosis who are most at risk for self harm or ending up homeless. They may be suicidal and in and out of mental hospitals. Their life tends to be one long crisis.Treatment of BPDThe good news is that Borderline Personality Disorder is very treatable. Obviously it is easier to do psychotherapy with higher functioning people with BPD, than those who are lower functioning. The therapy moves faster as well. DBT: I generally recommend that lower functioning clients with BPD who are having trouble tolerating their emotions, inhibiting their destructive behaviors, and organizing their lives begin with DBT (Dialectical Behavior Therapy). Marsha Linehan created it especially for these typical BPD issues. It is one of the easiest BPD therapies to teach psychotherapists, works well, is cost effective, and widely available. It is available in many different settings—hospitals, mental health clinics, and private practice. This increases the likelihood that you can find the setting appropriate to your level of functioning and that the practitioner will take insurance. Object Relations Therapy: This is generally based on the work of James F. Masterson and Otto Kernberg. It focuses on achieving “whole object relations” and “object constancy,” as well as dealing with the pain of childhood trauma, abandonment, and abuse. This is a very effective psychotherapy for those clients who are psychologically minded and want to understand themselves better. It works well with those BPD clients who are able to organize their life sufficiently to be seen in private practice and are not a danger to themselves or others. Fewer psychotherapists are trained in Object Relations Therapy for BPD and it takes more years to master than DBT. For this reason, it may be harder to find a well trained Object Relations therapists outside of major cities and they may not accept insurance. Gestalt Therapy for BPD: I developed a Gestalt therapy approach to BPD that I teach internationally and describe in my book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. It blends the creativity of Gestalt therapy with the insights of James F. Masterson’s Object Relations approach. Punchline: Everyone can evolve. Everyone can improve their coping strategies. Our past pains and traumas can be worked on till only a scar remains to remind us of our injuries. If you or someone you love has been diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder take heart! The only thing limiting your recovery is how much work you are willing to put into your psychotherapy. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com

column1: What client resources, coping strategies, personal strengths, and other characteristics can you draw on to facilitate the counselling process? How can focusing on these strengths help the client?
column3: Very often individuals join therapy in a state of disempowerment due to emotional challenges. That type of mind state disconnects people from their inner and external resources: people feel unlikable, unresourced, incapable, etc, plus they may find other people annoying, tiring, or undesirable. Things that were pleasant or easy before become difficult or unpleasant. That means that the person loses connection with their strengths and with what makes life enjoyable. Therefore, if the clinician helps to regain awareness of the positive characteristics in the person and their circumstances, the strengths and resources become available again. Anything that can activate brain circuits that produce healing hormones or neurotransmitters (like dopamine, oxytocin, serotonin, etc), is good medicine to alleviate emotional distress. It could be something like focusing on achievements, lovable memories, pride and joy, friends, financial stability, or the simple fact of watching the beauty of a flower or enjoying the sunset. Every time the brain engages in these experiences, it produces the right chemicals to find wellbeing and calmness. That’s empowering enough to motivate the person to keep going in that direction. That’s the hardwired self-healing capacity we all have; our innate wisdom.

column1: I was recently robbed at gunpoint. It scared the hell out of me, and I'm losing sleep because of it. How do I move on?
column3: Wow. I’m so sorry that happened to you. You really, really need to talk to someone about it. You don’t state any specifics, so I can’t give you more specific advice. You can learn a lot of good coping strategies specific to you by going to a therapist. It really is a deeply personal thing. I wish you the best of luck.

column1: How do people who have a high IQ deal with stress/pressure in comparison to people who have an average IQ?
column3: I have noticed by observing myself and others that how you cope with stress/pressure depends on your personality and the coping strategies that you have learned or have been taught over time. Intelligence does not seem to play the main role here, although it might help you develop personal insight faster than others and thus find successful coping strategies earlier in life. In my belief right now, there are two ways to develop insight: 1 emotional intelligence, and 2 reason. Some people have average conventional intelligence but high emotional intelligence, they tend to have good coping strategies and good relationships with people. If you have 'only' average emotional intelligence, then conventional intelligence may help you improve your emotional intelligence and coping strategies through imagination and reason. On the other hand, you may be more likely to notice issues that are not within the control of any single person: poverty, war, that extremely tough physics problem, disease and ruminate about them until the end of time. There is always something to think about and if you do not know healthy ways to channel the chatter in your mind and to distance yourself from issues, you may feel like you're going insane. And there is another catch. If you are depressed or in a delusional state of mind all the reason in the world will not help you. You will use it to justify your feelings and thoughts. You will find only evidence that proves your thoughts true and discard evidence that proves them false. Better reasoning skills then mean more difficult therapy because you can always find a reason why your therapist is wrong. Somewhat unhealthy ways to cope that I've seen people fall victim to (on TV, in real life, and so on): Avoid taking care of trouble and becoming impulsive and reckless: they run away, they move to another country, self-medicate, they party like there is no tomorrow and possibly overindulge in things that are not necessarily good for them (drugs, alcohol, food, sex). Becoming depressed and anxious and also behave in an avoidant way, but less external. They would like to take care of things but they feel unable to make a change in their lives, so they ask themselves, why bother at all?Trying to regain control, attempting to solve problems head on and becoming angry and short with people. They dig themselves in, the problem must be solved / stressor eliminated no holds barred and they have an idea in their heads about how it is going to happen.Retreating into their personal space, refusing to go out until they've found a way to deal with the stressor. It might or might not be healthy. I'd say if they forget to take care of themselves it becomes unhealthy.Thinking about it till the end of time but not taking action. Highly intelligent people are not different, they do break down. However, I believe that having a higher intelligence means that unless you feel truly defeated, you are more likely to suddenly realize the long term consequences, reconsider your behavior and restrain yourself or eventually return and apologize. You know what will happen to your family if you move to another country, you can visualize your children growing up without you, wondering who you are. You know that you'll destroy your liver if you drink too much alcohol and you know that you become impulsive under stress so you never touch the bottle. You know intuitively that running away doesn't solve your problems. Why do some intelligent people seem to calm under pressure? Some reasons: They realize that some influences on what they are trying to do are beyond their control. Fretting over them is a fruitless exercise. You can only do your very best within your circle of influence and luck is when preparation meets opportunity. Just keep preparing and eventually there will be a chance.Things that many people care about do not matter as much to them: grades, which uni to go to, having thousands of followers or friends, how popular they are, their looks and appearance, how much money they have/make.Compared to the vastness of what we call our universe they possibly view (some of) their problems as trivial.They have a passion that they work on tirelessly and they do not have time to focus on things that they cannot control anyway. Their passion can be anything: science, music, politics, human relations, animals, photography, games, sports, you name it.They know themselves and take care of their physical and mental well being. They take breaks when they need them, they exercise and eat relatively healthy foods. Why do other intelligent people reach for drugs or alcohol or commit suicide? Some reasons: They care about the world and people with all their heart and it pains them to see people destroying the planet and waging war.They feel trapped in a world that doesn't seem to care about them with people who don't understand them.They must do things that they don't care about to the point of mental torture. Paperwork, applying for grants, continuously having to convince people that what they're doing is worthwhile. Jobs that are bland and a poor fit for the person, bad work environment, bullies.Linking personal identity to matters that are temporary and then losing these things. For example something that they have built over many years which is suddenly gone, like a relationship with someone, their business, their reputation. Seeing their future plans die.Growing tired of the endless chatter in their minds and not knowing how to deal with it.

column1: What do I do if i've lost the passion to everything?
column3: Have you heard of Learned Helplessness? When you are trapped in an abusive situation--such as a relationship with a lover, a job, your parents, or your country--you begin to lose control. Your freedom, your health, and your happiness get metered and subjected to another's wishes. Did you cook dinner? NOT what I wanted. Did you finish the project on time? Well, WE wanted it early. Are you so hungry you want to eat? You'll eat when I FEEL like cooking. Are you so lonely in solitary confinement that you're hallucinating? You are inhuman, and deserve OUR punishment's for reparations. Maybe this kind of treatment happened when you were growing up. Think about that for a second: all ability and control you have, over your personal fulfillment and survival, is gone. It's surrendered to another who threatens your livelihood if you even try to take initiative. How do people deal with this or similar suffocation? It's called learned helplessness. It's supposedly a coping strategy for, and symptom of, depression. The kind of thinking where defeatist thinking in your head destroys everything you create, uprooting plants before they even have a chance to bloom. In the experiment linked above, dogs are conditioned to adopt learned helplessness. They hear a bell, and are given a shock in turn no matter what they do. (FYI, see That Dragon, Cancer). The next phase of the experiment has these dogs on a divided cage. They can hop from one side to another, and either side can be shocked. After feeling the shock, dogs who were SPARED this Pavlovian conditioning jumped to the safe side. But, the conditioned dogs surrendered to the shock. They laid down and accepted being helpless. They were used to feeling pain. You're turning to Quora because you think you've tried everything. So now you're going to Quora to see if there is help for you. Is it even possible to imagine being helped from this? I'm here to tell you that it is possible to escape this torture. And you might need help beyond Quora. You'll need friends, family, therapists--whomever you trust to provide you escape plans that you will believe in. But even if people hold out their hand, you gotta believe they're strong enough to help you pull yourself up. You gotta believe they got their muscles from success, not from deceit and delusion--just like you can, and will. Good luck, and rise anew. PS: If you want more, You Are Not So Smart has written about this. Their blog often points out how our own minds can work against us, instead of for us. This is one of those cases. :)

column1: What is the hardest thing about being a therapist?
column3: Arguably, the single greatest challenge faced by even highly-trained therapists is learning how to avoid developing "compassion fatigue". I experienced a brief period of compassion fatigue years ago when in a single month, I had worked with several clients who presented with distant and recent histories of severe abuse and trauma - including a family whose father and husband had recently taken their own life. This is was one of the key clinical experiences that lead me to really master and apply - not just to study good self-care skills - especially relaxation training.Here are some great resources from the APA for clinicians: Are you burned out?I learned how to quickly get and stay very calm in otherwise very stressful situations by strengthening my relaxation response. For example, a six/six-second vagal-diaphragmatic breathing pattern combined with repeated daily progressive muscle relaxation, practice to self-induced relaxation through a 5-second body-muscle-tension scan - was a personal and professional life-changer for me. it only took me a few months to really get good at it. Relaxation training allows me to stay much more clinically focused, responsive, and personally resilient when working with deeply emotionally distressed couples and in my work with individuals as a mental health counselor. I've now taught and coached hundreds of clients to master their own relaxation responses as part of a core set of stress management skills. The relaxation response, strengthen emotional self-control, and boosts cognitive flexibility. It empowers clients to more effectively manage their stress, anxiety, and anger before it manages them. It’s a foundational skill for effective couple-communication. It’s often essential in addiction recovery and behavioral relapse prevention. It’s also a critical leadership management and teamwork skill. Good emotional self-control enhances cognitive-flexibility and enables deeper empathy and other-perspective taking. It also drastically improves communication effectiveness and our ability to develop and implement solution-focused coping strategies - the work of real-world problem-solving. Compassion Fatigue:".. a state experienced by those helping people or animals in distress; it is an extreme state of tension and preoccupation with the suffering of those being helped to the degree that it can create a secondary traumatic stress for the helper." “We have not been directly exposed to the trauma scene, but we hear the story told with such intensity, or we hear similar stories so often, or we have the gift and curse of extreme empathy and we suffer. We feel the feelings of our clients. We experience their fears. We dream their dreams. Eventually, we lose a certain spark of optimism, humor and hope. We tire. We aren’t sick, but we aren’t ourselves.” - Dr. Charles FigleyHope that helps!

column1: What happens if trauma is not resolved?
column3: It never is. So you tell me, then, what happened to anyone who ever survived trauma? It depends on how they cope with it every day. Some have coping mechanisms. Some have coping strategies. Some go on to lead perfectly normal lives. Some go on to lead chaotic lives. Some don't go on at all, but take their own life to escape their pain. In any case, you either learn to live with it…or you don't…but it's never completely resolved. It doesn't go away any more than the past does. You don't just “get over it.” It leaves a scar that never fully heals, and “triggers” are what cuts it back open after any amount of time has gone by.. It's a weight on your shoulders you just learn to carry…it can make you stronger…or it can crush you under its weight. You have to exercise things like self-control and mindfulness, because the pathways and processes in your brain are just like the muscles in your body - use it or lose it. Some people go to therapy for the rest of their lives to learn how to cope. Some go for a long time and then can do it on their own so stop going after that. Some go a short time. Some don't go to therapy at all. Who do you suppose struggles the most and why? It depends on what happened, how tramatic it was, how much support a person has, and how they deal with it. It helps to have a good sense of humor. If you can find ways to laugh, it's not so bad.

column1: How does one comfort a friend who just lost a loved one?
column3: Knowing what to say can be very tricky. Some statements can actually be inflammatory without meaning to. Why? Because people have different filters and life experiences. If you’ve been through loss yourself, you can say “One day it won’t always feel this raw.” If you haven’t, then the best thing to say is “I’m so very sorry,” and then offer a long, heartfelt hug. Below are some of the worst things to say and why, and suggestions to say instead. I hope this helps. “How are you? Are you okay? This statement ignores the obvious. And demands an answer. Suggestion: “I’ve been thinking of you, how are you feeling today?” This invites us to open up. “I understand how you feel.” This statement tends to dismiss our emotions and is inflammatory. Suggestion: “I have absolutely no idea how you feel. But please know I have a good ear for listening and an available shoulder for hugs.” “Time heals all wounds.” Time doesn’t heal the pain. Instead, over the years our coping skills become stronger. Suggestion: “I’ve been thinking of you. Please know I have a good ear for listening and an available shoulder for hugs.” “At least he/she lived a long life.” When you love someone, their lives are never long enough. Suggestion: “Loss is so terribly painful regardless of age.” “It will get better every day.” Recovery isn’t predictable, nor is it a chronological process. One day can be good, but the next two might be very hard. Suggestion: “Some days will be better than others. When you’re having a rough day, call me and I’ll bring you coffee.” “Call if you need anything.” We aren’t thinking clearly, and we often have no idea what we need. Even if we do need something, we fear being a burden. Suggestion: “I’m going to the grocery store for toilet paper. Are you getting low?” Be specific, but not pushy. “Well, at least s/he is in a better place.” No matter how good another place is, we want our loved one right beside us. Additionally, this statement evokes guilt for feeling selfish about that. Suggestion: “I’m terribly sorry for your loss, it must be overwhelming on many levels.” “At least s/he isn’t suffering.” Our own suffering snuffs out all logic as to why we should be glad that our loved one can’t feel pain. Suggestion: “I have absolutely no idea how you feel. But please know I have a good ear for listening and strong shoulder for hugs.” “God must have needed him/her.” “God doesn’t give us more than we can handle.” “It’s God’s will. “When God closes one door, he opens another.” “God plucks a rose to make Heaven more beautiful.” No matter how steadfast we are in our beliefs, a profound loss often triggers an examination of why our faith didn’t protect our loved one. This statement can be quite inflammatory as it implies that our needs don’t count, regardless of our faith. Suggestion: “Just know that I’m praying for you. And I have a good ear for listening and strong shoulder for hugs.” “You need to stay strong for________” “You are so strong!” Both of these evoke guilt for wanting to cry. Suppressed sorrow leads to complications that not only hinder our ability to recover, but creates confusion over why we feel so weak. Suggestion: “You don’t need to stay strong.” Suggestion: “We will be strong for you.” “I miss him/her as much as you do.” This dismisses our sorrow and implies competition for the loss. Suggestion: “I miss them too.” “It’s time to move on.” This implies that you know what’s better for us than we do. Rushing through it can hinder long-term recovery. Suggestion: None. “We all lose someone at some point,” or “Loss is a part of life.” While both statements are true, they lack compassion and dismiss one’s right to move through the bereavement process. Suggestion: “Loss is so terribly hard!” “You can have another child.” One person doesn’t replace another. Also, while in great emotional distress, we are virtually incapable of looking ahead. Suggestion: None. “You’ll find someone else.” Again, one person doesn’t replace another. And looking to the future will feel too scary for a while. Suggestion: None. “I hear they are finding a cure for that now.” This adds disappointment and jealousy that a cure wasn’t found in time to save our loved one. Suggestion: “Are you going to continue your involvement with the organization for the disease your loved one had?” “Why didn’t the doctor suggest you go to the hospital?” We don’t know why. Suggestion: “What type of choices did your doctor offer for end of life care?” “Your loved one is flying with the angels now.” It’s best to avoid afterlife or spiritual references unless you are absolutely certain you know the person’s belief. Suggestion: None. “Tough it out. Telling us to tough it out is asking us to hide our grief. This is the worst thing we could do. Showing our emotions helps us heal. Suggestion: “It’s okay to be human” or “It’s okay to be sad.” “Everything happens for a reason.” This depends upon one’s spiritual beliefs. Suggestion: “I can’t imagine how heartbreaking this must be.” “At least they’re aren’t suffering anymore.” While intellectually true, this doesn’t change our need to process the loss. Suggestion: None. “They would want you to be happy.” Sometimes feeling happy isn’t possible, so this generates guilt. Suggestion: None.

column1: Can grief cause your hair to shed excessively?
column3: When my husband died suddenly from a heart attack I went into deep shock which triggered completely denial. Eventually, some weeks later, my head went through a hair loss tsunami. The Year Of Magical Thinking - The Tricks Your Mind Plays On You In the Year Of Magical Thinking, the late Joan Didion wrote about the tricks our minds play on us when spouses or family members died suddenly.Year Of Magical Thinking - Death, Grief And Dealing With Loss Didion’s husband, renowned writer John Gregory Dunne died much like my own husband. Joan Didion’s Husband Died Suddenly But I Don’t Remember Her Reference To Hair Loss One minute Dunne and Didion were getting ready for dinner together in their apartment in Manhattan and then he was gone. He died sitting in his favorite chair of a heart attack on December 30, 2003. Although Didion didn’t mention her hair shedding excessively, or at least I don’t remember her doing so, my own strands started coming out in handfuls approximately 12 weeks after my husband’s death. It really is true that grief is a personal thing. What one person experiences as grief, another person may not. Telogen Effluvium - A Type Of Trauma Triggered Alopecia The massive hair shedding was nothing new to me. I have already lived through onsets of Telogen Effluvium during other very traumatic times in my life over the years. The first time occurred when I was 7 years old and my mother almost chocked me to death. A few months later I had unexpected hair shedding. My hairdresser, who also happened to my aunt. was puzzled by the sudden thinning of my hair. Telogen Effluvium Can Be A Recurring, Chronic Or Persistent Type Of Hair Loss When asked if I had suffered any traumas lately neither my mother nor I were willing to volunteer the incident where I lost consciousness in the middle of the night due to assault. Eventually my hair grew back, but I discovered one you trigger Telogen Effluvium, it can be recurring, chronic and persistent. Over the years after a significant emotional, mental or physical trauma my head would start to rain hair. But approximately 10–12 weeks after the triggering event hair would explode from my scalp. Grief Is Not Just About The Death Of Loved Ones The work that Elisabeth Kübler-Ross did involving the five stages of grief tends to pertain more closely to terminal patients who are facing imminent death from disease.Peaks And Valley - Integrative Approaches For Recovering From Loss Grief is not only limited to actual death of loved ones. Grief that is not specifically related to the death of a loved one may follow more of a Grief Cyle rather than the Stages of Grief. Any Loss Of Life Or Physical Attachments May Trigger Grief CyclesPsychologist Sherry O’Brien wrote about the many ways people experience grief through the loss of an attachment. In her book, “Peaks and Valleys: Integrative Approaches For Recovering From Loss”, published in 2014, O’Brien explains that anytime there is any type of break in an attachment we hold, we experience mental, emotional and physical types of grief.Broken attachments which may trigger grief include, but aren’t limited to:The death of a loved one which is the worse type of grief.The loss of a job or a career (termination, layoff, retirement)Loss of any relationship from love to friendship to family (physical death may or may not occur). Example: A best friend or sibling who gets angry and cuts you out of their life may trigger deep grief even if your friend or sibling didn’t physically pass away.Loss of the use of the body through illness, paralysis, chronic illness, physical trauma from accidents or falls or similar When people can no longer use their bodies as they once did, they grieve the loss of that independence and freedom.Graduating from any level of school from grade school to college.Moving away from home, friends and family.The death of a pet.A major change in lifestyle including losing large amounts of weight or becoming clean and sober from drugs or alcohol. Some people find their lives are disorganized through the severance of a long held habit.Yes, people grieve the loss of weight and the use of drugs and alcohol. That grief can also trigger hair shedding. Who knew? Right? Telogen Effluvium Any attachment that is broken in any way may trigger grief which can then trigger Telogen Effluvium. Alopecia, whether it’s Telogen Effluvium or Alopecia Areata which is an immune system disorder can be directly connected to massive hair shedding and hair loss. Telogen Effluvium occurs when the body experiences some sort of shock, stress or emotional event which causes the hair to be forced prematurely into a resting and then shedding state. O’Brien has organized grief in different phases rather than stages. Her grief phases include:ShockProtest - Why Me, Why No, Why not someone else.AngerDisorganizationReorganizationRecognitionRecoveryGrief Can Trigger Hair Loss And Hair Loss Can Trigger Deep Grief Ironically, when someone loses their hair through the sudden onset of alopecia areata or telogen effluvium or a gradual loss through androgen alopecia (male or female pattern hair loss) people will experience grief over the loss of their hair. Loss Of Hair From Grief May Trigger DIfferent Grief Which Will Perpetuate The Hair Loss Cycle Yes, grief from losses in life can trigger hair loss, but hair loss from disease, shedding from grief, aging or other reasons can actually trigger a grief cycle, which perpetuates the shedding cycle. Many people who lose their hair either suddenly or over a period of time may lose their sense of identity and self-esteem. Any loss, including the loss of body parts of hair is traumatic for many people - both men and women. Hair Is A Critical Part Of Us - It Is A Part Of Our Body And Our Identity Hair is part of us. It is how we identify ourselves. Losing that part of us and that identify more often than not does trigger deep grief which ebbs and flows over a series of phases. The Takeaway - Grief Can Cause Hair To Shed Excessively Whether you are experienced the grief over suddenly losing your hair or the grief of the loss of some other attachment in your life, grief can cause hair to shed. If you hair is already shedding from some other type of grief, loss of your hair can intensify the shedding and grief cyle. Grief Cycles Of Ebb And Flow Yes, hair loss can trigger a deep period of grieving. Loss your hair, for whatever reason, is a loss of attachment and a loss of self. It is also triggering. It requires Reorganiztion of how to live life with limited or no hair. It also requires recognition that the hair may never grow back and the willingness to find a solution that works and move on towards recovery. As you can see, grief and hair loss or hair loss and grief had very deep and lasting ties. Best wishes to all. What I write is based on my own experience and belief in the techniques I share.”
