column1: My husband was just diagnosed with bipolar 1. His diagnosis includes substance abuse and hyper-sexuality. We have 2 young kids (3 and 6). How do I help/support him while making sure our kids are in the healthiest environment? Is divorce inevitable?
column3: Just my opinion, but when mental disorders are present in the family there is no such thing as a “healthy” environment. There are two types of trauma that interrupt emotional and mental development: addiction and/or mental illness. Not only do these factors interrupt the development process of the individual with them, but of those around him or her as well (i.e. nuclear family). This can lead to family members taking on dysfunctional family roles such as the resentful chief enabler that picks up the slack for the addicted or mentally ill member (usually the spouse), the hero (often first born child), the scapegoat (black sheep of family), and more; the more dysfunctional the family unit is, the more static these roles are among the family members. Not only can dysfunctional family roles be subconsciously taken on, but an enmeshed or estranged family system can also develop as a result of it all. In enmeshed families, for example, secrets from the outside world and from each other are common; an interesting dynamic erupts known as “don’t talk (to others about our family’s problems), don’t trust (others outside of the family unit), don’t feel (numbing or ignoring feelings is ideal).” Boundaries are often lacking in dysfunctional families along with respect for self and others. A strong (healthy) support system is very important for the individual with an addiction or mental illness. It’s a necessary component for their success in treatment. Not only should the individual with the addiction and/or mental illness be receiving treatment, but members within the family unit should be as well. If everyone in the family is not receiving professional help, the change in the unit from treatment of the one individual with the addiction or mental illness will only be temporary- if at all. As family theory states- “the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.” The husband with bipolar 1 disorder sounds like he has a dual diagnosis (addiction and mental illness) and would greatly benefit from treating both at the same time. The downside to this is that it can be difficult and expensive to find a program that has the resources to do so. There is also often waitlists to enter addiction treatment centers. Depending on the severity of the addiction, inpatient (also known as residential) treatment can be extremely enlightening (if first time) and effective (if the patient takes the program seriously and truly desires or is ready for recovery). There are different paths to recovery from substance use, but AA meetings can be a good start. Getting a sponsor (from these AA meetings) is even better after attending a couple of them. Working the 12 steps has helped countless individuals with substance use disorder to gain and maintain sobriety. A free and excellent resource for the family members in the unit that do not have substance use issues is Al-Anon. Al-Anon is an educational, support group for family members that live or have lived with a loved one that has an addiction. Like AA, it is anonymous and participation in meetings are optional (but, of course, very much encouraged). This is where a support system can also be found for the family members without an addiction -outside of the family unit itself. This is where they can learn how to deal and cope with their loved one’s addiction in a healthy way. One more note that I would like to bring up is this: if you do or don’t divorce, what are you teaching your children? The children in this situation, though very young, are absorbing and processing everything that they see. They learn the proper functionings and values of a relationship from their parents. If they are diagnosed as teenagers or adults with the same mental disorders as their father, wouldn’t it reinforce the idea that they are not good enough, worthy/valuable, or lovable because of it as their own mother could not or did not want to “make it work” with their own father? But if you stayed with their father even when he is not seeking treatment or sobriety, wouldn’t it reinforce the idea that it’s okay/normal to tolerate the abuse or dysfunction of another person? Would it reinforce the idea that it’s okay/normal for them to mistreat others in that same dysfunctional manner? Divorce is very traumatic for children. It’s actually one of the stressful events included in a study and evaluation known as ACEs (adverse childhood experiences) alongside growing up in a household with substance use. The chance that they will be diagnosed with the same mental illness is higher than average as there seems to be a genetic predisposition for bipolar disorder. Substance use, or addiction, is also genetic with the environment having an influence on its development. The statistics I have seen state that a child of the biological parent with an addiction has a 50/50 chance of developing an addiction themselves later on in life; it is unclear whether living together or separately from the parent with the addiction really does have a significant effect on the outcome. The chances of the child developing an addiction as an adult increases for a child with a biological and foster parent with an addiction. But you are the only one that can decide what is best for you and your family. There is no one on this Earth that knows the details of the situation better than you. Divorce does not have to be inevitable, but I have heard stories of child protective services stepping into the lives of families with one addicted parent (even if the spouse is sober). Trauma is inevitable in life, but there are ways of reducing and minimizing the effects of it. If you are not educated on mental illness or addiction and the effects of it on everyone involved, I strongly suggest professional help to guide you and the family along the way (i.e. AA meetings, Al-Anon meetings, in-patient/out-patient treatment, psychologist individual & family sessions, addictions counselor individual & family sessions, reading books on the following topics: co-dependence, setting boundaries, surviving addiction, adult children of alcoholics, etc). With the current opiate epidemic on-going within the USA as per the CDC, the area of addiction is getting a lot of attention at the moment; as drug overdoses are the leading cause of death in Americans under 50 years old, it is being looked at more seriously. Think about it all very carefully and thoroughly. Good luck!

column1: Since dealing with a narcissist, I have no more feelings, I don't care about anyone, and have no empathy. How can I be myself again?
column3: I was raised by a narcissist mom. I was also the scapegoat of my family. My most recent romantic relationship was also a narcissist. For me, my world crashed around me on many levels, all within a span of a few years. It was multi-faceted. It lead to my breakdown, which I would say is similar to what you described, except that I also had a nervous breakdown mixed in, full of very negative strong emotions like anxiety, panic attacks, hopeless, I felt insane, couldn’t understand what had just happened and why, my world caved in on me, and depression…. CPTSD for sure. With the depression I didn’t want to commit suicide. I just was a mess in my head. Foggy brain, couldn’t think. Couldn’t make decisions. Felt extreme negative emotions or else nothing and numb, bouncing back and forth between the negative and numb. This lasted years, but I could see improvement via therapy, albeit small levels. But still, enough to give me hope. I will explain what happened to me, and possibly you can resonate with pieces of it. My dad was the enabler and also the main scapegoat of the family. I bounced between scapegoat and golden child. My brother was the main golden child, so I was typically the SG more often. Mom didn’t want me, tried to abort me so she claimed, and told me more than once how she wished I had never been born. I was 7 years younger than the youngest of 4 brothers so I was like an only child. My 4 brothers had a life long before me and were friends, had stories, camaraderie, etc. I felt like an extreme outsider to my own family. I had to watch them all laugh and have fun together, reminiscing about their life before me. By the time I was in Junior High, they had all left home and so I truly was an only child. But, I wasn’t and so every holiday and get together left me feeling like an outsider to my own family. And then, mom didn’t want me and I was a burden to her financially, so she claimed. In order to combat feeling so unwanted, so abandoned, not fitting into my family, so worthless, not belonging, not safe… I became a workhorse. I had no “needs or wants.” I became exactly what mom wanted. I did what she said, predicted her bad moods and avoided them, I became a people pleaser, codependent, problem fixer, quiet, passive, workhorse who did things for mom, everything she wanted. I cooked at a young age. I cleaned house. I parentified mom, becoming her confident and best friend for her to confide in and complain about dad. I had no childhood. In order to do this. I HAD TO REJECT MY TRUE SELF FROM A VERY YOUNG AGE, not even knowing what I was doing. I also, at the same time, had to BUILD A FALSE SELF that was what everyone wanted me to be. The one difference between the narcissist and me, which was a big one, was that I loved, and I loved hard, and I was sweet, nice, caring and loving, while she was mean, unless she was faking her niceness for the public and people outside of our family unit. Otherwise, me and the Narc both had false selfs and pretended to be that which we aren’t. That is SOUL DEPLETING. My dad died, and I tried to save him during his illness from my family’s abuse… now turned on him. Of course, I couldn’t save him. I couldn’t save myself even. This devastated me. Then, when he died, I quickly realized just how much of the “scapegoat load” he had carried for our family. I now had the sole role of being SG to 4 brothers, their wives, mom. When I fought against my family for the sake of dad, I was rejected, with 2 of my brothers immediately going no contact with me… I then isolated myself and had to mourn his death alone. The very family I needed at that time wasn’t there for me. This further threw me further into CPTSD, with new and additional abuse, more abandonment, isolation, etc. I could barely cope, but was starting to recover gradually during the 2 years following his death. Then, at that time (2 years later) my spouse of 7 years cheated on me and deserted me emotionally, leaving for awhile. I had a nervous breakdown that lasted off and on for 4–6 months. Therapy and meds saved me. I still wasn’t over the death of dad when my spouse did this. He was narcissistic. After all of this, losing my family at once, and then my spouse 2 years later, I was as you describe. Numb, panic attacks, crying episodes off and on for days at times, often very sad and hopeless, confused, foggy brain, untrusting, high BP, couldn’t really leave the house very often, except for work, and then right home, etc. I truly couldn’t cope well. For me, I was taken down to such a low level, mainly by my dad dying. Him being the scapegoat, I called him the “glue that held our family together” and I really recognized this immediately upon his death. Our family has never been the same and is broken apart. Normally, I would help keep us together, planning events and smoothing over hurt feelings as they came up often between various brothers and their wives. But now, I had been so wounded, and suffered immensely from the loss of dad. He was the main one and pretty much the only one who really loved me. True love. I felt his loss immensely and deeply. I loved each member of my family, but could see how they did not love. I especially loved dad. My family was turning on each other like a pack of wolves. It was unreal and tragic to witness. Mom abused dad emotionally and physically during his dementia. Once I witnessed the extent of this, with dad being such a victim and like a child since he had dementia, I immediately no longer loved mom. The gig was up and I saw her for exactly what she was. She sent dad away, putting him in a nursing home when he was fine to be at home. I truly hated her and now resentment and guilt added on to the rest of what I was feeling. Just the loss of him alone, I believe would have sent me into this crisis as you describe. But, losing my family, holidays, and then my spouse, sent me into a deep crisis and years of therapy. I’m guessing you’ve had something similar happen. If you lose a scapegoat in your family system, they carried much of the family drama, and problems… they are the “trash receptacle” and you will feel this loss. Also, SG’s are capable of deep love, IMO. That is why they are the scapegoat. They do it out of love for their family. And then, I too was a SG. My family not only loaded me up with trash, but also sent me out to pasture AS THE TRASH. At least when you’re taking on the trash, but not yet BECOMING the trash, you have a worthy role in the family and feel useful. But, when sent out to pasture, now being considered the trash, this is SO REJECTING and SO DEMORALIZING and you feel so UNSAFE and your basic needs that were barely met, now are not being met at all. It’s a SHOCK TO THE SYSTEM. In order to survive, the body will shut down anything that isn’t desperately needed, and that would be your need to love. Belonging trumps love, and you’ve just been removed from belonging. Your safety has been very threatened according to your body. This is why you feel the way you do. The body goes into fight or flight, or freeze or fawn. Numbness, which you are describing, is a form of “freeze.” I’m thinking you’re experiencing a form of “freeze” in the fight or flight syndrome. Hopefully, you can resonate with some of what I’ve said in order to begin healing, which starts with understanding and recognizing what you’re going through. Understanding is the first step to healing.Don’t pressure yourself. It took you many years to suffer through abuse, possibly a lifetime of abuse. Go easy on yourself. You are the only one who can love and care for you, and now you really really need to do that. Allow yourself concessions, setbacks, mistakes, etc. It may take years to recover, but you will see gradual and steady growth if you work at it and be kind to yourself.Go to therapy. If they aren’t helping after the first few sessions, find a different one. Don’t tolerate one who blames you. I’m sure you blame you, and your narc blames you. WE CANNOT HAVE A THERAPIST WHO BLAMES US. If they do, they aren’t a good one, and they don’t understand. Find a new one.Take Meds if you need to and if they help, in order to speed up your recovery a bit and help you get through this.Read books on narcissism. Go to support groups if you like to do that. You can join online ones. Try to understand it. That in itself is empowering, and that is why I wrote out so much explaining my situation so you can understand it, and maybe resonate.Youtube is a great resource. Dr. Ramani, Teal Swan, Richard Grannon, Lisa Romero… there are many others I can look up that I follow. Just ask if you want more names.Practice and implement healing techniques. Inner child work. Boundaries. No contact or low contact. Learn to identify narcs in your life. Learn what healthy relationships look like.I would suggest you don’t start out “trying to get your old self back” yet. That is the END goal, and it’s too far away. It puts too much pressure on yourself. Then, you will beat yourself up, just like the narc beat you up, because you can’t achieve that in a week, or a month and you feel you should be able to. You can’t really realize just how much trauma you’ve been through until you start down your healing pathway. Small goals. Little improvements. Growth to a better you. Not just the “you before your narc,” but instead an OVERALL BETTER YOU. More healthy, not one who can be abused by a new narc. Try to set a goal to feel more at peace, more often is a good one for now. Or, to go no contact with your narc. Or, to learn how to set boundaries and to try to spot them. Seek out small wins and then cheer yourself on.Lastly, if you have any friendships left that are healthy, try not to talk to them too much about the narcissist. Don’t use them as a therapist or sounding board, too often. I’ve already made this post too long! So, I don’t want to go into all the reasons why…. but let this friendship be your sanity, your “Palace outside of the narcissistic relationship, that is healthy.” Let it be a place of refuge. Leave the incessant talking for your therapist, or for Quora. Let your therapist help heal you, not your friends. Don’t taint your healthy relationships with the narcissist information. It’s toxic. Keep those relationships sacred, positive, healthy and a retreat away from the narcissism. Also, that can be a place where you can practice “being your old self” slowly and in small ways.Much love to you. You will not only get back to a version of your old self eventually, but with healing and some time and work, you will be a new and improved, stronger and healthier version of your true self.

column1: I feel really bad since my grandfather died in September and I started to suspect that I have depression. How do I tell my mom about it?
column3: My heart goes out to you. I am very sorry for your loss. I know how hard it is to lose a grandparent you are very close to and it sounds like you two were very close. When my grandma died in the early 90’s, I was sure life as I knew it was gone. I loved her so much, she was my saving grace. She l;loved me unconditionally, and I knew it. She was there during the happiest times of my life and there for me during the saddest and hardest. She never wavered, she never abandoned me. Even now, writing this brings tears to my eyes. Fact is, I miss her, sometimes madly. I do not believe we get over the loss of our loved ones. I believe we learn to go on and we tuck them into our hearts and memories. You sweetie, as hard as it may seem to wrap your brain around it, are right where you are suppose to be. Grieving is a different kind of beast. Experiencing feelings of not knowing if you are the only one that feels this way is very normal. It has only been 4 months. If you are still where you are right now and not making any movement at about month 9 or ten then yes, I would begin looking for some help. Although, your mom sure would like to know. She knows you and will have a better gauge of how you are doing than I would. Give her a chance to support you. That’s her job and most mom’s are very good at the job God gave them to do. It’s okay to tell her. I’ll bet she has some of the same feelings and is trying to hide them as not to hurt you. It is okay for you two to grieve together. It will strengthen your relationship; not saying it’s not already strong. Hiding how you are feeling now will only give you encouragement to hide things from her later. The following is an answer to a question from a parent whom lost a child. I speculated and hope I was at least close in thinking that maybe they were feeling stuck. This group is for pretty much any age. I would imagine itty bitty’s not. Some people need it and some don’t. I did. And I am glad I did. It took me a long time to get there. Pride you know. I thought I should have been able to get through it all on my own. Grief, believe it or not, takes a while to go through. You must not rush yourself or let anyone rush you. It is done on your time. That is very important. If you are somewhat depressed, know that this will probably pass. Getting on anti-depressant’s may be jumping the gun if your normal self can take care of you on your own…if you get what I mean. We were, well most of us, born with what is needed to go through trauma. And, we pretty much know what we can handle and what we cannot. I’m thinking you might be a teenager. If you don’t need medication to get through this, then I would take my time, love myself as I am, be gentle with me and let it take it’s course. If you have had it, then absolutely, go see your doc. Okay? Your mom might ask you, do you weant to go see the doctor? Do you feel like you need counseling? Or, honey, what can I or what do you need me to do for you, how can I help? If you need her to hold you while you just cry, please ask her. In the late 1990’s, I facilitated grief groups within the facility I worked. I am a person who is able to go deep so I was in the place I was supposed to be. But, when my brother died, I had no idea what to do, how to act, do I talk about it, do I stay quiet, why do these people seem to want me to console them, am I doing this right, shouldn’t I be better by now??? Is this ever gonna end? Or, how about driving down the freeway and you suddenly feel like you have been hit head on by a Mac Truck? The weeping comes so hard and so fast that it practically knocks you down. Those are called waves. The waves come when they want, they don’t care if you are ready…or not. No, they won’t last forever. Grieving comes in waves. Mine hit’s me in the car driving, (I have a deal with God, somehow through the tears just at least let me see enough to go on or pull over) or, I wake up in the morning crying. Because of the way my brother died and I suppose because 6 others (two other family members and 4 friends) thought they needed to die that year, by the time 2016 came around, I was absolutely stuck, angry, depressed and so full of blame that I couldn’t move. I saw it and reached out to my church. Just so happens there was a grief group starting up in a couple of months. It gave me freedom from myself and my anger and it gave me back my tender, compassionate heart. Best thing I had found in a long time. GriefShare. That is the name and that is the correct way to spell it. Let me put some information in here for you. The groups are run by people like you and me. The videos are a God send. The following is taken from the GriefShare website: “How GriefShare works It may be hard for you to feel optimistic about the future right now. If you’ve lost a spouse, child, family member, or friend, you’ve probably found there are not many people who understand the deep hurt you feel. GriefShare groups meet weekly to help you face these challenges and move toward rebuilding your life. Each GriefShare session has three distinct elements: Video seminar with experts Each week your GriefShare group will watch a video seminar featuring top experts on grief and recovery subjects. These videos are produced in an interesting television magazine format featuring expert interviews, real-life case studies, dramatic reenactments, and on-location video. Support group discussion with focus After viewing the video, you and the other group members will spend time as a support group, discussing what was presented in that week’s video seminar and what is going on in your lives. Personal study and reflection During the week you will have the opportunity to use your workbook for further personal study of the grieving process and to help sort out your emotions through journaling. Your group will spend time discussing questions and comments from the workbook study. This can be a confusing time when you feel isolated and have many questions about things you’ve never faced before. Being a part of a GriefShare grief recovery support group “I’ve never been to a support group like this before. I don’t know what to expect.” Most people quickly feel comfortable and accepted in their GriefShare group. They discover there are others who have the same kind of feelings they do and who understand the hurt they feel and the loss they have experienced. Here is an overview of the GriefShare experience: You’ll probably feel a little nervous about going to GriefShare the first time.Those feelings go away quickly for most people, usually during the first session they attend. GriefShare is a warm, caring environment designed to help you. You’ll discover there are people who understand your hurts, emotions, and painful experiences! When someone you love dies, it’s common to feel isolated. In GriefShare, you’ll find that you are not alone, that there are others who understand what you are going through. You’ll learn helpful, practical information that will help you recover from the pain of grief and loss. The GriefShare DVD videos feature top experts on grief recovery subjects and case studies of people just like you, who have been through the grief experience. You’ll have the chance to talk about your experiences. It can be very healing to tell others what you are going through. The support group sessions include a time to talk about what you’ve seen on the GriefShare videos and what is going on in your life. And while you have the opportunity to tell your story, there’s never pressure for you to do so if you don’t feel like it. You’ll have a workbook for personal study and to write down things you’ve learned. The workbook provides opportunity for further study about the grief process and personal reflection about your grief. The weekly journaling questions help you sort through your emotions. You can tear out and carry with you the perforated “Care Cards” for words of encouragement during the lowest points of your day.You’ll begin to gain closure in your loss. It’s sometimes hard to move on in life when you are still dealing with the grief and emptiness that happens after a loved one dies. You’ll learn how to go through a healthy season of grieving, then begin transitioning to emotional and spiritual wholeness. We call this “your journey from mourning to joy.” You’ll become part of a “family.” GriefShare group members often tell us that they feel like their group has become a family, that they made new friends and are around people they can relate to. You’ll discover hope for the future. While things may look bleak now, you’ll learn ways to restore your hope and rebuild your life. Many GriefShare alumni tell us the program helped them move from deep grief to peace and a sense of joy again. Group leadership The leadership team for GriefShare consists of people who understand how you feel and have a real concern for individuals experiencing the grief of loss. Most GriefShare leaders have experienced significant losses in their lives and are examples of the healing and restoration that can occur as an outgrowth of deep grief.” I didn’t want to have to go to this group. I kept telling myself, “Kel, you used to facilitate these groups, you gotta pull it together, you know what you need to do.” No, I didn’t, I was stuck and angry. Not a good place to be. I went. The videos are amazing. They are not actors. They are people like you and me grieving and talking about it. I started to feel human again. By the end of 13 weeks I also found forgiveness for the person I blamed for my brother’s death. Today, I have compassion for her and someday, I hope I can meet her face to face…we need a hug. You will get a work book to help you with your feelings and the anger that will come up and every other emotion. I believe in this program. It works, every one of us in the group was given the gift of “growth” while we were there. And, we got to watch each other move from anger or guilt or complete sadness to the place of at least welcoming acceptance. I don’t believe we “get over” our losses. I believe we learn to live with them. But, isn’t it true also, for us to live with something don’t we have to find some acceptance first? GriefShare can help you begin to think about acceptance or they can help you achieve acceptance. I was elated that I was not the only one feeling the way I felt. That’s what grief does to us. It is a different kind of beast. Grief is an amazing emotion that puts you on a hell of a ride. But, that ride can be overcome. These groups are normally facilitated in a church, you do not have to be a member or a believer…just a griever. And there is never any pressure. Please, keep your heart open for yourself. You are the most important person in your life right now. If you need the support, it will be there. To find a group close to you call one of the numbers listed below, they will have the information you need to get you started. If GriefShare is not offered in your community, then please call a Hospice. They will absolutely know how to help you as well. And most of all…please know this…You are NOT ALONE! You can message me anytime. Please take care of you. Blessings! With Much Love! :) Kelly PS If you would like to chat, PM me, we can do that. It’s okay for all of us to support each other. So, here is the website: https://www.griefshare.org/about and some phone numbers: Email: info@griefshare.org Phone: 800-395-5755 International: 919-562-2112 GriefShare is a ministry of Church Initiative. © Church Initiative. column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: You learn to function again by absorbing the loss of that person as part of yourself. You move from being unable to think of anything else, to thinking of them several times a day, to daily, to weekly, to just every so often. I think of my mother and brother every so often, and hardly ever tear up except in certain emotive situations. There are no actions (as far as I know) you can take to accelerate recovery, but there are some attitudes that can prolong or delay grief, like denying how you feel or refusing to talk about the dead person. Interacting with people tends to remind that life goes on, and finding something important to focus on can help avoid depression. 'Time heals', they say, but really it just dampens the effects of pain. It never completely leaves, and that's part of who you are, and that's ok.
column9: Part if my lack of progress was fear of “forgetting”. I didn't want to let go of my memories to end up with a vague moment once in a while. Someone told me to write down everything they did while it was vivid. Best advice ever. Now I have them all tucked away in a book. I can visit any time I want to - and I was able to let go.

column1: How do you manage emotional triggers after narcissistic abuse?
column3: It’s fucking hard, so hard. I’m not sure what is an emotional trigger from the manipulation and lies and what is from my childhood. I am certain what she triggered in me, stems from my childhood and was brought out of the dark hole I had it locked in for years. Triggers are hands down the worst emotional pain a person can feel in my opinion, I haven’t had anything come close. Maybe the death of a child, but triggers are bad. I can’t even explain the feeling. They aren’t as bad as they were, but I can easily take myself back in time and relive it if I want to. But I try and stay out of that part of my brain. The visual triggers, smells and songs are getting less and less. but they are still resting ready to pounce when called upon. How do you manage them? You have to be aware of what it is. It’s an emotional response to abuse. I found a therapist that is working with me in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and EMDR. The purpose of the CBT is to become aware of your thoughts, and be able to process them. So many times I catch myself ruminating on something she said, did, or what she is doing, in return, I am tormenting myself with my thoughts. What the Narcissist has triggered was laying dormant the whole time, their abuse just woke up what you need to address to live your best fucking life. column1: What is the appropriate response when someone tells you that they are getting a divorce? With a divorce, it can be unclear if they feel happy or sad about the outcome.
column3: You should: Give them a hug*Spend some time talking. It can be about the divorce or about anything elseDon't feel awkwardCall them up in a few weeks First an aside: Nobody is happy about a divorce. Even if it's something that a person chooses, it still represents the dissolution of a relationship, some difficult division of property, and may include messy legal and custody issues. Every marriage starts with joy and hope, and no matter how much of a relief it is to be moving on, the end of a marriage represents the death of that joy and hope. Hug This is really important. There's a lot of sadness and shame for most people getting divorced, even if they did nothing wrong. A hug is a powerful way to communicate to your friend that she is accepted and loved. It's also important because if they're getting divorced, they're separating from the person that used to give them physical comfort. You don't always realize that you need a hug, but that doesn't mean the need isn't urgent. Talk Talking about the divorce itself, the causes, the fallout, and the recovery is something everyone who gets divorced needs to do. But they also need to talk about other things. Conversations on other topics still communicate "I'm your friend and I care about you," but they also offer a respite from the negative emotions that surround the divorce. Even people getting divorced need to hang out. Don't feel like you failed if you spend an hour talking and discover that you only covered political news and the local sports team. Don't feel awkward You might feel like you don't know what to say. Maybe you don't know how to act around a person who's getting divorced. Here's a secret: he doesn't know how to act either. After you give them a hug, say something that they can run with (toward or away from the divorce) like "how are you doing?" Wait for the answer, even if it takes a while. Follow their lead on what to talk about. If the conversation has run out, don't be afraid to start talking about something in your life. Sometimes a short soliloquy gets things back on track and gives your friend something to discuss with you. Call them again People often say "let me know if there's anything I can do." There is! The problem is that when you're in emotional pain (whether divorce, death, or disappointment), you're not very good at articulating your physical and emotional needs. Being sad usually means not being as proactive about spending time with friends. What your friend needs is for you to call her up and make plans in a few weeks. People are very responsive at the beginning of an emotional trauma, but your friend will need your support for weeks or months, not days. *I'll assume that if they're telling you about a divorce that they're still in the process, and that they're someone you would call a friend. If it's an overshare from a distant acquaintance, you should probably do something different.

column1: How does one recover from narcissistic abuse?
column3: Deep depression, the darkest place you’ve ever been. You are likely trauma bonded to your abuser, so even though she treated you like absolute shit, and property, and disposed of you like used toilet paper, you don’t remember how to function as a member of society without her. Now, you can stay there forever … or you can seek help. Therapy is a God-send. It helps clear your field of vision. You begin to see just what it was you were subjected to. For me, I felt ashamed at first - how could I be so stupid? Then anger - I hope she dies a terrible, horrible death. Then disgust - how can anyone look at themselves when they treat ANYONE like that, let alone someone who gave so much. Finally, indifference … fuck her, she’s my used toilet paper now. She’s going to keep on living her pathetic, shallow cycle, and I’m going to do me. At the end of the day, I’m proud of me - she needed me, I didn’t need her. I was able to provide joy to someone devoid of it for 5 years. I gave back to someone for nothing in return, and I owe her nothing now. She can thank me, or she can keep hoovering. But I did my part to make her life better for a short while. Hope that helps.
column9: I’m somewhere between hoping he dies a horrible death and finding the thought of him disgusting. My therapist gave me a useful tool today. I was telling her about the nice things he did in the beginning and I’m sorry to say it took some effort to come up with any. But each one she was able to trace back to his motives for doing them. Every single nice thing he did for me was for his own benefit. Every one. It was eye opening. The nice guy I thought he was didn’t even exist in the beginning. Everything was all about him from the start. It makes it easier to let go.

column1: Why is it that the narcissist remains in your thoughts over and over again? I can't seem to get him out of my head.
column3: This was quite a mind bender for me too because in the aftermath of a brutal discard, trying desperately to make sense of things after a 3 year relationship and FIVE breakups, having been manipulated, lied to repeatedly, cheated on, toyed with, insidiously abused, betrayed, proposed marriage to and then replaced within 3 weeks with all that horrendous soul destroying stuff I absolutely KNEW there was NO logical, practical or sensible reason for me to need or even want that relationship but YET I had this feeling deep down into my inner core that I would do almost anything to get it back. Why?? Why was I feeling that way?? It was an overwhelming feeling and the despair was unlike anything I'd ever felt… so why ?? I mean come on, I've had relationships, I've had breakups… but THIS was something else. And it was in that moment I realised something was wrong. Something was VERY WRONG!! As normal human beings we respond on all levels to what our five senses are perceiving and translating to us as reality… so during the love bombing stage we see, smell, touch, hear and even taste this individual as REAL and wonderful and the perfect soulmate that the universe has finally delivered. This person is filling your every desire and is so “into you” that you become consumed by this perfect love that is filled with passion and deep connection unlike anything you've known. In your mind you've connected with your soulmate but all it is is their dance of deception. Your brain, in response to this perfect love, is creating a drug addiction. Yes, an actual drug addiction!! Your surging brain chemicals during this phase are creating a highly addictive cocktail of dopamine, serotonin and oxytocin which is equivalent to using cocaine or heroin. Added to this chemical addiction forming in your brain their covert and insidious behaviours are causing rewiring in parts of your brain. This can now be seen with modern CAT Scan technology and shows up as blunt force trauma. So while they’re doing their dance of deception for you they are in fact planting a seed deep into your psyche and emotions and it's this psychological trigger that they use to keep you hooked in with expertly deployed intermittent reinforcement of ‘their love’ for you or to hoover you back in after a discard. Many survivors say it was like they were under some kind of hypnosis and yes, I concur with that fully. These individuals are parasites, set out to suck the soul out of you, to extract your personality because they don't have their own. Looking back, as long as everything and everyone complied to the narc's desires things were peaceful but I did watch the narcissism actually grow over a period of 3 years amongst family and the multi-residential arrangement she had carefully orchestrated to ultimately benefit herself at no cost to her. Really quite sinister. My narc partner was a pathetic individual with all the markings of a full blown narcissist, including a total absence of empathy, being a bald faced liar, had zero knowledge in her head, little conversation skills and fewer life skills. Refused to read a book or newspaper, refused to cook a meal, had no interests in life, no life in her, thorough alcoholic, couldn't organise a piss-up in a brewery, control freak, pathetic lover and honestly, I kid you not.. looking back she truly brought nothing of value to the relationship. And I mean nothing!! Everything was a reflection of me. I brought everything; the music, the laughter, the fun, the plans for outings, the romance, the seduction, the passion and everything in between so why the hell was I feeling the way I was feeling??? The person I'd been so deeply in love with had revealed herself as something evil that was capable of destroying good and decent folk. Yes, I had seen many red flags including the utterly deplorable manner in which she had treated my predecessor, many more horror stories I came to hear of only after our final breakup that were just unbelievable!! This realisation was shocking but even that did not eliminate the feeling of that longing and pining for the loss of something that didn't exist… This individual was apparently just an illusion… WTF??… the loss of an illusion, a fabrication, a figment of my imagination and simply a mirror reflection of myself that had shown up as an actual person, physical and tangible!! And after a brutal discard you are grieving the death of something that didn't exist but that person is still a living breathing entity and you know they're out there doing the same to someone else that they did to you. Talk about a mind fuck!!!! The abuse is unfathomable. I'm well aware the narc smears me on a regular basis. When things were good she'd say she was very attracted to my intellect, that my mind and knowledge was sheer brilliance BUT when I'd buck against what I later came to know as insidious abuse or if I caught her in a lie she’d tell me I psychoanalyse everything and my mind didn't work like normal people. That’s called gas lighting…. and then came the triangulations and the manipulations and the scary thing is; when the narc is playing this all out you have NO idea you're in a soul destroying abusive relationship. You realise from time to time something is a bit ‘off' but you put that down to bad day, bad week, let me make your mood better, can I pour you a drink… and so it goes. They will often use the ex as a triangulation tactic. Name dropping and comparing you to the ex is great for breaking you down. After a traumatic breakup the smear campaign is another horrendous form of abuse from these individuals. After going out of their way to crush you they then embark on further destruction by way of horrendous lies about you to anyone who will listen. For those in recovery; when you can deal with the drug addiction and understand it to be that and also to understand that the realationship caused some rewiring of your brain, with some retraining of your mind and psyche you will heal. As with any addiction there will always be a residual feeling but you will overcome this with time so give yourself at least a year to start feeling a little more normal because healing from this hell is a process. This is no ordinary relationship and no ordinary break up so support groups are vitally important for recovery. Few therapists know how to treat people with NVS (narcissistic victim syndrome) so knowledge of what has happened in your life is what will ultimately break you out of this hell. If you haven't done prayer or meditation for cutting soul ties please give it some serious thought as this has proven to be an important step both spiritually and psychologically. You can find many guided meditations for this on YouTube. And then forgive yourself too. And love yourself. Know that you are good enough, you are a wonderful and magnificent person of value to the world. That's why the narc chose you… because YOU ARE GREAT!! You are everything they will never be and that's why they try to destroy you so beat them by bouncing back. Keep moving in a forward direction, self care and self love are vital…. maintain no contact and God speed in your healing towards truth and real love.
column9: This was a very good visceral description of what it's like to be with a narc. Hell on Earth. Somehow, there should be a law against such evilness. This behavior on the part of a narc is abuse of the highest order. Through information and realization of who and what narcs are, they can be shut down before the misery begins. There is hope!

column1: What are the effects of Ketu on the 8th house in a birth chart?
column3: South Node or ketu in the 8th house for men and women The south node in the 8th house is reflected in the natal chart of the native - his fate, and life. This house suggests the need to learn how to use all your strength to the fullest. In this case, it is not so much about the strength that characterizes the fruits of ambition and success in society, but about the will of the spirit and the power that oozes from the dark, deep depths of the soul. At the beginning of the path, a person may not be aware of this energy, and even more so, he does not know how to manage it. The ability to breathe life into something is hard, deep work, and once awakened, this ability will change your life forever. Features of nodes and their phases in astrology You should refer to the ascending or north node, otherwise called Rahu and the Dragon Head, and the setting or south node, Ketu and the dragon tail, if you are interested in learning about previous lives and inner development. Such combinations in the natal chart began to be called nodes, based on an Indian legend. In it, a demon in the guise of a snake drank the sacred drink of Amrit and became immortal, but it was cut into two halves, each of which became a separate creature, connected by internal force with the second. This legend refers to the legends about the opposition of Surya and Chandra, or the Sun and the Moon. Lunar nodes in astrology are called the intersection of the orbit of the Moon and the ecliptic of the Earth, where we are talking mainly about the Moon. Lunar nodes are always associated with eclipses. In astronomy, lunar and solar eclipses always occur near the south or north node. This is exactly what is described in the Indian legend of the confrontation between Surya and Chandra. When a solar eclipse occurs, Surya wins, and when the Sun and Moon diverge and a lunar eclipse occurs, Chandra wins. In the horoscope, the nodes characterize the karmic movement of the soul. The south node symbolizes the collection of previous lives that can help to succeed in the present rebirth, which denotes the north node. By the location of the nodes, you can understand whether a person will be able to realize himself in life or it will be filled with problems. Important note phases:Every 18.6 years there is a return during which the first karmic results are summed up, which is why it is considered a difficult period. People, especially those born on an eclipse, may feel desperate and wish for suicide. The next time this period will come at the age of 37, but even then this time will not be easy for people.About once every 9 years, a semi-circulation occurs. At this time, the world begins to react to how the right path you have chosen for yourself. The next semi-conversion occurs at age 27, this event includes the "27 club" - people who committed suicide at 27 years old.So, in a person's life, half-conversion occurs at 9-10 and 27-28 years old, conversion - 18-19 and 36-37 years old, and further in their frequency. What do the lunar nodes show? The lunar nodes in the natal chart reflect what knowledge and practice the soul has acquired in previous reincarnations and what it should acquire in the next rebirths. The south descending node, or Ketu, reflects the experience gained in previous lives, and the north ascending node, or Rahu, reflects what a person must realize for himself in the present reality. At the same time, it is important to take into account the fact that it is not at all necessary to live as prescribed by the provisions of the knots. Professional astrologers study the natal chart in its entirety, and not just the nodes, which symbolize the knowledge that has been received and those that need to be received. You can’t stop after you have “acquired” the necessary information, you must constantly develop and gain new experiences, albeit not always positive. Life is ready to push you on the right path and put you in various situations while you are living your astrological destiny. So you should not make the realization of the tasks of the lunar nodes your meaning of life. Interpretation of the south node in the 8th house Of course, the 8th house holds many secrets, it was not without reason that it used to be called the “House of Death”. If we consider death from the point of view of reincarnation, then such a name is quite logical, because it symbolizes the death of the former “I” to acquire a more elevated state: from weak to strong, from sick to healthy. The power of the 8th house lies in careful introspection to find the energy in yourself for recovery and awareness of something. Apply it, and then you will see the light in the darkness and you will be able to order the chaos. In another way, you can say that for a while you become a shaman who goes to the primordial realm to find valuables there and share them with the world in which you live at the moment. an example is the Phoenix - a bird that, after death, is born every time from the ashes left from it. The eighth house is also referred to as the house of relationships. This is a symbol that you will have to find an ally who will be with you in this life. In the present, you should find a balance between the strengths and values ​​​​of you and your partner, but you will not be able to realize this alone. You will understand how powerful support for the development of relationships can be given by combining your means, whether it be emotions, money, strength, or anything else, the main thing is that thanks to this you and your partner will be able to support each other and get a sense of calm, security. If we are talking about the sexual sphere, then we mean not a short romance without a chance for continuation. The Eighth House symbolizes sexuality, which removes all prohibitions and makes it possible to discover something new, previously incomprehensible. The French called it "little death", which is a door to another world that cannot be perceived by the senses, but which contains the most inaccessible energy. This world opens when there is a strong emotional and spiritual relationship with a partner, where both people are equal. In such relationships, no one will hide or deceive, they can give impetus to the deep rebirth of everyone. It is worth mentioning concepts that can to some extent underestimate knowledge about the eighth house but are fundamentally important. It will be about trust - to accept for yourself that a person will keep an important secret from you; betrayal - the ability to turn away from another person in an attempt to build a strong relationship with another; risk - to decide to show your partner what you are. These include qualities such as dependency, suspicion, and possessiveness. They arise when a person fails to balance the area that is now being discussed. Of course, this includes fear. Fear of parting with a person if he decides to leave you, and fear of what awaits you ahead if you decide to continue your journey together. New difficulties arise with a detailed study of the descending node, which forms the principles of human behavior, given its karmic past from the second house in the horoscope. Probably, in the past, situations happened to you where you had to survive because of some dangerous incident. Such events can be an economic or social crisis, a natural disaster, or a dangerous disease that claimed the life of a person close to you. In such conditions, your main task was to survive yourself. After feeling the severity of the problems, inner energy opened up to you, thanks to which you can provide yourself with protection. Such a karmic inheritance will be very helpful in real life if you meet the tasks of the ascending node on your way. At the same time, it should be borne in mind that we are studying the descending node without covering all its characteristics.At the same time, we partially look through rose-colored glasses, because the level of protection and happiness is determined by the criteria established by the people themselves. You may have made key mistakes in judging something because you gave the wrong answer to the question of where the boundaries of what is acceptable are. For example, earlier you were so obsessed with your happiness that you forgot to take into account the needs and values ​​​​of the environment, and now the principles of your life have not changed much. Or perhaps you are materially and financially secure because you do not pay attention to the personal boundaries of people because of neglect or because of your frivolity. In the most unpleasant situation, your new life will not give you such happiness, and you will have to achieve it again. The eighth house is ready to tell you about the deep power and give you a chance to live this life with dignity. Before you help people, you need to understand what they want. A person is unlikely to be able to take a clear point of view regarding the basis and direction of the development of society until he balances his own and social ethical standards. In spiritual terms, a person can often experience stagnation in development, because the strongest subconscious programs are aimed at changing the rules of behavior in the outside world and the psyche, a normal life is evaluated precisely with their help and therefore may seem boring and meaningless - this is called the aspect of a professional revolutionary. And the programs of adaptation to the outside world and the creation of one's ethics are being studied and developed, and one's ethics may categorically disagree with the public, as it is perceived at the subconscious level as an indestructible base. Thus, the spiritual development of a person consists in balancing these two ethics. The south node in the 8th house is evidence of a lot of problems or stagnation in the professional field, problems with the excretory system, indicates a shorter life span, less mental stability, propensity for crime or conflict actions, loss of inheritance, and other troubles. Such a person can be addicted to emotions and make dangerous enemies. A person whose horoscope has the south node in the 8th house has no remorse or inconvenience when using other people's money, whether it belongs to another person or a bank. He should pay attention to the development of internal and external values ​​and property and not resort to the use of someone else's. Thus, he will begin to value his work higher, he can become smarter, close all debts and start life without financial problems. How to Harmonize the South Node in the 8th House Get over yourself and trust someone. While you are looking for a suitable partner for yourself to realize the power of the ascending node, higher powers send people to you who can help you. You just need to study all the candidates and choose the right one. So, you should try to fully trust your partner and devote yourself without a trace to relationships with him in all areas. It is important not to attribute to him characteristics that cannot be called positive. Thus, you will partially get rid of these characteristics and will not undermine relations with an ally. The journey you're preparing for can be intimidating, so you need to have a partner ready to go with you. Do not forget that when choosing a companion, the main role should not be played by his external beauty or gender, because we are talking about the most important choice. Of course, you can make a mistake, but subsequent troubles are unlikely to break you. So you will become stronger and will be able to make the right choice in the future, the main thing is not to give up. Don't be afraid to confide in another person, such an experience is extremely important, even if the results do not live up to expectations. If your ascending node is in the eighth house, expand your knowledge. Spend more time reading. If the south node is in the sign of Scorpio, you have probably already read everything you need to know, and if it is also in the 8th house, then it is a good idea to reread the books that you had before. For people who study the space of the 8th house, namely the occult, higher powers are ready to help in every possible way. The means of occult help have their dimensions, they can be compared with how clothes are selected. Someone will be content with the clear characteristics of the natal chart, for someone on a subconscious level, the results of the layout of Tarot cards will suit, and for someone, a logical approach to things in numerology that should be understood sensually will be an ideal option. Try all the variations of help from the Universe and decide on the ones that are most suitable for you. In this way, you will be closer to entering the inner world, which cannot be touched or seen but contains the knowledge and power of the universe. Talk to a medium that people you know may have told you about, r an astrologer who might give lectures on karma as a trial course. Try to find a fortuneteller in the area of ​​​​esoteric shops or shops who will read Tarot cards for you. Try to find out what they are dealing with in the "other" world of the eighth house. Be sure that you will find an inner response. Sign up for diving lessons. The 8th house wants you to be brave. Few people are not afraid to jump into the abyss from where their knowledge was sufficient for protection. Courage is also needed insight into what surrounds you and relaxation in it. Of course, the ascending node gives by no means simple tests, but you should not make them more difficult. The universe does not approve of the complication of life, it is already difficult. It expects you to seek reasonable support during the execution of the task. It is worth contacting a psychologist if the eighth house has filled you with problems, this is especially true at the beginning. After all, when you first dive with scuba diving, you must have an instructor with you. And one more thing. If your south node is in Scorpio, then the energy of this combination will be visible to the naked eye. It will not only double your strength and increase your options for solving problems, but it will also increase your challenges. If the ascending node is located in Taurus, the signs from the Universe and the situation will not be so obvious.
