column1: I have heard that being burned alive is not as horrific as it may seem as the victim's nerves are obliterated almost immediately and thus there isn't as much pain as one would think. Is this scientifically accurate?
column3: From those I've spoken with, and in most accounts I've read, being burned “alive” is the worst experience ever, though I have listened to the story of an Argentinian architect who was burned up in his pickup truck who didn't immediately feel pain at being engulfed, and personally treated a patient who was burned in his vehicle but didn't feel pain until a minute or so after he was engulfed, and have read the account of a woman who was in a plane that caught on fire with a fireball slamming through the cabin. She said she felt a “warm cloud” blow over her and she passed out, along with similar recollections in people caught in fireballs from large explosions, i.e., no pain before losing consciousness. It is possible the massive sensory overload from such overwhelming fireballs makes it impossible for the brain to immediately perceive pain[1], and it’s been shown how combined sensory inputs (noise, touch, vibration) can basically “drown out” the immediate sense of pain. What is impossible to tell is the role of post traumatic amnesia. But these are cases of overwhelming injury occurring all at once. Their REAL pain comes later, during months of treatment in hospital. If, however, you’re burned gradually - especially when you can anticipate it like a trapped firefighter or someone staked down by rogues like ISIS can[2], you will feel it. Horribly so, and the following accounts confirm this. Moreover, if burning wasn't so horrible, it would not have been, historically, one of the favored “worst things" that could be done to a person, by any culture anywhere on earth, whether as a means of execution or for torture. I attended a burn seminar, at the end of which a burn survivor—a physicist—spoke to us all. He had been in his truck when, for some reason, his vehicle burst into flame. He described the pain as…indescribable, and then he passed out. He woke up intermittently, felt the pain all over again, heard noises of emergency personnel, and went out. Over 18 months later he finally left rehabilitation facility, his story moving us all to tears. “Bullshit!” answered a guest speaker at my fire academy, in response to a questioner asking “Coroners always tell us guys caught in fires die of asphyxiation, and that you don't feel anything.” “You feel plenty”, continued the guest speaker, a firefighter who nearly burned to death during the 1987 Lauder Fire as he and his partners sheltered in “shake and bake” fire shelters all wildland firefighters must carry. Like so many burn survivors, this incredibly inspirational black man, covered with obvious scars over his face and scalp, described the situation and how, by ignoring certain warning signs, his group were caught by surprise when the fire blew up below them.The video above begins just before the burn-over. The firefighter interviewed here was not our guest speaker, but he echoes what is written below. PS: I don’t know why our speaker was not on this video—I cannot find him anywhere.About to be caught in this inferno, he and his partners struggled through thick vegetation to an area of “black” (an area of vegetation which had already been burned before and which was therefore considered relatively safe). Realizing too late this particular black was still super-heated ground covered with glowing coals like you find in a charcoal grill, they deployed their shelters, having little other choice. In the panic of the moment, partner Dennis Cullins pitched his shelter near a log that was still actively smouldering. The survivor firefighter said Cullins’ screaming went on for a long time, tormenting him. Eventually, Dennis’ screams weakened, and finally stopped.As guilty as this made him feel, he said it was a relief when the screams finally stopped. As for himself, he said the pain was indescribably intense, burning the fronts of his legs and his elbows down to his forearms. He began to smell cooking meat and realized it was him, and the the pain faded somewhat as his flesh charred. You may wonder why I mention the speaker’s race? It is funny. He described that for years after the fire, his skin was so sensitive he had to wear a ski mask whenever he was outside in the sun. “Imagine,” he joked, “A black guy wearing a ski mask and walking into the bank to get some money.” Former Firefighter Featured in Online Documentary After Surviving Severe Burns This guy was lucky in comparison, the fire whirl (think “Dust Devil” but carrying flames instead) hitting him so fast it was past within seconds. Nearby resources were able to get him into what looks like a sleeping bag, part of a “Santa Clara burn pack.” What he remembers is the unrelenting pain. As part of our fire academy and on-going training, all of us were exposed to many of these incidents as abject warnings of what would happen if we screwed up on a fire assignment. As a medic I've run on a fair number of burns, and not a single one didn’t involve excruciating pain. I gave this following guy the most narcotic medication I’ve ever given a person. Driving east bound on the I10 in a crappy truck, this guy was scalded when his radiator blew, the steam blowing through his firewall. I found him, skin peeling from his torso, as he danced around under a garden hose he was using to direct water over his body. He was hurting. I told him, “Dude, this isn’t going to make any sense to you, but we have to get you warm. So enjoy the water for a few seconds while we set up for you. I’ll give you plenty of pain medication.” I gave him all the morphine I had and it only eased his pain a bit.The screams of trapped victims in burning cars is something anyone who hears never forgets either. Apparently, the only pain worse than the pain of being burned, is the pain of surviving. The process of recovery and rehabilitation begins with what every burn patient remembers as physically and emotionally traumatic, and includes debriding (scraping) of damaged or scarred tissues, (watch this video to see how grafting and debriding is done), cleaning, and repeating over and over again for weeks to months, with later rehabilitation taking months or years. Some hospitals, including designated burn centers do this badly, allowing the patient to remain awake during the procedures, which, no matter how much pain medication they give, is still awful. Advanced burn centers such as Grossman Burn Centers just put you out each time, a much more humane process. Your scarred skin may take months or years before it can tolerate sunlight again either. The life-changing experience of severe burns is so powerful, it is not uncommon for those who’ve gone through the painful recovery process to become burn care specialists themselves, like this physician did, or join support groups who in turn try to help subsequent victims. In a nutshell, those who say burn victims died of suffocation are technically correct, but deceptively so, like telling you to “take comfort, because despite the fact he was tortured for hours by having every bone broken in his body, he actually died of shock, and shock itself doesn't hurt much.” There's a long time to feel the pain before the mercy of losing consciousness actually happens.Footnotes[1] Brain correlates of stress-induced analgesia - PubMed[2] ISIS video shows Jordanian pilot being burned to death
column9: I am a nurse and worked briefly in a burn unit. I pray that God does not take me home that way. It is excruciating and the surgeries, the infections, the grafts - burn patients that survive these procedures and lead productive lives - are amazing. God bless them!

column1: What are the most underrated life skills?
column3: My uncle’s a male nurse. Believe it or not, it’s a thing. In the many years that he worked at our local hospital, I’ve grown to watch him age quicker than his siblings. He’s only the middle child. I was old enough to legally smoke but too young to drink when he came back from work one day and spoke with his wife who was setting food on the table. I was nearby desiccating coconuts to be squeezed of its juices to be used in a dessert. “Me’a tatau aipe?” she asked him. He looked detached; we knew what it meant. “More. Three today. Two usual, and one drowning.” He has seen death walk through the hospital and claim the lives of others so many times before. You’d think that it would chip away at his own soul, but he was rather used to it. Just not quite used to it. “Stalin, can you ask Sansa for some lilies from her garden?” This was grave. The only time he asks for flowers is when a child dies in the hospital. A child drowned… When it happens, he goes out of his way to visit their families with a bouquet of flowers. He’s only a nurse—not even a doctor or a saint, but he has the heart of one. We visited the family the very next day at the morgue. It was miles away from the hospital. I stayed back in his beat-up old truck that he had since I was child. Hate me if you will, but I am not one to fake emotions if I truly didn’t feel it. I would look solemn, but you would think I was happy though I was not. From the vehicle, I saw tears, gratitude, more tears, and a gracious goodbye. He got back in and we left. After awhile of driving, an old catchy tune played on the radio. He sang along—off key—and was back to his usual self. Okay…talk about a quick recovery…just what the doctor ordered haha-ha? No? This Quora question sparked that memory. I now realize that with the amount of deaths he had witnessed over the years, with the countless flowers he had given in the name of a child taken too soon: He had never allowed that atmosphere to drown him. If at home, it lasted for as long as he spoke of it. It applied across the board for everything that he did. The most underrated life skill in my opinion, is the innate ability to bounce back from something that could drown you, and then push forward without looking back. It is resilience.
column9: Credit must be given where it is taken: A special thank you to Troy Mason for a comment which has been added to the answer “It is resilience.”

column1: Can a human live without any senses? I.e. you can't see or hear or smell or taste or feel? How would you perceive time?
column3: A person without 5 senses or completely defunct senses cannot live independently for long, unless a caretaker looks after his needs voluntarily & moment the support is removed, his slow death is certain. This type is very rare or not recorded in history so far. Learned people can throw light on this aspect. When he cannot sense at all, he cannot distinguish, past time, present time & future time. Please read further. His brain will be having no impetus to form impressions or patterns, understanding & analyzing various problems, in the absence of sense inputs.The word sense is derived from "Sensor", meaning a device to sense non electrical inputs & feed them to an electronic equipment to analyze & give an output to make "Sense" of a situation. Senses in the case of man are hearing, seeing, touch, smell & taste & if these functions are prevented, brain will have no work & mind becomes dull & inactive,though not dead. In the absence of inputs to brain, it cannot be active & cannot organize anything purposeful.The existence of such a person can be called as default conditions of life without exposure to senses. His case cannot be compared to transcendent form of self, which can manifest it’s presence despite the biophysical obstacles. The big question arises, whether it was right from birth & “was that possible in normal birth”? If these malfunctions are acquired later, probably medical team may be in a better situation to restore them later partly or fully. A person born without senses, loses all his capabilities to live on his own. He has to be aided by a care taker completely. His mind does not work, on external stimulations, but still alive with subconscious memory, even though the conscious sense outputs are not reaching the brain. The brain has no inputs from conscious mind & remains idle but very much alive. It is as good as coma. External stimulations will have no effect on senses.This makes his life abnormal, as he cannot protect himself from external attack, he cannot eat on his own, he cannot differentiate tastes, smells, he cannot feel touch & cannot hear. In these circumstances, he will be deprived of feelings & emotions,which are the basic traits of man.The brain remains like an empty machine waiting for customers from senses to reach, so that it can react analyze & send signals to mind. If the mind does not receive any input, he remains alive with subconscious memory, just like his internal organs are functioning subconsciously, without involving conscious attention or recognition from him. A brain without any input from senses is as good as ineffective to keep the person informed about impending dangers, pleasure & pain, hunger & thirst & left to himself, he will have a fast death, or until the caretaker withdraws the support to protect him from external dangers & looks after him in all aspects of survival including feeding, exercising, taking him to the toilet etc.His life is not in his hand but at the mercy of God & even living instincts like that of other species will be absent. Anything going wrong inside his system cannot be noticed & even the caretaker will be ignorant of what is happening & how to take corrective actions. A human without senses is a hypothetical case & the person is unlikely to remain for long after birth, since senses may not return to normal, whereas in a coma stage, a person can return to normal one day or the other & regain consciousness, so that he can put his senses to action subsequently. Coming to the 2nd part of the question, perception of time is totally absent, because nothing comes to his mind. If you call a person senseless, it may be a temporary affair,as he may become sensible some time or the other, because his senses are in tact, but not put to proper use. In the case of a person defunct with senses completely, there is no possibility of return to normalcy, unless it is a temporary shut down, due to some deficiency or defect, which can be set right subsequently by medical treatment or surgery. CONCLUSIONS:- If all the 5 senses are not functioning, he is still alive but his condition is more or less like that of coma stage with no effect with external stimulations. Due to absence of inputs to brain, it is totally unable to be active to perform it’s functions & mind does not react or functional, though alive & without a caretaker, continuation of life is doubtful after a certain period. If they are not permanently impaired, there is a possibility for recovery through medical aid or surgery. “With the blessings of Saptha Rishies & Almighty”.
column9: What about hunger, for example. Wouldn't such person feel hunger, thirst, breathing need…? That would give them the ability to perceive time passing. If that was true, we could even develop a language to communicate with them: For example, the person can breathe in a given rythm to communicate something, and we can artificially pump them air so they don't feel the need to breathe. If they ‘not sense’ the breathing need, they are receiving an external input that they can interpret. Of course I'm thinking this language should be agreed upon (imagine it is an international language we all learn, so if by one accident one day someone looses all their senses, they already know the language).

column1: How has dealing with grief changed you as a person?
column3: I lost my son only a month ago to suicide, so while I’m not sure yet where it’s going to lead me, I can talk about the changes I’ve made thus far. Prior to losing him, I did a little too much drinking. After losing him, that increased, but then something really good happened from the bad. The day I received his ashes was a drinking day. I had some of his ashes in a little baggy in pewter heart box in my pocket and would reach into the pocket to rub my fingers on the box. At one point, I reached in to discover that the box had opened and the ashes were missing. I panicked and in my panic to find them, I fell down the back porch stairs breaking two ribs, rupturing my spleen, and busting my head open along with a number of other injuries. I didn’t go to the hospital immediately which almost resulted in my own death. I haven’t drank since. Prior to his death, I was working hard to build a business he would be proud of. Since his death, I haven’t been able to work. I try, but my heart leads me to look into how to deal with my grief. In fact, that’s how I found this post. At the same time, I feel more inspired to succeed for him. I just don’t know how to focus right now. My inspiration has shifted from build my business to advocate and speak for him since he can no longer do it. My son suffered from depression. I clearly couldn’t help him. If I could, he’d still be with us. I feel the need to scream out his story and to bring awareness to depression. I feel the urge to vlog and blog about it. I write in my journal daily, but I want to reach out to others both to build support for my own recovery as well as other’s recovery. I want to build a platform where we can talk and share our stories. Now I spend more time with my remaining child, granddaughter, parents. I make it a point to reach out to my daughter everyday whereas before I put her on my calendar once a week. We did talk more than once a week, but there were times where I had to make an effort to set time aside for my children because of my focus on work. As for my parents, my mother and I had a falling out last fall and weren’t talking at all. Immediately, we set our differences aside and stepped in to help each other. She stepped in to help me. Now I realize how short time is and I want family to know that I think of them everyday. I realize since his death that I have relationships that aren’t worth investing in. That feels like an odd thing to say at a time when I should be building relationships that bring me support, but at the same time, I have discovered that one particular relationship has not only not provided support but has also kept me from getting the support I need. Since his death, I have begun to address my own depression. I am now seeing a therapist and taking medications that help me with my chemical imbalances. They also help me to sleep. Before, it was common for me to only get four hours of sleep at night. Now I’m closer to eight hours which is important for my mental health. I still smoke, don’t exercise enough, and eat a poor diet. I considered improving in these areas but have decided that until I have more control over the drinking and learn better coping tools I will keep the smoking. When the children were little, I exercised regularly. That will become on of those tools, but for now, I’m addressing my faults one day at a time, one step at a time. I suppose the next step will be my eating habits, but at the moment I can barely eat at all. Maybe a good way to handle it would be to take a day to fast and start fresh rebuilding my eating habits from scratch. I cry a lot and laugh none. It hits me when I least expect it. Music seems to trigger it most often. We listened to similar music and some of his favorites were also mine. When he was 17, he said “Mom, ‘Simple Man’ is our song.” He loved and Elton John, as do I. My stations play those songs often. At the same time, when a rare smile does appear on my face, I feel it. I feel both the muscles used to express pleasure and the guilt that I can feel anything good during a time when I feel so bad. I think of God and heaven more but not in a good way. I lay in bed at night wondering if he’s found peace. But I fear he has not. I worry that his suicide will keep him from heaven. I worry that his soul is lost, and if so, where is he? This is an irony because for the most part, I question faith. Yet hear I am hoping he’s in heaven where happiness is abundant. I feel guilt—so much guilt. I could have done more. I could have stayed at his place for a bit after he broke up with his girlfriend. I could have pushed him to see me on Christmas instead of just accepting his excuse that he had to work the next day. I could have called him at the stroke of midnight to wish him a happy New Year instead of waiting until the next morning. If I had seen him more, I might have been able to see his pain and done something to help him. I could have invited him to take a walk with me on the beach. I feel guilt at accepting that if it wasn’t now, it would have happened in the next few years. His suicide has always been a fear of mine. Even when he was a small child, I had the feeling—this overwhelming fear that he would do this. It’s so strange how I always knew. He was my little Eeyore—an introspective contemplative child. When I got the call that he had missed work (he never missed work), I reached out to everyone who might be able to help me find him. They all said, “Jeanna, calm down. It will be okay. Don’t think the worst until we know.” But I knew. I hoped that he had decided to drive away and disappear for a few days to think. I hoped he was unconscious in a hospital but still able to recover. I prayed he was still with us, but I knew what had happened. I feel guilt at getting and coveting the things he left behind—his pillow, the Grover doll he took to every surgery since his first at two years old, his camera which is much better than mine and given to me because I’m the one who deliberately looks for photo opportunities in the simplest things. I feel guilt at benefiting from his death. His car will be sold to fix my teeth. His insurance if it’s not void because of the suicide will help me get into a better, more secure living arrangement. His kitchen ware which I have no emotional attachment to will help me get a desperately needed fresh start. All these things he would want for me, but I would rather have him back. I feel anger at his father. He made a promise to me after our divorce that would have made my life more stable—a promise to sell our co-owned home. I intended to invest that money in a venture with my son. Because he broke his promise, I was never able to do that. I feel like his broken promise has stolen time from me and our son. I feel like the venture may have brought him hope to keep living or a sense of responsibility to see our venture reach success. I feel anger because he wanted his father to honor his promise to me and he openly expressed his frustrations with his father even while loving him. And I feel guilt because I lashed out at his father over this after his death even though he was a great dad and is grieving as well. I also feel resolved. So many times I made excuses and set my needs aside for his father when he set none aside for me. It’s a little selfish, but I’m grieving too. His father’s pain does not trump mine, so why do I put him first and continue to suffer so his needs are met when mine are not. Most of all, my life his come to a dead stop. I can’t focus to work. I don’t eat. I don’t want to socialize. I don’t feel anything but empty. I’m hiding, but also feel the most emotionally vulnerable that I’ve every felt. I want to talk about it. I’ve hugged more strangers in this past month than I have in my entire life. Homeless people, doctors and nurses, his friends, my friends. At the same time, I haven’t hugged my boyfriend once. I’ve come to realize that he isn’t a part of my support system, so I don’t bother. That relationship will be one of my changes either we fix it or we end it. I’ve decided that if I am going to have to do this alone, I’d rather do it completely alone without the burden of having to consider the needs of an unsupportive partner. I’ve decided that when my dad dies (he has prostate cancer), I would rather be able to cry alone at night than hear the words, “why are you waking me up with your sniffling?” And I’ve decided that in order to build something that matters, I have to either change or get rid of something that doesn’t. I know that this will all get better. I will never stop missing my son. I will never stop thinking of him. Every instance in which I would have thought of him while living will bring thoughts of him after death, but this will get better. It will become easier. I will learn to laugh again. I will become a better person for him and for my daughter. I will become a better grandmother and child. I will get through this, but not without having undergone great changes.
column9: Hi, Jeanna♥️ I have a son as well and came across this tonight as I’ve struggled with physical pain. I wanted to tell you that I feel your son is okay. I believe we existed spiritually before we came to earth and we continue on after we leave. I imagine your son in a special place with people set apart specifically to help him with whatever struggles he had here that led to his decision to take his life prematurely. However, I believe in heavenly parents who, in their great mercy, made a way for us to return to their presence. Can you see in your mind’s eye a place of learning in the next life? That we continue to grow? I also have assurance that my diseased body will one day be resurrected and I will have a healthy working body. That I will wrap my arms around my own son with a perfect body. ♥️And you will too. How wonderful that small things he left behind are helping you.. of course you would trade them to have him! Please don’t feel guilty about benefiting from these ‘gifts.‘ I can just see your son ‘giving them’ to you. Blessing your life somehow as you pick up the pieces right now. I love that you are making small goals to improve each day! This is what life is about, being better today than we were yesterday. You can do this. And you don’t have to do it alone. The Savior knows of your struggles. He suffered not just our trangressuons but all our suffering. Let Him help you- I know through prayer we can find the strength to live out our lives. And to know about the truth of all things.. one day you will reunite with your son and it will be wonderful.

column1: What is one thing you consistently do while answering Quora questions?
column3: The one thing I consistently do while answering Quora questions is cry. Yes, I usually am on Quora somewhere between 3:00 and 4:00 AM CST with my first cup of morning coffee. Sometimes I might also be eating a small cup of yogurt.Image From Unsplash Maybe it’s because I’ve just had a good night's sleep or maybe because I start each Quora session reading the answers of the people I always follow, but I am always much more emotional when I’m here. Quora has been incredibly cathartic for me in so many ways. Not only have I unearthed many of my own personal life demons and brought them into the Quora light, but I’ve also discovered others who bravely share their own pain of their lives. Even after many years of therapy where I’ve cried buckets of tears and gone through stacks of tissues, I still have tears left for Quora. More often than not when I’m sitting quietly in my office reading Quora questions and previous answers, my eyes begin to water. When I write about the death of my late husband, my recovery from my eating disorder, or living with my mentally ill mother, I have tears streaming down my face. I am very humbled by the amazing people here on Quora who so openly share their lives which brings so much help and healing to so many people around the world. Not everyone will agree with me about Quora, but for me, it has been a wonderful gift. Best wishes to all.

column1: From a legal and non-emotional POV, is the 22.5 years' sentence against former police officer Derek Chauvin lenient or harsh? Thanks to any lawyer or person with law knowledge.
column3: It was neither. I think that Cahill, throughout the trial, was, despite the high-profile nature of the case, determined to handle it like any other case before him. I think he was successful at that. Chauvin did not have any prior criminal record. That counted in his favor, as per the Minnesota sentencing guidelines. He normally, without such a record, would have received somewhere around fifteen years for his crime. Chauvin had the opportunity to have the jury decide whether there were aggravating factors to his crime, but waived that and had the judge do so. The judge found that there were four aggravating factors:Chauvin, as a police officer, abused his position of trust and authority during the commission of his crime.Given the lengthy period of Floyd’s death, during which he repeatedly said he was in pain and pleaded for his life, Chauvin acted with particular cruelty.Chauvin committed his crime as part of a group of at least three other people.Chauvin committed his crime in front of children.Watching the initial video was sickening. Watching it during the trial, combined with the body camera videos, was heartbreaking. Chauvin continued to kneel on Floyd for several minutes even after another officer told Chauvin that Floyd had no pulse. Other officers repeatedly asked Chauvin if Floyd should be placed into the side recovery position as their training and procedures require for handcuffed suspects. Chauvin nonchalantly refuses. As Floyd says he can’t breathe and begs for his life, Chauvin sarcastically replies “Uh-huh”, repeatedly. Chauvin acted with depraved indifference toward human life when he killed George Floyd. Under Minnesota law, that is murder. 22.5 years for murder is a comparatively light sentence; many murderers get a life sentence, especially when aggravating factors are found to exist. Chauvin should thank his lucky stars that he even has a chance of seeing the outside of a prison again.
column9: Considering he's an ex-cop, and considering the nature of his crime, he's not necessarily guaranteed to see the outside of that prison. I'm sure that he'll have plenty of people gunning for him every minute of every day.

column1: Should I wish my ex a happy birthday during no contact?
column3: No! No! No! Absolutely NO! I want to educate as much as possible on this wonderful site. There are ONLY 11 words in your question! But 3 of these words are incredibly IMPORTANT to ALL quorans (Especially you younger quorans). I do not wish to sound patronising either, but I feel that this is a great opportunity for me (43 years romantic relationship experience) to really ENLIGHTEN you all. The 3 words are EX, NO, CONTACT. I'm going to deal with the RIDICULOUS ‘NO CONTACT’ first. There is NO such thing as no contact! Not in the WAY people appear to view it. You see the problem with the ridiculous no contact is that far far too many people view no contact as a STRATEGY at the END of the romantic relationship! Here's the scenario so often foolishly played out: How's things with you and Jenny? ‘Me and Jenny have split up! ‘I'm so sorry to hear that Mike'. When did you and Jenny split up? ‘2 weeks ago' What's happening now? We've AGREED to go no contact! We have a plan! I want you quorans to really think about that scenario. (Of course) Jenny and Mike are fictional characters. 2 characters we can all IDENTIFY with. When I say we I mean you younger members of society. You see Jenny and Mike haven't ACCEPTED that the romantic relationship is OVER! It doesn't matter who ended the romantic relationship. The couple have NOT ACCEPTED that the romantic relationship is over! But it IS! And this ‘birthday' greeting EX question is an example of the unhealthy amount of ex partners, who simply have NOT accepted that the relationship is over. But EX = OVER! This is incredibly difficult for younger quorans to truly understand! There can be no such ‘construct' as no contact. The romantic relationship is over. Therefore the state of being is this: Complete separation between 2 ex partners. This is what the END of a romantic relationship really looks like. 2 people were simply not compatible enough to sustain their romantic relationship. What follows after romantic relationship dissolution is (and always should be) this: Acceptance that the romantic relationship is over. Grief at the COMPLETE LOSS of the partner. The EX partner! Romantic relationship dissolution = The LOSS of the partner. (Everything) Grief, heartache, tears, renewed strength, emotional equilibrium. This is WHAT romantic relationship dissolution is in reality. Yet we find approximately 60% of ex partners simply REFUSING to accept that the relationship is over and blatantly AVOIDING the one thing that leads to full emotional recovery. That my quoran friends is GRIEF! We grieve for the COMPLETE loss of the ex partner for the following reasons:(1) To adjust to a life of being completely SINGLE again. (2) To face the heartache, shed the necessary tears, GRIEVE for the incredible LOSS of not only the romantic relationship, but ALSO the ‘cancelled future' (that MOST people will have envisioned), and to finally regain emotional equilibrium. We must ALL go through this painful process to become strong and confident AGAIN. (3) Having negotiated this NECESSARY GRIEF, we set ourselves FREE again to LOVE again. If we love our ex partner and the romantic relationship has sadly ended, then we LET this person GO! We set him/her FREE! We do this because we truly LOVE our EX. We do this to allow our disorganised neurotransmitters the chance to regain stasis. (The state of being where we feel reasonably happy in our lives). We can ONLY do this if WE bravely FACE the incredible heartache and grief which are part of the human condition. So you see I've dealt with no contact and ex already! I'll reiterate: (1) EX = OVER and the COMPLETE LOSS of the partner. (2) NO CONTACT is a socio/psychological CONSTRUCT that can't possibly exist! No contact = nothing. What no contact really is IS the STATE OF BEING. (The incredibly painful state of being that is the complete separation) of BOTH EX PARTNERS post romantic relationship dissolution. It is the ONLY way to handle romantic relationship dissolution. Trust me on this please (you younger quorans especially). If you KNOW that the romantic relationship breakdown is PERMANENT, then you BOTH must walk completely OUT of each others lives. I'm not talking on/off relationships here. I'm not talking friends with benefits (casual dating) relationships here. I'm talking about the incredibly painful END to a SERIOUS romantic relationship. Recognise what a serious romantic relationship IS! Recognise that when this romantic relationship has ended, that you MUST go your complete separate ways immediately. Do this please. I am all for true friendship with an EX. My posts can appear brutal at times. But make no mistake romantic relationship dissolution is BRUTAL. (Brutal on our precious HEARTS). This applies to rejector AND rejected! ‘Friendship’ of sorts MUST wait until BOTH ex partners/lovers have fully recovered emotional equilibrium. This can't possibly happen with ANY continued contact when you KNOW its OVER! Never be a coward at the end of your romantic relationship. Be brave and accept that the romantic relationship was simply not MEANT TO BE. Because if you truly WANT to recover following the devastating end to your romantic relationship, then you must follow my advice. It is ONLY then that you come back stronger. Stronger and more READY for another romantic relationship that will surely come your way. Exes are exes for a reason. You've had your go at a romantic relationship. It probably worked well until irreconcilable differences emerged. No point hanging onto a romantic relationship that is DEAD! Think of the ex partner as a male/female CORPSE. That corpse IS your ex partner! You wouldn't hang on to a real life corpse, would you? MOURN the DEATH of your romantic relationships. But there is HOPE. You see once you've fully grieved the complete loss of the romantic relationship, (AND your partners very EXISTENCE in your life in ANY WAY) it is at this juncture that you CAN become friends with your ex! Both ex partners having fully recovered following the absolutely necessary COMPLETE SEPARATION in the immediate aftermath of the dissolute romantic relationship. But do you know what usually happens quorans? BOTH EX partners have now MOVED ON! At least one of the ex partners is now IN a new romantic relationship. And the other ex partner will soon follow. Do these EX partners become FRIENDS once their DEAD romantic relationship has been PROPERLY grieved? The answer is almost always NO! Why? Because they really DON'T CARE anymore about the EX. They are BUSY loving with someone new! This is how life is! So it is absolutely clear that this person should NOT send ANY birthday greeting to his/her EX. You quorans should never send any greetings etc. To any EX. The relationship is over. It's time to completely move on. (Move on completely OUT of each others lives). In 99% of cases the ex partners simply DRIFT OUT of each others lives completely! This is the post romantic relationship dissolution psychological concept of DELAYED DETACHMENT. (The other 1% have children together and/or work/study together). Move on at the end of your romantic relationships. Don't hold yourself back. Don't act like an obsessive stalker type. Just LET your ex go. Let bygones be bygones. No greetings ever. No greetings cards etc. To ANY ex who you were in a serious romantic relationship with. Not someone that you STILL HAVE strong emotional feelings for! Because all you achieve in sending disingenuous greetings cards etc. Is the proof that you simply WON'T LET GO! Who would send a greeting card to the DEAD body (corpse), that IS your FORMER partner who you had a serious romantic relationship with? I hope this exhaustive answer informs you (younger quorans especially) of what you MUST do to maintain your SELF RESPECT and to recover as QUICKLY as possible. Please stay safe.
column9: Great advice for us (young quorans).People like you have always been there for our every problem and seeking advice from you is what i am grateful for.

column1: What would be the reasons why someone suffering from mental illness (BP2, PTSD, BPD) think/feel that they are detached from the sense of loss (losing someone meaningful)? My friend said this to me in conversation a while back and it stuck with me.
column3: Right out of the gate, let’s clear up the fact that Borderline Personality Disorder is not a mental illness. It is an emotional disorder. If you’re a casual reader of these things, this might seem like a minor detail, but it’s not a minor detail. Either a person’s understanding of the disorder is accurate at a fundamental level, or it’s not. If your understanding of it is erroneous at the very basics, then it will certainly be completely off the mark when trying to make sense of it at higher levels. With all respect, I don’t care what you learned in Psychology class to the contrary. (I’m speaking to readers in general here, not to the author of the question, specifically.) If the only thing you learned at the university was how to accept everything you’re told at face value, and how to turn off your powers of reason, it’s a real tragedy. But please don’t dispute reason by sending me messages about what you’ve been told. I don’t care what you’ve been told - I care whether you can use your brain to reason. For the subject of mental illness vs emotional disorder, I discuss this in detail here: Brian Barnett's answer to I am confused, is borderline personality disorder a mental illness or a disorder?Now, about the question of being emotionally detached. Folks with Borderline Personality Disorder experience this because they subconsciously ‘run from’ negative emotions. Any emotion that makes them the slightest bit uncomfortable provokes behaviors meant to subconsciously distract from, and escape, the uncomfortableness of that feeling. I can’t give you an exhaustive list here, but creativity is a common thing this translates into. It can be bowling, drug abuse, knitting, alcoholism, adopting a new puppy every six months - anything that serves to distract from feeling a bad feeling. It’s really astonishing, but not surprising, how many people with Borderline Personality Disorder are artists. I myself have been a hardcore cartoonist since I was six years old. I was first published in newspapers when I was thirteen. What else is astonishing is how I can now look back at my fever-pitch love of cartooning and see, at least in large part, from where this love was born. It’s no coincidence. When I work on comic strips, I’m transported to a place where I’m in total control of everything that happens. I lose track of time, become totally absorbed - eight hours go by and it seems like thirty minutes. It’s an escape, in every sense. And a large part of that used to be escaping from negative feelings that I subconsciously did not want to feel, or process.Emotionally healthy people do not run from negative feelings. When they experience something like loss, they carry those bad feelings around mindfully. (Not obsessively, but mindfully.) They pair these feelings with memories and analytical thought to better understand them, and eventually come to peace with them. (You’ll hear this talked about as ‘processing’ the emotion.) So the feelings don’t get ignored, or set aside, but rather they get embraced - no matter how uncomfortable they are - and eventually absorbed. In effect, they become a permanent part of the person, helping define their overall life experience - not as an isolated representation of what life is, but in combination with all of the other aspects of the life experience as well, such as the joyful, the mundane, the bittersweet, and so forth. People with BPD, on the other hand, have no tolerance for negative feelings. It’s like flinching an open wound away from salt. They don’t even think about it. They’re not aware they are doing it. Why is this? Borderline Personality Disorder happens when parents subtly negate, or invalidate, their children’s feelings at a tender age when they are forming their fundamental core understanding of themselves and how the world works (between the ages of birth and about three or four). Some examples of this are, “That’s no reason to get upset.” “Oh, you think this is funny?” “Stop your crying. I’ll give you something to cry about.” “Don’t be sad...” Laughing at the ridiculousness of something a child ‘shouldn’t’ be scared of, like the vacuum cleaner, for example. Getting frustrated and angry when the child is crying ‘for no good reason’. These are examples of invalidating behavior on the part of parents. Now that you know what to look for, you’ll see it almost any time you go out, which is heartbreaking. The very real message is: Your feelings don’t matter. They are irrelevant. Your feelings are wrong - they are inherently shameful. And this is precisely the subconscious conclusion the child arrives at, the viewpoint they adopt, the lens through which they begin to view and approach everything in life.The first step they take after reaching this conclusion (which their parents are entirely responsible for) is to ‘turn off’ their feelings. Now, in reality, nobody can turn off their feelings. So these children do the next best thing; They deny them. They stop sharing any form of genuine emotional openness and intimacy with their caregivers and with anybody else. (This is what you do with anything you are ashamed of, if you think about it. It’s what shame is. If you have a hairy freckle on your foot that you are horribly ashamed of, you don’t go showcasing it at the beach. No, you buy sandals that will hopefully cover it.) These children grow up believing that the ugliest, most embarrassing, shameful aspect about themselves is their very feelings. Can you even begin to imagine the implications? They carry this unrecognized certainty right into adulthood. Every one of their behaviors, feelings, and thoughts first pass through this subconscious filter; My feelings are inherently shameful and irrelevant. This is the angle from which they approach every situation in life in which they find themselves. As a result, they don’t grow up learning to regulate their feelings like emotionally healthy people do, because for that to happen - for this mature skill of managing emotions to occur - feelings have to be acknowledged and mindfully experienced over time. For emotions such as loss, there is no way their systems are prepared to handle that sort of overload. A person with BPD isn’t even willing to process the negative feeling of a denied date request, or of getting cut off in traffic, much less the death of a loved one, or a divorce. As somebody who once had Borderline Personality Disorder, I can tell you that in the past, when people I loved have died, I felt absolutely nothing. I cried, I went through the motions. But inside, I simply felt nothing. Nothing at all. I knew I was supposed to feel sadness and intense pain, but I didn’t feel anything. Imagine an empty barrel. I felt like the inside of the barrel. I realize this comparison makes little sense, but it’s the only thing I can compare it to. Void. Nothing. The feelings were still there. I simply would not acknowledge them. So resolute was my subconscious willpower in blocking me from experiencing them, it was as if the feelings did not exist at all. After my recovery from Borderline Personality Disorder, this changed. A very dear friend of mine died with me by his side after three weeks together in hospice. I carried those agonizing feelings of loss around mindfully afterwards, processing them for nearly a year.As I have intended to do for quite some time, I have finally created a private Facebook support group specifically for folks who follow my Quora articles. It is named the following: Brian Barnett: Borderline Personality Disorder https://www.facebook.com/groups/BrianBarnettBorderlinePersonality/Afterword Nobody has to live with Borderline Personality Disorder. I was able to rid myself of the disorder after having lived with it unaware for the first thirty-five years of my life. I write openly about the experience here to save others from the same pointless theories and misdirection I once had to sort through. Please read my other Quora articles to learn more.
column9: I had already been having doubts about how much I was I really recovering from BPD, and after reading your answer I now realize that I really haven’t recovered much at all. I thought when I stopped drinking and started crafting, the peace I felt was a sign that I was improving. plus my family was finally happy with me, and were proud. column1: Does a narcissist get his karma? Do his terrible actions ever catch up with him?
column3: Yes, and he does, already! Look at his facial expression. Talk to him to hear grand amount of negativity in his conversation. Look at how nervous he usually is, how suspicious, scared, controlling, used to sky falling! I was subjected to horrifying lies from a covert narcissist, many-faced, chameleon, pathetic loser, parasite masked as a decent, misunderstood and humble. He surrounds himself with people he buys with small amount of money he has and deception, to build props around himself to conceal his true identify from the World. I knew this person for many years. When he was younger he was beautiful. Now, he looks unrecognizable. column1: How do people get out of a relationship and act fine?
column3: They just “ACT” fine. An individual’s relationship is a personal matter. You don't want to spread grief or sadness everywhere around yourself letting people know that you are suffering from adverse effects of a break up. The amount of pain suffered post breakup is directly proportional to one's degree of bonding with your significant other. Also, first time breakups hurt the most. I am not saying breakups do not hurt but subsequent break ups rarely hurt like the first one. Kindly leave room for some exceptions. Moreover discussing one's breakup requires a lot of emotional strength. Revisiting memories is not easy. So most people in order to avoid being questioned about their depressed state, making them answerable to a few, in the process rekindling memories, try to avoid that matter altogether by posing as if nothing has happened. Quite expected. You don't want to talk about something unpleasant with most folks except some extremely close friends or family members. I have started to discuss my own breakup after years. Now I can divulge some details, even laugh about it because time has healed the trauma but till one or two years after my breakup, I used to maintain a deathly silence about my blown up relationship. I think this is very natural. A part of healing. Although they say that you heal faster if you can talk about it. I beg to differ. Each of us has his/her own recovery mechanism. There's no universal approach to deal with tanked relationships. Other reasons behind a person acting fine. Well, he or she may actually be fine. This happens when they were never deeply involved in their relationship. Therefore its getting wreaked doesn't make much of a difference. Doesn't matter to them. Another reason, they've already started dating someone. I know people who jump from one relationship into another so as to overcome the pain of failing in a previous one. To conclude, some act fine, some are actually fine.

column1: In The Last Samurai's fight scene in the rain, what is Taka's emotion while watching? I think her face expression is quite hard to interpret.
column3: The scene where Ujio (Hiroyuki Sanada) orders Algren (Tom Cruise) to put down the wooden practice sword occurs relatively early in the film and shortly after arriving at the samurai village. At this point, with the exception of Katsumoto (Ken Watanabe), most of samurai want Algren dead. After all, he is the enemy. Katsumoto, however, decides he wants to “know his enemy,” and spares his life. Katsumoto orders Ujio not to kill Algren, so the most Ujio can do is to give him as much shit as possible without actually killing him. He yells at Algren to put down the wooden sword, but Algren doesn’t understand what Ujio is saying because he is speaking in Japanese. Ujio mistakes him not understanding for insolence and proceeds to beat the shit out of him. So all of the onlookers, including Taka, simply watch as all of this is happening. And, you’re right. Her emotions are hard to read.It’s a given that Taka hates Algren as much as a person can hate another human being. After all, Algren just killed her husband. Ironically, she is assigned to care for him during his recovery (you’ll recall he was pretty badly wounded at the beginning of the film), by her brother Katsumoto. At some point, she tells Katsumoto she wants to end her life if he does not kill Algren. But the conflict and mixed feelings I believe she was feeling was that Algren is the same as her husband. He is a warrior. His ‘duty’ is to kill the enemy, just like her husband’s duty is to kill the enemy. So, although she is torn up inside because of the death of her husband, she understands perfectly that Algren did what he had to do to defend himself. If Algren didn’t kill her husband, her husband would have killed Algren. So, while she wasn’t exactly cheering on Ujio to beat up Algren, I think she felt sympathy for her guest, given he was wounded, had no martial arts skills to defend himself, couldn’t understand what Ujio was saying to him and was only doing his duty as a warrior.
column9: I disagree that Algren doesn't understand what Ujio wants him to do. Ujio even takes the wooden sword from him several times but he keeps going back to pick it up in defiance.

column1: What can I do to help the pain of my pet passing away?
column3: Not just a dead pet but with anything you loved and now lost, applies this same rule. When you lose something most precious to you there comes an empty space that thing was holding in your life. You actually don't miss the thing itself that much but that empty space in your routine keeps reminding you about the loss. It keeps reminding the things and tasks associated with it you used to do. When you suffer the loss you start missing those tasks and it creates an emptiness in your emotional space too. Now to recover from this situation you need some or similar or same replacement to fill that empty space. Once you get that space filled, you once again will have something to do at same place, same time. This will hold your mind from running into memories. I know it still not easy but it gives you a great start towards recovery. So to revover from the pain of losing a loved pet you need to get another one to continue with your routine. Fill that empty space and you are good to go ahead. :-)
column9: I agree but I've always needed some of that empty time and space you refer to. No other dog will ever really replace what you lost. It can be just as wonderful but it will be different. I say no rush.

column1: How do I inspire others to donate their organs?
column3: In India once a person is dead, they cease to have ownership of their organs. Their nearest kin has all the rights to donate the organs or refuse organ donation irrespective of the wishes of the diseased even if the wishes are in writing. So no amount of convincing living people to donate their organs after death will yield any tangible results in the form of increased organ donation rates. Family education counts the most. So how can you as an individual help? Indian law recognizes the “brain death” definition of death. For a detailed explanation of brain death I'm borrowing from Dr. Vinay Kumaran post here: What is brain death? by Vinay KumaranThe main causes of brain death are head injuries (traffic accidents, falls, assaults) and strokes (hemorrhagic or thrombotic). The first priority in such cases is to try and save the patient’s life. As they slip into a coma, they are put on a ventilator. Emergency surgery or interventional radiological procedures are done to relieve the pressure on the brain and to stop bleeding. These measures are not always successful and in some of these cases brain death occurs despite these measures. Brain death manifests in the form of rapid changes in heart rate and blood pressure requiring medication to stabilize and dilatation of the pupils of the eye and their unresponsiveness to light. Every patient on a ventilator with fixed dilated pupils should be tested for brain death. The tests are simple but as a safeguard, Indian law requires that the tests be performed twice, at least 6 hours apart by a panel of four doctors approved for the purpose by the Ministry of Health. Mistakes in the diagnosis of brain death are practically unknown as compared to the usual cardiac death which is occasionally misdiagnosed by a careless physician in an unusual clinical situation. Brain death is not a coma. There is no possibility of recovery. If we do an angiography of the carotid arteries, there is not blood flow into the head. The brain is literally dead meat which will soon begin to putrefy. However, since the patient is on a ventilator which is breathing into the lungs and with appropriate medical management to keep the blood pressure and electrolytes within acceptable levels, the organs can continue to function reasonably normally and they can be transplanted into patients who need transplant if the next-of-kin of the deceased person agree. The time of death in the death certificate in such cases is the time when the second set of brain death tests is performed.Eyes and skin can be donated within 6 hours after death while other organs like Liver, kidney, heart, pancreas, lung, etc require brain death with a beating heart for the organs to be useful. Next time there is a death in your immediate family or close friends due to whatever cause in home or hospital, counsel their immediate relatives and help them contact the nearest eye bank if they want to donate the eyes or a medical college if they want to donate their whole body to the college. Both of these things can be done together. Skin donation can be done too but skin banks are very few and only present in metropolitan cities. For organs requiring brain death with a beating heart- this type of donation can occur only in a hospital death where the patient is on a ventilator but is certified brain dead according to the above explanation. So again you can counsel relatives of such patients to donate the diseased person's organs before they plug them out of the ventilator. Live non-related organ transplants are not allowed in the Indian Human Transplantation Act. Politicians like Sushma Swaraj can bend the law citing that some random person is “emotionally related” to her and get a live donor kidney transplant from a non-related donor. Common people however cannot avail this modality. In any case, convincing related people to donate organs is a difficult in itself, so convincing people to donate their precious organs to a random stranger is a tall task. The pledge cards of various organ donation websites and eye banks are nice things to bring awareness but a futile exercise when it comes to actual organ donations because the next of kin controls whether organs are donated or not. So our only hope of increasing organ donation rates in India are to help educate people to prevent these roadblocks. Educate your family and others. Create awareness about organ donation in your immediate circle of family and friends.

column1: How do I recover from a divorce?
column3: I’m so sorry. “Divorce is like the person died, but their corpse is still walking around.” It has also been called “the death of a mini civilization.” You are grieving the life you thought you’d have. Give yourself time and space to process your pain. Anesthetizing with drugs/alcohol will merely prolong dealing with it. Counseling helps. If finances are tight, as they often are in divorce proceedings, you might consider a divorce recovery workshop. I also found same-gender friendships became increasingly important in my life. You still need people! Meet-up groups can be a great way of connecting. Friends or family that you can call to vent to when the latest frustrating event happens helps so much. Self care is important. Please try to get enough sleep. Exercise, if you aren’t already. I would recommend not rushing into dating again. This will delay your healing. Journal. Listen to beautiful music that restores your soul. Try to plan at least one social outing for those long, quiet weekends. Above all, explore or lean on your faith, which can help you tap into that “peace that passes understanding.” I get it, as only one who has been there can. Tears instantly sprang to my eyes when I read your post. I didn’t want to be divorced. Four years post-divorce, however, I’ve healed to where I no longer cry every day. I embrace this life that is authentically mine. What I do and prioritize is true to myself. Sometimes it’s hard, but now the atmosphere in my home is one of peace and honesty. It is better than living with betrayal and deception. I was told I would accept things in time, but I felt so deeply hurt that I thought I would be the one freakish person who would never experience acceptance in healing. Thankfully, I was wrong. You will get there, if you give yourself sufficient time to grieve and open yourself up to moving forward. *Virtual hug*
column9: Thank you for your kind message. A lot of it resonate with me amd my healing journey. Forgiveness is one issue I am finding it hard to achieve, although I know it is for my own good. Still work-in-progess…

column1: What should I do to get rid of addictions?
column3: Addictions are a tricky thing in life. Once you deal with them when you are older, they are difficult to handle. They could have been triggered due to external events (death of a loved one) and due to lack of emotional support, you get a painkiller, and that painkillers numbs that pain for you, and *bam* addicted. If I was a father, I would shield my children from social media and the hollywood narrative of what they as industry depict as a success, and “good versus bad.” As the real world doesn't work that way. I believe (naively) this is a great cause of anxiety, depression and whatnot what fuels people to numb pain, hence drugs, hence addiction. Whether that is cocaine or sugar, no difference. I would try to teach my kids meaning in life, and if I had a friend who struggled w/addiction I would try to show him that as well. They need a counterweight as to the “why” they jump to xyz product or activity which they can't let go off. If pills or drugs addicted related, cold turkey might not be the way, so that would be tapering lower dosage with psychological help. If you seek ways to get rid of addiction, you have already done the most difficult part. Identify you are an addict. At this point I would seek professional help. For me, I have not been “addicted” except for a sense of always wanting to work and do things. I am a functioning “workaholic”. But I survive and thrive due to meaning. Purpose. Solving puzzles. I find addiction a very interesting topic, as Ive seen many friends and colleagues break and collapse due to addiction issues. I am always interested as to why a random person does what he does everyday. Once you find your way to live a healthy “addiction free life” I would ensure a strong social network which will not allow you to relapse. Your friends are a depiction of what success you might achieve in the future Moderation, as with everything in life, is key.
column9: “I would try to teach my kids meaning in life”. As a father, I think this is a great idea. Really difficult though. I sometimes try to share my idea of meaning but I don't think they are buying it, and to be fair why should they? So I try to help them find their own meaning….but it feels like a bit of a guessing game. Parenthood - it's a tough gig!

column1: How does your attitude towards death affect your attitude towards life?
column3: I have bipolar disorder, an illness where 1 in 5 people die. I've been close to suicide on several occasions. After 18 years, I am wanting to end my marriage. My husband's response was 'do you think you can survive living on your own?' I said I want a good emotional quality of life, and if I ended up dead because of it then that's ok. Being dead is better than living a compromised life. It does not scare me as it once did. Emotional recovery from the devastation that bipolar imparts has forced an evaluation in the way my life has been lived. With suicide sitting on my shoulder I am forced to face death head on. I now more than ever seek integrity in how I live. Fear of anything must not block the heartfelt need for the highest quality of life that can be achieved in a person's lifetime. Because 'here' is not the end of the story, I live in hope for the future. Although they still meet criteria for BPD (mostly due to fears of abandonment from the abuse) they are not the stigmatized version of BPD that most are familiar with. Therefore, I believe there are two types of borderlines. Type 1:A small percent (lets say 20%) of those with BPD are those who are unable to benefit from therapy, are abusive, and also have a comorbid diagnosis of narcissist personality disorder. They are unreachable in an emotional context. They have true personality disorders and are unable to change or get better. This is the stigmatized version of BPD that we mostly hear about. Type 2:These individuals show change through therapy, have insight, growth, and may not even meet criteria for BPD in the future as research has shown. They are not the abusers; they are the survivors of covert or overt narcissist abuse. Type 1is a true personality disorder. According to the DSM-5, personality disorders are pervasive, inflexible, and they are stable over time. Research has shown that treatment for personality disorders such as narcissistic personality disorder (NPD) and antisocial personality disorder, has little to know affect in changing symptomology. These individuals do not get better in therapy, remain abusive, and are unable to mentalize and grow. Type 2therefore, is not a true personality disorder by definition. They are fundamentally different than all the other personality disorders because these individuals are able to grow and change through therapy. The borderline experience in these individuals is not pervasive, inflexible, and stable over time. It is the opposite. They are highly emotionally intelligent, have empathy, high sensitivity and emotional attunement. However, they still look like and meet criteria BPD. Approximately 80% of individuals with bpd that are in therapy no longer have symptoms after 6-10 years, only 11% of those in “remission” have a recurrent episode after those 6-10 years. If 80% of those diagnosed with BPD are getting better they literally do not meet criteria for a personality disorder. So, 80% of these individuals are not true borderlines, they are something else. Let’s call it Emotional Dysregulation Abandonment Trauma Disorder! Research has reported that 90% of those diagnosed with BPD have a history of childhood abuse (that is self-reported). Borderline personality disorder is a pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, dissociation, and marked impulsivity that is potentially damaging such as substance use. The causes of BPD are still being studied, however, genetics and childhood environmental factors such as emotional, physical, and sexual abuse are known to be involved. According to a large number of studies childhood abuse is the most common psychological, physiological, or social risk for those with BPD. Ninety percentof those diagnoses with borderline report childhood abuse ranging from emotional neglect to physical and sexual ritual abuse. It is possible that the other 10% of those with BPD also had a form of childhood abuse, however, they do not recognize their childhood as abusive due to certain types of abuse being covert as well as children believing the abuse is normal. Moreover, these children enter into abusive relationships as adults continuing the belief that abuse is normal behavior and thus never recognizing or acknowledging they have been abused in childhood. According to Dr. Steven Farmer, author of Adult Children of Abused Parents (1989), children that come from an emotionally abusive childhood will have difficulties in adulthood. These difficulties most likely include depression, relationship issues, an inability to trust, low-self-esteem, alcohol and drug problems, and eating disorders. Each of these difficulties we see in the criteria or presentation of someone with BPD. So, we know that abuse and BPD or Emotional Dysregulation Of Abandonment Trauma Disorder go hand in hand during childhood. Children that were raised in homes by those with abusers with NPD or traits of NPD usually display signs of complex posttraumatic stress disorder (CPTSD). CPTSD children show signs of flashbacks, difficulty regulation emotions, hypervigilance, harsh internal critic, substance abuse issues, dissociation, anger, compromised immune systems, anxiety/depression, difficulty trusting others, and many more symptoms. A narcissistic parent disrupts a child’s ability to form healthy attachments, boundaries, self-worth, and self-love. The narcissistic parent changes from available and supportive to detached and enraged while the child unknowing is subjected to narcissistic rage and abuse. This type of abuse becomes normal to the child, increasing their tolerance for abuse and decreasing their feelings of worthiness and ability to feel loveable. Narcissistic abuse is covert, insidious, and manipulative. Idling back and forth between a disguise of love and care, to an erosion of control, dominance, intimation, rejection, gaslighting, jealousy, dishonesty, blame shifting, and complete destruction over the victim’s person sense of self-worth. The invisible scares inflected on those in relationships with a narcissists are so hidden, the victim themselves usually do not realize they are in an abusive relationship for over a decade. Survivors exposed to narcissistic abuse not only suffer from CPSTD, but many also suffer from Stockholm syndrome, as well as narcissistic abuse syndrome. Although narcissistic abuse syndromes has yet to be added to the DSM- 5, millions of survivors and licensed mental health professionals use this diagnosis to help describe the aftermath of those who survived narcissistic abuse. Symptoms of Narcissistic Abuse Syndrome include (or Narcissistic Victim Syndrome): Fog, pacing, confusion, "loss of self", panic attacks, angry outbursts, insomnia, weight gain or weight loss, obsessive thoughts, rapid heart rate, muscle aches, throwing up, getting sick, desiring death, possibly suicidal, no interest in previous interests or even loved ones, blaming self, second guessing self, may seem desperate and trying to reach for help, fear of Narcissist annihilating them. Narcissistic Abuse is a type of soul rape.“The ongoing impact of narcissistic abuse on victims is similar to being a prisoner of war (Brown, 2016). This is the fight or flight that we commonly see in those with BPD when triggered by feelings of abandonment. Research has found that 87% of those who have been abused re-enter into an intimate abusive relationships. So, this abused child with BPD traits or meets full BPD criteria most likely unconsciously and unknowingly continued on into another abusive relationship with a narcissistic. If the abuse is causing CPTSD and the expression of BPD symptoms and this person enters into another abusive relationship, the symptoms of BPD would also continue making it look like this individual who is struggling with CPTSD from narcissistic abuse and abandonment issues has borderline personality disorder. They have no idea they are being abused because this is how they were raised, the abuse is normal and they are used to being blamed for everything and they take on that projection and act in away that is borderline. This is why the therapist also believes this person has BPD and much of the time misses that there is even any abuse happening at all. If majority of women dealing with narcissistic abuse do not recognize the abuse for over a decade, then most therapists are missing the abuse too. This is especially true if the patient has been diagnosed with BPD. If an individual is unaware that they are being abused they will not be commenting on their partner’s abusive behaviors or in ways that allude to abuse. Moreover if these individuals are diagnosed with BPD they will primarily be blaming themselves for being “borderline,” unlovable, difficult, and mentally ill, leaving them the perfect victim for someone with NPD. Although it may seem that most mental health professional would surely be able to tell is one of the borderline patients were being abused, even if their patient didn’t recognize it themselves, this is most likely untrue. Due to the stigma of BPD being known to be overly dramatic, the cause of most interpersonal conflicts, untrustworthy sources, and difficult to love, most mental health professional will be blind to the abuse. The NPD individual blames the borderline for all of the conflicts in the relationship, leading the borderline to believe the same. Her/his stories would then be narratives of the chaos she created in which she may feel that she is taking responsibility, possibly metalizing her partner and on the right road to recovery. Nothing could be further from the truth. The borderline individual is being manipulated, groomed, and abused. Mental health professionals unfortunately have been fed the stereotype description of BPD since undergraduate training. This Instills fear, chaos, and creating the most mentally ill expression of BPD. It is extremely possible that many mental health professionals have multiple individuals with either BPD or BPD traits in their caseload and they are completely unaware. They have been training to only recognize BPD patients at the stigmatic view of the “difficult patient.” It is also probable that the “difficult patients” that are painted as the borderline patients are actually narcissistic patients with complex PTSD that expresses itself as appearing as a borderline diagnosis. In this case we could call these patients borderline personality disorder, however, they make up even a smaller portion of the original view of BPD. Meaning, these narcissistic patients with CPTSD are the ones that have low emotional intelligence, insight, boundary issues, demanding, hostile, invasive, and are usually in and out of treatment. They are more likely to be demanding, struggle with patient/ therapist boundaries, and are highly aggressive and entitled. These patients usually are not suicidal, dissociative, cutting, or struggling with affective instability. These are narcissist patients that had a traumatic childhood that are fixed, inflexible, and stable across time; they are true personality disorders. However, due to the stigma, most clinicians label them as BPD patients. The real BPD patients actually have insight, emotional intelligence, able to use mentilazation over time. Like all disorders borderline personality disorder is on a continuum. Many individuals with BPD may have traits and some will meet full criteria for five out of the nine symptoms. However, if these individuals are meeting criteria and are improving in symptomology over time it should no longer be considered BPD because it literally is then no longer a personality disorder and instead complex posttraumatic stress disorder should be considered followed by an understanding if narcissistic abuse syndrome if present. Looking at the criteria of CPTSD we see significant overlay with the criteria of BPD. Moreover, symptoms of narcissistic abuse syndrome my account for the other unexplained symptoms that appear to have BPD qualities. I believe once you take the individual with BPD out of the abusive relationship and environment (intimate partner, family dynamics) the individual with BPD symptomology will begin to improve. In particularly you will see marked improvement in their identity disturbance, impulsivity, recurrent suicidal behaviors, and chronic feelings of emptiness, dissociation, and anger and aggression issues. Then BPD symptoms will then present more as CPTSD with abandonment issues and emotional dysregulation still being at the heart of it. However, with the constant criticism removed, the manipulation and gaslighting gone, and the fight or flight system deactivated this person should be able to heal and begin to have a sense of self and self-worth. Through therapeutic work they will begin to understand and incorporate boundaries and learn to rebuild trust and understand distress tolerance for abandonment triggers and no longer meeting the diagnosis of BPD which leads us to the conclusion that they didn’t have a personality disorder all along. Instead they had CPTSD with abandonment issues manifesting into a symptomology of the expression of BPD from narcissist abuse. These individuals then should be given a new diagnosis since they do not just suffer from CPTSD and meet symptomology for BPD. A new diagnosis should emerge that incorporates the emotional dysregulation, the trauma, the abuse, and the fears of abandonment. Thus allowing therapist to see the problem more clearly with more empathy and compassion and with a deeper sense of education on psychological abuse.

column1: Which musicians have continued with their music career after recovering from a devastating accident or injury?
column3: When people think about the 1977 Lynyrd Skynyrd plane crash, what they usually think of are the deaths of Ronnie Van Zant, Steve Gaines, and Cassie Gaines. Few people consider the fates of the band members who survived the crash. The luckiest were drummer Artimus Pyle, who escaped with several broken ribs (and was the one who went for help), and pianist Billy Powell, who woke in the wreckage to find that his nose had been nearly severed from his face, but other than that and other facial lacerations, he was mostly unharmed. Guitarist Allen Collins broke two vertebrae in his neck, and his right arm was so mangled that the emergency doctors wanted to amputate it; Collins’ father, acting on his behalf, refused to allow it. Guitarist Gary Rossington broke both arms, both wrists, both legs, his pelvis, and several ribs; those ribs punctured his liver and stomach. Today he is the last surviving original member of the band, and still has steel rods in his right arm and leg. Bassist Leon Wilkeson fared worst. His seat broke loose on impact, throwing him, still strapped in, face-first into the same bulkhead that broke Steve Gaines' neck. Leon lost most of his teeth and needed extensive facial reconstructive surgery, including steel plates. He also had massive internal injuries, including a punctured lung, plus six broken ribs, a severe double compound fracture of his left arm, and a closed double fracture of his right leg. On top of that, because of where the plane had crashed, he was immersed in contaminated swamp water until rescuers arrived, and subsequently developed severe infections in his wounds. His heart stopped twice on the operating table due to extreme blood loss, and he needed to be resuscitated and given numerous transfusions. It would take almost two years of recovery — both physical and emotional —before the surviving band members would play together again. Leon in particular was never the same bassist he had been prior to the crash, due to permanent nerve damage in his left arm that severely limited his range of motion for the rest of his life, but he continued to play bass until his death in 2001. The surviving band members reunited in 1979 at Charlie Daniels’ Volunteer Jam for an instrumental performance of “Free Bird” in honor of Ronnie, Steve, and Cassie; it was their first time playing together since the crash. Subsequently, all but Artimus (who had recently had a motorcycle accident that left him recovering from a leg injury) reunited as the Rossington Collins Band, with a female lead singer, Dale Krantz (who later married, and remains married to, Rossington). They released two albums, both well-received, before they split due to personal tragedy and inner conflict, and in 1987, all of the surviving members, other than Collins, paralyzed from the chest down in a 1986 car accident, re-formed Skynyrd with Ronnie’s younger brother Johnny on vocals. They weren’t and aren’t the same band as they were before the plane crash; it’s impossible that they could be. The loss was too great, and the loss of cofounding member Collins (who died in 1990 at 37) compounded it. But all of them soldiered on. Here’s the video from Volunteer Jam in 1979 — with a lone spotlight shining on the place Ronnie would, and should, have been standing.
