column1: How do you go on after suddenly losing a young child?
column3: The answer is complex, and depends on a variety of factors. Generally, the more support a parent has in the aftermath, the better they’ll do over time. Support from family, friends, community are all critical. After losing a child, a parent is engulfed in an emotional firestorm. It takes 2 to 3 years for the flames to subside, though the embers remain hot for another 2 to 3 years. Only then does the parent begin to rebuild themselves and their lives. It’s important to recognize that the timeline above doesn’t apply to everyone, as each loss is unique. Further, it’s intertwined with the support a parent has. If they lack support, it takes much longer to process the loss and rebuild one’s life. Below are important steps that can help a parent rebuild. PHASE 1: First 2 - 3 yearsTalk about it. The human minds needs to talk about something in order to process it. We have to process the loss in order to rebuild. If a parent is denied this, it can stunt or halt their recovery.Find support groups, either on-line or in person. Surrounding ourselves with others who speak the same loss language is a comforting reminder that we’re not alone. It also allows us a safe place to talk about our loss, and gives hope that the journey is survivable. If one group doesn’t feel right, try another.Practice good sleep hygiene. A good night’s sleep helps us cope the next day. Lack of sleep impacts our coping skills. Talk with your doctor to discuss medication if needed. Avoid alcohol, which interrupts your natural sleeping pattern.PHASE 2: Years 3 - 6Using the Rule of 5, engage in pleasure by treating your 5 senses to something that looks, feels, smells, tastes, and sounds good: 5 things you can see that brings you joy (a sunset is one example), 4 things you can touch (wear luxury socks), 3 things you can hear (the sound of children laughing), 2 things you can smell (a scented candle), 1 thing you can taste (a favorite treat). This exercise serves as an important reminder that not all pleasure is lost, and helps to reintegrate the parent back into the world around him/her.Embody self love. If your best friend were in the ICU, how would you treat him/her? With tender loving care. Consider yourself in the ICU of Grief Memorial Hospital, and make yourself your own best friend. This step can be done in the first 2 to 3 years as well, but the brain is consumed with emotional pain and often not cognitive enough to focus on anything besides just breathing and getting out of bed.Engage in a good belly laugh at least once daily. Laughing is a powerful healing modalities. Watch comedy sitcoms, a funny movie, or YouTube videos for a good laugh.PHASE 3: Years 7 and beyondVolunteer. Giving is good for the giver in that it induces a natural high and offers health benefits such as lower blood pressure, less stress, improved sleep, etc. Helping others helps our own heart to heal. We also see that struggles come in many forms, which reminds us that we’re not the only one.Share your natural gifts. You get to exercise your talents and receive all the benefits of giving (see above) while others benefit from the giving of your talent. Win-win. Can you sew? Sew a memorial quilt for someone. Can you sing? Join a community choir. Are you a good hugger? Become a baby cuddler at the hospital nursery.Embrace your story. Don’t be distracted by someone else’s awesomeness. Our identity is tied to our experiences. Own your story and live it bravely. Your hard-earned lessons will inspire others in ways you’ll never know, and gives them hope that if you survived, they can too.It takes years to rebuild, but it can happen. Along the way we learn that the heart can hold joy the same time as sorrow, we don’t have to choose. So give yourself permission to create joy. Your future depends on it. Thank you for asking such an important question, Nikki. I hope this helps.

column1: My son died one year ago and today would be his 17th birthday. My son (15) acted like he was still there and celebrated his birthday by making cake and lighting a candle. Is this normal behavior?
column3: Yes, absolutely normal and acceptable, as we all cope with the death of family members differently. I have a family member that miscarried her son, and her and the rest of the family celebrate what would've been his birthday every year, her son would be 12 years old now. This same family member has as miscarried at least 2 other children, including her daughter's twin. We all deal with the loss of a child differently, and in your son's case this is his way of remembering his brother. It's not that he's acting like he's still there, he's acknowledging his brother was here and that he misses him, and still loves his brother and thinks about him. I'd be more concerned if your son didn't acknowledge thw loss of his brother.

column1: How does one comfort a friend who just lost a loved one?
column3: I take two different approaches. When my step-dad passed away, I immediately packed my bags and went to my mom's house for a week. I became a life assistant. She lost her partner and was just kind of floating. She was there and not there so I acted as the connection between her and the rest of the world. We made cremation and funeral arrangements, entertained guests, went grocery shopping, watched tv, went to eat, slept, did chores, answered phone calls, notified friends and family, and when she wanted to talk about him, we did that too. I think if you are intimately close (spouse, child, parent, best friend) to the person and are in the position to offer that kind of 24/7 support, it's imperative that you do so. Moving from one world to the next is the single most powerful event in our lives. No one should have to deal with their emotions or practical matters alone during the aftermath. On the other hand, when I don't know the person well enough to be intimately involved, I tell them to ask directly if they need something. Then I watch or listen to see if I can figure out what they need. Bianca mentioned some very specific and practical ideas. I agree. They rarely know themselves. If they already have a "connector" then I speak to that person, introduce myself if necessary, tell them I WANT to help, and ask what I can specifically do to help. Usually they are in a better position to answer than those closest to the deceased. Most importantly, I follow through.

column1: Why is it important for kids to be raised with pets?
column3: Something not mentioned in previous answers is how valuable pets can be in preparing children to deal with things like discipline, (ex, how to treat an animal who has eaten your socks), accidents, sickness, aging, and death. The life span of most pets is short enough for a child to gain insight into those subjects, and help prepare them to cope with the reality of aging family members, frailty, and life changing loss. Nothing reduces the emotional pain of those things, but i think they are easier if you've been through the process with a beloved pet.

column1: How does one recover after the loss of a child? Is it ever possible?
column3: Hello my friend. Please keep in mind that everything I share here is my own personal grief journey. I would NEVER tell anyone how they should grieve, recover, or ultimately cope with the death of their child. We are all different, and everyone grieves in their own way, in their own time frame. My hope and motive is to offer support, hope, and encouragement to anyone going through this horrific nightmare. Do we ever recover? Yes, in a way we do, but, we will never be the same person again. My oldest son, Jesse, was diagnosed with Asperger’s Syndrome at age 11 years. Life was tough with him, and for him. He was more stubborn than a bull, and yet, the most sensitive young man I ever knew. Quite the dichotomy within him for sure!Life for Jesse was always two steps forward to ten steps back. When he first went to Middle School, he was so overwhelmed and traumatized by the sheer number of people, the sights, the sounds, the smells in the cafeteria, that he spent the first six months eating his lunch in the quietness of the office, but he never gave up, and he started developing friendships, and blossoming, but the hair trigger that is a hallmark of Autism, was still with him. There were more days than I can count that, I received a phone call from school, informing me that Jesse had experienced another meltdown, and was banging his head against the wall, or, another kid said something to set him off, and he got into another fight. It was a daily, exhausting battle. Jesse saw many counselors, and he had a special educational plan allowing for him to be alone when he needed it. He was always in sensory overload. When Jesse got to high school, he was quite the friendly, cool kid, and very popular with the girls. He was also introduced to drugs, and got caught with pot at school. We had to go to court over that, and I hoped and prayed it would scare him enough to leave it alone.There were many times when, Jesse and I butted heads, and he would take off, but he always kept in touch with me via text, and he always came home. Despite everything, he was very much a Mama’s boy, and he and I had a very special bond. One Sunday evening, I went back to his room, to tell him that dinner was ready, and to my shock, there was his girlfriend, the new one he had introduced me to on Friday, in bed with him. They were not doing anything, and were fully clothed, but it hit me in that moment that, he had been sneaking her in through the bedroom window all weekend, right under my nose. I was livid. I made her call her mother to pick her up, and I left him in his room, telling him we would discuss this later. I went back about an hour later, and he was gone. He had climbed out the bedroom window. I immediately texted him. He responded back, said some very nasty things, and told me he would be home later. We kept in touch via text, just like we had so many times before, but this night would be different, and Jesse would never come home. I fell asleep around 10pm, and I woke a little after 1am. I went back to his room, expecting to see him asleep in his bed, but he wasn’t there. My heart dropped. No matter what, he ALWAYS came home. It was a cold, misty, February night. I jumped into my truck with my phone, and I began texting him. Nothing. I drove around everywhere I knew to look, nothing. I drove for hours, texting him over and over and over again. Nothing. The whole time I was driving around I was praying, and thinking about how cold it was, and that he should be at home, in his warm bed. I finally went home around 5am, and called the police. An officer came and took the report, and based on everything that had happened, we all assumed that he was with the girlfriend, so he was reported as a runaway. Around 10:45am, there was a very aggressive knock on my door. I opened it, and there stood the officer who had taken the report, and a woman was with him, in plain clothes, with a Homicide Detective badge on her belt. I knew. No one had to tell me. I knew. Neither one of them could look me in the eyes. They asked me to sit on the couch, so I did. No one said a word, so finally, I said, “Are you telling me that my son is dead?” The officer said, “Yes.” I remember slamming my fist down, hard, on the glass-top coffee table, looking skyward, and crying out, “Lord Jesus, please let him be with you!” over, and over, and over again. The tears wouldn’t stop. This was on Monday, February 8th, 2016. Jesse was 16 years old. I lost days, then weeks, then months. My memory is still very spotty. The pain was too great to bear. I did not get to see Jesse again until the funeral on Friday, and seeing him in that casket made it all too real. It was real. My son was dead. His death was not by Homicide, and through my own detective work, I found out the truth. My son’s girlfriend’s father had recently died of cancer. There were left over Fentanyl patches and Xanax in her house, which she had stolen from where her mother had hidden them. She gave them to my son. I had no idea that he had these drugs, and after receiving the final Coroner’s report, we knew that this was the first and last time that Jesse tried opiates, and that it was accidental, not suicide. My family, friends, co-workers, and employers could not have been more supportive during this time, and I was, and still am, very blessed. I was allowed all the time I needed, and then some, to process what had happened, and the ramifications of it. The crying jags, uncontrollable, came and went randomly, for a year and half, and my employers graciously gave me every moment off that I needed. I wanted the world to stop. I wanted the world to feel my pain. I wanted the world to know just how special, and loved, Jesse was, and still is, but time stops for no man. This was a harsh, bitter truth, that I slowly came to grips with. I started grief therapy right away. I went three days a week to start, then weekly, then monthly. This helped tremendously. My friends and family meant well, as time went on, but they often ended up saying things, or offering suggestions, that were so painful, and all I could do was smile, and say, Thank you. It is not their fault that they cannot understand, nor feel what I feel. I became two people, and I still am. I am the woman who overcomes, who smiles, who has hope, and faith, and keeps going, just like the energizer bunny, but I am also the woman who lives hidden inside, with a piece of her heart torn out, now living in heaven, and that piece of my heart cannot be replaced. I have three other children who love me and need me. I have a career to tend to, bills to pay, and a life to live, and doing it all without Jesse is quite painful. I try not to think about what could have been, what might have been, in his future. I try to remember the sweet little boy who loved insects, nature, and animals. The sweet little kid who couldn’t give hugs when he was little, so instead he would headbutt my shoulder, like a puppy. He couldn’t say I love you, so, he said I like you, and that was the sweetest thing, ever. Jesse was unique in every way, and I will always remember how blessed I was to have him, even if it wasn’t for as long as I had dreamed of. Grief will come and go, like waves in the ocean. Sometimes it’s a Tsunami, and leaves you drowning. Sometimes it’s gentle, just a reminder, that you miss them. I keep the clothes that Jesse was found in tucked away in my closet. It was a new shirt and new pair of jeans that he absolutely LOVED. I will not wash them. Every now and then, I take them out, and touch them, smell them, and look at the little bits of concrete paint that still cling to the shirt. It may sound crazy to some, but it is quite common for parents to do things like this after the death of a child. I slept in his bed for weeks, with his picture tucked under my arm, right after he died. I still keep his favorite crib toy, “Lammykins,” and his baby blankets, in my bed. One of my favorite pictures of him and his best friend is facing my bed, so every morning when I wake up, there he is, smiling at me. It’s been three years now, since my baby went to heaven. I know that he is safe, and I will see him again. I also know that, Jesse wants me, and all of his family, to live our lives, and be happy. Easier said than done, but, one day at a time. I can honestly say that I am recovering, and coping, and better able to handle those bad moments that inevitably come. I never know what might trigger a torrent of tears, and sometimes, there are no triggers, it just hits me out of the blue. I accept it, allow myself to feel it, and keep moving through it until I reach the other side. For me, I like it when people bring Jesse up. I like to talk about him, to remember him, and so often, people walk on eggshells, thinking it will cause me pain. Sometimes, sometimes not, but either way, it is very much appreciated when people remember my son. :)This picture was taken a few weeks before Jesse died, and is one of my favorites. He was having breakfast with his Aunt Judy. It was a lovely day for both of them!For anyone interested, Ellie’s Way, a grief group on Facebook, is where I got this necklace and key chain. Todd Nigro is the group owner, a beautiful soul who lost his precious daughter to a tragic accident when she was seven years old. He, and the group, are a God-send, and I would highly recommend this group to anyone experiencing any type of grief due to loss of a family member. With these people, you are guaranteed to receive 24/7 support, encouragement, and lots of love. I have come to a conclusion that, no matter what life throws our way, we can become bitter, or better. We can become victims, or victors. It is a DAILY choice, and I say that because, I don’t always succeed, but I try, and I don’t beat myself up for those bitter moments, and I hope and pray that anyone reading this, will be kind and gentle with themselves, and others, as you navigate through this journey. ♥ *5/27/2019-I am so overwhelmed with all of the love and support in the comments. I honestly don’t know what to say, except, I love you all, and you have no idea how much it helps me, to see the brighter face of humanity. I hope I have helped many of you, in your grief journey. The Sun still shines! THANK YOU ALL, so much! ♥* Kahlil Gibran On Children
column9: I’m sorry for your loss. I hope that sharing these details is cathartic to you. My 14 year old also has autism and there is not a day that passes that I don’t worry about him.

column1: How do I help a child with the loss of a pet?
column3: For most kids, pets are more than just animals their families own — they're members of the family and the best of friends. While it's impossible to shelter kids from the loss of a pet, you can help them cope with it. And because a pet's death might be their first time losing a loved one, the grieving process can help kids learn how to cope with other losses throughout life.

column1: What is it like to lose a child?
column3: Being a parent has been the most rewarding - and the most painful experience of my life. I can hardly imagine what my life would be like if I had not been a parent. I am grateful that my wife of over 36 years has been there to help me through every parenting experience. My heart goes out to those single parents who have to do this without the support of a partner. I have had countless opportunities for emotional growth as a result of raising children. Until now, I haven't written specifically about the experience of losing our daughter. Please forgive the length of this Quora Share. Up until now, I have limited my writing to mostly medical topics, but this question caught my eye. I assume many may not read this because of its length, but once I started writing, more and more memories came to the surface and spilled out on to the page. Following are some of the things I've learned about myself, some of the feelings I have felt, and how they have impacted my belief system. I have had the privilege of taking care of cancer patients for 35 years now (if you count residency). During the first five years after completing my residency, I was an associate professor of Radiation Oncology at the Baylor Medical School in Houston and director of the residency training program. We treated the kids with cancer at Texas Children's Hospital. My wife and I had three sons at that time, all under the age of seven. All of the young boys I took care of at work reminded me of my own sons. One of the main reasons I treated the children was because I was the youngest faculty member. It was a job that no one wanted to do. It was very sad, and it felt very threatening, so they gave it to the person with the least seniority. (They claimed that since I had taken my specialty boards more recently than anyone else, I was probably more current on all the pediatric treatment protocols, but I knew that they really just didn't want to do it). My wife and I were blessed with a fourth son a few years later and we debated about trying one more time for a girl. Finally, in 1991, our daughter was born. By this time I had made the move out of academia and into private practice. We had moved to Oklahoma City, which was a much nicer city than Houston in which to raise a family. We had the usual challenges that went with raising children in the nineties and two-thousands. Katrina was a really beautiful girl (see photo). She was never snobbish - she was friends with everyone in her class and managed to meet kids her age from all over the country. She was extremely bright, outgoing and enjoyed performing in the theater in high school. Her four older brothers loved her and always seemed to get along with her (even though they didn't always get along with each other).Everyone had made it through the teenage years before Katrina got sick, so at least there was a minimum of coexisting emotional turmoil during that time. Katrina had a breast mass when she was about fifteen which, on biopsy displayed some bizarre features that were hard to classify. Of course a biopsy is just a small core of tissue from a 14 gauge needle, so there wasn't a lot to process for special testing. Nevertheless, when the entire mass was removed, it turned out to be a fibroadenoma - a relatively common benign breast tumor and there was no sign of anything out of the ordinary. Whatever they hit with the biopsy needle, it was the only microscopic evidence of anything abnormal. Katrina was popular in High School (an experience that neither her mom nor I had had when we were that age). Everybody loved her - she was nice to everyone - especially those classmates who were insecure about themselves. She decided to go into nursing after high school - the only one of my children with any interest in medicine. (I am extremely proud of all my children. Unlike many of my colleagues, I didn't have any expectations that they might choose a medical career. I just wanted them to be happy and at some point be able to support themselves.) She went to the University of Tulsa, about a hundred miles from home. She joined a sorority, Chi Omega, and was admired and loved by all her sorority sisters. Just as in high school, she was kind to everyone, including the girls who were insecure - she had empathy for everyone. When we went for parents day, we walked with her across campus to the football stadium. She stopped every fifty feet or so to introduce us to some of her friends. There were just a few kids that we passed on the way that she didn't seem to know. I had the privilege of going to "Dad's Day" during her freshman and sophomore years - some of my fondest memories of spending time with her.While at college, she had noticed a mass in her breast in the same location as the previous one. She knew that fibroadenomas frequently recurred, so she wasn't too concerned about it. With her busy social calendar, she didn't see her doctor until it was several centimeters in size. Her doctor sent her for breast imaging right away and the radiologist called the breast surgeon immediately. She had it excised and we went with her to meet with the surgeon for a post-op visit. She told her that she had a phylloides tumor. She said these are almost always benign, but unfortunately hers was malignant. It's really hard to describe the feeling that immediately followed. It felt like the floor had fallen away and that the whole fabric of reality was unraveling. I have long understood that denial is an automatic response that takes over to protect us from being overwhelmed when we encounter some unacceptable aspect of reality - I guess that was what was going on - Nothing seemed real. No, I thought - I must have the cancer - that would be OK - she can't have cancer - Oh, God NO, please, this can't be real. This can't be real. This can't..... We went immediately to the pathology department to check out her slides. The Komen "Race for the Cure" happened soon after her surgery and a few of her sorority sisters came to visit her the night before. When we went to the event the next day, about 25 more of them surprised her at the race. A phylloides tumor arises from connective tissue in the breast (as opposed to carcinomas, which arise from the ducts or glands). An older term is cystosarcoma phylloides, since, like sarcomas, they arise from connective tissue - and look kind of like sarcomas under the microscope. Phylloides tumors (actually, they call them phyllodes tumors now, but when I went to medical school, they were spelled phylloides) make up less than 1% of all breast tumors - and malignant phylloides tumors make up a very small percentage of those. They are more common in women over forty, and rarely occur in twenty year olds. Overall, there are less than fifty cases in the US every year that are even remotely similar to what my daughter had. Malignant phylloides tumors are made up of an epithelial component and a connective tissue component. In her case the sarcomatous part looked like a rhabdomyosarcoma under the microscope. This is a sarcoma that most commonly occurs in children - I had treated many children with rhabdomyosarcomas when I was in Houston, so I kind of knew how to do that. As it happened, two world renowned experts (a pediatric oncologist and a pathologist) on rhabdomyosarcomas (rhabdos for short) practiced at our local children's hospital, so I took her slides to the pathologist the next day. I looked at them through the teaching head of his microscope - most of the tissue looked like the familiar "rhabdo" but parts looked bizarre - I had never seen a malignant phylloides tumor before. I talked to the pediatric oncologist at length. He said there was no precedent for treating a malignant phylloides tumor with the combination chemotherapy one would use for a rhabdo, but he was going to an international conference the next week and he would ask the other experts there and get some opinions. (BTW, I am the medical director for the Procure Proton Therapy Center in Oklahoma City. One nice thing about that is that we could get everything we needed done immediately.) We got staging studies, including a PET scan, which were all negative - after removing her breast, she had no measurable evidence of cancer in her body. Her surgeon put in a port for chemotherapy. We took her to the Dana-Farber Cancer Center in Boston. (The proton community is fairly small, so I knew quite a few docs at Mass General, where they have a proton center, so I was able to get her into Dana-Farber right away - the same group of Harvard Radiation Oncologists work at both places.) We met with a surgeon, a radiation oncologist and a medical oncologist in a very efficient multidisciplinary clinic. They summarized their recommendations - a combination of drugs like those used for adult sarcomas - very toxic with a pretty low response rate. Katrina was otherwise healthy, though, and should be able to tolerate treatment well. I got a call from the rhabdo guru I mentioned above. He was back from his conference. None of his colleagues who studied rhabdomyosarcomas had any better ideas about what to do. At least Katrina had the benefit of opinions from all the world's experts. I took her to a classmate of mine from medical school - a very good medical oncologist in community practice. Soon, she started chemotherapy (the chemo was so toxic, it could only be given during admission to the hospital). She was admitted to the hospital for five days for each round of chemotherapy - once every month. I think she was able to repress much of her fear, since, after all, her daddy was a cancer expert and would make everything turn out OK. I am grateful she felt comforted by that - even though it was just her perception - I knew it was not reality. (I had learned a long time ago, that there's really very little that doctors can do for people. A trillion cells are each running countless biochemical processes in every human being. What we can influence is an infinitesimal fraction of what we can't. Whatever you chose to believe about a Higher Power in the Universe, there's certainly one making all this happen. Human beings have a tendency to just look at what we can control and assume that that's very close to everything. We live our lives in a constant state of denial. Until we face something in our life over which we are clearly powerless, it's easy to maintain that illusion. It's the same way with knowledge. We understand only a little, but if we continually focus on what we do know, and ignore what we don't, we can create the illusion that we "know everything". For example, we have learned a little about how the brain works - functional MRIs, EEGs, PET brain scanning, understanding the biochemical mechanisms of neurotransmitters, developing drugs that alter those neurotransmitters, etc. So many people think that just because we understand what we do, that a complete understanding of how our mind works is just around the corner. The reality is that today we are no closer to understanding why consciousness exists than we were a hundred years ago. Until humans get even remotely close to an explanation for the phenomenon of consciousness, I will continue to believe that there is a benevolent Higher Power running everything. I frequently tell people to throw out everything about religion that doesn't work for them and focus on developing a practical relationship with whatever they conceptualize their Higher Power to be - as long as it's consistent with their experience.) Katrina was being admitted for her fourth cycle of chemo when she showed her oncologist a lump that had popped up in her mastectomy scar. Her surgeon removed it (and took out her tissue expander at the same time) and it was indeed a recurrence of her cancer. Restaging once again showed no evidence of metastatic disease, so we stopped the (ineffective) chemotherapy and my partner gave her radiation therapy to her chest wall to sterilize any residual microscopic cancer cells remaining after surgery. Everything was looking good. She could have her breast reconstruction performed further down the line. She had almost no side effects from her radiation therapy and her hair started growing back. She went back to school. She came back home for a follow-up PET/CT scan and we were once again looking forward to celebrating a good result. Katrina, her mom and I would always go into the radiology reading room as soon as her scan was done. The radiologist was delayed this time, so I pulled up the scan and started reviewing it. There was a hot spot on one of her thoracic vertebrae. I remember being baffled as I looked at it, wondering what could cause that sort of artifact - it wasn't there on her prior scan. The PET was hot, but the CT looked OK. When the radiologist came back, he was very kind and didn't just say something like "Well, this looks like cancer here." He could tell that I was involuntarily experiencing reflexive denial, so he simply suggested we do an MRI - just to clear up the "artifact" question. I watched the monitor as she had the MRI, my wife sitting beside me. The MRI was unmistakable - I felt the same way I had in her surgeon's office the day we first learned of her diagnosis. I told my wife - "It's cancer - it's metastatic - she's no longer curable." When Katrina got out of the scanner, she could tell by looking at us that it wasn't good news. I told her that there was cancer in her vertebra and that we would treat it with radiation therapy. She didn't ask if it meant that she was terminal and I didn't tell her. When my patients are ready to know the answers to the really big questions, they will ask me. I think it's unkind to take away someone's denial, just because I want them to "know the truth". Denial serves an essential survival function. It allows people to continue living from day to day, whereas knowing the truth might make them shut down and give up right then and there. When they are ready to move beyond denial, they will ask those questions. I showed my daughter the same compassion I would show one of my patients. She said, "Well, let me know when I have an appointment with Dr. P (my partner) - I'm going back to school tonight." She had Stereotactic Ablative Radiation Therapy to the vertebra, which controlled the cancer for quite some time. A little while later, she developed metastatic disease in her femur. Fortunately, we knew a world class orthopedic oncologist who performed a hip replacement. She had several more courses of radiation therapy and a few more surgical procedures over the next year and a half, but no more chemo. The usual treatment for a rare cancer is to have "best guess" chemotherapy and when that fails, there's always a "second line" chemo (it's second line because it has less chance of producing a response than the "first line" does). Then there's third line, etc. At least we knew enough to stop putting her through the discomfort of more chemotherapy. Her hair grew back. She finished her semester at school. As time went on, she came to understand that she wasn't going to survive the cancer, but we rarely talked about it. She decided not to take any more classes in college, but wanted to keep living in an apartment in Tulsa, because that's where most all of her friends were. We took out a home equity loan so we could afford to do whatever she wanted. She remained active in her sorority. She had a twenty-first birthday party in Tulsa and then we flew eighteen of her friends to Las Vegas with us and she had a twenty-first birthday party there as well. We went to Europe for an extended vacation, which included a cruise around the Adriatic Sea - she met a young man on the cruise (from Scotland) with whom she fell in love. He felt the same way about her and came to America to visit for six weeks - they had no illusions about her life expectancy, but both of them enjoyed being together. She gave him an "out" due to her condition, but he didn't want to take it. She loved the Oklahoma City Thunder Basketball team and we managed to get season tickets - she went to every home game including one that was only four days before she died. One day she was driving through an intersection and was literally "hit by a Mack Truck" - it was a dump truck that had run a red light. It fractured the vertebra that had been treated with radiation - over the next few months the residual cancer grew through the cracks in the vertebral body and around her spinal cord necessitating one more operation to remove the cancer and stabilize her spine. Toward the very end, her back pain required high doses of narcotics to control. She never wanted Hospice - she just wanted her family to take care of her. Her two brothers who lived out of town both came home for the last couple of months of her life, so she had her Mom, Dad and four brothers with her every day, not to mention almost daily visits from a host of friends. Finally, the cancer filled so much of her lungs that she became hypoxic and lost consciousness for the last 36 hours of her life. When she stopped breathing, I tried to clear her airway and was tempted to ventilate her, but I realized that anything I did would only add minutes - or at most an hour to her life - still, even though she had been unconscious for over a day, it was hard to let go - it made me realize how hard it must be to "pull the plug" on a loved one. We cried, we prayed, we thanked our Higher Power for the twenty one and a half years that we got to have her with us. We had a funeral in Oklahoma City and a Memorial Service in Tulsa. All together, more than a thousand people came to the services - a testament to how many friends she had (and how many friends we are blessed to have). About a year later, we went to Scotland to visit Mark, Katrina's Scottish boyfriend, and his family, whom we had gotten to know via the internet. We sprinkled some of her ashes at the origin of the River Dee, before it winds its way down through the Scottish countryside to reach the North Sea at Aberdeen - a place Katrina would have wanted to visit if there had only been time. There will always be a hole in my soul that will never again be completely filled, but today it is mostly filled with fond memories of our time together. The stages leading to Acceptance include Denial, Anger, Bargaining and Depression. I've come to understand how denial can take over and protect my psyche from being overwhelmed by realities that are too terrible to experience at a conscious level. Denial is like a parachute that slows my descent so that I don't suddenly slam into unpleasant truths. I experienced relatively little anger on my journey toward accepting my daughter's death. I think gratitude is the best antidote for self pity (I think that self pity and anger are two sides of the same coin), and I was fortunate to be able to feel grateful every day that I got to spend with Katrina - and now - everyday that I get to spend with all my other loved ones. I don't think that feeling grateful is something I can will myself to do - like all my other feelings, it is a gift. Nevertheless, it seems to displace anger, just as water displaces oil. I have seen thousands of cancer patients and their families spend much of their remaining precious time "Bargaining" for a cure - another round of chemo, an expensive new drug, a clinical trial (with little chance of success) or going to Mexico to take laetrile - motivated by their fear of death, they continue to grasp at straws, even though fighting the inevitable saps their strength and robs them of the enjoyment they might have today. I am grateful to all those who've demonstrated this behavior to me, so I didn't have to waste my time (and my family's time) "bargaining". Instead, we had that much more time to spend enjoying the wonderful gift of each day. It was reasonable to try the chemotherapy, but when we saw that it wasn't working, we were able to move on. Depression (or at least profound sadness) is an unavoidable part of the journey toward acceptance. I think this is what I feel while the chemicals in my brain re-equilibrate - while the synaptic connections reorganize - while the changes occur that allow me to get to a state of Acceptance - the state where I'm OK with what had previously been an unacceptable fact of reality. Acceptance is the answer to all my problems today. I believe that nothing happens in this universe by mistake. "When I am disturbed, it is because I find some person, place, thing or situation - some fact of my life unacceptable to me, and I can find no serenity until I accept that person, place, thing or situation as being exactly the way it is supposed to be at this moment." I don't waste my time arguing with those who wish to believe that "if I like something it must be God's will and if I don't like it, it must not be God's will" - or those who wish to believe that "God takes care of the big things, but leaves the little things to chance". Today, my Higher Power is everything - and I choose to believe that every sub atomic particle, every quantum packet of energy is in exactly the state it's supposed to be in at this instant. Of course, what I believe about these things is beyond the reach of investigation by the scientific method and I don't expect anyone to believe anything that can't be scientifically validated. This is just what I believe - and if it works for you too, please use it, but regardless, I hope you find some philosophy of life - some belief system - that gives you comfort when life brings you experiences that are so terrible, they seem impossible to survive.
column9: What an amazing story and you write it so well. I love that the radiologist gave you just a little more time for hope and deniability when he called the hot spot "artifact" knowing full well you knew otherwise. He was just trying to extend a few more moments of hope. I'm sorry you lost your gorgeous, wonderful daughter and that the world lost her as well. This world needs more, not fewer, people like her. The experience, I'm sure, has made you a better physician . . . and definitely a better writer!

column1: Do you believe that the royal aides and members of the royal family treated Meghan with the same amount of compassion as they did with Kate?
column3: Yes. Which is none at all. Both Catherine and Meghan chose to become members of the Royal Family Firm, and neither received in depth coaching to enable them to cope with the expected behaviours and losses. Catherine was going out with William for 10 years before they married, so she was much more aware of what the Royal life entailed, and willing to do it - and accept the bad with the good. As an upper middle class English girl (from a relatively humble background, her parents were entrepreneurs, and succeeded, climbing the social ladder as they did so) she knew what the public expected. She was clearly not self-centred, but giving, and generous. Meghan was in it for what she could get out of it. It is obvious now that she had no intention of staying in the Royal Family. It was a clear case of ‘grab the wedding, grab the limelight and the Royal ‘celebrity’ status (very cheap PR), grab the Prince and anchor him with the child and the brain washing, and then decamp to LA with the booty, and the means to make money amongst the media rich and infamous with whom she longed to associate.’ Catherine neither sought nor expected compassion - for what? What happened that required compassion? Meghan seeks attention all the time, and wanted the Royal family to ‘ask if she was all right’. Why? She clearly was. She had the money and the man, and having a baby does not invite compassion but congratulation. Compassion for what? Going through labour? Millions do that every day and she could afford the best help. Meghan is a narcissist. Catherine is not. That is the difference.
column9: I love this answer. Well said. Especially about how she didnt need compassion but rather congratulations.

column1: How do you cope with family estrangement?
column3: This is going to be raw and painful for me, but here goes. 4 years back I divorced my husband of 21 years. We had 8 kids together & home churched & home schooled. My family (also my church family) pulled the plug. I was on my own, no one from my Christian community would touch me with a 10’ stick for fear of “catching” whatever caused my marriage to go awry. Being estranged from my family & friends put me into severe depression. I didn't have a net to fall into, so I lay there, in bed day after day, only rising to do what HAD to get done. I went to a therapist and a psychiatrist, but nothing was enough. I was alone, I focused on my solitude and I stayed in my deep misery. I went into hospital for the psychological ward one night, in hopes that someone would finally save me from my hell —but they didn't. I was sent home (relieved!) to my children who were terrified mommy was so ill she was going to die. No one was going to save me. No saviour was there at the right moment. No god in the heavens was concerned for me. I was on my own. What changed? How did I pull through? •After realizing just how truly blessed I am to have these beautiful people (my kids) in my life I slowly became grateful for them, again. I cherished and cared for their problems, along with mine. •After abandoning my responsibilities as the caretaker of my home I took account of how fortunate I am to have a shelter. I have been painting, cleaning, and organizing little by little. •After laying in my bed, exhausted from merely living, I forced myself to accept my pain as worthy, accept my suffering as long enough, and forgive myself for grieving the loss of so many dreams; I started to live again. Losing my extended family through ignorance & theism has brought me to a new level of understanding. •Humans are assholes. I'm not going to conform! I'm going to be the mom I wish I'd had as a child. I'm going to be the friend I wish I'd had. I'm going to be the person I fantasize about becoming —right now! —not “when I'm ________ enough”! Now is the moment! • I became completely honest with myself. No more lying, “it's only a piece of cake” when it's the 3rd piece. Nor, “I can't stop smoking cigarettes, I need them for this stress” business. If I knew it was bad, I admitted and quit it. It was hard! • I started listening to my body a bit more. My body’s response to my drinking alcoholic drinks was severe lethargy, aches, pain and wouldn't you know it, depression! I had to fess up to myself & stop playing the part of the victim to quit. I'd been a victim far too long & no one had ever rescued me. I had to rescue me!!! •And, I joined a group therapy 2 months ago & it's been so good for me! I hope you good speed, consistency, strength & wisdom to pull you through! Find a good therapist [don't stop ‘til it's a good fit!], keep your closest friend (s) and become your own best, most reliable friend. Fall in love with yourself. Love you! (I listened to a lot of meditations from the Insight Timer app called “Living Awake” to forgive and start to love me.) It will work!
column9: Your amazing. Thank you so much for sharing your story. I have come to realise the same thing. There’s only one person responsible for your happiness and that is yourself. I have been through so much and I refuse to go through anymore. I haven’t had an alcoholic drink in almost 11 years. I still smoke, but I’ve cut right back. 3 a day. 1 joint, before I go to bed. Helps me sleep. I’m concentrating on my son. On his education. On being the parent I never had. Having as much fun as we can before he gets to old to play with dear old mum.

column1: What is your unpopular opinion on how Prince Harry really feels about leaving his duties as a royal family member?
column3: Prince Harry was deeply affected by the loss of his mother, Princess Diana. His mother was his most favorite person in the world. Put yourself in his shoes. You’re living this above average life as a royal child and the most favorite person in your world, the person who loved and cherished you more than any other disappears one day. The cause of her disappearing: due to being famous which led to her being chased by paparazzi. Would you want anything to do with an entity that caused your loved one to be killed?No, you’re going to want to live as normal a life as possible. You’re going to want to live a life that doesn’t entail frequent access to the royal rota and other press outlets who:Were a force which led to your mother’s deathTarnish you and your wife’s name by spreading false info about you to the publicConstantly invade your privacyYou would do your best to try to stay away from constant reminders of the worst day of your life. A day that brought about so much unhappiness.My unpopular opinion is that Prince Harry has wanted to leave royal life since the day that his mother died. The day she died is the day he probably began his intense dislike of fame and paparazzi. Being a royal family member brings fame and intense scrutiny by press and paparazzi. The 12 year old Harry was unable to separate himself from the source of his unhappiness. That is—until he became a grown man who’s lived and had enough life experience. A grown man who is able to think and make sound decisions for himself. So while the popular opinion is that Meghan is the one who influenced him to step back from the royal family, I believe otherwise. He also confirmed that it was his decision in his last speech, stating: ”The decision that I have made for my wife and I to step back is not one I made lightly," he said. "It was so many months of talks after so many years of challenges. And I know I haven't always gotten it right, but as far as this goes, there really was no other option.” My unpopular opinion about how Prince William really feels about his duties Another unpopular opinion that I have is that Prince William would also happily step back from his duties as a royal if it were his choice. People forget that William was always an extremely shy individual. He too had struggles coping with the loss of his mother and became much more introverted than he already was.Prince Harry has even supported this notion that William would probably not choose not to be a king if it were his choice. In a previous interview, Prince Harry said:[1] “Is there any one of the royal family who wants to be king or queen? I don’t think so, but we will carry out our duties at the right time.” Prince Harry had the choice to opt out of royal life. His brother has no choice but to remain a senior royal so long as there is a monarchy. Ironically, it seems that the shyest people are somehow always destined for the spotlight. This shy but dignified man will be a king soon!Is the British public ready for the reign of the future ‘His Majesty William the Fifth by the Grace of God of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland and of His other Realms and Territories King, Head of the Commonwealth, Defender of the Faith?’Footnotes[1] Who Wants to Be King? No One, Prince Harry Says

column1: How can I get over the sudden death of my dad?
column3: Hi, I understand Dealing with your dad's death is difficult, painful and sad for any person. When you are a young person, the loss of a father is extremely difficult because you are losing a mentor, the person who was meant to help guide you through many parts of growing up. It may feel as if the loss of your dad has taken away the person you are inside, has removed a piece of yourself that was integral to making you the person you are. Here are some ways to start working through your pain and sadness. Steps 1.Be accepting of the pain. The loss of your dad can easily take away your emotions and impact on who you feel you are. You won't feel the same after this loss and it is important to accept that this is a normal state. 2. Talk to others. Speak with family and friends as openly as possible. They know you are going through a really difficult time and it is important to share your emotions, your ups and downs and your fears with others. Remember that your inner circle of family members are probably experiencing similar emotions and maybe you can help one another through this devastating time. However, if you don't feel comfortable talking with family members or you feel that their own pain has locked them away from you so intensely, you should feel free to talk to your peers and people who can help at school such as counselors or a doctor. If you would prefer a more private setting try blogging or chatting online. It is best not to bottle it up inside; while you can still keep deep emotions and reflections to yourself, talking to some extent is vital to keep you connected with humanity and feeling the power of supportive friendships. 3. Talk to your mother. Many young people feel an overwhelming need to protect their mother from pain. Yes, she will be suffering intensely but she needs you and you need her. Remember that your reluctance to speak with her may be interpreted by her as a need for her to avoid upsetting you by talking too much about the loss. As such, this can turn into a vicious cycle of both of you trying to protect one another and neither one of you actually opening up and actively talking through what has happened and sharing your pain. Acknowledge it first if your mother cannot and tell her that you do need to talk to her about your feelings of loss. Also tell her that you want to discuss how you love her and how you still love your dad and that you want to keep the memories intact as a family effort. In this way, you can try to help avoid joint isolation in grief. 4. Seek professional help. It is really important to seek counseling if you are having feelings of depression and an inability to cope with your loss. It will not improve things for you if you allow yourself to be swept under by powerful negative emotions. 5. Allow yourself to cry. It is going to be hard and crying is a normal outlet. If you feel that you need to maintain a brave face in front of others, cry in your own personal space, whenever the urge takes you. But realize also, that there is no losing face or shame in crying in front of anybody during a time like this. Everybody can imagine how terrible it must be to lose a father and they will be supportive 6. Talk about who your dad was. Remember the good things about your dad and look at photos of him. Put together a memory album and write down all the wonderful things you have experienced together. Other ideas include making a collage, writing letters to your dad and saving them or disposing of them in a symbolic fashion and making a DVD of times spent together. 7. Integrate the loss into your life. Over time your grief will change in the way that it is expressed. Few people ever truly "get over" the loss of a close loved one but most people find a special place in their heart that guards the memory and essence of the lost person for life. Accept that you will faced with the heartache of the loss of your father time and time again through life, especially on occasions where you would have expected your father to be standing by your side, such as graduations, sports events, a wedding etc. You will also lack the advice on finances, planning, socializing etc. that a father would have provided you. Accept these realities and do your own planning and find mentors who are supportive, caring and capable of assisting you in these ways. 8. Know that you will always be your dad's child. He may have died but you still continue to have a relationship with him. You will always be his child and he will always live on in your heart. Others will know the person he was through you; so treasure the memories and be ready to share them with others as time moves on.

column1: Are you able to trust your partner again after they have cheated on you?
column3: No. Maybe to a point, but never to the extent that a life partnership should have. They have shown you that they are capable of betrayal and duplicity, you won’t ever be able to fully trust a person who is capable of such behavior. It may not impact the relationship on a regular basis, but it will introduce an insecurity to the attachment which limits your ability to bond, weakens your faith in them, and establishes a nagging doubt as it pertains to their motivations and integrity. Some people accept this reality and cope with it as an inherent aspect of their relationship. Some may assert their bond is strengthened as a result of infidelity. I, personally, believe those people have chosen to believe in a delusion, allowing them to believe in a fantasy preserving their desires and ignoring their reality, but maybe it works for them. From what I’ve seen, nobody escapes the consequences of infidelity - every relationship is permanently injured - trust being the inescapable casualty of betrayal. Even if it is minimal, it never completely vanishes. There are various accounts of the effects on the betrayed partner in subsequent relationships, for those that leave their cheating partner. It seems their ability to trust is largely dictated by how dedicated they were to healing themselves from the trauma of betrayal. There are many other factors that influence the betrayed’s ability to trust - how old they were, how invested they were in the relationship, the emotional intensity and degree of intimacy they believed existed with the cheater, how well the cheater handled disclosure/discovery, whether they shared children, if the affair partner was a friend or family member of the betrayed, if they were left for the affair partner, how much support they received from friends/family, etc. It seems, based on my observation, that betrayal leaves a lasting scar. The wounds merely scabs over if the cheater and betrayed partner reconcile the relationship. For those that leave, it scars over, but occasionally there are reminders of the pain that they felt where the scar now exists. There is a hesitation and skepticism, that serves as a survival instinct if something triggers that memory. Not all that dissimilar to a child that has touched a hot stove - they may still enjoy cooking, but will be cautious of the hazards in the kitchen, and may continue to suffer from heat or cold sensitivity or loss of feeling (reminding them of the injury and occasionally the lasting effects).
column9: There is also the never knowing the full knowledge of what happened, especially if all you have to go on is the cheating partners version they provide. You will never know the full length of time or how they really felt for the other person, so that would always niggle away. I'm not sure how anyone puts it behind them.

column1: What are some effective ways to cope with the grief of bereavement (due to the loss of family)? Are keeping busy and letting time heal the only ways?
column3: I’ve grieved the loss of a brother in his 40’s to suicide without warning in 2000, then the loss of a key employee and best friend (also in his 40’s) in 2001 to a sudden heart attack at home, then in 2005 we lost our then 20 year old son to a botched firefighter training accident in our small close knit community. Those were the untimely losses, we had several other losses of elderly family members and friends to cancer along the way. It’s challenging to grieve untimely death, but our society treats death at any age as a failure and something to be feared or delayed at almost any cost. Even at very old age we’re saddened to lose someone who has lived a long and loved life. None of us will escape death, and most of us will not escape grieving someone close to us. We arrive to grief completely unprepared and without a plan or experience. I’d like to see more teaching on preparation for grief, because no matter how unwelcome or inconvenient it is, grief can and should be an opportunity to learn about ourselves and about life. My belief is that we don’t simply “get over” the death of a loved one, so we shouldn’t try to close the door quickly. Keeping busy and waiting for time to heal us work slowly and ineffectively, in my opinion and experience. To heal well, we must come to understand how to incorporate the lost life and therefore the lost love into our own life and perhaps learn something from that lost life that we can carry forward in memory. Grief is initially a massive emotional overload that washes over us and pins us down, often to being completely numb. I liken the first experience to being dropped roughly into a dark and dangerous pit deep in a foreboding forest. We can’t see a way out, we’re surrounded by obvious perils, we’re uncomfortable and unprepared. We know we must move on, and get back to life, but we become afraid and our numbness keeps us locked in place. Slowly we climb out of the pit, perhaps sliding down as often as moving up. Over time we find our way and find paths to follow that others have taken before us. We still have no idea where we are or where we’re going, but if our life had a purpose before then we have a will to survive and heal. As we move away from the pit at the center of our loss we slowly learn to survive the loss. We walk at times with others who maybe are grieving the same death differently and we seek guidance and share memories. In the end, the worst of the emotions are resolved and as we walk into a place called Acceptance we have regained the logic in our lives and carry only the memories we wish to from that person we loved and lost. I tell people new to loss to focus on the years of life and not the days, weeks or month of the death. Don’t isolate yourself, and don’t allow those close to you to isolate themselves. Speak of the good life more than the inevitable or tragic death. There is nothing more beautiful to me than the capacity of humans to love so deeply that the wounds to our soul from losing that loved one are sometimes worse than anything we could have imagined. The capacity of the human soul to heal from those wounds and carry the scars of loss through life is amazing, if we allow ourselves to heal. I have a deeply scarred soul from untimely loss of loved ones. I love deeply and risk more loss because nothing surpasses the joy of love. I allow very few people to see my scarred soul, only the closest see it. But each scar has taught me wonderful things about life, about love and about the capacity of the human soul to endure loss and heal to be better and stronger. Grief of untimely death has changed me. I fear little, even my own death. I have fewer friends, but the ones I have are deeper and more valuable to me and I’m willing to risk the suffering of grieving them in the future for the value sharing the love of friendship brings to our lives today. I walk towards the friends and families who have suffered a suicide to share what I know and try to help them take the first steps away from that horrible and confusing loss. I gravitate towards those who have survived the loss of a child, especially the ones who can learn to laugh and love again. Outer beauty means little to me, I am attracted to the beauty of a battle worn soul that somehow survives and has learned the real value of love again. Am I better for loss? No, I would have preferred never to lose loved ones. But I have become who I am because the Universe randomly chose these challenges for me and I found a way to come back to a life that includes love and laughter. Wisdom is an overused descriptor, but many aspire to wisdom without understanding that most wisdom is acquired thru pain. We learn more about the value of life, the value of love and the value of our souls on the few worst days of our lives that we do on all the easy days we have. I am wiser for each journey through grief that the Universe chose for me. Be well and peaceful, find and share your inner strength with those who most deserve and best reflect your love.
