column1: Will I ever get over the loss of my dog?
column3: Hello and please accept my deepest condolences. Losing a pet is never easy. The broken heart that you have is just as real as the loss of a child or another loved family member. I have lost many dear pets through out my life and one thing for sure, it never gets easier. I had to put my dear Bischon (Gino) to sleep on 01/21/13. I cried so much I just wanted to die myself.I had him since he was 6 weeks old. He would have been 13 in April. I put him down in Jan. I have his pictures everywhere in my home. I talk to him everyday. He used to sleep on my bed and I have even felt him move on the bed. I have felt him brush against my legs. I have even heard him with his little growls. You might think I an totally crazy, (others might agree with you) lol. I got rid of most of his things.slowly.I donated a lot to the SPCA Canada. I then got a new little rescue fur baby, a few months later, he will Never take the place of my Gino,but he sure did fill a void in my heart. He needed a home and love, and I needed another pet to love. The first year was the hardest after my loss, I cried several times a day. Slowly, the tears stopped. I still cry sometimes when I think of him or see another dog that reminds me of him.I had Gino cremated. I have his ashes here in my home. I used to take him everywhere in my car and he loved to go with me. I take my other little baby Joey with me everywhere now as well. I got a doggie stroller that I keep in my car and we go galavanting. I fell in love with him too. It didn’t take too long. I wish you the best. Time has a way of healing the heart. My advice, when you feel ready for another pet, think of the ASPCA or any other shelter.There is a little heart beating and just waiting for a forever loving home. God Bless

column1: Can children survive being raised by two narcissistic parents?
column3: Yes. Children are resilient and can survive two narcissistic parents, but they won’t get away, without emotional “scars,” most likely. These children will have faced NPD in their parents, and it can be a very difficult road to travel, even after leaving their parent’s home. Some may never even know how truly brave they really are. If they have conquered the insurmountable odds of NOT being emotionally destroyed before adulthood, by these people, that is ALREADY, a huge accomplishment. If an adult-child of narcissists got out of their personal hell or the “house of two narcs,” with the ability to still love and empathize NOT “taken” from them, they have already endured a true hero’s journey. The children of narcissistic parents all deserve great respect for being able to survive that type of childhood and for escaping their parent’s home with their mind and heart still somewhat intact. That, in and of itself, is courageous! Children of narcissistic parents have had many years, at the very least, of emotional and/or psychological abuse by the time they leave home. They have often been trained to self-destruct on auto-pilot, or to be victimized into fostering unhealthy dependency on the disordered parents. These parents sabotage their children by means of controlling them, well into adulthood. These children might have some pretty serious emotional “battle scars” and endure some PTSD-like symptoms, as they have seen and experienced things from living with two narcissists that few people, probably even believe are possible. Spending your childhood in a home that is often described as a war zone of “emotional destruction”, by many victims of narcissistic parents, requires courage and indestructible strength to move forward. This journey is not for the faint of heart. It takes real power to face the limitations of your narcissistic parents and accept such a profound loss. The narcissistic parents did not love you. This has to be accepted, for healing to begin. The fortitude it takes to withstand the “lessons” narcissistic parents taught with so much zeal, is profound as well. Some people teach by example even if they don’t know it. “They always did their best to teach me everything I never wanted to know, everything I never wanted to do, and everything I never wanted to be.” Often times, Narcissist’s don’t acquire real wisdom or real discernment. They teach what is opposite of real love. No one who still can love at all, would ever wish even one narcissist parent on their worst enemy. But, two? That is going to be a tough road to walk. If you are now, an adult-child of a narcissist or even an older teenager and you can leave home just keep walking or even limping if you have too, just don’t lose hope and don’t look back. Narcissistic parents can “turn you into a pillar of salt,” as they often can emotionally drag adult-children back into their headspace and ask them for help, playing the vulnerable card. Just when their children are finally getting away and on their own for the first time, the narcissistic parent can manipulate when their child has a vulnerable moment with promises of an adult great relationship with rewards and attachment. Yet, given any amount of time, the narc parents will go back to their old tactics eventually, of blame, guilt, shame, and gaslighting ! They will not treat you better just because you are an adult overall, but it is positive that you also won’t have to spend as much time with them, behind closed doors, so you are safer already in so many ways just to have that physical distance. Children of narcissist’s need to be confident in themselves and in their own choices as well as their own independent intuitions and abilities. Children of narcissist’s were most likely made to doubt themselves, often because narcissistic parents set out to create more dependency so, the children could be controlled more easily over time. These disordered parents continue this dynamic with their children wether they are an adult or a child, it’s all the same agenda, just different approaches and power grabs. For the narcissist parent, it’s all about control and goes about undermining the child’s ability to feel confident in their independence and autonomy. It’s important to remind these children of narcissist’s to NOT be afraid to make mistakes. Even if they make mistakes, they are THEIR mistakes to make, and it’s ok to accept an error and learn from it and move forward with confidence in learning and growing emotionally. There is no shame in making a mistake if you are free. Any REAL freedom demands the occasional blunder, to fine-tune skills, learn and mature. The adult, who is a child survivor of narcissistic parents, must be truly brave, wise and internally strong to have endured these types of disordered parents, and not break completely. They will suffer, but, they will not be destroyed. They will weep, but, not give into despair. They will learn about this disorder and put a name on what their parents did to them, someday. This will be the day the narcissist is actually defeated. Everything changes when you find out what to call this “thing.” The very parents you thought DID love you, but was just misguided, angry and immature; actually were and are INCAPABLE of loving something outside themselves, in a healthy and responsible way. Although some part of you always knew the narcissistic parents didn’t love you like other parents loved their children and most are in deep denial, I just didn’t believe the other extreme either, of no love. That was a very hard but feeling pill 💊 to finally swallow and accept. It sure made more sense when watching their actions and behaviors. Adult children of narcissists may have a difficult time trusting others and figuring out who is safe or not, to be in their life. They may struggle with trying to self- medicate with inappropriate use of alcohol or drugs, or go from one relationship to another without a breath. There is hurt there and the damage has been done. Recovery from narcissistic abuse takes time. No one in the family of a person with NPD escapes that type of household unharmed. Only time will tell, to what degree of brokenness each individual child and family member will have to face. Sadly, the child of two narcs (the real ones with NPD), won’t make it to maturity without SOME psychological and emotional wounding from the NPD parents. How this manifests in their adult life or WHEN it does, will have to be dealt with eventually. It has been often reported often that when the adult-child begins to understand the magnitude of their losses for having two parents with NPD and the difficulty that will be the added to the road ahead for them there really is a grief and sadness that must be faced to move forward. The journey, after leaving a narc parent’s home, often feels exciting but can be very overwhelming to finally realize why they treated you so differently then someone who they loved. They may have said the words that they loved you. This was all a lie. They treated you exactly like they felt about you however that was. Always watch the actions of a narcissist never listen to the words. The way they treated you, is what they felt and the way they treated you, that’s how they cared. If they didn’t seem to love you and abused you it’s because they didn’t love you and hurting you was a way to try and force compliance and punish you. It’s simple and logical and all makes perfect sense once it’s acecpeted. No one that really ever loved you could ever have treated you the way they did. You were right all along. Their love was always a lie, just as you expected. They didn’t hurt you to try and help you. Help and Love doesn’t hurt. Often, children of NPD parents are accustomed to NOT having their feelings and or decisions validated or respected. Most of the narcissistic parents, certainly demand respect from their children, while they provoke them to wrath and violate their child’s trust. It’s such hypocrisy. These adult-children were often undermined and controlled through abuse and smear campaigns. Equally abusive, are the narcissistic parents that are over-enmeshed and are suffocatingly-indulgent and/or intrusive. These parents violate boundaries just as much as the physically abusive narcissists do. It’s all based on a parenting style of cruelty, discounting authenticity and abuse. Unfortunately, just for being born into double toxicity with two disordered parents, their child will have to summon all their strength just to cope and learn, to heal and then… to walk away and never look back. The adult child will then begin to rejoin humanity in all of its beautiful, heartbreaking symphony of life, and become a free person. They will have escaped the jail of narcissism. The family system of two narcissist parents, will be without appropriate role models and without REAL moral or REAL loving guidance. The parents will truly and completely, be unable to trust or be trust-worthy. Some children break-down emotionally, after years of abuse such as this. Others, although it is more rare than previously thought, become narcissists themselves. This occurs mostly with the child that was engulfed and idealized as the golden child and aligned their identity with the abusive narcissistic parent. Sadly, narcissistic parents are often so selfish, they were willing to sacrifice their favorite or golden child’s true self and real feelings, to exploit and show off their “mini-me” for narcissistic supply. This is often the sad carnage of a narcissist’s legacy. The severity of future problems with the adult-children of narcissists, depends on; where both the parents are on the spectrum of severity of narcissism, as well as the child’s own personal genetics, combined with other factors such as the intensity and frequency of traumas and abuses, and finally, if there were any safe and loving other role models when the child was growing up that loved them and they could confide in or feel safe with. The child’s natural temperament will play a role in which children develop NPD and who walks away from that insanity with the ability to still love and empathize with others and themselves. Most likely, if both of the parents are narcs; one parent will be more covert and one parent more overt. Usually, a child with one non-narcissistic parent can seek comfort from them, away from the disordered parent time to time. No such luck in the two narcissist parent scenario because both are probably equally unsafe at different times. Children of NPD parents, crave nurturing, love and stability, like all children. In this case, the child will have to find refuge in someone else besides the narcissistic parents, to get their emotional needs met. Siblings may be good mutual support resources for each other and could provide validation, companionship and encouragement for one another. That is, if the children haven’t been triangulated yet, by the parents, or “set-up” yet, to be enemies with the “golden child vs. the scapegoat wars,” always orchestrated by the narcissistic parents. NPD parents use triangulation and psychological abuse techniques to “divide and conquer,” in their unholy family -style war games. Narcissistic parents do all their “dirty-work” behind closed doors. Such a truly destructive family dynamic, perpetrated by such disordered personalities. Such parental self-interest and soulless cruelty, should never have access to or custody of ANY Child. This absolutely diabolical disregard for the best interests of their own children and their future, is so profound and destructive. This abusive division does a horrible disservice to their children. Narcissistic parents are just too cruel and dangerous, by their very disorder and symptoms, to not be abusive. These types will always abuse their children in different ways and with real NPD, and do not meet any criteria for even a “good enough” parent under any circumstances. Again, the truly narcissistic parent (pwNPD), will always abuse their children on some level. Always! Narcissist’s cannot, NOT abuse. Emotional abuse, of all the types at the very least, will be profound in these situations. The narcissistic parents will try to wound the children psychologically, if not physically (only not physically, for fear of the consequences of the law). So, these narc parents put in the place of physical beatings of their children, internal and psychological beatings of emotional and verbal abuse planted inside the child’s mind; along with gas lighting, smear campaigns, devaluation and discarding to destroy and destabilize their own flesh and blood children. For some damage control, the child will desperately need a strong, healthy support system outside the two dysfunctional parents, to survive and learn safe relationships from, if they are to have a chance at all. The narcissistic disordered personalities of these parents will often have major deficits and huge blind spots that impede their ability to function in a moral or compassionate way with their children. Narcissist’s lack and neglect empathy, and do not have sound reasoning or judgment like a well-rounded compassionate, loving and wise guardian needs. Only a healthy parent could provide these things. The child’s well-being will be as severely damaged from two narcissist parents, as it would be by a parent who was not providing enough food for nourishment, blanket for warmth or adequate shots to keep away disease. Research also suggests, narcissistic abuse can be so damaging, it can alter the child’s brain chemistry releasing stress chemicals for so many years, that a child will loose IQ points on tests over time with them, act out or develop ADHD, and actual shrink the frontal lobes in some children over time, with chronic abuse and cortisol stress chemicals flooding their nervous systems, that will eventually and often does create, a complex type of PTSD in many of these children, as adults. The chronic abuse and stressful environment of living with a narcissistic parent, creates fear within the child and can cause impaired thinking, difficulty concentrating, difficulty processing information and difficulty following directions. Other problems seen in many children of narcissistic abuse are other cognitive -behavioral problems like impaired concentration, impaired social skills, trauma bonds, phobias, eating disorders and drug and alcohol addiction. Without intervention and healing, this emotional/psychological abuse can have harmful life-long effects that are very harmful, in many areas of the child’s adult life. To sufficiently meet a child’s needs, a parent should provide for the safety, stability, security and love that creates secure attachments and healthy development. Narcissist parents cannot do this. They do not have the skills to give or the morality to teach and model appropriate behavior and actions with consistency and in a healthy and balanced way. Narcissistic parents cannot really love and cannot give their children the attention they so deserve and crave because the Narcissist’s needs are always more important than the child’s needs to the narcissist. Narcissist’s are not known for sharing or caring about what other people, even their own children, need emotionally. Narcissistic parents are stunted themselves. By the time their own child is around 6 years old, most are more emotionally mature than their parents who have the disorder, if they really meet criteria for NPD. Without other primary relationships with family members or mentors that are positive influences, the child will not be able to develop their own sense of security, sense of self and emotional growth. Kindhearted or involved extended-family members such as aunts, uncles, grandparents, cousins, family-friends or even a great teacher, can make all the difference in the child's life. These extended- family relationships are absolutely vital to the well being of this child and their future. Children need to know all parents are NOT like their parents. The hope is that, these healthy family relationships will provide the child with consistent, supportive interactions and healthy exchanges of love and compassion, so the child has other examples of positive and productive relationship models besides the disordered parents to refer to and model after. Loving extended family members can mirror genuine love to a child and the child back to them, creating a reciprocal exchange of positive emotions and healthy bonding. Attachment and love occurs naturally and the child experiences a healthy relationship. A child can also learn to regulate self-esteem by doing esteem-able acts. Helping and participating in the community, even when they are young, is so important. Volunteering for a non-profit organization like Habitat for Humanity or learning about poverty and serving food at a soup kitchen or assisting people with bagging groceries at a food bank, or feeding the elderly meals, are just a few examples for beginners and a good way to become interested in other people who are less fortunate or ill and be of service for humanity. Hobbies and common interests with peers, is another way to strengthen a child’s “outside-the-home” network of support. As a child joins groups and participates in activities of interest, they learn to share common goals and ideas, while gaining social skills. Children of narcissistic parents also need to develop appropriate socialization skills to be successful in peer relationships in school and beyond. These children often lack the socialization area of development because, they are often forced to spend so much time and energy just trying to survive abuse and spend so much time focused on the narcissist. Many of these kids live in the freeze, fight or flight modes and have difficulty connecting with peers later in life. All activities and time away from the home (away from the narc parent’s influence when young), lbegins to create a sphere of positive connections. These behaviors, experiences and connections will foster ideas and insights that the world is a big place and “not all people will hurt and torment you,” message of hope. These outside positive relationships and activities can build self-esteem and really help to offset some of the limitations and long-term narcissistic damage. Without these healthy bonds, self-esteem, service and socialization are even more important. getting our needs met by administrators. The child will have to rely on narcissistic parents for these examples or experiences. If this occurs, they will be bitterly disappointed. The child will be less at risk by not having to rely on dysfunctional parents to try and provide support for healthy needs when they cannot. Another predictor of how much resilience the child may acquire to cope at home and after leaving home, is to discover what role the narcissist parents will force the child into (if there is more than one sibling). Narcs always assign roles that are abusive, but if the child is a scapegoat or lost child, they won’t necessarily identify with the parents or want to emulate their parental behaviors and attitudes. These child-roles may be given to hurt them by their narcissistic abusers, but actually later, will enable them to see their parents for what they are, and escape the formation of their own personality disorder, by choosing to call the abuse for what it is and disengaging as soon as possible. The child not identifying in any way with the parent’s toxic behaviors or personalizing their criticism too deeply is important. So, because the child doesn’t look to his parents to model self-esteem, but has a system of help and safe people set up around them that works out, great progress will be made towards freedom of mind and healthy maturity in the future. I was the daughter of two very cluster-b personality-disordered parents. I had to find bonds and relationships with other safe-family members, to provide those insights and come to terms with the ability to be able to compare, contrast, review, discern and understand covert and overt behavior. Learning how other adult people or parents, (beside narcissistic parents) treated their children and how loving families didn’t bully or hit their children, even if they behavedmuch worse than I ever did. These experiences gave me a clear picture that there really was something very wrong with both my parents. For children, to eventually disbelieve the negative messaging of narcissistic parents, they have to have others they love, to show them the differences and contrasts. The big disparity between healthy love and unhealthy love is made clear by the contrast of character between those with NPD and those without. So, the love of my other close family members, helped me to survive and encouraged me to heal after leaving home. These relationships gave me a reference point of normality and a way to keep myself safe by knowing what it looks like and feels like when people love me. These type of relationships teach what is healthy and what was really abusive, growing up with my parents. I personally never remember wanting to emulate or identify with either one of my two disordered parents, except my father, when I was very young before the age of six years old. Narcissist’s can be some of the cruelest and most toxic people you will ever have to endure. It’s especially heartbreaking, when they are your parents and your first examples of what love and empathy are supposed to look like. Eventually, I did learn about empathy, felt it, conveyed it spontaneously and often while I also embraced it. I gave love to other good people in life and received so much more in return with gratitude and joy. Any child can heal if they don’t lose hope, are honest and do the abuse recovery work. Even on the dark days, all is not lost. The amazing resilience within each human and child to grow emotionally, even if they have only one other loving relative or person of substance in their life to counteract narcissistic influence, it can be enough and is so important. So, can a child survive two narcissistic parents? Yes, but not without great deal of suffering and some good insurance for all the therapy you will need to get started with, after leaving home. I knew I was really emotionally healing, when I could share my story without the intense hurt or emotional baggage, that triggered me for decades, before that day. I carried that old pain everyday since I had learned to walk and talk, and it was finally gone. I thought I would always have a half-depressed and half-anxious nature to deal with inside myself. I finally accepted my own freedom, did the work and that anxiousness was gone and never to return the same way again. Today, there are no narcissistic parents haunting my mind, criticizing and misusing their power and no anxious and depressed moods beating me up and making me feel weary. I also no longer have that “parental-inner-critical-voice” internalized and it no longer sabotages me. I choose life, not death, freedom not captivity. I look forward to what the Universe has for me to enjoy and I have no ill will towards my narcissistic parents but neither will I subject myself to their disrespect or disorder anymore. Freedom and Life await. I am enjoying the journey and I hope to see you on the road to complete recovery and healing. Don’t loose hope!

column1: Can a person develop PTSD after experiencing several major life stressers in rapid succession? (Loss of job, end of long term relationship, loss of custody of child, homelessness, betrayal by family members, witnessing the desth of a stranger)
column3: A person develops PTSD when for whatever reason, their normal ability to cope with the ups and downs of life is not available to them. A person may go through life dealing with traumatic events every day and not suffer from PTSD. The same person could be subjected to another event and develop PTSD from there. It is not the size or quality or quantity of events, it’s when normal copying mechanisms are not working, for whatever reason. Don’t fall into the trap of comparing events as a basis for PTSD. The mine is bigger than yours thing just doesn’t work here.

column1: How does a person go on after losing their only child?
column3: They live one step at a time, one day at a time. A couple I know, not close friends but we were neighbours for a while and then worked together, lost their daughter about three years ago. It was not a surprise as she had cystic fibrosis and she lived well over the expected time but it had a devastating effect on her parents all the same. I’ve watched them struggling, going through all the stages of grief and crawling on hands and knees emotionally. They are not over it. They never will be but they keep going. They have good support from family and friends which is important as they have also lost a family member, niece, granddaughter, cousin. But the pain is so great that family can often be a bitter reminder. There is actually nothing anyone can do for that … just be there if needed. The mother found facebook to be very helpful. Every step of the way has been shared with her facebook friends - recommended books, uplifting sayings, photos, memories, music, personal messages. She shared whatever she was thinking and asked people not to comment at all. Some friends could not take it and unfriended her but others have stuck with her, reading what she posted or scrolling past, did not matter. The mother has recently started a support group. I am not sure how effective those support groups are - for introductions and telling your story for the first time over a cup of tea is very good but meetings following that could be repeats of the first, and I wonder if repeating the story over and over as new members come in really helps. I suppose it works with some people better than others. But, their life is totally different. The father has changed careers and they have down sized and simplified their life. They did have a quiet trip to Canada, last year, mainly sightseeing which was good for them. I wish them well.
column9: Don’t judge support groups or repeating their story. The child lived and died. The parents often want to talk about it.

column1: What are some ways to cope with miscarriage and depression simultaneously? Are there any tips for managing both situations without feeling overwhelmed?
column3: So sorry you are coping with both a loss of a child and also depression at the same time. The grieving process takes time and is different for everyone. I would continue to use the tools you have for managing your depression already and give yourself more grace and understanding for grieving the loss of your baby. If you aren’t already in therapy it might help to process everything. Having a few close friends or family members that you can talk with about what you’re feeling is a good idea as well. There isn’t a one-size-fits-all solution for this. However, I believe there is power in prayer. I will be praying that you have comfort and peace during this time and that you can share with those you trust how you are feeling.

column1: Adult My 9 year old son says he doesn’t want to celebrate his birthday because his grandma died the day before, should I honor his wishes, and do nothing, or go ahead and celebrate it?
column3: My goodness, what a sweet son you have! Life will be hard enough to his tender heart without going out of your way to “toughen him up.” If he was close to his grandmother (or not) and wants to mourn her loss that is understandable. Frankly, it would be somewhat concerning if he wanted a big party the day after experiencing such a loss. It sounds like his concern right now is his relationship with Grandma. Maybe, instead of a traditional birthday party, you could host a small gathering of family members to share a meal and recount memories of what the grandmother meant to each person. Your son may not be feeling festive, but realizing that others also are going through this loss with him could be helpful in dealing with his grief. In future years your son can celebrate his birthday, but this might always be a time of reflection for him. Loss of a family member doesn’t ever go away, but it can get better as you find ways to cope. If your son hasn’t experienced much loss in his life, this death could be even more significant to him in bringing home the transience of life. Most adults have come to the understanding that they won’t live forever, but it can be a shock for children who don’t truly have firsthand knowledge of this fact. Grief, loss, and death are hard for adults and incomprehensible for children. Extend grace to your child during this time and realize that some somberness is to be expected. However, if you are noticing symptoms of depression that affect his appetite, sleep, and schoolwork then professional help can greatly assist your family in dealing with this loss. Don’t be embarrassed to seek help for circumstances that are outside of your parental control.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of my dog?
column3: Thx for the a2a. It is going to be sad for a long time. We went a year between dogs after Jack died because I (we) were too sad to get another dog. And it's OK. Anyone who says otherwise is full of it.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of something with a lot of sentimental value?
column3: What have you brought by birth? What will you carry forward after your death? The answer of both is—”nothing”. Then, there is no valid point to repent over losing any material. In reality, men are hankering for acquiring materials. These items become part and parcel of their life with deep sentimental value. As such, they are depressed in losing them. Such behaviour is common in most of the people. Somehow, it is humane. But too much depression or pain is unusual and avoidable. Just follow. 1. Nothing in this world is permanent, including life. In this light, any material is temporary. Hence, there is no reason to bother losing any material. 2. Time is the best medicine. Children forget their mother's death within a few months or a year. Priority changes from time to time. You will also forget the pain of losing your so called favourite things and wonder, how fool I was to depress so much on this petty matter? 3. What is your stake in this vast limitless world? Just a few feet. Like a drop in the ocean. And your favourite thing? Very very negligible and insignificant. Rabindra Nath Tagore realised the eternal truth on watching the vast moonlit world through the window of a night train. He regained his mental peace after the death of his favourite son. Is your loss more severe than his? 4. The material you lost was not your cup of tea. This is your destiny. What has happened, happened for good. You could have lost more valuable things. Thank God for this. 5. There is a balance in life. You have lost something. You will gain something. You should not lose heart. You should not depress. 6. The world is beautiful. But the life is short. Hence, time is precious. The life is solely yours. Now it is your discretion whether you can afford to waste your valuable time in depression for losing some insignificant material or not.
column9: I found this at the most rightful moment and can’t be more grateful. I recently lost a silver necklace that was very precious to me, so much so to lead me into depression and sleepless nights for a few days. I’m still not over it. I still can’t cope. But your valuable words did provide some comfort, and for that I thank you.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of my computer data?
column3: (First off, you have mentioned you had written countless story ideas, journal entries, and other thoughts in the "Notes" app - app's usually auto-backup - see if you can retrieve your data from the backup. Contact the app provider and ask if there is anyway they can help you retrieve your data.) Personal Experience: I have lost my computer date thrice. The biggest loss was the loss of numerous pictures that I had treasured from several years prior - especially with people that are not alive anymore. It broke my heart to learn that it's all gone forever, but slowly I had to accept the fact that no matter what I do - I am not going to get it back. My Advice: What's gone, is gone. Just because you sit and cry, or spend time worrying about having lost the data - it isn't going to come back. You just have to tell yourself "let this too shall pass." Sit down and, without getting frustrated, try to recall those story ideas, and journal entries you had written - write down what you can recall. Believe in yourself! You have a long way to go, and you will come up with better ideas that you had done previously - don't let this get you down. :) I wish you the very best!!

column1: How do you cope with the loss of your boyfriend? My boyfriend passed away. How do you cope with the loss of a loved one? How do you heal the pain? How do you handle the pain?
column3: Grief - and the way one experiences it - is personal. There is no right or wrong way AS LONG as you do not hurt yourself (or others) in any way (e.g., maintain healthy habits, etc.). For me - because I believe there is something after this human experience AND I had no unfinished business with those in my life who died (I make sure those I love KNOW that I love and appreciate having them in my life - and do so regularly while they are alive) - my grief typically manifests in moments here and there when I have something I want to share with my loved one - and realize I cannot - or when something reminds me of them. These moments never go away, they just become less intense over time. In talking with and observing others, it appears that everyone has their own unique way of grieving. Some people even enjoy being in the grieving process, and keep it actively going for as long as possible (I think they like the attention - but not sure about that). Some like to do it quietly. Some, after a time, want to live life fully again; others shy away from living. It seems all of those who grieve always remember their loved ones that have crossed. The memories become sweeter over time - but the missing is always there. SO - you might want to consider letting the passage of time soften your loss. You can talk to him as if he were still with you; you can write him letters; or you can find some other way to healthfully connect with your memories of him. Keep in mind that retribution rarely brings satisfaction; only grieving, love, and time heal the heart.

column1: Why is it often harder to cope with the loss of a beloved animal than the loss of a human family member or friend?
column3: I recently visited an elderly relative in a retirement home and struck up a conversation with a gentleman who was walking his small, white dog. We got into a conversation about pets, and his eyes watered when he talked about his dog and how she had been there for him for 15 years, more than anyone else in his life. His children visited regularly but his dog was the only one who was with him all the time, by his side through everyday ups and downs. He said that after his wife died, and after the funeral was over, and all of his relatives got back to their normal lives, his little dog was the one who licked his face as he cried every day for his wife. He explained that his dog wakes him up in the middle of the night when he became short of breath to remind him to put on his oxygen tank. He said that his dog was the one who was with him when he was recovering from surgery and would sit in his arms and look into his eyes. He told me in that moment that nothing would be more painful to him then when it came time to lose her, and he told me that he prayed that he would go first, and that he had already found someone to take care of her when he was gone. He told me that he had even lost his son 40 years before and although that was incredibly painful, he said he had a bond with his dog like he had never in his life before. I think the bottom line is that if you have that kind of relationship with your pet, no one will ever be there for you the way they will, adding to that their childlike dependency on you for all of their needs brings in that parental type of relationship as well. You feel an extreme responsibility for their well-being in every way. Finally, their innocence and joy and non-judgmental nature is unparalleled by anything you'll ever get from a human long-term. A spouse will do many things for you and love you deeply, but those relationships tend to be... complicated. You may experience this type of love with a child when they're very young, but that will soon diminish as they will move on with their friends and their life soon enough. And parental relationships will certainly get complicated as well! The point is there is no relationship like there is with a pet. A pet will remain faithful to you forever and teach you a type of Love that is not possible to get from a human.
column9: Thank you a million, and then a million times more. This is how I feel after having lost my young dog (she was only 5, nearly 6). It’s been almost five months, and you’ve written many of the things I’ve been trying to explain to people and make sense of myself. It’s been so SO hard. I had never suffered this much for a pet, or even a human. But as you wrote, it is so hard for me to really define that bond and give it justice. There’s no label for it. They feel like your baby/toddler sometimes, and other times they feel like the greatest friend you ever had. But it’s really an insult to call them your bet friend, because again, as you said, they love you so unconditionally, that it’s hard to ever replicate that with a human. She was there for me when I had no one. And I would’ve risked my own life to save hers. And honestly, if I met a genie, and he asked me if I rather have a billion dollars or my girl back. I would pick her every time. And I mean that. Thank you so much for writing this, Ripley. And for my girl, Potato, I love you, always forever.

column1: What do you think is the best way to cope with the loss of a dog?
column3: We had two dogs, Morgan and Charlie. Had them since puppies, Charlie we had since birth, he was raised on an eyedropper after his mother died whelping. They grew up to be awesome dogs, and we had many adventures over the next decade. Charlie grew up to be my wife’s constant companion and protector.early this year, Charlie the brown boy, developed a splenic tumour, and crossed the rainbow bridge. Morgan, his sweet, big, older brother was depressed and listless. My wife was devastated. Our daughter heard about a puppy mill rescue, a golden lab - and bought her out and dumped her. She was shut down, overweight, anxious. We named her Princess, and she followed Carrol everywhere, but as Carrol is largely bedridden currently - she moved into the bedroom with her. Over the months she has come out of her shell to be the most loving and gentle fur person imaginable. She and Carrol have bonded incredibly. When we first got her home she followed Morgan like a golden shadow to his black, and in his gentle way he seemed to be showing her what a dog’s life should be. Unfortunately (and I am tearing up here) one evening about a fortnight later, he was off his food and very listless. I sat up all night with him, not really expecting him to see the morning, but he did-and I took him to the vet first thing. He also had a splenic tumour, and secondary tumours. We were back to a one dog home, and very dejected - but it was only a few more days when we heard of some Catahoula puppies (Charlie had been a Catahoula X Rottweiler) at the local pound. we went there with the intent of getting one.but who can decide which one to leave?They don’t replace our beautiful old boys, but they have their own place in our hearts and lives. My advice, get another dog. It isn’t disloyal it is honouring your passed love.
column9: Rescue another one. Mine passed away, I said "No MORE, can't take the pain." That lasted 3 days…. Rescued Tanner, best decision EVER!! No more lonesomeness. 🥰

column1: How do you cope with the loss of a loved one while incarcerated?
column3: It is tough. Basically you have no choice but to deal with it. I mean after all most people in prison are in prison because of something they did. That doesn’t lessen the pain of losing a loved one Plus the fact that you are not allowed to attend the funeral . At least not in Missouri, Anyway I will tell two stories involving people coping with the death of a loved one. The last one involves me I had a celly. One day he was expecting a visit. It never came. Later that day he was called to the caseworkers office. He came back and was in tears, so I left the cell to give him time alone. When I came back he was still in tears. I did not know what to say. When the guards came by for count they asked if he was alright and he just nodded yes. Finally , I told him that it was obvious he was not alright and that I would listen if he wanted to talk. He didn't say nothing for a long time and finally said “ They are all gone” I asked gently who he was talking about. He explained that his parents were coming to see him and were involved in a horrible car wreck and both had died. I can not imagine the pain this man was in. He ended up talking to the chaplain and got better, or at least it seemed he got better. However he was never quite the same I have had several loved ones die while in prison . While all was tough , none was as tough as my little brother passing. I had finally gotten a release date and had told my brother. He was ecstatic. However , I still had 15 more months to go. I was sent to a low level prison to finish the rest of my time. With 8 months to go I was called to the majors office one day. I walked in and the room was full of C/Os ,Sgts, the Major and others. I was told to have a seat and told them I preferred to stand. I was concerned with all the people in the room. The major asked if everyone sat or squated if I would take a seat and I agreed. He then instructed me to call my sister in law . The was no answer. He then told me my brother had passed. I told him he had to be mistaken as I had just talked to him the day before. He asked if I wanted to talk to a chaplain and I said no. He asked if I wanted a room in the hole to myself. The last thing I wanted was to be in the hole . I went back to my housing unit and called my sister in law and she confirmed it was true. She could hardly talk. Later I went to the yard and talked to a guy who grew up with my brother and I . I told him what happened and that I wanted a little time alone. I went to the lower yard where there was not many people and cried .I went to prison for protecting my little brother and now it almost seemed pointless. I was angry, in pain you name it. I had all these emotions. I hope I have conveyed a little about coping with death while incarcerated. I know I can’t describe it completely. It doesn’t matter if you are incarcerated or free, death of a loved one is hard. But in prison it is a little different.
column9: Fucking hell mate. All the best

column1: How can I cope with losing my friend?
column3: I can relate but not exactly, my former friend and I still visually see each other but we do not speak at all. I cope with it by believing that she wasn't a friend because if she was, she would've apologized simply for her mistake and we'd be friends. But it obviously didn't matter much to her, so I tell myself, do not give attention to those who seek not for it, especially one who cares not for one others feelings. It hurt me at first to know that and I couldn’t believe she would be that person, but hey, I'm alive. With or without her, I will live my life. She wasn't there for me when I was born, nor when I needed her, so I guess I don't really need her. You have to believe in yourself, you have made it this far, nothing can stop you from continuing, you will either meet new people or see your friend again in the long run. It's hurts more to lose a friend you thought was a real friend, you should wish your friend a happy future and try to keep in contact with them. Maybe that'll ease you missing them. Losing a friend you speak to is okay, it's happened many times, especially when you constantly move, and I know what it feels like. You will find new friends and you can still have that friend(s).

column1: How do atheists cope with the moments of despair and loss in their lives?
column3: Hi, Stephanie. I'm very sorry to hear of your impending loss. I got similar news about my mom a little more than a year ago, and I wrote about that some here: My answer to Death and Dying: What does it feels like when doctor says you'll just live X days / months? You have a hard road ahead of you, and you have my deepest sympathies. To answer your question, I think the very most important thing I did was to face it as squarely as possible. It was important to me to be as present as i was able. Partly for her sake: dying is a hard thing, and she needed our support. Partly for my family's sake; we needed one another. And partly for my own. As I don't believe in an afterlife or reincarnation, this was my one chance to do some important things right. That said, there were plenty of things I did to cope. An important one was keeping a sense of humor. Our family has a big streak of black humor; it has gotten us through dark times. At the meeting where we decided there was no option but to move my unconscious mom to hospice, the very first thing said was, "Looks like I picked the wrong week to quit sniffing glue." The family all laughed, and our neuro-oncologist, used to us, chuckled and said, "Ah, an Airplane reference," so the younger doctors would know what the hell was going on. My mom's sister later mentioned that my mom would have been glad to see us handling it with the same humor she had handled all the dark times in her life. There was a great deal of laughter at her memorial service. And, especially after it was all done, there were the more usual things. Good whiskey, drunk with family. Quite a bit of ice cream. Long talks with the few friends who had gone through something similar. Fat novels to get lost in and entrancing movies to give me a little breather. Long walks and bike rides to wear me out. There was also some travel, as I mention elsewhere on Quora. But as an atheist, I think the major difference for me came after. To me, the pain wasn't just something to be gotten through. it was an opportunity to sharpen my understanding of the transitory nature of the world. Having seen very clearly how little time we all have, it inspired me to make some major changes in my life. I have also used the time of mourning to become more compassionate and more grateful. I believe this is all we have, and the loss of my mom has greatly deepened my commitment to making the very best of it. For all of us.

column1: As an atheist or agnostic, how did you cope with the loss of your loved one?
column3: I was close to my youngest Aunt who was approaching 96 years old and fell in her home just as I was coming to see her, a ten hour drive from my home. This aunt, my uncle and their ttwo children were extremely Christian. When I went to see her I would visit with her granddaughters, both of whom had married ministers in the same church, one the preacher and the other a music minister who led the choir and devised elaborate plays and musicals for celebrating the holidays. The girls’ children were/are involved in these events; the congregation is very friendly and had no qualms that I was gay. They were their own denomination I believe, though the ministers had gone through training. I have to say I had trouble with the ceremony, what with the new kinds of hymns, lyrics projected onto the walls,…and the passion, the incredible passion of the choir singing these hymns, really devoted and happy. I tried to sing the common songs, and participate in the question and answer ritual but I didn’t feel I was being honest or sincere. My aunt tried her best to walk again (with a walker), As a former PTA I was able to assist or at least monitor her progress. I stayed with her daily and sent emails to her family about what she was doing. I ended staying there for four months. The day came when she was so exhausted with trying to walk that she said she had decided to accept the end of her life, seen by her family of course as not a tragic decision. “You will see your husband again, and your daughter!” people told her. (Her daughter’s faith was so strong that she thought god would cure her of cancer, but she accepted her death when she was not cured. ) I sat by her bedside often, holding her hand, and we said little things to each other. She acknowledged how much I loved her because I wasn’t leaving her. I looked at her with compassion and knew she probably would not exist after death. Of course I never said a word about my non belief. That would have been cruel and unnecessary. She lives, as they say, in my heart and in the hearts of her family and friends. Her photograph on my wall here smiles at me, In that way, she still lives.

column1: Adult Who is the dearest person you've lost? How have you coped with the loss?
column3: The Story of Kisa Gautami: Kisa Gautami was a young woman from a wealthy family who was happily married to an important merchant. When her only son was one-year-old, he fell ill and died suddenly. Kisa Gautami was struck with grief, she could not bare the death of her only child. Weeping and groaning, she took her dead baby in her arms and went from house to house begging all the people in the town for news of a way to bring her son back to life. Of course, nobody could help her but Kisa Gautami would not give up. Finally she came across a Buddhist who advised her to go and see the Buddha himself. When she carried the dead child to the Buddha and told Him her sad story, He listened with patience and compassion, and then said to her, "Kisa Gautami, there is only one way to solve your problem. Go and find me four or five mustard seeds from any family in which there has never been a death." Kisa Gautami was filled with hope, and set off straight away to find such a household. But very soon she discovered that every family she visited had experienced the death of one person or another. At last, she understood what the Buddha had wanted her to find out for herself — that suffering is a part of life, and death comes to us all. Once Kisa Guatami accepted the fact that death is inevitable, she could stop her grieving. She took the child's body away and later returned to the Buddha to become one of His followers. Hope you got the answer, each one of us has untold story, which hurts , fill us void, but life has to move on:)

column1: I lost a friend due to my mental illness, what do I do about it?
column3: TO GIVE YOU CONTEXT, I had struggled for a couple of years with on and off depression (better periods changed for worse and even suicidal), that peaked after I got out of an abusive relationship. I developed PTSD from this and experienced regular severe anxiety attacks on the streets, memory loss, bad or no sleep, and very bad depression periods, including physical manifestations like migraines, chest pain, tremble, and uncontrolled cry. During this period, I had friends whom I trusted and whom I told about the struggles I went through. They never actually left me, but I noticed very soon, they were getting in touch less and less and even if I contacted them and tried to talk about different things, their replies were short, sometimes only GIFs. I managed to get through the worst part, although still experiencing regular anxiety attacks that I cannot very well control. However, it seems these relationships cannot be fixed. When I talk to some of these friends after some time, I was told I was too self-centered and exhausting (it was not a one-way relationship, I helped them a lot over the years, with similar mental health issues, school problems, even legal issues in two cases). They do not contact me by themselves anymore and I even found out one of my very best friends had a wedding recently and did not even tell me. It hurt so much on my chest as if I had a huge stone instead of a heart. Sometimes, I feel as if it would be better to just let go of these relationships, because they would not improve, no matter how much I try, and that I do not speak about my mental health struggles with them anymore. However, I also feel that I would be left completely alone, with no one, if I lose these people completely. I think they will not try to get back to me.
column9: I am so sorry for what you've been through. It must be so hard and hurtful. I also want to say that I had similar experience like you. All of my friends left me when they know I had mental illness. But it was also because of my behavior due to that condition. I didn't even understand what I did wrong. It happened 7 years ago when I was 14 years old. But now, I am 22 and I realized that how I acted in the past might be annoying for them. Even they knew it was because the mental illness that I had. Now, we still follow each other on Instagram (just few of them). However, they never initiated talk or etc. I tried few times to chat with them but ends up they didn't want to engage more. Like, didn't read my dm. Yes it hurts a lot. Especially seeing them hangout together without asking me at once. I'm sending you hugs and loves! I hope we will have good friends in near future.

column1: How do clergy cope with the loss of faith?
column3: It is or can be quite a difficult role as clergy. however many ministers and priests have good support networks or should do. These are much better than decades ago. Clergy often know about how to cope with doubt and faith loss issues, and often will confide in trusted others and the leadership within a church or parish. Obviously, some clergy will suffer in silence and spiritual pain if they do not have trusted mentors and friends. We see this sometimes in independent churches and amongst younger pastors and priests, who are still learning to be clergy or have to go through a faith crisis. Most clergy and mature believers go through a faith crisis at one or many points in their lives and ministries. It is called ‘the dark night of the soul.’ Many mystics have written well and honestly on this. The Psalmist wrote about this many times. Psalm 23 ‘Even though I walk through the darkest valley, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.’ This the Valley of Bacca, or weeping of the soul. God seems to use this time for many genuine believers to help them draw closer to God and begin to submit to God and learn to rely totally on God. It can be very painful and disconcerting for most. But to be a mature disciple of God and to be able to allow the Holy Spirit to flow through them ‘The work of Grace’, people must go through this. How clergy and people cope and respond to this weeping and doubt or questioning the faith or learning to rely on God rather than ones own intellect or self -reliance, depends on their level of theological understanding, level of communion with God, emotional maturity and strength as well as their confidence in God and their belief or learned belief. Some clergy and others can go into despair and lose the faith for a time or reject long held or inadequately held beliefs. This is honest spirituality. Why accent to a belief if one does not fully accept it and the implications. On average most Protestant ministers stay in leadership for 7–10 years. I am not sure about Orthodox or Catholic. However, often these people go on to more effective roles in their Christian life or other ministries or occupations; being the wiser for all they have been through. To be able to minister to a wide range of people and especially the most vulnerable and broken, requires experience of these for most clergy. Hence the ‘dark night of the soul.’ A number become atheists or agnostics and it is sad to meet some who hate the church and the idea of God from these faith loss crises. However, it does show and highlight that some people’s spiritual and theological foundation were inadequate or possibly shallow. However, when people know their Bible and that in context and the revelation history of the mercy and grace of God then these people can cope some what better. Obviously, it is essential that clergy and others are able to share and discuss their doubts and loss of faith or questions of faith with others they trust well. Non- judgmentalism is paramount here. And I have met some clergy and others who have lost hope because others did not understand or dismissed their fears and confusion. However, as these people seek the love and unconditional mercy of God they often grow deeper in their faith and communion with God. Mystics have often written about this. Clergy and others often grow through reading about others’s ‘dark night of the soul’ and also studying theology/Bible truth and psychology. Again, becoming more wise and spiritually literate or better understanding revelation and perception. Some others stay in the organisation but have less spiritual commitment to their faith and can become ‘just religious’ or ‘turn to more ritual’ faith. That is fine as some people find an equilibrium within themselves. They still believe and that is appropriate. However, over time some of these people re-find their faith and at a new level or a new level of contemplative and mystic revelation. God is responsible for this perception. So, clergy, missionaries and other believers cope in different ways and at different levels and extremes and periods. If, someone completely throws away their faith and becomes anti-God (anti religion is ok), then they need a lot of love and psychological help. Being prayed for and helped by the Holy Spirit are so important. I would encourage people who have suffered loss of faith and even hatred towards God to seek genuine help and in a secure and loving environment. There are many ministries, people and doctors who can help. God is still the best Dad to see and sit with and wait for the ‘night of the dark soul’ to pass and get ready for the next journey with God - mountains and valleys a like. Hope this is helpful. See lovely song

column1: Adult What are some ways widows cope with the loss of their spouses?
column3: I lost my husband very unexpectedly after 4 years of our marriage. He is the love of my life and my best friend. I'm more of an introvert person, so losing him was like losing the only friend I had, the only person whom I shared my fears, my happiness, my tensions...my life. I don't know if I have completely come out of that pain, but I think I'm dealing with the grief better. These are my ways of dealing with the loss; I'm not sure if it works for everyone. 1. I have accepted that he is gone and of course it is the worst thing ever happened to me. But apart from that, I don't think I have any other sorrows. There are plenty of positive things in life that I'm happy for. I have a healthy body, I am financially independent, I have a lovely 2 yr old son, I have a supportive family....and so on. So I have written all these positive things on a paper and pinned it near my bed. The first thing that I see when I wake up in the morning is this list and it reminds me that I am still luckier than most of the people in this world. 2. ‎Everyday before going to bed, I write a letter to my husband in a journal. I tell him how the day was, I share my fears and sorrows, I tell him how our son is growing etc...Trust me, this has really helped me a lot. I feel some kind of comfort when I do this. 3. ‎I set some goals/tasks for myself every 3 months time and try my best to accomplish them. These goals could be something that I wish to do before I die; like learn photography, give a meal to all the kids in an orphanage, visit a place etc. This gives a feeling that I have got something to do in my life, and that time is precious. 4. ‎I have been part of grief support groups in facebook and the experiences that others share has helped me survive. I could understand that I am not alone in my grief. Losing your partner is a horrible experience. In my honest opinion, I don't think you would ever come out of that emptiness you feel in your heart. But things would get better with time and you would learn to live with that pain. I hope my answer helps you deal with your loss.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of your young child (under 2 years old) and what are some appropriate forms of grief?
column3: My son and ex daughter in law are currently coping with the lost of a teenager. Katrez was our stepgrandson. I hope that they will remember the good times, 18 years. He was rebellious in his latter years and went to live with his biological father after his mom put him out at age 18. She had initiated the divorce from our son, calling him fat and disgusting. Many times she disrespected our son in front of his stepson. It is my understanding that the biological father just coming home from prison, not sure why he was serving time, included Katrez in the art of selling drugs. Apparently, a drug deal went wrong when Katrez was robbed of the drugs and had his gun stolen. The biological father supplied Katrez with another gun, put him back out into a crime infested apartment area where the grandmother and sister were living trying to bring up their own children. Katrez gets out the vehicle, his father Robb pulls off, hearing gun shots, he returns. He sees a young man shot, thinking it is a friend of Katrez, puts the young man in his vehicle and rush him to the hospital all the while, asking where is Katrez, to the wounded young man. After dropping the young at the hospital, he learns that the young man who kept reaching for his gun before he took it from him because he did not want the young man to go into a hospital with a gun, was the young man that his son had shot with the gun that he gave him. His son, Katrez, layed dying on the 2nd floor landing of the apartment building, shot by either that young man that he rescued and/or the young man's older brother. Katrez was shot in the head, twice. The mother knows the facts, yet, she has been pacified by the father giving $4000 toward the funeral. She threatened to share with the father the statement that I made that I could not stomach being around the biological father for the repast after hearing that he is involved in his son's death. I see it as a possible threat because she is aware that the biological father killed a man over her and got away with it before he went to prison for other charges. This is what Katrez's, my stepgrandson, biological father will always have to deal with concerning his son's death. Dealing with the death of an innocent 2 year old is sad and as time passes, the parents will feel less grief and heal and be able to smile at the beautiful memories of 2 years of joy that he or she brought to their lives. Some parents only have 2 days or 2 months with their child. Some moms died in child birth and only experienced the love of carrying and delivering the child. I pray that your family will find shalom from Father Yahveh, our heavenly Father, who will always be with us, knowing that we will see our innocent children one day, if we continue to live covered by the blood of Yeshua, when He gave His life for us.

column1: How do men cope with the loss of freedom when they get married?
column3: It really feels hard in the first few months up to an year into marriage. Or at least till you strike a balance on how to handle your wife. I learnt that keeping my wife occupied with something will get back my freedom. For example, I married her when she was jobless. I realized I am becoming her entertainer day by day. She felt bored at home all the day and when I come back home in the evening, i couldn't watch my favorite shows as she expected me to take her out, hang out or spend till late nights with her. I indirectly started motivating her to think about her career, work on setting some objectives and helped her work towards it. Now she has a full time job and doesn't seem to pestering me like earlier. She comes home as tired as me and does the minimal kitchen chores and go to bed. I get time to spend on my shows as well. Of course we go out for dinner, watch movies but once in a while like in weekends. So to answer your question, men really don't cope with the loss of freedom. They make continuous efforts to get it back. Another idea would be to get your wife pregnant. Once kids are born, they are more occupied then ever before and you know where your freedom is.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of a child? How do you deal with blaming yourself?
column3: You will never live with it if you blame yourself and are forever disecting the past. As the past is gone and can't be changed so there is little point dwelling there and living in regret and an eternity of misplaced guilt and continuing to make your own life even more of a living hell.. Torturing yourself with the endless thoughts of the ‘what if/should have/could have/would have and wish I had done’ scenarios! Whats done is done and nothing can ever change that but you must decide what you want to do about it now as in the here and now is the only place that you can ever do anything about anything that may effect the future. The past must be accepted in order to change it into something else and use it for the greater good of all in the future and gives you a future purpose and a far better and healthy way to deal with it, than to keep punishing and blaming yourself for something that was not within your control. An unfortunate unwarranted tragedy that no person would ever wish for but life never throws anything at us that we are not fully equipped to deal with …..

column1: How do people cope with the loss of a religion?
column3: Loss of religion does not mean loss of faith or relationship. Religion is the human backbone to the presence of God on earth. Humans are not perfect however, and humans are evil in some cases and they have distorted and perverted religion for money, and for other reasons so to be disappointed by a religion or a church is understandable. Understand that much of the degredation of a church is intentional, done by people who hate what the church stands for, defiling it on purpose. This has caused many who see everything at face value to turn from their faith, embarrassed or disgusted that God would let that happen. God does not interfere with what humans have the power to stop themselves. He gave us the tools, power, and wisdom to do so, so whatever happens in that aspect is on us. For example it would have only taken one bullet to stop Hitler from killing all those innocent people. One person, with the courage and the gun to stop all of it! Hitler was only one man. No one did it. What could they have done to the guy? And when you feel in your heart that what you are doing is right? How are we judged then? What if Hitler thought he was making humanity better? We do not know the answers to all that but no one has to lose their love for God just because they don't like what has become of their religion. Jesus was not a Christian. He was a Jew, so wouldn't His followers also be Jews who follow Jesus?

column1: How do you deal with the loss of a boyfriend?
column3: Write in a notebook. Write every memory, write a story of how you met, write the ups and the downs and finally write the reasons why you loved this person. By writing it all down you have released those emotions that no one else will ever understand, as your relationship was one of a kind between the both of you. If you ever need a laugh or a happy memory you can go back to the notebook. A ex boyfriend of mine died 11 years ago although time has healed me completely, I read that notebook and I get that same happy melting feeling that he may be gone but not forgotten.

column1: How do you deal with losing family?
column3: I coped with losing my family with LOTS of different things, both mentally healthy and not. I wrote letters to some and tied the letters to balloons to send into the atmosphere. I've prayed. I've been sexually provocative to fill voids, smoked weed, partied under various circumstances, opened myself to others I might not before, been a workaholic, the list is extensive. The reality is, nothing has ever healed loss. People don't just grieve in death. We grieve the end of a relationship, for example, because the termination of that relationship is equivalent to the death of the person. We've all heard the saying that time heals all things and I try not to be cynical towards any helping thought like that. Time does to all things what the ocean does to the seashore. The ocean doesn't make sand disappear. That's nonsense. It washes over it. It pushes and pulls it. I consiously go from one distraction to the next in life while experiencing periods of pleasure as often as possible. I got into the habit of letting pleasure happen vs planning it though because for me it's just not as pleasurable planned. Sometimes planned pleasure can become a major disappointment sadly lol. I side tracked there a bit without meaning to. I guess I just tend to connect pleasure with connection to family in the sense of family on goings. The traditions, the closeness, the feeling of someone having your back no matter what.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of a child? How do you deal with blaming yourself?
column3: I do not know the right answer nor do I know if there is one. I pray to God that I never know. I have came very close. My son overdosed on heroin in the next room one night while at home. I am a trained medical assistant & I couldn't save him. If it wasn't for my ex he wouldn't be alive & drug-free today. He had to be narcanned 7 times that night. I know how I coped during the overdose, I didn't! I checked out. I don't know if I knew my own name. In my opinion I think being able to cope after a brief check-out comes from knowing & being comfortable with yourself. If you are not comfortable in your own skin aren't you going to question everything? Including parenting? God forbid if I was to lose one of my two kids, I know I have done & loved them to the very best of my abilities. I do not question whether or not I could have done any more. I know I have! Anyone going through grief of a child & feels like they need help, please seek professional help. Good Luck❤️
