column1: How do you cope with the loss of a pet you’ve had for 11 years?
column3: I know it is hard…they take a piece of us when they go…hold onto ALL the incredible, silly, special times you shared together. I too have lost dogs and we all need to mourn…I lost my ‘soul dog’ a few years ago and she taught me so many priceless lessons…one of them was that our hearts are big enough to love again and again and again…she actually ‘found’ a dog in distress and I STILL have that dog today…she is almost 14 years old! In my ‘Zoe’s’ honor that I lost in 2015 I continue to adopt/rescue in her honor….the circle of life…there are SO many pets out there that need a second home…our hearts are big enough to love again and it does us so much good mentally and it helps an animal out at the same time…if you are unable to adopt, perhaps you can foster for a while or volunteer at a local shelter…remember ALL the amazing times with your pet…their lives were SO much bigger than this one last moment…we could’ve missed the pain, but then we would’ve missed the dance and I am certain you would not have traded in a minute of it!! Lastly, energy can never be destroyed…they are always around…xoxoxo
column9: Ohhhhhh so well said! Thank you! Love love ❤️ 🐾

column1: Why is coping with the loss of a loved one the hardest thing to overcome in the lives of many people?
column3: That is a very interesting question. Surely the answer is because you have given your heart and soul to that person and care about their well being. I am thinking more in terms of how you can overcome their loss, though. I shall take it in spiritual terms to test the waters. Not too many people can cope with a spiritual loss, and a lot of people will object to the suggestion even. However, the reason people find it so hard to cope and overcome the loss of someone they love is because of The Law Of Attachment. If we are attached to anything = we will suffer. The answer is to practice non-attachment. This is a very tall order for most people, but if you can separate yourself from the other person spiritually you will never suffer. The problem is that while they were here on earth you gave away too much and your bond was so precious that it is very hard to separate as two different people. I am not the world’s most spiritual person, but I do try my best not to get attached to anybody or anything. They are not possessions, after all. We do not own people. They are separate entities in their own right so it is only proper that we should let them be. The way to unattach from people or things is to Cut The Cord That Binds. We all have cords attached to other people. Your cord may be for your husband while his cord may be for your child. Either way, there is literally a cord (or rope or chain) attached to your belly button and the person you are attached to. In order to cut the bond you will need a pair of scissors, or a pair of pliers or even an axe. You will need whatever it takes to cut this cord. In your mind’s eye imagine the cord coming out of your belly button and attaching itself to someone. Then cut the cord! Just like that. That, of course is easier said than done, and it brings up much resistance. But if you want to be free of the pain of attachment that is exactly what you must do. Most people have many (even hundreds) of cords attached to people coming out of their belly button. They think they own them. Once they realize that you don’t own anyone in this life it will be easier to cut the cord and say goodbye for good.
column9: My Nephew committed suicide last month. He would have been 39 years old today.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of a twin?
column3: I have not suffered the loss of my twin so may not be able to answer your question satisfactorily. Grief is a natural response to loss. It’s the emotional suffering you feel when something or someone you love is taken away. The more significant the loss, the more intense the grief will be. People most associate grief with the death of a loved one, which is often the cause of the most intense type of grief. However, a loss of any kind can cause grief. The grief you are feeling is the knowledge that you had a twin and the chance to share something special was lost when your twin died before birth. This changed the course of your life. When you lose someone, it's an unfortunate fact that you'll never enjoy that person’s physical presence again. This doesn't mean that the person you lost never existed. You and your twin spent a number of months sharing a confined space before you were born. You were aware of your twin and in a way knew each other. It was unfortunate you didn’t get to enjoy a lifelong relationship with each other. Reclaim the idea of what you've lost. Nothing can bring back what you lost but your twin lives on in your thoughts, words, and actions even though you may not realize it. Embrace it.

column1: Can cats cope with the loss of a front leg?
column3: I had a foster kitten last year that only had 3 legs. She had a hard time with the litter box, but she managed. She was happy and got around fine. If you watch The Incredible Dr. Pol, their cat in the office is a 3 legged cat it does every thing a four-legged cat can do. So they can cope just fine.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of an important relationship?
column3: Hi Allie, Losing a relationship is very hard. I found that talking to close friends helped me through those tough times. Sometimes it was minute by minute, the hurt was terrible. Personally, in my desperation, I talked to God, which eventually led me to believing and asking Jesus into my heart. The pain was still there and it took a while but life changed that day for me. I have lost since then also, but now I have my soul mate and I feel so fantastic with her. I guess we all have different feelings and thoughts on life, but thats what changed for me.I wish you the best.

column1: Adult How do I cope with the loss of my lover?
column3: So very sorry to hear of your loss. Let me start by saying your harming yourself isn't going to fix anything, though I do understand feeling that way. When my fiancé died in 2010 I was never suicidal, but I didn't particularly care if I died. I remember going to sleep hoping I wouldn't wake the next morning because I just wanted to aching to stop and I truly didn't believe it ever would. I won't tell you time heals anything because that isn't true. It's been almost 6 years since he died and there are still days that it feels surreal. There are still days I expect him to call me to discuss the events of the day or something silly that has happened in the news. There are still days I get overwhelmed by grief that I can't tell him about something exciting that has happened and cry for a good, long time. No, time doesn't heal. But it helps. I needed to find a distraction, something which didn't have anything associated with him. I needed to get out of my head. It took me almost 2 years to get to that place, though. It's only been a few weeks for you. Give yourself time, not a timeline. Don't put pressure on yourself to move on, feel better, not cry, be happy, or anything else. All you need to do is wake up and get by. In time you'll find your way, but it takes time and it has to be your way. That timeline will be different for everyone and what makes you feel better will be different than what made someone else feel better. I found comfort in the music industry, that may not work for you. When you're ready, maybe try taking a class, painting, a book club, dinner with friends...something to get you in a comfortable, low-pressure, social situation. Go to a councilor. The best thing I did was go to a grief councilor within a few weeks of my fiancé dying. It helped me immeasurably. I tried a young widow's group, which didn't work out well for me, but groups are wonderful, too. Take care of yourself, whatever that means for you. Exercise, walking, swimming, massages, yoga, naps, sleep, eating well. Be good to yourself. You're allowed to spoil yourself now. I promise. You're welcome to message me, anytime. Email me anonymously, message me here...reach out to someone, especially if you're feeling like you want to harm yourself. If you'd like to read a bit more about my story, I've written about it quite a lot on Quora, but here it is at length. ~XOXO Grief & Resilience or: How Heartbreak Led Me Back to the Music Industry
column9: Thank you so much. I'm much better now. It's been more than 2 months now. And yes, time doesn't heal. Not a day goes by when I don't think about him. It still hurts. And I'm still trying to find out how he died.

column3: “LOSS OF LOVED ONE”—- the pain is hugee i understand but u need to move on and that can be done if u start distracting yourself from that loved one..u need to stop reviving the memories you had with him/her. column1: How does one cope with the loss of both their mom and dad?
column3: I have a very serious suggestion for you…Do not worry about their loss, and instead, honour them, love them, have fun with them now. The memories you create with them will give you strength when they are gone because you will know that you took advantage of every minute to show them your love. My father was my best friend. He died in December 1990…sounds like a long time ago, doesn’t it, but he is still alive in my heart. I loved him; we had a special relationship…we went for walks together; we went to yoga together; we went to tai chi together; we went to movies together. He came to my son’s soccer practices and games; he babysat my children and took them to music lessons and read to them. He was a wonderful father and grandfather and I still miss him every day. We suffer many losses in life, especially if we live long enough. Believe me, when bad things happen, they are most often not the things you expected to go wrong. Worry and anticipatory worry are such a waste of time. I had read that my entire life, but now that I am older, I realize how true it is. The bad things I thought might happen often didn’t, or they happened when I least expected them to happen. Good things are sprinkled throughout our lifetime. Friends appear when you need friends, and they might not even be the people whom you expect them to be. Please, please believe me when I urge you not to think about the bad things that may or may not happen. You have no idea when your wonderful parents might pass away, but you can take advantage of the time you have now. Make beautiful memories, laugh, experience life and love - the rest will take care of itself.

column1: How do retired people cope with the loss of their careers and developing a purpose again?
column3: Many people identify who they are with what they do for a living. So, it's not just that a job ends, but rather the feeling of emptiness that rises to the surface of “Who am I?” No one wants to feel like they are just putting in their time until death comes. Part of the answer is realizing that we all have seasons of life. Like seasons in a calendar year, it keeps changing. This morning I woke up to a cool, crisp morning with morning mist filling the valleys. Autumn is coming. I'll miss summer, but at the same time, I can look forward to the coming months. It's my choice to pick my attitude. But change is always hard. I missed teaching very much. But I know that I could not do that any more, so what am I here for? I prayed about it, and over time, a new purpose formed. Are you ready for this? I am here to help people. It's a simple purpose, with many ways to work it out. Occasionally I still substitute teach. I've also helped a family pack up to move out and helped the next family to move in. I spend time sharing encouragement with those who are depressed or overwhelmed. I've cooked, entertained, given money, and laughed with friends and strangers. Sometimes I sit outside and praise God for His creation, and I make time to lift up requests for those who are hurting. Helping others may not be your own preference, and I do understand. But as for me. I've found that in getting my focus off of myself and on to others, in genuine care and concern, my spirit is joyously lifted up, as well. Everyone has a different answer for this, as we are all unique. But helping others has many ways to bloom. There is a growing list of what I physically can no longer do. But there are still things I can do. I figure that if, at the end, I am confined to a bed, I can still pray. God uses our prayers to go where we cannot.

column1: What are some ways to cope with the loss of a loved one's memory?
column3: From experience with my own wife’s dementia, when she was confused about things, like wondering if we were married, I would dig out our wedding pictures, and that would trigger her memory, and she would start recalling details. That would do it for about a few hours! But then she wondered which “Vern” she was married to, the “Vern” she slept with, or the “Vern” that did the cooking, the cleaning, laundry etc., so then I would again use pictures and other events etc. to show that it was all the same person! It takes a lot of patience and love, to repeat, repeat, repeat! But in spite of it all, we were happy together. She died about 5 months ago. I hope this helps - anything that will help trigger the loved one’s memory connections. Once there’s a trigger of some sort, talking can help recall other details. I hope this helps.

column1: Can getting another dog help with coping with the loss of a previous dog?
column3: Definitely. I mourned the loss of my constant companion, a 7 year old cocker spaniel, for two years before adopting another dog. When the dog I adopted died at 15, my wife and I adopted another dog two weeks later. I was entirely unsure if it was the right decision, but certain seeming coincidences made it inevitable. (Same rare breed, same rare name, at a local shelter.) The second scenario (adopting a dog almost immediately) gave me an outlet for the care and love I could no longer bestow on my recently lost friend. It definitely took my mind of my loss. Losing your dog is never easy, but it is always worth bringing another one home. They are such incredible animals and they fill our lives with joy, laughter, love, and devotion. Knowing how many sad dogs are sitting in shelters, abandoned and unwanted, confused as to what they did wrong by just being themselves, I will probably never go more than a month without a dog (or many dogs) in my home. They complete my family and my life. Everyone thinks they have the best dog, and everyone is correct.

column1: How can I help my dog cope with losing another pet​?
column3: I’ve always been a dog person. I have four with me right now. They do most things together. They each have a unique personality and I’m sitting here imagining about how each one would handle the absence of one of the others. They don’t mind much when one goes off to the vet, or is even gone for a couple of days or more for surgery. Still, they do kind of look around a little when one is missing. Our dogs are pretty well adjusted. Ha, one just wandered over, the little one, and is standing on the arm of the sofa checking out what I’m doing here typing. It’s the baby — actually he close to a year old, but he still has come adorable puppy ways. OK, he just sniffed me, decided I was fine, and lay down on the sofa arm, facing away. He’s sleeping already. We know dogs aren’t pack animals, never were — that’s wolves — but they’re pretty good in groups. and if they’re with their humans, they can adjust pretty well to temporary or permanent loss (they often don’t quite know the difference.). We’ve always helped grieving dogs, if that’s what they’re doing, with what we called (when I was a priest) “the ministry of presence,” Or sometimes “the ministry of just showing up.” Being there, extra attention, not leaving them alone as long as we normally might.

column1: How will the EU cope with the loss of its second-biggest net contributor and exclusion from its biggest trading markets post Brexit?
column3: Brexit won’t cause any exclusion to business, I don’t think it’ll be good for anyone but life will carry on. There may be specific issues if border crossing slows down with goods that are perishable, but many business will not suffer any radical impact. What will happen is that unless a trade deal is in place (whether this March, or at the end of the “transition period”) there will be a change in tariffs. For example, say you want to buy a widget from France, it currently costs €100, let’s say the WTO tariff is 20%, so you’ll now pay €120 in total (€100 for the goods & €20 for the tariff). If there’s an increase in delivery costs due to customs agent fees & so on that will also be added in. Trade still happens, it’s just more expensive to be in business, so you either eat into your profit margin, or the costs to consumers goes up (maybe a mix of both). So what will happen to the EU? If the UK doesn’t pay what it has previously agreed, there will be a shortfall & this will need to be found from somewhere. It’ll be a short term crisis & it’ll likely be picked up primarily by the larger countries. After this the next budget will be balanced, as they’re losing a net contributor everyone will likely have to pay more, or cuts will have to be made. That said there will be some form of savings the EU will see by not having to accommodate the UK. As far as the trade goes either costs will go up (as above), or alternative suppliers will be found to maintain costs at or close to where they are, these may be in the single market or somewhere with a trade deal. The same will happen in the UK, I hope companies spring up to cater for needs that were previously met by suppliers in the EU.
column9: “Brexit won’t cause any exclusion to business”. This is not true for services where operational licences will need to be applied for in every individual Member State. Without the Single Market a lot of UK professional qualifications will no longer be legally recognised and firms will not have the right staff to continue business. A lot of contracts and insurances become invalid once UK does not come under the ECJ. A lot of the things that the EU exports to UK are not made elsewhere or made to the same standard we expect. BMWs and German kitchens etc. They also arrive “next day”. Outside the EU there are import costs; quality issues; transport costs and long delivery times. Falklands Islands order from UK, for example, and you have to order 6 months ahead. That means importers have to vastly increase longer term storage space to ensure supply regularity - all that costs extra. Most all countries have agreements in place to supply neighbouring countries as priority eg Australia and China. The worst UK companies have a productivity 60% below competitors - that means we will be importing (not making) EU goods for a very long time. Even if you can import something cheaper it does not mean the supplier will reduces selling prices. Most all UK politicians either ignore or talk total nonsense on these practical issues.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of a beloved dog? Any advice for grieving pet owners?
column3: It’s very hard, and very traumatic to navigate grief. My take on grief, apart from the obvious feelings of loss, is that grief is the process of the brain (mind) catching up with real life events. When the brain has caught up with, and accepted, the new status quo, the feelings of grief will lessen. To get to that point takes time, but you can help move the process forward. You must do things that will nudge your mind into accepting what has happened - some of these methods sound harsh, but I've used them, and the book I wrote advises them, and I’ve had many good reviews and messages of thanks from people who've lost a dog. the last one was from a man on his forties who has recently lost the first dog he’d loved. It was heart-breaking to read his words, but comforting to know I’d helped. The first thing I advise, and I did this with the loss of my beloved Marley, in 2021, is to remove the dog's belongings from the home. My wife and I sobbed as we bagged Marley’s bed and belongings less than two hours after he was put to sleep - completely unexpectedly, I might add. We woke that morning not knowing it was our last morning with him. It was hard to put those items in the cold garage, but nowhere near as hard as coming downstairs to his empty bed the next morning, or seeing the empty food bowl that didn’t need filling, would have been. Doing that helped our brains on the long path to the acceptance of our new reality. On the first morning after losing him, we came down to no sign of him. That broke us, but already our subconscious minds were noticing the lack of a dog’s bed and toys. Then, with heavy hearts and many tears, we walked the route we took him on each morning, taking turns to carry his lead. This also helped our minds begin accepting he was gone. We put the lead in the garage when we got home. This all may sound callous, but believe me when I say that out of all the dogs I’ve loved, Marley was the one I have loved the most - he helped me with my own mental health (he saved my life) and filled the gap in our lives after my wife had a third miscarriage. We, unhealthily or otherwise, treated Marley like a child, so to say we were upset is an understatement - our hearts were broken. They still are, but we can smile when we think of him. And we can have photos of him on the shelf, that don’t almost bring us to our knees when we glance at them. When he died, we were lucky that we had the advice I’d written to fall back on. Or I don’t think we’d have coped. I always say that love is love - it’s an emotion you don’t control, and if anybody belittles a person’s feelings towards a dog or any animal, that person is not worth knowing. To answer the question in a cold hearted. yet concise manner. I would say that you cope with the loss of a beloved dog by forcing your mind faster down the road of grief than it would naturally take. That means doing hard things, like getting rid of your dog’s belongings and not looking at photographs etc for a long while. There is more to it than that, but it can’t be written here. To anybody grieving a dog - I am so sorry for your loss, but please know this - it WILL get better. And I thought I’d add - this is not an advertisement for my short book - if you do want to purchase it for a few pounds or dollars, you can search for it and find it on numerous platforms - ‘Coping With the Loss of a Dog: Dealing with The Death of your Best friend’ -by Richard Oliver - 2016 (I donate 10% of book profits and my website profits to UK dog charities each month - although the website is in its early days and not earning much) If you are grieving a dog, and genuinely can’t afford to buy the book, please reach out to me, and I will send you a copy of the PDF with no questions asked and no judgements made.

Our other daughter has a friend who lost her 21 year old daughter and after 4 months she joined a grief group. She said is the best thing she ever did. The point is that only people going through the same difficulties can know how you feel.

column1: What are some ways to cope with the loss of a religious community after leaving a religion?
column3: I was raised as jehovah’s witness, but by the time I was about eight years old, I HATED everything it stood for! Sending little kids out door to door on Saturdays, prosletyzing could have led to some sad outcomes! Once a man in just a half opened robe opened the door and I could see everything. I was scared as sh*t and left right away! I missed out on birthdays, Chrsitmases, being told by my mom that I was going to “get destroyed at armageddon” because I was misbehaving…the fear they all installed in me still reeks to this day. Can’t vote, can’t salute the flag, can’t have blood transfusions, all of it was so ridiculous! So at age 17, I left home and that “religion” for good. They in turn, disfellowshipped me, meaning I was a non-person to them. So when my mom, still a JW when she died, was to have her celebration of life service, my dad told me their minister would come. I was a Catholic convert by then. I waited, we all waited and after an hour, I took my dad aside and asked when this minister was coming. He said he placed a call and the “minister” said he refused to come because I was there. Oh well. I finished the service myself. How to cope? Simple…be happy you are no longer a prisoner of their belief system.

column1: How can I cope with the loss of my adopted stray kitten?
column3: To me there is nothing more than losing a beloved pet. I have learned, in my personal case, that when I lose a pet, I must immediately adopt another pet and thus save a life. I do this because I loved my deceased pet so much and I want to show respect by giving life to a new pet. This way I continue to mourn for the first pet but at the same time I have a new pet to love. It hurts but it also helps the healing process. One time my dog passed on. I did not adopt another dog for about five months. It was sheer hell and I was in an extremely deep depression which greatly affected my life and way of living. It was horrible. I have learned never, ever to wait - I need one at once. I will always love and miss and mourn for those who passed - always. But I also have a live pet who loves me and whom I can love. This way I find peace and can live normally.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of property after a natural disaster?
column3: The monetary loss can be covered by insurance in a lot of cases. Other things can be replaced with the help of organizations like the Red Cross, the Saltation Army, and other charities that work with disaster recovery. Check with the people working the disaster itself. In the United States, the American Red Cross generally runs point on major disasters. As far as memories and sentimental loss, these things really cannot be replaced. Try to realize this and focus on the things that matter like the people in your life, the memories you have, and the experiences you have shared. Also, remember that you will have a chance to build new ones in the coming years.

column1: How do you cope with the loss of your forever favourite pair of shoes?
column3: You are a sad person if you cannot work through losing a pair of shoes! Hopefully you will live to wear out and/or lose uncountable things. You cannot be very happy if you’re so attached to stuff that you suffer long-standing bereavement when it’s gone. There is only one thing you will ever accumulate of value. That is love. Love can only be returned to you from another living thing. Stuff cannot satisfy our need to love and be loved. She/he who dies with the most stuff does not win!!! Focus on building strong relationships with people, animals, nature. Experiences and hobbies that you enjoy and travel also offer much more lasting happy memories and happinesses during your journey through this one life you will get. Grow up and look beyond TV, movies, commercials, magazines, etc… Don’t let cooperate marketing professionals continue to feed you the notion happiness can be found in material possessions or money. It’s important to have enough to live comfortably. Beyond what we need spending our time with people we love doing and experiencing new things. Learning new things that interest you. Don’t wait until you actually have to learn what bereavement after you lose someone you love, or face the end of your own time.

column1: How did you cope with your spouse suddenly leaving you?
column3: By relying on family and friends, who were wonderfully supportive when I needed them. My incredible therapist was a big help too, but I only saw her once a week - family and friends were available 24/7. I had to deal with moving, health problems, economic upheaval, and severe emotional trauma leading to serious depression. Without my family and friends I would have been lost. With them, I was soon back on my feet. I was dating again in about 9 months, and I'm with a marvelous new partner now. I have work that makes me happy, and I'm healthy. To have what I have now, I had to give myself time to grieve, but not allow myself to wallow in regrets. I had to give myself permission to be angry while resisting the lure of bitterness. I'm still hit now and then by pangs of grief for what was, but I've also acknowledged that the best times were long gone by the time he left physically. That helps to kick the might-have-beens in the teeth. You need to look forward now, and plan for your future without him or her. Analyze the relationship rationally and take what wisdom you can from it so that you avoid repeating any mistakes you made (there are always some, none of us are perfect). A therapist is a good idea - find one if you don't already have one. Draw your friends and family close around you. Open up to them and let them help you. Don't necessarily talk down your ex to them, but let them know that you're hurting and need their support. If you had kids together, DO NOT speak ill of their mother or father to them. Ever. If you do so, you'll come to regret it. Good luck in moving forward and healing. Edited to add: Someone assumed that I cheated or otherwise transgressed. He cheated and left me instead of staying to attend the therapy sessions that had been scheduled with his approval and work through the issue.

column1: How can I cope with the loss of a sibling as a teen?
column3: Just being a teen brings so much together physically and emotionally. The transition from child to adult is in a word messy. To have lost a sibling as a teen is a tough situation. So let’s start there. It’s not a easy road ahead, but if you successfully manage your way forward you will be an “old soul” among your peers. Let’s start with reality. Couples who loose a child tend to divorce. I am not trying to be negative at all, but embrace your family dynamics. So the strain between your mother and father will be high. Loosing a child means they loose the future of what your sibling would have added to their lives (speaking of graduations, weddings, grandchild etc.). You may feel a bit of survivors guilt. By this I mean, we don’t have a perfect relationship with our siblings. So you might remember every negative interaction you had with them. So don’t let yourself go down that path. You were probably a better sibling than you give your credit for. So don’t dwell on negative thoughts. You need to find a “safe place” to express your feelings and emotions, as there will be very low lows. Your peers are ill-equipped to understand the depth of your loss. Continue to be a teen and group up with your friends, but don’t expect them to be mature enough to understand your journey through grief. You need a friend (wise, potentially an older person in your life - teacher or pastor etc.) You may need to seek out a group. It would be great if you could find one for teens but I don’t of any offhand. However, if you are serious about growing through your grief journey even going to an adult group would be beneficial (thinking of Christian faith-based group: www.griefshare.org). Keep in mind as you develop as teen on top of going through grief. It’s not an easy task, but it will force you to become an outstanding adult. You will have depth and understanding beyond your years. Take the loss of your sibling and make it your own and build your life. 0

column1: How do you cope with the loss of your 2 year old and still have another child alive?
column3: I dont personally know. But I can tell you that there are support groups out there for child loss. I think it may be helpful just to be around other people who understand your grief. Grieving a loss… its just the worst. Coping is really just a fancy word for “managing your life in a healthy way, despite having a range of extreme emotions, as well as the temptations of addictions starting, or preexisting, amid other potential emotional and physical disabilities to deal with as well, while trying to maintain employment, your home life, and your social circles.” Its not easy. I know about coping, for sure. I do not know the grief of losing a child. But as far as needing help with coping, I personally would get into a support group and go to meetings, getting to know other parents, and maybe making friends with some who seem to be making it work, despite the huge emotional obstacles. Some might use a dry erase board in the kitchen as a monthly calendar to remind everyone of important appointments and social outings. Some may have a shrine set up in memory of their deceased child. Some may have added social things to their weekly schedule to help them to keep being around people who they know love them very much. These are healthy behaviors. Healthy is basically anything that is not destructive to your life or family, that is constructive behavior that you can feel good about, at the end of the day. If it was a baby, and moving the high chair away from the table is too much, try putting a doll into the high chair. I know thats weird sounding.. but at least it wont be an empty high chair. At least that baby doll will bring you fond memories of your baby. If its a kid, try putting a big picture of your child on the dining room chair. Or even on the wall. It might feel more normal.. These are bargaining tools. Its a stage of grief, where you kinda are in denial and also are pretending somehow that they arent really dead. Grief is an ongoing process. I know it all too well. My dad died when I was 9. I am 42 now. I still mourn for him. I stopped bargaining when I was about 10 or 11.. but there was a long time when we all just felt better, thinking daddy was on a vacation to Europe.. although it wasnt true, it was comforting, somehow. I also made a memory book about my dad. I drew pictures of him and shared memories of us. The only thing missing was the future. My guidance counselor wasnt really good at grief counseling apparently. He had died in february. The next ...

column1: How does one make up for or cope with the loss of a once in a lifetime opportunity?
column3: We are all having “once in a lifetime opportunities” every day. Most all the time we go blithely on, unknowingly. Twenty years ago, everyone knew that Amazon was going to be a monstrous powerhouse. Even people who had nothing to do with stocks knew it. How much would an investment of even $1000 then be worth now? The same is said now about Alibaba. Seventeen years ago, gold traded at its lowest value in history. Not the lowest amount, but lowest in value. A few years later it has risen 700%. Silver rose 1100% in the same time. I remember in 1994 I found out that silver mines dotted northern Idaho where I was a geology major. All of them were closed. I asked “why?” and was told that Silver had to trade at $20 an ounce to be profitable for the mines, and it was at something like $4. It was thought it would perhaps never reach $20 again. It did. How much would 1000 ounces of silver, which cost $4000 in 1999, be worth in 2012? Then there was Angie. Angie, if you're reading this, I was wrong and I'm sorry. Still. 25 years later. The list goes on and on. How do you deal with it? You GO FOR IT, next time. The final words of my grandmother in the 1980s and grandfather in 1990s were identical, and I never told anyone for years. “David, when you're dying, it isn't the things you failed at in life which bother you; it's the things you didn't even try.” Coming from a man who put men on the moon! (Huge story, for another entry) So, you feel this sting? Good. It's there for a reason. Next time, try. TRY! Try and fail miserably! Try and fail epically! Try and be humiliated! Try and break a bone! Try and regret it, but try! Try and make a mistake! Try and be wrong! Try and look like a fool! Try and be told you aren't good enough, but try! Try and overdo it! Try and be rejected! Try and go broke! Try and do too much and still be told it wasn't enough because life isn't fair, but try! Every successful person will tell you about how much they learned from failing. Every successful person will tell you how much they learned from succeeding. No successful person will tell you how much they learned from never having tried. As a final point, and very personally, take this last tidbit with you and apply it to every aspect of life…..from business to personal relationships to academics…… My mother was never asked out on a date and never went to one dance in high school. Years later, at a high school reunion, she talked with a classmate who asked her how well she remembered high school. He was amazed that she even remembered him, because he had always had a crush on her and had compared every woman he'd been with to her. She said “High school was very lonely for me. Of course I remember you. I always hoped you would ask me to a dance, but nobody ever did.” She ended up being a professional opera soprano, a ballet dancer, and a Miss America contestant! She was lonely because, as he said, everyone figured that she must have been doing something way too cool with someone way too popular and good looking than them, so they didn't bother ever calling. It took my dad, the roguish pirate that he is, to get the job done. Next year, he will celebrate his 50th wedding anniversary with the Miss America contestant whom nobody asked out on a date. How's that for trying? Let it sting. Next time you wonder how hard you should try to do something, remember this feeling you have and this story. And remember, sometimes God simply says “No.”

column1: How do I cope with the loss of my mother who was my best friend? Life has lost its meaning.
column3: Let me start off by saying that I'm so sorry for your loss. I know just exactly how you feel. I lost my mother who was also my best friend. My mom passed away on August 27th, 2017. Ten days after her 62nd birthday. I still have trouble coping with it. I feel like a 46 year old orphan who doesn't know where home is anymore or where I belong in the world. But I have just recently realized that the bond with my mother is still as strong as ever. Our earthly bodies can't interact like they did before, but our souls and hearts are connected forever. I know that you are going through one of the hardest things that you are ever going to go through right now but I also know that you are going to be able to make it through it. I have a feeling that you are a lot like me. We are strong women because strong women raised us. Keep your head up and please stay strong. We are living for us and them now. Let's make them proud.
column9: Hi Janet… Thank you very much for your kind words… I have searched so desperately for comfort ever since my angel passed a month ago and everyday is just a painful reminder. I don’t know if life will ever have meaning again but I really do hope that like you, my bond with my mom waxes stronger everyday. I believe we are a lot alike too and our angels are strong beautiful women.

column1: What are things people said or did to help you cope with the loss of a pet?
column3: Nothing. I’ve found, and have accepted, that grieving for a pet is a lonely grief, indeed. It’s all on just myself to process that grief, and to accept the regrets. Every pet owner has regrets…..did we wait too long to put the animal down? Did we put the animal down too soon? Was there something, (anything!), else that we could have done to save the pet’s life? Those regrets are part of the grieving. I think that most of us pet loving folks beat ourselves up a little. After all, we’ve lost a beloved member of our family so we turn to blaming ourselves. I’m old now, and have had to say goodbye to four past cats, six past dogs, and one tiny Netherland Dwarf rabbit, who lived for 15-years. Each and every time I was utterly crushed, but I’ve learned to lean into these losses like one would lean into a hard wind, and am able to accept the loss, the regrets, and the lonely mourning. After all, there’s not another choice, nor option. It doesn’t get easier but I do have tremendous empathy for those who have lost their pets…..even internet people who I do not know. When I read their stories I feel deeply for them because I know what it’s like…..I know. Have you lost a pet? Is that why you’ve asked this question? I hope not, but if you have, I feel for you too.
column9: I believe that you have done an excellent job. I know when I have lost a pet I have real feelings of loss and regret. Fortunately, all of them live on in my heart and I hope that we all meet again.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of a friendship with a narcissist? I have to cope with loss of friendship, wasted time, wasted energy, love & care.
column3: You are not alone. Coping with the losses you mentioned is the thread that connects all narcissist victims. Every victim of narcissists abuse has the same story of “What do I do now? How could I have wasted the time, energy, care and love on such an abusive relationship?” Or, “Why did I not see it sooner?” It is a very haunting revelation in itself. Once you are away from the narcissist and begin the healing process…ruminations will begin to cease if you allow. You can stay in the mindset of sorrow grief despair and hopelessness. Yes. You can. But this is what the narcissist wants. He gets fuel from bringing you (victim) being in the hopeless state. So…ask yourself this question. Do I want to stay in this horrible nightmare? No. No. No. Then, time to change your mindset. Change your thinking. Push the ruminations back onto the narcissist by speaking them away…keeping a journal…get out and start new and good things. Participate in new or even… long forgotten… old hobbies, exercise, new friends, connecting in new and fabulous ways. There is a big exciting world waiting to meet you. Yes you. You are worth it. You are different now, but only better for what you experienced. This is what has been waiting for you while you were stuck in his web of lies. Do not be hard on yourself. You were deceived from the get go. Peace🙂
column9: I saw your contribution to the discussion on Quora so I checked you out because I got curious about your intelligent comment. It turns out you are as beautiful as you are intelligent too, I want to get to know you. but it not going through, follow me so I can message you. Do reply.

column1: How do I cope with the loss of a career changing opportunity?
column3: I’m not really certain that I understand the full measure of the problem, so I will focus on the question. We all suffer losses in our lives. Some are more far reaching than others. Some hurt more, and hurt for a longer time. You do what you need to do to get through the hard time, the grieving time, the sad time. You put one foot in front of the other and keep moving on in your life. Force yourself to look at what you have and see the moments of gratefulness for what you have. Don’t look back. Turn your face to the sun and move toward the next opportunity in life.

column1: How do families cope with the loss of a loved one who has been missing for an extended period of time?
column3: I’ve told the story of my brother, Mitchell Dale Stehling, who went missing in Mesa Verde National Park, CO, on June 9, 2013. In spite of a massive search effort, Dale remained a missing person for seven and a half long years. He simply took a hike on one of the well-traveled and well-marked trails, and never returned. At first, we all thought he would turn up. We thought that maybe he was injured and couldn’t make his way back. We were assured by park rangers that nobody ever stayed lost for long, and that they were sure Dale would turn up. My family was devastated. We couldn’t fathom what must have happened. Weeks dragged by, then months, and pretty soon a whole year had passed since the day he went missing. My mother became like a zombie. She could barely speak. She carried some guilt, because Dale had initially decided not to go on the trip out west, but our mother talked him into it. I honestly worried that my mother would just fade away and die of a broken heart. My father was devastated too. He couldn’t speak of the incident, or of Dale, because it was too painful. Everyone grieved in their own way. As for me, I felt like I was walking through quicksand. My heart was broken like it never had been before. The days felt endless. I cried all the time for years. I just couldn’t come to terms with such a mysterious disappearance. Dale was my youngest brother and my best friend on earth. We were extremely close, and talked to one another almost every day, or Dale would come to visit me. He was a light in my life, which wasn’t a happy one; I was in an abusive relationship. For a long time, when something would happen, my first thought was, “I have to tell Dale about this”. But Dale wasn’t there. Everything reminded me of him. Oh, Lord, the tears I shed. Then after over seven years, we got a call from the park rangers at Mesa Verde. Dale’s remains had been recovered. We finally knew he was deceased. The not knowing had wrecked us. But when his remains were returned to the family, for me, it was like losing him all over again. You would think I would have gotten some closure, knowing his fate. But it didn’t work that way for me. I grieved hard for two more years, and it has only been for the last year that I can talk about him without crying. When a loved one goes missing, just disappears, you grieve, but with hope as its sidekick. There is always the hope that your loved one will return to you. You mourn, but you get stuck in the grieving process, because you don’t have a body to bury. Our family decided against a memorial service for Dale after he disappeared. We all held out hope that someday a miracle would happen and we would have him back. I’m thankful to the ones who found my brother’s skeletal remains and made sure they made their way back to us. A lifetime of not knowing would have killed me in tiny increments. Rest In Peace, Brother of Mine. You will never be forgotten.
column9: I’m so sorry for you. You lost not only a sibling but your best friend. Your story is really heartbreaking. I hope you find peace. xo

column1: How has New Zealand been coping with the loss of tourism due to COVID?
column3: The New Zealand tourism industry has, unsurprisingly, bourn the brunt of the economic fallout from the Covid pandemic. Domestic tourism has stepped in as New Zealanders are, for the most part, unable to travel abroad and thus are holidaying at home and able to visit attractions where they’d otherwise be crowded out by overseas tourists but that is only a fraction of the income that has been lost and many operators have either reduced or suspended operations or in some cases, they have closed down entirely. Fortunately domestic spending is up so overall our economy is doing very well, but that is little comfort to a hotel owner with no guests. Currently the tourism industry is pinning it’s hopes on a ‘Travel Bubble’ opening up with Australia in the next few months (A ‘Travel Bubble’ with the Cook Islands is likely to open up in the next few weeks, but the Cook Islands has a very small population that is relatively poor compared to New Zealand), this will allow Australians to travel to New Zealand without restriction (and vice versa) and Australia is a major source of tourists so that should give the industry the boost it needs. Since the latest community outbreaks on both sides of the Tasman appear to be under control (Australia has just lifted the travel restrictions it imposed after last Sunday’s community case was announced) I’d say we’re still on schedule for the trans Tasman travel bubble to be announced as originally planned.

column1: How do I cope with the sudden loss of my only son?
column3: My son hung himself at age 15 some years ago. I'm so very sorry for this tremendous loss and trauma. I know there's a hole in your soul. As lame as it sounds, time HELPS. It does not heal all wounds as if they never happened. You're likely in shock right now. My advice there is to enjoy its cushion. The day will come when you will face things without it. Mine lasted 6 months. No denial, but shock was my friend during my most horrific of days on this planet. You will need to know, there is no one path to grief resolution and you will always carry a bit of melancholy from here on out. But you will need to do YOU. This is life's grievous wound and sometimes no one can help but other times they will. You will see an empty chair at every occasion and it feels like the prick of a sharp knife. You will see and hear things that will do the same. These triggers reign while the wound you have is open and inflamed and bloody raw. During this time, I prayed to die many times. I'd beg God, “Just don't wake me up.”, crying and pleading not knowing how this would ever end. Speaking of God, I was so mad at him for 2 years, I couldn't bring myself to prayer beyond the scream. I knew it had been allowed, not caused but I did not care. Oddly enough, I wasn't mad at Jesus! LOL More like, “I know he's our dad but I feel betrayed.” Thankfully, my God eventually sorted all that out. Back to you. Eat when you can and try to just stand. You will go through all the stages of grief before you can start to breathe again. Honor your son with self care during these times so you stand again. Ask people to respect your boundaries but do not lock anyone out who wants to love you. It may turn out the people you thought would he there, aren't. It's because it scares them to think of themselves in a like position and also, many can't conceive of this level of pain. They aren't sure what to say in the face of it. (NOTE: The only right words are “I'm so sorry. I'll help however I can.” Or, if you can't help, leave the last bit off. Then FOLLOW UP.) Accept that there will be triggers back to that awful day, depending on circumstance. Know what to do. Accept the help. Be kind to yourself. A grief counselor is very helpful and you can video call, not even leaving your home. You need an impartial party to guide you without family filters etc. Pay attention to your heart health. Again, eat, even if just a few bites. After about 2 years, I spoke to God again. It still took me years after to feel normal, whatever that is now. I found my way in a way that I needed. Eventually the nasty wound scarred over. I did better at holidays and milestones. I grieved the losses of those too. Don't let people tell you that the wildly “real” dream is only a dream. You come out of those feeling awed. The bad ones are post traumatic stress. I can tell the story without tearing up and that's how I knew I'd healed. I had someone else in life to live for. I'd rather have skipped the lesson but we have no choice beyond honoring our loved ones. We often find a new purpose along the way. We find that the guilt we felt with laughter then, feels resolved now. My observance now is how very few speak his name unless I bring him up. He was a good kid. He was injured bullriding and had a traumatic brain injury that put it into motion. It only took a month to drop him to his bottom. Again, my condolences and prayers, too.
column9: Thank you Kathy, this really helps.

column1: What can you recommend to cope with the loss of a dentist?
column3: My dentist got quite old. He wasn't doing the job as well as he used too and it was a 45 minute drive to the office. I told him I was moving out of state and got a new dentist 10 minutes away. She is an Asian American and does an excellent job. My mouth and teeth are much improved. Just look around and find a younger dentist. They keep up on newer technology.
column9: Would you say the same about your physician? I loved dentistry and always stayed up to date.

column1: Hey Richard. I wrote to you a while ago about my spirit guides having me on a training program. I am not a medium and have never been involved in the spiritual world in earnest until this year. My spirit council has me going through a lesson plan which has been a wonderful experience. Recently, they started encouraging me to practice simple mediumship by connecting with loved ones who have passed. This is on behalf of their family members who are still earthbound. I wouldn't even think of trying this without the full consent of these bereaved people as I'm not about to play around with anyone's grief. This week, I just completed my second one with the amazing support, love and encouragement of a daughter who wanted to reach out to her mother. In the end, her mother, brother, and pet cat visited (another story for another day … but it was cool). After reviewing the messages from them, this kind woman told me honestly, what was incorrect and what seemed much more plausible. I'd say the interpretation of the messages I passed on to her was probably about 40% to 60% correct. So as disappointed as I was that the reading wasn’t more accurate, this woman has encouraged me to continue. Anyway, here's my question. The daughter asked me to ask her mother "Who did you meet when you first crossed over"? The response was that her brother, among others, greeted her. But at the time of her mother’s death, her brother was still alive, although he tragically died 11 months afterwards. Is it possible that the brother's higher self might have greeted her even though his earthbound self was still here? Based on my interpretational accuracy of about 50% for this connection, and that I'm extremely new at this, is this a plausible theory? My own spirit guide commented to us that not everything I interpreted was accurate, but "for our first attempt (with these folks) it was as good or better than expected". LOL. Now that's a resounding evaluation if I ever heard one. My spirit guide has quite the sense of humor. Still, the basic tone of her message was accurate and welcomed. I'll keep working at it with their encouragement and see where this all leads. I look forward to hearing your thoughts. Barry
column3: I recommend taking a look at DIVINE COUNCILS IN THE AFTERLIFE for a number of conversations with folks on councils… worth seeing what others have to say. The rules aren’t the rules, the percentages are estimates, change, fluctuate, so take them with a grain of salt - or a cup of salt. Not everything we see on the planet is accurate either so once one gets their mind around that - approximations of reality - then one gets a clearer view of what isn’t always clear to view. It’s great one is starting to chat with their council - as noted, I’ve been filming people doing that for fifteen years since I first chatted with mine.. Running out the door, will comment later.
column9: Hey Richard. Thanks. I appreciate you slipping in this quick comment before running out. I’ll check out some of those conversations tonight from your book. I’m getting a lot of great contact through my spirit guides but I’m so new at this that I really need a human reality check once in a while from some one who is more in tune with the other side. When I am doing this, pretty-well solo, I don’t have a lot to gauge about some of the things I’m experiencing, and I really want to stay on track. Your input is highly valued. B

column1: What are the effects of autism on an individual's ability to show/feel love for others, even family members? How can someone with autism overcome these challenges emotionally and mentally (if possible)?
column3: Autistic people don’t emote (show emotion) in the same way as non-autistic people, but that doesn’t mean we don’t have emotions. Some of us struggle to name, or recognise emotions, but that doesn’t mean we don’t have them. We show love in different ways, includingtelling the person all about the thing(s) that excite and interest us, because we want to share that excitement and positivity with our loved onesgiving that person cool things, like nice pebbles or cherished items. Again, we want to share the positive things that bring us joysending that person lots of memes or photos. Yet again, we’re sharing something with that person that makes us feel good because we hope it will also make them feel good, and feel connected through a shared experiencebeing physically affectionate, or tolerating a hug every now and then. Autistic people often have sensory processing issues that make hugs and touch physically painful. We’d hope that our loved ones care enough about us not to insist that we put ourselves through pain for their benefit, but you might get a hug every now and then. Some autistic people sensory-seek in relation to touch, because it’s pleasurable to them rather than painful, but it’s very much down to the individual. It can change for that individual too, and while someone might be Ok with 2 or 3 hugs in a day, more than that is overwhelming/painfulkeeping quiet and out of your way. If we feel, or are made to feel that our presence is challenging or unwanted, we’ll keep our distance out of love for you. I know this was how I tried to support family members after a bereavement because me being around is stressful for themAs for overcoming the challenge - the challenge really is having family members or friends who don’t accept us the way we are, and accept love how and when we show it. The challenge of maintaining any sort of positive self esteem when we are told we don’t measure up, and that the way we are isn’t the way people want us to be, is really difficult. In my experience, overcoming that challenge involved distancing myself from people who don’t understand or accept me, spending more time alone working on my inner self esteem, and trying to educate people (generally) about autism and autistic behaviour so that some good can come of my rubbish mental health.
column9: I would add doing things for the people you love. I would also add spending time with the people you love. Just know, spending time is being in their presence, not necessarily doing things together.

column1: What is something that someone said to you during your grieving that stuck with you?
column3: My husband and I met at community college in 1963; and we are still happily married all these years later. It was in April of 1965, right after our church wedding rehearsal, when my fiance phoned to say that his father had suffered a heart attack and died. Although our wedding plans weren’t fancy, there were still many things that needed to be changed. Relatives were on their way into town, flowers and wedding cake were ordered, etc. When my fiance and I went to see his mother early the next morning, we found that when she called their relatives and friends to tell them of the death, she also told them the wedding was cancelled and we would be getting married at the courthouse, sometime in the future. This was a bit of a shock to me, since we had not even decided yet what to do. We went to consult with our pastor, who advised that we still get married in the church; and not to delay too long, as it would make it even harder for the new widow to part with her son. He suggested we get married the following week. My fiance and his sister had just lost their father, their mother had just lost her husband, so I focused on their grief—supporting their needs—and the needs of their various family and friends. By the time of the visitation, funeral and burial, I barely remembered it was supposed to be my wedding day, my honeymoon, etc. But one kind soul said something I have never forgotten. At the funeral home, a dear friend of the bereaved family came through the receiving line. When she got to me, she leaned over in a hug and whispered, “Most of all, I feel sorry for you.” Me…not even quite a member of the family yet? How thoughtful! That has stayed with me for the past 57 years. It has made me aware to look around for the most forgotten in a group event, and making sure that they, also, are comforted, or celebrating, or whatever is appropriate for the particular occasion. It can make a world of difference to that person, to be recognized, to be included.
column9: Kinds words can make a difference in your life without the other person even knowing their words were just what you needed I was 25 with a 2 and 3 year old a week before my husband passing I had been offered employment which I definitely needed now I was a Widow so I learned a new job buried my husband my heart broke every time my boys were looking out the window for their dad to come home from work they just had not grasped daddy is in heaven yet I was feeling so overwhelmed as mom was not stay at home now and two boys without a dad. I had just got home from work had the two boys in a stroller with bags of laundry inserted between them and a lady in the complex where I lived came up to me and said You are the most capable Woman I know keep on Trucking that was a saying back in the day and for some reason when ever I felt like I was failing or not enough time in the day I would say to myself you are the most capable woman I know dont even remember her name but she was one of those angels on earth which is a message I desperately needed at the time .

column1: Is the pain of losing an adopted child the same as losing a biological child?
column3: To effectively answer that you would need to speak to someone who has lost both an adopted and biological child. I hope to never find that person, as that sounds horrific. However, it may help you to look at Steven Curtis Chapman’s organization, Show Hope, which is dedicated to supporting adoption and adoptive families. Part of their organization is called Remembering Maria, which is the Chapman family’s eulogy of their daughter Maria, who was killed in a car accident. I think if you read through the anguish this family faced, and their grief work through bereavement, you will find that it was just as difficult as losing a biological child, with subtle nuances related to adoption perhaps, but just painful. Macro level outlook - grief is grief, and if someone you love dies, then it doesn’t matter if they share DNA or not. If you related to that person as a family member, then your family member died. That’s why there are numerous accounts of those who didn’t feel as much grief when their estranged biological family member died as they did when their friend, their partner, or even their pet did. If you love, losing hurts.
column9: I lost my two year old daughter in a car accident many years ago (I was driving and was hit broadside due to loss of control on slushy, icy roads). I lost my 20 year old daughter to a drug overdose 8 years ago. I lost my step son at the age of 25 (he died in his sleep due to untreated sleep apnea). The pain is different for each…the pain is the same for each. It doesn’t matter that he was not my biological child. He was loved by all of us as were the other two. He too will never have a chance to have a family or to succeed in his life ambitions. I write…a lot…I walk…a lot. When someone asks “how many kids do you have” (oh…the dreaded question) I always say I have six girls and 2 boys. I also hope there is no request for more information because I may or may not cry depending on the day and the moment. But life can still be beautiful if you look for the beauty.

column1: Hi Richard, my son passed suddenly in January of this year. I found him. I won't go into detail but i can,t get the image of him deceased out of my head. My beautiful boy. I went to see him in the Chapel of Rest and he looked so different as to other people ive seen there who looked at peace and asleep. Im heartbroken. I want to be with him but i have 2 other sons that i can,t leave. Apparently my son had a heart attack ( my dad passed aged 31 of the same thing and my son was also 31) Ive begged to see him in my dreams, ive begged for signs he,s okay. Ive had nothing. Its killing me. Will he be alright?
column3: I am so very sorry for your loss. As a parent, I cannot imaging the grief that you are experiencing. Grief, especially after the loss of your son, is very complex. I cannot assure you that your loss will go away but it will change with time. You are experiencing grief, sadness, fear, anger, & depression. In my experience working as a therapist to grieving parents, this is a tremendous amount of tumultuous emotions to bear on your own. There are many groups for bereaved parents and I encourage you to explore them. I have two family members who lost their 20-something year old children suddenly and they have found support in these groups. I also encourage you to find a therapist, who specializes in bereavement counseling. This will be your support in processing the trauma you are experiencing. You ask if your son is okay. My answer is that your son knew you loved him. Your love made his time on this Earth wonderful. Be assured that he is your Angel looking after you. He would want you to live your life knowing he is okay.
column9: I am so sorry for your loss.. I too lost my 24 year old son in a car accident in January 2022, so I know the pain you are going through :( I haven't had any therapy as I believe it is within us to find the ways which bring us comfort during the times when we are low. But everyone is different and knows whats best for them :) Personally I turned towards spirituality. I find it very comforting to hear the perspective that our physical bodies are just vessels, that our spirit never dies, that we are just passing by earth for a little while and then our spirit will ascend to the next level of its journey. It gives me hope and comfort that my son was called upon his next journey and we shall see each other again. He had his own path to follow and I must not feel sad but proud! But..we are human! We feel, we cry, we miss tremendously, a million times more as mothers! Some days are good..some days are bad.. some days are very bad.. its a cycle we now have to live with for the rest of our lives. I truly wish you find the strength and comfort to continue ❤❤❤

column1: After all is said and done, what is your biggest take-away from the fact that Donald Trump is the President of the United States?
column3: Look at the people around you. The thousands of people you have known throughout your life. Your colleagues at work, your acquaintances and friends, family members including parents, siblings, your children, cousins, the workers who serve you in the shops, the people working at your bank. At first glance, they all seem so normal, so harmless, so average. However, if half the people - people that surround us - can vote for Trump without batting an eye then at least half the people around us are moral zeroes. I will not bore the readers by stereotyping Trump’s voters and supporters as racists, religious bigots, misogynists, traitors, authoritarians, etc. I am sure many of them are. I am sure that there are quite a few Trump supporters who - in their personal lives or way of thinking - do not conform to these stereotypes. We can be sure that Trump voters and supporters, who number in the tens of millions, are as diverse a group as any other large demographic category. Racism, bigotry, misogyny, disloyalty, authoritarianism are issues that matter. Trump clearly attracts this type of people. However, what the Trump election has exposed is something disturbingly novel. Above all he appears to attract people who seem incapable of contributing their bit in upholding even the most basic or elementary or obvious moral standards in the public arena. This is new territory. Trump voters have exhibited this capacity: the ability to vote for a man who is openly, unabashedly, and undeniably indecent. Now, the word ‘decency’ has a distinctly modest ring to it. In terms of its true meaning it is of fundamental significance. Decent defines as ‘behavior that conforms to accepted standards of morality or respectability.’ Moral and respectable behavior includes honesty, integrity, compassion, benevolence, loyalty. Trump’s behavior and language irrefutably violate the terms of decency. He is a pathological liar, a lecher, a swindler, cruel, petty, spiteful, crooked, and treasonous. It is not even possible to plausibly claim the contrary. He has publicly, unashamedly, and purposefully exhibited this behavior for all humanity to see. Just watch these examples below.Treason by calling on a hostile power to hack a fellow citizen’s emailsLechery by bragging about grabbing pussyCruelty by mocking a reporter with a disabilitySpitefulness and more cruelty by slandering a bereaved family of a Purple Heart and Bronze Star decorated army captain killed in warMendacity and slander by questioning their president’s place of birthTreachery by swindling hundreds of contractorsNo other candidate in America - including Hillary Clinton - has debased himself or herself in such a horrible manner and in so many ways in just one single election campaign. Do we know of anyone who would prefer a lecherous, treasonous, deceitful, crooked, cruel, petty, and spiteful parent or teacher or superior or spouse? We may not be able to choose our parents and teachers. We may lack the prescience to avoid bad employers, business partners or spouses. And yet, half of the population voted for precisely such a person, while fully aware of his true character as exposed by his own behavior in the public limelight way in advance of Election Day. However, the problem goes deeper. In making and then justifying their choice, Trump supporters are also unbelievably dishonest. The forensic marker of their dishonesty is the fact that they keep telling us that it was a matter having to choose between Trump and Hilary. The fact of the matter is that they never rejected Hillary for her own sake. Long before they ever got to voting against Hillary, they used their voting power in the Republican primaries to reject 17 REPUBLICAN CANDIDATES in favor of Trump. Every single one of these 17 Republican candidates was more decent and capable than Trump. On what grounds could one honestly claim that Trump was better than John Kasich, Jeb Bush, Rand Paul, George Pataki, or Bobby Jindal, just to name the better ones? However, even a certified lowlife as Ted Cruz never ever by any length managed to stoop as low as Trump did. And if one really did not like any of those 17 other Republican candidates, there were third-party and the independent candidates! How about the best of them, Evan McMullin? And finally, one could have decided simply not to vote, rather than vote for Trump. If someone votes for a man who is so obviously treasonous, mendacious, vile and cruel, it was because they lacked a moral core. It is because the filth and cruelty of this man thrills and pleases such people. So my take-away from the fact that Trump is now the president is that half the people around us - who seem so normal, so harmless, so average - are at the core - and by now openly so - moral zeroes, a danger to us and themselves and it shows:.
column9: “They used their voting power in the Republican primaries to reject 17 Republican candidates in favor of Trump.” Yes! This is something that Trump voters tend to skim over when using the “I didn’t like Hillary” excuse. I haven’t seen even one cogent, believable explanation for Trump winning primaries over more qualified candidates.

column1: Adult Should I attend my uncles funeral even though we weren't close? He voluntarily discharged from the hospital (blood cancer and diabetes) stubbornly.
column3: If you have an idea that your presence at his funeral would comfort his surviving family, then, yes, you should go. As the old saying goes, funerals aren’t for the dead—-they’re for the survivors. And, as anyone who’s ever been part of the bereaved family knows, it matters very much to them if other family member take the trouble to show up. All the more so if the deceased person didn’t have many friends or supporters.

column1: Who are some social activists in India and what are their achievements?
column3: Parveena Ahanger: The Iron Lady of Kashmir Parveena Ahanger is a Kashmiri activist who founded an organization called Association of Parents of Disappeared Persons (APDP), which advocates the struggle of the family members of the persons who went missing due to enforced disappearances by military and law enforcement organizations. She was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 2005 for her peaceful human rights activism. Parveena Ahanger used to be an ordinary illiterate woman, who rarely stepped outside her house. But a sudden turn of events changed her life forever. On 18 August 1990, her 17 year old son Javed Ahmad was arrested by the Indian Army during a raid in Batlamoo area of Srinagar. Since then no trace of Javed has been found. An undaunted Parveena has looked for he son in the jails of Jammu and Kashmir, Rajasthan, Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, but all in vain. She moved the court of law but no whereabouts of her son came out in a protracted trial. Her untiring efforts encouraged the family members of persons who went missing in a similar manner to fight for truth and justice. Thus the organization called Association of Parents of Disappeared Persons (APDP) was founded by Ahanger in 1994 to support the cause of the bereaved family members. In the wake of the militant uprising and separatist movements in the Kashmir Valley in the 1990s, which instigated massive military operations and crackdown, such incidents were not uncommon. According to official estimates, 3744 people went missing during 1992–2003. ADPD puts the number somewhere between 8,000–10,000 (1989–2006). A majority of the disappeared persons were young men and even minors who were not known to have any connection with extremism. ADPD currently comprises of family members of a thousand disappeared persons. One of their prime objectives is detailed documentation of their cases. On the 10th of every month, the members gather at Srinagar to hold a public protest and display support towards one another. The organization is also vocal against the controversial Armed Force Special Forces Act (AFSPA, 1990) which gives the Indian military special power in disturbed areas. The efforts of ADPD received international attention and Ahanger has represented ADPD in several countries including Philippines, Thailand, Indonesia and the UK.In the words of Parveena Ahanger, Nobody understands a mother’s pain. I'm a victim, there are many like us. APDP originated out of my pain, and pain of hundreds of mothers like me. (at the University of Westminster, London, 2014) Source: 1. Kashmiri mother vows to find son she lost when he was arrested in 1990 2. Association of Parents of Disappeared Persons
column9: I didn’t know about her. Thanks for sharing.

column1: What happens when someone dies in a hotel?
column3: Firstly upon identification the room is kept out of bounds for all staff. In some cases staff ( senior personnel ) may administer first aid to resuscitate the guest. Resident manager or the general manager is informed and in house doctors are called to confirm death. Local police authorities are informed simultaneously and a First information report is filed. This facilitates the issual of death certificate and further process of autopsy or embalming depending upon the cause of death & its nature. Family members are informed and further process are synced to provide all assistance to the members of the bereaved family. It is extremely scary to deal with death in a hotel. Personnel are kept on standby all the time and the General manager ensures that the hotel staff does not communicate anything which jeopardises the reputation of the hotel. It is very gruelling for the General manager and his supportive head of the departments.

column1: As a software engineer, what is it like to work at Microsoft or Google?
column3: Microsoft is a fun place to work for. Things have drastically changed since I joined almost 4 years ago under Satya’s tenure. Work Culture: I joined Microsoft straight out of school as a shy and introverted person. I was that person who’d rather spend 2 days figuring out stuff on my own rather than chin-up and ask someone for help. But that changed over years since people are more than happy to help others get unblocked and they spend quality time with you to make sure you are on-board rather than moving at the speed of a TGV and expecting you to jump on-board and deliver. My managers have always been very objective about my performance and given me great constructive feedback to improve myself and get better. Growth was an important factor for me in terms of job satisfaction and I feel far more emboldened now to chime in my ideas and speak my mind out about design shortcomings and offer new solutions. Compensation and Benefits: Microsoft is not on par with other major tech companies in terms of pay and they are aware of the dissatisfaction this has caused among employees. But the benefits are great - we get great healthcare benefits, prime discounts, Microsoft software and hardware with employee discounts and free gym memberships to fancy sports clubs. We have 3 months paid paternity leave for new dads and 6 months paid maternity leave for new moms. We also have paid family care leave of 1 month to take care of a sick family member and paid bereavement leave of 1 month to take care of a family member’s loss. I wouldn’t care about the extra money a company offers if I can take a month off to attend to my sick family member and still get paid. Work-life balance: Nobody expects us to reply to emails over weekend or after 6 pm. Work is very well planned out ahead of time and we always know what we are working on and what to expect over the upcoming months. Sure, occasionally we might work late nights to ensure that things are lit up for that big demo or presentation - but never to the point of exhaustion or feeling burnt out. I have never carried my work laptop to any of my vacation destinations (including long India trips). Flexibility: We have co-workers from all spectrum and Microsoft has a great way of accommodating it all. I have a co-worker who can work only from 7 to 3 since he commutes from a far place and has to pick his kids up from school - so we schedule meetings accordingly. We have few other teammates who work from home quite often since they have a young kid. We have 3 of our team members working from Vancouver, CA for h1B visa issues - Microsoft is great in terms of supporting its employees through visa issues. We always ensure that we schedule our team outings only when the Vancouver folks can join in. I believe people produce their best work when they are given the freedom and liberty to do that work from wherever they feel most comfortable in. Tech: I work in windows organization(now its all Cloud + AI) and thankfully, my team is pretty bold in terms of adopting and experimenting with the latest products out there. We use a lot of open source libraries and our SDKs are open-source as well. We are given full liberty to research into latest capabilities to make our applications run faster and better and implement them. People: Honestly, this is what makes Microsoft special to me. I always feel like the people in my team have my back and they are more than forthcoming to help me out when am stuck. My GEM (manager’s manager) is also super fun and last week, we watched all the FIFA semi-finals in our conference room with the whole team while she complained about people who scheduled meetings during the world cup semi-finals. You wouldn’t be surprised to run into people who have stayed at Microsoft for more than 10 years. Most of them I’ve come across put down roots in Microsoft and I can see why.
