column1: How did they remove the guns from citizens in the UK and convince those citizens to agree to it?
column3: Deep breath… ‘They’ (the UK government) did not ‘convince’ citizens to ‘agree’ to have their guns ‘removed’. Quite the opposite, in fact. British citizens called upon their government to control the sale of guns in order to keep them out of the hands of irresponsible people, especially those who might shoot kids. In Britain, handguns were effectively banned after a single school shooting (the Dunblane school massacre) in 1996. The massacre in Dunblane, Scotland, prompted widespread outrage and a surge in public support to ban private ownership of handguns. A grassroots UK Gun Control Network was established after the shooting and spearheaded the campaign. The bereaved families also started a petition, the Snowdrop Petition, which presented 750,000 signatures to Parliament. The campaign was flooded with public offers of support, including money, as well as media backing. The government bowed to public pressure and passed the Firearms (Amendment) Act 1997 and the Firearms (Amendment) (No. 2) Act 1997, which effectively banned private possession of handguns almost completely. So it’s not that some sinister, tyrannical establishment deliberately stripped ordinary British citizens of the ability to defend themselves. This is just a fantasy that NRA members like to tell each other. In reality, the vast majority of British people simply do not want anything to do with guns; they do not want to use guns as a means of self defence; and they certainly don’t want psychologically disturbed individuals being able to use guns to shoot random schoolchildren. But just to be clear, there is no law preventing British citizens from responsibly owning licensed firearms other than handguns — for good reason. Self-defence has not been considered a ‘good reason’ in Great Britain for many decades (though it does still apply in Northern Ireland). In free countries, people get to demand certain basic rights. In the USA, many people demand the right to bear arms. That’s their choice. In the UK (and most other democratic countries), most people prefer the right to live without ever worrying about being shot. The UK's gun control laws are among the strictest in the world because they reflect the will of the British people. We don’t need guns to defend ourselves because there are so few guns around in the first place. We like it this way. We have one of the lowest rates of gun homicides in the world.List of countries by firearm-related death rate - WikipediaFurther readingWe banned the guns that killed school children in Dunblane. Here’s how (New Statesman, 16 Feb 2018)After shooting tragedies, Britain went after guns. (Washington Post, 3 Feb 2013)What the UK and Australia did differently after mass shootings (CNN World Edition, 26 Dec 2017)

column1: What is the worst greeting card you have received?
column3: After my husband died in December of 2013, I received many cards, letters and donations consoling me and honoring him. Finally, in the dark days of January, I was able to sort through them and spent days taking in what everyone said. In return, during the next month, I answered each one with a distinctly personal note. And I was so emotional, it had to come out in my writing. It was a tearful enterprise but sending out a stack of letters expressing gratitude got me through each sad day. I was especially touched that an ex-husband of a divorce client sent a note of condolence after he saw the obituary in the newspaper. And my law colleagues all came through, I hadn’t realized what a close and supportive community they turned out to be. But there was one card I received that distressed me so greatly, I ripped it into little pieces and threw it out. It was a store-bought condolence card from a friend or family member (it’s not important which) with simply a signature. No “Dear Barrie,” not even, “Love” or “Sincerely” in the closing. And a cold wind just slammed me in the face. I realize that as a newly bereaved wife, my sensitivities were high and the truth was, I literally went out of my mind. I can still clearly see that blue card with the signature under the printed greeting. In those early months after losing my beloved life partner, his suffering still vivid to me, I deeply felt his presence. So that any perceived affront to me was an affront to us both. I needed to protect him still—as I did when I was his caregiver—from the world in which he was totally vulnerable. I see myself at my desk, holding the card, falling apart, alone and bereft, looking for a lifeline but not finding it that day. A year like no other, and that was just the beginning.
column9: So terribly relatable, as I lost my wife suddenly and unexpectedly in 2015. I wonder if the person who sent you that card when you lost Paul just didn't know what to say, but at least wanted to get the sentiment across to you. I know how hard it is just to say something when someone loses a loved one. I imagine them sitting before the card and laboring over what to say, and finally just signing it, and feeling that at least they tried and took the time to send something. Perhaps they felt badly that they couldn't find the words. Maybe it would help you if you spoke with them about it. And it might help them too. Bless you.

column1: Do teachers get vacation time during the school year? If so, how much?
column3: Teachers typically have the same vacations as students except for a number of professional days sprinkled through out the year (Professional days are when we come in to work without students and work on developing curriculum, reading up on state guidelines/mandates, or whatever other responsibilities we may have). Teachers do have allowances for sick days, bereavement, and personal days. These vary from school district to school district based on negotiations by teacher unions with the boards of education. I teach in northern New Jersey and have an allowance of up to 10 sick days, 5 days for the death of an immediate family member (2 for non-immediate), and 4 personal days per year. I have heard that a nearby school gives 2 personal days and 15 sick days. Any additional time will result in docked pay. I imagine there is large variation from place to place, depending on strength of unions and support for education.

column1: Adult Why do people laugh at funeral?
column3: A funeral is very stressful. Most people don’t go to funerals very often, and when they do it’s either part of the grieving process, saying good-bye, or supporting a friend or relative who is grieving. For the bereaved people (close family members and friends), the funeral in Western cultures is often up to three and sometimes even more days after the event. These people have therefore, either been nursing their sick loved one on their deathbed or received “out-of-the-blue” shocking news, in the case of a sudden death, for days or even weeks leading up to the funeral. That’s a lot of stress build up. You are confronting a new situation. How will family members cope without the loved one? Are there any threats? Are there now vulnerable people who will no longer be supported either emotionally or financially? How will the family be financially or emotionally stabilised? Who has needs? What work needs to be done? SO a funeral is actually the end result of a lot of new situations. Planning a funeral is not something we normally prepare for in advance. That takes work and concentration. People who don’t normally work together, are thrown together in order to manage the funeral, the event, and people’s emotions and any roles that would normally be done by the deceased. In some cases laughing is letting off steam, other times it’s part of the bond building process that a funeral provides. I remember being at the funeral of a person that I hadn’t spent a lot of time with, but I knew him well enough to know his sardonic, cynical personality, which was also the tone of his sense of humour. After the serious part of the funeral was over, I imagined him to be present in the room in spirit, being sarcastic about some of the interactions between his friends and family members. It made me burst out laughing……

column1: Do therapists/counsellors diagnose you by simply through word-of-mouth or send you a diagnostic document as a reference so you clearly understand about your diagnosis and re-evaluate your therapy process when needed?
column3: Diagnosis, presenting concerns and treatment plan/goals should all be transparent between client and clinician. Not that this would ever happen, but if someone barged into your session and asked each of you, client and therapist, why you were there, what you were being treated for and what your treatment plan/goals were, you should both have the same answers. Some clinicians who don’t bill insurance don’t use diagnoses, and that’s fine. And in most places, you need to have documentation of treatment plan and presenting issues, because it’s a part of ethical practice and informed consent. If your state, province, or country doesn’t have that, you might not get something formally written out. However, a client (and clinician for that matter) should ALWAYS know what the therapist’s idea of your presenting concerns are and how the two of you are working toward improvement, healing or change. As far as re-evaluation, Every time there’s new context for the therapist to see, or new information or hopes or goals shared by the client, a revisit to the treatment plan is really important. For example, let’s say someone presented to treatment for anxiety but then disclosed a binge drinking issue, or they presented for help with mood swings but suddenly are struggling with grief over a family member’s death, treatment may change. It’s an ethical MUST to be sure that client and therapist are on the same page with any changes. Otherwise the client hasn’t been *informed* and given a chance to *consent* to the change. As far as diagnosis, if a clinician is using diagnosis/diagnoses, they need to be documented in the chart and clients absolutely have a right to know what diagnoses are in their chart. And if there’s no diagnosis in the chart, a clinician would be remiss to make one up after the fact. There needs to be a consistent paper trail and, especially for serious or stigmatized ones, there needs to be documentation of thorough assessment and of the client being informed and consenting to proceed. — TLDR: If you have any concerns about whether you and your therapist are on the same page about what you’re experiencing (diagnosis, symptoms, or both), what your goals are, and what your path through it looks like, ask. An ethical therapist will offer this, along with the space to discuss, ask for clarity, process or collaborate on any modifications. If they deny you that information, get defensive, or act like you’re being problematic or critical, run run run far away.

column1: What is your best memory of your relationship with your therapist?
column3: I’ll go ahead and list my best memory with each therapist I’ve had. There have been four. All of them were necessary for me to be able to do the work I’m doing with R. I am so grateful for each of them. In order, then: J, my college therapist: He gave me a silver dollar as a transitional object because I was dissociating and losing time and feeling unsafe in between sessions. The giving of the silver dollar is a U.S. military tradition, and we shared a military background. So it was so meaningful to me. I carried that silver dollar with me for years, until I gave it to a kid I worked with who needed it more than me. I’ll write about this on my Space someday. F, J’s close colleague that I saw after college: She was so good at identifying and labeling my cognitive distortions - this was part of our CBT work. One day, I finally said the thing that I’d never said before because it felt so embarrassing to admit, and because I was afraid that if I did say it, she would confirm it. I said, “Everyone leaves me. There’s something about me that people don’t think is worth sticking around for.” F replied, “Sam, a relationship ending is not the same thing as being left. Sometimes things just end. You’re not leavable. It’s not something about you. People have their own stuff that forces them to pull away, sometimes. That’s them. Not you.” I needed that. I still think about it frequently. A, my first trauma therapist: One night, two years into our work, I showed up to therapy wrapped in another country’s flag, wearing one shoe (and holding the other), and extremely scared and confused. A smiled at me warmly and said, “Whatcha got there?”, which I found funny, though I couldn’t express that. What I did do was cry. And A held my hand while I cried. For almost the entire hour, she held my hand, saying, “You’re safe. You’re here in my office and I am with you. And you can hold my hand for however long you need to.” Holding her hand grounded me. And I learned in that moment that physical touch is the only thing that makes me feel real. R, my current therapist: We’ve had so many beautiful interactions and it’s so hard to choose just one. I think my best memory with R was the first time I really sobbed in therapy. I had cried before, a little bit, but never enough to make sound. I finally just let it rip one session. Grief poured out of me in the aftermath of discovering a family member’s body that morning. I had no real control over it. R crossed the room to sit beside me and she placed her hand on my shoulder and said so gently, “I hear you, Sam. I hear your pain. I’m right here next to you. You can make the sounds, you don’t have to be quiet. I’ll stay right here.” And when I started saying, “I’m sorry!” over and over again, because I felt that their death was my fault, all R said was, “I know. I know, Sam. I hear you. I’m here. I know.” She didn’t try to make me believe something different. She didn’t try to convince me of something I wasn’t ready to accept. She just let me have my emotions, and she stayed with me as they overtook me. She was the life raft. And that session changed both of our lives. I have so many more memories with all of them. This was hard!

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: “Get over” has several connotations here. I’ll go over the one most people mean, which is - How do you recover from feeling bad/sad/empty/angry/etc. as the result of a family member’s death? Simply, you just carry on. I know it’s a cliche, but it’s true. And here’s another true cliche - time is the best medicine. It’s the only natural healer. Time is in charge, and fixed, so you can’t rush it…it is what it is. Be patient…time is healing you, healing can happen so slowly that you don’t feel the progress, but it’s definitely happening. 1% better every week, for example, is progress, but hard to detect. But like a damaged nerve that needs a long time to heal, there is therapy you can do in the meantime to facilitate the healing, and to minimize the pain on a daily basis. Keep yourself busy. Take care of your health. Talk to a therapist if need be. Try to do things that make yourself happy. Socialize. Don’t bottle anything up…if you need to talk about the deceased, do so. By all means think about the deceased as much as you like. Cry as much as you like. Whatever works.

column1: How do you deal with unbearable grief?
column3: My father passed away in 2012. If you had told me six years ago that I would still occasionally endure waves of grief that leave me crying, silently saying, “I miss you so much - I wasn’t ready to lose you”, I would not have believed it. I would have thought that those intense waves would have long died out by now. Or at least died down to a level that didn’t still crash in to me without warning, wiping me out and leaving me soaking wet. Sometime last year, a friend of mine shared with me the story of the Japanese ‘wind phone’ - a disconnected rotary phone within a white, glass-paned phone booth nestled in a garden in the town of Otsuchi.A man named Itaru Sasaki had built the phone booth after losing his cousin in 2010 as a way to ruminate over his death. A year later, Sasaki’s hometown of Otsuchi was hit with a triple disaster: an earthquake followed by a tsunami, which caused a nuclear meltdown - and 1,285 people died or went missing. Many people from that town as well as all over Japan have since traveled long distances to use the ‘wind phone’ to speak to their lost loved ones. I read the article and then promtly listened to the This American Life podcast episode that shared some of the one-way conversations with people who used the phone and their reasons for making the pilgrimage to do so. I was so moved by the story because it seemed like a sad yet beautiful way to untangle the grief that remains knotted in my stomach, even years after my dad’s death. After that, I searched on Amazon to see if I could find a cheap push-button phone - the kind that I grew up with and often called my dad at work on. Of course I did find one (it’s Amazon, after all), and I sort of laughed at myself for even considering the idea of purchasing the phone. I went back and forth for a few weeks trying to decide if I wanted to complete the order. I think what held me back was the thought that buying a phone for one-way communication with the deceased seemed like something a sane, emotionally stable person would never do. Despite that thought, I did eventually make the order and the phone arrived two weeks later. But when it did, I decided that I would return it, again thinking that this was a silly method to deal with my grief. I left the phone in the box by the front door so that I could take it back to the post office when I got a chance. But I never did. Eventually the deadline to return it for refund passed, and I brought the box up to my ‘office’ which is a built-in desk in the upstairs playroom that overlooks a greenspace from a large window. I unpacked the phone and placed it on my desk. It sat there for a long time and got some great use by my 3-year old daughter as a play phone to call Santa and other characters. One day a few weeks ago, I took my two and a half year old son to get a speech assessment. We already knew he had a severe speech delay, but needed the official diagnosis to get access to the funding for preschools in the fall that would provide daily therapy for him. After the assessment, I was informed that the diagnosis would be ‘severe speech delay as well as severe receptive language delay’. This did not really surprise me. I expected the degree of the speech delay to be severe, and although I would have guessed the receptive language delay to be moderate rather than severe, I anticipated the overall diagnosis. Despite this, after dropping my son off back at the day home and returning home to where I mostly work from, I stood in the kitchen alone and began to cry. It wasn’t the first time I experienced tears over my son’s different developmental pace, yet I found myself again worried about my boy and his future. But my own reaction surprised me since I expected the very diagnosis that I had just recieved that morning. At that point, about one year had passed since first understanding there was a potential problem, and I was sure that I could handle this unexpected plan with grace and strength. I was sure that I was at peace with the possiblity that my son may be on a different developmental trajectory - but standing there in the middle of the kitchen that day, crying from his official diagnosis that I already knew about - perhaps I was not there yet. After a few minutes, I made myself a coffee and went upstairs to my office to continue working. I sat down at my computer but found it difficult to begin. I noticed the phone on the left side of my desk and stared at it.“Hmm. Maybe I will ‘call’ my dad,” I thought. My dad was a physician who spent 12-hour days at the hospital almost every day, so it made sense that his office number would be the one to call him at. But I couldn’t remember it. For some reason it didn’t feel right to dial another number, or no number at all, so I googled my dad’s name and former hospital location, and managed to find the office number. I dialed it, preceeded by the “1” plus area code just as you would for a real long distance phone call, and picked up the reciever. I couldn’t say anything for about a minute. I just sobbed. I finally found my voice and began a one-way conversation with my father. I told him how much I missed him. I told him about what I’m doing at work. I told him that I am writing lots again, starting a Toastmasters club and returned to coaching wrestling to little kids. And then I told him about my son. After I told him about my son and my fears for him, I found myself saying, “I know what you would say to me…” and then relaying the sound advice that I know my dad would have given me, about taking it one day at a time, trusting that I and my son are exactly where we are supposed to be, and that everything will be okay. After ending the conversation by thanking him and saying another “I love you and I miss you”, I hung up the phone and realized that I felt quite a bit better and calmer. It was an odd and interestingly comforting experience. I haven’t used the phone again since then, but I’m sure that I will at some point in the future. I also thought that someday, when my children are adults, I could tell them how this phone comforted me in my grief and that, if they wanted to, they could use this phone to contact me after I am gone.

column1: Is whatever written in Garuda purana true?
column3: One needs to continually be reminded that the Purānas are ENCYCLOPEDIAS. They contain everything from Atomic theory to Zoology so when asking a question about the verity of something one must be more specific about the subject. I assume you are asking about the Preta-kāṇḍa which deals with death and the afterlife. The answers is these are descriptive stories, narratives and legends which have an implication in defining cultural beliefs and asserting values, and which inform ideal practice and behaviour. According to the principles of exegesis (Mimāmsa) the primary function of Scripture is to give practical guidance in how to live a Dharmic life this is known as the VIDHI — and this is the most important part of Shastra. In order to support and encourage the desirable practice, the Shastra describes incentives and to discourage the negative acts they give disincentives. All the incentives and disincentives are called ARTHAVĀDAs. In other words they are metaphoric only and not to be taken literally. In the Preta-kāṇḍa it describes the journey of the deceased called PRETA or “hungry ghost” into the after-world and its exit interview with a panel of Judges Yama – the Lord of Death, Chitragupta – the celestial accountant and Varuna – the celestial Intelligence-gathering agent. The deceased person is asked to give an account, discussion ensues followed by judgment and then it is sent either to a heaven if its good deeds are excessive or to hell if its bad deeds are dominant and if neutral then one returns to earth to continue the spiritual journey. The underlying theme of all these stories is about DHARMA and ADHARMA. The only time when people’s minds are capable of full and attentive focus is when a close relative or beloved has died. So during the 10 days after death the Garuda Purana is read in order to emphasize the nature of Dharma and to re-orientate the minds of the listeners to true ethical and spiritual values and to reinforce their practice through the introduction of a post-death reward and punishment system. This is all ARTHAVĀDA - it is not to be taken literally! One needs to focus on the behaviour being eulogised and not the consequences of that behaviour. WHY are these stories told if they are not to be taken literally? Because there are different levels of attainment among the śrāvakas (listeners).uttama — the best and most intelligent with an academic and philosophical bent of mind – who instinctively know Dharma.madhyama – the middling who are bright, clever, intelligent, educated but not much inclined to abstract thought who get confused between Dharma and Adharma.kaniṣṭha – the “small” folk - those who are simple and non-academic, basic education, who belong to the masses and are not naturally inclined to Dharma and often mistake Adharma for Dharma and are generally following their natural instincts without the filter of Viveka (discrimination). They are prone to superstition and need encouragement and support.It is for these latter folks that the meaningful and metaphorical stories of the Puranas are told. When I conduct funeral ceremonies I quickly assess the caliber of the participants, their family and friends and then direct my explanations and teachings to suit their qualification as uttama, madhya or kaniṣṭha. The mere fact that the majority of readers of this post are on English Quora we would assume you all to be of the uttama or madhyama category and therefore can dismiss all these metaphorical narratives as ARTHAVĀDA. The practical outcome of the Preta-kāṇḍa is to prescribe rituals for the passage of death and process of grief. These rituals have a profound effect upon the participants from a psychological point of view. The are like a kind of Gestalt Therapy. Their function is to:–To help people to recognise the fact and the inevitability of death.To develop coping strategies to formally process their grief in the company of the close family and friends.To perform ritual i.e. stylized acts which they believe will contribute to the welfare of the deceased and thus free themselves from guilt pertaining to their possible neglect of the deceased person.To benefit the deceased who is believed to hover around for 10 to 40 days after death and to inform them of their altered state and to bid them farewell and to depart into the Great Beyond!(Whether they are actually benefited or not is speculative and not really important - the major positive effect of these rituals is on the family and their processing of grief.)

column1: What happens when we try to supress grief?
column3: My best answer is to share my own story. My parents died in a car accident nearly three years ago. I am a pastor, and we were approaching Easter. I felt that I needed to be strong and lead my church through the celebration of Easter before I could take time to mourn the loss. I did the normal rituals of the visitation and funeral, but then I went back to work. When people asked, I said I was okay. I stuffed those feelings for about three months. I kept thinking that avoiding the pain would make it somehow go away. It did NOT. Five months after the funeral, I approached a grief counselor. I could not focus in the office. Nothing seemed worth the monumental effort it took. Crying jags would hit me out of the blue. I was a mess. In therapy, I have learned that most of us are able to stuff our emotions, to bottle them up and put them away...for a while. I have also learned, that in those bottles the emotions remain, as potent as when they should have been experienced. And one day, inevitably, the bottle breaks. And those emotions, those thoughts, and all of the pain get loose. They will not be ignore any longer. When grief goes unacknowledged in its due season, it will come at you at an unexpected moment. And it will take longer to recover. Why does it take longer? This is just my theory, but I believe we were designed to experience grief within a supportive community. That community gathers around us in the immediate after death moment. That community support fades with time. If we wait until the community support has passed, we experience the grief alone. Another factor, is the guilt of unexperienced grief. We think "I should have..." We then have to face the guilt and maybe shame as well as the grief. Bottom line, when you experience a grief event, as much as it hurts to do so, allow yourself to feel it and live it as fully as you are able. Healing only comes as you have experienced your life experiences. May you find peace in your journey.

column1: What's your experience with Wellbutrin?
column3: I was prescribed Wellbutrin 14 years ago after my husbands death. I was vastly depressed and couldn’t pull myself out of it. I began grief therapy with a therapist who believed in combination group, individual and chemical therapy. Because I had to pick a doctor who was in my insurance plan, I had no personal referrals from anyone who knew her. Wellbutrin made me hyperactive! My house was never cleaner and clothing more organized then when I took Wellbutrin. I found myself scrubbing around sink faucets with an old toothbrush! I cleaned out my refrigerator and it looked like it was new. It’s an amazing drug, or it was for me, but it didn’t help one iota with depression. It did get me up out of bed, however it also caused me to lose weight I couldn’t afford to loose. My therapist decided I had an eating disorder (I weighed 119, down from 130 lbs and I’m almost 5’9”) and wanted me to go to impatient treatment. I could see the handwriting on the wall..talk therapy for an eating disorder I didn’t have, continued drug therapy and no real help, just more complications. After 5 months I slowly removed Wellbutrin from my pharmaceutical drugs, ceased the group therapy and stopped seeing the therapist. Nothing she’d done was really helpful. After I got back to normal - or as normal as I could be with depression that didn’t allow me to get out of bed, I went to another grief therapy workshop. It helped immensely and I went to this workshop every year for 10 years, until the workshop facilitator passed away. Wellbutrin isnt for everyone, my daughter has taken it for ADHD not depression. It is helpful for her. It doesn’t trigger weight loss in her.

column1: How do I allow myself to grieve and move on from the death of a loved one? It's been over 4 years.
column3: What does “allow myself to grieve” mean to you? To me it seems you have moved into a dark place and you are not allowing yourself to come back to live in the world to enjoy the happiness to which you are entitled, and to which your loved one would have wanted you to move into. When a loved one dies, they can stay in your heart forever, and there is a natural time to grieve. The Jewish faith has done what I feel is an excellent job of dealing with death and grief (I may be somewhat prejudiced since I am Jewish). The pre-burial period (which is as short as possible) is the time of highest grief, then the first seven days after burial are set aside for shivah - the period for extreme mourning. You are not to conduct any business, but you receive guests to comfort you, talk about your loved one, and grieve. You sit on hard chairs, you cover mirrors, you don’t answer phone calls, and you say prayers each evening (for those who are religious and observant). No music or dancing or amusements or attending festive events such as weddings, and you are not supposed to cut your hair or wear new clothing. Then there is a 30 day mourning period, when you may go back to work, but you are still not to enjoy entertainment, music, festive events. Mourning extends for a full year, after which the death is commemorated annually. Jewish tradition provides a framework to channel and express our grief over the loss of a loved one, one that over the centuries has proven to be valid and humane. The wisdom of adhering to the observances and timetables established has been attested to time and again by those who his process. These mourning laws provide the outlet and validation for grief so crucial to the healing process, as well as the framework to move on from one level of mourning to another, until our loss is integrated as a constructive, and not destructive, force in our lives. Why did the Jewish Bible, our Torah (the Christian Old Testament) need to make such strict rules and state them so specifically? Because you, dear heart, are not alone. Grief is individual. Everyone’s grief is different. Everyone’s heart is broken, of course, but some of us heal more easily than others. Four years is far too long for deep pain and grief and the inability to move on. You should seek help since you have been unable to do it yourself, either in group grief counseling or in individual therapy. May you have a short journey back to the other side, bubala!

column1: What is the kindest thing your therapist ever did for you?
column3: This year will mark five years of work with R. I’ve been in therapy for eleven years, in total, and almost half of them have been with her. It’s really hard to choose, but one interaction stands out to me at the moment. R and I have a shared experience of sudden traumatic death in our families - exploring the connection we both have to catastrophic loss has been a focus since August. She has shared a bit about losing her mom in a plane crash as I have opened up more about my grandparents, who recently died in a flash flood. R’s mom was deeply special to her as a child, and my grandpa was the closest person to me in my family. Grief can feel terribly lonely. I am so grateful that R has been willing to share some of the things she has experienced in her own grief with me. The Foundation puts together an ofrenda at the end of every October for Día de los Muertos. Clients and therapists can choose to bring in pictures of their deceased loved ones to be placed on the altar, along with candles and other items that represent them. This is entirely voluntary. I decided to participate this year. I printed two pictures of myself with my grandparents, and gave them to R for the ofrenda. She sent me a text the next day with a photo that showed where she’d placed the pictures. She had placed them right next to the picture of her mom. I cried into my latte at Starbucks as I realized what she had done. At the beginning of our next session, we stood in front of the ofrenda. I told R how much it meant to me that she would place my grandparents near her mom. Without hesitation she said, “It felt right. I wanted them with her.” Neither of us are religious, and I am only vaguely spiritual, but I understood what she meant and I was profoundly moved. I looked over at R, she smiled sadly at me, and I crumbled. She put her arm around me as we stood there together, and I cried. After a few minutes I had to wipe my eyes and make a joke. My window of tolerance for my grief around my grandparents is still pretty small. But I felt very loved in that moment. There have been so many kind moments with R, but as we approach the two-year anniversary of my grandparents’ deaths, this one stands out to me.

column1: If your loved ones have passed away, do you look forward to death in order to join them?
column3: Until November, 2015, I was very afraid of dying. After my son was murdered during a robbery in November, 2015, I look forward to the afterlife and seeing my son again. I am no longer afraid of dying. If I were to die, it would be a very sad and difficult time for my daughters, grandson, husband, extended family, and friends. My immediate family would require more grief therapy sessions. We have faithfully attended professional grief counseling over this past year, and another death in our family would keep them in therapy for even longer. I, however, would not be sad. Sadness is an emotion experienced by the living body. I believe that once our living bodies die, our life energy (soul) continues to exist on another plane, or in another dimension, which we humans cannot fathom, comprehend, nor prove. I believe my soul will join the souls of my son, mother, and all my other ancestors who have already died. So in answer to your question, yes, I look forward to death in order to join my son and other ancestors. However, I hope that I do not experience death until I am very old.

column1: How does it feel to be in therapy for a long time, and then not be able to see or contact your therapist again after they retire, because your therapist believes it is harmful?
column3: Jean, I can answer this from the therapist’s side since I’m about to retire and I have some very long-term patients. I let them know four month ahead so they’d have time to process their feelings of loss and to discover that they can continue on with their lives without me. I used the word “loss” deliberately because it’s analogous to grieving a death; in this case the death of the special relationship with the therapist, the person who knew your secrets and accepted you unconditionally. Loss and grief are parts of life and the termination process is an opportunity to experience grief fully and safely. Sometimes it’s the most important part of therapy, because it’s a lesson in how to grieve and come out whole. The goal of the therapist is to support the patient during this time and facilitate adjustment to a new reality. That may mean transitioning to a new therapist or accepting that a phase of life is over.
column9: I think that a long-time therapist’s retirement is bound to be worse than grieving a death. If someone dies, we can grieve and hopefully eventually learn to cope with the loss. If someone that we have cared about cuts us out of their life and we never see or hear from them again, there is no real closure. We don't have any way of knowing how they are or even whether they are alive or not. Just a once a year email or note exchange would be enough. I just don't understand how we, as patients, are supposed to stop caring about our therapists, no matter how many coping skills we've learned and how independent we've become. I think this applies to other people in our lives as well. For example, I haven't seen my mentally ill brother since 2008. I have no idea where he is or how he is doing or even if he is alive. There's a long story attached to his disappearance which I won't go into. Suffice it to say that part of me will always grieve the red-haired little boy that I grew up with. Living with the not-knowing is the hardest part of all.

column1: Did therapy actually help you?
column3: I have been in therapy several times. Sometimes it helped, sometimes it did basically nothing, sometimes it made things considerably worse. The first therapist I remember was, in hindsight, probably a counsellor, because she went by Mrs rather than Dr, though that could have been a deliberate choice. I saw her when I was 12–13. It was supposed to be my own therapy, but my mother insisted on coming to the first few sessions, and then wanted a few sessions with me, her and my at-the-time stepfather. The therapy was supposed to focus on why I didn’t want to go to school, why my relationship with my mother was failing, and why I didn’t get along particularly well with my stepfather. There is a reason why you hear it said, often particularly urgently: do not go to couples therapy with your abuser. Abusive partners - and abusive parents - will manipulate the therapist, and turn the therapist against you, unless the therapist is particularly skilled - and sometimes even then. Mrs Cullinan - that’s her name, because fuck her - was one of the worst things to happen to me in my childhood, and I honestly feel like she actually became more abusive than my mother was. My mother, at least, never intended to abuse me. She is an untreated Borderline, and as such is not capable of seeing a person as having a collection of positive and negative traits, or of maintaining positive feelings about someone while being angry at them. So when she was angry at me, she would vent to Mrs Cullinan about how lazy I was (didn’t want go to school), and how spoilt I was (always wanted mommy’s full attention), and how selfish I was (wouldn’t accept stepfather and stepsiblings). My mom didn’t mean any of this - or rather, she meant it for the hour or so that she was angry at me for - and was genuinely startled when Mrs Cullinan, for the entirety of our sessions, called me spoilt and selfish and lazy. Once my mom’s mood has shifted, she doesn’t remember any of the feelings she had - or even the things she said - when her mood was different, and, after initially disbelieving that Mrs Cullinan said these things to me, she was flabbergasted that a counsellor would have such an opinion of me. When my mom liked (loved?) me - which was most of the time - she thought I was an angel sent from heaven. (Literally. Religious/spiritual delusions have been a part of her life as long as I’ve known her.) She thought I was perfect and kind and loving and selfless. Because my mom forced her way into my therapy, and because Mrs Cullinan didn’t look at Mom’s history and mental health and decided to automatically believe her side of things, I wouldn’t talk to her. She never found out that I wanted more attention from my mom because after she met my stepdad, she stopped hugging me or touching me in any way, because my stepdad felt threatened and told her it made us look like lesbian lovers. She never found out that I didn’t accept my stepsiblings because one of them - in his late twenties or early thirties - was molesting me. And she didn’t find out that I didn’t want to go to school because I felt horribly ill all the time, because I had a severe, undiagnosed hepatitis A infection, which led to fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue. She was probably inexperienced, and probably wasn’t receiving the support and mentoring she needed. Still, fuck that bitch. On the other end of the spectrum, I had Dr Chris, the therapist who did a few hours a week pro bono at the youth centre where I was a youth worker and crisis worker for 13 years. He wasn’t exactly my therapist - we were colleagues - but I do consider myself to have been in therapy with him, as I went to him to talk things out whenever I had issues. He was, quite simply, one of the finest medical professionals I’ve ever known. He got me through a rape, an attempted murder, the loss of my budding surgical career, a stroke (possibly two), retrograde amnesia, and the deaths of my father, one stepfather, two partners and the miscarriage of my first and only child, with minimal emotional scarring. Yes, I have PTSD, but it is manageable, and I’ve remained functional throughout. I do not believe that would have been possible without a good (great!) therapist. Somewhere in the middle, Dr Morsley was a woman I saw once after I was raped, whom I was referred to by my GP. We were not able to find a rapport, and I chose not to see her again after the first session. I found her very book-bound - I did not fit the profile that her books told her I should, and she was unable to adapt to the me that was in front of her. During our hourlong session, she insisted that I must feel degraded by the rape, or that I must hate my rapist, or men in general, or sex. I told her that men were great, sex was grand and would remain grand, and that my rapist was incapable of empathy and other positive human emotions, and as such, I did not hate him because you don’t hate a shark for being a shark, or get angry when it bites you. We left our session with her believing that I was denying my true feelings because I always needed to control situations. I received a letter from her a week or so later, saying that she didn’t think I was ready for therapy, but when I was, I should give her a call. I disagreed about not being ready for therapy, continued to talk to Dr Chris at work, and never called Dr Morsley again. Two years later I got a discharge letter from her clinic, and that was the last I heard of her. She may have been a good match for some clients. Not for me. Sometimes therapists, or therapies, aren’t right for the client. Donna and Dionne were a pair of cognitive behavioural therapists who ran a group CBT class that I attended for six weeks, about seven years ago. They were excellent at their job, really knew their stuff, were able to form therapeutic relationships with everyone in a fairly large group and keep everyone feeling heard and validated - and despite all that, were of very little help to me personally, because CBT was absolutely the wrong therapy for me. I think that it’s a wonderful therapy for a lot of people - it’s something that many of the kids at the centre thrived in - but for me, it’s of limited use at best, and sometimes exacerbates my issues. By nature I’m a thinker (an overthinker?), an overanalyser, and almost all the CBT techniques that were taught - thought recording, cognitive reframing, identifying thought patterns, etc - were all things I’ve been doing naturally since childhood. I do think these are valuable things to learn - indeed, I think my natural tendency to do them is at least partly responsible for my emotional resilience and ability to stay more-or-less happy (for most of my life, anyway). I think many people would benefit from learning them. But the biggest thing I got from six weeks of CBT was a new appreciation for shoes. Dionne had amazing shoes. Whether therapy is helpful for an individual depends on so many factors. Is the patient ready and willing to do therapy? Is the therapist qualified to treat the patient’s particular issues? Is the therapist experienced? Is this the right kind of therapy for the patient’s issues? Do the patient and the therapist have any biases or prejudices that might not make them a good match? Does the therapist have a mentor who they can go to with any concerns or problems that come up, if the therapist isn’t sure what to do? Are there other issues in the patient’s life that will affect the therapy? My mother went to therapy several times in my own lifetime, and received only minimal benefits from it, because she never disclosed to her therapists that she was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder in her twenties. Her therapists thought they were treating her for grief and intimacy issues, and they didn’t have the necessary information to adjust her therapy, or refer her to someone specialised in personality disorders. My friend Zia, another person with BPD, has never received the benefits from therapy that she might have, because she has never been able to leave her abusive family, and is tied to them by a combination of love, trauma bonding and cultural expectations. If she had a therapist who was experienced in treating young Muslim women, who understood the context of her home life as a second-generation immigrant and the eldest daughter of a strict religious family, she might have found the help she so desperately needs. Therapy can be extremely helpful. It’s something that I generally recommend, despite my experiences with Mrs Cullinan and Dr Morsley. It’s horrendously underfunded in a lot of countries, and that makes people hesitant to go in the first place, or to change therapists when things aren’t working, but I do encourage people to do so if they’re not getting any benefits after a certain amount of time (usually several months). Therapists are people, and sometimes people have personality clashes, and other times people outright suck. Still, I encourage people to consider therapy if they feel it might be beneficial, to look for therapists who share their values (I specifically look for sex work-friendly and LGBTQ+ friendly therapists, for example), to stick with it for a decent period of time (unless they find their therapist outright harmful) - and to consider changing after that period of time is up if they feel like they’re not getting anywhere.

There is something beyond my book knowledge which I should accept and live rest of my life.. Though physically seems to be a single person.. Now we are a family of five in terms of love bond.. Me ( as a son) and my mom… Me ( as a mom) and my mom kid.. My mom's sister.. Her guest.. (Who came twice with my mom in vivid dream to pacify me) This is my family.. With complete bond.. I receive love from my mom.. I give love to my mom kid.. And we share the family happiness with our guest.. Its all happening through my household work.. Cooking.. Its my mom's role.. Never let us down even if the physical separation happens due to nature or any other odd situation.. Love is eternal.. My mom still teaches me through various means.. I express my love through various ways.. One thing we used to talk previously .. that am her only property and she is my only property in this world.. And that word saves me now whenever I feel low.. Previously I used to taste the food before I feed my mom kid in her last few years. So it's been easy for me to continue my motherhood. I take care of my health and fitness considering her presence. Since I got this motherhood experience with my mom, I can speak for a mother also. Your mom would never leave you.. She is closer to you than before.. Your bond with your mother is eternal and biological death cannot separate her from you.. “ Move on “ in life “ with her… “ Your mom's soul is with you… Live with her.. column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: Everyone deals with loss differently. Some people turn into blubbering messes, unable to leave the house without crying at every memory or interaction — an old man crossing the street with a cane can bring on hysterics, reminding you of your grandfather. Others hold it in; acting stoic, going to work, keeping busy. Some head down the path of self-destruction, using drugs, alcohol, and reckless behaviour to numb the pain. And some handle it entirely in regular therapy sessions, and maybe even a little medication. We’re all different. It’s never easy when someone dies. Never. Even when it’s a relief — when they've been lingering and suffering for a while, when their pain is so extreme that they just want to die, when there are mixed complicated feelings, it’s still SO. INCREDIBLY. HARD. In the very early stages of our grief, all we can think about is pain and sadness. We don’t even consider that there would be any lessons for us to learn as a result of losing someone. I have come to realize that there are things that we learn from our grief and that these lessons are part of our healing. I also know that if we choose to open our hearts to embrace these lessons, our life over time slowly but surely goes from a languishing life to a flourishing life. I would like to share 7 valuable life lessons with you to encourage you, to live your life to the fullest, to chase your dreams, to deal with the curveballs that life throws at you, to seize the moment and to treasure the gifts of life, love, and laughter. 1. Live Your Life to the Fullest As It Can Change In A Blink Of An Eye ‘Enjoy the little things in life, for one day you may look back and realize they were the big things.’ Embrace life, take the time to make memories and cherish the moments you spend with the people you love. Get your priorities sorted and know what is important to you. 2. Family and Friends - Your Precious Gifts in Life ‘Stick to the basics, hold on to your family and friends - they will never go out of fashion.’ All material things that you gather, your fortune and your power are easy to get and easy to lose. The people in your life who love and support you, once you lose them you can’t get them back. 3. Healing Is A Process – Don’t rush it. ‘If you desire to heal, let yourself fall ill let yourself fall ill.’ Grief doesn’t magically end after a set period of time. There will always be reminders in your life where your feelings of loss and grief will return. Over time, however, you will find that your pain turns to a dull ache, then to sad memories where you cry, and then, after awhile, you will have memories where you smile briefly. There is no right or wrong way to feel when grieving. Don’t fight it. Be kind to yourself and believe in yourself, your strength and your courage – the essential ingredients for your healing. 4. Use Your Power Of Choice - Choose to be hopeful. ‘There are two primary choices in life; to accept conditions as they exist, or accept the responsibility for changing them.’ We cannot control the bad things that happen in our life, however, we can control our reactions to these challenging events through our Power of Choice. Hope for a better future and then with hope optimism will come and then the positive attitude to life. 5. Find Your Purpose In Life ‘The mystery of human existence lies not in just staying alive, but in finding something to live for.’ Finding your purpose in life gives your life meaning. Knowing your purpose in life gives you clarity, focus, and hope for your future. Don’t be overwhelmed by the journey to find your purpose in life – it is a big journey. Make a plan and take action – don’t give up. Set realistic and achievable goals and take one step at a time. Celebrate your successes - each time you achieve your goal no matter how small or how big, celebrate it and share your successes with those you love. Happiness comes when you know what you are doing, believe in what you are doing and love what you are doing. The pursuit of your happiness is all about you living a meaningful life and when you find your purpose in life, you increase your happiness in life by 200 percent. 6. Don’t Let Your Past Rule Your Life Now And In The Future. ‘Renew, release, let go. Yesterday’s gone. There’s nothing you can do to bring it back. You can’t ‘should’ve’ done something. You can only DO something. Renew yourself. Release that attachment. Today is a new day!’ Your past is your opportunity to learn the lessons you need in order to deal with your present life. Let go of your regrets in life, make peace with your past, accept it and move on. Don’t waste your energy on what is not important. Focus on what you have, not what you don’t have. You are not what happened in your past, you are whom you choose to be now and in your future. 7. Don’t Run Away From Life – stay strong and embrace its unpredictability. ‘Running away from your problems is a race you’ll never win.’ When you run away the only place you can go is nowhere! The pain, the discomfort and the challenges of life will follow you where ever you go. It is ok to fall apart for a little while but only for a little while. Spend time with yourself, developing your strength and your resilience. Get prepared for life and be adaptable and flexible. Remember that everything that happens to you is a life lesson – embrace life and never forget how precious the moments in life are. ‘The most beautiful people we have known are those who have known defeat, known suffering, known struggle, known loss, and found their way out of the depths. These people have an appreciation, a sensitivity and an understanding of life that fills them with compassion, gentleness, and a loving concern. Beautiful people do not just happen.’ Don’t grieve. Anything you lose comes round in another form -Rumi Take Care! Peace :)

column1: Do you think Prince Charles planned the killing of Princess Diana, why?
column3: No, of course not. It makes absolutely no sense.She was the mother of his children. Say about Charles what you like, but he loves his sons and would never have deprived them of their mother.Diana was already more popular at the time, thanks to her flawless PR strategy, but her untimely death has frozen her in a state of youth, beauty and perfection. Let‘s be honest, that’s probably not what anyone would necessarily want for an ex-Partner.Charles got heaped plenty of blame on him for her death, including this ridiculous conspiracy. Other people were more pragmatic and simply pointed out that without the divorce it wouldn’t have happened.Diana‘s death left Charles to deal with a lot. He was suddenly a single parent who had to support his children in their grief, deal with a hysterical nation who wanted to share in their grief, and get through his own sadness. Diana had been his wife after all. It also seriously endangered his new relationship, which was now even more „impossible“ than it had been already. It has come to light since that after Diana‘s death, Charles went into therapy for 12 years to cope with everything that had happened.A car accident is not a very reliable way to kill someone. Diana‘s bodyguard survived. It could just as well have been her.Her driver caused the accident and died in the crash. Suicide killers for hire are a exceedingly rare for some reason…Two countries have investigated the whole accident. One came to the conclusion that it was entirely the intoxicated driver‘s fault, the other that it was the driver‘s fault, but the chasing Paparazzi have some share in the blame. Neither found any hints of foul play.It’s been 24 years. Can we please let the poor woman rest in peace and the living get on with their lives?
column9: Thank you for your clear-headed answer to this question. Conspiracy theories surrounding Diana's death have been around since the accident. Diana was a much admired addition to the RF. column1: What does it mean to be the adult child of an alcoholic? Will things never be normal?
column3: Hi, I'm Kelly, and I am the adult child of an alcoholic and a cocaine addict. I asked myself "What is normal?" through most of my childhood and early adulthood, even as I longed for some semblance of normalcy. Most children of alcoholics/addicts are chameleons. We learn to blend in and appear normal even though we aren't quite sure what that feels like. We develop all sorts of coping mechanisms that help us deal with our chaotic and often unsafe environments and our quixotic and often abusive parents. The problem is, once we get out into the Real World, those coping mechanisms are maladaptive and dysfunctional. I left home when I was 16 in an attempt to wrest control of my life from my parents and my role as their enabler, but certain patterns were set in me that sabotaged me for years. I was very controlling, I needed to be in control of everything and everyone around me. When I felt like things were beyond my control, I experienced anxiety and cold rage. I chose broken people as friends and lovers and tried to fix them, blind to the fact that I was acting out my role as enabler and trying to fix them as I had tried and failed to fix my family. I was a perfectionist and an over-achiever. I set unrealistically high expectations for myself and found fault in my achievements. I was never good enough, and I was so vicious in my self-criticism that I someone managed to turn success into failure numerous times. Does any of this sound familiar? I eventually realized that the coping mechanisms I'd developed in childhood were not working for me and started an extensive reading into the psychology and behavior of survivors of childhood adversity. I studied the tools and techniques of both cognitive and dialectical behavior therapies. I learned to reprogram my thinking and behavior, learned how to be mindful of my emotional states and what provoked/triggered inappropriate behaviors. I eventually went into therapy for grief counseling after 4 deaths in 18 months, and with the help of my therapist, pulled everything together and really started living my own life on my own terms, with gusto. The importing things I've learned that I want to pass on to you: 1-Once you are an adult, you own your life--stop blaming your parents for the choices you make and the feelings you have. The sooner you own your life--your choices, your thoughts and feelings--the sooner you can make progress toward loving your life. 2-There is nothing wrong with you. You need to practice radical self-acceptance. Accept yourself as you are and are not. Embrace your inner child, comfort it, and tell it that you're an adult, you've got this, and the tantrums and acting out have got to stop because s/he is sabotaging both of you. 3-Listen to and modify your inner dialogue. You are going to have to re-write your personal narrative, the stories you tell yourself that are negative and self-defeating, and look at how they are untrue. That negative little voice in your head is not your friend. It's an aspect of your personality that is afraid and angry. Ignore its babble. 4-Be the person you want to be. You don't have to be that person perfectly on the first try. But keep trying. Do your best to be the person you want to be--not the person you think you should be, but the person you _want_ to be. Put those fabulous chameleonic skills to work and fake it until you make it--until the negative voice in your head doesn't have anything bad to say about who you are. 5-It is ok to be afraid. It is ok to make mistakes. Fear lets us know we are alive. Mistakes help us grow. What is not ok is letting your fears, your anxieties and patterns from past experiences, keep you from doing what you want to do and being who you want to be. 6-It is ok to ask for help. You are worthy. You are worthy of help. Really. It is ok to say "I don't know how I'm supposed to feel about or react to adult life, my childhood was too dysfunctional. Can you help me?" Go find a therapist. Find an ACOA support group. Join online forums and support groups. You're not alone. 7-You get to decide if your parents are toxic to you or not. You get to decide if you want to have anything to do with them. You get to decide if you want to forgive them or not. It's best if you can let go of as much of the anger and upset and forgive them -- not for them, but for yourself. Holding on to the anger and pain just punishes you--not them. You feel how you feel and whatever you feel is absolutely appropriate. It is important to validate your emotions rather than push them aside, because they will come out one way or another, often out of proportion to whatever it is that provoked it. Good luck. You'll always wonder what Normal is. And that's ok.
column9: For #7, May I ask how much you’ve forgiven your parents and is it to the extent of being able to have a fully functional relationship with them currently? column1: When a spouse dies, what is the appropriate mourning time before dating?
column3: “When a loved one dies, they can stay in your heart forever, and there is a natural time to grieve. The Jewish faith has done what I feel is an excellent job of dealing with death and grief (I may be somewhat prejudiced since I am Jewish). The pre-burial period (which is as short as possible) is the time of highest grief, then the first seven days after burial are set aside for shivah - the period for extreme mourning. You are not to conduct any business, but you receive guests to comfort you, talk about your loved one, and grieve. You sit on hard chairs, you cover mirrors, you don’t answer phone calls, and you say prayers each evening (for those who are religious and observant). No music or dancing or amusements or attending festive events such as weddings, and you are not supposed to cut your hair or wear new clothing. Then there is a 30 day mourning period, when you may go back to work, but you are still not to enjoy entertainment, music, festive events. Mourning extends for a full year, after which the death is commemorated annually. Jewish tradition provides a framework to channel and express our grief over the loss of a loved one, one that over the centuries has proven to be valid and humane. The wisdom of adhering to the observances and timetables established has been attested to time and again by those who have lived by this process over the centuries. These mourning laws provide the outlet and validation for grief so crucial to the healing process, as well as the framework to move on from one level of mourning to another, until our loss is integrated as a constructive, and not destructive, force in our lives. Why did the Jewish Bible, our Torah (the Christian Old Testament) need to make such strict rules and state them so specifically? Because you, dear heart, are not alone. Grief is individual. Everyone’s grief is different. Everyone’s heart is broken, of course, but some of us heal more easily than others. Four years is far too long for deep pain and grief and the inability to move on. You should seek help since you have been unable to do it yourself, either in group grief counseling or in individual therapy. May you have a short journey back to the other side, bubala!” That being said, there is no “appropriate mourning time.” Everyone is different. Every relationship is different. The length of time people are married and the depth and breadth of their emotions, life together, the amount of time they were married, how they felt about each other, all factors make up the amount of time one mourns a beloved. Many never stop mourning and many never date again. That was a prior Content reply of mine.

column1: What’s the first thing a therapist does when they realize their client is a narcissist?
column3: I can speak of my own experience. Two years ago, I requested that my then-husband and I attend marital therapy. After years and years of covert, hidden abuse, I thought I was losing my mind. I had reached a point where my fragile sanity was questionning whether I was making the abuse up. This is what happened when we entered therapy for the first time.I sit down on the sofa first, my husband sits in the seat opposite before standing up to remove his jacket and stare idly around the room looking I know, for somewhere to hang his precious, expensive clothing. I note our therapist clocking this. He takes my husband’s jacket and hangs it on the back of his door. My husband has shown his hand. I wonder to myself if the therapist has noticed the first clue of my husband’s character — his unmistakable self-importance. As the three of us have never met before, I am sure this unknown expert in human-psychology will be absorbing every cue belonging to us both; both verbal and non-verbal. I am stiff as a board — my body is tightly wound up; muscles taught: unconscious expression of my hyper-vigilance — the fear that threat is imminent. Heartbreak, grief, anxiety and trepidation are scrunched up like a ball of old muddied paper. My mind and my soul are heavy with anguish. When our therapist asks us what has brought us here today, my husband — whom I once believed was the love of my life — answers coldly — “Well I think Amelie should tell us as I don’t even know myself.” A disinterested scoff leaves his possession. He has shown his hand again. How he — the smart and cunning one — doesn’t realise is beyond me. Despite the depth of heartbreak moving my soul, I still see him for all that he is — deeply self-loathing, and fervently motivated to prove that the opposite is the case to a human being that he has never met before. This drive being more important to him than loyalty to his own wife. I wonder to myself: doesn’t it occur to you that our therapist can see straight through you? Perversely, I feel for him. And I am reminded why we are still together; because I have forgiven a thousand sins in the name of empathy and understanding. I have chosen him above myself from the day we united.I open my mouth to speak and struggle to find voice. Heaving arrests my form; you can hear it in my vocal chords — the hoarseness coming from difficulty breathing, deep in my diaphragm. I tell the room in between erratic tears, that have I loved my husband more than life itself — that we have been together for 11 years, but we are broken. I tell the air-space in front of me, that my husband is aggressive and passive-aggressive, that I can’t discern what is real anymore and I don’t remember what is normal from what is not. And I say that I no longer feel safe in our union, that my spirit has been under attack for as long as I can remember. I break down. I literally, cannot cope. For all the seriousness of my words, they are underscored by a fear that our therapist will view me as the perpetrator and my husband as the victim — cognitive dissonance running amok and wreaking havoc in my broken mind. Do I speak of the abuse? No, I won’t be believed. None of it is believable. Our therapist spends time listening to my husband’s response, which I don’t recall. I just remember that he was complimenting him — on his intelligence, his powerful presence and his charm. My husband was confused, I was not. I knew what this man was doing — road testing his instinct that my husband may have NPD. I knew my husband agreed with our therapist’s compliments, a wry smirk betraying his haughty arrogance — relishing these affirmations of his distorted beliefs of self. But he so dislikes being swindled, or rather — having somebody one step ahead of him, so I see the cogs of his mind whirring fast — trying to verify the authenticity of our therapist’s comments.I don’t remember exactly, but I think around 40 minutes in, our therapist suggests that taking a personality profile test may be useful — he frames it well — “it may help for you to understand each other better.” We both agree to take the test. I know what’s coming. My husband and I spend the next week apart, and seven days later we return to our therapist’s little room, our eyes not meeting once as they have done day after day for eleven years. I feel like something or someone has died and he’s announcing the death to us much like a surgeon does to grieving loved ones in the waiting room, when he has failed to save the life of their beloved. Our therapist explains he will hand us our spouses reports before swapping to read our own reports, to then discuss whether each one is commensurate with our own perceptions, of each other, and of ourselves. We acknowledge the instructions silently and take the reports he hands to us. I read the first paragraph in milliseconds before collapsing into uncontrollable grief. I can’t cope with what I am reading. My brain hurts. I feel as though some sort of internal splitting is occurring. This is an internal, emotional pain like I have never known before. The assessment of my husband confirms that he has Narcissistic Personality Disorder. In this micro-instant, I think my heart is shattering. A million thoughts and fears race through my mind. I am heartbroken for my husband; the little I know about this disorder tells me that NPD is borne out of suffering and neglect in childhood. What fate befell him as a child? I am heartbroken for myself too — as I thought it was me that was the source of all our problems; years of covert gas-lighting have totally eroded my sense of reality and my sense of self, I have come to believe that everything my husband had said over the years is true —that in his words — I am “the damager of everything”. The bittersweet pain of relief is literally overwhelming. I finish reading the three pages of his report, whilst he is still reading the first of mine.Over the course of the following weeks, I watch as our therapist so carefully ‘handles’ my husband’s personality disorder. He is clear, firm, and plays along to all my husband’s character flaws; his need to be seen as all-powerful, supremely intelligent and superior, and his need to be seen as the victim. Our therapist plays into his hands. And this is for one reason and one reason only - that were he not to, he would lose this client - my husband would have abandoned the process of therapy if our therapist had tackled him and his personality issues head on. Instead I watched in admiration and awe, of how skillfully he brought out unconscious drives and behaviours in my husband. Clinical psychologists in particular, are trained at length to prompt self-reflection to lead one to make better decisions to better their lives. I haven’t in all my years known a therapist to instruct their client to divorce their spouse. After 5 one to one sessions between him and I, that is exactly what he did. A few weeks later I asked my husband for a divorce in the very office where I discovered the label that classified his personality which gave explanation for the sadistic abuse I experienced at his hands for 11 years. It was our marital therapist that urged me with firmness, that informing my husband of my intentions to sever our union should be done in this place of safety — this man who had freed me from the shackles of my marriage was himself concerned for my safety in the moments that I tell my husband I am divorcing him. My ex husband never returned to therapy after that moment - entirely normal for someone suffering from NPD. Why would they need therapy, when they are perfect after all?
column9: My heart went out to you as I read your answer. It is just terrible that one person can do so much damage to another. I remember when my ex was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder. We had been together for several years and were talking about marriage, in spite of the troubles we had in our relationship. He was adamant … he wanted to marry me. So I insisted on getting counseling first. We went together for our first appt, and as usual, my ex turned on the charm. Our therapist was a beautiful young lady, and my ex all but drooled on her. Next step was a session with my ex and the therapist. A week later, it was my turn to meet with the therapist alone. She told me that she couldn’t legally tell me anything that went on during the visit with him, but she said she had something she wanted me to read. She handed me a large book, opened and with a sticky note arrow pointing to the part she wanted me to read. Then she left the room and I read. I remember getting dizzy as I read, seeing my ex in every statement. He was all the things listed, and the page was all about Borderline Personality Disorder. I had never heard of it, and the diagnosis was almost more than I could bear. Later, my ex assured me that there was just a personality conflict between him and the therapist, and I fell for his excuses. We did marry. He did hit me, and mistreat me in so many ways. Three months in, I couldn’t take any more, and because of some issues with the rental contract, which I had never added him to, I was able to have him removed from my home. A while later, I received a petition for divorce, which I happily signed, and also got my maiden name back in the process. I had to be slapped in the face with the truth before I would believe he could possibly be such an evil person. I’ve never run across anyone else like this ex, thank God.

column1: How does a BPD person deal with grief from a death in the family, particularly a second mother figure?

I felt orphaned, alone abandoned here on earth to fend for myself. I fell right into dangerous grounds, the wrong people, drank excessively, I were a complete mess. Like a child left out in the cold. column1: Have you been to a counsellor and felt even worse after seeing them?
column3: Many years ago, I had a series of crippling, personal losses. I wasn't coping or healing, so I went for grief counseling. I'd had no experience, whatsoever, with any kind of therapy, so I didn't know what to expect. First, instead of giving me the help I needed, this man made me commit to twice-weekly, unending group-therapy sessions. Then, he proceeded to belittle, demean, and bully me nonstop. So many people in my life, who hadn't witnessed how I was being treated, told me that I had to trust and believe in the process. So, I stayed for a few months, spending too much money and feeling progressively worse. I finally got fed up and left after he'd repeatedly accused me of having been sexually abused by my father (absurdly untrue, and my father's recent death was one of the sources of my grief). I was a liar, you see, for not telling the truth about how I'd been molested throughout my childhood. Flash forward, and this guy is now a convicted and registered sex offender with a revoked medical license. He was the true child molester during those sessions, and he was projecting his own, sick proclivities onto me. He was also using me for his own therapy, rather than the reverse.

column1: Most people are aware of the fact that many therapists have been in therapy for themselves at some point. If you are a therapist and are not in therapy at this time, what would need to happen for you to go back to therapy? What value could it bring?
column3: I have a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder. I am also a therapist. I went to several therapists after the death of my 13 year old child. I had no concept what it meant to lose a child and my mental health was fragile and I needed help. I went from grief therapist to grief therapist and I was shocked that they were completely clueless how to deal with the severity of my grief. There is only so much a university degree can do if it is not working in conjunction with real life experience. There are just some things you cannot learn from a text book. If you have not experienced something no amount of empathy and compassion is going to help you help me. I went to a therapist and ended up counseling her in regards to her marriage, another therapist compared my loss to the death of her cat, and the last therapist I saw told me that my son went home to the place he originally came from. I found a support group of volunteers who have lost a child. No religious agenda, no charge for anything, and by sharing our stories we have healed as much as one can after losing a precious child. They saved my life because my pain was their pain and their pain became my pain and we could understand each other and no topic was off limits and there was no judgement. After speaking for 30 seconds heads were nodding because they understood because we all had the same experience. I have had tremendous loss and I am only stating this because I know no one else like me. Not even in my support group where people have lost two children. My losses are horrific and they have also given my life great purpose. Grief is my teacher. I have lost five children. My daughter at 8 months gestation. my son 13 by accident, my daughter 25 years from brain cancer, my son 29 years and two weeks to the day of my daughter's death by suicide, and my step daughter who has a beautiful bio mom at the age of 40 from cervical cancer. I also have a major mental illness and I am only on this earth because I found healing from those who have lost children and have suffered and heal along with me. There is no circumstances that would send me to therapy. I know all of the scientific terms, I have done the research and have earned my education however, nothing compares to experience and the insatiable need to continue to learn from those that are wiser and who have humbled me by opening up their hearts and their minds to me. My space on this forum is Child Loss which I just started. If you have lost a child I hope you will visit me there xo

column1: Did your life improve in any way whatsoever after you stopped taking antidepressants?
column3: My depression almost 16 years ago was situational- caused by my beloved husbands death. I took antidepressants for about 10 months. I also went to grief therapy one on one for the first 24 weeks and group therapy, which I continued to go to for 5 years. I got to a point where I was ready to deal with my loss without drugs. I decided depression was a natural consequence of my loss. I titrated off the antidepressant over a few weeks. I actually felt better, more alive and energetic off the Amitriptyline than on it. Of course the therapy helped a great deal. I still have periods of depression around his birthday and our wedding day but I accept the emotion and allow myself to process it. So yes, my life improved. I dealt with the cause of my depression through therapy and continued using the tools I learned when depression pops up again. I felt physically better after coming off Amitriptyline as well.
