column1: What incident shook you and made you cut back on your social life?
column3: My father’s death. I had a love/hate relationship with my father. While he was a skilled craftsman and the most honest man I ever met, and had the kind of steel self-discipline I can never hope to achieve, he was also spiteful, mean-spirited, negative and something of a beater. I got beat a lot as a child. A lot. It broke my spirit. When my father finally died after smoking 2 packs of Camels a day since he was 13, I felt nothing. At least I felt nothing at the time. However, in the time after his death, I started to ramp up my social activities to insane levels. I joined every possible organization so I could meet women and never spend a moment alone. I was meeting women everywhere I went: at the grocery store, on bike rides, through friends, at parties, everywhere imaginable. I was dating different women 2 - 3 times a week, every week. Sometimes I would have two dates on Sundays. I never took the time to learn anything about these women. I met them and moved on to the next one. I didn’t sleep with all or even many of them but I just kept moving. I did this at breakneck speed for 18 months. Then one day I was getting dressed for work as I did every day. I reached into the sock drawer and pulled out a pair of brand-new socks still in their wrapper. I had gotten them in a bunch from my dad’s sock drawer after he died. He didn’t need them anymore. And without thinking, I stripped off the wrapper and pulled them on. And before I could pull on the second one, I broke down in tears. It took 18 months but I finally succumbed to unresolved grief about my conflicting emotions with my father. I took off work that day and called a counselor and went through grief therapy. For the first time ever, in my life, I was able to tell someone my story, how I thought, how I felt, what I experienced, my conflicting love and hate for my father, a man who sacrificed everything he ever wanted to put food on the table every day and clothes on my body and who beat me with his fists and with 2x4s for the most minor of infractions. It’s extremely hard to balance out the contradictions within a mind, to square that my father was a good man who tried to do the best with what he had for his family while suffering his own dragons and observations about the world around him, seeing others do better, seeing his body fall apart and still needing to work every day, suffering long-term PTSD from WW2 where he woke up every night with screaming nightmares from combat. He never complained. He never explained. He just got up and did what he had to do. And along the way he punished us when we got out of line - his line. He judged us as harshly as he judged himself and when he found us wanting, the weapons came out and we suffered. As a result of the therapy, I stopped dating completely. I pulled back from almost every social engagement and only continued to run and bike with those groups. When you’re biking, even with a group, you spend a lot of silent time in contemplation and enjoying the fresh air and scenery. It was good for me. I finally met a decent woman and we went out for a while, about 18 months. By then, I had come to the realization that my dad wasn’t perfect and neither was I, and nor would I ever be. He didn’t have children and then decide to screw them up. He wanted what was best for us, and he was terrified of not being able to provide. Terrified. He didn’t care what others thought but he judged himself. From the outside, he looked like a stalwart of the community, a towering giant of honesty and integrity. And he was. He never suffered from petty jealousy or avarice. He just kept his eye on the weekly paycheck and did what he had to do. And took his hidden, unacknowledged frustrations out on us. It was hard to rectify that. My dad has been dead for almost 40 years now. I am an old man. What I am, he largely formed, for better or worse. But his death changed something in me and I became manic and unfocused for a long time. It took therapy and understanding to figure it all out and I am still trying. For better or worse, he was what he was, and I am what I am. I’ll never be young again. I’ll never be that confident bon vivant who could strike up a convo with a strange woman in a grocery store then go out on a date. All that is gone, maybe for the better. But for awhile, I changed my entire life and who I was.

column1: Should drugs be prescribed for grief?
column3: When my younger brother killed himself in his early 40’s without prior warning or even hints of problems, I visited my family doctor. I asked for two things: Drugs to help me sleep and a referral to a good therapist to help me find a solid base again. Grief , especially complicated or untimely death, can be a long and exhausting process. If grief pushes someone to become profoundly depressed and lacking forward progress, drugs may be part of the best solution. When grieving we tend to huddle with the wounded and lose touch with those around us living a normal life. We can get stuck. Good and well meaning friends can and often do burn out trying to help, and they are not professionals. If your grief feels like it’s moving and you’re returning to normal life functions a little more each day you’re probably fine. If you’re not sleeping, or you’re tense and angry, perhaps drugs and/or therapy would help. Five years after my brother’s suicide, we lost our then 20 year old son to a firefighter training accident. With the tools and knowledge I had acquired in therapy after my brother’s suicide, I felt no immediate need for therapy or drugs. Now 13 years later, and functioning well, I’m seeing my old therapist to help me finish the journey to acceptance. There is no timeline or standard path through grief, each case is different. Healing isn’t always the obvious choice, but to heal you must choose to work at healing.

column1: How did you change yourself after meeting a tragic death of a family member?
column3: My dad died in 1992. He died of emphysema from smoking 2 packs of camels every day since he was 13. It was tragic. The end of his life was a horrible for him and he died alone in the hospital before we could get there. I was very ambivalent about him since he beat me a lot when I was a child but I realized after lots of therapy that I did love him and I cried months later when the grief struck me. After that I decided to tell people I loved them (if I did), especially family members. Because you never know the day they are going to die and it will be too late to say anything, to ask anything, to tell them anything. So now, I say I love you to my family after every phone call, even my brother, who then tells me I am gay. (I am not). Don’t delay. Tell someone you love them right now because it might be your last chance.
column9: Wise words Jay. Sorry about the loss of your father. My little brother was living in Sydney and I in Auckland. He phoned me from a phone booth in Kings Cross. We’re not a demonstrative family. So it seemed strange when my intuition kept nudging me to tell him I loved him. I did and he went —-er um Jen love you too. These were the last words we spoke to each other. He passed away 6 weeks later aged 24. So you never know,

column1: How do therapists deal with patients who don't trust them enough to open up, but still want to keep seeing them?
column3: I suppose they keep on seeing them, and still keep on moving towards a relationship of trust. The Psychologist I saw for grief therapy after my son died never gave up on me, and he was worth the 200 bucks per hour I paid him. He made it very clear from the get-go that therapy can become very uncomfortable, but it is that discomfort that leads us right out of stagnancy, no matter what we seek therapy for. Eventually, my youngest daughter attended these sessions with me, as she was just as lost and traumatized as I was by the death of her brother, but she now speaks with a different therapist weekly, and I no longer attend therapy sessions. This Psychologist she speaks with is a woman, hand-picked by Abby, Ms. Cherice she calls her, and it isn’t just about the loss of her brother. My kids have been traumatized to no end, just like me. I told my daughter that she would have to have the sessions become bi-monthly due to cost. I carry my kids on my insurance, they are now 21 and 22 years of age, but we have a high-deductible plan with an HSA, and my need to see my cancer doctors is also a high expense. I am happy to report that I remain cancer-free five years out, and that my brilliant daughter is blossoming. I do not exaggerate in calling her brilliant, but she is also fragile, still trying to overcome all the trauma of her childhood, and learning to trust people. Why do I mention all of this, quite off topic? Because Cherice still counsels my daughter every week, for an hour, and she does it at no cost. I did not know this until last month, when I asked my daughter why the monthly statements regarding their sessions stopped coming to my email. It was then that my daughter told me that Dr. Cherice was counseling her for free. Why? Because she cares about my daughter, for real. Abby is not just an income source, she is a real human being who has bonded with Cherice in a very positive way, and Cherice has chosen to keep on counseling Abby for free, because she sees the beautiful person that my Abby is, and she understands the financial situation of our household. Kudos going out to all the real counselors out there who won’t give up on the people who are really in need. God bless you, Dr. Cherice. ♥

column1: Does complex post traumatic stress syndrome require treatment by a specialist in that area, or can a general therapist help? It seems impossible to find a specialist in that area.
column3: I have a diagnosis of major depressive disorder. I am also a therapist. I suffered from C-PTSD for a year after my 13 year old son died accidentally. I was in severe mental and emotional pain and I had not lost a child before so I thought I was suffering from grief. After a few months of flashbacks 24/7 of the death scene and dropping down to 87 pounds and not sleeping because my ribs dug into the mattress and sleep involved nightmares.worse than the flashbacks that left me sleep deprived and severely dehydrated I was very ill. I started to figure out in my brain fog induced brain that something besides grieving was simultaneously making life unbearable. I went to countless therapists and psychiatrists and not one of them picked up on the C-PTSD. I was tired of searching for help. Someone recommended a psychiatrist and I thought it was worth one last try. She is brilliant, compassionate, and as a young child she came upon a death scene and lived with C-PTSD for years before she was diagnosed. She prescribed medication that allowed me to sleep and eat and that was a game changer. The death of my son and the brilliance of my psychiatrist put me on the path to become a therapist. Once I could eat and sleep I had the energy to deal with the flashbacks. As you know they are horrific and you need a quiet and peaceful environment to heal from them. I had the flashbacks for just over a year 24/7. Every day and every night I relived the horror. One day I had the flashbacks and there was no pain and no reaction. It was like watching a movie that I had seen a million times and I knew every single thing that was going to happen. I kept having the flashbacks without pain for about a month and I never had a C-PTSD symptom again. I was so grateful and called my psychiatrist and she told me that she also healed the same way I did. I am telling you this because I want you to know that you will heal too. There is nothing wrong with asking a therapist if they are successful in treating C-PTSD and what their experience with C-PTSD clients has been. When you get the answers that satisfy you that is your therapist Experience is the key to healing. Let me know how your therapy and healing is going.
column9: That’s heart touching. Hope you are feeling better now?

column1: How did you cope with extreme grief after your spouse passed, besides "support" groups, counseling, and religion?
column3: I have not lost my spouse yet, and God forbid the day, but I have lost my son. I also lost my brother, and my mother. I like how you singled it out, as extreme grief. Its nothing less. It really breaks your spirit, and your drive. I am a college grad, in behavioral science, but I am a painter instead. I am a painter, because I don't want to deal with certain situations, so we have our own business. I can't do it some days. Its not because I haven't accepted my sons death. Its been 5 years, I am just so sad sometimes. I just have anxiety so bad. Also anger!! I subcontract work from a government funded company. You know the equal housing opportunity. I work so hard. Just to pay dumb crap that no one else pays, like insurance, and my phone plan. Just so I can work again, but I am not feeling it. I wish there was therapy for a broken brain. I don't want to forget, I just want to be happy. I want some gumption. I deal one second at a time. Truth is I can't help you. I can only relate. I can tell you, although our circumstances are different, the extreme effects are the same. Grief is a destroyer. We thank heavens that we got past the first year, but really it takes a long time to fully absorb the situation. Slowly we kinda just stop being anything, but aggrivated. You do find out who your friends are. You start seeing things way differently. You see things for what they really are, and sometimes you just gotta walk away. I have seen people lose spouses, and make some really bad decisions. I can say you should face the process of grief, before you make any rash decisions. People will take advantage of your empathy. Don't let people do that to you. You have been through enough. I wish there were some magic words, but there's nothing. I am so sorry for your loss. I cannot imagine losing my husband. I know how hard it is to do simplistic tasks, its debilitating. It makes you so angry at yourself, because you just can't function properly. I hope, I really do that, that things get better. I hope you have at least one person that understands. Good luck, and even though you don't want to hear it… God bless
column9: thank you Amanda for your heartfelt response. it really moved me, your empathy. my wife was everything wonderful in my life; after 40 years together she is irreplaceable. everyday is like moving a mountain, the simplest tasks like eating are incredibly hard (I’ve lost 15 lbs - nothing tastes good anymore)…well, I won’t go on as you well know how it is. again, thank you and I am so sorry for your loss, losing a child must be the worst.

column1: Is somatic experiencing an effective form of therapy? My therapist says I should trust her because it worked for her, but there is no placebo-controlled empirical evidence. If one doesn’t believe in it, will it be a waste of time and money?
column3: I started participating in somatic experiencing in the last six (6) months. Although I’ve spent many years working with other therapists to deal with unresolved traumas stemming back all the way to the age of 5 years old, I still felt there was more emotional junk caked at the bottom of my soul. When my late husband passed away suddenly, my therapist, Betty Erickson (daughter of Dr. Milton Erickson) utilized EMDR treatments on me over the course of a few weeks. My family and friends who cared for me as I struggled with the traumatic loss of my beloved husband were at a loss how to help me. I couldn’t eat, sleep, breathe or function in even the most simplest of ways. EMDR got me back to a level where I still struggled with soul crushing grief, but I could sleep for several hours at night, keep food in my system and even dress myself. It took time, ongoing therapy and being kind to myself to eventually get through the grief of my late husband’s death. Betty Erickson utilized conversational psychotherapy combined with conversational hypnotherapy to guide me through my childhood and unresolved abuse traumas. Sadly, she passed away in early 2019 after an illness. I started searching for a therapist who was trained in EMDR because I felt that if I ever needed those type of sessions it would be better if I was already working with a new therapist who had those skills. After searching for the best new therapist for my ongoing journey, I found my way back to a therapist I had worked with during my struggles with my eating disorder. He had helped me tremendously and I have been abstinent from that addiction since the very late 1980s. Over the years since I worked with him, Sam had taken Somatic Experiencing (SE) training and was certified. He had also did his own life-changing work with therapists throughout his life and that included Somatic Experiencing which he shared had helped him make a huge shift with past traumas. It’s hard for me to put into words how much Somatic Experiencing (SE) has helped me dig down deep into the well of lifelong grief I’ve sustained due to the abuse I endured in my early years with my mentally ill mother. The work is very gentle, safe and I feel completely protected. I am constantly amazed by the intensity of emotions which burst forth in a SE session from the very depths of my soul that I was unaware was still down there. After one session where my therapist and I examined a hiding space I constructed as a young child to avoid being physically attacked by my mother, my body started shaking so violently, my teeth were chattering. One session brought up such sadness and feelings of being lost that I sobbed to the point of physical exhaustion. For days after that session I was on the verge of tears at the most innocent moments in my daily life. I know that SE will not work for everyone. In fact, it may not have worked for me even a few years ago. But it works for me now and I can feel the most broken parts of my soul slowly being patched, mended and healed. With each session of SE I am discovering how my early life impacted the decisions and interactions I had in the past and have in my current life. Is it possible to remove all the remaining scar tissue I carry from the traumatic experiences in my early life? I’ll let you know later because I am going to keep pushing until either I’ve left this planet or feel that I have done everything possible to be the very best person that I can possibly be. I am driven to continue to grow towards peace, health and wholeness. It’s my journey and may not be true for any other. I am just grateful I found this type of work. Is it an effective form of therapy? For me, it’s helped me to move the needle which I thought couldn’t be moved any further. Everyone has to make their own decisions about the value proposition, but if anything helps you heal, isn’t it worth every penny? It certainly is to me. Best wishes and hugs to all who are dealing with any type of trauma. What I write is based on my own experience and belief in the techniques I share.”

column1: How to deal with Anticipatory Grief?
column3: Dealing with Anticipatory Grief Anticipatory loss or grief is the emotion a person feels while preparing for an upcoming loss, such as the death of a loved one. Inevitably, all of us will experience this type of grief at some point in our lives. Anticipatory grief is common among individuals whose loved ones are going through a terminal illness or degenerative disease such as cancer or Alzheimer’s. This can also be experienced as adult children witness their parents go through aging. In addition to the loss of a family member or friend, this type of anticipatory grief can be felt in other ways, for example, if a family pet is nearing the end of its life or if someone is preparing for an out-of-state move away from all things familiar.Anticipatory grief may also happen when a person receives news about their health prognosis, such as someone being told they have a terminal illness or when a pregnant mother is given the news that her baby may have serious health complications. No matter the circumstance, it is important to note that anticipatory grief will be felt before a person passes or an event takes place, which makes processing it different from the common form of grief we experience after a loss occurs. What Does Anticipatory Grief Feel Like Some common feelings or behaviors of individuals experiencing anticipatory grief include:AngerAnxietyDenialDepressionIrritabilityInability to think of things other than the impending lossGuiltLack of motivationLonelinessShockTearfulnessWithdrawal from preferred activities or socializationThe Stages of Anticipatory Grief There is no set way for a person to move through the grieving process; however, according to the University of Rochester Medical Center, there are four distinct phases that one may experience if they are dealing with anticipatory grief. 1. Acceptance that death is inevitable One may feel sadness or depression during this phase. 2. Feeling concern for the dying person Family and friends may experience regret during the phase, feeling sorry for past arguments or failed relationships. If someone is dealing with their impending death, this stage may translate to a fear of dying. 3. Rehearsing the death During this phase, a person may become focused on what will happen immediately after death. This can include saying goodbye, planning funeral arrangements, and preparing for the loss. 4. Imagining the future Survived loved ones may think about what their lives will be like when a family member or friend passes away. What will the holidays be like? Will special occasions continue? Will traditions stay the same? For a dying person, this phase will be similar, as they think about what life might be like for their loved ones when they are no longer around. They may even be thinking about their own experience with death and what will happen during this process. How to Manage Feelings of Anticipatory Grief? With anticipatory grief, one has a unique opportunity to prepare to manage their grief. There can be both positives and negatives when dealing with anticipatory grief. Ideal Way To Deal With Anticipatory Grief One of the most important things to do if you are experiencing this type of grief is to talk to someone, a friend, a loved one, or a therapist. Holding your emotions will only lead to feelings spilling over into other environments, such as at work or with family members. Little Research Is Helpful Figuring out what to expect can be a helpful technique. For example, if your loved one receives a cancer diagnosis, you may want to learn about available treatments and outcomes, potential side effects, survival rates, how to be a positive support in their lives, and how to help them focus on their life’s quality. The sudden death of a family member can be difficult for the remaining family members to adjust to. Still, some positive impacts may be felt if the deceased had time to prepare things, like who will manage finances or who will care for young children. Therapy For Anticipatory Grief Common forms of therapy that aid in working through anticipatory grief are cognitive behavior therapy and narrative therapy. Cognitive Behavior Therapy/CBT Cognitive behavior therapy is more skill-based and will help a grieving person learn ways to shift their mindset to something more positive Narrative Therapy Narrative therapy will allow grieving people to have the time and space to talk through their experiences of grief. Both types of therapy focus on helping grieving people re-frame their experiences to manage difficult emotions better. A therapist can provide appropriate space for you to talk through your grief, find comfort, and achieve a sense of acceptance for the anticipated loss. The therapist will also be able to provide support and guidance once the loss takes place. Original source:https://www.ammiraticounseling.com/dealing-with-anticipatory-grief/

column1: Have you ever faced numbness in your life?
column3: yes i have felt totally numb, for a little while, on occasion. these occasions have so far included states of intoxication, exhaustion, physical illness, trauma from violent incidents and accidents, and loss (particularly after deaths and breakups). regarding that last one: personally, after a loss, i tend to cycle through a whole bouquet of difficult emotions including no emotions. there are psychologists and especially pharmacology lobbyists who would call those lows depression, and also psychologists and psychiatrists who would call them grief, it’s a whole big debate among experts… the only thing they seem to be able to agree on is that when people lose people, they usually feel bad about it for a while, so i try to remember these difficult emotions will pass. but i digress. fortunately, feeling numb doesn’t usually last very long with me. i do have friends and sometimes clients for whom feeling numb does last longer, and that could be for a number of reasons ranging from neurological conditions to depression to trauma response. any particular reason you are asking this? because if you are feeling numb and don’t like it, there may be things you could do about it (treatment of an underlying physical condition, trauma processing, or therapy for depression, for example).

column1: How did you get through the unexpected death of your parent?
column3: I’m so sorry for your loss. This is such a tough question because after my mom died unexpectedly, I wanted to know the same thing! It was the first death I’d experienced and it was so devastating, I had no clue how to cope. I immediately signed up for grief therapy, which helped SO much. I knew that losing my mom would be traumatizing and had the potential to drive me totally insane and I knew I didn’t want to turn to alcohol or negative coping skills and I didn’t possess the ability to just get on with it, so I sought therapy to learn positive tools and coping skills to work through my grief. I googled articles, read books, blogs, listened to podcasts, all to do with death and grief and how to get through it. And then focusing on things that brought me joy was key as well. Being in nature helped me a great deal as it is a gentle reminder of how ‘All Things Must Pass’. After my Dad died four years later, unexpectedly, I turned to my friend and said, ‘I don’t know how I’m going to get through this.’ and he said, ‘You don’t have to know.’ And that statement just FREED me. It just made it okay that I wasn’t able to figure out how to get through it. The thing is, humans are resilient and grief is the price we pay for love. So we just get through it. The arrow of time always moves forward. It won’t rain forever Kris. Sending you a big hug. Also, I host a little show on the Good To Go! Facebook page every Wednesday (8pm ET/5pm PT/1am GMT) called “Grievers and Groovers” and we talk about death, grief and everything in between. Might help you to connect with others and hear how they are navigating their grief journeys? You can find a link to the G2G! FB page on my site: www.goodtogopeace.org

column1: My friend feels she is responsible for her friend's death as she made him stay back after school for an extra class and, as a result, they had to travel by a different medium and met with an accident and he died on the spot. Now she is afraid of even making close friends. What do I do to help her?
column3: It's normal to feel responsible for what happens around us, even if it's an accident. It's better than feeling that bad things happen at random. When you think about it, we're the descendants of people who were good at figuring out how things work and at protecting ourselves. Usually that's good for us, but sometimes figuring out how things work and how to keep bad things from happening leads us astray, makes us believe things that aren't true. If your friend is in the early stages of coping with this loss, try just being there. Listen when she needs to talk. Ask her how she's holding up and then wait for the answer. Use active listening skills, like repeating the gist of what she has just said, e.g., "You wish you could go back in time and do it differently." If your friend seems to be in extreme distress or if it's been going on a long time without getting better, it's time for professional help. Suggest she check in with her physician, ask others who have been in therapy, or look for grief groups in the community. She's lucky to have you in her life. Take care of yourself too.

column1: How do you deal with grief after 4 years of losing a parent?
column3: My dad passed 20 years ago. After a year I went into grief counseling which really helped. I made some changes in my life because I realized life was short. My mom passed 6 years ago and though mom and I weren’t close, and actually things ended badly between us, I had a tougher time getting past her death because now both parents are gone. It took me 5 years to get into therapy after mom died and now it’s been 6 years and I’m finally over the grief of it and can get on with my life. I wish I’d gone sooner but I guess I wasn’t ready. I miss my dad terribly and always have. It’s not a bad feeling though. I can think of him and cry a little and/or smile and remember something about him, what a good man he was, how he would have done anything for us even though we were raised to be strong enough to take care of ourselves. When I think of mom, I’m sad and sometimes angry how things ended up and can never be resolved. There is no time limit on grieving. Everyone is different, every relationship is different. If you are still having problems after 4 years please look into grief counseling.

column1: I originally started therapy after the death of my teenage son to cancer. I am now in the space of reluctant acceptance so is that my therapy goal achieved?
column3: I am so sorry about your son. Your “space of reluctant acceptance” is an achievement as your grief work continues. There are many aspects and phases of grieving, which is ultimately a healing and restorative process. You can never be quite the same again, but your can be just as good as ever, just a little different. It’s a slow process getting there, often measured in years, not weeks, but you’ll get there. Now how about therapy? Your’re stable now, reluctantly accepting, functional. Your family and friends may be saying “You’re doing so well!” and you may not always appreciate that sentiment. Is your therapy goal achieved? If your aim was “reluctant acceptance,” yes. Now you’re deciding what’s next. What’s the next objective, and do you think therapy will help you achieve it, or will you follow some other path. Maybe you could check in with the therapist who has been your companion on the journey to “reluctant acceptance,” and sort out what you want to do next, and when.

column1: Is it worth starting a relationship with someone knowing it will end in 2 years?
column3: I really could not answer that. Let me tell you my experience. I met my future husband at work. We dated 2 years. We were married 6 years. He died unexpectedly and suddenly. We knew each other for 10 years total. I grieved deeply for almost 10 years after his death. In the time I was grieving I functioned in life . Raised my family but felt incredibly guilty. It took some really good therapy and a twelve step program to regain my life back. I stayed in a long term loveless living arrangement for 23 years after his deat. I supported everyone but myself. The only thing I wished different about the last 25 years without my husband is I wish I had the courage to face the imaginary fear of lonilness and vulnerability sooner. So I guess I would say is this ….. do what makes you happy today. Be prepared for grief later and the consequences that come along. Don't feel guilty just know you lived your life in the moment and then the moment is gone. And that's ok. Or you can end it now and be available for love again. If this is not mutual then only you are choosing your own destiny. You see once I gained my life back and faced my fears and rid myself of the thingsand habits that kept me in the depths of sadness I found true love again. I was ready for it and available to take the chance on happiness and not worry about loss. Tomorrow will take care of itself. I only have today. Be happy.

column1: What are some signs of a strong therapeutic alliance?
column3: In my experience an individual can know after one or two sessions at the most if their psychologist is one they can feel comfortable with. One of the biggest factors I have experienced bringing a positive connection is shared experiences. I know when I was a child in foster care I felt a disconnect with the multiple therapists I had throughout my childhood because I felt like they didn’t truly understand what it was like to be in foster care…which at the time was crucial for me to feel a connection. In my opinion having a similarity that is of strong importance to you is the most important factor in having a strong alliance. This creates an in-group bias. In group-bias causes the individual to have a favoritism towards those in the same group. We naturally bond with those we feel are like us. We build our self esteem by belonging. The more distinctive and the more important to us the in-group characteristic is the more bonded we feel. For example we share an in-group with others that like the same color as us. However the bond between the individuals would be much stronger with an in-group that shares being alumni of the same university. An even stronger in-group bias would be towards those that graduated the same year. Additionally feelings of bonding release Oxytocin into our system. Oxytocin enables in the development of trust….trust being absolutely cruicial in a therapeutic setting. Studies have shown oxytocin plays a role in why we trust and prefer those in our in-group. We will feel more of an in-group bias when the characteristic is emotional in nature (such as others who have also experienced grief) and when the characteristic is more closely related and specific to our experience (such as others who have also experienced grief resulting from a spouse who died). This is why I feel shared experiences, especially shared experiences around the reason for therapy will always create the strongest bonds and most beneficial treatments. This is often not difficult considering many psychologist get into the field because of their experiences. Addiction counselors are usually former addicts, I work largely with foster children and I was a foster child my whole childhood. Although I don’t feel experiencing the same pasts in some way is necessary, but having a strong in-group connection is. Your psychologist could be an avid hunter like you are but you are seeking therapy for an unhealthy fear of death. Besides this key factor I think some other things that create a good relationship is a psychologist who is empathetic, who makes you feel like your emotions are valid. Even if it is the most irrational emotion….if you are depressed, upset and having anxiety attacks over losing your favorite lipstick (that can easily be rebought from the store for $9.99) a seemingly irrational set of emotions for the event…the important thing is it’s not irrational to you. The emotions are not irrational, they are very real and a therapist that understands that and can be empathetic to the individuals emotions despite the reasoning for the emotions I feel helps the relationship. This overcomes one aspect that can hurt a therapeutic relationship; having a difference of opinions. You may discussing your feeling regarding the possibility of having an abortion while your therapist may have a very strong opposite stance on abortion. When a Psychologist is empathetic to ones emotions, the topic is irrelevant. This helps the relationship and makes you feel validated, which is important. Another factor is the psychologist ability to be positive. Not saying every moment of therapy be positive and annoyingly cherry, but most of therapy is discussing negative isssues, events and experiences. I feel it helps the relationship and the progress of therapy when the psychologist is able to bring positivity into the sessions as well. You shouldn’t need to see a psychiatrist to get anti-depressants because of how how depressing a session of therapy is with your psychologist. Ideally you will look forward to your sessions. I think if you and the therapist you partner with share these characteristics you will have a solid foundation for success.

column1: How have you recovered from intense grief spanning years of time?
column3: I lost both my parents and my in-laws in one year. Then my brother died a year later. Five years after that, my wife died. I know grief only too well. I have no religious belief. I won't see any of them again. I loved each of them very much, but it happened and I accepted each death. (It takes a while to actually believe what just happened actually did happen, but in time you get there in my experience). I didn't fight grief, although I did of course feel rage at times. I spent a lot of time alone, just trying to exhaust myself physically and trying to come to terms with the losses. That strategy, plus being open and talking about the losses to friends willing to listen, worked surprisingly well. One issue would not go away though: I was very disturbed by dreams, especially concerning my wife's death. I had five therapy sessions a couple of years after she died (one was EMDR) and I felt a lot better. It's normal to feel grief. You don't have to accept hugely upsetting dreams every night though. I was traumatized by her sudden illness and I needed help to overcome that. I am mentally very healthy and living in the present. Having great things in my life and having an exciting future has all helped. My generally positive and happy nature has enabled me to move forward. My lost family members will always be with me in my mind, but in my day to day life I have a new relationship, three new grandchildren and exciting plans. I am not tormented by my grief…by my grandchildren occasionally, but not by grief any more. I hope everyone can find the peace and acceptance I have found.
column9: Living in the present and in the world, is much better for you than living in the past and in your head. I think you've done amazingly to be where you are after all that death and sadness, as it's easy to get stuck there and never really come out the other side. X

column1: How can I console my kids after their dad just passed away? I feel so helpless and lost myself. How can I get by?
column3: This is one of the hardest questions. I thought losing my dad was the most difficult thing I would go thru until I had to watch my kids go thru the death of their dad. I know first hand how hard this is. It is hard to look in their faces and see their grief and it is hard to look into their faces and see their dad. Then comes the kids needing all the things dad did and knowing you can't be him, all while trying to not drown in your own grief. You just be there for them as much as you can at this time. Show them their grief is ok by grieving with them. Know and let them know that even tho he may not be here in the physical world, he is always with all of you. Talk about his quirks or eventually even what dad would say in different situations. Reminisce with them about the good and funny times you had with him and share stories of him from before they were born. Be very understanding in the fact that we all grieve in different ways. Allow his few very good friends (you will find out quickly who they are) to continue to be in your kids' lives, even if it is just a phone call here and there. Do your best to maintain relationships with his family if possible. Most importantly, seek some therapy for you and the kids. My kids were 17, 19 and 21 when their dad passed Dec 20th, 2017. Despite them being a little older, he was our rock. As time goes on, you will figure out ways to deal with the things only dad could do (my kids' dad was a mechanic so we have never had to hire one or buy a car by ourselves) even if it isn't quite as good. All of us look for feathers as signs from dad that he is watching over us. And find a cool way to memorialize him so that everyone can have a part in it. Continue to seek support from family, friends and professionals for as long as any of you need to because at some point you also have to show them it is ok to live again and that is what he would want. I am deeply sorry you and your children have experienced such a profound loss. I hope this helps in some way.

column1: Should caregivers, doctors and nurses receive free psychological support?
column3: Yes! There are lots of situations that can, especially over the course of time, work to traumatize nurses,doctors, EMT’s and related professions. Everybody’s different. For me, it’s young people and children. Abused children. The kids who had a drink on prom night and came to my ER broken and not breathing. And one special little girl. She was a huge wonderful strong personality! Magnetic. She was the car accident survivor. She had lost the ability to speak. Had brain damage. Paralyzed on 1 side. Seizures. Ulcers from IV dilantin . She was alert, and like any child just wanted to play. She had a trach and recurrent scarring which had to be minimized periodically by laser. When I became her nurse after acute hospitalization, I gained a a lovely friend. I was her charge a few years. She learned to speak using a Servox and explained to the kids at school about using it and how she would breathe thru her trach. She was sassy and assertive. She was strong at the end of my care for her, no paralysis or sores. No seizures. We were often mistaken as mom and daughter. I attended school with her, keeping suction and other needs at hand. Another nurse and I were no longer needed after a few years and we moved on. Then it happened. About 2 weeks passed, my daughter and I were arriving home from the store, when my patients family member sped into the driveway behind us-the little girl was taken to the ER, not breathing. A failure to reinsert her trach tube (scarring blockage) during her scheduled cleaning and change. We dropped everything and took off to the hospital about 4 miles away. My mind was racing… all I can think of is that infection can be treated more successfully than death… and what can I use to open another airway?No matter how small? Unfortunately, this precious child was gone when we arrived. The nurses there were quick to explain to me (I knew them) all they had done as if a desperate apology……. This was a loss of a child who I’d spent 10–12 hour days with for the last few years. She’d come so far. My dear friend. Nurses need therapy for grief, trauma, burn out. And training to help manage stress.

column1: What are your views on the placebo effect? Do you believe we can truly ease or even heal ongoing health or mental problems with the help of psychology?
column3: Placebo effect simulates or replace the loss, temporarily, to ease the psychological pain or depression.Placebo effect removes the associated pain and not the direct pain. It can be used for (1)physical and (2)mental health issues. Let me give an example for each.. For physical health issues..In my understanding the mirror therapy which is used to reduce the pain of the lost limb is based on the placebo effect. Here the associated psychological pain registered in the brain at the time of impact is reduced during this therapy.Mirror therapy - WikipediaMirror therapy (MT) or mirror visual feedback (MVF) is a therapy for pain or disability that affects one side of the patient more than the other side. It was invented [ when? ] by Vilayanur S. Ramachandran to treat post-amputation patients who had phantom limb pain (PLP). Ramachandran created a visual (and psychological) illusion of two intact limbs by putting the patient's affected limb into a "mirror box," with a mirror down the center (facing toward a patient's intact limb). An occupational therapy assistant using mirror therapy to address phantom pain The patient then looks into the mirror on the side with the good limb and makes "mirror symmetric" movements, as a symphony conductor might, or as a person does when they clap their hands. The goal is for the patient to imagine regaining control over a missing limb. Because the subject is seeing the reflected image of the good limb moving, it appears as if the phantom limb is also moving. Through the use of this artificial visual feedback, it becomes possible for the patient to "move" the phantom limb and to unclench it from potentially painful positions. Mirror therapy has expanded beyond its origin in treating phantom limb pain to the treatment of other kinds of one-sided pain or disability, for instance, hemiparesis in post-stroke patients and limb pain in patients with complex regional pain syndrome . Post-amputation phantom limb pain edit Ramachandran (right) with his original mirror box A diagram of a mirror box. A patient inserts a whole hand into one hole and the "phantom" hand into the other. When viewed from an angle, an image of two complete hands is created in the brain. Based on the observation that phantom limb patients were much more likely to report paralyzed and painful phantoms if the actual limb had been paralyzed prior to amputation (for example, due to a brachial plexus avulsion ), Ramachandran and Rogers-Ramachandran proposed the "learned paralysis" hypothesis of painful phantom limbs [ when? ] . [ 1 ] Their hypothesis was that every time the patient attempted to move the paralyzed limb, they received sensory feedback (through vision and proprioception ) that the limb did not move. This feedback stamped itself into the brain circuitry through a process of Hebbian learning so that, even when the limb was no longer present, the brain had learned that the limb (and subsequent phantom) was paralyzed. [ 2 ] Ramachandran created the mirror box to relieve pain by helping an amputee imagine motor control over a missing limb. Mirror therapy is now also widely used for the treatment of motor disorders such as hemiplegia or cerebral palsy . As Deconick et al. state in a 2014 review, the mechanism of improved motor control and pain relief may differ from the mechanism of pain relief. Deconick et al., who reviewed only the effects of MVF on sensorimotor control, found that MVF can exert a strong influence on the motor network, mainly through increased cognitive penetration in action conhttps://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mirror_therapyFor mental health issues..Grafted calf that replaced after the loss of her calf, helps the cow to come out of her grief. column1: My son passed away 10 days ago and I'm supposed to see him not embalmed at the funeral home. What state would his body be in?
column3: Some days I am glad I seen our son before he was embalmed. He looked much better than he did embalmed. Now can I say 100% that was the smartest decision of my life….no. I made that decision from a broken hearted moms state if mind. He was my baby, my only son, the need to see him was equally as powerful as my grief if losing him. I didn’t care, I saw him into this world and I needed to see him out. I hate going to those visions in my mind. I can’t get them out, even through therapy they still won’t go. I lost a daughter 3 years after my son, the same battle and worse this time, I viewed her as well. Now I am doubly traumatized. It was my children, but not my children, if that makes sense. It’s caused so much more pain for me but at the time no one was going to stop me from seeing my babies. I needed that time with them. They both had been at the morgue for sometime so needless to say the refrigeration was did what it does, there were other things I will not put in this, things I can’t unsee now. Therapy is slowly helping with these images my mind will not leave me unsee. If I had not done what I did I would not have made my grief worse. My daughters death was more traumatic than my son’s, imagine that, at the scene I was going to fight a cop to see my daughter. He very kindly said mam, you don’t want to go up there, you don’t need to see that. The look in his eyes, how much compassion, love and kindness in his eyes is something I’ve become so grateful over. I listened to that officer and I spared myself an extra horror as it was going to be horrifying enough, for now my grief had taken on a new level. My grief was in a horrible state for my son and now I had lost my oldest child as well. My world was, is a mess. Thank God for therapy it has really made a difference not just for me but for my remaining child, husband and grandchild. I needed to be here for them so together we could find a state of mind that would allow us the strength to keep living. I had years of me existing, just going through the motions but not living. These years I played those images from viewing my children over and over again. I forgot what my babies looked like and just saw those horrible images of them in death. It’s not like that now due to therapy. I still see them but not as often as I did or as for long as I did. I’m rambling now, this is just my experience, everyone is different. Losing loved ones is never easy, the pain is horrible, however, losing my children is pain like I have never felt before. Each loss in my life was different, none feels like what I feel about my children. I hope this helps anyone who takes the time to read this small book. Sending a healing hug to all who’ve lost anyone, if it gets too much get help, therapy has saved me.
column9: I’d imagine this depends on what caused his death. Natural causes are less likely to look as bad for instance as an accident or overdose. I don’t imagine you want advise on if or not to go see him, he’s your son and you probably will regardless of the suffering from that. Sometimes we just do what we must and the stronger the bond the more likely we will be there for someone no matter what. This is how I felt about viewing my grandma but looking back on that I kind of wish I hadn’t because I adjusted her dress so the stitches wouldn’t show since she wouldn’t want them to. Now I remember her like the last time I saw her alive in the convelescent hospital as she was in the process of dying. She said people had been coming to take her on trips and I said that’s okay grandma, go with them, they are here to help you transition. Those people are you spirit guides/angles and they love you too. She seemed to find peace in this while knowing I was right about that and it was as if she relaxed finally, then she left contented. This is how I choose to remember her now and I push seeing those stitches into the cornfield where they belong with memories I’d asssume forget. You’ll get over going too, it may take time but you will heal from it. I’m so sorry for your loss friend.

column1: Struggling to conceive and keep losing babies with my husband (Miscarriage/Infant Death) Am I being punished for the two abortions I had years ago?
column3: No, you are not being punished. I’m sorry that you feel that way. I hope you have had a complete gynecologist examination and that your husband has also been checked over. Even a low grade infection can affect the fertility of either partner. Get the medical check-ups, get therapy for your grief. Ditch any doctor or counselor who says that you deserved to have a miscarriage. Do the same with any friends or relations who say the same, as toxic stress can also affect your body. I read your comment post that describes your situation. It seems that you and your husband have had one miscarriage. I don’t know how long you’ve been married, but some people try for years before they have their baby or babies. One couple had a child, then ten years later, the second one came along, even though the mom claimed that they had not done any form of birth control and they had a good romantic life. One thing I’ve noticed in the decades I’ve lived, is that there seems to be no correlation between pregnancy and the goodness of the people involved. A couple who marry, do everything right, with no health issues may not get pregnant or have one miscarriage or still-birth after another, while one of their sisters gets pregnant the first time she has sex at a drunken party and nine months later, pops out an eight pound baby. Life isn’t fair. Sometime it looks like some people have all the luck, and others don’t, until suddenly the situation gets swapped or evened out or thing get so turned around nothing seems the same, while for others, nothing ever seems to change. You say that you have a good husband, so enjoy your time together now and don’t look back. Life has many surprises in it. Keep yours eyes and your heart open and rejoice in every sunrise, be grateful at the sunset. This week (August 11) is the Perseid's meteor shower. Take time to watch for the falling stars. Peace.

column1: How do you go on after suddenly losing a young child?
column3: My son lost his child ten days before Christmas almost three years ago. He and his wife went to therapy where they could talk about their son. He still goes today. You never get over the loss of a child. He was my grandchild, 18, talented in any athletic endeavor he tried and an artist as well. His life was just beginning. The holidays approach. It is not a joyous time for us. My son already shows signs on his face of grief returning. He has three younger children who want Christmas as usual. The youngest does not even remember his big brother, since he was not quite three when he died. HIs birthday is Christmas Day. The now eldest son is ten. He was 7 then and my son’s only daughter was almost ten. There are pictures all over their home in an effort to keep his memory alive for his little siblings. How does my son go on? He moves forward. He keeps going. As do I. Last December I had panic attacks. I couldn’t breathe and went on an antidepressant. Children should not die before their parents and grandparents. It is against the natural order. My son and his wife are Evangelical Christians. I don’t see how they can go on loving god and believing god loves them. If I was a believer I would be so angry at god. I was angry for a long time. It is not fair. But I am old enough to know that there is no fairness about life.
column9: My heart is so sad for you all. Your son and his wife will always remember. Unfortunately his siblings won’t remember him and they will live with his ghost hanging on all the walls. The therapist might want to have a chat with your son about healthy remembering. Being angry with G-d doesn’t change faith in God because he knows your sorrow. My heart is so sad for you all.

column1: Are therapists who unilaterally end their client's therapy (for other reasons than sickness, death, retiring or moving) automatically bad therapists?
column3: No, they are not. I think the problem is not so much the act of unilateral termination itself as the way in which it is sometimes carried out. As patients, I believe that we deserve a comprehensive explanation as to why the therapy is being terminated. How are we supposed to learn from what happened and understand our therapist’s decision if we are not given information about our own treatment? Ideally this information would be offered to the patient verbally as well as in writing. That way if the shock is severe enough that the patient can’t remember what was said they will have a written document to remind them of what is happening and why. What’s not okay is when this information isn’t communicated directly in a caring professional tone. Being sent a form letter that has been copied and pasted from a Google search on “how to terminate a patient” is unacceptable. How impersonal! Such an act is a slap in the face because a generic letter fails to summarize the unique gains, ongoing challenges, and personal nuances of the work. It does not offer an adequate explanation as to the reasons why the therapist has chosen to end treatment, which does not help the patient find closure and also doesn’t offer much background for the next therapist they hire if it’s someone they weren’t referred to. Honesty may hurt but I’d much rather hear a complete account of why my therapist is terminating me than be left to fill in the gaps. I want to learn. I want to understand more about how I can take responsibility for my behavior. What is mine and what is hers? If she was anxious about my behavior or suspecting a diagnosis she isn’t qualified to treat, then fine, please, let’s be open about that. Don’t deny me the information needed to engage in deeper reflection and self-inquiry. This is how I find my own closure. If there isn’t proper closure after unilateral termination then all sorts of bad things can happen. The lingering grief and powerlessness can take all sorts of forms. In my case I suffered with intrusive fantasies of revenge (wherein I felt I had impact), urges to return to her old office as a means of pinning down my grief in time and space (like a funeral), obsessive googling, PTSD, and disenfranchised grief that still lingers. Plus it was harder for me to hire another therapist and trust them. In my case what happened was extreme. My therapist unilaterally terminated me without ever even saying goodbye or telling me I was being terminated. She simply took a vacation and disappeared. For context she did not make a referral or notify me that I would need to hire another therapist. In fact prior to the disappearance she told me that I was a complex and intimidating patient, that most therapists would be unable to manage me because I would challenge them. 🤣 (as though she was the best in the world, the only one who could possibly handle the challenge?) She then told me that if she ever found out I had hired a supplemental therapist she’d terminate me. From there we had two months of normalish therapy, though I was very anxious. Then she disappeared. As a patient who is terrified of crossing boundaries I never reached out or shared my feelings with her because she didn’t offer me the space to do so and I didn’t want to intrude. I sent one polite inquiry about the status of our work but she didn’t answer so I gave up. I waited three more months before hiring another therapist because I was still afraid that if she came back she would terminate me for having seen someone else. I was so afraid of losing her even though she’d already left. Later I found evidence she’d lied about in-state licensure. Her family member was writing about her in an online narcissistic abuse support group. This offered some closure but it did not absolve her of the trauma she caused me. Really it opened up a whole other round of betrayal and distrust. I’d consider that a very bad unilateral termination. That said, even when unilateral termination is done well, I think it is often incredibly painful. Bottom line: we deserve the courtesy of being offered a voice in the termination process, with the understanding that whatever we say likely will not change their decision if they made the decision for ethical reasons. in which case, they made the choice because they genuinely want what is best for us.

column1: How do I overcome grief and continue to live for my existing family?
column3: The popular understanding of grief is that grief has a beginning, some number of stages (depending on the clinician or author) and then grief concludes with acceptance. This understanding of grief treats loss of loved ones as an affliction or illness that is healed with time and perhaps therapy. We speak of healing grief. I accepted and embraced that popular path through grief after my younger brother killed himself in 2000 at age 43 without prior warning signs or calls for help. In 2001, my best friend and a key employee of my small company died suddenly in his late 30’s at home from a sudden cardiac event that had never been diagnosed or treated. Again, I embraced the popular mainstream path through grief. In 2005 our 20 year old son was killed in a firefighter water rescue training accident in our small close knit town. I struggled for a long time, a number of years, without finding a comfortable acceptance. The mainstream teaching on grief and the common modalities of therapy just didn’t resonate productively in healing that third untimely and unexpected loss in five years. I wanted to return fully to the life around me, to our marriage and family, but I felt unable somehow to just close the door with acceptance. I spent a long time searching my soul for better understanding. The short summary of what I understand about grief, some ideas that you may wish to consider as you struggle to live after loss.We grieve because we love.No love, no grief. Deep love, deep grief.When we love someone, from the love of family and friends to the lifetime passionate lover, we rarely speak the words but we understand that one of us will die before the other.The person died, the love we shared with them didn’t die but is changed.Grief is the final responsibility of loving someone.Grief is, at it’s simplest root, love continued after loss. Why would we end it, why would we close the door on that love?Grief is meant to teach us about love.We are meant to heal the initial painful fires of emotions that loss brings, we are not meant to excise and erase the memories that cause that pain.We are meant to learn from loss, to better appreciate life and love while we are still alive.We are meant to curate and incorporate the lessons and power of the love that we have shared with our loved ones, especially those loved ones who have died.We are meant to share the lessons learned with the living as examples or parables on love that add value to other lives around us.No good life that is full of love will escape what we call grief. We are all destined to die at a time and place that we have little or no control over.I will repeat: Grief is the final responsibility of loving someone.A good guidepost on your journey is to ask yourself: “How would my lost loved one want me to grieve? How many tears, how much pain, how much damage to my life would they expect me to bear? Universally, the path they would choose for you to grieve their loss will be easier than the one you choose for yourself. That is because they too loved you, the would want you to take the meaning of their life with you, not to take the pain of their death. Understand that your grief is simply love and try to find better and more positive expressions of that love to enrich your life. Share your love to add meaning to the life of your lost loved one and to the lives of those who surround you in life. Be well, love well, and you will find peace even in the most tragic loss.
column9: thanks for the great reply. yes, grief is an extension of love. I lost my only sibling- my younger brother , barely two months back. He had a heart attack in Jan2015 , symptoms of which he ignored. I feel guilt that I should have insisted upon him to go to the hospital. Another attack recurred in 3 days, in a much more serious way. He survived , but with lot of damage to his heart muscles. This resulted in progressive heart failure and resulting death in march 2020. His wife is already dead and he had left behind a 17 year old daughter. I feel guilty that I could have done better to save him, in 2015 itself. This feeling is eating me alive. Waking up every morning is a nightmare and gut wrenching. There is also a family dysfunction as wife does not comprehend the intense grief. Dont want to lose her too….

column1: How can we overcome the pain of losing someone very close?
column3: Grief: Coping with the loss of your loved oneCoping with the loss of a close friend or family member may be one of the hardest challenges that many of us face in our daily life. Imagine when we lose a spouse, or parent our grief can be particularly intense. Loss is understood as a natural part of life, Hence we can still be overcome by shock and confusion, leading to prolonged periods of depression. The sadness or depression typically diminishes in intensity as time passes, but grieving is an important process in order to overcome these feelings and continue to embrace the time you had with your loved one. Everyone reacts differently to death and employs personal coping mechanisms for grief. Research shows that most people can recover from loss on their own through the passage of time if they have social support and healthy habits. It may take months or a year to come to terms with a loss. There is no “normal” time period for someone to grieve. Don’t expect to pass through phases of grief either, as new research suggests that most people do not go through stages as progressive steps. If your relationship with the deceased was difficult, this will also add another dimension to the grieving process. It may take some time and thought before you are able to look back on the relationship and adjust to the loss. Human beings are naturally resilient, considering most of us can endure loss and then continue on with our own lives. But some people may struggle with grief for longer periods of time and feel unable to carry out daily activities. Those with severe grief may be experiencing complicated grief. These individuals could benefit from the help of a psychologist or another licensed mental health professional with a specialization in grief…. so you can do the following as a matter. Accept your feelings. People experience all kinds of emotions after the death of someone close. Sadness, anger, frustration and even exhaustion are all normal. Take care of yourself and your family. Eating well, exercising and getting plenty of rest help us get through each day and move forward. Reach out and help others dealing with the loss. ………….

column1: My mother-in-law passed away. My husband suffers so much. How can I help him?
column3: Helping another person through grief is particularly poignant when the other is your spouse and the grieved is an immediate family member. First, you need to recognize that you have feelings, maybe strong feelings, regarding the deceased. Both you and your spouse will most likely be grieving at the same time. Even though you may be grieving simultaneously you, most likely, will not be at the same place in the process. Therefore, recognizing your difference in pace, it is important to allow the feelings to come as they will and be patient with yourself. Grief takes time. Usually, a good benchmark is to consider that the sense of loss may be prominent up to a year, maybe longer. Living through family events one experiences the loss of a loved one. This is why many cultures have a year of grieving expected of the grieved. Sometimes even wear black or some reminder of the process. Now a word about feelings. The loss of an important person in your life elicits many confusing feelings depending on how complicated the relationship was for you. The loss of mothers, fathers, siblings, and children elicit the strongest feelings. Grief invites feelings of loss, anger, dissertation, relief, irritation, helplessness, vulnerability, impatience, peace, to mention just a few. Almost any feeling can be expected and sometimes will show up at unwelcome times. Grievers may have to leave the dining table, or the concert, or worship service. They may be overcome with grief while working, or reading, or playing whatever and need to self-isolate or take a moment. It is good for each person to have their own grief counselor for the first year following an important death. Believing that one needs no one is often a signal that there are complex feelings they are apprehensive about exploring. Some persons believe that the idea of working through grief is to find a way to “bottle up” or contain one's feelings so that they don't affect relationships, or work, or aspirations. Such a belief can indefinitely extend the length of recovery. The goal of Grieving is to feel the feelings and appropriate their meaning into one's future life. Often grievers come to understand that relationships never actually leave our memory, their memory simply gradually becomes less problematic and eventually adds to the richness and depth of life.
column9: That is beautiful, I always say that you never really get over it, you incorporate it into your being and it becomes part of who you are. I love your explanation. Thank You

column1: What are the psychological effects of breaking up with someone?
column3: There are psychological effects of breaking up with someone...whether you are the "dumper" or the "dumpee." When a serious relationship ends and it was either unwanted or not expected, the initial response is most often one of panic and confusion, because a sudden breakup is similar to other traumatic events a person can experience (where something familiar and trusted is taken from them, often without warning.) If the Break Up Was Unwanted (The Dumpee Experience): The most common psychological effects experienced by the person being dumped are: PainObsession/RuminationStress ResponseIdentity Shift Pain: The psychological pain experienced when we are rejected, betrayed, or abandoned is very real. The same part of the brain that processes physical pain is activated when the emotional pain of a breakup is felt, and the person feels, behaves, and reacts in a similar way as someone who is in a great deal of physical pain. It may be that people who say it feels like their heart has been broken are describing a real physically painful sensation. For adolescents, in particular, breakups can precede the development of major depression, partly because they may not yet have the life skills and experience to manage the psychological pain associated with the end of a significant relationship. Obsession/Rumination: Because romantic love actually activates the part of the brain which is associated with cravings for food and drugs, a similar experience of craving and withdrawal is to be expected following a breakup. The person experiencing a breakup can't stop thinking about their ex and their past, the "good times," going over and over what went wrong and what they might have been able to do to prevent the breakup. Seeking to reconnect with the ex-partner or continue to want to be some part of their lives is normal, and can include everything from the classic "drunk texting the ex" to the more dangerous forms of obsession and criminal stalking behavior. Stress Response: The person is attempting to come to terms with a traumatic event, the end of an important relationship. Like other traumatic events, a person can respond with feelings of shock, being in denial, attempts to bargain with the ex to reconsider, feeling angry and sad, grieving, and eventually coming to accept that it's over. The brain is wired to perceive disconnection from sources of love and attention as highly distressing. To be dumped on the savannah by your tribe, by your mother upon whom you depend completely, or by your partner whom you trust is psychologically scary, painful, and stressful. As the person is attempting to cope, all of the normal responses to being in a high-stress state can occur. The person's appetite and sleep, ability to pay attention and concentrate, energy and motivation, and immune system can all be affected. Identity Shift: The person experiences an immediate shift in identity from being a part of a couple to being single again. Rapid shifts in identity cause disorientation for most people, requiring time and emotional and cognitive processing to reorient to their new identity. There can be a loss of status, home, friends, time with children, extended family, places of worship, financial resources, and other changes and losses that must be dealt with, but are not often anticipated. Above all, the loss of "what might have been" must be grieved to acceptance. ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Many people think there are only psychological effects for the person being dumped when a relationship ends. Although the pain is different for the person who makes the decision to call it quits, it does exist and is often no less painful. If the Break Up Was Wanted (The Dumper Experience): The most common psychological effects experienced by the dumper are: Dread/Anticipating LossGuiltIsolationGrief Postponement Dread/Anticipating Loss: The person who makes the decision to end a relationship often (and hopefully) does not do so impulsively, but rather after long and careful thought. During this time, where the partner may or may not be aware of the contemplation to end the relationship, the person often experiences a great deal of anxiety and dread as they consider ending the relationship and all of the potential consequences involved. Because the dumper knows the end may be coming, there is less shock and trauma involved in the ending, but the stress of contemplating and disconnecting from a loved one is often no less stressful. This process of considering whether to end a relationship can take weeks to decades, during which time this stress and dread anticipating the end can be occurring. Many times once the dumper announces that it's over, it may appear they are able to move on very quickly, when in reality they have processed through many of the same kinds of emotions and grieved the end of the relationship for a long time already. The dumpee is just beginning that process when the relationship ends. Guilt: Many times the person who ends a relationship feels intense guilt over causing harm to someone they care about. They do not want to cause harm, but it is unavoidable if they have determined for whatever reason that the relationship is no longer tenable or healthy for them. If there were a way to end the relationship without anyone being hurt, they would do it. Often it is not possible, so the dumper has to be willing to accept that they have caused another person they care about to suffer. A sensitive, caring person is going to feel bad about this and have to live with this. Isolation: No one is going to be crying tears for the dumper, however, no matter how bad they feel about ending the relationship. The dumper is often perceived as the "bad guy" for leaving the dumpee feeling hurt and abandoned. Friends and family members often take sides, and the dumper is often seen as obviously strong enough to not need support if they were strong enough to leave, so it is usually given instead to the person who has been left behind, who is in shock. A similar shift in identity occurs for the dumper as for the dumpee, who must also navigate their surroundings when what is private becomes public, deciding whether and what to share about the reasons for leaving their partner. Although there are always two sides to every breakup, and partners share responsibility for their relationship problems, the "spin" about a breakup will likely become an oversimplified cliche that never adequately sums up the reality. The dumper will often be in the position of having to decide whether and how to defend their decision to end their relationship to outsiders. Refusing not to comment rarely garners support and often increases feelings of isolation. Grief Postponement: All of the eventual losses and changes in lifestyle that can result from a breakup (home, kids, family, friends, financial resources, etc) are experienced by the dumper as well as the dumpee, but cannot be openly complained about or openly grieved. The dumper often does not feel they are entitled to grieve those losses, because they were the one who wanted it to end. Grieving the end of the relationship can become complicated, because some losses cannot be grieved ahead of time, but by the time they are being experienced, that grief is not supported or allowed. Although the initial psychological effects of significant relationship breakups are almost always bad and painful, regardless of who initiates the end of a relationship, the long-term outcome for most people is positive. Most people not only survive breakups, but learn things about themselves, others, and relationships that are helpful for the future. If psychological pain does not appear to be lifting after a few weeks, or a serious decline in the ability to function occurs after a breakup, a person should seek professional counseling.
