Indeed, Thompson (1974) reviewed not only the psychological literature, but also the sociological and demographic literatures, and she concluded that, in the United States, if not around the world, having children is a moral imperative. If…parenthood is a moral imperative, then voluntarily choosing not to accept this responsibility should evoke moral outrage among perceivers. Furthermore…moral outrage should help account for any unfavorable evaluations of voluntarily childfree targets. Such findings would perhaps explain why perceptions of voluntarily childfree women and men have changed so little over time and despite the increasing typicality of their parenthood decision in the United States.This study underlined a couple of societal trends:Those that “violate” perceived societal norms will experience societal backlashSocietal norms are heavily imbedded in gender stereotypes - women and men are given “prescribed roles”A perceived societal norm is parenthood; motherhood and fatherhood are prescribed rolesWomen and men who voluntarily choose to not have children experience societal backlashThe backlash experienced by those who are voluntarily childless is rooted in societal backlash from the “failure” to fulfill prescribed roles, which are gender stereotypes“Failure” to voluntarily have children is seen to produce societal outrage - which produces behaviors of societal backlash - since parenthood is seen as prescribed roles/gender stereotypesAll of the above points reflects societal pressure towards parenthoodWomen that don’t want to have children seem to experience a societal pressure to change their mind. The fact that women are being pressured towards motherhood reflects that women are pressured to fit inside prescribed roles and/or gender stereotypes. A Times article covers the notion of parenthood and how those who don’t want to be parents are looked down on: [3]We rarely ask, 'Why do you have kids?' Instead it's 'Why don't you?' And that 'why don't you' comes with a ton of judgment.The article that I mentioned above in my excerpt received a host of negative reactions. Mike Huckabee, in an interview with Fox & Friends, had this reaction about the Times article: [4]Fox and Friends invited former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee on their show this past Saturday to discuss the Time cover story and its implications. The most terrifying thing about the article, according to Huckabee was that it might send the...message that it was actually possible for people who didn't have children to lead a fulfilling life. (Imagine the horror if childless women started to believe that their lives were still worthwhile.) As far as Huckabee is concerned, reproducing is "the highest particular calling that I think we can have as human beings" and anyone who rejects that calling must be in some way lacking.Tucker Carlson went even further, saying:Having children means less time for vacations and spin class, where the real meaning in life resides, right? I mean, have you ever seen anything more selfish, decadent and stupid?Yikes.In another study, “Gender-Role Attitudes and Behavior Across the Transition to Parenthood”, which was published in 2013, said this about societal pressures on motherhood: [5]The role of motherhood is seen by society as central to a woman’s identity.More specifically, a book called Singled Out, written by Dr. DePaulo in 2007, said this about societal pressures in regards to parenthood:There are…particular life tasks that people in a given society are expected to accomplish, and a corresponding timetable for achieving them. For example, by a certain age, you ‘should’ be married. Then, before too long, a married couple ‘should’ start having children. Violate those cultural mandates…and you get stigmatized.DePaulo, B. (2007). Singled Out: How Singles Are Stereotyped, Stigmatized, and Ignored, and Still Live Happily Ever After. This stigmatization that Dr. DePaulo points out is clearly seen in Tucker Carlson and Mike Huckabee’s reactions to the Times article on Fox & Friends (mentioned above). Motherhood is pushed to the point that people think it is an innate part of life: [6]Motherhood is so highly connected with adult femininity in the United States that many women feel that they need to be mothers.The above points, regarding societal pressures on motherhood, reinforce traditional gender roles which contribute to the inequality and oppression women experience. It is an inconvenient truth that women still can’t win; if women choose to not have children, they are seen as ‘cold’ and/or ‘frigid’. If women have children, they are expected to sacrifice their dreams and careers in order to let their husbands pursue theirs (if they are married to a man). If women are single mothers, society is quick to blame and resentful in offering help. If women choose to adopt, infertile or not, society shows a self-righteous pity towards them. It’s a mind-numbing cycle of devaluation compounded by cruel societal attitudes. But, why would society pressure women to have children? Why can’t society value women for more than their desire (or lack of desire) to be mothers? A woman who is not a mother is of no less value compared to a woman who is a mother; a woman who is a mother is of no less value compared to a woman who is not a mother. For some reason, society is having trouble understanding and/or caring that the current way women are valued or devalued is problematic and dehumanizing: [7]Society assumes that all women, with enough exposure to their babies, will feel the same sense of endless, selfless love. We’re thought to be biologically programmed this way. But the truth is far more complicated. It’s hard for any woman to escape the expectation to be a mother. The maternal myth suffuses every human culture, from Catholicism’s Virgin Mary to Hinduism’s goddess mother. It’s considered the most natural state of womanhood, leaving the childless woman the object of pity. Let’s not even mention the woman who doesn’t want or like children at all. At the weekend Thomasina Miers, chef and founder of the Wahaca chain of restaurants, suggested Theresa May had abandoned the fight against childhood obesity – including a ban on junk food adverts, and free primary school lunches – because she isn’t a mother. Miers’ implication was that motherhood somehow makes a person automatically care about not only her own children but everyone else’s as well; and that women who aren’t mothers don’t have the same caring sense towards future generations… For the sake of both mothers and children, we need to begin detaching the myth of motherhood from the reality. It’s unfair of any society to expect women to be the best mothers they can be without economic or emotional support, just because they should love their children. Not all women are happy to be mothers. And when it comes to abortion, it is also wrong of pro-lifers to assume that keeping a baby will always work out fine because some maternal instinct will inevitably kick in… The spectrum of human behavior encompasses those who want children, those who don’t, and those who aren’t yet ready to have them. The most unnatural thing of all is forcing a woman into motherhood in the anticipation that she will biologically fall into line when a baby arrives.An analysis that covers societal attitudes towards motherhood, “Myths of Motherhood. The Role of Culture in the Development of Postpartum Depression” (published in 2007), offers a powerful critique on the themes I have explored thus far as well as the concept in the original question: [8]In his treatment of sexual development and femininity, Freud designates the “female” in terms of lack and absence: men are whole human beings and hold the penis; while women are defined by the absence of the sexual organ and thus they are condemned to experience an unfulfillable desire that is constantly displaced onto substitute signifiers. In a nutshell, motherhood is thought to coincide with the female desire to retrieve what she lacks. It can be configured as a fundamental experience in women’s attempt to achieve wholeness by gaining what they do not possess… If we type the word “motherhood” in the British National Corpus and look for the adjectives which tend to co-occur with it, we obtain the following result: good, divine, free, greatest, great, important, radiant, welcoming, relevant, perceived, positive, etc…These examples bring to the fore the linguistic strategies that frame the social understanding and acceptance of motherhood and the difficulties which arise when it comes to comment on the complexity and the problematic of motherhood. Only by starting from women’s experiences is it possible to understand the complexity of motherhood. The key factor that allows a shift from an external and impersonal view to the cultivation of a female point of view is giving voice to one’s own secret doubts. The interpretation of motherhood as a female experience is a recent achievement, accomplished during the second half of the nineteenth century when more attention came to be devoted to women’s responses to the birth of a child, when it becomes necessary to deal with both the birth of a child and the birth of a mother. Only by starting from this conceptual turning point, can we discuss motherhood as a female experience. In this way, motherhood stops being considered as a natural event which has high chances of happening, and begins to be understood as a complex experience that brings about a crisis in women’s life. This shift in perspective…underlin[es] that the birth of a baby can be considered a phase in a woman life cycle that calls for a reorganization of her inner world and the search for a new mental space which may host both an idea of the child and an idea of self-as-parent…motherhood is first and foremost a life condition that entails a deconstruction and reorganization of one’s own sense of identity. Having a baby creates a state of vulnerability and insecurity which may upset women’s psychological balance. In this way, motherhood assumes a more complex connotation which conveys positive aspects alongside with some downsides: motherhood can be complicated, it may occasion conflicts and moments of crisis. This new perspective challenges an inveterate cultural prejudice that sees motherhood as the indispensable condition for women to fully express their nature, embodying the most powerful role in the formation of the feminine self and conforming to the stereotype of the happy and fulfilled mother. This prejudice is overcome by a more complex view that considers the birth of a child as a personal and subjective experience, rooted in a complex weave of past-present-future factors of a psychological, relational and social nature, in which conscious and unconscious phenomena intertwine. Not all women react to this experience with prompt readiness. In line with the theory of the birth of “the senses of the Self”, Stern argues that the physical birth of a baby corresponds to the psychological birth of the mother which expresses itself through the formation of a new identity: the sense of being a mother. He claims that this process of reorganization is finalized at the dawn of the motherhood mindset. A personal mindset is what helps us to organize our values, our distinguishing qualities and the peculiarities that turn a person into a coherent and unique individual. Having a baby brings about a change in one’s own priorities. It influences preexisting relationships and redefines roles formerly played…Mothers will have to redirect their previous mental organization, their previous set of values and needs, and cope with the duties and responsibilities of motherhood…Stern goes on arguing that the maternal mindset will have to learn to coexist with other identities to achieve a balance between pre-existing identities and the new identity as mother… Maternal skills and mothers’ willingness to derive gratification from the exercise of those skills are strongly interiorized and sustained on a psychological level. On an evolutionary level these skills are inscribed in the psychological structure of the woman. Nevertheless, the very skills and needs that create the woman as mother, also give rise to potential contradictions in the maternal function… What seems important to highlight is that the discourse on the ability of women to procreate, based on genetics and “biological facts”, are automatically projected onto another field of maternal experience: the rearing and education of children. Whereas it is a matter of fact that women are biologically constituted to produce offspring and feed them, the discourse on the biological constitution of women has nothing to do with the more subtle moral aspects of the maternal role, which is a cultural phenomenon and stems from a desire for order and social control. The fact that maternal love is considered a trans-historical fact of human existence does not provide proof that this attitude is universal. In other words, if it is a fact of nature that women are geared for motherhood, the way women have performed this role for centuries, including moral attitudes and social expectations, has little to do with biological facts and is probably a cultural phenomenon that derives from the male gaze on femininity and maternity. To sum up, the discourse on motherhood can be emancipated from social and cultural myths only on condition that women manage to find their own way of living this experience and arrive at a personal understanding of the interplay between social and cultural representations, on the one hand, their own expectations, values and social and cultural condition, on the other hand. In this way, the narrow dichotomy good mother/degenerate mother may acquire a host of intermediate evaluations thanks to which it is possible to understand the difference that exists between womanhood and motherhood. This discourse – which has been popular from the times of ancient Greece up to the present but also informs (albeit in part) the technical jargon of psychoanalysis – presents motherhood as the apotheosis of femininity and leads mothers into assuming a role which is functional to the stability of the family and social order… In the case of these hetero/hypernomic women, who tend to abide by social norms, play the established social roles and hide their inner conflicts and tensions, myths of motherhood contribute to suppress the contradiction which is intrinsic to motherhood itself making this contradiction invisible but still painful and hence uncontrollable and potentially devastating. The conception of motherhood as the fulfillment of female nature, rather than a period of existential crisis characterized by the dichotomy between social expectations – “how I should be” – and personal experience – “how do I feel with regard to this new situation” – is at the heart of this contradiction.The above analysis is summarized in the below bullet points:Patriarchal cultures have limited women by believing that all women “gain what they lack” through motherhood - this reinforces systematic oppressioni.e., Motherhood was/is positioned as a fulfillment of an innate need for all femalesThe ability of women to procreate was used as an excuse to automatically project the traits of motherhood unto all women - this created a myth, which insisted that motherhood is a “biological fact” instead of being a subjective choiceThe truth is, motherhood is part of a woman’s identity - motherhood is not the only identity that women have nor is it the most important one - identity is based on an individual, not genitalia or genderNeither gender or sex determines one’s destiny and/or roleMotherhood is not a necessity in order to gain Womanhood; women are not women just because they have childrenThe mindset that all women gain status/identity/what they lack through motherhood is literally equating women to cattle; “women should be bred as soon as possible because it is in their nature to be mothers. Whatever else they do in life is of little significance” - that’s a deranged and sick way to think about 50% of the world’s population.As someone that has parents who were not able to have children on their own (I’m adopted), people who think that women can only have fulfilling lives by reproducing is just as infuriating and harmful for women who have fertility issues. As a woman, I am disgusted that society seems to be so obsessed with what women do with their uteruses in general. As the daughter of a woman who struggled with emotional pain that her infertility caused her, I am angry at the implications that this type of thinking projects onto women who cannot become pregnant or who suffer miscarriage after miscarriage. My mother is not only my mother, she is also one of the bravest and most capable people I know. My mother being my mother is not her story; it is part of her story. Furthermore, my mother was treated poorly by most that she knew, including her family, when she first told them she might not be able to get pregnant. My mother’s own family ignored that my mother had graduated at the top of her class in high school and college, that she had started a construction company with my father with no help outside of a bank loan in a town where no one knew her or my father in her early 30s…none of that mattered - my mother was judged and looked down on because she was not able to become pregnant. The beliefs that this question asks about - "a woman's life will be complete once she gives birth to a baby" - not only shames those who are voluntarily not having children, it also shames women who have fertility issues: [9]Individuals who learn they are infertile often experience the normal but nevertheless distressing emotions common to those who are grieving any significant loss — in this case the ability to procreate. Typical reactions include shock, grief, depression, anger, and frustration, as well as loss of self-esteem, self-confidence, and a sense of control over one's destiny. Relationships may suffer — not only the primary relationship with a spouse or partner, but also those with friends and family members who may inadvertently cause pain by offering well-meaning but misguided opinions and advice. Couples dealing with infertility may avoid social interaction with friends who are pregnant and families who have children. They may struggle with anxiety-related sexual dysfunction and other marital conflicts. There are about 40 ways to treat infertility. About 85% to 90% of patients are treated with conventional methods, including advice about timing of intercourse, drug therapy to promote ovulation or prevent miscarriages, and surgery to repair reproductive organs. Only about 3% of patients make use of more advanced assisted reproductive technology such as in vitro fertilization (IVF). While medical interventions offer much-needed help and hope, studies suggest that they may also add to the stress, anxiety, and grief that patients are already experiencing from infertility itself… Treatment failure…may trigger a renewed cycle of grieving and distress. The distress may be especially severe for patients living in Western developed nations such as the United States, where the cultural assumption is that anyone who works hard and is persistent will succeed in achieving a goal.In summary, I think that the belief that "a woman's life will be complete once she gives birth to a baby" is a common societal judgement. Furthermore, I think that this belief is harmful and dehumanizing for many reasons, but specifically because women are taught that if they can’t have children naturally or do not have children voluntarily that something is wrong with them. This reflects how society does not value women as individuals; society values women if they carry out their prescribed roles - that is unacceptable.Footnotes[1] Childlessness Up Among All Women; Down Among Women with Advanced Degrees[2] http://www.readcube.com/articles/10.1007/s11199-016-0606-1?shared_access_token=o5-yjTCSXk2gmjGnHJtq-_e4RwlQNchNByi7wbcMAY6f7ucxWO4RvrMbWtzmxG22tYu1HcZulOE27rEa8ZrIws19coFsI0U8KTc4JHiFZ85O0Zvk2L8M9qN3nBZH-Azs_BLXZRS_b1kDadIYYk6PEy2UJRq8VN9IHTjs23JInPE%3D[3] Are Childfree Adults "Selfish"?[4] Should we care that smart women aren't having kids? | Sadhbh Walshe[5] https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3764615/[6] Child-free women feel intense pressure to have kids, but rarely stress over it[7] We need to detach the myth of motherhood from the reality | Angela Saini[8] http://www.scielosp.org/pdf/aiss/v48n3/v48n3a08.pdf[9] The psychological impact of infertility and its treatment - Harvard Health

column1: What is depression?
column3: Depression (major depressive disorder) is a common and serious medical illness that negatively affects how you feel, the way you think and how you act. Fortunately, it is also treatable. Depression causes feelings of sadness and/or a loss of interest in activities you once enjoyed. It can lead to a variety of emotional and physical problems and can decrease your ability to function at work and at home. Depression symptoms can vary from mild to severe and can include:Feeling sad or having a depressed moodLoss of interest or pleasure in activities once enjoyedChanges in appetite — weight loss or gain unrelated to dietingTrouble sleeping or sleeping too muchLoss of energy or increased fatigueIncrease in purposeless physical activity (e.g., inability to sit still, pacing, handwringing) or slowed movements or speech (these actions must be severe enough to be observable by others)Feeling worthless or guiltyDifficulty thinking, concentrating or making decisionsThoughts of death or suicideSymptoms must last at least two weeks and must represent a change in your previous level of functioning for a diagnosis of depression. Also, medical conditions (e.g., thyroid problems, a brain tumor or vitamin deficiency) can mimic symptoms of depression so it is important to rule out general medical causes. Depression affects an estimated one in 15 adults (6.7%) in any given year. And one in six people (16.6%) will experience depression at some time in their life. Depression can occur at any time, but on average, first appears during the late teens to mid-20s. Women are more likely than men to experience depression. Some studies show that one-third of women will experience a major depressive episode in their lifetime. There is a high degree of heritability (approximately 40%) when first-degree relatives (parents/children/siblings) have depression. Depression Is Different From Sadness or Grief/Bereavement The death of a loved one, loss of a job or the ending of a relationship are difficult experiences for a person to endure. It is normal for feelings of sadness or grief to develop in response to such situations. Those experiencing loss often might describe themselves as being “depressed.” But being sad is not the same as having depression. The grieving process is natural and unique to each individual and shares some of the same features of depression. Both grief and depression may involve intense sadness and withdrawal from usual activities. They are also different in important ways:In grief, painful feelings come in waves, often intermixed with positive memories of the deceased. In major depression, mood and/or interest (pleasure) are decreased for most of two weeks.In grief, self-esteem is usually maintained. In major depression, feelings of worthlessness and self-loathing are common.In grief, thoughts of death may surface when thinking of or fantasizing about “joining” the deceased loved one. In major depression, thoughts are focused on ending one’s life due to feeling worthless or undeserving of living or being unable to cope with the pain of depression.Grief and depression can co-exist For some people, the death of a loved one, losing a job or being a victim of a physical assault or a major disaster can lead to depression. When grief and depression co-occur, the grief is more severe and lasts longer than grief without depression. Distinguishing between grief and depression is important and can assist people in getting the help, support or treatment they need. What Depression May Feel Like Many people believe that depression needs to be debilitating and cause significant problems in their life in order to seek help. What they don’t realize is that some of the more subtle signs of this disorder are often the first indication that something is going on. Here are some examples of how depression may feel to you.Depression feels like there is no pleasure or joy in life. According to Anjani Amladi, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist, it’s so much more than being sad. According to Amladi, “depression robs people of things they once loved, and for many people, they feel like nothing will bring them joy again.”Concentration and focus become much more difficult, which makes any kind of decision-making challenging. Amladi says that sometimes people describe this as being in a fog as they are unable to think clearly or follow what is happening around them.For many with depression, it feels like there is no way out. Everything feels hopeless like there is no light at the end of the tunnel. Amladi says this can lead to a feeling of failure and worthlessness. In more serious cases, it can lead to suicidal thoughts or actions.Depression also has a significant impact on sleep. This often manifests as trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, frequent nighttime awakening, or feeling tired upon waking despite getting an adequate number of hours of sleep. “This can lead to a feeling of exhaustion and low energy which can prevent people from even being able to get out of bed, or perform daily activities like showering, eating and brushing their teeth,” Amladi says.Sometimes depression can be physically painful. Amladi says it is not unusual for people with depression to feel body aches, headaches, muscle tension, and even nausea. How It Feels According to People With DepressionLeela R. Magavi, MD, psychiatrist, and regional medical director for Community Psychiatry, says the most common question asked in her practice is: "How does depression feel?" “Some people ask me this question for comfort and to ensure that they are not alone with their experience, while others feel so confused by their tumultuous feelings that they struggle to clearly identify their inner experience,” she says. With that in mind, here are some of the responses Magavi hears in her sessions:"Depression feels like a weight on my chest, which brings me down everywhere I go.""Depression is receiving praise at work but still feeling worthless.""Depression is the loneliness I feel when I see other couples and families laughing and enjoying their lives.""Depression is feeling like I am a failure as a person, family member, and friend.""Depression is when I cannot take care of my children because I cannot take care of myself.""Depression is not brushing my hair and teeth because I simply cannot move.""Depression is smiling when others laugh, hiding behind the fabricated mask, and wishing I could just disappear.""Depression is my life and shadow, which haunts me every day."Christian Sismone, someone who has dealt with depression and anxiety her entire life, says it’s important to provide a non-clinical perspective. She shares these examples:“Depression makes my mind feel like a turtle running in chunky peanut butter.” Sismone says this is most evident when she is not able to have clear thoughts.“Depression feels like I'm suffocating in my emotions, and at times I feel as though I can breathe, but only through a straw.” Being someone who attempted to end their life 10 years ago, Sismone says the complicated emotion of depression can feel too great.“Depression can feel like an old friend that doesn't quite fit, but you know the ins and outs.” For Sismone, learning how to work with depression instead of running away from it, helped her move forward.

column1: According to your opinion, Which is the best character in Naruto Shippuden and why?
column3: Tobirama senju 千手扉間 Senju TobiramaSecond Hokage (二代目火影, Nidaime Hokage)Tobirama Senju (千手扉間, Senju Tobirama) was a member of the renowned Senju clan, who, together with his elder brother and the Uchiha clan, founded the first shinobi village: Konohagakure. Throughout his lifetime, Tobirama would work tirelessly to achieve political stability and implement the institutions that made the village system work, thus ensuring Konoha's continuity and prosperity. After his brother's death, he would succeed the title of Second Hokage(二代目火影, Nidaime Hokage, Literally meaning:Second Fire Shadow 千手扉間 Senju TobiramaSecond Hokage (二代目火影, Nidaime Hokage)Tobirama and his family. Tobirama was born during the Warring States Period, and was the second of Butsuma Senju's four sons. He and his brothers grew up on the battlefield waging constant war with their rivalling clans especially the Uchiha. After the deaths of their brothers: Kawaramaand later Itama, Tobirama and his older brother, Hashirama, decided a new shinobi system would need to be implemented to end the cycle of child deaths — a system that would require an alliance between the warring clans. [5] At some point in time, it became apparent that Hashirama got into the habit of disappearing into the forest for extended periods, and as such, Tobirama accepted his father's assignment to follow Hashirama and find out what he was doing.From tracking Hashirama, Tobirama discovered that he was meeting with a boy named Madara: a young Uchiha. After Tobirama reported this to their father, Butsuma pressured Hashirama to lead Madara into an ambush to be carried out by himself and Tobirama. Upon springing the trap, however, they were met by Madara's family — who had similar plans and while their fathers clashed — Tobirama fought Izuna Uchiha: Madara's younger brother. [6] Hashirama and Madara were able to negotiate a temporary ceasefire, allowing all of them to walk away without bloodshed. In the years following their families would continue to clash, Hashirama against Madara and Tobirama against Izuna. On one occasion Tobirama eventually mortally wounded Izuna.Tobirama about to kill Madara. Hashirama, by then the leader of the Senju, tried to use Izuna's fate to broker peace between their clans, but Madara — at Izuna's behest — refused. His refusal increasingly became the minority view, with individual Uchiha siding with the Senju in growing numbers. After Izuna succumbed to his injuries, Madara, wracked with grief, made one final stand against the Senju and was summarily defeated. Tobirama attempted to kill Madara to finally end the fighting, but Hashirama stopped him, knowing that would only renew hostilities between the Senju and Uchiha. Madara offered to surrender if Hashirama would kill himself or Tobirama. [7] Hashirama agreed to take his own life, and as he made preparations he instructed Tobirama, despite his protests, not to seek retribution. Madara ultimately withdrew his request and agreed to peace. The Senju, the Uchiha, and all their affiliated clans came together to found Konoha, a village of peace where children would never need to die in battle. [8] Although Hashirama was optimistic about the village's future, Tobirama remained realistic about how that future would be achieved knowing that it was not enough to simply bring all these clans together. He believed the Uchiha — Madara in particular — threatened that future. When Hashirama wanted to give Madara the position of Hokage, Tobirama forced him to open the selection to a democratic process rather than appointing a leader, leading to Hashirama's election instead. [9] Tobirama would continue to act as the voice of reason throughout Hashirama's tenure; during the first Kage Summit, Hashirama wanted to give Konoha's tailed beasts to the other newly-formed villages for free, but Tobirama insisted that the villages pay for the tailed beasts they received. [10] Under Hashirama's leadership, the new system of ninja villages achieved peace for a time. Eventually, Tobirama started training his own three-man teamconsisting of Hiruzen Sarutobi, Homura Mitokado, and Koharu Utatane. [11] Techniques he had created, such as the Shadow Clone Technique and Summoning: Impure World Reincarnation, he outlawed, their use no longer being needed. But peace would ultimately be temporary as Madara challenged Hashirama's authority and the two fought at what would become the Valley of the End. When Madara was killed in the battle, Tobirama took his body in order to study the Sharingan, and then buried it in an unmarked grave. [12] Conflicts would start emerging elsewhere in the world, and it was during one of these that Hashirama would die. [1] Before his death, he passed the title of Hokage to Tobirama and left him instructions to not mistreat the Uchiha. [13] Tobirama's role as Hokage included helping Konoha's shinobi transition from valuing their clan above all else to valuing the village and everyone in it. [14] To this end he created such institutions as the Academy, the Anbu, and the Chūnin Exams. While largely successful, enough that other villages adopted the same organisations, [3] the Uchiha resisted the loss of their autonomy. Already wary of the Uchiha because of his history with Madara, Tobirama created the Konoha Military Police Forcefor the Uchiha to run, publicly as a sign of trust but primarily so that the Uchiha could focus their energies into something beneficial. Others, however, would come to see this as a way to marginalise the clan. [15]Tobirama and his team during the First Shinobi World War. Like Hashirama before him, Tobirama tried to foster good relations with the other villages. He planned an alliance between Konoha and Kumogakure, but during a formal ceremony he and the Second Raikage were attacked by the Gold and Silver Brothers and left near death. [16] During the First Shinobi World War, Team Tobirama, as well as Danzō Shimura, Torifu Akimichi, and Kagami Uchiha found themselves surrounded by Kumo's Kinkaku Force. With no way for all of them to escape, Tobirama volunteered to act as a decoy in place of Hiruzen. As he departed, he passed the title of Hokage to Hiruzen, [17] before being killed by Kinkaku. [18]Personality Tobirama was a composed individual with a pragmatic approach to life. He believed that, through well-defined rules and laws, many of the world's problems could be solved. [5] In many ways he was a counter-weight to his older brother Hashirama's ideals; when Hashirama would get carried away with his headstrong optimism, it fell to Tobirama to mediate and force a more realistic alternative in order to achieve those idealistic goals. Hashirama was typically disappointed by Tobirama's intervention, but he usually agreed without much protest; [19] on the rare occasions he disagreed, it was a sign that Tobirama's methods were becoming too forceful, creating a mutual balance. [20] Tobirama likewise, despite how often he needed to undermine his brother and his personal opinion that Hashirama was something of an idiot, [21] greatly loved and respected him, and if anything wanted Hashirama to respect himself the same way he and others did. [22]Tobirama enraged by Sasuke's intent to destroy Konoha. Tobirama was a firm believer in the Will of Fire — a philosophy that held that all villagers of Konoha were part of a family. Any who threatened Konoha were subject to his rarely-seen but unbridled rage. [23] As Hokage, it was not only his responsibility to protect that family at all costs but also to encourage the disparate villagers of the same view: to move away from the idealism of only think about their clan and that they should think of the village as a whole. [14] It was for this reason that he came into conflict with the Uchiha and Madara so frequently, as he felt they too often valued their own desires over others'. [24] This often gave him the appearance of being prejudiced against the clan and its members, [25] but he was in fact perfectly capable of spotting and happy to cooperate with any Uchiha that could overcome their "Curse of Hatred"; he cited Kagami Uchiha as a perfect example of this transcended Uchiha. [26] In addition, when Madara was about to kill Sasuke, who was the last living Uchiha with the potential to restore the clan - Tobirama pleaded with him to stop, and displayed great anger towards him when he fatally injured Sasuke, and lamented his inability to use his kinjutsu to send his soul to aid Sasuke; [27] and later used the knowledge he gained from studying Madara's corpse to help Kabuto Yakushi heal Sasuke; showing that despite his continuous conflict with the Uchiha, Tobirama still cared about their well-being and had no desire to see the clan go extinct. He also later expressed happiness when Hashirama and Madara settled their differences as their reincarnated forms were being dispelled. Tobirama believed that aspects from both Hashirama and Madara's extreme personalities were necessary components to being Hokage: Hashirama’s indulgent nature and Madara’s ruthlessness. Learning from them, he tried to find a balance between Hashirama and Madara as he didn't have someone to balance him out, unlike his brother. Though they only knew each other for a short time, Tobirama and Minato Namikaze, the Fourth Hokage, got along superbly. Their mutual respect for each other seemed founded on their similarities: both of them famously moving and thinking quickly on the battlefield. [28] [29] While their actual personalities were quite different, Tobirama was nevertheless amused by Minato's quirks such as his complicated names for techniques, such as the "Spiralling Flash Super Round Dance Howl Style Three". [30] Befitting his composed and pragmatic nature, Tobirama was a stern man who spoke bluntly about most topics, never sugar-coating facts or the matter at hand. He was reasonable more than anything, remaining calm and even-handed in all situations, having acted as the voice of reason to his brother throughout his reign. He believed in letting bygones be bygones if it meant an end to needless death and conflict, reprimanding Itama for believing otherwise and claiming that such a mindset would only lead to him ending up dead. Nonetheless, he allowed his past experiences with Madara to affect his judgment of the Uchiha clan in many instances, and he never got rid of his suspicious attitude towards them during his lifetime. He could also be too far-sighted and ruthlessly pragmatic at times, having created the Summoning: Impure World Reincarnation, in spite of its extremely vile nature, as well as building the Konoha Military Police Force outpost within the Uchiha's compound, which, while giving them more autonomy, cut them off from having any political influence in the village. While not one to get blinded or hindered by emotion or petty notions, he had a streak of pride which presents itself in comical manners at times: he insisted Naruto use proper honourifics when addressing him and chided Naruto for claiming techniques Tobirama created as his father's and his own. He also got embarrassed when Hashirama forced his opinion on him in front of others. column1: Does anyone feel that after learning about narcissistic personality disorder you’re worse off than you were before learning about the disorder?
column3: It's tricky. Short term? Without question. Where it's tricky is that symptoms of narcissistic abuse can also include symptoms of Complicated Grief. Complicated grief - Symptoms and causes [ https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/complicated-grief/symptoms-causes/syc-20360374 ] In complicated grief, painful emotions are so long lasting and severe that you have trouble recovering from the loss and resuming your own life. Different people follow different paths through the grieving experience. The order and timing of these phases may vary from person to person: * Accepting the reality of your loss * Allowing yourself to experience the pain of your loss * Adjusting to a new reality in which the deceased is no longer present * Having other relationships These differences are normal. But if you're unable to move through these stages more than a year after the death of a loved one, you may have complicated grief. If so, seek treatment. It can help you come to terms with your loss and reclaim a sense of acceptance and peace. I'm not a licensed professional, so I won't get into that which I am not qualified to address. However, the link posted has some very good information regarding a condition that is very real and debilitating. For NPD Abuse Survivors, complicated grief can be even further exacerbated with the utter mind fuck of waking up to the reality that someone we loved never really existed. In the long term? No. I'm better off knowing. Even better than before, actually. The rewards of recovery give survivors a perspective of truth. Truth is the foundation for healing and thriving. It takes time and effort to reach that paradigm, but I was far better off knowing exactly what happened to me, so I could face the true challenge of conquering the survival of that experience. Is it painful? Of course. Our abusers intended it to hurt as much as possible, so we would forever...

column1: If you are a transgender person who has transitioned, and lived in your true gender for a long time, do you ever grieve for your former self?
column3: What former self? I’m still me. I’ll answer this in two parts, external view, and internal view.EXTERNAL VIEW ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ My wife grieved over my former self, as soon as she found out I was transgender, even two years before I started gender non-conformity in public, and four years before I started estrogen HRT. For several years, I was very confused by her response. To me, I was still the same person. “I’m still here!” To her, the person she thought she knew, had never existed.It's me Oh baby, it's me How in the world can tenderness be gone In the blink of an eye? … The girl in me, she's calling out Oh, the girl in me she's calling out To the boy in you... To the boy To the boy in you... Baby come back... Baby come back to me. — Sara Groves, “It’s Me” (YouTube)After several years, I realised and understood. In psychology, this is called complicated grief, and it can be debilitating over a period of years. I hadn’t lied to her about who I was, or at least no more than I’d lied to myself. I’d pushed my female gender identity under layers of denial for three decades. Though I hadn’t betrayed her, she felt betrayed. She had good reason to feel betrayed. From my wife’s point of view, my former self was gone. It would have been easier for her if I had died. The grief was enormous, and complicated by the following factors:Implicit sense of betrayal and blameNo funeralNo support groups and no help for spouses of transgender peopleReligious conservatives are utterly useless at providing personal emotional support to the spouses and families of LGBTQ peopleMarginalisation in her religious subculture … social isolationQuestioning her own identity and beliefsBroken dreamsSeparation and divorceStill seeing me for co-parentingSimilar issues lead to complicated grief for friends, parents, siblings and children of transgender people. Complicated grief is not a foregone conclusion. Many relationships adjust to gender transition after a normal period of grieving. Prepubescent children often experience no grief at all. When the normal healthy grief process is broken, it tends to break very badly. My wife grieved for my former self, who she thought I was.Naomi Lauren's answer to Does marriage end when one partner transitions?INTERNAL VIEW ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ The grief a transgender person experiences in gender transition, is the grief of lost relationships. Lost through misunderstandings, antagonism, fear, hate, controlling behaviour, lack of acceptance, uncomfortable distance, misgendering of pronouns, and deadnaming. That grief and loss we experience is enormous, but like most grief, it fades with time, whereas the pain of untreated gender dysphoria only gets worse with passing years and decades. My gender transition is not a change of who I am. It’s the fulfillment of who I am. Using a yin-yang diagram as analogy for gender identity, each man (upper left) has a seed of the feminine within him, and each woman (lower right) has the seed of the masculine within her. This is referred to as the Anima and Animus in Jungian psychology. In common parlance, this is referred to as:A man’s inner-feminineA woman’s inner-masculineIn heterosexual dating, it’s “normal” for a man to express his inner-feminine vicariously through his partner, because he doesn’t feel allowed to express his own feminine traits himself. The same occurs in reverse, and living vicariously through someone else is not entirely healthy, but it’s what we do. What is “normal” does not necessarily mean either good or healthy.By comparison, before gender transition, this is how my inner landscape looked, keeping my enormous inner feminine inside me, barely contained within the masculine shell approved by society.Does that look a tad uncomfortable? It’s worse than uncomfortable. It was a constant stress and pressure to keep my feminine self locked up inside. Over years and decades, that pressure grew stronger, and the stress mounted. In gender transition, from a psychological perspective, all I’ve done is:Taken my enormous inner-feminine, and put it on the outside.Taken my scant outer-masculine, and put it on the inside.That sounds easier than it is. It’s actually scary and new and disorienting, and it takes 2 to 5 years to complete, but immediately there is a sense of RELIEF. There’s room to move. There’s a reduction in chronic stress and distress. There’s a sense of authenticity, and a feeling that we are actually seen for who we really are. Both my feminine and masculine traits were there before transition. Identical feminine and masculine traits are there now after transition. The only difference is that I now display and express my feminine traits, to the praise or condemnation of society. My masculine psychological traits are all still there, but are somewhat more hidden now, because our gender binary society PUNISHES people who are not clearly men, or clearly women. My feminine side desperately needs human acknowledgement and recognition. That is a human need. Without it babies die, and adults wither.Naomi Lauren's answer to Are there people that don't strongly identify with either gender?Though I don’t like wearing skirts, nor makeup, nor heels, my authentic feminine self needs to be seen. Though I utilise a bare minimum of the trappings of the female role, I need to participate in our gender binary society through the female role. I need acceptance as a woman. My outer-feminine that people can now clearly see, was always there inside me. My inner-masculine that used to be on the outside, lives more-or-less happily on the inside. He hasn’t gone anywhere. :-)

column1: What should the spouse or partner of someone with complicated grief know?
column3: Firstly let me say to anyone who is dealing with a spouse or partner whose grief is complicated; you will need to be prepared to deal with an emotional rollercoaster and it will either strengthen your relationship or tear it to pieces. ‘Complicated grief is considered when an individual’s ability to resume normal activities and responsibilities is continually disrupted beyond six months of bereavement’. By this definition, your spouse or partner is experiencing profound loss made worse by various factors such as; The dynamics of the relationship with the deceased. If the relationship was complicated before death, it’s going to become more so. Any areas of discord that were present will be deeply regretted. There no longer exists an opportunity to solve disagreements and guilt will form because of this. Even if the disagreements were slight, the bereaved will magnify them until they berate themselves constantly. As the partner, your job is to listen, allow them to freely express those dark thoughts whilst resisting the urge to tell them not to feel guilty. Reminding them of all the good things that were done and said may help them to focus on positive thoughts. The trauma surrounding the death. If the death of a loved one was sudden and totally unexpected, trauma will be present. Death can be shocking at the best of times but loosing a child for example will have far reaching consequences. Loosing a child whether young or older will devastate most parents and although the definition of complicated grief states six months, that is conservative in my experience. It will take six months just to unfurl from under the blanket of shock and acceptance won’t be on the radar before a year at least. The bereaved’s coping skills and communication style. If your partner’s ability to cope with everyday stresses was good before the loss then that will help them form strategies to cope now. Not having the ability to cope with stress requires help from the professionals. You need to be the rock they can cling to during this storm. If your partner is good at expressing their feelings then you should listen without judgement, nor should you offer solutions because these feelings don’t follow a linear pathway. Thoughts and emotions will run in ever decreasing circles and you may hear the same things over and over. Inability to care for themselves. This is where you can be of practical help as your job is to make sure that your partner is eating, taking care of personal hygiene and getting out of bed even for a while. Grief is exhausting as the adrenal glands will be depleted and any pain will be felt acutely. You may have to be prepared to do all the housework, cooking and cleaning plus being the sole parent to any children you may have. Caring for yourself. This actually is the most important point and it should be the first thing that you do. If you don’t look after your own mental and physical health then you can’t look after anyone else. What use is it for you to become ill and stressed? You may also be grieving and although your partner’s grief may be taking top priority now, you must be able to talk about how you are feeling so I suggest seeing a bereavement counsellor or joining a group for the bereaved. My thoughts are with anyone who finds themselves in this situation.

column1: Is it normal to still be struggling 7 or 8 years later after losing your mother even though you were an adult with children when she died?
column3: The short answer is yes. Grief is very personal and extraordinarily individual. Personally, I don’t think we really grow up until we lose a parent. The long answer is more complex - did your mom have a complicated death? Losing a parent is one of the most distressing and, unfortunately, common experiences people face. Most people experiencing normal grief and bereavement have a period of sorrow, numbness, and even guilt and anger Gradually these feelings ease, and it's possible to accept loss and move forward. For some people, feelings of loss are debilitating and don't improve even after time passes. This is known as complicated grief, sometimes called persistent complex bereavement disorder. In complicated grief, painful emotions are so long lasting and severe that you have trouble recovering from the loss and resuming your own life. Different people follow different paths through the grieving experience. The order and timing of these phases may vary from person to person: Accepting the reality of your loss Allowing yourself to experience the pain of your loss Adjusting to a new reality in which the deceased is no longer present Having other relationships These differences are normal. But if you're unable to move through these stages more than a year after the death of a loved one, you may have complicated grief. If so, seek treatment. It can help you come to terms with your loss and reclaim a sense of acceptance and peace. This is known as complicated grief, sometimes called persistent complex bereavement disorder. I suffered from this when my dad died in January of 2017. A therapist that specializes in grief is going to be helpful.

column1: How long does it take for the urge to contact my ex narcissist to go away after the discard?
column3: Healing and moving on from pathological narcissistic abuse requires immense inner strength, the very strength that narcissists systematically try to strip from their victims. Survivors must rebuild what they’ve lost, or create what was never created in the first place. That is not an easy feat, but it is an attainable goal; something that must be done for personal sanity and peace of mind. It doesn’t seem fair. Survivors must do all the work; they need extensive counseling, must stay dignified under the pressure of unfair judgment, must take actions that feel contrary to their natural behavior or inclinations, and must accept the reality that they will never make sense out of the irrational behavior exhibited by their narcissistic abuser. Following are tips for getting over Narcissistic abuse. Learn grounding techniques and self-soothing methods Narcissistic abuse is an emotional trauma. It targets your primal abandonment wound. When you feel betrayed, rejected, and abandoned by the Narcissist, your amygdala hijacks your your rational thinking and sends you into fight-or-flight mode. You have a thought (I’ve been rejected because I’m not good enough), you experience an emotion from that thought (panic, sadness, depression), and then you run with it like a Running Back on crack with blinders on. Yeah…you’ll want to stop doing that. There’s not a lot you can do to prevent this from happening completely, but practicing self-soothing methods and grounding techniques will help damper this emotional hijack if repeated consistently. The best techniques are the same ones used to help with PTSD triggers and emotional trauma. Learning to self-soothe is the critical first step because otherwise, any activities you engage in to heal and move forward will be drained away by the emotional hijacking caused by your amygdala. Make sure you’ve implemented No Contact in its true form Once the Narcissist successfully reaches out and provokes a response, it’s back to square one. (If children are involved, a very strict plan for modified contact should be legally documented, entered, and enforced). Remember, narcissists are smug in their belief that you will surrender to their manipulations. Not going No Contact is the equivalent of volunteering in purgatory, where you’ll waste years of your life. Do you really want that? Probably not. Work on your self-esteem The number one, most important thing to realize is that the perceived rejection from your abuser is an illusion. Narcissists strive to take away every last shred of your self-esteem because that’s how they keep you hooked…to keep you thinking, “I am damaged goods. Better to have someone who treats me like crap than no one at all”. Remember, most of what comes out of their mouth is a lie, including the negative things they say about you. Seek professional help if you believe you may suffer from any form of psychological neurosis, such as complicated grief (Please note – complicated grief used to be attributed strictly to bereavement, but medical professionals now know that it can apply to any type of traumatic loss).

column1: Why is it that almost four years after my mother’s passing, I still cannot get over it, and it still hurts a lot? I miss her so terribly much.
column3: You are not alone. There are others that have experienced this type of grief. It’s called Complicated grief - Symptoms and causes . The causes of complicated grief haven’t been completely discovered. It’s likely that this is similar to other emotional disorders, where there are genetic, environmental and situational factors that contribute to being stuck. Your best choice as a first step would be to seek counseling, and a support group. Follow the directions of your doctor. I also think it’s in your best interests to accept that death is something you accept, not something you get over. It happens, and there is nothing anybody can do about it. It’s normal to miss what we have lost, and to feel helpless about having no power in the situation. We just have to learn to adapt. I am so sorry for the loss of your mother, and the continual intense suffering you’re experiencing.

column1: What indicates that grief manifested into complicated grief?
column3: There are three main features that distinguish complicated grief from normal grief. These features interfere with processing grief as follows:Ruminating. Rumination is similar to obsessing. One will ruminate about the circumstances of the loss. This may involve a lot of self blame, blame of others, or blame towards the lost loved one.Catastrphic Expectation. The person worries about what will happen now that the loved one is gone. Painful scenarios are conjured up.Avoidance. Pictures, conversations, keepsakes concerning the loved one are avoided.Each of these features would interfere with the grief process. Blame and anger from rumination would conflict with feeling the sadness and forgiveness one needs to feel. Worry about the future in catastrophic expectation takes one away from the here and now, removing oneself from one's feelings and replacing them with anxieties about a grim future. Avoidance obviously removes one from being reminded of the grief, as well as from the feelings one needs to feel.

column1: What is the most emotional and real incident you have ever faced?
column3: I was in Pondicherry with my friends and we were playing Cards and were enjoying a lot. I had kept my mobile to charge since the battery was low and I was completely involved in games. It was 3am when I came back to see my mobile and I had received 37 missed calls. I called back and I got to know that My friend had passed away due to dengue. I was shattered and completely blank and nothing I could do from there. Few days later, I came back to my native and I saw his parents. Bereavement, Mourning, Grief, and Complicated Grief Few days after his death, his sister gave a birth to baby boy. She was not even interested to see her baby. We all went to his father and started telling that “This new baby is your son. Your daughter gave birth to your son again” . His dad for almost 15 days ,did not even come out of his house and always looking at his Son's photo. Didn't even cry. He started crying when he saw his daughter's baby. Children take on great symbolic importance in terms of parents' generativity and hope for the future. All parents have dreams about their children's futures. When a child dies the dreams may die too. Three central themes in parents' experience when a child dies include the loss of sense of personal competence and power, the loss of a part of the self , and the loss of a valued other person whose unique characteristics were part of the family system. While guilt and self-blame are common in bereavement, they are especially pronounced following the death of a child. The parent's role competence as the child's caregiver, protector, and mentor is severely threatened by untimely death.

column1: Why does everyone deal with grief differently?
column3: Where do I start? There are many, many reasons. In training people in counselling skills in loss, I try to make the reasons as graphic as I can to show these. Draw a small circle, then another circle a bit bigger around it, then another circle around that and so in - will look like a donut with more rings. Then in the middle put yourself In the next circle around your ring - put those who are the closest to you - your inner circle. - your family usually and closest friends The next ring - colleagues from work/neighbours/ people you see regularly. The next ring - people you meet day to day, who you chat with - at the supermarket etc. Look at how many people you have on your chart. If you have lost someone close and your circles are full - they are in effect ‘circles of support’, people who will be there for you to call on. If you are an isolated older lady, maybe no children and have lost your husband. Your circles may be quite empty - less support. It is graphic - the more people in your life, the more support in dealing with your grief. Then take it further - look at your life - your ethnicity, your upbringing, your age, male/female, financial situation, religious believes - everything that makes you - you. Each will impact on your grief e.g.\ Children / youth / we know grieve differently to adults People can be left in financial hardship, following the loss of the wage earner - causing great stress Sometimes people who have religious believes get comfort from their believes, which help them to cope - Males often don’t open up as much as women (although this is getting better) THEN - there is complicated grief - Someone having an affair - loses their lover and can’t grief or go to funeral Someone who has had several close family losses close together - each one compounding the other. How the person died - suddenly, long slow illness, murder, suicide I am only scratching at the surface here, but hope you understand a little more on why people grieve differently.

column1: Can untreated complicated grief lead to self-destructive behavior?
column3: I am driven to answer this only because of the words “untreated” and “complicated”. Untreated implies that grief is an affliction or disease that can be treated. Complicated is a label that is so non-specific that it’s useless. My credentials are experiential and not professional. I have grieved the loss of a 40 something brother to suicide in 2000, followed by the sudden unforeseen death of a best friend and key employee in 2001, followed by the death of our 20 year old son in a firefighter training accident in 2005. All grief is complicated for the person experiencing it. Most of us lack significant experience with grief when it first grabs us, and there are precious few mentors and guides with experience. We avoid grief as something that is negative, yet in every well lived life of normal duration we will experience different degrees of grief. Here’s my simplified view of grief: We grieve because we love. No love, no grief. When we love someone, be it the love of friendship or the lifetime passionate lover or soulmate, we must logically accept that one of us will die before the other. Grief is the final responsibility of loving someone. We can learn much about life and love from loss of a loved one. Wisdom comes mostly from pain. The pain we feel in grief teaches us the true value of those we have loved and those we will love. Healing from grief is a choice we must make, a choice to not run away of close the doors on grief, but a choice to include the love of those we have lost in our lives going forward. Not healing from grief diminishes the enjoyment and value of our lives, so healing is important. Putting a timeline or defined path on healing from loss is impossible, because each journey through grief will be different, even among those grieving the same loss. Seek peace, seek love and allow your soul the time to heal itself. Your soul can carry immense scars gracefully and lovingly once it heals. Be well and peaceful

column1: How do therapists remember everything?
column3: Most therapists had to be fairly competent in school and in the United States had to attain a graduate degree, so their ability to retain information is already above the average. It is then extremely common for therapists to take notes after (and sometimes during) their sessions. They’re often not terribly extensive but are able to queue a more full memory when they read it. For example, I might just write some stray names of important people to my client with no other information on the off chance my notes ever get subpoenaed. If I’m being supervised, my notes have to be more thorough so my supervisor knows what I’m doing. For example, let’s say I had a meeting with a client who we’re processing grief with. Let’s assume it’s some complicated grief with a dead sibling who they had a contentious relationship with but who died suddenly. This client now finds that their sibling, after passing, has been idealized by their parents to the point that they no longer feel like a significant relationship exists between the client and their parents, so they’re mourning the loss of the entire family. My notes would be something along the lines of: “[Sibling name], grief. Feels abandoned by family. Follow up: friendships, extended family.” I’ll remember the client enough to be cued to everything we discussed by those notes I wrote immediately after the session. This has worked out so far with my client loads only being about 24ish clients. If I ever do full-time therapy, I might need to make my notes a bit more detailed to get by.

column1: What happens when someone with bipolar disorder loses a loved one?
column3: Just looking at the great article from The International Bipolar Foundation, Losing A Loved One ,… Going through the grieving process is very difficult for everybody. But for those who have bipolar, experiencing such a loss can be a very trying thing. The journey of grief can have lots of ups and downs and you might struggle to move on to the next stage of grief in a healthy, effective way. When you have bipolar disorder you're more likely to experience complicated grief. Complicated grief occurs when symptoms are more severe and tends to last a long time. Individuals with bipolar need to take time and space to grieve properly. That unfortunately, is not always possible for those in the workforce. You must take extra care of yourself at this time. Establishing a healthy routine can improve your well-being and make it easier for you to work through the stages of grief. Some of the best ways to deal with grief, when you have bipolar disorder include,.. expressing your true feelings to love ones. Finding an outlet to express yourself such as journalizing your feelings and emotions every day for at least 30 minutes. Exercising at least an hour a day. Eating a healthy diet. Not taking on any new commitments at this time. So all being said ,it's important to know that grief is a trigger for bipolar. There is some real potential for the manic state to kick in following bereavement or complicated grief. And as always counseling should be considered during this time to ease the grieving process for those with bipolar.

column1: What are your thoughts on Prolonged Grief disorder as an addition to the DSM? (Details in first two comments)
column3: My thought is that it fits in perfectly with the snapshot-in-time diagnostic criteria of every other DSM diagnosis. What I mean by this is, rather than accept symptoms as symptoms, the DSM has become such a steamrolling behemoth, with too much (financial) investment now in creating ‘disorders’, that its component work groups and committees must continue to create such in order to justify their own existence. In other words if I’m on the ‘Grief and Grieving Work Group’, of course I’m going to create some sort of disorder out of the ‘evidence’ before me, especially when the precedent is there for such non-specific criteria as ‘the presence of two of the following eleven criteria are present for more days than not over the course of six months’. This allows for the pathologizing of nearly every mental state. (Which subsequently allows for the monetization of nearly every mental state.) The simple truth is that in psychiatry we treat symptoms, not disorders. (But that of course would shrink the DSM back to its original fifty pages or so.) In the case of grief, or ‘prolonged grief’ or ‘bereavement disorder’, or ‘complicated grief’, or ‘complicated bereavement’, or choose your euphemism, they all boil down to depression in the context of loss. And for some people this depression will last longer than it will in others. I don’t think anyone needs a specialized work group of highly educated physicians and scientists to bargain and compromise their ways through their own psycho-pathologies to arrive at this simple homegrown knowledge.

column1: My friend told me that his brother passed away. How should I reply?
column3: I’m sorry your friend has lost his brother. I hope the following will help you comfort and care for your friend.Be a caring person for those who are grieving. Please be a light to someone grieving. It doesn’t take much. Here’s what may happen to the bereaved. The loneliness and pain during the first few months may cause them to isolate. Many become addicted to food, alcohol, drugs, spending, suicidal ideation and more. I believe addiction is a search for love, belonging, safety and acceptance—we all need and search for this, but more so for the grief-stricken. The grief-stricken can’t feel this—not for a time. I see this so vividly in the elderly and parents who have lost a child. Holidays are more salt in the wound. A caring person does not judge but checks in with the bereaved because loneliness is such a hellish part of grief—empty bed, no mealtime banter, songs that rip the heart out—holidays are the worst! My first Christmas after my husband died was bleak, empty and tear-filled. I couldn’t wait for Christmas to end! Sometimes faith is shattered. This is not the time to Bible thump. Your private prayer will work wonders. A hug and a little presence will too. A caring person builds trust and is safe for the grieving person to unload their tremendous burden. Rational thinking may not be there for some time. It’s another part of the grieving process. They will question everything they did or did not do, as if they could’ve prevented the death. Just reassure. A caring person may take them to lunch, a movie or bring a homemade meal. Shovel the walk. Walk their dog. Tell them a story about their deceased loved one. They matter. They need to find purpose. A caring person will not take outbursts of anger personally. A time-out is okay. Anger is part of the grieving process and part of healing, especially in the beginning. A caring person allows the grief-stricken their own space. Grief is not a “take this, do this, it’s about time to move on” experience. There are no steps to being grief-free. It takes a lot of time and is different for each person. They will never completely get over the loss. It’s part of who they are. They are learning how to have a different relationship with their deceased loved one. A caring person will check in with a grief counselor, hospice, pastor or someone qualified, should the grief be destroying the grief-stricken. They may be suffering from Complicated Grief or trauma. Listen to the experts and do what they advise. If your gut tells you they need emergency help, call 911 or a suicide hotline. I’d rather look foolish and bear their anger than lose them. It’s not easy. If it were, we’d all be caring people. Being as concerned as you are, you must be a very good friend.

column3: All the details are not evident in your question. However, therapists have ethical guidelines to follow for terminating. column1: It’s been 6 years since my dad left me but I'm just now missing him. I’ve had a private breakdown in the school bathroom 2 times by missing him and my depression is way worse. What do I do?
column3: When we deeply loved someone that we lost, grief is a natural part of the process. Even many years following the death of a loved one, we can sometimes be triggered by things like birthdays, anniversaries, etc. It’s normal for grief, like the tides, to ebb and flow. That being said, finding oneself in a deep depression after six years, or feeling debilitated by grief years after the loss, could mean that you are experiencing something called “complicated grief,” and my suggestion is that you talk to a counselor or another mental health practitioner. Sometimes we can navigate our way through complicated grief with talk therapy, and sometimes it requires more intensive treatment such as medication. I strongly advise you to see a professional that specializes in grief counseling. If it doesn’t work out, don’t give up! Another thing you can do that might help is to join a group called The Compassionate friends. They have chapters throughout the world. You can find information about them on Google or Wikipedia. They are a wonderful group of people that are suffering through many of the same issues you are experiencing. Participation is absolutely free. I hope this helps, and that you can find relief. Don’t allow your grief to take over your life. You can learn to cope with it but you will likely need to reach out.

column1: Why does grief sometimes bring up past traumas or old wounds?
column3: It does. It’s because we are so raw and vulnerable that everything comes to the surface. Like a tidal wave, it hits and knocks us down when it’s all we can do to get through our loss. Great! Another agonizing issue on top of the unthinkable. It is a big part of what is called Complicated Grief. Things we thought were dealt with, unconscious hurts and scars, disappointment with those you thought would be there for you, and that thing called “layers” give us sleepless nights and heavy hearts. Like the proverbial onion, we did deal with old trauma and wounds, but here they are again. It’s another unconscious event that pain and grief have said, “Deal with this.” Not today or tomorrow, but grief will have its way, eventually. You can bury it again. Drink, eat, and spend it away. Or, “Not this time, Pain. I’m going through Hell and I’m not staying.” With resolve, we chip away at it. I found the following quote by Yusif Ahmed helpful: “The darkest moments in life are often the ones that teach us the most. Just as a seed must crack open in darkness to reach the light, our minds must face negative thoughts to unlock the potential for growth and transformation. Embrace the shadows—they are the birthplace of your strength.” Hang on, pray, seek help, and it will pass with more knowledge and compassion as your helpmates. Blessings, comfort and peace.

column1: What are the dominant symptoms common to chronic grief?
column3: A state of chronic grief, more commonly referred to as “complicated grief,” is sometimes the case amongst individuals who have been coping with the loss of a loved one and seem unable to make any progress with the grieving process, usually after a minimum of one year’s time has passed following the death. The individual may experience prolonged depression and anxiety, an unhealthy desire to remain withdrawn from society, a preoccupation with death and particularly the events surrounding the death of their loved one (especially if the death was surrounded by traumatic circumstances), and a variety of other symptoms.

column1: What do young grieving males need the most?
column3: Grieving makes of all ages need a safe place of trust where they can open up without fear about their grief. Males are conditioned to feel weak when they are emotional, and grief is entirely emotion. As a result, most men won’t talk about their grief, it’s buried behind protective walls and has no outlet, especially other men. We, as a society, need to teach better grief before we need the tools to handle the loss of a loved one. As part of a couple that has grieved the loss of our 20 year old son since 2005, I know how isolating grief can be and understand the statistically very high divorce rate that grieving a child brings. But, grief at any time will change a person, we talk too much about returning to normal after loss and not enough about how we might learn and shape ourselves through grief. We see grief as an affliction that must end. We grieve because we love. No love, no grief. Deep love, deep and complicated grief. When we love someone, there is always the possibility that one of us will die before the other. The person we loved dies, our love for them doesn’t die. Grief is the final responsibility for loving someone. Grief will, if we allow it to, teach us about life and love in ways that we never imagined. But we need to talk about grief and to share stories of our love with each other so that all who grieve can learn from the loss. Young men, followed by men in general, have a deep fear of emotions that we cannot control, so we need to build a safe place of trust, a place without judgement, to encourage that journey. Ask simple questions, listen far more than you speak, share kind memories of the lost loved one, focus on the life not the death, and then ask more questions and listen again. Ask them how their lost loved one would want them to grieve this loss. That path will be easier than the one they will naturally choose for themselves. The loneliest time after any loss begins weeks after death when the rest of the world goes back to normal and the lack of normalcy in those grieving becomes isolating and overwhelming. So stay in for the longer term. Keep them safe, if they get dangerous to themselves or irresponsible, guide them quickly towards professional help. Be well, seek peace, and know that grief is love expressed by those who survive the loss. Grief is a beautiful emotion that honours life and love.
