column1: What lessons from trauma therapy can teach us about grief?
column3: Trauma therapy didn’t teach me about grief, my best friend committing suicide did! Here’s what I learned:It’s jagged. Don’t expect a straight line.The stages are for real and can come in any particular order.The only way out is through.It’s the most painful human emotion one can process.There are no shortcuts or one way through.It never disappears, only lingers in the distance.It’s the price for having loved.I’d do it again.Trauma itself comes with its own grief, however, and it’s more complicated than any other loss. It’s a loss of self. Grieving a loss of self comes with some additional attributes, some are listed as follows:Grief of loss of self is the most complicated grief of all.It’s often confused or comorbid with emotional disorders such as depression, PTSD, borderline personality disorder, and narcissism to name a few.It creates a deep sense of despair.The anger stage felt in this process resembles rage.Ruminating about what could have or should have been.An inability to forgive oneself.It is difficult for loved ones to approach someone in this state of Being, causing deeper isolation.Trauma induced grief is complicated and requires support from other people. It is wise to build a network of support people, so no one is particularly burdened with this challenging work as a supporter. Remember, no one else has the solutions, you do…inside. It’s about reclaiming what is lost, not finding it in another. If the grief includes a loss of self, it’s instrumental to take loving care of oneself. Be patient and kind to yourself. Know you’re not alone, we all experience self betrayal and there are many mechanisms available to support the journey into self alignment. You won’t get there through self and other shaming, though. This is a soft, not a tough, love calling! Godspeed! ***Share, expand upon, do not reproduce***

column1: What are the best ways to handle your grief independently?
column3: Understanding the possible experiences that may be symptoms of grief is a good place to start. They don’t necessarily go in any specific order but often include the following phases: Denial/Shock, Depression, Irritability/ Anger, Negotiation, and Acceptance. There are a couple of different models that are widely accepted and the things I listed above are generally included in both. Understanding that there’s really not “an appropriate amount of time” for someone to grieve is important, because we all process grief in different ways. People who still have past childhood traumas which remain unresolved have more of a tendency to have difficulty dealing with grief, but the significance of the lost relationship also matters (it’s typically more difficult to lose a spouse than a friend). Generally, most grieving for a death falls into the time-frame of a few months to a couple of years. Grief that extends into 3+ years is not healthy or normal. That’s not to say that a person’s sadness should be completely gone or dealt with, but hopefully it’s no longer something which still debilitates the person past the point of being able to get on with the normal activities of daily life. Sometimes people suffer such a great loss, or a series of losses all in a row, that they are said to have “complicated grief.” This kind of grief often requires professional help and/or temporary care under a psychiatrist to treat successfully. If left to your own devices, there are many self-help books available to help people better understand what they are experiencing and various methods of coping with your feelings.

column1: Is there any way to reduce whipsaws in a moving average based trading system?
column3: Your question refers to trends flattening into sideways markets. Solution is not in the signal. Disclaimer: i abandoned moving averages in 2010, precisely for that problem. I happily thrashed all indicators as well at the same time. They are redundant derivatives of price. Most market participants use a combination of 2 or 3 moving averages. Whether they use simple, weighted, triangular, harmonic or exponential, it is a variation on the same spaghetti with different sauces. I copiously backtested them all. None of them solve the core problem of flattening trend. Rule 1: complexity is a form of laziness. So adding Fibonacci, RSI or whatever makes it more fragile, not more robust. Keep your christmas trees for December Sequence of events: you follow a crossover. So, You are out. Then signal to get back in, then out. Flip flops like a career politician, lose a big portion of your previous gains. Immediately after giving up that thing breaks out again. Been there, not a happy place Change of perspective Solution is rarely in the signal itself. There are three types of trends: up, down, and sideways. Accept that there are sideways trends and deal with them. Here are four ways to get you through a sideways/range bound market:Define the range:Box dimensions: look for the lowest low since the beginning of the sideways market. That is the bottom of the range. look for the highest high since the beginning of the sideways. That is the top of the range. We have our box dimensions.If You are in a position && if longer MA is congruent with your position, lower than Long or higher than Short, suspend trading. Just hold still as long as price remains in the boxStop Loss: this is a good case where stop loss setting does matter. Once you have the dimensions of the box, place a stop loss n*ATR away so as to not to be triggered easily. Stop loss is likely to be a bit far from pricePenalty bet size: no-one knows when price enters a sideways market. So, you will probably suffer a few losses. If You do not want to see your gains evaporate, trade smaller, much smaller. We have a penalty ledger precisely for that purpose. We know we can’t avoid sideways so every time we hit a loss on an instrument, we reduce size next time. The rest is proprietary, sorryReject trades: distant stop loss combined with a depreciated risk budget makes positions smaller. We apply a rejection hurdle. Anything too small is a waste of ammo and should be discardedSo, as you can see, we are not trying to be cute with moving averages. We accept sideways for what they are: a big swamp. We accept initial flip-flop too. She looked nice and sweet but things did not work out. It’s complicated Mindset As Scott Phillips said MA systems have around 30% win rate through the cycle. This means YOU WILL FAIL 70% OF THE TIME. It is important to enter a trade thinking You will lose for the following reasons:you will naturally size smaller if you think this is yet another losing tradeyou will be happily surprised when it works, but not discouraged when it does notit keeps you focused on the process. You will be less attached to the outcome when you know you lose more often than notthis is called pre-mortem. You pre-package your Kubler Ross grief. Just another frog you need to kiss before it turns into Princess Charming

column1: Is it wrong to not have compassion for someone who decides to be depressed when you try and show them how not to?
column3: Depression is not something that can be switched on and off at will. If this person is depressed, chances are that nothing you can say to them will make them stop being depressed. Telling them to snap out of it just doesn’t work. Reactive depression is related to events in a persons life such as loss or death of an important person in their life. It can be the loss of a job, a relationship or even failing an exam at Uni. It is doubtful that anything you can suggest will change the depression that this person is experiencing. They need to go through the stages of grief and eventually that depression will likely resolve. Having said that the 5 stages of grief, denial, anger, bargaining, depression and acceptance are not necessarily followed in that order. It is also common for people to revisit the stages they have passed through over and over before they finally reach acceptance. All you can do here is to be a good friend and listen. No one wants you to solve their problems, they usually just want someone who will listen as they go through the stages of grief. Unresolved grief may lead to Major depression or clinical depression. Major depression Clinical depression is another matter altogether. Most people feel sad or low at some point in their lives. But clinical depression is marked by a depressed mood most of the day, sometimes particularly in the morning, and a loss of interest in normal activities and relationships -- symptoms that are present every day for at least 2 weeks. In addition, according to the DSM-5 -- a manual used to diagnose mental health conditions -- you may have other symptoms with major depression. Those symptoms might include:Fatigue or loss of energy almost every dayFeelings of worthlessness or guilt almost every dayImpaired concentration, indecisivenessInsomnia or hypersomnia (excessive sleeping) almost every dayMarkedly diminished interest or pleasure in almost all activities nearly every day (called anhedonia, this symptom can be indicated by reports from significant others)Restlessness or feeling slowed downRecurring thoughts of death or suicideSignificant weight loss or gain (a change of more than 5% of body weight in a month)Showing a person how how not to be depressed is possibly not a useful action. If anything it may make them feel guilty because they are letting you down by “staying depressed” despite your best efforts to “ cure them” Depression is not simply the result of a 'chemical imbalance', for example because you have too much or not enough of a particular brain chemical. It's complicated, and there are multiple causes of major depression. As such there are many forms of treatment for Major Depression, from medication, talk therapy, ECT, light therapy and many other therapies. It might be a good idea to give your friend an ear to listen to them and leave treatment to the experts.

column1: How do I overcome grief faster after my mother’s death? I already go to a counselor, and have family helping me. However, I cannot stop thinking of her and I keep crying.
column3: There is no time schedule for grief from loss. You can’t expect to just get over it and move on. the process for grieving is complicated, and not the same for everyone. You won’t get beyond this if you think you’re supposed to. Grief is something that follows its own course, though you do have to get up and get into your life, you can still feel the loss and mourn. Traditionally, the course of mourning for a spouse’s death was considered a year. That seems about reasonable. but generally the first few weeks are the hardest. And the next few months you’ll have constant reminders. You need to not fight it, unless the grief is so overwhelming that you are unable to function. You need to feel. But you are still here, and that means you also need to keep living. One of the reasons we have wakes, funerals and memorial services is in order to address all our feelings of loss. It hurts deeply, and it’s not something you just get over, or just move on, it’s something you have to make passage through. You’ll always have those feelings, but the more time that passes, the softer the pain will be. And then one day you’ll find yourself remembering something your mom did and you’ll smile. And that’s when you are on the other side of grief. Allow it to be, don’t fight it, but don’t stop living. It’s okay to cry, but it’s more important to live.

column1: Is there a difference between grief and mourning? If so, what is it? What are the differences between them in terms of their causes, symptoms, treatment etc.?
column3: Mourning vs. Grief: What’s the Difference? Updated 4/29/2022 Certified Grief Counselor American society has a hard time actively dealing with the discussion of death and loss. Many people may not know that there are different ways in which death affects us and that there’s a difference between mourning vs. grief. Jump ahead to these sections: Mourning vs. Grief: What’s the Difference? Although sometimes it can be a fine line distinguishing the two, there are some apparent differences. While grief is typically described as a normal and natural emotional reaction to loss, mourning is considered to be the outward manifestation of those emotions. When a person is said to be grieving, they are likely to experience emotions like sadness, pain, worry, and anxiety. But, when grief turns into mourning, it's generally defined as the public showing of that emotion. However, even with the distillation of inside versus outside, there are many differences between grief and mourning. Overview: Mourning vs. Grief Dealing with loss is painful and challenging. Most people will experience the death of a close loved one, and how they react to that loss can have a lasting effect in the months or years to come. Society generally interchanges grief and mourning to describe the feelings, emotions, and behaviors following a significant loss. Although these two words are related, they aren't interchangeable. Grief represents how an individual thinks and feels after suffering loss, while mourning is the outward manifestation of grief-related feelings. When you know and understand the differences between the two, you equip yourself to better cope with your loss. Mourning, grief, bereavement, and loss are all normal responses to loss, and we understand grief as the psychological or physiological response to bereavement. These reactions transform as time passes, and no two people will experience loss in the same way. Symptoms of grief may include some or all of the following:Profound sadnessLonging for the deceased individualShock and disbeliefAnxietyGuiltDepressionBy contrast, mourning is how an individual expresses their grief to the outside world and may include:Preparing for a funeralDonning black clothingSharing memoriesPlacing flowers at a gravesideCrying in publicWithdrawing from society for a time period» MORE: Show you're thinking about them with the perfect sympathy gift What Is Grief? Every person who has lost someone or something meaningful to them may experience grief after suffering a loss. As you learn to cope with your loss, you may experience the different stages of grief associated with the healing process. There are eight main types of grief generally recognized by therapists and scholars alike, which are the following:Anticipatory grief. Feeling grief before a loss occurs. This is common when a loved one is suffering a terminal illness, when cognitive decline starts to happen to your loved one, or when you sense that your marriage is headed toward divorce.Normal grief. When you’ve suffered a loss and everything seems “normal” with you to the outside world, this is referred to as normal grief. It appears that you haven’t been affected much by the loss, but the symptoms of grief come and go as you go about your normal routine. You still experience loss, sadness, and mourning, but the feelings come and go without affecting your life in any major way.Complicated grief. When grief overwhelms you and takes over your thoughts and ability to function in your daily life, this is known as complicated grief. Complicated grief is uncommon and only a small number of people may experience it. This type of grief makes it difficult to function and may cause you to have irrational thoughts linked to self-harm or other unusual behavior.Delayed grief. Some people don’t experience grief until weeks or months after having suffered loss. The delayed reaction may be because of other things going on in their lives that have taken over their ability to focus on the current loss. For example, a person who has lost someone to death while concurrently welcoming the birth of their child may delay their grieving until the joy of the birth settles in.Inhibited grief. When you focus your time and energy toward new or different things and away from the pain of your loss in hopes that it’ll go away, this is called inhibited grief. You may, for example, not want to face the reality that your child has died, so you volunteer all of your time feeding the homeless. You hide your feelings and emotions from everyone as you go about filling your schedule with distractors.Disenfranchised grief. This type of grief is when you are grieving the loss of someone or something that is dear to you, but others don’t recognize your grief. This type of grief can be typical following the loss of a pet, a job, or a romantic partner whom you can’t openly grieve such as in cases of extramarital affairs or other types of relationships not openly recognized.Absent grief. When grief doesn’t exist or you haven’t allowed for it to manifest in a timely and healthy manner, this is considered absent grief. It’s different from delayed grief in that with absent grief, you may not have accepted the loss and haven’t yet experienced the grief that ensues. Or, it may be that the grief expected just doesn’t exist such as when a parent dies whom you’ve never met or weren’t close to.Exaggerated grief. When several losses occur right after another, or all at once, you may feel an overwhelming loss that you’re unable to cope with. This is considered an exaggerated type of grief and may lead to further complications later on if left untreated.What grief may feel like When you’re dealing with grief on your own for the first time, it can feel rather unusual. You’re plumbing the depths of your emotional pain of losing someone or something, which may not be typical in your day-to-day life. Though grief can be synonymous with sadness, there are a few other emotions that you may also experience that may not be considered part and parcel of the grieving process.Sadness. Feeling sad after the death of someone you love is a normal reaction and symptom of grief. When your emotions are heightened beyond what is considered a normal part of grieving, it’s possible to become depressed if your grief is left untreated.Longing. Longing for someone after they’ve died is when you miss them so much that thoughts of them consume you. You typically suffer deep emotional distress wishing they were still alive. You can also experience longing for other types of losses such as pet companionship, your job, or a partner who’s left the relationship.Thinking and remembering. Thinking about your loved one who has died and you remembering them is a normal and healthy part of the grieving process. When thoughts of them consume you and you feel like you don’t know how you’re going to live without them, this is when your grieving transforms from something that is normal, to a more complicated type of grief that would benefit from outside help.Anxiety. Feeling anxious is also a normal part of grieving. There’s nothing wrong with admitting that you’re scared or unsure about what the future holds for you, especially when you have lost someone you depended on. You should expect to feel this way during the first few weeks or months after losing your loved one. With time, these feelings should lessen as you learn to navigate your new reality.Anger. It’s normal to feel anger toward others or your loved one who’s died when you’re grieving. This is especially true if you’ve lost your loved one in an unexpected way, or if they’ve contributed to their own death. Whatever the reason, know that you can find healthy ways to work through these emotions.Examples of grief Describing the emotions that one goes through is one way of defining grief, but experiencing grief can be another thing entirely. If you’re unsure as to what grief for you may look like, here are a few ways that grief can show up for others that may ring a bell for you as well. One such example is crying whenever someone mentions your deceased loved one. Even if you’re not crying outwardly, you can be grieving if you feel angry toward your loved one who died of a drug overdose. Here are some other examples:Cursing at the world and life in general for being so unfairWithdrawing from your normal routineConsuming drugs or alcohol to lessen the painWhat Is Mourning? Mourning is when you outwardly exhibit your grief-related emotions, and/or participate in external acts related to grieving. Depending on your culture, family traditions, and societal norms, mourning can take on a very formal approach that includes certain grief rituals and time-periods in which mourning is expected to take place. Needs of Mourning Dr. Alan D. Wolfelt is a grief counselor who penned the term “Needs of Mourning.” The needs of mourning are things that are considered essential to mourning similar to the stages of grief that are important for healing to take place. The Needs of Mourning can be described as follows:Accepting the reality of the death of your loved one or acknowledging the loss of something meaningful to you.Feeling the pain of that loss.Remembering the person or the thing lost.Developing a new identity after a loss.Searching for meaning within your new reality.Allowing others to help you overcome your pain and suffering.One need of mourning that is rarely discussed is the need for validation of the importance of your deceased loved one’s life. Especially when someone dies at a very old age, friends and family may no longer be alive to attend their funeral or memorial services. In order for the family left behind to feel that they’re honoring the memory of their loved one, they hire professional mourners to fill the seats at the funeral. Professional mourners may also interact with the few people known to the deceased who are still alive and able to attend. 🌻 Express your condolences with a sympathy gift. Show your support to a grieving friend. Browse our hand-picked selection of gifts.https://www.joincake.com/blog/sympathy-gift-baskets/Examples of mourning With grief, you may mourn your loss externally at certain places, but to mourn on the whole implies an activity related to the loss. With mourning, it is typical that you would attend a funeral to honor a loved one that has died. You might also wear clothing that outwardly shows your mourning, which is another way of displaying grief to the outside world. Some other examples of public mourning can include:Sharing stories of your loved oneParticipating in grief ritualsVisiting the gravesite of your loved oneGrief vs. Mourning: 5 Differences to Know Even with the definitions and examples given above, grief and mourning can exist at the same time and blur the boundaries that define each one. Colloquially, it may be easy to interchange the words when talking to someone about loss, but they do have some important distinctions. Here are some you should take note of when dealing with grief and mourning. 1. Internal vs. external Feelings and thoughts are what you experience and process internally when you are grieving. The outward acts associated with grief rituals such as lamenting and attending funerals are part of the mourning process. 2. Natural reaction vs. participation Grief is a natural emotional reaction to loss while mourning is more of the ceremony attached to your suffering. External acts such as wearing mourning clothing for a period of time or flying a flag half-mast are examples of some things that may be expected while crying in the shower is an example of a more personal way of expressing your emotions. 3. Grief comes first vs. mourning comes after The grieving process typically begins with the initial loss and the feelings and emotions tied to that event. Most people will begin their grief journey trying to make sense of their loss before finding acceptance of it. Mourning is the process that follows death and sometimes overlaps with grief. » MORE: Meaningful sympathy gifts that aren't flowers 4. Grief lasts for several months vs. years of mourning Simple, uncomplicated grief usually lasts for several months before the bereaved may find healing. By contrast, a person who is in mourning can remain in this state for many years or even for a lifetime. 5. Personal vs. ritualistic When you grieve it’s often very personal. Many times you may find yourself internalizing your feelings and emotions while learning new ways of expressing your hurt, anger, and sorrow. As you move toward the mourning stage, you may find yourself participating in all of the rituals and events planned around the death. Grief usually requires no formal process. How Can You Tell if a Loved One Is Mourning or Grieving? Knowing when your loved one’s grieving or in mourning is an integral part of the grief journey. Although grief and mourning are two very distinct aspects of loss, it may be useful to know that grief is considered to be the internal processing of loss-related feelings and emotions. In contrast, mourning is the external expression of pain and suffering that follows loss. Both of these processes are necessary for someone to heal after a loss. Sometimes they overlap, and symptoms of both may continue well after experiencing a significant loss. Each of these roles will have an equal, yet completely different, role in helping your loved one deal with death. The grief process aims to heal the internal conflicts and emotions following a loss, while acts of mourning focus on honoring and remembering a loved one who died. After suffering a significant loss, you can expect your loved one to experience a combination of the two. Grief and mourning often go hand-in-hand, and it may be difficult to tell the difference between the two in the early stages of grief. Following the death of a loved one, an individual can experience different feelings and emotions that they may be uncomfortable or unfamiliar dealing with. Many won't know how to deal with their loss, and their grief reactions may reflect this. The holding in of loss-related reactions may lead to your loved one reacting in ways that are out of character for them or that make you feel shut out and rejected. Generally, the feelings that accompany loss may range from profound sadness to anger and irritability. You may already recognize some of these symptoms in your loved one's behavior. They're all normal and natural reactions to loss and shouldn't be a cause for alarm. An individual struggling with coping with their loss will typically keep these feelings to themselves. A person mourning may also display some of their feelings and emotions out in the open. Acts of mourning are a display of an individual's pain and suffering after experiencing loss. Mourning rituals and behaviors contribute to emotional and physical healing after loss and are an essential aspect of the overall process. When your loved one's in mourning, you can expect them to participate in death rituals, cry in public, or continuously talk about their loss. Some grief-related experiences will overlap, making it difficult to tell the difference between grief and mourning. You'll start recognizing some of your loved one's patterns of behaviors as the weeks and months go by. In time, both grief and mourning will begin to lessen as healing begins to take place. In the meantime, consider keeping an open dialogue with your loved ones to gauge how well they're coping with their loss. The mourning phase typically lasts a few weeks and will gradually begin to meld into the grieving process. Once your loved one starts settling back into their daily routine, mourning turns to grief. Keep in mind that the two phases will look very much the same in the beginning, and there’s no need to try and figure out exactly where in the process your loved one’s in. Grief and Mourning Work in Tandem These two processes work together to help you heal when you’ve suffered through a life-changing loss or event. Either way, these timelines are not as important as finding your inner peace and healing after loss.SourcesWolfelt, A. D. 1997. column1: Adult Do you feel that there is an unhelpful societal expectation for parents' lives to be permanently ruined after their child's death?
column3: No, I do not feel there is an unhelpful societal expectation. A parents life is ruined for quite sometime following the death of their child. You have lost your child, a part of you, which does ruin the life you thought you were planning on having. You are reminded several times a year of your loss: holidays, their birthday, and their date of death. You can’t escape it, you try to brace yourself for those times, to be there for your other children, who became adults and still have days where they are just broken. Sometimes, you smell a cologne they once wore, or sometimes a very strong feeling of loss hits you, years after they died, it breaks you all over again. It is not as raw as it was initially, but it hurts, it hurts in ways there are no words to explain. I don't think parents are ruined following the death of their child, but they will never be the same people they were prior to the child’s death. Society has little to do with it, love of a dead child does it to us. Only those who have lived through the trauma of a child’s death should comment, otherwise you are only guessing at the impossible… and something none of us who live it would want to happen to anyone else. If you settle into grief more than two years, it is called complicated grief, and you DO NOT WANT TO BE THERE. Many have experienced it and continue to struggle with the vicious grips of depression for decades. We are members of a group no one should be in. Please say their name, quit looking through us, don’ t feel required to offer a word or phrase of wisdom unless you are one of us. Listen to us tell our stories of them, we know you tire of the same stories all of the time, it helps us hold on to the memories of a life too short, in time we will smile and laugh. Society; isolates us, reprimands us, guilts us, and erases us from relationships we had prior to losing our child. Society, conditions us to deal with our loss on our own, they were our child, the rest of you know what happened, but are neglent in knowing how often we are triggered, do not understand why we have tears in our eyes we are trying to gain control over, because to you it has been five years, to us five years means we have lived five years without touching, hearing their voice, or smelling their presence in our lives- it is tourture, but something we must learn to live with and without. RIP KHR I love you, my dear son.

column1: Will I ever be happy again after the loss of my only child?
column3: I just lost my daughter Starilyn to complications from cerebral palsy this past August. My father followed in October My ex fiance just last week to suicide. He couldn't cope with the loss of Star. You will be happy eventually. Pain never goes away. We just learn to deal with it better as time goes on. The problem is we as human beings expect a certain order in the chaos that is death…older goes first. There actually IS no order to it, humans created that based on life experience and basic biological understanding that as you get older, things stop working properly. People go when its their time to go. Those left behind get upset because THEY didn't think it was their time, and they are left with emotions they have no closure for since the person in question is now decreased. Please, understand there is a life after death FOR YOU. We will all figure this out one day, but until we do, take a deep breath, look around at the world and realize that the same genius mind that created it will also have answers for every question you have, but you must be patient. I hope and pray you understand happiness after losing someone you love is not a sin.

column1: Is there a life after breakup?
column3: Ofcourse... Breakup is not the end of life. Why do breakups hurt so much, even when the relationship is no longer good? A breakup is painful because it represents the loss, not just of the relationship, but also of shared dreams and commitments. Romantic relationships begin on a high note of excitement and hope for the future. When these relationships fail, we experience profound disappointment, stress, and grief. An ex is a very important part of one's life. A person learns a lot of good and at times bad things during a relationship so keeping mementos is a very complicated issue. Emotionally speaking, losing a partner to a breakup is very similar to losing one to death, and in both cases the only way to get over the loss is to let yourself grieve. Give yourself the time you need to process your feelings. Breakup involves suffering for few days. Yes its normal to feel bad after a breakup but its not the end of your life. Actually, It is the beginning of your life..Believe in time, it can give you some space so that you can breathe again. Self care and self love are the best way to heal from a breakup and build up the courage to start a new relationship... Just move on..!!! Get your ex out of your life. Get rid of the old memories: Burn the pictures, eat the chocolates, delete the music and stop going to the places that remind you of him. Do something you enjoy! Believe it or not, time alone isn't as bad as it feels after a break up, in fact, time alone is one of the best things you can get before you re-enter the single life. Take that time to make yourself a better person. There are thousands of things you can do, Always remember.... ● When you are crying for them. They are laughing with someone else. ● Not everyone is meant to be in your future. Some people are just passing through to teach you more lessons in life. ● Life is too short to waste pining after someone who isn't making you happy. If you have followed all of the steps above, you will surely have been a happy and independent life. You can start going on a date and build a brand new relationship. It is that easy to survive break up, as long as you see it as a 'break'. It's not the end of the world, your life will still continue. Focus on your life as a process of becoming the best of you. And one more thing...... Your ex gf/bf is not oxygen. So, you can survive without them...

column1: How do I fill the void left by someone who was once my everything and is now married to someone else?
column3: 1. Practice releasing regrets. When a relationship ends, it’s tempting to dwell on what you did wrong or what you could have done differently. This might seem productive—like you can somehow change things by rehashing it. You can’t. All dwelling does is cause you to suffer. When you start revisiting the past in your head, pull yourself into the moment. Focus on the good things in your current situation: the friends who are there for you and the lessons you’ve learned that will help you with future relationships. It might help to tell your friends to only let you vent for ten minutes at a time. That way you’re free to express your feelings, but not drown in them. 2. Work on forgiving yourself. You might think you made the biggest mistake of your life and if only you didn’t do it, you wouldn’t be in pain right now. Don’t go down that road—there’s nothing good down there! Instead, keep reminding yourself that you are human. You’re entitled to make mistakes; everyone does. And you will learn from them and use those lessons to improve your life. Also, keep in mind: if you want to feel love again in the future, the first step is to prepare yourself to give and receive it. You can only do that if you feel love toward yourself. And that means forgiving yourself. 3. Don’t think about any time as lost. If you looked at that unhealthy relationship or the following decade as time lost, you’d underestimate all the amazing things you did in that time. True, but that made it easier to travel and devote myself to different passions. If you’ve been clinging to the past for a while and now feel you’ve missed out, shift the focus to everything you’ve gained. Maybe you’ve built great friendships or made great progress in your career. When you focus on the positive, it’s easier to move on because you’ll feel empowered and not victimized (by your ex, by yourself, or by time.) Whatever happened in the past, it prepared you for now—and now is full of opportunities for growth, peace, and happiness. 4. Remember the bad as well as the good. Brain scientists suggest nearly 20 percent of us suffer from “complicated grief”—a persistent sense of longing for someone we lost with romanticized memories of the relationship. Scientists also suggest this is a biological occurrence, that the longing can have an addictive quality to it, actually rooted in our brain chemistry. As a result, we tend to remember everything with reverie, as if it was all sunshine and roses. If your ex broke up with you, it may be even more tempting to imagine she or he was perfect and you weren’t. In all reality, you both have strengths and weaknesses and you both made mistakes. Remember them now. 5. Reconnect with who you are outside a relationship. Unless you hop from relationship to relationship, odds are you lived a fulfilling single life before you got into this one. You were strong, satisfied, and happy, at least on the whole. Remember that person now. Reconnect with any people or interests that may have received less attention while you were attached. The strong, happy, passionate person you were attracted your ex. That person will get you through this loss and attract someone equally amazing in the future when the time is right. Not a sad, depressed, guilt-ridden person clutching to what once was. If you can’t remember who you are, get to know yourself now. What do you love about life? 6. Create separation. Hope can be a terrible thing if it keeps you stuck in the past. It’s not easy to end all contact when you feel attached to someone. Breaking off the friendship might feel like ruining your chances at knowing love again. It’s helped me to change my hopes to broader terms. So instead of wanting a specific person to re-enter your life, want love and happiness, whatever that may look like. You will know love again. You won’t spend the rest of your life alone. In one way or another, you will meet all kinds of people and create all kinds of possibilities for relationships—if you forgive yourself, let go, and open yourself up, that is. 7. Let yourself feel. Losing a relationship can feel like a mini-death, complete with a grieving process. First, you’re shocked and in denial. You don’t believe it’s over and you hold out hope. Next, you feel hurt and guilty. You should have done things differently. If you did you wouldn’t be in this pain. Then, you feel angry and maybe even start bargaining. It would be different if you gave it a second go. You wouldn’t be so insecure, defensive, or demanding. Then you might feel depressed and lonely as it hits you how much you’ve lost. Eventually, you start accepting what happened and shift your focus from the past to the future. You have to go through the feelings as they come, but you can help yourself get through them faster. For example, if you’re dwelling in guilt, make forgiving yourself a daily practice. Read books on it, meditate about it, or write about it in a journal. 8. Remember the benefits of moving on. When you let go, you give yourself peace. Everything about holding on is torturous. You regret, you feel ashamed and guilty, you rehash, you obsess—it’s all an exercise in suffering. The only way to feel peace is to quiet the thoughts that threaten it. Letting go opens you up to new possibilities. When you’re holding onto something, you’re less open to giving and receiving anything else. If you had your arms wrapped around a huge bucket of water, you wouldn’t be able to give anything other than that bucket, or grab anything else that came your way. You might even struggle breathing because you’re clutching something so all-encompassing with so much effort. You have to give to receive. Give love to get love, share joy to feel joy. It’s only possible if you’re open and receptive. 9. Recognize and replace fearful thoughts. When you’re holding onto a relationship, it’s usually more about attachment than love. Love wants for the other person’s happiness. Fear wants to hold onto whatever appears to make you happy so you don’t have to feel the alternative. You might not recognize these types of fearful thoughts because they become habitual. Some examples include: I’ll never feel loved again. I’ll always feel lonely. I am completely powerless. Replace those thoughts with: All pain passes eventually. It will be easier if I help them pass by being mindful. I can’t always control what happens to me, but I can control how I respond to it. 10. Embrace impermanence. Nothing in life lasts forever. Every experience and relationship eventually runs its course. The best way to embrace impermanence is to translate it into action. Treat each day as a life unto itself. Appreciate the people in front of you as if it were their last day on earth. Find little things to gain in every moment instead of dwelling on what you lost. When I feel like clinging to experiences and people, I remind myself the unknown can be a curse or an adventure. It’s up to me whether or not I’m strong and positive enough to see it as the latter. –

column1: Adult Do the five stages of grief follow a specific and definitive kind of order or can they be varied and change from moment to the next?
column3: The 7 stages of grief The seven stages of grief are another popular model for explaining the many complicated experiences of loss. These seven stages include: Shock and denial. This is a state of disbelief and numbed feelings. Pain and guilt. You may feel that the loss is unbearable and that you’re making other people’s lives harder because of your feelings and needs. Anger and bargaining. You may lash out, telling God or a higher power that you’ll do anything they ask if they’ll only grant you relief from these feelings. Depression. This may be a period of isolation and loneliness during which you process and reflect on the loss. The upward turn. At this point, the stages of grief like anger and pain have died down, and you’re left in a more calm and relaxed state. Reconstruction and working through. You can begin to put pieces of your life back together and carry forward. Acceptance and hope. This is a very gradual acceptance of the new way of life and a feeling of possibility in the future. As an example, this may be the presentation of stages from a breakup or divorce: Shock and denial: “She absolutely wouldn’t do this to me. She’ll realize she’s wrong and be back here tomorrow.” Pain and guilt: “How could she do this to me? How selfish is she? How did I mess this up?” Anger and bargaining: “If she’ll give me another chance, I’ll be a better boyfriend. I’ll dote on her and give her everything she asks.” Depression: “I’ll never have another relationship. I’m doomed to fail everyone.” The upward turn: “The end was hard, but there could be a place in the future where I could see myself in another relationship.” Reconstruction and working through: “I need to evaluate that relationship and learn from my mistakes.” Acceptance and hope: “I have a lot to offer another person. I just have to meet them.” This is a pattern observed, but people are different and there is no set time or reaction. Many ways of doing the same thing. column1: How do I overcome grief and finally accept the situation?
column3: Acceptance and “getting over” are quite different. There comes a point, which is different for everyone, during which you accept that your loved one is gone. That doesn't make it less surreal and it certainly doesn't equate with getting over the loss. A lot of the early months in the grieving process are muddled through in a total fog. It's a bit like someone is manipulating you remotely as you're always distracted and walking in a cloud of sadness and borderline-catatonia. Depending on your relationship with the deceased, this fog may mast a few weeks, months, or upwards of a year. As an example, when my fiancé died I spent more than a year in that state. I can't tell you hardly anything that happened the year following his death and found myself doing absent-minded things, such as leaving my car running when I went out or getting lost in my own neighborhood. When my father died I was sad but far better equipped to function. Now for the more complicated part of your question- getting over it. I hate to be the bearer of bad news but there is no getting over it. It changes, gets different, morphs into more of a dull ache than poison-laden knife constantly stabbing you, but it's always there. Even when you find some type of happiness or semblance of peace in something new there's always a little hint of that memory. An emptiness, a twinge of heartache, and bittersweet longing for what you had with that person are always there. Some days it's more prominent than others. Let yourself feel however you need to and know that in time you won't get over it but it will become more navigable. You're welcome to email me if you need someone to listen. ~Much love to you.
column9: When you finally accept that your love one isn't coming back, is gone until you join them in eternity, you will gain a small measure of peace. You won't look for them every time you come home or won't wait to tell them something about your day. You will still miss them but the pain has lessened just a little so you can breathe again. You certainly will never get over the loss because of your memories, the finality of the person not being present, in your life, your loneliness, the miss of their touch, the encouragement they gave you when you needed it most, the heartache you have endured since they left you nor the desire to talk to them one last time. Your heart cries out in pain over the memories when you look through old photographs, find their Christmas stocking with their name on it you made for them or see your grandchild being born when in the back of your mind you are thinking about him missing this event and your grandsons life. The only comfort I have is to know that when I die I will see them again through the death and Resurrection of Jesus Christ on the cross. Loving God and depending on him has been the saving Grace through this hellish experience of losing your soulmate. I can't blame God because I know that he is doing his will and cares for me in a way I can't understand. He has never left me wanting nor forsaken me in any way so I must ensure and press through. For my riches are in heaven!

column1: What is it like to lose a child?
column3: This is a tough question to answer as it brings all the pain I try to push back (he's just on a long vacation; he's busy with work, etc., AKA denial) with as much force as I can muster until I'm lying in bed alone with my thoughts, trying to hold on to every detail I can about him. The fear of forgetting his voice one day drives me insane. I had my firstborn son, Kenneth Wayne III, when I was 19 years old. I loved him before I laid eyes on him. I couldn't wait to meet him and, when I heard his first breath, I instantly realized the meaning of unconditional love. I knew right then & there that nothing would ever change this deep love I felt. I was a child myself at the time so I refer to his upbringing as he and I growing up together in a sense. I learned the meaning of maturity, responsibility, selflessness, compassion, empathy, protection and many more traits. In turn, I taught him the same. It was he and I together during the day until his dad joined in after work. We explored nature, played hide-n-seek, went to the beach, made sand castles, watched Sesame Street, Disney movies, danced, read books, sang songs and listened to lots of rock-n-roll music. Two and a half years later his brother was born. Ken's first words when he laid eyes on him were "Can you put him back in there now"?! Of course that changed immediately. Not only did they form a bond as brothers, they were the very best of friends! It was awesome watching them grow up together. I never imagined loving someone as much as I loved Kenny. Of course, my love for my younger child was also instantaneous (such as when my daughter was born). It was the boys and me together during weekdays and dad taking over when he got home and joined in the fun. Those years were really some of the best of my life. Being a mommy was what I wanted and here I was, at 23, with two incredible boys. I'm sure we had our ups and downs back then, but looking back now, the stresses of those days seem rather silly. Kenny was born with a drive to succeed. He had an extraordinary gift of gab, having long detailed conversations with adults starting at the age of 4. People were fascinated by his vast vocabulary and his drive to learn all he could. His questions were numerous (e.g., at the beach, "how many grains of sand do you think are here"?). He was a sponge, soaking up each reply we gave. It was obvious he would listen intently to your answer. He was incredibly loving, very respectful, silly and funny, spontaneous, athletic and extremely ambitious in his academic pursuits. Beginning in elementary school, he was a 2x Spelling Bee Champion, won 1st place in the Greater San Diego Science Fair in physics, SCHS (highschool) Science Olympiad Grand Champion and made the principal's Honor Roll for 16 consecutive quarters. He achieved various other awards in academics along with awards for baseball, wrestling, and competitive pingpong. He graduated from high school as Salutatorian in 2007. In his senior year, he and his dad worked endless hours on his college applications. Their hard work paid off when Ken was accepted to each college he applied (5 UC schools). He chose USC for their world class business school, the Marshall School of Business, and entered the prestigious Lloyd Grief Center of Entrepreneurial Studies. He joined Delta Chi his first year and held positions on their Board. He befriended all walks of life and ended college with numerous close friendships. Ken was looked to for advice in many different areas and respected everyone he came in contact with. He appreciated the beauty of life and was positive in his surroundings. Everyone Ken met considered him their best friend. He lived more in his short 23 years than most do in a lifetime. He traveled to Hong Kong and Greece, fished in Mexico, attended countless music festivals/concerts and academic debates, never missing out on anything he wanted to do. He came home often to spend time with his brother and the rest of his family, always stopping to visit his old friends from SD. Obviously to try and answer this question, I needed to give a bit of background first. I thought about how to answer a question of this nature and found that, from my own personal experience, I don't believe words could truly describe this pain, horror, loss, and anxiousness I feel without my boy. I can identify with the pain and sorrow in each answer written here. I believe one can only know the pain of losing a child if you've lost a child yourself. How could I possibly put into words the difficulty of life without him, the breathlessness felt each morning I wake up knowing he's gone, the guilt I feel for not being able to save my firstborn child, my lil buddy, one of my 3 favorite people in this world? How does one go about life without their child? After the loss, I didn't leave my bedroom for nearly six months. When I did it was because I had spoken to a man that lost his daughter and had written a book about the loss and also opened a center for people grieving the loss of their child. He graciously invited me to his home to speak with me. We sat on his veranda and I asked him how he was able to go on with life after his loss. He looked at me and without hesitation said ‘Rebecca you're fucked and that's just the way it's going to be. You have to learn how to deal with the rest of your life knowing this”. At first his honesty was shocking. However as the years have gone on, I realize his words that day struck a chord. I'd much rather hear honesty than the other lame things I've heard ‘he's in a better place.” No, the best place is here living life with his family, ‘God needed him back’; how selfish of God in my eyes, etc. For me, to attempt to explain the emotions of a mom and/or dad when they lose their child is way too complicated. Words like sadness, despondency, and misery don't scratch the surface of emotions. I'm left wondering how to console my other two children when I can't understand nor accept this grief myself. The instant the two people from the Coroner's office knocked at my door, the life I had was over. No longer would I be the same person. There's a distinct difference between who I was before his loss and who I am now. When I reached the top of the stairs and saw them in my living room, everything about me ceased to exist. The stresses of the day before no longer mattered. Had he been in an accident? No. Was he murdered? No. Did he have a hereditary disease unknown to us? No. Suicide? No. We had to wait four months for the autopsy conclusion. What a fucking nightmare not knowing. Why I didn't immediately get in my car and drive the 3 hours up north disturbs me to this day. Why we asked my siblings and father to go up and clean out his room of his belongings makes me very angry at myself. What was I thinking not going myself? Was I in shock? Denial? The guilt is overpowering. No matter how many people try and persuade me that his passing is not my fault, somehow it still is. I'm supposed to protect my children. I'm the mom! The love I have for my children and life itself is buried under a heavy load called GRIEF. The comments I've heard about 'having two other children to live for, Kenny wouldn't want me to live like this', are well intended yet don't have an effect and can't penetrate into my numb mind. The endless nights of terror imagining the what-ifs: what if this happens to Nate or Kay? What if I had just gone up to his house that day to surprise him? Why hadn't I gone to him after finding out? What if he never met the punk that was with him the evening before? The thoughts have left me an insomniac. I'm more comfortable in my own surroundings with pictures and memories of a different time. I try as best as I can to hide my sorrow from my other children and family. It's all I can think of. I'd never want my kids to think they aren't just as important. When they come tell me about their accomplishments, I'm proud. The moment of happiness is followed by a gut wrenching feeling, 'why isn't Ken here to share and enjoy these moments'? I'm left pulled into different emotions. If I don't show how proud I am, I'm a shit mom. If I smile and let my happiness show for my other children, I'm worthless to Ken because he'd think I wasn't devastated about his loss. Does it make sense? Nothing makes any sense in tragedy. What would he feel if he could see me smiling? I still don't know the details of the night my son lost his life. I know what caused his passing but the roommates he lived with told us they were 'too shaken up' to speak of any details. While I can only imagine the panic and despair they felt upon finding him, can and do they imagine the anxiety we as parents feel not knowing? Will they ever tell me? Each night I try and piece together his last day and night but I'm only left with a story I created. I created this wonderful human in my body, witnessed his first breath but I'm not worthy enough to tell me about his last moments? I'll never know what he was thinking or the whys that surrounded this tragedy. It was 3 years on July 6, 2015. Some say time heals but that hasn't been true for me. The first and second year were shock and denial. When January 1st came this year all I could think was 'UH OH' here we go again. I believe that's when I finally realized he wasn't going to come home. How I long for that denial to come back and protect my mind. Perhaps in time I'll have learned to incorporate the pain into life. I don't see the light at the end of this tunnel. Maybe this year was the year of realization. I don't want another year of birthdays, holidays, anniversary dates, and celebrations without my firstborn child. Losing your child leaves a hole in your very soul that cannot be filled. It leaves you numb, breathless, anxious, sobbing, apprehensive, angry, bitter, hateful and many other emotions tied up in the word 'bereavement'. Getting back to an answer to this question (finally) here it is: I pray that the reader never has to personally know an answer to this question and if you are on this same path, I'm so very sorry that you have to live with this pain. I wish for you peace on your journey.

column1: I’m at the stage of grief where I’m upset. Upset at my parents . I swear I hate them. How do I get over this stage?
column3: Ok, why should you listen to me when I speak about grief when I'm not a mental health professional of any kind. Because Murphy and the fates have colluded to give me a great deal of experience with the stuff. I had already been a widow for eight years when my brother and both parents died in a four year period. The order of their passing required that I give up my job, my home and all of my retirement dreams so that I could take care of my parents. It was complicated. Suffice it to say that I have experienced grief regarding the loss of all of these people and things. So, my perspective, hummm. Some folks say that there are stages of grief. The word “stages" implies that there is an order to things and that a grieving person walks through each stage, in order, until that stage is complete. It implies that they then walk on to the next stage with the final goal being a lack of grief and a sense of moving on as if nothing happened. I'm sure that makes for nice neat lectures and presentations in some class or book…but…it isn't realistic. Grief is messy. Nothing follows any real plan. There are good days and bad days. There are days of anger and rage. There are times of overwhelming sadness that can get so bad it is hard to breathe. There are also days of empty numbness. Just when your spirit starts to stabilize a birthday, holiday or anniversary rolls around and you can start to react again. I say “react” because a great deal depends upon the nature of the relationship you had with the person, thing or dream. Then there are times when a wry smile sneaks up onto your face from within as a happy thought or memory pops into mind. Of course in the beginning, that wry smile and happy memory may lead to sadness as you realize that those times can't ever come again. Slowly tears become wry smiles much more frequently. If your relationship with the person was not a good one then there are matters of unfinished emotional “stuff" that are suddenly left hanging. This really complicates things. Give yourself a huge break! Grief isn't easy or neat. It changes form on you when you least expect it. When asked, I tell people not to make any major decisions for at least the first full year after the loss, when at all possible. This doesn't mean that grief will be “over" in a year. I also tell them to allow themselves to feel whatever feelings that they have. That is crucial! The only way “through” grief is to walk through it and experience it as it comes and goes on it's own terms. Do not look for a return to normal. You will eventually emerge into a new normal. Eventually grief and those sneaky burps of intense emotion do end but not with the sudden completion of some list of stages. A sense of peace and that new normal sneaks up on you. It is time to seek help if you feel as though you are stuck, out of control, completely shut down or a inability to function at all continues past a couple of weeks. When I say “ability to function" I am talking about eating, sleeping, paying Bill's, going to work or school and basic self-care. Give yourself a period of time to “fall apart" as you experience what “falling apart" is like for you. Just don't get stuck there without seeking help from a grief counselor. I wish I could tell you that the course that grief takes is predictable but it isn't. It is unique to every person and again to every loss for each person. Cut yourself some slack. Find a grief counselor if you need to. I saw this image on the web one day. I don't know who made it. It spoke to my experience.Like I said. Grief is messy. Peace Y'all Q: I’m at the stage of grief where I’m upset. Upset at my parents . I swear I hate them. How do I get over this stage?
column9: You are Absolutely positively correct . I lost my son 4 yrs ago and my husband a year ago. Unless you have list a lived one how can you empathsize with them. Our emotions are all over the place. The professionals know text book. Not life’s shitty lessons in How to get past a day without wanting to throw up with pain. I’ve been seeing a Psychiatrist for years nobody can prepare you nobody can feel it for you the people that been through it understand. When people ask about my don or where is your husband. column1: Can huge losses and tragedies (loss of home, death of a loved one) be considered spiritual awakenings or at least the catalysts that throw us into an awakening?
column3: Major losses can become a catalyst for major changes in life. In a five year period starting in 2000 I lost my younger brother to suicide in his early 40’s, a best friend and key employee to sudden heart attack in his late 30’s and then our 20 year old son was killed in a firefighter training accident in our small close knit town. Three untimely and unexpected deaths that each had complicated implications on my life in five years. I am a technician and engineer at heart and was casually religious but certainly not spiritually very connected or believing. While I still contribute to our church, I have pulled away from organized religion. I have instead become far more sensitive and connected to my spiritual side. Based on experiences I believe in much deeper invisible spiritual connections that we can form between living souls if we allow them to. I have no evidence of life beyond this one, just a deeper appreciation for the subtleties of this one. I was far more materialistic before these tragedies. Money and possessions brought me no comfort in my grief and have far less value. I am now a firm believer that we are here to love life and to love other souls, and that the love we build in our life will be all that survives our death. That is the only immortality I have confidence in. I believe that the Universe is a completely random place without inherent logic or emotion. Life delivers us challenges randomly and we must choose to survive and heal the tough ones. or allow our souls to be broken and empty themselves. Life is not promised to be fair or easy. I believe that each of us is gifted an empty soul at birth. With the help of families, community and loved ones we fill that soul with a purpose to our lives that we each build. Each new day is a gift that we can use, abuse or waste as we wish. In the complicated aftermath of our son’s death, I was invited to write in our local weekly on any subject I wanted. Prior to that I was publicly very quiet, and a natural introvert. Over the decade that followed I wrote over 200 columns with many on life and love and built a respected voice in our community. I have received the gift of trust from several people that I’ve helped find help and walk back from the edges of what could have been suicide. I have no idea what my life will bring. I have no fear of my own death because I know that mostly the Universe will choose the time, place and method to end my life. My greatest fear is that I will not live my life to the best possible while I am alive today. I live each day stronger than I ever thought I might be. I carry the pain of love lost comfortably because I see grief as the final and lasting expression of love shared. Grief is the final responsibility of loving another human. I caution those with sudden loss to not make sudden changes in their lives, but to look through the huge holes opened in your soul by loss and look for happiness and love of life to re-find their purpose. That re-found purpose may look nothing like the life they had before loss, and we need to be open to those changes happening.
column9: Well said. You have a way with words and I appreciate all your writings. Have a great new year and thank you for always helping explain to others this unimaginable loss. I changed from mine and it is the five year mark. I am very happy with my choices so far. I am hoping this is only the beginning to a new prosperous career. As you stated, this is really only important to me for one thing though, and that is my loved ones and own happiness.

column1: I've been in dealing with my daughter's death. A lady just stopped to check on me & said get over it already. If I slap her will I go to jail?
column3: Hello, I too have lost a child, my son- I DO KNOW how it feels. I can say people try with good intentions to support you, or others will leave all together- we belong to the club no one was to be a member of. People are afraid of us, because they see “the woman or man who lost their child”, we scare them because “loosing a child all of a sudden became a real possibility for them”. Two weeks after our son passed I tried to return to work, a friend (once a very dear friend) said “You got to pull up your big girls panties.” We are from the western portion of USA, and the phrase is common for “getting over things and moving on”. I was so angry I yelled at her “ MY SON IS DEAD I WILL NEVER EVER SEE HIM AGAIN- F(*& YOUR PANTIES AND F*&^% YOU TOO!” I didn't slap her, I wanted to choke the life out of her- I was so angry and I had that anger for a very long time. The four year anniversary will be here in a week, I can say life gets livable and sometimes you will even laugh again, there are days you will almost not think about “it” (being the death), and feel tremendously guilty about it. All of my social circles changed following his death, my best friend and I are only cordial to one another. The death of your child- changes you, changes how you think, changes how you treat people, and how people treat you. I was not one to go to counseling, where I live it is standard practice to deal with things yourself. I literally could not do it- I stayed in my bedroom and in bed sleeping (thanks to pills) for three years. I wanted to die- I lost all hope, all desire, all joy I lost my son, I didn't want to, and could not go on. I did seek counseling (at the time I didn't think it helped). My official diagnosis: Complicated grief- I could not let go of it, because I think somewhere deep inside I needed to continue to feel guilty for our son’s death. He was a suicide- two inches between life and death, and he held out for death- I still tremble when I think of the choice he made. It breaks me all over again- yet, if I can share it with someone, or help someone- I try because that is the gift of his death and life to me. It is a way I attempt to honor him for the wonderful person he was. Later, when I flushed all that medication for depression, anxiety, and a handful of other prescribed medications I began the acceptance process. Journal, write, spend time alone, draw, paint, get busy- that helped me, I don’t know what helps others. I found several people who also lost a child and began speaking with them- they understand us, because they are us. As a parent, I want people to remember our son, to say his name, tell a good story about him, confirm he was important to them as well. It is the single most difficult experience I have been forced to live through, I am sorry you are living it as well. Life is so completely unfair sometimes, and it destroys people for a very long time and for some it does. I found, I have to let people “do their thing, say their comments, they feel the need to communicate something” just let them, attacking them does nothing, but assign a “crazy label to us”, we are not crazy, we miss our children, we want to see, feel, smell them one more time. It is enough to make us feel as if we are going crazy. I will tell you about the most beautiful comment someone said to me following our son’s death. I was on facebook a lot, trying to express my loss, understand it, process it. Anyway, one day I decided I had to let him go, I had a blanket of his I had kept in a bag- when I missed him I would go to my closet, shut the door, and wrap his blanket around me, breathing in his smell…I would sob, and be angry, and sad, and all the things that crash and smother our very breath in those moments. I took the blanket to the laundry room and sat on the floor for hours holding and loving it, I could not put it in the washer- for hours I fought with myself and the image of giving up the only thing that smelled like my son. I finally placed it in the wash, turned it on, and fell to the floor in a puddle of tears and despair. Later, I posted the experience on facebook. One girl, who had gone to school with my son said “ I loved him too.” I’m so sorry you are going through this, please contact me. I did, and we spoke for many days following this experience- she loved him too… isn’t that what we want to know? That our child was important to someone else too. It is a long painful process, you do what you need to, in order to get through the process, and that is exactly what it is. About the slapping of the person, let it go- that person doesn’t have a clue as to the depth of your pain and the battles you confront each and every day. I wish you all the best, and hope one day you will have less hurt to be confronted with, I am so very sorry for your loss of your beautiful child.
column9: Thank you so much! I'm sorry about your son as well.....Lord have mercy, put your big girl panties on?! Yes, I would have rock it inside out. If anyone had told me how drastic of a turn my life was about take honestly I would've said yeah right. I've always tried to live right but it hasn't worked out so well. I was accused of being a witch and murderer for absolutely nothing. I don't believe in either and my family meant the world to me. I gained nothing & ended up homeless. From 06-10 my mom, dad, grandma, husband & daughter died I was 29. I'm remarried and we've had our two girls Aahviaughn died last year & Laila 2 months ago so it's hard & it hurts so bad.
