column1: What are the most common triggers for depression?
column3: What Triggers Can Cause Depression? By identifying depression triggers, people can identify and be aware and be alert to signs of depression in themselves and in others. 1. Grief and Loss Grief and loss – known as bereavement – are a significant situational trigger of depression. However, diagnosis may be tricky because the symptoms may just be taken as being a normal reaction to loss. Handling grief is a personal experience. How grief is managed depends on the individual’s age, life experience, personality, state of mind and the situation being grieved. Grief can manifest itself in physical and mental symptoms, such as:Depressed mood and full depressionAnxietyAngerHigh blood pressure and heart rateHigh-stress hormone levelsSleep disturbancesImmune system changesSubstance useWhen grief becomes prolonged or intense it is known as complicated grief or prolonged grief disorder. Grief can become particularly complicated if it is accompanied by rumination. It can be difficult to tell when the usual sadness of grief crosses the line to depression. People who are grieving should discuss the issue with their physician, particularly if they are having difficulty coping. Related Topic: Complicated grief treatment 2. Rejection People have an innate need for approval, affirmation, and acceptance from others. Rejection and social exclusion can be very stressful for people and have been associated with low self-esteem. Some people are especially sensitive to social rejection and have a high rejection sensitivity (RS). A person’s level of RS depends on their genetics and their prior experiences in life. People with a high RS are more sensitive to social cues and pick up on the smallest hint of rejection. They respond intensely to any hints detected. Any perceived failure in being accepted causes anxiety. With perceived repeated failures, eventually social withdrawal and depression results. Even people without a high RS can try hard to gain others’ approval, and feel down after being rejected. Anger and aggression are common rejection reactions as well. This response is especially true when rejection involves a love-interest. Conversely, depression itself causes an elevated RS, because people with depression tend to feel lower self-esteem and are therefore more sensitive to rejection. Their negative depression symptoms (such as depressed mood, lack of energy, social isolation and loss of interest in activities) may make them more likely to be rejected socially. The widespread stigma against depression and other mental health disorders may magnify the likelihood of rejection. An individual’s RS is not necessarily fixed at a certain level. Counseling may help treat depression and prevent relapse. 3. Stress Psychological stress is a major cause of depression because of its physical effects on the body and brain. In particular, stress causes hormonal changes that are present in about 70% of depressed people. The hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal glands are disrupted from their normal regulation of mood and emotion. Stress releases the stress hormone cortisol, which results in physical changes to brain cells. Stress can even result in changes to the size of the hippocampus, the part of the brain that is known to be reduced in depressed people. Psychological stress also activates the immune system, including the release of immune system chemicals (cytokines) that are associated with depression. These immune chemicals are active in brain tissue, including the hippocampus, which explains their role in producing symptoms of mental illness. 4. Illness Illnesses may contribute to up to 10-15% of all cases of depression. This correlation can happen because:The illness itself may be tragic, and receiving the diagnosis can be traumatic (e.g., cancer, HIV infection, Multiple Sclerosis)The illness may cause depressive symptoms (e.g., hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, mononucleosis)The illness may have an inherent association with depression (e.g., Parkinson’s disease, erectile dysfunction, heart attack)The medications used to treat the illness may cause depression (e.g., some heart medications, hormones, certain antibiotics)There is a reciprocal relationship between illness and depression. Many illnesses or their treatments can be triggers for depression, and depression is known to slow recovery and cause a higher risk of death in many illnesses. In the case of a chronic or terminal illness, co-occurring depression can magnify the suffering brought on by the illness itself. Physicians should make their patients aware of a particular illness or medication that can cause depression and should watch for this side effect. Likewise, people who are ill should be aware of this common and debilitating effect of illness. 5. Lack of Sleep Sleep has a reciprocal relationship with depression. First of all, sleep changes are a core symptom of depression. An individual has either increased or decreased sleep. About 75% of depressed people have insomnia, and about 40% sleep excessively (hypersomnia), with lots of overlap. Sleep problems are some of the major reasons that people seek help for their depression. Conversely, a lack of sleep is a known trigger for depression. Insomnia increases the risk of developing depression by four times. A clinical trial in adult twins showed that a sleep duration of five hours or less doubles the incidence of depression. Because these were twins, the genetic predisposition for depression was not a factor. Another large study with adolescents showed that sleep duration of six hours or less per night increases the risk of depression by 25% to 38%. Developing depression can cause sleep disturbances, so a vicious cycle can ensue. Adolescents seem to be especially prone to sleep deprivation, usually self-imposed. Addressing sleep problems appears to be an effective way to prevent depression, as well as treat depression and prevent relapse. Also, given the association between sleep problems and suicide risk, addressing sleep symptoms in depressed people is especially important. 6. Rumination Rumination is grief that has gotten out of control. The ruminating individual dwells on the grief rather than trying to embrace and deal with it healthily. The grief and pain become an obsession that interferes with normal life functions. People who ruminate get stuck on thoughts like, “Why did this happen to me,” and, “How terrible is this?” They get caught up in self-pity and exaggerate the negative. They may also get angry with others who are handling their grief in healthier ways. It is not surprising that rumination has been identified as a major trigger for depression. It can cause depression, worsen and prolong existing depression, and it is a risk factor for suicidal ideation. Conversely, the impaired emotional regulation that is characteristic in depressed people can lead them to ruminate. Experiencing grief is a normal part of life, but many people are poorly equipped for handling it, especially if it is a new experience for them. Their expectations of grief may be unrealistic. Researchers found that hope — internal confidence and motivation to succeed — is the antidote for rumination. People with high hope have better self-efficacy and a focus for continuing on with life despite the loss that they are grieving, rather than ruminating. People who are ruminating should receive grief counseling. 7. Money Problems Financial problems can cause depression in several ways. A study that tracked 35,000 Americans to study the effects of money on mental health found that low household income is associated with increased risk of mental health disorders, especially depression. The study found that a drop in income increases the risk of depression. Additional research found that financial difficulties and financial stress are associated with depression, which appears to worsen financial difficulties, beginning a vicious cycle. People experiencing financial difficulties, such as drops in income or financial loss, should consider measures to improve their ability to cope with the stress associated with these changes. 8. Life Transitions Life transitions, even positive ones, can have negative effects on a person’s mood. People are creatures of habit, so even positive life changes can take them out of their comfort zone and cause stress. For example, a job promotion can involve leaving a familiar and comfortable job for one that is unfamiliar and difficult. The new job can involve leaving behind familiar people and being surrounded by strangers. It may also be more stressful and involve a steep learning curve. The collective effect is stress that may precipitate depression, despite the positive event of getting promoted. If the life transition is a negative one, such as losing a job or getting divorced, then the stress and depressive effects will be even more of a shock. There is a subtype of depression called adjustment disorder, where the individual develops depressive symptoms or even full depression after life changes. People should anticipate the stressors of life changes, and be prepared for them. Those who are having difficulty coping should consider engaging their support system and even counseling. They should also be vigilant in looking for symptoms of depression that may follow these life changes. 9. Substance Use Substance use and depression are closely related. Many of the mental and physical changes seen in depression and addiction are similar. They also share many risk factors, have overlapping symptoms and each can cause or trigger the other. Recent discoveries revealed that drug and alcohol abuse can cause physical changes in the connections between the brain cells so that new pathways are formed that support addiction. Many people use substances as a way to self-medicate their mental health symptoms. In many cases, people aren’t even aware that they have a treatable mental health disorder and have been living with their symptoms for so long that they assume that it is just normal. When substance use and depression (or other mental health disorders) occur at the same time, it is referred to as comorbidity. When comorbidity occurs, it is crucial to treat both conditions at the same time. Trying to treat depression in the presence of active substance use is difficult. Likewise, trying to treat addiction in the presence of untreated depression greatly lowers the chance of success. Managing Depression Triggers One of the most important aspects of managing depression triggers is awareness of them so that individuals and their loved ones recognize them promptly and act accordingly. Even if people are subjected to a trigger that they can’t immediately change — such as chronic illness, financial troubles, or a life transition — they can take action to reduce the stress from the event. Given the range of severity and things that can cause depression, people who struggle with bouts of depression require professional help. It is a serious illness that can become chronic, and it is associated with disability, reduced quality of life, physical illness and even death. Comorbidity is especially dangerous and requires specialized care. 9 Common Depression Triggers and Causes | What Causes Depression?

column1: Adult How does one end grief, and how long does it normally take for one to grief over a loved one?
column3: How does one end grief and how long does it take for one to grieve over a loved one? Grief is the price we pay for love. The deeper the love; the deeper the grief. Grief doesn’t end. Initially when we lose a loved one or loved ones…we go through various emotions. My Grandpa died unexpectedly. He walked 5 miles the day he died and rode his bike for 2 hours. He he returned home and had a heart attack. He was healthy. And then he was gone. My sister called and left a message that Grandpa died. I dropped screaming. I went from shock and disbelief to begging God to bring him back to me. I bargained with God…if I could have Grandpa back…I will give anything for one more moment. If I had known the last time I saw him was the last time I saw him…it would not have been the last time. I would do anything to roll back time. Command life and death…and beckon him back to me. I was on my knees trying to bargain with God. Then I got mad at God. I screamed at God…cursed God for taking him from me. And then I realised if I didn’t stop cursing God…Grandpa wouldn’t come back to me. So I begged God to forgive me for cursing him…and promised I would never do anything wrong again. And begged him to bring Grandpa back to me. When Grandpa didn’t come back to me; I screamed at him again. What kind of God would take him away from me. I once again tried to bargain with God…roll back time and I would never sin again. I would be perfect. I even tried to bargain with God. Asked him to switch Dad for Grandpa. It seemed a fair trade at the time. Then when God still didn’t send him back to me…I decided God didn’t exist. I stopped believing in God…even as I cried and sobbed and begged him to send Grandpa back to me…I told God I will never believe in him again. Then I panicked and begged God to forgive me. If I didn’t believe in God there was no way Grandpa would come back to me. So…I promised never to disbelieve again…and promised once again…if he would just bring him back to me. I won’t ever question God’s existence again. My anger subsided. And was replaced with depression. Without Grandpa I had no reason to live. I begged God to take me instead of him. This went on and one for about let’s see…only about 27 years. I am not ok. It is not ok that Grandpa died. How can I exist in a world where Grandpa was no more? Then MiMi (my grandma) died. And I begged God to bring her back to me. Whatever the price I would pay it. Nothing was ever the same. The thing is…I went back to the same begging and bargaining with God to bring Grandpa back to me. At the very same time that I was begging God to bring MiMi back to me. The grief of losing Grandpa came flooding back and I was stuck in a never ending cycle of disbelief, bargaining, begging, anger…depression and acceptance…that’s not true…never accepted that Grandpa died. And I never accepted that MiMi died. I buried it. Then dad died. It all came back. The pain of losing dad compounded the pain of losing MiMi and Grandpa. I felt the hideous grief of losing both of my grandparents while trying to wrap my mind around the death of dad. I was wracked in grief…and 2 years after dad died…mom died. I am spinning out if control. But no one knows. I hide it well. Unless I go to a store. Where there are mothers, fathers, grandpa’s and grandma’s. Or people who have mothers, fathers, grandpa’s and grandma’s. Everywhere I go…my grief follows me. Sometimes I am good at stuffing my grief..I put on a smile and move on…then a memory will hit me. A whiff of perfume…a song…white hair..the smell of cigarette smoke. A raspy voice…a giggle. Long nails painted red…and I am lost in nostalgia. I go from the highest of highs to the deepest of lows. Nostalgia sweetens the breeze and breaks my heart all at the same time. And my heart is broken again. The cycle of grief shows it’s ugly head and I spin out of control once again. The grief of losing Grandpa, MiMi, Dad…and mom engulfs me. My body and essence know the anniversary date of all of my losses. As well as birthdays, holidays, Monday’s , Tuesdays , Wednesdays, Thursdays, Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Grandpa and dad died on Sunday, MiMi and mom on Wednesday. And Grandpa’s funeral was on Saturday, MiMi’s funeral was on Friday and Mom’s on Monday. I didn’t find out dad died until after his wife had cremated him. It’s complicated. There was no service for dad. I just mourn him every moment of my life: The magnitude of our grief is only matched by the magnitude of our love. As long as we love…we grieve. Grief is the price we pay for love. We don’t stop grieving. We stuff our grief. Keep it close to our heart. And then we go back through all the stages we went before. We just get better at hiding it. And as painful as it is to lose loved ones…nothing compares to the loss of our children. There is nothing worse then losing a child. All the grief we experience in the loss of our parents, grandparents, siblings and friends does not even come close to the grief of losing a child. I can’t even speak it…lest the thought or word beckons our children. Beautiful Soul…you love and you lose…and the nostalgia lifts us to to highest of highs and drops us to the lowest of lows. Grief ebbs and flows…but it doesn’t leave. And for this we are blessed. We only grieve because we love.

column1: How can I stop grieving? I don't want to feel this anymore.
column3: By living. I know that sounds like a dumb answer, but it’s the truth, and yet far more complicated than it sounds when you’re dying inside. I don’t mean go through the motions, though definitely keep doing your daily tasks. I mean shake it up a little and live. It doesn’t have to be anything big. What got me through grieving one of my grandfathers was playing solitaire a lot and making red beans and rice. It brought me comfort and reminded me of his good qualities which helped me bring those into my life and helped quell my sadness. But it can be bigger things too. It can be following a dream you used to talk about with them, knowing that if it’s possible that they are cheering you on from somewhere. It can also have nothing to do with them and be you going out to try new things and meet new people. Grief is a slump, a track. Easy to get caught into. We get lost in thoughts of sadness and life can become depressing and monotonous easily. Do not wear yourself out trying to force change. I have tried that before and you can legitimately make yourself sick that way. But do shake things up some. Remember god things you once loved and give them another go. Trying new things. See old loved ones and meet new people. A little here and a little there will get you there in time. And if you do choose something big, a big change, remember that the initial excitement will easily cover the grief, but that you may cone back to it a few times later and that that is okay and normal. Healing grief i us a process. The pain of loss never fully goes away, but it does become manageable in time.

column1: How does an INFJ handle a breakup?
column3: As an INFJ, this is how I approach and navigate through breakups successfully within 2 weeks to 3 months (it happens in the following order):I set up no contact and refuse any offer for friendship. Because unless we have kids together and unless things aren’t completely toxic, I don’t believe in staying friends with an ex. It only makes things more complicated than they need to be.I keep reminding myself that I don’t need my ex to feel safe, whole and complete because I know who I am and can generate those feelings within myself and without the ex. That I experienced this before and came out of it stronger each time. This is how I let go very fast and bounce back from breakups.I accept that it’s over.I allow myself to feel and express the grief of the loss. Because keeping it in isn’t a good strategy. So I give myself a few weeks to max 3 months off to grief and adjust to the changes the breakup initiated. This is the most intense stage. Most get stuck there for a long time.I reflect on everything this relationship taught me and take note of how much I have grown through it. Because we are never the same person after breakups since relationships shape our personality.I actively work through unhealed or hurts parts in order to heal them through the power of awareness and letting go.I take a break from dating and prioritize solitude until I am in a mentally & emotionally stable place. I can’t stress enough how powerful it is to learn to enjoy solitude after breakups rather than immediately jumping into another relationship.Once I‘m done with all the above, I do a life audit, revise some goals, get back on track and then take action to build an amazing life.

column1: Why didn’t Hannibal attack Rome after the Battle of Cannae?
column3: Attacking Rome after Cannae would mean a siege. Hannibal’s first act of the Second Punic War was the siege of Siege of Saguntum. This was in friendly territory for Hannibal and it took him over six months to subdue the city:Rome had seven miles of walls, 33 feet high:Hannibal did not have the engineers and specialists to create siege engines. He would have to starve Rome out. How many troops did Hannibal have to seal off this wall? His losses were 6,000–8,000 at Cannae. Optimistically, he would have at least 2:1 ratio of wounded to killed. If he fought with 50,000 at Cannae, afterwards, he would have an army 30,000 men left. Military men claim, one man on top of proper wall is worth 8–10 below it. That is why people have always built walls, forts and castles. They are massive “force multipliers.” By straight military analysis, he had far too few men to even consider storming the walls of Rome. Central Italy was still loyal to Rome. How was Hannibal to feed these 30,000 men in hostile territory? He could not ship in supplies; Rome controlled the Mediterranean. Hannibal figured halting his army around the gates of Rome would lead to its destruction. Instead, he gathered his strength in Southern Italy, areas friendly to him. Capua had allied with Hannibal. Hannibal decided to make his move towards Rome by eliminating the holdouts in the Campania region (cleaning up your rear is always a good idea). The area that had allied with Hannibal is in blue below:During the second half of 216 BC, Hannibal made his move:He did not breech the walls of Naples. Acerrae was taken because its inhabitants had abandoned the town. Casilinum was poorly defended and was taken after a costly fight. The maps is complicated because Hannibal’s movements were complicated, The History of Rome, Book 23:…the Carthaginians retired from the territory of Nola and marched down to the sea close upon Naples, eager to get possession of a maritime town to which there would be a safe course for ships from Africa. But hearing that Naples was held by a Roman prefect, Marcus Junius Silanus, who had been invited thither by the Neapolitans themselves, he left Naples as he had left Nola, and directed his course to Nuceria, which he at length starved into capitulation, after having besieged it for a considerable time…Hannibal tried his siege skills at Nola, again, in 216 BC. He lost the Battle of Nola (216 BC). The History of Rome, Book 23:….some authors have declared, that two thousand eight hundred of the enemy were slain, and that the Romans lost not more than five hundred. Whether the victory was so great or not…2,800 men lost in a failed attempt to take a small Italian town? The Romans claimed it as a minor victory. Still, his losses were 10 percent of his remaining manpower. Hannibal’s assessment was correct. If, his army was incapable of successfully taking a small walled town, if the defenders held their ground, trying to take Rome would destroy his army. He made two other attempts on Nola and those failed too: Battle of Nola (215 BC) Battle of Nola (214 BC) The only way Hannibal marching to Rome could have succeeded was if the Roman leadership lost their nerve and refused to fight. According to Livy, they almost did. That was where Quintus Fabius Maximus Verrucosus, the Delayer, comes in:Livy claimed the days after Cannae were hard for Rome. Women clogged the gates looking for their brothers, fathers and sons. The Senate refused to convene. The guards at the city gates were instructed to stop anyone from leaving. And many more extreme measures were instituted to prevent panic from spreading. But, the death of so many Roman men, in their prime, was a horror show. Fabius plunged into the grieving masses and restored order, Plutarch • Life of Fabius Maximus (Cunctator):…when all were plunged in boundless grief and helpless confusion, was the only man to walk the city with calm step, composed countenance, and gracious address, checking effeminate lamentation, and preventing those from assembling together who were eager to make public their common complaints. He persuaded the senate to convene, heartened up the magistrates, and was himself the strength and power of every magistracy, since all looked to him for guidance. Accordingly, he put guards at the gates, in order to keep the frightened throng from abandoning the city, and set limits of time and place to the mourning for the dead, ordering any who wished to indulge in lamentation, to do so at home for a period of thirty days; after that, all mourning must cease and the city be purified of such rites.Livy has a slightly difference account but largely confirms the situation, The History of Rome, Book 22:Publius Furius Philus and Marcus Pomponius, the praetors, called the senate together in the Curia Hostilia, to consult about the defence of Rome; for they made no doubt that the enemy, after wiping out their armies, would be advancing to besiege the City, which was all that remained to do to end the war. But when, amid dangers at once so immense and so incalculable, they failed to think of even any tolerable plan of action, and were deafened with the cries and lamentations of the women, both the living and the dead in the lack as yet of any announcement —being indiscriminately mourned in almost every house, then Quintus Fabius Maximus urged that light-armed horsemen be sent out along the Appian and Latin ways, and questioning those they met -for some there would surely be who had dispersed and made off in the rout —bring back word of the fortunes of the consuls and the armies, and if the immortal gods, taking pity on the empire, had spared any remnant of the Roman name, where those forces were; [whither Hannibal had gone after the battle, what his plans were, what he was doing and was likely to do. To discover and ascertain these facts was a task, he said, for active youths; what the Fathers themselves must do, since there were not magistrates enough, was this: quell the panic and confusion in the City; keep the matrons off the streets and compel them each to abide in her own home; restrain families from lamentation; procure silence throughout the City; see that bearers of any news were brought before the praetors —every man must wait at home for tidings that concerned himself; —and, besides this, post sentries at the gates, to keep anyone from leaving the City, and make the people rest all hope of safety on the safety of Rome and of its walls. When the tumult had died down, then the Fathers must be convened again and consider how to defend the City.For those that wonder, some of Hannibal’s men thought he should have marched on Rome, immediately. His cavalry commander advised immediate and aggressive pursuit. Livy again:Hannibal's officers crowded round him with congratulations on his victory. The others all advised him, now that he had brought so great a war to a conclusion, to repose himself and to allow his weary soldiers to repose for the remainder of that day and the following night. But Maharbal, the commander of the cavalry, held that no time should be lost. “Nay,” he cried, “that you may realize what has been accomplished by this battle, in five days you shall banquet in the Capitol! Follow after; I will precede you with the cavalry, that the Romans may know that you are there before they know that you are coming!”However, even at that point, Hannibal had decided not to march on Rome. Maharbal’s words have gone down in history:To Hannibal the idea was too joyous and too vast for his mind at once to grasp it. And so, while praising Maharbal's goodwill, he declared that he must have time to deliberate regarding his advice. Then said Maharbal, “In very truth the gods bestow not on the same man all their gifts; you know how to gain a victory, Hannibal: you know not how to use one.” That day's delay is generally believed to have saved the City and the empire.So, at the time, many Romans and Carthaginians thought Hannibal should have gone in for the kill. It would be hard to explain to a subordinate, such action would throw away a great victory by starting a venture that he could not successfully complete.

column1: What would you say to someone who is not grieving as much as others think they should?
column3: What would I say to someone who is not grieving as much as others think they should? Grief is a personal matter. We carry it deep in our heart. Grief is a journey we take alone. We don’t ask anyone to come along for the ride…because we only process grief….alone. No one else will ever know how we are processing grief. There are no rules when it comes to grief. There are no right ways or wrong ways in our experience of grief. There is only our grief. And it’s ours. So…we decide how we grieve. Whether we scream, sob, drop to the floor, feel nothing…it’s the best way for us grieve. When I was working Children’s Protective Services, I had cases where a baby or child had died. And what I observed in parents who have lost a child (I only received fatalities if there were suspicions of child abuse or child neglect surrounding the child’s death ) their are absolutely no rules, and a parent’s response to the death of their child varies. In 15 years, I only saw one mom cry (I had multiple fatalities)…the dad’s that i worked with cried…screamed…sobbed…but only one mom cried. Sometimes when we lose someone we love…in particular a child…the body won’t release the tears. We can’t squeeze one tear out…but we are screaming inside…it’s so loud it’s deafening. I have observed mom’s open their mouth and nothing comes out, or sometimes what comes out…is laughter. And that can look like mom or dad didn’t care. This is the furthest from the truth. Mom’s and dad do care. Desperately. Grief is numbing. Grief is stabbing. Grief is a constant punch in the gut . Grief follows no definitions or rules. And rarely presents us in a positive light. There is simply too much darkness that tries to drag us under and bury us. And we present to others as if we don’t care. Because frankly…we don’t. We don’t care about anything except one more chance to get it right. To be in the right place where we can command yesterday…and change the outcome. If only…If only kills. No matter the scenario…we cannot go back and do something different or say the right thing that will change the outcome. This is what we care about. We just want one more moment…and that moment happened…a moment too late. There are various stages of grief. Disbelief, bargaining, anger, depression and acceptance. These stages are not linear. We can go back and forth through the stages over and over. Or we may skip some stages. Or we may be in a stage, and get stuck in that stage. Or we may at some point work through some stages of grief. And this is done in solitude. We experience our grief…alone. Our grief isolates us. Even if we are surrounded by others. And this may look like we don’t care…Things are rarely as we see them. We search inward. We have already looked outside of ourselves and that didn’t help…so we pull back. And this looks like we are not grieving…as others think we should. If we show too much emotion…we are not handling our grief as we should…we should be “getting over it”. Others have so much to say about something that isn’t about them. My mom died on 10/13/21. Our relationship was complicated…and those complications were not resolved. They only got worse the closer it came to mom dying. When mom died…we hated one another. And we loved one another so deeply…we couldn’t hold on strong enough to make it right. Our life together just slipped through our fingers. There were no death bed confessions of love and regret. She was here one moment…and the very next moment she was gone. In a blink of an eye. The chains of regret that bound her in life were released when she died. Those chains are strangling me. I couldn’t cry. And then I couldn’t stop crying. I couldn’t eat…and I couldn’t stop eating. I couldn’t get up, and I couldn’t stand down. To one person, I looked like I was devastated…and to another…I looked like I didn’t care. It’s all about perspective. I couldn’t scream or even squeeze a tear out…I finally was able to cry. I finally cried at mom’s graveside service. For my sister’s dog. My sister’s dog died the morning of mom’s service…and we sobbed at the service…for the loss of her dog. Her graveside service was before her funeral (long story). The following day was her funeral. I spoke at her funeral. I read a poem I wrote to her at her, and then I read a scripture about love. After I read it I added “such beautiful lies “…and I kept saying “beautiful lies”. So…then I sat down…my sister took me in her arms. I started crying and saying beautiful lies over and over. The day of her graveside I didn’t cry for her…and at her funeral I couldn’t find the love. To me…that scripture about love, mom’s love for me and my love for her had nothing in common. Our life together was one beautiful lie…amid the ugly truth of our shared hatred for one another. And my grief looked like I didn’t care that mom died…I can’t breathe since mom died…and some were concerned that I wasn’t upset about her death. I can’t stop the tremors that threaten to upend me. The panic stays dormant…until I get into a car. And I am terrified of the ride. I rock back and forth and cover my face (I don’t drive now…until I do)…and then I start screaming. I only scream in the car while my husband is driving. Needless to say this is not pleasant for either of us…I’m working on bracing myself against the dashboard or my seat…to replace screaming. I did this on the way to my mom's graveside and funeral services. And I did it yesterday and I may do it today…so…I’m working on remaining silent as I hold on for dear life to the dashboard. I didn’t screams yesterday…I only repeated “oh my God I’m dying….” I am nothing if not dramatic. To some…I don’t care that mom died. I even had one person tell me it’s good that I wasn’t upset since I hated her so much (hate and love are the flip side of one another). One can’t hate if one doesn’t love. The opposite of apathy. And I have been told it’s been almost 2 years…I should be over it. People have a lot to say about something they know nothing about…our grief. You are handling your grief the very best you way can. There are no rules about how you should experience and display your grief. It is very very personal. And for the record…we don’t “get over” grief. We try to manage it the very best way we can.

column1: What positive changes have you made in your Life, what was the effect?
column3: Change is inevitable. When we think of change having an impact on mental health, we typically think about the stress caused by loss -- the death of a loved one, the end of a relationship, the pressure from family/friends, and other endings hold a finality that can be difficult to accept. But sometimes, things change for the better. Positive change can create stress as well, even when it's something we've looked forward to for a very long time. Regardless of what type of change is taking place in your life — positive, negative, or somewhere in between — there are strategies you can utilize to cope with the stress of those life changes and come out the other end a stronger version of yourself.“Change is painful, but nothing is as painful as staying stuck somewhere you don’t belong.”Dealing with Positive ChangeWhen most people hear the term “positive change”, they automatically think happiness is associated with it. However, that is not always true and even major positive changes in a person’s life can cause depression and anxiety. (That’s why I always mention not everything will work in your favor just because something worked in my or someone else’s life.) Some common examples of positive changes that many people encounter throughout their lives are: going to college, getting a job, and having a significant other in life.Going to collegeWhether going to college three miles away or 3,000 miles, it will always be a huge change. This huge change can cause people to develop depression and anxiety. It can stem from multiple different things such as the harder school work, balancing social and academic life, and being homesick. How to deal with it: For support, turning to close friends and family can help. There are also trained professionals on every college campus to help students transition and get the help they need.Getting a new job (in my case career change that I made - still working on it so giving more details related to it is difficult so will explain concerning a job)A common belief is getting a new job causes happiness and joy, while that is the case, it can also cause anxiety. Anxiety can stem from all kinds of different thoughts. A prevalent thought maybe “Is this the right job for me?” or “Am I doing everything correctly?” These thoughts are completely common and most, if not every young person has these exact thoughts as well. Something else about a new job that may cause anxiety is a new schedule to follow. Humans are creatures of habit and having to start a brand new schedule can be tough. How to cope: Adopt a new schedule to develop habits that will help you be successful in your new job. Having something stable to rely on -- even if it just means waking up and going for a walk before work at the same time each day, or spending a few minutes reading before bed -- can make a world of difference when everything feels like it's up in the air.Having a significant other (I thought this but things didn’t work out for both plus it was just a relationship, not marriage so stepping out of it was easy)Starting a new relationship is exciting, but it can also be nerve-wracking. Everybody's had the butterflies, but for some, the better you feel about your future with a new partner, the more pressure you might experience not to mess up. You may find yourself with less time to devote to friends or hobbies, more responsibilities, or going through related life changes — moving in together, getting hitched, and so on. Yes, all of these things are exciting! But like any change, they can be stressful as well. How to cope: Maintain some time for yourself. Set some time aside to be apart from your significant other -- spending time with your friends, working on an independent hobby or project, or just relaxing on your own. A little bit of space to maintain the interests that made up a larger part of your life before you met your partner can give you much-needed stability and take a bit of the pressure off.Dealing with Negative ChangeFor all the good that it can bring, change can also be incredibly painful. We all experience moments that alter our lives or our futures dramatically, and in the aftermath, we might find ourselves struggling to accept our lives or our path forward. When dealing with these negative changes, the scale of the change hardly matters — maybe it's a small change, maybe we've been expecting it, but it can still have a dramatic impact on our mental health.Losing a loved one (Past 2 years have done this damage as I lost someone I loved the most - I’m sure many must have experienced it and I have no words to make anyone feel better life is difficult)Coping with the death of a loved one is always difficult. There's no way to sugarcoat it. It just sucks. It doesn't matter how old you are or how long you've been expecting it — losing someone close to you is deeply traumatic and can take a toll on an individual's mental health. Managing the loss and establishing a new "normal" without the person lost can feel insurmountable at times, but it is not insurmountable. It may take time, but you will get through this period of grief. How to cope: Grief is personal, so coping with grief is personal. Take your time. Be gentle with yourself. Give yourself the time and care you need to heal. If your grief lingers, make sure you're dealing with complicated grief rather than depression — and take steps to get the support you need.Moving somewhere new aloneWith jobs, family, and significant others, moving around may occur during life. Moving can be fun and exciting in some ways, but also can be scary and intimidating. Moving can be especially scary if you move to a new place and do not a single person. Making friends after college can be difficult enough, but in a completely new place without knowing anyone can be even more challenging. When feeling lost and alone, depression may start to occur. How to cope: There are ways to make friends in a new place. Consider downloading an app dedicated to finding new friends. Check out local community organizations related to things that interest you — it's a great way to jump into friendships where you already share some common ground.Not all change has a silver lining. Sometimes it's necessary to deal with downright painful changes.An important part of managing stress effectively is knowing when you're experiencing more stress than you can effectively deal with on your own. If the change-related stress in your life has become overwhelming, know that it is okay. We all need extra support sometimes. Whether that means spending some extra time talking to loved ones or seeking professional treatment for anxiety, there are plenty of avenues available to explore. Life is truly a rollercoaster and there will be thousands of ups and downs and changes throughout it. Both negative and positive changes can affect the mind and body and cause depression and anxiety. I hope with the above tips, coping will become easier! for everyone. Don’t ever choose to run from the situation first evaluate how you can bring change and if still things don’t change choose therapy sometimes it helps. Bhavya Bist

column1: How's it like to lose your baby while he or she is still unborn?
column3: It all depends on how you’ve come to think about your pregnancy. I was very lucky to attend an amazing support group for women who had lost their children prior to birth, and I did notice that a couple of women were sad, but not heartbroken. They had one thing in common, and it wasn’t how for along they were when their babies died. They hadn’t really begun to think of their fetuses as children yet, and their pregnancies hadn’t seemed quite real to them. I have no doubt that they would have loved their children as much as the rest of us once they were born, but for various reasons they just hadn’t connected with the life inside of them yet. They were grieving, but we also had one conversation where they explained that they just couldn’t relate to the level of pain that some of us felt. There were other women who had lost a pregnancy so early that they’d been unable to even spot the fetus or embryo, and some of them were as lost as devastated as I was after losing a baby when I was nearly full term. They had felt connected to their baby from the moment they learned that they were pregnant and they had lost the entire future they had begun to imagine for them. I lost two pregnancies at around 8 weeks and one at 13 before my perfect little baby died inside me. I felt deep dispair and sadness with the first two, and I only left the house to go have an ultrasound (to make sure that everything had come out) for the first few weeks. I was grieving the loss of a pregnancy rather than a child, though. My feelings of failure were almost worse than the actual grief, and I felt like my old self within a month. The third pregnancy ended at 13 weeks and 1 day, and it was a lot worse. We had made it so far and we told our family and friends less than five days earlier. The earlier miscarriages both happened at night, as I was sleeping in my own bed, but this time I was at work when I started to experience serious cramps. My heart stopped (it didn’t really, but it sure felt like it did) and I walked to the bathroom in a daze. No blood yet, but the cramps were bad. I called my husband and told him to meet me at the doctor’s office. I was sitting at a red light when it felt like the pain was beginning to subside, but as soon as I registered the relief, I felt something running out of me. There was a visible bloodstain on my pale gray pants when I arrived, and I saw all the pregnant women in the waiting room look at me with a mix of sympathy and relief that they weren’t me. I pretended that it never happened. I didn’t want to sit at home and cry again, and it just so happened that I soon began to experience severe pain from my endometriosis. My doctor referred me to a pain management specialist and he had the perfect solution for my problems: Oxycodone and fentanyl. It felt like a miracle because the drugs numbed my emotional pain along with the physical, so I never truly got to process that loss. It was really the worst thing that I could have done, but I grasped at the chance to ignore my grief. The drugs also provided me with a convenient excuse to stop trying for a baby, because I really didn’t want to lose another unborn child. It turns out that life doesn’t give a damn what we want, so after years of difficulties conceiving, I got pregnant when I wasn’t trying. Thankfully I never realized, because this one hadn’t implanted in my uterus so I ended up losing a fallopian tube along with it. My doctor now told me not to get pregnant again, but I got sober and we decided to try again. I had another surgery to remove as much of the endometriosis as was possible, followed by six months of hormone injections to give my body a rest. My periods never returned after the last shot because I conceived as soon as I began to ovulate again. That seemed like a good sign, and the pregnancy went well. My baby hung on through the first trimester, and then the second. Then a complication arose, one that can be fatal for women and their babies, but we thought that it was under control. Everything went went well for a while, but then my doctors decided that we should deliver a few weeks early. It was less than 24 hours before I was scheduled to deliver that my baby just stopped moving inside me. It was the worst feeling imaginable, and I don’t think that there would be any real point in trying to describe how it felt. If you aren’t familiar with that kind of grief, you won’t understand anyway – and I envy you that. If you are capable of understanding it, it means that you won’t need any explanation – and I am so, so sorry for that.

column1: Adult How do you know when you've reached the acceptance stage of grief?
column3: Several people have already talked about how grief doesn’t have stages and it’s individual, to me the important part of this question is “how do I know that grief is over?” For me there is a key difference between sadness, or even deep sadness and grief. Sadness is completely normal and is what we feel when grief is done. Grief is also completely normal following any loss, however it is more complicated than sadness. The Grief Recovery Method defines grief as “the conflicting feelings following a change or end in a familiar pattern of behaviour” so in grief we may be experiencing lots of different feelings all at the same time. for example relief the suffering is over, anger that they died too soon, lonely with them to talk to etc. When grief is complete it is possible to have fond memories not turn painful so that you can talk about the person and be happy recalling good things, sad remembering they’re gone but it doesn’t hurt and the feelings aren’t conflicting. If there is pain or conflict in your heart then there is still some unresolved grief. As unresolved grief is almost always undelivered communications of an emotional nature eg what if? if only? why? would’ve, should’ve, could’ve the Grief Recovery Method teaches how to complete these in a safe way so that grief can be resolved and the person move forward in their life.

column1: My girlfriend passed away last month and I can't seem to move on. Every time I approach a girl I feel like I'm cheating on her. What should I do?

You'll get involved with wrong women and carry extra baggage that you could've avoided easily. Don't date anyone now for your own sake. Instead focus on investing on your personal and professional growth. Don't force yourself to forget her. Allow yourself the time to heal. And time is the greatest healer.

column1: Adult What is anticipatory grief?
column3: Anticipatory grief is the grief that comes in anticipation of a loss. Perhaps, someone you love have just received a diagnosis of a terminal illness.
