column1: How do you cope with watching your dog age? My dog is 14 sometime last month and I can see how old he’s getting. He has gone deaf and developed a breathing problem. Nothing major but it’s just hard seeing how old he is compared to what he was before.
column3: It is so hard. I go through it with all my pets, as does everyone who very much loves a dog or cat. Today, we have three cats, aged 6, 4 and 3, and a dog, 2. As I said a year or so ago to our vet, having young pets is like being at the beginning of a long vacation. A young pet means you haven't yet entered that period of vague dread that your days together are hurtling past. I remember that feeling. Five years ago, I had a terminally ill 12-year-old cat, a 14-year-old cat and an almost 12-year-old dog. Every ailment, even something that turned out to be mild, caused me great anxiety. I even felt jealous and a little resentful toward people with young pets, though I'm ashamed to admit it. What I was experiencing, and what you're experiencing, is anticipatory grief. It's a normal part of the process of getting ready to say good-bye to something or someone that matters a lot. And it does help temper grief when the loss happens, at least a little bit. I've experienced the deaths of human and animal loved ones that were long coming, but as painful as those deaths were, there is an extra wildness to grief that is compounded by the terrible shock of a sudden death. So I think that simmering dread we feel when a pet is getting old is helping us get through some of the grief, because we're getting ready for an expected loss. But the problem with anticipatory grief is two-fold. First, we don't know for sure when the end will actually come. After our 12-year-old cat died 5 years ago this week, the other cat and the dog lived another very good and mostly very healthy 3 years. I spent those 3 years preparing to lose them, feeling very regular pangs of sorrow. But--and here's the other problem with anticipatory grief--I look back at photos and think back on memories of those 3 years, and we had some really great days with them. Fun, funny, happy and loving days. I wish I had worked harder to stay right there in those moments--just like our pets always do--instead of letting myself wonder mournfully if this was to be the last Christmas together or whatever. I'm going to try that with our current pets, and ask me in about 8 or 9 years how I'm doing with it. Because how you're feeling, as I said, is how we all feel with an elderly pet. But try to help yourself be more like your dog, and join him in the perpetual present, where our pets live, as much as you can. He's still here today. And I wish you lots more todays with him.

column1: What is grief, and what are the forms of grief?
column3: Grief is an emotional response to the loss of someone. It can impact you physically and emotionally. You have to work through the stages at a pace that is comfortable. Typically this can include going through various stages, such as denial, depression, anger, and acceptance. You typically go back and forth from one stage to another. There’s no set timetable for grief and it’s important to be easy on yourself. Accept that you’re going to deal with different uncomfortable emotions and get the help you need to work through your loss. There’s also anticipatory grief. For example, that can happen when you know someone is terminally ill and you start grieving while they are still alive.
column9: When you’re grieving you may need to set healthy boundaries with people to help reduce your stress. You may also need to identify how to avoid loneliness and isolation while dealing with everyday challenges. Many people also struggle trying to cope with lingering feelings of survivor’s guilt and unfinished business, along with other issues. It takes work to put your life back together after loss, especially now. I discuss ways that people have worked through their grief in my latest book, Beyond Loss in a Pandemic: Find Hope and Move Through Grief After Someone Close to You Dies.

column1: Adult What is anticipatory grief and how does it differ from immediate grief?
column3: It seems anticipatory grief contains the element of dread (worst case scenario) or is preparatory for the inevitable (best case scenario.) I am applying this comment to the case of terminal illness of a loved one or oneself. There is fear of the unknown, and of loss. We can also grieve for lost youth, lost career (termination or retirement), lost relationship such as marriage failure, loss of a beloved home, community, or friends when we move, and this list surely goes on. The good thing about anticipatory grief is that grief is a process. We may begin anticipating a loss before it occurs. This gives us time to process, say goodbyes, reminisce, and find closure once the loss finally does happen. It's often said at funerals of very ill people that loved ones have been grieving for a long time. Once the loss is reality, the grief-stricken are prepared to heal more quickly. This is not true in the case of sudden, unexpected loss.

column1: Why are the grieving scrutinized for how they show their grief?
column3: Because people want you to grieve in a way that validated their feelings, not talking your feelings into consideration. When my husband died, I heard it all. From I have to strong to support his friends and family ( most of which never visited when he was sick ), to I am not sad enough ( I had a lot of anticipatory grief since he had a terminal illness. So while still devestating when he died, I was at a place where I could control my emotions when around other people ). I have also got, from other widows, “ I hated it when people told me how to grieve. But this is how you should grieve “. And being told it wasn’t fair that I was not letting someone help me grieve. And being told that I should comfort someone my husband had only met once because she was so sad, and it was disrespectful that I wouldn’t visit her less than 24 hrs of my husbands death. My young son has also been subjected to this, with lots of family trying to force him to grieve a specific way, and trying to use him to gain sympathy, and money, for themselves. It is my belief that people can’t handle it when the attention is not on them, so they have to do whatever they can to draw that attention back to them. And the way to do that is to tell you that you are wrong and should listen to them.

column1: Did you mourn your loved one as soon as they passed on, or did it take you a while?
column3: It depends if I knew that they were diagnosed with a terminal illness and they were in hospice I experienced anticipatory grief. If they died suddenly I was in shock and disbelief so it took time to mourn. Every death is different and the reaction to the deaths are different and each person grieves differently. There is no right way to grieve. 🦋

column1: Is anticipatory grief of losing a loved one to a terminal illness actually worse than the grief of their death?
column3: It can be, yes. My cousin and I have joked that she’s outlasted her doctor’s “expiration date” by two years. But it’s not funny anymore. It’s difficult to watch someone who is 100% mentally there and engaged and WANTS to fight but the body is wasting away. Watching their prolonged suffering is painful when you know there’s nothing medically that can be done. It’s difficult to tiptoe around the awkward conversations about faith healing or “when I’m better” let’s do…whatever… because I can see the grey palor of the skin, the wasting away of muscle and sinew. Every bone is pronounced, cheeks hollow, no fat left on the body, how long can one survive like this, literally starved of nutrients? The clock is ticking and I am holding my breath. I am at a constant state of dread/readiness for “the call”. I don’t know which is worse, to be fully cognizant and aware of everything while you’re dying a slow and painful death, or to be suddenly gone. Sadly our family has experienced both types of loss and both are traumatic in different ways. Today I grieve for my cousin who battles cancer. I grieve for her mother, my aunt, who will lose a second child. I grieve for my aunt who is losing her eldest child to terminal cancer just as she lost her husband to cancer a couple of years ago. I grieve for my aunt and cousins who will lose their daughter/sister slowly to cancer just a few years after losing their son/brother instantly in a plane accident. I grieve for the loss of time, one never having a family of their own, and the other dying when their children were too young to have more than a distant memory of the parent. I grieve for my still-living cousin as much now as I did for her brother and father who preceded her in death. Actually even more so because she is more to me than a cousin, she is the sister I never had, the best friend I always needed, and the best prayer warrior, confidante and advocate in my life, and I can’t imagine her gone. Yes, I grieve prematurely anticipating her death.

column1: What strategies can families employ to ensure that their loved ones receive quality care at home during terminal illness?
column3: First off - this is a difficult thing to do at home, in particular without help. But, many hospices do home health hospice. Hospice is often payed for by insurance or various government programs, so most of the cost is covered. This is the most comfortable place for a dying person to be, and home hospice can make it even more comfortable - they can bring in a hospital style bed along with a bed table like those used in hospitals, equipment for oxygen if necessary and equipment for toileting and body cleaning needs. It can be cheaper because you are not paying any facility costs as well. But it does mean having someone available 24/7 to take care of the person’s needs. If you have family willing to help, this works much better - it can be very difficult for one person to do, in particular if they are already grieving (this is called anticipatory grief, by the way, and is fairly common). It can be a good idea to bring in more family or someone else to assist with the person’s needs as well.

column1: How do you cope with being a caregiver to your terminally ill wife or husband? How do you deal with the loneliness and deteriorating companionship?
column3: Hi! I am an anticipatory grief coach and I help people in your position As a caregiver you are managing a fine balance, on one end you need to care of yourself and on the other end you still need to be there for your partner What I tell the caregiver is that you need to start planning as if your partner is no longer with you. It is hard, but getting a sense of what is to come is the best way to deal with anxiety. Remember to reach out to friends and family. At this time you need as much support as you can get. However, when you are spending time with your partner is the complete opposite. You need to help them manage their emotions, fears, anxiety, worries. I am happy to help you if you are interested! My website is www.titipoza.com

column1: Adult How can I overcome unrelenting anxiety, panic attacks, & irrational fear? My mum is dying from cancer and I'm struggling to deal with this, but it's starting to make me paranoid & fearful of losing other people I love such as my kids.
column3: Everything that you mentioned above is normal! The world that you have known has had it’s foundation pulled out from under you! Your Mom is dying of cancer! That’s not the normal way life is supposed to happen, she is supposed to be here to take care of you! I’m not speaking to the “? “ old you are! I’m speaking to the little girl or little boy who is struggling to deal with this, the unreality of this potential loss! Since your foundation is being pulled out from under you, you don’t trust your reality. Your inner child (and adult) is screaming: “If this can happen to her, maybe it could happen to my partner or God forbid, even my kids!” Your paranoia and fear are perfectly normal, but this new normal is foreign to your heart, your mind, and your psyche! You are overcome! At this point , if you were my patient I would get a release to speak to your personal physician and have him or her start you on a benzodiazepine on an as needed basis. Xanax or Ativan would be most helpful for you to deal with the “unrelenting anxiety, panic attacks, and irrational fears.” As a cognitive-behavioral therapist I would also normalize your reactions (REALLY NORMALIZE THEM). I would then have you start with some breath meditation to help you keep some of your anxiety in check. I would also teach you a deeper meditation to take you to a safe place to counter your current level of unrelenting fear! At the same time I would start to challenge some of your irrational fears! “Can you tell me what evidence that you have that your partner or your children are going to die? What, let’s do a reality check that you know they are going to die? I’m not talking about the possibility, but what real evidence do you have that leads you to some real probability that your partner or children are going to die! Do either have a terminal illness or a progressive CA? Do either want to take his/her own life? Are you still their Mum and feel that you can care for them? Of course you do! You can do this, we will talk to your Mom’s doctor and if it is what she wants we will take every means to treat her Cancer/ or if she is terminal and she wants to die in her own home without pain,nor stress then maybe Hospice and palliative care will be the best for her! She will be free of pain, without respiratory distress, and without any anxiety! You need to take it five minutes at a time and focus on taking care of you and your children/partner and then spread out the care of you Mum to others. Everything that you are going through is normal. See my posts about my first Hospice patient and her waiting to die when her loved one were not there, or a recent post of how long we grieve. I agree with one of the responders that working with a Cognitive-Behavioral therapist may be helpful. The first step may be allowing yourself the anticipatory grief of the impending death of your Mom and just finding a therapist who has experience in grief and bereavement and spend some time processing the impending death of your Mum! Eat, try to keep a regular time to go to bed and to get up. Take some time for the normal things with your children and your partner. It’s O.K. to have some fun or relief from all of this stress even while your Mom is saying her final goodbye!!! Spend some one-on-one time with your Mom and if you can tell her what she has meant to you, don’t try to undo sh_t that may have occurred in your past! It’s the past, focus on now! When you leave the room say to her if you believe it: “ I love you, goodbye for now!” Should she die when you are not there, you will have said goodbye! If your are a primary caregiver for your Mom, spread out the responsibility, that may include Hospice. If you have siblings meet with them and have them come up to the bat so you are not feeling all of the burden. My dear one, so much courage for you to reach out to Quora! I pray for peace, love, and healing for you and this intimate journey with your Mum! Please take care! Be Well! Lawrence J. Schulte, Ph.D.,C.Ht. Ph.D. Clinical Health Psychology (2009-Present) C.Ht. Certified Hypnotherapist (2016-Present)

column1: If you're married and your partner is fatally ill, how do you prevent yourself from emotionally detaching from them?
column3: It is a day-by-day thing, some days are better than others. in my case I have been told multiple times during the last 5 years that my husband was terminal. With a prognosis ranging from he won’t make it home again (when in the hospital for over 60 days), to he has less than 6 months. And yet he is still with me, I have been angry, broken, shattered, scared, but I have been with him every day. Initially he had cancer but the treatment caused massive pulmonary embolisms that caused two massive heart attacks. I have been through tube feeding him, picking him up off the floor when too weak to walk, but also too stubborn to use his darn walker. I have performed CPR multiple times, have torn my rotator cuff and destroyed my back caring for him. So I have had every emotion from denial, to acceptance, to detachment, praying, begging, and anger at him, Hod and anyone else blame at any given moment…… In the last 18 months his heart has almost completely failed, he has lost over 100 lbs (cardiac wasting), and he has developed dementia and can’t remember most of our life, our marriage or the way we once were together. I sought a counselor and he told me that the waves of detachment are both self preservation and what is called anticipatory grief. Kind of like standing in a contained space and seeing a 10,000 lb weight falling directly for you, and you have no way to escape, you know what is coming but you have to try to believe it won’t be as bad as you fear, but you are still bracing for impact. So there is no normal reaction, grief, pre- or post- loss is a very heavy burden. In my case we have very little family and no one close enough to help not even with emotional support. I have already lost my mother, father, 3 brothers, niece, great nephew, ex-husband and quite a few friends, but the one thing I have learned is being experienced at loss does not help a darn bit, each new loss, whether death, unexpected divorce, betrayal or whatever else may happen is a brand new can of grief you must open and deal with. one day at a time…. For as long as necessary.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: How to deal with the grieving process While grieving a loss is an inevitable part of life, there are ways to help cope with the pain, come to terms with your grief, and eventually, find a way to pick up the pieces and move on with your life.Acknowledge your pain.Accept that grief can trigger many different and unexpected emotions.Understand that your grieving process will be unique to you.Seek out face-to-face support from people who care about you.Support yourself emotionally by taking care of yourself physically.Recognize the difference between grief and depression.The stages of grief In 1969, psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross introduced what became known as the “five stages of grief.” These stages of grief were based on her studies of the feelings of patients facing terminal illness, but many people have generalized them to other types of negative life changes and losses, such as the death of a loved one or a break-up. The five stages of grief Denial: “This can’t be happening to me.” Anger: “Why is this happening? Who is to blame?” Bargaining: “Make this not happen, and in return I will ____.” Depression: “I’m too sad to do anything.” Acceptance: “I’m at peace with what happened.” If you are experiencing any of these emotions following a loss, it may help to know that your reaction is natural and that you’ll heal in time. However, not everyone who grieves goes through all of these stages—and that’s okay. Contrary to popular belief, you do not have to go through each stage in order to heal. In fact, some people resolve their grief without going through any of these stages. And if you do go through these stages of grief, you probably won’t experience them in a neat, sequential order, so don’t worry about what you “should” be feeling or which stage you’re supposed to be in. Kübler-Ross herself never intended for these stages to be a rigid framework that applies to everyone who mourns. In her last book before her death in 2004, she said of the five stages of grief: “They were never meant to help tuck messy emotions into neat packages. They are responses to loss that many people have, but there is not a typical response to loss, as there is no typical loss. Our grieving is as individual as our lives.” Grief can be a roller coaster Instead of a series of stages, we might also think of the grieving process as a roller coaster, full of ups and downs, highs and lows. Like many roller coasters, the ride tends to be rougher in the beginning, the lows may be deeper and longer. The difficult periods should become less intense and shorter as time goes by, but it takes time to work through a loss. Even years after a loss, especially at special events such as a family wedding or the birth of a child, we may still experience a strong sense of grief. Source: Hospice Foundation of America Symptoms of grief While loss affects people in different ways, many of us experience the following symptoms when we’re grieving. Just remember that almost anything that you experience in the early stages of grief is normal—including feeling like you’re going crazy, feeling like you’re in a bad dream, or questioning your religious or spiritual beliefs. Emotional symptoms of grief Shock and disbelief. Right after a loss, it can be hard to accept what happened. You may feel numb, have trouble believing that the loss really happened, or even deny the truth. If a pet or someone you love has died, for example, you may keep expecting them to show up, even though you know they’re gone. Sadness. Profound sadness is probably the most universally experienced symptom of grief. You may have feelings of emptiness, despair, yearning, or deep loneliness. You may also cry a lot or feel emotionally unstable. Guilt. You may regret or feel guilty about things you did or didn’t say or do. You may also feel guilty about certain feelings (feeling relieved when a person died after a long, difficult illness, for example). You may even feel guilty for not doing more to prevent your loss, even if it was completely out of your hands. Fear. A significant loss can trigger a host of worries and fears. If you’ve lost your partner, your job, or your home, for example, you may feel anxious, helpless, or insecure about the future. You may even have panic attack. The death of a loved one can trigger fears about your own mortality, of facing life without that person, or the responsibilities you now face alone. Anger. Even if the loss was nobody’s fault, you may feel angry and resentful. If you lost a loved one, you may be angry with yourself, God, the doctors, or even the person who died for abandoning you. You may feel the need to blame someone for the injustice that was done to you. Physical symptoms of grief We often think of grief as a strictly emotional process, but grief often involves physical problems, including:FatigueNauseaLowered immunityWeight loss or weight gainAches and painsTypes of griefSince the experience of grieving following the loss of someone or something important to you tends to be unique to you, it’s difficult to label any type of grief as either “normal” or “abnormal”. However, there are types of grief that fall outside the expected symptoms and reactions described above. These include: Anticipatory grief As the name suggests, anticipatory grief develops before a significant loss occurs rather than after. If a loved one is terminally ill, for example, you have an aging pet, or you know that your retirement or job loss is imminent you may start grieving your loss before it has fully unfolded. Like conventional grief, anticipatory grief can involve a mix of confusing emotions, particularly anger. Some people even equate it to giving up hope and refuse to allow themselves to grieve before their loss has occurred. However, anticipatory grief can also give you chance to prepare for your loss, resolve any unfinished business, or say your goodbyes, for example. Disenfranchised grief Disenfranchised grief can occur when your loss is devalued, stigmatized, or cannot be openly mourned. Some people may minimize the loss of a job, a pet, or a friendship, for example, as something that’s not worth grieving over. You may feel stigmatized if you suffered a miscarriage or lost a loved one to suicide Disenfranchised grief can also occur when your relationship to a deceased is not recognized. Some people may consider it inappropriate to grieve for a work colleague, classmate, or neighbor, for example. As a close friend or same-sex partner you may be denied the same sympathy and understanding as a blood relative. This can make it even more difficult to come to terms with your loss and navigate the grieving process. Complicated grief The pain at a significant loss may never completely disappear, but it should ease up over time. When it doesn’t—and it keeps you from resuming your daily life and relationships—it may be a sign of complicated grief. Complicated grief usually arises from the death of a loved one, where the loss has left you stuck in a state of bereavement. You may be unable to accept your loved one has gone, search for them in familiar places, experience intense longing, or even feel that life isn’t worth living. If you’re experiencing complicated grief and the pain from your loss remains unresolved, it’s important to reach out for support and take the steps that will enable you to heal. Seeking support for grief and loss The pain of grief can often cause you to want to withdraw from others and retreat into your shell. But having the face-to-face support of other people is vital to healing from loss. Even if you’re not comfortable talking about your feelings under normal circumstances, it’s important to express them when you’re grieving. While sharing your loss can make the burden of grief easier to carry, that doesn’t mean that every time you interact with friends and family, you need to talk about your loss. Comfort can also come from just being around others who care about you. The key is not to isolate yourself. Turn to friends and family members. Now is the time to lean on the people who care about you, even if you take pride in being strong and self-sufficient. Rather than avoiding them, draw friends and loved ones close, spend time together face to face, and accept the assistance that’s offered. Often, people want to help but don’t know how, so tell them what you need—whether it’s a shoulder to cry on, a listening ear, or just someone to hang out with. If you don’t feel you have anyone you can regularly connect with in person, it’s never too late to build new friendships . Accept that many people feel awkward when trying to comfort someone who’s grieving. Grief can be a confusing, sometimes frightening emotion for many people, especially if they haven’t experienced a similar loss themselves. They may feel unsure about how to comfort you and end up saying or doing the wrong things. But don’t use that as an excuse to retreat into your shell and avoid social contact. If a friend or loved one reaches out to you, it’s because they care. Draw comfort from your faith. If you follow a religious tradition, embrace the comfort its mourning rituals can provide. Spiritual activities that are meaningful to you—such as praying, meditating, or going to church—can offer solace. If you’re questioning your faith in the wake of the loss, talk to a clergy member or others in your religious community. Join a support group. Grief can feel very lonely, even when you have loved ones around. Sharing your sorrow with others who have experienced similar losses can help. To find a bereavement support group in your area, contact local hospitals, hospices, funeral homes, and counseling centers, or see the links below. Talk to a therapist or grief counselor. If your grief feels like too much to bear, find a mental health professional with experience in grief counseling. An experienced therapist can help you work through intense emotions and overcome obstacles to your grieving. Beware how you use social media Social media can be useful in letting others know about your loss and reaching out for support. However, it can also attract Internet trolls who post inappropriate, insensitive, or even abusive messages. To spare yourself additional pain and heartache at this time, you may want to limit your social media use to closed groups rather than public postings that can be commented on by anyone. Taking care of yourself as you grieve When you’re grieving, it’s more important than ever to take care of yourself. The stress of a major loss can quickly deplete your energy and emotional reserves. Looking after your physical and emotional needs will help you get through this difficult time. Face your feelings. You can try to suppress your grief, but you can’t avoid it forever. In order to heal, you have to acknowledge the pain. Trying to avoid feelings of sadness and loss only prolongs the grieving process. Unresolved grief can also lead to complications such as depression, anxiety, substance abuse, and health problems. Express your feelings in a tangible or creative way. Even if you’re not able to talk about your loss with others, it can help to write down your thoughts and feelings in a journal, for example. Or you could release your emotions by making a scrapbook or volunteering for a cause related to your loss. Try to maintain your hobbies and interests. There’s comfort in routine and getting back to the activities that bring you joy and connect you closer to others can help you come to terms with your loss and aid the grieving process. Don’t let anyone tell you how to feel, and don’t tell yourself how to feel either. Your grief is your own, and no one else can tell you when it’s time to “move on” or “get over it.” Let yourself feel whatever you feel without embarrassment or judgment. It’s okay to be angry, to yell at the heavens, to cry or not to cry. It’s also okay to laugh, to find moments of joy, and to let go when you’re ready. Look after your physical health. The mind and body are connected. When you feel healthy physically, you’ll be better able to cope emotionally. Combat stress and fatigue by getting enough sleep, eating right, and exercising. Don’t use alcohol or drugs to numb the pain of grief or lift your mood artificially. Plan ahead for grief “triggers.” Anniversaries, holidays, and important milestones can reawaken painful memories and feelings. Be prepared for an emotional wallop, and know that it’s completely normal. You can plan ahead by making sure that you’re not alone, for example, or by marking your loss in a creative way.
column9: The support group that helped me was Griefshare, and there may be one near you. Check out GriefShare - Grief Recovery Support Groups - GriefShare. May God comfort you as He did for me.

column1: Why do I feel like I can never cry? Why do I feel like I am numb?
column3: If you’re not crying you may feel you’re not grieving as you should, and it can make you uncomfortable. Yet, grief can be surprising and unpredictable; you may well feel emotions you hadn’t expected. It’s good to remember that your relationship with the person who died was unique, so the way you grieve this person will be unique also. If someone dies after a long terminal illness, it’s possible that those who were close have already experienced something called anticipatory grief . This is an emotional response to loss before it actually happens. There’s usually been acceptance of the death for some time. If this has happened to you, that is, you’ve felt some grief before the actual death, then it may ease your sense of loss at the time of death, and affect the way you grieve. Some people feel numb when someone dies, and feel intense grief much later. These intense moments can be triggered by celebrations, anniversaries, surroundings, or even people who remind you of the one who died. There may be no trigger at all. It’s hard to predict whether grief will come later. Grief can be very private and people often wonder how their feelings compare with others’. You may find that sharing your experiences of grief helps you to understand what you’re going through. You can talk with friends about the death, join a grief support group, or see a grief counselor. You may find that keeping a journal helps you work through what you’re feeling or not feeling about death, loss and grief. We all find our own way of coping with the feelings that surround death. It is important to remember that if you feel overwhelmed, there are people who can help you try to understand what you’re going through. It may help to see a counselor to talk about your experience and the feelings that you have. Consider joining a grief support group. Many people find it helps to know they’re not the only ones grieving, to see how others are grieving and to hear how they’re managing grief. If there’s a hospice or palliative care association in your area, or if you were involved in such a program before the death you may want to reconnect with them. They may offer grief programs, or can refer you to services that meet your needs.

column1: What is the kindest thing a pet has done for you?
column3: Getting cancer was the second worst thing to happen to me on that particular day. Having to eat hospital food was easily the worst. This is just the story of a boy with Leukemia. And a dog who didn’t give a fuck.Dogs give unconditional love. Every story in this wonderful thread proves that. But that’s an understatement. Especially when my perfect pup was concerned. His name was Achilles. And he was a moody, emotional little shit. If he was still with us (bless his wonderful doggy heart) he wouldn’t be offended at that though. In fact he’d agree. Then he’d give me those pleading eyes that all dogs have mastered. The ‘I’m so hungry’ eyes that appear literally seconds after a full bowl of dog food is reduced to crumbs. I’m a big believer that we don’t choose a dog. They choose us. And yes I’m aware that sounds like some sort of hippy, bumper sticker bullshit. But when a strong, handsome staffy followed my brother home on his bike one day, it felt like the universe was giving us a gift. Because that’s what dogs are. They’re gifts that we borrow. But never keep. Nothing that loves you so powerfully and permanently can last forever. We get them, knowing we’ll outlive them. And that’s what makes them so special.We tried to find Achilles’ real family. We even found the house he’d been sitting in front of when he took a fancy to my brother’s bike. But they wanted nothing to do with him. They’d found him wandering in the bush with no collar. Starving. Sad. So he became part of our family instead. He was a shy and skittish boy at first. A sudden noise would send him into convulsions of fear. While the sound of a gun shot in a movie reduced him to absolute rubble. Dad thought he might have been a farm dog. One who associated the sound of gunpowder with a beating he might soon be receiving. We didn’t care that he was full of emotion though. Because he had a new home. A home with us. And it would be nothing but love from here on out.We’d had Achilles for 3 or 4 years by this point. I’d named him. I was studying History and the name felt appropriate. He was strong and rugged and good looking, just like the mythical Greek Achilles. His only Achilles heel? Loud noises. Oh, and he LOVED cheese. The little shit couldn’t get enough cheese. He was always begging for a slice like a crack addict chasing just one more high. And when I was diagnosed with cancer and spent 244 days in hospital, he was probably begging for cheese at home. That little shit.For anyone who doesn’t know what chemo does…it fucks you up. My body was a bomb site. Worse than the phsyical pain, I felt so incredibly, desperately alone. It’s impossible to feel anything but isolation when you’re literally separated from the world. You just can’t risk catching anything when the slightest infection poses such a threat to your mortality. And that was my life for pretty much a year. Days turned to weeks and weeks to months in hospital. Alone. Always alone. But there was a hope. Small that it was. See, every month, I got 3 days back at home before the cycle of destruction tore into my body at hospital again. Just 72 hours to live like a normal kid, before I resumed my battle with death.I was still alone at home of course. I couldn’t risk any family member slipping me something deadly under the table. Only, I wasn’t really alone. Because I had Achilles. This little shit sat with me. Ate dinner with me. Watched movies with me. Slept in bed with me. I don’t know how he knew of my pain but he never strayed from me. Dogs have a sense for shit like that. For 72 hours he was with me. I’m sure he had things to sniff and plants to piss on. But in my brief excursions home, he was there. He was always there. He was there when I was in quarantine and he was there when I had no one. It might seem like a minor act of kindness. And in the grand scheme of life it probably is. But the kindest thing my pet ever did for me, was just being there, when no one else could be.Achilles died in 2014. Not a day goes by when I don’t think of him. But I read a story once that I want to share. It was about a place beyond a Rainbow Bridge. Which is a place where pets go when they pass away. They have each other. They have all the treats they ever wanted. They get to chase postmen and smell each other’s butts and pass the time in heavenly bliss. Then, when we pass away, they cross back across the Rainbow Bridge and join us in forever. I don’t know what happens when we die. No one does. But I managed to beat Leukemia. By the grace of God. So when my time comes and my second chance comes to an end, it’s not my last breath that occupies my thoughts. It’s the hope that the first thing that greets me in the world beyond our world, is a flash of blinding rainbow light And a little piece of shit begging for cheese.Image Credit: Pixabay
column9: That’s pretty much just like my story. I had leukemia in 2016 (AML) My roommate was a dick and basically didn’t acknowledge my existence, so I was lonely. Except for my dog and his 2 dogs. They were my lifeline and my company, all day every day when I wasn’t in the hospital. Dogs are the best! No better companion during cancer treatment.

column1: What does it feel like to get divorced?
column3: Getting Divorced was EXTREAMLY Painful Getting divorced after 23 years was the second most painful event of my life. I was the person “filed upon”, and while it didn’t come out of the blue, the experience was jolting emotionally, psychologically, financially and in every other way. The divorce itself was fairly amiable. We agreed we would use mediation and each of us hired attorneys who were supportive and experienced in mediation. Financial “Readjustment” Our daughter was in college so custody and child support were not issues, but paying for college was. We agreed to split all assets 50/50, so over a million in retirement investments were split. Effectively, my 401(k) became a 201(k). While painful, most of the financial split was simply business. The most contentious financial part was determining spousal support now and into the future, but we worked through that. She Moves 3,000 Miles Away Immediately after divorce my ex-wife moved to California and told my daughter not to share any detail of her life with me. I simply sent money each month. Deep Grief and Depression I went into what I see now a very deep depression. I felt the marriage was my failure. I felt guilt, shame, regret and nearly every negative emotion imaginable. I was sure I had alienated my daughter for the rest of my life. I eventually stabilized a bit, but I’m still not sure I’m over it to this day. But The MOST PAINFUL EVENT……. As I said, my divorce was only the second most painful event of my life. About four years after the divorce, I lost my job of almost 19 years. A few days later I innocently called my daughter to let her know the news. My daughter was unexpectedly in an airport waiting to fly to California to see her mom. Her mom (my ex-wife), was in intensive care, and doctors had called my daughter to come immediately. I learned that my ex-wife had been batteling an autoimmune disease for over two years. She had lost over 100 pounds, and was fighting for her life at that moment. In tears, my daughter asked me that if this did not turn around, would I, could I, come to California to help her. In a state of some sort of emotional shock, I said of course! Remember, I had no knowledge of my ex-wife’s life or condition as per her wishes. At her request, I had been outcast from all members of her family. The news deeply saddened me and took me immediately to very dark places. The next day I got a call from my daughter. My ex-wife had passed away with her daughter by her side at age 56. I went to the airport and purchased a one way ticket to California, not knowing when I might return. When I got there, I consoled my 26 year old daughter as we made memorial and funeral service arrangements for California and Pennsylvania where she is buried. At both services , I was NOT considered a family member. I sat several pews back, mixed in with others. In my grief, I felt the two people closest to my ex-wife were my daughter and myself. At the first service, in California, I mourned more deeply than I ever have, sitting alone on a distant park bench on the church campus, crying more intensely than I’ve ever known with sorrow, grief, regret and shame. I felt as if...

column3: Yes but they died unnecessarily only two weeks apart, not months as your question asks. They got back together and my sister obviously had her assets in her name and kept it that way. However, he was well taken care of by her, lovely cruise holidays etc. He never went without but she made sure his previous stupidly would not have the opportunity to repeat itself. The authorities were in contact with her regarding the funding for his care and she explained as above. During his time in short term care he realised this was not for him even temporarily and he walked out to go home but they came after him and took him back. Soon after he was dead! Another case of covert euthanasia? “Never go into a hospice,” I told my sister who lived one hundred miles away, “you will come out in a body bag!” “Don’t be so stupid, they wouldn’t do that,” she said! I called the Coroners office before the double funeral but they wouldn’t take me seriously. I was too emotionally drained, exhausted and saddened by the ignorance of the condescending person on the other end of the phone to argue after begging for an investigation before the funeral. Heartbreaking! Pope Francis wrote eloquently about covert euthanasia online, please read it! column1: Atheists, isn't it inconsiderate to tell your theist family members you are atheist? Once you do they will ask why, you will explain to them and this may convince them to turn atheist and take away afterlife beliefs that give them so much comfort?
column3: I found it essential to tell my parents, as it happens. My mother is a Methodist lay preacher, and tried to forcefeed me her religious views since I was born. When I told her in my mid teens that I am an atheist, it certainly shut her up. I engaged her in debates on the topic and thrashed her every single time. She doesn’t talk to me about god any more, mainly because she knows that I’ll tie her beliefs in knots within about 3 questions that she knows she can’t answer. As for me, I’ve stopped doing that, for exactly the reason you mention. I could see that it really hurt her to have the flimsiness of her beliefs laid bare. She has been unable her whole life to process grief, and she’s had plenty of it - a baby killed by a drunk driver, another son who drank and ate himself to death, a brother-in-law who killed himself and the death of both her parents. Like all theists*, her only coping mechanism is to comfort herself with the self-deceptive lie that she will see them all again one day in heaven. All theists* know deep down that this isn’t true - you don’t really think you’re immortal, do you? But it stops you having to fully face up to your loss, and this cowardly avoidance tactic is one reason why religion is so popular. This has done her no end of harm, with her bottled up emotions and her stunted feelings, which is why I used to try to get her off it. However, I came to realise that she is terrified of confronting these feelings and her own fear of death, and that her religion is the placebo with which she substitutes emotional maturity. Even though she would be better off without this nonsense, I don’t want to take that away from her, so we don’t discuss religion any more. *EDIT - Thanks to The SOWER for pointing out that I should not claim to know “all theists”. So I’d like to rewrite these sentences thus:In common with what I suspect is true for many theists, her only coping mechanism is to comfort herself with the self-deceptive lie that she will see them all again one day in heaven. I also suspect that a lot of theists know deep down that this isn’t true - you don’t really think you’re immortal, do you?
column9: I am atheist, but I don’t go around advertising it. If someone is comforted and receives solace for their beliefs (either theistic or otherwise) I would never have the arrogance to deprive him of that solace, and in fact would be devastated had I, however accidentally, actually done so.

column1: What do you predict will happen in the U.S. over the next 2 weeks with the coronavirus?
column3: The US is headed for an economic crash the likes of which most of us haven’t seen in our lifetimes. Even though the stock market will be buoyed by the congressional stimulus plan, it’s not enough. Once individuals and companies start declaring bankruptcy, losing their health insurance, (most can’t afford COBRA), the economic situation is going to be very bleak. You just can’t keep printing money to ease the situation, either. Hard times will be coming economically and the stock market will dive once again. Doesn’t matter if most people go back to work immediately either because so many industries and the health care system will be affected by the sheer numbers of people who become sick. This may not occur in the two week time, but it will happen. It’s going to be a recession/depression. We weren’t prepared for this and everyone globally will see long lasting effects.You will realize you know an immediate acquaintance, co worker, friend or family member that has COVID-19. You may even realize you’ve been exposed to the virus, or test positive for it. We are starting to see more reports already of celebrities who have been diagnosed. Some of these people will die and we will grieve their loss.Supply chains will be stressed but new ones will be created due to overwhelming demand. Workers that are still considered essential will be working more overtime and in more stressful circumstances. Think of the staff at the stores, security services, transportation and healthcare and emergency services.Panic buying will remain the new norm in the states. People are confused by mixed messages in the media and how often do we see a world wide pandemic? It’s shocking right? People feel comforted by what control they can exert in a situation where it’s chaotic. If that means ordering three freezers and stocking the pantry and hoarding toilet paper, at the end of the day, they feel they controlled their security as much as possible. Same with guns and ammo. No one is going to take away their security blanket of food and whatever they deem to be their necessities. I suspect many of us will remember this for a long time, no matter if all the toilet paper came back miraculously tomorrowLife in the states will change as we know it. There is no vaccine and there is no cure. Lots of unknowns. Social distancing will only work for so long before people refuse to stay home, etc. Since we don’t live in an authoritarian country like China where they locked everyone down, we can expect that our curve will not flatten as quickly or as successfully. People in this country were already deeply divided over the country’s leadership and this is a time of fear, worry and isolation for many Americans. It ain’t getting better in two weeks.Small businesses will immediately struggle and some may not survive, but this is also an opportunity to think out of the box to flourish if you are an entrepreneur.People will rely more on streaming services, video games, entertainment, food and alcohol as coping mechanisms but especially social media because they want the feeling of belonging to something (social media) to express themselves to a trusted audience. That’s why we are all on Quora right ;)Life will go on. Sadly it will go on without some of us.

column1: Why are some nurses cold and uncaring with patients? Isn't it their job to be comforting and kind?
column3: If we became emotionally involved with our patients I doubt we’d last a week until we burned out. Too much pain and loss to endure. As kind of a weak example, when I start an IV, I look at the vein and nowhere else. If I got even a glimpse of the patient’s face as I stuck him or her, I wouldn’t be able to do it. By focusing on the task at hand and removing myself emotionally from it, I’m able to get the work done. This doesn’t mean we have to be cold. I’m always friendly and perhaps my sense of humor tends to be politically incorrect. But I can’t afford to go beyond that. How would you do if you lost a friend or family member every couple of weeks? How many weeks would you hold up knowing there was no limit to the number of family members who were going to die on you? I’m guessing not long, because you’re only human. As are we. Those nurses who appear cold and unfeeling I’m guessing are anything but. The external mask is their coping mechanism. One other thought before I stop: work load. Their employers may have stacked so much on them they don’t feel they can afford to stop and comfort somebody. I’ve worked in places like that.
column9: Exactly, Jay. I was a nurse in a nursing home. Most of the residents have some form of dementia. We had to be on our toes for our shift, and sometimes, beyond. Yes, I have been kicked, punched, bit, spit on, had my jaw cracked, chased around the nursing station, almost got killed by a resident “demonstrating” how to kill a enemy, had a resident bleed out on my uniform, and so on. Yes, you have to have a thick skin. Death in a nursing home is the norm, not the exception. I can’t tell you how many times I’ve had to call a loved one, to tell them to come to the home ASAP. We don’t tell them that their loved one is dead—not over the phone. We go into the kitchen, make up a pot of coffee, and if we have them, a donut, or something for them to eat, before they get there. Then, we tell them in person, after they get to the home. Most of the time the family will want to see their loved one one last time before we ship them to the funeral home, and, of course, we comply. They can be with their loved one for as long as they wanted. If we nurses seem aloof, it’s not because we don’t care, it’s because we care too much. If we fell apart each time something happened, we wouldn’t be nurses for long. It’s merely a coping mechanism, so we can do what needs to be done. But, that doesn’t give nurses license to be so mechanical, and not give patients one word of kindness. Fortunately, in the nursing home, we could be MORE caring than a hospital nurse could. I did work in a couple of hospitals, and it turned my stomach with the caliber of nurses that I worked with. I quit those jobs, and went back to the home. I tried to treat my fellow nurses, aides, residents, and family members, with courtesy and dignity. I recall when I was in a hospital with cellulitis for about 3 days. My roommate was about to be discharged. One of the nurses said to her, “Now, you can go home and suck down your smokes, so you can quit having the DT’s”. This nurse was hateful, nasty, insensitive, and rude. If I could have, I would have jumped over my barrage of IV’s, and throat punched that nurse. Yes, smoking was (and is) banned from hospital grounds, but, did that nurse have to say that? The answer is, NO. I hope that she got fired. She was what gave good, compassionate nurses a black eye.

column1: What are the indications for family therapy?
column3: Conditions for family therapy tend to include conflict of interest and opinion, psychological and emotional health issues, fidelity issues, issues about addiction, loss and bereavement, personality or behavioural change, etc. Misunderstanding, unwillingness, and un-readiness to accept a change to the status quo in a family tend to be at the bottom of family crisis. Resistance to change is a natural defence or coping mechanism in the sense that it gives both the family member/s at the receiving end of the change and the member making the change, time and space to see if the change is a phase and transient or permanent. column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: People grieve differently. There is no one right way to grieve. The death of someone you love is one of the most traumatic events in one’s life, specially if it was unexpected. My best friend passed away about a year and a half ago at the young age of 28. It was completely unexpected. He just didn’t wake up one morning. As much as I may want to forget that morning, it is seared into my memory forever, almost as if I could go back in time and relive it. The night before he passed, he and I had gotten into a little tiff, and he called me during Game of Thrones, which I ignored, and I figured I’d just call him the next day. The next morning, I woke up at around 8 am (super early for me) and saw a missed call from his mother. I didn’t think too much about it because he would call me from his mom’s phone to get me to pick up. But something inside me told me to call back and that’s when I heard “Rose, I have some bad news. Matt’s dead.” Have you ever had a moment in your life, where it was so clear, but so tragic, that you knew your life was never going to be the same again? I pray you never do. Even though I was numb to my absolute core and it seemed as if time stood still, I KNEW that my life as I knew it was over. Matt wasn’t just my best friend; he was my soul mate. We were not romantic in any sense, he was gay, but I loved and still love him. I was truly and utterly heartbroken. The first month after he passed, I barely got out of bed. I prayed that Matt would come and take me while I slept. I had zero desire to live. I contemplated suicide multiple times a day. The amount of guilt I had about not answering his phone call, and not resolving our fight nearly killed me. I didn’t go to work. I didn’t eat. I isolated myself from everyone except for Matt’s mom and his sister. Being with them was the closest thing to being with him and I took it. I slept with his sweatshirt because it still smelled like him. But during all this, I kept hearing him talk to me. He was talking as if he was right next to me. Initially, I brushed it off as a mind game; a coping mechanism for my grief, but it was then when my gifts started. Even though, I was hearing and speaking to Matt, I didn’t fully grasp the magnitude of what was happening. For about 8 months, I cried every single day, often multiple times a day. I was still consumed by guilt. I knew I didn’t want this life anymore. I also knew that Matt did not want this for me one bit. I slowly started to sleep less. I went back to work. When I was invited out, I went. My other best friend was planning a wedding and I got involved. I took an amazing vacation to Bali and to Tokyo with 2 great friends and made even more great friends. I reconnected with long lost friends and made new ones. I honed my gifts and started to help people. Throughout all this, I also went to a psychiatrist, a grief counselor, all of which helped, but eventually, what helped me the most was the realization that Matt really never left. If I can still hear him and still talk to him and I can feel his presence, then he’s still here. He may not be here the way I want him to be, but he is and he shows me signs on a daily basis. Don’t get me wrong, I still miss Matt tremendously, and I still cry every now and again, but I know with certainty he is still around and that is what comforts me. I don’t know how I will grieve when the next person I love will pass away, but I’ll know that they never really left and that’s a beautiful thing.

column1: How does a person develop a lack of empathy?
column3: Empathy can be lost and likely also re-gained if you've ever been able to experience it in the first place. Empathy is nothing that a person themselves can shut off, but is lost due to severe trauma, often during childhood. However, trauma during adulthood can lead to loss of empathy, at least temporarily. This is a way for the brain to protect the person from the pain they have experienced as well as the pain of others around them; a coping mechanism. Severe trauma during early childhood, such as abuse, never experiencing love or security and being very neglected in other ways can cause a child never to develop empathy the same way a loved and nurtured child would. People who have lost their empathy as adults have willingly or by force had to go through terrible trauma. An example is during military training in dictatorships where the trainees were made to rape and kill their own family members as an example. This trauma forced them to shut off their empathy to survive it, and made them very effective soldiers.

column1: What are warning signs that you are going to be a hoarder when you grow older?
column3: Risk factors play in here more than so-called “warning signs.” Such risk factors include a childhood wrought with fear of loss - be it familial, material, monetary or otherwise - and such a significant and repeated loss breeds the coping mechanism for hoarding later in life. The warning signs you speak of may be seen by a fly on the wall as the child ages, but chances are that the familial environment largely contributed to the conditions which would lend the child to develop these tendencies and would thus go likely unnoticed by the surrounding family members who created the environment to begin with (although it is most likely not done with intent, and further, many factors which would contribute to a child developing hoarding tendencies down the road would be outside the family’s control - I.e., death of loves ones, poverty, lack of resources including education, etc.)

column1: How do I deal with reactive attachment disorder in adults?
column3: I’m not quite sure what you’re asking. Have you been diagnosed with reactive attachment disorder? Are you a caregiver? Therapist? Partner, family member, concerned other? Just curious? Please feel free to provide missing context and details in a comment to this answer. I hope this broad overview of RAD proves even marginally useful. Reactive Attachment Disorder (RAD) is caused by early, profound, and (very often ) extended neglect. Over-crowded, under-staffed orphanages and serial dysfunctional foster homes provide fertile ground for the seeds of RAD. Conversely, responsive and consistent primary caregivers allow children to develop trust, empathy, healthy attachments, a solid sense of self, and pro-social behavior.Children with RAD don't trust adults because they didn't trust adults to take care of them when they were small. They use coping mechanisms to help them feel safe which may include lying, manipulating, stealing, impulsivity, aggressive or controlling behaviors. They are charming or charismatic, which deceives others into thinking that they are being socially appropriate. In reality, children and adults with RAD may lack empathy for peers, other people, and animals and can sometimes be cruel to them. source: Therapy for Attachment, Therapist for Attachment (links to goodtherapy article)RAD is considered extremely difficult to treat. Many children with RAD fail to develop healthy attachments and become deeply unhappy and angry adults who crave control, lack empathy, and exhibit indifference or cruelty to others. Many adults with RAD can make (varying degrees of) some changes in these core issues with the help of a therapist specifically trained to work with attachment disorders.…(A)dults who have never addressed problems with attachment and who see the result of attachment issues in their lives might, in treatment, identify and explore early losses, grieve for the childhood bonds that were not experienced, and gain closure while learning how to develop healthy attachments and accept love, if they have difficulty doing so. Through therapy, adults who have experienced attachment issues may become able to build stronger bonds with friends, children, and partners. source: Therapy for Attachment, Therapist for Attachment (links to goodtherapy article)For additional credible information about healthy attachment, child development, and RAD, check out the following Amy E.
