column1: In the movie, "A Star Is Born" (2018) what would be the likely diagnosis for the fictional character of Jackson Maine?
column3: The character of Jackson “Jack” Mane in the movie A Star Is Born (2018) is a fictional character who serves as a wonderful example of the borderline male struggling with substance abuse and addiction. He is a wildly romantic, rock & roll Peter Pan terrified of abandonment, overflowing with intense feelings, and on a constant mission to run from his pain. Jack’s core borderline personality disorder (BPD) features:·Lack of object constancy and unstable sense of self.Severe early trauma and abandonment from the early deaths of his parents (mother during his birth and father when he was 13 years old).His resulting intense fears of abandonment leading him to keep his older brother with him at his side, employing him, etc.His inability to take on the age appropriate tasks leading him to parentify other people around him to constantly take care of him, like his brother, and eventually his wife Ally.His impulsivity and difficulty sitting with a bad feeling without immediately acting it out, leading him to drugs and alcohol as a means to cope with his overwhelming feelings.Playing out the classic “I hate you, don’t leave me” pattern, firing his brother in a moment of rage, telling Ally that she is “F------ Ugly” as a means to push her away when his fears of abandonment kick in.Instantly forming intense attachments to people in order to avoid abandonment, typically much faster and more intensely than someone without this disorder would do.Difficulty taking care of himselfSelf-harmExamples: Parentifying others: There are many examples of Jack parentifying other people in life to take care of him. For example, his brother taking on the complex role of father, manager, caregiver, lecturing adult who he also rebels against in the classic borderline pattern of “I want you to take care of me, but I will rebel against you like a child who doesn’t want any rules.” His brother (like many caring family members of someone with this disorder) takes on the role of concerned, yet resentful adult who puts him to bed when he gets too drunk to do it himself, lecturing him about taking care of his hearing loss and trying to make sure he is taking care of his physical health, etc. During one of the more romantic and positive times in his relationship with Ally after they get married, he tells her, “thanks for making me a home.” This was particularly symbolic, because despite actually being older and more financially stable than she was, and even owning his own house, internally he very much felt like a child who needed an adult to move in and take care of him. Previously to this, he didn’t feel like he had “a home”, and would avoid going home as much as possible, (instead spending time touring, partying, going to bars and using drugs and alcohol as a means to avoid spending any time alone with his own thoughts or his own space). He hated the idea of being alone at home even for a moment and was grateful for her to move in, take care of him constantly, cook and clean and take on the complicated role of wife and mother to him. Once she did this, he appeared to feel like he finally had an adult (his wife) there so his child-like internal self felt safe and taken care of. Lack of Object Constancy and Unstable Relationships: Like most people who suffer from borderline personality disorder, Jack has very little object constancy, (the ability to maintain a positive emotional tie to himself or others the moment he feels hurt or angry), and struggles to sit with any bad feeling that he has without immediately acting it out towards others, including self-medicating with drugs and alcohol. He has major issues with attachment due to his early childhood trauma of losing both his parents at such a young age. As a result, he learned to protectively and instantly attach to others, like Ally, in an attempt to avoid abandonment and loneliness. However, due to his lack object constancy, he proceeds to throw people out of his life the moment they do something that hurts or disappoints him. Some examples of this was how he called his wife Ally, “F------ Ugly” (among other completely unrelated insults) when his intense fears of abandonment were triggered by her success, and her not being at his side every day. Another dramatic example was during a outburst of rage towards his brother, instead of finding a way to communicate with his brother about his intense feelings of hurt and anger, he said every deeply hurtful thing he could think of to him, and then fired him, despite the fact that he could barely take care of himself without his brother’s help (and eventually trying to hire his brother back to be with him every day again). Addiction: Like many people who suffer from BPD, Jack struggles with substance abuse and addiction, which serves a multitude of functions in his life. Some of these include: a maladaptive means of self-medicating himself in an attempt to numb the pain and trauma in his life, something to do when he feels lonely and cannot handle his feelings of abandonment, a way to avoid taking on a more adult role in his own life (parentifying others around him to take care of him), as an escape when he is overwhelmed, a method of self-harming, and even as a means to “connect” to others without having to be vulnerable. Self-harm: Many people who struggle with BPD learn to use self-harm as a maladaptive coping mechanism for dealing with overwhelming emotional pain. Jack frequently self-harms when he is overwhelmed with negative emotions that he has not yet developed the ability to cope with. This includes using drugs and alcohol, not taking care of his hearing loss (often making it worse), and most tragically taking his own life when he is soberly facing the reality of his intense feelings of self-loathing about his own role in his life, his fears that he will not be able to overcome his addiction, feelings of being fundamentally unlovable, and fears of Ally abandoning him for fame. The Borderline Appeal: Jack is a great example of just how appealing some people with BPD can be. He is wildly romantic (knowing just how to make Ally fall in love with him, but also pursuing her aggressively until she finally gives in), and brilliantly creative. Jack made beautiful, raw, and intoxicating music which served as one of his only healthy vices for coping with all of the tragedy and pain he felt in his life. Like many people with this disorder, he lived hard, loved hard, and sadly he died in the same way. The point is… Jackson “Jack” Mane is a tragic fictional character who beautifully depicts the intense struggles of having borderline personality disorder and addiction.
column9: I found this article interesting and Quite accurate, but as someone with BPD I don’t think Jack actually “wanted” someone to take care of him: (Clean cook etc). People w/BPD are not incapable or afraid of being alone-We’re afraid of being alone w/OURSELVES!!! We are our own worst enemy- so we look everywhere for someone to save us ( from ourselves ). We want what 90% of people want: home, family life, stability, security…& LOVE. But we are constantly being mind-f*cked by our own brain. As a loving caring sensitive woman… BPD has created a chaos in my life that is hard to explain. It’s horrible. I don’t wish this on anyone . Ultimately, although families (& ourselves) pay the price… It is US that put ALL all the blame on ourselves- ( whether you believe that or not)…Even tho it was NEVER our fault!

column1: Can you help me understand anorexia? How is restricting a coping mechanism?
column3: This is a good question. I can only speak for myself and others who have shared their stories with me. I personally dont believe anyone starts out on a path to weight loss and decides to have anorexia. The power weight loss, of this magnitude, has over you is profound. Yet it goes from being powerful to completely out of control very quickly. It becomes an obsession that is indescribable. Unable to eat or drink normally or function at all. Everything revolves around loosing weight, not losing weight, and not eating. So when you do eat, your world feels like its caving in. Your a failure. When I began trying to loose weight at 14, it was because I needed to loose some weight to be healthy. People had called me fat or chubby-which i despise-and i was so hurt by those comments. My life with my family was in complete chaos. I had no control over anything or anyone that hurt me. Over time, i did feel quite powerful when I had lost weight and refused to eat because suddenly people were paying attention to me in my family. I have to say that I never felt loved enough or that anyone ever considered how I felt about anything they did to me or around me, in my life. Anorexia was a real rush of power and control. Nobody could force me to eat and their pain at watching me starve myself, was very satisfying. I mean i didnt intentionally set out to hurt anyone, but today I can look back in retrospect and see things i didnt then. I finally could focus on something i got good at. Weight loss, starving myself, throwing up if i had to, and people noticed ME for my massive weight loss. (Anorexia never solved any family problem, fyi) Do I think this is a coping mechanism? No, not at the onset. However, once the obsession has a hold of you, I can see how it does. You have something thats yours, people pay attention to you, you feel worth something for the first time because your skinnier than anyone else, and you get this rush from not eating that doesnt come from any drug. So, all in all, I do think poor coping mechanisms do play a huge part in this. Psychologists and Psychiatrists have studied this at length and have all come to that same conclusion. We all dont start at the same point and yet somehow we get our needs met in this way. I was hospitalized three LONG times for this. Spent more than a year total, inpatient. Met many girls with the same illness. We all had control, or lack of control issues. We all used food-eating or not eating-to cope with our “issues”. We can even see this in society today. All over women are being photographed and focused on for their bodies. Your worth more skinny and beautiful than anything else. Is the perception of our society. Why dont we ever congratulate someone for gaining 20 pound like we do when you loose 20 pounds? (Other than the obvious health implications of weight gain ) Those things may allow you to see how we women, often derive our self worth frim our weight. Although I no longer derive my worth on my weight, I do work very hard to be healthy and happy overall. If you have any specific type if questions, as they pertain to a family member, I would be happy to explore that as well.

column1: Have you ever lost respect for your parents? If so, why?
column3: My parents would always argue and it was so painful watching them in plain sight, in front of me. They were yelling on the top of their lungs, to the point where it brought tears to my eyes. It’s like they didn’t care I was there at all, or if I was feeling bad. My mother would always talk ill of other people despite the many issues she has herself. I’ve only heard her once apologize about an arguement, only because I was sitting right behind her, and she had no choice since were right next to each other. Even if she apologized , that doesn’t mean that my hurt is gone. I have a stepdad in my life, but all they do is argue as well. This is really painful to watch, and I thought having another parent in my life would fix this arguing problem. I understand parents get frustrated with each other, but for them to be so involved in who is right or wrong, than rather the child that is standing beside them, hearing every word? Even when I use my headphones to block out their arguments. But even on full volume, yet I still hear them. It’s just a lot to handle, especially when I just turned 13. I hate the fact that none of them are willing to change. I’ve lost all of my respect for them because of that. I’ve been threatened twice to get kicked out of the house and live with my father because I was using unhealthy coping mechanisms (cutting myself, over-eating, violence, and burning my body.) just so I could deal with everything that was going on. After all this, I just wish I could move on. I don’t like my father either. I feel like I’m trapped. My family members always talk bad about something, as if I’m not good enough for anyone to hear what I have to say. I feel like crap. It’s like my mouth is sewed shut, and saying anything causes me to hurt. I’s like a dead end , and the only way out is the self harm, or the cliff. I just can’t wait until I move out and live my own life. I’m trying my best to be happy, even if I don’t have supportive friends.
column9: Hang on dear !!!I know it's easy to say …securing a job should be your goal and try to get away from all the negativity as soon as possible. I know it's hard .been there .living it .Do everything that makes you happy .Love and hugs !!xoxoxoxo

column1: Do you think hanging on to text messages and voicemails of family members and friends who have passed away is mentally healthy? If yes, when does it become unhealthy?
column3: I see nothing wrong with hanging on to text messages, voicemails, letters, little momentos, that a loved one that has passed has given you. Even wanting to hang on to some of their personal effects. There's nothing wrong with that, it's hanging onto a memory of a person that you loved and cherished and it also helps trying to come to terms with the loss that you're grieving. I have kept some things that are very important to me and also some things that because they were his or in his possession I'm not ready to release or give to someone and when I do get ready I will make sure that they get it but until then I will take care of it. I'm not actually sure when it becomes unhealthy unless you're making a shrine to it and you're trying to go after someone I mean it's a coping mechanism or part of one, it's a part of the grief process. And it's also part of letting go.

column1: What do I say to someone whose family member dies to console him and make him feel better?
column3: Because I've felt such loss, I tell them the following (paraphrased) as earnestly as I can: “. . . Please know you and your family are in my thoughts and prayers. The love we feel for loved ones does not diminish with their passing. Whatever coping mechanisms we have available may be used as tools for our aching souls. Sadly, such tools can help, but never cure. I believe a piece of our heart and soul goes with a family member to the grave. I know mine did. We, in turn, get to keep a piece of their heart and soul with us as long as we live. So, we try to cope and survive to keep them alive in us as long as possible . . .” E.M.

column1: How do I know if I'm in a bad enough mental health state to take a day off of work/school?
column3: I am not a trained professional in ‘the mental state required levels of health’ for taking a mental health day but in my experience, and I tend to push myself to the brink before admitting that I need a break, it will become obvious. If I find myself unable to concentrate or learn something new, if I am too tired to have a simple conversation with someone, if food doesn’t really perk me up or if each time I see a couch, I just want to lay down and sleep on it, I know that I need a break. Also, if a close friend or family member dies, that can indicate that it is a good time to take a mental health break. I was working my way through a heavily loaded semester when my Grandma passed away. I had accidentally registered for 21 credit hours and every moment of my life had to be planned out. After she died, I was in a fog. I went through my classes, I turned my homework into a coping mechanism for her loss. I let one of my speeches in speech class jut go - I just didn’t bother to do it - because I knew that it wouldn’t affect my grade much and I needed to give myself some reprieve. I had a lot going on. You also can see a school counselor/psychologist. They are there to help students with school issues and can help you see what things can help you make that decision for yourself. As for work, I would say the same thing. If you find that you are floundering and you start to cut corners or you stop caring about quality of work performance, you may need to take a break. It’s really all up to you and how you feel. What you can handle and what YOU need to be at your best. That’s my experience anyway.

column1: What will it take for an INFJ to move forward after a family loss?
column3: Time. After a loss of a family member, the most effective medicine which cures the grief is 'time’. While coping with such a loss, they keep saying how they miss the family member or the incidence of how the person passed again and again. It actually acts a coping mechanism for that person, to digest the gravity of the situation. For an INFJ some other things that might help are —Engaging their mind in other things, be it something like solving puzzles, learning to solve a Rubik's cube, learning to crochet or even studying. When these things are not very distracting, they ail they sadness and emptiness felt by the person.Helping others — INFJs tend to forget all about their problems when they see others in a fix and divert all their attention to help others. It ends up more like an altruistic therapy. This I would suggest is the best method for an INFJ to cope with a family lossHope this helps ☺️

column1: What coping mechanisms do you use when dealing with grief?
column3: I give myself time to grieve and never bottle up my feelingsI keep memories of loved ones that passedI spend time with family members and friends who can support me and I can share how I feel with themIt takes time to cope with the loss of a loved one. Give yourself time and do not bottle up your feelings because it will make it worse. Don’t stop yourself from crying because it’s part of grief.

column1: Can reading be a helpful coping mechanism for dealing with grief?
column3: Yes, it can. At least you would know that there are others who have loss family loved ones like yourself. I have read a couple of books on death, dying, and grief. I am so sorry I can’t think of any of the titles at this time. I’m sure you can find some on Amazon. When I loss my mom in 2015, I decided I needed help from my local hospice. They have grief counseling services. It’s free to the family members. The counselors specialize in grief counseling. They are supportive and very compassionate. They have individual and group sessions. During the summer they have sessions for little children from age six to eighteen. Think about attending a session or two. It helped me.

column3: I don't. Everyone coping mechanism is different

column1: How do successful people handle or hide their emotions on their daily routine?
column3: The important thing is to keep moving forward. Showing or even having negative emotions will lead to a detrimental dominoe effect. It could result in the loss of customers or business partners. It is positive in a business for people in our surrondings to be successful. However, when certain tough situations occur, it is necessary to continue with the daily business routines, and to analyze ways to improve. Likewise having a trusted family member and/or friend with whom it is possible to communicate with about certain situations will be helpful. The process of keeping busy and having normal periods of rest is part of the coping mechanism. If we communicate fairly and openly, then the chances of misunderstandings that lead to negative emotions will decrease.

column1: What are the most emotionally powerful paintings?
column3: I can not think of anyone more suitable to be mentioned here than Edvard Munch - the artist whose paintings are the epitome of emotions; felt rather than just seen.By The Death Bed, 1896 Munch's childhood was clouded by death and suffering; his mother died from tuberculosis when he was a toddler and later he lost his sister as well. He himself wasn't spared from the illness either:One Christmas Eve, when 13 years old, I lie in my bed. The blood trickles from my mouth - the fever rages in my veins - fear cries out deep within me. Now, now, in just a moment, you will meet your Maker and be sentenced for eternity.Death in the Sickroom, 1895 Here the focus changes from the dying person to the aftermath. Each of the family members possessed with grief reacting in their own way, not interacting with one another.My father was temperamentally nervous and obsessively religious — to the point of psychoneurosis. From him I inherited the seeds of madness. The angels of fear, sorrow, and death stood by my side since the day I was born.This is reflected in almost all of his artworks:Anxiety, 1894Separation, 1896 Separation is one of my favorite paintings by Munch. I can feel the man's suffering caused by the loss of his love. I can see her disappearing from his life, leaving behind traces that will haunt him in the future. She seems so light, heading in a new direction, while he on the other side is deeply hurt, unable to move on, overwhelmed by his pain. The contrast of colors and lines/strokes in his and her side of the painting is amazing: her — vibrant and with so much movement; his — dark, static, overcast, you can almost smell the heavy air he is breathing. His hand on his heart adds to the feeling of his heartbreak, it’s almost like it is burning.Melancholy, 1894Ashes, 1894And of course, The Scream, 1893 . Remarkable “behind the scenes” story and interpretation can be found on edvardmunch.org:His painting of a sexless, twisted, fetal-faced creature, with mouth and eyes open wide in a shriek of horror, re-created a vision that had seized him as he walked one evening in his youth with two friends at sunset. As he later described it, the "air turned to blood" and the "faces of my comrades became a garish yellow-white." Vibrating in his ears he heard "a huge endless scream course through nature."Munch had a habit of repainting same motives and paintings (often in different media), returning to all the deeply traumatic events again and again. That is why, in Munch’s art, it is possible to find many similar representations of the same events that had happened to him.Without anxiety and illness, I am a ship without a rudder... My sufferings are part of my self and my art. They are indistinguishable from me, and their destruction would destroy my art.Yes, his illness was fueling his work but I guess, his art was also a coping mechanism in his life. I remember reading him say how hard it was for him to process his father’s death since he wasn’t there when he died — he was unable to express himself through paintings like in the case of his mother and sister. Finally, whether you like his paintings or not, you can certainly not deny the powerful emotions they portray.
column9: As a Norwegian and someone who has even guided tourist groups at the Munch museum, it was amazing to read your interpretation of his art. I knew the basic facts, of course, but adding your impressions to it gives it a whole new dimension. Thank you!

column1: How accurate is the portrayal of Alzheimer's disease in Still Alice?
column3: I don't have enough experience to comment on its generalizability to all Alzheimer's patients, but as I watched the film, I constantly made comparisons to my own grandmother with Alzheimer's and our family's situation. (Some spoilers ahead, obviously:) I struggled with one of the fundamental messages of the movie - that after a period of turmoil Alice would be able to find some sort of peace with her disease because at her core, Alice was "still Alice," regardless of what changes were taking place. I guess my skepticism stems from the fact that the idea that Alice could eventually reach some sort of nirvana and quietly accept that every day will be steeped in compounding confusion and loss of control is just light years away from my grandmother's experience. In contrast to Alice's satisfying epiphany, 10 years into her disease, the woman who raised me - once the undisputed matriarch of our family - continues to fight every change and accommodation tooth and nail. She's in an assisted living center now, in diapers and on anti-psychotic medications, always asking for dead relatives and not recognizing living ones. And on a daily basis she cycles through negative emotions and behaviors: fear, anger, manipulation, violence, depression. She might be sobbing like a sad child, cry herself to sleep, then wake up roaring angry that anyone would treat her so patronizingly. Yes, with effort we can still elicit a laugh or a smile, but it's literally gone within moments. Maybe it's not fair that I'm answering this on her behalf and maybe you're hearing my own coping mechanism reflect my biases, but she is not who she always was. Or who she ever was. She's a zombie with the same body, a fragmented soul and a different mind altogether. As far as I'm concerned, the woman that raised me is already gone. When Alice's misguided suicide attempt failed I didn't feel the expected sense of relief audience members were meant to experience in that moment. I only felt sadness. Sadness that Alice, like my own grandmother, never had the chance to exercise the control she had wielded her whole life to preserve her own dignity and make a graceful exit. Sadness that our society thinks it's more noble to hang onto the end, no matter how painful or undignified or expensive or burdensome than to choose our own death or choose for someone else out of love. I also only felt sadness when Alice's daughter made the decision to give up her life in Los Angeles to move home and be her mother's caretaker. Sadness that society expects and applauds the vibrant, productive life of a healthy adult (daughters, in particular) to come rolling to a stop in order to care for a dying one. The one thing I think the movie did well was the portrayal of the evolution of family relationships before and after diagnosis and deterioration. As I've seen, family members and friends react in varied an unexpected ways - the closest friends might disappear off the earth and mere acquaintances might suddenly become regular visitors. It usually depends on how well the other person can - or wants to - suspend logic and fabricate fibs to provide comfort at a basic emotional level. In short, I thought the movie was too redemptive to be realistic - at least as interpreted through my peripheral experience. There is no peace, there is no continued core of who the Alzheimer's patient is - just a terrifying, heartbreaking and undignified dismantling of their identity.
column9: You have expressed some real truths here. That angry, confused, frightened person is mostly NOT having a good time.

column1: How does the grief of losing a pet compare to other forms of loss, and what coping mechanisms have proven most effective?
column3: Jessica, thank you for the question. While losing a pet can certainly cause grief there really is no comparison to that of losing a human family member. DO NOT go out and purchase another pet immediately. No other pet will compare to the one you lost so give it time before getting a replacement. Perhaps 3 to 4 months. To cope, talk about your beloved lost pet with other family members and friends. Reminisce about the fun and good times you had with your pet. In time as your grief subsides then you can consider obtaining another pet. All the best.
column9: Lisa, thank you.

column1: Is psychiatry a stable job in the Philippines? If so, how many years does it take to become a licensed psychiatrist?
column3: Cheers! I have had some experience assisting with psychiatry cases, both in my internship years, and with friends and families. Plus, I once considered treading that path. Once. Anyway, here’s my answer. I have a feeling that there will be an increasing demand for psychiatrist in the coming years. Points to consider:Certain occupations and industries, particularly the Business Process Outsourcing (BPO’s) have begun to provide professional care for their employees’ mental health. Sometimes, employees with mental health issues were only able to approach a psychiatrist once they were referred by their company. Performance must have improved which is why more companies are looking for licensed psychiatrists and occupational physicians to cater to their needs.At least in urban and semi-urban areas, more and more Filipinos are becoming aware of psychological and mental health. People are now less hesitant to acknowledge that they need help and to ask for it. Families sometimes initiate referring a member with a condition rather than hiding it from the community.A lot has been happening lately: pandemics, online schooling, social changes, misinformation and election propaganda. Coping mechanisms that we used to have are no longer viable because pandemic, you know. We couldn’t just go out with friends and rant about that toxic job. Worse, children are growing up with zero social interaction other than their gadgets. I’ve been seeing a lot of child behavior problems that parents are at a loss to deal with.So, if you define stability as never running out of work opportunities, then psychiatry is and will be a very stable - even busy - job in the coming years. Now, how do you become a licensed psychiatrist? The most important step is by becoming a licensed physician/doctor. Here in the Philippines, that means 6 years of elementary education, 4 years of junior high, 2 years of senior high, 4 years of a bachelor’s degree, then another four years of medical school. After that, there’s 1 year of medical internship before you can take the licensure exams for doctors. After that, you choose a residency training program that specializes in Psychiatry or Neuro-psychiatry which takes a minimum of 3 years. Once you pass the specialty board exams, you will be considered a psychiatrist. That’s a total of 20 years of education to be a licensed psychiatrist. There are ways to shorten it but it would take another long discussion. In a nutshell, yes psychiatry is a stable job (as far as opportunities go) here in the Philippines. Though it takes long years of education, I think it’s worth it if you think you’re up for the task. Fight on! Keep safe!

column1: What mental health problems can cause a person to feel emotionally dead?
column3: Feeling emotionally dead is also feeling emotionally numb. The article below gives additional symptoms associated with feeling emotionally numb or dead. Neuroimaging shows that the same brain chemicals and brain areas are involved in processing each of the shared traits of the condition; a lack of emotion, empathy, and interoception (the ability to understand and sense what is going on inside the body). People who experience emotional numbness and dissociative disorder ( DD ) are so overwhelmed by stress, outside chemicals, or medications that emotional responses become diminished. Most studies into the matter have found that people with emotional numbness or DD are less responsive to emotional cues, lack social understanding, and lack emotional awareness. PHYSICAL OR EMOTIONAL CAUSES: Causes of temporary emotional numbness that are NOT considered to cause DD include:drug abuse, especially marijuana, LSD, and ketamineseizures, especially those caused by epilepsy, medication, or drug overdosepanic or extreme anxiety attackssevere depression, especially as seen with major depressive disordersevere anxietypost-traumatic stress disorderMedications Common medications that are known to cause emotional numbness include:Anti-anxiety drugs (SSRIs): A 2014 study found that 60 percent of just over 1,800 adults who had taken anti-depressants within the past 5 years had experienced emotional numbness.Anti-depressant medications: A 2015 study concluded that one of the predominant, long-term side effects of antidepressant use in young adults is emotional numbness.Trauma and stress Some research suggests that DD and emotional numbness may develop as a sort of coping mechanism, acting to desensitize individuals exposed to extreme or continual stress. In 2016, an article in Developmental PsychologyTrusted Source outlined the results of a 6-year study that had followed nearly 3,500 children who had been exposed to violence. The study found that the young people became increasingly desensitized, or emotionally numb, over time regardless of age or gender. Causes of numbness that may also potentially cause DD include:traumatic experiences, such as a car crash, a near-death experience, fire, or terrorist attackdeeply emotionally disturbing events, such as the sudden or progressive loss of a loved one or friendphysical abusesexual abuseemotional abuse or neglect, especially in childhoodhaving a mentally ill or severely physically impaired parent or spouseextreme interpersonal conflict or stress, usually with a spouse, close friend, family member, co-worker, or bossfinancial crisis or stressTreatment depends on the cause. Most of the information above is extracted from the following article : Feeling numb: Causes and how to manage emotional numbness Thanks Wen for your A2A

column1: I am cheating on my spouse and don't want to stop. What should I do?
column3: So, you’re cheating and you don’t want to stop…chickenshit move, all the way around. I’m answering this assuming you are the only cheater. If it’s both of you, that is a whole nother set of problems. Pull on your grown up panties and BE HONEST. With yourself, your spouse, your kids and other family members. No matter what you do, you have destroyed the trust that is vital to a committed relationship. Since you don’t want to stop..don’t, you selfish whore! But do your partner the courtesy of a quick and clean divorce if that’s what they want, and all the alimony/child support you can muster. Don’t expect to be trusted by anyone, even your current affair - after all, you have proven that you will lie if it gets you laid. Your spouse has been publicly and personally humiliated and embarrassed. Been there, and it absolutely sucked. Whatever the reason, there is no excuse. Mid life crisis, job loss - whatever. If the best coping mechanism you’ve got is to unzip your pants, you’re in deep trouble. If you are fortunate enough to have a partner who is willing to forgive and reconcile, you are one of few. Your relationship will have to be different because the path that got you here has got to change, or you’ll end up right back here again. My biggest gripe with committed relationships? Its not enough to commit to each other - you have to commit to taking care of this relationship that you have said is the most important one in your life. Relationships are fragile creations; they can be damaged by inaction or neglect. We can damage them by our bad choices, and doom them to slow death by refusing to grow as individuals, as a couple, as life rolls along its sometimes unpredictable road. Spend the time it takes to keep your relationship fresh and interesting - do something new together, take up new hobbies, grow TOGETHER. That includes a little time alone, as we all need a bit of space. You want a grown up, rock solid, committed, rewarding relationship? Play to your personal strengths and work on your weaknesses. BE the kind of grown up you want to have as a partner, and enjoy.

column1: What are the similarities and differences between BPD and DID?
column3: Dissociative Identity Disorder, as described by the DSM-V, is a disorder in which there is the presence of at least two distinct and separate personalities within an individual, each with its own memories, behaviors and life preferences. Dissociative Identity Disorder occurs when a child **under the age of 8** (before the brain develops a “whole” sense of self) is subjected to intense trauma over a sustained period of time (often sexual or ritualistic in nature, but occasionally severe childhood illness requiring multiple surgeries can also have an impact). The child has no ability to handle this trauma (would likely die from it) so the brain creates a coping mechanism and unconsciously erects amnesia barriers, allowing the formation of additional “selves” or alters (alternate personalities). These alters replace the child in times of trauma, allow them to live a normal life without memory of the trauma. It is not possible to develop DID after the age of 8. A traumatic event experienced after this time could result in other disorders, such as PTSD but not DID. This is something that can only occur before the brain has fully developed a cohesive “self,” thus professionals say 8 is the oldest age at which you can develop DID. The symptoms of DID, as described by the DSM-V are:Inability to recall large memories of childhoodSwitches between Apparently Normal Personality and one or more Emotional PersonalitiesLack of awareness of recent events, and if they do remember, inability to explain them, for example not being able to explain how the patient got somewhere, or how the acquired a possessionLost time or frequent memory lossFlashbacks or sudden return of memoriesFeelings of disconnection or detachment from body or thoughtsHearing of voices coming from within the mind (not auditory hallucinations coming from without)Dissociative, “out of body ” experiencesSelf-harm or suicidal ideation (individuals with DID have the highest rate of suicide of any other disorder listed in the DSM-V)Changes in handwriting and vocal tonesFunctional changes: from nearly disabled to highly functioningMood swings and depressionAnxiety, nervousness, panic attacks or phobias (often concurrent C-PTSD symptoms)Unexplained sleep disorders; including night terrors, sleep walking, and insomniaHeadaches that come with switches and unexplained general body pain (somatic remembrances)Like DID, people with Borderline Personality Disorder report experiencing traumatic life events, such as abuse, abandonment, or adversity. This is one of the reasons most people with DID are misdiagnosed with BPD before getting the correct diagnosis. According to the DSM-V, BPD is “a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, and marked impulsivity, beginning in early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts.” It is unclear what the causes of BPD are, but there seems to be a genetic component as people who have a close family member are at higher risk of developing it. The symptoms of BPD, according to the DSM-V are:Fear of abandonment, whether real or imaginedFrantic efforts to avoid such abandonmentMarked black and white thinkingSuicidal ideationFrequent and intense changes in relationshipsSelf-destructive behavior. often undermining their own effortsStruggle with emotional regulation, most frequently expressing disproportionate or inappropriate angerWeak or distorted sense of selfStrong sense of emptinessImpulsivity, which could lead to substance abuse, self-injury, reckless driving, gambling, binge eating, and unsafe sexThe key difference between the two is that in DID is the presence of at least two distinct and separate personalities within the individual, as well as the amnesia barriers mentioned above. Patients with BPD have a suicide rate of around 8%, while those with DID have a suicide rate estimated around 70%. Both occur in around 1–3% of the global population, making them as common as schizophrenia. As far as treatment is concerned, dialectical behavioral therapy (DBT) is the most effective intervention for treating borderline personality disorder. With DID treatment relies on three stages: Phase 1: Establish safety, stabilization, and reduction of symptoms Phase 2: Confronting, working through and integration of traumatic memories Phase 3: Integration and rehabilitation, or Functional Multiplicity.
column9: Suicide rate is about 75% for BPD and about 10% actually are successful in their attempts. One thing that is similar with DID and BPD is DID has multiple personalities or alters, BPD has multiple altered states. They can easily get confused for this reason as well…those with BPD actually do switch and get triggered into altered states, but not actual alters. It's kind of like one part of someone with BPD is a wounded child concious that never fully formed, the “you" core conscious, and the psychopath with no emotions conscious that was developed to protect the wounded child. BPD switch between these when triggered. It can appear as if someone with DID may have BPD or vice versa. Only BPD is the same person in different states and DID is the same person as different alters/personalities.

column1: What is the best way to break off a relationship with someone that has borderline personality disorder?
column3: Source: SavanasDesign/pixabay The Short Answer: There is no one best way to break off a relationship with someone with Borderline Personality Disorder because many factors besides the person’s BPD diagnosis affect the relationship and need to be considered. Gestalt Therapy Field Theory and Relationships Everything we do happens in a context. As Gestalt therapists, we talk about things emerging from a “field.” There is no event that is not field related. In the case of a romantic relationship this “field” at the very least involves:History of the Relationship— as it is affecting the present situation.Individuals’ Past Histories— individual histories of both people in the relationship and how these past experiences are affecting how this couple interacts with each other in the present.Current Needs and Desires— the needs and desires of both parties involved in the relationship.Personalities of both People—including coping mechanisms and habitual ways of responding to conflict and loss.Relationship—The way both people actually relate to each other now.Additional Factors—Any additional factors in the environment that are affecting the way the couple relates—jobs, money issues, other people, lovers, children and other family members.Diagnoses—Psychological and emotional patterns that affect how each member of the couple reacts in the present.As you can see from the above brief list, a diagnosis, such as Borderline Personality Disorder is only one of the 7 factors the field that need to be considered when contemplating how best to break off a relationship. Let’s look at an example of how different aspects of the “field” affect breaking off a relationship with someone with BPD; Example 1—History of the Relationship Bob met beautiful, warm Betty and fell passionately in love with her almost immediately. She appeared to be the woman of his dreams. He pursued her with gifts and promises. Betty had been diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder and was very emotional and needy. She had been abandoned as a child and desperately longed for her mate to provide her with unconditional love and emotional security. She was clear about her needs and her diagnosis with Bob. Bob was so besotted with Betty, that he did not stop to seriously think about what Betty had told him about herself or how her past history might affect their relationship (#4 Bob’s Personality factors and #3 Bob’s Current Needs and Desires).Bob “Over Promised” to BettyBob saw himself as Betty’s “Knight in Shining Armor.” He promised her exactly what she wanted to hear: I will love you forever. I will never leave you. I will always be there for you! Unfortunately, once Bob had sealed the deal and Betty was his alone, his feelings started to shift. He began to find Betty’s constant need for reassurance of his love stifling. When he tried to claim some alone time, or even if he had to work late, this set off Betty’s fear of abandonment. Reassuring Betty started to feel more like an unwanted demand—not a romantic adventure. This “Knight in Shining Armor” thought he would be able to dismount and relax once he and Betty were actually in a relationship. Instead, he found that Betty’s need for reassurance continued and was now an ever present part of their relationship that he resented.The Break-upSo…Bob wants to break off his relationship with Betty. Now he knows that Betty will experience this as an enormous betrayal. He also realizes that he promised Betty more than he could actually deliver. From the point of Gestalt therapy field theory, this break-up will be affected not only by Betty’s diagnosis and her history, but also by Bob’s history and personality and his willingness to promise Betty his undying love—no matter what. So what is the best way for Bob to handle this breakup? Bob needs to acknowledge his own flaws to Betty and that this break-up is actually a part of something he needs to work on and improve—his unrealistic expectations of his own abilities. He owes Betty a huge apology and anything else he can do that will make their disengagement smoother. Finances and Responsibilities: Depending on their age, financial situation, and how long they have been together, Bob might consider paying for the psychotherapy Betty is certain to need to get over his betrayal and her abandonment by him. If he has been financially supporting her, he will need to think about how he can realistically transition out of this situation without Betty landing up homeless because he changed his mind. In this instance, Betty was the realistic one, despite her diagnosis of Borderline Personality Disorder. She was honest and forthcoming about her insecurities and neediness. Unfortunately Bob did not stop to process what she had told him and made up a wildly unlikely story in his head that went something like this: My love will save Betty and she will get over her insecurities and we will live happily ever after. When that did not happen, Bob became disenchanted with the relationship. Yes, Betty had her emotional difficulties coming into this relationship (Past History + Diagnosis), but the relationship actually failed because Bob’s Current Needs and Desires (#3) had changed, while Betty’s had not. The history of this relationship is the “field” from which the current problems emerged:Bob’s pursuit of Betty.Betty’s clear expression of what she would need to commit to Bob.Bob’s promises to her of undying love and security.These are important factors that need to be taken into consideration by Bob when he contemplates how best to extricate himself from this relationship. Example 2—Personalities Angie—Angie is an attractive, divorced professional woman. She makes an excellent salary and likes having control over her life. She is decisive and very organized. She has no children, but has told herself that: Someday when I meet the right man, I will want to have a baby. Mike—Mike is a disorganized dreamer. He was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder during college when he kept missing classes and not turning in assignments because he started smoking pot every morning to cope with his anxiety. His dream is to make it big as a singer songwriter. He occasionally plays gigs in small clubs. He supports himself by taking free lance jobs as a waiter for a catering company. He has never been able to hold down a 9–5 job without getting fired.The RelationshipUptight, ultra-organized Angie and impractical, disorganized, and dreamy Mike are introduced by friends and fall in love. Angie finds Mike’s relaxed approach to life a welcome antidote to the hyper-driven and tense professional men she has been dating (Personality Factors). Mike moves in with Angie, gives up his catering jobs, and Angie agrees to pay the bills so Mike can pursue his dream career without having to worry about the mundane details of practical reality. They talk about having a child together. Mike will be the main caregiver and house husband so Angie can continue her career. Mike says: This will be perfect! I love kids. I think I am still a kid myself. I can write my songs at home, sing to the baby, and together we can make it work.Leading Up to the BreakupMike settled in and stayed home writing songs and watching a lot of daytime television. He still liked to smoke dope in the morning. Angie started to resent the fact that Mike actually did almost nothing around the house except—if she asked—he might pick up her dry cleaning or call for some takeout food for dinner. She began to realize that it was wildly unrealistic to imagine Mike taking care of a baby while she was at work because he could barely take care of himself. He was sloppy, disorganized, and stoned most of the day (Current Needs and Desires).The BreakupWhen Angie started confronting Mike about how little he contributed to the household, he made typically Borderline excuses—I’ve never been good at that stuff. You are too hard on me. I love you. That we love each other should be enough. As Mike started to feel unloved and emotionally abandoned by Angie, he sought affection elsewhere. When the women at the club where he sang flirted with him, he started to flirt back. Eventually, he started a torrid affair with someone and spent more and more time away from home and Angie’s nagging (Additional Factor). Meanwhile, Angie started therapy with the goal of extracting herself from this relationship (Another Additional factor). Ever practical and decisive, she decided to ask Mike to leave by the end of the month and offer to pay for the movers to sweeten the deal. Mike surprised Angie by jumping at the idea. His new girlfriend had asked him to move in with her—something he had never mentioned to Angie—and within a month, he had moved out. Punchline: It is overly simplistic to ask “How best to break off a relationship with someone who has been diagnosed with Borderline issues.” The relationship emerged from and is inextricably affected by a variety of field factors that affect how the breakup will be understood by the people involved. In the above examples, Betty was devastated, but Mike was able to smoothly move on to a new woman. Both were diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder, but they had a very different set of reactions to the end of their relationship. A2A Elinor Greenberg, PhD, CGP In private practice in NYC and the author of the book: Borderline, and Narcissistic, and Schizoid Adaptations. www.elinorgreenberg.com
column9: Dear Elinor, your analysis is not only brilliant but impeccable in the observation of variable factors. This makes so much sense instead of categorizing people in to neurotypicals or otherwise. It's a delight to read your answers. Thank you for writing so clearly.

column1: Can someone be so empathetic that to cope in this world, eventually becomes slightly sociopathic?
column3: I have found that I share some of the characteristics and points of view expressed by Quorans who identify as being on the ASP spectrum. I also have extreme empathy, as you describe. Strong empathy is impossible to express fully. Suffering and misery are common. The tears of the world never stop falling. If your ears are tuned to that drip you are not going to get much sleep. If you have very strong emotions and you learn to cope with them, naturally you are going to have much in common with individuals who experience a more muted emotional palette. Both types are able to operate free of emotional constraint. Both can view the world without the lens of emotion - depending on just how well the empath in question has learned to cope. If you are confused about where your feelings are, if you believe that you are unable to process grief, then your coping may be out of balance. Shedding a tear is external behavior. That has a social aspect. Your internal experience is more significant (unless you are the protagonist in Camus’ The Stranger). You said that you really cared for family members; so you have feelings. If you have a problem processing grief, you may be in need of some clarification sought with a counselor of some kind. But if you simply have enough perspective on life and death that a loved one moving on did not break your heart, that is not necessarily a bad thing. I spent much of my life being afraid of my own feelings. How I would feel was the basis of all my plans. This is not an effective way to live in the real world. As an empath you may know that fear. Now it has turned around on you, and you are afraid of not feeling. Small wonder sociopaths are sometimes envied. You cannot turn yourself into a sociopath. You can develop emotional dysfunction. You can develop coping mechanisms that overdo it. You might also be perfectly healthy, but have social problems because of your style of coping. From your question, it’s not clear if you are actually experiencing problems. If you cared but you didn’t shed a tear it is not a problem in itself. If you are locked in dry grief, unable to process loss—big potential problem. Only you know which is the case.

column1: How do I deal with a child who constantly gets into people’s belongings?
column3: I’m always wary of putting in my five cents in questions that really should be a talk to a licensed professional about instead of posting on online platforms… To add onto previous answers to this—depends on the developmental maturity of the child—consider the child’s prior life experience. Some children recovering from adverse childhood experiences, such as forcible removal from primary caregivers, death of an immediate family member, or extreme poverty, develop inappropriate coping mechanisms and behaviours as a self-defense mechanism. The child may also exhibit attraction to specific objects or physical qualities of objects if they have challenges in sensory processing, social disorders, or delays in development. Please also note that this question doesn’t give any context in the relationship the child has with the OP. If OP is a childcare provider, then I’d encourage working with the child’s parent as much as they’re willing to cooperate to address this behaviour. Getting into people’s belonging is probably the lesser of the other evil—taking of other people’s belongings. Respecting of other people’s boundaries and property is an important life skill to develop as soon as it is developmentally appropriate, as disrespecting others’ boundaries and properties will be interpreted as criminal behaviour at adulthood. If this is OP’s own child and is at a loss, research what kind of free resources are available through your local parent groups, your child’s pediatrician or other licensed medical professionals, community associations, municipal and regional governing bodies, medical associations. The amount of support you can find as a parent/primary caregiver will depend on where you are.

column1: What are the differences between DID and BPD? They seem so closely related, but how would one differentiate one from the other, if there's even a way?
column3: Dissociative Identity Disorder, as described by the DSM-V, is a disorder in which there is the presence of at least two distinct and separate personalities within an individual, each with its own memories, behaviors and life preferences. Dissociative Identity Disorder occurs when a child who has disorganized attachment and is under the age of 8 (before the brain develops a “whole” sense of self) is subjected to intense trauma over a sustained period of time (often sexual or ritualistic in nature, but occasionally severe childhood illness requiring multiple surgeries can also have an impact). The child has no ability to handle this trauma (would likely die from it) so the brain creates a coping mechanism and unconsciously erects amnesia barriers, allowing the formation of additional “selves” or alters (alternate personalities). These alters then replace the child in times of trauma, allowing them to live a normal life without memory of the trauma. The symptoms of DID, as described by the DSM-V are:Inability to recall large memories of childhoodSwitches between Apparently Normal Personality and one or more Emotional PersonalitiesLack of awareness of recent events, and if they do remember, inability to explain them, for example not being able to explain how the patient got somewhere, or how the acquired a possessionLost time or frequent memory lossFlashbacks or sudden return of memoriesFeelings of disconnection or detachment from body or thoughtsHearing of voices coming from within the mind (not auditory hallucinations coming from without)Dissociative, “out of body ” experiencesSelf-harm or suicidal ideation (individuals with DID have the highest rate of suicide of any other disorder listed in the DSM-V)Changes in handwriting and vocal tonesFunctional changes: from nearly disabled to highly functioningMood swings and depressionAnxiety, nervousness, panic attacks or phobias (often concurrent C-PTSD symptoms)Unexplained sleep disorders; including night terrors, sleepwalking, and insomniaHeadaches that come with switches and unexplained general body pain (somatic remembrances)Like DID, people with Borderline Personality Disorder report experiencing traumatic life events, such as abuse, abandonment, or adversity. This is one of the reasons most people with DID are misdiagnosed with BPD before getting the correct diagnosis. According to the DSM-V, BPD is “a pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, and marked impulsivity, beginning in early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts.” It is unclear what the causes of BPD are, but there seems to be a genetic component as people who have a close family member are at higher risk of developing it. The symptoms of BPD, according to the DSM-V are:Fear of abandonment, whether real or imaginedFrantic efforts to avoid such abandonmentMarked black and white thinkingSuicidal ideationFrequent and intense changes in relationshipsSelf-destructive behavior. often undermining their own effortsStruggle with emotional regulation, most frequently expressing disproportionate or inappropriate angerWeak or distorted sense of selfStrong sense of emptinessImpulsivity, which could lead to substance abuse, self-injury, reckless driving, gambling, binge eating, and unsafe sexThe key difference between the two is that in DID is the presence of at least two distinct and separate personalities within the individual, as well as the amnesia barriers mentioned above. Patients with BPD have a suicide rate of around 8%, while those with DID have a suicide rate estimated around 70%. Both occur in around 1–3% of the global population, making them as common as schizophrenia.
column9: 70% suicidal rate is alarming. Is that the rate of success or attempt?

column1: How can I find out whether or not my family has any intergenerational trauma? What should I do if I find out that we as a family are indeed facing some intergenerational trauma?
column3: If there is intergenerational trauma in your family then there will be lots of clues to this in your family members’ behaviours and maybe your own. Often people minimise or suppress trauma and may think that they are ‘fine’ ‘it wasn’t that bad’ or ‘I have dealt with all that.’ Even when we try to suppress our emotions they ‘leak’ and we can often get clues from our thoughts, feeling or behaviours that we are traumatised. Trauma manifests itself in symptoms and these can include: Depression Irritability Numbing Loss of interest Decreased concentration Chronic pain Headaches Hopelessness Shame and Worthlessness Substance Abuse Eating Disorders Nightmares Flashbacks Hypervigilance Mistrust Feeling Unreal or Out of Body Generalised Anxiety Panic Attacks Emotional Overwhelm Addictions These are all clues that we may be traumatised as they are evidence of coping mechanisms and those ‘leaky’ emotions.

column1: Why is it often harder to cope with the loss of a beloved animal than the loss of a human family member or friend?
column3: "I was more sad when my dog died than when my mom/dad/sister/brother/wife/husband/son/daughter died." In a 2013 survey that we conducted on pet loss, we heard this sentiment from numerous respondents. Your question reflects a true issue for many pet owners. Echoing some of the comments below, I suspect that Pet loss is incredibly difficult for two reasons: 1) the human-animal bond is strong and continually increasing and 2) the mourning process for pet loss is often insufficient 1) The Human animal bond is strong – more so now than ever From ancient Egyptians’ cats to the Chinese emperors’ dogs, pets have bonded with humans for a really long time. In the last two decades in America, however, this close relationship has become more mainstream and prominent. Pet ownership has risen to its highest levels, and total pet spend is over $60B/year in America alone. Our pets have migrated from sleeping outside the house, to inside the house, to in the bedroom. Many of our pets eat grain-free food, receive top quality medical care, and travel with their family. We celebrate their birthdays, talk to them, and treat them like people – they are truly humanized in many households. A recent NYT Article was aptly titled, "Dogs are Humans, too" So why are pets so close to us? They can’t talk, and they don’t reason with us and challenge us like our fellow humans. My research in the pet industry (and raw gut feel) indicates that the increasing intensity is due to a few factors: a) A pet’s love is not a function of our success – they have unconditional “love” Our society is increasingly fast paced. Millennials (and other generations) image craft on social media, move from job to job, and are always “connected” - all in the name of forward progress. Keeping up with the Jones’s has reached new heights. But for all of our success (and all of our failure), our dogs just. don’t. care. Bad day at work? Don’t care. Good day at work? Still don’t care. A saying in the pet world says, “I just aspire to be the person that my dog thinks I am.” Bottom line: pets don’t care about all the stuff that stresses us out. They are there for us no matter what in this rat race of life. Whether our pets feel “love” in the same way as humans may be debated, but what we do know, is that their feelings are not subject to our image or success in the other aspects of life. b) Time enhances closeness Pet owners: quick, name 5 people that you will spend more time with than your pet over the course of his 12 year life…waiting….nope (unless you have a lot of children). In general, the amount of time spent with your pet is greater than any human outside your immediate family that LIVES in the house. In most cases, significantly more. Say you work 40 hours a week. That leaves over 100 hours around the house. For many pet owners, those hours are spent with your dog sitting in your lap, sleeping on your head, or begging by your feet. Over the course of 12 years, that means that you've easily spent more time with your dog than almost anyone in your life. c) Physical touch also strengthens our bonds – and our pets are our most touched companion We live in a digital world. We love social media, and we prefer to text, rather than talk. We over work and under play. With the exception of some cool recent pet webcams, our pets don’t have this same luxury. All they have is physical interaction. Fortunately for them, our brains and bodies happen to like that type of interaction. Article: http://www.cnn.com/2011/HEALTH/01/05/touching.makes.you.healthier.health/ Our interactions with our pets help us reach a chemical and perhaps primal part of ourselves, which today’s digital environment may not satisfy. Do you touch your dog more than your spouse (if you indeed have a spouse)? The answer is probably yes. This physical touch further enhances our bond. 2) The mechanisms for coping with pet loss are sparse. While we have spiritual, ritualistic, and secular ways of coping with human death, most of these do not fully extend to our bonded animal friends. a) Spiritually, most major religions do not address pet loss Because the human animal bond has increased exponentially since the advent of most major religious texts, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam do not robustly discuss what happens to pets after death. While many console ourselves with our religious beliefs when our grandparents pass, it raises more questions than answers for our pets. b) For humans, we have funerals, which help in the healing process These serve not only to allow a sense of mourning, closure, and in some cases, celebration, but they also provide the immediate family with a support from other family, friends, and the surrounding community. There is an outpouring of love that helps to support the survivor with the grief process. Despite our close bonds with our pets, rarely do we have this funeral ceremony with the support of family and community. c) Inconsistent understanding requires us to bottle up emotions For humans, there is a relatively consistent empathy for the pain that the person is going through. For the loss of a pet, however, there are two ends of the spectrum. While non-pet-parents think (and sometimes say), “it’s just a dog” or “why is (s)he so sad,” there are others that fully understand. As a result, pet parents are often compelled to keep their grief to themselves, lest someone think that they were weird or overly-dramatic. This prevents them for being able to undergo the grieving process properly. Therefore, the pain is greater…or at least, lasts longer. In summary, pets are really close to some of us, for reasons that have both pre-dated us, and that are unique to today’s society. Further, we don’t have the same systems to deal with the pain. Combined, this can make the process for pet parents as difficult or more so than a human loss. Fortunately, there are organizations out there that are bridging this gap. Pet memorial centers and pet loss support groups are developing throughout the country. The Pet Loss Professionals Association (PLPA) and the International Association of Pet Crematories and Cemeteries Association (IAOPCC) are leading the charge in providing that support. It will never be easy to lose a cherished pet. They are our rock and our support, throughout the highs and lows of our lives. But it’s okay to feel grief. And it’s okay to find people that will support you along the process. I’ll leave you with this poem from Jimmy Stewart on the Johnny Carson show.
