column1: Recently, a close family member died. I don’t feel sad at all, but everyone around me is crying. Maybe I’m still in shock, but I am typically a very emotional person. Is there something wrong with me?
column3: Sometimes the horror of losing someone is too much to take on board! Everyone around you crying may just make you feel guilty or unfeeling , but it may either hit you when you least expect it, or you have mentally shelved it until you can cope. So don’t feel there is anything wrong with you, people just have different coping mechanisms. So sorry for your loss. Your loss is Heavens gain!

column1: Can losing a family member cause PTSD?
column3: That depends on some factors that are not included in the question. Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) is a brain disorder that changes the brain following a traumatic, highly stressful, or life-threatening event.Was the family member close to this person?Does the individual have one or more mental illnesses before the event? Do they have a history of dissociation? Do they have a repertoire of healthy coping mechanisms?Has this loss been preceded or followed by other distressing events?Are they in an environment which itself is perceived as dangerous?Does the person have a support system established around them before the loss?Will the loss create a radically different circumstance of their own circumstances, such as a minor losing their parent?Is the passing of their family member sudden or after a terminal illness?Is this person a witness to seeing their family member die in a tragic way?One example would be Dr. William Petit who’s family (wife Jennifer Hawke-Petit and their daughters Hayley, 17, and Michaela, 11) were victims of a sadistic massacre, being bound, tortured, raped and murdered on July 23, 2007. After beaten unconscious and escaping the fire set by the perpetrators, he was the only survivor. DR. Petit was so overtaken with flashbacks, night terrors, and hypervigilance so that he could only sleep 2 hours a night. Yet, gradually he learned how to turn darkness into light. How did he accomplish his recovery? Growing up, Dr. Petit developed his social and life skills through experience at quite an early age by helping his father work at their family-owned general store. Dr. Petit, a diabetes specialist, was actively involved in his community. He operated a private practice while also volunteering/working with other organizations and serving as the Director of Public Health (1994-2008) Following the tragedy, he advocated for himself and his loved ones until he saw justice served to the perpetrators - Joshua Komisarjevsky and Steven Hayes - now both sentenced to death, in 2010 and 2011 respectively. Not all family members of murder victims have such resolution. In the US alone, there are approximately 6,000 unsolved murders every year. Understandably, he did give up his practice for good following the incident, but in-between therapy and survivor’s guilt, he established the Petit Family Foundation to remember those he lost. This 501(c)(3) organization honors Jennifer Hawke-Petit, Hayley Elizabeth, and Michaela Rose by funding the education of young people, especially women in the sciences, to improve the living standards of all. William continues to serve as its President even today. When he met Christine Paluf while she was volunteering at the Petit Family Foundation as a photographer, he was ready again for family life and remarried in 2012. Shortly thereafter, the couple welcomed into their family a new son William Petit III. The 65-year-old has in no way forgotten his first wife or his daughters, but time has eased his grief. Dr. Petit says he worked through his grief so that one day he will meet his beloved family in heaven. By 2016, the doctor has since stepped into politics and is currently serving his third term as a State Representative from the 22nd district. So you can see that the outcome following the loss of family members has many factors. Can losing a family member cause PTSD? The confounding answer is in some cases, but not all. If you have lost a family member and need help, please seek a grief counselor and get the support you need. Best Wishes!

column1: What are some healthy coping mechanisms for dealing with grief and loss?
column3: I’d recommend finding a GriefShare group near you.https://www.griefshare.org/In USA culture we have little general knowledge about how to grieve in a healthy way. These 13 classes (~45 minute video, group discussion, workbook) offer you the knowledge you need to grieve in a healthy way - and people to talk with who understand! Its not just for widows(ers) - its for anyone who has lost someone important to them that they love; children, uncles, grandparents, siblings, close friends etc. It is faith based but people of no faith are welcome and not proselytized. There are many good books to read. Look at the reviews (on Amazon for instance) to help decide if a book is a good fit for you. Find a few friends and family members who will patiently listen - DO talk about your lost loved one with them. That’s therapeutic to do. Also, looking at scrapbooks, photo albums etc. are therapeutic to cry over. Having a beloved pet can be very helpful if you live alone. DON’T just distract yourself! Some distraction is fine - but its a mistake to always try to get your mind off of the pain of your loss. That avoids dealing with it - it WILL come back at you if you don’t deal with it! When you're alone feel free to scream and yell your pain and sorrow out to God! He understands. Recovery takes years. But if you address your grief in a healthy way you will see it get less painful in a year or two. If you are a widow(er) and desire to remarry, a general rule of thumb is not to do so for a couple years. I know that may be the first thing that comes to your mind! To refill that empty spot in your heart with someone else! But that would be another form of unhealthy distraction. You need to wait until you have dealt with your grief enough before you start another serious relationship. Having close family and friends who you allow to tell you the truth are helpful for knowing when you are ready. Regarding grieving a beloved pet - sure! Get another one to fill that hole in your heart as soon as you want! I do not minimize the pain of losing a pet - I mourn my beloved fur babies too! But in my opinion its fine to get a new pet to love as soon as you can, if that’s what you want to do.
column9: Griefshare was very helpful to me twice. It was interesting that the second time, the videos had been updated, so it was still the same wonderful support, but a fresh look.

column1: I have a friend who still sobs and sad 10 years after losing her husband. She is 82 and Alzheimer's runs in her family. Is this a sign or what’s wrong with her?
column3: No. Grief is a very personal and emotional loss. People feel it to a varying degree. There is neither a set period for mourning, nor there is a certain acceptable manner in which to feel and express the enormity of a loss. The old lady at this point in her life is more lonely than ever, and consequently feeling the loss of her husband even more intensely. Also, if she has a only few close family members or a few surviving friends—her contemporaries, then she might feel all alone. Shedding tears is cathartic. They bring her some semblance of comfort and relief. Many Grief Counselors recognize crying as an acceptable and quite common coping mechanism…. because keeping the pain bottled up is worse…lot worse BTW crying has nothing to do with Alzhimer’s. However, DEPRESSION has a close connection to it, but it is third only after BRAIN TRAUMA and a HISTORY OF HEAD INJURIES.

column1: Does family depression really exist? Why and how does family depression occur? Can you provide clinical and real life examples?
column3: I’ve never heard of the term “family depression.“ I presume it refers to depression as a characteristic of the family system versus as an individual trait of a specific family member, or of the specific members in a family unit. I further presume it’s distinguishable from a family state in which one clinically depressed member “causes” a depression-like state of the overall family (insofar as individual depression can be considered separate from social dynamics—it usually cannot). If I’m correct in all my conjecture, then family depression is a state resulting from maladaptive intrafamiliar dynamics, or from maladaptive familial function within the sociological system (aka, tension between the family and the overarching ecological system, such as overall society, institutions, communities, and organizations). In other words, “family depression” is to take a clinical, or psychological phenomenon and translate it into a sociological one. So does family depression exist? I suggest that it does, at least as much as any individual depression or clinical depression does. If depression exists, then of course depressed people will have an impact on the function of the systems in which they exist, or on the individuals and systems with which they interact. However, “family depression” suggests that depression is not an individual phenomenon, but a systemic one arising from dysfunctional systems, or dysfunctional interactions between those systems (or between the individuals comprising those systems). Why might family depression occur? I’ve answered that above, but to be more specific, it would be caused by stressors on the family unit exceeding the family’s capacity to cope with said stressors. Those stressors might originate within the family system (e.g., intra-familial discord) or externally, (e.g., discrimination, poverty, and community violence, etc). I suggest that any family-level depression which occurs in the absence of intrapersonal problems within the family (which are often caused or exacerbated by extraneous forces, anyway), is true “family depression.” However, I cannot imagine any real life scenarios where a person or family can be depressed without both internal and external stressors and limited coping resources. How does family depression occur? From a systems perspective, it would originate in the processes individuals and families are involved in, and not in the content of the individuals or families involved. Like other social systems, the origins of any systemic problem is usually a matter of problematic interactions between entities rather than dysfunctional parts. In this case, the family can be considered to have the capacity to function well, but may not have the skills, the tools, or the access to do so, resulting in a depressed state for the entire family unit. Any notion that a dysfunctional family member, or the dysfunctional brain or thinking of a family member might be the cause of family-wide depression is valid, but likely false. Social systems are not like mechanical systems, and people are not machines. They can be similar, but ultimately, a system-wide malfunction is seldom, if ever, the cause of one dysfunctional part. In mechanical terms, even wear and tear does not isolate a particular part, unless that part sees more use (which could be considered a system dysfunction, rather that a mechanical malfunction). Below are real life examples of family depression I’ve encountered personally and professionally.Undocumented/immigrant families: While undocumented and/or immigrant status does not automatically make a family (or individual) depressed, it is certainly a risk factor for depression. In fact, many immigrant families, particularly those that are undocumented, do tend to have high rates of depression and other “behavioral health” problems affecting multiple family members simultaneously. That said, not all immigrant families, even undocumented families, can, or should be considered depressed. Some families manage to cope better with stressors related to immigration and/or undocumented status, or have access to sufficient community support wherein they do not experience depression at the family level, even if certain individual family members do. Families affected by poverty and/or community violence: Same as with undocumented/immigrant families, except the particular stressors may vary. There’s usually much overlap between immigrant and undocumented families and poverty and community violence. Again, exposure to poverty and/or community violence does not automatically make a family depressed. Families with poor interpersonal dynamics (including well-off families): Families plagued by discord are susceptible to family level depression, even wealthy ones (and maybe especially wealthy ones, as they may lack certain protective factors poorer families may not, such as access to community resources, spirituality, etc). Interpersonal conflict, especially when contained within a family system can easily derail any and every member’s mental health and ability to cope with stressors, including their ability to functions outside the family system. It wouldn’t surprise me if you see this a lot among prestigious or famous families, in which each individual’s day-to-day life is highly politicized and they are subject to constant scrutiny, both within the family and in their dealings with other prestigious individuals, families, or other communities. Families affected by loss, especially unexpected loss or tragedies: This is probably the most common, and perhaps the most relatable of all the examples. Tragedy does not discriminate, despite it having a greater impact on more vulnerable families. Natural disasters, crimes, accidents, war, and other tragedies happen anywhere and everywhere, and can significantly impact individuals, families, communities and whole societies. During such events, wide-spread depression can certainly take root, and the family unit is especially vulnerable. During global and regional events like the COVID pandemic, Hurricane Katrina, 9/11 and other large-scale disasters, many individuals and families may experience pervasive group-level depression for myriad reasons. And even in more isolated events, such as accidents or violent crime, the loss of a breadwinner, or of a home, or of a caretaker, can significantly impede a family’s ability to cope with other stressors, resulting in family-level depression or mental health problems. Chronic illness or disability: This is another challenge many can relate to. Taking care of a chronically ill or disabled family member can put a huge strain on a family. It can cause all sorts of conflicts and suffering for everyone involved. These situations are difficult and it’s easy to see how families affected by chronic illness or disability could become depressed, especially given the life-long challenges they pose. but it’s important to note that the ill or disabled family member is not the cause of the family’s problems, nor is the illness or disability the cause of any problems. Inadequate individual, familial, communal, and/or societal resources are the cause, and they can and should be addressed.Often families can access resources to buffer against any long-term mental health problems caused by some of the problems above, but in many cases, aid is limited and the impact of life-altering circumstances or events can affect not just the nuclear family, but extended families, entire communities, and even future generations. This is especially true for families dealing with multiple problems without adequate support or resources, resulting in hopelessness, helplessness, and ultimately, a depression-like familial-state. So I return to my original point, familial depression exist only insofar as depression exists. However, depression of any variety is not just a matter of character, or of content, but of the processes and functions of social systems, the interactions between individual entities within those systems, and the various entities’ (in)ability to meet the needs of the people within them, or the people or other entities with which they interact (including the family-system). Ergo, depressed families like depressed individuals are not inherently dysfunctional, though quite often, society has failed them.
column9: Thank you for you submission. It was really informative and useful. To clarify some areas you refered to in your submission: Family depression can be understood and explained using Family Systems Theory. Murray Bowen, a Psychiatrist, broadened Freud’s theories and developed family counselling using psychodynamic principles. Family Systems Theory emphases the family as an interconnected system. Therefore, the behaviour or changes in the behaviour and functions of one family member can directly affect and impact other members. Bowen’s family counselling treatment was not developed to treat a struggling individual outside of the family context. Rather, the treatment focused on the family as a whole, viewing the family as an interconnected system. In a nutshell, Bowen research and clinical research found that there was so much more to therapy than just studying a single individual- leading to the creation of Family Systems Theory. On a similar matter, many psychodynamic psychology clinics that specialise in treating children (like theTavistock clinic in the UK, as well as the psych clinic I completed my clinical Masters in) insists that parents undergo child-focused-parent-therapy at the same time their child engages in their own psychotherapy. Family depression is present in many households around the world. You gave many examples of situations where family depression many occur including mainly people that come from disadvantaged backgrounds. However, like attachment profiles, and mental illness in general, we find family depression does not discriminate. Family depression is often influenced by both genetic and environmental factors and is linked to intergenerational factors. I have worked with many families that met the criteria for family depression. Dorothy Heard, an attachment theorist also broadened Freud’s, Bowlby and Ainsworth’s work to encompass Family systems and the attachment dynamic. Using attachment theory as a theoretical framework, she introduced the concept of the attachment dynamic as a model to explain: “ (1) how individual members of a family behave as though they constituted a system (2) the extent to which the complementary activities of attachment and caregiving Behaviour (a) govern the movements of family members towards or away from each other; (b) affect the degree to which they each engage in creative exploratory activities: and (c) influence the internal representation each family member builds of him or herself in action with others or acting alone.” I will stop there but should mention that other theorists have their own understanding of and interpretations of family systems theory, including Bowen, Fogarty, Wardle and Skinner and Guerin. In fact, I believe that Object Relations Theory closely fits into both attach and family systems theory. The theories mostly complement each other and can be used to develop a psychodynamic formulation and to treat people.

column1: How do I act towards a person who has bipolar disorder?
column3: It depends a lot on the severity of the illness, and what your connection to that person is. The first thing that I would suggest is that you educate yourself on the illness. In simple terms, people suffer deep depression, followed by mania. Everyone is different. Like any illness some people have mild symptoms, and don’t need medication, just support. Other peoples symptoms are more extreme, and medication is needed to try to control the extreme mood swings. So, lets assume that you are asking about someone suffering at the extreme end. Encourage them to get treatment and medication if prescribed, and then to continue to take that medication, even if they feel better. Support them if they are depressed, and keep an eye on them in case they are sui*idal. Clean their house, and do other chores. Encourage them to eat. Watch their pets for them. Talk to them, and help them to seek help, if necessary. When they are suffering with mania they can sometimes exhibit dangerous behaviour, or do unusual things that are worrying. If so, get them help. For families living with someone with severe bi-polar it can be extremely disruptive to their own lives. Parents can feel guilty thinking it is their fault. Siblings can feel left out as all the attention goes onto the bi-polar sufferer. A spouse can be worried about their partner, and the negative affect on their children, especially if the children are dragged into dangerous situations. Money could be tight if the sufferer can’t work, or the medical bills pile up, or sometimes during mania some sufferers go on excessive spending sprees. The stress obviously strains the relationship, but also puts a mental strain on all of the family, leading to exhaustion, anxiety, depression, and breakdowns. People will grieve the loss of the person they knew before their bi-polar symptoms surfaced, and have to get used to a new reality. Friends often walk away from sufferers eventually, because it causes too much disruption to their own lives. Marriages can break down too. However, families can also put into place coping mechanisms to deal with extreme events, and can discuss what actions they will take with their relative when they are well. IE: Moving out with the kids for a time, or locking credit cards, etc. This can help them feel as if they have some control. I have experienced a different kind of illness with my family member for over forty years (Schizophrenia). Different symptoms, but same stresses on friends and family. So, the same processes apply to other mental illnesses too.
column9: What ever you do dont treat them any different just cuz they have bipolar

column1: Can you describe the rehabilitation programs you have taken part in while in prison? How have they helped you?
column3: During my 18+ years in prison I’ve participated in, completed, and facilitated dozens of educational and self-help programs but my work in “No More Tears” stands out. Founded at San Quentin in 2001, No More Tears is an organization comprised of incarcerated men and community volunteers, that believes former perpetrators of violence are responsible for helping curb violence in the communities where we were once the cause of it. As my friend, mentor, and founding sponsor of No More Tears the late David Lewis once said, "We planted the mines in our communities, now it's up to us to go back and defuse them." The very first No More Tears workshop I attended was titled, “Putting a Face on Violence” and it was there that I met the Ortiz family. That day the Ortiz’s opened their hearts and shared with us the gut wrenching story of their family member who had been killed in a senseless act of violence. Hearing the raw pain in the family member’s voices, and watching the tears stream down their faces as they described how their loved one’s dreams and aspirations had been cut short, all resonated deep within my soul. Without question, the most memorable moment of the workshop for me was the way I felt when the grandmother looked at me. Her eyes spoke to me in a way that only a grandmother’s eyes can, and in a few brief seconds taught me a life-long lesson about love, family, and the need for me to get involved in the movement to end violence in our communities. From that moment forward, I knew exactly why they named the workshop “Putting a Face on Violence.” That Saturday afternoon I sat in a room filled with about 50 other men who’d committed violent crimes, and there were very few dry eyes in the house. The Ortiz’s pain and loss transcended the hyper-masculine male role belief system that dominates incarcerated settings like San Quentin, and touched each of us in a way that reminded us of our own humanity. Listening to the Ortiz’s story moved me and made me think of how much I love my own family and how I would feel if one of my family members were murdered. Right there in my seat I felt anger, sadness, helplessness, and pain just “thinking” about the loss of someone in my family. However, the most important thing the Ortiz’s story did was make me think about the crimes I committed against my victims and how the impact of those crimes made them feel. How were they feeling at that very moment? Were they feeling the same kind of pain as the Ortiz’s? Were they crying? How many tears had they cried? Were they afraid? Had they been living in fear? Were they able to go back to work? The questions were and still are endless. That day I walked out of No More Tears with a profound emotional connection to the Ortiz family but more importantly, an emotional connection with the victims of the armed robbery I committed in 1991. You see, for years I had avoided thinking about and connecting with the pain I had caused in my victim’s lives. Looking back, I see denial was a coping mechanism I used to minimize the fact that my choices caused harm. Consequently, my denial prevented me from making an emotional connection with the seriousness of the robbery I committed, and the far reaching impact of the trauma I inflicted upon the lives of my two victims and their families. Going to No More Tears and meeting the Ortiz family helped change all that and in the process helped change my life. The Ortiz’s story helped me to understand that when I pulled that gun out of my pocket and pointed it at my victims, I did much more than just rob them. I disrupted the physical, emotional, and spiritual well-being of my victims, their families, and their entire community. The robbery I committed lasted five minutes but the fear, pain, and stress of the traumatic event that I caused could last for the rest of my victim’s lives; perhaps carrying over into the lives of future generations of their families as well. The fact that I am responsible for causing so much harm is something that I can no longer deny and from the bottom of my heart I truly am sorry. In the months following that workshop I struggled with feelings of guilt over the crimes I committed and the harm I caused. I had been in denial for so long that it was hard to face what I had done. But rather than shut down emotionally I sought help and found it in programs like No More Tears, the Victim Offender Education group (V.O.E.G.) and V.O.E.G. Next Step. Because of the support I’ve received and the work I’ve done, I am much more aware of my emotions. In turn, my awareness of other people’s feelings and emotions, especially of those I’ve harmed, has become an important part of my life too. Even as I sit in my cell and write this, the thought of my victim’s pain is a constant reminder not only of what I’ve done in the past but also of the importance of what I’m doing today. Since meeting the Ortiz family, my work with No More Tears has afforded me the honor and privilege to meet and work side by side with many other survivors of violent crime, police, elected officials, clergy, teachers, and concerned citizens. Together we are assisting each other in our individual healing processes while at the same time making collective efforts to stop the violence at San Quentin and in our communities. Through my active participation in No More Tears, I’ve experienced an awakening that has set me on a trajectory of awareness, healing, and responsibility that would have been unlikely had I not come to prison. For this reason I see my time in prison, especially my time here at San Quentin, as a blessing of the greatest kind. ### All communications between inmates and external channels are facilitated by approved volunteers since inmates do not have access to the internet. This program with Quora is part of The Last Mile San Quentin. Twitter: @TLM

column1: Why do people get fat when they know it isn't healthy for them?
column3: I am fat. I don’t want to be fat. I have struggled with good food choices from the age of 8. For some food is an addiction, a way to self medicate. Heard of emotional eating? Sometime people struggle with aspects of life and use food as a coping mechanism, or a self soothing activity. Eating habits often change with depression. Some people struggle to eat, some eat too much. For some people eating helps with concentration… some people with ADHD use food to help with focus. Think about when you are not getting a lot of sleep, eating can help you push through exhaustion. I was a skinny kid, to the point my mother was worried about my health. My problems started as a child when I was about 8 when I was abused (not by a family member). I started stealing candy mainly from around the house and home business. Emotionally puberty hit me hard. I could not stand the weight gain, having fat where I only had muscle and skin before. Eating these bad foods did not help I was still a healthy weight at this stage, but I felt fat and unhappy about my body. As an 11 year old I started skipping meals, trying to keep my weight down, but still addicted to sweet and salty. By the age of 15 I started developing anorexic traits, by 19 I was bulumic, with anorexic episodes and needed hospitalisation. I was trying to control one aspect of my life…my body, but the reality was everything was out of control, I was severely depressed. Hospital “cured” me of my eating disorder…the purging. Anorexic phases were always hard for me to maintain. Back then Binge Eating Disorder was not recognised as a problem. Years of yoyo dieting followed. I could not and still cannot maintain healthy eating habits. I am now morbidly obese. I do not want to be this way, it does affect my health, I am unhappy about my weight, and cannot seem to get my eating habits under control. Pain and balance issues make exercise unpleasant and difficult. I have tried many diets, exercise regimes, medication, and weight loss surgery. I have gained 50 kg in the past two years. Despite this my weight is currently not the biggest problem in my life by a long shot. For some people it is healthier mentally to accept themselves and the body they have than to focus on weight loss. Fat is a very subjective term. Most people who are obese, particularly morbidly obese like me will eventually experience some health issues related to their weight. Not necessarily the case for active overweight people with a fairly balanced diet and healthy lifestyle. The answer to your question is not simple, and is probably as varied as the number of people out there. One thing that does not help is shaming or judging people on issues such as weight.
column9: Actually fat shaming works great. In Japan, it’s universal, so their obesity rate is less than 1/10th ours, which currently stands at a jaw dropping 42.4% which is Fucking Disgusting.

column1: Why don't I remember actions I do or things I say, like I have multiple personality disorder or being possessed?
column3: Hi and thank you for your question. I can feel how distressed you are and how frightening this must feel. I’d like to phrase this as kindly as possible so first I’ll address the fact that it is no longer called MPD. DID (Dissociative Identity Disorder) was once referred to as Multiple Personality Disorder. It has not been referred to as MPD or Split Personality in about 30 years, as research as progressed and shown it to be a valid traumatic dissociative disorder (like Complex-PTSD) rather than an actual personality disorder. Second, as someone who went through a very traumatic exorcism because my parents preferred to think I was possessed rather than that I was experiencing a very real, valid psychiatric disorder due to CSA I can say with confidence that it can be extremely painful to draw a parallel between DID and demonic possession. This can be a huge trigger for a large part of the DID community. That said, your question is quite valid and it does sound as if you are experiencing some sort of dissociation… the extent of which I’m not able to determine given the limited information I have to work on. I would strongly encourage you to seek the opinion of a skilled trauma-informed therapist. However, if you think you may have DID, ask yourself if the following applies to you:A history of childhood trauma or sudden remembrance of childhood traumaLapses in memory of day to day events, as well as important personal details/information of which you should be awarePeople accusing you of saying or doing something of which you are unaware (I think this is a box we can check from your question itself)Loss of timePoor memory, missing appts, not remembering things that have been discussed in previous sessions, etc.Switches (meaning reported to you by a family member/caregiver)Hearing voices coming from within (this is distinct from auditory hallucinations that come from without the mind, as that would indicate schizophrenia)Intense shame surrounding and avoidance of issues involving switchesFeeling disconnected from the body or the feeling of being a “guest in your own body” (for ex. seeing through someone else’s eyes)Periods of amnesia, most often during a childhood time periodSevere mood swingsSevere headachesPTSD symptomsNight terrors, sleepwalking, other sleep disturbancesIf these symptoms feel familiar to you, please do seek the counsel of a therapist. DID is a very serious disorder, regardless of the fact that it is actually a coping mechanism, and it can disrupt every aspect of your life. You would need help in navigating through therapy. What I mean by coping mechanism is that Dissociative Identity Disorder manifests when a child **under the age of 8** (before the brain develops a “whole” sense of self) is subjected to intense trauma over a sustained period of time (often sexual or ritualistic in nature, but occasionally severe childhood illness requiring multiple surgeries can also have an impact). The child has no ability to handle this trauma (would likely die from it) so the brain creates a coping mechanism and unconsciously erects amnesia barriers, allowing the formation of additional “selves” or alters (alternate personalities). These alters then replace the child in times of trauma, allowing them to live a normal life without memory of the trauma. It is not possible to develop DID after the age of 8. A traumatic event experienced after this time could result in other disorders, such as PTSD but not DID. I hope this helps answer your question and that you find healing. Best wishes.

column1: Can a death in the family make loved ones feel hollow inside?
column3: Yes, the death of a family member can make you feel hollow inside. In 2008, I lost my baby brother28, my baby sister33, and my husband41 all within eight months. After their deaths, I felt numb. It was all I could do to get out of the bed and get dressed in the morning. Everything from that time period was just one big blur. This hollowness or numbness is a coping mechanism. It allows your mind to slowly process the loss you've experienced and gives you time to grieve. You've just been through a life-altering event, and it will take some time to feel whole and normal again. Share with your loved ones so that the grieving process isn't so difficult. Try to be each other's support so that you're not going through all of this alone, and remember time often heals what reason cannot.

column1: Are the Uchiha clan genetically predisposed to the "Curse of Hatred", or was it a lie perpetuated by Black Zetsu?
column3: I have seen no evidence to convince me of his honesty. Instead what we must understand is that the Uchiha as a clan did not survive the Warring States Period unscathed. Each loss brought them immense sorrow and to cope with it they developed a very flawed coping mechanism. This is the Curse of Hatred.It is self perpetuating curse because those that fall prey it to immense hatred are rewarded with the power to survive. Over time this developed into something resembling generational trauma. By the Third Shinobi World War many were still effected with clear signs of self isolation and judgmental behaviour. The alternative is to grow and accept the fragility of live. This technique rewards people with a clear head that’s uninfluenced by strong emotions. But suffers from complacency because as Hashirama Senju proved this is not a world anyone should accept.Uchiha Clan by Indiandwarf on DeviantArt Kagami Uchiha is a first generation Konohagakure citizen who broke this circle of hatred. There are reasons aplenty. Some have suggested the cause to be nature, nurture or institutional brotherhood. I believe that it is all three and more. In the warring states period you could wipe out twenty members of a clan if you knew how they fight. But in Konoha you have to deal with an various combinations of twenty different clans and unaffiliated shinobi. It also means that the clans suffer proportionately less if a unit is lost. It was from Kagami’s line that Shisui Uchiha was born. He exemplified what the Uchiha could be. When his father suffered a slow and excruciating death, he accepted fate for what it was. When his best friend died, he did not respond with logical acceptance. He felt all the emotions common for child soldier. And he even managed to unlock the Mangekyō Sharingan. But he did not let these emotions consume him.Itachi and Madara are two sides of the same coin when it comes to hatred. Itachi internalised his hatred while Madara projected it outward towards the whole world. They did terrible things for the good of the many. And yet it was at the end of their lives when their Mangekyō Sharingan withered as they had lost sight of the connections that gave them such a power. Sasuke grew from small child who hated himself for letting Itachi run amok to a teenager who despised the world for destroying his family. As an adult he would not let either consume him. But the emotional damage was done and he left the future of the Uchiha Clan in safer hands.Sarada Uchiha was raised by Sakura Uchiha of the Haruno Family. She did not know her father. But her mother gave her all the love and attention she deserved. She was content. But in the back of her mind there was something missing. Eventually she sought out her father and found a man who had kept his distance to protect her from the dangers of the world and his broken heart. It was during this ordeal that Sarada awakened the Sharingan. Her emotional state was complicated to say the least. There was anticipation, uncertainty and perhaps even a bit of pain from missing out on a loving parent. But it was not trauma. And that’s important because the Curse of Hatred is predicated on the idea that it offers something in exchange for extreme suffering. People want to believe in it because it justifies all the needless pain they have gone through. In reality the power was always within each Uchiha. They just need to open their heart for it. Slava Ukraine and have a nice day.

column1: My former classmate is 28 and never met her dead mother. How did she survive without her mother?
column3: Coping with the loss of a parent at a young age is unbelievably challenging. Your classmate might have found strength through support from other family members, friends, or from therapy. Developing resilience and finding ways to remember and honor her mother's memory could have played a significant role in her survival and emotional healing. Human beings despite our emotional fragility, can prove amazingly resilient, under the most difficult a traumatic circumstances! Especially when the loss of a parent occurs at a young age, obviously it get’s more difficult the older she was when she lost her mother. But given the fact that childbirth was one of the most common causes of death before the mid 1900s, a great many people grew up, never knowing their mother. Human beings. Find a way to survive emotionally. The human brain is an incredible organ with an incredible ability to defend against Trauma. Today we called these defense mechanisms. Nonetheless, I’m sure that the loss of your classmate’s mother was tremendously traumatic, and may still be a cause of pain to her. Be careful when bringing this up as it could trigger a profound, emotional response, which she may not be ready for. I sincerely hope your classmate is doing well, emotionally, and has come to terms with the loss of her mother, and has developed coping mechanisms sufficient to deal with the loss of her mother! Laura.

column1: Is it normal for a woman that lost her mother at a young age to makeup memories about her and then actually believe them?
column3: A child losing her mother — or any parent figure for that matter — is practically the most jarring and traumatic experience she could ever have at her age. As human beings, even at a young age, we tend to revert to coping mechanisms to deal with the ensuing trauma, it would not be surprising to see that a child would make up memories of that lost parent figure, in the subconscious attempt to take back that part of her that she lost. As much as with would seem easier to forget any thought or memory that child might have about her lost mother / parent figure, for some children, it would be easier to make believe, and move forward in their lives with that belief. The question though that begs an answer is that when the child does come around, will there be someone to help them transition to a life without these made-up memories. It is up to the remaining parent and the surrounding family members to care for and nurture the child, so that even with loss, the good memories — be it manufactured or otherwise — would remain with her and shape her into the best version of herself in the future. Have a blessed day!

column1: What are the effects of losing a parent on siblings?
column3: It depends upon age and environmental background: Young, dependent children experience fear when they lose a close family member- their whole world is upset and their future may be uncertain- plus if a Mother or Father, or sibling died- they are scared because it could happen to another family member- or even to them. They may experience nightmares and become afraid to go to school- what if something bad happens- becomes an ongoing theme. Young children have few coping mechanisms and cannot comprehend the big picture, so they feel abandoned and alone; unless there was a close bond with other adult caregivers. Some children may think they were somehow responsible, especially if the parent was running an errand for them. It is similar with a sibling- it’s hard for them to understand the concept of death. If the child was being neglected or abused- they are coming from an unsafe place to a less safe place in their lives; so it’s traumatizing. If the ‘child’ is a young adult just beginning an independent life, they are overwhelmed by the loss plus having to cope as a new adult- they may resort to escape measures.. such as addictions. Grieving is difficult for anyone of any age, but more complicated when the person suffering a major loss is a child- or if there was complex trauma and unfinished business. In addition, if poverty and lack of resources are part of the mix, depression and hopelessness may become an issue . The mental health of the individual before the loss is critical- if they were stable before- it will be easier for them to see through the grief.

column1: Am I immature for growing to hate losing friends?
column3: It is not immature to feel upset or disappointed when losing friends. It's a natural part of life to experience loss and change in our relationships. It's important to remember that people come into our lives for a reason and leave for a reason, and that it's okay to grieve the loss of a friendship. It may be helpful to talk to someone about your feelings, such as a therapist or a trusted friend or family member. It may also be beneficial to focus on self-care and healthy coping mechanisms during this difficult time.

column1: How would you describe what it feels like to have your heart broken?
column3: The question is so easily asking to quantify 'the king of worst feelings'. The pain, anguish, trauma one undergoes immediately after a breakup cannot be quantified so easily. As I write this, my mind rewinds, trying to recall the exact state I was when the girl I was in love, 'broke up' with me. Our brain is a wonderful organ when it comes to coping with breakups because we have a magic mechanism called "forgetting" which saves each one of us from the clutches of 1000 deaths. Background: I was 25, very reserved, intelligent and good looking guy. It was my first love with an average looking girl with whom I took a long time(2 years) to decide that she was the one. I never dated anyone and had very few friends. She was my first date and after she came into my life, she became my only world (friend, enemy, philosopher, guide, wife,whore,witch, bitch and mom). Though I took her for granted sometimes and dominated her, I truly loved her. She kept saying "you are so handsome and i am so average"....will it work out? I never believed external appearance mattered so much for her. Most importantly, I never thought she would go after another guy even in my wildest dreams. But, knowing me, she planned for long, broke up with me quickly and married a very rich and ugly guy within her family and settled in a different country. To give an analogy, "the feeling of breakup" was like going through death helplessly. The remotest resemblance to quantify this broken heart feeling would be the DABDA theory of Coping with Death. DABDA stands for Denial, Anger, Bargain, Depression and Acceptance. (Most people will enter these stages after receiving a terminal diagnosis of their medical report.).Being a guy, the first reaction was a combined Denial-Anger-Bargaining with severe mood fluctuations. Then I experienced Depression and finally Acceptance. Denial: The first stage of breakup. I could not accept it is happening to me. How can a part of me behave so differently as if ignoring me ? my love 'hating' me? going away from me ? saying it's not part of me ? Wait a sec...she IS part of me. I know every movement of hers. I understand what she wants. A kid can poke my eyes sometimes, but it's not intentional. Everyone changes. She can't do this...deep inside she is part of me...I can FEEL it. Being a guy, during this stage, I isolated myself from family and friends to avoid discussions. I believed by not acknowledging, the issue will cease on its own and she will come back. Anger: "Why me?" Why now? Where did I go wrong? The realization that all of my hopes, dreams, and well-laid plans aren't going to come about brought anger and frustration. This anger is often directed at myself and people who loved me. I rarely saw people in their faces, neither did I display any enthusiasm and sometimes exhibited fits of rage. Even strangers weren't immune to the actions my anger brought about. Seeing people laughing and dancing was a cruel reminder that I am not going to have my hand anymore. Bargaining: I tried to convince myself that if I call her, she would accept me. Just one chance. Maybe I have wronged her so much that I would correct myself. I would do as you say and correct myself....just give me one chance. Is it because that day...I spoke like that ? I didn't mean to hurt you. Trust me. Just one chance to see you face to face and explain myself. Prayed to God, please, please make this work. Whether I believe in you or not, just this time, just once, make it work. Even when the obvious reality kept staring at my face, I refused to accept it. Depression: Its a deep sense of loss leading to high negative feeling. Seeing meaninglessness in everything. Lack of personal hygiene, hunger and a desire to dress. Every small things (from gifts, children pics, souvenirs, food, tv scenes, colors, sounds etc) reminding of her making life more miserable. Crying, crying out loud sometimes within a pillow (so that voice is muffled)....and sleep being the only escape from reality. Hating myself seeing in the mirror and loosing focus on everything. This was the most difficult time to cope. This stage was accompanied by strong feeling of committing suicide after killing her (especially after being told that she is married with another guy. Mentally playing out the part of slitting her throat and seeing blood all over my hands and feeling good. Mood fluctuates....reality seeps inside....cry...cry...how can I think like this to the girl with whom I dreamt of babies...named the babies together? ... I was in a shattered state. Acceptance: Though there was a painful realization that she was gone, it was yet to sink in fully. Head understands quickly but heart takes a long time to accept as reality. 'Time heals' they say and so slowly and gradually I changed. This might be due to some true friends and family members who got scared but understood and respected my silence. They ensured that I didn't stay alone too long and ensured that I ate at-least little. Slowly and gradually, in six months my focus shifted and I started smiling at little things. My family got a kitten with which I liked playing. It was a new beginning like a child getting adjusted to a new environment, I adjusted to the world back again. Note:I have expressed only a fraction of what I went through by these "limited words and sentences". It is by far the worst feeling (state of being) anyone can undergo. Would request anyone reading this to show empathy and understanding for your friends / family members who are going through a breakup. Update: I became a better person after the breakup. I became bold, assertive, outgoing and passionately went after my professional goals.I truly believe that the love I had was pure and she helped me bring it out for the first time. I trust and believe in true love always because I know I am good. Time healed everything. I fell in love with a beautiful girl after 5 years and I am happily married to her with a beautiful kid.

column1: What are some unhealthy coping mechanisms for fear and anxiety?
column3: Unfortunately, in stressful situations, we too often rely on negative coping mechanisms instead of positive coping mechanisms. It would be great if we could all be distracted when a crisis hits, but most people instinctively choose to engage maladaptive coping mechanisms. can affect your own life and the lives of those around you. Of all the negative coping mechanisms out there, these 7 are the most common and arguably the worst. 1. Avoid the problem altogether Anxiety avoidance is a very common strategy for dealing with situations that frighten people. On the surface, it makes sense to stay away from things that make you anxious or worried. However, over time, this fear is amplified and persists if not confronted. Avoidance can give you immediate relief, but learning to face your concerns is the best thing you can do in the long run. 2. Smoking Many people turn to smoking to deal with stress, as it provides an immediate sense of relief. You can also keep your hands busy by focusing on something else. Smoking is a form of recreation, but it is negative and has serious negative economic and health consequences in the future. 3. Compulsive Spending A common way to deal with stress is compulsive shopping. Buying new shoes and jewelry can lead to good happiness in the short term, but can cause a lot of her problems in the long run. Some people hide their purchases from family members, or take out loans or credit cards to continue spending even when their bank accounts are empty. As a result, the entire family could face the financial burden of her 4. Drinking too much caffeine Much like smoking, coffee gives you an immediate sense of relief. This helps against herstress in the short term, but can cause problems in the long term. Can develop caffeine dependence, causing caffeine crashes and sleep disturbances. Immediate situations that evoke fear of being able to escape provide an immediate sense of relief. The next time a similar situation occurs, will remember the relief from the previous escape, and will attempt to escape again. However, this is a terrible strategy and can lead to increased isolation. It can also be distressing for family members because they don't know where you are going or when you will be back. Even if you keep avoiding panic-inducing situations, fear won't go away naturally. 5. Excessive Alcohol Consumption Excessive alcohol consumption numbs the emotions and senses, so alcoholism is common for stress relief. However, excessive drinking has many negative effects on health. There is also This may not seem like an overly destructive problem, but the human body needs external stimulation and exercise to stay healthy. 7 Celebrity Some believe that going out for meaningless sex is a way to shut out stressful situations. However, this is a dangerous act and can cause many problems in your life. Promiscuous behavior can result in the loss of stable relationships and friends, and can lead to sexually transmitted infections. 7. Eating Disorders A very common negative coping strategy is to use food to forget the problem. Some take the form of overeating, while others take the form of severely restricting caloric intake. Either way, eating disorders can have serious health consequences and can be life-threatening. The Importance of Developing Positive Coping Mechanisms Most of us need to look for more positive ways to deal with stressful and difficult situations, rather than relying on negative patterns of behavior. Unfortunately, as humans, we have an instinctive tendency to resort to maladaptive coping strategies in times of crisis. Therefore, recognize which coping strategies are negative and which are positive, and take proactive measures to discourage the use of negative strategies and focus on positive strategies instead. is important. Whenever you feel stressed or anxious, you should try to face your fears and stop running away. By staying in the situation, you will eventually learn that your fear will decrease over time. You should also maintain a positive lifestyle, exercise, and eat healthy in moderation. By engaging in productive pastimes such as knitting, woodworking, or baking, you can divert your attention away from stress in positive ways, rather than engaging in negative distraction techniques such as impulsive shopping or excessive drinking. You can also learn how to distract. Negative coping mechanisms can bring immediate relief, but only do more damage in the long run. Therefore, seeking a counselor may help you identify more adaptive mechanisms that can help you live a happier life and achieve happier outcomes when faced with stressful situations.

column1: What one thing makes someone a very mature person?
column3: I would rather answer this question with an example which happened in our lives. In march 2008 our beloved son-in-law breathed his last breath. He left behind him his wife(our daughter) and two sons. Elder one P was nine years old and younger one J was four years old then. During their father’s last hours these two boys were left in the house with some relatives ; while all of us were in the hospital. While returning from the hospital all of us promised to each other that we would not reveal the fact to P until next day morning before his father’s body is brought home. We returned home keeping our faces as sober as possible. Whenever anybody could not control, they would go to some other room and cry silently. Next day morning we gave the elder one early breakfast and prepared our selves to reveal the fact to him. Our son some how gathered courage and told him every thing. P cried hard for half an hour. After half an hour, he wiped his tears and announced that he will tell his younger brother about his father’s death. He fetched from somewhere his father’s shirt and wore it. He went to his brother and woke him up. The conversation went like this: “Annayya(big brother) why are you wearing daddy’s shirt?” “J ! from today on wards I will be your daddy” “But why annayya?” “Because our daddy is no more.” “What is that no more annayya?” “He went to meet God and will never come back” “Then you will be my daddy?” “Yes .That’s why I am wearing this shirt” J sat on his bed and hugged his annayya tightly. “chinna daddy!” (little daddy) he said still hugging. From that day on wards P behaved like a father with his brother. Today J is afraid of nobody except his brother. What one thing makes someone a very mature person? Responsibility! How did my daughter cope with her grief? Please see Sridevi Datta's answer to How can a lady get back to being strong after she loses her husband or her child?.

column1: What does it feel like to have your sibling die?
column3: TL;DR In my experience of suddenly losing a sibling, you go through a range of emotions, especially: detachment, heartbreak, shell shock, numbness, anger, failure, loneliness and realisation. Eventually, the warmth and inspiration of others who have been through the same or more, takes the place of all those feelings and what remains is hope. You are forever changed, but we endure. Marc & Daniel Surreal: the first feeling is detachment from normal life I pushed the phone harder onto my ear to better hear the call from overseas; I was speaking to a policeman who slowly explained that my little brother had been killed in a horrific car crash. Within a few seconds, I could feel that my brain and nervous system were shutting down – totally overcome by raw emotion. Struggling to concentrate, I clenched my jaw and willed myself to focus on what the policeman was saying, I knew I had to relay the details to the rest of my family. Daniel, my brother, had hit a big pause button on my life – nothing really mattered and all direction had completely dissolved. Heartbreak: the second feeling is actual, physical heartbreak The only thing harder than hearing that my brother had been killed at 23, was telling my mother. She had heard me on the phone and knew that something was wrong, she watched me with her pained eyes as I sat on the side of her bed and looked at her. My mother had lived a hard life, she lost her husband (my father) to a heart attack and was left to bring up two young boys; wanting the best for us, she uprooted the family before developing ovarian cancer. Here she was, thin and in constant pain with less than two months to live, wondering if Daniel had twisted his ankle playing rugby. When I told her what had happened, she screamed; then wailed for a long time and then screamed. I don’t think I will ever forget her cries, and in that moment a piece of my heart broke off. Not same as when someone decides to end a relationship, which is a momentary crack that gets sealed by the next person. This is a physical feeling that a part of your heart is gone forever; someone who you've known every day, for almost your entire life will never come home again. Shell shock: the third feeling is severe shock As soon as I finished telling my mother what the police told me, my body started showing signs of shock. The first was hyperventilation; this came unexpectedly with heavy onset; stranger still was my heart pounding fast and hard with cold running through all my veins. Finding it hard to control, I jumped in the shower and focussed on slowing down my breathing. Later on, I would lose focus mid-sentence and forget things that I did earlier in the day. At night, I would only fall asleep from exhaustion; when I did dream, the images were those of the car crash – screeching, flames and burning bodies. Numbness: the fourth feeling is no longer feeling anything The man next-door said that he was having trouble losing those last 5kgs, a woman at the checkout till mentioned she was irritated that her cat vomited on her new carpet; I felt nothing. My emotionally-drained brain reasoned that all these insignificant things are changeable. Losing the one person who you can depend on no matter what is immutable – no amount of effort or money will bring them back. Friends shared with me that losing their grandmother changed their life and they couldn't believe how that upsetting it was. I understood that it was natural to show empathy but it isn't comparable; I was sad when I lost grandparents and shattered after losing my parents - but for me, losing a brother was something that changed the deepest part of me. Selfishness: the fifth feeling is irrational anger and selfishness Often, my brother and I used to talk about who would be a better uncle to each other’s kids, how we would be each other’s Best Man at our weddings, or about starting a business together and living in the same city. Whatever it was, we were going to do it together. Suddenly, I was irritated and angry at him – we spoke about these things and agreed that we would do them, why has he left me here with these broken dreams? Why did he have to be in the car at that time? Why hadn't he just broken his leg? How can he be so selfish? It's a lot of deep anger but once the initial grief has passed, it’s clear that these feelings are completely irrational. Failure: the sixth feeling is complete failure As a sibling, and especially an older brother, it was my job to protect him. This was even more true in my situation as Daniel didn't have a father figure past the age of 7; everyone always told me to look out for him and set an example. As the realisation of his death set in, so did a profound sense of failure. I started to over-analyse all the advice that I’d given him and every time I left something risky unchecked, connecting all the dots and coming to the unavoidable conclusion that it was my wrong advice that put him in the situation where he died. I had failed. I had failed my late-father; I had failed my sick mother. I had failed him. People cautioned me not to take on any blame but it’s impossible not to; every day I force focus away from it but deep down I know it’s a scar – it lightens after time but never truly leaves. Loneliness: the seventh feeling is being truly alone One of the best feelings about having a brother is that if he was in trouble, had no money or was sick – he could rock up, sleep on the couch, share my food and stay as long as he needed to. I know that my brother would've done the same for me. Parents naturally get old and pass away, so having your sibling to depend on no matter what, is true security in life; now there’s a void in my life where that feeling lived. To fill this, I surround myself with things he owned and I find myself wearing his t-shirts; they can’t replace him but just a little bit, it quietens the loneliness. Realisation: the eighth feeling is coming to terms with reality He has died; this has really happened. He’s not coming back and he’s not coming home. Siblings share memories and experiences of birthdays, family holidays, sports, hobbies, events and are there to remind each other when they forget. But now it’s only me that has those memories; I carry his memories. The hardest things are photographs and memories; knowing that every year I will grow older, have more candles on my cake, my skin will weather and my hair will grey, but Daniel will always be 23. Echoes: the penultimate feeling is questioning if it was a pretence Try as you might to come to grips with reality - your brain doesn't always play fair. Sometimes you'll be on a train pulling into a platform and you'll glance at someone as you pass by who could be your brother - and for a moment - your heart stops. You test yourself: Could it be him? Could he have somehow survived? But it isn't true. Also, he comes into my dreams - unannounced, unchanged and naturally as if he has always been with me. Coming back to reality and waking up from these is hard - like being pulled out from a warm bath into a cold, empty house. These situations, or echoes of the person, happen regularly - and I'm not sure they ever really quieten. Hope: the last and most important feeling is hope Someone dying is a natural way of life – and even though there are times when it’s especially unfair, like losing a brother at a young age, a parent having to bury their child, or losing your whole family, people have walked those difficult roads and survived. And I’m sure that most go on to create their own families, being happy and fulfilled as anybody, despite losing someone so close. Knowing that there are people who are worse off than me and yet succeed in life (people I grew up with, Ashley Buerkett, etc…) keeps me focussed on living and the future. As Daniel used to say, “Go forth, be strong”…
