You wanted to do a certain job or you envisioned your life to be to look like a certain way at a certain time in your life. But what happened after meeting the narcissist? When you lose your years, you lose opportunities and you are not able to do things even after leaving. And that is what you have to grieve because last time cannot be recovered. Once lost, it's gone. And also the narcissist promised you so many things. The dream of togetherness, the dream of having a family, the dream of being together forever. That is what they told you. But they ended up delivering a nightmare. So they destroyed your dreams. The hope was gone. You lost so many things collectively. column1: Does depression cause emotional detachment?

They are closing down emotionally and need help urgently. Depression means depressed emotions or crushing of or closing down to emotions as the body and mind cannot cope with anymore stress or disappointment. This can initially be helpful in crises and trauma, but more than a few days like this is not right. The person is suppressing or crushing the ability to feel and experience. column1: Is it normal to stop caring about things and people? Why do some individuals lose interest in everything and everyone around them?
column3: I don't believe it is normal to stop caring about things and/or people. I think it's possible that someone can get hurt emotionally enough that he (or she) withdraws away from people and puts up an invisible wall to keep the hurt out or to let any new hurt, in. It's also a sign of severe depression when a person supposedly stops caring about anything or anyone. It is natural to want, desire, and crave affection and connection from others. It is natural to want to be a part of something greater than just one's own life. A person not caring anymore is most likely someone who has shut down emotionally and psychologically as a coping mechanism to deal with unimaginable pain and grief from the past.

column1: Do narcissists call you stubborn when they realize they can no longer control you?
column3: A narcissist will call you everything THEY ARE always. Narcissists project.And they cannot see outside of themselves. They had bad dreams, were highly paranoid, got easily spooked, and were all afraid of ghosts. They also landed themselves in prison a time or two from it.) It’s for a mask, a fraud. Only real love is power. And that’s why they are always trying to harm those who have the ability to emotionally attach and love. Yet their golden child abuse made love and attachment impossible for them—being too dangerous—so they yearn for what they didn’t feel they had in childhood: the power their abusive parents had. When any person discovers fraud, they typically revert to self-protection. So the love that supply feels for a narcissist, and therefore the fantasy of their control, collapses on the narcissist every time. This happens to every narcissist, a million times over, all throughout life. And they still never learn they can’t control anyone or that their “power” is illusion and flimsy AF. Though I have known narcissists to get lonelier and more isolated as they age, more hesitant to have a lot of friends, but they always need some form of supply…and it always goes to 💩.This even happens when narcissists are able to amass systemic power or form cults: look at the Nazis, or the American slave owners, or the fall of Rome….narcissists, narcissists, narcissists. They can do damage and cause pain, but they never maintain power or control, because a human soul, and the power of love, cannot be owned, silenced, or controlled. History refuses to have its crimes silenced or erased. There are always Champions of truth. They’ll never kill us or control us all, as they fantasize.More so than name calling, the sign that a narcissist is losing control of supply is VIOLENCE. When violent, a narcissist is GIVING YOU POWER. In that state, the loss of their fantasy of power and supremacy causes them to have an adult temper tantrum, which manifests as narcissistic rage. In this mental state, their masks are off and they lose all SELF CONTROL. All you need then is evidence of the brutality and heartlessness of the violence, and you have what is needed to expose their inhumanity and injustices to make them face either consequences or shame. This is how the American Civil Rights movement succeeded: in being nonviolent, the narcissistic rage and racism of white supremacist police brutality was exposed to the world. The emotion behind narcissistic rage is FEAR. Of love, of loss of control, of being unmasked, of someone being better than them in some way, of grief, of shame, of abandonment, of YOU. They use violence in an attempt to project their fear. It is their desperate grab for power, their despair over their own fantasies of grandiosity proving false, their grief over their inability to love…their ultimate unmasking. They reveal themselves to be not the heroes and gods they fantasized, entitled to everything… …but the villains, entitled to nothing. In a narcissistic rage, they go into such a state of PTSD from their childhood that they risk everything and lose all touch with reality. They have you on their conscience, evidence of their deep shame, and they have to bury you. Every day their mind must bury what they did to you to survive. They can only do so through denial and delusion, since they can’t survive shame. And in lashing out in anger and delusion, they officially lose the war and transfer all their power into your bodily lacerations. The trauma in your wounds, once healed, becomes both a mirror to reveal truth… …and something that makes you stronger than ever before.SOMETHING THAT MAKES YOU POWERFUL AND RESILIENT. People rarely talk about this, but with every narcissist I endured, many of whom were very abusive and violent, my life went through a tremendous upgrade, even as I was still trauma bonding. My health would improve, I’d create better art, I’d reach for new goals and attain them with ease. I suffered a lot of grief with my BPD, and survival didn’t always look certain, but I had faith and gratitude and blessings whenever I survived a toxic enmeshment. I got smarter every time and I devoted myself to self awareness of my own mental health and understanding of others. I committed to social justice causes. I read tons of books. I took up new hobbies. I won awards. I traveled the world. I made a life I’m proud of, and I did it all on my own, without sacrificing my heart, while feeling and processing my grief from narcissistic abuse, from loving those sitting farthest from the light of love. I have deeply loved a lot of narcissists, starting with my parents. It’s ingrained in my DNA to love them and it’s ingrained in theirs to hate. But once you are covered in scar tissue from betrayals and abuses, nothing much hurts anymore after that. You become even more unbreakable, and loving, than before. You become a walking embodiment of the full throated, fearless TRUTH. You become REAL power. The narcissist will hate you for that. Forever.You can’t even blame them. column1: How do aging women come to grips with loss of attractiveness?
column3: Well for one thing, it’s all about perspective. What’s considered attractive by one may not be so to another. But really, is the mission of life bound up with attractiveness? Some of the greatest people who’ve ever lived were not particularly beautiful, but they made a difference. Ultimately, looks don’t matter. Or they shouldn’t. But it seems we are hardwired to look for things that are attractive to us. It’s natural for us, men as well as women, to notice the physical attributes of someone of the opposite sex. (I am not bashing gays, just making an example) Because a woman who appears to be in good shape means the probable ability to bear children. And a man who appears to be in good shape is perceived as healthy and able to provide for a family. It’s just nature. It’s some part of us that we aren’t even aware of that makes us naturally look for beauty in others. The animal kingdom contains many animal species where there is a dominant female. She is the boss. But as she ages, she weakens, and she will be tested by another, younger, more fit female. Eventually she will have to give up her place as matriarch and will be demoted or even kicked out of the pack. Tell me it isn’t the same in our human society. So on another note, how do I as an aging female, come to terms with losing my attractiveness. Well that has happened in stages. I have always had a young looking face. Even up into my 50s people mistook me for being several years younger than my actual age. But when I hit 30, I got my first grey hair. I will never forget the day I stood talking to my mother and she suddenly reached up and plucked a hair off the top of my head. I was shocked to see a steel grey, wiry hair. She laughed and said now they would grow in faster. Always gotta be messing with me. That is when I began inspecting my hair for grey all the time, and while I was at it, I noticed little wrinkles at the corners of my eyes. I developed a deep frown line that runs down the middle of my forehead. As time passed, some little brown spots began to show up on my face, and wild hairs came out of nowhere and sprouted on my chin. The area around my eyes has darker pigmentation than the rest of my face, and I have bags under my eyes and look perpetually tired. All through the years, I have fought the signs of age on my face. I began using a facial moisturizer early on, and over the years have tried them all from high dollar to drug store brands, and not one of them has ever made me look any younger. I have always gone light on the makeup. I like a natural look, not a heavy make up look. But as I aged, the products I had always used worked differently. Foundation would settle into creases and show off dry patches. When I was going through the “change”, I perspired so much that make up ran off my face and even the strongest waterproof mascara wouldn’t stay on. Now I don’t bother with makeup. My eyes tend to water at times, which inevitably makes my mascara smudge, and I have yet to find a make up that doesn’t show off my big pores. So I go natural. But I would like to wear makeup sometimes. It’s just that I no longer can. My poor body has been through the mill too. Two babies, some surgeries including a total hysterectomy, which robbed me of hormones. I didn’t do hormone replacement therapy. I have been skinny as a rail and over 250 pounds. I have been a body builder and a fat lazy slob. I have used illegal drugs. I have gone on drinking binges. I have done fad diets, including starving myself. I once had prediabetes, but managed to lose weight so it went away. I have some kidney trouble due to a huge kidney stone that completely blocked my ureter and my left kidney was swollen and damaged and doesn’t function as well as it should. I’ve had heat exhaustion and nearly froze to death. I have been very hard on my body. And my body is complaining to me these days. I have a bad knee, sciatica, and pain in my right hip. I get tendonitis in my achilles tendon which is so painful. I walk for about 40 minutes to an hour every day, but I still have cellulite on my thighs. I’m carrying an extra 20 pounds. I noticed the other day that my stride is not as long as it used to be. Seems like I take more steps now. And I’ve shrunk in height. I’m only about 5′3″, down from 5′ 5 1/2″. I have suffered with bad posture and rolled shoulders since I was a kid, and now I have a small hump high on my back. I could go on. Even as I wrote all those things, I felt my heart sinking because I am describing a worn out old lady who can barely get around. I guess to sum it up, I haven’t accepted aging in any kind of good way. I’ve been fighting against it for over 40 years, and now, I have to admit I’ve lost the battle. I look every one of my almost 64 years. I can’t change that. I’m not up for plastic surgery. I’m starting to convince myself that I deserve every wrinkle and grey hair. Life has not always been kind. And that brings me back to perspective. I know how I look. I see the sags and bags. But I don’t think I am ugly, which I did for a long time when I was young. I think I just look like me, a short little lady with a little slump and a long grey ponytail. That’s it. Just me. I accept it now. I accept that my body droops here and there. I’m not repulsed by it, which I was when I gained an extra pound when I was young. I accept that I’m not as strong as I used to be. After all, I have been driving this body for 63 dang years, and it’s bound to show a little wear and tear. So I don’t pay much attention to my physical appearance. I’m content and feel like I look like an average person. The good part of aging is what I’m paying attention to these days. I’ve been there and done that, pretty much. I have stories to tell and experience under my belt, which gives me the wisdom of my years. I never wanted to live alone for most of my life. I thought I had to have a man in order to be whole. That belief caused me a lot of grief. Now I am living alone for five years and I wouldn’t change it for anything. I am perfectly happy with my own company. I have time on my hands because I don’t have to run to work every day. I can sit at my computer and muse and answer questions at my leisure, with no one to disturb my train of thought. So. I don’t feel unattractive. I feel like myself. I don’t feel like I’m old and of no use. I have a purpose in my life that keeps me on my toes, and I am needed. I am surrounded by people who hope the best for me and who treat me with respect. I have my own home, my own car, my own income, and my little four footed cohort, Ted. I have all I need or want. I wouldn’t go back to my younger years for any amount of moolah. I am happy to be right where I am today, and there’s a smile in my heart. I’ve always thought that people who have a heart that shines through their smile are the most attractive people. That’s all I hope for now. I hope people don’t pay as much attention to my wrinkles and age spots as they do my heart. Because that’s the important part of all of us. That’s what makes us attractive, the glow. Be happy.

column1: Other than shouting back, what's the best thing to do if your boss screams at you about something you did wrong?
column3: I’m a physician. I have been screamed at by patients’ families, more times than I can count. (Trust me. They were all, “my boss”.) It was almost always something over which I had no control. (No, I can’t help it if the ice machine in the ED is loud.) Here’s how I deal with anyone who screams at me I remind myself that it’s not about me. People who are screamers, are screamers to everyone. A stressful situation can bring out the worst in anyone. Fear of losing control, of a situation, can make people do some outlandish things. Does this mean that I condone this behavior? Absolutely not! I think it denotes a lack of sophistication of thought and poor coping skills. Surprisingly, not everyone wants to be me when they grow up, so strangely enough, it happens. Stay calm. Don’t yell back, no matter how unjust the situation. The louder they get, the calmer you get. Adopt an expression of polite interest. (No eye rolling or pursed lips.) Is there any truth in what they are saying? If there is, own up to it. If you can get a word in, ask questions. It will make them slow down and think. It looks like this… I walked into the ICU, one morning. A family was just about to discontinue care on a patient. (Pull the plug) I was the doctor assigned to that patient, that day. I had not previously been involved in his care. I read through the chart. The poor man had horrible chronic lung disease, at baseline. He was quite ill, at the time of admission, with his fourth big bout of pneumonia. He was “found down”, in his room. He had lapsed into a state where his heart was not beating but the electrical activity was registering on telemetry, as though it was. This was a limit in the existing technology, not hospital negligence, that led him not to be discovered for a short while. When found, they called a code blue and resuscitated him. It was too late. He was brain dead. The man’s son was going off the deep end. I introduced myself, calmly. “I’m Dr. Boehm. This is a truly awful day for you. How can I help?” “I WANT ANSWERS, NOW!” Quietly, I replied, ”Sure. Let’s sit down in the conference room and talk.” “This f-cking hospital, killed my father! You aren’t going to get away with this. I’m going to sue your ass.” (I had not been involved in his care.) I listened to him rant and rave, a polite look of interest on my face. When he had yelled himself out, I explained what had happened. “YOU ARE ONLY SAYING THAT BECAUSE YOU WORK FOR THE HOSPITAL!” (I didn’t work for the hospital.) He jumped up and ranted some more. I took out my card. It had my practice name and address on it. I, silently, set it on the table in front of him. “OK, so you don’t work for the hospital. Still, “you people killed a healthy man!” (His dad was anything but healthy.) More ranting and cussing. I sat quietly empathetically listening. This guy didn’t know up from down. All he could think about was the loss of his beloved father. Again, he yelled himself out. “Sir, I can see how very upset you are. I can’t imagine how sad this day is for you. Unfortunately, your poor dad was not a healthy man. He had end-stage lung disease.” “YOU'RE JUST SAYING THAT!” “Sir, did your dad have an oxygen unit that he dragged behind him?”, I asked gently. “Yeah.” “Was he a life-long, heavy smoker?”, I asked quietly. “Yeah.” “Was he hospitalized four times in the last two years for severe pneumonia?”, again, quietly. “Yeah.” “Are these the sign of a healthy man?” “Well, no, I guess not.” “I’m so very very sorry for the unimaginable grief you are experiencing.” “Thanks.” “Would you like to go be with him, now?” “Yeah.” This was a pretty common occurrence, at the hospital. I didn’t take it personally. Now, if I had done something wrong, I would have admitted it. I would have asked how to make it right. On the other hand, if the person, screaming, were a colleague or someone in hospital administration, who was not distraught, I still handled it the same way. Only difference was that I would sit down with that person, perhaps the next day. I would approach them when they were calm. I would very calmly explain that it is not acceptable to treat me that way. I would and I have told people not to ever treat me that way again. No one with whom I had that conversation has ever screamed at me again. (This includes an attending physician, when I was a resident.) Once I calmly called a bully out, I found that they cut it out. Peace.

column1: How does it feel when someone close to you dies?
column3: I know this by experience. In 2000 I lost a 43 year old brother to suicide without warning or prior signs. In 2005 we lost our 20 year old son to a firefighter training accident. We have suffered the more usual losses of aging and ill family members and friends. Here’s what I know: We grieve because we love. No love, no grief. Deep love, deep grief. When we love someone, we understand that one of us will die before the other, but this understanding is rarely spoken. When a loved one dies, they stop living, but the love you shared doesn’t die. Grief is the final responsibility of loving someone. We carry the memories of love, and the lessons from love, for our lifetime. Grief is love now expressed and cared for by the lucky one who has loved and still lives to remember.

column1: Why is public accounting so stressful?
column3: You did it! You followed the education and career path bread trail carefully laid out for you by the Big 4 Public Accounting Firms. Nibble nibble, sign up for accounting by being told how much partners make. Nibble nibble, complete an internship. Nibble nibble, complete a master’s degree in taxation to get to 150 credits.Photo by Marcus Ganahl on Unsplash Finally, the exit! The big prize! A job offer for $65k to work 80 hours a week. Prestige! Gloryyyyyyy! Goodbye sun, hello cubes! While getting a job in public accounting seems like setting course for a successful career- beware. For many, the unspoken realities of working in this environment are unsettling. Once recognition sets in and the euphoria wears off; professionals often experience trauma and inner turmoil once they recognize how public accounting really works. Here’s how understanding the 7 stages of grief can help you with the grieving process. The 7 stages of grief 1. Shock Maybe you figured the first few weeks ran late because you were just settling in and learning the who’s who and what’s what of your new job, but over time, reality sinks in. These people are here until 8 pm each day… no one complains, and no one dares break rank until the big honcho leaves- That is to head home, grab a quick bite, and log back on later. You heard there was a busy season, a seasonal sprint where everyone puts in extra effort, but no one mentioned that the extra sprint comes on top of an extended workweek. Your significant other is threatening to leave, you haven’t seen your friends in weeks, and you are already running on fumes. What the experts say:Feelings of shock are unavoidable in nearly every situation involving grief, even if we feel we have had time to prepare for the loss. We know it’s going to happen, but not right then, not on that day. People in shock often appear to be behaving normally without a lot of emotion, because the news hasn’t fully sunk in yet. “Often there is a sense of numbness and a self-protective detachment from your feelings because they are too intense to deal with,” says Nathan.2. Denial Well, maybe it will get better over time as I adjust…Maybe I’ll get promoted and more money won’t make it seem so bad…Maybe I can hang around a few years and transition into industry at a higher level… No matter how it goes, the denial stage has the same themes where you doubt the realities of your present circumstances. You try and discount the bad and see the subhuman treatment in a brighter tint. But, deep down, you know something isn’t right. You came with high expectations and a willingness to put in the work to get ahead, but what they’re doing here isn’t sustainable. You become more distracted at work and less enthusiastic with each assignment as your intuition tugs at you, trying to self-correct.What the experts say: Many people experience denial after a loss: they know something has happened but it doesn’t feel real. “For me, the denial was not that I didn’t believe it — it was more a sense of, ‘But how can they not be here? How can they have been here, and now they aren’t?’” says Sherene. In addition to experiences of shock and denial, people often describe having a ‘mental fog’, says Nathan. “This can include forgetfulness, lack of concentration, sleeplessness, lack of motivation, repetitive thoughts and inability to make a decision.”3. Anger You scream to yourself, “I’m not staying to *#^#^$# 9 pm again!!” This is outrageous- Your work is done, but you know you’ll be an outcast if you try and leave before the rest of the team. Each day driving in and driving home, both likely in darkness, you rage internally. You are angry at your boss, coworkers, professors, and yourself for where you’ve landed. You’ve tried working more efficiently, but that only earned you more work. You tried working harder, but that, too, only earned you more responsibilities. No matter what you do, the flood of work never ceases. You are never done. Even more, the work sucks more than the day before. You bounce between clients, gaining a superficial understanding of what each does, and you try your best not to mess up. Your manager seems partially checked out, and they aren’t much help, either. You’re angry because you know it’s too early to leave the job without adding an asterisk to your resume, and you’re angry that you have to stay so the work looks good when interviewing for another role.What the experts say: It’s perfectly normal to feel anger in times of loss, but often people try to keep this stage of grief hidden. “Anger is a difficult emotion to deal with and can be minimised by others,” says Nathan. “But it’s important to find someone with whom we can connect in an honest way.” “I felt frustrated that my experience of grief was different to that of those I was close to,” says Sherene. “I was angry with myself — that I was taking too long, and wanting to talk about Mum and Dad to people who felt I should’ve moved on.”4. Bargaining At this point, you’re looking to make deals that likely won’t materialize. “Please, God,” you pray, “send me a recruiter to make me a bird and take me far, far away from here.” “Where are you freshy?” you can hear your manager howl in the distance, stomping around the office, looking to assign more work to you at 10 pm. You remain behind the door in the stairwell, staying hidden. You begin to admit you are desperate for a change. Things are falling apart and falling through the cracks in your life. “I swear that if you make him go away, I’ll never touch accounting again. I’ll join a convent and go to church every day.” You feel there is no escape. Trapped, exhausted, and realizing your only path now is to continue grinding away, getting one day closer away from Hell with each minute.What the experts say: The bargaining stage is about making promises to yourself or a higher being, asking the universe for a chance to put things right. A bereaved person may seek reason where there is none, and may feel guilty about how they behaved, or feel in some way to blame. “There’s a sense that, ‘Maybe I could have done things differently’,” says Nathan. “If only I’d stopped them leaving the house or I knew more about their medical condition, I could’ve intervened. We may feel helpless and hopeless, and consumed by thoughts of, ‘What if?’”5. Depression Now, when your manager comes around, you have the 1,000-yard stare of an inmate receiving a 50-year sentence. You can’t hear the words as your manager tells you something or another- You’re checked out. Each day you feel the air leave your lungs as you step into your car and even more once you step into the office. You’re going through the motions and feel as if all is lost. You’re so tired that you’ve forgotten what a full night’s sleep used to feel like. You haven’t had a free weekend in months, on your computer every day, losing track of where one-week ends and another begins. You go home, alone, or to find your spouse or family sleeping, you sleep-barely- and then you’re up again for the grind. I deserve this, you think.What the experts say: The jumble of emotions that usually accompanies the grieving process can typically lead to feelings of depression, isolation, anxiety and a feeling of dread. Sometimes the suffering seems too much to bear. “Someone may question the meaning of life, or feel they want to be reunited with the person that’s died,” says Nathan. In cases like this, it’s so important to ask for help. “People are often unsure of how to help us in our grief, so if you can accept an offer of help or ask for help, it will have the effect of strengthening those friendships,” he adds.6. Acceptance and Hope “You know what, I don’t deserve this. No one deserves to work and live like this.” Today, you feel fresh and re-energized. “Damnit, I’m a human being, and I’ve studied too long and worked too hard to be treated like an animal.” “Yes,” you think, “this DOES suck. But, it doesn’t have to suck forever.” You’re back and feel like yourself again. You begin to make a plan to escape. You’re stilled pissed, but now you’re ready to do something about it. You call in sick; you sleep, really sleep, and then think ahead. “I’m going to work where I’m appreciated and valued.”What the experts say: Humans, by nature, crave contact, connection and support, and at some stage in the grieving process will want to engage with friends and family again. Acceptance is about realising you can’t change the circumstances, but that you can gain some control over how you respond. “At times, we may need to distract ourselves from the grief, or place it to one side, so we can get on with work or social situations,” says Nathan. But this is also a stage where you might slip backwards and find yourself feeling overwhelmed from all the emotions again. It’s normal to move between any of the stages of grief from hour to hour, or even minute to minute. Says Sherene: “I gave myself permission to grieve. I felt that patience was a gift to myself.”7. Processing grief After resting and stepping back for a few days, you see the world in a new light again. Things look good, and you feel good. You reach out to your friends and family, and it’s nice to hear their voices and reconnect. Your computer stays shut, and you go for a walk in the park and treat yourself to Starbucks and a nice lunch at the cafe you love. When you return home, you update your LinkedIn, you make a few calls to people in your network, and you start to put out feelers for new opportunities. Yes, public accounting has sucked the life from you, but you’re determined to live again. You’ll stick through the short transition period until you find freedom, but until then, you’re going to do things on your terms.What the experts say: There is no right or wrong way to grieve — the process is highly individual. In addition, there’s no quick fix; the healing process takes time and varies from person to person. Importantly, there is no “normal” timeframe, so be patient with yourself. Wendy also suggests the following coping strategies that you may find helpful. Express your grief in words or another creative outlet, such as painting or drawing. Connect with others — this can be loved ones or community support groups. Ask for help, in whatever form. Practise deep breathing regularly. Set small, realistic goals. Ensure you’re getting enough sleep and aim for some form of movement each day. Eat a healthy, balanced diet and keep hydrated. Rehearse how you respond to questions and new situations.The Bottom Line Public accounting is a highly-profitable machine designed to make the partners rich and to suck your soul dry until you can’t take it anymore and leave. Once you’re gone, no one breaks a sweat because there is a long line of other victims eagerly waiting behind you. Or that is how things have worked in the past. Today, accountants are waking up to the realities of public accounting and choosing to study a different college major or work elsewhere. At the same time, Public Accounting Firm Partners are grinding their teeth and admonishing the laziness of millennials and GenZ, tone-deaf and colorblind to the shifting winds, while shopping for million-dollar beach houses. The times; they are a-changing. *My name is Ben Wann, and I’m on a mission to knock sense into the public accounting industry. Get this, if you want to hire and keep talent, pay partners less and workers more. Hire more help, reduce workloads, and your problems will disappear. You probably won’t listen, so in the meantime, I will make as many young professionals aware of your working conditions as possible.* Source:https://benjamin-wann1.medium.com/the-7-stages-of-grief-after-joining-public-accounting-e6b1b6042f7

column1: How did Hitler die?
column3: April 20th: Hitler’s BirthdayIt’s Hitler’s birthday, and it’s not a good one. Berlin is under Soviet attack, and all hope seems lost. Most top Nazi officials have fled the city, but Hitler has chosen to stay and make his stand. Desperate, sick, and sociopathic, he believes he can find a way to turn the tide of the war yet despite the facts. Hitler lived in the Führerbunker in Berlin, a central underground bunker in the city center. On his Birthday, he emerged for perhaps the last time to award children for acts of bravery. The German military was now relying on Hitler's youth to fill the ranks. He would never leave the bunker again, largely because the city was under constant aerial and artillery attack going forward. Hitler's reaction to defeat was very human. That is what disturbs many about Hitler most; that he was indeed human. Rather than accept failure and submit he continued to order children to their deaths in some vain effort to have the US switch sides and save the day. Instead of admitting defeat, he would combine the remnants of tattered divisions with Hitler Youth, cops, mechanics, and pilots and declare these mobs of ragged men “Army Groups.” In the past, a German Army Group was something to fear- it could topple a country. These new German Army groups could not move, let alone fight. April 21st: Hitler’s attempt to save Berlin Hitler ordered Army Group Steiner, one of these new Army Groups I mentioned, to attack the Soviets and save Berlin. He thought that Army Group Steiner could advance South and break the Soviet lines. If Berlin were saved, it would prove to the Americans that the Germans could stop the communists, and the Americans would switch sides. Hitler maintained that with FDR dead, the new US President, Harry Truman, would decide to switch sides and declare communism as the true enemy.The idea of the US switching sides was ludicrous. Hitler might as well have hoped for angels or aliens to intervene on his behalf. Regardless, here we are. April 22nd: No attack comes Hitler meets with the top brass, hoping to hear that Army Group Steiner is nearing Berlin with a sea of fleeing Reds before them. Instead, Hitler is told the truth. Army Group Steiner did not attack and indeed cannot attack. There are no trucks, no tanks, no air cover, not enough guns, too many injured, and no fuel to run anything anyway. The unit was under attack as is and cannot hope to hold out long, let alone perform an offensive operation against overwhelming odds. Hitler receives this poorly. He flies into a tearful rage and declares that his Generals and, indeed, the German people have defied and failed him. He finally declares that all is lost, resolves that he will die in Berlin, and retires for the day. This is finally the point at which Hitler accepts defeat. Berlin is days away from falling, Germany is out of men and weapons, and what remains of the military is in tatters. Hitler begins spending a lot of time discussing suicide and different poisons at dinner, and the bunkers chemist gets to work making some lethal concoctions. April 23rd to April 29th: Hitlers last week During this final week, Hitler oversaw the defense of Berlin to some degree but left it more or less to the city's commanders. Generals would inform him that the men were out of supplies and could not fight, and Hitler would just tell them never to surrender. Toward the end of the week, Hitler is informed that Berlin will fall in a matter of days. The Soviets vastly outnumber the Germans, and the Germans are bone dry out of supplies. Hitler orders everyone to keep fighting to the last and begins in earnest to prepare for his own death. Outside Berlin, Himmler, Goering, and other top Nazis either made moves to secure control of the German government or conduct peace talks with the Allies. Hitler viewed this as a betrayal and ordered that Himmler and Goering be executed. More than that, Hitler viewed this as a sign of the times. These had been die-hard loyalists, and they were now conducting peace talks behind his back. A stark reminder that the end, indeed, was very near. April 30th: Hitler ends his life By April 30th, Berlin's defense had nearly collapsed entirely. Hitler had resolved to kill himself for various reasons.Surrender was unthinkable: A core pillar of Hitler’s belief system was that surrender was an impossibility. He believed the Aryan people were the “master race” and thus were undefeatable. The only way the “master race” could lose to an inferior race was a lack of willpower or, in the case of WW1, a conspiracy committed by Jews. This, of course, is not true, but regardless, it was a central factor in Hitler’s thinking.Mussolini’s fate: Benito Mussolini, the first fascist, had been caught in Italy. The people of Italy had brutally executed him, and his final moments were that of humiliation. Hitler believed a worse fate awaited him. Unlike Mussolini, Hitler had started WW2 and the Holocaust and would certainly be held accountable.Defeatism: The war was lost. In the end, Hitler blamed his Generals and even the German people. Everyone had lied to him, and the German people had abandoned him. Even as children fought and died in the street for a lost cause, Hitler still believed the German people deserved death because by losing the war, they had proven to be inferior.Darwinism: This ties into the idea of surrender being unthinkable. Hitler had this warped concept of Darwinism guiding many of his decisions and beliefs. He believed that if a person, leader, or nation surrendered, they deserved death because this surrender was proof of their inferiority. You can imagine how this worldview may impact a desire to surrender.By now, the Bunker’s chemist had whipped up some poisons Hitler could use to kill himself. With his chosen poison in hand, he tested it on his dog, Blondi. Maybe this seems like the callous actions of a cold sociopath, but I disagree. Blondi had been Hitler’s dog for years and loved that dog as profoundly as any person can. Indeed, he thought Blondi was more intelligent than most people, and generally, Hitler loved animals and nature. This act of killing his dog- his companion- was a sure sign of what he intended for himself. These are desperate actions taken by a sick and desperate man. Hilter went to his personal guard, Otto Günsche, and issued him his final order. He was to find some gas and ensure that Hitler and Eva’s bodies were cremated so they could not be mutilated. Hitler ordered a few more officials to kill themselves and then retired to his room with his new wife, Eva Braun. Moments later, a gunshot rang out. Hitler’s room is investigated, and his corpse is found there. The corpse is seen by everyone in the bunker, from his personal secretary to his guard, Otto. Hitler and Eva’s bodies are brought to the surface, covered in gasoline, and burned.There have been documentaries and books written about Hitler’s supposed survival. The thinking is that he fled Berlin like so many other top Nazi officials. In reality, Hitler killed himself, and that is simply that.There are lots of witnesses to this, including Hitler's guard, secretary, and everyone else in the bunker. They not only saw Hitler’s corpse but then attended the makeshift funeral. These people survived the war and would recount what they witnessed for historians.Hitler was not the only suicide. Understand that Goebells was grief-stricken because he believed a world without Hitler to lead him wasn’t a world worth seeing. Goebells had been ordered to leave Berlin but stayed out of loyalty- he was Hitler’s most loyal friend. Would Goebells kill his 6 children, his wife, and then himself if Hitler had scampered off to Brazil? Moreover, other major Nazis in the bunker, including SS officers and Generals like Hans Krebs, also killed themselves.Hitler was not some little-known camp doctor or Einsatzgruppen officer. Everyone on earth to this day knows what Hitler looks like by heart. Many lower-ranked officers and officials who escaped were eventually caught, so how would Hitler maintain his hiding? None of the high-ranking Nazis escaped. Every General, politician, and leader was caught or took their own life.Joseph Goebbels had been in the bunker with Hitler. He had been ordered to leave and refused, remaining loyal. Goebells even brought his wife Magda and his 6 children into the bunker. Magda herself was perhaps more die-hard than her husband. She begged Hitler to flee and continue his work but was rebuffed. After Hitler killed himself, Magda was beyond grief. She decided a world without Hitler is not a world worth seeing. She would kill all 6 of her children, and then both she and her husband would take their own lives. Would this make sense if Hitler was alive? Even if Hitler’s escape was secret, it would have been known by Goebbels. Hitler did what anyone would expect. He took the easy way out and that is one of the greatest crimes ever.
column9: It should also be noted, that the people who were with Hitler in the Bunker and witnessed his and Eva’s death, were not all ‘made of the same cloth’, that is, they are different people, with different thoughts, who after the war matured in very different ways considering their political opinions, you have die hard Hitler apologetics like Guensche and die hard opponents of Nationalsocialism like Junge and somewhat mushy on the subject describing Hitler as nice and kind human with an evil ideology like Misch. The point is, even if these people were to make some secret pact of pretending to everyone that Hitler killed himself, while he magically teleported himself to Brazil, as the opinions on the subject Hitler would grow apart with these people, they would not all keep up the sharade, either Guensche goes one day ‘nananananana my idol just died 1999 (or whatever) you fools’ or Junge goes one day ‘that evil murder is still around’ or Misch goes, ‘now I’m the last one left, I can tell you he didn’t die’ . But that never happened. Even if they all had complotted to lie about his death, it’s unthinkable that they would keep up the lie considering their different stance on the subject. All their accounts match up, even the slight differences (Junge said she heard a shot, Misch said you couldn’t hear a shot cause the generator was so loud), that just confirms that they didn’t make up a story. There is absolutely no doubt whatsoever, that he killed himself.

column1: What type of personality disorder or mental disorder does Gollum from Lord of the Rings have? I’m afraid I might have that same disorder he has since I have Autism and possibly BPD given how needy I’ve become for someone to love me in recent years.
column3: While it’s true that Gollum had his fair share of issues, and not all of them stem from The One Ring, being love-starved was largely a cage of his own making.During his time in The Two Towers and The Return of the King, it’s easy to see that Gollum is starved for affection and approval, as just the slightest bit of tolerance and mercy from Frodo coddles him to the point where it almost completely suppresses his Gollum alter-ego, though not completely. Tolkien once wrote that though doomed, Gollum would have met a much more heroic end had Faramir also treated him with more kindness, but that’s not to say that Faramir was wrong to distrust the creature. Smeagol started out as a local troublemaker who was largely disliked in his community, with his fellow troublemaker Deagol being his only friend, aside from his grandmother. Upon viewing The One Ring, he jumped to murder rather fast, and used it for evil afterwards. Though one might blame Sauron for this more than Gollum, my point is that he wasn’t a very nice person to begin with, perhaps a malignant narcissist. After losing The One Ring, Gollum didn’t get better and shed his evil ways, he crept into the huts of the Mirkwood woodsmen and stole babies from the crib to devour to regain his strength. Though we see a pitiable abuse victim in the later portions of the story (Sauron had tortured him horribly) Gollum was firstly too enthralled with his precious to ever be trustworthy around Frodo, and his base personality was foul. I’m no psychiatrist, but I will say that Gollum shows signs of Dissociative Identity Disorder, partitioning his persona to cope with the grief and loss of losing The One Ring, though I’d say he had it earlier, to try and justify Deagol’s murder and his own actions, deluding himself into believing The One Ring was his “birthday present”. Gollum is a mess, and a horrible wretch, but to the questioner - you are at least self aware enough to be aware of your own issues, and it should be said there’s nothing inherently wrong with having ASD, it’s just you’re wired differently. If you’re worried you might also have BPD, my best advice is to seek a diagnosis and see about treatment, since these are things that can be managed with proper therapy and medication.

column1: "She became a broken girl after her mother's death." Is this correct English and does this mean a girl who is suffering from emotional pain after her mother's death?
column3: The meaning is recognizable, but it seems clearly written by someone who is not a native speaker. Closer is “Her mother’s death broke her.” You can also say “She broke after her mother’s death,” but the meaning can easily be taken to mean something more specific than generalized emotional pain, such as the girl relenting to a specific pressure to do something. edit: You can also say “She became heartbroken after her mother’s death,” but that is just bad writing, because in a serious circumstance like this, you should avoid extra words, and should avoid passive words like “became.”

column1: How painful is death?
column3: I died recently, I did not experience any pain. Let me explain. I had meningococcal septicaemia, a fever and knee pains. My wife took me to hospital because the St. Jonh’s Ambulance Service “was busy.” Upon reaching the emergency Department I was taken to Resuscitation Bay. I became unconscious soon after that and I was placed on life support. I do not remember feeling any pain. I could have been dead. I was on life support for about 20 days and I do not recall any pain. I do not recall being intubated or extubated. As a matter of fact I was unconscious for about a month. During this period I did not feel any pain or discomfort. My view is that a person becomes unconscious before death. Therefore, there is no pain when the brain and heart die.

column1: Why is breaking up so painful?
column3: Let me teach you some binary first. I hope many of you know the “AND” operation in binary. In simple terms, it is like this:0∗0=00∗0=01∗0=01∗0=00∗1=00∗1=01∗1=11∗1=1What do you observe here? And if still you couldn’t figured it out yet, then let me tell you. Not all breakups are painful. It is only painful when you are in love and your partner has moved on.I understand, your life is not binary. It doesn’t revolve around 0 and 1, there are some grey areas which you have to deal with it. Here, I am giving only simple explanation about painful breakup. But, why is it painful? You two have created a world of illusion, where in your fairy tale you are the king or queen. You see magic in your life because of their presence. Future is endorsed with your happiness index. But this is not the problem actually. Problem is “Idea of Love” which you have created from your surroundings. Where you get an idea from movies, TV serials, books etc. Your situation is more or less similar to Abhimanyu’s half knowledge of the “Chakravyuh”. You get an idea of falling in love, but you are clueless about getting out of it when everything goes wrong. And you meet similar fate, which is more brutal than death. So, one day you wake up from your dreamland, where your partner decided to leave you/already left. It’s a wake up call, but it is already late. You are left with wonderland, where you have no idea what to do with it without your partner. Suffering starts. Because “1” is there, but your partner’s love has become “0”. You are holding one end which is giving you tremendous pain but you are holding it tight. Because, you have hope. “What if” he/she will come back to your wonderland. Your suffering turns into frustration, then frustration turns into anger. It is unending loop of pain. The day you decideTo let it go,You have enough bullshit in your life,They have moved on and you are on your own.That day will be the end of your suffering.Sometimes, you just have to accept the fact That some people only enter your life as a temporary happiness.

column1: After losing a parent, why can’t I feel anything at all, when I know I should be in pain? My dad died almost two years ago from cancer. Whenever I remember him/his death, I draw a blank emotionally. I know I’m devastated, but I don’t “feel” anything.
column3: I was 18 when I lost my mother. Even though she had been struggling with a plethora of diseases from as long as I can remember, I always envisioned her as an invincible superhuman. She died of renal failure. I woke up with my grandmother screaming hysterically that something has happened to my mother. I was numb when I saw my father driving her to the hospital. I was numb when my brother came to my room and told me she is gone. I was numb when I held on to her cold hand, as I stared at her dead body. I was numb when my extended family started pouring in- screaming, crying, lamenting her loss. I was just numb, and for the life of me- I could not muster a single memory of her, despite her body being right in front of me. After a day or two, people kept on looking strangely at me; wondering why I seem unaffected. That’s when a cousin of mine took me to the side and asked me to not feel pressurized into ‘feeling’ a certain way. She asked me to cry when I wanted to, and laugh if I felt like- without getting consumed in guilt. An year passed by, and I had spent the last year focusing on my weight loss. I lost 100+ lbs in that span; by dedicating each day to frantic calorie- counting, working out, reading on health and fitness. I was 19 when I stepped onto the scale, and I realized I had hit my goal weight. And suddenly, all the distractions I had so diligently aligned in my life just vanished, and my house of cards came crumbling down. There was no particular day when it happened, but my heart was suddenly filled with a grief I never knew existed. Every once in a while, I would hear a friend talking to their mother on the phone, or smell the fragrance of e certain perfume wafting in the air, or step into the room where I had last seen her- and my heart would get shattered into pieces. It’s been 8 years since then, and it still hurts as much. Losing a parent is not something you get over, but you would eventually get used to the pain. It would be like a pulsating grief that would haunt you, comfort you and would eventually remind you of the relationship that you once had with your parent. I’ll just repeat what my cousin had told me all those years back- Don’t feel pressurized into feeling anything. Let it be. Breathe in. And breathe out. You would feel what you would feel, when you are ready to embrace it.
column9: This was so helpful because this is exactly how I am feeling. I can’t feel anything. But I can still laugh and I still carry on about my day… sort of… I feel drained and kind of depressed. I feel a sadness but I can’t cry. If I do it’s only for a second. I can’t remember any memories at all and it makes me feel so terrible. Everyone kept saying that we must not have been that close but she was my world. so I don’t know if numb is the right word because I’m still able to eat and laugh. But I can’t feel anything. I look at pictures and I love her but I seriously feel nothing and it’s so uncomfortable.

column1: Can a person fall in love again after breaking up with someone they loved deeply?
column3: This is a personal experience and it may vary subjectively. I have heard about a lot of people getting devastated after a break up. I completely understand the wreckage that you go through after you have to part ways with someone you were very close to. The intensity of havoc will vary depending on the reason behind the break up, irrespective of that, it is but a painful phase to go through. A break up is very similar to a death. It is in fact the death of a bond, and to come to terms with the trauma does need insurmountable strength. Nonetheless, I will admit it is not impossible to come out of the inflicted pain. Associate optimism with everything. Take your break up as something you were direly in need of to rediscover your lost self. Try to channelise that negatively strong energy in a more productive way. Keep yourself engaged. Think again about the purpose of your life and the great heights you always wanted to accomplish. Never try to find refuge in anything. Face it boldly and accept that something unexpected happened. Analyse the positive aspects of it. Your break up made you a stronger and a less vulnerable person, gave you an experience, helped you focus more on your dreams, you got rid of a person who was not right for you and gave you your personal space. Don't give up as the flow of emotions is terribly mighty to shatter you. Repair your heart. Don't blame or curse anyone for anything. Just accept that you've lost someone and you've to live without them for the rest of your life. As for myself, I can say, yes, I did fall in love again after my break up. I fell in love with myself. It was difficult going through those days but once I chose not to cry over something that only stole my peace and happiness, I haven't looked back since then. I am happily working for my goals. I enjoy my solitude more. Introspection helps me grow as a better individual. I have come to the realisation that some things are essentially needed. A break up is one of them. I wanted to make it one of the best things that ever happened to me. It can motivate you or vandalise you. But, the choice is yours. Choose wisely. Life is much more than tying yourself to a single person. Pragya Choudhary.

column1: What did you assume was exaggerated until you experienced it?
column3: The addictive abilities of prescription painkillers.My sister was addicted to prescription painkillers. (And meth and probably other things as well.) She was so addicted that she was arrested for writing fake prescriptions and couldn’t attend my wedding because it was out of state and she was under house arrest. I figured that she and people like her were just weak-willed or depressed and looking for an escape. I had little sympathy for people who were addicted to things that were legal. If it was really that addictive, it wouldn’t be legal, right? It’s not like it’s cocaine. They’re just painkillers. I was wrong. When I was 27, I pulled a muscle in my back. It was so painful that I couldn’t walk straight. I’m not entirely sure how I even made it to the doctor’s office, but as soon as I hobbled in, they said: “Pulled muscle, huh?” I suppose I had the tell-tale walk of a man who tried to lift too much without bending his knees. Anyway, the doctor prescribed me two prescription drugs. I believe one was a muscle relaxer, and one was a painkiller. I recognized the names as soon as he said them. I knew these were some of the things my sister was addicted to. And within 30 minutes of getting home and taking the first pills, I could see why she was addicted to them. I didn’t judge her and anyone else who was addicted to them as “weak-willed” anymore. I remember lying on my bed, after being in intense pain for a day, suddenly feeling great! Not just the muscle pain, but every physical and emotional pain I had seemed to disappear. The stress of work and bills and being a husband and father just went away. The bed felt like a cloud, and I felt like I was floating. I was so happy. When the first round of pills started to wear off after a few hours, I started to get depressed. Not just because the physical pain was coming back, but because some of my emotional worries and stress started to creep back in to my mind. I started to think about how much income I would lose from taking a few days off for my back pain. I started to think about the cost of the pills. I started to think about the domestic chores I’d been neglecting during my prescription painkiller trip. But mostly I was thinking about if it was safe to take the next round of pills yet. The doctor said every six hours, and it had only been four hours. Could my liver handle it? Did I care if it could or not? Then it hit me: I need to stop this before it gets worse. I didn’t want to end up like my sister. I liked my stressful life just fine. I didn’t need to escape from it. So I quit taking the prescription pills, and decided to go with over-the-counter painkillers, stretching, and patience instead. When I got back to work after a few days, a coworker offered to buy the leftover pills from me. But I didn’t want to be “that guy.” I didn’t want ANYTHING to do with those things anymore. So I flushed them down the toilet. But I had newfound sympathy for people who can’t quit them. I understand the attraction they have. My sister ended up overdosing on morphine a few years later. When we cleaned out her house after her death, she had over 300 empty prescription pill bottles in her room. The worst part was that those were just the empty ones. Some of her addicted “friends” had already come into her room and got the full bottles before we got there.

column1: Will dying always be painful? As in, even when you die of old age, it will be painful or at least feel weird, right? Are most natural deaths painful?
column3: I was the Catholic priest chaplain at a big city hospital for 11 years, mostly in the 1970’s — starting around age 27. I lived on campus, and got called for most deaths — maybe 3–4 per week — and spent a lot of time with dying people and their families. It increased when we opened an inpatient hospice program. I lost my fear of death after just a few months of that, and it hasn’t come back. I fear being helpless and a burden if I die from a long illness, but not due to physical pain or the dying itself. In that hospital setting, and especially hospice, pain was medicated and skillfully managed, and I rarely saw a person in great pain, certainly not for long, except sometimes people coming into the ER due to trauma. For a lot of folks, not actually dying, but with a terminal illness, there was emotional pain in getting used to the idea, but as often as not it came from love and concern for the people would would be left behind. We were training chaplains in those days too, in a kind of residency program called Clinical Pastoral Education. The student chaplains interacted with real patients almost from the beginning, and discussed their experiences in daily group sessions and classes. Many were surprised and some were comforted by their first experiences of being with dying people, and how their ministry was often directed to the family, as much as the dying patient. So my answer: No, dying is not necessarily painful, especially when you are in a health care setting. If physical pain is an issue, it can normally be handled quickly and comfortably. Grieving family members certainly experience the pain of loss, and even patients who are on good terms with their own deaths, may grieve for their loved ones’ pain.
column9: There is a secret about this, implied in your answer, that older folks know. My wife has asked me to outlive her, and I take good care of my health, including lengthy walks each night as well as a fistful of medications for that purpose. If I succeed, it will be my last and greatest gift to her—that she not be left to grieve.

column1: Do we still feel pain after death?
column3: Yes, we do feel pain after death, but not physical pain. It is emotional pain or turmoil, and that is far more “painful” than physical pain. Pain is associated with a body. Its and external disturbance of some kind, that impinges on the body. Why we “wear” a physical body (when we are living), the external disturbance or intrusion is transmitted to the brain which then translates it as “physical pain” which we then experience. When we die, we lose our physical body, together with the brain. But we continue to wear a body that is subtler in comparison to the physical body. It is our astral body, the Fourth Principle of Man, according to theosophical terminology. This is our emotion body. Our emotion body is the seat for all emotions, and it experiences irritation of some kind too. Gross vibrations (like anger, hatred, fear, jealousy etc.) are irritants than “disturb” the astral body in almost exactly the way, when a needle pricks our physical body or when a burning object is thrust on our physical body. So the astral “irritation” is a kind of pain too, though emotional in nature. Emotional pain being subtler, is actually far more painful and hard to tolerate as compared to physical pain. Let me give you an example, which readily comes to my mind. Imagine a fight or an accident in which you get severely injured. You experience pain, and even great pain. But when you know that your loved one is tortured and killed in the fight or accident, the pain about the loved one far exceeds your own physical pain. That's because emotional pain is far worse than physical pain, though physical pain being gross in nature is bad too. That's the kind of pain one experiences after death. It is not physical pain, but emotional pain. That is why, the immediate after-life realm is often referred to as “hell”.

column1: What is the worst kind of pain anyone can go through? Be it psychological or physical or any other form that it may manifest.
column3: From an Emergency Department perspective, the most severe 'physical' pain that I have witnessed patients experience tends to be related to burns. Although 'full-thickness' burns are, relatively, painless because the nerve endings have been destroyed, most patients with severe burns will also have 'partial thickness' burns which are excruciatingly painful. This is incredibly distressing for the patient, it is also distressing for witnesses (relatives and staff) as the patient often cries out in pain. The most severe emotional pain that I have witnessed is experienced by parents after the loss of a child. In an Emergency Department, the death may be the result of an illness, a sudden infant death or trauma. There seems to be little differentiation between the response. Parents are devastated and inconsolable and the staff members involved find these the most difficult cases to deal with.

column1: How did you find your cat?
column3: In the course of his work in property management, a man named Joe found a gray kitten in a closet, near death. I begged him to bring the cat home to me. The kitten had been abandoned by previously evicted tenants. He had been there alone in the apartment, surviving on dried beans and toilet bowl water for 3 weeks. Once in my care, I cuddled him in the bathroom for days. I believed since the water from the toilet kept him alive, he would have a strong emotional bond with the bathroom. He did. After 3 weeks of feeding him oil laden canned seafood and cuddling with him every moment I could, the kitty was able to fully expel the dried beans clogging his bowels and release the emotional pain of his experience. Brian (named after Monty Python “Life of Brian”) is now a mighty man cat. I estimated that he was four months old when found. But after he gained much needed weight during the 3 week rehabilitation period, I saw how developed he was and changed my estimation to 6 months old. Here is a picture of Brian then and now.

column1: Why do heavy drinkers continue to drink, despite the obvious damage they are causing themselves and to others? Is it really that hard to stop even when the addict is at the point where choosing to drink or quit/get help means life or death?
column3: Both my father and stepfather were alcoholics. My stepfather eventually went to sobering clinic, my father got cirrhosis of the liver and died. I had beat my head for 30 years, trying to figure out why my father didn't stop. Especially after I found myself in bed with him. He promised many times to stop, but it didn't last. I think it isn't the alcohol itself, but the impossibility to deal with emotional pain when sober. He had lots of unresolved trauma. People drink as a strategy to get some functionality. I had a fling with alcohol in my 20s, but stopped, only to switch to self-harm. Then stopped that, only to switch to shopping. Now I am wondering which is worse. It is the unresolved need, the pain that drives addiction. Humans will do anything to stop the pain, death included.
column9: I’m so sorry for your traumatic experience. I am an alcoholic in recovery. People debate whether or not alcoholism is an illness. For me, I believe strongly that my compulsion to drink was a physiological mental illness. Quite apart from the horror of physical withdrawal (which I went through countless times) there is an insane belief that you cannot function on any level without alcohol. The dopamine messaging system in the brain creates extremely strong connections to the chemical ethanol. This results in the compulsion to drink which overrides all other frontal cortex reasoning. Part of me knew that if I had just one drink it would always result in a binge, bringing pain and damage. Despite that, I HAD to have that drink and totally convinced myself that this time I could manage it. My obsession and need eventually progressed to 24 hour drinking. Everyone in life has difficulties - my childhood wasn't perfect but it was okay. Some alcoholics I know experienced trauma, some didn't. I was, however an introvert, hugely lacking in self-esteem. Alcoholics may be avoidant of emotional and mental pain and so self medicate with drink at the beginning. They have no idea it is their personal road to hell. Once established, alcoholism is a progressive, terminal physiological condition. A few of us, reaching the losses and horrors of rock bottom, may in a lucid moment seek help. Recovery at this stage,, as with other mental disorders, is not possible on one’s own. Only then, and with time sober, can we truly appreciate the extent of the damage we have caused to ourselves and loved ones. With help we can learn how to maintain sobriety on a daily basis - always in remission, IF we don’t take that first drink which will reignite the flame of our condition immediately. For those of us fortunate enough to receive help and escape the prison, life is precious, beautiful and we learn how to be comfortable in our own skin at last. We remember with sadness those who didn't make it and eagerly help those in desperation who want what we have.

column1: How do I overcome or move on after a breakup?
column3: DISCLAIMER: This is from personal experience and not everyone will agree with these methods, but I did find them to be useful. Everyone is different in how they handle certain situations. AND - I am not a professional :) From personal experience, the only way I found to move on from a broken heart is time. Yes, it seems like it’s not a short-term solution but as the days move on and time passes, you will eventually wake up one morning and realise that you have so much more to live for and he/she actually wasn’t that special. As Bess Myerson once wrote: “To fall in love is awfully simple, but to fall out of love is simply awful.” You have to go through the pain instead of trying to go around it. There is no shortcut without the share of obstructions in your way. You have to grieve in order to move on. By going through the pain you will become a stronger person. Detaching yourself and revealing your independence is key. You don’t need anyone or anything to make you happy, because at the end of the day the only person who is going to be there for you is yourself. Surrounding yourself by the people that you love enables you to see the people that are there to support you. The distraction of being with your friends and keeping busy allows you to realise that you don’t need any man or woman in a relationship to fulfil that emptiness, because you and your love ones can fill it. Remember to laugh and cry. Laughter heals on many levels, yet so does crying. Do you think it’s a coincidence that you always feel better after a good cry? No. ‘There are many physiological reasons that contribute to the healing power of tears.’ - Tears contain toxic biochemical byproducts, so that weeping removes these toxic substances and relieves emotional stress. So grab that box of tissues and cry the days away. Most of all, remember to love again. Once our hearts are bruised and burned from a relationship, we have two options:We can close off pieces of our heart so that one day no one will be able to get insideWe can love againHenri Nouwen once wrote: “The more you have loved and allowed yourself to suffer because of your love, the more you will be able to let your heart grow wider and deeper. When your love is truly giving and receiving, those whom you love will not leave your heart even when they depart from you. The pain of rejection, absence, and death can become fruitful. Yes, as you love deeply the ground of your heart will be broken more and more, but you will rejoice in the abundance of the fruit it will bear.” Hope this was helpful. :)

column1: How does a person with borderline personality disorder (BPD) feel after a relationship break up by the other partner?
column3: I felt an overwhelming sense of pain and grief, like a death had happened. I felt like I was so fragile that someone could poke me gently with their pinky finger and I’d shatter into a million tiny pieces. I felt so angry that I couldn’t handle it. I loved him so much and hated him so much at the same time. I felt so much emotional pain, and I felt desperate to be loved, and by him. I felt like part of my identity was gone. I felt like I wasn’t good enough. I felt like their was an empty and aching hole in my chest where something was now missing, and I was desperate to fill it. I also felt crazy and out of control. Lastly, I watched my friend go through a divorce at the same time, and I couldn’t hold it together like she could. I didn’t understand. In theory, her situation was worse. So I couldn’t even explain to anyone how much pain I was in, because it would sound crazy for me to say that. But I knew the pain was almost more than I could ever bare. It’s been 10 years and I haven’t told any other guy I loved him since. Now I’m 35 and I’m just tired.

column1: How did parents in the past deal with the death of their children, given the high childhood mortality rate before the age of modern medicine? Did they have particular ways of handling the emotional pain?
column3: I've been to a lot of wakes and funerals for older aunts and uncles and I'm always surprised when the names of predeceased children are read out loud during the religious service. For the most part, these aunts and uncles never discussed their predeceased children and their existence was a surprise to me. After one such occasion, I went home and asked my mom (who was too sick to go to the service) about "Cathy". Without missing a beat, she stated Cathy's full name, date of birth, and date of death. That world war 2 generation who survived the Great Depression was just stoic. They mourned quietly, but mourned for a lifetime
column9: What you just said - "mourned quietly, but for a lifetime", is the most succinct and insightful answer I've seen. My grandmother had four children that are still living today,with their own grandchildren now.. But my grandmother also had a little girl, her third pregnancy, named Suzanna. She was a stillbirth at just under six months. My grandmother had her buried in the family plot and even now, 40+ years later, she visits Suzanna's grave every year in the anniversary of her death, Leaving flowers.
