column1: If gender dysphoria does not completely go away even after transition, why bother? Does dysphoria get easier to manage?
column3: Yesterday was a bad day. Even after gender transition, yes, gender dysphoria can be hard to bear.About 20 minutes later, I called my friend, in tears. Good friends are so important. I’d spent most of the day lying in bed, alternately reading, dozing, meditating and dissociating. I learned how to dissociate from my pain back in 2011, during a time when my insomnia was so bad I was averaging 2½ hours sleep a night. It’s not a dissociative episode, as in there is no dissociative fugue. It’s deliberate, in the sense that it’s my choice to enter the dissociative state. It’s completely circumstantial, that the emotional pain I experience is sufficient to make that dissociative state possible, and desirable. I can stay there for hours, keeping the pain at bay, but completely incapacitated by the pain I’m avoiding. If I come out, the pain is waiting for me. Even just sending that SMS, “No but I’ll be ok”, was painful, because it required exiting the dissociative state I was using to protect myself. Calling my friend was painful, for the same reason, but it was time to come out. This is complex, a long post. Scroll to the bottom if you just want to see my TL;DR.Can emotional pain be worse than physical pain? ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ Before I experienced it, I would have said, “No, surely not!” Of course, there is pain and there is pain. Some people experience emotional pain of such enormity, that causing themselves physical pain brings a sense of relief. I’ve been tempted, but I never went down that road. Some people experience emotional pain of such enormity, that suicide looks attractive. Suicide involves physical pain. At the point that suicide becomes a real risk, the emotional pain experienced, is greater than the physical pain involved in suicide. At least that’s the way it was for me. 17 years ago, my Mum died of cancer, suffering physical pain sufficient to tear involuntary screams from her. I was so close to my Mum, though cancer took her away from me years before she actually died. She was still my Mum. That was the worst emotional pain I’d ever experienced, but it was temporary. It still has the power to make me cry, but the power of that emotional pain is much less now, 17 years later. Gender dysphoria is remarkably like grief, debilitating, powerful. It comes in waves, sometimes unendurable, sometimes overwhelming, sometimes just an ache in our hearts. Unlike grief, which fades and heals with time, untreated gender dysphoria does not fade. The waves come and go. Sometimes the tide goes out, but over the course of our lives, the sea level is rising; each storm crashes over us with greater intensity. If we don’t transition, we die from suicide, or we sink into something, anything, that eases the pain. At 39 years old, that intense emotional pain that I didn’t realise existed, crushed me, with an intensity of roughly 100 times that of my Mum’s death. Was my emotional pain from gender dysphoria, worse than my Mum’s physical pain as she died from cancer? No, I don’t think it was, though both of us screamed from the pain.Why then, is extreme emotional pain so bad? ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ Emotional pain is hard to bear, because the physical shell of our existence is still alive, with no end in sight. Because modern end-of-life treatment is effective at easing physical pain, though it doesn’t remove it. Because we have people look at us, and say:“There’s nothing really wrong with you.”“You’re just lazy.”“Why can’t you just get your act together?”“You’re deluded and confused.”“You’ve chosen a hard path.”After my “friends” gave me their advice, and all the reasons they refused to call me Naomi, I’d go home and lie on the couch … and dissociate to escape the pain. At sunset, I’d go walk off into the deserted bushland tracks at night, and cry, and pray, and scream.Naomi Lauren's answer to If you suffer from gender dysphoria, did anti depressants help before transition?In the Bible, Job had friends like that. I no longer have those friends.Looking for any other solution ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ For 4½ years, I sought every option I could, to find relief from that pain, to rise over it, rather than to sink under it. I wasn’t even 100% sure that the pain was caused by gender dysphoria. Through my reading, I realised it was extremely likely, because my experiences mirrored that of many other transgender people. I tried every option I could, except full gender transition, because I was afraid of risk and loss. In September 2015, I realised I’d already lost every reason to avoid gender transition:Lost my marriage.Lost my conservative church, where I’d attended, tithed, served and taught for 18 years.Lost almost all of my old friends.Lost my career.After 4½ years of trying, I lost hope that I would find another way to escape this pain AND get my life back. So, I started estrogen HRT, and found relief from about 85% of my symptoms and distress overnight. Estrogen affects the brain, and it was the effect on my brain (not my body) which delivered the greatest benefit for me.Naomi Lauren's answer to As a trans woman taking estrogen for the first time, will I feel anything?In my case I’d already found some acceptance of my name and pronouns, so I think it was the combination of estrogen HRT and social acceptance as a woman that delivered this 85% relief. For other transgender people, the relief they seek comes through other means, in addition to the direct benefits of hormones and/or social acceptance:Biological or anatomical changes through hormones and/or surgeries.Authentically expressing our gender identity and individuality, through body language, mannerisms, voice, activities & interests, clothes, accessories, grooming and hairstyle.Even with 85% relief, gender transition is still really hard. It carries it’s own challenges, which are different for each and every one of us.Naomi Lauren's answer to How did you come to know you needed to transition your legal gender?The remaining 15% of symptoms and distress can still be debilitating, and the waves and the tide still rise and fall. I still have difficult life circumstances, and must still cope with attention deficit disorder without using medication, and recover from trauma I experienced in these last 8 years. I’ll get there. My bad days now, are substantially better than my good days from before I started estrogen HRT.Gender transition is not a panacea ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ Gender transition does not fix every problem in your life, or even every debilitating problem. If you are expecting gender transition to fix everything, then you are building yourself up for disappointment. There is more to life than gender. Gender transition also makes some things much worse, with gender transition usually taking 2–5 years for an adult, but those circumstances are temporary.“Out of the frying pan, and into the fire”We exchange the chronic stress of gender dysphoria, for the chronic stress of gender transition, but the difficulties of gender transition are temporary. To escape the frypan, we have to face the fire, because that’s the only way out. I postponed gender transition until my life was at it’s lowest ebb. That is not an approach I recommend, because gender transition is hard. If you can see that you might be transgender, I highly recommend you take tentative steps toward a partial gender transition as a priority. For trans women and transfeminine peeps, I talk about how to do a partial transition in this post, no estrogen required!Naomi Lauren's answer to I do not experience gender dysphoria, but I feel more comfortable when I am wearing female clothing. l think l will live better if l am a woman. Should I start my transition?TL;DR, Why bother with gender transition? ¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯¯ Because it’s the only hope we’ve got. The alternative is pain and hopelessness — death or addiction. In my case, I’ve looked for, and found, concrete benefits of gender transition. This is why I can never go back to the life I had:Improved short term memory, better than it’s ever been.Improved medium term memory.Improved visual recognition and social communication.Most of my generalised anxiety is gone.Most of my depression is gone.Panic attacks are down, from several times a day, to a few times a year!Dissociation is down, from every single day, to a few times a fortnight.My insomnia is down, from every single night, to a few times a month.I handle financial anxiety better now.I can do public speaking now.I hardly ever feel a need to scream now.The aching need to exit this world is now entirely manageable, even though it’s not completely gone.For these benefits, I’ve had to pay a huge price, socially, emotionally, financially. I’m still paying that price, and it causes me huge stress, but it’s getting better. These benefits are getting better, as the stress of gender transition declines. As I said before, it bears saying again. Gender transition is not a panacea. Gender transition doesn’t fix everything. For a time, gender transition often makes things worse, throwing enormous new social stresses onto shoulders already weary of this life. But it gets better, unlike untreated gender dysphoria, which only gets worse.

column1: Why is emotional pain more hurtful than physical pain even if it doesn't hurt in the body?
column3: Let me answer this… Pain caused by emotional distress is more deeply felt and last longer than that caused by physical injuries. And those in the emotional pain, their condition performed worse than those thinking about physical pain.Similarly, painful emotional experiences shape people much more than painful physical experiences, impacting their mental health and self-esteem. A bullied child may grow up to be an introverted and under-confident adult; someone who lived in fear at an early age might avoid all kinds of situations which provoke uncertainty;. We need a more open dialogue about how severely heartbreak impacts our emotions and functioning. And for such discussions to be productive, we have to disavow ourselves of the notion that there is something childish, embarrassing or inappropriate about feeling severe emotional anguish when our heart is broken, because heartbreak is devastating, at any age. We suffer emotional pain that is nearly “unbearable” for days, weeks and even months on end. Our body experiences stresses that can damage both our short-term and long-term health. Our grief activates circuitry in our brain that causes withdrawal symptoms similar to those experienced by people who are addicted to cocaine or heroin. Our ability to focus and concentrate, think creatively, problem-solve and generally function at our regular capacity becomes significantly impaired. We start doubting on ourselves that we are living or not. ?If you broke your leg many years ago, you’ll likely experience little if any distress when you recall the event. However, if you recall an event that caused psychological pain – the death of a loved one, a cruel comment from school or work bullies, being rejected by a romantic love interest – you will likely experience a fair degree of emotional pain. And The biggest question is “why we are always suffering from emotional or unbearable pain by recollections of social betrayal and other forms of emotional pain. ? Because obviously we are expert or pretty good at keeping those memories stable in mind which gives us more and more pain. Physical pain can be temporary or lasts after passage of time. But it is not sure that one who is going through emotional or mental pain should relief after the passage of time. Physical pain can be healed by medicines, therapys and all. But emotional pain hurts lifetime until our last breath. I can relate with it literally.Thank you so much for this beautiful question. 🙏🙏

column1: What are the most disgusting signs that someone has a narcissistic personality disorder?
column3: Thank you for the A2A, Daniel. In my opinion, the most disgusting sign that someone has a Narcissistic Personality Disorder is that their children are a wreck. The most disgusting aspect of NPDs is their hatred and maltreatment of their children. A home ruled by an NPD parent is loveless, hostile unpredictable and cold. Emotional pain of the children is the norm, warmth comes only from heaters, food is served with a dose of malice, which gets stuck in the throat, and chaos and drama determine the daily experience. The first and most important job of a parent is to provide safety for their children. NPDs instead pose a major threat and inflict huge harm on their children, and the children are trapped in the abusive hands for years. At an early age, children cannot seek help – they are even unable to identify the fact they experience emotional pain. An adult target may suffer with a Narcissist, but they can at least (at some point) understand they are not happy with a Narc and eventually leave. They are often unaware, but a close friend or even a stranger could tell them the Narc is not treating them well. They can theoretically ask for help and leave, once they realize their life with the Narc hurts. They have that option. Not easily accessible to the brainwashed target, but the option is still there. Narcissistic abuse is especially devastating for NPDs children, because they have no chance to get out and learn any better. They are supposed to learn the best from their parents and feel best with their parents, but they receive a vile enemy instead. These children invariably receive the opposite of normal. Their world is upside down, inside out, unstable, destructive and unsafe. Unlike adult victims, NPD’s young children cannot learn any better or receive advice from their friends. Their close friends are the same young age and cannot tell them the Narc is abusive, because they are too young to know it themselves. Adults outside the family are either unaware of the abuse or are aware, but have no hard evidence, or are unable to intervene in the abusive family. column1: What is something your parent said that made you die a little inside?
column3: “You have a death sentence.” I was born with hemophilia (1974). In the early eighties, HIV was introduced into the blood supply. Back then, hemophiliacs depended on the blood supply in order to stop our bleeds. Our blood doesn’t have a specific clotting factor…thus our body can’t always stop internal bleeding from a bump, an accident, a bad nosebleed, or even anything in particular. Most of the time it’s spontaneous, suddenly your elbow or thumb or calf starts hurting. That was life with hemophilia in the early ‘80s. I was infected by the tainted blood supply when I was 10 years old. Back then, before HIV, hemophiliacs were treated much like asthmatics or diabetics were treated. Everyone felt a bit bad for their lot in life, and were sensitive to their disease issues. That changed for hemophiliacs almost overnight. Now, they were suspect. Adults who were once warm and friendly toward me suddenly looked at me from a distance. I was 10 years old. I had no idea why. This was a time of fear. As a boy, I recall many television news programs talking about AIDS. In the early days, they called it “gay cancer.” A lot of gay folks called it “blood cancer,” so to save face to their parents and communities (as they lay dying). I lived through that time (during my formative teen years). In 9th grade health class, I sat in the front row sweating as the health/gym teacher told everyone that one avenue for infection was having hemophilia. I walked out of class that day in a daze — wondering who, in my small town, knew that I had hemophilia…and would connect the dots. I miraculously left that classroom with none of my classmates being wiser (I believe). In 11th grade, I met a girl who made my heart flutter. Like any other teen, we dated. I struggled between love and fear. I wanted to kiss, explore, etc., just like we all did. My parents (pre-baby boomers) saw the writing on the wall. They didn’t have the emotional maturity to help me through these times (they were of the time where kids were seen, not heard). I was a smart kid, and I knew I needed to be super careful around my girlfriend (like, it was on my mind constantly). Since I was still an (older) kid, I loved Christmas (barely 17 years old). I loved everything about it; family together, a wonderful meal, happiness, and gifts. This Christmas Eve was different though. My older siblings weren’t quite home yet (I was so excited to see them, as they didn’t live here any longer). And, the most special part was my girlfriend would be coming over right after opening presents. I was super excited for my girlfriend to meet my siblings. My parents were doing last-minute spot-checks/clean up (clearing wrapping paper remnants). I was just out of the shower (as we were going to church in a bit). I had my best church/Christmas clothes on, and I was walking around with a hair brush, getting my hair in order. My dad called me downstairs (my mom was next to him). I was a teen, so I went about halfway down the stairs and sat on the landing, fooling around with the hairbrush. I called to him, “What, Dad?” There was a slight pause as I fumbled with the hairbrush impatiently. He said, “You know you have a death sentence, and it would be best to be very careful around your girlfriend.” The hairbrush I was holding unexpectedly snapped in my hands, I had broken it in half without even realizing it. I didn’t say a word, I just walked up the stairs with tears streaming down my face. That was the last Christmas I ever felt innocent joy. My family did meet my girlfriend that evening, it was quite uncomfortable for me. Six hours previous, I was on top of the world. I was finally in a boyfriend/girlfriend relationship…just like everyone else. I was normal (just for a moment). Post script - My girlfriend became my wife. That was 1991. We married in 2000. I don’t believe my parents ever realized the pain those words caused me. They do seem pretty happy I made it through though, and it wasn’t a death sentence. The phrase my dad uttered still stings, and I’ve never really felt the joy of Christmas that I once had.
column9: Dear Mark, I cannot imagine the pain you have had to endure having hemophilia during that time. column1: What is it like to have complex post traumatic disorder (CPTSD)?
column3: I can answer this as someone who is diagnosed with C-PTSD and has spent a number of years in treatment with a therapist, as well as reading about it and learning to observe my feelings and behavior. In some ways, C-PTSD looks similar to BPD, but there are some definite differences. Because of the similarity, it can take a mental health professional months or even a couple of years to recognize that it's actually C-PTSD, not BPD. I have attachment issues related to unmet needs from childhood. I have conflicting feelings of needing love and connection but intensely fearing it. I control my emotions very well until something triggers me. At that point, emotional pain floods me, and if it is bad enough, I will dissociate and feel emotionally numb for hours or even days. My nervous system always feels hyped up and on edge. Even though I am often exhausted, I have trouble sleeping. I have nightmares regularly and sometimes wake up drenched in sweat. It's hard to feel an emotional connection with someone else, even if I know they care about me. My mind has trouble understanding that a relationship is made up of many, many experiences tied together. I determine the state of my relationship with someone based on whatever happened between us the last time we were together. It's hard for my mind to connect everything before that and understand the relationship as a whole. My self-esteem is very low, and I don't trust my own perceptions. I am terrified to getting emotionally close to someone because I've experienced so much rejection. A loss of someone I love feels like a death. Unlike someone with BPD, I don't self-harm, threaten suicide, or have angry outbursts. I don't actively seek someone to nurture, rescue, or help me. My desire and need for love and connection is INCREDIBLY strong and painful, but my protective system is stronger. Plus, I don't feel entitled to impose on other people to help me when I am suffering. I loathe having such deep emotional needs and try to hide it from others. I choose to suffer alone rather than seek support. I think I'm likeable, but only as long as I can keep up a mask of normalcy. Friends and coworkers (even some family) who have seen me as competent and self-reliant can be quite shocked or even scared if they happen to witness one of my PTSD-triggered episodes. I become someone they do not recognize. They don't understand what happened or how to help. Because I seem so different when I am triggered, some friends have become suspicious and think I'm putting on some kind of an act for attention. But this is far from the truth. I have only partial awareness of what it happening. I am not really even there. I am lost in a past trauma that I am reacting to. After I come out of it, I feel terribly vulnerable and embarrassed, and regret that others witnessed me that way. This makes me try even harder to keep up the strong, in-control mask that hides my inner pain and issues. Even with hard work in therapy, I am still in need of treatment. I have been in therapy for well over 10 years, and I still struggle to trust my therapist or allow the vulnerability necessary to drop my armor even for short periods of time. I don't know how she has stuck with me this long. For some reason, she still believes in my ability to heal.

column1: Is it possible for people with C-PTSD to be emotionally unavailable?
column3: We talk a lot about people who are "emotionally unavailable," but what does that really mean? Sociopaths and narcissists are normally emotionally unavailable because they don’t "have feelings" or are disconnected from higher-order emotional experiences that could guide their acts, but what about the others? Those without pathology? Do they count? We say that someone is emotionally unavailable when they are either incapable or unwilling to connect with others on an emotional level—understanding, sharing, and empathizing with the emotions and experiences of others—probably based on the fact that they struggle to know or express their own emotions. They can be separated into those who are incapable and those who are unwilling. Most of the time, it’s due to a certain level of incapacity more than unwillingness. Most people who have trouble identifying and articulating their emotions feel or find themselves misunderstood and frustrated in their relationships, and they may end up avoiding conversations or situations that require vulnerability, fearing that it will make them appear weak, cold, disconnected, and rejected. That’s a vicious circle that makes them even more emotionally unavailable. That can also cause a loss of empathy, which could damage their self-concept and create a conflict about wanting to feel but knowing they cannot. Can this unavailability be caused by C-PTSD? Traumatized individuals, especially those who suffered traumatization for a very long time and developed C-PTSD, require strategies to survive their environment that involve emotional detachment or avoidance as a way to protect themselves from further emotional pain. I have noticed that people get lasting consequences after traumatic occurrences when their level of fear reaches the point of over-activating the parasympathetic nervous system, the one in charge of slowing down many functions, and of producing endogenous opioids and cannabinoids that cause numbing, dissociation, disconnection, and disengagement. So, yes, it is not only possible but very frequent that individuals who suffer from C-PTSD are somehow emotionally unavailable. They may have difficulty trusting others and opening up emotionally, and be constantly on guard, making it hard to relax and connect. But always remember that trauma is not a death sentence. If it has been resolved, even when there could be some symptoms left, the person recovers functionality step by step. Becoming aware and connected to their emotions may gradually happen until they engage emotionally again. Also, some people that meet criteria of C-PTSD may be very emotional, and may be very interested on the emotionality of others, and may be extremely empathetic to compensate. We, humans, are so complex that it’s almost impossible to generalize. Some people with C-PTSD are very emotionally available because that may be the strategy thet helped them navigate their traumatic circumstances.
column9: I have CPTSD , and my experience is that the person I was emotionally unavailable to was me. When I experienced traumas , I didn’t react at the time and at times disassociated, but to those around me my behaviour remained consistent with how they experienced me in their lives. It took me years to figure out that when I felt distress I need to sit down and work backwards over the previous days or weeks to make it rational in my mind.

column1: How do I stop grieving for my beautiful mom who passed away after a surgery and coma? I buried her in December 2020. It is still so hard for me to go on in life. I feel so lost without her company.
column3: You don’t. You just don’t. Grief is a living thing. As such, it changes over time just like all living things. It blossoms initially with an intensity that can be crippling. It evolves into an emotional pain that feels like it will never end and given enough time it turns into an emotional scar of sorts. It never truly goes away and your emotional state can no more return to “normal” than you can return a piece of aluminum foil with a hole in it to it’s prior, pristine state. Our current society doesn’t really recognize death as it once did. Most people in various cultures in the past observed and expected a full year of acute grieving for a loved one. At a minimum. It seems like as we become more “connected” in the digital age our attention spans are as short as our memories. Our emotions have not evolved like that however and they come under particular assault in this environment because it can lead you to unrealistic expectations of yourself in this regard. I for one am glad that we have much more depth than an emotional Twitter feed for a heart. I am so sorry for your loss. Most of the time, the pain one feels is directly related to the amount of love you experienced. That is a very real blessing. I suspect that your mother felt that love and was proud of your capacity to experience and create it. Give yourself time and most of all, give yourself some grace. Your mom certainly would.

column1: When was the hardest you have cried?
column3: In 2009, I was 26 years old and had a 4 year old son, and 2 year old and 1 year old little girls. My son had been sick for weeks. I'd taken him to the pediatrician every week for 4 weeks, and taken him to the ER once when he collapsed in pain and was screaming and begging me to make it stop. I was told repeatedly he had an upper respiratory, and the pain was just because he was constipated too. When he collapsed a second time, I took him back to the ER again and told them I wasn't leaving until they figured out what was happening. This time we had a different doctor, and as soon as she did her initial assessment, I could see on her face that she was concerned. She immediately got the doctor supervising the ER that day to come check him out as well, and I saw them making eye contact with each other throughout, and I knew they were very worried, although they didn't tell us what they suspected yet. They ordered bloodwork, and only an hour or so after entering the ER, they both came back and had someone come take my son to another room to color while we spoke. They asked me to sit down, and as soon as they started talking about his blood counts I started to feel like I was gonna faint. When they actually said the word “leukemia”, I started screaming and sobbing. I had forced my husband to come (he thought I was being paranoid and the previous doctors were right and it was just a virus), and I remember gripping his shirt as I screamed and wept. I had no experience with cancer, and as far as I knew, my 4 year old little boy could be facing a death sentence. I had always seen the St Jude ads, and listened to the stories on the annual telethon on the radio, and used to cry hearing the parents talk about losing their children. I remember pulling over and praying that my children never be that sick as I cried for those kids. My baby going through that was my worst fear, and it was suddenly coming true. I cried a lot during his treatment (never in front of him), but that first evening was shattering for me. And a side note: Cancer is NOT a death sentence, that was just what my inexperience and fear told me at the time. My precious little boy is now a healthy 12 year old who's about to pass my height. column1: How do I get over the break-up of a long-term relationship in which I was dumped?
column3: You take it hour by hour at first, then day by day. Give yourself licence to cry and feel the full range of emotion going on inside. Spending time in the shower having a good cry helps very early on too. You are also mourning for the end of the relationship and all the plans and dreams you had. It is a loss as significant as a death. What makes it even more difficult, is that you no longer have your significant other to share this emotional hurt for comfort. What helped me when a 20 year relationship ended was trusting in myself that I was going to be fine. Once the emotions begin to abate, you will begin to see the benefits of the end of the relationship. It was a time for deep introspection and finding my way to true authenticity and honesty with myself first, then with others. I did a lot of work to heal and the many benefits continue to this day. Friendships became deeper as we learned shared our most raw emotions with each other. I had to learn to navigate life solo in what I thought was a couples world - no more planning for the weekend as a couple, much less life. For me, being in a long-term relationship creates 'emotional memory' much like long-term repetitive motion creates muscle memory. Your decisions, habits, small day to day things are tied to another being, and finding your way to a new normal is hard. You learn to make new habits, new thoughts, opinions and choices. It was a painful way to lose my fear of being single and of experiencing deep heartache. For those who like predictability and security like me, I came out of denial and began a dialog with my partner. I knew that leaving the relationship was the right thing for both of us, and we continued our relationship as the closest of friends until he passed away several years later. I figured that if it was going to hurt, then suck it up, go ahead throw yourself on the sword and embrace the changes to come. I now know that I can take anything on in life and I will be fine - it will hurt, but at the end of the day, I will absolutely be fine. I began to delve into what I really needed out of life and a life partner vs. what I wanted or thought I wanted. I found myself on an unknown path with no plan "B" in mind - for me, like finding yourself at the precipice and not knowing what was to come was unthinkable. I once watched Dr. Oz on his very early appearances on TV. One episode in particular I remember to this day. He talked about his experience and a cardio-thoracic surgeon and what he has learned that science cannot explain. He talked about the saying that someone had a 'hard heart' and that there is medical basis for it. Angry, constantly stressed, unloving and cold people will indeed have hard heart muscles. People who are loving, kind, happy, surrounded by family and friends will have a beautiful, strong muscular heart muscle. This was borne out by his history with his thousands of patients. He went on to say that the heart is a muscle that needs exercise, love and a full range of emotions to keep it healthy. Keeping emotions in is not healthy. A loss of a loved one or relationship gives you a chance to feel the full range and depth of human emotions. I embraced this thought whenever I go through heartache. The silver lining in all of this is that if you do it right, you will grow emotionally from this and be emotionally healthier, stronger and much more resilient. You'll find that you will be able to see that it is better to live with the one where the love and commitment is mutual and will continue to grow|evolve over time. Give yourself time to heal. The raw emotional hemorrhaging will begin to modulate and abate, and one day, you'll find yourself smiling again, then you know you are on the mend an on your way to finding your own happiness again. I wish you well on this part of your journey.

column1: What was it like meeting a Holocaust survivor? What was her/his story?
column3: My grandma watched her own mother starve to death in Auschwitz. Apparently, if you feed people only potato peels and days’ old breast crust, that happens. Maria, a Polish friend from before the war who worked in the camp, snuck clothes in for her. My grandma, after changing in the bathroom, walked out in broad daylight, marching right past rifled SS guards and their vicious attack dogs.Her father was gassed later on. But she lived out the war in a tiny village in the southeast of the country, pretending to be a good Catholic while working as a secretary at a lumberyard. The problem: no one knows what happened during those years. What she had to do to survive. She’s never talked about it.In June, she’ll be 96. She hardly leaves the house, has to use a walker, and gets strong pain medication to alleviate all the aches that come with having your spine compress and decompress for nearly a century. Plus, the weight of knowing that your parents, cousins, friends—and everyone else you grew up with and loved—were slaughtered because some bloodthirsty lunatic managed to convince enough people that the Jews are an inferior race that must be exterminated but you couldn’t do anything about it. And, the guilt that while she managed to escape, her father stayed behind.A few years ago, I asked her what she thinks about me coming over, interviewing her, and writing her story. “I would be open to that,” she said. I was surprised. I thought it was something buried so deep that even if it festered there, sending out currents of emotional pain, there was no way it was ever coming to light. Or maybe she was just entertaining me. Impossible to say.But I didn’t go. It was hard to find the time between family and work. Or maybe that’s an excuse I tell myself because of my own guilt of not having pursued the opportunity—even if nothing would have come out of it. Anyway, the dementia is too advanced now. A conversation with her resets every twenty seconds. “How is your family and work?” “My family is healthy and my work is going well. I’m happy.” “I’ve gotten so old. Can you believe that?” “I can.” “But anyway, how is your family and work?” And I will have to live with the fact that soon, one more survivor’s story will be lost, and that maybe—just maybe—I could have done something about it.

column1: How do police officers deliver a death notification to the family of someone that just died? What type of reactions do you usually see?
column3: Making a Death Notification 1. The importance of duty A properly delivered death notification will have a significant impact on the surviving family members. Learning of the unexpected loss of a loved one is an extremely traumatic moment. Handling this properly can aid in the grieving process. The moments spent delivering the news will remain with the survivors for the rest of their lives. 2. Good Information is essential The first step in the process is the gathering and verifying of information. How was the decedent identified? Some of the best methods include identification by fingerprints, DNA, and dental records. Less reliable methods include identification by witnesses or by identifiers found on their person or in a crashed car. This is a question that is often asked by the family. It usually is a denial reaction, but you need to be sure that the identification is conclusive. The next step is to gather as much information surrounding the death as possible. Including, the circumstances, the location, when and how it incident occurred. If it was the result of a criminal act, was an arrest made, or has the perpetrator been identified? Determine where the deceased is currently located and the procedures for identification or viewing of their loved one. The final step is identifying the legal next of kin. This seems straightforward but it may not be. Who is the person’s legal guardian? If it’s an adult who is their closest relative? Once this is determined, you will need to locate the residence of those persons. If they are older, you should check any available records for indications of medical problems. A death notification to a person with a heart condition may become a medical emergency. In these situations, it is wise to have an ambulance nearby to respond as needed. 3. Notifications—Always made by two, always in person Two people, one of which will be a police officer, must deliver all death notifications in person. The first step will be picking the team. Hopefully, it isn’t simply the first two officers who are clear of calls. The investigating officer is a good choice, as they will have the most facts about the case. If the investigating officer is not available, then a superior officer will be a good second choice. Whatever officer is selected must be able to deliver a compassionate, respectful, and dignified notification. The police officer may take a civilian with them in certain circumstances. If the person is known to be deeply religious, taking their local pastor, or a police Chaplin may work well. Most hospitals have grief counselors available which may be a comfort to the surviving family members. In some circumstances, a close personal friend of a single survivor may be taken to provide comfort and remain with them after the officer leaves. 4. Plan notification, who will speak, what will be said Each of the two persons making the notification will have pre-planned roles. One police officer will do all of the talking, making the notification. It is easier for a person to follow when only one person speaks. The other officer or support person will watch for a reaction which may indicate a medical emergency—such as a person going into shock. Death notifications are not to be delivered at a person’s front door. When the person answers the door, first make sure you are speaking to the right person. Ask permission to enter the survivor’s home conveying the message that you have something of great importance to tell them. Being a uniformed officer will prevent any confusion. The presence of someone they know such as their pastor or close friend will also help put them at ease and allow entry. If there are young children present, you should ask to speak with the survivors outside of their presence. It may be best to allow a neighbor to watch them. Once inside the home, try to lead the survivors to a comfortable area where they can be seated. Generally, the living room is a good choice. The first words delivered are the most important. “We are here to deliver bad news.” This simple statement partially prepares the survivors for what is to come. The next words must be spoken plainly with compassion, but without vague terms. Using vague terms to describe death will only be confusing at a time when clarity is paramount. Terms such as passed-away didn’t survive or didn’t make it should not be used. 5. Tell the person what happened—the circumstances and the result Here are some examples of a proper death notification statement: 1. Your son John died of what appears to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound. 2. Your daughter Melissa was killed in a car crash last night. 3. Your father Allen died last night after falling down the basement stairs. 4. Your brother Robert was shot and killed last night during a robbery at his store. In each example, the delivery is short, direct to the point. Each uses the person's name and then immediately states that they died with a short explanation of the circumstances. After the initial delivery, it may take several minutes for this heartbreaking news to sink in. You may have to repeat the notification statement or clarify something they don’t understand. 6. Be prepared for almost any initial reaction There is no right or wrong way to react to devastating news. Everyone is different and the reactions will be unique to the individual. If a person immediately becomes quiet staring into space and shows no reaction, they may be in shock and need medical attention. Other normal responses include screaming, crying, falling onto the floor, punching, or breaking things. They may become angry with the officer as the messenger of the news. Others will retreat to another room. Do not judge the persons' actions, as they are their normal reaction to a devastating event. If you fear that they are in danger of harming themselves then the officer needs to step in and gently restrain them until medical assistance arrives. 7. Provide time to answer questions and provide assistance. After several minutes have passed and they are recovering from the initial shock, it will be time to answer any questions they may have. Be prepared to answer the four most common questions asked: 1. How do you know for sure it’s their family member? 2. What happened to them? 3. When did this happen? 4. Where are they now? Answer all of the surviving family member’s questions honestly and compassionately. Be mindful of their fragile state. Be careful when explaining the circumstances surrounding the fatal event to be generic and non-graphic in your description. If you don’t know the answer to a question, tell them so, but indicate that you will work to find the answer to their question. Never promise to do anything and not follow through. Provide assistance to the survivors as needed or requested. It is often helpful to make telephone calls to other relatives who may respond and offer additional support. If the deceased is able to view at the hospital the notifying officer should make these arrangements and provide transportation to and from the hospital. There are also times when visual identification of the deceased is needed by the next of kin to confirm the identity. Depending on the circumstances, an autopsy may be required. If asked the notifying officer should be able to explain the reasons for an autopsy and a general non-graphic explanation of the procedure. In some cases, organ donation may be a viable option and the notifying officer should be able to set up communication between the hospital and next of kin. Questions regarding the release of the body of their loved one may be asked. The notifying officer if asked should know the procedures involved in this release and provide guidance. If requested the notifying officer may make contact with a funeral director of the survivors' choice to set up arrangements for the removal of the deceased from the hospital. 8. Special circumstances If the next of kin lives a distance away from the officer's jurisdiction, then the in-person death notification should be made by the local police department having jurisdiction where they live. Care should be given to preparing the necessary information to be transmitted to the notifying agency. This should include; 1. The full name date of birth and identifiers of the deceased 2. The full name and address of the legal next of kin to be notified 3. A synopsis of the circumstances surrounding the deceased’s death. 4. The name and address and telephone number of the hospital where the deceased is located 5. The name addresses and telephone numbers of the police department, and the investigating officer. Some departments will provide this information over the telephone to the department making the notification. This may not be a best practice as some information may be lost or misinterpreted. Some departments will fax an initial police report of the incident along with the death notification request. This is better, so long as sensitive investigative information is redacted. The investigating officer should be available by telephone at the time of the notification to answer additional questions the family may have. There will be times when the next of kin are at work when a death notification has to be made. The timeliness of a death notification is more important now than ever before. Living in the age of social media it is common for the next of kin to find out through social media before police can even attempt a notification. At this point, the officers are merely confirming the loved ones' worst fear. For this reason, a death notification might have to occur at a person’s place of employment. This still requires a two-person team and the same procedures as a residential notification. Upon arrival at the business, locate the person’s supervisor. The officer will ask to meet with the particular employee regarding a family emergency. A quiet location should be selected, where the survivor can sit and listen. It will be up to the employee how much information the officer shares with the person’s supervisor. The officer should arrange for transportation from their place of employment to their residence or the hospital. When the deceased is not a resident of this country and their family resides outside the United States police should contact the proper foreign embassy. The consulate will arrange to locate and notify the next of kin. 9. Clearing the assignment A police officer must never leave a person at home alone after a death notification. They must arrange for a friend or family member to stay with the grieving person. The officer must not leave until the designated person arrives. Before leaving the officer and second-team member will leave their names and contact information. They should also stress that if they have further questions to call them directly for assistance. When the officer is confident they have done all they can to comfort and assist the surviving family members, the officer is free to clear the assignment. Receiving a death notification from a police officer will be a once in lifetime event for most survivors. It will be one of the worst days of their life. The loss of a child or teenager is especially difficult. Accept the survivor’s reaction and emotions as you accept your own. Police officers are not cold or unfeeling. If a notification moves you to shed a tear understand that it is not a sign of weakness but rather a genuine gesture of emotional empathy. Nothing that a police officer can say or do will ease the extreme emotional pain of such a loss. However, a proper death notification that is direct yet compassionate will aid in the grieving process. It must be viewed as both a duty and an honor to participate in such a difficult assignment, to ease the pain of the message we are entrusted to deliver. Author of the 2020 book “One Cop’s Life” available on amazon

column1: What spiritual practices help overcome addiction?
column3: My father was an alcoholic. Six years before he died, he had a heart attack, followed by triple bypass surgery. Against the advice of his doctor, he checked himself out of hospital early, went home, poured a large whiskey, and lit a cigarette. He never fully recovered from the surgery. Death moved in and waited patiently to claim him. I begged him to sober up. But no matter how hard I tried (and I really did) I couldn’t make him see clearly. Nothing in my arsenal of so-called helpful practices could rouse him from his ignorance. He liked being intoxicated. Or so I thought. Then one day he explained it to me clearly. And it was I who saw the light. Or rather, the absence of it. It wasn’t that he liked being intoxicated. To him, alcohol was medicine. Physical pain was more tolerable than emotional pain. In his mind, he was simply choosing the lesser of two evils: die a physical death or die an emotional death. Either way, death is inescapable. After spending nearly seven years confronting my own inner demons and navigating the death of ego in a quest to find a reason to keep living, I couldn’t argue with his logic. A caterpillar can’t become a butterfly without first coming completely undone. The natural evolution and maturation of our psyches can be psychologically demanding, especially when unresolved trauma is present, coupled with a lack of emotional resilience—factors that fuel addiction. My father had no desire to confront the childhood beatings he suffered at the hands of his own father—an essential ingredient in overcoming addiction. He was content to let death take its toll on his body, while alcohol numbed his mind. Simply put, he didn’t love life enough to care to prolong it. And therein lies the cure to addiction… Love. You can’t practice love, any more than you can practice being human. You can only be it. Addictive behaviours are adaptive responses to a lack of love. The only real cure is confronting the darkness that consumes the light.

column1: Have you ever walked out of a doctor's office because the doctor was being disrespectful to you?
column3: I went to see a dermatologist at Keesler AFB in Biloxi, MS, when my ex was active duty. I’d had a mole on the back of my neck that would bleed every time I dried my neck after a shower. After telling the doctor I was assigned about this and that my mother had a history of skin cancer, he began berating me for taking up his time for something so small and insignificant when there were REAL people with REAL problems, blah, blah, blah... There was an airman med tech standing in the room because he was anticipating a mole removal and so he began setting everything up. When the doctor finally wound down, I said, “Are you done?" Him: “Yes.” Me: (As I’m standing up, knowing I was taller than him as I’m six feet tall.) “Now you listen to me, you self righteous, self important weasel... You don’t know me and you don’t know my life, who I am or what’s important to me.” He is now inching his way towards the partially open door while the med tech’s eyes are as big as saucers, mouth agape, because military doctors and officers in general are treated like GODS in the US Air Force, so I’m sure neither of them were used to hearing someone show such contempt for a butter bar Airman Basic with a college degree. Seriously, the US Air Force truly believes officers can do no wrong. And he’s trying to make his way out the door, because I’m really ranting as I tell him about a grandfather and older brother who both died of cancer, the former at 59, the latter at 28, a mother who had lung cancer and survived, a father who had a melanoma removed from his leg a couple years earlier, and my possible death from skin cancer was a VERY real problem to me, a REAL person. I finished my rant with,"Now, how about going to get me a REAL doctor so I can get this mole taken care of?” By this time, the entire waiting room is staring because the room I was in was the one opposite the check-in desk, and another dermatologist came out to see what was going on. This one had very pretty birds on his epaulettes. The first doctor tried to tell him I just went off on him for no reason but this airman, bless his heart, with a shaking voice because he was going up against an officer who could make him miserable on many levels, told the colonel what REALLY happened. I was shaking at this point and on the verge of tears. Whether it was anger or genuine emotional pain by being told I didn’t matter to this doctor at all, I don’t know. The colonel put his hand on my shoulder, looked the first doctor in the eye and said, “Wait for me in my office while I take care of this poor woman. You won’t be seeing any more patients today.. We need to discuss your future as both a doctor and as a member of the Air Force.” Turns out the second doctor was the clinic commander. A few days later, the colonel called me personally with the results of the biopsy on the mole. It was malignant and he wanted to do a second procedure to remove more skin around the original area to make sure they got it all. It was done the next day. By this point in my life, I was an extremely abused wife. My standard MO when confronted with a hostile man would have been to meekly accept the first doctor’s treatment of me and do nothing else. I thank God every day I managed to find my voice that day. It saved my life. EDIT: thanks to all for the upvotes, but also for the good wishes and “atta girls”! Women are treated horribly by male doctors because they still live in the Victorian age, where every female medical emergency revolved around the uterus. “Oh, my, Mrs. Smith! You seem to have severed an arm. I’m sure it has to do with your monthly. Let’s discuss that, shall we? “ Thanks again! I appreciate it all! Second edit: I’ve completely enjoyed all the discussion here on an important issue- self advocacy. And it’s. Not just women who need to do it. It’s equally important for men.. That day at Keesler taught me an important lesson and while I wish it hadn’t been under these circumstances I’m glad I learned it. Third edit: all the editors in the world can edit my answers, correcting grammar, spelling, etc. and I’m not going to accept them. I did this answer on my cell phone and I don’t care what you do to “fix” it, I’m going to decline it. If you want to edit stuff so bad, go get a job as an editor. Oh, and see a therapist to find out just why you have this overwhelming need to fix other people’s posts. My guess is your desire to feel superior at the expense of other people. But I was married to a narcissist for 23 years...

column1: Can a relationship get back to normal after someone cheats?
column3: I was cheated on by my wife. When I found out, it was like my entire life was lopsided and upside down. I was sick, angry, hostile, so deeply hurt. I felt dizzy, everything felt unreal. At first, I decided to try to make it work. It was super rough. I tried to forgive her but all of her lies and deceit throughout the years were intruding into my brain. I had to know everything and demanded she tell me everything. It was to the point that even if she didn’t do something, I broke her down until she admitted she did something she didn’t do. I would yell at her on trips and tell her how awful she was and ruin the trip. I left her then got back together with her about 20 times. Every time I thought I could forgive but something would trigger me and I would rage. I would find the smallest things to be mean about - “I’m hungry for a pizza, did you guys have pizza after you had sex, I bet you did you slut! I bet you guys were real hungry after a marathon!” She would cry. I would tell her she deserves worse. Then I would leave angry and come back feeling sorry, sad and confused. Yes, it was toxic. Yes I didn’t feel we could make it. I would ask for explicit details and then get super pissed off and call her a whore. It all came to a point when I told her the only way I could ever forgive her was if she experienced my pain. I told her that I was going to cheat on her to show her how it feels. She begged me not to. I reveled in her pain and I did it anyway. Then I went home and told her everything we did. I watched her cry. At first it felt good, then I said to myself, what the hell am I doing? I’m becoming just like her. I’m awful. What a crappy thing to do to someone. Maybe I was a cheater too? Maybe I wanted to get cheated on so I could cheat? All these thoughts, real or imagined, ran through my mind. I didn’t know who I was or who she was anymore. We caused each other so much pain over a period of 8 months then we separated for 2 months. After that break, and talk of divorce, we began to talk about everything. I had already filed for divorce so what difference did it make to find out why this happened? We really talked, like we never had before. We talked like friends talk to one another - without judgment, without anger. We talked about how we ever got to where we were. Why we cheated and hurt each other. We finally started understanding all the problems in our marriage - the lack of intimacy, the cruelty, the resentment over problems we never dealt with, the neglect, the disrespectful comments, the way we abused each other verbally. We would laugh at stuff we shouldn’t laugh about - the cheating. The losers we cheated with. We didn’t pick winners. We picked - throw away people. It was weird that we chose the people we did, it was almost like we wanted to just pick disposable people to destroy what we had. Yes, very sick and even cruel to the people we used to facilitate our destruction, but I think many people do this. They just want an exit and look for the easiest and most desperate people to cheat with. Any port in a storm, they say. We were finally understanding how it all blew up. Somehow, over a few months, the anger, lies and resentment turned into forgiveness. Maybe it was that we were being honest, completely and brutally honest for the first time in our lives. We had both been liars to that point. We lied that we were happy. We lied about things we did or didn’t do. We finally laid it all on the table. It was refreshing to say things like, “yeah I did this or that!” Without holding back. And to have someone reciprocate and be honest themselves and know for the first time ever - neither of you were lying. Somehow we learned from it all and became better people. We stopped lying and deceiving each other. I stopped the progress of the divorce. We created an environment that was safe to say anything, even things that sting and hurt. We didn’t move back together for a while but we would meet and go have dinner and talk once a week. Sometimes one or both of us would have a breakdown and say, “no it can’t work!” But we kept meeting and I don’t know how, but patience came out. Time heals all wounds and I do believe that but I don’t think it can heal someone that is determined to hang on to their hurt. After a long time, we no longer had a Disneyland idea of what a marriage was supposed to be. We talked about all the couples we knew that had cheated - some never speaking again, some staying together. We now didn’t take each other for granted but took care of one another. We unlocked our phones and shared them. We gave each other our passwords and secret emails. We talked about private things that we kept from each other for over a decade. We admitted wrongs that the other person never knew about. It has been over 10 years since then and she is now my best friend and we are so happy. We are both not even the same people. We wouldn’t recognize our past selves. We both died spiritually and emotionally. Our first marriage ended and we had to literally start a completely new chapter of what was now a new marriage. It sucks that we had to destroy ourselves to rebuild ourselves, but sometimes your problems are so deep and so swept under the rug that you need to literally destroy what you thought you had and start from zero. People who say “once a cheater always a cheater” are people who don’t understand that life is more complicated than that. They prefer bitterness over forgiveness. I’m here to say that forgiveness is possible but you have to be willing to put in a lot of work, have patience and be willing to forgive. In response to guys who will say I was a simp, a cuck, whatever, that’s fine. I just laugh because I know a secret - you have been cheated on in your lifetime, you just didn’t realize it. The argument I always hear is, “don’t you care that your woman had another dick in her?” If you are an adult human, every woman you’ve been with has had another dick in her. There will also be people who will say, “oh my spouse could never do that to me, they are a good person, they have had opportunities and declined!” People are in serious denial if they think their spouse would never do it. I know cookie baking, church going, PTA soccer moms that are doing it right now. I know supposedly honorable men who would never do it, who did it. Then they go online and are like “once a cheater, blah blah!” It’s estimated that 80 percent of people will cheat in some manner in their lifetime. Don’t be naive. We are non monogamous beings. When it happens to you - you won’t even know it’s happening because many people are excellent at keeping secrets. Don’t assume your loved one would never hurt you. Yes people in love can hurt each other deeply. I am so tired of hearing the same old, “you wouldn’t have done it if you truly loved them!” This is just the thinking of hurt people who are trying to rationalize the cheating. The only way it makes sense is if they never loved you. This is defeatist thinking. The people we love and who love us, will hurt us the most in our lives. And yes you can cheat and be cheated on, even while loving someone, due to resentment, anger, loneliness, you name it. Side note: I am not advocating being a door mat. If you give someone another chance and forgive them and they cheat again, your sanity and a good exit plan should be number one, in my opinion. Yes there are people out there who will take advantage of your kindness. My story is unique but hopefully will give people another idea for a way through the darkness.

column1: Why did Harry Potter tell his son Albus that Snape was the bravest man he ever knew?
column3: This phrase is Harry’s way of saying “I’m sorry” to Snape—or at least his memory. Harry, after Dumbledore’s death in HBP, followed and confronted Snape; there, enraged and in terrible psychological and emotional pain, he called him a coward and urged him to kill him as he had killed Dumbledore. Snape, who had until then retained his composure and had even offered some advice mingled with taunting to Harry, became mad with anger and pain when he heard the word “coward”, probably because he knew how full of dangers his double life was and how terribly unjust this judgement was.Harry: "Kill me then. Kill me like you killed him, you coward —" Snape: "DON'T — CALL ME COWARD!"So, when Harry tells Albus Severus that his namesake was the bravest men he ever knew he is in fact apologising to Snape and admitting that he had totally misunderstood him. It shows even to us readers that Harry not only forgave Snape for whatever mistreatment had experienced at his hands but also came to deeply respect and love him. It’s like a moment of reconciliation which was very necessary.
column9: I think it is going to far to say Harry loved Snape. But he did have enormous respect for him

column1: Will I ever be happy again after the loss of my only child?
column3: My only child had a chronic illness that could have been fatal for over seven years. I don't think I have ever experienced more emotional pain and sleepless nights than during that period. Even though our son was healed by a radical experimental treatment at age 10, I had spent many days in children's hospitals with parents who had eventually lost their child. They continued to meet with me to talk through the emotional pain of their grief. I then chose to make it a focus of my Commissioned Lay Ministry in the Episcopal Church and eventually recareered as Therapist specifically trained in Marriage and Family Therapy. I work with families with chronically ill children which so often culminates in the child losing their fight for life. I sit with the family during the initial and ongoing grief. In this regard they have some time to begin grieving over months or even years before the tragic death. It appears your grief was from a sudden loss from "awful circumstances." This makes the grief more intense because there was no period for preparation. As a parent of an only child I can only imagine how devastating that loss was for you. I often have to help parents and their surviving children though the blame they put on themselves for not intervening to prevent the consequences and tragic death. Older siblings say "I should have walked home with him instead of running to catch up with my friends." Parents say "I should have been more careful or more observant" or a thousand other blaming statements. Finding ways to forgive yourselves and/or others involved is a long process that takes both time and effort. It is paradoxically both emotionally draining and spiritually freeing. It is hard to understand tragic accidents or the behavior of others that led to the "awful circumstances" because of the grip of emotional pain. Even though there may be emotional support initially from friends, a faith community, or caring professionals, after a while this support falls off. The one organization that seems to be the most helpful to my grieving families is an organization called "The Compassionate Friends" http://www.compassionatefriends.org/home.aspx They have local chapters in all 50 states and Washington DC. They also offer 18 online meetings a week. They will meet your needs wherever you are in your process of healing. I hope this helps you through your loss. Sincerely, Grayson Miller MA, MBA, LPC Licensed Professional Counselor On Google+ at: gplus.to/Grayson
column9: I lost my only child, my daughter Danielle Monique at age 28. She had been suffering with poor health five years before she passed. column1: What's the most inexplicable experience you've ever had, whether supernatural, paranormal, bizarre coincidence, mysterious intuition, prophetic dream, or unexpected lab result?
column3: I had an experience that made me wonder about psychic connections. I’d broken up with a man and hadn’t communicated with him at all in 2 or 3 years. I had moved about 180 miles away. One day he came to mind out of the blue and I felt a strong urge, a compulsion to find out if he’s OK. I felt that he was hurting and needed help. After a couple of days struggling with this because I really didn’t want to disrupt my life or his - I left him for a reason and didn’t want to open a can of worms - I caved and called his sister. I told her I didn’t want to know where he was, but I just needed to know if he was OK. She said that he was and after a short conversation we hung up. Couple of days later my phone rings, and it’s him. He was not OK. He was in extreme emotional pain. We did reconnect with a few phone calls over a couple of months. Then again, I had ‘a feeling’ and reached out to him because I thought he was in trouble and needed help. He’d just had a car accident. When we were together I’d felt connected to him in a way that I’d never, and still have never, felt with anyone else on this earth. Not even my children. FF about 10/12 years and I get another feeling. I use the internet this time. I find his death notice. I knew before I looked that he was not ‘here’ anymore, but I couldn’t believe it and I had to find out.

column1: Can you ever emotionally heal after losing a baby to miscarriage?
column3: Yes I have had a miscarriage, and I have also buried a six year old. Having a miscarriage was sad, and unfair, but doesn't hold a candle to losing a child that you have actually raised, bonded, and loved. Now I don't want to discount anyone's pain. A miscarriage is a low blow, but you will get better. As a matter of fact I would not have the older child I have now if it weren't for the miscarriage. He was born the day after my miscarriage, one year later. I am glad I have the child that I have. I certainly would not swap given the chance. However, losing a child is the worst mental abuse, ever! You cannot change the situation, and no person is pulling the strings. i.e if you were in a situation causing you mental torment, you can remove yourself from the situation. Grieving a death of a child is something you have to do. You have to follow through. It's sink or swim. So for 4 agonizing years I made zero progress. My bedroom became my living room, and my bed became my couch. Nothing was normal. Actually it still isn't, and never will be… I just decided that I was tired of being a miserable victim, and I decided to change it. It has been the most grueling task ever. Mother's day is wretched. It probably always will be. I could go bowling with the lump that formed in my throat, and stays for days. To whomever reads this mourning in any form is bad, but there is definitely happiness after a miscarriage. If God chose to take a child, that would be the best time to do it, yet it's not easy. There is an aftermath to get through. I'm sorry about your loss, there will be better days ahead.
column9: I’m so sorry about your losses.

column1: If you used to be an alcoholic, what do you do now when you have to deal with emotional pain, boredom, and personal celebrations?
column3: “if you used to be an alcoholic…” Well, after 35 years of not drinking I am still an alcoholic. Alcoholism is a chronic condition that does not go away. It reworks some basic neurology in the brain as well as alter the basic structure of the mind. It’s something I will have to my dying day. I also have diabetes- that doesn’t go away either. Part 2, “what do you do now when you have to deal with emotional pain, boredom, and personal celebrations?” When I was drinking the emotional pain was constant and savage. On a daily basis, I was one sorry human being. Alcohol didn’t help me deal with the pain; in fact, it was the major cause of an extended bout of depression. It made my life miserable. Boredom. My life revolved around alcohol. I lost my appetite for fun and all the other small gifts of life. Bored? I read and reread the same book for 20 years. When I wasn’t bored, I was in crisis- a victim of my personal, never-ending train wreck. Lastly, personal celebrations? Easy, I didn’t have any. In recovery, I have had to deal with severe emotional pain without the pseudo-palliative of alcohol. Death of loved ones, a failed career, poverty. I still had pain, but pain leavened with dignity and hope and the love of family and friends. Boredom. I love it. Life can be so full that those rare moments of down time are welcome. Personal celebrations. That day I receicved my Masters degree, climbed Kartahdin, the birth of my children (a son, a daughter and a gaggle of grand-kids, a loving marriage… and so much more. Triumphs. AA has an applicable saying. My worst day sober is better than my best day drunk. This is true.
column9: Excellent answer. I’ve had some days in the last 3 years that really test the theory. However, looking back, I can see that I never would have survived them if I was still drinking Thank You Robert 🙏🏻

column1: Did Darth Vader feel remorse for killing Jedi?
column3: I don't know about him feeling remorse for slaying any Jedi, but Darth Vader did once express a silent display of remorse when he had to kill two Imperial Inquisitors. The two fallen Jedi in question had developed feelings for one another, and actually fell in love. The price for this treachery in the eyes of the Sith Lords was death, and so when Vader learnt of their treason he immediately went to hunt them down and eliminate the pair.After a brief confrontation Vader suspends the lovers in mid air using the force, at which point the two Inquisitors realise their fate has been sealed. Before Vader executes them, they display a moment of love between one another.These two panels below show Vaders body language speak much more than words when it came to his emotions on the subject of killing the exposed Inquisitors. As he uses each victims lightsaber to mortally wound the other, he cuts the males final speach short in the grim process. Vader knew they cared for one another, but had to hide their feelings from everyone around them. This would have stirred his emotions, and made him think of the exact same struggle that he and Padme had faced long ago. He didn't want to hear the last expression of love between the two.We see Vader solemnly lower his head as he commits the grim deed, almost as if he can't watch the final moment between the doomed lovers. His method of execution is also interesting, as it suggests that for the lovers to die simultaneously, looking into each others eyes for that one last time, would be better than just dying by Vaders lightsaber. He showed remorse by giving the two lovers that one last courtesy. He even lingers near the deceased bodies immediately after their deaths...pondering possibly regret, remorse or even thinking back to his own memories of pain and loss.
column9: I have read these particular comic issues several times, and yet it had never occurred to me to look at Vader’s actions here in that light. Yet, when I think back to who he is - who he really is - it makes perfect sense.

column3: I’m sorry for your loss. The best advice I’ve heard about grief comes from Jennifer Shaffer’s father on the flipside. We were doing a session one day and tears filled her eyes - and I realized she was sensing her father. Instead of waving the emotion away, I said “Can I ask him a question? How can we help people like your daughter, deal with grief?” She paused a moment and said “He’s saying “try to move grief to nostalgia.” I said “What does that mean?” She shrugged, “I don’t know” she said, wiping away a tear. I said, “Well, ask him. What do you mean?” She paused and said “I’m hearing “Grief is only sad memories, but nostalgia is both sad and happier memories. If you try to move grief to nostalgia you begin the healing process.” It was a profound thing to hear, first because neither one of us understood what he was saying until he explained it, and secondly, because literally, here was someone no longer on the planet giving us both new information. If it’s new information it cannot be cryptomnesia or something someone heard, thought or saw in a movie. It could only be him reporting this - as she was hearing him, in his voice, say it in her mind. So instead of going into a philosophical discussion of why anyone would choose a lifetime that included mental issues, psychological problems, brain issues - because we cannot answer “why” someone chose a lifetime, only they know the myriad of reasons from previous lifetimes, how the 3D chess board looks - but we can ask them how they are doing now. Literally. Now. Because what the research shows, what the footage shows, what my own experience shows is that they return home. They aren’t stressed over health issues - because all of those health issues were left on stage when they left the props and costume onstage. People don’t take those fears, worries, problems, issues with them - because they were all related to how the brain is wired, how the brain became wired due to outside or internal factors - that doesn’t matter to them at all, because they are no longer navigating the stereo receiver. column1: Why would grief continue growing more painful and stronger after a couple of years?
column3: Sometimes after a death of someone we love we do everything we can to avoid feeling anything. We walk around numb, sometimes we do this with substances, activities, behaviors and/or people. Sometimes our brains just do it for us. Because there is no way around, over or under grief you have to go through it. You have to experience, the loss and everything that goes with it. Grief is awful, I think it’s one of the worst emotions there is. My suggestion would be to seek out a grief group, call your local Hospice, I’m sure they could steer you in The right direction. There are also online support groups. I love on line support groups because they operate 24/7, you may have to try on a few before you get the right fit. My hope for you and anyone experiencing grief is that in your exploration of grief you find Peace
column9: The first mistake this comment and others do make is thinking that grief is a bad experience or a negative emotion. I am a retired hospice director and have dealt with many families who have lost loved ones. I have prepped my families with the understanding prior to their loss to see clearly that their pending grief is the emotion of love. It is all about the love they have for their spouse or parent or child or friend or whomever. Why would we feel grief in this situation if we did not have love for the person who passed? Once it is understood that it is their own love that drives their grief it is better accepted and not seen as such an awful experience. I ask them to remember their loved one with photos or videos or stories that relive their experiences and express their love. They do this as they are able and it is a great release of their love they are feeling. I also tell them to realize the pain is due to the missing experiences they will have in their future that will now occur since their loved one has moved on to the next stage before them. Once they accept it is more missing them and they will be together again, it is not as hard for them to look forward to what they believe the afterlife entails. Each person is different in this perspective. So two very important things to process. One is love drives our grief so turn in into something positive because it is rather than negative because it isn't. What is always negative is indifference. If no one cared if you died that would be the worst of reactions of course. Grief is love. Two is placing pain of grief in the right frame of mind. We miss our loved ones once they pass. Do what you need to review your time with your loved one to keep them close to you. Why this is not more understood by people boggles the mind. It may be because then grief counselors and therapists would lose many clients. What matters to me is the health and well being of the families of those who pass. Take care and try my efforts. They have a great track record. ❤️
