column1: Do animals grieve?
column3: I would like to start by quoting Marc Bekoff [1] who is a Professor of Ecology and Evolutionary Biology and a leading scientist studying animal emotion and animal cognition: “When animals express their feelings they pour out like water from a spout. Animals' emotions are raw, unfiltered, and uncontrolled. Their joy is the purest and most contagious of joys and their grief the deepest and most devastating. Their passions bring us to our knees in delight and sorrow.” Marc Bekoff, The Emotional Lives of Animals: A Leading Scientist Explores Animal Joy, Sorrow, and Empathy - and Why They Matter I highly recommend that book where the quote comes from from. It is very entertaining and moving in addition to being scientific. Dr. Bekoff is really a pioneer in breaking through the ceiling of anthropodenial [2] and calling an animal emotion exactly what it is, an emotion. There is absolutely no reason that highly intelligent social mammals, who share a common evolutionary lineage (yes, go far back enough and we are related to mice and elephants too!) with us, would be devoid of the capacity to feel and express emotions. Emotions are at the root of survival, after all. Emotions are ancient. Attachment to offspring and mates creates very powerful bonds. Those bonds (call it love if you will) were selected for during evolution because they are adaptive. If a mother elephant loves her babies, she will protect them and feed them properly, and she will leave more offspring. If she is part of a herd, the whole herd will protect the babies. A male osprey that protects his nest and shares the fish with his mate and their babies, will be more successful than a neglectful bird. Thus, it is not surprising that an animal can feel deep sadness for the loss of babies or companions, or members of the herd or pack. Of course, not all animals grieve, and this is a behavior that is most prominent in social species. Dogs have been observed being depressed or sad after their human parent or doggie friend dies. Elephants in the wild have been shown to touch the bones of dead relatives when they walk by them. Mother chimpanzees are reluctant to let go of the rotting corpse of their dead baby. I think it's fair to call these expressions of sadness at the loss of a beloved animal in their social group grief. I'm not arguing that their capacity for grief or understanding death is exactly like ours, or as deep as ours, but they do feel the loss. And unlike humans, animals can't really fake feelings and emotions. See also this YouTube video: Animal Grief: how animals mourn - a ground-breaking book about animal emotion by David Alderton [1] Home[2] Are We in Anthropodenial?

We are animals, we are apes, and share much more with both of them than what historically humans wanted to accept.

column1: Can I marry a person who was a drug addict 2 years ago when all I want is a peaceful family life with a caring husband? He had no mental trauma leading to drugs, he did this just to enjoy life. Still an alcoholic, but promises to stop after marriage.
column3: The people I have met who became addicted to drugs and/or alcohol were running away from their emotional problems and personal issues. I never met an addict or alcoholic without mental problems who took up the terrible life of an addict with all its risks “just to enjoy life.” If you believe that story, I have a bridge to sell you. The reality is that when addicts gave up their addictions, they are still deeply troubled human beings. Drugs and Alcohol are coping methods The usual reason that people get addicted besides any genetic predispositions is: PAIN The pain can be any form of emotional pain. Of course, as they age, physical aches and pain get added to the mix of emotional pain and become another reason to drink and drug. I have known quite a few addicts in my life. Every one of them is dead today. One of the first rules I learned from my experience is: Never trust an active drug addict. The only former addicts I know who made it out safely went to rehab at least twice, are in ongoing effective psychotherapy with someone who understands addictions, and also attend AA and NA meetings every week. These are not people looking for recreation. Here are some of the main reasons I have heard for why people ended up drinking and drugging enough to become addicts and/or alcoholics:Childhood traumasSexual abuseSeverely low self-esteemExtreme social anxietyFear of being an inadequate adultA sense of aimlessnessHere is how a very bright friend of mine explained his addiction to heroin to me: Heroin structures my day. It solves all my problems and I don’t have to make any decisions. But it is mainly about my pain. I DO NOT want to think about my past or my problems or ………anything. Thinking is painful. Feeling hurts. When I get up in the morning, I know I need to hustle someone or steal something to get the money for a fix. Then I get my excitement for the day: I go uptown to a dangerous neighborhood and give some stranger on a street corner my money. Then I wait. I don’t know if I am going to get ripped off and he’s never coming back, or he will bring me something that will poison or kill me when I take it. Then, I take whatever I get and make another stupid life and death decision. I cook the dope and shoot it and wait to see if I get high or die. If I live, its time to start the whole process all over for the next fix. Add still being an alcoholic to this mix and you can see how desperate the person you are thinking of marrying must be to get away from himself. I do not think you understand what is actually going on in his brain and what his life as an addict and alcoholic was really like. Even if his plan works, and you marry him while he is still actively using only alcohol to help him cope with life and his inner demons, once he gives up drinking—if he ever gives up drinking—he will still need extensive psychotherapy to deal with the issues he has been avoiding. They will surface. What then? Danger of Relapse The danger of relapsing and becoming addicted to drugs and/or alcohol is very high. Multiple stays in a rehab center are not uncommon. Some Questions for YouWhy are you in such a rush to marry him?What is his plan for getting sober?Is this going to be his first attempt?What drugs was he addicted to?How did he get off those drugs?How many attempts did he make before he succeeded?Why is he waiting until after you are married to stop drinking?Why not at least wait to marry until he is off alcohol and sober for a year?Why do you believe he had no mental traumas?Punchline: Ex-addicts face a lifetime challenge to stay “clean.” If you add to the mix that he is still an active alcoholic, why are you in such a rush to marry him? You need to be more realistic about how deeply troubled this man is and the issues he will bring into your marriage. My advice is to either leave him and find someone else or at least delay marrying until he is no longer an alcoholic and has been clean and sober for at least one year. Elinor Greenberg, PhD In private practice and the author of the book: Borderline

column1: How does a narcissist handle a breakup?
column3: To consider how narcissists handle certain things, it can be helpful to consider their idealized false self and how important maintaining the image of that false self is. Narcissists have been emotionally abused/traumatized/neglected at a very young age, causing their emotional development to be stunted at the age of the trauma. They manifest a false self to appeal to their primary caregiver who neglected them hoping “maybe Mommy will love me now.” The idealized false self must be propped up at all costs. The narcissist cannot bear the pain of ripping the scab open to expose the wound of the real self which was rejected by the primary caregiver. The false self must be propped up. Whenever the narcissist hears “You're such a beautiful person!” (or whatever comprises the particular false self) the false self receives a boost. The false self is balanced precariously. There is a part of the narcissist that knows the truth of the real self, with its attendant shame and rejection, which can never, ever be encountered. The reality of the narcissist is dominated by the idealized false self. This, in a nutshell, determines the difference of how a narcissist and neurotypical (NT) handle breakups. An nt is in pain because of the loss involved, based on having love and empathy for the other person. The pain involves the pain due to oneself, the pain of the loved one, the sorrow attached to the death of a dream, and such things. When two lives are bound together as one, a breakup inevitably results in great pain. The narcissist doesn’t care about such things. The narcissist is self-involved, and is concerned about himself, especially in terms of the idealized false self. The narcissist will be thinking about things like: 1. How can I justify my behavior? 2. How can I prove I wasn’t to blame? 3. How can I prove my partner was to blame? 4. How can I benefit from the breakup? (e.g. financially, or can I bag any children, so I’ll have them to take care of me). 5. How can I cause pain to my partner to get back at them for treating me so unjustly? And so forth. Narcissists do suffer pain in breakups, but the pain is due to feeling unjustly treated, not getting what they were entitled to, no longer having the person around to get them to do what they want, and so forth. All of their thinking is self-referential. Their slogan is “I want what I want when I want it,” and their sense of loss is due to being unjustly denied what they want. There is no shred of emotions like grief or remorse or a broken heart or such emotions which are too mature or self disinterested for them to comprehend or experience. column1: Can morphine reduce emotional pain?
column3: Morphine is an extremely potent medication. I have been given it after orthopedic surgery involving my knee. It's pretty wonderful and really takes you away from it all. It is given to people in sever physical pain, including people who are suffering greatly and near death. Morphine is prescribed for physical pain. Please see an actual human doctor or psychopharmacologist if you are in emotional pain. No one on Quora can advise you about emotional pain, which is a very serious concern and can be life threatening. Having said that, there are many psychologists, psychiatrists and other empathic friends and loved ones who you can talk to about emotional pain. Eventually, you can learn how to talk to yourself to reduce your own emotional pain, but you need to learn what tools are available to help. Cognitive behavioral therapy is one such tool. There are also many medications that can help with depression and anxiety and other forms of emotional pain. It takes time. Good luck.

column1: Why is it so hard for addicts to get off of heroin?
column3: Not only is withdrawal hell itself, but life happens. I was clean for over two years when I relapsed, six months after my fiance suddenly passed away. By that time, I felt like everyone had moved on and forgotten about him, while I still had this gaping hole inside me, felt completely hopeless and lonely, and I knew something that would take all that pain away… heroin. So back to hell I went, not caring if I died or had to go through withdrawal yet again, because I only cared about getting relief from that horrible emotional pain I couldn’t bear to feel anymore. I even hoped for death because that would relieve me of all pain, and at least death gave me the hope that I would be with my fiance again, no longer alone. I’ve been through withdrawal many times, and the pain of withdrawal progressed rapidly each time. Addicts know there is an easy way out of withdrawal - simply use again. Even when I could get through the physical torture, the mental and emotional pain hit me even harder. Usually by the third day of withdrawal, even if I was starting to physically feel better, my brain kept yelling at me to go back. That’s exactly why addiction is a disease of the brain. I feel like it is nearly impossible to describe addiction, withdrawal and relapse to anyone who is not an addict. Our brains don’t work the same way, so of course anyone who’s never experienced addiction would question why we continue to use. For me, my brain tells me that drugs are the solution to anything. Feeling down? Heroin will make me feel better. Feeling awesome? Heroin will make me feel even more awesome! Until I’ve been clean for a decent amount of time (more than six months) and I see how living clean makes me feel better than being high, drugs remain my solution.
column9: I can totally relate with you. I am 8 years sober now. Life is much more bearable now. But the addict mind still exists in me. Some days are better than others. Yet I still have the desire to use in the mental aspects. But I don't use. Because I hash through the various things that have changed in my life. Which I am willing to share. 1.) Trust. People that I have know for a lifetime trust me now. Once they didn't. 2.) Love. I have learned to love myself now. Which means I can love others again. Because it is hard to love anyone else. When you don't love yourself. 3.) Respect. At one point in life I had no respect for myself or others. Now I do respect myself and I have the respect of family, friends, co-workers and employers. 4.) Safety. When I used in the past. I didn't care about mine or anyone else's safety. 5.) A home. When I was at my worst. All I had was a sleeping bag and a sidewalk. Now I have a home to be safe and warm in. 6.) Credit. After many years of not having anything to show for myself. Because anything of value always ended up sold. Now I have nice things. Like being able to buy myself new car. Not anyone else's problems. Which became my own. 7.) A real relationship. All of my prior relationships were based on a co'd addiction. Now I have a beautiful lady in my life. She knows all about my own past. Accepts who I use to be. Forgives me for my prior sins. Even though she was never a part of that past. I worked hard to become a real life responsible person. It was not an easy task. But the rewards are great. Yet I still have those old desires. I just do an evaluation of who I once was. Then I look at who I have become. Then I look at everything I can lose. I love who I am now and the life I rebuilt.

column1: What is it like to lose a child?
column3: I lost my husband March 30, 2016 to Gliobastoma Multiforme brain cancer. He was the love of my life and I had spent the previous nine months desperately trying to save his life. After his funeral on April 8, 2016, my fifty third birthday, my father went home looking for his Health Directive, he announced to no one in particular he was next. One week later, he collapsed from a massive stroke and died five days later. He was in the same hospital, with the same doctors. Less than one year later, my thirty two year old daughter, who had five children under the age of 10 had her gall bladder removed after severe pain. One week from surgery, after a routine biopsy of her organ, she was diagnosed with metastatic melanoma Stage IV. She had thirty tumors in her lungs, over fifty in her brain and one in her breast. She was given two months to live. In complete disbelief, I fell to my knees in the driveway as she told me on the phone, and sobbed until my face was numb. I went into denial until she took her last breath. This time, I was not in control of treatment. I had no power at all as none of us did, including her husband, who I watched go through the same frantic pace to save her life just as I did one year previously to save my husbands. Ultimately, despite all the latest cancer drugs she qualified for that gave us hope, she died on December 17th, 2017. The brain tumors killed her in nine months in an eerie re-enactment of my husbands death, who also only lived nine months from diagnosis. I watched her take her first breath at birth and her last upon death. The horror of watching my child die will live with me until I am no longer on this physical plane. I have not stopped sobbing, wailing or crying every day since. There is no way to stop the grief and it never goes away or gets easier. When my body goes into a numbness out of sheer instinct to live, one thought or memory sends it right back to stabbing pain that radiates throughout my body. I lost my will to live. One day, I could not take the sadness anymore. I understand now why mentally ill or depressed people take their lives. When pain is chronic, emotionally or physically, it gets to a point where it can’t be tolerated. I got out the end of life packet that hospice gave my husband and pulled out the morphine. I googled how much was needed to kill myself, making sure I had enough. My youngest daughter called. I told her what I was about to do. Her anguished cries woke me up. I was being selfish. So I stopped. I take it one breath at a time now when the pain becomes unbearable. I meditate, seek mediums and lean on my spirituality. It is life, and to expect things to remain the same forever is stupid. I am one of the unlucky ones, losing half my family in less than two years at such a young age. But it was a wake up call. I am still here for a reason, I just have to finish my lesson so I can go home.
column9: I lost my newborn daughter a year ago, reading your answer made me tear up. You have been through so much and you have fought so hard against the pain, but losing your daughter was the straw that broke the camels back. Your other daughter is so lucky she still has you, and you her. You will have a beautiful bond from all you have experienced together. My other children gave me a reason to get out of bed each day (8, 9 and 12 at the time) a reason to be happy and to create happiness even in my darkest hours. I told my children there will be times when I’m a bit ‘quiet’, I called it my ‘mummy time’ and they would give me a few minutes peace to gather my thoughts. They needed me to guide them through the grief also, which was both a blessing and a curse - but a strong reason to avoid giving up. I wanted to give you a hug when I was reading that, my heart broke for you. I’m so glad that your daughter phoned you, and I hope that love helps you both through this xxx

column1: How do you deal with having a miscarriage?
column3: Every day is different. Like the stages of grief, some days I am sad, some days I am mad, some days I am weepy, some days in denial, solumn, grey, angry at feeling cheated out of having children, introverted, the shame in wondering why my body doesn’t work like it should, hopeful to see my babies someday… I grew up in a very religious community and family, being told my whole childhood that my entire purpose is to grow up and bear children. I got married at 21, and a few years later was pregnant, though I didn’t recognize the signs until I was cramping and bleeding one night. I texted my mother-in-law, asking her if I was having a miscarriage, even though I knew I was. It was Valentines night. I told my husband, and he let out a cheer, told me he was “relieved,” and I was to never talk about it again. I grieved in silence, no one knew. So much pain, heartache , and tears that I had to keep to myself. We divorced a few years later. I remarried at 29, my new husband and I both anxious to start a family. I was pregnant about a year later, and we told everyone. We were so excited, and both felt that it was a girl. We announced it to our families, began planning, and putting together a nursery. Five weeks later, the bleeding started. Which turned into excruciating cramps that made me cry out and scream in pain. We went to the ER the next day, they did an ultrasound and there I saw my little bean of a baby and heard it’s heartbeat. They told me it was irregularly shaped, and would have problems if it survived. It’s sweet heartbeat was slow, at 40bpm. I cried as I saw my baby, struggling to live. They eventually sent me home. The following day was Christmas Eve, and was more of the same pain, blood and crying. Christmas Day came, and I felt better. The blood slowed, the cramps eased, and I thought everything was turning around for the better. That night, I miscarried in the toilet. I stared at the embryo, completely numb. My husband cried and grieved immediately. We buried our precious baby in our frozen garden in Christmas Tupperware. The reality that my baby was gone didn’t set in for me until the next day. My belly felt empty and I was very aware of the void. I cried so many tears for my baby I’d never get to raise. I went to my doctor, they said everything was clear and they couldn’t know why this happened. About six months later, I was pregnant with my daughter, my angel baby that lived. Every day is different, but there isn’t a day that goes by that I don’t think about my two babies that are missing. Mother’s Day is especially hard. I remember their due dates and death days, and lay flowers in my garden for them. They will never be forgotten. Miscarriage happens more than we realize, and if you chose to talk about it, you will find yourself surrounded by others that have experienced the same as you. Some it doesn’t seem to bother, others are immobilized by it. I know I am hesitant to try to have another child, I’ve always said three strikes and I’m out. I think the emotional pain of a third miscarriage would kill me. I don’t think I could handle the grief. Most days I am sad, and ache for my babies. I have a box in my nightstand of the positive pregnancy test, ultrasound, and announcement; I like to keep it close. I am so grateful for my daughter that I get to hold and watch grow. I “deal” by never forgetting, and openly talking about my miscarriages and be a support to others that have to deal with this awful pain. It’s a pain I wouldn’t want anyone else to know, a pain I wouldn’t want anyone to be able to share in. But we can carry each other on until we each find our own peace. I hope you find yours.
column9: Hugs & tears! Very early pregnancy losses aren’t really much recognized by society as sources of “legitimate” grief. There are no “Miscarriage Sympathy” cards & no memorial gatherings or life celebrations for those who never get the chance to live. We grieve mostly alone. I had two almost back-to-back ectopic pregnancies 28 & 30 years ago, & (like you) sometimes think who they might have been now, had they made it to birth. Hang in there! Yeah, there is the old saying about “three strikes”, but there’s also “Third (fourth?) time’s a charm.”

column1: After finding out and researching NPD, I have decided to let my narc back into my life this one last time just to be 100% sure that he is a narc. I intend to document everything. Is this advisable, and what can I do to speed up the cycle?
column3: After finding out and researching NPD, I have decided to let my narc back into my life this one last time just to be 100% sure that he is a narc. I intend to document everything. Is this advisable, and what can I do to speed up the cycle?Oh dear, dear. This is definitely not a good idea. You are planning to walk back into a pit with a poisonous snake, wagering that you can determine if the snake is poisonous without the snake striking you dead. I don't mean literally "dead," but acquiring some death. I understand why you feel compelled. I sometimes think back to 2015. I had left the narcissist a year and a half earlier and I remained haunted by thoughts of, and feelings for, him. What if he wasn't a Cluster B disordered personality, or what if he "only" had BPD and could be helped? Was there a chance we could have made it? Had I left even one stone unturned? I went back to find out. I left again 2 years later, crippled by neck and back injuries, chronically ill from poisoning, and with PTSD. The upside is that I know he is a malignant narcissist, and that nothing can ever change this. The downside is a loss of quality of life. I look back at the emotional pain I was in then, and weigh it against the physical pain I am in now, and I suppose it's a toss. I don't know if I ever could have worked my way out of that pain without going back. But I would advise you to give this option all you've got because, if you go back, it is highly likely you will pay a steep price for the answer you seek.
column9: Thank you Kris, I really hear and appreciate you. See, we’re in a long distance relationship across continents and we’re engaged to be married. It started with the emotional unavailability. And then he showed his lack of empathy several times. And then the subtle insults, criticizing everything about me, talking down on me and my achievements while praising himself. I also believe there’s a lot of lies going on. What finally made me go on to google his symptoms was when when he gave me the silent treatment for 2 weeks to “punish” me for complaining about his emotional unavailability. During said silent treatment, I was so hurt I missed my period due stress related hormonal imbalances. I told him this and he read my messages and ignored me for another one week. I ignored so many other people because I was being loyal to him even though he is in another continent. I feel so betrayed and so hurt cos I loved him so damn much. He was the man of my youth. Or rather, his false self was the man of my youth. Such a mess.

column1: Why did Snape stay loyal to Dumbledore when he didn’t protect Lily? That was their deal. Dumbledore clearly did nothing. If anything, Snape should’ve turned against Dumbledore and freed the death eaters at Azkaban.
column3: Dumbledore kept Snape loyal through a keen understanding of human nature — and some deft manipulation. Dumbledore recognized what he had in Snape: a potentially peerless asset, if only he could be properly motivated. At first, Lily’s safety was the carrot; after her death, however, Dumbledore had a very narrow window in which to assure himself of Snape’s continued cooperation.After a moment or two, Snape raised his face, and he looked like a man who had lived a hundred years of misery since leaving the wild hilltop. “I thought…you were going…to keep her…safe…” “She and James put their faith in the wrong person,” said Dumbledore. “Rather like you, Severus. Weren’t you hoping that Lord Voldemort would spare her?”Dumbledore didn’t merely deflect any culpability from himself here. He flipped the blame game around before it could even get fully started, and did so far more pointedly than Snape had attempted to do. He did not offer words of comfort, did not express regret that the Potters had died on his watch and he had not seen the betrayal coming, but instead reminded Snape of his own failure — of the role (and quite a significant one) that he’d played in Lily’s murder. In scarcely a few sentences he stoked Snape’s guilt, then struck while the iron was still hot.“Her boy survives,” said Dumbledore. With a tiny jerk of the head, Snape seemed to flick off an irksome fly. “Her son lives. He has her eyes, precisely her eyes. You remember the shape and color of Lily Evans’s eyes, I am sure?” “DON’T!” bellowed Snape. “Gone… dead…”This was the big sell — and it required the big guns. At the first mention of Harry’s survival Snape brushed it off; this was James Potter’s child, after all, and he didn’t care a whit about him or his son. But Dumbledore found the open wound and probed, pushing Snape into an emotional spiral before pressing his own case.“Is this remorse, Severus?” “I wish…I wish I were dead…” “And what use would that be to anyone?” said Dumbledore coldly. “If you loved Lily Evans, if you truly loved her, then your way forward is clear.” Snape seemed to peer through a haze of pain, and Dumbledore’s words appeared to take a long time to reach him. “What — what do you mean?” “You know how and why she died. Make sure it was not in vain. Help me protect Lily’s son.”Throughout Harry’s first six years at Hogwarts, Dumbledore was a warm personality, fond of candies and nonsensical jokes and with those ever-twinkling blue eyes; here, with Snape, he was precise and cold. His diction, too, was deliberate and careful; he referred to Lily as Lily Evans, not Potter, and to Harry as Lily’s son. James was deliberately omitted from the conversation because Dumbledore wanted to harken back to the days Snape spent with Lily as children, as friends, with a hope of something more, and doing so ensured that Snape was beside himself with grief and guilt over Lily’s death. The mere mention of the child alone (James’ child) had elicited little reaction, but the memory of Lily — as Snape wished to remember her — was a powerful motivator. Dumbledore’s masterstroke was making Snape’s protection of Harry evidence of his love for Lily — everything he said, from dwelling over Lily’s distinctive bottle-green eyes to the challenging if you truly loved her was meant to hurt, meant to prod and provoke Snape into agreeing. He had loved her as best he knew how, saw no purpose to living once she was gone, and Dumbledore pounced upon the opportunity to define how that love would pave Snape’s way forward. This is not to say that Dumbledore did not appreciate the magnitude of what he was asking of Snape. He acknowledged it himself. But he never forgot who and what he was dealing with: a Death Eater who had carried the prophecy to Voldemort knowing that it spelled the violent doom of a young family and an innocent infant; a man who loved a married woman and would do anything to save her life, yet cared not if the man she loved and the child they’d had were killed. Dumbledore said it in the end; this was the best thing Snape would ever do, and it was a pity that his hatred of the father meant that he could not bear being known to be the protector of the son — and yet that secrecy and that sacrifice, in the end, were what truly saved Harry.There was a long pause, and slowly Snape regained control of himself, mastered his own breathing. At last he said, “Very well. Very well. But never — never tell, Dumbledore! This must be between us! Swear it! I cannot bear…especially Potter’s son…I want your word!” “My word, Severus, that I shall never reveal the best of you?” Dumbledore sighed, looking down into Snape’s ferocious, anguished face. “If you insist…”

column1: Do you believe in black magic? Do you know someone who suffered from its effects?
column3: Sometimes I used to think the entire incident as a mere coincidence and at times not. Story of a widow family. My great grandmother had 4 sons and 1 daughter, my grandfather was the eldest of all. By the year 2000, the second eldest son died in a car accident, after picking up his guests from the airport who was returning back to India from Malaysia. Other than him, everyone sustained minor injuries. Two years later, the second eldest son committed suicide by drinking alcohol, which was mixed with poison. He took this decision to end his life after his 3 sons blamed him for their mother's death, who died of cancer some years back. By 2004, the youngest son died of Jaundice. It was only at this funeral, my parents came to know a story of how my entire great grandmother's family was cursed and bounded by a chain of spell that had lead to the death of his 3 sons. My great grandmother lived in a rented house and in the same compound there lived another family who had the same landlord. On the utilization of space,erupted a problem and had turned to be a verbal abuse. My great grandmother used to fight with her neighbor along with his 4 strong sons. The fight went to a peak, where my great grandfather who was very close to the landlord, complained to him, somehow convinced him and made him to vacate his neighbor. The aftermath of the incident made the neighbor very furious that the family cast a curse on my great grandmother’s family by infusing some evil in few lemons and was rolled inside the compound of the house. My grandfather with no clue picked up the lemons and that's how the entire spell was unleashed.Image Source: लौंग-नींबू के यह अचूक टोटके, रातों रात दूर करेंगे आपकी परेशानी The curse was like, “ The women of the family will witness all her son's death, will go through terrible emotional pain and then she will die, leaving behind no sons to do her last rite at her funeral”. By the same year 2004, somehow I got to hear this story from my parents and I was very reluctant in believing this story. I was like, “Had the story been true, if the black magic works, my grandfather should be next (out of curiosity)”. I waited until the end of the year 2005, but nothing bad happened to my grandfather. I thought it to be a pure coincidence and the story to be a bluff and I brushed it off from my thoughts. By the year 2006, we got a call from my grandmother that, my grandfather was hospitalized due to increase in blood sugar level. And he wasn't serious by then, but within next few days, his condition was worse, went unconscious and died later. All DIL's of my great grandmother became widow. Being a mother, she witnessed all her son's death back to back with a gap of 2 years between the months of September and October. It was just two years back, my great grandmother died at the age of 92 and her last rites were performed by her grandsons. She often used to give us only one advise as never to mess with anyone, especially with neighbors and to have faith in God.

column1: Which is less painful: drowning or burning to death?
column3: I've had the misfortune of being burned over 20% of my body. I was bad enough that I couldn't be treated at a level 1 trauma center. I've also had the misfortune of coming very close to drowning many times. I can tell you that there is simply no comparison. They are also very different. When you start to drown, you mind is filled with panic. You can't really think. Your mind understands that you can't breath in water. You start to realize that your body is running out of air. You want to breath in - badly. You have to fight the urge to breath. Fighting the urge gets harder the longer you're under. Eventually your chest muscles start spasming like they are trying to force air in. That's when it gets very hard to keep your nose and mouth closed. You don't feel pain. You feel panic. Thankfully it's generally over fast. Burning is horrible. It's far worse. When I was burned, I understood what happened instantly (a radiator burst and sprayed me). Instantly the level of pain is beyond description. I could see skin falling off my hands and body. It's almost surreal. You see what happened. You see your body literally falling apart in front of you. You can hear screaming. After a few seconds you realize that it's you that's screaming, but you aren't conscious that you are actually screaming. You want the pain to stop. But you can't make it stop. You realize you need to do something, so you do everything you can. But it doesn't help. Most people pass out and then the smoke kills them. The mind really isn't prepared for that level of pain. It's also not prepared for seeing your body coming apart in front of you. It is worse than you can possibly imagine. Movies, TV, and books really don't get this right. There is no way for people to act with that level of emotion. Up until very recently, most people didn't survive either, so there was no way to write about it. If you burn to death, god help you to make sure it is quick. If you survive, god help you to make sure you go to actual burn hospital. There is no comparison in the level of care.
column9: I've often wondered what it must have been like for people in the Twin Towers to make the decision to jump out a window rather than burn to death. I've often thought I'd make the same choice. Your answer deepens my understanding. Thank you. I'm glad you're well.

column1: Has your adopted child ever left you for his/her biological parent after you raised him/her as a young child?
column3: This is a rewrite of my previous post here. [New update below - 12–24] Our beautiful, outspoken, fearless daughter, whose birthmother chose us to parent her when she was a newborn, moved out of state at age 17 in 2016 to live with her birthmother. The years before had been tumultuous. Where she had once been a kid who exclaimed nearly every day, “This is the best day ever!” she became someone we didn’t recognize. She was bitter, angry, sullen…raking us over the coals with cursing and spite. She was also a talented competitive cheerleader whose coaches loved her. She hated school and many days it was impossible to make her go. Her counselors tried to help, and said she was a good girl with bad friends. I didn’t learn until years afterward that a boy had molested her while she had a sleepover with his sister. She told her friend's father, and the idiot laughed it off — saying it was normal for boys to do that! I was so clueless. I knew something was horribly wrong and began taking her to therapy. We even moved to a different county to get her away from bad influences. Things escalated after we moved to the supposed ‘wholesome’ new area. It turned out drugs were available everywhere. I didn’t know that till much later, either. I kept her in cheerleading because it was the only area of her life where she was succeeding. But in every other way our family was falling apart. Therapy for her, in-home therapy for our family, recommendations to get her an IEP, an uncooperative school, and then I learned she was cutting. Finding her in the bathroom with dozens of cuts on her arm and blood dripping on the tile was a horrifying moment. She wanted to die. She spent a week in a mental hospital. Then another week, and another in outpatient care. I let her get in touch with her birthmother, thinking that having a relationship with her and her siblings might help — but after a year of constant contact with her, her birthmother fell off the face of the earth — no contact. We later learned she had resumed her meth habit. But being cut off with no explanation really hurt our daughter. Then one night she threw a vase of roses her father had given her for Valentine’s Day, gathered shards of glass and ran out into the night. Police, a helicopter search for her…not knowing if she had taken her own life with the glass… Her dad, my husband, couldn’t take it anymore. He moved away, saying I could join him when she was done with high school. I couldn’t be angry at him — I often wished I could run away. But alone with her I completely cracked up — I had no power over her, and lost myself, while she filled the condo she and I lived in with drug dealers and weed, and other drugs I had no idea she was using. A psychiatrist said she had ADHD and put her on Adderall which simply became another drug for her. I had no idea she was sneaking boys in the condo and having sex in exchange for drugs. I had no idea what was going on most of the time. I begged her new school to consider an IEP — by the time they agreed to test her she simply quit going. Then we visited her dad and she accidentally set the house on fire. It burned to the ground, along with our cat and two kittens. She was in agony about it — I was numb. After that it was like she doubled down on destructive behavior. When she stole my car and drove friends and her new boyfriend several hours away to the beach, the police found a gun in a backpack belonging to her boyfriend. The two of them were arrested. That was on her 16th birthday. I was such a sucker. All she had to do was be nice to me and I was like a beaten puppy who was desperate for love. The shopping trips, the movies, the eating out I did with her — all to experience her love again, the fun again…only to discover she was using me — something she shared when cursing me out. The worst was being told I was never supposed to be a mother because I couldn’t have children- that I wasn’t even fit to be a mother at all. My self-esteem was so low by then that I believed her. She refused to attend school anymore and quit cheerleading, so after a lawyer managed to have her put on probation, we moved into the temporary quarters where her dad was living while our home was being rebuilt. It was an isolated area and we thought she’d stay out of trouble there. It turned out GED class was a great way for her to find drugs, sex partners, and trouble. And stepping outside of restaurants so she could smoke was a great place to meet people who know where drugs are. I found a wonderful therapist, but it was too late. She began disappearing for days at a time. Her dad and I were wrecks — was she even alive? Over the past few years she had been held at gunpoint by drug dealers, raped, and abducted. Only her quick thinking and outspokenness saved her life in each case. We were in agony wondering if she was ok. She decided to return to the state and town where she was born because her family there smoked and drank and had plenty of weed. They were more her kind of people than we were. So we put her on a plane and let her go. Watching her walk away from us with out a backward glance was devastating. Yes, the stress of living with her was gone, no more police, or wondering if she was dead or alive when she’d disappear for days, or dealing with lies and manipulation, but once again we didn’t know if we would ever see her again. I sank into deeper depression. Sadly, unbeknownst to us, not long after she moved there her birth mom met a guy and got hooked on meth again. Our daughter ended up taking care of her younger siblings. She was beaten and threatened by the adults. In her misery she hooked up with a couple of drug dealers — the first of which was murdered after being deported. The other’s mom let them live with her for awhile, then kicked them out. They were homeless. Then managed to get an apartment in a bad neighborhood. They both sold drugs. Then our daughter called to tell us she was pregnant. It was the first time in almost two years that she called us mom and dad. She wanted me to come to her. She had quit drinking, drugs and smoking because she knew these things might hurt the baby. I flew out to see her immediately, and, because I had had a lot of therapy, I kept my mouth shut. I helped them with baby things, and tried to get close to her boyfriend. He was a smart and engaging person, but I learned when he was drunk he beat my daughter up. He even stomped her stomach to try and kill their baby. I flew out again to help her birth family throw her a baby shower in the spring of 2018. That same night her boyfriend was murdered — possibly shot to death by a rival gang member — while they were out together. I suppose that was when our daughter reached bottom. She was in agony over her baby’s father’s death, but because she was pregnant she had someone to live for, someone to change for. I can’t say the next couple years were easy. While she regained her trust in us, she discovered her lifestyle had brought very few people she could trust. But she never gave up, and without drugs and alcohol in her system she could think clearly again. Her little daughter brought joy to her life again. She loves her siblings, and stays because of them. I miss her tremendously, and at times I mourn for the years we lost, and long for the days when she was little and we loved life together. I’d give anything to relive those days, when she was so innocent, funny and enthusiastic about everything. To hold her as she sleeps, to have her arms around my neck, her head on my shoulder, for the days when I was the center of her world. Even writing that helps me see that I was too bound up in her, treating her as a best friend rather than a daughter. It is no wonder she wanted to get away — first by becoming everything I had never been, and then by leaving. I needed her too much to fill up my own lonely heart and it wasn’t right to put that burden on her. I am still struggling with depression — it is part of who I am, and the cause goes beyond all that happened with my daughter. But that is my problem, not hers. I hope and pray she continues to be stronger than I am, and I believe she will be. She often says she isn’t going to let her daughter get away with any of the stuff I let her get away with — but at the same time, she forgives me for being who I am. And I never needed to forgive her — I’m her mom. I have enjoyed reading all the comments so much. Thank you all for feeling so strongly about what I’ve written. A few thoughts: After our daughter left, I cried for a year, and then found a therapist. I also started reading everything I could about the experience of adoption through the adoptee’s eyes. The information was eye-opening, to say the least! Part of our ‘healing’ as mother and daughter came because I educated myself on adoption trauma, and began to see she that she wasn’t this terrible daughter who’d rejected her loving parents; she was our daughter who was in terrible emotional pain which caused her to act out in extreme ways. Her actions were a reaction to her emotional pain! It wasn’t about US. It was about HER. My change in perspective made all the difference. I still had a lot to learn about HOW to respond, but I had the right place to start, finally. Update, February 2, 2022 Our daughter is nearly 23 now, and her dad and I are now 60. I’m not sure when I first made this post, but it has been several years. Some people have been rather judgmental in their comments, and all that I can say about that is until you have been an adoptive parent it is hard to understand the emotions and challenges we face. Most people fall hopelessly in love with their children, and adoptive parents are no different. We do the best we can, and when things don’t turn out the way we thought they would we blame ourselves. How could any parent do everything right? When children hit adolescence everything you thought you knew about them goes out the window. I doubt it is any different in families where adoption isn’t part of the story. All I feel now is gratitude. Our daughter is everything and more that she was as a child: a loving and gifted mom of three girls, a devoted wife, outspoken, assertive and beautiful, inside and out. All her therapists in the past referred to her as ‘a tough cookie,’ and that she is. That tough inner strength brought her through years of turmoil, and the loving, warm heart she was born with is in full flower, now. She has found peace. To see her eyes bright and lively again on Facetime, hear her laugh and joke and share her life, her husband and her wonderful little girls with us is a parent’s dream come true. Personally, I am still struggling to find the joy and enthusiasm in life that I once had. Trauma will do that. I know I have not exorcized all my demons when the only bright spot in my days is talking to her. I know that is not how it should be, and I pray I find a way to enjoy life again, so that loving her is only one of many joys. UPDATE: 12–23–24 Two years ago my husband and I moved to the same town where our daughter and her family live - the town where she was born. Now she has us along with her birth family - including her birth mother and father, six half siblings, birth grandparents, cousins, and US nearby - the best of all worlds! Her birth family has overcome many of their own demons, as well, and we are grateful for the relationship we have with her birth mother. Also, our daughter - now 25 - and her husband now have FOUR little girls! Her husband adopted her oldest - so adoption is part of their family, too. And that will be all - my daughter would LOVE more children but they recognize they can't afford it. This fall she started taking classes in hopes of getting into nursing school. Because she didn't finish high school - but got her GED - she needs A LOT of support academically. Finally my degree in education and college experience have been put to good use as we sat side by side by the computer as she took two online classes. Lots of coaching and encouragement from me and her dad resulted in As in both classes!! One of the classes was psychology which gave us many opportunities to discuss our experiences. She said many times in regard to her behavior. "Mom, I don't know what I was thinking! I don't know why I did what I did! I was so full of myself - I thought I knew everything!" She also apologized many times for what she put us through - something that means a lot to us. Many commenters thought I placed too much blame on myself - and I appreciate that. Her career goal: to be a midwife. She gave birth to her last child at home with several midwives present and it was such an incredible experience she wants to become one herself! My son-in-law let me cut the baby's cord…it was incredible to finally see a baby born…what a miracle. I am in awe of how much interest this posting has gotten over the years. Thank you all. PS I have found my joy and enthusiasm again - living here, having four beautiful granddaughters to spoil, and finding peace thru the love of family has brought it back. And our son is moving here to this state, as well!
column9: What an amazing journey you’ve been on and what kindness you’ve shown. My husband and I went through unsuccessful IVF and decided adoption was not for us. This story, despite the reallly difficult bits, is making me reconsider. In awe of you.

column1: If the owner of a cat died, will the cat know, or will the cat think her owner left her and escaped? In both situations, how will the cat feel?
column3: Yes, the cat will know. I run a cat rescue group. We have taken in cats whose owners have died. Some were admitted to the shelter by the extended family who didn’t want to continue to care for their decesed relative’s cat for whatever reason. Others have come to us directly from family members seeking to avoid further trauma to the cat by surrendering them to the shelter environment - which can be very scary and traumatic for cats over the age of 4 months old. So traumatic, in fact, that most older cats - even if they’ve not been surrendered there due to the death of their owner, develop what we call KPTSD - Kitty Post Traumatic Stress Disorder. Much of the work we do with cats post-rescue from the shelter is rehabilitation - both physical as well as emotional/behavioral. Older cats who have developed a deep bond and established routine with a person who later dies and leaves them behind absolutely do grieve the loss of that person. Most will eventually bounce back provided they find themselves in a new secure, loving and caring environment where they can re-group, de-stress and develop new bonds with new people. It can, however, take time - anywhere from 6 months to 2 years. Every cat is different. However, we’ve also had cases where, when their person dies, the cats give up their own will to live. Siggy was a large 10 year old female kitty who had been adopted by her owner when she was a kitten. Her owner died and the family decided they didn’t want to continue to care for her so they surrendered her to the shelter. Shelter staff described her as “a big girl” - and she was. At the time we rescued her, she weight about 18 lbs. As is common in the shelter environment, contagion is rampant and Siggy developed an upper respiratory infection (URI) prior to her rescue so that, on the day she was rescued, I called my vet and told her I’d be bringing her in as soon as our transporter delivered her to me so that they could prescribe antibiotics and administer fluids. However, when our transporter arrived, it was clear to me she was so snotty and sickly that it would be a good idea to have her admitted for a few days for observation. While there, they couldn’t get her to eat. She flat out refused food. Initially we speculated this was because her kitty cold was causing her to be so congested that she wasn’t able to smell the food and probably felt pretty crappy and wasn’t interested in eating. But after a week in veterinary care and a significant improvment in her health thanks to the antibiotics and fluids she’d been receiving daily, she still continued to refuse to eat. Appetite stimulants were administered. Different kinds of foods were tried. Still, Siggy refused food. So veterinary staff began syringe feeding her. She fought them. Gradually, she began to lose weight. She dropped from 18 lbs to 15, then 12, then 10. We decided drastic measures needed to be taken because without nutrients, her organs would begin to shut down. Siggy had a tube surgically inserted into her neck so that pureed food could be syringed into the food and, via the tube, directly into her esophagus. After a week and a half of this method of tube feeding - and attempts daily to put food directly in front of her to see if she would eat, we decided to remove the tube when she began to eat ever so slightly on her own. Unfortunately, once the tube was removed, she continued her hunger strike and nothing could entice her to eat. She was also severely depressed. She sat in her kennel with her face turned to the wall. She showed no interest in interacting with me, with staff, with the doctors. And she continued to lose weight. After a month - and close to $3000 in veterinary expenses in the effort to save her life - her organs did begin shutting down. The day I had to make the difficult choice to agree to euthanize her was tough. She looked nothing like the cat I’d brought them a month earlier. She was skin and bones and just a shell of her former self. At least, when we’d rescued her, there was a little light in her eyes. Not anymore. She had checked out. And it broke my heart to hold her while they administered the medication that would sedate her and then mercifully end her life… because, at that point, euthanizing her was the most loving and merciful thing we could do for her to prevent further suffering and a painful passing (organ shut down). I believe Siggy lost the will to live and wanted to die when her owner died. Life without them wasn’t something she wanted to face - and nothing we could do could give her that will to go on. And that’s one of the saddest and most difficult experiences I’ve had in rescue - when you save a kitty from being euthed at the shelter and still, try as you might, still can’t save them… because they’ve decided they don’t want to be saved. Siggy wasn’t our only case like this - but she was the most extreme. Most cats do eventually bounce back… although they do so tentatively and are much more cautious with people, less willing to form new bonds, far less trusting, can be anxious, can exhibit behavioral issues and can very much go through periods of depression and withdrawal from interaction and activity.
column9: My dad died in October 2017 and left three cats behind. Two were about two years old and the other was much older. I had told him for many years that I would take in any of his cats when he died, and that’s exactly what I did. It took me a while to arrange my house so I could move them in. I needed to make room for catpans more than anything. Every night about the same time, the younger boy yells for all he’s worth. He did it while he was still in his former home, he still does it. I think it might be the same time my father died, though there’s no way of knowing. He was the most uncooperative about leaving, too. I had to trap him in my father’s bedroom and grab him and place him in the carrier in one fell swoop. He yelled all the way to my house. He has taken up a place in one corner on a cat tree that he almost never leaves, except for food and water and (presumably since the spot stays clean) cat pans. He does everything necessary to continue through life, but nothing more. Edit update: Louie (the cat I mentioned above) still yells at the same time every single night and the top of that cat tree is still his favorite spot in the house, but he leaves it to get petted and knock pictures down off the mantel.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: I have accepted it as a part of life. I am 76 and have lost great grandparents, grandparents, parents, great aunts and uncles and aunts and uncles, even 2 nephews and a niece. My boyfriend of 35 years died. Next, I expect my two brothers to go. Most are expected so even if sad you aren’t so surprised. My older brother used to smoke 5 packs a day, he quit but has had heart attacks and half a lung removed. He is 78 and having trouble breathing. Younger brother is 75 but had cancer, liver damage, diabetic nerve pain and water on the brain. He gets tired easy now. I wouldn’t be shocked to lose both in the next 10 years. I stand on my own two feet and not depend on other people, except paid professionals. So far, the saddest besides the little kids was my boyfriend. He was my companion, but he smoked. He started smoking as a child. His parents let him, he knew it wasn’t healthy but kept smoking, after a stroke he was told to quit or he would have another stroke and that scared him, but he got stage 4 lung cancer anyhow. I stayed with him for a year to take care of him and watched him die. It is human nature to die, we all do so need to get used to it.

column1: My parents still don't refer to me with my preferred name and pronouns, how do I approach this?
column3: Parents can be tough. Personally, I’d say it’s time for a frank conversation. I talked to my mother at length about her grief at losing a son and I know that it’s not easy. I’m fortunate, however, to have a mother who got it, who knew that my name and pronouns were important and who worked to make that change. It took her about six months and I don’t think I’ve heard her stumble over it since. So, after 2 years on HRT… your parents have had plenty of time to grieve, it’s time for them to move on to acceptance. They may just need a little shove. Step one, like I said, is a very frank conversation. Sit down with them and explain that it hurts when you’re misgendered and deadnamed. Tell them how it makes you feel. If it helps, share a comic:It’s important that they understand that this is important to you. There are some things your parents may say that are fairly common and it’s important to respond to those: Parent: You’ll always be my son You: No, I’ll always be your child and I love you, but I’m not your son anymore. Parent: I’ve called you [insert deadname here] since before you were born, it’s hard to change You: I know, and I know you’ll make mistakes, but it’s important that you try to change the habit and it will get easier with time. They may have others, just keep bringing them back to the fact that this is important to you, that this is part of respecting the person you’re growing up to be and that while you are their daughter instead of their son, it’s not like you’re a completely different person or that you’ve died… They haven’t lost you, they’ve just lost an idea of you. It’s okay to grieve for that for a little while but after that, they have a daughter that they’re not being very supportive of and that’s not okay. Step two is the really uncomfortable part. Call them on it when they screw up. Start gently and interrupt when they use the wrong thing. Don’t let it slide. You don’t need to make a big deal out of it, but every time they say ‘he’ interrupt with ‘she’, if they use your deadname interrupt with your name. If your parents had invested the effort from the get go to retrain themselves, that wouldn’t be necessary. Since they haven’t, if they still don’t make effort on their own, then start prompting them. After a while, if they still aren’t making an effort, push back harder. I’ve found that getting up from a conversation and walking away from people has a fairly significant impact. You decide how much you need to turn up the heat and how fast. After a frank conversation, you may not need to turn it up at all, they may step up. Correcting parents, grandparents and other family members who watched you grow up is never easy but sitting back and letting them wound you is just going to make it worse.

column1: I recently lost my fiancée whom i was in a relationship with for six years. He died right next to me in his sleep in our bed. I woke up that day and tried waking him to see what he wanted for dinner, completely oblivious to the thought that such a thing could ever happen right.... then i touch him and he’s soo cold, i look for a pulse and nothing. I then looked at his face and that alone confirmed he was really dead. How do i deal with my PTSD? IS HE OK? HOW DO I DO MY PART ON EARTH FOR H I M?
column3: Oh Dear, I’m so so sorry for your sudden loss!! I have been where you are. My husband, (aged 42) died suddenly as well. We were talking in our living room and then he went to let the dogs out. After about 10 mins I went to see why he was taking so long. There he was, sitting in a chair blue. Called 911 and gave CPR until EMT’s arrived. He was dead on the scene. I too had PTSD for a long long time. I could not stop seeing what happened on my back patio in my mind, nor could I stop talking about it with anyone I would be talking to. Now, mind you after he died, I had nobody there for me. After a few weeks, my family told me to literally stop calling and find a grief support group. I have chronic pain issues so I wasn’t working either. With your fiancé’s sudden death, I’m sure you are still in shock. The very best thing you can do is take care of YOU right now. The first 2 years at rough. The grief physical pain of things starts to finally get better after you get through those first 2 years. No major decision making is a good rule during this time. I ended up in grief counseling as I was such a mess I was barely functioning. There, I told the same story over and over again. I basically told the story so much that eventually I got over the need to keep telling it. Then, I went to a grief support group. You can find all the info on grief support groups/classes through any local hospital. I say classes because they start on a specific day and end on a specific day about 3 months later. So, once a week you go and meet with the same people who are in your same shoes. The person running the group is a professional grief counselor as well. During this time, you all share your experiences. There’s usually a topic or exercise for each class. Like…taking a bunch of magazines and cutting out pictures that relate somehow to your fiancé. (Like a vision board) Or, the topic may be how to go through the pain you’re feeling and talking through it and not “going around” the pain by distraction ie., alcohol or drugs etc. At the end of our class there was a memorial event for anyone in our community that had lost a loved one. We got to bring pictures and at the end of the event there was like a movie theater there and it was a slide show of all the people who passed with their full name and pictures up on the big screen. It was very powerful. At this point in time and for the next 2 years it’s all about you and you processing your grief and surviving it. Make sure you are eating healthy and sleeping when you need it. Grief dear one, is WORK! Your body is working on grief 24/7. Right now you need to process the PTSD, (not everyone gets PTSD with the death of a loved one so that’s why you should get one on one counseling for that) grieve for him in the past, and grieve for the future that was taken from you. I was so alone and completely lost on what to do or how to handle it. Even if you have family or friends for support, they have not walked in your shoes. They may feel that they can relate because a grandparent had passed for example. They truly don’t know about sudden death and the PTSD that goes along with that, nor what it’s like to lose someone who shares your life like a fiancé or spouse. It’s different. You are experiencing the 2nd worse person to lose. The worst would be losing a child. Don’t expect people to completely understand it. They won’t unless they have lost a spouse, fiancé or boyfriend they were living with. So, back to your question…the answer is to take care and nurture yourself FIRST. Then, honoring his memory like when my father died of ALS, I helped others with a family member who had the disease. People get together to find a cure for whatever took your loved ones life, and they hold fund raising events where you can honor him with a t-shirt with his name and picture on it. I got a professional sticker over the back windshield of my Jeep that said “In memory of” then his name and below that was his birthday and the day he died. I found some comfort in doing that. Sorry this is so long, but I had a lot to say. Just know that this pain (I imagine it to be a separate being living inside my chest and it’s black and red and oozing.) I call a grief ball, you have to cry it out, talk it out, exercise it out and even scream it out will go away. The grief will always be there, and after dealing with it in the ways I have explained here, 2 years the physical pain of the grief ball will be gone. The beauty of the things around you will return. I promise! So, hang in there!! If you have anymore questions just message me. Hugs, Kari
column9: Hi Kari, I just read your response and it gave me some hope! It has been 9 months and I lost my 52 year old husband to suicide! He was bipolar and manic at tgat time! I found him! I miss him so much! I am seeing a psychiatrist and a therapist and taking medications! Nothing helps! We had no kids together! I am in physical pain too and taking care of my 88 year old non! I guess I am living for her because life is unbearable without my husband! I can’t even get a tombstone for him, it will make it final! I pray to God everyday to turn back time! I want him back! I loved him so much! He had a heart of gold!!

column1: Why is it often harder to cope with the loss of a beloved animal than the loss of a human family member or friend?
column3: I was more sad when my dog died than when my mom/dad/sister/brother/wife/husband/son/daughter died. In a 2013 survey that we conducted on pet loss, we heard this sentiment from numerous respondents. Your question reflects a true issue for many pet owners. Echoing some of the comments below, I suspect that Pet loss is incredibly difficult for two reasons: 1) the human-animal bond is strong and continually increasing and 2) the mourning process for pet loss is often insufficient 1) The Human animal bond is strong – more so now than ever From ancient Egyptians’ cats to the Chinese emperors’ dogs, pets have bonded with humans for a really long time. In the last two decades in America, however, this close relationship has become more mainstream and prominent. Pet ownership has risen to its highest levels, and total pet spend is over $60B/year in America alone. Our pets have migrated from sleeping outside the house, to inside the house, to in the bedroom. Many of our pets eat grain-free food, receive top quality medical care, and travel with their family. We celebrate their birthdays, talk to them, and treat them like people – they are truly humanized in many households. A recent NYT Article was aptly titled, "Dogs are Humans, too" So why are pets so close to us? They can’t talk, and they don’t reason with us and challenge us like our fellow humans. My research in the pet industry (and raw gut feel) indicates that the increasing intensity is due to a few factors: a) A pet’s love is not a function of our success – they have unconditional “love” Our society is increasingly fast paced. Millennials (and other generations) image craft on social media, move from job to job, and are always “connected” - all in the name of forward progress. Keeping up with the Jones’s has reached new heights. But for all of our success (and all of our failure), our dogs just. don’t. care. Bad day at work? Don’t care. Good day at work? Still don’t care. A saying in the pet world says, “I just aspire to be the person that my dog thinks I am.” Bottom line: pets don’t care about all the stuff that stresses us out. They are there for us no matter what in this rat race of life. Whether our pets feel “love” in the same way as humans may be debated, but what we do know, is that their feelings are not subject to our image or success in the other aspects of life. b) Time enhances closeness Pet owners: quick, name 5 people that you will spend more time with than your pet over the course of his 12 year life…waiting….nope (unless you have a lot of children). In general, the amount of time spent with your pet is greater than any human outside your immediate family that LIVES in the house. In most cases, significantly more. Say you work 40 hours a week. That leaves over 100 hours around the house. For many pet owners, those hours are spent with your dog sitting in your lap, sleeping on your head, or begging by your feet. Over the course of 12 years, that means that you've easily spent more time with your dog than almost anyone in your life. c) Physical touch also strengthens our bonds – and our pets are our most touched companion We live in a digital world. We love social media, and we prefer to text, rather than talk. We over work and under play. With the exception of some cool recent pet webcams, our pets don’t have this same luxury. All they have is physical interaction. Fortunately for them, our brains and bodies happen to like that type of interaction. Article: http://www.cnn.com/2011/HEALTH/01/05/touching.makes.you.healthier.health/ Our interactions with our pets help us reach a chemical and perhaps primal part of ourselves, which today’s digital environment may not satisfy. Do you touch your dog more than your spouse (if you indeed have a spouse)? The answer is probably yes. This physical touch further enhances our bond. 2) The mechanisms for coping with pet loss are sparse. While we have spiritual, ritualistic, and secular ways of coping with human death, most of these do not fully extend to our bonded animal friends. a) Spiritually, most major religions do not address pet loss Because the human animal bond has increased exponentially since the advent of most major religious texts, Judaism, Christianity, and Islam do not robustly discuss what happens to pets after death. While many console ourselves with our religious beliefs when our grandparents pass, it raises more questions than answers for our pets. b) For humans, we have funerals, which help in the healing process These serve not only to allow a sense of mourning, closure, and in some cases, celebration, but they also provide the immediate family with a support from other family, friends, and the surrounding community. There is an outpouring of love that helps to support the survivor with the grief process. Despite our close bonds with our pets, rarely do we have this funeral ceremony with the support of family and community. c) Inconsistent understanding requires us to bottle up emotions For humans, there is a relatively consistent empathy for the pain that the person is going through. For the loss of a pet, however, there are two ends of the spectrum. While non-pet-parents think (and sometimes say), “it’s just a dog” or “why is (s)he so sad,” there are others that fully understand. As a result, pet parents are often compelled to keep their grief to themselves, lest someone think that they were weird or overly-dramatic. This prevents them for being able to undergo the grieving process properly. Therefore, the pain is greater…or at least, lasts longer. In summary, pets are really close to some of us, for reasons that have both pre-dated us, and that are unique to today’s society. Further, we don’t have the same systems to deal with the pain. Combined, this can make the process for pet parents as difficult or more so than a human loss. Fortunately, there are organizations out there that are bridging this gap. Pet memorial centers and pet loss support groups are developing throughout the country. The Pet Loss Professionals Association (PLPA) and the International Association of Pet Crematories and Cemeteries Association (IAOPCC) are leading the charge in providing that support. It will never be easy to lose a cherished pet. They are our rock and our support, throughout the highs and lows of our lives. But it’s okay to feel grief. And it’s okay to find people that will support you along the process. I’ll leave you with this poem from Jimmy Stewart on the Johnny Carson show.
