column1: What are the advantages and disadvantages of caring for an Alzheimer's patient at home as opposed to in a nursing home?
column3: I up voted the other answer as it is a very thoughtful perspective from what appears to be a healthcare professional, and exactly the kind of thing I wish I'd found years ago when I reached out to answer that kind of question. My answer may not help as much, but it will be heartfelt and what happened to us during attempting what you are asking about... My grandfather masked the signs of my grandmother's depression and Alzheimer's for several years from the majority of the family. I found out a few years before most others and made a big effort to visit every weekend I could, even once I had married and was dragging my wife along. My grandad realised that getting my grandma active and interested in doing the chore type stuff, brought her back to "reality" and he really appreciated our visits, even when it felt like we were making work for them, we only stayed away when we were sick with a cold or something. Inevitably, he could not keep up the deception forever and it eventually took its toll on his health. During the fairly short course of his illness, he and my grandmother ended up sleeping in twin beds, after sharing one their entire adult lives, to eventually sleeping in separate rooms once he was released from hospital and she rapidly forgot who he was and mistook him for her own father. When my grandfather first became seriously ill, it got to the point that I was driving from Cambridge to Suffolk virtually nightly and every weekend for a couple of months until the rest of the family found out properly and got involved. His deathbed wish was that she stay in the family home as long as she could, which was the most difficult thing possible to achieve at this point of her illness. Without dwelling too much on that immensely sad time for us all, what happened to try and keep my grandma in her home was that my mum, uncle and aunt at first hired a carer for a short period who didn't work out. Then my cousin who was a nurse agreed to put her life on hold for a bit and move in to look after them both, something I don't think, through our grief, many of my family ever truly managed to express our gratitude properly for (myself included). Throughout this period, my grandma (who thought her father had died, once my grandad had passed on) eventually started trying to escape the house (thinking she was now being held captive by somewhat benevolent strangers) and of course that led to whoever was on watch locking her in. I remember one weekend where she climbed into bed with me and my wife and told us conspiratorily that she'd put on three pairs of trousers, two blouses and three jumpers so that we could all be ready to escape in the middle of the night and she could carry her belongings with her. On two other occasions I received worried phone calls from another cousin as my grandma had gone out for a walk together and had "bunkered down" in a neighbours house refusing to let my cousin reason her back into her own home. On both occasions I was already planning a visit the next day so just had to drop everything to get down there and deal with the situation. Perhaps due to the repeated visits over the preceding years seeding some knowledge of me, or maybe because she just preferred boys, she was willing to listen to me a little more than my (female) cousin so after longer and longer negotiations each time she eventually returned home. Eventually the risk of escape or taking a chair to the glazing in the middle of the night was the tipping point, more so than the havoc it was wreaking on our lives (and this was with three families helping out on alternating weekends, AND a live-in family member) and the three "children" decided to put her in a home. Weirdly, I think the timing was more or less right, and while there was a lot of grumbling about being abandoned at first, she was so reverted to her childhood memories that she forgot all notion of family and wound up with a "boyfriend" in the home. He had lost his wife but still wore his wedding ring, and the two of them at first spotted each other's rings and thought they must be married, and a little later, thought they were just dating... They would hold hands etc, and in a slightly odd way, I'm pretty sure she was quite happy in her own little world for a time. She died once she had "lost" her false teeth, with the general consensus that they must have either been stolen by another resident or went down the toilet. The home made no attempt to replace them, inform the family or even mash her food. Once we found out it was just too late and combined with a fall and another hospital visit (even though a brief one) the decline was very rapid. In the later stages of her disease, hospital visits seemed to be the polarising moments... She went in twice for her own accidental injuries, and once with my grandfather towards the end of his life. Each time, she came out radically advanced in her Alzheimer's progression. As per the other post on this question, we (as in the family members) had the opportunity to ward off our guilt by at least trying to honour my grandad's final wishes for a while, but didn't keep it up until the bitter end. If we hadn't taken her to the care home, she wouldn't have had that odd but largely positive experience with her boyfriend in there. As the glue that held out family together, the deaths of my grandparents, or perhaps the money that was left behind basically ruined the best of the relationships, and the separate families drifted apart. I took my little unit and left the UK entirely; thoroughly disgusted with the hospital and the palliative care systems, not to mention the lack of care provided for my grandma at her care home at the end. Um... The moral of the story is that while you should perhaps try to keep someone in their home as long as possible, you have to realise there comes a time where it is not possible any longer. When my grandma went into the care home she was no longer "coming back" to us at all, and at best had some recollection that the people visiting were related to her. My aunt, I think, became one of HER aunts, my mum was referred to as "that nice lady who visited me" and I became her son for a short time in the care home. She took great pleasure in introducing us to the other residents each time, although I sometimes wonder if it weren't quite a clever ploy to get us to say our own names... Dealing with this time is about trying to be there for them, when they don't know who you are and not just saying goodbye and driving away from that awfully compromising place you have had to leave them in... Cherishing the little things and forgiving the childish tantrums and other oddities. It's a horrific disease and probably one of the most painful ways to lose someone, as you have to watch them slowly lose you first; and then themselves, until eventually you end up meeting them as a child. If you can grow to love that child, then when they die... It seems to me that the care that needs to be provided to an Alzheimer patient will actually differ a lot depending on the individual, and strangely, will be based upon things you will never be able to second guess. As the memories start to dissipate, leaving only the earliest behind over time, if we are truly all just shaped by the sum of our experiences, inevitably those people who suffer from this form of dementia will go back to who they were before you were a twinkle in their eye and you just won't know that person, their motivations or what's important to them; or what their care requirements may be.

column1: In "Mary Poppins", why did Mr. Banks have so much money at one point but then lose it all later on?
column3: This must have to do with the sequel as the original Mr. George Banks never lost any money in the movie. (He lost his job at the bank but never any money). And in Mary Poppins the book, it’s made perfectly clear that Mr. Banks never has any real money from the get-go.“…Mr. Banks…said to Mrs. Banks that she could have either a nice, clean, comfortable house or four children. But not both, for he couldn’t afford it.”Mr. Michael Banks, in Mary Poppins Returns, explains to his sister Jane, when the lawyers have come to deliver the notice of repossession, that he had to use his home as collateral for a bank loan he took out when dealing with the loss of his wife and other expenses. This seems to explain that his wife got sick so that her medical expenses racked up, and then her death caused even more expenses. Anyone who has ever had to deal with an expensive sickness like cancer, or the loss of a close loved one can come away with the impression that both sickness and death are thriving businesses, from the burial plot to the coffin, to the flowers and not to mention the obituary and a wake or some kind of funeral, death can take a small fortune to pay for. As the Banks children head out to purchase groceries, we hear the daughter say they will buy day-old bread from the bakery as it is sold at a very discounted price and “that’s what mother did.” This seems to suggest that the family has never had much money at all. We later hear Michael say he’s a painter but that painters aren’t making any money lately. So, it’s explained that he’s a struggling artist with three children and that his wife has had to be extremely frugal, even before she got sick, so they’d manage to get by and put food on the table. It’s possible that, at some point prior, the family did have some money as Michael still has the strand of pearls that his wife once wore. Real pearls, especially the size as they are in this movie, are extremely expensive! I’ve rarely seen a strand of real (saltwater) pearls for less than 2 or 3 thousand dollars. That necklace is the only clue in this movie that this family may have ever had any money. And the fact that they’ve sold off everything else in the house that might’ve fetched a price, yet his wife kept her pearls to the death, seems to indicate that there was sentiment behind them. They are possibly a gift from a loved family member, either her own parents or his, and that’s why, even facing poverty, the family refuses to sell that pearl necklace. [The family also has a Royal Doulton porcelain bowl which the mother said was priceless, but upon research, we find out it isn’t really worth much money. Even today, you can find Royal Doulton bowls or plates for less than $50 online]. The Banks parents have vacated the home and aren’t present as grandparents in this story, seeming to indicate that they’ve also passed away. We can assume that George Banks, who was a keen investor and hoped to be a “giant in the world of finance,” did all he could to set up his children in life. We are told that he put a great deal of his investment in Bank shares that he left to his children, as well as his home, and if there were life insurance companies in business in 1910, you can bet he would’ve had policies for all of his family members. So, for Michael Banks to have ended up so destitute that he can barely afford food means he has really been extremely careless with both his inheritance as well as any profit he’s made from his paintings. It’s almost infuriating that he could’ve ended up so bad off! It’s likely that, despite having very little money, he gave his wife a lavish funeral well outside of his means. He took a bank loan to pay for it, and while the terms of the loan may have been fair and within his means, his grief after her death rendered him temporarily even more careless to the point where he completely forgot to make his monthly payments on the loan, oblivious to the reality that the terms of the loan would default at three months and his home could be taken from him since it was what he used for collateral. While he’s most likely a very loving and doting father and husband, Michael Banks is extremely stupid with money and he’s very, very lucky his father came before him and managed to invest very wisely for him and that he earned the loyalty and respect of his colleagues at the Bank where he worked. Those investments end up saving his son from financial ruin by the end of the story.

column1: How did you handle the death of your grandmother?
column3: Part 1 of 3:Getting Closure 1. Feel your emotions.You will go through the process much more easily if you do not try to fight or hold in what you're feeling. There is no right or wrong way to grieve. There is no time-frame in which grief ends. Try to open yourself up to the anger, sadness, confusion, or abandonment feelings that come over you. As time passes, you should begin to heal and feel better. Some grandchildren may take a grandmother's death harder due to the duration and closeness of the relationship, the cause of death, or how other family members are reacting. Adults should be sure to demonstrate authentic grief and let any children or adolescents know that it's okay to cry or be sad. 2. Think about what you learned from knowing her.Take some time for yourself to understand your thoughts about your grandmother's death. Write them down in a journal if you feel like that helps. Remember the good memories you had and the impact she had on your life. Ask others to share stories about the long, full life she had. This should bring you comfort knowing that her time on earth was filled with family, love, and interesting experiences. 3. Attend the memorial.Attending the memorial service is a terrific way to get closure from your grandmother's death, and offer support to other family members. If you are a minor, it will be up to your parents and your age as to whether you are allowed to attend the funeral or memorial service. If you have a desire to attend, express your opinion to your parents. Then, they can explain to you what will happen at the service and determine if you will feel comfortable attending. They should know that attending the memorial can help you get closure and celebrate your grandma's life. 4. Create a memory box or book.It can be helpful to process your feelings about your grandmother's death while making a memory box or book. Choose some of your favorite memories in the form of photos and mementos that you shared with your grandmother. Ideas for what to include in your box are endless--try using recipes, favorite song lyrics, or collecting short stories about her life to put inside. Decorate your box/book to your liking. If you are younger person who was not allowed to attend the memorial service, this can be a creative activity that brings you closure. However, even if you did attend the memorial service, it could still be helpful to connect with your memories and talk it over with someone while doing this creative activity. 5. Understand the death.Ask questions to come to an understanding of your grandmother's death. You might get closure by learning that, after a long illness, your grandmother is no longer in pain. Depending on your age, your ability to understand death will vary. Really young kids, around age 5 or 6, often think in literal terms, so saying "Grandma went to sleep" might make them worry that the same will happen to them when they sleep. Parents should reassure kids that they were not responsible for the death because some kids fear a death happened because of something they did. For example, the child might think Grandma died because he didn't visit her often enough. Older children and adolescents above the age of 9 can often understand the finality of death and that everyone eventually dies. Part 2 of 3:Getting Support 1. Spend time with family.The grieving process is only intensified when you pull away and isolate yourself from others. Remind yourself of the people still here and that they, too, lost an important family member. Fight the desire to pull away or appear strong and seek comfort from loved ones who are also mourning. 2. Turn to your faith.If you have religious or spiritual beliefs, now is the time to search out those verses or quotes that remind you that things will get better soon. Participating in religious/spiritual functions can further help you find closure, connect with others, and provide you with hope for the future. Research has shown that people with strong spiritual beliefs--because of the principles described about human life and existence beyond--tend to resolve their grief sooner than those who do not. If you are a non-believer, secular rituals, such as packing up grandma's things or regularly visiting her grave, could help you resolve your grief and find comfort. 3. Join a support group.A bereavement support group can help you and other family members come to terms with the loss. In the groups, you will be able to listen to and share your own feelings and stories with others who are also grieving. These support groups will provide coping resources for overcoming grief over the next several weeks and months after the death. Many communities have free support groups for people who are grieving. These may be held in a local church, hospital, or hospice. 4. Go see a grief counselor.If you find that you continue to heavily mourn the death and cannot function in your daily life, you may need to seek professional help. A grief or bereavement counselor can be effective with helping you process the loss of your grandmother and learn how to properly cope. Grief counseling is especially useful if you're experiencing prolonged grief or if your grandmother's death was especially traumatic in some way. Part 3 of 3:Moving Forward After Loss 1. Relive the memories.The best way to feel better after losing a loved one is to remember the good times that you shared. The times you laughed, did silly things together, whatever fond memories you have of the person who has passed away. It also may be helpful to revisit your memory box or book as time passes, so that you don't forget all the great times you had with your grandmother. 2. Take care of yourself.When we're mourning a loved one, it becomes easy to neglect ourselves in favor of lying in bed all day with a box of tissues. Try to get up and get outside to get some fresh air. Eat regular, balanced meals and aim for some physical activity a few times each week. Self-care activities also mean nurturing your body and spirit. Get a massage, take a relaxing bath with scented oils, meditate, write in your journal, or steal a few hours away to read a good book. 3. Support other family members.Concentrating on helping out others can help you process and move through your own grief. Try to be there for your parents and siblings when you are all going through this. One of your parents lost their mom, which is a terrible loss to bear. Remind them that you love them and offer to do small things that bring them comfort like making tea or lighting a fire. 4. Channel some part of her into your life.It can be gratifying to know that your grandmother lives on in your memories. You can continue to celebrate her life by picking up some activity or hobby of hers and making it your own. Consider learning to sew if she was really good at it, or take the time to make some of her traditional family recipes when you cook or bake. Try introducing someone special in your life to an activity you used to enjoy with your grandmother, like baking or doing a craft. That can be a way to celebrate her life while still moving forward. You might also keep fresh flowers in the house or light a candle each day as a way to remember her. 5. Know that it's okay to smile again.You may feel guilty for having fun or laughing after your grandmother's death. You might think it's disrespectful to her memory to be happy. That's not true. Hopefully, your grandmother lived a nice, full life and she would surely want the same for you. The grief process can feel very dark and bleak; don't be afraid to let a little light seep in by way of fun nights out with friends or board games with your family.

column1: How are you ever supposed to move on from a parent dying? My dad died less than 2 weeks ago from stage 4 pancreatic cancer. He had just turned 50, he should've lived so much longer. I feel like I was robbed of him. And I don't know what to do.
column3: First of all, let me offer my condolences to you for your loss. ❤️ Losing a parent while they’re still fairly young is so very difficult. I lost my dad when he was only 14 years older than your dad 3.5 years ago now. It’s still not easy, even years later. It’s hard enough to lose someone when they’re a little older and have lived their life through. I lost my last grandparent almost a year ago. My grandma was 87 years old, and she and I were close (despite a few disagreements over the years). In a lot of ways, she’s the one who really raised me, since my mother was less than thrilled about having a daughter instead of the son she expected to have. But it was her time to go. She was in a lot of pain, even though she didn’t want to admit it, and stubbornly refused help from the nearby family members (I lived about 4 hours away and couldn’t do it myself). When she passed away, I was very sad, but she had seen a lot over the years. She had lived to see her 2 children grow up, then her 10 grandchildren, and then saw her 5 great-grandchildren. She was very loved, and I think she flew away at the right time for her. My dad, in contrast, had lost both of his parents and his older sister years before. Losing his mother 5 years before, my other grandma (a sweet but sassy lady who I take after quite a bit) broke his heart, I think. He took care of her alone for years before she passed away. After she passed, he was at something of a loss. I could tell something was off, but he wouldn’t tell me. He wouldn’t talk about it. I couldn’t move closer to him, but I tried to encourage him to move closer to me. He only smiled his little smile and said he would think about it. That was his way of saying no. Then Covid hit and the whole world shut down. He was still hanging in there. I knew he wasn’t doing so well, but I couldn’t go to him due to travel restrictions. It didn’t help that he lived almost 13 hours away by car. Nobody was going anywhere. Then, as everything started slooooowly opening up, he had his final heart attack and passed away. Like you, I felt robbed. I should have had 15–25+ more years with him, but I didn’t get that. It was like a cruel joke. I had to clean out his apartment, tears running down my face the whole time. I had to make all the arrangements, sign everything with Dropbox, drive out to California to pick up his ashes, and deal with an unholy legal mess that I won’t get into here. That last bit was like insult to injury, and the guy who caused that whole tangle, I would love for him to get hit by a bus. Repeatedly. At any rate, moving on was rough. I’m not going to lie. My dad and I were close, and losing the last of my family on that side was hard. Losing one of my parents when still at a relatively young age was even harder. My dad was 22 years old when I was born. He should have been able to live longer than 64 years. He wasn’t very old, just like your dad wasn’t very old. It isn’t fair, and you have every right to be angry. I wish I could say that it gets better, but you’re always going to miss him. What I can tell you is that someday it won’t feel so raw. You’ll probably always think it was terribly unfair. You’re going to see others with their fathers, and you’re going to feel that pang of loss. Father’s Day is going to be excruciating for a while. Your dad’s birthday and other holidays are going to hurt. But, as time goes on, you’ll find yourself smiling at the memories more often than not. The time you did have with him will become precious. Physically he can’t be with you anymore, but he’s still there in your heart. He’s always with you. Nobody can take that away from you. What can you do? Put one foot in front of the other, and breathe in and out. Remember to breathe. Write about him. Write to him, if you’d rather do that. Make a shadowbox for his memory. See a therapist or join a grief support group. Do whatever you need to do to get out your emotions. I remember dreaming about my dad a few weeks after he passed away. We were standing in the old neighborhood near the old house where I had spent 14 years of my life, with the night sky full of stars that I remember from my childhood (where I live now doesn’t have as many stars), and I talked to him about everything that was in my heart. I don’t remember the conversation, but I do know that I told him everything that I needed to say. The love just flowed between us. Then I woke up. You’ll be ok, darlin’. You’ll be all right. It may not seem like it now, but you will be. Promise.

column1: How do you comfort your friend/someone close to you who's mourning and grieving from the death of their family member? What should I do?
column3: Listen to them. Allow them to cry and to speak of what the loss means to them. If they want to talk for an hour, just listen and show kindness. Be patient with your grieving friend. Don’t be embarrassed by their grief, don’t worry about saying the right thing. There really is no right thing to say. The best thing you can do is to offer a shoulder and an ear and a hug. Don’t let their grief run you off. Be present. Be available. Be patient. Grief is never easy to deal with. Be kind.

column1: How does the narcissist feel when a loved one dies?
column3: Narcissists view the death of a loved one from the perspective of a victim mentality or a “what about me?” point of view. A self-absorbed person will still feel the pain of loss but will do so from an entirely different viewpoint in comparison to someone suffering from seemingly normal grief over the death of a loved one. NPD distorts the reality of loss and turns it into something that the narcissist must now learn to adjust to despite the adverse effects on their overall well-being. For example, a spouse may mourn the death of their partner because now they must live with half the income they once had. A parent who tragically loses their child may view the child’s death as a punishment to them for past wrongdoings. column1: What is the history behind shaving one's head after the death of a loved one in some Hindu traditions?
column3: Possible scientific perspective: After a person dies, the body starts getting attacked by the elements and the process of decomposition is initiated. This may lead to several potential threats to health and hygiene of the ones in the same house as the deceased. This is why the family members of the deceased shave their heads and bath after the last rituals are performed. Further, it is also common practice to wash and clean the home that housed the deceased person's body and to close the kitchen for a day. All these sound like health related precautions to me.

column1: Harry and William are to press ahead with an emotional reunion. When will the brothers reunite?
column3: In the light of HRH, Prince Philip, the Duke of Edinburgh’s death yesterday, there has been news that Prince Harry wants to return for his beloved grandfather’s funeral, to mark his death and pay respects to him. Therefore, it seems that Princes Harry and William will, at last, reunite on the day of Prince Philip’s funeral, or a few days before, when Harry arrives in England. Now, I don’t know how reliable Harry’s return may be, but I truly think he will return to mourn his grandfather, as the two used to be incredibly close and had a similar sense of humour. Both princes were hilariously funny, and I think that created a close connection between the Duke of Edinburgh and his grandson. However, I genuinely don’t think that Meghan Markle will be accompanying her husband, if you’re wondering, for quite a few reasons. But anyway, back to Prince William and Prince Harry. The two haven’t seen one another in over a year, and the bombshell Oprah interview didn’t help in their reconciliation, either. The brothers are going through a tough time in their relationship, as Harry is now based in California with his wife and son, and Prince William remains in London with his family. It is unsurprising to me that Prince Harry wanted to go back to England to see his dear grandfather for the last time, as we all are, I assume, shocked at the news of the Prince Consort’s death.It will possibly, if Prince Harry does attend Prince Philip’s funeral at St. George’s Chapel, be a very sad reunion for Princes William and Harry, as the both of them loved the Duke of Edinburgh terribly. Seeing their wonderful grandmother, Her Majesty, the Queen be devastated will be difficult for the brothers as well. As of right now, we cannot be sure if the funeral will help join the brothers together again, or if it will pass with no improvement of their relationship. I find it extremely sorrowful that the Princes may have to go through the death of a family member together once again, as they did for the mother, the Princess of Wales, in order for them to heal their brotherhood. With the rule being only thirty attendants at funerals due to the COVID-19 pandemic at the moment in the UK, not many people will be allowed into the private service commemorating and remembering the brave and lovely Duke of Edinburgh. Hopefully, Prince Harry, Prince William and the Duchess of Cambridge will all get to see each other again and seek comfort in one another, as these are clearly terribly sad times for the Royal Family. Meghan Markle on the other hand? There is an EXTREMELY slim chance that she would return, and to be honest, I don’t think the Windsors need her there to ruin an already devastating moment and day for them.I and so many others were sad to hear of Prince Philip’s passing, and I, in particular, was very upset to have lost my favourite member of the Royal Family. The Duke of Edinburgh lived a great life of service and purpose, and he will always be remembered by the people of Britain as a brave man, who was always funny and himself at every engagement. Best of wishes to the Windsors, this must be so very hard for them to come to terms with. Long Live Prince Philip: June 10, 1921 - April 9, 2021.

column1: What is the most extreme example of human willpower and discipline?
column3: A Woman Finds Her Daughter’s ‘Dead’ Rapist: people are in awe of her “willpower” A woman from a remote village in Bihar, India tracked down her daughter’s rapist after he was declared dead leading to the closure of the case. The rape convict, Niraj Modi, has been sentenced to 14 years of imprisonment for raping a minor girl and his father to seven years for forgery, cheating, and dishonesty. Modi, a 39-year-old man who was a school teacher at a government school, was accused of raping his 12-year-old student, a minor girl, in October 2018. The girl was attacked while she was by herself in a sugarcane field, and her assailant threatened to post a video of the assault online to keep her silent. Soon after a complaint was lodged by the survivor’s mother, and Modi was arrested. But, he was out on bail after merely two months in prison. In February 2022, Modi’s father Rajaram Modi, who is over 60 years old and works as a farmer, travelled to a court nearly 100km (62 miles) away from the village, with a lawyer to claim that his son died on February 27, 2022, at their village home. In order to get a death certificate issued, he provided two pictures from the cremation, receipts of the firewood bought for the ritual as evidence, signatures and the unique biometric identity number of five villagers as per Indian laws. However, as per a 54-year-old law, the authorities didn’t question the cause of death.Two months after this, the local authorities issued a death certificate and the court closed the case in May 2022 as the “only accused in the case” was dead. However convinced that this was a forgery, the girl’s mother was the only person who suspected that the teacher had faked his death with the help of his father. The mother said that she went from one home to another in order to enquire if Modi was really dead and not to her surprise, nobody had heard of the news. Following which, she went to the court urging an investigation into the matter. In May 2022, she also wrote a petition to the local official claiming that the death certificate was issued based on forged documents and it needs to be investigated. Soon, investigation began and the authorities demanded more and fresh evidence from Modi’s family regarding his death including photos of the "deceased after his death, of the cremation, of the burning pyre, the last rites and [fresh] testimony of five witnesses". As a part of the investigation, members of the village council met the inhabitants of the 250 families in the village. It appeared that no one was aware of Modi's death. Hindus often only shave their heads as a sign of mourning if a close relative passes away. However, none of the Modi family members had done so. In fact, Modi’s own relatives did not have the information regarding his death.After Rajaram failed to provide fresh evidence of Niraj’s death, he was questioned by the investigative office again. Following the investigation, it was confirmed that Modi’s death was faked. The officers found that the teacher had falsified the signatures of the parents of five of his students' parents on a document requesting his own death certificate. He informed the parents that in order to set up the students' scholarships, he would need their biometric identity numbers. The officials, then, cancelled Niraj Modi’s death certificate and charged his father with forgery and in July 2022, the case was reopened. The mother’s relentless battle to track down her daughter’s “dead” rapist came to an end finally and in October last year(2023)he was convicted for his crimes. Keep smiling Keep shining

column1: In the Godfather movie, how would someone approaching Michael with a peace summit - be an indication that such person (Tessio), was a traitor? What was it about an invitation to such that would trip Vito and Michael into realizing he was a traitor?
column3: It was the simplest, cleanest way for a powerful, experienced gangster to overcome a weaker, inexperienced one, by pretending to extend a hand in peace, while holding a gun behind one’s back with the other hand. Offering a meeting under the guise of suing for peace, as a setup to perform an assassination, is the Mafia’s version of baseball’s, the “hidden ball trick.” If you know anything about the “hidden ball trick,” then you’re probably aware, it almost never works, except against amateurs and rookies — and veterans who have become full of themselves and think they are bigger than the game. But most veterans know better than to take their foot off the base before they see exactly where the ball is. It’s the amateurs and rookies who tend to make the mistake of not paying attention. And, while he lived, Vito Corleone would never have been fooled by such a ploy. As others have pointed out, the ruse has a long and distinguished history within the annals of the mafia. But because of Michael’s perceived lack of experience, no one believed he would see it coming — Tessio included. That’s what Tessio was banking on. Vito had passed away unexpectedly; the Corleones were in mourning; Vito’s sons had been particularly close to him. It was to be expected that Michael would be in turmoil emotionally, to not be thinking clearly, and to assume all members of the Five Families to consider this moment to be a ceasefire by all parties. Sure, they were technically no longer at war, but tensions always run high in the underworld; there’s always someone with a finger on a trigger and their eye peering through the crosshairs. It would be easy for Michael to assume that after the death of someone as important as Vito Corleone that all the other families would sort of bow their heads in respect and order their soldiers to set their rifles on their stocks in the at-rest position. And to be fair, that is… what happened. It’s just that the ceasefire only lasted through the end of the day of the burial. After that, all bets were off. The ace Michael had up his sleeve was that he wasn’t viewed by anyone in the underworld as a veteran of the business and that included Tessio. No one thought Vito might tell his own son how to play the game and call anyone’s bluff. Someone in another answer mentioned, quite accurately, that Vito and Tessio had employed this ruse three decades before in finally assassinating another head of a competing family, and Vito had seen other gangsters fall to the ruse. Tessio and Barzini both knew how it worked and because the rules of the Five Families required a meeting to resolve issues before going to war, it would look like a general, feel-good get-together to wipe the slate clean and set the new Corleone regime off on the right foot. It appeared to be the easiest way to get rid of Michael, by catching him unaware, when he was supposed to be mourning the death of his father and could be assumed to be at his most vulnerable psychologically. Vito just happened to be a man of far-reaching vision and he passed on his knowledge and experience to Michael, who was, himself, never anyone’s fool to begin with.

column1: Why do people get upset when celebrities die? Why do we mourn the loss of celebrities we never met in person?
column3: This is a great question that is very popular on the internet. To me, it seems ridiculous that some people get so upset by the deaths of celebrities like Prince, Robin Williams, David Bowie, Carrie Fisher, etc. Don’t get me wrong — I like all these artists and their works, but I don’t understand the level of intense emotion exhibited online by people who obviously didn’t know these celebrities personally. Here’s what I found on the internet which explains the phenomenon of heavy celebrity mourning: 1. Given the nature of media, we may have the illusory feeling that we have a personal relationship with celebrities. Excerpting from Decoded Science:In the 1950’s, two sociologists, Donald Horton and Richard Wohl, coined a term: parasocial interaction. The term describes the phenomenon in which the audience feels they have a relationship with the celebrity, despite their actual distance. Mass media gives the viewer the illusion of having a face-to-face relationship with the performer. The association with the celebrity is so strong, that the viewers sense that the celebrity actually exists in their physical world. Although the relationship is one-sided, people can strongly identify with celebrities. When a famous person dies, the significant relationship feels especially strong. The sense of grief can be overwhelming to fans, especially if their peers don’t understand why they are so sad. Social media can help fans connect in their sadness, to offer tribute to the dead celebrity and solace to one another.Excerpting from The Huffington Post:We see a big outpouring of grief when a celebrity or public figure dies especially on social media sites. The expression of grief is as if they were part of our family or group of friends. In a way, famous people are an extension of our friends and family. Although we don’t know them and probably have never met them, they are very much a part of our lives as we know so much about them. Online we could watch where they shopped, dined and took holidays. They were readily available to us on gossip sites as well as in their day job in drama series, films and TV shows. As we have such a lot of access to people’s lives they become part of ours. In the case of James Gandolfini, he was the main character in The Sopranos which was one of the most successful TV shows of the late ‘90s and early “noughties.” We watched and loved the program discussing the twists and turns of the plot over six series until the last episode. Then as the final episode finished airing, a bit of us died; it had been a constant in our lives for eight years, and it had come to an end. The program and characters are a part of us as they have been around for eight years, longer than some friendships! In our memory, it is part of a particular time of our life and the memories that are evoked remembering where we lived , who our friends were, parties, holidays it is all part of a big picture, a part of our youth revisited. It also affects on a more personal level if they are close in age to our own. In the cases of Whitney Houston and Michael Jackson, it was felt that at around 50 years of age they were too young to die. We grew up listening to their music and looked up to them as role models even when perhaps they were not appropriate ones. Diana Princess of Wales not only was very young, but also had two young boys; the fact that she was in such an awful car crash was a big shock. A a celebrity death can remind us of friends or family who have died and can replay all the feelings of grief and loss. . . The effect of a celebrity death feels like part of our youth has died and with the loss of Lou Reed this week that is very much reflected in the tributes to him. A loss of a little bit of what makes us who we are, the people who helped form how we are now. We align ourselves to famous people who are similar to us, we aspire to be like and who we look up to as role models and so they have an impact on us at certain times during our lives. When they die it is like a part of us has gone too and we will never get that back. It reminds us we all mortal and that we are still here and to make the most of our life, at least for a while.2. When someone who contributed so much to our culture dies, many people experience this loss like a family member dying. Excerpting from Vice’s April 2016 interview with Theresa Martinez, an associate professor of sociology at the University of Utah:[Discussing Prince’s death] It's not that Prince died, it's that an icon died. When David Bowie died, same thing, when Glenn Frey [of the Eagles] died, same thing—or when Robin Williams died. All these people are related to our understanding of ourselves, as a culture. We feel like it's a family member. I mean, people cried when John Lennon died. They didn't know him personally, but he was like a friend in their head, a person that they listened to and they absolutely loved and felt connected to. . . The thinking is, I loved that song! I loved that film that he was in! Awakenings is one of my favorite films and I can't believe Robin Williams is dead! As opposed to the people who are talking about "celebrity." (That thinking is, to me, very douchey.) For me the death of Prince is about when I was dating my ex-husband and we were listening to "Little Red Corvette" and Purple Rain and going to see Purple Rain in the theater. That's a memory for me. It's a memory of family. It's a memory of America, of American culture. That's why I think Bowie's death and Glenn Frey's death and all these deaths are significant to us. Not just because they're celebrities but because we've been listening to them since we were children, since we were adolescents. It's bigger than a celebrity question, and more important: It's an ethos question, of what our culture is.

column1: Who had the saddest life in history?
column3: Her mother died when she was six years old. She had a bad relationship with her father and stepmother. She battled depression, bipolar disorder and chronic migraines. She watched her husband and nearly all of her children die in front of her. She tried to kill herself and failed. She slowly became more unstable and was later institutionalized. She became estranged from her last living son until her death. She died alone.Mary Todd Lincoln is one of those strange historical figures who never really caught a break in life. If there was any way to sum up her existence it would the phrase “She didn’t deserve what she got”. Mary was born the daughter of a wealthy American merchant and received a good upbringing. She was well educated, witty and despite having a strange relationship with her family had a stable life. She was courted many people due to her social standing and she found a lifelong companion in a rising local star, Abraham Lincoln.Though certainly not a perfect couple, the Lincolns were damn near close to it. Abraham and Mary loved each other dearly. Both supported each other to the best of their abilities and both understood each other. Through toil and trouble they stayed together, even when it seemed the world was ending. At least for a while. Many people through out time have experienced tragedy and have pushed through their sadness and moved on to success and better mindsets. Mary Lincoln was not one of those people. It wasn’t one thing that broke this woman. It was many terrible things in her life that slowly destroyed her stability and state of mind. The first event came when her and Abe’s second child Eddie died of tuberculosis at barely 4 years old.The death of Edward left the Lincolns nearly inconsolable and even after the birth of their next two children, Thomas and William, the memory of Edward haunted the family. And then came an even greater tragedy, the American Civil War.The war had come about due to long standing national issues related to the system of Slavery in the United States, finally boiling over after Abraham Lincoln was elected to the office of Presidency. Eleven American States seceding from the United States and forming the Confederacy. What should have been a moment of happiness for the Lincolns was tarnished by this new catastrophe. Now war is terrible, but so rarely has a war tested people so much as it does during a Civil War. The Lincoln family especially suffered this time. It was honestly stacked against them from the start, especially against poor Mary. Mary was silently hated by the majority of the government Since her family were Confederate sympathizers (and several of her brothers even fought for the Confederacy), Mary Lincoln was intensely disliked by many members of Lincoln’s cabinet. She was unpopular and many of her detractors took any opportunity to criticize whatever they could about her, especially her spending habits. This hatred was entirely unfounded however. Mary was loyal first and foremost to her husband and would never betray him or the country he served. The Lincolns lost another son. The straw that nearly shattered the Lincoln family was the death of their third son William, who died after a terrible battle with Typhoid Fever in 1862, the darkest days of the Civil War.Abe and Mary fell into a great depression. Abraham wept in private and Mary was bedridden for weeks after. After William’s death, Abe threw himself into his work and his remaining children, desperate to distract himself from the loss of a second child. Mary on the other hand was beside herself. This is where her mental problems began to become more apparent. She became irrationally afraid that somehow her remaining two children would die and her depressive episodes became more common as she mourned her second son. She withdrew from her expected duties as First Lady and was prone to public outbursts and emotional instability. Mary watched her husband die. The photo on the left is Abraham Lincoln before the Civil War and the photo on the right was taken after.You can literally see him age 15 years in two photographs. The war weighed heavily on Lincoln. War is hell and the men who fight it are burdened beyond years. Lincoln was fighting to preserve the country he had grown up in. He loved the United States and was not about to let it be divided by the evils of slavery. He worked his ass off to save his country (small wonder he’s still beloved so many years later) and he paid the price. Now consider his wife. Imagine choosing someone to spend your life with, raise their children and comfort them in their most intimate moments. Imagine being the shoulder to lean on for the person who must be strong. The person who has to not only save the nation they love but take responsibility for an entire war. The victories, defeats and the effort to keep the fight moving forward. It’s on them to do the job no one else can. Mary Lincoln loved her husband. She watched him bear the weight of the future of America on his shoulders. She was there for him as he wept to the thousands dying in the field. She stood with him as he wrote speeches and advised him on the right words to say. She saw his face wrinkle from sleepless nights and his once mighty frame fade from the burden of leadership. The war killed Abraham Lincoln. It killed him the way a severed limb drains blood from a body. Slowly. Mary was there for him, hoping with all her heart that his sacrifice would be worth it. That he would win the war and then they could spend time together and heal. And then all of that was stolen away.During an excursion to a play alongside friends, the President and Mrs. Lincoln were noted be sat close together in a high rise balcony at Ford’s Theatre, holding one another’s hands. Mary whispered to to Abraham "What will Miss Harris think of my hanging on to you so?" The president replied with a smile, "She won't think anything about it". That was the last conversation Mary had with her husband. Minutes later she was covered in his blood. Abraham Lincoln was assassinated April 14, 1865, just days after the Confederacy had been defeated. He was shot in the back of the head at point blank range and died a few hours later.Mary was inconsolable. She was so consumed with grief that she had to be forcefully removed from her husband’s deathbed. She was dragged away sobbing. It’s almost cosmically perfect that Lincoln died just as he had won the war and ended all the suffering. He should have been given time to celebrate and be with his loved ones. Instead he got his brains blown out and Mary was left bereaved. At this point it just becomes a long train of tragedies that continue till Mary’s death. I’ll try to sum them up as best I canShe had to fight for compensation. Being widowed meant that without Abraham, Mary had limited income following the war’s end. She had to basically beg for money to prevent her and her remaining sons from becoming destitute. Even then she almost didn’t get anything from the US government.She lost another son. A few years after Lincoln’s death, Mary’s youngest son, Thomas “Tad” Lincoln succumbed to Tuberculosis. Mary didn’t even attend the funeral. What else can be said other than she was an emotional wreck? Her last son Robert attended, but by this point, Mary was done with funerals. She couldn’t stomach another one.Her mental problems worsened. Mental health knowledge was non-existent back then and Mary suffered various conditions. Issues that had surfaced following the deaths of her first two children now became more prominent. Manic and depressive mood swings. Extreme migraines. She also developed an irrational fear of poverty and was known to stitch huge amounts of money into her clothes. She wore black clothes constantly to show she was still grieving. She became more paranoid and isolated. She even consulted mediums trying to contact the spirits of her dead family members.Her own son turned on her. Mary’s remaining son, Robert Lincoln, became increasingly concerned with his mother’s mental state. In 1875, this culminated in him having her institutionalized. Shocked at what she saw as her son’s betrayal, Mary attempted to kill herself with a drug overdose but was stopped when the drugs she used turned out to be placebos. Her stay at a mental hospital was only for 3 months, but it permanently damaged her relationship with her last son. From then on she lived with her sister.She died slowly. After her stay at the asylum, Mary slowly disintegrated over the next few years in the care of her sister. She suffered migraines, chronic pain and dealt with spinal cord injuries from several falls, on top of her still present mental issues. It was just a long decline of health of all the accumulated years of pain, no different from watching a old person slowly die from simple old age. On July 15, 1882 (eleven years to the day after her son Tad had died) she collapsed in from a stroke and died the next morning in a coma. She was 63 years old.She was buried next to her husband and her children. Even nowadays she is often overlooked given the status of her husband and those who came after.The sheer drama of all that this woman had to endure broke my heart when I read about it. She deserved better than this. She shouldn’t have had to bury her husband and so many of her children. She shouldn’t have been tormented by the demons in her own mind. She should have been remembered more today. She just…shouldn’t have been dealt so much tragedy.Mary Todd Lincoln

column1: Will I ever get over the loss of my dog?
column3: You have my deepest sympathy for your loss. First, understand that it is perfectly normal to grieve for a pet. You’ve lost a friend and family member who was a big part of your life. It might help to find a support group. Here are a few on-line support groups. You may be able to find in-person support by Googling “pet loss support (your location).” Association for Pet Loss and Bereavement Pet Loss Grief Support Community Resources at Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Support and services Ten Tips on Coping with Pet Loss There are many more. Most of these and similar sites offer ways you can memorialize your pet. You may find doing so helpful. If you are having difficulty functioning day-to-day or are having thoughts of self-harm, then seek professional help. Don’t hesitate simply because you lost a dog and not a human. Several Quorans have suggested that you get another pet. That is what I would do, and have done. But I am not you, and this is a very personal decision. Some people find that getting another pet right away gives them relief, while others may take years to be ready for another pet. Some never do. I will say this: should you choose to get another dog now or in the future, understand that you are not betraying the memory of your old pooch. Your new dog is not a replacement. The great thing about love is that it is not zero-sum. There’s an infinite supply, and you can love a new pet while still loving and honoring your departed one. You will not be loving one dog more or less than the other. You will love them differently, because they are different dogs. If you are not ready to get another dog just yet, consider volunteering at a shelter or rescue, transporting, and/or fostering. You can think of it as a memorial to your old friend. Good luck. Remember that your dog loved you and he/she would want you to be happy.

column1: How do you support someone who is going through grief?
column3: When my husband passed away from cancer 8 years ago, I was so numb from the event that it didn't dawn on me at the time but once I thought about it, I was really shocked by people's reactions. He died of Anaplastic Large Cell Lymphoma after more than a 2 year battle. It was his body but WE went through the sometimes painful treatment, hospital stays, doctor consults, body scans all the while having our hopes dashed for a cure/remission. Seeing your spouse of 30 years deteriorating right before your eyes is so surreal. Where were the mourners when things were touch and go, stressful to the point you thought you would lose your mind? Comforting someone who has recently lost a close family member is paramount to their mental health. In my grief, I thought if one more person said how sorry they were, I was going to scream. It didn't help me when people said they understood what I was going through or he's in a better place now. No one can understand how you are feeling unless they are standing in your shoes. Understanding this time is about the griever and no one else will allow them to feel your earnest compassion. Don't tell stories of your grief experiences or anyone else's. People have well meaning words but they don't got the mark on most grief situations. Let the griever know that's alright for them to be upset, mad or feeling like screaming. It's perfectly normal to have a mixed bag of emotions and there's nothing wrong with showing them. Crying in public is acceptable. My answer to the question on how to help those grieving is simple. Make your words take action. If you tell someone you would be happy to help them don't leave it up to griever to call you to ask for help. They never will. Make a special effort to call them and offer to come sit with them and hold their hands if necessary. Make a meal and take it to them. Check on them often to see if they are doing well. It's possible they could help with lawn Care or just need someone to talk to. In general the average person has no idea what to say or what to do in the presence of someone grieving. They tend to get foot and mouth disease. Sharing a story about their loved one can be a great comfort to them.

There is stigma, and there is a feeling that “if only I had done more” that things might have been different. I would say that mental illness and addictions are illnesses that are just as deadly as cancer. Except when someone is diagnosed with cancer, there is a LOT more support and love from friends, family, and the medical establishment. When the illness is related to mental health, that support seems to evaporate. People who do not understand mental health issues can only see that a person is making bad decisions and “resisting efforts to help.” To them, it really looks as though the patient is willfully making choices that are wrong—but that is not the case. They are not ABLE to make the right choices because their mind is not functioning as it should. For a family that loses a loved one from mental health problems, including addictions, it is so important to understand that it is an illness just like any other illness. It is a brain disease. Sometimes, treatment fails.

column1: What is the difference between a person suffering from CPTSD and BPD?
column3: Complex Posttraumatic Stress Disorder and Borderline Personality Disorder are often viewed as very similar to each other. Indeed, there are certain qualities and characteristics of each that are similar; however, the disorders are actually quite different. I believe the confusion results from a basic misunderstanding of the causes, nature, and criteria of each malady. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) is classified as one of the Trauma-related and Stressor-related Disorders. These syndromes are broadly distinguished from other psychological disturbances by the following characteristics: exposure to a traumatic or significantly stressful event accompanied by difficulties experiencing joy or attaining contentment, outward expressions of anger, overt aggression, and/or dissociative symptoms. The commonly recognized Trauma-related and Stressor-related disorders are Reactive Attachment Disorder, Disinhibited Social Engagement Disorder, Acute Stress Disorder, Adjustment Disorder, Prolonged Grief Disorder, and PTSD. These psychological illnesses, though in the same family, may manifest in very different ways. Moreover, the same condition may manifest quite differently among different patients as well. For example, anxiety and fear may substantially manifest is some patients but may be relatively subdued in others. Whereas PTSD definitively results from exposure to a traumatic or significantly stressful event, the underlying causes of Personality Disorders are less concrete. The ten commonly identified Personality Disorders are Paranoid Personality Disorder, Schizoid Personality Disorder, Schizotypal Personality Disorder, Avoidant Personality Disorder, Dependent Personality Disorder, Obsessive-Compulsive Personality Disorder, Antisocial Personality Disorder, Histrionic Personality Disorder, Narcissistic Personality Disorder, and Borderline Personality Disorder. Personality Disorders are broadly distinguished from other mental disorders by their enduring detrimental impact on thought, emotion, relationships, or impulsivity as well as their manifestation by early adulthood. Personality Disorders may have a familial component to them and may or may not be clearly associated with trauma/stressors. Regarding the current specific question being answered regarding the differences between Complex PTSD (cPTSD) and Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD), two very significant criteria have now been noted: cPTSD must develop secondary to a traumatic/stressful event and cPTSD need not manifest by early adulthood. Furthermore, though trauma and stressors in early life definitely often seem to be implicated in certain cases of BPD, the type and degree of challenges that may result in BPD is generally understood to be more variable. For example, the emotional stressors of recurrent invalidation, chronic neglect, parental loss, and abuse have all been theorized to be possible contributors behind BPD. However, the trauma and stressors that result in PTSD have been more narrowly identified as related, directly or indirectly, to threatened death, serious injury, and/or sexual violence. BPD and cPTSD are similar in that both may involve episodic dissociation, rage, cognitive disturbances, emotional instability, feelings of emptiness, relationship difficulties, self-destructive behaviors, and/or paranoia. However, BPD and cPTSD differ in that BPD must have developed by early adulthood, must always be enduring/long-standing, may have a significant familial component, and is, at least currently, more nebulous in cause. Furthermore, whereas those with cPTSD tend to be more haunted by distressing memories and triggers, as well as tend to be notably hypervigilant or startle easily; those with BPD struggle more with intense fears of abandonment and with whole object relations. Finally, despite the length of this post, there are actually several more key differences as well as notable similarities between these two devastating conditions. That noted, I still hope that this was a helpful survey. Thank you. Dr. Gregory Serfer Physician and author of I Am Still Right Here

column1: Why is Holden Caulfield afraid of growing up in the novel "The Catcher in the Rye" by J. D. Salinger?
column3: The Catcher in the Rye is a divisive little book, and it can be interpreted in a lot of different ways. For some, it is a pompous and self-centred rant of a whiny teenager. For others, it is a reflection of universal teen angst, and moreover, an accurate portrayal of certain aspects of the world we live in. Of course, there are those who dismiss this book altogether, regarding it as an over-rated piece of second grade literature (but let us not think about them for the moment). The obvious reason for Holden’s fear of adulthood is that he associates childhood with innocence, and he wants to protect these vulnerable souls from the corruption inflicted by age. But I was fascinated by the character of Holden Caulfield for a somewhat different reason. You see, having studied psychiatry and psychology in some detail as a medical undergraduate, I was more interested in how his thought processes evolve over time.A little detour first. Grief is a response to the loss of a loved one, and is an essential part of healing. This response is primarily emotional, but has behavioral, social, and philosophical aspects as well. Although the incidence is not high, some forms of grief are actually debilitating, rather than restorative. Some psychiatrists and health workers are of the opinion that these warrant special attention. [A new diagnostic group of 'Prolonged Grief Disorder (PGD)' or 'Complicated Grief Disorder (CGD)' has been proposed for inclusion in Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM), but lack of substantive research prevents this, as of now.] In 1969, the Swiss psychiatrist Elizabeth Kubler-Ross introduced the ‘five stages of grief’ which are:DenialAngerBargainingDepressionAcceptanceStages of grief are not always so clear-cut, and this model has been criticized on the grounds of lack of empirical research. Still, it does provide a (very rough) framework to understand how people cope with loss.From the very beginning of the novel, it is apparent that Holden is struggling with himself to maintain a semblance of control in his life, and it is a battle which he is losing. Gradually, we learn that his brother has died a few years back, and he has witnessed the suicide of a classmate. If we go by the Kubler-Ross model, Holden is somewhere near the bargaining-depression phase. Holden’s attachment to Allie’s baseball glove is a form of bargaining; the glove has — in some sense — replaced Allie in Holden’s life. But this is not sufficient to rein him in. Holden is depressed, and is close to a nervous breakdown. Mr. Antolini, his old teacher, is perceptive enough to realize this, when he remarks that:I have a feeling that you're riding for some kind of a terrible, terrible fall. But I don't honestly know what kind …Throughout the novel, Holden also displays certain defense mechanisms which are often seen in depressives. More relevant to this discussion are:Minimization: When complete denial is impossible, people try to discount the importance of the problem. Deep down, Holden is aware that he needs help, but tries to ignore his problems by deflection (sarcasm, for example) and faulty rationalization (“people are phony”).Dissociation: People lose track of time and/or people, and just ‘go with the flow’, in a manner of speaking. They want to keep their past and present separate, unrelated to each other, seemingly oblivious of the fact that the present is, in fact, dependent on the past. Past is, for them, static, and a precious property which will always be with them, if they hold on to it tightly enough. This is actually a very important theme in Catcher in the Rye. Holden is afraid of grown-ups, and refuses to grow up, because he feels that time will wrench his blissful past away from him. This is precisely why the museum is so important to him — it is his link to the past.Interestingly, Holden’s attachment to and treatment of past as a discrete, preservable entity has some similarity with ‘Eternalist’ or ‘Block Time’ theory[1]. This conception of universe holds that 'past' and 'present' — but not 'future' — exist as four dimensional blocks of time and space. Universe is always growing, in a temporal sense, as blocks of ‘present’ are added to the existing one. This idea was presaged by the Greek philosopher Parmenides[2] who held that change is impossible; anything which exists is entirely existent, and anything which does not is absent. By this logic, Allie exists (in his block of space-time), and nothing — not even death — can make him non-existent. Were Holden a philosopher, he might have been comforted by this view of time. Of course, Holden is not interested in philosophical aspects of time (and would most likely call me a phony if he ever read this post). There is another conception of time, which emphasizes its constant flux. Time passes — past leads to present which is transformed into future. This is summed up by Plato’s famous quote in Cratylus (attributed to Heraclitus[3]), “One can’t step into the same river twice.” If Holden subscribes to this view, Allie is already gone, and nothing he does will fill the void in his heart. That is why Holden is often repulsed not by adults themselves, but what he sees in adults, not realizing that they too have problems of their own. As an instance, he likes Mr. Spenser well enough, but hates what he represents (i.e., old age). In a sense, what we interpret as Holden’s refusal to grow up can be seen as the rejection of the changing nature of time, subscribing instead to a Parmenidean view.Footnotes[1] Time (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)[2] Parmenides (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)[3] Heraclitus (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

column1: Is it normal for depression to come in waves?
column3: The waves you describe can also be called episodes. The term depression is often used to describe a low or discouraged state of mind resulting from disappointment (eg, financial crisis, natural disaster, serious illness) or loss (eg, death of a being). Dear). However, the most appropriate terms for these moods are demoralization and grief. Negative feelings of demoralization and pain, unlike depression, do the following:They occur in waves that tend to be linked to thoughts or reminders of the inciting eventThey are resolved when circumstances or events improveThey can be interspersed with periods of positive emotion and humor.They are not accompanied by widespread feelings of worthlessness and self-worthDepressed mood typically lasts for days rather than weeks or months, and suicidal thoughts and prolonged loss of functionality are much less likely.However, the events and stressors that induce demoralization and grief can also precipitate a major depressive episode, particularly in vulnerable people (eg, those with a family history or history of major depression). There are several types of depressive disorders. The most common are:Severe depressive disorder: Also called severe depression, it is characterized by a combination of symptoms that interfere with the ability to work, sleep, study, eat, and enjoy activities that were previously enjoyable. Severe depression disables the person and prevents him from functioning normally. An episode of severe depression can occur only once in a lifetime, but is usually repeated from time to time.Dysthymic disorder, also called dysthymia, is characterized by its long-lasting symptoms (two years or more). Although less serious, they may not incapacitate a person, but they can prevent the development of a normal life or feel good. People with dysthymia can also suffer one or more episodes of severe depression throughout their lives.Adaptive Disorder: Depressive symptoms are mild, are present for a short period of time and are due to a specific problem that has been suffered. Other depressive disorders: are those depressive syndromes that can be part of the set of symptoms of other psychiatric diseases (for example, bipolar disorder, social phobia, etc.) and non-psychiatric (anemias, multiple sclerosis, hypothyroidism, cancer, etc.). ).If you found this answer helpful, please leave an upvote.

column1: What is schizoid personality disorder (SPD), and what are the symptoms?
column3: There are very good answers from experts here, so I’ll just try to give my personal view as a schizoid. SPD is, to sum up, an emotional disconnection from the real world. It is supposed to have both genetic an environmental causes, and it works as a defense or adaptation system for the child to survive a world that is too menacing or overwhelming for him. The visible consequences (the symptoms) would be an abnormal tendency for solitude and a lack of emotional expression. You can check the DSM-IV criteria for a more complete list of features. Anyway, there is still a lot to know about this disorder, particularly about the “mechanism” behind it, the causes, the boundaries with other disorders, its evolution and posible treatments… All we have is theories. It is supposed to be a split between your inner true self and the false self that relates to the real world. In my experience, I can say I usually feel the real world as “fake”, as something that (I consciously know) is real and here, but somehow I am not totally awake in it, not actually connected to it, maybe like a good virtual reality system. I don’t feel significant emotions despite living significant events in my life, meanwhile I can feel more intense emotions by imagining situations, watching movies or listening to music, which belongs to my inner world. I am not interested in 99% of the people, because human relationships are boring and absurd to me, unless there is some interesting or funny, intellectual or physical feature in them, which is very rare. I prefer to be alone, focused on my private bussiness and interests, rather than spending time with people. I have (and I like having) a total logic control on my actions. I can feel fear, but I can control it. I feel more like a robot than like the rest of the humans. Many of the human behaviours are totally alien for me, as they are driven by emotions, just as I probably look alien for them (and so, I have wear a “mask” to avoid problems). I have never known what people call “love” nor “joy”, or even “fun”, as they understand them, but I have never known depression nor grief as they do, either. So, this personality presents both advantages and disadvantages.
column9: Thank you for sharing your personal perspective. It really is helpful in capturing the nuances of the Schizoid experience that someone theorizing or simply “outside” might never notice.

column3: “SUFFERING FROM TRAUMA IS A RULE RATHER THAN AN EXCEPTION.”The effect of unresolved trauma is not only limited to ‘signs’ ie. which you can see visibly but also includes ‘symptoms’ which the patient experiences psychologically and physically. The prevalence is 2-3% after 1 year of the traumatic experience. And from WHEN do you start putting symptoms experienced by an individual in an unresolved category? If after 1 MONTH of the traumatic experience the symptoms still exist, then they can be put under the unresolved category.Medical fraternity initially considered trauma in such cases as only a ‘One-time experience’ but now, it also includes multiple traumatic experiences ie. chronic trauma. So, Trauma can be classified as follows: Type 1- One time like eg. rape, war, accident etc Type 2- Repeated trauma like abuse by spouse or parent (This can be mental or physical both) SYMPTOMS OF UNRESOLVED TRAUMA Unresolved trauma can have symptoms ranging from anxiety, disturbance in sleep to even developing physical symptoms. column1: When is grief abnormal?
column3: Abnormal grief is not a thing with professional grief counselors. However, complicated grief is. A normal grief response for the death of a loved takes an average of 13 months. Symptoms begin to improve around 6–8 months after the death. There are no linear stages of grief. That’s a huge misconception. There is a beginning, middle, and end, but that doesn’t mean you get over the death. It means you get through it to a place where you incorporate the death into your life as you move forward. column1: What is the difference between psychopathy and being emotional numb?
column3: It’s very difficult to describe. Thanks for the request to answer. There is a vast difference. Emotional numbness is usually temporary and can be a symptom of many things, depression, various personality disorders, autism. just having callous/unemotional traits. Psychopathy is a brain abnormality which causes many more symptoms other than just subdued emotions. I recently learned about the existence of alexithymia which I found very interesting - looks as though there is a similarity between psychopathy and autism which relates to the wiring between the language part of the brain and the emotional part. I avoid answering questions like “what does X feel like” for this reason - I can’t find words to describe feelings, despite having a language degree! I also feel like I don’t have emotions most of the time, unless they really whack me in the face (which quite frankly, I hate). To me, “emotions” have to be extreme - anything else just doesn’t actually count. I am saying this because I think oftentimes we believe we are emotionally numb when in fact we’re just not aware of our emotions, we are blocking them or just not actively allowing ourselves to feel them. Psychopathy entails many other traits and is more permanent. It affects all emotional responses all the time, including fear, guilt, anxiety, nervousness - everything is “turned down”, permanently. Even the most emotionally numb person would feel intense fear in some situations as this is a primal response. Psychopaths can actually feel more intensely if they pay attention to their feelings (so I read), as can everyone else - but what I am getting at is that they just can’t experience the extreme highs and lows of other people (excitement at getting engaged, grief at someone’s death, intense romantic love, remorse at hurting a loved one etc). There are also other brain abnormalities with psychopaths such as dopamine sensitivity, which means that they feel way more pleasure from “rewards” than most people. There is more to psychopathy than just lacking in emotion. (otherwise all the male members of my family would be a bunch of psychos lol)

column1: What is it like to be a schizotypal? What would be a mild manifestation of this personality disorder?
column3: you kind of feels like you’re the only person who actually understands anything, but at the same time you’re constantly questioning everything. there’s lots of ways to experience it because
