column1: I hear voices/snippets of random conversations in my head when I close my eyes at night but I’m not falling asleep and very aware of my surroundings. Is this early stages of schizophrenia?
column3: The same thing happens to lots of people, and i suppose that it would depend on your chemical balance in your brain at the time while experiencing this, how your reaction to it would be, or what kind of sounds or conversations you are hearing. As a kid no matter how tired i was it would always take me hours (most nights up to 5 or 6 hrs) to fall asleep every night, even some nights now as a 31yr old, but as a kid it would be every night. as soon as my head hits the pillow BAM i feel wide awake with thoughts of anxiety, depression, replaying situations of the day that didnt sit well with me and ive not yet had the chance to process it, or thoughts of terrible things happening to me, imagining burglars or monsters creeping around outside the window, etc. I always thought i just had plain old insomnia all that time and that it had partially gone away as i grew up, as i still have a bit more trouble sleeping now compared to most people i know, but as a kid it was maddening and always a constant. When i was 23 i was dating a girl who had really bad clinical anxiety, aswell as her own unique basket full of other most likely undiagnosed mental disorders (as is often the case with mentally unwell people) and i recommended she switch to the doctor that i use, so we went together as she consulted with him about her anxiety attacks. He explained to us that as humans, our brains have neurons (a specialized cell transmitting nerve impulses/waves) and in return, receptors which receive the impulse and carry out the function of that impulse within our nervous systems. Mental disorders in general once diagnosed are hard to treat as there are numerous underlying physical or mental abnormalities which may be causing the observed symptoms, and the ‘disorders’ are moreso a classification regarding the symptoms themselves, then based on the knowledge of what the abnormalities that cause them might be, treatment plans are experimental case by case, and youd find more often so, the wrong medications are given initially, and hopefully through the process of elimination eventually the right medication will be given, and the problem improves and is pacified. He suggested to us that because she had not been having luck with her current anxiety medication, we switch to a new drug which was designated as an agent to help regulate the thought patterns that occur during an alpha brainwave state. there are four different electromagnetic waves (along with neurons and receptors for each) in the brain; alpha, beta, delta, theta. and depending on tbe activity being produced by the brain, a person can be observed as being in one of four different ‘states’ based on which brainwave is being most active at that time. ill skip the other three but alpha waves are most present when the brain is undergoing minimal activity, meaning that while not being highly engaged, you would be in an alpha state. sufferers of mental illnesses or imbalanced brain chemistry, have an abnormal amount of beta waves occuring during an alpha state, (beta state occurs while the brain is being actively or highly engaged) and this can lead to psychoactive thought patterns. he theorised high beta activity during her alpha state was causing her psychoactive thoughts, leading to her anxiety attacks and wanted to try a drug to reduce her beta wave interference. We broke up before she had given the drugs a proper run through, and to my knowledge she is still fairly crazy so as much as id like to know if he was correct or not, we will never know 🤣 . it wasnt until years later i had an epiphany, and did some follow up research that actually forms a very relevant conclusion to all this in depth explanation ive written. Those of us who are considered to be (and/or consider ourselves to be) of balanced mind, and brain chemistry is in good order, at most points in our daily lives are experiencing enough brain engagement, even during our alpha states (even small amounts of engagement such as sensory input; sight sound touch, smell, taste etc) to ‘pacify’ our beta waves from causing interferences to our alpha state. But at times of extremely low brain activity, even those without any type of a mental disorder or imbalance, can experience psychoactive dissolution such as hearing things, voices, conversation, thoughts/voices/feelings that feel like they dont belong to you etc, while trying to get to sleep, as all your basic sensory inputs that are functioning even during alpha state in normal day to day activities, are no longer pacifying the beta interferences. I was starting to suspect that this had always been the main cause of what id describe as nearly full blown insomnia as a kid (and less frequently as an adult). this was confirmed for me when that same doctor perscribed me quetiapine to help me sleep, as i was experiencing insomniana quite bad again at the time due to depressive onset and no other sleeping pills seemed to work at all, quetiapine isnt a sleeping pill, but he perscribed it as it is a powerful antipsychotic that balances or regulates the output of serotonin and dopamine, and is commonly used at higher dosages to treat bipolar, depression, or schizophrenia. but at a lower dosage, regulates brain chemistry and neurotransmitters to pacify the delta activity, which had been causing me mild schizophrenic, depressive onsets during alpha state while trying to sleep. quetiapine worked amazingly to get me to sleep but has its side effects too so i only need to rely on it on odd occasions where insomnia is giving me grief. by understanding the inner working of the brain through all these realisations, and determining a possible cause to what you are experiencing, can sometimes be enough to help keep severe symptoms at bay, as you can take a step back from a situation to scan your surroundings and determine if any triggers are present to be causing the symptoms (such as low brain activity while trying to sleep causing delta inteferences to produce what can easily be considered as “textbook scizophrenic dissolution”) and accepting that with this knowledge, we are capable of understanding that what are known to be symptoms of diagnosable serious mental illnesses, can also occur under certain conditions, naturally within the brains of clinically balanced people with a clear bill of mental health. most people wouldve given up reading long ago, but anybody who made it to the end of this answer, must surely relate this experience, and i would hope that youve gained enough mental acquity from this to develop your own drug free way of pacifying the ill state of mind that comes with this kind of occurance OR if you have a completely different abnormality to what i experience, have gained enough insight to the basic principles of the brains inner workings to lead your thoughts to your own epiphany or research to understand yourself better and synchronize your brain and body your own way and find a sense of relief, personally ive found that keeping myself engaged daily with my passions, interests, hobbies, responsibilities, and setting lots of goals for myself, that i can rest at night with ease on a normal daily basis.big goals are important but are pointless without little bite sized goals along the way there, so that if you get knocked back a step, you can still have tangible evidence of how far youve already come and not lose sight of the eventual success ahead. you can accept that you cant win the battle every day as sometimes things pile up too fast and can defeat me on certain days, and if im struggling to deal with it, quetiapine gets the job done when i cant do it myself. and that doesnt make me (or you if this happens to you aswell) crazy, or mentally ill, as sometimes mental illness can simply be commonly mistaken for the human brains natural response to hardships and personal struggles or grievances. and if more people knew what was going on, they might be able to summon the willpower within themselves to overcome their own state of mind for their own betterment. and if your problem is more severe, and requires a doctor or professional to oversee treatment. that doesnt always mean you have a disorder, that youre crazy, or weak, you may just need a helping hand to understand yourself and thats okay also

column1: What are some somatoform disorders?
column3: First off, somatoform disorders are physiological disorders where the patient experiences physical symptoms like pain, which seem to be inconsistent, or cannot be explained by medical diagnoses of any known neurological or physical conditions. These disorders, while they don’t typically affect the overall functioning of the patient, may cause issues and interfere with daily life between home, school, work, etc. 1.) Somatization Disorder Somatization Disorder usually develops within 18 to 30 years of age. It is a continuous pattern of physical complaints made by the patient, caused by psychological stress, that often result in unnecessary medical treatment (requested by the patient). These symptoms typically do not have an explanation related to actual physical diseases/conditions, and are not intentionally made up by the patient. 2.) Conversion Disorder This disorder describes physical symptoms felt by the patient that affects voluntary motor/sensory functions such as walking, which are actually caused by psychological stress. While these symptoms may suggest neurological disorders, there is not actually enough evidence to formally classify it as a verifiable physical issue. Conversion disorder is caused mostly by stress, typically pertaining to family issues, such as unresolved grief, as well as traumatic experiences, such as a car accident. This disorder is most common in adolescences, women in particular, and generally does not affect those under the age of 5. 3.) Pain Disorder Patients will be diagnosed with Pain Disorder instead of conversion disorder when the primary symptoms exhibited by the patient are pain, instead of impaired motor and sensory functions. 4.) Body Dysmorphic Disorder Body Dysmorphic Disorder is when there is a repeated, excessive concern surrounding slight anomalies or abnormalities, on any part of the body, for example scars, acne, excessive amounts of facial hair, etc. 5.) Hypochondriasis This disorder deals with the obsession that one has a serious medical condition or illness. This is often caused by the misjudgement, or inaccurate perception of bodily symptoms. Hypochondriacs may over think small physical and mental symptoms in fear that something more serious must be wrong. These individuals may obsessively self-examine and self diagnose.

column1: How can someone with BPD be so cruel?
column3: I think the real question is why can humanity be so cruel? Why do tragedies have to occur, why does child abuse exist as to where people develop things like borderline, why does mental illness exist…? Why didn’t anyone care enough to step in and save someone from trauma, why didn’t anyone realize the importance of emotional invalidation.. And of course, I can ask why neurotypicals are so cruel and have no regard for an understanding but I know why; they don’t know what it’s like to not have control of your emotions… But what good does asking these questions do, aside from more miserably, make you feel?… To think of all the “why” and “what if’s”, when what is, is and now, the matter of fact is, I am in late adolescence and have this disorder. We don’t just go out thinking, “I wonder who I can lash out on today.” “Whose life can I miserably make?”… If you thought we do, you are thinking of malignant narcissism… A borderline brain, damaged by childhood trauma primarily from excess cortisol release, does not filter correctly of emotional stimuli.. Rather than a borderline being cruel, the sometimes arising cruel behavior is reflective of a brain that malfunctions in emotional control. Assuming the borderline was cruel and you getting angry at their outbursts may have been perceived as invalidation, which greatly triggers borderline symptoms and thus, could have had role in the relational dysfunction.. People, especially in America, love to blame someone for having a mental illness like it somehow is the fault of their own, like they somehow chose it… Simply, because it cannot be seen through physical eyes, without access, to an MRI... This mentality need stop. Because this mentality leads to stigma, criminalization rather than treatment, and also impedes oftentimes, recovery. Rather than hold someone accountable for treatment, people are held “accountable” for being ill. Punishing someone for being mentally ill is not accountability; it is anger and anger makes the people perceive that they are holding someone accountable, but what they are doing is acting from a place of hurt that they their own selves, like how a mentally ill person need accountability for treatment, must take accountability for processing their anger and grief. Its All In Your Head: Borderline Personality Disorder and the BrainAmygdala The primitive part of the brain which regulates fear and aggression. In the general population it’s a vital tool for survival; even in the comfortable, safe, clockwork cities of modernity, emotions can be lifesaver. However: Brain scans have shown people with BPD have amygdala’s that are noticeably smaller than the general population, and may even have undergone atrophy. The smaller the amygdala, the more overactive it is. This means when people with Borderline Personality Disorder, experience an emotion, they do so more intensely than the general population, and the ‘cooling down’ period takes much longer. Hippocampus Latin for ‘seahorse’ the hippocampus is a pair of seahorse shaped tubes located in left and right hemisphere of the brain. Associated with long and short-term memory, spatial-orientation, and most importantly emotional reactions, it is the body’s data processor. This means, when an enviromental event is relayed via the visual cortex, the hippocampus decides the correct emotional response. Approach or avoidance. For people with Borderline Personality Disorder, the hippocampus is in a state of continuous hyperarousal. Uncoordinated and dysfunctional, it consistently misinterprets threats, and relays faulty messages back to the amygdala. This means people with BPD are more than likely to encounter other people, and the world around them, as threatening, when this very well may not be the intent or the reality. Hypothalamic-pituary-adrenal axis. A complex name for three interconnected glands: The hypothalamus, the pituitary, and the adrenal gland all interact with each other. Especially in managing the pressures of daily life and maintaining homeostasis. The ‘Hypothalamic-pituary adrenal axis’, is primarily responsible for the body’s production of cortisol. Cortisol is a natural chemical released during times of stress. Studies have shown people with BPD have abnormal levels of cortisol in their bloodstream. Too much Cortisol production, means stress levels in daily life are always overwhelming. Psychologically, resilience and coping skills are undermined, chemically, the body is overwhelmed. Prefrontal Cortex The prefrontal cortex is the pinnacle of human evolution, not only because it’s responsible for reason, rationality and decision-making but because it is also inhibits our primal nature. People with BPD have prefrontal cortexes which are inactive and inefficient. This is one of the reasons for some of hallmark symptoms of BPD including impulsivity. As Francisco Goya said, the ‘sleep of reason breeds monsters,’ and with a sleeping prefrontal cortex, individuals with BPD find themselves assailed by emotions, which make us feel out of control. Conclusion Of course this appears a raw deal for someone suffering Borderline Personality Disorder: After all, we are stigmatised with pejorative labels as it is without needing mental impoverishment added. But heres the twist: The heritability of Borderline Personality Disorder is estimated to be 40–60%, however, 70% of BPD sufferers have experienced some form of childhood trauma; often sexual, physical or emotional abuse. It remains to be seen whether structural abnormalities in the borderline brain, are the cause of the condition, or a consequence of trauma. An indelible imprint on our brain of suffering. To give just one example of why it is feasible the brain is ‘injured’ by trauma, is in the chemical cortisol. As we’ve already seen, cortisol is released in a response to stress; and so it goes to reason, extreme stress, especially experienced in childhood and over long periods of time, will lead to abnormal levels of production. Furthermore: The reason for the atrophy of the amygdala and hippocampus, and prefrontal cortex, is because high levels of cortisol have eroded parts of it away. This is the cruel irony: The brain is a mirror to life, and if cortisol has chemically eroded the most prized assets of the mind, then this is because stress has eroded core aspects of our lives. In order to address these startling discoveries about the brain, we need to acknowledge the nature of labels. That BPD is not someone twilight state between sanity and insanity, but a mind that has been worn away by developmental trauma. When we stop blaming individuals, we may start looking more at society. For now, I’ll just keep listening to the experts telling me It’s all your head. When I look at the brain scan I can’t help but agree.Stigma is bad all over the world, but it seems lesser so in European countries…

column1: In a hypothetical scenario, would a person be diagnosed with insanity if the person believed that they saw members of the angelic host disappear out of thin air?
column3: If the person was functioning very well at home, doing well at work and had no other symptoms of any mental illness, the person would not get diagnosed with a mental illness. It's that simple. There is no mental illness that has one symptom. There are mental illnesses in which hallucinations are a prominent symptom, but again, no mental illness has one symptom. And having hallucinations can be due to many other things than mental illness. Substance abuse and alcoholism are two very common causes of hallucinations, though the hallucinations usually go away when those behaviors stop. Dementia, though rare in the young, may cause hallucinations in the elderly. Brian injury, brain tumors, prescription medication for Parkinson's Disease, can cause hallucinations. Blindness can cause hallucinations. So can some kidney diseases, ovarian tumors, the list goes on and on. High fever, poisoning, dehydration… Some hallucinations are cultural. People can be conditioned and trained for years to have hallucinatory experiences without abnormal signaling in the brain. They become suggestible to the experience over time, largely because such experiences carry considerable social value. Some hallucinations are due to grief. About 20% of Americans will have a grief hallucination at some point in their lifetime. The good diagnostician knows how to determine step-by-step which disorder is causing hallucination, or if it is a cultural phenomenon or due to medical disease, substance abuse etc. No one can get diagnosed with insanity. There is no such diagnosis. Insanity is a legal concept, not a diagnosis.

column1: Are cognitive mental health problems triggered by experiencing too few emotions or too many negative ones?
column3: The answer is BOTH. It might sound impossible, but depression and anxiety happen when people feel strong negative emotions then find a way to not feel them. Before explaining, let me first clarify how I understand your phrase “cognitive mental health problems.” Many mental health symptoms interfere with cognition. Anxiety and depression in particular impact attention and fluidity as well as clarity of thought. In other words, if you feel anxious or depressed, you might have a difficult time concentrating or sitting still, and you will probably feel a mental dullness and/or fogginess at times. In the case of depression, the severity of cognitive symptoms can be so bad that they mimic the effects of Alzheimer’s or other forms of dementia. But let’s get to the meat of the question. How can you have both too many negative emotions AND experience too few emotions?You numb yourself.You deny the feelings.You detach from your emotions.You mask your feelings.You distract yourself from your feelings.In short, you employ any number of mental gymnastics to avoid experiencing the core emotional experience. To use the original analytic term, you use defense mechanisms. Defense mechanisms aren’t inherently a problem. Defenses allow for constructive, disciplined, predictable, and dutiful responses to social demands. We expect ourselves and others to self-regulate and be relatively even-keeled and predictable in social situations. It’s abnormal for someone to display a sudden, unexpected outpouring of emotion during ordinary life events (when tragedy strikes, that’s a different story). There are a few problems though with defense mechanisms:Not all defense mechanisms are created equal.If you are constantly avoiding feelings through defense mechanisms, you may be disregarding vital emotional information and eventually stop recognizing as well as understanding your emotions.It’s one thing to stay calm in a stressful situation in order to meet its social and physical demands. It’s another thing to never cry, feel fear, or express anger. In quiet moments with yourself or your loved ones, you need to be able to feel and express pain, hurt, grief, and sorrow. If you don’t, then stress accumulates. Tension between mind and body builds. You start making choices that are about avoiding pain rather than pursuing meaning. You accumulate more disappointments and fewer rewards. And what’s more, when you numb yourself to negative emotions, you also numb yourself to joy, intimacy, laughter, and excitement. Depression and anxiety ensue. Mental clarity gives way to foggy, blurry dullness. In short, when you encounter big feelings AND don’t feel them, you’re on a path to cognitive symptoms by way of anxiety and depression.

column1: What's the difference between a normal reaction to a traumatic event and PTSD?
column3: Thank you for the request. With all due respect…you’ve misunderstood something. Your question infers that there is a ‘normal’ response to trauma and…then there is PTSD which is apparently NOT a normal response to comparative trauma. The premise itself is incorrect. PTSD IS A NORMAL RESPONSE to ABNORMAL traumatic events. It is the TRAUMA that is not normal. I promise you it is very normal to have the effects of PTSD after enduring the extreme trauma that people have endured to ‘earn’ that diagnosis. The things these people have had to survive are often unimaginable to the average person. It is not simply normal stress, or normal grief over a normal loss, normal sadness over a normal life circumstance, normal anxiety over a normal life challenge, or normal fear over a normal threat dealt with just by being human. The very words ‘trauma’ or ‘traumatic’ have been diluted, I think. Granted, there are certainly degrees of trauma. But I think society uses that word so that they don’t have to NAME the actual beast. It’s a generic term people have glossed over with little thought or deep emotional attachment to it’s horrible evils. I don’t mean to be cheeky here. There are multitudes of information out there about PTSD and COMPLEX PTSD. Anyone who sincerely wishes to learn about it’s inception and how it moves and breathes once born, can find all the information they need. That includes the very scientific neurochemical responses of the elevated stress response in a brain which develops PTSD. Yes, the brain of those with Complex or Traditional PTSD are different from others. Particularly in those who’ve suffered extreme abuse from a very early childhood. Their tiny brains never had a chance. The ‘normal’ stress response in any human being…the Fight, Flight, Freeze response…get stuck in the ‘ON’ position for people who endure ongoing severe ‘trauma’. Whether that’s a war-zone in the military, native peoples living in a country laden with violent civil war, those in gang ridden areas, those who serve on our emergency services teams such as police, firefighters, emergency medical teams, etc., children being tortured by sexual abuse, rape, physical abuse and/or emotional gaslighting, or women, men or children who endure domestic violence in their homes, etc etc. These peoples brains do not ever SHUT OFF that emergency stress response. Imagine (try) not being able to fight. Oh but…wait. Can’t fly either! So the brain and the soul are overloaded by horror that WILL…NOT…QUIT! A scenario which they can not conquer, and from which they cannot escape. Enter the only response left…freeze. That’s dissociation. PTSD is hallmarked by the (sometimes rapid) cycling between what is called ‘activation’: the ON of flashbacks and overwhelming emotions, nightmares and reactions….and the ‘dissociation’: the shut OFF, numb, detached, thousand-mile-stare, depersonalized, dead nothingness. These responses are not a choice. They are what the brain does as a survival instinct. I assure you it is not only ‘normal’, but thee most base and primal, biological response to ‘trauma’. So maybe your question is really more along the lines of ‘Why do some people who go through a trauma have PTSD while others who go through the trauma generally NAMED or categorized as the same thing, don’t?’ ?? If not, feel free to stop here. Otherwise…: Trauma is a fickle monster. It can never be quite defined or predicted. It can’t be boxed, bowed or prettied up. It can’t be controlled, packaged, decorated or prescribed. It is a very PERSONAL experience for EACH and every individual who endures it. Every victim has unique nuances, dynamics, colors and flavors of that traumatic environment. In other words, there is no such thing as going through ‘the same thing’. Trauma and it’s effects cannot be used for negative comparative studies. It can be observed. Similarities can be documented in how people with (C)PTSD ‘tick’. Certainly there are common denominators. But that’s just surface. How this manifests for…what it ‘looks like’ on each person is unique. For one, their abuse began before they could even talk. For someone else, they had a decent childhood and didn’t encounter their trauma til they were 24, or 47. For one, it was their primary caretaker who was also their abuser…so, relational, betrayal trauma. For another it was a natural disaster or a nameless stranger with a gun. One of them was never even believed that it happened, let alone supported or avenged with justice. The other had a supportive family, friends and a whole government program to help them. Some already had a solid sense of identity, system of spiritual belief, healthy emotional regulation and a balanced view of the good and bad in the world. The other never had a chance at knowing what an ‘I’dentity even was, had no opportunity for a faith when worlds collided in contradiction, no construct of safety and grew up knowing the world was unsafe and learned people can’t be trusted before they ever hit kindergarten. Even siblings who grew up in the same home with the same parents experience that household and those relationships uniquely. Their levels of trauma can vary, as can their symptoms. That’s a very long answer to a very fluid question. I don’t know if I even answered you satisfactorily. Hopefully someone can use something I’ve said, however.

column1: What is the medical condition known as “broken heart syndrome”?
column3: What is broken heart syndrome? Broken heart syndrome is a temporary and reversible heart condition whose symptoms mimic those of a heart attack. Unlike a heart attack, broken heart syndrome happens when a sudden physical or emotional stress causes a rapid weakening of your heart muscle. You may think you’re having a heart attack because symptoms, such as shortness of breath and chest pain, are similar in both conditions. However, in broken heart syndrome, you (for the most part) don’t have blocked coronary arteries or permanent heart damage, and usually make a fast and full recovery. Broken heart syndrome is also called stress cardiomyopathy or Takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Takotsubo is the Japanese name for an octopus trapping pot with a wide bottom and narrow neck. The pot resembles the shape of the distressed left ventricle of the heart seen in broken heart syndrome. Cleveland Clinic is a non-profit academic medical center. Advertising on our site helps support our mission. We do not endorse non-Cleveland Clinic products or services. Policy What kinds of emotional and physical stress can cause broken heart syndrome? Examples of sudden emotional stressors that can bring on broken heart syndrome include:Grief from the death of a loved one and other large or meaningful loss (eg, divorce/relationship, job, home, money, beloved pet).Good news (e.g., surprise parties, winning the lottery).Bad news.Intense fear (e.g., public speaking, armed robbery, car accident).Extreme anger.Examples of sudden physical stressors that can bring on broken heart syndrome include:Severe pain.An exhausting physical event.Health issues, including asthma attack, difficulty breathing (dypnea), seizure, stroke, high fever, low blood sugar (hypoglycemia), large blood loss, surgery.Can I die from broken heart syndrome? Although death has happened, it’s an extremely rare event (about 1%) and therefore highly unlikely that you will die from broken heart syndrome. In most cases, broken heart syndrome is a short, temporary condition with a full recovery. Cleveland Clinic is a non-profit academic medical center. Advertising on our site helps support our mission. We do not endorse non-Cleveland Clinic products or services. Policy Who is gets broken heart syndrome? Broken heart syndrome mostly affects women (about 88%), especially in later middle age (after menopause; mean age range 58 to 77). One possible explanation is that the female hormone estrogen protects the heart against any harmful effects of hormones released in response to stress. As the level of estrogen declines with age, women might be more susceptible to the effects of sudden stress. How common is broken heart syndrome? The medical literature reports that broken heart syndrome occurs in about 2% of patients who were seen with a suspected heart attack. However, this figure is thought to be an underestimate of the true number of cases because the condition is often not recognized. Cleveland Clinic is a non-profit academic medical center. Advertising on our site helps support our mission. We do not endorse non-Cleveland Clinic products or services. Policy SYMPTOMS AND CAUSES What causes broken heart syndrome? The exact cause of broken heart syndrome is not fully understood. When you react to a physical or emotional stress, your body releases stress hormones in your blood like adrenalin, noradrenalin, epinephrine and norepinephrine. Experts think that these hormones temporarily interfere with your heart’s function. Broken heart syndrome:Disrupts your heart’s normal, steady rhythm (pattern of heartbeats).Causes part of your heart to temporarily enlarge (the lower part of your left ventricle).Leads to even more forceful contractions in other areas of your heart.These changes cause temporary heart muscle failure. What are the symptoms of broken heart syndrome? You may feel symptoms within minutes up to hours after the stressful event. In broken heart syndrome, the release of stress hormones temporarily stuns your heart muscle, producing symptoms similar to a typical heart attack. Signs and symptoms of broken heart syndrome include:Sudden, severe chest pain (angina) – a main symptom.Shortness of breath – a main symptom.Weakening of the left ventricle of your heart – a main sign.Fluid in your lungs.Irregular heartbeats (arrhythmias).Low blood pressure (hypotension).A small percentage of patients diagnosed with broken heart syndrome can’t identify any stresses that may have triggered their episode. What are the complications of broken heart syndrome? Complications are rare, but those that have been reported include:Rupture of the left ventricle (free wall) of the heart.Blockage of the blood flow from the left ventricle.Heart failure (your heart can’t pump enough blood to meet your body’s needs).Blood clot in the wall of the left ventricle.Left ventricular outflow tract obstruction.Cardiogenic shock.Complete atrioventricular block.Death.DIAGNOSIS AND TESTS How is broken heart syndrome diagnosed? After completing a physical exam and reviewing your medical history, your healthcare provider will order several tests including:An EKG (electrocardiogram) to measure your heart’s electrical activity.Coronary angiography (uses a dye and type of X-ray to look at your heart’s arteries).Echocardiography (uses sound waves to create moving images of your heart’s pumping action).Chest X-ray (shows the structure of your heart, lungs and blood vessels).Cardiac MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) (produces both still and moving pictures of your heart).Ventriculogram (uses a dye injected into the heart’s left ventricle, then X-rays show the size and pumping efficiency of this heart chamber).How does broken heart syndrome differ from a heart attack? Unlike a heart attack, in broken heart syndrome your heart muscle is not permanently damaged and your coronary arteries are not blocked. The tests your healthcare provider orders help reveal if your symptoms are broken heart syndrome or a heart attack. You have broken heart syndrome and not a heart attack if:Your symptoms appeared suddenly following a stressful physical or emotional event.Your EKG was abnormal – your heart’s electrical activity showed some abnormal changes – the changes are the same as those seen during a heart attack.Your blood work shows a rise in cardiac enzymes levels, the same enzymes that would be high in a heart attack.The arteries supplying your heart are usually not blocked and there’s no scar tissue present in your heart.The lower part of your left ventricle is enlarged – shows a ballooning of this area – and there’s unusual muscle wall movements.MANAGEMENT AND TREATMENT How is broken heart syndrome treated? Treatment depends on the severity of your symptoms. Broken heart syndrome is usually treated with medicines until full recovery. Medications include:ACE inhibitors to lower blood pressure (long term).Beta blockers to slow the heart rate (short term).Diuretics to decrease fluid buildup (short term).Anti-anxiety medicines to manage stress. (These medications may be long term, if needed.)Depending on how much your heart muscle was weakened, your healthcare provider may also recommend cardiac rehabilitation. Managing your stress with yoga, meditation and other relaxation techniques can also be helpful. Ask your healthcare provider for information on these methods and possible programs and services available. PREVENTION Can broken heart syndrome be prevented? There are no known treatments for preventing broken heart syndrome. However, learning stress management and problem-solving techniques can help improve physical and emotional stress. Engaging in relaxation techniques can also be helpful. Some examples include:Practicing yoga, meditation, journaling, or mindfulness.Taking a warm bath; lighting scented candles; and taking long, deep breaths and slowly exhaling.Depending on the source of your stress, there may be a support group you can join to talk about your stress and share coping skills with others who have had similar experiences. Seeking the help of a professional counselor might be considered too. In addition, managing physical or emotional stress can be helped by following general healthy habits too. These include:Eating a healthy diet, such as the Dash diet or Mediterranean diet.Getting regular exercise (at least five times a week for 30 minutes).Getting seven to nine hours of sleep each night.Spending time with others.Keeping your medical appointments, for both follow up and preventive health screenings. Finding and treating any health problems early always leads to the best outcome for a long and healthy life.Avoid – or better yet – stop unhealthy choices such as smoking, illicit drug use, and alcohol abuse.Source: Cleveland clinic from Google

column1: How long does a bipolar episode (depressive or manic) take to kick off, i.e. how long is it from the appearance of the first signs till symptoms reach maximum severity?
column3: Only a history of our mood swings can offer any indication of the time that will be needed for significant changes in mood.There are no fast and hard rules. Even with this knowledge, we will not be protected entirely from our mood swings. Predicting us from these ups and downs; from depression to hypomania (or mania) and vice versa. When we add medications to the mix, we have another factor that may cause a completely different rhythm of mood changes. Hopefully, most of the abnormal and troublesome symptoms will be limited and intensities are lower. It is best to be prepared for some difficulties while looking for the most effective medications. Several months, and longer, might be necessary to find the best combination and dosages. After the least number of symptoms has been established, there may or may not be a repeating pattern of symptoms; only time will tell. A complete disappearance of symptoms may not be possible. Personally, I discovered that I needed to lower my expectations. I would still have to vigilant for the signs of hypomania so that I didn't experience an looked of mania and possibly a psychotic break. Depression is a sneaky devil. Without recognizing the somewherechange in symptoms, my mood can slowly, unnoticed, fall into despair. My target is in the middle of elevated and deflated moods. Those times when looked is in that sweet spot are called euthymic moods. It is a place where we function best and under the least strain. There are a few things that can create a shift in bipolar episodes. They can trigger happiness or depression, fast or slow. The most common are chemical triggers such as pharmaceuticals, food allergies, other medical conditions, grief and stress. Truly, predicting when a mood will escalate or become gloomy and dispirited, is a guess. As mentioned earlier, someone's psychiatric records might help but in most cases, we must learn to live with a moving target that may be relatively calm, with bright mornings and peaceful night. We don't know how long such an episode will last.

column1: What are the main causes for blood in your urine while being pregnant?
column3: Found this post helpful Bleeding during pregnancy is more common than we first suspect. As many as one in three women will have some sort of bleeding during their first trimester of pregnancy. This can range from a few brown spots to bright red blood loss and for some, passing large clots. Bleeding can occur at any stage of pregnancy, though it is most common in the first trimester. It is important for women to remember that it is not necessarily a sign of problems. However, bleeding in the second and third trimesters can indicate a pregnancy complication. Any bleeding, at any stage still needs to be investigated. There are a number of reasons why vaginal bleeding during pregnancy occurs. Bleeding during the first trimester Bleeding during the first three months of pregnancy can be a sign of miscarriage. Around 1 in 5 pregnancies results in miscarriage before the 12th week of gestation. Although the statistics are high, for the individual couple who have experienced a pregnancy loss, the effects can be significant. Not all bleeding is a sign of inevitable miscarriage though. Around half the women who experience bleeding do not miscarry. Sometimes within the first 6-12 days of pregnancy there is what is known as an implantation bleed. This occurs when the thick, bloody lining of the uterus is disturbed by the embryo nestling its way into the uterus. An implantation bleed generally only lasts for a day or two before it settles down. Signs of miscarriageVaginal bleeding. This often starts off with spotting but can increase to large amounts, with or without clots.Uterine cramping, which is similar to period pain.Feeling a sense that something is not right; worry and anxiety over the pregnancy.A loss of pregnancy symptoms such as nausea and breast tenderness.In cases of threatened miscarriage and bleeding, sometimes women progress to the stage where miscarriage becomes inevitable. This means that nothing can be done to retain the pregnancy or support it continuing. It can be fairly safely assumed that the majority of miscarriages which occur are as a result of major problems with the development of the embryo. Miscarriage is often seen as “nature’s way” of ensuring that more healthy embryos survive and are able to progress into the later stages of development. By definition, a threatened miscarriage is when the embryo is still inside the uterus. A complete miscarriage is when the uterus is empty and the embryo has been passed. Many times, it is necessary for women to have a D & C – a dilatation and curettage of their uterus – to clear out the products of conception. Retaining these in the uterus can lead to infection and ongoing bleeding. What is important to remember if you are bleeding during pregnancyWear a pad or a panty liner so you can monitor your blood loss.Keep a tally of how many pads you are using and how often you need to change them.Don’t use tampons and avoid having sexual intercourse when you are bleeding.Seek advice from your health care professional.Don’t assume you are going to lose the baby. Many women bleed during pregnancy and progress to having a healthy baby on or around their due date.Ectopic pregnancy Occurs when the embryo implants outside of the uterus. The fallopian tube is a common site and because the tubes are not designed to expand like the uterus is, the tube can rupture as the embryo grows. An ectopic pregnancy occurs once in about every sixty pregnancies. It is more common in women who have had surgery to their fallopian tubes, had an ectopic pregnancy previously, or have a history of pelvic infections. Molar pregnancy Although this is a rare condition, it can still occur and is another reason for bleeding during pregnancy. Instead of an embryo forming within the uterus, clusters of abnormal tissue, known as a “mole” grow and take up the space. Bleeding, pain and a lack of foetal signs can all cause suspicion. An ultrasound can distinguish if a molar pregnancy is present. Occasionally women who’ve had a molar pregnancy require chemotherapy due to cancerous cells which have developed. Uterine infection Occasionally an infection is responsible for pregnancy bleeding. Identifying the cause of the infection is important so that the appropriate treatment can be initiated. If a bacterial infection is present then treatment is given with an appropriately sensitive antibiotic. Depending on the extent of the bleeding, hospital admission may be necessary. Urinary tract infection A U.T.I. can cause bleeding during pregnancy, both from the uterus and the bladder. Treatment with antibiotics is usually very effective, but it may be necessary to stay on these long term. Untreated urinary tract infection can lead to premature labour and kidney damage. Post coital bleeding Many women experience light vaginal bleeding after having intercourse. Most commonly, this is because the cervix is inflamed and engorged with blood. Most women are advised to stop having sex for as long as the bleeding continues. Placenta praevia This is a condition which occurs when the placenta lies over, or partially over, the cervix. Instead of the placenta adhering to the wall of the uterus so there is a firm seal where the blood flows between the two, there is a leakage of blood. There are different degrees of placenta praevia, each measuring the extent to which the cervix is covered. If the coverage is complete, there is no way the baby can be born vaginally, so caesarian section delivery is necessary. Older women, having had a previous history, and multiple births, all raise the odds of having placenta praevia. Around 70% of women with placenta praevia have painless bleeding, 20% will experience some cramping with bleeding and 10% have no symptoms. Placental abruption This is an obstetric emergency and can threaten the life of the baby and the mother. In placental abruption, the placenta separates from the wall of the uterus and causes bleeding and abdominal pain. In most cases, caesarian section delivery is necessary. Women who have had four or more children, who use cocaine or tobacco, who are aged 35 or older, who have a history of placental abruption or surgery to their uterus are more at risk. The odds of having placental abruption are around 1 in every 200 pregnancies. Around 80% or women with placental abruption will experience heavy blood loss and clots from their vagina and 20% will not have any visible blood loss at all. Premature labour Having an ante (before) partum (childbirth) bleed can also occur when the baby is coming before its due date. Before the 38th week of pregnancy is classified as premature labour. Blood loss at this time may be more watery and tinged with mucous. This is because the membranes may have ruptured as well and the amniotic fluid is mixing with blood. Uterine rupture Can occur in the later stages of pregnancy and is more common in women who have had four or more children. Where the uterine wall has been weakened, because of previous surgery or caesarian, it is more common for the uterus to separate. A uterine rupture is classified as an obstetric emergency so immediate transport to a hospital is critical. Varicose veins Occasionally, varicose veins of the vagina or lesions on the cervix can cause bleeding during pregnancy. But this tends to be a rare occurrence. Women who have had vaginal trauma or varicosities to the extent where bleeding is possible, usually have some degree of forewarning. Foetal bleeding Can be differentiated from the mother’s blood with a special test on the blood. Foetal cells can be identified as being present in the mother’s vaginal blood, rather than maternal cells. When to get medical help Any bleeding during pregnancy needs to be investigated. Although it can be more common for women to bleed during the first trimester, it is still important to seek the advice of a health care professional. Self diagnosing is common, but it doesn’t help to establish the true reason for blood loss. Ultrasound is a commonly used means of identifying why bleeding has happened. It can also help to work out where the bleeding has originated, if the baby is still viable and what to expect. Seek medical help if:You are experiencing any vaginal bleeding.You feel any cramping or pain.If you do not feel your baby moving or there is a change in the pattern of their movements.If you have an elevated temperature. A normal temperature range is 36.1-37.3 degrees Celsius.If you bleed heavily, pass blood clots or obvious pieces of tissue.If you feel dizzy, faint or lightheaded.If you become breathless or develop pain in the tip of your shoulder/s.If you have had a termination of pregnancy (abortion) and you develop heavy bleeding, an elevated temperature or abdominal pain.Some women don’t realise they are pregnant and find out they are when they present to their doctor because of vaginal bleeding. This is more common with women who have irregular periods and are not using contraception. What you can expect to happen if you are bleeding during pregnancyA check of your medical and obstetric history.A vaginal examination, probably with a speculum.Blood tests. These commonly include a pregnancy test, full blood count, and blood type assessment. Identifying the Rh factor is important, especially for women who are Rh negative and who are carrying an Rh positive baby.A urine test which includes culture and sensitivity to check for infection.An ultrasound to check if the baby is still present, where the embryo has implanted and if there are other issues causing the bleeding. If you are still within the first trimester of pregnancy, you may need to have a full bladder so the uterus can be more clearly seen by the sonographer.Your emotions It can be devastating for couples who are keen to have a baby to experience bleeding during pregnancy. Although many women go on to deliver perfectly healthy babies, there is no guarantee. Supportive counselling can be immensely useful for couples who experience grief and loss issues. Hope it'll help you. Take care

column1: Why doesn't the mental health system work?
column3: We are underfunded. Severely. Whether it’s federal funding or grants or getting paid by an insurance company, we consistently get the short end of the stick. For instance, during the Reagan years our state hospital system was “deregulated” so a lot of people housed in that system were put out into the community. As a result, a lot of patients who were unable to function were dumped into a community which was unprepared and underfunded to handle them.For some reason, in the United States, mental health, optometry and dentistry are separated from a person’s overall health. So people get insurance for mental health coverage that doesn’t include these three, so coverage may be inadequate, require you to purchase a separate policy or missing all together. (And the parity law has not done much to alleviate this.)Our mental health system often works under the “medical model” which requires that a disease be diagnosed before we can “treat” you. A lot of mental health issues are coping skills people have developed to get through life. These behaviors should not be pathologized, nor should the person have to be diagnosed as being “mentally ill” before we can help them. Trauma disorders are an excellent example of this. Trauma symptoms are a normal person’s reaction to an abnormal situation. Unfortunately, insurance billing and other systems require that I diagnose you with a mental health disorder, PTSD, before I can treat you. There is also no preventative element to mental health. We can’t treat someone who has been in a horrific situation in order to prevent trauma symptoms from developing. We have to wait until they develop symptoms first.We have allowed ourselves to be compromised by the pharmaceutical industry. We are working to address this, but it needs to be addressed and that is on us.We allow our culture to pathologize behaviors which are not pathological; i.e. diagnosing and “treating” children and young adults for ADHD or autism spectrum disorders when the real problem is bad or inadequate parenting. This too is our fault.Mental health is the bastard stepchild of the health industry. Trainings in any given topic are often geared only toward medical providers with no inclusion of mental health providers. Whether the information is regarding working with transgender clients, HIV clients or HIPAA requirements, it’s extremely difficult to find information that is not tailored only for medical procedures and providers.Mental health is not included as a valid piece of a patient’s treatment nor are we considered a valuable part of a treatment team. See 5.The medical profession does not seem to be trained in basic psychology. They drive therapists mad with some of their practices. Whether they are:causing trauma with their procedures/processes Actual Example: They don’t seem to recognize that there is a mind connected to the “diabetes patient” which harbors thoughts and feelings about the potential need to amputate their foot.or treating psychological issues with medical solutions Actual Example: the patient is grinding their teeth to the point that they are causing severe nerve damage to their face and severe damage to their teeth. The doctor does not suggest counseling to see if there are stressors in the patient’s life or to screen the patient for anxiety and teach them anxiety reduction techniques. The doctor does not refer them to a dentist for protective guards to protect their teeth. The recommended solutions? 1) muscle relaxers, 2) botox injections, or 3) surgery. Actual Example: A patient has just received a terminal diagnosis and is experiencing a great deal of anxiety, grief, anger, etc. about their impending death. Instead of referring them to a counselor they just prescribe Xanax.
column9: You missed one very huge piece of this puzzle: making people feel like they are mentally ill when in fact we're all living in a toxic culture/society/world where our "mentally ill" reactions are just us adapting to things we have no control over.

column1: What is the standard to diagnose a person as normal? Like not a sociopath, borderline, narcissistic, psychopath, etc., but a regular normal, functional person.
column3: There is none. You either have psychiatric symptoms, or you don’t. A psych will tell you if they feel you are having a normal reaction to an event, like grief… An ethical one. Most important word, ethical. But a psych’s job is literally, well… To diagnose and in the case of psychiatrist, medicate people. There are some psychs (haha autocorrect originally put psychos— check my edit log, and well, to a degree, that can be true. Mental health professionals are “psycho” when it comes to certain things) who practice therapy, but it’s more common to find LMFT’s and LCSW’s who are the therapists, and probably because there’s lesser competition for when it comes to the need of assessments and diagnostics as a result of there being less people able to diagnose, and a doctorate will always be more expensive than a masters, and thus, that will turn a lot of people off.. Everyone to a degree has behavioral patterns. That is why there’s a thing such as psychology, and why there’s an entire science behind it. If a person doesn’t have abnormal psychology, they will not meet off anything in the DSM criteria.. You cannot just assess if someone is “normal” or not, and I also should say many people go to a professional when they need not to, and end up misdiagnosed. Take someone who just lost a loved one… The person now doesn’t have anyone to support them, as the person they had lost was their only support. Doctor puts them on antidepressants, and tells them to go to psychotherapy. They were grieving normally… Didn’t have suicidal thoughts… Just had a “depressed mood”. But the psych wants money, and it’s their job, quite literally, to prescribe.. Now the person is wasting money and time, and not truly getting what they’re in need of. They need consolation and hands on support, which a therapist and antidepressant pill is not going to give them. They need to be embraced. They if they are spiritual, need spiritual care. They need to have a break from work, school, or the liking… They need to be treated gently. ANYONE who doesn’t get these things in response to something like the death of a loved one, is going to depress, and not feel very well, because it’s a literal NEED. It doesn’t make them “abnormal”, but now they feel abnormal.. When they are having a perfectly normal response to grief.. Now, they’ve convinced themselves they are “sick”… When they to begin with, were not. They just didn’t have the support. And yet they’re being treated (intentional pun), as if they are ill and abnormal.. Get a diagnosis of depression for insurance purposes, when truly, they are just grieving.. Grieving over the loss of their loved one, and an additional grieve of having no one there to comfort them. This is one of many reasons why I despise of western psychology. Western psychology convinces perfectly normal people they’re ill.. Western psychology kills people by teaching you to cope with things, when it’s not actually healthy to cope with them, and you need to directly address the root, or else it’s always going to be there and you’re going to always feel empty.. It is like putting a bandaid on a mole that is undesirable for your appearance, but never checking to see if the mole is cancerous.. How do I know? Because I’ve had western psychotherapy.. It convinced me I am ill, when really, I just am a normal person, who is a bit different than others… And I got abused by my parents, bullied and never had friends. I would be healthy if I had of those things. It’s a normal response to be as how I now, am… Not healthy, but normal and understands.. But because most people have friends, and grew up with non-abusive parents, I am seen as “abnormal”, because most people won’t have developed defenses like me. I was forced on antidepressant meds against my will.. Mother put it in my food (not with intent of malice), and was forced on the psychiatric pills in hospitals.. I had always refused, is why mother put it in my food. I intuitively have known they’re bad for you.. And I also knew that if I had what I NEEDED I wouldn’t have been “depressed”. That if I had a friend… Someone to hold me as I grieve and cry.. I wouldn’t be low… I was having a perfectly normal response to pain and abuse, but because most poeople don’t get abused and most people have support from at least someone, I was seen as abnormal because compared to the general population, I look abnormal being sad and depressed… But it’s a normal reaction to a situation as I had been in. Rather than “treat an illness” that they don’t have, you treat their lack of support— you help them find friends, who can give them what they actually need; hands on support (quite literally, even. There are no words when it comes to losing someone, only physical gestures). If this person had someone to lean on and help them cope with daily obligations they cannot handle during this time, and also to provide comfort and support, I am pretty sure they would not be as “depressed”. I put depressed in quotations, because clinical depression is a lot different than just being inconsolable and feeling hopeless and low over someone dying, in my opinion. They don’t need antidepressants, they don’t even need psychotherapy.. These things are distractions from the real problem; them not having the support and basic needs met that are necessary, and psychotherapy and antidepressant pills are teaching them to “cope” with that, when the root is never being tended to. (Looks like autocorrect agrees with me… It is “psycho” in my opinion, to medicate and give someone therapy, in place of what they TRULY need).
