column1: What are some signs that your cat is not happy with the way you are treating it?
column3: Copied and pasted from Rover.com : How to Tell If My Cat is Depressed: Signs and Symptoms Before you can determine if your cat is depressed, you should rule out health concerns. Dr. Mikel Delgado says that although there are some clear symptoms of cat depression, they might not tell the whole picture. She says “we can infer, but we can never truly know what’s going on in our cat’s mind.” These symptoms can indicate a larger health concern and a need to take your cat to the vet:not eating or drinkingexcessive scratchinggrooming to a point of hair losswithdrawal or hiding may indicate a health concernIf you suspect your cat has become apathetic, you may also want to keep an eye out for other potential symptoms of depression, such as: Disinterest in normal activities If a cat loses interest in playing with their toys or engaging in normal behaviors, it could be a sign that they’re not feeling well. Dr. Delgado refers to these normal behaviors as “good welfare signs.” She goes on to say that if your cat is depressed, they tend to have lower energy, lose interest in playing or interacting with you, and fail to engage in other species-specific behaviors. While it’s common for cats to want some alone time to relax, if there’s a significant change in what’s normal for them, they might be depressed. Increased hiding or withdrawal It’s common for cats to hide out from time to time.“[But] cats should not be sitting or hiding in one spot all day,” says Dr. Delgado says. If a cat becomes significantly more reclusive than usual, it may be a sign that they’re feeling down. Hiding can also indicate that a cat isn’t interested in activities they usually enjoy, such as playing with toys or cuddling up with their humans. Cats with depression are generally more fearful, and they may hide to soothe and protect themselves. Sleeping more or in different locations Cats sleep an average of 15 hours a day, so if you notice they’re sleeping a lot, it’s not always cause for concern. Dr. Delgado says cats love to sleep and need lots of it, but if they sleep too much, it might signal depression. Also, a change in the location where they normally love to doze off can be a clue that they’re not feeling like themselves.Tanchic/iStock Verbalizations Cats can be pretty vocal animals, but if you notice a change in their vocalizations, it could indicate that something is awry. In particular, a loud, mournful yowl low in pitch can be their way of saying that they’re unhappy. While purring often means a cat is content, depressed cats may purr more than usual to comfort and soothe themselves. Additionally, excessive purring can also indicate that a cat is unhappy. Tense body language Cats speak volumes through their body language, and they have a number of ways of physically communicating that they’re unhappy. If you notice that a cat’s ears are back, their fur is standing on end, or their tail is tucked instead of raised high, they likely aren’t feeling their best. It’s common for cats to tense up while they’re playing, but a happy and healthy cat will relax afterward. Increased or decreased appetite Like humans, if a cat is feeling low, it can directly affect their interest in food. If a cat is depressed, they may suddenly stop eating. They may even turn down their favorite treats. While less common, unhappy cats may also increase their food intake as a way to self-soothe. Regardless of whether they’re eating more or less, a change in eating habits can indicate that cats aren’t feeling like their normal happy selves. Aggression Pet parents often think that aggression in cats is simply a response to a threat, but it can actually communicate a number of things, including their mood. Aggression stemming from depression isn’t just a “stop it bite” or occasional hiss; it’s a consistent series of behaviors. Unhappy cats are more likely to perceive things as threats, whether or not they actually are. Subsequently, if a cat is feeling depressed, they often become more hostile and frequently lash out at all you or other cats or pets in the house. Over- or under-grooming Grooming is part of a normal and healthy cat routine. However, when a cat is feeling down, their grooming habits can take a sharp turn. A depressed cat may increase or decrease the amount that they groom themselves. Some cats may even stop grooming completely. As a result, unhappy cats often have gnarly, unkempt coats. If they start over-grooming, you may start to see bald patches on your cat. A trip to the vet can help them get their grooming habits back on track. Your vet can prescribe your cat Clomipramine, used to treat anxiety and depression in cats, to help reduce overgrooming behaviors.SilviaJansen/iStock Spraying Spraying might seem like an act of rebellion, but it can actually be intended for a cat’s own comfort. According to the Veterinary Ireland Journal, cats will sometimes spray their urine to self-soothe. Surrounding themselves with their own scent can help reduce anxiety. As unhappy cats tend to be more fearful, they will do whatever they can to mitigate the fear, including urinating outside the litter box. This often happens if a particular situation is causing the cat’s low mood. Destructive scratching Scratching is a normal cat behavior, and they scratch as a marking behavior to deposit their scent from glands on their paws. According to the Cornell Feline Health Center, cats also scratch to remove the translucent covering (the sheath) from their claws. While scratching is normal, excessive, destructive cat scratching is when cats scratch at household objects that aren’t their scratching posts or acceptable scratching spots rather than their usual, acceptable spots. Dr. Delgado says this could indicate the cat is stressed or upset. To help with destructive cat scratching, pet parents assess what their cat needs and try redirecting their cat to scratching posts or other normal scratching items. 5 Causes or Triggers Behind Cat Depression Dr. Delgado says the following are several of the most common reasons for cat depression.A change in a cat’s environment. Cats are very sensitive to any change in their lives, big or small. Some changes that might cause a cat to be depressed include a big move to a new home, new furniture, or a partner moving into your home.Stress. Like humans, stress is a common reason for cat depression and other feline illnesses. When a life stressor happens to a cat, they can develop symptoms of depression, including aggression and other behavioral issues.Other cats. Cats are very particular, so introducing a new cat into their home can lead to all sorts of problems, including depression, because it’s a drastic change. Pet parents wanting to bring another cat into their home should do so properly to avoid unnecessary stress for both felines.Grieving. When we lose a precious companion, we grieve their loss. Turns out cats do the same. Cats might not show their grief the same way, but the loss of their companion can make them show signs of depression, such as withdrawal, a change in appetite, overgrooming, changing sleep patterns, and more. To help, pet parents should understand that grief has no timetable, but including extra playtime, extra attention, and patience can help.Separation anxiety. Sometimes, pet parents have to spend time away from their cats. There’s a belief that cats can easily cope with long absences from their parent. However, recent studies have shown that cats are more sociable than we think and form special bonds with you. Therefore, they are more likely to show behavior changes, like depression, when you’re gone for long periods.What’s normal for one cat may not be normal for your cat, so look at changes in their specific behavioral patterns to see if something is amiss. Cats are generally creatures of habit, so when there’s suddenly a shift in their behavior, it’s very unlikely that it’s random. Other family members, as well as your cat sitter, can also help alert you to alarming changes. If you notice changes in your cat’s behavior, it’s best to consult with a vet right away. Talk with them about the changes you’ve noticed in your cat, and they can help you come up with an appropriate treatment plan.sdominick/iStock How to Help a Depressed Cat Dr. Delgado outlines the following checklist pet parents should follow if they suspect their cat is depressed:Go to the vet to rule out other medical conditions. It’s important to make sure your cat doesn’t have a serious health problem with the same signs as depression.Assess the environment for changes or unusual events that may be happening outside your window. Ask yourself: Has there been a new cat roaming around outside? Has your work schedule changed? To help your cat adapt to these new changes, it’s best to make them feel comfortable by not changing too much at once and maintaining a spot of refuge for them.Encourage interactive play and activities.Enrichment is providing the necessary environment for your cat to satisfy their instincts and is important for a cat’s overall wellbeing. Try to initiate different play activities and use new toys. In fact, pet parents who play with their cat more frequently and for longer report fewer behavioral problems in their cat.Foster social interactions. It’s a myth that cats are antisocial pets. They desire consistent social interaction and love to show affection to you. Carve out quality time to spend with your cats, such as cuddling on the bed or couch.Purchase medication to deal with stressors. If lifestyle changes don’t help, work with your vet to buy the appropriate medications for your cat to help with stressors that might be causing depression. One of these medications is Venlafaxine; studies have shown this medication can help treat depression and other behavioral disorders in catsConsult with a behavior professional. Dr. Delgado and other cat behavioral specialists are trained to spot behaviors that can signal depression and work with pet parents on how to help their cat. Cat behaviorists closely monitor any behavioral abnormalities. They observe your cat closely in their environment and then develop an appropriate treatment plan, sometimes in tandem with a vet.Takeaway Cats are often thought of as mysterious, but they communicate just as clearly as other pets do. If there’s a change in their normal behaviors, the root of the problem could be emotional. Knowing your cat and being able to pick up on the signals they give you is important, especially if you ever want to bring a second cat or other pet into your home.

column1: How can a doctor be so sure of a mental illness when diagnosing one?
column3: I am certainly no psychiatrist, but I do know a bit about this. It is not always so easy to be sure of some mental illnesses. The criteria try to be clear, but it is an intrinsically “fuzzy” area. It is not like, say, infectious disease where you see clear things like a fever, an abscess, or a bacteria growing in the blood. That said, there are some disorders, like schizophrenia, that have pretty dramatic symptoms that are fairly consistent from one patient to the next. With experience, these things start to become quite clear when you see them. Other disorders, like narcissistic personality disorder, can be hard to pin down with certainty. There are criteria listed but they are pretty subjective. The best psychiatrists and psychologists, I believe, will keep an open mind and not be too quick to make a specific diagnosis unless things are really obvious. If someone is hearing the voice of the devil and believes everyone is trying to poison them, they are probably schizophrenic. If someone is unable to function “normally” (whatever that means…) because they are terrified of germs on every surface out in the world and stay at home all day wiping their house with bleach, then they probably have a form of obsessive-compulsive disorder. The major conditions are clear — the patients are unhappy with their lives, and people around them are affected by their behavior in a consistent way that everyone sees. But many conditions are not so clear, and many patients have mild disorders that overlap with “normal”. Unfortunately, the way medicine works, we have to make a diagnosis of something, since it is unethical to treat a patient for nothing. So labels get attached to a patient that may not be quite right. After losing a close loved one, it is “normal” to have a period of grief and some degree of depression. How long should someone stay at home grieving after their mother dies, or their child? A week? A day? A month? For cases where this grief is affecting the patient in a way they feel is uncomfortable for them, there is the diagnosis of “adjustment disorder not otherwise specified” or something along those lines. When this kind of situation crosses over from a normal reaction to something that can be called an “illness” is a very subjective thing, and mostly it is determined by what the patient feels…if they feel that the feelings are out of control, unwelcome, abnormal, then they start to seek help. Whether that qualifies as an illness is a hard question to answer. I have known someone who had a significant fear of being confined in small spaces. She panicked one day when we were driving through a car wash, and nearly opened the car door to try to get out, right in the middle of the car wash! Another friend got very anxious when stuck in traffic. Another person I knew was cheated on by her ex-husband, and that left her quite scared of getting close to men again, seeing warning signs about possible cheating in every little thing anyone did. These reactions can have a label attached to them, but are they an illness, or just an individual quirk, or a normal reaction to a stressful event in life? If they affect someone’s ability to function, like say someone is unable to ride in a car at all because they fear they might get stuck in traffic, so they stay home all the time, and start sweating and shaking at the mere sight of a car, maybe that is an illness. A big part of this is how the patient experiences it. If they find their feelings are out of control and impeding the way they want to live their life, then it starts to become a mental illness, and it will be clear because they will tell their therapist that they are unhappy with how they are and want help to change. On the other hand, there are disorders where the “patient” feels just fine, but everyone around them is suffering because of their behavior. Many of us, for example, are thoughtless or selfish from time to time. We may forget to run an errand we promised to do, or not perceive that someone close to us is in a bad mood, or not notice that our spouse is getting frustrated with washing the dishes all week and we have not offered to help. These are things I think most of us would say are normal, and we feel bad about our mistake and try to fix it. But then there are people who actually have no empathy at all, do not perceive other people as real beings with their own feelings and needs, and who blame everyone else for their problems and feelings and even their actions. To those people, if you are unhappy it is your fault. If they forgot to do something they promised, it is your fault. If you are unhappy because they have not offered to help with housework for a month, it is your fault. They feel superior, entitled, and above everyone else. All problems are from something outside themselves. They feel fine, except maybe frustrated that the world is not following their wishes, but everyone around them is miserable. Is this selfishness, immaturity, or a personality disorder like narcissistic personality disorder (NPD)? Here, the diagnosis is not so easy, despite having clear criteria for NPD. But again, an experienced therapist (psychologist or psychiatrist) will have seen similar cases before, and will probably be able to make the right assessment after enough time. So, I guess what I am getting at is that it is a matter of experience and training, having seen enough clear cases of the different mental illnesses, that leads to a degree of certainty about what is and is not a mental illness. But it is not a completely objective field, for sure.

column1: Why are we sometimes in a mental condition where we don't like anything to do?
column3: Please, do not assume because one does not have a desire to do nothing at all, that one must be suffering some form of mental health condition. I am a Doctor of Psychology, who holds multiple degrees within 10 of 14 sanctioned fields of Psychological studies, plus Doctorate degrees in Philosophy and Social Anthropology. I spent 20 plus years in academic institutes and studied other fields as well under dual majors of Science and Arts. I have obtained as much knowledge one can garner regarding the human psyche of human behavior within the human condition. Otherwise, I am about as sane as they come. I often take pleasure in doing absolutely nothing at all. It is both a choice and a privilege. It is an exercise of my free will. Now on the other hand, if you have chosen to do nothing at all, and it causes you grief and discomfort, then it is very possible that there is something that is the reason for that discomfort. Then I would advise you to first see a medical practitioner and get a complete and full medical check up including a complete blood and urine panel done. These are tests done in a laboratory that will check to see if they may be any hidden physical health issues. Sometimes when there is something wrong with our body, we don’t always get familiar physical symptoms, so instead the brain sends out a signal mentally that something is not right. The blood and urine test will discover any physical abnormalities. Now if there are none, the medical practitioner can then provide you with a series of questions to test for depression, or refer you to a medical mental health professional called a Psychiatrist who can determine any mental health diagnosis. But remember what I said. If you choose to do nothing just for the sake of doing nothing, and feel no guilt of shame. That is absolutely okay. Just do not make it permanent. It serves no purpose and everyone must have a purpose in life.
column9: Yes, or maybe people just need to let go of the guilt and shame in doing nothing, and then they could enjoy the pleasure of a state of being… instead of doing.

column1: How does medical science define the pathophysiology of a "broken heart"?
column3: This is a bit of “it can’t” and “here’s what it can say”. Emotions influence hormones and nervous system function. Different people have different physiological responses to grief, although they come in fairly predictable patterns. For example, in immediate responses people often cry, their faces and eyes turn red, etc, which are functions of the parasympathetic nervous system, while they might also feel anxious, have rapid heart rates, breath quickly, and feel light-headed, which can all be due to sympathetic signals (which oppose parasympathetic). Both types of signals can influence things in the heart and the differing strong parasympathetic and sympathetic signals make one feel very odd and uncomfortable, which is part of the reason for the comparatively abnormal feelings during heartbreak, but it doesn’t truly explain it all. Exact feelings of “heartbrokenness” are difficult to define or pin down, and not everyone feels the same when they say they are heartbroken. Some people literally have an aching chest pain chronically, some have it only when they think of that person, and some people don’t really have it. It is important to keep in mind that one’s perceptions and emotions can influence one’s sensations: a phenomenon referred to as somatization. You may feel the loss or emotional ache/pain of break-up or losing someone and your body can turn that into a physical chest pain or other symptoms. These don’t really have medical explanations besides the brain making it happen as a somatic expression of mental/emotional upset. All that to say emotions influence the body’s functions. Some are more logical, some appear completely irrational, and a lot of it varies in type and intensity by person.

column1: Am so depressed in these days, I need an escape what should I do, am so lonely and I don't want to talk to anyone and am behaving very badly?
column3: If you are truly depressed, you need professional evaluation. I always recommend seeing a board-certified psychiatrist with proven experience with symptoms you are experiencing, before you do anything else about this. It is very typical for someone with depression to feel lonely, yet avoid human interaction. There are many such paradoxes with authentic depression. Sadness and grief are a normal part of the human experience, while depression is a clinical illness that almost always requires professional management. Usually the clinician sorts out what is “normal” and what is actual illness and physical causes must also be considered, so that’s why it’s crucial to start with a qualified MD; then if physical causes are ruled out and psychotherapy is recommended, a therapist can take over from that point. If there are physical causes or medication is needed, the first MD can handle that for you. Non-MD therapists tend to forget about other possible causes and often are not trained to consider them, so an MD needs to be your first stop. Such issues as Vitamin D deficiency or thyroid abnormalities can cause all kinds of so-called mental illness which disappear once the primary issue is corrected. It is very important to have all possible aggravating factors addressed and ruled out as part of the evaluation. Please follow through; if behavior has changed, there is always a reason that can be addressed with proper care. My best to you…

column1: In the show "The end of the ****ing world", does the character James show traits of autism?
column3: I work with adolescents with autism, and I definitely recognized them in James. (And possibly also in Alyssa) I’ll do what the other answerer did and give my take on the diagnostic criteria… Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple contexts, as manifested by the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text):Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, ranging, for example, from abnormal social approach and failure of normal back-and-forth conversation; to reduced sharing of interests, emotions, or affect; to failure to initiate or respond to social interactions.Clearly yes. James has a flat affect, and most of his social approaches in the show are awkward and uncomfortable. (He’s also very charming, and that dissonance is part of what makes the show so funny and great. Also true for many of my students.) I think he talks about not knowing what to do in social situations, but I can’t remember any specific examples.Deficits in nonverbal communicative behaviors used for social interaction, ranging, for example, from poorly integrated verbal and nonverbal communication; to abnormalities in eye contact and body language or deficits in understanding and use of gestures; to a total lack of facial expressions and nonverbal communication.James’s body language is very still and turned in on himself, and he doesn’t express much emotion with his voice, face or body. This is pretty typical for someone with poor understanding of non-verbal communication who is trying to do the bare minimum with their face and body so they seem as normal as possible.Deficits in developing, maintaining, and understand relationships, ranging, for example, from difficulties adjusting behavior to suit various social contexts; to difficulties in sharing imaginative play or in making friends; to absence of interest in peers.James doesn’t appear to have any friends, and doesn’t express interest in anyone but Alyssa. His last line in the first season is “I’ve just turned 18, and I think I understand what people mean to each other.”Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests, or activities, as manifested by at least two of the following, currently or by history (examples are illustrative, not exhaustive; see text):Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects, or speech (e.g., simple motor stereotypes, lining up toys or flipping objects, echolalia, idiosyncratic phrases).James sits in a very specific way - very still, facing forward with his hands on his knees. This is typical in students who have been taught not to stim, or who understand the social penalties associated with it. I have one student who has two settings: Repeatedly hitting himself in the balls or sitting perfectly still and staring into space, because that’s the only way he can stop repeatedly hitting himself in the balls.Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines, or ritualized patterns of verbal or nonverbal behavior (e.g., extreme distress at small changes, difficulties with transitions, rigid thinking patterns, greeting rituals, need to take same route or eat same food every day).When young James says he needs to feed the ducks, even though it’s obvious that it’s creating a problem for his family, he says it in exactly the same way my students do when they are worried the schedule is going to change. This was the most clearly autistic moment for me in the whole show. The other answerer felt that James was calm about the total lack of routine in his time with Alyssa, but I’d argue that literally all he can do under those circumstances is follow Alyssa. He’s not coping with the situation at all, he’s just…following Alyssa. Following Alyssa takes the place of routine and ritual in giving him a way to structure his life.Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus (e.g., strong attachment to or preoccupation with unusual objects, excessively circumscribed or perseverative interests).Yes, obviously, he's obsessed with killing things. Until he isn’t, and then he’s completely destabilized by the absence of that interest to focus on.Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment (e.g. apparent indifference to pain/temperature, adverse response to specific sounds or textures, excessive smelling or touching of objects, visual fascination with lights or movement).He puts his hand in a pot of boiling water so he can feel something. I know a lot of viewers attribute that to an expression of grief, but most people grieving a parent don’t stick their hand in a pot of boiling water.Symptoms must be present in the early developmental period (but may not become fully manifest until social demands exceed limited capacities, or may be masked by learned strategies in later life).The ducks, the boiling water, the killing things.Symptoms cause clinically significant impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of current functioning.James’s life is not going well. He lives in his car. He doesn’t have a job or go to school. He killed someone.
column9: I think this is a very well thought out answer, I generally agree that James does share traits, I disagree more so with Alyssa but I always thought James had it

column1: Why do some people have positive thoughts, and others have negative thoughts?
column3: Upbringing and life experiences can also play a significant role in shaping an individual's mindset, as positive or negative patterns of thinking may be learned from family, friends, or societal influences. One of the most common reasons behind negative thoughts is our past experiences. Our past experiences shape the way we view the world, and if we have had negative experiences in the past, they can impact the way we think and feel in the present. Those who were more attuned to danger and who paid more attention to the bad things around them were more likely to survive. The evolutionary perspective suggests that this tendency to dwell on the negative more than the positive is simply one way the brain tries to keep us safe. Intrusive negative thoughts can be a symptom of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) or another mental health condition. Negative thinking is also symptomatic of depression ("Negative Thinking and Depression fuels the Other"). How do I rewire my brain to stop thinking negative? Be Aware of Your Thoughts. Turn Negatives into Positives. Understand What Triggers You. Pactice Daily Gratitude. Switch Up Your Environment. In the Islamic faith, scrupulosity (and other intrusive thought subtypes) are often referred to as “wasawis.” Wasawis describe unwanted thoughts that are whispered into the mind and hearts of people by Shaitan (Satan). There is no punishment over uncontrolled dirty, negative or abnormal thoughts as only consciously done actions are recorded for good or bad deeds of a person. (Qur'ān 26:72). They said: 'Nay, but we found our fathers doing thus (what we do). '" (Qur'ān 26:74). Hence, as confirmed in the following Qur'ānic verse, their worship is not based on any spiritual attitude of mind, but just mere imitation of their ancestors. Since the Quran informs us that those negative people “..might become conscious of God” (6:69), i.e. they could change for the better, Muslim activists should contemplate on how to engage them in a manner that would not invite negativity from them or cause them to be defensive. It's a fact that whatever we do or say on a daily basis becomes part of our subconscious mind. If we say good things to ourselves even in bad situations, it will turn the situation. So, we must make a habit of using positive affirmations to feed positive energy to our minds. Stop overthinking. You are stressing yourself too much & instead you should trust Allah. Where is your trust in Allah? He loves you, He won't let you dow Many times the Quran reminds one that there is no grief or fear if one remains steadfast and that the Hereafter is free of all those negative and overwhelming feelings and situations (Quran 43:68, 46:13). The Quran acknowledges the reality of these emotions and, by extension, acknowledges the reality of depression. The Power of Negative Thought Patterns Shayṭān can make the most ridiculous things appear as acceptable through this process of negative thoughts.That is why it is so important for us to be aware of what we are thinking of and work hard to filter out bad thoughts quickly. Once you have spent time thinking about something often, it becomes a lot harder to fight that thought; your mind will be able to revisit those dark places more easily because it knows they exist.Negative thoughts – and sometimes overthinking as well – can take up a lot of people’s time and lead to problems like stress, anxiety, and insomnia. It takes a lot of willpower to fight and change, and results are not attained it is important to note here that these kinds of problems do not usually arise from a place where people are spiritually weak; this means that telling a depressed person that their problem is due to a lack of īmān is ignorance. Rather, this state arises from an emotional problem, and as a secondary effect it can have a negative impact on spiritual, mental, and physical aspects of a person’s life.There is a lot of information available on things you can do to try and combat negative thoughts and become a more positive person. But it is essential to recognise that the brain is like a muscle and it will take time to strengthen; you will have to be patient with yourself. As much as we would like there to be one, there is no immediate stop button for overthinking and negative thoughts. But these symptoms can become much more weakened by a good routine and schedule that involves increasing emotional, mental, and spiritual well being.Whether this is your personal struggle, or that of someone you know, you must remember that the real enemy is always Shayṭān.Verily Shayṭān is for people a clear enemy.Do not lose hope in yourself or in others, and do not think of people as all evil. There is a call to both good and evil inside everyone; sometimes people lose that battle, and they do things that are morally wrong. But that does not mean that they will always lose.The brothers of Yūsuf thought of killing him, left him down a dark well, and did not show much remorse for years. But they did eventually see how wrong they were and then sought Allah’s forgiveness.For as long as we are alive then we have a chance to fix up. For as long as we are alive there is hope.Beware of your thoughts, for they can become words. Beware of your words, for they can become your actions. Beware of your actions, for they can become your habits. And finally, beware of your habits, for they can become your destiny.

column1: Is neuroscience going to replace psychology?
column3: Neuroscience will replace the field of psychiatry in the areas of diagnosis and treatment of “mental illness”, but there will always be a place for psychology. One day we will completely understand the brain’s function and its specific connections that result in the spectrum of human behavior and mental processing. But while waiting for that, people are diagnosed as having a mental disorder because a consensus of a small group of people voted that way. Until we can develop definitive medical diagnostic tests to find these, psychiatrists use a standardized guide for consistent diagnoses of mental problems. This is currently provided by the American Psychiatric Association’s (APA) very subjective and controversial Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) first published in 1952 with 132 pages. In that version, homosexuality was listed as a sociopathic personality disturbance. The most recent 5th edition, the DSM5, was a major revision published in 2013. In over 950 pages, hundreds of mental disorders are labeled with descriptions of symptoms. None have a description of what the brain is doing anatomically and physiologically to cause these behavioral symptoms except when they note symptoms that “can be related to” various (presumably non-“psychological”) medical problems. This is the current standard for diagnosing mental illness – consensus opinion and no biological investigation. Diagnosis by descriptions of symptoms would be like diagnosing kidney failure, or adrenal gland disease, or extreme thirst, or diabetes, or pituitary disease (take you pick!) because a patient is drinking water excessively. Here is an excerpt from the book “What Am I and Why Do I Do the Things I Do?” Psychiatrist Allen Frances warned that DSM5 could "medicalize normality and result in a glut of unnecessary and harmful drug prescription." In a pre-publication blog he listed some potentially harmful entries, including diagnoses of Disruptive Mood Dysregulation Disorder (temper tantrum), Major Depressive Disorder that includes normal grief for a deceased person, Minor Neurocognitive Disorder (age-related forgetfulness), Binge Eating Disorder (eating too much), classification of introversion as a form of autism, first time drug users lumped in with addicts, Behavioral Addictions that make a "mental disorder of everything we like to do a lot”, and Generalized Anxiety Disorder to include everyday worries. A bereavement exclusion for people that lack energy and self-esteem during six months after losing a loved one was removed. That makes it a diagnosis of depression. You are mentally ill if you grieve for someone that recently died. Things that used to be variations of normal now have diagnostic labels, and therefore potential treatments. (also, see Allan Horwitz and Jerome Wakefield’s book The Loss of Sadness: How psychiatry transformed sorrow into depressive disorder and Gary Greenberg’s book Manufacturing Depression: The secret history of modern disease) The DSM5 lists Caffeine Intoxication as a mental disorder. It is simply not. It is a physiological toxicity. Caffeine Withdrawal is also now a mental health disorder. If you stop drinking coffee and get a headache you now have a mental illness rather than just suffering a physical symptom that is biological and normal. Neglecting a spouse or partner is a mental illness, and interestingly, it can result in mental illness in the neglected partner. Smoking pot is a mental disorder with about 10 subcategories. Seriously? You are diagnosed as having a mental disorder because a consensus of a small group of people voted that way. In over 950 pages, hundreds of mental disorders are labeled with descriptions of symptoms. None have a description of what the brain is doing anatomically and physiologically to cause these behavioral symptoms except when they note symptoms that “can be related to” various (presumably non-“psychological”) medical problems. This is the current standard for diagnosing mental illness – consensus opinion and no biological investigation. Biology tells us that we all lie somewhere along a spectrum that spans from incapacitating mental illness to extreme mental health. The vast majority of us act normally only because the majority decides the definition of normal. We all see ourselves as neurotypical, although most of us are somewhere off the exact center of normal. We judge the outliers as mentally abnormal. Similar to the way that autism is considered a spectrum disorder, and affected people are on “the” spectrum, it seems apparent that all mental illness is similarly on a spectrum. We are all on the spectrum of all mental disorders. A person with a brain abnormality that does not affect personality, such as epilepsy, is seen as similar to someone with any other physical abnormality. But when the defect affects a part of the brain that controls social behaviors or personality, the assessment changes. A “mentally ill” person is judged as a defective “self”, even though they also have a biological (genetic and epigenetic) abnormality or dysfunction like any other medical condition. But it defines who the person is as a person instead of just describing something that affects one body part; in this case his or her mind. The heritability of many personality traits, such as depression (30-40 percent heritable) and bipolar/manic depressive disorder (80 percent heritable), has been determined. There are multiple genes involved, many of which are yet to be identified, and the environmental influences on those genes are also complex. Much work is currently being done to learn about the physiology and anatomy that causes various disabling syndromes to one day make definitive and scientific diagnoses. When we finally get diagnostic ability by looking at the brain’s connectome, we will see exactly what causes what, and can medically determine the need, and direction, for intervention/correction. It will not involve consensus opinion and diagnosis-by-symptom, but will be diagnosis-by-medical test. It will not be shoot-in-the-dark medications to treat symptoms, but directed corrective addressing of the etiology – the cause of the problem.
column9: “Neuroscience will replace the field of psychiatry in the areas of diagnosis and treatment of “mental illness”, but there will always be a place for psychology.”. 😂👏 psychiatry is clinical neuroscience…

column1: Should I ask him to apologise for abusing me?
column3: SYNOPSIS: Based solely on what you’ve described, it sounds as though you are suffering from Narcissistic Abuse Syndrome. No, you should NOT contact your abuser for any reason.
