column1: Why does food intolerance from irritable bowel syndrome cause diarrhea and aggravate my gut with belly cramps? How do I improve my tolerance to foods?
column3: IBS isn’t causing your food intolerances. Food intolerances may contribute to IBS and make it worse but are not the cause of IBS. IBS is its own disorder. People with IBS have abnormalities in the colon that make it react in ways it should not. So it only makes sense to avoid eating anything that gives you symptoms and work with a gastroenterologist who works with IBS patients to find out what works best for you to control the symptoms. I was diagnosed with a very long list of genuine food allergies, the kind that show up on skin tests, ( not just intolerances ) and went on a diet that eliminated everything I was allergic to for about 13 years. No it was not fun to do that but I got used to it and it made an unbelievable difference to the severity of the problem and I go years without an attack now, though when I get one it tends to be a long long time before it resolves and I never know what triggers them those attacks. It’s just the damn disease. Now I can eat a few of the foods that once bothered me, so long as I don’t overdo it and I’ve learned to simply avoid eating most of the things that will give me digestive grief. Eliminating all foods that give you trouble for at least a few years is the only way I know that you might improve tolerance to SOME of those foods but NOT all of them. It’s better to learn to live without most of them instead and I can promise that is not the worst fate that can befall a person.

column1: Why do some people get depressed?
column3: I am a simple layman. I don't have many insights on psychology and psychiatry. In my 38 years of existence, I have seen enough. Earlier I didn't have a slight knowledge about depression let alone different kinds of human emotions and sensitivities. Growing up, Humans naturally face different situations which make them sad, anxious or stressed. It is completely normal. What is abnormal is when the degrees of those emotions heighten and turn into frequent episodes. Many things can trigger depression. I will write what I have seen.Fat shaming, Bullying which leads to inability to mingle with other kids. I never knew I had depression during childhood. I was fatter than most kids. I have curly when 99.9% of children around me had straight hair. I also have ugly eyes which made me look like I am angry. I felt alienated. My father's side was poor and my mother's side was rich. I was in the middle and didn't fit anywhere. I was lonely and turned into a bookworm. I had eating disorder which in turn made me fatter and fatter each day. I developed serious inferiority complex. I tried hard to be funny and comic and always laughed to attract attention but deep inside there was always a fear. That was the beginning of a life-lonh fight against depression.Unfortunate events like loved ones passing away, cheating partner and betrayals, break ups. It is said that time heals wounds. The person actually going through such incidents only know how slow time passes. Each movement of the second-hand of a clock can become real slow. Living a day can be compared to a year when you are living in sorrow. Not all of us have strong hearts that can help us cope with the sorrow and overcome grief to continue with our normal lives. We feel lost when the person who was by our side everyday suddenly disappears and we don't know how to get used to their absence. The present becomes dark and future bleak. Many can recover with time yet, many have PTSD and stay imprisoned in the past.Many housewives caught up in the cycle of family, family and family tend to suffer from depression. Once a woman gets married, she is no longer her own person. Long years of monotous life with no more dreams, no mode of venting the emotions, no person to talk to leads to depression. Everybody needs a break. I used to edit videos of various yatras at Yamnotri and other pilgrimages. The women dance crazily in a trance to the drumbeats. Sometimes, I feel that their dances are a mode of venting their stress and anxiety. (I know it is not so and it is related to faith and religion. It was just a fleeting thought)City Life and post-modernism have turned human beings into machines. Office to home, home to office, laboriously working the whole day and you come back to an empty room only to go to sleep for a while and go back to the busy workplace the next day makes the human mind dull. If you have family or friends around you, it is not sad. However, millions of us live alone. The fast life made us incapable to have a social life outside work. The only way to know about the world is through social media where everybody is uploading happy pictures. You yearn for that fresh mountain air or the sunny beach. You yearn for a good friend to talk to or simply hangout without any worries. Reality is the opposite. Many of us don't get that much salary which might allow us to take a holiday to travel. Some workplaces might not even give us long paid holidays. Some of us have homes in distant places that would cost a month or two's salary to go back. Socialising is also expensive. To eat out at a good restaurant or going to the movies or hanging out a fun place makes a heavy dent on our monthly budget. What do we do? We neighter have the luxury of time and money. We miss home, we miss freedom, we miss carefree days. We become more and more frustrated with our lives. With time, we get depressed.Pressure put on students to gain higher marks or get into a specific course by the parents is a major cause of depression. Children are supposed to be playful and childhood is supposed to be fun. We see parents these days putting too much focus on school education. They seem to have forgotten the notion of 'travelling a thousand miles is better than reading a thousand books ’. They seem to have forgotten that all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy. We all have noticed the rising number of suicide cases. No kid with a healthy mind will ever attempt suicide.There are various other causes of depression and mental illness. We for fear of social stigma never think of consulting a psychiatrist or a psychologist when we feel suffocated with our emotions, when we notice the slight symptoms of insomnia or trauma. Mental well being is very crucial for our health. I have suffered from depression and later mild PTSD. I had insomnia for many years. I still have the fear of closing my eyes and letting my mind idle. Uncomfortable past experiences have haunted me for the past ten years. The initial four to five years were the most difficult. I couldn't cry for almost three years. Not a single year could be shed. Then, I understood what poets meant by the term 'stone-hearted’ I went through different phases, I was on medication. I later decided that medication is not the final solution. I need to fight back. I took the resolution that however hard it gets, i will never let the darkness in my mind win everytime. Till today, i go through episodes where I feel like completely giving up. I sometimes stopped caring and feeling. Even doing daily tasks of cleaning the house or cooking becomes laborious during these episodes. Every time, it lasts for a month to two. Everytime, I try hard to get out of the state. Everytime, I try to find a new purpose of my existence. This way, I created my Youtube channel. I love videography and walking through villages and filming whatever I want to film give me joy. I do it when I am free. The best therapist is I myself and the best therapy is self-healing. When you are in the dark, try to find the light. Grope your way towards it. Depression might not go away but it would never kill you if you keep yourself strong.

column1: What are effective ways to release emotional trauma?
column3: Emotional and Psychological Trauma When bad things happen, it can take a while to get over the pain and feel safe again. But with these self-help strategies and support, you can speed up your recovery. What is emotional and psychological trauma? Emotional and psychological trauma is the result of extraordinarily stressful events that shatter your sense of security, making you feel helpless in a dangerous world. Psychological trauma can leave you struggling with upsetting emotions, memories, and anxiety that won’t go away. It can also leave you feeling numb, disconnected, and unable to trust other people. Traumatic experiences often involve a threat to life or safety, but any situation that leaves you feeling overwhelmed and isolated can result in trauma, even if it doesn’t involve physical harm. It’s not the objective circumstances that determine whether an event is traumatic, but your subjective emotional experience of the event. The more frightened and helpless you feel, the more likely you are to be traumatized. Emotional and psychological trauma can be caused by:One-time events, such as an accident, injury, or a violent attack, especially if it was unexpected or happened in childhood.Ongoing, relentless stress, such as living in a crime-ridden neighborhood, battling a life-threatening illness or experiencing traumatic events that occur repeatedly, such as bullying, domestic violence, or childhood neglect.Commonly overlooked causes, such as surgery (especially in the first 3 years of life), the sudden death of someone close, the breakup of a significant relationship, or a humiliating or deeply disappointing experience, especially if someone was deliberately cruel.Coping with the trauma of a natural or manmade disaster can present unique challenges—even if you weren’t directly involved in the event. In fact, while it’s highly unlikely any of us will ever be the direct victims of a terrorist attack, plane crash, or mass shooting, for example, we’re all regularly bombarded by horrific images on social media and news sources of those people who have been. Viewing these images over and over can overwhelm your nervous system and create traumatic stress. Whatever the cause of your trauma, and whether it happened years ago or yesterday, you can make healing changes and move on with your life. Childhood trauma and the risk of future trauma While traumatic events can happen to anyone, you’re more likely to be traumatized by an event if you’re already under a heavy stress load, have recently suffered a series of losses, or have been traumatized before—especially if the earlier trauma occurred in childhood. Childhood trauma can result from anything that disrupts a child’s sense of safety, including:An unstable or unsafe environmentSeparation from a parentSerious illnessIntrusive medical proceduresDomestic violenceNeglectExperiencing trauma in childhood can result in a severe and long-lasting effect. When childhood trauma is not resolved, a sense of fear and helplessness carries over into adulthood, setting the stage for further trauma. However, even if your trauma happened many years ago, there are steps you can take to overcome the pain, learn to trust and connect to others again, and regain your sense of emotional balance. Symptoms of psychological trauma We all react to trauma in different ways, experiencing a wide range of physical and emotional reactions. There is no “right” or “wrong” way to think, feel, or respond, so don’t judge your own reactions or those of other people. Your responses are NORMAL reactions to ABNORMAL events. Emotional & psychological symptoms:Shock, denial, or disbeliefConfusion, difficulty concentratingAnger, irritability, mood swingsAnxiety and fearGuilt, shame, self-blameWithdrawing from othersFeeling sad or hopelessFeeling disconnected or numbPhysical symptoms:Insomnia or nightmaresFatigueBeing startled easilyDifficulty concentratingRacing heartbeatEdginess and agitationAches and painsMuscle tensionHealing from trauma Trauma symptoms typically last from a few days to a few months, gradually fading as you process the unsettling event. But even when you’re feeling better, you may be troubled from time to time by painful memories or emotions—especially in response to triggers such as an anniversary of the event or something that reminds you of the trauma. If your psychological trauma symptoms don’t ease up—or if they become even worse—and you find that you’re unable to move on from the event for a prolonged period of time, you may be experiencing Post -Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD).While emotional trauma is a normal response to a disturbing event, it becomes PTSD when your nervous system gets “stuck” and you remain in psychological shock, unable to make sense of what happened or process your emotions. Whether or not a traumatic event involves death, you as a survivor must cope with the loss, at least temporarily, of your sense of safety. The natural reaction to this loss is grief. Like people who have lost a loved one, you need to go through a grieving process. The following tips can help you cope with the sense of grief, heal from the trauma, and move on with your life. Trauma recovery tip 1: Get moving Trauma disrupts your body’s natural equilibrium, freezing you in a state of hyperarousal and fear. As well as burning off adrenaline and releasing endorphins, exercise and movement can actually help repair your nervous system. Try to exercise for 30 minutes or more on most days. Or if it’s easier, three 10-minute spurts of exercise per day are just as good. Exercise that is rhythmic and engages both your arms and legs—such as walking, running, swimming, basketball, or even dancing—works best. Add a mindfulness element. Instead of focusing on your thoughts or distracting yourself while you exercise, really focus on your body and how it feels as you move. Notice the sensation of your feet hitting the ground, for example, or the rhythm of your breathing, or the feeling of wind on your skin. Rock climbing, boxing, weight training, or martial arts can make this easier—after all, you need to focus on your body movements during these activities in order to avoid injury. Tip 2: Don’t isolate Following a trauma, you may want to withdraw from others, but isolation only makes things worse. Connecting to others face to face will help you heal, so make an effort to maintain your relationships and avoid spending too much time alone. You don’t have to talk about the trauma. Connecting with others doesn’t have to involve talking about the trauma. In fact, for some people, that can just make things worse. Comfort comes from feeling engaged and accepted by others. Ask for support. While you don’t have to talk about the trauma itself, it is important that you have someone to share your feelings with face to face, someone who will listen attentively without judging you. Turn to a trusted family member, friend, counselor, or clergyman. Participate in social activities, even if you don’t feel like it. Do “normal” activities with other people, activities that have nothing to do with the traumatic experience. Reconnect with old friends. If you’ve retreated from relationships that were once important to you, make the effort to reconnect. Join a support group for trauma survivors. Connecting with others who are facing the same problems can help reduce your sense of isolation, and hearing how others cope can help inspire you in your own recovery. Volunteer. As well as helping others,voluntaring can be a great way to challenge the sense of helplessness that often accompanies trauma. Remind yourself of your strengths and reclaim your sense of power by helping others. Make new friends. If you live alone or far from family and friends, it’s important to reach out and make new friends. Take a class or join a club to meet people with similar interests, connect to an alumni association, or reach out to neighbors or work colleagues. If connecting to others is difficult… Many people who have experienced trauma feel disconnected, withdrawn and find it difficult to connect with other people. If that describes you, there are some actions you can take before you next meet with a friend: Exercise or move. Jump up and down, swing your arms and legs, or just flail around. Your head will feel clearer and you’ll find it easier to connect. Vocal toning. As strange as it sounds, vocal toning is a great way to open up to social engagement. Sit up straight and simply make “mmmm” sounds. Change the pitch and volume until you experience a pleasant vibration in your face. Tip 3: Self-regulate your nervous system No matter how agitated, anxious, or out of control you feel, it’s important to know that you can change your arousal system and calm yourself. Not only will it help relieve the anxiety associated with trauma, but it will also engender a greater sense of control. Mindful breathing. If you are feeling disoriented, confused, or upset, practicing mindful breathing is a quick way to calm yourself. Simply take 60 breaths, focusing your attention on each ‘out’ breath. Sensory input. Does a specific sight, smell or taste quickly make you feel calm? Or maybe petting an animal or listening to music works to quickly soothe you? Everyone responds to sensory input a little differently, so experiment with different quick stress releaf techniques to find what works best for you. Staying grounded. To feel in the present and more grounded, sit on a chair. Feel your feet on the ground and your back against the chair. Look around you and pick six objects that have red or blue in them. Notice how your breathing gets deeper and calmer. Allow yourself to feel what you feel when you feel it. Acknowledge your feelings about the trauma as they arise and accept them. HelpGuide’s Emotional Intelligence Toolkit can help. Tip 4: Take care of your health It’s true: having a healthy body can increase your ability to cope with the stress of trauma. Get plenty of sleep. After a traumatic experience, worry or fear may disturb your sleep patterns. But a lack of quality sleep can exacerbate your trauma symptoms and make it harder to maintain your emotional balance. Go to sleep and get up at the same time each day and aim for 7 to 9 hours of sleep each night. Avoid alcohol and drugs. Their use can worsen your trauma symptoms and increase feelings of depression, anxiety, and isolation. Eat a well-balanced diet. Eating small, well-balanced meals throughout the day will help you keep your energy up and minimize mood swings. Avoid sugary and fried foods and eat plenty of omega-3 fats—such as salmon, walnuts, soybeans, and flaxseeds—to give your mood a boost. Reduce stress. Try relaxation techniques such as meditation, yoga, or deep breathing exercises. Schedule time for activities that bring you joy such as your favorite hobbies. When to seek professional therapy for trauma Recovering from trauma takes time, and everyone heals at their own pace. But if months have passed and your symptoms aren’t letting up, you may need professional help from a trauma expert. Seek help for trauma if you’re:Having trouble functioning at home or workSuffering from severe fear, anxiety, or depressionUnable to form close, satisfying relationshipsExperiencing terrifying memories, nightmares, or flashbacksAvoiding more and more anything that reminds you of the traumaEmotionally numb and disconnected from othersUsing alcohol or drugs to feel betterWorking through trauma can be scary, painful, and potentially re-traumatizing, so this healing work is best undertaken with the help of an experienced trauma specialist.Findung the right therapist may take some time. It’s very important that the therapist you choose has experience treating trauma. But the quality of the relationship with your therapist is equally important. Choose a trauma specialist you feel comfortable with. If you don’t feel safe, respected, or understood, find another therapist. Ask yourself:Did you feel comfortable discussing your problems with the therapist?Did you feel like the therapist understood what you were talking about?Were your concerns taken seriously or were they minimized or dismissed?Were you treated with compassion and respect?Do you believe that you could grow to trust the therapist?Treatment for trauma In order to heal from psychological and emotional trauma, you’ll need to resolve the unpleasant feelings and memories you’ve long avoided, discharge pent-up “fight-or-flight” energy, learn to regulate strong emotions, and rebuild your ability to trust other people. A trauma specialist may use a variety of different therapy approaches in your treatment. Somatic experiencing focuses on bodily sensations, rather than thoughts and memories about the traumatic event. By concentrating on what’s happening in your body, you can release pent-up trauma-related energy through shaking, crying, and other forms of physical release. Cognitive-behavioral therapy helps you process and evaluate your thoughts and feelings about a trauma. EMDR (Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing) incorporates elements of cognitive-behavioral therapy with eye movements or other forms of rhythmic, left-right stimulation that can “unfreeze” traumatic memories. Helping a loved one deal with trauma When a loved one has suffered trauma, your support can play a crucial role in their recovery. Be patient and understanding. Healing from trauma takes time. Be patient with the pace of recovery and remember that everyone’s response to trauma is different. Don’t judge your loved one’s reaction against your own response or anyone else’s. Offer practical support to help your loved one get back into a normal routine. That may mean helping with collecting groceries or doing housework, for example, or simply being available to talk or listen. Don’t pressure your loved one into talking but be available if they want to talk. Some trauma survivors find it difficult to talk about what happened. Don’t force your loved one to open up but let them know you are there to listen if they want to talk, or available to just hang out if they don’t. Help your loved one to socialize and relax. Encourage them to participate in physical exercise, seek out friends, and pursue hobbies and other activities that bring them pleasure. Take a fitness class together or set a regular lunch date with friends. Don’t take the trauma symptoms personally. Your loved one may become angry, irritable, withdrawn, or emotionally distant. Remember that this is a result of the trauma and may not have anything to do with you or your relationship. To help a child recover from trauma, it’s important to communicate openly. Let them know that it’s normal to feel scared or upset. Your child may also look to you for cues on how they should respond to trauma, so let them see you dealing with your symptoms in a positive way.
column9: “Due to the entirely nonverbal nature of the limbic brain, experiential rather then cognitive methods are required for successfully engaging and changing its schemas.” (Ecker, B., 2011). “A dynamic neural process now known as reconsolidation can actually unlock the synapses maintaining implicit emotional learnings” (Nader, K., et al. 2000). (Pansskepp, J., 1998). The amygdala compares current perceptions to these attachment related implicit memories triggering a self-protective response. When the child is at his/her worst behavior an opportunity for healing is created only if caregivers understand what is happening as a process. One can see how difficult this can be because the normal response by caregivers is counterintuitive. So then what is the solution? “Further research has established that in order for synapses to unlock, the brain requires not just the experience of reactivation of the memory—it's also necessary for a second, critical experience to promptly take place while the memory reactivation experience is still occurring. That second experience consists of perceptions that sharply contradict and disconfirm the implicit expectations of the reactivated memory. (1) Fully reactivate the target implicit memory so that the emotional experience is occurring. (2) While the target memory is fully reactivated and the emotional experience is occurring, promptly create an additional, concurrent experience that sharply mismatches (contradicts and disconfirms) the expectations and predictions arising from the implicit memory.”(Ecker, B.2010, Psychotherapy Networker)

column1: Have you witnessed real life exorcism?
column3: I have heard about exorcism but never had seen the rituals of exorcism. Spirit possession and exorcism exists worldwide.Exorcism is the act of expulsion of an evil spirit from possessing a person or from a haunted house. I have seen spirit possession thrice and I believe that two of the cases could have been due to extreme stress which i would explain later but one of the case was probably genuine and not caused due to extreme stress or sexual abuse. The first incident occurred when I was very young and was about eight years old.There was a group of khatal owners who operated an unauthorised cattle shed near our property. Several petitions were sent to the corporation of Calcutta by some residents of the locality but the authorities did not take any action. The corporation referred the matter to the police and the police referred back to the corporation. The cattle shed was held responsible for malaria and other diseases.The matter was getting delayed. The police informed that they had limited powers and could seize stray cattle but the cattle owners got the cows and buffalows released and things were back to square one.The corporation finally informed that unless we could get the owner of the vacant plot to complain they could not do anything about it.The corporation was infact asking the local residents to trace the owners of the vacant plot which had a small derelict building more than a hundred years old.Some said that the owner was Rustamji parsee a businessman of the early nineteenth century and no one knew who were his legal heirs.The people who ran the cattle shed and sold milk were Goalas or yadavs and tried to defend their expulsion.The government inaction prompted some people to seek the help of antisocial elements and soon the cattle shed became a battle zone and ultimately one of the cattle owners suddenly had a change of personality and began to call himself Kal Bhairav and attack any one who approached the cattle shed with stones ,metal rods .My grandfather visited the owner of the cattle shed .I saw that man who called himself kal bhairav and he did never appear normal. He may have been possessed by a demon.My grandfather well intentioned approach to settle matters met with failure and he could have been killed but for the timely help of a few local youths who overpowered and bound him and gave him a good beating and handed him over to the police.The police were reluctant to keep him as he appeared deranged and was disturbing the other prisoners. Ultimately they sent him to jail where he became a nuisance and was beaten by the hard-core criminals and for his own safety they sent him to a solitary cell but in the cell he was incredibly dirty and refused to take food and covered the cell walls with his shit and banged his head against the wall repeatedly and was removed to jail hospital and before his bail petition for attempting to cause murder of my grandfather came up ,he died. My grandfather during his lifetime was always intrigued by this incident. The second incident happened in Burtolla police station area. Although I never worked in Burtolla and was in Jorabagan which shared common borders with Burtolla.Both these police stations had certain areas filled with brothels and whorehouses. In those days there was rampant exploitation of women and girls and there were no social organizations to look after their welfare. They were under the mercy of goons who exploited them in every way.Most of their earnings were taken away by the brothel owners and goons but the picture has improved now. Today they like to call themselves as sex workers and prostitude has become a derogatory word.One day while patrolling ,some young girls who were prostitutes came running and informed that there was a murder near a brothel. The area was within Burtolla and a man was sent by me with one of the girls to the Burtolla police station. The body of a young girl lay dead and it appeared that she was thrown down from the building. One person who appeared to be a Bheruah (caretaker of the girl )told us that the girl lived in one of the rooms in the 3rd floor. A very narrow winding starcase led to third floor and a glance at her room was sufficient to indicate that there were two persons inside her room and there must have been some dispute for which the girl was thrown out from the veranda. The criminals must have fled immediately as no one could say who they were.The Burtolla police had arrived and they took over the case.The girl next door to the deceased prostitute was inconsolable with grief as they belonged to nearby villages of Hoogly distict of Bengal. Later after a few days while patrolling I met the Bheruah who looked dejected. These Bheruahs are the girls best friends and are not goons. Probably fate had brought him close to the girl and many such girls had such men who are contemptuously called Bheruahs as they form a bond with a girl as mutual love develops.The Bheruahs sometimes work elswhere in small time jobs and stay with the girl during the spare time.They turn a blind eye to the girls activities and when the girl loses her charm they turn to the Bheruah and migrate elswhere where they stay as husband and wife. In India every woman needs a man unlike the west.The woman without a Bheruah or any other support would be forced to beg after retirement. Plenty of such old women would be seen begging during the day near the brothels and working as assistant to the girls during the night. The Bheruah told me that the best friend of the deceased had developed mental problems and was hallucinating in broad daylight. I asked the investigative officer who was probing the case and he confirmed the fact.The brothel owner wanted to send her back to her village but her family would not take her.The girl appeared to be possessed of the deceased girl and sometimes spoke about the names of her killers but the information was inadequate for the police to act.The girl was sent to a mental hospital.The murder case had to be closed for want of evidence. In those days no one cared for the death of a prostitute. The third case related to an incident in the port area.The Moninpur morgue before it's modernization was a terrible place for holding autopsies. Dead bodies of males and females were piled upon each other and the rotten stench could be felt from a considerable distance. The Doctors hardly cared and had tea and snacks inside the building and were used to the smell and the autopsies of important persons were done swiftly and the unclaimed bodies of beggars lay there for days to be devoured by large Rats who were so strong and well fed that even cats would not dare to touch them.There was a large pond which no longer exists now which was full of overfed cat fish and snake head fish .These fishes were fed with dead meat from the corpses by the DOMS (assistant of Doctors).The fish were unafraid of people as no one cared to eat them.The morgue was a dilapidated building of the British times and was surrounded by large marshy tracts of land and bushes and trees and lonely even during the day.The inside was equally dilapidated and the tables were old and dirty and resembled the given picture .No one came to place except those who came to claim dead bodies after the autopsies and after the closure of the morgue in the evening there was total silence. Even anti socials avoided the place.I had to visit the morgue sometimes in course of my work. One day I had to visit the morgue to identify a man who was brought to the place. He was killed by the people while attempting a dacoity in a village. His accomplices fled the place but not before firing indiscriminately and killing three villagers. The authorities got information that he was the notorious dacoit Baggan.After viewing the body there was no doubt that he was Baggan .The postmortem of the three villagers who were killed by Baggans men were held and their relations took away their bodies but no one came to identify Baggan.I visited Baggans village but his father refused to take the body.”I do not want to claim his body” the old man said.”He had left my house at a very early age and never kept any link” he said. “He has spoilt my name ,you can do whatever you like”I had to return and if there was no claimant the body would remain unclaimed. Baggan had a mistress who was the wife of his associate named Raju , who had become a reformed criminal. This mistress was the daughter of a reputed Doctor who fell for this ex criminal and her doctor father severed all links with her.Later She became Baggans mistress. She was stunningly beautiful but whenever I see such women I am amazed at their low tastes.Chanakya had rightly said that even the Gods did not know the workings of the mind of a woman. She did not want to claim the body, as a distant relative though she and her husband identified the body. After the postmortem the Doctors were asked to preserve the body for fifteen days and then dispose it. As a general rule unclaimed bodies are purchased by certain companies who sell the skeletons to medical students, medical schools or export them. A week after, the husband of Baggans mistress visited me and said that his wife was showing symptoms of spirit possession and he could have brought her but she was unmanageable. She claimed that Baggans spirit was haunting her and demanding why she did not claim the body.I told him to show his wife to a psychiatrist and the psychiatrist treated her for some time but the situation worsened. Someone told him that the psychiatrist will never cure his wife as they received few patients and held on to those patients like glue during their lifetime .He showed a homeopath who gave two medicines Hyoscyamus and stramonium but failed. He then visited an exorcist who promised him to rid her of the evil spirit . I was thinking about his case .Sometimes spirits from Morgues or crematorium or graveyards or forests suddenly follow and attach themselves to vulnerable females or children who start behaving abnormally ,being possessed. Sometimes such spirits could be exorcised. I promised to witness the exorcism but could not due to certain unavoidable reasons. The exorcist achieved temporary success and we all thought that she was cured but after several months she was again possessed and her husband was trying to figure out the next course of action when she committed suicide. I do not know if any of the cases related to spirit possession but in the last case there was an exorcism but without any fruitful result.

column1: What do you take for granted the most in your life?
column3: I know what I used to take for granted most in my life – my health. Just before my 41st birthday, I had something very strange happen to me. Out of the blue in the gym one day, as my heart rate was increasing to meet the demands of the increase in physical intensity, I felt a strong and painful lump in my throat - the kind you feel sometimes when trying to hold back tears. But there was no thought of sadness or stress in that moment, and I noticed that I could not get enough air in. I assumed that it was just a “one-off”, or that I was getting yet another cold (I have two young children so picking up colds is a pretty common occurrence for me). But the inability to get air in on exertion happened again in the gym the next day. But this time it came with a distinct noisy inhale – so much so that I noticed the people around me were noticing too. I used to be a physiotherapist and remembered what this symptom is called – stridor. This happened every day in the gym for about 4 days, but took a little less exertion to induce each time. By this point I had made a plan to see a doctor the next day to investigate. On the fifth day, my workout included a stint on the rowing machine, but after the first minute, I stopped because it was impossible to get enough air in to sustain any sort of rowing pace. Before I could see the doctor that afternoon, I noticed that this stridor and difficulty breathing were occuring at rest during normal conversation. Then to my dismay, I realized that I could not drink water without choking on it. I worried that my airway was slowly collapsing. I went to the closest hospital emergency room where they admitted me very quickly. Anyone who presents with difficulty breathing, even a healthy 40-year old, is presumed to possibly be having a heart attack so I was first given an ECG to measure my heart function, which turned out to be normal. Blood tests were taken, as well as a soft tissue neck x-ray, both of which showed nothing abnormal. I was given epinephrine mist to inhale and a strong dose of steroids to open up the airway and make breathing easier. They diagnosed me as having tracheitis (inflammation of the trachea) caused by a virus or bacterial infection and sent me home. But the inability to breathe and swallow normally did not go away and I felt that something was very wrong. Two weeks later I saw a pulmonologist who agreed that this was not asthma nor viral or bacterial-induced, and ordered a bronchoscopy plus or minus a biopsy. Three days prior to the bronchoscopy I ended up in the ER again with worse difficulty breathing. I was given the same treatment but doubled in dose. The doctors were still stumped. My throat looked normal, so the only thing I could do was to wait for the more invasive bronchoscopy and possible biopsy to get a better look. By that point I was thinking about the possibility of a mass compressing my trachea, which is what it felt like. I could not run up stairs without getting out of breath. I had not heard my normal voice in three weeks and I was still regularly choking on water. I also had new onset heart burn on a daily basis. My fear of these symptoms being caused by cancer was increasing with each passing day. One night I looked at my children as they were falling asleep and was overcome with grief at the thought of leaving them too soon. From then on I found myself constantly living in my imaginary and undetermined future, unable to stay in the present. I had a number of well-meaning friends who told me that it was nothing – that probably all I needed was some inhalers for asthma. I felt badly for complaining sometimes, but most of the time I was so debilitated by my symptoms. I couldn’t play with my children without becoming out of breath. I couldn’t coach my 4-6 year old wrestling class because I couldn’t project my voice loudly enough for them to hear me. I couldn’t train trampoline anymore. One morning after taking big gulp of water, I began to choke and spat all of it out on to my daughter by accident. Some moments felt like I was in a bad dream that I wanted to wake up from but couldn’t. On the day of the bronchoscopy, the fear of what they would find was overwhelming. My doctors were very kind and supportive, and a nurse held my hand as I sobbed until the sedatives took effect. The procedure itself was painless due to the anesthesia and sedatives given. After the procedure when the anesthesia had worn off, I was informed that there was no mass in my throat and that the bronchoscopy revealed what the problem was – paradoxical vocal cord motion. I was overcome with relief of knowing that this was not cancer and cried for a few minutes in the recovery area. Normally the vocal cords pull apart to let air in when you inspire, but mine were now doing the opposite and closing in. Knowing that I have a medical background, my doctor provided me with a handout of the most up to date knowledge on this condition. I began to read through the information. I learned that paradoxical vocal cord motion is rare, and not a diagnosis per se, but more of a description of what is occuring. The condition is found in both children and adults, but far higher incidence in women. Paradoxical vocal cord motion can have different causes, but also no cause at all. Some of the direct causes included inhaled irritants, post-extubation, and nerve injury. But none of those sounded like they fit what happened to me. I also read that a large number of these cases had no pathology – the paradoxical motion had no apparent reason and was considered a learned, maladaptive behavior. Therefore, even though it may be started by a physical cause, it can be completely perpetuated psychologically. Difficulty breathing is stressful in and of itslef, which leads to more difficulty breathing. You come to expect it and it becomes a self-fulfilling profficy. Most of these non pathological cases are associated with anxiety and stress. Now it made sense as to why all my doctors were asking about my stress and anxiety levels. I am a mother of two young children, one of whom has autism, and I work part time as a data scientist. Therefore it was not out of the realm of possibilities that I could fall in to this category, however, I couldn’t recall any of my exacerbations being associated with stressful thoughts or incidents. Despite this, I started to second guess myself – perhaps my mental health was not as good as I thought. Then there were the 15% of cases where this non pathological kind occurrs in athletes. These athletes typically have multiple trips to the ER presenting with difficulty breathing, stridor during exercise, and no history of cough or reflux. Well, this sounded exactly like me. Although my pulmonologist did not weigh in on what he thought the etiology was in my case, I was convinced that I was in this 15% athlete population with no known pathology. As I eagerly read the section on treatment for this condition, my heart began to sink. This non pathological kind is so rare that there are no trials and no evidence based treatment, only anecdotal. The mainstay treatments for this etiology include breathing exercises to learn how to control and relax the vocal cords during exertion, stress management/meditation, medical hypnosis, visualization, speech/voice therapy, and occasionally botox to the surrounding larynx muscles. I was so disappointed to learn there was no medication to cure this condition that was having such an impact on my day-to-day life. I began to read as much as I could about the experiences of other athletes with this condition. As grateful as I was that this was not cancer, I was still disheartened believing that I had a life changing condition where I literally had to relearn how to breathe normally. Many athletes were describing how their condition improved somewhat with breathing retraining and self-hypnosis, yet never fully went away. One competitive swimmer who had this condition commented that he would not wish it on any athlete. I continued going to the gym and trying to train as per usual, but now applying the diaphragmatic and resistance breathing exercises as soon as my heart rate increased and I felt out of breath from lack of required oxygen to the muscles. I tried hard to relax my neck muscles, breathe diaphragmatically and visualize the normal breathing pattern, but I was unable to get more air in. And as soon as I realized the failure of my attempts, I could feel my airway and neck muscles further tighten and the stridor even louder. Every day in the gym now felt like mental and physical torture. I was having a hard time and becoming depressed. I could forsee this depression and frustration taking over my life if I didn’t change something. To gather the re­solve to accept and adapt to my vocal cord dysfunction instead of continually curse it, I adopted strate­gies that fed my spirit and supressed the focus on my frustration and sadness. I started writing again. I started meditating again. I reached out to a few friends who kept me grounded when the panic became overwhelming, and checked in on me regularly to make sure I was not going off the rails with worry. I also read about Zen Bud­dhist phi­los­o­phy, be­cause it resonates with me. It has taught me to prac­tice liv­ing in the mo­ment, to rec­og­nize and set­tle into joy when it’s there, and to be less hard on my­self. All of these things helped me to get through having to sit down to catch my breath, asking my assistant coaches to take over when I couldn’t speak loudly enough to my class, the frustration and pain from choking when drinking water, and having to give up training trampoline for a while. My laryngoscopy was scheduled two weeks later. This procedure was necessary to get a more detailed look at the vocal cords and larynx. I was seen by an ENT (ears nose throat) doctor who performed the laryngoscopy. Before the procedure I updated her with the history of my symptoms and explained that I presented just like the athletes with no known pathology, and that I was desperately hoping that she could help me because my quality of life had been so severely reduced. With a camera inserted through my nose to view the cords up close, the ENT doctor observed the cord motion while asking me to make certain noises, swallow, and cough. After pulling out the camera, she said, “you do indeed have paradoxical vocal cord motion, but there is a clear reason for it. Your right vocal cord is paralyzed.” I started to cry and said, “But that’s worse, right?”, thinking that this condition was now permanent with no treatment options. She replied, “no, that means it will likely recover. I can see occassional flickers but othewise it is not moving, likely due to damage of the nerves innervating the cord. It can happen sometimes after a virus.” I told her that I was in fact sick with a virus shortly before the onset of the first symptoms. The ENT doctor likened what I had to Bells Palsy – a temporary facial droop from a facial nerve injury after the Polio virus. She thought I should expect to get approximately 90% function back within 6 months, but explained that I am essentially working with half an airway until then. It also occurred to me after hearing “right sided” that all of the tightness, the need to clear my throat and the hoarseness had been originating from the right side all along - I just never thought to say anything because I was not aware that single sided vocal cord paralysis even existed. I started to cry in the doctors’ office again from relief of knowing that there was an end in sight. Although she also wanted a CT scan of the throat to rule out the possibility of a tumor pressing on the nerve that an x-ray would not pick up, she felt that this was very unlikely, especially given my history of a virus before the stridor first began. The ENT doctor answered the rest of my questions and made some recommendations for additional breathing exercises. I drove home that afternoon in tears. It felt like nothing I had experienced before – like opening the floodgates of built up emotions that came flowing out. All the stress and fear and pain I had felt in the previous month were released during that cry. I arrived home and felt so emotionally exhausted that I fell asleep. I unintentionally slept for 3 hours in what felt like the deepest sleep of my life. I did have the CT scan a week and a half later, which showed a perfectly normal throat. It’s been about 2 months since the start of my symptoms, and I have noticed a very slight improvement in breathing during exertion, and no more difficulty breathing at rest. I can train trampoline for short periods of time and any other training is modified so that I don’t have to get my heart rate up too high. My voice is much closer to normal and I also rarely choke on water now. But the more significant change I noticed is that I wake up each morning feeling very grateful to be here, for my health and to have a functioning body. Maybe it really is all about perspective and appreciating the miracles right in front of you. When I’m tuned in to the right per­spec­tive, I can appreciate the qualities of myself and life that are so worthwhile, no matter what is happening to me or around me. I don’t think that I will take my health or body for granted ever again.

column1: Around how long does it take to come to terms with the death of a close family member? I am not looking for reassurance.
column3: I’d say it would depend on the way they pass on. It’s not possible to give you any number because it would depend on the individual coming to terms with the death of a loved one. Not everyone has the same outlook on life and death and what happens after. For the loved ones, someone dying from a sudden accident is not the same as someone dying from a terminal illness. For someone with a terminal illness we get the time to prepare ourselves to face the coming reality. But that is not what happens when we lose someone suddenly. For my late father who died from cancer, he came to terms with his passing long before the rest of our family did. I see the same thing with my uncle also with his terminal cancer.

column1: What did a family member say or do that you don't talk to them anymore?
column3: My brothers and sister tried to hide my mother’s death from me. I left home at 17 for college and served in the Army as an infantry officer. I never moved back. My one brother lived with my mom having two divorces and dozens of low paying jobs. My mother and I had a completely different relationship as I was the oldest son, a retired Army Colonel, and very financially stable. We were on good terms before she died. My sister promised to call me if she went into hospice. She didn’t. My other brother and I haven’t spoken in decades since he feels superior to everyone, despite being a thief and self centered. I felt the need to come see my mom, but when I told my sister I was flying in, she texted my my mom had died. My life is much simplified since I never have to bother with anyone in St Louis.
column9: What a crappy thing to do, depriving the oldest brother of being able to say goodbye to his mother.

column1: I didn't understand the ending part of The Godfather (1972). What is the explanation?
column3: What was the point of the ending to The Godfather, when Michael Corleone was in his office with his capos, Peter Clemenza, Rocco Lampone and Al Neri, and the door was closed on his wife, Kay? The point was to demonstrate that Michael was no longer the man he was in the beginning of the story and how he had finally and irrevocably cut himself off from the life he and Kay had once planned for themselves. And he had cut himself off from Kay, as well.“…my father … offered him $10,000 to let Johnny go, but the bandleader said no. So the next day, my father went back, only this time with Luca Brasi. Within an hour, he had a signed release for a certified check of $1000.” (Michael Corleone) “How did he do that?” … (Kay Adams) … “Luca Brasi held a gun to his head, and my father assured him that either his brains or his signature would be on the contract. ... That's a true story. … That's my family Kay, that's not me.” The Godfather (1972)Except that was Michael. Or at least, that’s who he eventually became. By the time we reached the final scene, Michael had personally killed two men in cold blood, seen his first wife die in a car explosion, dealt with the deaths of his oldest brother, Sonny Corleone and the eventual death of his beloved father, Vito Corleone. That kind of carnage would change anyone. All of that put into motion the changes in Michael to become the gangster who would order the deaths of four other dons of the members of the Five Families of New York. But Kay didn’t understand how all of this affected Michael. She just saw him coming to the rescue of his father, and taking on responsibilities for the Corleone Family that should have fallen to Sonny. And she still saw Michael as the same man she had originally fallen in love with; she had believed him when he said he wanted to take the Corleone Family legitimate. In fairness, that always was a goal of his. He just knew such change would require a great deal more bloodshed before he could accomplish that. Kay had to come to terms with who Michael was at some point, but before that could happen, she had to recognize what he had become. That’s why she confronted him after Connie accused him of murdering Carlo Rizzi. Kay still saw only the boy she had come love in college and it scared her to think she had been duped into marrying a monster. When Michael denied Connie’s accusations to his wife, Kay’s fear was visibly broken; we could see the relief break over her. But that was short-lived; immediately, that relief was replaced by a sense of impending doom as Kay realized Michael was completely guilty of Carlo’s death and was no longer the man she had once known.
column9: Kay’s look on her face before Al Neri shuts the door says it all without a word spoken from her.

column1: Was Led Zeppelin musically finished when John Bonham died?
column3: Led Zeppelin wasn't musically finished. The surviving three members, after the death of drummer John Bonham in 1980, were still among the most talented and prolific musicians of the entire era. In fact, guitarist Jimmy Page continued to be very active with solo work, guest work, and live shows with the likes of Eric Clapton and Jeff Beck, as well as forming original band The Firm. Singer Robert Plant released 5 solo albums in the 80's, spawning several charting singles. After a brief hiatus, to spend some much overdue time raising his family in privacy, as well as coming to terms with the loss of his friend and bandmate, multi instrumentalist, John Paul Jones, became a session player for a ‘who's who’ list of 80's stars. R.E.M., Lemmy Kravitz and many, many others invited Jones to bring his inimitable talents to their own projects. So, no, the deeply talented and motivated surviving members of the mighty Led Zeppelin were not finished musically.They were however, finished spiritually, with absolutely no consideration of continuing as a group without their brother and fallen comrade, John Bonham. Zeppelin was no more.

Oliver Starr	If a pack of wolves attacked you, and you somehow have managed to kill the alpha male and survive, would the pack still track you down?	9y	Oliver Starr	It depends... Are you food or a threat? Most wolf biologists now avoid the term alpha" and instead use "breeder" or breeding female/male. The term "beta" is now considered to be factually incorrect. Wolf "packs" are really families -- in fact most compassionate conservationists now refer to wolf "packs" simply as family groups. If there's any single most important animal in a wolf family group, it's the breeding female. In fact, I recently did a large study of the impact of different types of losses on wolf family groups and the two things that have the greatest impact are 1) loss of the breeding female and 2) loss of either breeding animal by non-natural causes. More than 1/2 of all wolf family groups break apart if the breeding female is killed. This goes up to 74% if the breeding female is killed by non-natural (i.e. human-mediated) causes. Beyond this I think you need to dig deeper. Wolves typically only attack things for two reasons: eating them or defending themselves against them. Since humans are not food as far as wolves are concerned that means any attack would be defensive. There would be no "tracking down" because once the threat is driven off the wolves would have no interest in continuing the pursuit. On the other hand if you managed to kill a breeding animal (assuming you could even tell which animal that was while being attacked since they don't wear a sign that says "I'm the breeder") but remained a threat, the other animals would not stop defending themselves in spite of the death of a breeding animal. In the wild wolves most commonly have serious and even lethal contact with other wolves. These encounters are usually very short lived, many things happen at the same time and the violence is significant. I've added a video of wolf family group conflict so you can see what I mean. You'll also notice that there's no "tracking" down. Once the initial conflict and chase have ended it's over. If wolves ate people the situation might be different. Assuming you were something that was "on the menu" and were injured in the attack, the wolves would likely follow and eventually find a moment to pick you off. However, the loss of a family member during a hunt is an incredibly rare occurrence so it's very hard to predict what would happen. Wolves are deeply emotional creatures and they form familial bonds that in my own experience are as strong and altruistic as our own. If I were struck dead while we were on the trail of game my malamute would stop instantly to see what happened. Our ambassador animal, Aqutaq, would probably continue to chase but very quickly return and probably not leave my side. Wolves are deeply impacted by the loss of a family member, just like we are. Biologists are generally reluctant to use words like "grief" when it comes to their topics of study, but I've found in the last few years that there's been a huge shift TOWARDS acknowledging that many other species have complex emotions, and we are now seeing this trend reflected in how things like the loss of a breeder impacts behavior of family groups, including notations on their perceived "demeanor". For anyone that wants to deeply understand wolves, I suggest you read "Among Wolves" by the late Dr Gordon Haber (who died in plane crash in 2009 while tracking his beloved wolves).

column1: How do I continue living after my husband has died?
column3: YES. I know a middle-aged women who was unfortunate to lose her husband due to a road accident. His husband was sole earning member in their family. column1: What are incels doing wrong?
column3: They’re listening to other incels.This is, or rather was, Elliot Rodgers. He was reasonably handsome. Well dressed. From a wealthy family. But he had deep seated mental health issues. On May 23, 2014 he went on a killing spree in Isla Vista, California. He killed 6 people and injured a further 14 more. After being injured by police in a gunfight, he finally took his own life. He and I were both born the same year, 1991, which meant that he was only 22 when he died. Rodgers had been a member of the online “incel” community, short for involuntary celibacy. Before his death he mailed out copies of his 137 page manifesto, My Twisted World, in which he talked about his inability to get a girlfriend, his hatred of happy couples, and the fact that he was still a virgin at age 22.Alana's Involuntary Celibacy Project In 1997 a woman identified only as Alana created a simple website, Alana’s Involuntary Celibacy Project. She’d only begun to date in her 20s, and was struggling to learn the social norms most people learn a decade earlier. So she began posting articles online, what would later be called blogging. And she created a forum where people with similar issues could share their experiences. Eventually Alana drifted away from the community she’d created. She’d come to terms with her own bisexuality. Learned how to forge stronger connections with people. And gotten a long term partner. As did most of the people in the community she created.A typical post in a modern incel forum. I’ve censored the racial slurs, for my own sake. But this left behind the most mentally ill members. Over time that became all who were left. And once you have a community entirely composed of mentally ill loners, they drive each other to become worse. Without knowing the exact problems you’re having with dating, I can’t offer much advice beyond simple platitudes. Wash regularly. Dress better. Be more confident. And try to put yourself out there. But there is one single, solid piece of advice I can give everyone, and it’s advice that could save your life one day. Don’t be part of the incel movement. Don’t talk to them. Don’t join their forums. Just pretend they don’t exist. Because whatever problems you have, hanging around people who identify as incels will only make them worse.
column9: I have a lot of sympathy with genuine people that struggle romantically. I’ve been there, indeed I suppose realistically I never left, I just grew up and had more experiences. It is a terrible feeling, especially when you may already have issues with your self image, depression, anxiety and other mental health issues. But to go fully down that rabbit hole, you have to refuse to self-reflect. There is no way that the guys who are out there who think they are repulsive, yet also that they deserve 18 year old virgins with the bodies of lingerie models, have ever critically examined their own ideas. They feel awful, completely insecure and inadequate. They desire porn stars and celebrities. So they go with that. For me, where my own journey and that of the red-pilled community went different paths was that I as a young man realized how contradictory my thoughts were. It was unfair, I thought. I’m not bad looking, not terrible anyway, I’m funny, I’m clever, I’m a nice guy, I wouldn’t ever do anything to hurt a girl (hovering around that fine line of being proud of my morals and being willing to be a doormat if it would get me female attention), I’m genuine, etc, all the things I could see or lie to myself about me. I could see how if the world was a better place, I’d be at the top of desirability charts, not these flash, self-confident, socially-comfortable pretty boys. But then I would want to be matched up with the girls who were at the top of the desirability charts now - not a female version of me, a socially-retarded, insecure weirdo, with a deep sense of inadequacy. I wanted things to change so it would be easier for me. So that the girls I fancied would approach me. It wasn’t a coherent argument, just some weird convoluted rationalization about I did not want things to be the way they were. I’m not sure where I would be if I was surrounded by people reinforcing those thoughts, reassuring me, offering me the validation and connection I was lacking in real life - especially in a community where you would be rewarded for misogynistic acts (like sharing private pictures of “reluctant porn stars”). Where every whining complaint from another insecure guy would resonate in me like a struck bell, and the counter advice would be “be yourself” and “don’t be a pussy”. Where influencers and other douchbags are deliberately stirring things up to make money. I’m not sure what would be the first lie to themselves would be, but I am pretty sure once they start it just keeps getting easier. They transfer their self-hatred onto other people - the girls they are attracted to, the men that show actually getting a relationship is not some sort of lost cause. It is depressing, as I can easily see how it can happen. But only if you lie to yourself, you must make that conscious decision to lie to yourself so that you feel better about your situation.

column1: What is the best advice you’ve ever received about getting over an ex who dumped you?
column3: I'm sorry to see that you're struggling with getting over your ex. I read your other question yesterday regarding this and you feeling that you were coming to terms with the breakup (only to relapse into further despair). I'll answer both questions here. You must first of all recognise that what you're going through is a GRIEVING process. The end of a serious romantic relationship is akin to the DEATH of a close family member or very close friend. You will therefore have ‘good’ and ‘not so good’ days as far as coping is concerned. I know it's cliched, but you/we really must take things one day at a time. Recognise that what your feeling is normal. If the romantic relationship is definitely over then you must AVOID ANY contact with your ex. This is crucial to your recovery. It's only been about a month remember! You should start to begin feeling like your old self again in about another 2 or 3 months. I can't emphasise how important it is for you to see what you're currently experiencing as a grieving process. Recognising the grieving process is the very best advice in your situation. Things will slowly improve I can assure you. Please don't despair as we've all been there. It sucks! You WILL get there. Stay strong and stay safe.
column9: Thank you Tony, it’s great to hear advice from others as this is my first heartbreak. I have faith that I will feel happier soon.

column1: What is something people misunderstand about being single? (Why is it looked at negatively?)
column3: In my unprofessional opinion one thing a lot of people dont understand about being single (and that includes some single people) is the longer you are single the harder it is to not be single. To be clear, when you say “single” in the context of the question I am assuming we are talking about people not living with someone else. Most people when they start out single because of a breakup /divorce/ tragic event/ whatever/ mourn the companionship of a relationship. As time goes on though it is almost like the death of a family member. When it happened it felt like the world is ending but eventually you move on and accept it. Then comes “me “ time. A lot of people when first becoming single after being in a long committed relationship will decide not to jump in to another relationship so as not to be involved in the classic rebound relationship.That leads to isolation. Isolation is a word with a lot of bad connotations but along with isolation comes a lack of stress and a new definition of what comfortable means to you. Isolation doe not mean you become a hermit living in a cave. In this respect it just means not living with another person. That may sound counter intuitive but consider how much work is put in to being in a committed relationship.People in committed relationships have to do a bunch of things they would rather not to please their partner. If you have a live in partner their quirks become part of your daily routine. Their problems become your problems. You share their pain, the ups the downs, the highs and lows, Being single frees you from most of that and as time goes on the prospect of having to do those things and share those feelings becomes less appealing. Older singles in particular fall into a comfort zone with that isolation and stress free life living alone brings. This is the reason why more older people choose to remain single than younger singles. When you are younger you have the energy and stamina to survive all the drama and what not of a committed relationship. When your older those little drama moments are a lot more taxing. You wont find many of the over 50 single crowd without pets though. Most wont admit it but in my strictly non professional opinion we have swapped animals in as substitutes for committed relationships.If you have a jaded view of that I guess you could say being single for long periods of time makes you commitment lazy or even commitment phobic. Speaking strictly for myself since I have been divorced this has been the happiest time of my life. I can finally do what I want to do when I want to do it on my schedule. I dont have to check in with anyone and I am not responsible for anyone else but me and two slightly nuerotic cats. I do sometimes miss not having a live in. As I get older there are times when I wish someone was here right now to share some bit of information I just got or to share an opinion or even just to cuddle when I feel like cuddling. But that is the “sometimes” the “most of the time” is (to be honest) I just dont want to be bothered. I dont want to talk about someone else's problems at work unless I am in the mood to talk about that. I dont want to stay up half the nite because someone else is snoring, I dont want to see that disapproving look when I decide to pig out and eat a half gallon of ice cream. I dont want to be told I shouldn't drink milk right out of the container.I have been free of those types of things so long that the thought of jumping back in is pretty daunting. I can be honest enough with myself to come to terms with that. That is not to say these singles I am talking about dont date. One of the longest post divorce relationships I was in lasted 3 years. But it lasted that long because we rarely saw each other. At best maybe we were together one weekend a month. We lived in different states and only saw each other when it was convenient for both of us. I cant speak for the entire single population of the world but for me the longer I am single the harder it is to imagine myself sharing a home with someone else. I think I have just gotten to lazy or selfish to do the things I should do if I lived with someone else. Do you know anyone that is commitment-phobic? What do you think causes them to be unable to maintain a relationship?
column9: I can relate totally to your answer .

column1: What does it feel like to become poor after being wealthy?
column3: A family member went from having a >US$5mm net worth and living in Beverly Hills to being a taxi driver The short answer is that it’s incredibly embarrassing. It’s one thing to lose your high-paying Wall Street job after the 2008 Financial Crisis, people get that, it’s another to piss away several million dollars through poor investment choices, profligate spending, and multiple divorces. From the outside perspective, people can’t really comprehend how someone can lose such a large sum of money. Their reaction is often “all you had to do is put it in the bank!” They assume that you did something wrong (true), and they firmly believe that it would never happen to them (probably also true). As for the jacka** in question, he can’t quite let ago of his glorious past. In fact he tells his taxi passengers about the mansion he used to live in. For a while he was holding out hope that he can “turn things around” by betting on the right stock. Now he’s worried about how he will make ends meet once he can’t drive a taxi anymore. He has purposely lost touch with all his friends because of the embarrassment. Going from being wealthy to being poor isn’t necessary a death knell – plenty of people have bounced back from bankruptcy. In fact many have bounced back from their setbacks even stronger than before. Unfortunately, this relative of mine chose to blame everyone else for his problems instead of coming to terms with his predicament. Sadly, age 68, time has run out. The lesson for me is to stay conservative in my investments, live below my means, and most importantly, DON’T GET DIVORCED!

column1: What is it like for a loved one to pass away?
column3: It is the single most devastating and life changing moment a person can experience. That being said, it varies on so many levels depending on the relationship you had with the person, how close a family member they were, how much time you spent together and the circumstances of their passing. I say the latter for the simple reason that should it, for example, be a parent that passes away, it is an expectation in life and the natural order. How a person dies can have a great impact on the grieving process. If you have began to prepare yourself for their dying, be it through illness or injury, you have already began the grieving process and can accept things a little more rationally. If however, the persons death is outside the natural order, or is sudden and unexpected, then it becomes a daily struggle to accept the circumstances you now find yourself, and be able to see a future without that person being a part of it. I personally am approaching 5 years without my son, an only child, who died aged 16 from a sudden brain hemorrhage. I still struggle on a daily basis to come to terms with this, and despite the incongruous positives that have arisen since, I would gladly sacrifice everything for just one more hug. See other answers I have given in this topic to get a fuller picture.
column9: Dawn - Thanks for such a heartfelt and accurate comment. The pain never goes away - it is just covered up with more life. Some of beautiful memories last while others, alas, fade. Good luck to you with your ordeal of coping with this tragedy.

column1: Is it considered rude or inappropriate to ask a close friend the cause of death of one of their family members?
column3: Depends on how the conversation is going. If they told you personally that their family member died, you can simply say: “Oh, no. That’s terrible. What happened?” And they’ll tell you. If you’re past that stage and they’re close friends, you can just ask them what exactly happened. I don’t really see a problem with this, but try to wait for a bit. Let them grief for a while and come to terms with their loss. If they haven’t told you personally that their family member died, you definitely shouldn’t confront them with it. They’ll tell you if they want you to know.

column1: What are our best memorials?
column3: I'd argue that the Vietnam Veterans Memorial is the most interesting memorial of the 20th century. It's powerful because it is in fact a memorial, rather than a heroic sculpture. 75 meters long, 58,272 names are etched on it, listing those either killed or missing in action chronologically. Built in 1982, the Vietnam Memorial was designed by Maya Lin, then a college student. Her design was chosen from 1,421 entries. It encountered substantial opposition at the time, with one critic calling it a "black gash of shame." Some critics opposed the design because she was Asian-American. Here's Maya Lin's original proposal (click on it - it's high resolution enough to read). See Sites of Memory: hatlie.de Vietnam War Memorial on the Mall in Washington, D.C. I think what marks the Vietnam Memorial as powerful is the fact that it is a true memorial, and not a triumphant structure like the sculptures before it. That is, we don't have a pompous building or a general on a horse here. And I think that's the main reason it was controversial when it was proposed. That's also its power, that and its essentially democratic nature: each name is the same size and importance and each name represents a life sacrificed. One of the things that struck me when I visited is the alphabetical directory of names. You can look up the names of the fallen and find out where on the memorial they are. I'm lucky not to have a family member who died in Vietnam, but for those who did, I'm sure visiting this memorial can be a true moment of coming to terms with their loved one's life and death. Maya Lin has gone on to have a successful career with many creative accomplishments. But the Vietnam Memorial is special, and it has given a whole new set of possibilities to the memorial as a form, and I think helps us make sense of this war.
column9: One story I read about it was that she came up with the idea while eating mashed potatoes. She took a scoop out and looking at the empty space she had an epiphany. In hindsight it really is a great memorial. It is one of the few (that I know of) that actually lists as close to all of a nation's losses from a particular conflict of such a scale. The "black gash of shame" is also fitting since as I read in the article it literally and figuratively represents a chunk of America ripped right out of the country.

column1: When you turn 65 years old, what will matter to you in life?
column3: Let’s see, that was in 2009 for me. Work mattered: I was working full-time at the practice of divorce law, aiming to close the office at age 70. I told my husband I couldn’t take the pressure of deadlines and Clients from Hell for more than five years. He was nervous about my plan, uncertain that we were secure enough financially. So I studied for certification as a Divorce Mediator, a way to ease the stress of my litigious profession and enjoy the more positive and satisfying results before my exit. Children mattered: Our youngest child, our daughter, was in law school, taking loans and working to make her way through. We supported her in her endeavors, visiting her often and being there for a devastating breakup, as my nurturing instincts remained strong. This would be the last graduation in our family. On to the empty nest. Our son had moved to Israel. I visited at least annually, and always upon the birth of a new baby. They rolled out the red carpet the minute I touched down as a new grandmother. The revered older generation mattered: My mom Rose was in her nineties and living in a subsidized senior citizens complex. By that time, I supported her in her chores of daily living that she could not handle alone, such as grocery and clothing shopping, laundry, showers, changing linens, reminding her to go to the dining hall for dinner, taking her to medical and dental appointments. Members of the extended family visited her often for the mutual joy of companionship. My home mattered: I enjoyed the security of our down-sized home, a small ranch with a yard big enough for a vegetable garden and plenty of room for my husband to play with his toys (tractor with five different attachments) and Legos (boulders to build stone walls). And we were able to provide a safe haven for one of our adult children who needed to return. My circle of close and supportive friends mattered: I treasured friendships built up and strengthened over the years. I found my college roommate Diane after decades and discovered that we both had lived in Massachusetts all along. We resumed our relationship in a heartbeat and continue with affection. My lawyer friend Neila helped me with her perspective on difficult cases. I supported her in her efforts to adopt and raise a troubled child as a single mother. The future mattered: My husband and I looked forward to the future that we thought was ours. Looking back, the past seems like a dream and the future is now the reality. I could not have predicted the path my life would take. My mom is gone, after a long and blessed life (not really a surprise). I became caregiver for my husband and had to close my office, effectively ending my career before the seventy year old target date. He succumbed to his illness when I was sixty-nine years old, but my law practice had been on hold for the year. I fought with everything I had in me to come to terms with his death. My son’s fifteen year marriage fell apart, a shock to me. Our other adult son continues to live at home out of health necessity. My lawyer friend Neila was killed in a freak accident while on vacation on a cruise ship two years ago. The future I could in no way envision in 2009 when I was 65 has sorted itself out, no longer a mystery. And I am humbled at the course of events that brought me to this day. What matters now: I am here.
