column1: Why have you decided to not speak to your family anymore?
column3: Growing up, I was fairly close to my mother's side of the family. She was one of five. I had eleven cousins who all married. We mostly stayed in touch. Everyone idolized my mother. She was the one who represented “home” to everyone. She sewed, cooked, baked, made wedding gowns and wedding cakes. She played the piano, knitted and crocheted. Plus she was the one everyone turned to for medical advice because she was a registered nurse. Mom was the last of her siblings to survive. Every aunt and uncle proceeded her in death. There was always a major gathering of the family following the service. Every. Single. Time. Many cousins stayed in touch as she struggled through colon cancer. When she came to live with me, just before she lost the battle, everyone was welcomed to come and say good-bye. I was the consummate hostess, cooking myself to a frazzle. I welcomed everyone, even cousins I had not seen in years,, to come for the day to say good-bye to mom. I was so upset at losing my mom, I lost 30 pounds in 3 months. The end inevitably came on a cold January morning. People came for the service. The gravesite was 45 minutes away, where mom wanted to be. I made sure that everyone knew that my house would be open for dinner following the internment. However, all but 2 cousins went out to lunch together without inviting me. Yes, I went home to my house, now without mom, and they refused to be there, choosing instead to enjoy a lunch among themselves. That's why I no longer speak to those terribly mean, selfish people.

column1: What is best to park an emergency fund, bank account, FD, or any liquid/debt mutual fund?
column3: I would divide the funds into three (a) Minor Emergencies - Tuition of a Kid, Wedding of a Relative, Urgent Trip by Air This cost is usually capped to around Rs. 2,00,000/- at the most. A Fixed Deposit by E-TDR would be the best solution. You get interest and you can break it using your cell phone and get credit to your account in 30 seconds. Dont deposit a Single FD - but 10 FDs of Rs. 20,000/- each so that you can selectively break 2–3 and not the entire lump sum of Rs. 2 Lakhs. Then replace this with your salary (b) Major Emergencies - Hospitalization, Death of a close member etc This cost would be a significant chunk and you may need some money until Insurance kicks in. This cost should be around Rs. 15,00,000/- to be on the safe side for a Family man and Rs. 5,00,000/- for a Bachelor. This sum would be also ideally parked in a Bank Term Deposit against which an OD can be taken easily so that the Deposit does not get broken. (c) Cash Emergencies - Always Keep a chunk of money in Cash. Police Trouble, Bank Strikes, Connectivity could lead to Cash requirements The Cash on Hand should be around Rs. 3,00,000/- for a Decent Emergency and should be available at Home in a Cupboard with a Locker Safe and Key.Its unwise to park emergency funds in Mutual Funds or Equities. The reason is these funds can also reduce in value - so if you place Rs. 10 Lakhs and MFs crash - then you could get only Rs. 8.5 Lakhs. Wherever there is any speculation - best to avoid it when it comes to Emergency Funds STATE BANK OF INDIA FIXED DEPOSITS OR PUBLIC SECTOR BANK FIXED DEPOSITS is the best bet.

column1: What are some books to stay away from, and why?
column3: Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close by Jonathan Safran Foer. This is a generally well-received book by both readers and critics, and I loathed it. The premise is that the protagonist, a kid named Oskar, lost his father in the September 11th attacks, and he wants answers. His only clue is that his father may have had contact with someone named Black, and so he sets out to interview every single person in NYC who is named Black. Spoiler: this actually works in the end, somehow. In the meantime, the reader is treated to endless bouts of nonsense that are supposed to come across as whimsically creative but more often just seem silly. They include the following: Oskar does not swear, but instead says "shiitake."Oskar's cat is named after Buckminster Fuller.In his school's production of Hamlet, Oskar is cast as the skull.Oskar practices tambourine wherever he goes.One character cannot speak, and for convenience he has "yes" and "no" tattooed on his palms, in spite of the fact that even speaking people often use simple head gestures to communicate these terms. John Updike summed it up best in his review of the book: "Playful inventiveness can come down with a case of the cutes." Add onto this a variety of gimmicks including photos, a flipbook, and "handwritten" annotations on the pages, and suddenly your silly, sentimental story is also a daring experiment in formalism for no good reason. It's just a sappy, superficial piece of nonsense that panders to the emotions of the 9/11 generation. Dreadful. Recommended instead: For a book about a child trying to understand the death of a family member: Mathilda Savitch by Victor Lodato. For a book about someone rebuilding a life after a terrorist attack: Incendiary by Chris Cleave. For a much better book by Foer: Eating Animals by Jonathan Safran Foer (a nonfiction examination of meat and the meat industry)

column1: Will I come to terms with having a disabled baby?
column3: This has been a thought-provoking question for me. I've been thinking about the horrifying but commonly accepted inference in the question: that the possibility exists that you might not come to terms with having a disabled child, that you might reject or resent your child for their disability. I've been thinking about why that possibility is allowed to exist, and what might reduce its presence in society. Expectations and the visibility of disabled adults For a lot of people, their idea of what it means to have a happy and fulfilled life is very rigid. You have to have XYZ characteristics and be able to do ABC things and have achieved DEF by the time you're 18 and so on. We believe this because this is all we've seen and all we know, and we simply have no scope to imagine how wrong we are. Amy Sequenzia is an autistic adult who is a leading figure in the autistic self-advocacy movement. Her writing is, in a word, ausome (not a typo). She is non-verbal, cannot live alone and needs significant assistance with daily living. The same is true for Stephen Hawking. Being disabled, even profoundly disabled, doesn't mean you can't have a happy and fulfilled life making a significant contribution to society. The visibility and acceptance of disabled adults is crucial to this simple fact becoming more broadly known and accepted. Tragedy narrative If you've read my answers before, you probably know I have an autistic son. When we first got his diagnosis, there was certainly an adjustment period. Overall I think this was a really positive process for us, since we had to throw out all our baseless expectations and learn about who our child actually was and what he actually needed, as opposed to our fairly lazy assumptions about him which were based on who we are and what we need. But the tragedy narrative was present. The “oh no, how awful” from well-meaning acquaintances. The “I told you there was something wrong with him” from a family member. This goes back to a large extent to my first point. These people assumed that autism was a fate worse than death. (A couple of them had actually refused to vaccinate their kids based on the nonsense Wakefield paper and the false link between vaccines and autism.) These examples, while distressing at the time, pale into insignificance beside a much darker iteration of the tragedy narrative. This is the direct excusing and pitying of parents who murder their healthy, happy disabled children. Parents who murder their typical children are monsters, while parents who murder their disabled children are overwhelmed, desperate, in need of more support and respite and so on. Don't get me wrong, parents certainly do need breaks, but if we believed that a disabled child mattered just as much as their able siblings, we would never excuse their murders in the way we routinely do. This article discusses the point further[1] And again, circle back to my first point for the reasons why we dismiss disabled children as being intrinsically worth less than their able siblings. We cannot imagine their lives as being genuinely precious and worth living, because they are different from the mental model of A Good Life that we’ve got stuck in our unimaginative brains. The failure, in case it's not clear by now, is in us, and not in the disabled person. Harder work Everyone's experience on this point will be different and I'm not going to say my view is right, but I've observed other people with their typical kids and I'm by no means convinced that my road is spectacularly harder than theirs. I mean, it has its own challenges and sometimes those can catch me unawares, but actually parenting is pretty hard work no matter what variety of kid you get. So when people say compassionately “that must be so hard….” well, ok, sometimes it is. But sometimes all kids are tough going. That's more or less intrinsic to the process, unless you get spectacularly lucky and have a single extremely easy child. Parenting takes patience, resilience and flexibility. That's just how that works. Probably should wrap up now I may come back to add more to this but it's pretty long already, so I will end with this: You absolutely can come to terms with having a disabled baby. Whether or not you do depends on whether you choose to let go of your preconceived ideas about parenting and about your child and accept the kid you have for who they are. This is completely within your power. You can make the conscious choice to accept and love your child, to learn about adults like them and to surround them with support and community. Or not.Footnotes[1] Why Are We Sympathetic To The Murderers Of Disabled Children?

column1: What is an extremely shocking cultural practice practiced in Europe?
column3: S'accabadora was a woman who, called by the family of the terminally ill patient, arranged to kill him, putting an end to his suffering . A merciful act towards the dying person but also a necessary act for the survival of relatives, especially for the less well-off social classes: in small towns many days away from a doctor, it served to avoid long and atrocious suffering for the patient. A female accabadora always arrived at the house of the dying man at night and, after having sent out the family members who had called her, she entered the room of death: the door opened and the dying man, from his bed of agony, saw her enter dressed in black, with his face covered, and he understood that his suffering was about to end . The patient was suppressed with a pillow, or the woman delivered the blow of " su Mazzolu " causing death. She went away on tiptoe, as if she had completed a mission, and the patient's family expressed deep gratitude to her for the service rendered to their relative by offering her products from the land. The blow was almost always aimed at the forehead . The term "accabadora" comes from the Spanish "acabar" which means to end. “Su Mazzolu” was a sort of stick specially constructed from an olive branch, 40 centimeters long and 20 centimeters wide, with a handle that allowed a safe and precise grip. In Sardinia s'accabbadora practiced until a few decades ago, especially in the central-northern part of the island. The last known episodes of "accabadura" occurred in Luras in 1929 and in Orgosolo in 1952 . In addition to the documented cases, there are many those entrusted to oral transmission and family memories. Many remember a grandfather or great-grandfather who nevertheless had to deal with the lady dressed in black. Its existence has always been considered a natural fact, just as there was a midwife who helped to be born, there was a s'accabadora who helped to die. It is even said that she was often the same person and that her task was distinguished by the color of her dress (black if she brought death, white or light if she had to give birth to life). This figure, an expression of a socio-cultural and historical phenomenon, and the practice of euthanasia in the small rural towns of Sardinia is linked to the relationship that the Sardinians had with death, considered as the conclusion of the natural cycle of life.

column1: Is discrimination against men real? Can you give any example of discrimination against males?
column3: “Do you have a life insurance?”, a friend asked me. No, I said. My husband has one. “But why don’t you?”, asked the friend. “I don’t know… I don’t have any dependents. I am pretty sure if I die, my husband will be able to take care of himself well”, I replied, doubting my own answer. The friend seemed to buy into the logic, but my mind threw more questions at me. Isn’t this a selfish attitude to have? You have ensured your future, but what about husband’s future? What about the loans you have taken together? What about the loss of your income which will hit him hard? Aren’t you being discriminatory?I asked a few married female friends if they have a life insurance. Most of them said the same thing - No, I don’t think I need it. That’s the point- Life Insurance is not meant for you. It is meant to support your family if you leave too early. As per a survey conducted by an insurance company in 2017, women are far more uninsured than men.The report said that as of today, only 50 percent of women in the urban internet population in India have life insurance coverage as compared to 72 percent of men who have purchased life insurance solutions. [1]Isn’t this being discriminatory against men?Just this week, the Motor Accidents Claim Tribunal awarded a husband compensation for his wife’s accidental death. The 35 year old woman was a housewife with a young family. BUT, the compensation awarded was based on the salary of a maid.The Mumbai tribunal reached a figure of Rs 4,500 per month after taking into consideration prevalent charges of a house help for choresThe other factors considered in calculating the compensation included loss of consortium, funeral expenses and loss of estate[2]A woman is like family manager. Her role in the household cannot be determined solely by her financial contributions. She binds the family together. She is like the lubricant of the engine. When she is gone, the family must be compensated not just emotionally, but also financially. Just like women, men also need time to come to terms with the loss of a spouse. He might need to spend more time at home. The grief might render him less productive at work. But the Supreme Court order does not take this into account.The notional income of a housewife was to be taken to be up to Rs 5,000 per month and that the services rendered by a mother, sister, wife are immensely valuable and unparalleled and cannot be calculated in terms of money since they are rendered with natural love and affection. The death of such a female member creates a great vacuum in the family.I feel this attitude is absolutely against men. It is after all they who have to suffer twice- one, the loss of their life partner, and two, their life support. By not insuring our lives, we women are discriminating against men!Footnotes[1] Women underinsured than men:Birla Sun Life Insurance survey[2] https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/mumbai/damages-for-housewifes-death-based-on-maids-pay-salary-taken-to-housewife-to-decide-payout-to-says-housewife-to-maid-orders-5-5l-payout/articleshow/62076282.cms

column1: A family member of mine died mainly due to a result of a long term mainly vegan diet. (Low in B12, B6, and iron). For this reason I dislike talk about the vegan diet. What do I tell my vegan/vegetarian friends, who wish to talk about veganism to me?
column3: If this is likely to happen to you often, if you are reeling from the loss of your family member while having to cope with a topic that brings you pain, that does put you in a bind. But you can help yourself out of that bind. If you research the topic on your own, you’ll probably come to know that if someone dies of an eating disorder, and they were also following a mostly vegan diet, the second probably didn’t have much if anything to do with first. The more thoroughly you can separate eating disorders and veganism in your mind, the better you will be able to cope with conversations that really have nothing to do with the demise of your family member. And once you are really there mentally, it will be safe to bring up the death of your family member in those conversations with vegan and vegetarian friends. If they are decent sorts, they will be sympathetic and reassuring that they have no intention of trying to convert you. However, if you lean in and ask them if they’re getting enough protein, or if they’re supplementing the vitamins they no longer get from meat, deceased family member or no deceased family member, you will come across as a condescending jerk. It’s like meeting someone who rides a motorcycle, and immediately demanding to know whether they wear a helmet because your cousin didn’t wear a helmet and now he’s dead. So however you engage these friends, it’s crucial for you to approach the topic with the same respect you demand of others. Engage them with the assumption that they’ve got their health in hand.

column1: If you register to donate your organs upon your death, can you also then donate the remainder of your body to science?
column3: Usually not. Original question:If you register to donate your organs upon your death, can you also then donate the remainder of your body to science?The exception is cornea donation. If you donate your corneas, then you can still be eligible for whole body donation. If you donate your main organs (heart, liver, kidneys, etc.) or tissues (skin, bones, veins, etc.) then most whole body donation organizations (that I know of) will not accept you. Most whole body donations are either used for medical school cadavers to train new physicians, to researchers, or by medical companies for other training. I think it would be too hard for them to find schools or researchers who needed a body without the organs. If they had the need, they would probably ‘reuse’ a cadaver that had previously had the organs in place. Other donations to ‘body farms’ would still need the organs in place. Most of their research depends on observing decomposition, and the organs are an important part of that process. Donation of the main organs can only be done in perfect (and fairly rare) circumstances. They have to be a “Beating heart” potential donors. This can only be achieved in 2 situations. They must also be medically suitable with no signs of infection.People who have been declared ‘brain dead’ but are being kept perfused on machines. This is usually while families come to term with the death or they are waiting for another family member to arrive, or they are still deciding if they will allow organ donation.DCD (death before cardiac death) donors. These are usually people who are in a persistive vegetative state, and the families want to withdraw care. They know their loved one would not want to exist that way. In these sorts of cases the patient is taken to the operating room, and all of the surgeons are present. Ventilation is removed and they wait for the patient to die. After they are legally pronounced, then they hook up the ventilation again (to keep organs viable) and begin recovering (the term ‘harvest’ is no longer used). If they do not die after ventilation is removed, (the time given is usually 45 minutes) then they are returned to hospice care. Most die within a day.There is a HUGE shortage of these sorts of donors, and they are desperately needed to save lives. If your choice to be a donor is to help society, then I would urge you to always choose this. If you are choosing to be a scientific whole body donor to save on cremation costs (and that is a perfectly fine reason), then do that. Organ Procurement Organizations (OPO’s) legally cannot pay for cremation after donation, like organizations that coordinate scientific or whole body donation. Tissue (skin, bones, veins, heart valves) and cornea donation can occur on many more people who die. There is a very strong need for these donors, and you can still save lives, but they are not as rare. We have a limited time to recover after death is pronounced (usually before 20 hours) and there are still many situations that would make someone ineligible. Sign up to be an Organ, Tissue, and Eye Donor! Let your family know your wishes.
column9: When my father died, he didn't have any organs anybody would want except his eyes. I was asked and I granted donation of his eyes to researchers on macular degeneration. I'm glad his worn out old body did something good for society.

column1: When the police go to a house to tell a woman that her husband was killed in a car accident, do they stay with her until someone comes to be with her?
column3: As a Family Liaison Officer, (FLO), I’ve had to take the loneliest walk more times than I would ever want to! Knocking on the door, knowing you are about to effectively destroy someone’s entire world is the hardest thing you will ever do. I’ve found over the years that there’s no point beating around the bush. I’m not being unkind but if I knock on your door at 3am wearing my white topped hat that denotes me as a traffic officer, it’s pretty obvious I’m not there to tell you that you’ve Won the lottery. (I’d much rather be doing that). I just sit the person down, confirm they are the persons next of kin and then explain that they’ve been involved in a road traffic collision and as a result their loved one has passed away from their injuries. It sounds cold written down but it really isn’t. It’s actually the kindest way to convey the message. Being vague or indirect can give false hope and that’s much worse. Part of what follows next is to ensure that person is taken care of. I will always ask if there’s a friend or relative they would like us to call. If this involves a trip to collect someone or to take them somewhere then that’s what we do. The last thing I would want is for that person to be alone or to try and drive somewhere whilst they are in no fit state due to their grief. If it means sitting with them for several hours, then so be it. They are my only concern. Edit 28/01/2022 Thanks to everyone who has taken the time to read and upvote this. I have had some amazing comments but also a few disparaging ones so I thought I’d set the record straight. First of all, this question should be set out in more gender neutral terms. I’m not a snowflake but the simple fact is this isn’t gender specific! As a FLO I’ve broken the news to, and comforted all members of families regardless of gender, husbands, brothers, fathers, mums, sisters, wives. It matters not, as an FLO, it’s my job to deal with that family (including estranged families), convey the news and guide them through the process. Being a roads policing FLO is the best worst job in the world! Unbelievably challenging but incredibly rewarding as you build a relationship of trust with the family. Depending on the circumstances of the road death it’s my job to talk the family through what happens next! If this is a single vehicle collision and no one else is involved or the investigation determines that the circumstances were such that the collision was unavoidable then the process will be dealt with by a coroners inquest. The FLO will arrange things like viewing and formal identification of the deceased, supporting the family through this traumatic time. It is the FLO’s job to keep the family updated with progress of the case, including talking them through the post mortem results and the forensic collision report. They will attend coroners court to support the family during the inquest. If a criminal act is identified, then the matter will be referred to the crown prosecution service (CPS) for a charging decision. After all this is a homicide investigation. During this time we will keep the family updated as above and then support them through the prosecution process. it’s the FLO’s job to act as the liaison between the investigation team and the family and support them throughout. FLO’s may also be called to attend forensic post mortems to record the pathologists notes.

column1: My mother died and afterwards I saw my 15 year old son asked a girl if she would come over and cuddle to help him cope. Is he definitely dating or crushing on her or could they just be really close?
column3: Do not try and read anything into what you saw between your son and this girl,it is perfectly normal for teenagers to have friends their own age group rather than family that they confide in,especially in times of upset and hurt like the death of a close family member who they will seek comfort in,because they don’t want to add to the grief of other people in the family, it is good that he feels he has someone out side the family to talk to about his feelings and emotions at this present time,who will help him come to terms with it. Your son is 15 years old so it is perfectly possible that he has met a girl he is keen on and likes spending time with,but at 15 he is not dating her yet as they aren’t really old enough to date in any serious sense(but they think they are),so don’t say anything to him about ti as that may embarrass him just watch quietly from the side lines,for now,and see how things develop,he may only be 15 but he is growing up if he comes to you for advice on how to deal with things in a relationship give it to him in way that helps him understand his feelings and what is going in in his life now.

column1: Why do some Hindus/Indians observe Sutak for 13 days after a death in the near family to mourn? I don’t understand the parts like untouchability or not being allowed to go to a temple. Isn't that the time when the family needs the God even more?
column3: Thanks for the AtoA. Most of the previous answers have stated the reasons well. Let me give you a few examples to put certainn things in perspective. There was an interesting case of a young lady, with a one year old who brought her mother in law to a psychiatrist . She said, that her mother in law always keeps telling that her son, who was employed in a guf country, was dead. So the daughter in law wanted the doctor to treat her mother in law. The interesting fact was, her husband had actually died in an aircrash or some such calamity(I forget the actual cause) .She was in absolute denial .The body of the dead husband was not recovered, and the death rituals were not performed, as the girl was pregnant when the misfortunate incident happened. She kept telling that her husband calls her through phone and he would be coming soon to see his new born. So the doctor had asked the mother in law to bring the daughter iin law for consultation under the pretext of treatment for the mother in law . After a few visits of maintaining the facade, they orchestrated a fake call, while in the clinic , to inform the girl that her husband had died in the foreign country, as if the incident had just taken place.The girl absolutely broke down there, and the fact that her husband was dead sunk in to her psyche. There was another instance in a family, with very ‘educated' offsprings, who absolutely forbid anyone from crying at the death ceremony, as they could not bear to see their mother cry. But, lo behold. That poor old woman keeps crying to this day. It looks like she cannot stop herself from crying 24/7. This explains the reason for Rudalis and the various Pattinathar songs sung during the death ceremonies.For them to accept the incident, and to come to terms with it. So:Quarantining an infectious familyProviding them with the presence of friends and family for comfort, condolence and a sense of belonging.Dealing with financial and inheritance issues within the family.Psychological acceptance of the loss of the family member. column1: As a member of law enforcement, how often do you have to tell someone that their loved one has died?
column3: Probably more than 60 and fewer than 100. Death notifications are truly one of if not the worst part of the job. I awakened to a reoccurring nightmare of one such call tonight as I do many many nights.I can't tell you how many times I've stood outside darkened porch of some poor family at 3:00 in the morning waiting to ring the doorbell and trying to gather my thoughts on what I will say when they come to the door. I'm always very aware that the people inside are living the last few moments of happiness in their life that they will probably ever truly have. Until you've had to look a mother and father in the eye and tell them that their child was killed and will not be coming home again is one of the most horrific things that a person can be asked to do in the line of duty. Even worse is that we really can't use euphemisms of any kind like they are no longer with us for example. You must use the word dead or died or killed. Saying passed away or some other kind euphemism often seen in everyday speech just doesn't do the job. The loved ones will not even hear it or comprehend subtlety. For the loved ones in shock you must say “died, dead or killed" simply so their mind can even comprehend the message. This makes it even more difficult because you naturally want to be delicate. In our training we're taught that delicate wording and euphemisms just don't cut through the shock and trauma the loved one is experiencing. Anyway, it's truly a soul-destroying moment for them and to an extent for us. After one child who died in a particularly horrific way, I recall sitting in my squad car for what must have been an hour. I could hear laughter and joy in the living room as I walked up. It's impossible to explain the feelings that I get when my duty requires me to tear someone's soul and put them in pain that will never end. Often I would sit in my car after and just want to cry. The time I'm speaking of in particular that always comes to mind (and my nightmares several nights a week) a beautiful 8-year-old boy was eaten alive by a pack of feral dogs in a Park. I lied and said he died of a dog bite and went quickly with no pain. A blatant lie but of course every loved one’s first question is “how"? If you ever tell a family member that there has been an unexpected death in the family and they don’t demand to know how and where it’s almost always true that they killed them or knew in advance. Off topic but interesting. Regardless of cause the most common means of death in order of frequency were vehicle accident, medical issue, miscellaneous accident and murder). Seemed like murder made it much worse by the reaction. People are always scared their loved ones will get killed in a collision or drop dead of a heart attack. Murder is time brutally cut short and many times is associated with for lack of a better term, a “worse death”, involving more pain, terror. When they told me my Grandfather dropped dead in a Piggly Wiggly store from a massive heart attack it didn’t haunt me like it would if someone had killed him. You soon learn there is no way to ease their pain and the best method is to be brief, direct, absolute and straightforward…then leave them to their grief. Honestly they don't hear a word you say after “they're dead and how it happened”. People have literally no idea how difficult the job is. If they did people that despise us would be a very infinitesimal minority instead of the enormously popular hobby that it is today. I'm retired and haunted nightly by such things as this topic as well as seeing horrible images in my nightly dreams of things like a young boy totally devoured by dogs like a pack of hyenas eating a gazelle. I know this is off-topic but it is after 4 a.m. as I write this. I awoke to a dream of a time I arrived at a vehicle accident just in time to watch an elderly woman confused and sitting in her car as flames reached her and she burned alive 3 feet from me while making eye contact and screaming in agony. The flames that started in the leaking gas tank ruptured when her son-in-law rear-ended her after he was rear-ended by a drunk and slammed into her car by the force. I broke the window and was 3 seconds from cutting her seat belt and yanking her head-first out the window (the door was inoperable). Then as I reached in to use my seat belt cutter I always carried since my Fire Rescue/Auto Extrication days, it was as if a man with a flame thrower standing in the rear of the car suddenly blasted her, engulfing her body and the front seat in a huge volume of intense flame so hot I was burned on my face and arms standing outside the vehicle. As the flame totally engulfed her she kept gripping the steering wheel and turned to me and gave a haunting scream of intense agony. Her grown son-in-law was standing at my side. Knowing if I had taken the correct on-ramp to I-70 I would have been there just in time to pull her out with no injuries. Ten seconds between life and an agonizing death. An hour later I was at a nearby Fire Station with this man who essentially rear-ended and killed his mother-in-law (not his fault but still) giving him emotional support as he had to call his wife. Imagine explaining to your wife you crashed into her mother and she burned to death as a result of the collision. I ended up taking him to OT Hodges (a local 24-hour diner that Cops, Firemen and Drunks frequent at night to get chili, chili cheese fries, dogs and coffee). We just sat there in silence for what must have been two hours after I was off duty trying to process in our minds what we had just seen. He was barely able to function and I was slightly better because I wasn’t related to the victim we had just watched be cremated alive 36 inches away. I took him to the Adams Mark (a luxury hotel by the Arch downtown) and had a Concierge friend of mine check him into a suite with gratis room service. I made sure department trauma counselors and Red Cross disaster response professionals got over to see him in those first critical hours the next day as well as contacting the Police in his hometown to make sure the wife received help as well. I don’t know why it never occurred to me to get help. I think I thought that it was just part of my job and I needed to “suck it up” and deal with the calls on the job myself (i.e. push those horrors into a dark recess of my mind and ignore them). I could go on and on. Last messages from husbands for their family as they lie bleeding to death in my arms. One time working as a Firefighter on a nearby departments ambulance to accumulate medical experience necessary in Trauma to be qualified as a Paramedic (Granite City Illinois) taking down the last words of a man cut in half by a truck’s rear bumper. He was on a loading dock and would die instantly when the truck was moved which was the only thing keeping his organs from his bladder to his diaphragm from falling out when it backed into him pinching his waist line between the bumper and the dock. Delivering those last words to the wife and children. Talking to a man on a roof and not finding the words that would convince them to not jump followed by the horrible thud sound of a man hitting concrete. Cutting a family out of a car crushed between two semi trucks compacting it to a 5 foot by 5 foot cube, removing the parents and two kids one piece at a time - the biggest chunk the size of a soft ball. The last gasps of breath of a teenager, shot I was holding as he died. The sound of the blood pooling in their lungs as they slip away first looking at me …then off into the distance right through me. You know when people are dying when you have seen it happen a lot. I always tried to keep them calm and kind of, I don’t know how to describe it in a word…be there as they died. I always try to prompt them “do you want me to give a message to anyone” (they don’t always know just how fast they’re circling the drain and often won’t realize that if they have any last words they should be now …kinda thing). Really watching what must have been over a hundred people’s life slip away waiting for an Ambulance after every conceivable way to die from falling off a roof to being shot or hit by a car. Not to mention just the average things that stick in your mind like finding the eyeball of a guy who died after a head shot from a 12-gauge and having to pick it up and bag it. Finding fingers and legs/arms and other parts on the side of the road after motorcycle accidents and having to drive them to the morgue to put with the rest of the body. Being at the morgue as a Detective having to watch a victim be autopsied so I can maintain the chain of evidence and collect the bullets pulled out of them to bring to the ballistics lab for analysis. I luckily didn’t do the Morgue thing often. I wasn’t a Homicide Detective and rarely had business at the Morgue. The place creeped me out. They’re pretty gross. Our was built in the 1920s or something with weird old tiles and greenish fluorescent lights. Picture the Morgue in 7 Deadly Sins with Brad Pitt. I avoided it when possible and was lucky I spent a lot more time as a regular Beat Cop in there than as a Detective. One gross thing people don’t know Cops do is get called to any body that is found. Someone finds an old man that lived alone 3 weeks in a 98 degree room dead. Usually the smell 3 floors away initiates the call. Then the Cop has to sit there. With that body. That decaying, slipping, oozing maggot infested body for hours of just “maintain the scene”. What you’re really doing is just waiting for the Coroner’s guys to get around to coming and collecting the body cause our Detectives are done. So whichever Cops particular Beat that is, he wins the “you’re gonna smell that body in your nose and not eat right for a couple days contest”. Best way to deal with dead body smell is a 3 pronged attack. 1. Vicks UP IN that nose. Not on your lip like on TV. 2. Take coffee grounds, put them in a pan and turn heat on medium. The smell of burned coffee cancels out dead body. 3. Cigars. Smoke em up. Cigar smoke + burning coffee + vicks up in that nose and you can sit and have your bag lunch watching the guys TV with him in the other lazy boy. I read so so much rage and hate for Police here in Quora and it really does hurt and aggravate those open wounds we suffered protecting the very people who live to insult and hate us. People we would give our lives to save. I saved so many more lives as a Cop than I ever did as a Marine, Paramedic and Firefighter combined and am left with the nightmares, mental and physical wounds (spinal cord injury and chronic pain for life) but it is the ingratitude and hate of Americans that is my most horrific wound. Sorry for the rant but it's just where my mind is tonight as I try to center myself and get through the flashbacks as best I can. I know there are bad people in every profession but if just one reader sees this and has just a small moment of empathy and connection with the pain we bear in the emergency services it will be well worth it. At least I’m still alive and coping. I have lost many many friends/co-workers who couldn’t cope. One of my best friends packed up all his belongings in his home and wrote and addressed several letters to family and friends. He took report sheets from work and wrote his own death report for the officer that would get the call for his suicide so all they had to do was sign it. He left us a case of Scotch with the letters to his families as well as belongings he wanted his Detective Squad to have. Things from cash to gun/photographs of sentimental value, etc. He drove his car onto the Poplar Street Bridge over the Mississippi between St. Louis and Illinois. He left his wallet, side arm, badge and ID on the seat of his car with a note giving his address and instructions making identification and the investigation easier for the responding Cop…then jumped off the bridge into the icy swift current of the Mississippi channel in December. In the end all he cared about was the impact it would have on the Cops that caught his case and making it easier for us. He worked as a City Copper for over 30 years and absorbed more poison and trauma than his mind could cope with. He was a wonderful man. He was my friend and I considered a mentor. He left me a note apologizing in his way . It was the final lesson of an old school Cop who made sure his life saving experiences were passed on to a newly minted Patrolman he took under his wing right out of the Academy and guided for years until he couldn't take the suffering the job caused a day longer. He said he lived years longer than he might because he knew the effect his suicide would have on me and some others. I ended up disabled years many years later by a good hit to the back by a man on PCP (or in some kind of extreme diabetic crisis) who was freaking out in berserker mode in a fight that lasted 15 minutes and ended up injuring my spine. Best job I ever had. I miss it everyday. Having worked every job on the other end of the 911 line it was the one where I had the most power to save lives and help people. As a fireman/medic I could only wait for disaster and try to mitigate the harm. As a Cop I could intervene and stop the most evil monsters lurking among us from walking free and preying on the people I swore to defend. I only wish people wouldn’t lump in all 1.3 million of us with the truly tiny percentage that tarnish the badge and disrespect the honor we worked so hard to uphold. For a comparison with another profession…Physicians, MD’s kill over 250,000 Americans each year due to incompetence and professional errors. Police kill fewer than 100. Imagine hating your doctor because you heard that they’re all incompetent and cursing all doctors for the actions of the bad ones. Yet Police are frequently grouped together as malicious and brutal killers and the tiny bad percentage of our profession is no where as lethal as Doctors just as an example. Yet hate and derision for us is literally an American pastime. You would never dream of lumping your Doctor in with the others that kill a quarter of a million (the numbers they maim from malpractice and improper med doses could be in the millions) and number in the tens of thousands if not more in terms of numbers that kill and maim people with incompetence and lack of skill/training. For every Cop that makes a mistake that kills a citizen there are thousands of Doctors that kill…and not just one or two but repeatedly kill hundreds or more in a career, maim thousands and are never punished or lose their credentials. I offer this not as an excuse for the terrible and disgusting behavior of the minority of Police we all see caught on camera, but as a comparison to other professions and how they’re treated as compared to police despite their racking up hundreds of thousands of kills compared to fewer than 100 questionable deaths Police are responsible for. Not making excuses, just comparisons to show the absurdity of the obsession/hate/disrespect for my profession. I have lost 5 friends gunned down in the line of duty. I lost 4 friends as a Firefighter killed in buildings they were in rescuing victims…1 ran out of air or burned to death and 3 at one time, crushed by collapse of walls and floors. I can't begin to count the number maimed and disabled like me. I won’t even address the PTSD, suicides and mental trauma on both the Police and Fire side. *Edit 9/16/20 Since June 1st this year my department alone have had 9 Police shot in the line of duty with 1 dying. 10 shot and 2 dying if you count a retired city Police Captain who was now working for another department who came back to the city to help stop the riots and was murdered by looters at a pawn shop. He was a friend of mine. The last Cop killed last week, shot in the forehead leaving 3 kids. Barely on the job a year and was trained by a good friend of mine I went to the Police Academy with. When one of us dies we have family like connections to each other. I feel so bad for Cops today and thank my lucky stars I left with a pension before people stood outside the hospital where two shot Police are in surgery fighting for their lives chanting “WE HOPE YOU DIE”.Crowd gathers outside hospital, chants 'We hope they die' after 2 LA County deputies were shot It was incredibly difficult job. Now it’s actually impossible to do correctly. Thanks so much for the nice comments and up votes. When I log in and see the upvotes and comments it really makes my day and I feel like I’m connecting with people through my writing. It’s much appreciated everyone. I moved my family to Paris France in 2022 and live in France full time since being disabled on the job. I have a lot to be thankful for and being Police was the best job I ever had.
column9: I appreciate all of the work that you did. Police save lives, and because of police officers like you we place a lot of trust and power in the hands of the police. I hail and praise those who honor that sacred trust. Thank you.

column1: How much can elephants memorize in the wild? How much in captivity?
column3: It goes without saying that the first animal you think of when speaking of excellent memory – to the extent it actually surpasses that of a human being – is definitely the elephant, whether of the African or Asian subspecies. Truly, an elephant never forgets.First off, elephant herds are led by a matriarch, who is generally the oldest and biggest female in the group, and has 40–50 years of experience to survive (and let her family survive) in a most hostile environment. Sure enough, her excellent long-term memory allows her to remember the routes towards every available waterhole or green pasture she visited during her own youth (something particularly useful during the dry season and the pachyderms’ annual migration), as well as to recognize the places to avoid due to strong human presence (mainly poachers and hostile farmers) – gradually, this knowledge passes on from mother to daughter and granddaughter, generation after generation.Moreover, research suggests that adult elephants are able to calculate and memorize the whereabouts of up to thirty of their family members… by smelling their urine! It’s no joke: an elephant can recognize dozens of its kin by the signature smell of molecular urine, and thus keep track of their whereabouts[1]. This helps the species stick together with its congeners, and upholds its reputation as an amazing memory machine.But the complex phenomenon that is elephant cognition gets all the more true when it comes to interacting with humans. Indeed, because of their long-lasting memory, elephants can remember for years specific people who provoked them or caused a too great amount of harm, and can even suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a mental health condition long thought to be solely human.In more severe cases, the damage is too much to handle, and the harm too much to be forgotten, to the extent that most individuals resort to ruthlessly attack humans whenever possible, either out of revenge following years of persecution (poaching, mass killings for their tusks, habitat loss, ever-increasing conflicts, separating calves from their mothers and families, deliberate mistreatment for tourist entertainment…), or to avenge the death of a beloved family member. Scientist Dr. Joyce Poole, from the Amboseli Elephant Research Project in Kenya, gives further information:[Elephants] are certainly intelligent enough and have good enough memories to take revenge. Wildlife managers may feel that it is easier to just shoot so-called “problem” elephants than face people’s wrath. So an elephant is shot without [hunters] realizing the possible consequences on the remaining family members and the very real possibility of stimulating a cycle of violence.[2]In captivity, things get a whole lot worse: a lot of captive elephants are often seen constantly swaying their trunks and heads, as a means to show stress due to a lifetime of abuse – something referred to as “stereotypic behavior”, a reminder that our need for entertainment isn’t worth an animal’s pain. At some point, many of these elephants may snap and attack, or even kill, at any moment…Such was the case with a circus elephant named Tyke (see above), who went on a deadly rampage in August 1994, killing her trainer before the eyes of aghast spectators, brutally attacking any man who tried to stop her, and wreaking havoc in the streets of Honolulu (Hawaii), before getting shot at by the police – later reports confirmed that Tyke was suffering from PTSD, given that her alcoholic trainer greatly abused her when intoxicated; since then, Tyke became the emblem of animal rights and circus tragedies, and animal-driven circuses are now completely banned in Hawaii[3].All of this clearly shows that when traumatized and threatened, these normally gentle giants quickly become aggressive.On a lighter note, elephants remember kindness too. As a matter of fact, many of them never hesitate to show ever-lasting gratitude to the very people who saved their lives and/or provided them all the care (medical, nutritional and the like) they needed – at a point of developing a friendly bond with these humans –; whilst others in India recently resorted to genuinely thank the men who rescued their calves from pits and wells[4], raising their trunks into what appears to be some sort of salute[5] and gratitude (this shows that animals do have souls just like us). The following quote, pronounced by a wildlife rescuer from India, says it all:Just a little bit of love, and you can change an animal’s life forever…Footnotes[1] Elephants sniff urine to tell who's who[2] Study: Elephants might seek revenge[3] GRAPHIC VIDEO: Remembering Tyke, The Rebellious Circus Elephant, And Her Tragic Death[4] Baby elephant rescued from ditch, mother returns to thank helpers. Internet hearts viral video[5] Mother Elephant Thanks Humans Who Rescued Her Baby From a Well (Video)

column1: Do midlife crisis affair realtionships last?
column3: I think you don't understand what midlife crisis means. Those who go into a midlife crisis might experience a range of feelings such as:Unhappiness with life and the lifestyle that may have provided them with happiness for many years.Boredom with people and things that may have been of interest to them before.Feeling a need for adventure and change.Questioning the choices, they have made in their lives and the validity of decisions they made years before.Confusion about who they are and where they are going.Anger at their spouse and blame for feeling tied down.Unable to make decisions about where they want to go with their life.Doubt that they ever loved their spouse and resentment over the marriage.A desire for a new and passionate, intimate relationship.Most people who have a difficult time during midlife and go into crisis mode do so because of external factors. They may be experiencing stress in their life that makes the transition more difficult or they may have childhood issue that were never dealt with that come to the surface during this time. External factors that may cause midlife to be problematic for some people are:Debt:It is easier to accumulate debt due to the availability of credit cards and loans. A person who is finding it difficult emotionally during midlife might find it easier to walk away from their family in order to rid himself of what he feels is the cause of all the debt.Significant Loss:The death of a parent or family member can cause grief, which is difficult enough to come to terms with, without having to also cope with the feelings of a midlife transition. Put the loss of a loved one with the feelings that accompany midlife and the whole process becomes bewildering and overwhelming.Avoidant Personality:If a person has a tendency to avoid conflict in their personal relationships, suffers from feelings of inadequacy, are emotionally distant and has low self – esteem they will find midlife transition harder to navigate. This personality type has a deep fear of feeling shame and rejection. Such feelings will keep them from seeking help should their emotions become overwhelming. More than likely, they will run from their problems instead of trying to find solutions to them. It’s this personality type that normally ends up in divorce court during midlife. So would that person have a lasting relationship with their younger lover? HELL NO! See, the thing is younger women have higher expectations and are full of life and energy compared to their older counterparts who have lowered expectations because of experience and wisdom that the young woman hasn't yet gotten. Now here is a man who is feeling a failure and full of negative energy dating a young woman full of life, happiness, expectations and positive energy. He may keep her at bay with expensive gifts but that won't last for long. Sooner or later, she'll feel his negativity and then begin resenting him. Resentment will lead to fights and passive aggression on a daily basis. Result is a bad break up and spending all their lives trying to erase that relationship from their heads permanently.
column9: Phill Ip is absolutely spot on. My ex husband is textbook. It is a real and serious, devastating situation. My life has been turned upside down and inside out. My husband endured retirement, empty nest syndrome, cancer, and death of his mother..When all this came together after 36 years of marriage, he told me he never loved me and he was not happy. From then on he has gone back to being a teenager. If a troubled teen would do it, so did my husband (and he is 63 years old). He hates me and has done the most awful cruel monstrous things to hurt me…I don’t even know the man. This is not a diagnosable condition; yet it mimics one that is diagnosable. Midlife transition.. If you have not experienced being on the receiving end of a spouse in midlife crisis, you don’t have the understanding of how destructive it is to spouses, children, friends, jobs, etc. Words cannot describe someone who is in a deep classic midlife crisis.

column1: During the meeting of the Five Families in The Godfather, what does Vito Corleone mean when he suggests that he will hold Barzini and Tattaglia responsible if Michael gets struck by a bolt of Lightning on his way home? Did Vito really believe this?
column3: When Vito Corleone said that he would hold a number of people responsible should anything have happened to Michael Corleone before he could return home from Sicily, did The Godfather really mean he would act out if Michael was struck down by the Hand of God? Of course not. The term we want to keep in mind here is the word, “metaphor.”“…I forgo the vengeance of my son. But I have selfish reasons. My youngest son was forced to leave this country because of this Sollozzo business. All right, now I have to make arrangements to bring him back here safely cleared of all these false charges. But I'm a superstitious man and if some unlucky accident should befall him, if he should get shot in the head by a police officer, or if he should hang himself in his jail cell, or if he's struck by a bolt of lightening, then I'm going to blame some of the people in this room, and that I do not forgive…” (Vito to the heads of the other members of the Five Families on the day he sued for peace.) The Godfather (1972)The key phrase was “…if he should get shot in the head by a police officer, or if he should hang himself in his jail cell, or if he's struck by a bolt of lightening …” Vito was letting Barzini and Tattaglia know that he had been playing the game of vengeance with far greater success than either of them for a much longer time, and that he would refuse to believe any claims of innocence in the event of the death of a second son. He was, in essence, leapfrogging the nonsense that would come along with the common practice of refusing obvious responsibility of a hit that is the standard modus operandi in the mafia. “…struck by a bolt of lightning…” was a metaphor, not unlike the crude, modern saying, “Don’t piss on my leg and tell me it’s raining.” Vito would have assumed guilt of Barzini and Tattaglia without discussion, had anything happened to Michael. Barzini tried to play that game anyway, as the attempt by Fabrizzio to off Michael that ended with the car bombing that killed Apollonia came after the meeting of the Five Families, so Barzini clearly felt himself equal to the task of clashing with Vito, had the opportunity arose. Barzini was wrong. Michael would, of course, take care of Barzini on his own after Vito’s passing and with Vito’s whole-hearted approval.
column9: Yes, it was a stronger way to say “you better not let anything happen, and if something does, even if it is not your fault, I’m coming to get you.” So you best make sure nothing happens.

column1: Adult If an adult son sends his grieving mother information about a bereavement support group after she lost her husband, should she thank him for it?
column3: In a normal situation, etiquette would say one should thank another person for any gesture meant with good will. However, a death is not necessarily a normal situation. Feelings are amplified all around and everyone is raw. Suggesting a bereavement group is not inappropriate, in my opinion; but it may be a suggestion that the bereaved might take offense to as too personal, or not be interested in. It might also be a suggestion she has heard three times already from friends concerned about her. I’m not sure whether the person asking is the adult son or the grieving widow. If the first, please let it go but continue to let your mother know you are there for her. Your mother has a great deal to think of right now, as do you, since you are both dealing with a loss. If you are the mother in question, it would be thoughtful to acknowledge your son’s concern for you. Remember that doing so does not commit you to attending the group if you don’t wish to. On a side note, everyone grieves and recovers differently. I attended a bereavement group after the death of a family member, and I found it made me feel much worse. I was better off grieving and coming to terms with things in private. We must all find our own path back to peace.
