column1: What did the Harry Potter movies get wrong that drives you insane?
column3: Ugh, where to start? I just re read the books and there are plenty things that the movies got wrong. Here are my four top pics.The labyrinth in the Triwizard TournamentThe Triwizard Tournament’s final test was way more interesting in the books. The labyrinth was designed to test the champion’s ability in battle as well as their intellectual skills. An example of the latter was Harry’s standoff with a sphinx-like creature that challenges Harry with a riddle.In the end, what happened in the movie happened in the book as well, but there were a few differences:The labyrinth itself is more dynamic and not just a boring maze of bushes.Cedric does not defeat Krum in battle. Rather, Harry surprises Krum using the Cruciatus curse on Cedric and quickly incapacitates him.Cedric is not dragged down by the maze’s roots and does not beg Harry to help him. That was pathetic. Book version: after their encounter with Krum, both Harry and Cedric are attacked by a huge spider. They manage to defeat it, but Harry is left incapacitated with a severe leg injury. The cup is just meters away from both of them at this moment.Harry and Cedric DO NOT race each other to the cup. They go on a heated exchange as to who is more deserving of the cup based on how much they helped each other. Despite the fact that Cedric seemed greatly tempted to take the cup for himself and that Harry was unable to stand on his own, Cedric steps farther and farther away from the cup while arguing with Harry. Once Harry proposes taking the cup together as Hogwarts champions, Cedric helps him get up and they go for it together. We know what happened next.My greatest discomfort here is that Cedric’s gentle and fair character is not at all shown in the movie. This is important, given that the guy was murdered 5 pages after this. By this point, book readers probably cared a lot more about Cedric than movie watchers did or at least held him in high regard, which made Cedric’s death a more uncomfortable moment in the book than in the movie. 2. The battle at the Department of Mysteries Oh dear god, I could write a whole book about it and I probably will. Book 5 was not the greatest, but the ending kicked ass. It featured one of the best action scenes in the entire saga, and the movies… well, blundered it.Here comes my long list of grievances:Lucius Malfoy and the Death Eaters are never, ever scared nor intimidated by Neville’s bravado. For Christ’s sake, we are talking about the cartels of the wizarding world. The movies did little to respect the Death Eaters.Rather than just chasing them through the prophecy corridor, the Death Eaters fight Harry and his friends across the utterly bizarre rooms in the Department of Mysteries in a series of cool action scenes. Slowly but surely, they incapacitate each and every one of Harry’s friends, with the exception of Neville. This is in stark contrast with the Death Eaters just suddenly appearing in the veil room and holding Harry’s friends captive. Boring.Bellatrix uses the Cruciatus curse on Neville to force Harry to give them the prophecy. Just as Harry is about to give it to Lucius, the Order arrives and engages the Death Eaters.. The prophecy is destroyed later in the battle.Lucius and Sirius never cross wands. I wouldn’t have an issue with this were it not for the fact that it seemed to replace Sirius’s duel with Bellatrix. Speaking of which…Bellatrix does not show up out of nowhere to cowardly deliver a killing curse to Sirius. She first incapacitates Tonks, then faces Sirius one-on-one in a fair fight and finishes him off.Speaking of which, Bellatrix does NOT kill Sirius with the killing curse. What actually killed Sirius was the fact that Bellatrix’s curse sent him flying through the mysterious veil. While we never get an explanation in the books, we can infer that this veil is a one-way portal to the world of the dead. Hence, crossing the veil is what killed Sirius.NOTE: Someone on the comments section mentioned that Rowling confirmed that the curse itself killed Sirius. I find this a bit confusing, because after Sirius was thrown beyond the veil, Harry was expecting him to return from the other side of the veil and continue his duel with Bellatrix. Why would he believe that if he had been hit with a deadly curse?Dumbledore shows up actually before Bellatrix killed Sirius. He helps the Order round up the Death Eaters and capture them.Bellatrix’s escape was not hassle-free after killing Sirius. Kingsley tried to stop her as well, but not even the experienced Auror was a match for her. This is when Harry snaps and decides to chase her on his own.It is worth mentioning that Dumbledore threw a curse at Bellatrix as she tried to flee…which she deflects.Ugh, here comes the worst part. When Harry does catch up with Bellatrix, he basically hides behind a statue to try and land a curse on her. After Bellatrix makes fun about killing Sirius, Harry loses it and successfully lands a Cruciatus curse on her. Rather than wimpering like a coward, the curse does little to Bellatrix, who quickly gets up and fights Harry again, much to the latter’s dismay.Brief pause. Sorry, but Bellatrix looking imploringly at Harry just infuriated me. Book readers… what do you think about Bellatrix being scared of Harry in the movie? It is insulting. Derogatory. Moving on…Harry kept hiding behind the statue, trying to catch Bellatrix off guard. Naturally, he failed miserably. Their “duel” is interrupted by the appearance of Voldemort, who of course does not encourage Harry to kill his best lieutenant. He barely speaks to Harry and moves in for the kill.This is when Dumbledore faces off against Voldemort. Dumbledore quickly moves a statue to protect Harry and instructs another one to trap Bellatrix during his duel with Voldemort.Dumbledore vs. Voldemort was more even. I got the feeling that in the movie Voldemort was superior. In the book, Dumbledore never loses his cool and Voldemort actually decides that this is a battle he cannot win and opts to escape.Here comes another horrible crime. Harry NEVER FUCKIN’ EVER tells Voldemort this “I feel sorry for you cuz you don’t feel love” crap. Voldemort does try to possess Harry in an effort to bring him immeasurable pain and have Dumbledore kill him out of mercy. However, Harry starts thinking about Sirius and these feelings of love are what “ejects” Voldemort from Harry’s body.There’s way more cool details that happened here that I missed. You may have noticed that I mentioned Bellatrix a lot. This is because I believe that was the main point of this scene: to introduce us to Bellatrix Lestrange.Movie watchers… did you really feel that Bellatrix was an overpowered witch? Did you think she was horribly cruel? Did you feel raw hate as the entire chapter unfolded? If you did, you felt it 10x less than book readers, trust me. After this scene, I was seething with rage. For one, I found her use of baby tones unbearable. Secondly, I was pissed off by how powerful she was and how she all but defeated the Order’s finest. On top of that, she had the gall to survive the encounter!Nah, this didn’t happen. What actually happened was that Neville got tortured by Bellatrix in front of Harry. “Give us the prophecy, Potter, or watch your friends die the hard way!” - Bellatrix Lestrange, after using Crucio on Neville. Bellatrix was way scarier than Voldemort. The movies did not make full use of Helena Bonham-Carter’s skills to accurately depict this unbearable villain. 3. Snape and Draco’s escape in the end of Book 6 I would not say the movie ruined this scene, but I did find it a bit more interesting in the book.Draco does not let in a half-dozen Death Eaters to Hogwarts… he lets in a whole battalion. A battle ensues between them and the Aurors patrolling the castle, as well as some students.Thankfully, Bellatrix was not present in this battle.Harry did not witness Dumbledore’s murder from below; he did so a few meters away, immobilized under his invisibility cloak. What he thought happened was that, while being disarmed by Draco, Dumbledore’s jinx hit him by accident. We can all infer that Dumbledore purposefully immobilized Harry so he would not interfere in his self-planned murder.As I mentioned, this was not a quiet thing. There was a huge battle going on in the Great Hall. Snape urged the Death Eaters to flee, as the job was already done.When the Death Eaters set fire to Hagrid’s place, he’s actually there. He bravely defends his home by literally tossing away the invaders.Harry vs Snape went more or less the same. It is slightly more meaningful in the books, as Harry consistently calls Snape a coward. We all know now Snape was anything but a coward. This kind of pisses Snape off, who finishes Harry off with a bit of Sectumsempra. That did the trick and Snape escaped.I do not have that much beef against how it was done in the movie. Rather, I was a bit surprised. Movie versions tend to make things a lot more visually attractive, and a full battalion of Death Eaters fighting Aurors and Order members in the Great Hall was a great opportunity for some epicness. My guess is that they did not want to “reuse” scenes. After all, in Book 7 we get the battle of Hogwarts in all its glory. It might have been less special for movie watchers to see our beloved Hogwarts under siege in movie 8 if you had already seen something similar in movie 6. 4. The final battle Ah, best for last. If something was horribly different in the movies it was the final confrontation between Harry and Voldemort. My list of grievances here is also long, so bear with me.The battle doesn’t restart with Harry “coming back to life” in front of everyone. The Death Eaters don’t find this so frightening that they decide to flee. Again, show some respect to these guys! The battle restarts with a classical deux machina moment, when all sorts of reinforcements appear out of nowhere to fight the Death Eaters, who are overwhelmed and have to retreat to the castle.Harry does NOT show himself at this moment. He uses the diversion to get up, hide himself with his cloak, and hex Death Eaters and protect people from Voldemort’s curses.The Death Eaters are quickly outnumbered and outgunned. Only two people remain fighting: Voldemort and Bellatrix. Voldemort fights McGonagall, Kingsley and Slughorn at the same time while Bellatrix fights Hermione, Ginny and Luna at once.Bellatrix does NOT FUCKING TURN TO CONFETTI when she dies! While I hated that it was Molly who killed her (wtf), the way she died was okay-ish. She gets killed while mocking her much less powerful foe, making fun of how she would kill her family after killing her. Molly’s spell hits Bellatrix straight on the chest, her lips still half-smiling. Guess who died in the exact same way? Sirius.Witnessing his best lieutenant get wacked infuriates Voldemort, who sends his three combatants flying away and tries to kill Molly. Harry blocks him and it is until this moment that he finally shows himself, in front of Voldemort and ALL remaining survivors in the middle of the Great Hall.And here comes the good stuff…The final battle between Harry and Voldemort in the books is… a conversation, really.Harry thoroughly explains Voldemort how he is wrong about everything, how Snape was never his man, how Dumbledore planned his own death to keep him from getting the Elder Wand.Harry calls him “Tom” the whole time, which greatly infuriates our narcissistic villain.Another curious thing that our hero attempted was to try and get Voldemort to feel some remorse, to repent. After all, during his visit at “King’s Cross”, he saw the part of Voldemort within him that died. He knew what would become of him and he was now certain he was going to kill him.More interestingly, Harry goes into a lot of detail as to why HE is the master of the Elder Wand and not Voldemort. In short, he kind of says: “Dear Tom, because of XY events, which led to Z, I am the master of the Elder Wand and not you. You should not attempt to kill me with it.”Voldy, being Voldy, completely snaps and throws an Avada Kedavra at Harry, while our hero counters with Expelliarmus.Lo and behold, Harry was right! The Elder Wand refused to kill his own master. Voldemort’s killing curse goes straight back to him, reminiscent of his very first encounter with Harry. With no horcruxes left this time, the killing curse hits Voldemort and kills him for good, the Elder Wand flying straight into Harry’s arms.When he dies… Voldemort DOES NOT TURN TO FUCKING CONFETTI! He becomes a rigid, stupid corpse.This is how it went in the books. Voldemort is killed by Harry in the Great Hall in front of everyone. He does NOT turn into confetti. So, movie version better? Perhaps visually. It is of course more epic to have a heated battle between the hero and the villain. However, this was not the point. Harry was never to be a match for Voldemort, man-on-man. Rather, it was Voldemort’s own arrogance that got the better of him. He was still arguably the most powerful wizard that ever existed. Having Harry fight him on equal terms in the movie was a bit insulting of Voldy’s capabilities. My deepest complaint here is the fact that both Voldemort and Bellatrix turn to stupid confetti when they died. WHY?! SERIOUSLY WHY?! Why am I so obsessed with this? Despite all his rhetoric and immortality efforts, in the end Voldemort was just a man who could die. Seeing his spread-eagled corpse was a sign for everyone witnessing the event that the great Lord Voldemort was unequivocally dead. Same goes for Bellatrix. There is a degree of humanization in seeing a rigid, lifeless corpse. It speaks of our fragility and inevitable mortality, something that not even Voldemort could escape from. It was very fucking important that everyone - students, Order members and Death Eaters - witnessed Voldemort’s demise and gazed at his probably ridiculous-looking corpse. Why the directors missed this is beyond me. Also, as mentioned by Gimi R in the comments section: there were no witnesses to Voldemort’s death in the movie, nor a corpse to show as proof. I find this very relevant. Imagine the following scenario: “Harry, you did kill Voldemort right?” “Yes, I owned the nose-less bastard.” “Great! So, where is his body? We did not see you actually kill him.” “Oh, his body disappeared. He turned into confetti.” “Umm…his body disappeared?” “Yes.” “Kinda like when he attacked you 17 years ago in Godric’s Hollow? When everyone else thought that he was dead despite not having a body to show as proof?” “Pretty much, yes.” It was important for people to witness the event and see his corpse to understand that Voldemort was really dead this time. It would have been the ultimate morale booster for the good guys and the final shock to demoralize the Death Eaters who worshipped him as a God.Ah yes, this is much better.That’s it! There are a lot more things worth mentioning. Other top contenders would be the character of Barty Crouch Jr, the aftermath of Sirius’s death at Dumbledore’s office and Harry’s subsequent grieving, the whole scene at Malfoy Manor... My main beef with these changes is that they altered the nature of the characters themselves, sometimes considerably. It is of course unrealistic to expect that the movie would be 100% true to the book… or even 50%. Adjustments had to be made, but you can make those while staying true to the characters’ natures and traits. Thank you for reading.
column9: Great points. I do prefer certain scenes in the films such as Harry's return with Cedric corpse as it's such a powerful and tragic moment. We never see Amos initial reaction to his sons death, we get to see it in the film amd it was brilliantly done.

column1: How can I get over the sudden death of my dad?
column3: This is a very big loss and one month is not enough time to grieve. It will take you quite a while to begin to heal. We don’t get over losing a close loved one. You will come to terms with it, at some point. Everyone grieves differently and no one can tell you to get over it. You will never get over it, but you will get on with life once again. Even though it seems insulting as hell that the world is still turning, you will get back on it and begin to live again. In the short term, for me, I couldn’t look at pictures or talk about memories. I had to deal with my losses in my own way, just as you will have to do. Whatever it takes for you to get through it, that’s your way of doing so. Don’t let it be with drinking though. Booze is actually a depressant and will make things worse. If you have your mom or another close family member to talk with, do it. Don’t isolate yourself. Everything you are feeling right now is normal. Your emotions will get to a better place. Get yourself a massage, listen to music, do whatever makes you happy. Sometimes we just want to give up when we’ve lost a loved one, but you can’t do it. I promise you, it’s okay to live again. Everyone has to do it. But for now, try to be kind to yourself, do things that distract you from thinking too much. You have barely come out of shock, if you even have, so you have a few months to go before the rawness of the pain begins to subside. You may hurt, but it’s because you love him so much. That love is never wasted. Don’t make any big decisions for at least a year. Many people make rash decisions after their parents pass away and some of them shouldn’t be made. you aren’t thinking clearly yet. Grieve in your own way, do what you have to do. For me, it’s been 27 years since my dad left. 33 for my mom. I still talk, out loud, to them. I believe they can still hear us. If you listen, you may even get a message or a visit from your dad. My sister passed last year and I’ve gotten many messages from her. It’s a real thing. You may start to notice things once your not completely consumed with your grief. What helped me through the loss of my sister, (my baby sister, ugh.), is, I made a memorial garden for her. Being able to physically do something about it, helped me a lot. I’m a pro-active person and being at a loss is not good. So, I put in the memorial garden with a small fountain, flowers, angels, lights, and signs. It’s lovely. You could do something in your dad’s memory also if you feel like you need to be doing something. Your dad wants you to be happy and to continue with your life. It’s what I would want for my son when I pass. I know the path you are walking and I know you are in pain, but in time, you will once again be able to speak about your dad and all of your memories. For now, stay busy. When we are busy time goes quicker and time heals some of the pain. You have my very deepest sympathy for the loss of your dad. Hang in there, my friend.

column1: What is the truth behind the death of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose? How did he disappear? What was the political scenario at the time of his death?
column3: Netaji Subash Chandra Bose’s death is still shrouded in mystery. But the various conspiracy theories about it make it even more mysterious. While recently the news about Gumnami Baba, a revered saint of Faizabad, Uttar Pradesh, who was believed to be Bose himself, came to the fore, we never cease to imagine how the great man must have spent his last moments on earth. Here is a look back at some of the most intriguing conspiracy theories: At 2 pm on August 17, 1945, a Mitsubishi Ki-21 heavy bomber took off from Saigon airport. Inside the aircraft were 13 people, including Lt Gen Tsunamasa Shidei of the Imperial Japanese Army, Col Habibur Rahman of the Indian National Army and one man who sat in a seat a little behind the portside wing – Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose. After an overnight halt in Vietnam, on August 18, the plane arrived to refuel in Taihoku, Formosa (now Taipei, Taiwan). Moments after the flight took off again, passengers heard a loud ‘bang’. Ground crew saw the portside engine fall off, and the plane crashed. The pilots and Lt Gen Shidei were killed instantly, Col Rahman fell unconscious. Bose survived, but his gasoline-soaked clothes ignited, turning him into a human torch.The Mitsubishi Ki-21 twin-engine heavy bomber that Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose and Col Habibur Rahman boarded at Saigon airport around 2 PM on 17 August 1945. A few hours later, in coma in a hospital, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose passed away. This is the established account of how one of India’s most famous freedom fighters died. But is it true? “There were no official reports released by the Governments of India or Britain,” historian Leonard Gordon says, “Even members of India’s Interim Government in 1946 waffled on the matter. Bose had disappeared several times earlier in his life; so rumours began again in 1945 and a powerful myth grew.” What you will read next is a saga of secrets, political vendetta, outrageous claims, half-truths and full rumours that strive to prove that Netaji did not die on that fateful day in Taiwan. No dead body In the immediate aftermath, an intriguing, and perhaps damning fact emerged: Netaji’s other lieutenants, who were to follow him on another flight, never saw his body. No one took photographs of Bose’s injuries, or his body, nor was a death certificate issued.Netaji with Mahatma Gandhi. As news reached India, senior INA officer JR Bhonsle rejected the news. Mahatma Gandhi said, “Subhas is not dead. He is still alive and biding his time somewhere.” Soon, rumours began doing the rounds that Bose was either in Soviet-held Manchuria, a prisoner of the Soviet Army, or had gone into hiding in Russia. Lakshmi Swaminathan, of the INA’s Jhansi Regiment, said in 1946 she thought Bose was in China. The Sadhu story In the 1950s, there emerged stories that Netaji had become a sadhu. And, the most elaborate of these took shape a decade later. Some of Netaji’s old associates formed the ‘Subhasbadi Janata’, and claimed Bose was now the chief sadhu in an ashram in Shoulmari in North Bengal. Through well-crafted newspapers and magazines, the organisation was able to, quite convincingly, recreate Bose’s post-war activities. According to the ‘Subhasbadis’, Bose returned to India after the war, became a sadhu, attended Gandhi’s funeral unseen in 1948, lived in a temple in Bareilly in the late 1950s, before finally settling in Shoulmari as Srimat Saradanandaji in 1959. Other versions, too, began gathering credence. Bose remained either in Maoist China or the Soviet Union. He attended Jawaharlal Nehru’s cremation in 1964, of which there appeared to even be photographic evidence.There were claims that Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev told an interpreter in Delhi that the Soviet Union could produce Bose in 45 days if India so desired. The Soviet Connection and a Conspiracy After independence, Nehru took the Foreign Affairs portfolio himself and appointed Vijayalekshmi Pandit as the ambassador to Russia. After her term ended, Dr S. Radhakrishnan took her place. There are reports that Dr Saroj Das, of Calcutta University, told his friend Dr RC Muzumdar that Dr Radhakrishnan had told him that Bose was in Russia.Hindustan Times news report, Nov 17, 1970. In another report, former Indian ambassador Dr Satyanarayana Sinha met CPI founder Abani Mukherjee’s son Georgey, who said his father and Netaji were imprisoned in adjacent cells in Siberia. In 1995, a team from Calcutta’s Asiatic Society, researching Indo-Soviet ties in Moscow, found a bunch of declassified files that hinted at Bose having been in the USSR after 1945. Dr Purobi Roy, a member of the team of scholars, said she found a document stamped “most secret”, dated 1946, in the military archives of Paddolosk, near Moscow, which mentioned Stalin and Molotov discussing Bose’s plans — whether he would remain in the USSR or leave. Dr Roy also said she found a KGB report in Bombay from 1946, which said, “it is not possible to work with Nehru or Gandhi, we have to use Subhas Bose”. This implies Bose was still alive in 1946.This photograph allegedly shows water room-heaters behind Netaji. These heaters were in use only in the USSR at the time. Gumnami Baba, aka ‘Bhagwanji’ Of all this, the most enduring legend is of a sadhu in Faizabad whom the locals called Gumnami Baba, who went by the name Bhagwanji. Bhagwanji, they say, was a monk who lived in Uttar Pradesh – Lucknow, Faizabad, Sitapur, Basti and Ayodhya – for more than 30 years till his death on September 16, 1985. He maintained contact with Dr Pavitra Mohan Roy, the former top Secret Service agent of the INA. However, more than his life, what Bhagwanji left behind after his death seems to confirm that the sadhu and Bose were one and the same: Gold-rimmed spectacles identical to what Netaji was always pictured wearing, powerful German binoculars, a colour photograph of Swami Vivekananda, Bengali books, the original copy of the summons issued to Suresh Chandra Bose to appear before the Khosla Commission, a map of undivided India, an album containing family photographs of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose.Left: Netaji’s handwriting. Right: Bhagwanji’s handwriting. Forensic expert Dr B Lal told the Mukherjee Commission that both handwritings matched. Other items recovered included a torch pencil generally used in map-making by military personnel, newspaper clippings about Netaji’s ‘death’ probe, letters from Netaji’s followers. One of the more intriguing finds was a letter from a person who accompanied the Khosla Commission to Taiwan, which reads: “We got only 15 days in Taihoku (Taipei). Formosa’s (Taiwan) task is over… I cannot write everything in this letter, if you permit, I can come over for a week.” Photographs found among Bhagwanji’s belongings indicate he celebrated his birthday on January 23. There was no plane crashClipping from a Japanese newspaper, published on August 23, 1945, reporting the death of Bose and General Tsunamasa Shidei. Netaji could not have died in a plane crash because no aviation accident occurred in Taipei on August 18, 1945. In 2005, the BBC reported that not only did the Taiwanese government reject the Bose-died-in-a-plane-crash-in-Taipei story, it also denied any plane crashes occurred between August 14 and September 20 that year. Stalin killed Netaji Most recently, the BJP’s Subramanian Swamy has alleged that Bose did not actually die in a plane crash in 1945, but was killed by Soviet dictator Josef Stalin in 1953. “According to the papers that exist with us, Bose had faked his death and escaped to Manchuria in China which was under Russian occupation, hoping Russia would look after him. But Stalin put him in a jail in Siberia. Somewhere around 1953, he hanged or suffocated Bose to death,” said Swamy, demanding that the Netaji files be declassified. However, he conceded, “Declassification of Netaji documents in haste and without judging the consequences would be difficult. India’s relations with Britain and Russia may be affected. “But I will persuade the Prime Minister to disclose the documents.” Inquiries and Commissions The Figgess Report of 1946, the first official probe into Bose’s death, said: “As a result of a series of interrogations of individuals named in the following paragraphs it is confirmed as certain that S.C. Bose died in a Taihoku Military Hospital (Nammon Ward) sometime between 1700 hours and 2000 hours local time on the August 18, 1945. The cause of death was heart failure resulting from multiple burns and shock.” In sum, the Figgess Report confirms: 1. The crash near Taihoku airport on August 18, 1945, in which Subhas Chandra Bose was a passenger 2. Bose’s death in a nearby military hospital on the same day 3. Bose’s cremation in Taihoku 4. Transfer of Bose’s ashes to Tokyo The Shah Nawaz Committee of 1956 was India’s first inquiry, comprising three people – Member of Parliament Shah Nawaz Khan, West Bengal government-nominated ICS officer SN Maitra, and Suresh Chandra Bose, Bose’s elder brother. The committee interviewed 67 witnesses in India, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, including the ‘survivors’ of the plane crash. Most importantly, it interviewed Colonel Habibur Rahman, Bose’s companion on the flight. Based on these testimonies, Khan and Maitra concluded Bose had died in a plane crash in Taipei. The committee’s third member, Netaji’s brother, however, disputed the report, claiming Jawaharlal Nehru orchestrated the inquiry to infer death by plane crash.Hindustan Times news report, Jan 21, 1971. 14 years later, the Government of India sanctioned another inquiry, this time by a one-man team – the Khosla Commission of 1970. Deposing before the Khosla Commission, Dr Satyanarayan Sinha had said Colonel Habibur Rehman had confessed to him in 1946 that he lied about Bose dying in a plane crash. However, the commission chose to concur with the two preceding inquiries into Bose’s death. More than 25 years later, yet another Government of India enquiry was constituted — this time, however, by a BJP-led government. In 1999, the Mukherjee Commission, led by retired Supreme Court judge MK Mukherjee, began his exhaustive probe into the Bose mystery. In 2005, after perusing hundreds of documents, taking oral testimonies, and visits to Japan, Russia and Taiwan, the commission reported that the Japanese and the USSR made a secret plan to grant Bose safe passage into the USSR. The commission also said that the ashes kept at Renkoji Temple, believed to be Bose’s, actually were of a Japanese soldier who died of a heart attack.

column1: What causes mental illness?
column3: Imagine someone falls down the stairs, and breaks both their legs. What now? We tell them to move on with their lives? To just keep going? That walking is not so complicated, that it just needs to be done one leg at a time? We ignore their screams of agony, belittle them, talk to them about not giving up? If their legs are stuck at weird angles, is that really going to help?What about if someone loses a friend or close family member, or something like that? Do we recognize that there has been a potentially traumatic experience? If there is pain, do we do a more thorough check, to see if there is a bigger injury? Do we recognize trauma when it is still fresh, provide appropriate care, and allow people to take time off to heal from injuries?Or what if someone is constantly getting sick. All people in a certain family and area are constantly getting sick. The thing they have in common is they all have lead based paint in their house. And we know lead is toxic. What do we do? Give them a 45 min counseling session once a week, and some meds to mask the symptoms?Or if someone is in a constantly stressful environment, and gets sick, and many people in that environment constantly get sick, and we know that stress is toxic, do we take measures to mitigate the stress factors? Try to make sure that people live in healthy and clean environments, free from toxins and pathogens? From early childhood on, not from when they are old enough to figure out themselves that they might have issues?Do people have a regular check-up once a year? To try and catch things before they progress too far?We really don’t do much about mental illness tbh. It’s kind of treated as an act of god, something that just happens, without any relation to anything else. We know it’s happening more and more, but we don’t look into what might cause it, apart from trying to identify if it has a genetic component. We are not really looking for a solution, it’s not like finding the gene gives us a way to change anything, it’s a scapegoat, something to blame. Selling self-help books is great, selling pills and drugs and anti-depressants and booze and anti-anxiety meds and so on are all lucrative. And the stuff that stresses people out are also money money out of it. Since both creating the problem and helping people deal with it create avenues for profit, trying to change things to not have the problem at all would be upsetting for a lot of people.

column1: What is it like to undergo depression? How does it feel? How does one deal with it? How important is it to be patient when dealing with depression?
column3: I never wanted to answer this but seeing too many queries regarding this, so I had to. Also many people claim they are in depression but some are real and some are just sympathy stunts. I will tell you about the real depression how it looks like as I have seen it everyday for 6 years. I am not a mental health expert. I realized anybody literally anybody can go into such states. It’s very very difficult to tell how you get into such state of mind and much more difficult to treat. Some relate it to hormones, some to situations but the exact reason will always be unknown. Depression can have many forms but I will tell you what I have seen very closely. Let me tell you how you go into depression and what depression is:You face some loss either in your business or you are very stressed in your job or something else.You are unable to sleep, you are anxious now about your sleep as well.You start taking sleeping pills, deterioration starts here, a point comes when even sleeping pills don’t work, you had hidden that from your family but now you have no option but to take help.You start seeking help from your relatives, they don’t take you seriously, mock at you because even they haven’t seen such things. They take it lightly.You start feeling more depressed, your state of mind worsens.You feel you are not performing according to your expectations or things haven’t worked out as you planned, you consider yourself as a failure.Shit starts getting serious, people try to console you, make you happy, it’s all blurry, you hear nothing, you are in your own state of mind, you cannot even express where you are, depressive thoughts goes on and on, you have no control over them.Fear of future is the dominating thought, you are just stuck, stuck at your failures, again and again saying sorry by saying “I was a complete failure, please forgive me, please take care of your mother”, you have forgotten all your abilities.Your relatives/friends might have said something in the past in a taunting manner and you took it personally (It’s pretty obvious, who likes to listen to taunts, no one). Your thoughts are again and again taking you to those crossed roads.You are just walking, thinking something, murmuring something, when asked about your murmurs, you just stare and that stare is sometimes frightening for others. You cannot sit, you feel extremely anxious, you just cannot eat properly.You wanna commit suicide but thoughts about your family after you, are not even allowing that. Still you say I am going to commit suicide, you open the door, your family tries to prevent you but your strength is too much that even 2–3 people combined cannot stop you (There I realized Mind is very very powerful). You go to terrace and come back after sometime.Nothing inspires you, you don’t feel good in anything and you are uncontrollable, uncomfortable. Sometimes you even try to hurt yourself by taking a stance as if you are running a 100 m race, you run and bang your head with a wall, on top of that you laugh after getting hit.You family members consult a Doctor, the doctor prescribes you some medicine then you just sleep, when you wake up, your family offers you something to eat, your family is terrified about your next step, they just want you to eat and sleep again. You somehow forcefully eat, take medicine, sleep again and the cycle continues.One of your family member is extremely terrified seeing your present situation, stress and anxiety of that family member will cause him/her a health complexion in future. This is bound to happen.You remember nothing except for the hurting past. You forget your goals, you tend to forget everything except that fucking past.You are sometimes referred to as mental, you are suggested to go to a mental hospital. This doesn’t affect you much as you are in a different world but it certainly lowers the morale of your family members.Your family members keep on changing doctors, you show some improvement every time, but the sudden panic attack destroys everything.Slowly and gradually your family members start losing hope.Your family refrain from going outside, they try to cut themselves from the social world afraid of suggestions and unnecessary questions.Your financial situation, mental condition with physical health everything worsens. The family is broken, everything starts falling apart. Your presence feels nothing to your family members, you cry, your family cries too but secretly.Good doctors say exercising is the only solution to recover completely from depression, but you are not even present in this world, how will you exercise, but you and your family has to make you do it somehow.If you are lucky, your family members’ consistent efforts somehow finds a good Doctor, your treatment changes, you show a positive change. Some stars align and you start improving slowly and gradually.You yourself show some positivity, you yourself try exercising, you yourself are eager to go out of this loop, to stop medicines completely. You are now on the right path.You try making new friends who don’t know much about your past, they try making you cheerful, some of your old friends try to remind you of your past abilities. Now the real recovery starts.You need this much patience and you need to keep even a slightest of the hope to revive a depression patient. It’s really hard, easier said than done, for many it becomes an infinite loop, only a few are able to come out of it, but when they come out of it, it is worth it. Depression is a disease where a patient suffers unconsciously and his/her family members suffer consciously. The only thing that is common is suffering. THE D-PAIN.

column1: Is internet addiction considered as mental disorder?
column3: Not exclusively and not generally. However, addiction, whatever the subject, has the capacity to generate into a disorder. Life makes many demands of us. We are functioning members of a family unit and the varied roles that that implies; we are students or workers and these too create demands. Addiction is such that it corrupts all of those relationships. It demands constant attention - doesn't take 'no' for an answer. Ultimately it takes over the self - the addict is the addiction and the addiction the addict. This is the point at which a mental disorder will mutate. One major concern about the cyber world is that the line between that and the 'real' world become blurred. Sadly, there are those that lose the capacity to separate and function in an confused state. Internet addiction is anti-social. It cuts the addict off from the 'real' world and real people. It offers an artificial and contrived escape from the (sometimes) mundane everyday life. As with others things, a little now and again is a welcome relief. The warning signs include a feeling of compulsion to log-on. I turned mine off for a couple of days last week - other demands. My world didn't crash.

column1: What does it feel like to have your sibling die?
column3: Note: As always with these particularly personal posts, I am in two minds about whether I should post it. The side of me that grew up always providing a calm, smooth façade finds spilling feelings deeply uncomfortable - the emotional version of puking all over everyone's nice clean shoes. Yet I am on Quora to learn, and with learning comes change and growth, and none of that can be achieved without a degree of openness. So be it. Having a sibling die feels like someone or something came with a hammer and chisel and with one blow, fractured your family into hundreds of pieces. I was just a toddler when my brother died. Old enough to love him, young enough to not have anywhere near enough memories to sustain me. Mama and Daddy married young. They kind of got forced into it by her parents. They had some issues right from the start, but they stayed together for a while and had my brothers - Anthony when Mama was 21, and Michael when she was 22. Over the next few years the marriage broke down, though they tried. When the boys were maybe 8 and 9, they separated and Daddy and the boys moved out. They didn't divorce, but they dated other people. When the boys were in their late teens, Mama became friends with my biological father - my Papa - and became pregnant with me. She was fond of my Papa, but she still loved her husband, and somehow when he found out she was pregnant he realised he loved her too, and they reconciled. They were a comfy family again. Two parents who loved each other, two teenage boys - Tony the golden child and Micky the lively hellion - who were equally adored. And one baby girl, sort of a cuckoo in the nest, who was loved nonetheless. Micky loved to party. He had a wild streak in him. Nothing terrible, but he liked that bit of danger. One night he came home from a party sort of drunk and woozy, but nothing to set off alarms. He said goodnight, and went to bed. Nobody ever saw him alive again. The cause of death was listed as asphyxiation due to aspiration of stomach contents. The story we got, which was pieced together from accounts of friends in addition to the coroner's report, was that some of the boys had found some pills in the medicine cabinet of the house they were partying in. I'm not sure exactly what, but some sort of sedative. Because they were eighteen, and wild, and really fucking stupid, they thought they'd down the lot and see what happened. They also drank a lot of beer. All the kids went home to their respective houses and slept it off. All of them were fine, except my brother. My brother got sick from the beer while he was unconscious from the pills, and choked to death. Well, shit, it was good enough for Jimi Hendrix. My family broke that day. Families always do when they bury a child. If they're otherwise healthy units, filled with generally healthy people, they manage to put themselves back together. The cracks are always there, but they manage to hold together, even when they're missing a piece. My family didn't. Couldn't. Their marriage had been shaky pretty much since they got married - yes, they loved each other, but love alone is not enough. Daddy was from the tail end of the Silent Generation, from a family who were hardworking and stoic and rarely showed their pain - or their affection. Mama had abandonment issues from her awful childhood, bipolar disorder, and borderline personality disorder. Add the loss of a child into that, and we never had a chance. Mama needed affection, reassurance, someone to grieve with her. When she didn't get those things, she collapsed emotionally. Daddy turned to stone, and the more she clung, the more he withdrew. The day Mama tried to kill herself has always been one of my most crystal-clear memories, even though I can't have been more than two and a half. I remember the clothes she was wearing, the tropical fruit squash and raisin biscuits Daddy gave me to keep me quiet when Mama disappeared, the poem in the children's book I was reading. I remember the frost under my feet as I wandered over the frozen grass outside, and the way she looked when I found her, and Daddy screaming as he came up behind me into the shed. I'd never heard him scream before, or since. Never heard him express any real emotion, honestly. I guess she went to hospital then. I don't remember that bit. By summer, everyone was saying she was better. You could tell that she wasn't really, but she smiled, and wore bright clothes, and that was good enough. When she decided to move the two of us abroad, everyone said it would be good to have a fresh start. They patted my head, said, "Be a good girl and look after mommy," and waved us off. And so I became my mother's carer at age three. We had a few good years in Spain, where I was genuinely happy, and she seemed mostly peaceful. We probably shouldn't have returned to England, but by the time I was five I was showing promise as a gifted child and needed more intensive schooling than I could get on a small island, and my Papa had just married and wanted to see more of me, so back we came. I've spent a lifetime being good and taking care of people - first my mom, and then everyone around me. It's a combination of guilt and fear, I think. Fear because her first self-harming wasn't her last, only her most dramatic, and I grew up all too aware that I was often the only thing standing between life and death for her. Guilt because in my child's mind, I was to blame. I was born, and my brother died. As an adult - even as a teenager - my rational mind recognises that those two things are not connected. My gut still hasn't got the message. Tony and I have never been close. He liked me well enough as a small child, and then started to dislike me when I began to approach my late teens. I think I reminded him too much of Micky at that point. We had a few really bad years, where he blamed me - out loud - for everything from his relationship breakups to my own poor health. By the time I reached my mid-twenties, things were a little better. He's married now, with three step kids, and it's mellowed him a bit. Sometimes he actually seems pleased to see me, which always surprises me. I know Tony loves me. He probably always loved me, even when he hated me. I also know that if some higher power gave him the choice, he'd trade me for Micky in a nanosecond. Mama had a lot of bad years, though she's strengthened with age. My teenage years were particularly difficult - I've written a little about that before, in another post - and my twenties were no picnic, but in the last year or two she's actually begun to loosen her grip on me and encourage me to have a life. In the last twelve months I've taken not one but TWO solo vacations, after not having a vacation in fifteen years. I'm trying to cultivate hobbies and a social life, although it's slow going after so many years of saying no to everything. I've been a recluse for the last decade, and it's not easy to break out of that pattern, but I'll get there. Daddy maintained a good relationship with Tony, and he met a new partner when I was about fifteen. Like Tony, he found me harder and harder to face as I got closer to the age Micky was when he died. He never could face Mama, and we only saw him occasionally, usually at Christmas, or at my niece and nephews' birthday parties. I don't think he ever told me he loved me, but I know he had some affection for me - he built me a few computers when I was in high school, made sure I had internet access (Mama has never even turned on a computer), taught me how to make decent coffee, and bought me jewellery for birthdays and Christmas - pieces that suited my personality, that he'd clearly put some thought into. Daddy died in June of this year. He'd found out he was terminal in summer of 2014, although the doctors expected him to have another five years or so. I found out he was sick by accident, from my niece - Mama and I weren't supposed to know. I was mad about that for a long time. It wasn't a nice feeling to know that the whole family, and several of my niece's friends - people who'd never even met Daddy - were allowed to know, and Mama and I weren't. We didn't get to see him during the eleven months he lived after his diagnosis. I was pretty mad about that too, though not mad enough to force myself on a dying man against his wishes, even if he was my father. At the wake, they showed a montage of photos, the majority of which were from his later life with his partner Margaret. Pictures of him and Margaret, pictures of him with friends, pictures of him with Tony's family. Having barbecues. Swimming. Holding my niece's baby. The thing that shocked me was that he looked so happy. I had never seen him happy. I guess he just couldn't be happy around me. We had him cremated, and after a long legal kerfuffle, Tony got permission to bury his ashes in Micky's grave. It was what he wanted, and in some strange way it feels like the only thing to do. Part of Daddy died the day we buried my brother, and now the rest of him is there too. Tony will be okay. He has a good marriage and a good relationship with his step kids. We see him and his family occasionally, mostly for Mama's sake, although I imagine that when Mama's gone I'll stop. Mama, as I said, has grown mentally and emotionally stronger with age, even as her physical state gets weaker by the day. Her bipolar and borderline conditions have eased as she's gotten older, and she's considerably more functional than she was in my younger years, though she's always happiest when you leave her alone with her books and her garden. I don't know how many years she has left, but I imagine we'll remain close for the rest of them. And me? I take care of Mama, and the house, and try to save the world in my spare time. I laugh about it, call it my Catcher-in-the-Rye complex, though for the most part I seem to stay more upbeat than poor Holden Caulfield. And I write. Mama was blessed with a sort of selective amnesia about painful issues in the past. She doesn't remember anything about her suicide attempts, only that she was "sad" after Micky's death. Tony was away at uni at the time, and with Daddy gone, I think I'm probably the only person who remembers what happened during that winter. I write about it so that it doesn't fade; so I never have a day when I wake up and wonder if I imagined it all. I haven't quite worked out whether it's better to remember or to forget, but until I do, I'm keeping my options open. Some families manage to put themselves back together after losing a member. We never could. We were a shattered mirror, and in trying to keep us together, we only managed to cut all of us to pieces on the edges of the cracks. Maybe we can stop doing that now.

The COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted or halted critical mental health services in 93% of countries worldwide while COVID-19 affecting mental health demand for mental health is increasing, according to a new WHO survey. The survey of 130 countries provides COVID-19 affecting mental health first global data showing COVID-19 affecting mental health devastating impact of COVID-19 on access to mental health services and underscores COVID-19 affecting mental health urgent need for increased funding. The survey was published ahead of WHO’s Big Event for Mental Health ̶ a global online advocacy event on 10 October that will bring together world leaders, celebrities, and advocates to call for increased mental health investments in COVID-19 affecting mental health wake of COVID-19. WHO has previously highlighted COVID-19 affecting mental health chronic underfunding of mental health: prior to COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic, countries were spending less than 2 per cent of their national health budgets on mental health, and struggling to meet their populations’ needs. And COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic is increasing demand for mental health services. Bereavement, isolation, loss of income and fear are triggering mental health conditions or exacerbating existing ones. Many people may be facing increased levels of alcohol and drug use, insomnia, and anxiety. Meanwhile, COVID-19 itself can lead to neurological and mental complications, such as delirium, agitation, and stroke. People with pre-existing mental, neurological or substance use disorders are also more vulnerable to SARS-CoV-2 infection ̶ they may stand a higher risk of severe outcomes and even death. “Good mental health is absolutely fundamental to overall health and well-being,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of COVID-19 affecting mental health World Health Organization. “COVID-19 has interrupted essential mental health services around COVID-19 affecting mental health world just when they’re needed most. World leaders must move fast and decisively to invest more in life-saving mental health programmes ̶ during COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic and beyond.” Survey finds major disruptions to critical mental health services The survey was conducted from June to August 2020 among 130 countries across WHO’s six regions. It evaluates how COVID-19 affecting mental health provision of mental, neurological and substance use services has changed due to COVID-19, COVID-19 affecting mental health types of services that have been disrupted, and how countries are adapting to overcome these challenges. Countries reported widespread disruption of many kinds of critical mental health services: Over 60% reported disruptions to mental health services for vulnerable people, including children and adolescents (72%), older adults (70%), and women requiring antenatal or postnatal services (61%). 67% saw disruptions to counseling and psychotherapy; 65% to critical harm reduction services; and 45% to opioid agonist maintenance treatment for opioid dependence. More than a third (35%) reported disruptions to emergency interventions, including those for people experiencing prolonged seizures; severe substance use withdrawal syndromes; and delirium, often a sign of a serious underlying medical condition. 30% reported disruptions to access for medications for mental, neurological and substance use disorders. Around three-quarters reported at least partial disruptions to school and workplace mental health services (78% and 75% respectively). While many countries (70%) have adopted telemedicine or teletherapy to overcome disruptions to in-person services, there are significant disparities in COVID-19 affecting mental health uptake of these interventions. More than 80% of high-income countries reported deploying telemedicine and teletherapy to bridge gaps in mental health, compared with less than 50% of low-income countries. WHO has issued guidance to countries on how to maintain essential services ̶ including mental health services ̶ during COVID-19 and recommends that countries allocate resources to mental health as an integral component of their response and recovery plans. The Organization also urges countries to monitor changes and disruptions in services so that they can address them as required. Although 89% of countries reported in COVID-19 affecting mental health survey that mental health and psychosocial support is part of their national COVID-19 response plans, only 17% of these countries have full additional funding for covering these activities. This all highlights COVID-19 affecting mental health need for more money for mental health. As COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic continues, even greater demand will be placed on national and international mental health programmes that have suffered from years of chronic underfunding. Spending 2% of national health budgets on mental health is not enough. International funders also need to do more: mental health still receives less than 1% of international aid earmarked for health. Those who do invest in mental health will reap rewards. Pre-COVID-19 estimates reveal that nearly US$ 1 trillion in economic productivity is lost annually from depression and anxiety alone. However, studies show that every US$ 1 spent on evidence-based care for depression and anxiety returns US$5. Note on World Mental Health Day: Mobilizing COVID-19 affecting mental health global community to #MoveforMentalHeatlh On World Mental Health Day (Saturday 10 October), as part of its campaign Move for mental health: let’s invest, WHO is inviting COVID-19 affecting mental health global community to take part in The Big Event for Mental Health, an unprecedented online advocacy event that will call for increased investment in mental health at all levels ̶ from individuals to businesses to countries to civil society ̶ so that COVID-19 affecting mental health world can begin to close COVID-19 affecting mental health gaps highlighted by today’s report. The Big Event is free and open to COVID-19 affecting mental health public and will be broadcast on 10 October from 16:00 to 19:00 CEST on WHO’s YouTube, Facebook, Twitter, TikTok and LinkedIn channels and website. For updated information about COVID-19 affecting mental health Big Event for Mental Health, including COVID-19 affecting mental health latest lineup of performances and participants, visit COVID-19 affecting mental health Big Event web page. To learn more about World Mental Health Day, visit WHO’s campaign page. As COVID-19 affecting mental health coronavirus pandemic rapidly sweeps across COVID-19 affecting mental health world, it is inducing a considerable degree of fear, worry and concern in COVID-19 affecting mental health population at large and among certain groups in particular, such as older adults, care providers and people with underlying health conditions. In public mental health terms, COVID-19 affecting mental health main psychological impact to date is elevated rates of stress or anxiety. But as new measures and impacts are introduced – especially quarantine and its effects on many people’s usual activities, routines or livelihoods – levels of loneliness, depression, harmful alcohol and drug use, and self-harm or suicidal behaviour are also expected to rise. In populations already heavily affected, such as Lombardy in Italy, issues of service access and continuity for people with developing or existing mental health conditions are also now a major concern, along with COVID-19 affecting mental health mental health and well-being of frontline workers. As part of its public health response, WHO has worked with partners to develop a set of new materials on COVID-19 affecting mental health mental health and psychosocial support aspects of COVID-19.The COVID-19 pandemic and COVID-19 affecting mental health resulting economic recession have negatively affected many people’s mental health and created new barriers for people already suffering from mental illness and substance use disorders. During COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic, about 4 in 10 adults in COVID-19 affecting mental health U.S. have reported symptoms of anxiety or depressive disorder, a share that has been largely consistent, up from one in ten adults who reported these symptoms from January to June 2019 (Figure 1). A KFF Health Tracking Poll from July 2020 also found that many adults are reporting specific negative impacts on their mental health and well-being, such as difficulty sleeping (36%) or eating (32%), increases in alcohol consumption or substance use (12%), and worsening chronic conditions (12%), due to worry and stress over COVID-19 affecting mental health coronavirus. This brief explores mental health and substance use during, and prior to, COVID-19 affecting mental health COVID-19 pandemic. It focuses on populations that were particularly at risk for experiencing negative mental health or substance abuse consequences during COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic, including young adults, people experiencing job loss, parents and children, communities of color, and essential workers. We draw on KFF analysis of data from COVID-19 affecting mental health Census Bureau’s Household Pulse Survey (an ongoing survey created to capture data on health and economic impacts of COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic), KFF Health Tracking Poll data, and data on mental health prior to COVID-19 affecting mental health COVID-19 pandemic. Key takeaways include: Young adults have experienced a number of pandemic-related consequences, such as closures of universities and loss of income, that may contribute to poor mental health. During COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic, adults in households with job loss or lower incomes report higher rates of symptoms of mental illness than those without job or income loss (53% vs. 32%). Non-Hispanic Black adults (48%) and Hispanic or Latino adults (46%) are more likely to report symptoms of anxiety and/or depressive disorder than Non-Hispanic White adults (41%). Historically, these communities of color have faced challenges accessing mental health care. Compared to nonessential workers, essential workers are more likely to report symptoms of anxiety or depressive disorder (42% vs. 30%), starting or increasing substance use (25% vs. 11%), and suicidal thoughts (22% vs. 8%) during COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic. Prevalence of Mental Illness and Substance Use Disorder During COVID-19 affecting mental health Pandemic During COVID-19 affecting mental health COVID-19 pandemic, concerns about mental health and substance use have grown, including concerns about suicidal ideation. Suicide rates have long been on COVID-19 affecting mental health rise and may worsen due to COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic. Early 2020 data show that drug overdose deaths were particularly pronounced from March to May 2020, coinciding with COVID-19 affecting mental health start of pandemic-related http://lockdowns.As was COVID-19 affecting mental health case prior to COVID-19 affecting mental health pandemic, adults in poor general health (which may reflect both physical and mental health) continue to report higher rates of anxiety and/or depression than adults in good general health.1,2 For people with chronic illness in particular, COVID-19 affecting mental health already high likelihood of having a concurrent mental health disorder may be exacerbated by their vulnerability to severe illness from COVID-19. column1: How should someone handle living with a narcissist, especially if it is a family member?
column3: While the word narcissism has become a popular term in the wider public, NPD is a mental illness. It is hard to handle and almost impossible without receiving personal damage. Some of the reasons are that:Everyone in the close social circle is affected, not just the narcissist - especially if the narcissist is a parent or spouse.Within the wider family circle, any relatives or close friends who are in contact with the narcissist are oblivious to the problem, tricked by the narcissist, support him/her, and also hinder them from going to the doctor. These people are unofficially called "the flying monkeys" of the narcissistNPD is hardly treatable.The narcissist does not think they are ill.The narcissist will avoid going to the doctor. Instead they crazy-make others.The narcissist will continuously make the positive actions and contribution of others disappear by not talking about them, while at the same time he/she projects their own problems to them. They will turn every interaction with others into a personal matter, and then blame them for it. The results of such behaviour include thatThe people around live in emotional turmoil and lose the ability to concentrate.They lose their roles in interaction with others.They start arguing with one another.Eventually they all get worn out and break down, and usually develop some illness: depression, PTSD, a personality disorder (such as becoming co-dependents / co-narcissists), a mental illness such as schizophrenia or bipolar disorder, or something similar. They may also start doing alcohol or substance abuse. Some of the best ways to handle a narcissistReport the problem immediately to the local police station: Even if they may not do something about it, it is better if they are aware in advance. Don't wait for the next argument to find an excuse.Cut contact: become as independent as possible - financially, socially etc. - and leave that environment immediately and cut all ties.Take legal action: keep records of things happening - with mobile phones, cameras, written records, pictures etc., gather witnesses, and report all kinds of abuse straight to the police.Join forces: Talk to all other people who know about the problem and together take action against the narcissist - take them to the doctor's and inform all others about it.Seek psychological support: Anybody who has spent time with a narcissist in their family will need psychological support. It is best to see a specialist at all times - during and after.Educate yourself on the topic: There are more and more books coming out explaining narcissistic disorder and how to handle such people. Look at some of my selections here: What are some good books about recovering from narcissists?Further support informationTechnically and legally, the behaviour of narcissists in a family is Domestic Violence and specifically Emotional abuse. You can use this term to refer to it. Also contact services related to Domestic Violence who know how to deal with this.Emotional abuse has become a criminal offence officially in the UK as of 2015. This means that the police, at least in the UK, take it quite seriously. Here are some articles (these are old, the law was passed). Note that it does not refer only to women, but also to men and children.New laws in the UK in 2015 to make emotional abuse illegalEmotional abuse of children to become criminal offenceBid to make 'emotional blackmail' a crimeIf you are confused and unsure what you have, the most likely ones are: severe anxiety, depression and PTSD. These are the most common things people around narcissists. If left for a long time, they may cause other disordes. You may also notice that you feel extremely angry and tense all the time. You may also feel helpless, terrified, isolated, controlled. All of this is the result of interacting with the narcissist. Also report all of this to the police.Domestic Violence contact numbersUS National Domestic Violence Hotline: The National Domestic Violence HotlineHotlines in America, Canada, Australia and New Zealand: CrisisUS hotlines for Domestic violence: National 1-800 Crisis HotlinesList of crisis hotlines across the world: Global Hotlines ListDomestic violence hotlines for all US states (not only for women): Domestic ViolenceList of domestic violence lines worldwide (US, Philippines, Canda, Scotland, England, UK, Sweden, Switzerland): Domestic Violence International Resources : The Zero 5.0lafMore resources about family individual counselling: http://www.princegeorgescountymd.gov/sites/Family/spotlight/Documents/Domestic%20Violence%20Resources%20Full.pdfThe MIND organization in the UK can offer advice and support on how to deal with them and alternative solutionsMind, the mental health charity - help for mental health problemsFree suicide support via telephone & email (Note: Not a good place to talk about the experience with a narcissist. They often do more damage than good.)The Samaritans: Samaritans | Samaritans This is a free 24/7 line with offices in the US and the UK that can help prevent suicide.Befrienders worldwide: Emotional support to prevent suicide worldwide (again, it's not only for suicide)When you talk to others who do not know about NPD, use the term "Family bully" or "Serial bully" instead, as it is vastly easier to understand than Narcissistic Personality disorder. These are unofficial terms for it. There is information about this behaviour on this website: verbal abuse and emotional abuse through power, control, domination and subjugationLook on the internet for forums about "Narcissistic survivors", "Narcissistic abuse recovery" or "Narcissistic abuse victims" where you can learn about the problem, discuss with others about this problem and find further information.Find a good therapist, ideally one who specialises in NPD and people who suffered narcissists. If one does not prove that they know about NPD immediately, go to another with no second thought. A doctor who has dealt with someone who has been in an environment with narcissists for a long period of time will know what to do and how to handle this matter. The others are literally talking nonsense, wasting time, trying things which do not work, and even worse, they misdiagnose and do all sorts of irrelevant treatments.Speak with someone who knows what NPD is or someone who has been in your position and gone over it. You will find that they know exactly what has happened, and may have more information.A good website to find out about NPD is the new website of OutoftheFOG (which stands for out of the Fear, Oligation and Guilt): Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD)For some specific information about how to interact with a narcissist, read my answer: How do you defeat a narcissist? There are also some good books on the subject. Read my answer: What are some good books about recovering from narcissists?

column1: Can you have empathy and have ASPD?
column3: Interesting question. I have ASPD myself, so I'll share what I know based on my knowledge and research, as well as my personal experiences. First thing to know here is that empathy is not a catch-all term. There are many types of empathy. In summary, empathy can be split into two main types; cognitive empathy and affective empathy. • Cognitive empathy is mainly logical, and involves putting yourself in someone else's shoes and understanding their feelings. • Affective empathy is more emotional, and involves being able to connect with and share another person's emotional experiences. Like all mental health conditions and personality disorders, ASPD (formerly sociopathy) is on a spectrum, so everybody with this disorder is different and their experiences are unique and diverse. When it comes to ASPD, most individuals on the antisocial spectrum have either intact or heightened cognitive empathy. The deficit here lies in affective empathy. However in some cases (perhaps more so low-functioning individuals) there can be a cognitive empathy deficit as well. It's dependent on the person. To my understanding, affective empathy is largely dependent on genetics. It would make sense that I have ASPD, considering that it runs in my father's side of the family, and so I am genetically predisposed to having a deficit in affective empathy. I also experienced intense trauma my entire childhood and most of my teenhood: physical, verbal, and emotional abuse, as well as emotional neglect at the hands of my parents, bullying and some sexual assault at primary school for three years, severe major depression in my teens that went mostly untreated for almost two years... All of these experiences were quite traumatic for me, and severely impacted my mental health. Traumatic experiences like this can effectively numb and sometimes completely switch off any affective empathy the individual might've had to begin with. So when it comes to ASPD, you can either never develop affective empathy due to genetics, or lose the ability to feel it due to severe and/or repeated trauma. In my case, I never had it to begin with due to genetic predisposition, and on top of that, I never even got the chance to develop it later due to such traumatic experiences that subconsciously taught me my own pain was already too much to deal with, so it would be even worse to have to feel the pain of others as well. Emotions were too painful, and so my feelings became numb and shallow, and my affective empathy never developed to prevent further suffering on my part. This is how the lack of empathy happens. The DSM states that people with ASPD have a "lack of empathy", though this is very vague and not further explained. Allow me to elaborate here... Like I explained earlier, empathy is not a catch-all term. There is very much a spectrum of affective empathy in which an individual with ASPD can feel. • Some might still have affective empathy, but it might be reduced to some extent. • Some might only feel it for their loved ones or people whom they have a strong bond/connection with, but not feel it towards anyone else. • Some might not feel it at all. Everyone with ASPD is different. Generally, most of us have cognitive empathy but impaired or absent affective empathy. I'd also like to add that some of us can and do experience sympathy and compassion. It really just depends entirely on the individual, everybody is unique. I personally do not experience affective empathy at all, and I never have, since it never developed for me. But I do experience cognitive empathy, sympathy, and compassion. I only feel it for the ones who I have a close bond with though (my cat, partner, family members). I don't feel it towards people I don't know unless I choose to do so. And when I do, I have to consciously put the effort in to involve myself with that person and their struggles. It's practically second nature for me to feel cognitive empathy, sympathy, and compassion towards animals though. I have a soft spot in my heart for animals, as they have never hurt me in the way that humans have, so I view them as quite innocent and deserving of my cognitive empathy, sympathy, and compassion. I'm kind of the same towards children, though to a much lesser extent. Those are just my personal experiences and the knowledge I have regarding ASPD and empathy. I also want to clarify as a friendly reminder that individuals on the antisocial spectrum are not inherently evil/abusive/dangerous people. A majority of us have either been genetically predisposed, have undergone severe and repeated trauma, or maybe even both (in my case), which has caused us to develop ASPD in the first place. It is not our fault. We do not choose to have this disorder. We cannot choose our nature. We can, however, choose our actions. A lot of us are just trying to get by in life like everybody else. Just because we lack the ability to feel someone else's pain, it does not mean we are monsters. We just have a hard time connecting with other people's feelings, and it's not an active choice we make. It is simply how we are. So yes, you can, in fact, have ASPD and still experience empathy. It just depends on the person. Hope this has helped. :) --Kody~☆
