column1: Why do people put their parents into nursing homes when they could just take them in to their own homes? Especially those who have the space.
column3: It's really not as simple as simply having the space. There are some people who only need a little support that could very easily move in with a family member. But generally, they're the ones that have few significant health issues and are more in need of companionship, someone to keep an eye on their general health, less space and housework/gardening to maintain, or someone to make sure they're eating properly. They won't need someone there 24/7 — so they move in and life basically continues as normal — just with an added family member (or sometimes two). That option is much cheaper than retirement villages or independent living/assisted living. But it still requires willingness of both parties. Not everyone is thrilled to give up their own space (whether they're the ones moving in or the ones offering to share their homes). Inviting a disabled or elderly family member to move in also may have the additional pressure of what happens if they need more care in the future that can't be provided at home. It's great you've asked Mom to move in while she's still healthy, but what happens when she can no longer use the stairs or has a health crisis that affects the level of care she requires? Can you afford it? Do you have the financial and physical means to adapt your home and provide 24 hour care? It's also worth pointing out that a person can have a significant disability or even really poor health for a very long time. Even a terminal diagnosis can take several years. I am all for people living and dying at home, or at the home of a family member, but it's not always feasible. But once they've downsized and given up their independent life — they're generally there until they pass or their family can no longer provide the care they need at home. And that brings me to the level and quality of care the family can provide. There's a huge difference between minor incontinence issues (needing a pad because you're not always quick enough to the toilet or leak when you laugh or cough) and people who have no bladder or bowel control. “I've changed plenty of diapers after having kids!” does not mean that you will be great at cleaning up adult size waste in adult sized incontinence products. Leaks and “blow outs" still happen and sometimes the most sensible solution is to strip entirely and shower it off them and their clothing. I've also known elderly people who insist they can handle their most intimate cleaning on their own (and often they don't want the opposite sex, but especially not a son or daughter, to do it) — only to later discover that they're red, raw, and sometimes have ulcers or pressure sores because they're protecting their modesty rather than getting as clean as necessary. Severe infections are possible — sometimes fatal. They may be fine with an outside carer or nurse doing it, but completely reject the idea of family doing it. But I can promise you that bodily functions won't wait for an outside carer to arrive — and even sitting with a bit of urine in a pad can cause skin irritation and burns. It's something that needs discussing before agreeing or offering to care for them at home, really. And finally — dementia. If you have a family member diagnosed with dementia there is a tremendous amount to consider and I highly recommend sitting down with someone that deals in elder law, as well as someone that deals in dementia, as soon as possible after diagnosis. Time really is of the essence. There can be years when it's more of a frustrating nuisance, but you do not know how quickly varying stages will occur and you will want to do this while they still have the capacity to make their wishes known. But, unless you have the means to provide a safe environment or they succumb to a different health condition, many people with dementia end up in nursing homes because it can be extremely difficult to provide the right environment at home. Wandering is a big safety issue — there will come a time when they are too vulnerable to go out alone and if they are left unsupervised they may not know the risks they're taking by leaving. Some develop traits that you may not want your children or visitors to witness. (e.g. sexual comments, public masturbation, aggression, racism/bigotry, playing with feces, spitting, etc.) Others will repetitively cry or shout that they don't know who they are or where they are, or even just a single word for hours on end. They may have sleep disturbances and need supervision all night, every night. And of course, staying with family requires dementia-proofing — which is like baby-proofing at adult height. Most of the assisted living facilities I worked at had some residents that were still independent enough to dress themselves or open a bag of snacks — but their kitchen had the stove disconnected because they were not safe to handle hot pans or may cause a fire if they forget they're cooking or don't remember what to do while cooking. That's not really feasible at home with a family. And leaving notes that say “Don't use" or “I'll make your dinner at 6pm” often aren't enough. There is a point when their mental faculties decline and they can't “connect the dots" — their brains become more primal. They feel hunger and may still know that means to eat something — but they may eat something inappropriate, they may no longer connect the words “dinner" or “eat" with hunger, or understand that they can't do it safely themselves. Of course dementia can also be distressing for families, as well. It's not so bad when they still recognise you, even if they get your name wrong 10 times before landing on the right one. But one day you will likely be a stranger to them. They may like you and assume your intentions are good — or they may be wary and see you as an intruder or threat. Either way, it's not a nice feeling. Some people are better at accepting it than others, but this is often around the point that families start looking at residential care. Families can learn to help elderly or disabled family members to safely move, to attend to hygiene needs, to flush ports, change and use feeding tubes, look after ostemies, provide respiratory treatments, or even do a good amount of end of life care for someone terminally ill. But caring for an adult with dementia as they lose their abilities and their memories is heartbreakingly difficult beyond a certain point and there's no set in stone road map that can predetermine all of the obstacles and if/when they'll arrive. Several years ago one of our neighbours came by specifically to tell us that her husband had early onset dementia and that he'd been moved into residential care and that his doctors had told her to focus on rebuilding her life as though she was single. That wasn't to say “abandon him" but that there was nothing left of the man she loved — she could carry on loving him and visiting him, but that love was never going to be reciprocated again as he no longer knew her or remembered her. My heart broke for her and it broke again when I realised she was afraid we'd be judging her for “acting single" or for putting him in a home. None of us had any idea that he had dementia as it seemed to have progressed very quickly from forgetful to forgotten. Hard decisions have to be made sometimes because not everyone is equipped with the space or ability or time to do it alone. I have met patients in nursing homes who are actually happy to be there. They have their wits about them and know that their medical needs are beyond what they could safely manage alone and either they don't have family they could move in with or their family can't manage their needs. But many in nursing homes don't know they're in nursing homes — and those that can recognise “this isn't home" usually aren't in distress because there are nice people to help them and their basic needs are being met.
column9: You really covered all the territory with your answer. Only those who have had to deal with caring for elderly relatives, especially those with dementia, understand what is really involved in keeping them safe, and how difficult or even impossible it can become to manage that plus a family or/or a job at the same time. Sometimes professional care is the optimal decision for the health and well-being of all those involved.

column1: What is the most neglected aspect of life?
column3: Mental health Means stress,overthinking because our lives doesn't go in our way... column1: What does it feel like to have no family?
column3: What does it feel like? It feels like torture. Like a bottomless well of overwhelming sadness and loneliness. A part of me is angry with God because, I didn't ask to be here. My life has consisted of those who were suppose to love me, deciding that they simply didn't want me. My biological parents didn't want me. My father desperately wanted my mother to have an abortion but, she decided to have me instead. They created an excuse as to why they didn't want to take me from the hospital after birth. That's where my Grandmother stepped in and decided to take care of me straight from the hospital. She wanted to do something kind so I wouldn't end up in foster care, but sadly, she had her own issues with mental illness and was abusive to my sibling and I, as well as my two cousins. At one point, she was taking care of all of us because in my family, people love to neglect their children. My grandmother loved to beat me into submission. A hanger. A belt. An extension cord. A switch (a branch from off of a tree in the backyard). Slapping me multiple times. Digging her nails into my arms and breaking the skin leaving behind imprints. Beating my bare legs, arms and hands causing painful welts. Sitting on me so I couldn't move so she could beat my bare bottom. She would tell me to shut up repeatedly if I disagreed with her about anything. If I didn't comply, she would hit me until I was broken down and collapsed in pain. She would hit me until I wept, sobbing and could barely catch my breath. Only then she would stop. She would later call me into her room and tell me that she beat me because she “loves me.” She controlled everything about all of us incessantly. Our opinions, putting up a simple poster on the wall, listening to music…everything. We had no friends or social life. It took me years to figure out who I was because with her, you were not allowed to explore or have your own autonomy or you would immediately be labeled as disobedient. A word she loved to use as a devout Bible toting Christian. Anything would grant you that label. That just meant you were going to be beaten even more. She was also a master of manipulation. When you wouldn't do her bidding, she would tell anyone who would listen how “disobedient ” you were. A smear campaign designed to make you feel so far beneath her. We all walked on eggshells. We were stifled, unheard, and it felt as if I was suffocating under the pressure to behave as a perfect child. To do everything she wanted regardless if she was hurting me, neglecting me, emotionally unavailable to me and causing trauma. Our relationship was extremely complicated because on one hand, I loved her for “taking care” of me. On the other, I greatly despised her because of the damage she was doing to all of us. My biological mother came around occasionally. My first memory of her was maybe when I was about 5/6 yrs old. I was trying to play with her and she wanted me to leave her alone. I kept trying to play until she got a hold of a magazine, rolled it up, and smacked me in the mouth with it. The force was so blunt that it knocked out my front tooth. Our relationship was never good. Years later, we found out she was diagnosed with Schizophrenia. Her behavior towards me was problematic, short fused and aggressive. I have no actual memories of her other than the incident of her hitting me, a nose ring, a loud laugh, silver jewelry, brassy blonde hair, and the smell of cigarettes. I resented her so much that I excommunicated myself from her. My entire childhood was spent yearning for her to nurture me, and trying to understand why she rejected me and didn't come around often. I couldn't make sense of our relationship and I would cry often not understanding my place in this world. My father came by every now and then. He would take us to McDonald's and give me $100. That was it. He never paid child support so sometimes, we didn't even have food. Sometimes the electricity was shut off due to past due balances. He was physically abusive to my biological mother when they were married and it was always speculated that he married her for a green card. They eventually divorced. I didn't have a great relationship with him either because he never wanted me and his actions proved it throughout my life. The rest of my family are plagued with mental illness on my mothers side. They are broke, destitute, and one of my cousins who my Grandmother was taking care of went off to prison for some time. Felony Armed robbery. His brother was accused of sexually abusing someone. Some of my family who I adored have passed on. We have a rather small family as it is. I have never met my fathers side. My biggest fear growing up was my Grandmother abandoning me too. Even though she was quite abusive in many ways, I didn't want her to abandon me like her daughter and my father did. When I was 11/12, she did just that. She married a man who quickly destroyed what little good we had. She stopped parenting me, caring about me, and began regularly threatening to throw me out of the house because I protested the things her husband was doing that negatively affected us. All she wanted was to be married. She simply never stood up for me. Nothing. She even let him physically push me a couple of different times and never said a word. I felt like no one loved me or even cared. One day, her husband put his hands on me and I lost it. I grabbed a knife because I was ready to stab him. Never have I ever been violent. I was so tired and felt as though I was losing my mind. I was around 15/16 and never had a normal life. I wanted to k*ll myself and was severely depressed and done with it all. I wept everyday and prayed to God to leave all of the hurt, abandonment, and abuse behind. When I was 17, I was finally able to leave my Grandmother and the mess she created. There were times that I even thought I was going to hit her. I seriously contemplated it once. I stood over her, frozen, with a cast iron frying pan running the scenario through my mind and thinking… what if? I was exhausted of being physically and emotionally abused. But, just like the abuser and manipulator she was, all of a sudden she wanted to be “nice” once she knew I was leaving. I left and never looked back. My Grandmother has since passed on. But the damage left behind is immeasurable. Her husband passed on a year later. Good riddance. My cousins, we have not spoken and I don't have a desire to. My Grandmother always incenuated that one of them possibly did something inappropriate to me when I was very young. The same one who was accused of sexual abuse in his adult life. Other family members are toxic, in abusive relationships and other unsavory situations. A few other family members are dealing with mental illness. My Grandmother was the link to everyone else. When she died, there was no reason to speak to the others. The problem with my family is that there is unresolved generational trauma and unchecked untreated mental illness. Sadly, when you grow up the way we did, there are issues that stem from it. My brother whom I was closest to, we are no longer on speaking terms. I see in him some behaviors that was akin to my Grandmother. Gaslighting. Never taking responsibility for his actions. Anger. I had to leave him behind as well. I have no family. All I ever wanted was to be loved given the circumstances of me being brought into this world. All I ever wanted were parents/family who loved me fully and unconditionally. But the very people who were suppose to love me and take care of me, willingly threw me away. Abused me. Shamed me. Took away any resemblance of a normal positive childhood. My childhood was full of fear and abandonment. Struggle. Pain. Depression. Disappointment. Feeling unworthy. No self esteem. No confidence. Feeling like a burden to everyone. I struggle alone with depression and anxiety even to this day. Many times, I wouldn't even be able to get out of the bed for months at a time or even do the basics of taking care of myself. My mental health issues became so severe over time (I've spent years not fully processing childhood trauma, and unconsciously choosing relationships/friendships that mimicked my Grandmothers very conditional love and abuse) that I recently had to reach out for additional help. I now have a psychiatrist and therapist as well as access to appropriate care to treat my mental health. I was diagnosed with Major Depression, Anxiety and CPtsd. The abandonment issues… I try to keep them at bay but, I see it in how I deal with people. I don't feel extremely close to anyone. In the back of my mind, I think people will leave or disappoint so I don't allow myself to get too close. I can cut people off rather quickly. In the past, it was a defense mechanism. Now, it's because I realized that subconsciously, I kept people in my life that behaved like my Grandmother. So anyone I cut off now, it is rooted in purpose. The purpose of bettering my life. So that is progress I suppose. I currently don't have many friends. I'm down to about two and then there are acquaintances like coworkers. I had to remove alot of so called friends who always made me feel unloved. How does all of this feel? I would never wish it on anyone. I am lonely on the holidays. Many times, lonely in general. Something deep within always feels missing. I never properly and healthily bonded to a parent which is necessary in a childs life. I was also never taught the fundamentals of starting friendships and relationships with people. Often, I feel like a burden to others so I isolate myself. I am uncertain if my introversion is naturally a part of my personality or if I feel forced into it as a means to feel….SAFE. I do most things alone. Sometimes, I'm exhausted from the energy it takes to push myself to feel normal. I've been pushing myself since I was a child, and I am fatigued from the mental and emotional energy that takes. It's almost as if I want to give that responsibility to someone else. To take care of me for once. My entire life has always been me in survival mode. Many times, I feel like a child still longing to be nurtured and made to feel safe and loved. It's a hole I don't think can be filled. I was robbed of it. In regards to dating, I panic because deep within I wonder, who is going to want someone like me? Someone who has been abused, deals with mental health issues, doesn't have family and has a life of so much tragedy? Who wants to be with someone like me when you can be with someone who has a family and a fairly “normal” life? I hate that I feel this way about myself because, I really do have so much love to give despite my circumstances. It may take me a lifetime to move past what has happened to me. Part of me wishes I would have been put in foster care. Maybe I would have had a chance to be so much more as a person. Maybe I wouldn't have been abused. Maybe mentally I wouldn't struggle the way I do. I didn't ask to be born into this. I didn't ask for any of these experiences. Much of what negative occurred, happened as a direct result of my Grandmother, the consequences of her actions, and me trying to pick up the pieces. That's the difficult part. Now, I am another one on my Grandmother's side of the family with mental illness. I feel guilty complaining. There are people who have it worse in life. But I guess, pain is pain so one shouldn't feel guilty for how they feel. People do not understand how it feels to live this type of life. Often, I don't even know who to put down as an “emergency contact” just in case. Who will be there for me when I get married? Who will care? Will I even find a partner who understands that these things that occurred are not my fault? Will they judge me for it as if it was my own doing? Will they be able to see me? The real me? My higher self knows and understands that I…. SURVIVED. Regardless of how others view my life and or experiences, I survived. I didn't take my own life. I didn't end up having a substance abuse issue. I didn't end up homeless on the streets. There is of course a tremendous amount of trauma in my life, but I do what I can in the form of therapy etc to get better. Sometimes I feel sorry for myself on holidays and at other times. Times like right now as I write this. I try to block out all that has happened. But… My higher self believes… For those of you who are dealing with the same thing, having no family for whatever those reasons are, please be encouraged. Know that you are loved. Family doesn't have to be your blood. Family can be the amazing friends you have made along the way. And not everyone will reject you because of your past or experiences that others in your life have caused. Embrace your friendships. Know that you are loved even if you don't feel like you are. Seek therapy. Seek healing. I don't know if I will ever fully heal from everything that has happened, but I sure do feel better about myself through putting in constant hard work. In my life, I have already done more than everyone in my family. I'm already beating the odds. I am breaking the cycle. All you can do is the best you can to live the best life you can. Create new memories. And sometimes, not everyone can go on that journey with you. Sending love and hugs to all of those without family. Stay strong. You are loved.❤

column1: How will ACA affect career and job choices of young people, and their lives in general?
column3: Let's get past all of the rhetoric of the others promoting or opposing ACA. The bottom line is that most Americans will have more choices about how they approach their health care and more choices means freedom. Some companies have very publicly changed the terms of the plans they offer to employees, doing things like excluding spouses on plans. However, you can now purchase your own plan and can not be rejected or charged higher fees for existing conditions. This is critically important. For example, I have a family member who was diagnosed with Cancer in his last semester of law school. He was stuck in the family business because the risk, after remission of losing coverage from another employer was too great to consider other career choices. I know a number of small business owners who are unhappy about the implementation of ACA and how it ties their hands on new hires, but at the same time, they appreciate the wider gains that the law represents. Personally, my own insurance costs have been cut in half. The extension of mental health benefits have helped because of the costs associated with Autism. I don't believe the ACA is perfect. It needs to be fixed, but it moves us in a very important direction. As a young person today, you no longer face financial ruin if you get sick. It still won't be free or cheap, but you will recover your health and your finances. Just a few months ago, that was very uncertain. I don't know many people who have been seriously ill who argue against those points.
column9: Jonathan- You say, "The bottom line is that most Americans will have more choices about how they approach their health care and more choices means freedom." Please defend this statement in light of the fact that millions of Americans who had individual plans lost their plans. Defend it in light of the many more millions (predicted to be 93 million) who will lose their employer-sponsored plans after the administration's delays end. I think the exact opposite of your statement is true. Prior to ACA, I had a zillion choices (i.e. freedoms) related to my health insurance AND health care. The choices have and will continue to narrow for millions of us. Per the pre-existing condition of your family member who stuck with the family biz, he could have always used COBRA if his employer fired him or laid him off. He chose not to go that route. It's not right or wrong, but it's just what he chose to do. "I don't know many people who have been seriously ill who argue against those points." -- you might not know the right people. Again, my experience differs from yours. I know plenty of people who have been seriously ill or have chronic illnesses who despise the law. Thanks for writing a pretty balanced answer to this "shill question."

column1: How does having PTSD/C-PTSD affect one's daily life, including career choices, friendships, and relationships?
column3: Your nervous system is stuck in the past while the Earth is turning. Stomach is churning, you may feel nauseous, because your digestive system takes hits too. Along with muscle pain and tension, TMJ lock jaw, and irregular hormones due to high levels of stress and anxiety. All types of stuff goes on in the body. To answer your question… CAREER You're too depressed to even consider a life path for yourself. Your mind is racing with intrusive thoughts and flashbacks about the trauma like pop-up ads, so how can you figure it out when you can't focus. You may lose faith in humanity and decide to give up contributing on the system. Everything seems pointless because no matter what you do, the joy for life has disappeared. The state of hopelessness can get you into alcoholism or drug addiction. You're stuck in a deep depression where you don't want to do anything anymore. When you do have to leave the house, you feel all types of emotions of anger and sadness, all kicking your ass at one time. FRIENDSHIPS The lack of trust and the need to self-isolate can ruin our ability to form bonds with people. We can't fit in or we tend to feel out of place like no one can relate. RELATIONSHIPS This is the hardest one. Lack of trust is definitely a HUGE factor here. Feeling alienated can make it hard to connect with people. Getting hurt by people who were supposed to love you can deeply traumatize you to where you start to think everyone is out to get you. You feel like no one loves you, and this feeling is deep-rooted if your parents, step parents, caregivers, foster parents, or other family members have abused or neglected you. Constant betrayals and emotional pain really take a toll on your mental health to where you become cynical. You build barriers around to protect yourself. You might push everyone away because you don't know how to accept love because you view all love as fake because that's all you know, or that's mostly it. Your traumatic experiences can make you feel isolated. You feel like no one can understand you or empathize with you in any way because most people appear shallow. Those who lack emotional depth cannot comprehend how deep our pain is and how severe traumas hurt us to our core. Their ignorant and callous remarks will only trigger us and piss us off because it's like “How in the hell do you not understand me!? Do you ever feel anything? Why don't you feel what I feel? Why doesn't anyone else feel me?” That's what goes through your mind, and this makes you want to be alone, but that can also put us in a dark place if we're not healed.

column1: What is the most scared you have been of a member of your own family?
column3: I have a cousin who made unfortunate choices to use street drugs. Consequently, his ability to function has been affected and his life is now a consistent cycle of going to jail for committing various crimes ; transfer from jail to mental health facilities after being found incompetent; being declared lucid after an extended stay and consistent drug therapy; released with med prescriptions; failure to maintain drug therapy which results in another criminal episode (i.e. broke into a home or store; trespass; assault,etc..) and a trip back to jail, where the cycle begins again. On one such occasion, at the point of the cycle where he hasn’t maintained his drug protocol, but has not yet committed a crime, he showed up at our family’s home. It is where our grandparents used to live, in a different state. Family members stay at the home whenever visiting the area. At this time, his father; my mom; my daughters an I were there. How he got into the house is not clear, but when I returned from a store run, he was there. And, now we couldn’t get him to leave. He would go into the restrooms and incessantly brush his nearly bald head, for an hour. He has an explosive temper. So, we were very careful in attempting to persuade him from staying in the bathrooms. The concern was that he’d find something to use as a weapon, and emerge from the room in a dangerous state. We locked all bedroom doors and did all we could to keep him away from the kitchen. At some point, we all left the house to “go shopping”. He attempted to stay behind, but we told him that we were all going to dinner afterwards, so there wouldn’t be anything for him to eat after coming back later evening. While we were out, we did all we could to lose him in the mall, but he stuck to us like glue. Unfortunately, we found ourselves stuck with him for the night. He stayed in the house with us, and no one slept. Throughout the night, he made continuous long-stay trips to the bathroom. soon as daybreak came, I told him we were preparing to go to church so, I would drop him off wherever he was staying; and, advised him to come back later to join us for dinner. Along the way, he asked -“Are you afraid of me?” I very confidently called him by his name and said “No, Sxxxx. We grew up together. Why would I be afraid of you?” I said it with a tone of indignation. Like, what an insulting thing to insinuate! I maintained the attitude as the ride continued. When we reached the destination, he got out of the car but tried to continue a discussion while holding the door open. I said, “Listen! It’s really upsetting to me that you have some idea that I, who grew up with you like a sister, is afraid of you and don’t want you around. I have to get ready for church and can’t be late. So close the door. I’ll be back to pick you up after church.” He then closed the door. When I returned to the house, everyone had already begun packing. Within the half hour, we were on the road headed back home. We later heard he’d assaulted someone and was arrested just days after we left.
column9: You listened to your intuition, and handled him, and that whole situation really well. I’m sorry. It’s very upsetting to know someone all your life, then watch them become something that you need to protect yourself and your family from. Awful feeling. I’m sure you have memories of childhood where you laughed and played together as kids do. I’m not sure many people realize (because of the anger and fear) that they’re also grieving? I mean, you’ve lost someone. It’s like a death. This person you grew up with, and knew, is gone. It makes sense that you’d grieve the loss of him. I guess I wonder if people realize they might be experiencing grief. You know? Hope you’re well.

column1: How can we identify that someone close to us is going through mental stress or mental illness and needs our help and support?
column3: How can we identify that someone close to us is going through mental stress or mental illness and needs our help and support? Everyone goes through physical and emotional changes throughout life. As humans, our development is marked, in our way of dealing with our feelings about psychological and biological changes within us as we get older and go through different phases of life. So, sometimes it can be difficult to differentiate between developmental changes and behavioral changes that are of concern. For some people who have a predisposition for mental illness, emotional or mental life can change abruptly, with the onset of mental illness. Nevertheless, it can be hard to know how to recognize that mental illness is present. According to APA, Mental Illness is “health conditions involving changes in thinking, emotion or behavior (or a combination of these) .Mental illnesses are associated with distress and/or problems functioning in social, work or family activities.” They include depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorders, among others. Mental or emotional distress is something everyone experiences at some point in their life.Feeling sad or downExcessive fears or worries, or extreme feelings of guiltSignificant tiredness, low energy or problems sleepingProblems with alcohol or drug useMajor changes in eating habitsExcessive anger, hostility or violenceSuicidal thinkingAccording to SunriseHouse, the steps that can be taken to recognize whether or not there is a mental health problem underlying an individual’s behaviors involve looking out for the following elements of the individual’s personality:Thinking processes : If you think someone close to you has difficulty in paying attention, a feeling of disorientation, or problems making decisions. It can also affect the ability to access short-term or long-term memory. Ex : If your friend seems lost or irritable during lectures or your family member is not able to contribute in family discussions and is always quiet.Mood swings or major emotional shifts : If there are extreme mood changes and mood swings are occurring on a regular basis, and fluctuating wildly, it can indicate a mental health concern. Ex : If your loved one is happy one minute and angry/lashing out or restless the other without a particular reason.Behaviors, eating and sleeping patterns: Some changes in behavior are readily apparent i.e. a formerly quiet child having angry outbursts or formerly a good, healthy eater suddenly begins leaving meals uneaten, changes in sleeping patterns. Noticing whether or not there are changes can help to identify more subtle behavior changes.While this may simply be a phase the individual is going through, changes that are extreme or put the individual’s health at risk should be investigated.Delusions or hallucinations : A less subtle sign that someone is experiencing a mental health problem is hearing voices or seeing things that aren’t there. Ex: If a family member complains of seeing someone standing by the window or constantly hearing voices of deceased relatives.Social relations or withdrawal : Any unexplained changes in social circles or withdrawal from activities with friends may indicate a mental health issue. Ex : Lack of initiation of plans to go out and socialize, avoiding situations where there will be socializing expected i.e. marriages, functions etc.Daily activities or responsibilities : People who develop mental illnesses may begin to have issues maintaining daily responsibilities, this may be severe enough to create a physical inability to perform certain activities, or they may be mild enough to simply cause the person to feel overwhelmed by simple tasks. Ex : Getting irritated with washing their own dishes, unable to bathe, brush teeth etc.Complaints about physical ailments: According to MayoClinic, mental illness can often manifest symptoms of unexplained physical pain or ailment, discomfort etc. Ex : constant headache or feeling of one losing their balance.Drug or alcohol use: A person who is experiencing disturbing mental health problems may turn to drugs or alcohol to self-medicate – that is, to help diminish the disturbing feelings that come from the disorder.Ex: Increased (more than usual) alcohol consumption after a long stressful day.These steps enable an individual to recognize if someone close to him is going through concerns underlying mental health. With this it is very important for one, to talk and catch up with the individual as well as always look out for signs and symptoms that may show that the individual is going through something that needs help and will benefit from help. However it is recommended that one need not infer anything directly from signs/symptoms without talking to the person and understanding their side of the story. Once you have the conversation with your loved one, suggest to them that seeking help will benefit them. Do not impose your opinions and conclusions of their conditions on them.

column1: How is (CPTSD) complex post-traumatic stress disorder diagnosed?
column3: It has to be diagnosed by a psychiatrist or a psychologist. I'm not a mental health professional but here is what I have learnt from personal experience and therapy So there is PTSD and CPTSD. PTSD results from going through a threatening event where you fear for your life(safety) or the life(safety)of a loved one. And as a result you experience severe distress that impairs your life after the event has passed. Having flashbacks, nightmares. Being jumpy and on edge all the time,… Complex PTSD usually starts from childhood and also usually caused by our caregivers or close people to our family, people who were supposed to protect us. It's going through traumatic events repeatedly over a long period of time, could be years. Like, being abused by a parent or an older sibling or a teacher or a family member. It happens more than once and as a kid you feel trapped and scared. You don't know who you can go to or who can take you away from this. You live your childhood in fear. You don't trust anyone. And this affects your personality even after the trauma ends. As an adult, you can develop unhealthy destructive behaviours to cope with this pain inside, to numb yourself. Being Impulsive in your actions, addiction, eating disorders, self harm, suicidal thoughts. Deep down, you feel that something is broken even though you keep telling yourself that no one is hurting you now. You get these feelings of unworthiness, hopelessness, emptiness, loneliness. You have no self-esteem and no self confidence. You feel you are not good enough for anyone or anything. You feel like a failure. Unexplained feelings of guilt and shame. Feeling like you are still stuck in the past. You lose sense of who you are. You have trust issues with people, you have fear of abandonment and rejection. It's very similar to Borderline Personality Disorder but the main difference is some people have BPD but they haven't been exposed to traumas as kids or even adults. And I have met some of those. I hope this answers your question.

column1: What are the symptoms of borderline personality disorder? How can you tell if someone has borderline personality disorder or if they are just an angry person with another type of mental illness?
column3: Here are some common identifying characteristics. Borderline Personality Disorder If a commenter is triggered by this list, and you feel yourself feeling defensive, this may inspire a commenter to post an ad hominem attack. If that happens, I will delete you and block you. You’re free to disagree. You are NOT free to attack. I’m going to answer this original question with both widely-accepted, peer-reviewed characteristics and the results of my nearly 20 years of professional experience as well as extensive personal experience. There will be some who will read my answer and will claim I trigger them, I paint with too broad a brush, or I lack the SME to answer with authority. Additionally, they will claim I am mean and hateful toward people with BPD and that most people with BPD are normal, healthy, and well-adjusted people who are harmless. Ok, so be it. The data doesn’t lie. **Borderline personality disorder BPD** **DISCLAIMER**: I’ll repeat this disclaimer often. Please don’t skim over it. **Not everyone** with BPD will exhibit all of these traits, and the severity of symptoms can vary from person to person. If you or someone you know is experiencing these symptoms, seek help from a mental health professional. BPD is a treatable condition, and with the right treatment, people with BPD can learn to manage their symptoms and lead fulfilling lives. Thank you for reading the disclaimer and for taking responsibility for your own emotions and for being accountable for them. **BPD** People often ask me what the MOST destructive emotional and mental health disorder **I’ve counseled and experienced personally. ** Outside of sociopathics and psychopaths, it is the Axis II disorder known as BPD. Since 2006 I’ve intensely researched, counseled, and interacted with people, both the famous and relatively unknown, with Borderline Personality Disorder. Over that time frame, I’ve seen BPD crush otherwise strong and intelligent people into dust. I’ve personally seen its behaviors and manifestations destroy marriages, families, businesses, and careers. **WHAT IS BPD?** Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is an Axis II mental health condition characterized by pervasive instability in moods, (evidenced by instantaneous wild mood swings) volatile interpersonal relationships, and wild vacillations of their self-image, and erratic, dangerous, and highly dangerous promiscuous behavior. People with BPD most often, **but not always** have intensely wonderful but habitually unstable relationships, struggle with plunging self-worth, and engage in impulsive and self-destructive behaviors which most often destroy the ones they claim to love and adore. They have difficulty self-regulating their emotions, which can lead to feelings of emptiness or anger. They are completely self-contained one moment and the next they're exploding in uncontrollable anger and they lash out at those they claim to love. BPD is a very serious condition that can be debilitating, but **with proper PROFESSIONAL treatment, some people with BPD can lead fulfilling lives and be a blessing to their family and friends. ** A mental health professional, such as an experienced therapist, psychologist or psychiatrist, can diagnose Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) by conducting a comprehensive evaluation that includes a clinical interview, psychological testing, and a review of the individual's medical and psychiatric history. **However, some tell-tale signs that MAY indicate that a person has BPD include the following:** * Intense and unstable relationships may change rapidly between idealization and devaluation. * Impulsive and reckless behavior, such as substance abuse, binge eating, reckless driving, or risky compulsive sexual behavior. * Self-destructive behavior, such as self-harm or suicidal threats or gestures. * Chronic feelings of emptiness or boredom. * Difficulty regulating emotions, which may lead to sudden and intense anger or mood swings. * A fear of abandonment, which may lead to clingy or needy behavior. * A distorted self-image or sense of self may lead to rapid changes in goals, values, or interests. They are often body metamorphic. * A tendency to blame others for problems or setbacks rather than take responsibility for one's actions. It's important to note that BPD is a severe condition and requires professional help. ***Don't try to self-diagnose.*** If you suspect that you or someone you know may have BPD, it's essential to seek help from a qualified mental health professional with strong experience with BPD. A relationship with someone with Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) can be challenging and emotionally intense, first to the great and wonderful, then suddenly unexplainable to the destructive and bad. It can also destroy YOU if you don't recognize it and either hit the eject button or learn as much as you can about it. People with BPD have difficulty self-regulating their emotions and have intense but unstable relationships. They idealize & idolize (love bomb) their partner with compliments and intense sexual attention at one moment and suddenly switch to devaluing or criticizing them leading to wild nonsensical arguments out of thin air. This makes it excruciatingly difficult for their partner to predict how they will be treated and leads to feelings of crippling insecurity and paralyzing confusion. You may feel like you're losing your mind as the partner. Additionally, people with BPD may fear abandonment, which can lead to extremely clingy or hyper-needy behavior. They may also engage in impulsive or self-destructive behavior, which can strain or destroy the relationship. They're often habitual liars and most often highly unfaithful to multiple simultaneous relationships they secretly have in motion. That is, until it all crashes down taking innocent people with it. Suddenly all of the unexplained and bizarre behavior makes sense yet the explosive damage is already done. On the other hand, people with BPD can be extremely loving, caring, and affectionate. Although rare, they can also have empathy and insight into their condition. With *the right kind of help* when it is **wanted** and **consistently** accepted, people with BPD **can learn to regulate their emotions** and improve their relationships. It is important to note that it is not easy to maintain a relationship with someone with BPD; it takes a lot of patience, understanding, and empathy. It’s actually really, really exasperating. It is also crucial for both partners to be willing to consistently work on the relationship and to seek a competent, BPD experienced and professional therapist. In an upcoming article, I will share some of my experiences with psychopaths and sociopaths. Here is a more detailed and potentially triggering list to someone with emotional health issues such as BPD. In my past practice I was a subject matter expert in Borderline Personality Disorders. In that capacity I was often asked to write academic and simple guidelines for people who might be dealing with someone in their orbit with Borderline Personality Disorder, or BPD. Here is a less-egghead version of my papers that might help you clear up some questions you may have about a mate, romantic interest, friend, family member or boss that you just can’t pin down what’s wrong with them. I included several disclaimers. Please don’t skip them. Also, I tried to make this as rated PG as possible because it’s a very mature subject with some very mature ramifications and I wanted this to be appropriate for a broader audience. But, it’s still for mature audiences only. Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is an Axis II mental health condition characterized by intense and unstable emotions, impulsive behavior, distorted self-image, and difficulty with relationships. (See (a) below for helpful information.) Here are some **general** widely accepted traits of BPD: 1. Intense emotions: People with BPD often experience intense and rapidly changing emotions. They may feel intense anger, sadness, or anxiety that can quickly escalate and be difficult to control. 2. Impulsive behavior: People with BPD may engage in impulsive behavior, such as substance abuse, binge eating, reckless driving, or risky sexual behavior. They may also engage in self-harming behaviors such as cutting or burning themselves. 3. Distorted self-image: People with BPD may have a distorted sense of self-image, which can lead to feelings of worthlessness, shame, or self-hatred. They may also have difficulty understanding their own emotions or motivations. 4. Fear of abandonment: People with BPD often have a deep fear of abandonment, which can lead to clingy or controlling behavior in relationships. They may become extremely upset or angry if they feel that someone is rejecting them or pulling away from them. 5. Unstable relationships: People with BPD may have difficulty maintaining stable relationships, due to their intense emotions and fear of abandonment. They may idealize someone one minute and then devalue them the next, causing confusion and instability in their relationships. 6. Identity disturbance: People with BPD may have an unstable sense of self, which can lead to feelings of emptiness or a lack of purpose. They may also experience frequent changes in their goals, values, or career path. 7. Dissociation: People with BPD may experience episodes of dissociation, which can cause them to feel disconnected from their surroundings or their own emotions. They may also experience periods of depersonalization, where they feel like they are outside of their own body. I’ll repeat this disclaimer often, **not everyone with BPD will exhibit all of these traits**, and the severity of symptoms can vary from person to person. If you or someone you know is experiencing these symptoms, seek help from a mental health professional. **BPD is a treatable condition**, and with the right treatment, people with BPD can learn to manage their symptoms **and lead fulfilling lives.** **Romantic relationships with BPD** How is a romantic relationship with a person with BPD in the beginning? Romantic relationships with people with borderline personality disorder (BPD) can start off in a variety of ways, just like any other relationship. However, people with BPD often experience intense and rapidly changing emotions, which **can** affect how they approach relationships and how they are perceived by their partners. **Here are some common patterns that may be seen in the beginning stages of romantic relationships with someone who has BPD:** 1. INTENSE attraction: People with BPD may feel an intense attraction to their partner right from the start. They may feel like their partner is their "soulmate" and may express their love and commitment very quickly. 2. IDEALIZATION: People with BPD may idealize their partner in the beginning stages of the relationship, putting them on a pedestal and viewing them as perfect. They may see their partner as their savior, someone who will rescue them from their emotional pain. 3. High sensitivity to REJECTION: People with BPD often have a deep fear of abandonment and may be hypersensitive to any signs of rejection or distance from their partner. This can cause them to become clingy or possessive early on in the relationship. Often they will preemptively end a relationship to head off impending rejection or they will engage in multiple other secret relationships to provide an ‘other’ or ‘supply’ of attention, love, affection and sexual excitement. 4. IMPULSIVE behavior: People with BPD may engage in impulsive behavior early on in the relationship, such as spending money recklessly or moving in together quickly. They may also engage in risky sexual behavior or substance abuse. 5. UNPREDICTABLE emotions: People with BPD often experience rapidly changing emotions, which can make it difficult for their partner to understand and respond to their needs. They may be very loving and affectionate one moment, and then become angry or upset the next. People with BPD can be dangerous and destructive to your life, your work, your family. (See (a) below.) **I** said I’d repeat this, and here I am again, repeating this disclaimer. **** It's important to note that **not everyone** with BPD will exhibit these behaviors, and the severity of symptoms can vary from person to person. However, it's important for partners to be aware of these **potential challenges** and to seek support when needed. With the right treatment and support, people with BPD can learn to manage their symptoms and develop healthy, fulfilling relationships. **Being a friend or family member of a person with BPD.** It **can be** difficult to identify whether a friend or family member has borderline personality disorder (BPD) without a proper diagnosis from a mental health professional. However, there are some common signs and symptoms associated with BPD that you can look out for. ****Here are some of the signs and symptoms of BPD:**** 1. Intense and unstable relationships: People with BPD often have intense and unstable relationships, characterized by frequent arguments, breakups, and reconciliations. 2. Fear of abandonment: People with BPD often have an intense fear of abandonment and may go to great lengths to avoid real or imagined abandonment. 3. Impulsive behavior: People with BPD may engage in impulsive and potentially harmful behaviors, such as binge eating, substance abuse, or risky sexual behavior. 4. Mood swings: People with BPD often experience intense and rapidly shifting moods, which can be triggered by minor events or perceived slights. 5. Distorted self-image: People with BPD often have a distorted self-image and may experience feelings of worthlessness or emptiness. 6. Self-harm: People with BPD may engage in self-harming behaviors, such as cutting or burning, as a way to cope with intense emotions. 7. Suicidal thoughts or behaviors: People with BPD may experience frequent and intense suicidal thoughts, and may engage in suicidal behaviors. Are you noting a pattern yet? Any bells ringing or red flags yet? If you’re getting angry or defensive right now, you might like to seek a competent and experienced therapist to examine why you’re so triggered by this post. And again with the disclaimer, it's important to remember that **not everyone** with BPD will exhibit all of these symptoms, and that other mental health conditions can present with similar symptoms. If you are concerned that your friend or family member may have BPD, it's important **to encourage them to seek a professional diagnosis from a mental health provider.** With the right treatment and support, people with BPD can learn to manage their symptoms **and live fulfilling lives.** ****How do I know if my manager at work has borderline personality disorder?**** This one has two disclaimers because in a workplace setting, identifying and pointing out mental health issues in others can be the third rail of HR no no’s. **ONE**: It's important to remember that it's not appropriate or ethical to diagnose someone with a mental health condition, including borderline personality disorder (BPD), without their consent or a professional assessment from a mental health provider. However, there are **some common behaviors** that **may be** exhibited by a manager with BPD that you can look out for: 1. Intense emotions: Managers with BPD may have intense and unpredictable emotions, which can be difficult to manage in a professional setting. They may become angry or upset easily, and may struggle to regulate their emotions in response to stressful situations. 2. Impulsive behavior: Managers with BPD may engage in impulsive and potentially harmful behaviors, such as making rash decisions without considering the consequences. 3. Splitting: Splitting is a common behavior in people with BPD, in which they see people as either "all good" or "all bad." This can lead to extreme reactions to perceived slights or mistakes by employees, and may cause the manager to engage in erratic or inappropriate behavior. 4. Fear of abandonment: Managers with BPD may have an intense fear of abandonment, which can lead to them being overly critical or demanding of their employees. They may have difficulty trusting others, and may react strongly to perceived betrayals or rejections. 5. Intense and unstable relationships: Managers with BPD may struggle with building and maintaining stable relationships with their employees. They may have difficulty managing conflicts or giving constructive feedback, and may have a high turnover rate among their staff. **TWO**, it's important to remember that **not everyone with BPD will exhibit all of these behaviors**, and that other mental health conditions can present with similar symptoms. If you are concerned about your manager's behavior, it may be helpful to seek support from a human resources representative or a mental health provider. Now for the tough question. ****When should you leave a BPD mate or create distance from a BPD friend or family member?**** Dealing with a loved one who has borderline personality disorder (BPD) can be a difficult and exhausting experience. People with BPD often exhibit intense emotions, impulsive behavior, and difficulty with interpersonal relationships. While it's important to offer support and understanding to those with BPD, there may come a time when it's advisable to leave the relationship. ****Here are some signs that it MAY be time to consider ending a relationship with a mate, friend, or family member with BPD:**** **1. Your own mental health is suffering:** If the relationship is causing you stress, anxiety, or depression, it's important to prioritize your own mental health. Constant conflict and emotional upheaval can take a toll on your well-being, and it may be necessary to take a step back from the relationship in order to protect your own mental health. **2. The relationship is toxic:** If the relationship is characterized by abuse, manipulation, or other toxic behaviors, it may be necessary to end it in order to protect yourself. It's not healthy to be in a relationship that is emotionally or physically damaging, regardless of whether or not the other person has BPD. **3. The person is refusing treatment:** While BPD is a treatable disorder, some people may refuse to seek help or engage in therapy. If the person is not willing to work on their issues or is resistant to treatment, it may be difficult to maintain a healthy relationship with them. **4. The relationship is one-sided:** If you feel like you're constantly giving and the other person is not reciprocating, it may be time to reassess the relationship. Relationships should be a two-way street, and it's important to have your needs met as well. If you find yourself in a situation where leaving a relationship with someone with BPD is necessary, it's important to **do so in a way that is **respectful and compassionate**,** which is often extremely difficult because there are aspects of a person with BPD that are extremely attractive and desirable. *However, that which is extremely attractive and desirable is also very dangerous. * It may be helpful to have a support system in place, such as a therapist or a trusted friend, to help you navigate the process. Remember, ending a relationship with someone with BPD is not a decision to be taken lightly, but it may be necessary in order to protect your own well-being. column1: Why do people in Western countries leave their elderly people at care homes and nursing homes?
column3: The generalizations in this question are astounding. As a Westerner who is both a citizen of the United States and a European country, I can say the following:My 86 year old maternal grandmother has been living with us for over a year. She suffers from severe schizophrenia and for several months experienced multiple episodes per week that would keep us awake for over 24 hours. Her condition is now somewhat stable, but she is bedridden (by CHOICE, might I add) and the daily diaper changes take a toll on both me and my mother physically as well as mentally. The cost of senior care homes in this country is extremely high, otherwise we would have put her in one due to the fact that her mental illness and bedridden state impinge on our ability to move on with our lives and stay out of the house for more than a couple of hours at a time (this applies to my mother more than me).My 85 year old paternal grandmother is still extremely lucid and somewhat mobile. She recently sold the family home after living on her own for several years and moved in with my Uncle and Aunt. My Uncle, her son, spent the better part of a year building an addition on their house so that she would have her own space and independence, whilst simultaneously being able to have someone nearby at all times to keep her company or take care of her in the eventuality that something happens.My second cousin’s mother (i.e. my great-aunt) suffered from Alzheimer’s for many years before passing away in 2013. She lived at home with my cousin, who was also able to hire someone to come by daily and help care for her. Her twin sister, my other great-aunt, lived in Florida, in an elderly retirement community, where she had been for decades BY CHOICE before passing away last year. Nevertheless, my cousin would fly down to see her every month. As my great aunt’s condition deteriorated, other members of our family began to take charge of her wellbeing and spend more time in Florida, as well as hiring a personal caretaker to look after her when they themselves could not be physically present.The whole point of this is to counter this idea that Westerners simply abandon their elderly family members as soon as they get the chance. I mean, seriously, what complete and utter BS. Yes, many elderly people are abandoned daily, but that doesn’t automatically make it the standard. True, I am speaking from my personal experience in giving you the above examples, but much of what I’m conveying is not unique to me. Many friends and acquaintances have gone through similar things. Furthermore, these examples illustrate that there are levels to the care that the elderly can receive. Many end up living with and being cared for by their families, but others (such as my great-aunt in Florida) choose to live independently whilst being administered a certain level of care and having their families keep an eye on them. Honestly, is that so wrong? I hate this idea that just because you’re old you should automatically be pitied or looked upon as “lonely,”when many actually try to prolong their independence for as long as possible, or even make the CHOICE to move to a retirement center. Being old shouldn’t mean you lose a sense of yourself as a person. As you can see, money is also an important factor in how an elderly person might be cared for by their family. Many of my family members have the privilege of having enough money for things like retirement communities or building additions on houses, but then there is my first example, wherein my mother and I are stuck caring for a bedridden elderly lady with an exteme mental health condition. My mother has been relegated to sleeping on the couch and her back is suffering enormously from the physical strain of changing a grown woman’s diaper twice a day, amongst the many other strenuous tasks. I’m not saying that we are poor by any means, but as stated before, the costs of elderly care homes (including the State-funded ones) are sky high. If we had the funds, would it be so bad to put my grandmother into a home? A place where PAID PROFESSIONALS would care for her, as opposed to two unqualified women who are being held back from many of their other duties in life. I really take issue with romanticizing the sacrifices you make for your family. Sacrifice is indeed a noble thing, but when it consistently comes at such a great cost (and often falls upon the WOMEN of the family), it affects society as a whole. There are limits to how much one can give. Putting an elderly person into a home also does not automatically equal abandonment. Many family members make efforts to visit and spend time with their elderly relative at whatever home they’ve been placed in. If a home ends up being the healthier option for specific individuals, why automatically label it a bad thing? Apologies for the extemely long response. I just felt that, by highlighting my personal experience in regards to caring for the elderly, some stereotypes about how Western society functions could be challenged.

column1: What is the scariest situation you've been in?
column3: I’d seen my fair share of awful things up until 2021. I had lived through several incidents that easily could’ve landed me dead. Yet, I had never felt an unrelenting, urgent sense of fear until I was committed to an “institution”. My life, for a few weeks, was a psychological horror. I can’t condense it all, but I’ll try. As a woman, I’m used to underlying misogyny affecting my social interactions. I’m used to people being misinformed about depression and PTSD and addiction in general. I’m used to seemingly mundane social nuances that arise from these identities, but for the most part, I could always choose to block the encounters out and continue with my day. It becomes a totally different matter when the bias affects you systematically and you can’t run away. One day, I was committed to a behavioral reform drug rehabilitation center, funded by the state and partnered with the Department of Corrections. Ironically, I was not sent there through a criminal court process. A family member petitioned for it in civil court, and I was taken away for involuntary commitment through what’s known as Casey’s Law, an emergency avenue to have people involuntarily committed to rehab in the wake of the opioid epidemic. I did not have the same rights I would have in a criminal court. The petitioner chose the facility without realizing it was not appropriate for my needs. I had no chemical dependence on alcohol, but I did have a serious problem - I would drink to black out once a week at my worst, and had been arrested, which was more than enough to meet the criteria for substance abuse disorder in the DSM-V. I won’t go too much into the process, but originally, the deal was that I was to be released when the center said so, but not held for more than a year. Few people “graduated” from the program before 8 or 9 months. I had always known at an intuitive level that alcoholics and addicts are treated as subhuman, like children, like nothing, but I had never had to face the stigma before. Suddenly, I had nurses who wouldn’t believe me when I said I didn’t have any withdrawals. They didn’t believe me when I said the amount I usually drank. They didn’t believe me when I told them I don’t need religion. Of course, they wouldn’t call it religion. To me, there is nothing more terrifying than hearing these words as an adult who is of sound mind:“You think you’re suicidal, but you’re just spiritually sick, Amy. What did therapy ever do for you? You need to find a higher power.”“You think ‘science’ is the answer to everything. You need to abandon your pride and trust us. We know more about the solution than you.”“You don’t know what’s best for you. You don’t have to question everything, you know. Have faith.”“Don’t call your family complaining about this place or you will lose all contact with the outside world until further notice.”“Until everyone can stop gossiping, you’re all forbidden to speak until further notice. Anyone caught speaking extends the time for everyone.”“We know you smoked weed. Don’t lie. You’re not well. Either you’re lying, or you don’t know.” (I did NOT smoke weed. The closest thing I can think is that I ran a 5K like a good program participant, which spiked the THC levels in my system.)“Shh, don’t say that out loud. You’ll get in trouble,” or, “I can’t say what I want. I don’t want to get restarted or get a contract.”“You are a criminal, or else you wouldn’t be here. You need to abandon your ways. We know you lived in the madness, and you think you’re better than the rest of us, so you lie. You need to find God or you’ll always live an unmanageable life.”“Your ‘sister’ left because you all told your war stories, and now she’s going to go back out and use. Her blood is on your hands.”“You are no different than anyone else here.” False. I was no better. My needs were still wildly different than the majority of the women there, most of which having served long sentences in prison or having lived on the streets for years and years. I needed mental health treatment for PTSD, not criminal mentality reform. So, like the others, I ended up writing a mandatory paper on my criminal/jail mentality every night, and I had to make stuff up.I knew I would never graduate the program unless I either let myself be brainwashed (not possible) or pretended to go along with their cult-like process. I had to shush my family on the phone for discussing drawbacks to the program, but the person sitting in on the call had heard, and the damage was done. The next day, staff sat me down and told me I had failed a drug test for weed, and they know I snuck out and smoked, so they were restarting me in the program and I had to walk around in scrubs in front of everyone and start the months long process again. IMPOSSIBLE. They didn’t believe me! It was a conspiracy and I was powerless to fight it. I finally felt myself going mad and began to have self harm urges, and suicidal ideation. My dissociation worsened, and it all felt like a horrible dream. I begged the program director to let me go to a psych ward. She finally relented after trying her “you’re just spiritually sick” approach on me so many times. She said I’d go for a couple days and come back. The people at the crisis unit were horrified at my experiences, and although normal policy was to send me back after a couple of days, they held me until I could organize a transfer elsewhere with the court and local legal authorities. I spent a month at a normal rehab, where they respected that you were an adult and an individual, addressed mental health concerns, and offered multiple pathways to recovery. I’ve been sober ever since. Every day I take a walk outside and I’m grateful for the personal freedom I have. Once, if you’d asked me my personal hell, I couldn’t have told you. Now I know for sure. I still have nightmares about that place every couple of weeks, if not more, but I’m sure they’ll fade with time. I’m proud of myself for keeping my head and sticking to my guns, but I worry that the program director, in all her vindictiveness, will completely refuse to get help for another person in need of psychiatric intervention, because I was the one that got away (and didn’t go to jail for it).

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: I have suffered personally.But I do not want to go specifics. Death visits one's family and take away some.There are no specific rules.There is no seniority based on age,(a boy of ten may precede a man of seventy.)Health,richness or poverty, responsibilities, position,rank,country,caste,creed,colour,nothing matters.Again it comes in various times…..while sleeping,eating,travelling,playing,working,flying in the air,diving in the water,etc Then the way it comes also varies..natural,accident, various diseases..heart attack,cancer etc. Death has no consideration for age..earliest could be immediately after birth and latest 100 plus years. Again no differentiation..between a saint and a Satan, a good person and a bad person, between kind and cruel, man and woman, person of good habit and a person of bad habit. Another peculiar aspect is no advance warning is given to anybody. It just comes and takes away. Somebody will be hale and healthy..one minute..no more. Somebody is bed ridden.. but years pass by before death makes its presence. No analysis possible and hence no answer. Such being the case what one can do in life.Know very well that one has to go along with death. Unknown factors..time,date,year,cause,place,how and why. Be ready to welcome it anytime. That is mental PREPARTION. Know death will take away oneself,parents,children.etc etc just like that.Nobody knows what will be the order since there is none.DECIDE NOT TO BE AFRAID OF DEATH. Now the question is how to face the loss of a family member. A million dollar question. In spite of knowing the philosophy of death in detail, it is very difficult to bear the loss. Again this depends on various factors.. very old,very sick where death will minimise suffering,..anyway loss affects one.Face it philosophically and continue living.Otherwise one's life will become miserable.
column9: When near and dear ones are snatched away by death we are simply lost. There is a vacuum which cannot be filled ..Though we know the philosophy of death this tremendous clinging on to life exists. Somehow,we do not know why, we cling to life,; we cannot give it up. We think we shall live eternally. So in spite of the loss, however terrible it is,our life has to move on. This moving on varies from person to person.Those who can understand the philosophy of life could make this movement smooth and easy. (of course with the memories of the departed one keeping our mind busy). Here is another factor..the loss cannot be brushed away. People would say “”time will heal everything"” Absolutely wrong. This is like the burning charcoal. When there is no activity for some time it is covered by ashes giving an impression that it has burnt out.The moment there is a wisp of air the ashes fly away and you can see the burning charcoal.This is the case with those who have lost somebody dear.The sorrow may not be visible outside but at times it pours out.Time has no relevance. Even twenty or thirty years do not make any difference.

column1: Can parents' mental health get worse as they age?
column3: Yes or it could get better, it all depends on the individual. Certain medications that people take for other medical conditions may cause mental health issues as a side effect. If parents are aging, they may be taking more medications for health problems that come with age. Other reasons why a parents’ mental health may get worse are that some older people feel lonely, which would cause depression to get worse. They may feel that the signs of aging are depressing to them as well. They lose family members and friends through the years and that can affect mental health as well. There are some people whose mental health gets better with age. They may feel less pressured because they no longer have to work and have a ton of responsibilities. So this gives them more free time to themselves to work on their mental health and well-being. It all depends on the circumstances in your parents’ life as well as other factors that might be beyond their control.

column1: Is it true that everyone suffers from some mental illness?
column3: The study of psychiatry if a fairly young field, in the sense that it only really took off after Freud, who made the subject have mass appeal with his books which were daring and (to some extent) scandalous in his time. Since then, much theory and study has gone into the intricacies of human nature, the organic and behavioral problems which constitute mental health impairment, and its proper management. Serious mental illness was barbarically treated in antiquity, and in our current age, there are still huge flaws in the treatment of the mentally ill. Yet the mind is as vulnerable as the body, there are few who have not suffered from a viral infection, currently have a disease, or will develop a disease sometime within their lifetime. Yet less stigma is associated with the vulnerabilities of the human body than the human mind. Lets take for example the evolution of chronic and traumatic psychological stress in combat. The term posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has become a household name since its first appearance in 1980 in the 3rd edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-lll) published by the American Psychiatric Association, In This diagnosis is associated with the legacy of the Vietnam War disaster. Earlier conflicts had given birth to terms, such as “soldier's heart, ” “shell shock,” and “war neurosis.” The latter diagnosis was equivalent to the névrose de guerre and Kriegsneurose of French and German scientific literature. This condition has been observed since antiquity, but proper identification of its symptoms, its progression, prognosis and treatment have only recently been elucidated despite having been briefly mentioned from the Bible, the Tale of Gilgamesh, and the writings of Shakespeare. This condition was treated in different manners, but it is a legitimate psychiatric condition, not one borne of cowardice, but of the fragility of the human mind to acute intense stress. It’s easy to see a broken bone sticking out of some patients skin due to excessive trauma or stress, but the illnesses of the mind are not readily apparent. There is no shame in having mental health illness, and chances are most will suffer some form of mental illness or another during their lifetime. The point of defining these illnesses is that they impair social functioning, cause distress, and inhibit normal functioning of a patient. This may not affect the patient, but can cause collateral damage to close members of a patient, and in some cases cause inter-generational mental illness. It is a very common aspect of the human condition. Take for example, an elderly couple and one of the partner dies. The normal response of grief, medically referred as Bereavement. Bereavement may be temporary, but is still best served by social support and support groups. Bereavement can also become Complicated Bereavement in which symptoms may include suicidal ideation, depression, and severe impairment which would require more intense treatment with the possibility of psychiatric medications. Losing a loved one is common, and failure to understand the condition of the surviving spouse is detrimental, considering the adverse consequences that can arise. The attitude of indifference (a just walk it off mentality), is not only insensitive, it is based on a woeful lack of understanding of human psychology. And losing friends, family, loved ones, etc. Is an almost quintessential part of being human. Mental health is like physical health, you want to beef up your mental health, then dissect the framework of your mind and find your weaknesses, flaws, and failures in social functioning and address them. Strengthening of the mind, just as one would strengthen the body at a gym, allows oneself to improve social functioning and handle greater strength as well as develop insight and introspection into oneself. Most people don’t even know what their defense mechanisms are, their coping strategies, their links between cognition-feelings-and behaviors (addressed in Cognitive Behavior Therapy), etc. Mental health is the dominion of the human mind and requires work, as does the improvement of the human body through exercise and proper diet, and its strengthening through exercise. Simply put, we have become better at identifying diseases of the mind in the same manner we have of the human body. The diseases were always there, we simply have become far better at recognizing them and learning to treat them.
