column1: What is "borderline" about borderline personality disorder?
column3: I would have to say borderline of thought processes and emotions. It's the border of what an average person would think and feel and someone who is suffering from BPD. The Mayo Clinic says this about BPD. “Borderline personality disorder is a mental health disorder that impacts the way you think and feel about yourself and others, causing problems functioning in everyday life. It includes a pattern of unstable intense relationships, distorted self-image, extreme emotions and impulsiveness. With borderline personality disorder, you have an intense fear of abandonment or instability, and you may have difficulty tolerating being alone. Yet inappropriate anger, impulsiveness and frequent mood swings may push others away, even though you want to have loving and lasting relationships. Borderline personality disorder usually begins by early adulthood. The condition seems to be worse in young adulthood and may gradually get better with age. If you have borderline personality disorder, don't get discouraged. Many people with this disorder get better over time with treatment and can learn to live satisfying lives. Symptoms Borderline personality disorder affects how you feel about yourself, how you relate to others and how you behave. Signs and symptoms may include:An intense fear of abandonment, even going to extreme measures to avoid real or imagined separation or rejectionA pattern of unstable intense relationships, such as idealizing someone one moment and then suddenly believing the person doesn't care enough or is cruelRapid changes in self-identity and self-image that include shifting goals and values, and seeing yourself as bad or as if you don't exist at allPeriods of stress-related paranoia and loss of contact with reality, lasting from a few minutes to a few hoursImpulsive and risky behavior, such as gambling, reckless driving, unsafe sex, spending sprees, binge eating or drug abuse, or sabotaging success by suddenly quitting a good job or ending a positive relationshipSuicidal threats or behavior or self-injury, often in response to fear of separation or rejectionWide mood swings lasting from a few hours to a few days, which can include intense happiness, irritability, shame or anxietyOngoing feelings of emptinessInappropriate, intense anger, such as frequently losing your temper, being sarcastic or bitter, or having physical fightsWhen to see a doctor If you're aware that you have any of the signs or symptoms above, talk to your doctor or a mental health provider. If you notice signs or symptoms in a family member or friend, talk to that person about seeing a doctor or mental health provider. But you can't force someone to seek help. If the relationship causes you significant stress, you may find it helpful to see a therapist yourself. Causes As with other mental disorders, the causes of borderline personality disorder aren't fully understood. In addition to environmental factors — such as a history of child abuse or neglect — borderline personality disorder may be linked to:Genetics. Some studies of twins and families suggest that personality disorders may be inherited or strongly associated with other mental disorders among family members.Brain abnormalities. Some research has shown changes in certain areas of the brain involved in emotion regulation, impulsivity and aggression. In addition, certain brain chemicals that help regulate mood, such as serotonin, may not function properly.Risk factors Some factors related to personality development can increase the risk of developing borderline personality disorder. These include:Hereditary predisposition. You may be at a higher risk if a close relative — your mother, father, brother or sister — has the same or a similar disorder.Stressful childhood. Many people with the disorder report being sexually or physically abused or neglected during childhood. Some people have lost or were separated from a parent or close caregiver when they were young or had parents or caregivers with substance misuse or other mental health issues. Others have been exposed to hostile conflict and unstable family relationships.Personality. Personality traits that include impulsiveness and aggression may play a role in the development of borderline personality disorder.Complications Borderline personality disorder can damage many areas of your life. It can negatively affect intimate relationships, jobs, school, social activities and self-image, resulting in:Repeated job changes or lossesNot completing an educationMultiple legal issues, such as jail timeConflict-filled relationships, marital stress or divorceSelf-injury, such as cutting or burning, and frequent hospitalizationsInvolvement in abusive relationshipsUnplanned pregnancies, sexually transmitted infections, motor vehicle accidents and physical fights due to impulsive and risky behaviorAttempted or completed suicideIn addition, you may have other mental health disorders, such as:DepressionAlcohol or other substance misuseAnxiety disordersEating disordersBipolar disorderPost-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)Other personality disorders”But always seek help and understanding from a licensed therapist, counselor, psychiatrist or psychologist for any confusion about any mental illness.

column1: Is it possible to diagnose a person with borderline personality disorder if they became emotionally unstable when they were manic or depressed?
column3: I wish I knew why people think diagnosis is worth doing. I wish I knew why people ask so many questions about diagnosis. I think that people misunderstand what diagnosis is and what purpose it serves. Diagnosis in mental health does not imply effective treatment. Diagnosis does not work the same way in mental health as it does in physical health. In physical health, the implication is that if you have a correct diagnosis you can provide a treatment that will fix the problem. Even if that were the case in physical health, it is most certainly not the case in mental health. You can treat mental health problems whether you have a diagnosis or not. That's because the only person who can fix a mental health problem is the person who is sick. The treatment process is always experimental. Try things to see what works. Diagnosis does not help psychiatrists or therapists figure out what will work in advance. It really doesn't matter what label to put on a pattern of behavior that fits in the category of mental illness. What matters is support for that person. What matters is the person coming to understand themselves and figuring out how to change their behavior so they can get what they want out of life. What matters is making an effort and not getting immediate results, but still trying. It takes years to make changes. There are no pills that fix mental health problems. The only things that work involve changing relationships, which means it is a group process, not just an individual process. But it's a group process where you can only change yourself. You can't force others to change. So that makes it very difficult. A lot of people despair at the impossibility of having control over others and then give up on themselves. So treatment involves having hope that if you work on yourself, it will also affect others, but the effect on others will be very indirect, as will the effect on yourself. Diagnosis doesn't affect this process. You can work to recover whether or not you have a diagnosis. The accuracy of the diagnosis is irrelevant. The only thing that matters is the work the individual does and the compassion they get from others. But they can't control whether other people are compassionate. Maybe they can try to find compassionate people, but no one has control over the people currently in their lives. Either those people are compassionate or they aren't. And if they aren't, it is easier to find compassionate people than it is to wait until the existing people in your life become compassionate. That's why so many people with mental illness lose all their friends, and often lose connection with family members. Often, we end up starting over and making new friends. If we're really lucky, we might be able to learn how to share ourselves honestly with family members. Sometimes family members might become more compassionate over time. But we have no control over that process. Diagnosis doesn't matter. Treatment does matter. The treatment that works is the same no matter what mental health diagnosis you have. You have to come to understand yourself and take action to change your behavior. You need to surround yourself with compassionate, non judgemental people. Unfortunately, looking to the psychological profession for compassionate non judgemental people is not a guaranteed solution, since unfortunately large number of people in that profession really don't know how to be compassionate and non-judgmental. So, for the most part, people identified as mentally ill have to fix themselves. It's the only realistic solution.

column1: What is the best early morning habit for success?
column3: 1. Wake up early There are a host of benefits for early risers. They get better sleep, tend to eat fewer calories, and are less prone to depression. Also, early risers are more productive and have time for exercise, eating breakfast, and other positive morning activities like reading, time with family, and reflection. Start by getting up five minutes earlier a day for the first week. Slowly set your alarm back by a few minutes a week until you reach your optimal time. 2. Drink a full glass of water in the morning Drinking a big glass of water immediately after you awaken has many health benefits. It purifies your colon and improves the stomach’s ability to absorb nutrients. A healthy digestive system hydrated properly gives you glowing skin, as water removes the toxins from the blood. Drinking water also improves the creation of new blood cells and muscle cells, and helps you lose weight. Before you go to bed at night, put a glass of water by your bed. After your alarm goes off, but before you get out of bed, drink the full glass. 3. Make your bed According to a Navy Seal, Admiral William McRaven, making the bed may be the best way to start off your day. He says, “If you make your bed every morning you will have accomplished the first task of the day. It will give you a small sense of pride and it will encourage you to do another task and another and another. By the end of the day, that one task completed will have turned into many tasks completed. Making your bed will also reinforce the fact that little things in life matter.” Making your bed every morning is correlated with better productivity and stronger skills at sticking with a budget. 4. Set 3-4 daily goals Setting three to four big goals for your day first thing in the morning gives you benchmarks for daily productivity. It also helps you create specific tasks to address your bigger monthly or quarterly goals. Three or four goals is a good number, as they can be spaced out during the day. You can do two in the morning before lunch and two in the afternoon, or complete one in the morning, one at midday, and one in the late afternoon. Three or four goals isn’t overwhelming — it’s realistic. If you finish them early, you can always set more. 5. Eat breakfast with your family Research shows eating breakfast as a family has a positive impact on the health of family members, particularly adolescents. A University of Minnesota study found that eating together as a family improved diet quality and lowered the risk for becoming overweight. It’s also beneficial for your family relationships, as you begin your day with connection and communication. 6. Perform your hardest goal first Mark Twain suggest, ““Eat a live frog first thing in the morning and nothing worse will happen to you the rest of the day.” You don’t have to eat a frog, but getting that weighty, dreaded task or goal out of your way gives you energy for the rest of your day. Procrastination creates anxiety and makes you feel bad about yourself. 7. Exercise early It’s not easy to get your body moving first thing in the morning, but research shows people who exercise in the morning stick to their workout plans better than those who wait until later. Also, working out in the morning can actually increase the positive impact that exercise has on your heart, and morning exercise helps your body burn calories faster and more efficiently throughout the day. 8. Set a timer for productivity To increase your productivity, set a timer for a period of time during which you work on a project or goal without stopping. The timer motivates you to work harder without quitting, and it gives you the comfort of knowing you’ll have a break within a certain amount of time. This is known as the Pomodoro Technique, developed by Francesco Cirillo in the late 1980’s, whereby you work in timed intervals of traditionally 25 minutes, separated by short breaks. This time management method is based on the idea that frequent breaks improve mental agility. 9. Remove distractions Sustained focus is the cornerstone of productivity and success. The increasing number of distractions around us make in nearly impossible to focus unless we mindfully eliminate them. Over 90% of (the US) population reports they multitask, performing one task while distracted with another. These distractions affect memory and performance, but resisting distractions builds a strong bond in your memory, allowing you to hold on to your original task. 10. Batch your tasks Batching your tasks is a form of time management where you dedicate blocks of time to similar tasks so you can decrease distractions and improve productivity. Batching helps you boost creativity and mental sharpness, as well as decrease fatigue, procrastination, and stress. After each batch of similar tasks, you take a planned break to recharge, and then move on to another batch of tasks. Developing these morning habits will be life-changing. Over time you’ll notice you’re getting more done, you feel more relaxed and focused, and you feel happier and more motivated in general. If you want to begin creating these morning habits, begin with one habit at a time. Work on it for six to eight weeks until it becomes automatic, and then begin another new habit.my channel: https://www.youtube.com/c/korchipatikishorekumar

column1: What is the difference between anxiety, stress, and tension?
column3: I’M SO STRESSED OUT! From the NATIONAL INSTITUTE of MENTAL HEALTH Feeling overwhelmed? Read this fact sheet to learn whether it’s stress or anxiety, and what you can do to cope. Is it stress or anxiety? Life can be stressful—you may feel stressed about performance at school, traumatic events (such as a pandemic, natural disaster, or act of violence), or a life change. Everyone feels stress from time to time. What is stress? Stress is the physical or mental response to an external cause, such as having a lot of homework or having an illness. A stressor may be a one-time or short-term occurrence, or it can happen repeatedly over a long time. What is anxiety? Anxiety is your body’s reaction to stress and can occur even if there is no current threat. Stress vs. Anxiety If that anxiety doesn’t go away and begins to interfere with your life, it could affect your health. You could experience problems with sleeping, or with your immune, digestive, cardiovascular, and reproductive systems. You also may be at higher risk for developing a mental illness such as an anxiety disorder or depression. More information about anxiety disorders is available at Anxiety Disorders. So, how do you know when to seek help? STRESS: • Generally is a response to an external cause, such as taking a big test or arguing with a friend. • Goes away once the situation is resolved. • Can be positive or negative. For example, it may inspire you to meet a deadline, or it may cause you to lose sleep. BOTH STRESS AND ANXIETY: Both stress and anxiety can affect your mind and body. You may experience symptoms such as: • Excessive worry • Uneasiness • Tension ( muscle tension, feeling tightness) • Headaches or body pain • High blood pressure • Loss of sleep ANXIETY: • Generally is internal, meaning it’s your reaction to stress. • Usually involves a persistent feeling of apprehension or dread that doesn’t go away, and that interferes with how you live your life. • Is constant, even if there is no immediate threat. It’s important to manage your stress. Everyone experiences stress, and sometimes that stress can feel overwhelming. You may be at risk for an anxiety disorder if it feels like you can’t manage the stress and if the symptoms of your stress: • Interfere with your everyday life. • Cause you to avoid doing things. • Seem to be always present. Coping With Stress and Anxiety: Learning what causes or triggers your stress and what coping techniques work for you can help reduce your anxiety and improve your daily life. It may take trial and error to discover what works best for you. Here are some activities you can try when you start to feel overwhelmed: • Keep a journal. • Download an app that provides relaxation exercises (such as deep breathing or visualization) or tips for practicing mindfulness, which is a psychological process of actively paying attention to the present moment. • Exercise, and make sure you are eating healthy, regular meals. • Stick to a sleep routine, and make sure you are getting enough sleep. • Avoid drinking excess caffeine such as soft drinks or coffee. • Identify and challenge your negative and unhelpful thoughts. • Reach out to your friends or family members who help you cope in a positive way. For more information about stress, visit 5 Things You Should Know About Stress. Recognize When You Need More Help If you are struggling to cope, or the symptoms of your stress or anxiety won’t go away, it may be time to talk to a professional. Psychotherapy (also called “talk therapy”) and medication are the two main treatments for anxiety, and many people benefit from a combination of the two. If you or someone you know has a mental illness, is struggling emotionally, or has concerns about their mental health, there are ways to get help. Find more information on the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH) website at Help for Mental Illnesses. If you are in immediate distress or are thinking about hurting yourself, call the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline toll-free at 1-800-273-TALK (8255) or the toll-free TTY number at 1-800-799-4TTY (4889). You also can text the Crisis Text Line (HELLO to 741741) or go to the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline website at Home. column1: Why would a mother lose affection and love for her children? Like becoming numb and not feeling any affection or desire to be with them or have them near her. She just wants to be left alone.
column3: Depression is a common cause of those type of symptoms. If it’s shortly after childbirth, it could be post-partum depression. Both are treatable but require support. If this is you or a close friend or family member, find a local support center, talk to a doctor, or in the US, call a local depression or suicide prevention hotline; either can help you find the mental support you (or your friend) need to get and stay mentally healthy. If you’re religious, also (not in replacement of, but in addition to) talk to a local religious leader. Many are trained in helping with mental health conditions, and some churches and synagogues have mental health support services (with trained and/or certified) counselors, usually for free. For new moms, local Moms groups can also be a wealth of information and support. Search the Internet for one in your area or ask around. People are here here to help. column1: Is it expensive to be poor in America?
column3: Living in poverty is expensive emotionally, mentally, physically and financially. This can mean:becoming isolated from family and friends;lacking hope and feeling powerless and excluded with little control over the decisions that affect your day to day life;lacking information about the supports and services available to you;having problems in getting your basic needs met and accessing decent housing, health services and schools and life long learning opportunities;living in an unsafe neighborhoods with high levels of crime and violence and poor environmental conditions or in a remote and isolated rural area;going without very basic necessities because you may not be able to afford essential utilities like water, heat and electricity or to buy healthy food or new clothing or to use public transport;being unable to afford to buy medicines or visit the dentist;living from day to day with no savings or reserves for times of crisis such as losing a job or falling ill and thus falling into debt;being exploited and forced into illegal situations;experiencing racism and discrimination;being unable to participate in normal social and recreational life such as going to dinner or cinema or sports events or visiting friends or buying birthday presents for family members.Alcohol & substance abuse, from kids in African slums to adults in the US, this is a very common self-destructing habit often taken as a way to cope with huge amounts of stress and... well, despair;Too many people believe that being poor is easy. After all, the poor get profound government benefits, right? It's not as easy for them as you may think. Being poor is more expensive than being in the upper or middle classes in more ways than one. In America, we villianize the poor.

column1: Which K-pop group made you cry?
column3: This is Super Junior. You’ve probably heard of them. They are one of the most respected and famous K-Pop groups.And this is their leader Leeteuk. The group as a whole have suffered a lot, but him especially.When Super Junior debuted, they received a lot of hardships, because they were the first group to have so many members (12 at debut, but Kyuhyun joined a year later), and they were the first group to have a fully foreign member, Han Geng. They received a lot of backlash and were branded a flop, and told by Lee Soo-Man himself that they would only last 6 months. This surely would have taken a toll of Leeteuk, seeing his group suffer like this. But that isn’t the main part of this sad story at all. In 2006, while returning from Donghae’s fathers funeral, Heechul crashed his car when a tire malfunctioned. He fractured his leg in five places, including his femur, knee and ankle. He also ripped his tongue. He had 6 hours of surgery. He had metal rods inserted into his leg, most of which are still in there. Because of this injury getting worse over time he hasn’t been able to fully participate in comebacks since 2015. You can assume this would also really affect the leaders mental health. But again, this wasn’t the end of Leeteuks hardships. Then, in 2007, Super Junior had another car crash. Leeteuk, Shindong, Eunhyuk and Kyuhyun were driving together when their car overturned. Shindong and Eunhyuk suffered minor injuries, but Leeteuk and Kyuhyun were badly hurt. Leeteuk was bleeding a lot, and required 30 stitches on his face, and 150 stitches on his hip. Kyuhyun was hurt the worst. He was flung 20–30 metres out of the car and he said his lower body was paralysed. He suffered many injuries, including one of his ribs puncturing a lung. Kyuhyun went into a coma. The doctor said he would have to do a surgery on Kyuhyuns throat, which would mean he would never sing again. Kyuhyuns father begged them to find another way, as Kyuhyun loved singing so much. Another doctor found another way, but Kyuhyun was given a 10% survival chance. Luckily, he survived. Also, Leeteuk was really badly hurt in the car accident, but when the ambulances came, and when they rushed to him first, he told them to help Kyuhyun. Despite his own pain, he wanted to save the others. If you watch the video, you can faintly hear him call for Kyuhyun when we is being stretchered onto the ambulance. Then, in 2009, Han Geng left the group and sued SM for mistreatment. He said that because of SM, he got gastritis and kidney disease. Kibum also became inactive in 2009, and he left officially in 2015. This surely would have affected Leeteuk knowing his members suffered like this.In 2014, Leeteuk suffered extreme tragedy within his family. He was serving in the army at the time. Leeteuks father was looking after Leeteuks grandparents, who both had dementia. Leeteuks father was low on money and severely depressed. On the 6th of January 2014, Leeteuks father killed his grandparents before committing suicide. Leeteuk said he was already suffering depression at the time and this only could have made it worse. He was given emergency leave to attend their funeral. After returning, he was said to be so severely depressed that he was offered early release from the army, which is extremely rare in Korea. I’m censoring the faces in the photo out of respect. In 2017, Leeteuk suffered another suicide of someone close to him. SHINee Jonghyun committed suicide on December 18th 2017. I could easily write an answer about how this makes me cry, but this answer is mainly about Leeteuk. Leeteuk had to carry his close friends coffin into a hearse, and given his public fight with depression, I’m sure this really hit him hard. Again I’m censoring faces.This story does have a happy ending though. Leeteuk seems to be much happier now. Sungmin and Han Geng are both married now, Kibum and Han Geng are still friends with the rest of Super Junior. Han Geng is publicly friends with Leeteuk, Heechul and Siwon still, and Kibum is publicly friends with Heechul. Zhoumi and Henry are both successful soloists, and again they are still friends with Super Junior. Not much is public about Kangin anymore, but I hope he is reflecting and improving himself. Also I know that Heechul was very close with Sulli so maybe Leeteuk was close with her but I’m not sure so I didn’t include that. Edit: Thanks for all the support on this post. I realised i completely forgot to mention the debt his father left him, the milk club and more. His father left him loads in debt after he died, which Leeteuk took hears to pay off. The milk club was a group formed by Leeteuk in 2009 for idols suffering from depression and anxiety. He wanted to help put idols who, like him, were suffering a lot. Some of the members were Yoona, Taeyeon, Onew and Yoochun. If there is one main thing people should take away from this, it is to be kinder to idols. While Leeteuk, Super Junior, and most idols may seem fine on the surface, you never know what they are feeling behind the scenes. I always see a terrible amount of hate for Leeteuk, Shindong, Yesung, Heechul, Siwon, Kyuhyun and Kangin, even though they are all lovely people. Please show some support to them as Kangin in particular is quite worrying. He is losing weight at an unhealthy rate, and he has not been practicing or promoting for 5 years, so it clearly is a separate issue. After the Caroline Flack tragedy, we all promised to be kind, so remember that, before sending hate to idols, or anyone.

column1: What is mental health?
column3: Your mental well-being affects how you think, feel, and behave. When you feel good about yourself and can cope with the pressures of daily life, you are in good mental health. If you have trouble coping with ordinary situations, it may be a sign of a mental health condition and needs to be treated right away. There is a range of mental health conditions a person can suffer from, including: bipolar disorder, anxiety, depression, schizophrenia, obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) There are several early warning signs that can indicate something may be affecting your mental health that you should be aware of. these can be one or number of the following: Thinking life is not worth living, losing interest in things you used to enjoy,mood swings or constantly feeling low, disturbed sleep, either not getting enough or sleeping too much, have difficulty concentrating or remembering things, eating less than normal or overeating: If you can relate to any of these warning sings, it's important that you seek help. Talk to a friend or family members or see a Psychiatrist. People can and do recover from mental health problems, recovery can be a process, does not always mean getting back to where you were before.will have ups and downs. requires commitment from you and support from your family and friends can allow you to lead a normal life. will involve finding your own ways of coping with life's challenges!

column1: Is the gun violence problem in America too far gone to solve, even if comprehensive gun control laws were passed with unanimous support by the house and senate?

column1: Do doctors lose empathy towards patients over time?
column3: I went with my uncle to a doctor’s appointment a couple of months ago. He had kidney stones that adversely impacted urine flow and caused troublesome symptoms. The doctor recommended having surgery, and there was nothing wrong with that. What clearly caught my attention is how he urged us to go for the operation. He looked silently at the scans and blood tests without bothering to look us in the face or explain anything. He had this unwavering grimace that I believe was truly startling, not only to his patients but also to his staff and assistants. His face was expressionless and cold. He didn’t elaborate on any of the details that are related to the operation or the risks that might come with it. It is as if empathy parted ways with his facial expressions a long time ago. Looking back, the whole experience was quite unnerving. If it were my decision, I would not have gone for the operation; at least I might have chosen the operation, but with another surgeon. I would never choose to go for an operation that is to be done by a surgeon with whom I feel frightened. It makes no sense. When I remembered this incident, I honestly thought of this bizarrely random question. Should physicians be more or less empathetic? It is hard to tell. This is a very confusing question that I do believe most senior doctors might turn their backs on and refuse to answer. The main hurdle with empathy when it comes to healthcare service is that oftentimes it is a double-edged sword. Sometimes, it could be beneficial for patients to feel that the physician in charge of their health problems is subject to the same intense emotions as they are. That he/she possesses an adequate level of compassion so that they feel safe and secure around him. At other times, it could prove to be fatal. When a patient suffers from an atrocious disease with a slim chance — if any — that he or she will recover completely, it is quite important as a physician to be as compassionate as you possibly can. At such times, when your hands are tight and there is very little you can do, compassion should be your closest friend. The one you lean on during those extremely dark times. And that is exactly why, as a junior physician, I have already decided not to pursue certain specialties, such as oncology. That is because I assume that many patients, if not most, have a bad prognosis. They are going through mental and physical anguish that is quite hard to comprehend. And hence, it will be remorselessly draining to have this kind of unwavering empathy towards each of them as you go through your daily work. But at other times, when you are overly empathetic and don’t control your emotions, this can lead to you making inaccurate decisions that might adversely affect the patients’ conditions. For instance, in most healthcare systems, particularly in developed countries, as a surgeon, it is not permissible to operate on one of your family members.This is greatly attributed to the fact that when you do so, things can be very tense in ways you can only imagine.When emotions get in the way, you are more likely to lose focus. And this could be catastrophic at times. You might start to panic when things go badly or when complications arise, and hence you lose that sharpness of thinking that you inevitably need to get back on track and fix whatever issues have arisen. That is why in certain medical specialties, such as emergency medicine, neurosurgery, and cardiac surgery, when the physician or surgeon in charge has little — if any — room for error, it is profoundly fundamental to gain control over your emotions. To not let your emotions take over and let you make the wrong decisions. It is an integral part of the training that we as physicians dread but yet have to go through, and many patients and their relatives might feel furious about it, but it is ultimately for the greater good.
column9: A good doctor will always be empathetic without being emotional. They are two very different things.

column1: How can I help my friend with depression?
column3: By getting them professional help. Period. Here is one of the harshest truths of life. Most people can't really be there for you. It isn't humanely possible. They will post about I am always here for you statuses and be there for people who are close to you, but in reality most of them aren't. Yes the world is full of good people, doesn't mean they are going to care about you. And whether they should or shouldn't, is not my thing to judge. And even if you want to be there for your friend, and they are going through clinical depression, and if you do not know how to protect yourself, and stay sane while caring for them, it can just be counter productive. Because depressed people can be very difficult to deal with. No amount of reassurance is sometimes enough for them. Depression isn't a fever that will just go away in a day, It's a long drawn chronic illness which is going to stay around for a long time, always lurking in the background rearing its ugly head the moment you slip up. You can't really get rid of it, the best you can do is learn how to deal with it, and life gets better after that. The battles become easier. So the moment you say you are going to be there for them, they are going to call you incessantly, and at all times and many a time give out sos calls when they are going through an episode. And they relapse. All the freaking time. Will you be ready for that kind of responsibility? Are you even prepared for that? That is something to ask yourself before promising something like that to a person with mental illness. What I can tell you from being a depression and suicidal ideation survivor, that this is your battle and many a times you will have to be alone. Thats why you should be counting on people who can actually help you as opposed to people who are supposed to help you. Like I never really count on my family or friends when I am having an episode. Why? Not because they don't love me. Because they aren't trained to help me and sometimes their conditioning is not enabled to help me or give me what I need. So I depend on my therapist. Who is professional, detached and does her job well as long as I keep paying her. Do you go to your parents and friends when you have a physical condition? No you go to a qualified doctor. The same way, when your mental health is affected, you need to find someone who is trained to help people like you and knows exactly what you need. Having said that, a support system is indeed essential. Family, friends, peers who understand you, are empathetic towards you, is a vital part of getting over depression. But it comes only after professional help. It can only act as an enhancement and not the core part of the treatment which can help you recover. If you have someone who is depressed in your family, stop with the talk with me, reach out to me shenanigans. Because you must realise you aren't equipped to help them, and by taking on responsibilities, you aren't capable of taking on and promising things you won't be able to stand by on, you are only going to worsen things further and screw them for good. So the most sensible thing to do is to refer them to someone trained to help them. And you must realise this, even though talking to people can feel very lofty and nice and give you the impression that you are helping them, actually you are not. Words aren't gonna do a lot in clinical depression, except perhaps give them a very short term rush of positivity that isn't going to last for long. And all they are going to do is relapse again. The only person who is trained to be your therapist, is your therapist. Professional help unfortunately has no substitute. Normal people around you ( and that includes Sadhus, shady life coaches and people with no qualification whatsover, trying to dupe you) cannot help you, in the way a professional can. Yes its costly. So I have to keep working hard to afford it. What if you don't have the money or cant afford it? Thats absolutely okay, you have to keep trying to find someone who can give you something close to therapy. Like friends going through the same thing. Like support groups both offline and online. There are many people on Facebook who give therapy for free or in return for donation to a charity of their choice. There are a lot of NGOs working for people with mental health issues. Please message me if you need information on that. Look up on that. But if you are only looking upto friends and family to help you, you are going to be disappointed because it will take sometime for you to find the right kind of people in your life who will understand what you are going through. I saw a ton of psychiatrists before I found the right one to help me. I had to wait for 8 years battling depression before I found a therapist that worked for me. You have to keep trying. But I completely agree that the mental health awareness in India is shitty. Parents, Teachers, and colleagues often don't understand. Mental health is still a huge stigma. Most schools, colleges and offices don't even have a certified therapist where the students and employees can go and talk to, if they are facing a mental crisis. My college, despite being a medical college didn't have a counsellor, let alone a therapist. Mental illness is looked down even more in medical colleges, and among the community of doctors so you can imagine the situation elsehwere, where people don't bother to educate themselves on mental health. And the problem with psychiatry is, most high rankers in Medical entrance examinations don't want to take psychiatry. My psychiatrist friend often jokes that “Jisko kuch nai milta woh leta hai psychiatry, par jiska koi nai hota uska hota hai psychiatrist!” ( People don't take psychiatry by choice, but a person who has no one to turn to, turns to a psychiatrist). And because of that, a lot of psychiatrists often focus on minting money, rather than treating the patient, because the doctor you are seeing probably didn't even want to sit on that chair. Talking helps. Being kind and empathetic helps. But if you want to get a grip on your life, you need to get therapy. Also sometimes many of our psychosomatic symptoms are actually normal reactions to the situations and environment we are put in. That is why therapy is important to figure out what exactly is triggering your depression, and what do you need to change, something within yourself or the environment surrounding you, or both. I feel, even if one person in your family is going through depression, there should be therapy for the caregivers as well, that is the family, so that they know what behavioural patterns are triggering the episodes in the person affected, and how to deal with them. Just as people with physical conditions tell everyone about their condition, depressed people should absolutely come out with their depression, without no shame or guilt whatsoever, so that people know that the person is going through something tough. And depressed people should drill it into their heads, that its not their fault. Asking for help doesn't make you weak, or an attention seeker, or crazy. Asking for help is one of the sanest and smartest things to do. This is your battle to fight. Help yourself before it gets too late. Stay aware so that you don't go beyond help. Protect yourself and your life before anything else.I know I might sound a bit harsh here.But if you don't understand the ground realities, you will never understand that the only one who can save you is you. Others can just help you figure out how to do that. So choose these ' others ' carefully. Stop expecting help from people who aren't capable of helping you. You have to structure your life around your depression. You cannot afford to lose control and let your depression take over. You have to sleep on time, get up on time, take your meds if you need to, take your therapy, do your meditation, do your breath work, exercise every single day and find ways to deal with the stress you are subjected to. And sometimes its okay to accept that perhaps your body is able to take only a certain amount of stress and not beyond that. Its okay to have a normal, average life and stay functional and alive, rather than chasing things which are beyond your control and wreaks havoc in your body and mind. You have to design a life which is optimum for your needs. Irrespective of how everyone else is living their lives. Because only you are going through, what you are going through. No one else is in your shoes fighting your battle for you. Yes I believe in living big and chasing my dreams, but not at the cost of my sanity. Self care should come before anything else. Living sane should be your foremost priority. Once you fix that, you can actually chase your dreams in a mentally healthy way. You cannot afford to be callous and casual about your life, because there is a line in mental illness, and if you cross over that, its very difficult to come back. The more you sink in, the more no of episodes you have, the more you relapse and face recurrence of episodes, the more your body has a chance of succumbing to depression. Thats why you have to be extra, extra careful about protecting your mind. And it's really the time now, to be selfish and pay attention to your own life, because no one else will. If you are depressed, please make it a habit if reaching out. I know depressed people don't, mental illness doesn't work like that. But please try. If nothing works, put it out on Insta or Facebook that “I am depressed, Please help". Someone will reach out to you. Do not give up hope. Do not give up fighting. Because I know for sure, that depressed people do not want to die. No one wants to die. People commit suicide because they are not aware of other options. Because they cant figure out a way from the pain, sadness, the incessant thoughts rampaging through their minds. There is always a way out. All you have to do is think straight, ask for help being absolutely shameless, and keep hanging on. Its sometimes not you doing, what you are doing. Its the illness talking. And with therapy, you can actually go back to being quite close to the person you once were. So Do not give up. Better days will come. You just gotta keep breathing, and think about taking one step at a time. A depressed person can look like this.A depressed person can also look like this.So stop judging people, and assuming things about them. You can never, ever guess what's going on underneath, unless you care to to give them the space to trust you, and open up to you, and when they do, you listen to them without gaslighting them, without judging them, and without making them feel like shit for feeling the way they do. People with mental health issues already go through tons of shit every single day, silently suffering. The best way you can help is not contribute to their suffering by being insensitive. Its okay if you dont want to take out time for them, its absolutely okay because you are a human yourself, and have issues of your own. So get them help, refer them to someone who can help them. Be kind. Be empathetic. Be sensitive. And please, please educate yourself on mental health. So that you know how to deal with a friend or family member going through something difficult. I have been a patient of mood disorder and battling with depression for over 12 years now, and I am on therapy and medication. I am not trained to help you, since I am not a psychiatrist but I can connect you to people who can. Please DM me if you need help.

column1: What is it like to be in a relationship with a psychopath? What are some common behaviors or thought patterns?
column3: It starts out as the most amazing soulmate experience ever, with you being unable to believe your good luck in meeting someone so perfect. You will be in the middle of a whirlwind of romance and attention. Then, gradually, the intensity cools off and you notice little things that cause you moments of concern. You brush such thoughts away and redouble your efforts to make the relationship work, blaming yourself for not being attentive enough or for forgetting how badly ‘he was abused in a previous relationship’. Meanwhile you keep everything hidden from your parents, siblings and other members of your family, aware that they’ve had some hostile things to say about him in the past. They now keep their mouths shut as it was causing tensions between you. One day your partner tells you with great seriousness that he has concerns about your friends who don’t seem to be treating you respectfully, and he thinks it might be better for your mental health if you stayed away from them for a while. You’re surprised at the mention of mental health but he assures you that he’s been watching you with great concern recently because of your irritability and forgetfulness. You weren’t aware that you were irritable or forgetful but over the next few weeks you mislay your purse and keys multiple times again and again (‘gaslighting’), and your anxiety levels begin to rise. Over the next six months you gradually lose contact with your family and friends, though you’re not quite sure how. Increasingly your partner seems to lash out at you for no reason at all before making lavish amends, telling you how much he loves you. When you tell him that this doesn’t seem like normal behavior he laughs and says that you’re being ‘over-sensitive’. You get a growing sense of unease though you can’t put your finger on it. He keeps saying and doing almost abusive things that don’t quite fit in with the loving person you know, and you keep forgiving him because you know that you’re in love and you think that he’s having a hard time at work or that you haven’t yet ironed out the wrinkles in your relationship. But you yearn for the old days of romance and being wined and dined. One day he’s in the bathroom and his phone’s unlocked (he’s normally very secretive with his phone) and you scroll through the messages and realize that he’s been having an affair. You spend the next week or so walking round in a daze while he acts as if everything’s perfectly normal. When, finally, you confront him he smirks, then laughs and says that it was nothing, just a misunderstanding, there was never any intimacy and that you shouldn’t take it seriously. Convinced by his words and behavior you resume the relationship. For the next month your relationship is perfect but then it starts taking a darker turn. You don’t seem to be able to do anything right. He very subtly criticizes and belittles you and accuses you of being manipulative. You do your best to correct all your faults. Then he’ll be randomly nice and you’ll wrack your brains trying to work out what you did right so that you can do it again. You gradually begin to feel your self-esteem slipping away and you find making decisions harder and harder. You’ve always been a strong and independent person so you’re not quite sure why you feel like this. You sleep badly at night, have digestive problems and have high blood pressure. One day, coming downstairs half asleep, you almost trip over a pair of your own shoes left on the stairs. You have no idea how they got there (a set-up designed to create ‘an accident on purpose’) and your partner tells you in all seriousness that it might be time to see a doctor (more ‘gaslighting’). Another day your car gets a puncture and your partner mends it. He tells you that he’s discovered something wrong with the brakes and tells you that you shouldn’t be driving it. You need the car to get to work. An instinct tells you to call out a mechanic even though it costs you a lot of money, and the mechanic tells you that it’s quite strange how the brakes were malfunctioning. Afterwards your partner makes a great scene, accusing you of showing him up in front of other people and saying that he was only trying to help. Six months later you chance to see your partner outside work kissing another woman. Dazed and angry you go home, pack your most treasured possessions and head for your Mum’s. There you walk around as if in a fog, feeling as if you’re not attached to the ground while trying to make sense of it all. You gradually realize that he’s not what he seems to be. When he gets home your partner sees that you’re not there and phones you. You tell him that you’re leaving but he’s very persuasive and tells you that you misunderstood what you saw and that it was just him being friendly, the woman he was kissing was in a dark place and needed some comfort at that time. You feel a magnetic, hypnotic yearning to go back to him but you steel yourself and refuse. Eventually he slams the phone down. Your Mum tells you that you seem to be a shadow of your former self. She advises you not to have anything to do with him. You exchange stories – because she made it her business to learn as much as she could about him - and you realize that he’s a Jekyll and Hyde character. Your partner rings and texts you multiple times. He sends you cards. You see him standing outside your Mum’s house. He calls at your workplace. You have no terminology to describe his behavior. You have no idea that he is and always will be a psychopath. Deconstructing the story above The soul mate experience – ‘love-bombing’, an intense display of interest and affection combined with ‘mirroring’ (reflecting back to the target their own personality, needs, desires etc.) and the ‘mask’ (the creation of a false persona tailor-made for the target). Moments of concern – these are ‘mask slips’ where the false persona no longer makes sense and the reality of the cold psychopath underneath is revealed. Forgetting how badly he was abused in a previous relationship – lies and ‘the pity play’ where he gets your sympathy in order to manipulate you. In this case you cut him lots of slack because you were manipulated into feeling sorry for him. Your family keep their mouths shut – in an abusive relationship it’s important to stay in contact with the target and to support them. They will need you when they finally emerge from the ‘cult of two’. Concerns about your friends and your mental health – the psychopath is ‘isolating’ you from your support network as it’s then easier for him to manipulate and control you. His concern about your mental health is the beginning of ‘gaslighting’ where he gets you to distrust your own perceptions. You didn’t think you had mental health problems – now you think you do. You mislay your keys and purse multiple times - more gaslighting, getting you to distrust your own perceptions as the psychopath hides your keys and purse. When you no longer trust your own perceptions – perhaps you think you’re going crazy or getting forgetful - then the psychopath’s ‘truths’ start to become your truths as you begin to believe what he tells you. You’re not quite sure how you’re losing contact with your family and friends – more ‘isolation’. Behind your back the psychopath has been telling your friends that you have mental health problems and need some space, while he called your parents on the phone to complain about them interfering in his and your life. He says you’re over-sensitive – a form of ‘gaslighting’, getting you to distrust your instincts / perceptions whilst normalizing his behavior. Saying things almost abusive that don’t quite fit in with the person you know – you see more mask slips and you begin to see ‘devaluation’, where the psychopath emotionally abuses the target. His phone’s unlocked – it was deliberate. The psychopath wanted to play a game with you. Psychopaths play with targets like cats with mice. He smirks – ‘Duper’s delight’, a feeling of contemptuous glee that the psychopath feels when outwitting or hurting a target. You don’t seem to be able to do anything right – the emotional abuse in the ‘devaluation’ stage is now ramping up. Randomly nice – random good / bad behaviour leads to ‘the trauma bond’, a magnetic, hypnotic desire to be with the abuser. Self-esteem slipping away and decision-making becoming harder – you’re beginning to suffer from Complex Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (CPTSD) as a result of the emotional abuse. The poor sleep and other physical problems are also due to CPTSD. You almost trip over your own shoes – the psychopath was trying to create an ‘accident on purpose’ in which you’d fall down and badly hurt or kill yourself. He deflects blame and simultaneously gaslights you by telling you that you need to see a doctor. Your partner mends a puncture – he lets the tire down on purpose and then ‘discovers’ the brake problem. He deliberately sabotaged the brakes. His intent is to harm you or at the very least make it difficult for you to get to work because he wants you to lose your job so that you’re further isolated. You walk around as if in a fog – you’re suffering from Cognitive Dissonance. This is when you’re trying to make sense of two opposing truths – he’s so nice and loving and yet he’s so horrible. If the answer ever comes – he’s a psychopath in this case but in other cases perhaps a narcissist or suffering from brain tissue damage – then the cognitive dissonance will go away. Your partner phones you – he’s trying to reel you in again. This is known colloquially as ‘hoovering’. I use the term ‘retrapment’ (it’s not a copyrighted term. ‘Hoover’ is). You have a magnetic, hypnotic yearning – the trauma bond. There’s not much about what it feels like in the research literature so I’ve used my own experience. You refuse to go back to him – it’s colloquially known as ‘No Contact’. It gives you space away from the manipulator to get your head straight. ‘No Contact’ means no checking his Facebook page, no answering texts or phone calls, no driving past his workplace. In extreme cases it means moving to a new city, breaking off contact with mutual friends and even breaking contact with family members who stay in touch with him. You seem to be a shadow of your former self – a result of the emotional abuse which in turn led to CPTSD. You are unable to see yourself accurately – you are no longer aware that the abuse has escalated to the point where it ‘s blatantly obvious to everyone else and that ‘you’ had disappeared. Jekyll and Hyde character – refers to psychopaths and narcissists. Rings and texts you multiple times – more hoovering. More often than not it’s successful. In her weakened and disorientated state the target doesn’t realize that the cat is going to play with the mouse again. Targets can go through the cycle described above in the story multiple times before they finally get the strength to escape. No terminology – without the terminology the world can’t be described. Without appropriate education we won’t know about psychopaths. Unless you live in a cave you WILL have a bad experience with at least one psychopath in your life. Whether or not you realize it was a psychopath is a different matter. * * For more insights into the masks of psychopaths, their so-called ‘relationships’, defences against psychopaths and psychopaths in the workplace visit my Quora page Richard Smith
column9: Thanks for this great post 👌 “You have a magnetic, hypnotic yearning – the trauma bond. There’s not much about what it feels like in the research literature…” I couldn't agree more with the point above. This is a very significant part of the whole process, from the unhealthy bonding to the hoovering falls, and very little is said about this in clinical literature or research. Even for those who are very clear minded and doubtless about cutting any ties before getting too close, it can be absurdly difficult to avoid or get rid of that magnetic pull & hypnotic yearning . I think this abnormal attraction to someone and to thinking about them against our own will is the major red flag of all 🚩to identify a psychopath or a narcissist or a heavy borderline who are as well on the spectrum of psychopathy. There should be more specific information and clarity on how it happens because, besides everything else, it's felt very metabolically. I'm sure the guys in Marketing Research know better but they don't share it Interdisciplinary nor to the general public. It's draining and disturbing far beyond any reasonable proportion to the relevance that person has for one's life, and it seems to come from a sort of celular information that goes up to the brain and mess it up… No wonder people are caught off guard.

column1: What is a brief reflection about the negative effects of separation of members of the family? Minimum of 2 paragraphs. Each paragraph has 5 sentences.
column3: I think you meant “the negative effects of separation on members of the family”. Not “of”. The meaning is “how separation negatively affects family members.” This sounds like the prompt for an essay. I don’t know if this essay is supposed to be about families in general, or a family in a story, or your own family. But let’s say it is about families in general, you should still give specific examples wherever you can, in order for your essay not to sound vague and meaningless. You should first make an outline which includes at least two points that you will discuss. Each paragraph should have a central focus or idea, and every sentence in your paragraph should relate to that focus. You should think of two ways in which being separated from each other badly affects family members — not just one family member, but at least two. You might want to talk about the mental health of the family members who miss each other and could fall into depression if they are apart from each other. Don’t forget to give specific examples either from your own life, the life of someone you know, or a book. Make sure to follow the instructions exactly, so when it says “no more than five sentences per paragraph”, be sure to do exactly that, or you may lose points. Avoid repeating the same idea.

column1: Do you think that Donald Trump is just a major symptom of a larger problem in America?
column3: Donald Trump is merely a symptom of the fact that we’ve long ignored not just one major problem but a host of festering problems in the US. This list is in no particular order as some items work in tandem with others and I don’t claim it’s exhaustive.Unequal economic opportunity - Many Americans suffer from an inability to prosper in the richest country that has ever existed. They come in a variety of flavors:Rural folks - Farmers and miners have long been ignored by coastal elites (from which most politicians arise). They work damned hard to drag food/resources from the ground only to see meager profits from their work. The family farmer has struggled for decades while the big corporate farms expand, receive corporate welfare, and leach profits away from the small guys. Infrastructure spending neglects rural areas. Rural folks are more likely to have poor electrical hookup that fails frequently, no water or sewer, and intermittent internet if they have any at all. Certain types of mining are fading due primarily to the shift of economic factors, but given the rural issues with education, these folks don’t understand the macroeconomic environment so they don’t know they have to change direction. Plus, if they are older, it’s difficult to shift from being a coal miner to a computer programmer. They want to know why urban elites live such fine lives while they do not. They are angry because they believe that the urban poor soak up all the social benefits while they miss out.Urban poor - These folks are primarily of color. They start out in life behind the starting line due to the poverty of their parents which becomes a generational legacy. Because they are clustered in rundown areas of cities, they suffer from poisons related to industrial activity and lead paint which can affect the intellectual development of their children. A lack of role models for young people that look like them means many young folks don’t know what to strive for and so they don’t. Policies related to marriage and family can drive these people to make poor but expedient choices such as not marrying to obtain better benefits. Because they live in areas with poor school funding, their schools are below par, another shackle holding them in poverty. They are run down. Some are frustrated and angry. Others have simply given up and survive on welfare or illegal activities to get by. They’re detached from the greater community of this nation.The neglected middle - The middle class has been eroded at both ends of the spectrum. Some folks have risen up into the ranks of the wealthy, but many more have sunk down into poverty. This can be because of job losses, divorce, substance abuse, or medical calamities. Like the rural folks, these people have always worked hard. They’re bewildered that there’s no protection for them when they fall. Instead, they see subsidies for farmers, corporate welfare programs, tax laws that benefit the rich and social programs that go to the poor. There they stand in the middle asking, where’s mine?Race relations - While we as a society have advanced beyond the days of public lynchings and the KKK burning crosses with open disdain, we’ve still got a long, long way to go. We’ve got:Outright racists - A certain portion of the white population believes people of color are inferior to them. They resent seeing POC having any type of success, because that implies perhaps those POC folks aren’t, in fact, inferior. They also tend to believe that if a person of color succeeds, it’s because that person received some unfair advantage they didn’t receive. These people hate that the US is steadily trending browner. They want what they perceive as the good old days, when white folks ruled all, to come back.Annoyed white folks - some white people who aren’t outright racists, nevertheless have reasons to dislike the browning of America. Most of that comes back to economic problems. They tend to be poorer and less educated so their jobs are more at risk. When a flux of new people enter the market to challenge them for those jobs, it causes pain and dislocation. Among the more elite whites, there’s still a belief that minorities are soaking up a bigger piece of the pie, costing them taxes, and they feel that’s unfair.Militant minorities - some members of minority groups believe in protesting their second class status. BLM is a good example. While the majority of the marches that take place are peaceful, not all are. Those that break into violence or physical damage infuriate people not involved in the protests. People of color are demanding more of the economic pie, but that can mean a qualified white person loses out, which causes more turmoil as a society.Poor educational systems - The US has some of the best of the world’s schools and some of it’s worst. Which one you attend depends primarily on your economic status. Some inner city schools are almost war zones between gangs, making learning impossible. In the poorest districts, teachers aren’t well paid, leading to only the worst teachers at those schools. The physical plants are deteriorating, which doesn’t lead to a good learning environment, and some even suffer from problems such as lead paint. The US also has a mentality that all children learn at the same rate. We’ve “mainlined” kids of various talents into a single pool. While this might help lift some of the less endowed children, it also holds back those with greater talents, leading to a waste of lost abilities. Underfunding of schools leads to huge teacher-student ratios, further undermining education.Diversity versus tribalism - humans seem hardwired to collecting themselves into tribal groups. We group by language, religion, political affiliation, economic strata, age, race, geographic location, or ethnicity. The US, being such a salad bowl of various cultures, has a greater diversity than pretty much any other nation on earth. With that comes the friction inherent in tribalism. As a nation, we’ve done a poor job of trying to break down the barriers tribalism creates.Mental health failures - For whatever reason, the US has a confrontational approach to dealing with mental health. Once upon a time, people were locked up in terrible conditions and left to rot. When that was determined to be inhumane, they were released into society. However, that dumped the problem of “treating” them to families, most of whom are unprepared for how to do so. This has led to the massive increase in drug and alcohol abuse as people with untreated mental health problems self-medicate to survive. Mental health resources are woefully underfunded. Quality beds are too few. Families have no where to turn. Homelessness can result.Immigration failures - The US has always attracted immigrants from the very start. Abundant land and resources beckon compared to the cramped quarters of Europe or Asia. When those that got here first decided too many of those that followed were arriving, they tried to slam the door on them. But the pressure to come arises from societies that are war torn, mired in poverty, or suffering from outbreaks of violence. Blocking them from coming won’t stop the pressure. It merely causes that pressure to rise to the boiling point, causing such issues as the mess at the border.None of these issues is new. We’ve dealt with most of them for a century, some since the US began. All of them cause certain groups of people to be angry and frustrated. They blame the government for failing to address the issues. So when Donald Trump appeared, saying “I hear you!” and declaring himself an outsider, millions grasped at the chance to make a change. column1: How is COVID affecting your life?
column3: I am working in a PSB in village around 400 km away from my hometown where my parents live alone. 17th April was the date when I came to know about the health of my mother. She was having headache and feeling difficulty in in breathing. Even on working days I have phone call with mom and dad at least 3 times a day. my father was of opinion that what will I do even after coming back they are taking care so I should stay away. I was feeling helpless, all I could do is to force my parents to take it seriously and seek hospital care. Seeing the condition of hospitals especially in Delhi my father didn't wanted to admit my mother in any hospital. To support his point my cousins from pharmacy stream advised to instead buy an oxygen concentrator and take care at home only. Still I kept on making the pressure. And then lord Hanuman sent Hemant bhaiya to the rescue. Hemant bhaiya was the school mate of my sister. Nobody will believe me if I tell you that neither me nor my sis was in contact with him. We just called him once and he stood by my family. He took my mother to various hospitals in Delhi where everywhere everyone refused to admit her due to lack of bed. He took my mother to Faridabad and admitted her in a local hospital. I boarded a bus to Delhi , the same night. Reached hospital the next day, spend some time with mom but the vibes in hospital were very negative, also the carelessness of staff, unavailability of doctors and the atmosphere there signalled us to look for another option. Hence we shifted mom to a bigger and better hospital in the same city. From 19th April 2021 it's almost been a month.Inspite of all the government regulations, we are paying daily fees which is most of the times more than my monthly salary.I am in hospital since day one. Seen both joy of discharging your patient and sorrow of losing their loved ones. From a 30 year old boy who was going to marry next month to a senior citizen uncle the pain on their family members face was unbearable. And would make anyone cry.The day she was admitted her HR CT score was very bad around 18 and the way doctor talked about her reports I was devastated but again gathered some courage to take on the challenge. Because I was the only one meeting my mother, giving her all the hopes and positivity I could within those few minutes.I have seen my mother getting admitted in emergency, later being shifted to Highly dependable unit and then to Intensive care unit. For almost 15 days there was no improvement and she was on continuous Oxygen support, that too 30l i.e the maximum they could give without ventilator. While many were getting discharged, i was daily meeting my doctor to hear the same line wait n watch.When she got RTPCR negative report for covid, her health started improving slowly. oxygen requirement also decreased. She was shifted to general few days back and doing well. She is still on oxygen support but improving. Also now I can be with her 24*7.Covid-19 not only infected my mother's lungs, it has affected our lives very badly. Seeing your mother in hospital is not anyone would like to experience daily seeing deaths around you also gives you mental trauma and weakens your hope but then you have to stay strong. No matter what happens throughout the day you chant god's name and get ready for the next day hoping for something better. Even a single notification or ringtone makes you awake you look at your phone and thank god that the call isn't from hospital. Like others, I don't have a pic from hospital as any evidence of something. I believe it is a trauma, something I won't wish even my enemies to go through. The day we admitted her in emergency and when she was shifted in HDU covid ward. I was standing outside and trying to get a look of her from the small glass window there was a man probably 50 standing besides me. He advised me “ you shouldn't come here too often" And all I could say was “she's my mother"मेरी हज़ार उलझनों के बीच, माँ को मुस्कुराते देखना सुकून देता है ❤️

column1: How do veterans feel about Trump after his first year?
column3: I am not a veteran — nor FWIW am I Democrat; I’m independent — but I do come from a proud Navy family (father was a Captain), so veteran issues are very important to us, and the GOP have a sad history of giving our vets and active service members the short shrift, despite their flag-waving. After the Affordable Care Act, a.k.a. “Obamacare,” kicked in, the number of vets without insurance dropped by almost 40%. That would be reversed if Republicans get their way. Forgetting “Trumpcare” and POTUS himself for the moment — he’s merely a useful idiot for Republicans to have their agenda passed — the GOP has a pitiful record regarding their actual, long-standing lack of support for America's war veterans and active service members. R. 2875). Educate yourselves, and then let your elected officials HEAR FROM YOU. Technology and medical research has progressed exponentially in the last few decades. Today, doctors are not as helpless as they were even 10–15 years ago when it comes to Cancer care. On most occasions, they are in a position to help which is why doctors don’t necessarily have to internalize patient suffering as much as the general public think they do. Later this week, I’ll be operating on a man in his late 80s to remove a cancer of the eyelid which has spread to his eye socket. I will need to remove the affected eyeball along with the cancerous tumour to make sure that I have removed every part of the cancerous growth- so that the cancer doesn’t spread elsewhere. I spent quite a bit of time over the last 3 months trying to convince the patient and several of his family members that the eye needed to be removed. The elderly gentleman would rather prefer death than live as a one eyed man in his last years and his family seemed to agree. It took a mammoth effort to convince everybody concerned that if they sat on it, the cancer would likely spread to other parts of the body and would eventually cause a lot of pain and sufferring before him actually succumbing to the disease. If we went ahead with the surgery now, we would have a realistic chance of curing the man of that deadly cancer and add a few more years of quality life. My job above is not sympathize with the situation the man has got into. My job is to do something for the condition that has brought him to me. My job is laying out his options -Surgery, Chemotherapy, Radiotherapy- including the consequences of not doing anything at all (which is sometimes a reasonable choice). My job is to give a realistic picture of his prognosis and make him (and his family) understand that losing an eye is nothing compared to what he might suffer if the tumour spreads- this is the toughest part! In all this, my role is to take in all the data that is available to me about the patient, make sense of it and help the patient make the best possible decision. In bargaining with the patient and his relatives, we were all losing precious time. I may hope that the cancer wouldn’t have spread in the time it required to convince the patient but I cannot do anything about it because the decision for surgery is the patient’s choice-not mine! Despite the delay not being my choice, I still get to bear the yoke of responsibility for his disease. In doing my job, patients sometimes may not agree with the options I may give and may prefer to live in denial. In most cases, they do agree, but there is no guarantee that things will go according to plan like clockwork. Cancer is notorious for recurrences which again complicates treatment further. My role again here is not to worry about things going south but it is to ensure that they don’t and to be on top of the disease and treatment. It is painful to lose patients and it upsets all of us greatly to lose our patients to disease. It is especially painful when we put in significant amount of our skill, knowledge, intelligence and emotional investment in the treatment of a patient. However, we know more than anyone else that everybody dies eventually no matter how good the medical care is. When it happens, we need to find ways to cope with that and move on to our next patient who needs our help. Our work doesn’t stop. Also, suffering is a relative term. Many times mental agony far overwhelms physical ailments including pain. A man with a blinding cataract may not seem as bad as a man with stage IV cancer. A cataract blind man in a remote place may not be able to take care of himself or be able to work to feed himself because he’s poor and cannot have access to cataract surgery while the patient with stage IV cancer may have dedicated nurses, help and family members to take care of him and give him access to comfort care. How can we stand in judgement as to whose suffering is greater? It is also not true that only oncologists have to deal with psychological issues related to patient sufferring. Neurosurgeons have to deal with a lot of their patients dying on table and sometimes doing an excellent job at surgery only to find the patient to slip into coma later in the ICU. Pediatricians deal with sufferring of small babies who cannot even voice out their problems and babies die too despite their best efforts. Obstetricians have to deliver not just babies but also sometimes bad news of stillborns and congenital defects in a new born. Psychiatrists deal with the most challenging mentally ill patients with their patients not remembering their work and sometimes taking their own life. Nearly every field of medicine have patients suffering and some of them dying! Medicine is inevitably full of stories of suffering, pain and death. However, doctors have a job to do. They get it right most of the times, but sometimes things don’t go according to plan or the disease just runs it’s inevitable course. They get to be heroic sometimes and at times, fallible- like all humans can be. But, that’s the job! Disclaimer: This answer is not a substitute for professional medical advice. column1: How does losing people we love change us?
column3: The loss of my brother in 2000 when he was in his early 40’s was completely unexpected. He left behind, a wife, two preteen children, two parents, three siblings and hundreds of family, friends and work associates who had no idea that he was in pain or needed help. Whenever we saw him, he was smiling, laughing, joking and proud of his successful career and family. That taught me that mental health issues are a cancer of the human soul and to allow myself to be vulnerable and to seek help if I ever needed it. We offer sympathy for patients of disease, but mental health carries too much shame and stigma. In 2005, we lost our then 20 year old son when he was killed in a firefighter training accident in our small close knit town. A million small pieces of love kept us afloat through a parent’s worst nightmare. Our souls were empty and bleeding, but we found our way back to life. The power of the human soul to be wounded and heal is a wondrous thing. I love well healed wounded souls because they have been tested by life and proven resilient. Live without purpose won’t survive such wounds, so we rebuilt our purpose and changed. I follow in the idealist footsteps of my son as I journey through the rest of my life without him. That allows me to embrace grief as an extension of love shared. The deeper the love shared, the harder the grief will be. Grief is the final responsibility of love, a sacred opportunity to carry and incorporate the essence of a soul into your own life. Life is gifted to us one dawn at a time, we can waste it or live it, and the best thing we can do is build love. Love is the only thing that will survive our death, and therefore a life without love is a life without real purpose.
