column1: How important is it to keep track of where you leave things around the house, and does it affect a person’s mental health?
column3: I will not speculate on whether my spouse’s tendency to lose things around our house affects his mental health, but I know it affects mine. Several times each month, I and/or our son spend some time helping him find his keys (or watch, wallet, glasses, phone, work papers, etc.). It seems it is always at a point in time when we need to be somewhere like off to work or school (because that is when you need these types of things handy). Some days I take it well -- like a challenging treasure hunt. Other days, searching in pockets, under papers, in trash bins, under the car seat, anywhere hard to get to, turns me into an ill-tempered, ill-mannered family member (the kind who would get kicked off Twitter if I typed out the commentary playing in my head). Solutions to the problem, as you will know if you live with someone who has difficulty keeping track of things, are hard to come by. It is easier said than done to put things down in the same place consistently for him, and tools like Tile (small units that you put in your wallet or attach to your keys, for example, and then link to your phone to beep when you need to find things) only help some of the time. Additionally, this is not a problem limited to the home. Someone who loses stuff around the house, loses stuff outside the house as well. We have had to cancel and replace my husband’s credit cards multiple times, for example. So far, we have always been fortunate enough to have his wallet and/or phone (or even one time, a new camera) found by an honest person who turned them in wherever he left them. But it is difficult – I now irritate my family a lot by constantly asking if they have their stuff when we go somewhere. I am no fun much of the time. So, long answer to a simple question – that yes, this problem is probably affecting someone’s mental health even if it’s not the person who has trouble keeping track of stuff. (And I will take any and all suggestions that have worked for others in helping solve this type of issue.)

column1: What are some ways to deal with a family member that suffers from schizophrenia and how does it affect your daily life?
column3: Give that person great love and support. Mother Nature has kicked them in the head. Schizophrenia is a lifelong, incurable neurological illness due to biochemical and sometimes structural problems in the frontal lobe of the brain. Nobody deserves that. It is not a “mental health issue,” a term the media likes to use. No, it’s a severe illness just like diabetes or leukemia. The most important step to keep them well is to make sure that they take their medications. If side effects tempt them to quit their drug regimen, take them to their psychiatrist who will work with the patient to find a tolerable mix. Also, avoid high expressed emotion, i.e., screaming, intense criticism, etc. They need peace and quiet, a healthy diet and exercise. If the person is ill, ignore hallucinations and delusions. Arguing about them can implant the mistaken ideas in their memories. To remain well, the patient must severely limit intake of alcohol, which can undermine their medications. Marijuana and illicit drugs can provoke psychotic episodes. Once stabilized, if they cannot work, help them apply for Social Security Disability and learn all the rules. A disability attorney can help with the application and an appeal, if the application is initially denied, a common occurrence. Once on SSDI, they cannot earn more than about $1,000 per month or they will lose their benefits. Ask a lawyer to draw up a health care power-of-attorney and HIPAA release naming a responsible family member as the attorney-in-fact. If the patient should suffer a psychotic episode, that person can act on their behalf to get them to the doctor or an ER. The most dangerous symptom of psychosis is lack of insight, which means that a psychotic person does not know that he is ill. “It’s like sleeping with your eyes open,” a patient told me. That is why someone must be able to act on their behalf. Having a family member diagnosed with a psychotic disorder is a heart-rending tragedy. The primary care giver should carve out time for himself, give himself time to grieve, keep in contact with friends, and not dwell on the patient’s lost potential.

column1: How can you be a perfectionist people-pleaser and not be stressed out?
column3: You can’t. If you are basing your decisions and how you live your life on others you will be a stressed out mess. I am slowly learning how to keep my autonomy while still being a kind person. People pleasers are many times afraid of abandonment if they say no or set up boundaries basically this person may not like me anyone so instead of having a confrontation I would rather concede. The problem is yes you may have more people in your life but not necessarily true friends. This behavior actually attracts very toxic people. You are basically abandoning yourself in order to please others. In the short term yes you may lose some people by being true to yourself but it will be those people never really cared about you as a person anyway. Someone that cares about you listens to your opinion and what you value. They don’t just like you when you agree with them and do what they ask. That is a fake friend or family member and they are sometimes the people you would have never guessed. If you continue to people please it will eventually affect your mental health and possibly even your physical health. It erodes who you are as an individual over time and ultimately leads to unhappiness.

column1: Is any ENHYPEN members struggling or depressed? (I'm new to being a fan so I'm just curious)
column3: It’s no doubt the ENHYPEN members are struggling, maybe even depressed, but they seem to hide it behind closed doors. I’m going to answer for each member based on MY observations. I’m no professional psychologist (yet), so feel free to disagree with my opinions. Heeseung: I feel like Heeseung is a really fragile and sensitive person. Normally off-camera he’s always incredibly quiet and is by himself a lot, especially during dance jams when he’s just standing by the side or wandering by himself. Jake said that Heeseung is someone who needs a lot of care and attention, so he tries his best to spend time with him and show him care. He really takes words to heart, especially in I-Land when Heeseung cried because the others were constantly criticizing his leadership skills despite him leading them on as best as he could. He tries to be as perfect as he can for us, and it’s sad how he doesn’t love himself as much as he loves Engene (coming from his own words). Plus all those disgusting comments about him on Twitter (the ones shaming his appearance and his plastic surgery procedures) no doubt have an effect on him, it's obvious he’s seen them considering his demeanor has been quite different after what occurred and he often hides his face under a mask and pulls it all the way up to his eyes. I don’t want to assume anything about his mental health but it’s clear Heeseung is a very sensitive person who has his own struggles. Jay: Now Jay seems like a rather confident person. He’s incredibly patient, keeps his calm, takes care of the other members well, and is charming and bubbly. Although he has a rather tough exterior, he probably goes through his own share of struggles. The ongoing issue is that Jay is constantly seen as being the ‘clown’ or ‘meme’ of ENHYPEN. A lot of Engene don’t take him seriously and constantly make memes about him, especially those horrible I-Land memes (R.A.S and that crying meme, bleugh) and he’s clearly expressed his discomfort time and time again, respectfully telling Engene to stop. He said he wants to be taken seriously and not as a joke all the time. Yes, Jay likes to be the mood maker and he likes to make people laugh but we need to understand the boundaries and realize there are certain limits we shouldn’t cross, especially when he himself has said to stop. Jake: Jake is also an incredibly happy and bubbly person. He is so caring and he takes care of all his members as best as he can. He literally raised Ni-ki throughout their ENHYPEN journey since Ni-ki’s parents are far away. He looks after Heeseung and generally is the most comfortable person to talk to according to all the members in various interviews. I think he is very mentally stable, but I also think he’s hurting a bit inside. During their fan live, he broke down on stage and cried uncontrollably because of his grandma passing away just a few days before their concert. How horrible is that? He didn’t even get the chance to grieve, to take a day off and process his loss. That was BELIFT’S fault on that. Idols are human too, not robots. Jake’s grandma clearly meant a lot to him, depriving him of grieving her then making him perform live on stage was a cruel thing to do. Sunghoon: Honestly, I haven't yet seen any signs of discomfort within Sunghoon yet. He’s always joking around with the members and does his own thing. He doesn’t speak much about his personal life or feelings, just keeps things moderate. This doesn’t mean he doesn’t have his own struggles, I’m sure he does. Maybe the pressure of being the Music bank manager, maybe desperately missing his parents and sister, there are a tonne of possibilities. Sunoo: Now with Sunoo, I can say with conviction he had quite a few things going on with him. I remember in the middle he became quite withdrawn and quiet. During Dance Jams or Vlives he kept to himself and sat alone in a corner or barely said any words. The other members say he’s sensitive and at home, he often spends time by himself watching Kdramas or something else, quite a stark contrast to his usual bubbly and sunshiny personality. He has the pressure of being the ‘sunshine’ of the group and it isn’t easy, especially when he has those days when he isn’t feeling so great. Once again, Idols are humans. I don’t particularly like that agencies make certain idols act in a certain way to appeal to their fans. For example, making Sunoo talk all cutesy and do a tonne of aegyo. Right now Sunoo doesn't do any of that, at least not often and he’s showing more of his personality than before. So that’s good. Another thing is his weight obsession. I feel really sad that Sunoo thinks he’s fat or he needs to lose weight. He DOESN’T. Sunoo is perfect as is, I don’t like how Engene and some members make comments about his body. I’m sure the members don’t mean it in distaste, but it shouldn’t be said regardless. Sunoo takes it to heart and has gone on many diets to lose weight, I feel horrible for him because he’s sensitive and listens carefully to what others have to say about him. In a way, he reminds me of Heeseung. Jungwon: Honestly, Jungwon in my eyes is the most stable member. I’ve never seen him falter, never seen him act or look sad, never seen him talk about his feelings in a way that indicates he has depression or is greatly struggling. Sure, he talks about his leadership responsibilities and yes it’s definitely a pressure on him, considering he’s incredibly young and he is responsible for leading the team, so those are definitely struggles he might be hiding for the sake of not worrying us. He’s talked about himself being happy and content with the way things are, so I don’t usually worry about him. Ni-Ki: Ni-ki, the young maknae of the group, has not seen his family since he first came to I-Land to debut. Can you believe that? Imagine a young 13/14-year-old, coming by himself to an unknown country leaving his entire family behind, people he’s grown up with and has extremely close bonds with. Imagine participating in an incredibly tough survival show, debuting, and working incredibly hard for a total of around 2 years, and not a single time during that period, you haven’t seen the people you love the most? A literal child!. There are so many times, more than I can count where Ni-ki has expressed how much he misses his family and how he desperately wants to see them. He’s cried a lot too, breaking down on the same stage as Jake because all he wanted was to see his parents, his sisters, just once. From 14 years old to 16 years old, Ni-ki didn’t get to see his parents at all and BELIFT is not giving him a single chance to. Japan and Korea are literally neighbors. They could send him on a plane for a single DAY, or bring his parents over and have them reunite for a short while at least. I feel so bad for Ni-Ki. He’s definitely struggling a lot from the feeling of missing his parents, from the pressure of being in the K-pop industry at such a young age, from being in an unknown country all by himself without anyone to rely on but his members. It’s sad. (EDIT: He finally met them!! :) I’m so happy for him, he seems so much happier nowadays) In short, I’m sure every member in ENHYPEN has their own share of struggles. Some more than others, some get over them fast enough, some can’t. We as their fans and loyal supporters must be mindful of these and remember not to cross limits with them or say hurtful things that would affect their mental health. Always be kind! Because you never know if a member is reading your words or not.

column1: What are the consequences of keeping a family secret?
column3: The environment that is created when family secrets are kept is poisonous for the entire family. It can be very damaging, causing tension, resentment, remorse, worry, and occasionally the use of addictive substances as a coping technique. The existence of secrets, which inhibit open communication and ultimately result in major health and mental health issues for family members, is one of the most poisonous issues that many families face. In the end, family secrets cause some families to lose their ability to remain together. It is crucial to emphasize that there are instances when it is preferable to keep a secret from others if doing so will result in unneeded harm and no gain. Therapists thinks that most secrets are better kept out in the open, though. Consequences Intimacy made difficult Distrust and anger Keeping secrets can affect children’s lives. Keeping secrets can cause illness. Keeping secrets can create a false sense of reality.

column1: Is divorce overrated?
column3: Divorce is going from one terrible situation to another terrible situation. I don’t know what planet Steven is from, but as far as I’m concerned, divorce should be your absolute last resort. If you don’t think you can survive one more month in the situation you are in, your health, safety or sanity is in jeopardy-then you should file for divorce. But you should try everything else first-mediation, counseling, psychologists, couple’s therapy, getting extended family involved, medications for mental health issues, living in separate homes, limiting time together—anything but divorce. All of those things are preferable to divorce. Do you want to know why? Divorce is the most stressful and nasty experience you will ever survive. It will take years off of your life because of worry and stress, and it will affect your health in a negative way. Not even a death in the family can equate to the amount of pain you will experience during a divorce. Secondly, your children will suffer, no matter what you do. You will lose friends. Your work will suffer. You will lose family members over this. Divorce should be the answer only if you feel that you won’t survive the current situation, because it will be nasty. Sorry to have to tell you this, but I prefer everyone know what they are getting into.

column1: When a person is battling depression and decides to open up about it, what are some things that I, as a friend, must absolutely never say to them?
column3: This is an excerpt from an email I received way back in 2004 or 2006 with regards to what to say or do to a person diagnosed with depression. I can safely say that some of these should be common sense. For more information, please visit any site that deals exclusively with mental health or mental illness. Best and Worst Things to Say to someone who is suffering from Depression (Disclaimer: I am not the original author of the list of do's and don'ts on what to say to a person who is depressed. I am simply the messenger. In other words, I'm not responsible if you think it's right or wrong. However, I would invite the reader to read this with an open mind, and try to put themselves OUT of their own point of view for a moment, and look at this from another perspective. That is all!) Earlier this morning (around 2am), mom and I were talking about some things, mostly about one of my cousins on her side of the family, who is suffering from depression. We talked for over an hour about that, and other sub-topics that won't be shared here. Suffice it to say, it sparked something in me to post a list of things that are best and worst to say to a person who is depressed, and believe you me, I'VE BEEN THERE! This is not just me saying "Been there, done that, got the t-shirt." kind of message. I mean I actually lived it and survived, thankfully. These are not intended a rule of thumb, but rather a guideline so that the next time you come across someone who has more than the occasional "blues" of the day (perhaps for a couple of weeks or more), you can be prepared on how to deal with that person better. Perhaps it may be a family member, a relative, a co-worker, a friend, or just someone who needs that proverbial punching bag. Remember, depressed people already know the solution to their problem. They don't need YOU to fix it. They just want an open ear, someone who will LISTEN to them vent, and in the end they will come up with their solutions, but you can certainly give them support, guidance, and perhaps a little encouragement. Once again, I'm not trying to be preachy. Just trying to put out there what I know from experience! Here it goes. Best Things to Say to a person who is Depressed It is most tempting, when you find out someone is depressed, to attempt to immediately fix the problem. However, until the depressed person has given you permission to be their therapist (as a friend or professional), the following responses are more likely to help. Acknowledge my depression for what it is (No 'it's just a phase') and give permission for them to feel depressed (No 'but why should you be sad?')Here is the list from contributors to a.s.d. and Pendulum: "I love you!" "I Care" "You're not alone in this" "I'm not going to leave/abandon you" "Do you want a hug?" "I love you (if you mean it)." "You are important to me." "If you need a friend... (and mean it)" "you look great ! (say it and mean it)" "It will pass, we can ride it out together." "When all this is over, I'll still be here (if you mean it) and so will you." "Don't say anything, just hold my hand and listen while I cry." "All I want to do now is give you a hug and a shoulder to cry on.." "Hey, you're not crazy!" "May the strength of the past reflect in your future." "God does not play dice with the universe." - A. Einstein "A miracle is simply a do-it-yourself project." - S. Leek "We are not primarily on earth to see through one another, but to see one another through" - (from someone's SIG) "If the human brain were simple enough to understand, we'd be too simple to understand it." - a codeveloper of Prozac, quoted from "Listening to Prozac" "You have so many extraordinary gifts--how can you expect to live an ordinary life?" - from the movie "Little Women" (Marmee to Jo) "I understand your pain and I empathize" "I'm sorry you're in so much pain. I am not going to leave you. I am going to take care of myself so you don't need to worry that your pain might hurt me." "I listen to you talk about it, and I can't imagine what it's like for you. I just can't imagine how hard it must be." "I can't really fully understand what you are feeling, but I can offer my compassion." "Depression is like a very dark storm... you are in the middle of the storm now and can't see your way out... but it will get better. One day you will be able to turn around and see that the storm has passed..." "I'm sorry you're having to go through this, I care about you and care that you are hurting. "Don't torture yourself with your feelings, I'm here to listen." "I'll be your friend no matter what so it's okay to talk about your feelings-- it'll make you feel better." "I'll be with you at all times." "With friends, joy is multiplied and sorrow divided." "I cannot understand the pain you're in, I cannot feel it. But hold onto my hand while you walk through this storm, and I'll do my very very best to keep you from slipping away." "I love you unconditionally and will always be here for you." "Keep kicking against the darkness until it bleeds daylight." - Preacher, "I'm never going to say 'I know how you feel' unless I truly do, but if I can do anything to help, I will." Worst Things to Say to someone depressed! Some people trivialize depression (often unintentionally, and sometimes hurtfully) by dropping a platitude on a depressed person as if that is the one thing they needed to hear. While some of these thoughts have been helpful to some people (for example, some people find that praying is very helpful), the context in which they are often said mitigates any intended benefit to the listener. Platitudes don't cure depression. "What's your problem?" Will you stop that constant whining?" What makes you think that anyone cares?" "Have you gotten tired yet of all this me-me-me stuff?" "You just need to give yourself a kick in the rear" "But it's all in your mind" "I thought you were stronger than that" "No one ever said life was fair" "Pull yourself up by your bootstraps" "Why don't you just grow up?" "Stop feeling sorry for yourself" "There are a lot of people worse off than you" "You have it so good - why aren't you happy?" "What do you have to be depressed about?" "You think you've got problems..." "Well at least it's not that bad" "Lighten up" "You should get off all those pills" "You are what you think" "Cheer up" "You're always feeling sorry for yourself" "Why can't you just be normal?" "You need to get out more" "Get a grip" "Most folks are about as happy as they make up their minds to be" "Get a job" "You don't 'look' depressed" "You're just looking for attention" "Everybody has a bad day now and then" "Why don't you smile more?" "A person your age should be having the time of their life" "The only one you're hurting is yourself" "You can do anything you want if you just set your mind to it" "Depression is a symptom of your sin against God" "You brought this on yourself" "Get off your rear and do something" "Snap out of it" "You're always worried about your problems" "Just don't think about it" "Go out and have some fun" "Just try a little harder" "I know how you feel - I was depressed once for several days" "You'd feel better if you went to church" "Shit or get off the pot" "What you need is some real tragedy in your life to give you perspective" "This too shall pass" "Go out and get some fresh air" "We all have our cross to bear" "You don't like feeling that way? So change it" "You're a real downer to be around" "You are embarrassing me" "You'd feel better if you lost some weight" "You might feel better if you stopped being so negative." "You're too hard on yourself. Quit being such a perfectionist" "Don't take it out on everyone else around you" "You are going to lose a lot of friends if you don't snap out of this" "You're dragging me down with you" "You're just being immature" "You are your own worst enemy" "That is life - get used to it, cupcake!" "My life isn't fun either" "Life isn't meant to be easy!" "Life is just tough, and it doesn't get any better!" "You don't care about the rest of us - you're so self-absorbed" Here are a few more added by someone in the group: "Cheer up, it might never happen." "No use crying over spilt milk." "I wish you weren’t so unhappy all the time." (Bad as the person is a) ignoring those times your depression affects you less, and b) places an accidental burden on you to not be unhappy FOR THEM). "What’s the worst that can happen?" (Very bad if you also suffer GAD etc). "Stop moping around!"

column1: Why milennials tend to have more mental health issues?
column3: PREFACE (UPDATE): After receiving some initial feedback on my answer, I thought it was important to provide some context. I spent 7 years studying behavioural, evolutionary, and neuropsychology. My studies have shown me how critical mental health is to our well being not only as individuals, but as a society as well. My answer below is in no way meant to suggest that I do not believe that mental health is important, that mental health issues do not exist, or that mental health services are not important tools that can be used to help people struggling with mental health issues. My personal belief, however, is that there are aspects of the western, capitalist system that have negatively impacted mental health through the degradation of communities. Without strong social support networks, my belief is that most professional interventions will ultimately fail. I believe that our over-reliance on government programs, divisive social policies, and overemphasis on the importance of individual performance in the capitalist rat race have weakened communities and robbed people of these critical social support networks. I also have a pretty healthy level of skepticism when it comes to how the psychological community defines and treats “mental health issues", as we all should given our ever changing understanding of the topic. After all, the American Psychological Association (APA) listed “hysteria" as a psychological disorder until 1952, and the manual that they publish to guide the classification and treatment of psychological disorders has been revised numerous times as our understanding progresses. The APA also has a nasty history of involvement in government initiatives to improve the effectiveness of torture techniques, and there are plenty of controversial collaborations between psychologists, governments, and industry that continue today. So, while there are certainly aspects of the field that have been immeasurably beneficial, we should never stop being critical of our psychological institutions. ORIGINAL RESPONSE: We are a generation that believes in “logic” and “science”. Scientists tell us when and/or if a given behaviour or thought process constitutes a mental health issue, and we trust that they are correct. What is a mental health issue? Here is a definition from Mental health problems (introduction) “In many ways, mental health is just like physical health: everybody has it and we need to take care of it. Good mental health means being generally able to think, feel and react in the ways that you need and want to live your life. But if you go through a period of poor mental health you might find the ways you're frequently thinking, feeling or reacting become difficult, or even impossible, to cope with. This can feel just as bad as a physical illness, or even worse. Mental health problems affect around one in four people in any given year. They range from common problems, such as depression and anxiety, to rarer problems such as schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.” Essentially, even if a thought process is very common (most people will feel that way at some point in their lives), it is pathologized. For example, every single person on this planet will lose someone that they love, or will be lost themselves. These experiences are unbelievably heart breaking, and cause a period of immense sadness for those with the ability to feel emotion. In the past, communities were extremely important during these periods of time. Neighbours volunteered to help with day-to-day tasks. Family members and friends brought over meals and checked-in on the bereaved. In my hometown, there was a large Tornado a few decades ago that decimated a few homes and barns. The entire community came together to rebuild, on their own time, with their own money. It was a beautiful homage to the extraordinary level of cooperation that we are capable of. In our current society, individuals move more frequently, and often away from extended family members, in the pursuit of personal goals. Thus, the strength of communities has been greatly diminished, and many people lack strong social support networks. Instead, they rely on paid professionals and the government to ineptly mimic a pseudo-community. Yes, we all have problems, and some definitely have more than others. But, I can tell you that your psychologist will not rock you to sleep after you find your mother, lifeless on her living room couch three weeks after a cancer diagnosis. Corporations will do nothing but obstruct you from receiving your entitlements. Governments will do nothing but ensure that they receive their fair share of the pie. Millennials have more mental health issues because they rely on the wrong people and institutions for help, and because the term has lost all reasonable meaning.

column1: How common is it for people to regret having children?
column3: I have wondered about this. For the sake of kids, it's often a taboo topic. Moms might share how stressed they are about specific incidents in their talks/chats, and that's a good way to vent, or some may find therapists, and that's another great way to cope. Some would have other family members step in, or receive support emotionally, financially etc to get through the difficult ways, and they are all so important ways to cope. I think another aspect to remember is that time is changing so quick. What our parents and grandparents have survived and applied, may very well NOT be the case for us. The societla structure, the toys kids play with, the way they connect, the way information comes in.... so so much change. I do remember my husband saying at one point he feels envious about his friends and colleges that have only 1 or 2 kids - that's when our surprise baby #4 came at Urgent Care testing I went in for something else. That was a shocking surprise to me, as I thought that he and his family was the reason I had even felt positive or entertained the idea of having kids. He is a good dad, a wonderful guy, but the challenging situation can make us easily overwhelmed. No families in the states, living in the South where family bonds are strong and people are not very friendly or easy to connect. And I could see how too much stress could negatively affect anyone, and in the worst case, can lead to mental illnesses, which then can compromise good decision makings and possibly leading to the next generation to suffer some more. Just for quick general background, I am an East Asian immigrant, that come from a good and stable environment once I went back to live with grandparents. In my younger first years, my parents conceived me (mistake/surprise baby) in the US, where they have had big financial difficultes. Living with grandparents had been a big blessing for me and I do think that has rescued me a lot. Growing up in the stress filled Tokyo by a heavily stressed mother despite the economy was still good back then, was still enough for me to pick up so much more of the sorrows of living than the joy of it. In middle school, some kids from less unfortunate backgrounds would gang up, and at one point I remember them half-threatening classmates to get them to contribute for someone's abortion. I have had multiple friends and acquaintance die from various reasons (traffic accident, being murdered, losing battles to quick developing cancer), friends losing their parents and since this is Tokyo, not where they had their family support, the children's generation's life quickly declining. I was ready to not have kids, until my innocent husband who grew up happy said, he thinks it would be fun to have kids - apparently he and his sister got along well, he has good relationship with him parents, and they had much hope for life and not much worries. When my mother in law seemed so happy and loving and supportive when I first shared the news of being pregnant, I questioned myself of my belief, that it wasn't worth having kids. My MIL's strong belief that kids are great and babies are the best thing you can have all affected me. I come from a background where we're supposed to respect elders, and I had not know that I was probably feeling the change of economy better than her. I know there was a sense of "I really hope that's true - with her support, I think I can make it, and perhaps things are not so bad after all." But the night I borough the baby back home I was starting to have postpartum depression, which only got worse with each pregnancy. However, the great uplifted mood during pregnancy has really made me wonder: which is the true me? What's the truth and reality around here? I had the most blissful pregnancy time, yet overwhelming post-partum where I have not gotten around to life-planning successfully. I've gone back to give birth to my kids twice with her, leaving my husband behind in the US, thinking those times when you're pregnant and after birth is so important in the kids formation Ends up we're not going to live close to my MIL, not even in the same country or continent. There comes a point when she can no longer continue to offer the support she'd had hoped to give or that I was longing to get - and the reason I even had kids. I felt so nurtured, and cared for while living with her, and once I realized that was a thing of a past and not to be continued unless we were planning on paying multiple Ks for the airfare per ticket, it was very very difficult. She has had many family members around, and have had the full social support structure, as well as stable finances. We lack them. Then when kids come with their difficulties which is not always predictable, there's a tipping point as to how you can survive or get overwhelmed. I do understand both sides. For those who say kids are so valuable, my speculation is that they have been blessed with good health mentally, spirtually, emotionally and or physically, or have good support to cover in times of diffuculty, whether it be a financially stable situation, or family members who can come to their rescue when needed. I am very happy that things are going well for them. I was hoping that would be the case for us as well. As someone said, "kids can bring so much joy as they turn out good." And when that's not the case - when we get overwhelmed, yes there's so much grief. I have come to lower my expectations. I used to think there's no way my kids will be stuck in front of screen, that we'll have a good balanced discipline, that we could continue to love and support them the way both me and my husband have received support all the way through college easily. Now I am realizing my youngest one may not have bathed for so many days up to two weeks, and my older two are constantly on their screen (who isn't too? They say many of their friends have iPhones - my 8th grader just got a tracfone for Christmas - and they're not happy at all with what they get and think we're poor, and are hard on the parents.) Holidays are stressful as all the entitled kids are at home bored with more screen time, we're not really able to spend much quality time with any of them, parents are overwhelmed, we don't get to be fed but we have to constantly feed and clean, I worry about how the kids are growing mentally as I try to figure out my own. Now I am so much more appreciative of the environment that we both grew up in (surrounded by extended family members, with seniors being healthy mentally and physically). We grew up in good economic times too. That's something that I think everyone should be aware: how much it costs to raise kids for them to not feel inferior and deprived. Due to overwhelm and not being able to take too much good care of myself, I find myself being very sad and frustrated. For me, I take it as a process of letting go, growing in faith and trust (which is not easy). In the end, I think it's how much support you have, as kids should not be just the product of parents themselves. Unless you have good structure, the way it is in the US (or at least what I'm experiencing right around myself), when parents are isolated and overwhelmed, it's so easy to get into that questioning even regretting. I love my kids. Love them so much that I wish they were in a better environment. Wish I had the chance to establish a better community to raise them together. I could see how much more easy, fun, happy and joyous that experience would be. One thing that has brought so much comfort to me is the thought that they are their own spirits, coming to this world to have their own journey, and that it is not "my fault" to have birthed them into this rather cold/hostile/un-kind environment. If there are any mental health issues parents are feeling, (I'm saying this to myself), it's helpful in the long run and worth the investment to receive care in that arena. I believe it is wise to have good awareness of your own upbringing, see it as it is, not as you've made believe it to be (i.e. kids are so much joy - yes, but that's when you're surrounded by other people who can love them as much as you do and are committed to raising them with you), and have a realistic picture and know your boundaries. Let's do the best we can and hope for the best. (If you're feeling desperate, I personally want to say I have benefited so much from Energy Healers. They get down to the core and can help in amazing ways that I would not have been open to unless I was really down in the lowest point of my life, so desperate to have aid.)
column9: Four kids are a lot for anybody and especially if you are experiencing postpartum depression. The first order of business is to get this treated, because otherwise you will never stop feeling overwhelmed and all your kids need a mother who is fully present, not sinking in quicksand. I hope your husband is helping you in this. He should be. Once that's taken care of, I think you both need to enlist your children in running the household. You didn't say how old they all were, but you'd be surprised that even very young children can contribute -- and this is important for THEM. They need to feel like part of the team. You need to teach, coach and encourage them in tasks you give them and accept they are learning and what they do will not be perfect. With gentle guidance, you can help them get better over time. The older kids should be helping with the younger kids -- somewhat. I do not like when parents assign all the parenting work to other children BUT they can and should help. Also, the older ones have learned a lot. Ask them to teach younger ones (how to tie shoes, fold clothes, put stuff away, teach ABCs, count numbers). Kids like to show off their knowledge and teach others. Let them. You need to run your home like a kind but firm CEO -- get up a list of chores for each of your children that is age appropriate. Some tasks will be daily, some weekly, and some monthly -- but hold them to it. Again, they need to feel they are contributing. Be reasonable. Don't eat up all their time with chores. And be a good manager by training them in the tasks, following up that they've done it and kindly giving them pointers for doing better next time. Increase their responsibilities over time. In their unstructured time, let them use TV, tablets, computers or whatever for a VERY LIMITED TIME each day -- say 30 minutes or 1 hour (again, make it age appropriate). Remember, YOU and YOUR HUSBAND are in control. If you're not, then no one is. This makes children feel very insecure. IMPORTANT: Have weekly family meetings. Don't skip this! They can be just 15 or 30 minutes. All gather round the table and talk about what happened during the past week, talk about the chores and give the kids feedback about how they are doing (always try to find something encouraging to say) and listen to their concerns and suggestions and make adjustments. Try to listen twice as much as you talk. Kids sometimes have a hard time finding the right words to express their thoughts so ask them questions to clarify. It also shows you're paying attention. Perhaps one child would rather do dishes and another fold laundry and maybe they could switch tasks. Find out if there is other tasks to help you with they might find fun -- like helping you cook, chop vegetables, set the table etc. Your children need to know that their feelings matter to you and are willing to accommodate their wishes if you can. They want to know that you SEE them and that you HEAR them. Isn't that what adults want in their relationships too? Also, at the end of the meeting, go round the table and ask each child what they are grateful for. You have to encourage this mindset. In reading your post I fear that your underlying thoughts of "birthing them into a cold, hostile, world" is a vibe you are unfortunately going to pass on to your children. I'm not sure if you were referring to your home or the world in general but in any case you MUST change YOUR mindset and the children will follow your lead. Look for the positives, the small moments of joy, seek out the good -- you find what you're looking for. Are you looking for the bad? You'll find it. Are you looking for the good? You'll find that too. Kids will listen to what you teach them, but they'll also watch you for what you're not teaching. What do you want them to be... unhappy? moody? depressed? overwhelmed? -- or -- happy? strong? confident? loving? Display in yourself what you want them to copy. They are watching you. Closely. You will be amazed at the shift in your kids' attitude and gratitude. And you will find it changing in you too. Remember, most of the stuff that needs doing in the home are simple tasks that children can easily master but YOU need to assign them and TRAIN them. You will need a lot of patient repetition -- this is how ALL people learn -- and since children are new to everything, they need lots more of it. No yelling please. Only bad managers need to yell. Don't underestimate what children can do. I was just reading an article in the Wall Street Journal where German parents send their 3 YEAR OLDS to camp (no parents allowed). These kids learn to do for themselves, including whittling wood (yes, with knives!) so they can put food on a stick and cook over a campfire. It concerns me that you say: "That's something that I think everyone should be aware: how much it costs to raise kids for them to not feel inferior and deprived". They aren't going to feel inferior / deprived unless you let them. It's your job to guide their mind to one of abundance . . . to teach them to regularly focus on what they have, things they have accomplished, their ability to be creative, to have them always think of what they can be grateful for. YOU can't let them wallow in a "deprived" mindset. They need your guidance to steer them on the right course, but it seems you are lost in this regard which doesn't bode well for your children. So, change YOUR mindset first, then teach it to your kids. It will help you immensely to keep a "gratitude" diary .... at the end of each day jot down at LEAST one thing you're grateful for. One moment in the day that made you feel joy (did your baby smile for the first time? did your son say "I love you mommy"?). You'll have to work at it to start with, but it'll be easier and easier until it becomes part of you. Then, you MUST teach this to your children. It is the foundation on which they can build a life. Also, just like adults, kids need a hobby. Get art projects and encourage them. If they don't have something to fill their time they will revert to the easiest thing which is the TV and computers. Don't leave them up to their own meager devices . . . steer them in a creative direction. Can you get some cardboard boxes so they can build a Fort? How about some sheets so they can create a tent? Is there a playground or sports activity they can do? Their creativity is their most valuable asset and it should be intensely nurtured by you while they're young. Yes, it is easier to raise children when you have extended family close by. I'm truly sorry that didn't work out for you. It's a loss for the children not having a grandmother in their lives too, so it's not your loss alone. Perhaps you could create your own by seeking out other mothers and support each other, trade babysitting, put on parties, etc. Make your own "family" wherever you are. Your children don't have the ability to create this network, but you do, and should, for their sake. Make that effort. When you became parents you became a coach, teacher, manager, entertainment director, cook, psychologist, nurse and so much more. Get your kids involved in all aspects of the home. They shouldn't just be little people sitting on the sidelines absorbed in their own little world. (How would you like to go to a job each day where the boss hasn't given you anything to do, but everyone around you is hustling and bustling and getting stuff done? You'd probably start playing computer games just to fill your time, but wouldn't you rather be part of what's going on and contributing? Children are the same. They want to be meaningful too). Another tip: when you look at your young children, try to visualize them as the grown men and women they will become. Ask yourself what it will take to get them from here to there successfully. Break down the steps and do it. Start now. Reinforce their strengths and help them overcome their weaknesses. That's what a good coach does. Try to give each child one-on-one time with you. They place a very high value on your attention (one day they won't) so don't be stingy with it. Or with your love and affection either. It's free, so you can afford to be very lavish with it. Have a ritual at the end of the day where all the children gather before bedtime for a story or just talking. It's up to you to create these moments that your children will cherish and sustain them. They only get one childhood -- what do you want them to see when they look back on theirs? Remember, these people will all be your friends one day! Your job is to get them to adulthood with a sense of happiness, strength, independence, confidence and optimism. Always keep the end goal in mind!

column1: Why do I feel no interest in anything anymore? Is it apathy or depression?
column3: Everyone loses interest in things at one time or another, but when it happens a lot, it can affect your relationships, your job, and your ability to enjoy life. You may be able to see the signs of apathy or depression in yourself, or a friend or family member might have pointed out that you don't seem as interested or engaged as you used to be. If this has happened, instead of you diagnosing yourself I would encourage you to seek professional help, such as going to a medical doctor who is able to give you a proper diagnosis and treat you. Treatment will make a big difference, so talk to your doctor or a mental health professional to get the help you need.

column1: Has mental illness become the "new normal?"
column3: I have a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder. I am also a therapist. We have two pandemics happening at the same time. Obviously the Covid-19 pandemic and the mental health pandemic. The pandemic has increased isolation and anxiety in children and adults. Contact with peers is crucial for good mental health. Children have lost a year of education and although experts are claiming that children are resilient and can snap back to “normal" how is that even possible when this era of Covid-19 is anything but normal? Losing a year of freedom is something most adults are experiencing and they are not doing very well so how can we expect children to do better? To suggest that the pandemic has not traumatized children and professionals are not taking into account the emotional and mental impact the pandemic has had on our and our children's emotional and mental health is deeply concerning. Children and adults who have suffered from depression and anxiety cannot just put the genie back in the bottle and carry on as if nothing has happened once everyone is vaccinated and everything and everyone is just supposed to go back to “normal.” Mental illness does not work that way. We know that children and adults are suffering from mental health symptoms associated with the pandemic and those symptoms and illnesses are not going to go away. We also have no idea what the long term implications of what this pandemic has done to our mental well-being and we need to be able to set up crisis areas in schools were children can go if they are afraid or anxious while at school. When the pandemic was upon us and everything shut down and we were locked down overnight it shocked me and I am educated in mental health. Children are going to have to learn to trust that their whole world is not going to change again and we cannot promise them that this will not happen again because it can. This rush to get children back to school is ill conceived if we do not start by focussing on their mental and emotional well-being. The first thing we have to do is to take our children's emotional and mental temperature and provide them with the mental and emotional help they may need before we add academic pressure on top of a pot that is ready to boil over. The emphasis on getting back to “normal" is unrealistic and particularly to students who cannot keep up academically and who will not to no fault of their own be graduating with the rest of their class. Before children go back to school funding needs to be in place to evaluate each and every child's mental and emotional well-being. We also have to emphasis that the pandemic and everything associated with it is anything but normal so children understand that what they have been through is not fair and they deserve and need to openly express how the pandemic has affected their lives. The impact that Covid-19 has had upon our lives is the “new normal" and the new normal has to be acknowledged and we have to navigate carefully and compassionately as some children are not as lucky as others. Parents are divorcing, children have gone hungry, and children have lost family members to Covid-19. Just one of these horrors will have life-long implications for a child. Some children will have experienced loss, divorce, and hunger. The government cannot allow a child who is suffering to go back to school as nothing has happened and neither can we. I am asking all therapists to volunteer a few hours a week in schools because our children are going to need it and they deserve nothing less.

column1: How can I choose between my parents' health and my own mental health?
column3: Doctors aren't allowed to disclose things to members of your family without your consent if you have mental capacity/able to think and understand-at least that's where I live. I'm still unsure how you are affecting their health through this. maybe The best thing to do is focus on the other issues here like why can't u prioritise both? Can you make it so that you don't neglect either one, that your relationship leaves u in a good mood and not affect the others in your family? Can you work on finding a purpose in your life so it's not just someone else? Like doing what makes u happy or you're good at or feel fulfilled in? 18 is basicslly an adult so u may not be too young but I guess it depends on person to person. Maybe unless they get angry u can explain To your parents or siblings how much they mean to you and that you may not find another? Or tone down the relationship so it's not affecting everyone? Let's not forget also ur probably at end of high school and so it's an important time for your education and future career and life too so don’t lose focus on that.
column9: Sorry I wasn't clear on why it's affecting my parents. My mom has high blood pressure, so her heart beats really fast and she gets nauseous. And to be honest I really don't know how I can't let it affect them. Because they ask whether I'm meeting with someone or am going somewhere and then I have to tell them where I'm going. And I did tell my dad how important this is for me, but he's really concerned about my mom. Everyone is. So now I feel especially bad because I have the feeling all of this is my fault.

column1: Do you think that young people are more depressed than older people?
column3: That can be the case, but isn’t always. The world has changed in a lot of ways, some of these ways are percieved as negative and some are percieved that way for good reason. Younger people are more likely to spend large amounts of time on social media which can often give them the impression that things may be worse than they actually are which can become a self fulfilling prophecy in some very tragic ways. Social media is one of the main drivers of the political polarization that is making people hate and fear each other so much. Older people are less likely to have this constant bombardment of negative messanging influences, yet many people suffer from lonlieness due to losing many friends and family members over the years. This can often make older people feel like they don’t have much to look forward to and many older people also being mentally and or pysically sendentary can often make this much worse. My 71 year old mother for example has been struggling with depression because of how many family members she has had die on her as well as being depressed due to health challenges making her not able to do as much as she used to. The bottom line is that depression can affect anyone of any age group, though admitedly the mental health challenges among the young are especially troubling due to them leading to alarming increases in youth suicide rates. Quite frankly we are failing both older as well as younger people by doping them up on SSRIs with dangerous (often permanent) side effects instead of getting to the root of the problem.

column1: How do you detach yourself from someone but yet be attached? How can you not be affected by their actions or behavior?
column3: Maybe I’m weird, but your question makes sense to me. It could be a case of a family member who behaves in a way that brings out the worst in you. Things can get a bit complicated..a person might annoy the hell out of you, and cause you to become frustrated and angry, but that person may also have good qualities that you at times, have to admit are admirable. So back to the question.. It’s tempting to try to completely detach yourself from someone, but due to certain circumstances or relationships, that may just cause more problems. And in the end, how practical would it be to completely detach ourselves from every person who possessed some quality that annoyed or angered us? If we rephrase the question to, how can I best keep my sense of peace, while spending significant amounts of time around someone who has caused me to lose it at times? All I can say is it takes a tremendous amount of self-awareness to choose to not react negatively when certain buttons are pushed. When you feel that familiar irritation or anger starting to boil, focus on your breathing, “watch” your feelings at that moment as kind of an observer from the outside, and don’t react negatively with words or physical actions. Don’t add fuel to the fire. This takes a lot of mental focus, especially in the beginning, but it becomes easier each time you’re successful at doing it. You basically replace useless (and often destructive) habits with more useful ones. This is obviously not easy…but worthwhile! (Unless you live completely alone on a deserted island, with all your needs cared for, in which case you may live a peaceful existence, but a very limited one). The key is that calming your outward reactions is not enough. You could be calm on the outside but boiling mad on the inside. This isn’t good for your health, and it will come out in some form, sooner or later. In other words, we need to be able to calm our negative reactions on the inside, as well. In this way, it is possible to detach yourself (emotionally) from certain aspects of someone you have a relationship with (whether family, spouse, friend, coworker), but also remain attached in the sense that you are in a relationship with that person (whether by circumstance, or because you’ve decided that it’s still worth being in a relationship with that person). All that being said, it is a challenging process that requires constant attention to your inner state (I’m personally still very much in the “work in progress” stage), but it is such a worthwhile endeavor. Some might say that it is connected to the true purpose of being alive as a human. Don’t get discouraged! I sometimes find myself stumbling back a step, but we make progress by stepping forward two more steps. Even when we “lose it,” (by not paying attention and letting the anger or frustration completely boil over), it can be a great reminder and motivation that we don’t want to go back there again. Hope that makes sense..and I hope I interpreted your question correctly.

column1: Have you ever realized that you were wrong about someone?
column3: Who hasn't? Most people have had a friend or significant other that they thought were wonderful people, only to discover that they really aren't. Others peg someone as awful or criminal and find out they are a kind hearted person. As for examples: We'll go back to my first long term boyfriend way back in high school. I was in love with him. Handsome, sweet, smart, not to mention had a cool car, cool friends. We were together all the time unless he was working. Well, some friends spied him at a carnival with a group of girls and he refused to answer his phone. After confronting him I believed him when he said they were just friends. Several months later, I found out that he cheated on me with some random girl. After we broke up, I found out about 2 more. I never would have thought he'd be the type, but he absolutely was. Example 2: a family member with mental health issues seemed to be doing fantastic taking care of her issues. Really coming along, taking meds, working, steady relationship. Really an improvement from her worst days. Then I noticed the lying, manipulation, using other people, if confronted she'd flip out. I was wrong, she was only taking meds sometimes, lied to make herself look good. Refusing to acknowledge her wrongs, she's been in a downward spiral and slowly losing everything that matters to her because as an adult she can't be forced to get help. Example 3: guy dressed all in black…liked metal music, huge ear piercings….call him goth. Obviously a freak, had some issues….turned out he was really chill, laid back, sweet, dreamed of becoming a photographer, was pretty good at it. People have their dark sides, light sides, and we see what they choose to show us. How wrong we are about them only affects us to the same degree as we are close to them. A mere acquaintance you always thought was a decent person being arrested for drugs…you may think oh wow I never would have guessed & move on. If that person is your boyfriend, you're going to be devastated.

column1: An in-depth investigation into Prince Harry's latest claims and discrepancies during his latest interviews has been published in Buzzfeed News. Does this suggest that Prince Harry and Meghan might lose support in America too?
column3: Why would he? Because some buzzfeed person took a break from writing about the “37 things from amazon that will change your life”?
