You do it while they are still there.Harry notes in the docuseries about beginning therapy, which he says he did four years ago.Um, no. He has been in therapy before. He started therapy *again* a few years back. Much like I started therapy *again* in 2018.this highlights another contradiction in Harry’s recent interviews: his claim that his wife was the person who encouraged him to seek treatment for his mental health — even though he has long credited William for making him realize that he needed to confront his emotions about the traumatic death of their mother.It’s almost like you can hear the same message from different people, and comprehend it differently. Talking about his mother is one thing. Really seeing how it’s affecting your intimate relationships is another. My ex had been in therapy before he met me. They wanted him to talk about certain things about his life. He wouldn’t. Then we met, got engaged, and broke up. Before we got back together, I encouraged therapy. This time he talked about those things, and had some breakthroughs. And we were able to get back together because I didn’t feel like he was an emotional ticking time-bomb. Different reasons for therapy, different therapists, and a different time in your life = different results.I always thought to myself, What’s the point of bringing up the past? What’s the point of bringing up something that’s only going to make you sad? It ain’t going to change it. It ain’t going to bring her back. And when you start thinking like that, it can be really damaging,” he said. “You [William] always said to me, ‘You have got to sit down and think about all these memories,’ but for me, it was like, I don’t want to think about it.”That’s from 2017. After he had already gone back because Meghan mentioned it. But Meghan wasn’t in this interview. He was talking to William, who had indeed said those things to him, and Catherine. So it makes sense that he would mention William as having spoken about these things. It does not mean Meghan didn’t say anything. It does not mean that he only had the one person talking about it to him. It simply means that at that interview in that moment he only felt it was relevant to mention what William had said to him.“Absolutely not,” Levin quotes Harry as saying in the recent Telegraph article. “She had nothing to do with it.”He obviously didn’t wish to share everything about his life with her at that moment. Now he does. No famous person has to share every single thought with us. Ever.Harry noted in The Me You Can’t See that he initially rebuffed the concerns of “a couple of people close to [him]” who had encouraged him to seek help for his mental health, noting, “It’s all about timing.” He reiterated this in the May podcast, saying that “you need to feel it in yourself” to get treatment.This author is writing all these things, but I don’t think they are hearing what they are writing. Harry is literally saying that he knows people had mentioned it before, but he didn’t “feel it in” himself at the time, and the author is still saying that’s a contradiction. I can know that I need to lose weight, but still not do all of the hard work to lose weight. I can know that I don’t fit into my favorite clothes, and still sit on quora instead of doing some pushups. Humans are weird. But it doesn’t mean we’re lying about things. It just means we have to wait until the time is right to do something, and it means that we sometimes share this part of ourselves and other times share that part of ourselves. I don’t want to even discuss the last thing they bring up. There is a massive huge difference between just getting therapy and getting in-patient help for a pregnant newlywed in the Royal family. William and Catherine had to announce babies well before 12 weeks because they knew the press would eat her alive if they noticed she had been admitted to the hospital just for hyperemesis. Can you even imagine what they would have done if Meghan had become a patient for suicidal ideation? That’s not something that was ever going to be possible. Meghan was embarrassed to have those feelings. Many people are. Many people don’t talk about them. Do you know what happens to those people? They quite often die. They feel weak to have such emotions and they hide them until they do something about them. I lost a friend to suicide last August, and no one knew what was going on because he wasn’t talking about it. When she was brave enough to talk to him about it, he didn’t know what to do, either. Most of us wouldn’t know. And in a family where, I remind you, they know that the press would swarm like crazed yellowjackets regarding a hyperemesis hospitalization, there was no way she was going to get the help she was asking for, so of course he wouldn’t have brought it up with the family. Again, there is a stigma in the family about talking about mental health; that’s precisely why the younger ones of the family are trying to change that. What a mess of an article. I hope she was able to do something good with the money she got for writing it, so that something good can come out of the drivel she came up with. In a few years she’s going to look back at it with the shame that I look back on things I wrote in my diary in junior high.

column1: What are the criteria for BPD (EUPD)?
column3: If you have BPD, everything feels unstable: your relationships, moods, thinking, behavior—even your identity. But there is hope. If you have borderline personality disorder (BPD), you probably feel like you’re on a rollercoaster—and not just because of your unstable emotions or relationships, but also the wavering sense of who you are. Your self-image, goals, and even your likes and dislikes may change frequently in ways that feel confusing and unclear. People with BPD tend to be extremely sensitive. Some describe it as having an exposed nerve ending. Small things can trigger intense reactions. And once upset, you have trouble calming down. It’s easy to understand how this emotional volatility and inability to self-soothe leads to relationship turmoil and impulsive—even reckless—behavior. When you’re in the throes of overwhelming emotions, you’re unable to think straight or stay grounded. You may say hurtful things or act out in dangerous or inappropriate ways that make you feel guilty or ashamed afterward. It’s a painful cycle that can feel impossible to escape. But it’s not. There are effective BPD treatments and coping skills that can help you feel better and back in control of your thoughts, feelings, and actions. BPD is treatable In the past, many mental health professionals found it difficult to treat borderline personality disorder (BPD), so they came to the conclusion that there was little to be done. But we now know that BPD is treatable. In fact, the long-term prognosis for BPD is better than those for depression and bipolar disorder. However, it requires a specialized approach. The bottom line is that most people with BPD can and do get better—and they do so fairly rapidly with the right treatments and support. Healing is a matter of breaking the dysfunctional patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving that are causing you distress. It’s not easy to change lifelong habits. Choosing to pause, reflect, and then act in new ways will feel unnatural and uncomfortable at first. But with the time you’ll form new habits that help you maintain your emotional balance and stay in control. Recognizing borderline personality disorder Do you identify with the following statements?I often feel “empty.”My emotions shift very quickly, and I often experience extreme sadness, anger, and anxiety.I’m constantly afraid that the people I care about will abandon me or leave me.I would describe most of my romantic relationships as intense, but unstable.The way I feel about the people in my life can dramatically change from one moment to the next—and I don’t always understand why.I often do things that I know are dangerous or unhealthy, such as driving recklessly, having unsafe sex, binge drinking, using drugs, or going on spending sprees.I’ve attempted to hurt myself, engaged in self-harm behaviors such as cutting or threatened suicide.When I’m feeling insecure in a relationship, I tend to lash out or make impulsive gestures to keep the other person close.If you identify with several of the statements, you may suffer from a borderline personality disorder. Of course, you need a mental health professional to make an official diagnosis, as BPD can be easily confused with other issues. But even without a diagnosis, you may find the self-help tips in this article helpful for calming your inner emotional storm and learning to control self-damaging impulses. Signs and symptoms Borderline personality disorder (BPD) manifests in many different ways, but for the purposes of diagnosis, mental health professionals group the symptoms into nine major categories. In order to be diagnosed with BPD, you must show signs of at least five of these symptoms. Furthermore, the symptoms must be long-standing (usually beginning in adolescence) and impact many areas of your life. The 9 symptoms of BPDFear of abandonment. People with BPD are often terrified of being abandoned or left alone. Even something as innocuous as a loved one arriving home late from work or going away for the weekend may trigger intense fear. This can prompt frantic efforts to keep the other person close. You may beg, cling, start fights, track your loved one’s movements, or even physically block the person from leaving. Unfortunately, this behavior tends to have the opposite effect—driving others away.Unstable relationships. People with BPD tend to have relationships that are intense and short-lived. You may fall in love quickly, believing that each new person is the one who will make you feel whole, only to be quickly disappointed. Your relationships either seem perfect or horrible, without any middle ground. Your lovers, friends, or family members may feel like they have emotional whiplash as a result of your rapid swings from idealization to devaluation, anger, and hate.Unclear or shifting self-image. When you have BPD, your sense of self is typically unstable. Sometimes you may feel good about yourself, but other times you hate yourself or even view yourself as evil. You probably don’t have a clear idea of who you are or what you want in life. As a result, you may frequently change jobs, friends, lovers, religion, values, goals, or even sexual identity.Impulsive, self-destructive behaviors. If you have BPD, you may engage in harmful, sensation-seeking behaviors, especially when you’re upset. You may impulsively spend money you can’t afford, binge eat, drive recklessly, shoplift, engage in risky sex, or overdo it with drugs or alcohol. These risky behaviors may help you feel better in the moment, but they hurt you and those around you over the long-term.Self-harm. Suicidal behavior and deliberate self-harm is common in people with BPD. Suicidal behavior includes thinking about suicide, making suicidal gestures or threats, or actually carrying out a suicide attempt. Self-harm encompasses all other attempts to hurt yourself without suicidal intent. Common forms of self-harm include cutting and burning.Extreme emotional swings. Unstable emotions and moods are common with BPD. One moment, you may feel happy, and the next, despondent. Little things that other people brush off can send you into an emotional tailspin. These mood swings are intense, but they tend to pass fairly quickly (unlike the emotional swings of depression or bipolar disorder), usually lasting just a few minutes or hours.Chronic feelings of emptiness. People with BPD often talk about feeling empty, as if there’s a hole or a void inside them. At the extreme, you may feel as if you’re “nothing” or “nobody.” This feeling is uncomfortable, so you may try to fill the void with things like drugs, food, or sex. But nothing feels truly satisfying.Explosive anger. If you have BPD, you may struggle with intense anger and a short temper. You may also have trouble controlling yourself once the fuse is lit—yelling, throwing things, or becoming completely consumed by rage. It’s important to note that this anger isn’t always directed outwards. You may spend a lot of time feeling angry at yourself.Feeling suspicious or out of touch with reality. People with BPD often struggle with paranoia or suspicious thoughts about others’ motives. When under stress, you may even lose touch with reality—an experience known as dissociation. You may feel foggy, spaced out, or as if you’re outside your own body.Common co-occurring disorders A borderline personality disorder is rarely diagnosed on its own. Common co-occurring disorders include:depression or bipolar disordersubstance abuseeating disordersanxiety disordersWhen BPD is successfully treated, the other disorders often get improve, too. But the reverse isn’t always true. For example, you may successfully treat symptoms of depression and still struggle with BPD. Causes—and hope Most mental health professionals believe that borderline personality disorder (BPD) is caused by a combination of inherited or internal biological factors and external environmental factors, such as traumatic experiences in childhood. Brain differences There are many complex things happening in the BPD brain, and researchers are still untangling what it all means. But in essence, if you have BPD, your brain is on high alert. Things feel more scary and stressful to you than they do to other people. Your fight-or-flight switch is easily tripped, and once it’s on, it hijacks your rational brain, triggering primitive survival instincts that aren’t always appropriate to the situation at hand. This may make it sound as if there’s nothing you can do. After all, what can you do if your brain is different? But the truth is that you can change your brain. Every time you practice a new coping response or self-soothing technique you are creating new neural pathways. Some treatments, such as mindfulness meditation, can even grow your brain matter. And the more you practice, the stronger and more automatic these pathways will become. So don’t give up! With time and dedication, you can change the way you think, feel, and act. Personality disorders and stigma When psychologists talk about “personality,” they’re referring to the patterns of thinking, feeling, and behaving that make each of us unique. No one acts exactly the same all the time, but we do tend to interact and engage with the world in fairly consistent ways. This is why people are often described as “shy,” “outgoing,” “meticulous,” “fun-loving,” and so on. These are elements of personality. Because personality is so intrinsically connected to identity, the term “personality disorder” might leave you feeling like there’s something fundamentally wrong with who you are. But a personality disorder is not a character judgment. In clinical terms, “personality disorder” means that your pattern of relating to the world is significantly different from the norm. (In other words, you don’t act in ways that most people expect). This causes consistent problems for you in many areas of your life, such as your relationships, career, and your feelings about yourself and others. But most importantly, these patterns can be changed! Self-help tips: 3 keys to coping with BPDCalm the emotional stormLearn to control impulsivity and tolerate distressImprove your interpersonal skillsSelf-help tip 1: Calm the emotional storm As someone with BPD, you’ve probably spent a lot of time-fighting your impulses and emotions, so acceptance can be a tough thing to wrap your mind around. But accepting your emotions doesn’t mean approving of them or resigning yourself to suffering. All it means is that you stop trying to fight, avoid, suppress, or deny what you’re feeling. Giving yourself permission to have these feelings can take away a lot of their power. Try to simply experience your feelings without judgment or criticism. Let go of the past and the future and focus exclusively on the present moment. Mindfulness techniques can be very effective in this regard.Start by observing your emotions, as if from the outside.Watch as they come and go (it may help to think of them as waves).Focus on the physical sensations that accompany your emotions.Tell yourself that you accept what you’re feeling right now.Remind yourself that just because you’re feeling something doesn’t mean it’s reality.Do something that stimulates one or more of your senses Engaging your sense is one of the quickest and easiest ways to quickly self-soothe. You will need to experiment to find out which sensory-based stimulation works best for you. You’ll also need different strategies for different moods. What may help when you’re angry or agitated is very different from what may help when you’re numb or depressed. Here are some ideas to get started: Touch. If you’re not feeling enough, try running cold or hot (but not scalding hot) water over your hands; hold a piece of ice, or grip an object or the edge of a piece of furniture as tightly as you can. If you’re feeling too much, and need to calm down, try taking a hot bath or shower; snuggling under the bed covers, or cuddling with a pet. Taste. If you’re feeling empty and numb, try sucking on strong-flavored mints or candies, or slowly eat something with an intense flavor, such as salt-and-vinegar chips. If you want to calm down, try something soothing such as hot tea or soup. Smell. Light a candle, smell the flowers, try aromatherapy, spritz your favorite perfume, or whip up something in the kitchen that smells good. You may find that you respond best to strong smells, such as citrus, spices, and incense. Sight. Focus on an image that captures your attention. This can be something in your immediate environment (a great view, a beautiful flower arrangement, a favorite painting or photo) or something in your imagination that you visualize. Sound. Try listening to loud music, ringing a buzzer, or blowing a whistle when you need a jolt. To calm down, turn on soothing music or listen to the soothing sounds of nature, such as wind, birds, or the ocean. A sound machine works well if you can’t hear the real thing. Reduce your emotional vulnerability You’re more likely to experience negative emotions when you’re run down and under stress. That’s why it’s very important to take care of your physical and mental well-being. Take care of yourself by:Avoid mood-altering drugsEating a balanced, nutritious dietGetting plenty of quality sleepExercising regularlyMinimizing stressPracticing relaxation techniquesLearn to control impulsivity and tolerate distress The calming techniques discussed above can help you relax when you’re starting to become derailed by stress. But what do you do when you’re feeling overwhelmed by difficult feelings? This is where the impulsivity of borderline personality disorder (BPD) comes in. In the heat of the moment, you’re so desperate for relief that you’ll do anything, including things you know you shouldn’t—such as cutting, reckless sex, dangerous driving, and binge drinking. It may even feel like you don’t have a choice. Moving from being out of control of your behavior to being in control It’s important to recognize that these impulsive behaviors serve a purpose. They’re coping mechanisms for dealing with distress. They make you feel better, even if just for a brief moment. But the long-term costs are extremely high. Regaining control of your behavior starts with learning to tolerate distress. It’s the key to changing the destructive patterns of BPD. The ability to tolerate distress will help you press pause when you have the urge to act out. Instead of reacting to difficult emotions with self-destructive behaviors, you will learn to ride them out while remaining in control of the experience. For a step-by-step, self-guided program that will teach you how to ride the “wild horse” of overwhelming feelings, check out our free Emotional Intelligence Toolkit. The toolkit teaches you how to:get in touch with your emotionslive with emotional intensitymanage unpleasant or threatening feelingsstay calm and focused even in upsetting situationsThe toolkit will teach you how to tolerate distress, but it doesn’t stop there. It will also teach you how to move from being emotionally shut down to experiencing your emotions fully. This allows you to experience the full range of positive emotions such as joy, peace, and fulfillment that are also cut off when you attempt to avoid negative feelings. A grounding exercise to help you pause and regain control Once the fight-or-flight response is triggered, there is no way to “think yourself” calm. Instead of focusing on your thoughts, focus on what you’re feeling in your body. The following grounding exercise is a simple, quick way to put the brakes on impulsivity, calm down, and regain control. It can make a big difference in just a few short minutes. Find a quiet spot and sit in a comfortable position. Focus on what you’re experiencing in your body. Feel the surface you’re sitting on. Feel your feet on the floor. Feel your hands in your lap. Concentrate on your breathing, taking slow, deep breaths. Breathe in slowly. Pause for a count of three. Then slowly breathe out, once more pausing for a count of three. Continue to do this for several minutes. In case of emergency, distract yourself If your attempts to calm down aren’t working and you’re starting to feel overwhelmed by destructive urges, distracting yourself may help. All you need is something to capture your focus long enough for the negative impulse to go away. Anything that draws your attention can work, but distraction is most effective when the activity is also soothing. In addition to the sensory-based strategies mentioned previously, here are some things you might try: Watch TV. Choose something that’s the opposite of what you’re feeling: a comedy, if you’re feeling sad, or something relaxing if you’re angry or agitated. Do something you enjoy that keeps you busy. This could be anything: gardening, painting, playing an instrument, knitting, reading a book, playing a computer game, or doing a Sudoku or word puzzle. Throw yourself into work. You can also distract yourself with chores and errands: cleaning your house, doing yard work, going grocery shopping, grooming your pet, or doing the laundry. Get active. Vigorous exercise is a healthy way to get your adrenaline pumping and let off steam. If you’re feeling stressed, you may want to try more relaxing activities such as yoga or a walk around your neighborhood. Call a friend. Talking to someone you trust can be a quick and highly effective way to distract yourself, feel better, and gain some perspective. Improve your interpersonal skills If you have a borderline personality disorder, you’ve probably struggled with maintaining stable, satisfying relationships with lovers, co-workers, and friends. This is because you have trouble stepping back and seeing things from other people’s perspectives. You tend to misread the thoughts and feelings of others, misunderstand how others see you and overlook how they’re affected by your behavior. It’s not that you don’t care, but when it comes to other people, you have a big blind spot. Recognizing your interpersonal blind spot is the first step. When you stop blaming others, you can start taking steps to improve your relationships and your social skills. Check your assumptions When you’re derailed by stress and negativity, as people with BPD often are, it’s easy to misread the intentions of others. If you’re aware of this tendency, check your assumptions. Remember, you’re not a mind reader! Instead of jumping to (usually negative) conclusions, consider alternative motivations. As an example, let’s say that your partner was abrupt with you on the phone and now you’re feeling insecure and afraid they’ve lost interest in you. Before you act on those feelings: Stop to consider different possibilities. Maybe your partner is under pressure at work. Maybe he’s having a stressful day. Maybe he hasn’t had his coffee yet. There are many alternative explanations for his behavior. Ask the person to clarify their intentions. One of the simplest ways to check your assumptions is to ask the other person what they’re thinking or feeling. Double-check what they meant by their words or actions. Instead of asking in an accusatory manner, try a softer approach: “I could be wrong, but it feels like…” or “Maybe I’m being overly sensitive, but I get the sense that…“ Put a stop to projection Do you have a tendency to take your negative feelings and project them on to other people? Do you lash out at others when you’re feeling bad about yourself? Does feedback or constructive criticism feel like a personal attack? If so, you may have a problem with the projection. To fight projection, you’ll need to learn to apply the brakes—just like you did to curb your impulsive behaviors. Tune in to your emotions and the physical sensations in your body. Take note of signs of stress, such as rapid heart rate, muscle tension, sweating, nausea, or light-headedness. When you’re feeling this way, you’re likely to go on the attack and say something you’ll regret later. Pause and take a few slow deep breaths. Then ask yourself the following three questions:Am I upset with myself?Am I feeling ashamed or afraid?Am I worried about being abandoned?If the answer is yes, take a conversation break. Tell the other person that you’re feeling emotional and would like some time to think before discussing things further. Take responsibility for your role Finally, it’s important to take responsibility for the role you play in your relationships. Ask yourself how your actions might contribute to problems. How do your words and behaviors make your loved ones feel? Are you falling into the trap of seeing the other person as either all good or all bad? As you make an effort to put yourself in other people’s shoes, give them the benefit of the doubt, and reduce your defensiveness, you’ll start to notice a difference in the quality of your relationships. Diagnosis and treatment It’s important to remember that you can’t diagnose borderline personality disorder on your own. So if you think that you or a loved one may be suffering from BPD, it’s best to seek professional help. BPD is often confused or overlaps with other conditions, so you need a mental health professional to evaluate you and make an accurate diagnosis. Try to find someone with experience diagnosing and treating BPD. The importance of finding the right therapist The support and guidance of a qualified therapist can make a huge difference in BPD treatment and recovery. Therapy may serve as a safe space where you can start working through your relationship and trust issues and “try on” new coping techniques. An experienced professional will be familiar with BPD therapies such as dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) and schema-focused therapy. But while these therapies have proven to be helpful, it’s not always necessary to follow a specific treatment approach. Many experts believe that weekly therapy involving education about the disorder, family support, and social and emotional skills training can treat most BPD cases. It’s important to take the time to find a therapist you feel safe with—someone who seems to get you and makes you feel accepted and understood. Take your time to find the right person. But once you do, make a commitment to therapy. You may start out thinking that your therapist is going to be your savior, only to become disillusioned and feel like they have nothing to offer. Remember that these swings from idealization to demonization are a symptom of BPD. Try to stick it out with your therapist and allow the relationship to grow. And keep in mind that change, by its very nature, is uncomfortable. If you don’t ever feel uncomfortable in therapy, you’re probably not progressing. Don’t count on a medication cure Although many people with BPD take medication, the fact is that there is very little research showing that it is helpful. What’s more, in the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved any medications for the treatment of BPD. This doesn’t mean that medication is never helpful—especially if you suffer from co-occurring problems such as depression or anxiety—but it is not a cure for BPD itself. When it comes to BPD, therapy is much more effective. You just have to give it time. However, your doctor may consider medication if:You have been diagnosed with both BPD and depression or bipolar disorder.You suffer from panic attacks or severe anxiety.You begin hallucinating or having bizarre, paranoid thoughts.You are feeling suicidal or at risk of hurting yourself or others.

column1: I am living with my terminally ill dad. He's a jerk; I feel trapped; what can I do?
column3: I’m so sorry for you in this situation. My father passed away earlier this year and he could also have been aptly described as a jerk. He said some extremely hurtful and downright shocking things to me in his last few weeks. I don’t know if you’re an adult or a child, a caregiver or just a family member in residence, so my advice will need some interpretation to fit your specific situation. First, I would see about hospice. Most terminally ill patients wait far too long before taking advantage of hospice services. Your father’s doctor should be understanding of the problem and may help you if you need a hospice provider. Hospice providers help family members, too. Talking to a mental health professional can help you cope (and your father, too, if he’s willing). At least it’s someone to hear your side and help carry your burden. If you don’t have insurance or money for therapy, contact your local mental health association or see if your local hospital can direct you to someone. I had to set some boundaries with my dying father, which was the last thing I wanted to do. I was empathetic and you probably are, too. However, my dad was abusive and sometimes even dying people have to stop and consider how they’re affecting others. I told my dad I loved him and was doing my best, but I can’t allow him to verbally attack me anymore. He actually apologized and things between us were better…for a few days. Meditation is very helpful to me. Five minutes a day can make a big difference. Writing down your thoughts and feelings may bring some clarity or at least allow you to do a brain dump. It’s hard to carry everything you’re going through in your head. Writing can be a release. Be kind to yourself. Allow an hour or two of self-indulgence to help power you up. See a movie, take a walk, visit friends, watch tv, whatever you want. I understand feeling trapped. I felt trapped and confused. It was brutal sometimes. If you’re a child, you may need to get an adult’s help. If you’re an adult, you may need to let yourself be free to go. Of course, most of us empathize with the terminally ill. We must also empathize with those who are living with a dying person. I won’t guilt you or tell you to hang in there. I don’t know your situation as I trust you do. I wish I could give you a hug and take you out to dinner. Don’t lose sight of your own needs. You’re important, too.
column9: engage him, poke him if you will, in metaphysical conceits.. if he uses a word that hurts you, try to dispassionately explore the etymology of the word or phrase that is hurtful. Read Gibran and other contemplatives and so-called metaphysical poets. You do not have to be a poet to be an adept with metaphysical conceits. If this piques your interest feel free to ask me more questions. if not, thank you for reading my reply. I send my best wishes for your difficult situation. All things pass and whatever trapped feeling is inside of you now will die with your father. Try to be unafraid to really get Stoic and deep about death itself. It seems at first undesirable given the situation but the truth is it’s the only opportunity you may have. Remember that these are, his last days, but truly none of us can be promised a tomorrow. We all die.

column1: Did gun control work in the UK? Why?
column3: I moved to the UK from the US after the gun control laws came into force. I've shot a gun a few times in the US for fun (target, not hunting) but have never owned one, so I really didn't notice much of a difference my first year in the UK. My British husband and I were visiting the US when the Columbine massacre occurred. We were both very saddened by it, but I think my husband was more affected by it. In 1987, in Hungerford in England a perpetrator killed 16 people and injured 15 more in random attacks, using a handgun and two semi automatic weapons. In 1988, centre firing semi automatic weapons and shotguns with more than a 3 cartridge capacity are written into an amendment of the Firearms Act. In 1996, 3 years before Columbine, the UK had a school massacre, too, at a primary school in Dunblane in Scotland. It was an adult perpetrator against children and teachers, but the death toll was similar to Columbine. The murderous spree in Hungerford was enough to get the Government looking seriously at gun control. And school kids dying in Dunblane was the last straw for hand guns. First came restrictions in the same year, then those were tightened a year later in 1997, and when Tony Blair became Prime Minister in 1997, he banned all handguns except muzzle loading, historic weapons, and specific sporting weapons. And in 23 years, I've not met a single person who objected to the ban. So in 1999, as we watched the details of Columbine unfold on the TV, it brought back memories of Dunblane for my husband. He, of course, thought this would be the impetus for the outlawing of guns in the US. It, of course, was not. I can't remember what prompted me to do it, but a few years ago, I tried to tally up the dead and injured from US school shootings. It may have been after the shootings at Marjory Stoneman Douglas highschool. I started with the massacre at Columbine. I don't recommend doing this if you like children or plan to have them one day. There were so many — when one should have been too many. Flash back to 1998 or 1999 — my first years in the UK. My husband and I were walking home late from the pub. We are in a “rougher" part of town and we reach a narrow passageway. He gallantly said, “Let me go first, people have sometimes been jumped going through here.” And I doubled up laughing, which may have bruised his ego a bit. Only a few years before I moved abroad, I was living downtown in a major city and regularly slept on the floor because of gunfire outside my building. Usually it was just morons shooting up the bus shelter, but you never know when a stray bullet might come through your window! I replied to him, “What are they going to do? Pull a knife??” The thought had me in tears of laughter. I could outrun a knife, but I couldn't outrun a bullet. I now have a better appreciation for knife crime, but when you come from a place where knives are tools more often than weapons and if someone really expects trouble they bring a gun — I found it difficult to take knife crime seriously for a while. Yes, gun control has worked in the UK. Not because we do as we're told (as I've seen suggested before) but because I think maybe we're just small enough to appreciate that Hungerford or Dunblane could have happened where we live. To our friends. To our family. To our children. And that's just not acceptable. Yes, knife crime is an issue — in some places much more so than others. But I live in a fairly underprivileged place and in over 20 years, I can count serious incidents locally on one hand. And of course, you can't obliterate 15 people huddled together in 5 seconds with a knife. In 1996, a mentally unstable man leapt a fence into a schoolyard in Wolverhampton in England, armed with a machete and began slashing at children and teachers while parents collecting their children tried to distract him. There were injuries to teachers and children, but no fatalities. If he had brought a gun instead, it would have had a much different result. If you look at incidents like the 2019 London Bridge stabbing, yes two people died, but people also fought the attacker — even when it appeared he was wearing a suicide vest. Several people chased him down with whatever weapons they could find — including one using a fire extinguisher and another man grabbing a 5 foot narwhal tusk off the wall and stabbing the attacker with it. Even though he had already killed people and threatened to detonate his vest. That is so much more unlikely to happen if the attacker has a gun — a knife can't easily pick off people one by one. Also, in the UK only certain members of the police force carry guns. These officers are members of Armed Response Units and are trained marksmen. If someone is reported to be in possession of a firearm in public, these are the fellas that turn up. There have been times when they have turned up to investigate children with realistic looking toy guns. (Most toys now have obvious features to help people determine if they're real or not.) But recently they were called out locally for a man having drug related mental health issues who was brandishing a weapon as he raved at his neighbours. When AROs arrive on scene, you have two options:You listen and follow directions to the letter, calmly and correctly ORYou are likely to leave in a body bagThere is often an element of trying to deescalate the situation as part of option 1, but continuing to brandish the weapon or make sudden moves or do anything that makes it look like you may have another weapon or anything they deem an imminent threat and they will immediately assume you prefer option 2 and they won't lose sleep over it. I know a few people who have decommissioned or replica historical firearms and even they very carefully and securely store these, even though they are incapable of firing anything. They don't mess around with them except at sanctioned events and they're kept out of reach, if not sight, of their children and even passers-by. It's not worth a visit from the boys with real guns and live ammo. So gun control has worked in the UK. There are still people who illegally own guns and there are sometimes shootings still — but from what I'm aware of these overwhelmingly tend to be criminals killing other criminals. Parents in the UK send their kids to school without fearing they won't come home. Children here have never experienced active shooter drills or threats. Chances of kids bringing handguns to school or having access to them at home are minimal. People willingly surrendered weapons to the police when the changes to firearm laws were made. No one wanted a repeat of Dunblane again and many people here can't comprehend how the US has seen so many shooting rampages targeting random individuals and especially so many school shootings without everyone being outraged, heartbroken and demanding substantial change to the firearms laws in the US.
column9: This is one of the best replies on British attitudes to gun laws. I'm also glad you didn't shy away from the issue of knife crime, which is our equivalent.

column1: How can I maintain mental health this covid period?
column3: Coronavirus, also known as COVID-19, is a disease that can be transmitted from an infected person's nose discharge to another person and affect the lungs and airways of a human. We have been facing COVID 19 related challenges since the year 2020 because the virus has been spreading rapidly among countries, regions, and worldwide. The sudden changes like isolation and social distances, and other challenges have affected most people's mental health. Therefore, COVID 19 and mental health has become a popular topic among the world. In this article, we will discuss everything about COVID 19 and mental health, including how to overcome mental illness and how to take care of your mental health during this time, and the coronavirus for people with mental health diseases.COVID 19 pandemic and your mental health Reports have shown that many people seem to feel depressed, stress, anxious, lonely, and fearful during this coronavirus pandemic. People tend to lose control over their emotions and feel weird stress facts, and people with mental illnesses have worsened their conditions due to self-isolation and social distancing. However, there are some particular strategies and tips on taking care of your mind during this difficult time. We will now explore how to stop feeling sick from anxiety, stress, and depression during COVID 19. How take care of your mental health?Taking care of your physical healthEating healthy food – You must take a healthy and balanced diet to get essential nutrients that can fight against infections. You will also have to limit foods and beverages with caffeine because they can increase stress and anxiety. Besides, you should avoid junk, fast food, and refined sugar. Exercising regularly – Engaging in regular exercise can reduce stress and anxiety. You can follow exercise plans online, or you can do some other activities that contain movements. Getting enough sleep – You will have to get enough sleep to maintain a healthy body. Getting enough time to sleep can make you feel relax. Engage in relaxing activities – You can do meditations, yoga, listening to music, or reading books or whatever you can feel relaxation.Taking care of your mental healthFocusing on positive things in your life – Make sure you always focus on the positive and avoid negative thoughts to take care of your mental health. You can get rid of negative feelings like sadness, loneliness if you focus on positivity. Be thankful for what you have in life, and stop worrying about things you do not have. Limiting getting exposed to media – When you get COVID 19 related news such as false news and rumors regularly, you might get feared and lead to depression. Therefore, you must only listen and read trusted news from WHO or your local authorities. Maintain your regular activities – You can engage in your usual schedules throughout the day to avoid unnecessary and weird emotions. If your area is not in isolation, you can go to work, school, or other places under the safety rules and regulations, and if you are staying at home, you can stick to your usual activities and other routines. Keeping in touch with others Stay in touch – You should keep connections with your loved ones even if you want to stay home to keep your distance. You can always connect through calls, texts, or any other communication apps to talk and share your feelings with them and update them. Help others – If you think someone you know requires help during the pandemic, you can help them while obeying safety measures. Worst things to do for your mental health Addicting to smoke, alcohol, and drugs – As you already know, coronavirus can badly affect your lungs and airways; if you are smoking, you are at a high risk of complications if you get infected with the virus. Also, you must not addict to alcohol and other drugs because they can harm your physical and mental health. Overusing electronic devices – You must not use your mobile phone, tablet, laptop, or any other electronic device 30 minutes before sleep. And also, you should not overuse the devices even if you are spending more time at home during this time. Not getting enough sleep – You might not maintain your regular activities properly. You might be spending more time doing unnecessary activities and avoid your sleep time. It can affect your mental health badly. COVID 19 for people with mental health diseases We all are aware that mental health affects how someone behaves, acts, thinks, and talks. Mental health illnesses have a significant impact on your emotional, psychological, physical, and social well-being. Therefore, if you or someone you know is already going through mental illness, COVID 19 pandemic is an additional challenge for you. We are going to discuss how to maintain mental wellness during this time. Are you running out of your medicines? If you are running out of your medicines, you will have to contact the health care team to arrange a prescription for you. They will take the necessary actions to send an electronic prescription directly to a pharmacy so that you or someone else can collect it for you. In some situations, they will give a paper prescription to get your required medications. If you have difficulties going to a pharmacy, then you can look for a delivery service. Most of the pharmacies have started delivery services due to pandemics. Do you need to contact your health care professionals? If you need to contact your health care professional, try contacting them through phone calls because if your area has travel restrictions, you might not be able to reach them unless you have an urgent matter. From where can you get support other than health care services? You can get support from volunteer support teams, local authorities, or local coronavirus support teams if you cannot reach health care providers. Can you have visitors if you are in supported housing? You might be able to have visitors under special instructions if you are in supported housing. The staff will arrange safety procedures to let your family members or friends visit you. If not, they will also help you stay in touch with your loved ones via video calls or phone calls. Do you need urgent help? If you need urgent help, you must contact the local mental health helpline as soon as possible. Also, you can make emergency appointments for a health care professional. Always try to get in touch with the support line if you are going through a mental health crisis. Do you need emotional support? If you need emotional support, it is always better to talk to someone about your feelings. It can have a positive impact on your mental health. But you can also speak to local support teams if you need additional help. Stress and anxiety are completely normal conditions in everyone's life. All of us can have such feelings during a time like this. But if you feel that you are having too many depressing thoughts, you must seek help as soon as possible. Therefore, if you always feel depressed, stressed, sad, feared, and if you cannot stick to your regular work, if you lose appetite, unusual aches or pains, and sleeping problems, you should look for help from professionals. Ignoring such symptoms can lead to severe conditions like suicidal thoughts and hurting yourself or others soon. Final Thoughts The mental health of a person decides how he or she behave, talk, act or think. We can say mental health has a significant impact on a person's behavioral, psychological, physical, and emotional life. COVID 19 pandemic has become a threat to almost everyone in the world and their mental health. Sudden changes like social distancing, self-isolation, losing your loved ones, getting infected with the virus, and career changes can affect your mental health and cause stress and anxiety. This article discussed how you should take care of your mental health during this pandemic. You can follow mentioned instructions to overcome mental disorders like depression, stress, and anxiety. If you are a person with a mental illness, you can also follow the tips on how you should behave during this time.

column1: What are some ways for a scapegoat to cope with feelings of anger and resentment towards their family?
column3: As someone who has been the victim of childhood trauma, gaslighting and scapegoating these are my suggestions: The first thing that you need to do to help you cope with the anger and resentment you feel toward your family because they scapegoated you: is to END your relationships with all of your family members completely and permanently for the rest of your life. Once you close that door, then you are not allowing them access to you or your life anymore. This way they can be no further damage to you. From this point on you can start focusing on your Healing Journey. NEVER forgive anyone who has harmed you in any way. Because when you start forgiving people, you open that door again, and you will allow them back into your life to hurt you over and over again. You need to focus your forgiveness on YOURSELF for not being aware of the fact that childhood trauma, narcissistic abuse, and scapegoating exists. No child is aware of these things. Our family members are supposed to love us— and when they betray us—by abusing us and scapegoating us then they damage us in ways that are extremely difficult to cope with for the rest of your life. But you need to face the harsh reality of what has happened to you and not make excuses for their behavior. Only by being honest with yourself about what happened will enable you to begin healing. The more you try to shut out the bad memories, or fall into the Trap of trying to convince yourself that it didn't really hurt as bad as you think it did, then you are trapped in denial and delusional thinking. That will just keep the turmoil inside of you roiling around, and you will just keep flailing through life feeling like you are sinking into a quagmire quicksand all the time. The best way to start coping with the anger and the resentment you feel is by acknowledging it and giving yourself permission to feel those emotions. Journal about it on paper where only you are the one that reads it. During your alone time: talk everything out so that those emotions begin to be purged from your mind and your heart. The most important thing is: Focus all of your love, understanding, kindness, compassion, empathy, and determination on YOURSELF. Let other people worry about their own problems. It is your job to rescue yourself from adversities that happen in your life. So your focus is on rescuing yourself and creating a better life for yourself. Don't let others distract you from that very essential goal. Keep telling yourself: I am the priority now and from this day forward. You are not being selfish! If you have been scapegoated then you have been brainwashed and manipulated into prioritizing the needs of others— while ignoring all of your own needs—since you were a child. You have done that to no avail. Because no matter how much you turn yourself inside out to please others—all they ever did was ridicule you, denigrate you, insult you, ostracize you, exploit you, manipulate you and make you feel shattered inside. So it is the OPPOSITE of selfish to decide that people who have harmed you so badly deserve one more moment of your time and consideration. People whose scapegoated you— harmed you in dozens of different ways. They alienated you. They have been mangling you all of your life— so why would you want to waste one more precious bit of the energy you have left by focusing it on a black hole of a person who will never appreciate anything you do for them? Abusers who traumatize and scapegoat people will literally absorb all of the light inside of your soul until there is nothing left of you but if flickering cinder which CAN and WILL burn out— and leave you empty and suicidal if you allow these people to continue to have access to you and to continue to harm you. If somebody was coming at you with a knife to try to stab you: you would either try to run away and save yourself, or you would try to fight back and save yourself. But your goal would be to save yourself from harm. That is called self-defense. And it is absolutely no different when we are discussing self-defense when your enemy is a narcissist or other kind of abuser who is traumatizing you and scapegoating you. Because the abuser's words and their actions are dangerous as that knife in a slasher scenario. If you're honest with yourself, don't you feel like you've been cut up into little bloody pieces time and time again by the cruel people in your life who are tormenting you? If your answer is “yes”, then you need to prioritize Protecting Yourself. Removing yourself completely from any situation where somebody can do you more harm means that you are defending yourself in the best way possible. You're not seeking Revenge because that only leads to more violence. You are walking away to deescalate a harmful situation. Yes, technically, this is a retreat. Retreat Does Not Mean Defeat you are discussing maintaining your sanity, your mental health, and your integrity. A Strategic Retreat means that you are pulling back to a safer position, you are reevaluating the situation, and figuring out better strategies to protect yourself and build stronger fortifications inside of yourself so that you can withstand the adversities of life better. Once you disengage from these battles with your abusers: you have won the battle. Because you have declared a truce with yourself. Because you are telling yourself that it is pointless to keep fighting a never-ending battle trying to make people who are not capable of love understand that you are worthy of love. You cannot make somebody love you if they don't want to. That is an exercise and futility. It is a lost cause. And that kind of an endeavor is always a losing battle. Because you're pitting your ego needs against somebody else's ego needs. And if they've already been harmful to you than they are dangerous. You have to get over the fixation of wanting to prove that you are right and they are wrong. You know that what they did to you was wrong. But no abuser or narcissist will ever admit that. So basically, what you're doing when you get fixated on the right and wrong of this kind of an issue is: you're asking a pig to fly. Pigs Can't Fly. And there is a great deal of Truth to the old saying: You Cannot Make a Silk Purse Out of a Sow's Ear. Silk is a totally different thing. A sow's ear will always be a sow's ear. Silkworms need to eat lots of mulberries from specific types of mulberry trees to create real genuine silk. Read about it. Forget about expecting apologies, remorse, or contrition from your abusers and focus all of your attention on loving yourself. Once you have learned to love yourself, then you can go out and seek other people who are more loving by Nature. And then, very cautiously, if you feel that you want to attempt it, you can start initiating relationships with others. But you have to educate yourself about the dangerous types of people that are out there who could trick you into another relationship that could turn out to be harmful to you. People who have been scapegoated have been conditioned to accept Intermittent Reinforcement and little Crumbs of Love shown to you sporadically (and grudgingly) by your abusers. This means that the tiniest bit of attention or affection that you receive is so desperately welcome by your parched love-starved soul that you get so excited and so hopeful things will change, that you convince yourself that your abusers are finally realizing you ARE worthy of love. Only to find out, that it was a trick—to lure you into a false sense of anticipation or security—just so that your abusers could shatter you again with their abuse and watch you crumble while they gloat and snicker and thoroughly enjoy the devastation they just caused inside of you. THAT'S WHY you need to be very cautious when initiating new relationships. Because vanity and narcissism are becoming very common due to the proliferation of social media. People spend their days taking selfies and bragging about inconsequential events in their life such as: I had a bagel for breakfast. Who cares? People all want to think that they have the charisma to become the next influencer on social media. Obnoxious people who drone on about their political beliefs so aggressively or their religious beliefs so sanctimoniously mistake their opinions for facts. Because everybody wants to be the next talking head on social media that racks up those “likes”. People who have endured and survived childhood trauma, gaslighting, scapegoating and other forms of abuse have a void inside of them that makes them crave love and affection because they have never really received it in a genuine way. As long as you are aware of the fact that your traumatic past makes you ripe for exploitation, manipulation, and deception then you can cautiously evaluate your interactions with people to determine if they are genuine. The crucial thing is is don't rush into any relationship. Take your time to let the relationship develop. Because the one thing that you will notice about narcissists and other deceptive people is that they are very impatient. They crave instant gratification of their ego needs. They want something from you. Your attention, your affection, your admiration, your concern, your money, your talent, your ideas, your insights. Anything they think is valuable is something that they want to exploit. They want to take credit for all your ingenuity. And they definitely want to exploit your kindness. Anything manipulative people think that they can get from you— they want it right NOW! That's why it's so important for you to protect yourself by pumping the brakes and slowing everything in your life down when it comes to interacting with other people. Whether you believe it or not, YOU can take control of your destiny in relationships. YOU are the one who is in control of how any relationship is going to progress. So if you look at every interaction you have with people from a detached point of view (as if you are a scientist conducting an experiment) then you have the ability to analyze: How did that interaction go? And you analyze that after the interaction is over. Use your memory of what just happened and replay the interaction back in your mind as if it's an instant replay on television. Focus on what was said by you and the other person. And remember all the things that you noticed about that person's facial expressions and body language that will reveal to you lots of important information about what their real agenda and intentions actually are. Trust your instincts when they warn you that the expression on somebody's face was condescending, or smug, or smirky, or devious, or sly or any other negative thing that makes your internal warning system doubt what that person said or did. We all have internal lie detectors in the forms of instincts and intuitions telling us to pay more attention to something— but we ignore those warnings and second guess ourselves. Why? If you've been subjected to fhildhood trauma, gaslighting, or scapegoating, then your abusers have made you question your sanity in so many different ways that you can't trust your intuition. The truth is: you're intuition and your instincts that warn you to be cautious are your best friend. They are YOU talking to yourself in the most primordial, protective, compassionate way possible. So trust your instincts, even if you doubt them at first, and they make you anxious. Keep trying to figure out what your instincts are warning you about and why— and those answers will startle you and protect you. I guarantee it. Because everything human being on this planet has Survival Instincts. And that's what those instincts are trying to help you do: survive and thrive! You can relax and be genuine with people when you're interacting with them, as long as you're very cautious about not giving up personal information that they can use against you to exploit you. When people are asking you a bunch of personal questions: you are not obligated to answer any of those questions. Most people are not really trying to get to know you. They're looking for things that they can find out about you so they can gossip about you— and try to harm you in some way— because they want to compete with you. Especially in job situations. So be extra careful not to think about coworkers as potential friends. Because they're not. Anytime you're on a job: circumstances will create many potential adversarial situations. No matter how insignificant you think your job might be, I guarantee you that somebody else is going to want to TAKE your job. Even if all you're doing is cleaning toilets. There's going to be somebody out there who's also a janitor who's going to want your job. I've seen this happen time and time again to people who do everything from janitorial work, to food service work, to clerical work, healthcare work, up to an including professions that most people in America think are the pinnacle of employment professions, such as being a doctor, or a lawyer. Doctors and lawyers will tell you all kinds of stories about how competitive their professions are from the time that they are in school throughout their entire working career. Throughout my life I have been friends with people who do all kinds of jobs for a living. People like to tell me what's going on in their lives. They are very candid and very open with me cuz I'm a good listener and I'm a compassionate person. So I get to hear all of the stories about backstabbing coworkers who are trying to undermine people so that they can steal that person's job. This happens to truck drivers. It happens to people who work in beauty salons. Happens to construction workers. You name the profession and I've talked to way more than a few people in those professions on a personal basis. That's my nature as a human being and it's also part of the professions I have done in my life. I've been the scapegoat of my family since I was born. So as a fellow scapegoat, I am being very candid with you about ways that you need to learn to protect yourself. Because I've had to learn how to protect myself the hard way too. It is an ordeal. And it's an ordeal that really will be part of your life until the day you die. You cannot let your guard down. As soon as you let your guard down that gives people an opportunity to harm you again. That kind of vigilance is very exhausting but it is absolutely crucial to your survival.

column1: How do you handle your own mental health when in a relationship with someone who also struggles with their mental health?
column3: So you have to have a balance, right? Like you have noted already, just by asking this question, you aren’t just worrying about your partner— you’re worrying about yourself also. Therefore, that’s how you need to treat the situation. You need to have a support system around you, that spans further than your partner first of all, it can be anything from a family member, close friend or pen pal, as long as it isn’t cause for concern. (WARNING, when asking for advice, note if your family is projecting how they would feel in the situation onto you, before you accept that advice) The reason I give this warning, is because how you might phrase something, may come across as your partner is just being lazy, unwilling to make a change, or whatever the case, but another’s perspective is always valuable, granted they know what they’re talking about. Researching their illness is always a good option, they’ll appreciate the concern you’re showing, but just as they’re responsible for getting themselves back to where they need to be, you need to do the same, maybe you could even research with one another, if you’re interested of course. (Includes researching about it, for yourself too) Do not create false narratives and compromise on the responsibilities of your partner, so with this point, don’t begin to hate or resent your partner for not pulling their weight whenever they’re having a crisis, I know times are tough, you know, as well as I know, that better days are to come, you just need to get there, so don’t be so hard on yourself if your efforts don’t produce the results you were expecting, for example, showing a lot of love to someone who is depressed, doesn’t just rid them of their illness, it’s definitely a good thing, just not the answer and you might get burnt out. A lot of the time, depression can be narrowed down to something that is expected to happen, maybe a job promotion or down payment on a house, a personal setback, etc. Radical acceptance, is very much needed. We need to accept what is and not let ourselves (again) create a false narrative and try to predict the future, this will exacerbate any generalised anxiety that you might have, this will be undoubtedly projected into the workplace, panicking over mundane or maybe less important details, snapping at peers, that’s not to say ignore your partner whilst at work, but keep your work, strictly about work. Can you accept what your circumstances are? Can you accept that things might be different for a bit? Can you accept more responsibility? etc. If you cannot, then you may need to leave, as to not risk your own mental health deteriorating any further, being in a household with a sick person, will have its affect on you.Living With Someone With Mental IllnessIf you live with someone with a mental health disorder, you may have found yourself thinking, "Their mental illness is killing me!" Here are some tips that can help.https://www.verywellmind.com/coping-with-a-mentally-ill-spouse-2302988Much of what I’ve said can be find in this article, but it’s always nice to hear it from an individuals perspective. Just remember, you are NOT a bad person for taking care of your needs, in fact, taking care of yourself before you take care of anyone else is easily demonstrated in an airplane analogy— when they tell you to secure your mask, before you help secure somebody else’s (I.e. your kids) Last point, do not make them your persecutor, you are a team, but you cannot and should not, lose yourself in one another completely, that’s great when you’re being intimate, but when it comes down to taking care of business, when the boat gets rocked and someone is seasick, you need to take the wheel and steer it for the time being, yes that was a terrible ship analogy, hopefully it makes you laugh a little.

column1: What are the symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis?
column3: What is arthritis? Arthritis is the name given to over a hundred conditions that cause joint pain. There are 2 main types osteoarthritis or degenerative arthritis and the inflammatory or rheumatoid arthritis. The cause is still a mystery to doctors. Osteoarthritis is the commoner type; other types are infectious or metabolic. They share common symptoms of pain, swelling, stiffness and warm to touch. Having these symptoms in multiple/symmetric joints differentiates rheumatoid arthritis from others. Rheumatoid arthritis Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is an autoimmune disease. This means that the body’s immune system has gone awry and decides your healthy cells are foreign and thus destroy them. Our immune system defends our body against disease; their role is to attack foreign substances like bacteria and viruses. In the case of RA the immune system mistakenly attacks the joints and other healthy tissues or organs. This creates inflammation (swelling, pain, warmth, redness) in and around the joints and other body systems, such as the cardiovascular or respiratory systems. This makes rheumatoid arthritis a systemic disease. A systemic disease affects the “entire body.” Rheumatoid arthritis can thus affect the blood vessels, bone marrow, skin, lungs, heart, eyes, salivary glands or nerves; but most commonly affects the joints of the hands, feet, wrists, elbows, knees and ankles, sometimes the shoulder, hip, jaw, and neck may also be affected. The joint effect is usually symmetrical. That means both knees and hands are affected. This symmetry helps to set it apart from other types of arthritis. If this inflammation goes unchecked, it can damage the cartilage that covers the ends of bones in a joint, as well as the bones themselves. This makes the joints become loose, unstable, deformed in some cases, painful and lose their mobility. Joint damage cannot be reversed; therefore doctors recommend early diagnosis and treatment to control rheumatoid arthritis. Who’s affected by Rheumatoid Arthritis? Nearly three times as many women have the disease as men. In women, it most commonly begins between ages 30 and 60. In men, it often occurs later in life. Having a family member with rheumatoid arthritis increases the odds of having it; however, the majority of people with rheumatoid arthritis have no family history of the disease. Causes The cause is not yet fully understood, although doctors do know that an abnormal response of the immune system plays a leading role in the inflammation and joint damage that occurs. No one knows for sure why the immune system goes awry, but there is scientific evidence that genes, hormones and environmental factors are involved. Some include exposure to cigarette smoke, air pollution, insecticides and occupational exposures to mineral oil and silica. Symptoms of rheumatoid arthritis RA is a chronic disease; the symptoms may vary in severity and the effects of inflammation may come and go. A period of increase in inflammation and other symptoms is called a flare. A flare can last for days or months. Symptoms can come on gradually or start suddenly. They're often more severe than with osteoarthritis. It can be difficult to detect and diagnose RA because early symptoms are subtle and nonspecific. Symptoms appear differently in every patient and many will experience spans of no symptoms at all. In the early stages, you may not initially see redness or swelling in the joints, but you may experience tenderness and pain. These following joint symptoms are clues to RA:Joint pain, tenderness, redness, swelling or stiffness for six weeks or longerMorning stiffness or stiffness after long periods of rest lasting for 30 minutes or longerLimping due to pain and/or joint deformity or joints shift out of placeMore than one joint is affected (polyarthritis)Small joints (wrists, certain joints of the hands and feet) are affected causing pain and loss of range of motion and loss of joint functionThe same joints on both sides of the body are affectedFatigue, irritability, depression. Fatigue can be caused by the body's reaction to inflammation, poor sleep, low appetite and medicationsFlu-like symptoms, such as feeling generally ill, muscle aches, feeling hot and sweatingAlong with pain, many people experience loss of appetite and a low-grade feverInflammation of the cricoarytenoid joint - this is a joint in the larynx (voice box) can cause hoarsenessSystemic effects of rheumatoid arthritis:Eyes - Dryness, burning, itchiness, eye discharge, pain, redness, sensitivity to light and impaired visionSalivary glands - Dryness and gum irritation or infectionSkin - Rheumatoid nodules – small lumps under the skin over bony areas that may be painful or painlessLungs - Inflammation and scarring that can lead to shortness of breath or even chest painBlood Vessels - Inflammation of blood vessels that can lead to damage in the nerves, skin and other organsBone marrow- Anemia, a lower than normal number of red blood cellsNerve tissues –skin damage, tingling sensation, numbness, pins and needle sensation on the hands and feetKidneysPsychological Symptoms RA affects every person differently. Symptoms differ in severity and frequency, and may cause emotional and psychological symptoms. This may leave a person unable to function for long periods of time without pain. Jobs that involve a large amount of moving or a large amount of time sitting still can be difficult for a person with RA. Mental health disorders such as depression, anxiety, low self-esteem and feelings of helplessness are common among RA sufferers. This fatigue results in low levels of energy and can adversely affect emotions and mood, occupation, relationships with people, sex drive, productivity, attentiveness, creativity, and peace of mind. Fatigue from rheumatoid arthritis may be related to poor appetite and weight loss or even the autoimmune disease that may be the primary cause of rheumatoid arthritis. These symptoms could all be the result of any number of different illnesses such as Sjogren’s disease and more. This is why it is important to be aware of rheumatoid arthritis and all its potential symptoms to ensure proper diagnosis as early as possible. If you have painful, swollen joints and stiffness in the morning that lasts for longer than half an hour, you should see your doctor. A lifestyle modification is in place for prevention and treatment of RA. I hope this was helpful. Dr Nse Onyebuchi

column1: Why do so many people have depression nowadays?
column3: On the radio this morning, I heard more than 10% of Americans take anti-depressants. I’m sure twice as many are depressed, simply slogging through life. The factors usually tied to optimism and happiness is having enough food, housing in a safe area, job security, sufficient income or money to purchase necessities, access to healthcare, and of course, strong, loving, and supportive ties to family and friends. In America, in the 1950’s, a man could work in retail or manufacturing, and earn enough money to afford a small house (or quality apartment), car, food, and other essentials so his wife could stay home, and raise their children. The family might go on vacation once a year. The father would come home from work, after an 8-hour shift, and enjoy being with his family, maybe tossing a baseball to his kids, who played outside, until it got dark. The family would save up for large purchases, such as appliances or a new car. While healthcare wasn’t particularly advanced, most people weren’t concerned about going bankrupt because they were having a baby, needed an appendectomy or medication for a chronic illness. At one time, General Motors was the largest employer in America, paying in today’s dollars around $50 per hour. Today, the largest employer in America is Wal-Mart, which pays $7-$10 per hour with few benefits. While Americans have always faced challenges – including in the 50’s – today’s jeopardize the welfare and contentment of great swaths of people who live in poverty (46 million Americans), have severe food insecurities (over 14% of US households), don’t have sufficient housing, and access to healthcare (including care for minor episodes of depression). They live in towns and cities of all sizes, yearning to pull themselves out of their predicaments, but unable to secure higher paying jobs, obtain additional education, afford childcare, pay-down mounting debt, recover from bankruptcies or foreclosures, and pay for necessary medical care. Hopelessness and depression is a way of life for these people. Just a step up the economic ladder are people who live paycheck-to-paycheck, one calamity away from losing their home or being contacted by bill collectors. They too experience depression. People who are on higher rungs, are also wrought with depression, feeling the pressure to work longer hours, be available on weekends and evenings respond to work emails or learn new skills to dodge being laid-off. Maybe they already lost their jobs, and are now working for less money (and few to no benefits) as a contingent or temporary worker. They might have multiple loans to pay for education, health expenses, household and car repairs. Perhaps, they’re paying the mortgage on a house “under water.” Adding to peoples’ anxiety is seeing how people with more money and resources live. Dissatisfaction can lead to depression. Finally, depression can be the result of an illness, life experiences (i.e. death of a family member, moving to another school), environment (i.e. abusive spouse, living in a high crime area), side effect of a medication, and especially genetics. Some people are more prone to depression because of their family history. Even with availability of anti-depressant, people deal with depression by withdrawing, running away, overeating, binge shopping, drinking, taking drugs, engaging in dangerous behaviors, contemplating, and sometimes committing suicide, such as Sylvia Plath, Virginia Wolf, Kurt Cobain, and Robin Williams.
