column1: What do you think of the new Ohio law banning abortions for Down Syndrome children?
column3: There are so many angles from which I could approach an answer to this question. All of them, of course, are biased by my own personal position on abortion: I am pro-choice. Reading about this makes me want to cry, because it so offends my sense of what should be the priority. But a woman’s right to self-determination on the reproductive front is my priority, and I need a better argument than “because I said so” to take a position that my priority is more righteous than someone else’s. So my argument is that this law does not best serve the individuals it purports to protect. Yes, it is true that aborting a fetus because it has been diagnosed with Down Syndrome is discriminatory. I will not even try to argue that it isn’t. But I have some problems:I believe it has a strong potential to do as much harm as good.It will unnecessarily cause the abortion of healthy, wanted fetuses, potentially in numbers high enough to rival the numbers of Down Syndrome fetuses that have been ‘saved’.In itself, it is discriminatory towards those whose support systems are inadequate, either personal or economic.Until we as a society show that we value and do not discriminate against non-average but normal presentations in children who have already been born, it is self-defeating to direct our efforts to combat discrimination against the unborn who have an unarguable abnormality.Over 15 years ago, I received a triple screen[1] result that showed that my baby had a 1 in 200 chance of having Down Syndrome. As this test was only a predictive test and not a diagnostic test, there was no way to confirm whether or not the baby actually did have Down’s; an amniocentesis was the only way to actually diagnose the condition. I was fortunate that my amnio showed that the fetus did not have Down’s, and I did not have to make any kind of decision about what to do. Not everyone is so fortunate. The following quote is from what I consider to be one of my best ever answers on Quora:Having a child with Down Syndrome often means giving up at least some of one’s dreams for the future:Most parents dream of a retirement where they will not have children living at home and dependent on them, yet more children with Down Syndrome continue to live with parents once they are adult than move out and live independently.[2]If it is a first pregnancy, many parents of my personal experience who dreamed of having multiple children found that after having a child with a significant disability, more children were not within the range of what they could handle.Many parents have budgeted for a family and done their best to ensure a comfortable standard when raising their children, yet 40% of parents of a child with Down Syndrome report financial issues due to the child’s condition.[3]Jennifer Edeburn's answer to How do I convince my wife to terminate a Down Syndrome pregnancy? When I was faced with the loss of my dreams, I had the option to confirm the diagnosis and then choose afterwards whether or not to continue the pregnancy. Had I not been able to choose after the diagnosis, it is possible that it would have occurred to me to consider whether to terminate the pregnancy in advance of the diagnosis and simply try again; I was certainly young enough. In the reality of a world where a bad triple screen result or ultrasound cannot be followed up by amniocentesis without losing the ability to abort the pregnancy, the following will be the outcomes:Parents will decline the amnio and continue the pregnancy. There was always a group of these parents, but maybe now there will be a few more.Parents will have the amnio, and if it is positive thenSome parents will choose to continue the pregnancy and keep the child anyway. These parents might always have made this choice; many who know they will keep the child have an amnio so that they are able to prepare themselves for the outcome.Some parents will choose to continue the pregnancy, and make arrangements for the adoption of the child. These are the babies most likely to have been ‘saved’ by the law; although some parents with an in utero diagnosis of Down Syndrome do this now, it is reasonable to expect that in the absence of a termination option many of those who would choose to terminate would go this route.Parents will choose not to have the amnio, and they will abort the undiagnosed fetus (still legal) and try again.My odds based on the triple screen were 1 in 200. If just two out of a group of 200 women with that same probability from the triple screen choose the third option, then the mathematical expectation is that more healthy babies will have been sacrificed to the harshness of this law than Down’s pregnancies will have potentially been rescued from abortion. Further, even if the odds are 1 in 50 and it is a group of only fifty women, that number — two in group three for the law to sacrifice more healthy fetuses than protect those with Down’s — does not change. I wrote above about the loss of one’s dreams, and I think the following from the same answer is also applicable:… other respondents to this question have shared their positive experiences with friends or family members who have Down Syndrome or relatives with Down Syndrome. Those are important and supportive, but it is crucial to keep in mind that they are anecdotes. I have seen many heartwarming true stories of people who have dropped a wallet on a crowded street in a major city and received it in the mail with any money intact when whoever found it mailed it back to them. I’m sure you see where I am going with this; these are someone else’s experience that indicates the possibility that you will have that same experience, but doesn’t guarantee it.When we consider the potential for a woman to choose the third option under the new law — to forgo the amnio, abort, and try again — I think we can see that parents who have little in the way of financial or personal support systems in place are the ones who can least afford the gamble that they will come out on the ‘winning’ side with respect to the level of disability that their child will exhibit if it is born with Down’s. They must employ the most realism, see past the heartwarming story; I think the law discriminates against parents who find themselves in this situation, as it applies more pressure on them to consider aborting what might be a healthy fetus as they are less able to sustain the risk of having a child with a disability. My second issue with the law is related to a fairly standard pro-choice argument: it is insufficient to care about the outcome of a pregnancy without also considering the life that the child will live after it is born. As a society, we already provide less and less tolerance for deviation from the average. ADHD is diagnosed in some 10 percent of children of elementary age or above.[4] Statistically speaking, that means 3 kids in every class of 30. Although ADHD is referred to as a disorder, in the USA it about twice as likely that a school age child will have ADHD as it is that they will have blond hair.[5] [6] Think about that: ADHD is more normal than blond hair. Yet, my experience and that of others is that teachers do not adjust their methods to simultaneously serve both those with ADHD and those without; but rather management of ADHD from an educational perspective is based on either medication or specific accommodation. We also discriminate against children based on their aptitudes; not everyone’s natural leaning or interest is to a career in a STEM field, and yet average salaries are higher in those areas.[7] From a career and self-sufficiency perspective, as the well-paying jobs in our culture go increasingly to those who fit a standard definition of intelligence, the consequence is that on the playing field of access to success there is discrimination against those with any kind of mental challenge. In the specific case of Down Syndrome, this is not discrimination that can be covered by the Americans with Disabilities Act: it is based on a real disparity in the ability of these individuals to do the jobs that bring home a substantial paycheck. In the face of all this discrimination against people who are already born and aged 5 or older, based on a normal range of variation that can be traced to components of an individual’s genetic makeup, I find it difficult to accept the validity of an argument that we should fight against discrimination in utero by ensuring the birth of an individual with abnormal genetic variation who will inevitably face discrimination in areas that affect their quality of life. As a society, we can’t currently guarantee that those born with Down Syndrome will have a reasonable quality of life. Until it is true that we can, I think that those concerned with discrimination against individuals with Down Syndrome should focus their advocacy in that area, and not on behalf of the unborn.Footnotes[1] Triple or Quad Screening for Birth Defects-Topic Overview[2] Independence and employment for adults with Down syndrome[3] A population-based assessment of the health, functional status, and consequent family impact among children with Down syndrome.[4] General Prevalence[5] Are only 5% of Americans naturally blonde?[6] 11 Brilliant Scientific Facts About Blondes[7] Science And Math Majors Earn The Most Money After Graduation

column1: How does disclosing a mental illness affect your career?
column3: It really depends on your employer and the degree of stigma against mental illness in your region/culture/religion. I disclosed my bipolar disorder to my supervisor at my current job. I had to: I was in a hypomanic state and couldn’t concentrate on anything because of the racing thoughts, and she wanted me to manage a project with our most difficult client. I had to tell her because I knew I wouldn’t be able to do a good job in my current state. I was fortunate that she was accepting and understanding: she and her husband have family members with bipolar disorder. I was also fortunate that it hasn’t harmed my career with this company and they didn’t find some bullshit reason to fire me. I did not disclose my illness to any of my other supervisors because a) the stigma was so strong within me that I didn’t want to tell anyone I had one of the “scary” mental illnesses (my family didn’t even know my actual diagnosis because I was scared they’d gaslight me and condemn me for getting a “chemical lobotomy”); b) because in my generation (Gen X) and the place I grew up (Maine), I was raised to believe you just don’t talk about “personal problems” at work; and c) I was afraid I’d lose my job (see “bullshit reason to fire me”). Now I’m really open about my mental illness. I talk about it on LinkedIn, where potential employers can see it. I talk about it on other social media channels, too. I do so because I’m trying to build a career as a mental health advocate and public speaker, so in this case it’s part of “building my brand,” so to speak. I probably will lose some job opportunities because of it, not gonna lie. But I don’t care because I don’t want to work for a company that doesn’t actively support employee mental health (and by that I mean REAL support, not a free subscription to a mindfulness app).

column1: Why do people insist you must love and forgive your family no matter what even if they're abusive or manipulative? I always hear things like "well they're still family!" when anyone makes any sort of statement about despising their abusive relatives.
column3: Dear Questioner, As someone who is estranged from his family and my wife hers, I can tell you that not having a family is hard to acknowledge; it’s like voluntarily becoming an orphan that won’t ever be adopted. It really does affect your mental/emotional health. You should love/forgive everyone, but I don’t believe you should stay in an abusive environment; there is nothing good that comes from that. If you don’t forgive/love your family, then the family will fall apart: Who wants to be without family? My wife’s from an abusive family: She met me and broke away; she stood up for herself, but there were consequences like the family disowning her as a daughter. Now, every holiday, she has to know how she no longer has a family to celebrate with; she has to acknowledge that her family doesn’t love her as they should, so all her memories, good or bad, bring sadness and despair. At times, I wonder if being in the abusive family was better than having no family at all for her— now she has to deal with the PTSD problems of the abuse with having no family, as well. Therefore, I imagine that people don’t want to lose their family and will forgive/love them to prevent that from happening, even though you should be that way with everyone. I find that the most abusive members of a family usually has the support of other family members, so they can go on abusing without fear of losing family, as the abused one will be alienated since the abuser is usually the one everyone else supports. Abusive people usually try to make their image perfect to outsiders, yet tell the one being abused that they will be abused when they get home; they try to do their abusive acts when no one is around, so the abused one will seem crazy/insane for talking bad about such a “sweet” person: Society is really blind. Take Care, With Love Through God and Jesus and The Holy Ghost, Not having a family anymore and being a victim of abuse is very hard mentally/emotionally— They usually just want their family to love them and be sorry: My dad was like this all of his life and now my wife is becoming like this, where she can’t resolve that her family doesn’t love her and that she was abused without them being apologetic about it— It’s as a dream that can never be true that you long for.

column1: What does patriarchy mean? What does patriarchy have to do with Rhea Chakraborty’s case?
column3: The Wikipedia definition of “patriarchy” is thus: “Patriarchy is a social system in which men hold primary power and predominate in roles of political leadership, moral authority, social privilege and control of property. Some patriarchal societies are also patrilineal, meaning that property and title are inherited by the male lineage.” In India, patriarchy assumes a unique connotation because of our historical, socio-cultural development, combined with our history of colonialism. All of these cannot be fully explained within the scope of this answer, so I will confine myself to aspects that are directly relevant to Rhea’s case. We must remember that besides being patriarchal, Indian society is also hierarchical, homo-phobic, feudal, collectivist, authoritarian and casteist. All of these structures operate in tandem, and they bolster and reinforce each other in a cascading structure of privilege/lack of privilege and power/lack of power. You can be simultaneously privileged because of your caste; but disempowered because of your gender or sexual orientation. You can be disempowered because of your gender but empowered by your position in the caste, class, family hierarchy. Your position as an oppressor/oppressed depends on the role that you play on the socio-cultural totem pole. Not all women are oppressed simultaneously. Not all men are oppressors simultaneously. The same person can be a perpetrator and victim, based on the roles he/she plays in the socio-cultural-economic-caste-class hierarchy. I have maintained, for fifteen years, that you cannot fix socio-cultural-political and economic inequality unless you fix power structures within the Indian family. Unless you acknowledge and erase dysfunctional power structures within the family, your efforts at large-scale social, cultural, political and economic reform are destined for failure. Since 2014, a lot of liberal hand-wringing has focused on why Indians have rejected liberalism as an ideology. Look no further than the flawed dynamics of the Indian family, an institution that the Singh-Rajput family has inadvertently come to symbolise. Dysfunction and unequal dynamics within the family affect large socio-cultural-economic and political inequalities, and we liberals, have always enshrined the family as a sacred, private space that is immune from scrutiny and reform. The flawed dynamics of the Singh-Rajput family have coalesced into a perfect storm that has transfixed the nation for three months. Three national investigative agencies, the Mumbai and Bihar police, two state governments, the Union government, the Supreme Court itself, have joined the Jamboree. Fun Times! We must ask ourselves why the suicide of a young actor, no matter how unfortunate, has caused an entire nation to loses its marbles! What’s going on? How much public money has been spent on investigating a suicide caused by mental health issues? Fellow Indians, we’re the patsies. The money that the Enforcement Directorate, the Central Board of Investigation, the Narcotics Control Bureau, the Mumbai Police, the Bihar Police, has spent on investigating Rhea, has come out of your pockets. Why are you not outraged? Need I remind everybody that Rakesh Asthana, of rather uncertain past glory, is the director general of the NCB? Need I also remind everyone that elections are imminent in Bihar, that Nitish Kumar is an NDA ally, that the BJP has an interest in toppling the coalition government in Maharashtra? Need I also remind everyone of the unproven allegations of rape, swirling on sock puppet social media accounts, against none less than the young Environment Minister of Maharashtra? Should I really connect all the dots now, folks? Do we really not see “the foreign hand”? My answer is necessarily going to be long and complex, because I must tie disparate narratives and causes together to explain why #JusticeforSSR is trending, when the economy has contracted by 23.9%, when India is the worst-hit by Covid economy in all of the G-20, when the Chinese are at our doorstep, when Covid is claiming a 1000 lives everyday, when young people are forced to take the JEE-NEET in person, when we are the second worst-hit by Covid in the effing world!Yet, what do we want? Yeah, that’s right! #JusticeforSSR! Why do you need real news when you have this:Why am I highlighting flawed family dynamics when referring to the economy? Here’s why: In very few Indian families, are traditional power structures that originate in gender roles and kinship patterns, ever questioned. In a typical Indian family, all members do not enjoy equal rights, responsibilities, privileges and freedoms. All family members are not presumed to enjoy an equal footing. Indian families are not democratic; where conflicts, disagreements, opinions and choices can be debated and aired, without stigma and consequence. The family environment does not encourage authenticity, independence, originality, autonomy or any deviation from convention or social norms. There’s no focus on critical thinking, on fostering open dialogue; on open, respectful communication and exchange of opinions. Most things are taboo: Sex is taboo. Questioning “the elders” is taboo. Questioning the sanctity and rightness of “the family” is taboo. Going against “the family” is taboo. Young people cannot question “the elders” or defy them. You cannot violate “social norms” or do things that will invite “criticism” of the family. Indian families functions like mafia organisations, not as organic units where each member is unconditionally loved, respected, accepted and supported.Vito Corleone would approve! If this is not tragic, what is? What is more tragic than being forced to wear a mask, be someone else, by your family, the people who ostensibly love you the most? What therefore happens is that Indians are indoctrinated into a herd mentality, indoctrinated into unquestioning group-think, vital parts of your being and psyche are hidden from “the family”. Your sex life is hidden from the family. Your struggles, your conflicts, your mental health issues, are all hidden, or only partially revealed, to your family. You must be told what to think. Because Indian families frown on disagreement, openness, independence and critical thinking, the consequences are catastrophic for the quality of public discourse. Most Indians never learn to analyse political, social, cultural, economic and personal problems critically. They never learn how to form independent opinions. To go against the grain. To challenge received wisdom and convention. To think for yourself; without being manipulated by media, the political class, the family, society and culture. We follow the herd. We think how everyone else is thinking. Our views are those of everyone else. We do what everyone else does. We follow. Not lead. We are sheeple. We therefore, become a nation that has a macabre obsession with vilifying a young woman against whom we do not have a shred of evidence. Why? In Indian families, women are simultaneously deified and vilified. They are simultaneously revered and shamed. As mothers, sisters and daughters, Indian women are revered, deified, and cherished. As wives, daughters-in-law, girlfriends and as ordinary women on the street, we experience a horrendous amount of vilification, slut-shaming, demonisation and abuse. This is why Indian patriarchy is so unique and so toxic. It conditions women to alter their behaviour and priorities based on the roles they occupy. Therefore, Indian women are simultaneously perpetrators and victims, and this experience alters their ability to think and behave rationally. Look at the millions of educated Indian women baying for Rhea’s blood. How would you feel if you were her? How would you feel if an entire nation convicted you without a shred of evidence? The end result of a sustained media witch-hunt, independent investigations by three national agencies, the Mumbai and Bihar police, is that we know that Rhea was once in possession of 59 grams of marijuana. There is no evidence that this was for commercial purposes. For this to happen, we would need to seize and forensically examine the weed. Said quantity has been consumed already. The only reason why we know that Rhea was in possession of marijuana, is because she told us! A confession before the Police is not admissible as evidence under Section 25 of the Indian Evidence Act. Practically, from a strictly legal viewpoint, there is no evidence against Rhea. Yet, we are now holding her responsible for Sushant having smoked weed. Umm, he was a 34-year old adult. We are also accusing her of being a gold-digger, a social-climber, for controlling Sushant, for wrongfully confining him, abetment to suicide, using criminal force, practicing black magic, exploiting him to further her own career, sabotaging his career, forcing him to consume psychotropic medication, extortion and blackmail, and yes, murder. From theft to cheating: Sushant Singh Rajput’s father charges against Rhea Chakraborty Sushant’s family has accused her of not being sanskari enough because, gasp! She never wore salwar-kameez. How inexcusably heinous. Rhea wouldn't have ever worn that kind of salwar-suit: Sushant's family's lawyer A lot of these accusations are contained in FIRs and chargesheets, that are legal documents subject to judicial scrutiny. We actually expect a judge to try her for being a gold-digger, a controlling girl-friend and a non-wearer of salwar-kameezes! Based on what evidence? Zip. Zilch. Zero. Yet, we are a country that “worships” women. We treat women as “goddesses”. Yes indeed. What really breaks my heart is that none of the young, educated women writing social media tirades against Rhea, think that it could be them, one day. As women, we have internalised misogyny to such an extent that we are the proverbial frog in boiling water. We will boil slowly to death, never suspecting that anything is amiss. This is why Indian patriarchy is so noxious. It sets one woman against another. All our lives, we are gladiators in an arena that we did not design, playing a game that we did not design, in which the loser will always be a woman. We are locked in fierce battle, mother-in-law against daughter-in-law, sisters against brother’s girlfriend, a man’s sister against his wife, as co-sisters, as bhabhis, behens, saas, bahu, jethani, devrani, nanad, beti, maa. Have you noticed that all the relationships that Indian women are known by, are in relation to men? We are known as some man’s mother, some man’s daughter, some man’s wife, some man’s girlfriend, some man’s sister, some man’s “gold-digging, social-climbing, blackmailing, extorting, sociopathic girlfriend”? Yet, we women participate gleefully in the nation-wide maligning, slandering and destruction of another woman, and then sleep peacefully at night. How can you? How can we do this? It’s because we have internalised the roles that patriarchal society wants us to play — as sister, as mother, as the hated girlfriend or wife. We don’t question them. We don’t feel any solidarity or empathy for a woman who is a victim of patriarchal brutality. A woman like Rhea. A woman like Nirbhaya. A woman like Priya Ramani, who is fighting a lonely legal battle against MJ Akbar. Feminism will always fail in India, because Indian women cannot see themselves outside of the golden cages that patriarchy has built for them. As long as we can participate vicariously in the destruction of another woman, we will never question the golden chains that bind us, convinced that what happened to Rhea, will never happen to us. There are two last point that I want to make. Sushant’s family has insisted all along, that he could not have killed himself. That he was not mentally ill. That there is a conspiracy, a cover-up. They have painted themselves as the perfect Indian family, living the perfect Indian dream, until Rhea came along.The perfect Indian middle-class family This is the blog of Vishal Kirti, Sushant’s brother-in-law, who has consistently driven the narrative against Rhea, accusing her of being a narcissist, a sociopath, a criminal, a monster who drove his brother-in-law to suicide. The family has vehemently denied that Sushant has mental health issues, and accused Rhea of forcing psychotropic medication on Sushant. The blog is expertly crafted, to home in on middle-class Indians’ most cherished tropes — our hunger for success, wealth, success, fame. Our desire to see ourselves as “self-reliant, hard-working people who dream big”. The family have been consistently forging a certain narrative that paints Rhea as a monster and Sushant as a victim. Why? What are they hiding? Sushant and the journey of the middle class It now emerges that Priyanka Singh, Sushant’s sister, was illegally supplying him prescription medication. The drugs Librium, Lonazep and Nexito. Well, if Sushant had no mental illness, if he didn’t have anxiety, depression or bi-polar disorder, why was she supplying him these drugs, illegally, might I add? New Twist In Sushant Rajput Case Over Sister's WhatsApp On Medicines Rhea left Sushant’s apartment on June 8th. She blocked his number on June 9th. His sister Meetu lived with him between June 8th and June 12th. He killed himself on June 14. These dates thread together an interesting narrative. It appears that the family was well-aware of Sushant’s precarious mental state, but chose to leave him alone anyways. Several psychiatrists have now confirmed that Sushant sought treatment intermittently between 2013 and 2020. His family was also provably aware of his mental illness. Yet, somehow, they chose to paint Rhea as a murderous monster. Why? Why was the image they were trying to project so important that we witnessed a national media circus? This is why I alluded to dysfunctional families. Families that cannot accept uncomfortable, unsettling facts about their loved ones. Families that would rather orchestrate and cooperate in a nation-wide witch-hunt against a young woman and her family, than accept that their beloved successful son and brother, a movie star, was mentally ill. Families that seek to camouflage their guilt and grief as a vengeful, blood-thirsty vendetta against another hapless individual and her family. Their blood-lust and callousness has driven Rhea to Arthur Road Prison, in flagrant violation of well-established judicial precedents. All because their darling boy chose a woman they did not approve of, or trust. All because they could not accept that their darling boy had actually killed himself. Fellow Indian women, how many of us are hated or disapproved of, by our husband or boyfriends’ families? How many of us have in-laws who distrust us? Are we all monstrous criminals then? It would seem so. If Rhea is, then so are we. Should Rhea Chakraborty get bail? What do we care if our greatest institutions are compromised? What do we care that due process and the law have become malleable instruments in the hands of the ruling class? What do we care if another human being has to endure unspeakable horror, as long as we are entertained? Sushant will now be known for scandal, for his mental illness, his weed-smoking, being forced to choose between his family and his girlfriend. That’s his legacy now. Not his dreams, his intelligence, his talent or his success. This murky, macabre, indescribably horrifying freak-show that his family has actively participated in. Talk about desecrating a dead person’s memory. Sheesh. Robin Williams committed suicide. Anthony Bourdain committed suicide. Why is it so hard to accept that successful, intelligent men can be depressed to the point of killing themselves? Toxic masculinity, anyone? When Deepkia Padukone confessed to depression, the nation said “meh”. Yet when it emerges that a successful and promising male actor was depressed, we scapegoat the girlfriend. Fellow Indians, nicely done! Lastly, the machinations of The Powers That Be: We must ask ourselves why we are being sold this narrative by mainstream media:Mr Modi’s genius lies in his uncanny ability to tune into the public pulse. His genius lies in his ability to craft narratives that the Indian masses will swallow, hook, line and sinker. He knows that millions of middle-class Indians are aspirational. Sushant was a shining emblem of a middle-class boy tasting undreamt of success. Who he was, as a person, doesn’t matter. What matters, is what we, the ordinary Indian, want him to be. We want him to be invincible. A shining movie-star. The beautiful Bihar boy who headlines Rs 200 crore films. We don’t want to know about the lowest growth rate since 1952. We don’t want to know about 18.9 million salaried employees who’ve lost their jobs since April. 18.9 mn salaried people lost jobs since April, 5 mn in July, says CMIE The media gives us what we want. This is why, had our families encouraged us to think critically, think rationally, think independently, millions of educated Indians wouldn’t have swallowed the bilge that we are being fed. We would have learned media literacy. We would have distinguished between news and propaganda. We would have known the difference between good journalism and journalism masquerading as entertainment. We would have known “how consent is manufactured”: Does this ring a bell?

column1: What did you love and hate about “Peaky Blinders” series 5?
column3: Like most people, I have been waiting to be transplanted back to the crazy world of the Peaky Blinders Gang and this season saw more inner turmoil brewing in the Gang instead of the turf wars that we are used too. Things I loved:Tommy Shelby Our favorite gang strategist was at it again. I love Tommy and how he is usually 5 steps ahead of those around him. However, we can see the change in Tommy. Tommy’s ambition is affecting how he conducts his business as several members of the family pointed out. Tommy’s ambition has him in league with the fascist (on the surface ) which even on a superficial level is enough to piss off Polly. Polly GrayPolly is never a disappointment. The beating heart of the Peaky Blinders gang, they would be nowhere without Aunt Pol who is facing a great conundrum because of the potential war between Tommy and Michael. Polly will choose her son which would put Tommy and the rest of the gang at a huge disadvantage. However, I can tell Polly is pissed at Michael because of his disloyalty to the family and how he is dealing with Gina. Lizzie Shelby :Previously, I didn’t care for Lizzie, I didn’t hate her but I didn’t love her. However, she really grew on me this season. I liked her character evolution and the fact that Lizzie has always truly loved Tommy. I think Lizzie wants Tommy to let her in and trust her the way he would Polly and Its possible next season that he will. People may not understand the marriage between Lizzie and Tommy but they actually make more sense to me in some ways than Tommy and Grace. Tommy can be his truest, crazy self in front of Lizzie and she may not understand everything but she doesn’t really judge. What I find funny is the two different worlds Tommy and Lizzie are trying to maneuver through. They are in the gang life but they are also members of High Society and they struggle with reconciling their new positions. I burst out laughing at the look Polly gave Abarahama Gold when Lizzie couldn’t make an important meeting of family business because she was at a violin recital for their son.Abarahama Gold: Abarahama Gold is Littlefinger in a tougher form. I like Abarahama and the fact he loves Polly. What really got me is how he told Tommy, Polly was of better blood than he was. Haha that was funny. Abarahama would have made a good fixture for the Shelby family but I am curious as to why Polly would marry him and what the plan was with that.Brilliant Chang: We were introduced to the Chinese this season. I liked that a lot actually because black characters were introduced on Peaky Blinders long ago. I am glad to see them add Asian cast members because there were quite a few Asians in UK too around this time. I enjoyed Chang’s introduction and how he came into Tommy’s Bar. Things I hatedhe’s better at smoking than Tommy at least 😂 Michael Gray - Funnily, I love Michael as a character but I hated him this season. Michael was the 3rd most intelligent person in the Shelby clan behind Tommy and Polly. I honestly saw him as a successor to Tommy but he screwed up major this season. Michael lost a fortune on the stock market which could have been prevented had he listened to Tommy. Michael was also being managed by his wife and I thought he was smarter than that. There were some scenes that made me wonder if this is apart of a bigger plan. I knew Michael would be upset about his exile to America but I didn’t think it would play out like this. I hate Tommy and Michael being enemies.Gina Gray – Excuse my language but I HATED THIS GIRL!! Gina came off as a self righteous, self entitled bi*** and honestly, she just made American women look bad. Right from the start with her introduction to Polly ( Michaels Mother) she left a sour taste in my mouth. Polly had her number from the beginning though. Gina is self righteous, self entitled.. I am not sure if they are trying to market her as Polly’s equal but she just came off as a bi*** and she is controlling and turning him against his family. Eww she has got to go.Sir Oswald Mosely – he is a hateful character but interesting to watch. He is your typical British upper class Prig who spouts fascist rhetoric. My take on his character (besides echoing many traits of a certain American President) is he is of a lost generation. Sir Oswald is Downton Abbey gone wrong where you have a developing, changing society and the “upper classes” cannot afford or keep up with it. During this time, many of the “Great Houses” of England were dying dynasties which I believe laid the seeds for the Fascist movement because people always find people to blame for their misfortunes. After the crash, they blamed the Jewish people, in modern times its usually African Americans who are blamed for American misfortunes as well as Jewish people. Its ludicrous really but alas its easier to blame others for your failings in life than to blame the real culprit (yourself). What I found interesting about Sir Oswald is his fascination yet deep hatred of Tommy Shelby. Sir Oswald hated that someone like Tommy Shelby of Gypsy blood was able to rise so high in the World with wealth, success, and respect of his community. Oswald hates Tommy Shelby and tries to put him in his “place” by always making snide remarks about the class differences and his wife. My anger at Tommy is he lets it slide for the most part. Tommy Shelby from season 1 would have killed him at the first remark but Tommy has changed. Anywho, great job done by Sam Clafin!! Tommy Shelby- Yes, Tommy is on my list of characters I loved and hated this season. Tommy is genius strategist but he is stretch way too thin now. Yes, going to politics has helped Tommy climbed to new heights but at what cost to his mental health and his family relationships? I like how Tommy has intel on almost everything and everyone, but this is also why he is stretched thin. There lies the question for Tommy and the crux of his problem, is it harder to get to the Top of the World or to stay at the top of the World with all your enemies waiting for you to fall. Tommy is so worried about remaining King of Birmingham that we saw a lot of death foreshadowing and inner turmoil monologues. Honestly, I found that boring. I like Tommy the strategist out thinking the most educated of men. Arthur/Linda Shelby – Ugghhh both got on them were on my nerves. Takeaways : So I loved and hated a lot of characters this season. I wish they would lose some of that “ woe is me” dialogue and get back to the Peaky Blinders they once were. I also found it interesting is it was Michael who told John before he died “ We aren’t the Peaky Blinders unless we are together”. This is a very true statement. The Peaky Blinders are first and foremost a family and if the family dynamics is screwed then the gang is screwed. I hate how the family is not working together.

column1: What do you do if you've noticed a very close friend showing increasingly serious signs of mental decline - not simple memory loss, and you have discussed it with them, asked them to see a doctor, and they refuse, and remain in denial?
column3: Contact a close family member with your concerns. Before you do, keep a dated log of things you've observed and note your concerns so you're prepared to have a detailed discussion. They may need that information if they are going to take over caring for this individual. Try to keep closer tabs on your friend and keep trying to persuade them to seek help but be supportive. A person who's functioning is declining may cut you off before being pushed too much. They may anger easily. Sometimes observation is enough and keeping interaction as casual as possible will help you assess behaviors. Note forgetfulness, comprehension issues, and changes in personal care, household duties and personality. Particularily note bizarre or disruptive behaviors and moods. (Laws, protocols, policies and cultural norms vary. I'm in the US, Midwest) If substance abuse has been an issue, learn about the adverse affects that can occur long term even after being clean for awhile. Being a ‘dry-drunk' or alcoholic dementia can impair a person and it's progressive. Physical health might be at issue. For example, for older women, simple urinary tract infections can lead to a decline in functioning and even psychosis. This is a difficult time --a gray area between getting a person help they need, but don't want and when you can't take action legally. A person can be impaired a long time before the law recognizes that there's sufficient evidence that they lose their autonomy. In the maintime, they live alone, cook, drive, pay bills, make financial decisions--and it's not necessarily safe. But friends and family are helpless. If family isn't available, start to consider how much responsibility you want to take on as a friend. Find out the local resources for assistance and perhaps talk with neighbors. You may find yourself in the position of having to call adult protective services if your friend's functioning seriously declines, especially if basic safety is an issue. That may be the only way to eventually get them help. You risk losing a friendship, but a person not in their right mind will not be able to see that. With the right help, and depending on the condition itself you can work towards repairing your relationshop. Until then, you'll know you did all you could to help. You're in a difficult and challenging position. Best wishes to you.

column1: Can I describe mental wellness as the ability to perceive and appreciate happy moments? I’m sure that when a person has serious mental health problems they can’t really be positive about anything.
column3: As I read some of the responses to your question, it seems that people do not understand the various types of mental illnesses and how those struggling with, for example, bipolar, have little control over their moods. I have family members and relatives who have bipolar. The following information from Mayo Clinic is very informative. Bipolar disorder, formerly called manic depression, is a mental health condition that causes extreme mood swings that include emotional highs (mania or hypomania) and lows (depression). When you become depressed, you may feel sad or hopeless and lose interest or pleasure in most activities. When your mood shifts to mania or hypomania (less extreme than mania), you may feel euphoric, full of energy or unusually irritable. These mood swings can affect sleep, energy, activity, judgment, behavior and the ability to think clearly. Episodes of mood swings may occur rarely or multiple times a year. While most people will experience some emotional symptoms between episodes, some may not experience any. Although bipolar disorder is a lifelong condition, you can manage your mood swings and other symptoms by following a treatment plan. In most cases, bipolar disorder is treated with medications and psychological counseling (psychotherapy).

column1: How can I deal with my younger brother being a conceited jerk and constantly being rude towards my other family members and me? It’s beginning to affect me, mentally, and I can’t take it anymore. My mother seems to take the situation lightly.
column3: I’m not sure I understand what mental issues you are experiencing when you say he is effecting you mentally. If your feeling angry and frustrated by him behaving like he knows it all, and he teases you and aggravates you all the time, then he has won. You have given him control over your emotions. Your doing exactly what he set out to do, control you. When your mother takes his behavior lightly, and doesn’t do much interfering, she is letting you find a way to handle the situation on your own. Maybe she feels that this it your battle, and that it’s time you learned how to deal with it yourself. All your life there will be people that are going to treat you in ways that you don’t like. And you’ll treat people in ways that they don’t like. There are jerks all around us. Some you’ll never even meet but they can still cause you misery if you let them. Even though we are a social people, we seem to have a hard time getting along with others. It’s important to learn how to not let the behavior of others make your life miserable. Instead of complaining to your mother about how your brother is making you mental, ask her how she manages to not let his behavior effect her. Keep the conversation about what you can do and not about what he is doing. Determine what it is exactly why your brother is making you feel mental. If he’s making you mad because you don’t like how he treats others by being rude, is there anything you can do to make him behave the way you would like him to behave? No, there is no way to make someone else behave like you want them too. So the real reason this makes you mad is because you can’t do anything to change how he acts. You don’t have the control over him that you want. Understand that you can’t make anyone change. You can’t make someone behave the way you want. If we could, parenting would be so much easier. Once you accept that you don’t have the power to control others you stop trying to change them. What they do or say won’t effect you. And when someone’s behavior doesn’t effect you, you aren’t giving them control of your emotions. You not allowing them tho make you mental. They no longer have won. You win. You keep control of yourself, not them. We have two choice, give people the power over our emotions or keep the power. If I gave power of my emotions to everyone that I wished didn’t behave like they do, I’d bevangry all the time. I’d be miserable. I’d be fighting a losing battle trying to make people behave like I want them too. I would never succeed because I can’t make someone do something they don’t want to do. Just like your brother can’t make you do something you don’t want to do. Be grateful for your brother. He is teaching you a valuable life skill that will make your life much more enjoyable. Once he realizes that he can’t control your emotions, he will learn to respect you. But he will always be your brother and will probably continue to treat you like a sister but you can teach him a valuable lesson as well. Maybe he’ll learn that his behavior isn’t getting him the attention and control he wants and he’ll decide to change how he treats others. Maybe, maybe not. But that’s not your concern. Your concern is your well being and emotional health.

column1: Do people get more lonely as they grow older?
column3: How to Prepare to Age Alone According to a 2012 study in The Gerontologist, about one-third of 45- to 63-year-olds are single, most of who never married or are divorced. That’s a whopping 50 percent increase since 1980, the study found. What’s more, about 15 percent of 40- to 44-year-old women had no children in 2012 — up from about 10 percent in 1980, U.S. Census data shows. So what do you do when you step back from your work, or just look at your future and realize there is no one to take care of me when I get older? It can be a scary question to face, and as the statistics show, there are many more people today that are in this situation. In research presented this year at The American Geriatric Society’s annual meeting, found that nearly one-quarter of Americans over age 65 are or may become physically or socially isolated and lack someone like a family member to care for them. The term elder orphans is being used to describe this new group of the elderly. The consequences are profound, older adults who consider themselves lonely are more likely to have trouble completing daily tasks, experience cognitive decline, develop coronary heart disease and even die. Those who are socially isolated are also at risk for medical complications, mental illness, mobility issues and health care access problems. But growing older without kids or a partner doesn’t mean you’re doomed — just as aging with kids and a partner doesn’t mean all’s clear. You never know what will happen, life is a game of roulette, you could be married and have seven children, and you could still wind up alone. Keep in mind that 69 percent of Americans will need long-term care, even though only 37 percent think they will, according to SeniorCare.com. Here are some ways to help yourself to be prepared for the chance that you could become an elderly orphan. 1. Speak up. Talk about your choices with your friends and family members, it is a discussion that needs to be had so stop waiting for it to go away, or magically resolve itself. It will not, you will get older and eventually you might be alone and talking about what could happen and having a plan in place is important. 2. Act early. You need to look inside yourself and know yourself and your family history to determine when you should start planning. Someone with a family history of Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s’, heart disease, and other serious conditions should start planning much earlier than someone whose family genes are strong. No matter what type of family tree you have, it is never too early to start planning for long-term care, because just like car insurance, you may never need it, but will be thankful if you do! You can create a long-term care plan by socking away money for medical emergencies, or invest in a long-term care insurance policy that will give you peace of mind that you will be financially taken care of later in life. 3. Make new friends and keep the old. Your social connections can help with practical health care needs, like driving you to the doctor when you’re unable. But they also do something powerful: keep you alive, research suggests. In a 2012 study of over 2,100 adults age 50 and older, researchers found that the loneliest older adults were nearly twice as likely to die within six years than the least lonely — regardless of their health behaviors or social status. Connections can also help ward off depression, which affects nearly 20 percent of the 65-and-older population, according the National Alliance on Mental Illness . The more social activities you have, the more friends, the more things you can do to keep your body and mind active — that’s the best protection you have against mental illness.” 4. Appoint a proxy. Find that person who you trust most in the world and ask them to be the keeper of your personal information in case of an emergency. They should have your Social Security number, where you keep your insurance card, which medications you take, everything you would need in the event of an emergency. Also, revisit the information with that person every so often to update any new medications or other pertinent information. Before you start losing any cognitive capacities, consider designating that person as your durable power of attorney for health care, or the person who makes health care decisions for you when you’re no longer able. If no one comes to mind, hire an attorney who specializes in elder care law by asking around for recommendations or searching online for highly rated professionals. Unlike your friends, they have a license to defend and are well-versed in elder care issues. 5. Live well. The two biggest things you can do to stay healthy as you age is exercise and eat well. Some of the foods that we eat are really, really bad for the body and that’s one of the major causes of chronic conditions — and not exercising. Keeping your brain sharp is also critical if you want to be able to make informed decisions about your health care. Participate in activities that challenge you — math problems if numbers trip you up, or crossword puzzles if words aren’t your forte. “The old adage, ‘If you don’t use it, you lose it,’ is 100 percent correct..

column1: How has the world changed since covid?
column3: COVID-19 has turned the world upside down. Everything has been changed. How we exist and interact with each other, how we work and communicate, how we move around and travel the world. column1: How can schizophrenics have more self-confidence?
column3: Schizophrenia is a serious mental illness that affects how a person thinks, feels, and behaves. People with schizophrenia may seem like they have lost touch with reality, which causes significant distress for the individual, their family members, and friends. If left untreated, the symptoms of schizophrenia can be persistent and disabling. However, effective treatments are available. When delivered in a timely, coordinated, and sustained manner, treatment can help affected individuals to engage in school or work, achieve independence, and enjoy personal relationships and thus gain self-confidence. Psychotic symptoms include altered perceptions (e.g., changes in vision, hearing, smell, touch, and taste), abnormal thinking, and odd behaviors. People with psychotic symptoms may lose a shared sense of reality and experience themselves and the world in a distorted way. Specifically, individuals typically experience: · Hallucinations, such as hearing voices or seeing things that aren’t there · Delusions, which are firmly held beliefs not supported by objective facts (e.g., paranoia - irrational fears that others are “out to get you” or believing that the television, radio, or internet are broadcasting special messages that require some response) · Thought disorder, which includes unusual thinking or disorganized speech Cognitive symptoms include problems in attention, concentration, and memory. For some individuals, the cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia are subtle, but for others, they are more prominent and interfere with activities like following conversations, learning new things, or remembering appointments. Specifically, individuals typically experience: · Difficulty processing information to make decisions · Problems using information immediately after learning it · Trouble focusing or paying attention Treatments and Therapies The causes of schizophrenia are complex and are not fully understood, so current treatments focus on managing symptoms and solving problems related to day to day functioning. Treatments include: Antipsychotic Medications Antipsychotic medications can help reduce the intensity and frequency of psychotic symptoms. They are usually taken daily in pill or liquid forms. Some antipsychotic medications are given as injections once or twice a month, which some individuals find to be more convenient than daily oral doses. Patients whose symptoms do not improve with standard antipsychotic medication typically receive clozapine. Psychosocial Treatments Cognitive behavioral therapy, behavioral skills training, supported employment, and cognitive remediation interventions may help address the negative and cognitive symptoms of schizophrenia. A combination of these therapies and antipsychotic medication is common. Psychosocial treatments can be helpful for teaching and improving coping skills to address the everyday challenges of schizophrenia. They can help people pursue their life goals, such as attending school, working, or forming relationships which again build up self-confidence. Family Education and Support Educational programs for family members, significant others, and friends offer instruction about schizophrenia symptoms and treatments, and strategies for assisting the person with the illness. Increasing key supporters’ understanding of psychotic symptoms, treatment options, and the course of recovery can lessen their distress, bolster coping and empowerment, and strengthen their capacity to offer effective assistance. Having treatment through self-management, many individuals with schizophrenia gain confidence, skills and knowledge to better manage their mental health and gain more control of their lives at a time when they may feel they have lost control.
