column1: I’ve been made aware that I’m a covert narcissist (NPD), but can’t change or find the motivation to keep trying. Am I stuck this way? Should I avoid contact with people to control the damage I do?
column3: While I’ve never been diagnosed with NPD, I have been diagnosed with C-PTSD in the past due to childhood trauma. My Mother is extremely narcissistic and I was the child victim of Munchausen by Proxy Syndrome through her. As a result, I developed strong tendencies and symptoms of both NPD and BPD based on the criteria. I check almost every box. The simplistic answer given by Lou Wales is very well put. I want to add and expand on her sentiments about trying by giving you my personal thoughts and story. Why? Because I am so sick of reading narc haters preaching that a pwNPD (or one high in narcissism) cannot grow into a better person. Things aren’t this black and white… oh, the irony. lol The way you worded your question saddens me. I'm assuming you're buying into all the hate and believing you're stuck. This is hogwash. You are aware therefore it IS possible to get better! I understand how rare it is to transpire. But me and others are living proof you’re not alone. It depends on the person and how bad their tendencies are and how much effort they are willing to put in. Evaluate this sentence as it applies to you and figure out what you want to do. There's no one size fits all. Moreover, I got wrekt and mind-flayed by a highly narcissistic guy recently (my guess NPD w/psychopathic tendencies) and it hurts like hell. He’s aware of himself, too. In hindsight, it was all so juvenile from both our ends and kind of funny tbh idk I started imagining him sometimes as an angry, pouty little boy with his arms folded, refusing to say what's the matter lol Especially when he’d give me the silent treatment. Gotta find ways to make light of it. We both knew what was going on but unspoken. And what came first? The chicken or the egg? xD Doesn’t matter at the end of the day. He came out on top and that’s that. I’ve experienced firsthand both sides of the same coin so I hope you and others will hear me out. Motivation will manifest if you work hard enough and dig deep. Don't count yourself out just yet. Don't throw away the chance at enhancing your life and relationships. There is hope. Yes, the unfortunate truth is a big chunk of you will never change but you have to keep trying and little victories will emerge the more you practice. You can evolve to an extent that is noticeably beneficial and worth it. No, don't avoid people! That's the worst thing you can do for yourself!!! You can't avoid your problems, life lesson 101. Doing so will leave you isolated and disturbed. Being alone is not how humans operate. We are social creatures - accept the scientific fact and apply it. You have to learn to socialize in healthier, more productive ways. Maybe keep in touch with a select few people that you deem worthwhile so you don’t overwhelm yourself. Given you’re not intentionally sadistic, choose those who have high levels of empathy and understanding if you can. I’ll probably get flack for that statement lol But it’s a huge contradiction to those who do want to improve… what other types of people can realistically help? Be open about your condition if you're comfortable enough or simply roll with the punches. It's horrifying and humiliating when you become aware. Do not downplay any discomfort you may be feeling. It’s important to go through a grieving period if you are capable of doing so. Regardless of how deep your feelings run, you have lost many potential opportunities and experiences. It is a whirlwind of emotions in the beginning, at least for me it was. You are seeing the reality of who you really are for the first time. It was delusional thinking before and that's scary as fuck to analyze. Your brain gets flooded with images of moments in time you wish didn’t happen. In my experience, I saw all those times I was off my rocker in rage over god knows what. In your case being predominantly covert, maybe you'll recall times where you were being insidious... cold, critical and demeaning. Their were times where I made ultimatums to others in attempts to control them. Or maybe for you it was subtle things you'd do and say that added up overtime, where you indirectly conveyed it’s my way or the highway. Perhaps a family member, a friend or SO pointed these sort of things out to you or whatever you did in general. You go on the defensive each time. Personally, I would and sometimes still do think thoughts such as, “No I’m not any of these things! I don’t act that way! You're seeing it all wrong. It’s your fault. You’re too sensitive to my criticisms. Man up or accept the fact that you are failing at life in one way or another. You deserve your misfortune and pain because of your failures. You’re hopeless and useless.” I was a terrible person. I was unbearably stubborn and controlling. I hated affection. I hated kissing. I hated sex. I hated having to compromise. I believe and still believe I’m unique, unlike anyone else, and therefore entitled to special treatment. It’s hard for me to not see everyone as inferior. The list goes on. My ex boyfriend was dealt one of the shittiest hands in life (his dad was the abusive one) and I was beyond cruel to him at the beginning of our relationship. He had it hard and his own emotional issues to deal with. All he needed was unconditional support and love which I was unable to provide. I was young and naïve. I thought I was being a loving, supportive girlfriend. I mean, I was — but intermittently! Everything in between was complete disdain. Sometimes it was slights and passive aggression. Yelling and name calling was my jam. When shit hit the fan, I’d scream at the top of my lungs and start finding stuff to throw at him. Typing this makes me cringe. When people point out “shame” is at our core, this is very much the case. You have to forgive yourself and let others forgive you! Do not avoid others because you're afraid of the shame you will inevitably feel time and time again as you try to get better. You may fail often and even feel guilty as you keep hurting others. It will sting but one must fail in order to succeed. My ex and I started dating senior year of high school. It wasn’t until my early 20s that I had the epiphany that would alter my perception and created a new way of navigating. It was an instant moment of full on clarity (Makes me wonder how others become self aware. Is it a slow progression or sudden realization?). For the millionth time, my ex emphasized how I was turning into my Mom. Like mother, like daughter… carrying out the abuse she taught me. It all became transparent. Anytime I interacted with my Mom after that, I could spot the ways in which I mirrored her behaviors. Kind of trippy, really. Long story short — even though I’ve already made it long lol — my ex and I were together for 14 years. I improved myself as time went on. He acknowledge my improvements so it's not like I'm talking out of my ass. lol The problem was as I kept improving, he kept regressing. Like I said, he had his own mental health issues. I believe the compounding effect of the years of damage done by me turned him into an overly attached vindictive monster. Sure, he had a choice, but this was the reality of the situation. All the built up resentment he had towards me was too much for him to handle. Being treated like shit for years is painful and you can easily become an angry individual, especially if you're mentally ill. Wanting revenge is a normal feeling/response to abuse. But you're not suppose to act on it or else you are no better. So the tables were turned in the end. He became emotionally and physically abusive and “stuck” in a rut. I'm not blaming him for our demise, it takes two to tango. We split up last year because I emotionally cheated on him (I was 100% faithful up until that point). I don't want to make excuses for myself or point fingers. All I can say is, I had mentally checked out long before this happened. I was on autopilot. The sad irony is that he is the reason why I became aware. I betrayed the person who I have everything to thank for. No matter how poorly he treated me in the end, this does not justify my betrayal. Infidelity of any kind is wrong! Plain and simple. Without him and our years together, I'd still be living in my bubble. He was a kind soul and meant well. Very affectionate. Also quite intelligent. I enjoyed the way he shared his knowledge with me. He had a lot of promise or I wouldn't have stayed with him for so long. I learned much from him. He taught me how to melt the cold with warmth. His family helped a lot, too. His Mom was more of a Mom to me than my own. My Mom would never hug me or tell me she loved me like his did. I actually can't remember a single time my Mom did either of the two. When his Sister got married and had kids, I observed and admired what a growing, healthy and loving family looks like. I became an Aunt to 3 nieces and a nephew. You need people in your life to show you the way. The more people, the better. Btw it wasn’t all kitten and rainbows with his family. I embarrassed myself in front of them a few times before I learned to wise up and stop acting out. While our relationship was one long, drawn out shit show, I don't regret it. Despite all the bad, there was a lot of good. He was my best friend and made me a better, smarter person. Point is... I tried. I tried hard every day to absorb anything I could that would help me and I still do. I try to be more mindful and less impulsive. Tomorrow is a new day. You need to know this is a life long commitment to yourself due to the ever changing nature of life if you actually want to improve. Your brain is wired differently so it can be stressful. I think because of how I’m half borderline I kind of lucked out because the magnitude of which I feel things is intense lol The volatile shifting of moods matched with the intensity made it obvious for me to see my narcissistic tendencies. It’s pretty interesting. I do like Psychology. Being single and dating for the first time, I started recognizing my patterns of unintentional love-bombing, gaslighting and manipulation. I can reel in almost any guy effortlessly but I typically want nothing to do with them after a brief period of assessment. I’ll admit that I am having a lot of trouble in this department. Though I always try to be good natured and honest. I never have ill intentions. The worst part that’s effecting my dating life is I feel entitled to special treatment and I seldom meet guys because I see very little value in 99% of them. It’s no coincidence the one guy I got involved with is of high social status, very narcissistic and pathologically comparable. Like attracts like and the BPD/NPD coupling is hot press. Early on as I embarked into dating, lack of attention when I NEEDED it in that VERY moment would crush me and my knee jerk reaction is to act out. Doesn’t matter if the guy was of value or not. I was alone and I needed validation at every chance I could get. I have practiced controlling my emotional upheavals over the years and its still the hardest thing I struggle with as well as validation/reassurance seeking. I’m accidently self absorbed in conversation and don’t ask enough questions to get to know the other person because there’s a void of caring in that moment of time. I’m just excited and want to talk about my myself when I engage with someone new. These symptoms can annoy some guys which is understandable. I annoy myself with it! Ha! So I started to tone it down and make a point of asking a question or two. I don't stop trying to find new ways to practice being less co-dependent and happy with myself. I can sometimes with certain hobbies and whatnot. It comes and goes now, where before it was static for the first 6 months. I lived on the dating apps fishing for attention lol xD My mood swings are something fierce and I don’t want to take out my onslaught of emotions onto others. I’ve done enough of that with my ex and have no interest in repeating past mistakes with new people. I try to eternalize things by writing my thoughts out as they come to me until I calm down and can think logically again. It started with how I’d be ready to fire off a text message, but then I'd stop myself and reread it multiple times. “This is dumb and embarrassing. Or I don’t want to cause conflict or be mean. It’s not worth it.” This is what I try to do when I notice questionable things I'm about to say. But there are times where I mess up. That's just how it goes. Notice how the word TRY comes up often? You have to drill into your head so as to not lose sight. You try and you try. And then you try some more. Constantly trying is what you have to do. When I catch myself in the moment and adjust my behavior, it’s a great feeling. You begin to develop an internal locus of control, something you've may have never experienced or had before. This is important for improvement to take place. Don't mind the fact that an external locus of control will remain dominant. That's who you are but the fact that you're creating a foundation so you can practice self control will free you and allow you to form genuine connections. Typically you’ll see your actions in hindsight and reflect on how you could’ve carried a conversation better, how you could’ve handle a situation in a more selfless way, etc. Even hindsight and introspection is a form of trying because you are gathering information to help you in the future. This is going to be the case 90% of the time. And that’s ok. It is very, very difficult to control your natural way of interacting in real time. But it can happen the more you remain mindful and keep track of your maladaptive behaviors. If you know you hurt someone or noticed how you were acting selfishly with little regard for the other person’s feelings, then apologize! Always, ALWAYS say sorry when you know you’ve done wrong. It doesn’t matter if it’s forced or comes off as shallow. Ignore the haters who cry about "fake" apologies. This stance is incredibly toxic. Who are they to say it's entirely fake? Can't they see that the pwNPD is trying to be aware of someone else’s feelings other than their own? It might be surface level but this is what is happening. Admitting fault, no matter how shallow, isn't something that comes naturally. Any smidge of remorse should be acknowledge. You might not know what else that person is thinking and feeling if they cloak themselves with overt anger or radio silence. The only thing grounded in certainty and reality is the fact an apology is being made! Advising people to dismiss apologies makes my blood boil because it hinders potential growth, whether its desired by the person or not. Anyway, that was a tangent lol… Just always say sorry. You’ll find in time that the once difficult thing to do is actually the easiest thing to practice because it usually comes with instant gratification. When someone accepts your apology, it makes you feel good for doing the right thing. You might start noticing how you can use your innate narcissism to your benefit instead of your destruction. That’s the whole point of healthy narcissism and that's what you want to aim for. Remember, you are aware, so that means any apology you are giving is stemming from... awareness. lol THIS IS A GOOD THING!!! Keep practicing! You have to stay dedicated to saying sorry imo. It helps condition yourself to develop deeper remorse and empathy, which are the most important functions you need to learn in order to get better. Owning up to your transgressions will help you identify what areas you need to work on. You can also look at it this way - you're practicing mitigation. Change is a strong word. I’ve been self aware for about 7ish years. 6 out of 7 was with my ex. This past year came with a new learning curve with dating and being single. Also - don’t be hard on yourself. You will be learning how to care and acquire empathy for the first time in your life. Think about that. This is something that “normal” people innately have because they were raised accordingly. You don't have that luxury. It’s a shitty thing to come to terms with and you’ll often feel low. You’ll hate the world and everyone in it because it’s not fair you’re decades behind emotionally. Ya, its not fair. You didn't ask for this. It fucking sucks. So you need to adjust your lens from “It’s not fair and I'm a hopeless case” to “I am grateful that I’m no longer blind and now have a choice.” Many pwNPD like my Mother are oblivious. There is no choice in existence for those types. They can't learn. But you can!!! However, don't expect this huge change or you’ll be back at square one. Its not realistic to think big picture. It's going to take time and due diligence. Improvements will be minimal yet very IMPACTFUL on your life, impactful in a way you once thought would never be possible. Instead of inflicting hurt, you’ll be caring. Instead of being selfish, you'll be selfless. And so on and so forth. It wont happen all the time but there will be a handful of times where it will and you’ll recognize the difference in yourself. This will make you happy and proud of your efforts. You start to accept yourself the way you are and do your best everyday to be a good person towards others. That's all you can do and that's all any DECENT HUMAN BEING will ask for. If someone is making you feel low even though you are making an effort to be nice and communicate effectively, then they aren't a decent human being. One of my best friends is the most overt narcissist I’ll probably ever come across but you know what? He’s also one of the most hilarious people I’ve known and really fun to be around. He’s not that bad, I know his true self and his overall presence in my life is very positive. I owe him a lot because it was through him I developed a support system of good people who look out for me and my best interests. They urge me to not give into BS. They know I have strong personal values and morals I want to uphold. Recall when I said if you feel comfortable enough to be completely honest? I’ve been myself and outright with my new friends. So I instinctively served everything on a silver platter to the new dude… oops lol I put my trust into him like I have with others. I was open about everything. Literally everything and other private details. I don't need disloyal people like this in my life so it’s a good thing he finally dropped me like a sack of potatoes =P It was a 7 month long Quasimodo situationship full of silent treatments, future faking, push/pull, lying, etc., all initiated by him. The worst part was the physical avoidance in the second half paired with seductive with-holding. The guy cannot do intimacy and it’s sad to witness because I remember being that cold once. He’ll have to be nicer and more honest if he ever wants back in. My prediction is he’ll be too much of a coward to return after I forced him to face himself. The funny thing is we never fought once. There was just constant, underlying conflict that was never addressed authentically. The door is open and my motto is to not burn bridges. Naturally you'll begin to surround yourself with people who love you unconditionally and will aid you in becoming the best version of yourself. Once you notice progress, it'll be felt and motivation will grow. Little by little, you'll learn how to love yourself in the process of learning how to love others. It’s a pretty cool thing that unfolds. Don’t overthink or question if you are feeling deeply enough because ANY amount at ANY magnitude is progress!!! I promise you that life will be much more fulfilling and meaningful if you TRY to bond with others. Start today and never stop trying!
column9: Thank you for being so brave and honest. This has been so helpful to read.

column1: In what ways might reincarnation change our perspective on the cards we’re dealt in life?
column3: This one hits close to home. Having gradually come to believe we reincarnate, my view on the purpose of life, including the cards we’re dealt, has indeed changed. I’ll share my shift in perspective, but feel I should begin with a caveat: This topic is a potential landmine. I genuinely apologize in advance if any of the ideas I express are upsetting, which is not my intent. People born into difficult circumstances, such as extreme poverty, poor health, mental impairment, or abuse could possibly be provoked by any suggestion that our soul plays a part in selecting the difficult circumstances in which we find ourselves. If reincarnation is true, we never die. Consciousness may never end, but it doesn’t mean we can’t or don’t suffer. Can there be purpose and meaning in such suffering? If you’re open to that possibility, you may want to keep reading. If not, you may wish to skip this answer and I apologize for any offense. The Story of Rachel Imagine for a moment learning that a close friend was involved in a tragic car accident, losing her ability to walk. This very thing happened to a close friend of mine – a girl I dated in college though we eventually lost touch. Years later, I ran into her and discovered she’d been in a horrible car crash. The crash permanently crippled her, relegating her to a wheelchair for the rest of her life. We talked about life since college and she explained that after her accident, she went through a long bout of depression. Finally, she said, she woke up one morning, looked out her window, and decided to move past her pain and resentment. When I saw her, she was in her first year of law school and was very excited about the future. I never did see her again, but I like to imagine that she’s done quite well and had found peace in her life. My Father’s Tragedy Her situation reminds me of a tragedy in my own family that involved my father and took place before I was born. My father grew up in a small town in the deep south (US). His friends described him as a fun loving and a great athlete. They claimed he was a great baseball player – maybe good enough for the majors. It’s hard to tell whether they were exaggerating to impress me, but it’s a story they all relay. When he was 16, he was riding a motor scooter down a country highway when he was hit head-on by a semi, catapulting him through the truck’s windshield, out the passenger window, and onto the side of the road, where he lay crumbled, broken, and comatose. An ambulance was summoned and he was taken to the hospital and placed in a full-body cast. He remained in a coma for several weeks. Four weeks later, he awoke.Pictured: Not my dad, but close to how he appeared As you can imagine, he was horrified at what he discovered (he had no memory of the event). His entire body was scarred and he had developed expressive aphasia, a communication disorder that makes it difficult to speak. Even more devastating than the loss of his once-good looks, was the loss of his ability to play ball. He was angry and resentful. Fast forward to today. These days my father tells me and my brother that his motor scooter accident was the best thing that ever happened to him. He had managed to channel that resentment, anger, and competitiveness into mental and spiritual pursuits. He was the first member of his family to attend college, and he later attended law school. He became deeply spiritual and invested a great deal of time teaching my brother and I. Were in not for that accident, I can’t honestly say I’d be the person I am today. I’m not suggesting we experience suffering to direct us to law school (!) Everyone has their own path. The Story of Lisa In Dr. Michael Newton’s book, “Journey of Souls,” he relays the story of a patient – an athletic woman I’ll call “Lisa” – who suffered from a mysterious pain in her legs that caused her to be depressed. She had seen many physicians, but none could identify a cause. Finally, a physician suggested the problem was psychological, leading her to seek treatment from Dr. Newton. Under hypnosis, Lisa revealed an interesting story that cast light on her condition. Lisa had earlier relayed to Dr. Newton the details of a previous life in 800 AD where she was a massively strong, athletic Viking named “Leth.” The following conversation involves her most recent life as a young woman in New England. When she was six-years old in this recent life, she was involved in a tragic accident in which she fell out of a moving carriage, which then rolled over her legs, crushing them. She was never able to walk or stand again. Dr. Newton: In your history of body choices why did you wait a thousand years between being a physically strong man and a crippled woman? Lisa: I developed a better sense of who I was during the lives in between. I chose to be crippled to gain intellectual concentration. Dr. Newton: You chose a broken body for this? Lisa: Yes, you see, being unable to walk made me read and study more. I developed my mind… and listened to my mind. I learned to communicate well and to write with skill because I wasn’t distracted. I was always in bed. Dr. Newton: Was any characteristic about your soul particularly evident in both Ashley and Leth the Viking? Lisa: That part of me which craves fiery expression was in both bodies. Dr. Newton: I want you to go to the moment you were in the process of choosing the life of Ashley. Tell me how you decided on this particular damaged body. Lisa: I picked a family in a well-established, settled part of America. I wanted a place with libraries and to be taken care of by loving parents so I could devote myself to scholarship. I constantly wrote to many unhappy people and became a good teacher. Dr. Newton: As Ashley, what did you do for this loving family who took care of you? Lisa: It always works two ways – the benefits and liabilities. I chose this family because they needed the intensity of love with someone totally dependent upon them all their lives. We were very close as a family because they were lonely before I was born. I came late, as their only child. They wanted a daughter who would not marry and leave them to be lonely again. I was struck by the similarities to Lisa’s story and what happened to my friend and father. What other tragedies are deliberately planned? Patients under hypnosis often describe life on Earth as “a grand play.” A Personal ExperienceConsidering these stories leads me to reconsider many of the events of my own life. Like my father, I was raised in a small town in the deep south. Where I was raised, people were expected to be Christian and attend church – which we did. There was a saying I heard growing up I find kind of funny: “you can’t throw a rock without hitting a Baptist.” That’s a lot of Baptists. I was expected to study the Bible in depth – we weren’t the sort of Christians who showed up in church once a year on Easter. My family expected me to be a biblical scholar, and a week did not go by in which I did not study the scriptures in depth. Even so, I never fit in with my church or community, and others noticed I was different. I always questioned what I was being taught rather than just accept the dogma I was being fed. This caused many problems for me and, ultimately, I was kicked out of my house at age 16 for refusing to go to church. Incidentally, that was the same age when my father had his accident. For years I resented the controlling upbringing in which I was not allowed to question and it affects my personality today. But now I have a different perspective, and it relates to my purpose on Earth. I believe I needed that experience to understand what it’s like to grow up under the shadow of fundamentalist Christianity because, in a former life, I was heavily involved in codifying and spreading the Christian message. In that former life, I meant well, but failed to understand the long-term, downstream impact of what I was doing which played a significant role in modern day fundamentalist thinking. In this life, I was meant to learn that lesson firsthand and help correct my earlier mistakes, but it necessarily involved my being raised in a hardcore, fundamentalist community. Conclusion I can’t say that all life’s suffering involves a soul’s choice made in the Spirit world prior to reincarnation. There are so many variable and so many possibilities. However, it appears that many times the obstacles we encounter in life are there for an important reason that relates to our soul’s development. Even so, I would not presume to claim this is always the case – particularly as it relates to the life of others. I’m an eternal optimist and, perhaps for that reason, I find it comforting to think that at least some of our suffering is a deliberate challenge placed before us to allow us to fulfill our purpose in life, which I believe is to grow spiritually. For me, this gives meaning to grief. And I’d rather live in a world where suffering is endowed with purpose and meaning than one where it’s meted out with no rhyme or reason, a world devoid of reason or purpose.
column9: I’d rather live in a world with purpose, too, and I believe that every experience allows our souls to learn.

column1: What happens when trauma remains untreated?
column3: Trauma is defined as any kind of physical, emotional, or psychological harm caused by someone else's actions. Trauma can happen at any age, including childhood. In fact, children who have experienced trauma often experience symptoms of PTSD later in life. The effects of trauma can last a lifetime. Trauma can cause a person to feel anxious, depressed, angry, sad, guilty, ashamed, confused, or hopeless. These feelings may lead to self-destructive behaviors, substance abuse, eating disorders, and suicidal thoughts. Trauma can take many forms, including physical, sexual, verbal, and emotional abuse. Physical abuse includes being hit, kicked, burned, bitten, choked, strangled, or beaten. Sexual abuse involves unwanted touching or penetration. Verbal abuse includes name calling, humiliation, threats, yelling, and blaming. Emotional abuse includes neglect, abandonment, isolation, and rejection. Trauma can occur in different ways. A child might witness violence between their parents, or they could be abused by a family member. Someone close to them might die unexpectedly, or they could lose a loved one due to illness or accident. There are many reasons why people suffer from trauma. Trauma can affect anyone, regardless of race, gender, religion, socioeconomic status, or nationality. However, certain groups of people are more likely to experience trauma than others. People who live in poverty, are homeless, or are victims of domestic violence are among those who are most vulnerable. If you or someone you know is suffering from trauma, here are some things you can do to help yourself heal: • Talk about what happened. Share your experiences with a trusted adult. You don't need to go into detail, just let them know what happened. • Get professional help. If you're not sure where to turn, call your local mental health clinic or hospital. Ask if they offer counseling services. • Find a safe place to talk. If you're having trouble talking about what happened, find a quiet space where you won't be interrupted. • Take care of yourself. Make sure you eat well, get enough sleep, exercise regularly, and manage your stress levels. • Don't forget to love yourself. column1: Do drugs truly affect our emotions?
column3: Drug addiction exacts an emotional toll on sufferers and their family members. Addiction grows in a bed of pre-existing emotional turmoil, and the feelings of anxiety, shame, guilt, and worthlessness that increase risk for addiction will only become worse as the chemical dependency deepens. Drug abuse also creates fresh emotional complications for everyone it affects. Emotional pain and disruption is inevitable for drug addicts and their loved ones, and only through treatment and recovery can families escape the pernicious effects of chemical dependency. Drug addiction is a physical disorder with profound emotional ramifications and dimensions. Addiction, alcoholism, and substance abuse can be harmful to your mind and body. While many people understand how addiction hurts your appearance or other physical changes that take place due to prolonged substance use, the emotional effects of drug addiction and alcoholism are often less understood. What Addiction Does to Your Emotions Addiction typically exists hand in hand with negative emotions like depression, anxiety, loneliness, and even anger. When a person who is struggling with addiction or alcoholism feels these negative emotions, they often abuse substances to quell the emotions. Then as withdrawal sets in, the emotions worsen, and they must use more just to feel normal. The emotional challenges aren’t limited to withdrawal; people often experience greater difficulty controlling their emotions at all stages of alcoholism and addiction. The very mechanisms of addiction, cravings, and impulse are linked to changes in the brain that only intensify as the addiction continues. People who are struggling with addiction may face heightened feelings of sadness, anxiety, worthlessness, and anger. Active addiction can worsen existing mental health challenges, such as anxiety the same pathways that reinforce addiction. As a person’s addiction worsens, their emotional challenges and changes often worsen as well. Emotional Effects of Prescription Drug Abuse Different substances affect the brain and emotions in different ways. Prescription drugs, such as prescription opiates, lead to a different set of emotional changes. Opiates, for example, are prescription drugs that can lead to striking emotional changes. Long-term opiate use was found to alter blood flow between both hemispheres of the brain, with one hemisphere receiving slightly more blood than the other. In patients who have greater blood flow in the right hemisphere of the brain, these blood flow changes caused by opiate abuse are linked to more negative moods. Other prescription drugs like benzos are also associated with emotional changes like mood swings, increased anxiety, and depression. Treating the Emotional Effects of Drug Addiction and Alcoholism This includes support for the physical effects of substance abuse as well, such as addiction's effect on the skeletal and nervous system. Healing the emotional damage done by addiction and alcoholism requires dedication, therapy, and support. Over millions of people are dependent on some type of illicit drug or misused medication, and the effects of their addiction are like ripples in a pond, spreading outward to cause pain and misery for everyone in the addict's social and family circles. The emotional devastation of drug addiction is experienced most directly and acutely by addicts themselves. Bur spouses, children, parents, grandparents, siblings, extended family members and close friends also feel addiction's impact and their emotional reactions range across a broad landscape of pain, stress and discouragement. Oftentimes, people are driven to excessive use and abuse of drugs by a desire to escape or forget. They may have suffered some type of trauma in the past, or may be undergoing some trauma in the present, and leaves them plagued by feelings of stress and anxiety. Some of the common emotional risk factors of drug addiction includes: •Being subjected to emotional, physical or sexual abuse in childhood. •Exposure to distant or neglectful parenting styles. •Multiple instances of being bullied. •Being a victim of domestic abuse. •Suffering thorough a natural disaster, possibly involving a loss of life. •Losing a loved one to death, divorce or desertion. People who've been through such experiences may feel guilt or shame if they somehow blame themselves for the advise they suffered or the loss they experienced or the circumstances they created that led to the emotional injuries. Drug addiction can easily develop among people using illicit substances to numb their pre-existing emotional pain, but this is not a strategy that will work for long (if it works at all). Eventually, tolerance for the drug advances, and users have to take more and more of their substance of choice to experience the same effects---which is the primary reason why these substances are so addictive. Another problem is that drugs themselves create fresh chemical imbalances in the brain---or reinforce the old ones---which can lead to increased emotional instability. In every city and state help is available for addicts and their loved ones, so no one who has suffered the emotional impact of drug abuse should have to go through it alone.

column1: How has the coronavirus affected you?
column3: A bit personal one. The lockdown had an up and down effect on me. On the one hand, I reconciled with some of my hobbies (PC Gaming, book reading), also grooming some more along the way (poetry and video editing), my mental health and academic productivity took quite a hit. That is not the point of this answer though.ContactFor most of the lockdown, I have been away from direct contact with COVID-19 fortunately. I did go out 4–5 times by a car with my brother, taking enough precautions, to buy some things and had to siphon chicken to satisfy our buds, but other than that, I haven't gone out for any recreational activity or a meetup. My parents, both of them, being doctor, have been at risk for contracting it for a long time now. They take all the precautions, rushing to the shower after coming back home immediately and doing all kinds of errands. The bomb dropped last Friday when my Father came home early feeling weak and having fever. My mother, coming back at her usual time, quickly got my brother shifted into my room to cut his contact and herself shifted into another room. He got tested next day and by Saturday’s night, his report was positive. Now, I knew the circumstances were extreme so I reluctantly gave up on my privacy and freedom to accommodate my brother. Its not easy, because the most comfortable space in my house is my room, it's my little kingdom, I , the sole king there. Anyways, I managed with him, watching movies with similar interests, trying to just adjust with him and I was doing an okay job so far. Saturday and Sunday went this way and we were getting along well. During Monday afternoon, my mother came to my room to check up on us and observed that he had a fever. She immediately rushed him out, took out a temperature reading. Turns out he was having high fever and she got him tested too. By that night, he was confirmed positive too. Turns out, now I was at risk for COVID. I had been with him for two days, relatively close except when using the table, watching movies together, sharing the bed, so it is highly likely that I may have it. I use “may” because I don't have any symptoms now. I did have fatigue, malaise and GIT issues on Tuesday but they have since subsided and I feel energetic enough now. I didn't have any episode of fever yet, hoping it stays that way.My turnAs a protocol, you are required to get a test 5 days after a family member is infected. So today was the day I went to have my test. We went to the auditorium of PGIMS, Rohtak, where a special area for COVID checking specially for healthcare workers and their families has been established. My mother had registered for the test for herself and for me. She went first, they gave her a sampling tube and she sat on the chair where the doctor was taking samples. They put a swab in her mouth to get a oropharyngeal sample and then in her nose to get a nasopharyngeal one. During the mouth bit, she had a gag reflex which made me tensed but I remembered that my mum has a very sensitive palate so it may not be an issue for me. Then came my turn. Timidly, I took my sampling tube and went to the chair. The doc took some time to get new gloves now pointed me towards her. I knew it was coming. Truth be told, the mouth part was easy for me. For the initial 80% time period, it felt like nothing. But the remaining 20% felt like something had choked my trachea. I felt an irrestible urge to cough but maintained myself and let it through. They twisted it around to get a good sample. Then came the real pain in the nose, nasal swab. The doctor told me to turn my head somewhat to get easy access to my nasal opening. I knew this was it. The first 30% or so felt like it was cleaning my nose, nothing to look here. But hell broke lose for that 70% time. It felt like something had gone too far into the abyss, where it doesn't belong and it was causing a lot of sensation, all the neurons were firing at the same time. It felt so uneasy at that time. And they twisted the swab too, adding salt to the wound. Thankfully, it was over in about 10 secs so it wasn't a major hassle. Not gonna lie, on the day after my brother got positive, I was pretty cynical, that, combined with the general weakness and gut problems made me think negative for pretty much the whole day. I am more positive and optmistic at present fortunately. The test result is yet to come. Will update the answer. Edit: I am negative for COVID 😀
column9: I have chosen the nasal swab as to me it is quicker. However, I have felt as you have aptly described. My oldest is an Emergency Room Physician. The middle son is an attorney and on Christmas Day I was with him and his family. He called the next day to report a sore throat and fever. His test was positive, and therefor I isolated myself for almost 2 weeks. My test was negative at 5 days. His family is fine and he now is afebrile for 3 days today. He described the illness as “never felt so ill”! I pray you will remain well and your parents will regain their health. Lynn Barlow (pediatrician for 45 years)

column1: When did you learn your parents did not care about you at all?
column3: My parents refused to get me psychological help when I started experiencing depression and started hurting myself at 10 years old. I would punch myself and leave bruises on myself, and I would dig my fingernails into my skin until I bled. My teacher noticed and referred me to my school’s psychologist. I told her that my parents were alcoholics and all about the verbal abuse, neglect, and occasional physical abuse going on at home. Apparently she was a family friend, so she called my mom instead of reporting it. My mom told her I was overdramatic and that I had a habit of lying for attention. My parents were furious at me. They told me that if I told anyone else that they’d lose their jobs and go to jail, and my brother and I would have to live in a foster home and never see any of our biological family again. My maternal grandparents would’ve been happy to take us. Anyway, I kept quiet and continued to experience two or three depressive episodes a year. I became suicidal at 13 years old. Then my parents divorced and my mom got sober for a while. I was finally able to get therapy from a psychologist during that brief time. For the past 12 years she has been repeating a cycle (1) 4 months of sobriety (2) Relapses and starts drinking again (3) Binge drinks one night and calls a family member (mostly me) to verbally abuse them (4) Apologies and says she’s trying to get sober (5) The cycle repeats. I moved out of her house when I was 19 for the sake of my mental health, but I still fall into her trap sometimes. My dad continued his alcoholism after the divorce and spiraled into a drunken misery until he almost died of alcohol poisoning 8 years ago, went to rehab, and has been sober since. I choose stay away from alcohol, and I get myself psychological help when I need it since depression, anxiety, and PTSD from childhood trauma continue to affect me sometimes.

column1: Does the pro-life movement oversimplify adoption?
column3: The short answer: Yes.The longer answer: Adoption should not be classified as an easy solution to abortion because, for obvious reasons, adoption and abortion are no where near being the same thing. Women who choose to place their biological child for adoption do not do so for the same reasons women choose abortion. Yet, for some reason, adoption is labeled as something that fixes something else. When adoption is seen as a solution to abortion and not as a solution for a child who does not have a home or biological parents who are capable for caring for them, we start to see flawed thinking. Just like abortion, adoption is a complex decision. Other than that, the similarities between the two end. Why? Simple:The opposite of abortion is to give birthThe opposite of adoption is to raise the child you already gave birth toYes, many women who do not want/can not raise a child may consider both options - abortion or adoption - before they settle on one, but this doesn’t make adoption the solution. People continue to conflate that taking away access to one choice is fine because another choice is still there…that makes absolutely no sense, period, and I have numbers to back that up further. However, logically, the “adoption solves abortion” argument is inherently flawed thinking in its entirety. The thing about the anti-choice movement is this: forcing women to give birth is not “pro life”.I think it is very telling when you see the focus of priorities of anti-choice law makers. For instance, with abortion, there are laws that favor pressuring women who are pregnant to reconsider abortion:There are 27 states that make pregnant women have “Mandatory Waiting Periods” before they can have an abortion: [1]Many states require waiting periods between provider counseling and the abortion procedure. These mandatory waiting periods may require a woman to make two trips to the health care provider if the state requires the woman to receive counseling in person (as opposed to telephone, video call, or another avenue).“Informed Consent”: [2]A state may require a physician to provide a woman with such information such as alternatives to abortion, sources of financial aid, development of the child, and the gestational age of the child. Prior to 1992, informed consent provisions were unconstitutional.Another unethical thing with “informed consent” laws is that some states make doctors tell women that abortions will likely cause mental health issues: [3]In several states, including Kansas, Michigan, Nebraska, North Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah and West Virginia, "informed consent" laws require health care providers to tell women seeking an abortion that the procedure can lead to mental illness. These laws are based in part on a 2009 study by psychology researcher Priscilla Coleman, who found a higher incidence of depression and other psychological disorders among women who had abortions. Since that time, many scientists — including Weitz herself — have published papers showing how Coleman's research methods were flawed. She made the basic "correlation equals causation" error, said Weitz. "You may have higher rates of depression in the population of women who choose abortion, but that's part of why they choose abortion. You can't make a causality argument, but that's what these studies try to do."Why is this weird? Because there are no informed consent laws regarding adoption. Why should there be? Because women should not be bullied towards one choice, period, especially if they do not have reliable information on either. So far, I see vulnerable women being taken advantage of, either way:Birth mothers can sign their rights away (permanently) as a mother to their child shortly after they give birth in these states: [4]Alaska, Arkansas, California, Colorado, Delaware, Georgia, Indiana, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, North Carolina, North Dakota, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Wisconsin, WyomingWhy does this matter? Because a birth mother can still be under the affects of pain medication, hormone fluctuations, etc. when making this choice. Birth mothers are also not informed that their biological child placed for adoption will more likely struggle with identity issues, learning disabilities, low self esteem, depression, anxiety, addiction, abandonment issues, ADD, ADHD, suicidal ideation/attempts:Identity Issues: [5]Identity formation begins in childhood and takes on increased importance and prominence during adolescence (Grotevant, 1997). Adoption is a significant aspect of identity for adopted persons, even when they are adults (Evan B. Donaldson Adoption Institute, 2009). The task of identity development may be more difficult for an adopted person because of:the additional issues related to adoption, such as why he or she was placed for adoptionwhat became of the birth parentsdoes he or she have siblingswhether he or she resembles the birth parents in looks or in other characteristics.Learning Disabilities: [6]Low Self-Esteem: [7]Often accompanying these issues of identity are issues of self-esteem—that is, how the adopted person feels about him or herself. A number of studies have found that, while adopted persons are similar to nonadopted persons in most ways, they often score lower on measures of self-esteem and self confidence (Borders, Penny, & Portnoy, 2000; Sharma, McGue, & Benson, 1996). This result may reflect the fact that some adopted persons may view themselves as:differentout-of-placeunwelcomerejectedSome of these feelings may result from:the initial loss of birth parents and from growing up away from birth parents, siblings, and extended family members.They also may be caused by an ongoing feeling of being different from nonadopted people who know about their genetic background and birth family and who may be more secure about their own identity as a result.Additionally, some adopted persons report that secrecy surrounding their adoption contributes to low self-esteemDepression: [8]Cubito (1999) compared adoptees to normative data utilizing the Brief Symptom inventory as a measure of overall distress, the Zung Self-Rating Depression Scale, and the Anger Content Scale of the MMPI-2. Adoptees were compared to two normative scales; one for everyday people in our society, and one for a sample of outpatient mental health clinic patients. The overall finding was the adoptees scored about halfway between the outpatient and normative data on all of the test instruments. The same author found another sample of adoptees to score significantly higher (p<.01) on the same measures of overall distress and depression but not on the anger scale when compared with normative data for these tests (Cubito, 1996).Anxiety: [9]Another surprising conclusion that the Minnesota study produced was the fact that children adopted from within the U.S. are more prone to behavioral disorders than those adopted from overseas. Some 40,000 children worldwide annually emigrate from more than 100 countries through adoption, a trend increasing rapidly in the U.S. since the 1970s. But these foreign adoptees are far more likely to internalize their problems, suffering more commonly from depression or separation anxiety disorders. Domestic adoptees, on the other hand, tend to act out. While consistent with adolescents studied in both North America and Western Europe, Keyes says, this finding "goes against preconceived notions that kids from foreign cultures would have a harder time adapting to new families."Addiction: [10]Data collection included the Childhood Problems Scale, the Minnesota Substance Abuse Problem Scale, and the Minnesota Substance Abuse Treatment Questionnaire, and the Michigan Assessment-Screening Test/Alcohol-Drug. Findings showed that the prevalence of adoptees among SUD patients was 14 times higher than expected (95% Confidence Interval, 10 to 18 times). Adoptees reported childhood histories similar to those of non-adoptees with "any parental SUD", but they more closely resembled non-adoptees without parental SUD in regard to SUD severity and SUD treatment. Conclusion is that adoptees and their adoptive families should be alert to the increased risk of SUD among adoptees. Clinicians can expect that adoptees should manifest milder levels of SUD morbidity, similar to "non-heredity" SUD.Feelings of abandonment: [11]There can also be significant concerns about feeling abandoned and "abandonable," and "not good enough," coupled with specific hurt feelings over the birthmother's choice to "reject" the child" to "give me away" or "not wanting me enough." Such hurtful and vulnerable feelings may be compounded should the child learn that the birthmother later had other children that she chose to raise herself.ADD & ADHD: [12]First, most individuals adopted as infants are well-adjusted and psychologically healthy. Nevertheless, there exists a subset of adoptees who may be at increased risk for externalizing problems and disorders. The odds of being diagnosed as having ADHD and ODD were approximately twice as high in adoptees compared with nonadoptees. This excess of clinically meaningful behavioral problems in adopted adolescents has significance for researchers who examine the effect adoption has on individual functioning, for adoption agencies and their workers who counsel and advise members of the adoption triad, and for physicians who are dealing with an overrepresentation of adoptees in their clinical practices.Suicidal Ideations/attempts: [13]The study of more than 1,200 teens, all living in Minnesota, found that those who were adopted were almost four times more likely to attempt suicide. Out of all the participants, 47 out of 56 who attempted suicide were adopted, and girls faced a larger risk. Of the 47 adopted teens, 16 were boys and 31 were girls, and among those who weren’t adopted, four were boys and five were girls, Medscape reported. “Adolescence, in general, is a period of higher risk [for suicide attempt],” Dr. Victor Fornari, director of child and adolescent psychiatry at North Shore-LIJ Health System, told HealthDay News. “And now there’s evidence that the risk may be relatively higher for adopted adolescents.”American Academy of Pediatrics Study: [14]According to a 2001 survey conducted by the American Academy of Pediatrics, it was found that attempted suicide is more common among adolescents who live with adoptive parents than among adolescents who live with biological parents. This does not mean that most adopted kids will venture down this route; merely that there are commonalities with adopted children that separate them from birth children and might make them more prone to the causalities of suicide.I want to make it clear that I am not saying that adoption shouldn’t happen; I am saying that the birth mother is led to believe that her biological child will live happily ever after when it is more likely they will suffer - this is important because women are told that one option has x amount of risks but the other option is regarded as perfect. This shows a gross disregard about women making informed decisions, period. In fact, it shows that many law makers are willing to exploit and bully women based on a falsehoods. I’m adopted - in no way am I suggesting that people should not adopt - I love my parents and feel sick to my stomach when I even think about the possibility of them not adopting me. I am making the point that women are bullied into not aborting and that is not how it should be. Women should have access to reliable information for all of their options - it should be illegal to try and control what choice the woman ultimately picks.Birth mothers are also not told how they might feel after placing a child for adoption: [15]3/4 of birth mothers still experienced feelings of loss 12 to 20 years after placing their newborns.A study from the Donaldson Adoption Institute shows extensive data regarding the pain that birth mothers feel the rest of their lives regarding placing their child for adoption [16]In essence, women are pressured to carry a pregnancy to full term and then lose their biological child due to information that is purposefully deceitful and manipulative.The following will be based on information available in the United States. As an example of anti-choice people oversimplifying adoption, consider this quote from Mike Pence: [17]"There are so many families around the country who can't have children. We could improve adoption so that families that can't have children can adopt more readily those children from crisis pregnancies."The falsehoods in Pence’s quote:The terminology of “Crisis pregnancies” is faulty because “crisis” shouldn’t be assumed to mean that the issue is the lack of a parentPence alludes to a false reality; he asserts that there is a shortage of kids to adoptPence also objectifies women by talking about them as if their bodies should be seen as property for reproductive reasons - that is dehumanizing and misogynistic.Pence is wrong in alleging that not enough children are available for adoption. For instance, just considering the Foster Care system alone, here are the numbers: [18]Of the 400,000 children in foster care, more than 100,000 of them are waiting to be adopted.The former VP of public policy at the Guttmacher Institute, Cory L. Richards, said: [19]“Increasing the rate of completed adoptions, however valid on its own merits, is irrelevant to the abortion rate. And increasing the rate of newborn relinquishments, even assuming it could be done in an ethically and socially acceptable way, at best would be tinkering at the margins. Even if relinquishments doubled, and each one of them represented an averted abortion, it would make hardly a dent in the abortion rate.”And even if there were a shortage of children to be adopted, this is still unethical and misogynistic thinking; this logic ultimately produces a narrative that women are like cattle to be breed to produce offspring for others. That is a disturbing and corrupt way to view women and their bodies period.The people that do adopt are not adopting in rates that would put a dent in the abortions that currently occur. There would still be hundreds of thousands of children that aren't placed into families: [20]Adoptions in the U.S. in 2015:Comparatively, 699,202 abortions were done in the United States in 2012. [21]Based on the above numbers and the other statistics I included, I think it is clear that anti-choice argument regarding adoption is disingenuous and irrational.Footnotes[1] https://www.kff.org/womens-health-policy/state-indicator/mandatory-waiting-periods/?currentTimeframe=0&sortModel=%7B%22colId%22:%22Location%22,%22sort%22:%22asc%22%7D[2] Abortion laws - Information on the law about Abortion - State Of The Statutes[3] Why don't we know more about the long-term effects of abortion?[4] Consent to Adoption: What Biological Parents Need to Know - FindLaw[5] https://www.childwelfare.gov/pubpdfs/f_adimpact.pdf[6] The Paradox of Adoption[7] https://www.childwelfare.gov/pubpdfs/f_adimpact.pdf[8] Internet Scientific Publications[9] Breaking News, Analysis, Politics, Blogs, News Photos, Video, Tech Reviews - TIME.com[10] Substance use disorder among adoptees: a clinical comparative study.[11] Long-Term Issues for the Adopted Child[12] The Mental Health of US Adolescents Adopted in Infancy[13] Adopted Teens 4 Times More Likely To Attempt Suicide: A Stark Reminder That Clinicians Should Take Parental Concerns Seriously[14] Attachment and Trauma Specialists[15] Impact of Adoption on Birth Parents: Responding to the Adoptive Placement[16] https://www.adoptioninstitute.org/wp-content/uploads/2013/12/2006_11_Birthparent_Study_All.pdf[17] The Mike Pence vs. Tim Kaine vice-presidential debate transcript, annotated[18] About the children[19] The Guttmacher Institute Mourns the Loss of Cory L. column9: It's curious to me that you're essentially saying that just because some people who are adopted have hard lives means we should have had the option to abort. It certainly won't convince any prolifers, since they'll say that any life is better than being killed. Also, I fail to see how abortion would frequently be less traumatizing for a mother than adoption. Abortion is no less of a permanent decision plagued with eternal “what ifs”, and in the case of the mother seeing it as killing her own child, certainly would be more traumatic for her than any wondering of how her child ended up in adoption could ever be. With adoption, there is some chance of reuniting with the child, so in some sense it can actually be less permanent of a decision(yes she missed out on the years up till a reunion, but at least there would be time after reunion). Finally, I don't believe prolifers trivialize adoption like you seem to think they do. They just see any imperfections of adoption as preferable to what they see as murder in abortion. And indeed, I am sure that some have personal experience with adoption, either adopting the kids themselves or being the ones that gave a kid up for adoption. Remember, these are millions of people you're talking about, just as varied and diverse as any other group you care to mention (like your own side of the issue!). So thinking they all think exactly the same is unlikely to be true. P.S - It'd be easier to convince prolifers if you don't call them antichoice. Saying antichoice for prolifers is just as bad as saying antilife for prochoicers. It'll make prolifers uninclined to believe you respect their views enough to have a real dialogue that might change their mind, and it can easily make you look blatantly partisan to any undecided people.

column1: How can I cope with my loved one's addiction?
column3: “… the family's unity, mental health, physical health, finances, and overall family dynamics,” says the National Council on Alcoholism and Drug Dependence. And with more than 22 million Americans in need of treatment for alcoholism or a substance abuse problem in 2013*, a lot of families are at that breaking point. There are a lot of moms, dads, siblings, and spouses out there trying to deal with their loved one’s addiction, asking themselves, “What did I do wrong?” The short and long answer is … nothing. The 3 C’s of Recovery can help families remember that. What are the Three C’s? I Didn’t Cause It. I Can’t Control It. I Can’t Cure It. Cause Addiction is a disease. It may be difficult to think of addiction as a disease, but it is. For many people, however, addiction is viewed as a moral failing or a lack of willpower. Or they feel that the addicted person was “raised wrong” or spoiled. The National Institute on Drug Abuse defines addiction as “a chronic, relapsing brain disease that is characterized by compulsive drug seeking and use, despite harmful consequences.” And much like diabetes or cancer, it can’t be caused by any one person’s presence, behaviors, or words. Drugs increase dopamine in the brain, mimicking a biological response to a natural reward. In other words, the drugs make the addicted person feel euphoric, and the brain teaches that person to keep seeking that feeling. When some drugs are taken, they can release 2 to 10 times the amount of dopamine that natural rewards such as eating release, reports NIDA. How then can normal rewards compare with the highs associated with drugs? They can’t, and the user becomes depressed over time, unable to enjoy what they once did. So, they seek more and more drugs to get the feeling of euphoria they felt early in their addiction. Alcoholism also causes physical dependence, with the craving that the alcoholic feels for alcohol being the same as the need for water or food, according to the National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism. The biological evidence supporting addiction as a chronic disease should reinforce for families that they are not the reason behind their loved one’s addiction. There is nothing a mother, father, sibling, spouse, friend, or caregiver can say, do, or think that can cause his or her loved one to become addicted to drugs or alcohol. Control Addiction as a disease also means families can’t control their loved one’s addiction. Physical dependence is in charge. If an addicted person suddenly stops drinking or using drugs, withdrawal symptoms like nausea, tremors, hallucinations and convulsions will kick in. Focusing on and trying to manage an addicted person’s behavior will not control the disease. Laying blame won’t work, and neither will family members adapting their own behavior to accommodate their loved one’s addiction. In fact, adapting – also known as enabling – is a strategy many families use to try and control their loved one’s addiction. Sometimes, this manifests as family members protecting their loved one from the negative consequences of his or her behavior by making excuses or by cleaning up any messy situations caused by the addicted person. In some instances, family members give the addicted person money or purchase alcohol for the addicted person to consume in a safe place. These attempts to directly or indirectly control the addicted person’s behavior don’t change it and can have the opposite effect. Some families lose their sense of what a “normal” life is. They adapt their behavior to hide the truth of their loved one’s addiction from themselves – and because of shame, from others. And by hiding from everyone in their lives, they lose much needed support. Other families stop expressing genuine feelings in an effort to contain the problem. Eventually, the emotions break free from suppression, resulting in an inevitable outburst. The emotional disconnect also causes families to miss out on making real connections with each other and being present in each other’s lives. Meanwhile, none of these actions change the reality of a loved one’s addiction. No one can control someone else’s addiction or how that addiction affects the addicted person. Cure And no matter how much families love their addicted family members, their love can’t cure addiction. There is no cure. Recovery is a lifelong process, and as the American Society of Addiction Medicine explains, “… because relapse is possible even after many years of remission, we cannot use the term ‘cure.’ ” Like other chronic diseases, addiction is managed through aftercare programming, relapse prevention, and a strong, ongoing support system. When a person in recovery relapses, this is a re-emergence of symptoms requiring treatment. “Addiction treatment should be held to the same standards of success used to judge treatment of other chronic diseases, such as diabetes, hypertension, and asthma where relapse and noncompliance with therapy and medication are common,” noted Thomas McLellan, former adviser to the Office of National Drug Control Policy and the World Health Organization. Families that change their perspective on addiction – seeing it as a chronic disease rather than an acute illness that can be cured – are less likely to be disappointed if their loved one relapses. Family members can always offer support, but they should only do so in a way that equally values their own self-care needs. Struggling with a drug or alcohol addiction is one of the hardest things anyone can do, and each person’s journey of recovery is their own. The same holds true for families. If you need help dealing with addiction in the family, Al-Anon Family Groups and Nar-Anon Family Groupshave some great resources. *Source: Samhsa.gov

column1: What are some possible causes of mental illnesses such as depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia, which may carry a stigma in society?
column3: Thank you for the question. I’m JIM and I’m 70 years old and I’m a retired Structural Engineer and General Contractor. I was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in 1972. I have had four major manic episodes since 1996 and all four were a result of me making the decision to discontinue my medication. Don’t be like me. Stay on your medication. Please. More than Half of people with mental illness don't receive help for their disorders. Often, people avoid or delay seeking treatment due to concerns about being treated differently or fears of losing their jobs and livelihood. That's because stigma, prejudice and discrimination against people with mental illness are still very much a problem. Stigma, prejudice and discrimination against people with mental illness can be subtle or obvious—but no matter the magnitude, they can lead to harm. People with mental illness are marginalized and discriminated against in various ways, but understanding what that looks like and how to address and eradicate it can help. Stigma often comes from lack of understanding or fear. Inaccurate or misleading media representations of mental illness contribute to both those factors. A review of Studies on stigma shows that while the public may accept the medical or genetic nature of a mental health disorder and the need for treatment, many people still have a negative view of those with mental illness. Researchers identify different types of stigma:Public stigma involves the negative or discriminatory attitudes that others may have about mental illness.Self-stigma refers to the negative attitudes, including internalized shame, that people with mental illness may have about their own condition.Structural stigma is more systemic, involving policies of government and private organizations that intentionally or unintentionally limit opportunities for people with mental illness. Examples include lower funding for mental illness research or fewer mental health services relative to other health care.Stigma not only directly affects individuals with mental illness but also the loved ones who support them, often including their family members. Stigma around mental illness especially an issue in some diverse racial and ethnic communities and it can be a major barrier to people from those cultures accessing mental health services. For example, in some Asian cultures, seeking professional help for mental illness may be counter to cultural values of strong family, emotional restraint and avoiding shame. Among some groups, including the African American community's, distrust of the mental healthcare system can also be a barrier to seeking help. Media representations of people with mental illness can influence perceptions and stigma, and they have often been negative, inaccurate or violent representations. A study published in 2020 looked at a recent example, the popular film Joker (2019), which portrays the lead character as a person with mental illness who becomes extremely violent. The study found that viewing the film was associated with higher levels of prejudice toward those with mental illness. Joker may exacerbate self-stigma for those with a mental illness, leading to delays in help seeking. The stigma of mental illness is universal. A 2016 report on stigma concluded "there is no country, society or culture where people with mental illness have the same societal value as people without mental illness." Stigma and discrimination can contribute to worsening symptoms and reduced likelihood of getting treatment. A recent extensive review of research found that self-stigma leads to negative effects on recovery among people diagnosed with severe mental illnesses. Effects can include:reduced hopelower self-esteemincreased psychiatric symptomsdifficulties with social relationshipsreduced likelihood of staying with treatmentmore difficulties at workA 2017 study by Pew Research Center involving more than 200 individuals with mental illness over a period of two years found that greater self-stigma was associated with poorer recovery from mental illness after one and two years. An editorial in the Lancet notes that the impacts of stigma are pervasive, affecting political enthusiasm, charitable fundraising and availability, support for local services and underfunding of research for mental health relative to other health conditions. Some of the other harmful effects of stigma can include:Reluctance to seek help or treatment and reduced likelihood of staying with treatment.Social isolation.Lack of understanding by family, friends, coworkers, or others.Fewer opportunities for work, school or social activities or trouble finding housing.Bullying, physical violence or harassment.Health insurance that doesn't adequately cover your mental illness treatment.The belief that you'll never succeed at certain challenges or that you can't improve your situation.Jim Whittington

column1: Is living with people who have undiagnosed and untreated mental health problems difficult?
column3: The problem with your question is your choice of the words “undiagnosed”, and “untreated”, which implies that there is a reliable, and scientific system, or process for approaching and helping the troubled, confused, and conflicted among us, which some believe are merely reactions to adversity. Some sociologists, and social workers say they are “Normal reactions to insane circumstances”. For 10–24 year olds, the second leading cause of death is suicide. So, something is probably not going the way it should for them. When internal conflicts cannot be resolved, this very tragic action may result. But “Family” members, are sometimes the cause of these conflicts, especially when it comes to historic child abuse, and walking away, for good, may be the only solution, to keep sane. This is the “Nurture” side, or lack thereof, of the “Nature/ Nurture” debate, or environmental upbringing. Denial is the another point of view about this. The affected person will not admit there is something not quite right within. And this is the hardest part, because it brings up the issue of forcing treatment, and the possibility of losing that relationship, after trust has been broken, when “Us”, and “Them” replaces any kind of fond affection, or even love that may have existed before the ambulance is called. Psychiatric treatment is by no means a pleasant experience. Side effects to medication is the #1 reason for going off pills. And then a negative, possibly more and more permanent attitude towards psychiatry may start. And the end of that dark path is not pleasant at all. If police are called, there is a very good chance the individual will be shot. This is the very delicate business of trying to “Help” another with problems, who has not agreed to co-operate with authorities, and officials, who have the legal power to force treatment upon them, even if they are kicking and screaming. Good luck.

column1: How can someone deal with a toxic person who constantly brings up past mistakes and holds them against you?
column3: Dealing with someone who constantly brings up past mistakes and holds them against you is both a punishment as well as a mechanism of control due to the guilt and shame it causes. As a result, navigating a relationship dynamic with such a person will be extremely challenging and emotionally draining due to the added devaluation such behaviour causes.First and foremost, it is extremely important to clearly communicate your boundaries to this person by asserting the constant bringing up of past mistakes is not acceptable. Seek to discuss how you expect to be treated and always remember it is important to be assertive but calm when communicating your boundaries. In maintaining your boundaries, seek to avoid engaging in arguments or defensive behaviour when past mistakes are brought up. The past is just that the past. By continually apologising for past mistakes, this creates fuel for the toxic behaviour and arguments to continue. Additionally, by continually apologising, you are essentially unable to move forward while also inadvertently allowing the toxic person to keep you anchored to the past. While it is very normal and even healthy to acknowledge the mention of the past in a neutral tone, always try to steer the conversation away or disengage completely if the behaviour continues. ➡️THE PAST IS A PLACE TO LEARN FROM NOT A PLACE TO EXIST WITHIN⬅️ Sometimes, even in toxic behaviour, there may be a kernel of truth therefore, take this opportunity to reflect on any feedback to determine if there is indeed anything constructive you can away take from it. However, always remember to separate useful feedback from harmful criticism. Remind the person (and yourself) that your focus is on the present and moving towards the future instead of being anchored to the past. Emphasise the changes you've made and your plans for improvement. Surround yourself with supportive friends or family members who understand your situation and can provide you with the emotional support you need. Sometimes, just talking about the issue can help you gain perspective and strength and if possible, limit your interaction with the toxic person. If you must interact with them such as within the contexts of a coworker or family member etc, try to keep your interactions brief and focused on the task or topic at hand. Additionally, applying the ‘grey rock’ method will help in keeping things neutral and less emotionally reactive.’If the situation escalates or does not improve and you find it affecting your mental health, always seek third part support such as a psychologist and/or counsellor as this can be an excellent source by which to gain additional strategies to effectively address the situation with the toxic person. Doing this will not only provide you with strategies but also significantly contribute to helping you build resilience. Building on this, always seek to engage in activities that boost your self-esteem and help you maintain your emotional balance. This essentially means that you invest in ‘you time’ such aa exercise, hobbies, meditation, or anything that makes you feel good about yourself. ➡️LEARN FROM THE PAST, BE MINDFUL OF THE PRESENT, LOOK TO THE FUTURE⬅️ Always remember this one fundamental and inalienable truth, the past is in the past. The past exists as a reference point from which we grow and develop. Anyone who uses the past against you is essentially a toxic person who focuses on the past rather than the potential of future possibilities. A person who focuses on the past is unable to place their focus on the future and will likely lose the significance of the present. While you are not able to control another person's behaviour, you can control how you choose to respond to it. In understanding this, you are better able to protect your mental health and prioritise your overall well-being.
