column1: What can I do to protect my son who is transgender from my mom? My son came out 1 year ago (FTM) and as a result everyone in our family was accepting, except my narcissistic, uber-religious mother.
column3: My son is a trans man, and I am a trans woman. It runs in the family in our case, with autism likely to be part of the reason why, given we both have an autism diagnosis.Naomi Lauren's answer to Can people on the autism spectrum be transgender?Being both transgender myself, and the parent of a transgender child, I’ve heard so many sad stories of family rejection, but there’s also happy stories, too.Names and pronouns are the primary accommodations required for gender dysphoria, and are the primary symbols of acceptance or rejection. Gender transition can be a difficult and fragile time, so when someone was likely to disrespect my son’s name and pronouns, I was ready to defend him. He commenced social transition-to-male at 18 years old, so he handled many things himself, but he always knew I had his back. We’ve lost some family along the way. More subtle types of rejection are rudeness, guilt trips, and passive-aggressive behaviour. Overall our experience was good, but the people who had trouble respecting his name and pronouns, were the same ones being rude or passive-aggressive in other ways. Most tellingly, they weren’t rude or passive-aggressive before his transition. Your son probably expects to lose some relationships along the way. Rudeness or rejection from a grandparent at this time can be a big deal. The closer the relationship between grandparent and grandchild, the more intense the risk. Close relationship amplifies the power of acceptance or rejection. In a similar way, your own supportive parent-child relationship is a highly protective influence, because the closeness of your relationship amplifies the effects of your support. Interestingly, age seems to be no predictor of acceptance or rejection, with plenty of grandparents adjusting more easily than other family members. In my experience, conservative religious beliefs are the biggest predictive factor for rudeness and rejection, with about 70% accuracy. Do comment below if you’d like help with Bible verses about respecting transgender people.What to do? I can’t give you direct advice to your situation, but these rules of thumb tend to work:During the early stages of transition, people often respond better if they are told ahead of time. Hearing before seeing. Having time to adjust to the new gender presentation, and the new name and pronouns, can help people to respond well.Some people respond best to a medical framing of gender dysphoria, as a developmental disorder like autism or dyslexia that needs accommodations. Some others respond best to a psychological framing, with acceptance and kindness being important for mental health. Some very few respond better to an individualist framing, supporting the child in their own unique journey of self-discovery. I’ve more information on these if you think that might help you.One month elapsed time, or 2–3 visits, is highly predictive of future acceptance or rejection.Rejection destroys trust, and relationship cannot function without trust. If your mom is expressing rejection, whether by misgendering or by passive-aggressive behaviour, she’s destroying the relationship with her own grandchild. Relationships with her other grandchildren are also likely to be negatively affected.It’s usually best to be guided by your child, collaborating to figure out the best approach and timing. In particular, be careful to check with your child what they are happy for you to disclose to your mom.You’ll probably need to hide your own fears, in this and other areas, but it’s really good that you are planning carefully. This is a journey for you, too, and you’ll almost certainly need support from other parents of transgender kids. Here’s one such resource you might find helpful.►http://www.howtobeagirlpodcast.com/episodes-1
column9: This answer brought me to tears. Thank you so much for this support. Yes, I would love to read some bible versus that may help me communicate clearly with my mother about people who are transgender. Thank you again. I will work on building friendships with other parents of transgender children.

column1: What must be the reason that anyone keeps isolating himself from people?
column3: Isolation can increase the risks of mental health issues such as depression, dementia, social anxiety, and low self-esteem. ... For example, a person might develop depression because of intense loneliness, then feel even more isolated because of their depression. Social isolation can lead to feelings of loneliness, fear of others, or negative self-esteem. Lack of consistent human contact can also cause conflict with the (peripheral) friends the socially isolated person may occasionally talk to or cause problems with family members. The Difference Between Isolation and Loneliness First, let's start by defining key concepts. Isolation is defined as a state or situation characterized by being physically separated from other people—whether intentional or not. Loneliness, on the other hand, is defined by an internal feeling—it's about quality, not quantity. In this way, one can socially isolate or separate themselves from other people, but not necessarily feel alone or lonely. In a similar way, one can be surrounded by many people and feel as if they were the only person in the room. Social isolation can be desired or sought out by an individual, but loneliness is normally not a choice. Having said that, how do they relate? The Relationship Between Social Isolation and Loneliness A recent study published in the journal Health Psychology found that both concepts—though normally studied through the lens of how they differ from one another—have an interdependent relationship. What does this mean? That instead of seeing them as isolated concepts, it's better to analyze and study them together, with the goal of understanding our physical and mental health. The researchers found that a higher level of social isolation usually produces higher levels of loneliness; high levels of loneliness make people prone to socially isolate themselves, as well. When the two manifest together, a higher risk of mortality is associated. These results can give us valuable information about the frequency with which we decide to socially isolate ourselves from others and its effect on our mental health—especially with the copious evidence associating loneliness to several mental health conditions—and our physical health. So, what to do about this? With the increasing popularity of online personality tests and the curiosity of finding out what's our Myers-Briggs personality type, society has gained a new understanding of individual differences and the various ways in which people operate. While there are some who feel energized when socializing with others, there are others who feel recharged when they spend time by themselves. There's no "right way" or "wrong way," but this post is intended for the latter: those with a tendency to isolate themselves and choose to be physically alone. Believe me, as a fellow plan-canceling aficionada whose ideal Friday night involves staying at home and watching a movie or reading a good book, I completely get it. There's no feeling quite like staying in. But, with what frequency are you isolating yourself? How can you know when this is becoming potentially troubling or dangerous? How can this repeated behavior affect your health? How is this related to the feeling of loneliness? frequency with which we decide to socially isolate ourselves from others and its effect on our mental health—especially with the copious evidence associating loneliness to several mental health conditions—and our physical health. So, what to do about this? Honoring Alone Time While Protecting Health The positive aspect of these studies is that they offer us a space to act preventively. They give us enough information to develop an action plan. In that vein, here are some tips to make the most of your time alone, without over-doing it:Give yourself a timeframe. How many outings a month are you comfortable with? For some people, it's 1-2 a month, while for others it can be more. Whatever the time you give yourself, try to keep at it and be patient with yourself. Remind yourself that while nothing is set in stone, it's still important to know yourself and know if you're predisposed to falling in the isolation trap.Talk to a close friend. My closest friends know exactly when to push me a bit further to socialize with others and when to respect my personal space. This isn't something that was formed overnight; it's a product of years of close dialogue and honest conversations about what I am and am not comfortable with. Talk to a friend who you can trust about all of this so they can help you avoid an isolation trap.Do something for your community or for others. Volunteering and engaging in selfless activities has been shown to have positive effects on mental health. Whether it's belonging to a group, foundation or a community, think about doing something positive for others as a way to do something positive for yourself.Enroll in a book or cultural appreciation club. The positive thing about these groups is that the frequency with which they meet is a complete sweet spot: not enough that it might be overwhelming for you, but just enough to keep you interested. If you already enjoy reading, for instance, why not kill two birds with one stone?Effects Of Isolation : An Explanation. There are countless negative effects that social isolation and extreme isolation can have on our minds and bodies that a range of side effects, including changes to his sleep cycle, and hallucinations. But why is isolation so difficult for humans to withstand? One of the reasons that living in isolation is difficult is because humans are social creatures. such as researchers stationed in Antarctica – report that loneliness can be the most difficult part of the job. Yossi Ghinsberg, an Israeli adventurer and author who survived weeks alone in the Amazon, said that loneliness was what he suffered from most and that he had created imaginary friends to keep himself company.Many people that have lived in isolated environments. some people said isolation is a bliss to connect with nature and its originality but sometimes loneliness can be damaging to both our mental and physical health. Socially isolated people are less able to deal with stressful situations. They’re also more likely to feel depressed and may have problems processing information. This in turn can lead to difficulties with decision-making and memory storage and recall. People who are lonely are also more susceptible to illness. Researchers found that a lonely person’s immune system responds differently to fighting viruses, making them more likely to develop an illness. The effects of isolation can become even more pronounced if you experience it in total darkness, causing both physical and psychological consequences. One impact of being in complete darkness is that it can wreck your sleep cycle. Two of the key mechanisms for sleep cycle regulation, the hormone melatonin and the brain’s suprachiasmatic nucleus, both rely on light to function. Daylight reduces our levels of melatonin, helping us feel awake. Daylight also helps the suprachiastmatic nucleus to reset our waking time if our sleep cycles start to drift. Without daylight, our 24-hour circadian rhythm can change. This explains why people exploring cave systems, for example, may find that their sleep-wake cycle becomes disrupted. This means that the time they feel like going to sleep doesn’t stay in a regular pattern and can shift each day. People placed in isolation may also experience hallucinations. The lack of stimuli causes people to misattribute internal thoughts and feelings as occurring in the outer environment. Essentially, hallucinations happen because of a lack of brain stimulation. While the impact of total isolation can be severe, the good news is that these effects are reversible. Exposure to daylight can normally correct sleep-wake patterns – though this might take weeks, or even months Reconnecting with other humans can reduce loneliness and help restore us to good mental and physical health. However, some people who have been held in social isolation against their will may develop long-term mental health conditions, such as post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). But some people who have faced the challenge of being alone for an extended period of time may show personal growth – including emotional growth, feeling closer to family and friends, and having a better perspective on life – as a result of their experience. How to Stop Isolating Yourself From Other People Isolation is a vicious cycle: we isolate ourselves because we don’t want to be hurt by others who might find us unlovable, but we are hurt even more when we find ourselves alone. Shutting people out isn’t only a mental decision; our actions, body language, and tone of voice reflect our attitude to others. We are left alone, to our constant relief and sorrow: we aren’t being hurt, but we aren’t being loved or accepted either. We soon learn that being alone is worse than interacting with others, even when there is a risk of being hurt or abandoned. As social animals, we can’t live our lives in shadow, hiding from interaction. Loneliness is unsustainable and destructive. I learned this after about a month of isolating myself. 1. Identify the root cause of your isolation and determine why you view yourself as unworthy/incapable of interaction. What is it about being social that scares you? Did you lose a friend or get in a traumatic argument that made you believe you will only be hurt or abandoned if you get close to people? Consider the thoughts that run through your head as you interact with someone. Do you tell yourself that you are unlovable? Do you feel that you will bore, upset, or annoy the other person? Do you convince yourself that you will be hurt or abandoned because you always are or now deserve it? 2. Try to reconnect with an old friend or someone you haven’t spoken to since before you began to shut others out. Once you identify the cause of your isolation and address it, you can reconnect with people again. 3. Talk to a trusted person about your isolation. This step was extremely difficult for me, because I thought of my depression as shameful and a place of weakness. I thought that being honest about my problem was the surest way for me to be abandoned. Find someone you trust and feel close to and let them know how you’re feeling.Once again, learning to reconnect with people after depression and antisocial behavior isn’t easy. It takes time, tears, and a lot of self-reflection. The process may seem tedious, but there is no short cut to healing for any illness, especially mental ones.

column1: How does a person with borderline personality disorder (emotionally unstable personality disorder) behave?
column3: That is a very good question. BPD behaviors are based on a very complex interaction or intense emotions, fear of abandonment, black and white thinking, emotional amnesia, projection, and even disassociation and hallucinations under stress. There is no simple way to describe it. I had created a summary that describes how BPD affects behaviors. I hope it helps: Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) is a hereditary, genetic condition that significantly affects emotions, sense of self, memory and interpersonal relationships. Studies reveal extensive differences in brain structure and function. BPD is often triggered from the interplay of genetics with trauma during childhood. It is suspected that during early childhood, increased levels of cortisol caused by stress (trauma) permanently change the brain structure and function of those genetically predisposed to it (such as increased gray matter in the amygdala area, among other things), causing BPD. While there is no cure, BPD is very treatable with Dialectical Behavior Therapy that was specifically designed for people with BPD (by a person with BPD) and can give someone the tools to recognize and manage the symptoms. BPD is a disorder of Dysregulation made up by Emotion Dysregulation (the core of BPD), as well as, Interpersonal, Identity, Behavioral, and Cognitive Dysregulation. More specifically, BPD causes intense emotions that are difficult to control and manage (i.e. “Emotion Dysregulation”) including unreasonable Fear of Abandonment which is central to BPD. BPD is primarily noticed through interpersonal relationships (“Interpersonal Dysregulation”): Persons with BPD (PBPD) feel all emotions intensely, therefore, when they like someone (either in friendship or romantically) PBPDs will love that person intensely. If the other person reciprocates then they will both be enmeshed in a very intense and personal relationship. PBPDs see the world through Black and White Thinking. Themselves and others are viewed as either “good” or “bad”. There are very few gray areas, if any. For example, it is difficult for a PBPD to be angry at a loved one and recognize that - while the PBPD is angry at them - the PBPD still loves them. Conversely, if a loved one is angry at the PBPD then the PBPD will view either themselves or the loved one as “Bad”, because for them, someone who is “good” would never criticize or make them feel sad. Thinking is generally Black and White or Good vs Bad. When a PBPD loves you, they will make you the center of their lives. This phase is called “Idealization” and the loved one is viewed as “all good”. PBPDs also feel intense fear of abandonment - and in order to avoid the possibility that a genuine loved one will abandon them - they will unconsciously suddenly start to hate (“devalue”) their loved ones in a process called Splitting (which will also completely change their memories of such a person). Splitting occurs primarily against those people PBPDs feel like “they cannot live without”. At the suspicion of real or imagined abandonment, suddenly (overnight), the loved one will be viewed as “all bad” and all their behaviors become suspect with malevolent ulterior motives. The entire relationship is completely forgotten and replaced with an alternate reality where the former loved one was always “all bad” and the two were never enmeshed in an intense, loving and personal relationship. This phase is called “Devaluation”. PBPDs also Devalue people they feel threatened by or who make them feel insecure. It is important to note that BPD causes fragmentation of memory including, lack of object constancy, lack of whole object relations, “emotional amnesia” as well as outright False Memories (things that never quite happened, but feel as true to PBPDs as anything else). This peculiar problem with memory means that PBPDs only remember others based on their last encounter and continuously color the entire relationship based on each last encounter (i.e. they are unable to link the past with the present. Because of the lack of object constancy, they can only live in the present). Because PBPDs memories are fragmented, it becomes exceedingly difficult to trust others. PBPDs experience difficulty intergrading what they know about someone into a cohesive image. It is not uncommon for PBPDs to believe that loved ones, who have proven themselves to be trustworthy, will betray them at any moment. For reasons that are not yet fully understood, the PBPD mind cannot integrate a consistent perception of others based on past experience. The past cannot be integrated with the present. For a PBPD, given the opportunity, anyone may do anything, no matter how absurd under the circumstances or how out of character it would be. As such, PBPDs are unable to exhibit normal levels of trust. PBPD memories are based on their present feelings and not the actual past (i.e. for PBPDs, their emotions and feelings dictate their reality, instead of facts.). A distorted view and understanding of reality is one of the major issues of BPD. Without treatment, PBPDs are generally unaware that their memories and perception of reality are distorted. If a PBPD Devalues you, then you will be remembered as always having been an unworthy person who they don’t particularly like (even though up until yesterday you were the center on their lives and could do no wrong). Any attempt to remind an untreated PBPD of the past will cause them confusion and cognitive dissonance. Untreated PBPDs will ultimately rationalize their behavior even against overwhelming facts. For PBPDs, how they presently feel about something, makes it the absolute and only truth. In short, when a PBPD loves someone intensely, the fear of abandonment will be so overwhelming and all-consuming that the mind, in order to protect itself from those overwhelming emotions, will suddenly “flip a switch” and cause to PBPD to suddenly feel nothing for loved one, hate them and lose all their memories of ever loving them. Sadly, unless treated, the effects of BPD on a PBPD can only be called tragic. Once Devalued, the loved one will notice a very drastic, sudden change in the PBPD’s behavior towards them– the person who was extremely loving yesterday and the two of you were inseparable, now treats you like a persona non grata for no apparent reason while denying anything is different. The Devaluation phase completely erases the loving and close relationship. The PBPD will be unable to remember that they once had strong feelings for you. For those close to a PBPD (such as close friends, life partners, family members etc.) it may feel as the PBPD has two personas, a Dr. Jekyll and a Mr. Hyde, where neither the Dr. Jekyll nor the Mr. Hyde persona is aware that the other exists. When the Mr. Hyde persona (i.e. the persona with BPD) comes out, the PBPD loses all recollection that the loved one is actually a genuine love one. Again, the loved one is instead viewed as having always been an unworthy and manipulative person who the PBPD never really cared for. At the exact moment of Devaluation, PBPDs may start planning and implementing their exit strategy from the relationship (since they now hate/dislike the other person). This can take form of an unconscious Distortion Campaign that creates a false and negative narrative regarding the former loved one, justifying any actions the PBPD takes. Typically, the Distortion Campaign involves a lot of rationalization as well as the elaborate manipulation and gaslighting of the former loved one that PBPDs are known for. Rationalization, manipulation, distortions and gaslighting are not done consciously or with malice, but are simply the result of whatever the PBPD feels is true at the time. As mentioned previously, PBPD perception of reality is based on present feelings (and during Devaluation, they will believe, beyond any doubt, that the former loved one is a person with little to no worth). The Distortion Campaign happens as part of the famous “I hate you, don’t leave me” phase. In this phase the PBPD will be emotionally distant and very mean to the former loved one (“I hate you”), but at the same time, due to the Fear of Abandonment, they will also take steps to convince the former loved one not to disappear from their life (“don’t leave me”). Needless to say this is a very toxic phase. Alternatively, a PBPD may suddenly disappear from the former loved one’s life completely (they now want nothing to do with the devalued loved one) while the Fear of Abandonment may cause them reappear later. It’s possible for the PBPD to slowly love the devalued person again (after all, the person they liked initially is still the same person, despite the distorted view that BPD caused), starting the cycle of idealization and devaluation all over again. Until the PBPD receives treatment, devaluation of loved ones is inevitable and at some point, this cycle will break into permanent devaluation. To those familiar with Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD), all this is almost identical to the famous NPD cycle (popularly known as the “Idealization, Devaluation, Discard, Hoover” cycle), but it is rooted in completely different reasons (those reasons are explained above). Another important aspect to remember which is common with many PBPDs is that the Black and White Thinking causes PBPDs to Project their own flaws or bad behaviors on others. Here is a common example of a BPD unconscious thinking pattern: Something “bad” happened and it makes me feel uncomfortable, and since the world is Black and White it must mean that a “bad” person caused it, which means either that the other person is “bad” or I am actually the “bad” person. This type of thinking is the reason why many PBPDs find it difficult to admit fault even against overwhelming evidence. For a PBPD, admitting fault in anything would, in the PBDP’s mind, mean that the he/she is “bad”. Therefore, the “bad” actions or behaviors are often Projected on others. PBPDs will often unconsciously generate a false narrative that absolves them of all responsibility for their actions and they will believe in that narrative as truth. Furthermore, the PBPD will try to convince others of such alternate version of reality (even though that narrative might not make much sense). There is also a distinction in behavior between Traditional and Quiet BPD. A person with “Traditional BPD” will express intense bouts of anger and rage towards the former loved one, while a person with “Quiet BPD” will simply become cold and distant. (Note: Quiet PBPDs experience the same hard-to-control intense anger as Traditional PBPDs, but instead of expressing those feelings outwards, they are internalized). It is important to note that PBPD s Idealize and Devalue themselves as well as others. They may confident and proud in themselves one moment, but the next moment see themselves as terrible persons who do not deserve love, friendships or success in life. BPD can cause a host of other symptoms, such as: Getting angry or upset very easily and finding it difficult to calm down (“Emotion Dysregulation”); unstable sense of self (due to the intense emotionality, PBPDs have a hard time knowing who they are or what they like and dislike) as well as strong feelings of emptiness ( “Identity Dysregulation”); impulsivity, drug use, promiscuity, binge-eating or shopping due to the intense emotions and feelings of emptiness; self-destructive behaviors such as sabotaging close relationships or even self-harm (the self destructive behaviors are called “Behavioral Dysregulation”); difficulty to admit fault (“projection” of fault to others); disassociation from reality under stress (and/or hallucinations) as well as incorrect perception of reality (“delusions”) (called “Cognitive Dysregulation”) ; and ultimately an extremely high rate of suicide (up to 70% of PBPDs will attempt suicide and 1 in 10 will commit suicide). BPD can range from Mild (people with Mild BPD are considered “high-functioning”) to Severe (people with Severe BPD have trouble functioning, i.e. holding doing a job, taking care of themselves etc.). Not all PBPDs exhibit the same symptoms and in fact, there is great variation of how BPD manifests in different people. For example not everyone with BPD will experience Disassociation under Stress and Hallucinations. Nevertheless, everyone with BPD will exhibit certain BPD aspects, such as Intense Emotions that are difficult to control, Fear of Abandonment, Idealization and Devaluation (and Splitting), Black and White Thinking, Distorted Perception of Reality, Lack of Object Constancy / Emotional Amnesia and Memory of the Past being shaped by Present Feelings. Those are the core side-effects that make up the disorder and they are all inter-connected. For example, it is impossible to have ongoing Devaluation if Emotional Amnesia did not prevent the PBPD from connecting the past with the present. If the PBPD could accurately remember the past, then Devaluation would immediately cease. Also, Devaluation would never happen in the first place if the Intense Emotions did not cause an overwhelming Fear of Abandonment where the mind felt it had to paint the loved one as “all black and evil” rather than face the possibility of a “genuine” loved one abandoning them. The BPD core symptoms are all based on each other and “feed off” each other. BPD is a serious and dangerous condition and one of the four “Cluster B” Personality Disorders (Antisocial, Narcissistic, Borderline, and Histrionic) that are characterized by dramatic, overly emotional or unpredictable thinking or behavior. It is imperative that PBPDs receive professional treatment. Unfortunately, many psychologists appear to lack to skills to properly diagnose BPD and it is often misdiagnosed or even left undiagnosed. Besides Dialectical Behavior Therapy which is absolutely necessary, it is said that yoga, meditation and breath-work can help manage the intensity of the BPD emotions. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM–5) lists 9 easy to spot BPD behaviors. A psychologist will diagnose someone with BPD if at least 5 of those 9 behaviors are spotted. The DSM-5 is used for diagnosis and should not be confused with a summary or a description of BPD. Laypersons should avoid looking at the DSM-5 in attempting to understand BPD; it is a tool for professionals used for the limited purpose of diagnosis. Furthermore, there have been several recommendations in updating the DSM in regards to BPD based on our updated understanding of BPD. It is also important for the loved ones and former loved ones of PBPDs to seek help for themselves. The trauma of suddenly being treated in a horrible way by a loved one and losing them for no apparent reason often causes PTSD and/or other mental health issues. For this reason, people who have been through a relationship with a PBPD are often called BPD survivors. Once someone is aware of what BPD is, it is relative easy to spot due to the intensity of the interpersonal relationships and the sudden devaluations that follow. It is through these interpersonal relationships that high functioning PBPDs often realize that a problem exists.

column1: Since narcissism is a personality disorder, should we be publicly outing a narcissist? Why or why not?
column3: Since narcissism is a personality disorder, should we be publicly outing a narcissist? Why or why not? I don’t have a definitive across the board answer to this question. But one thing I do know is the devastating trauma and ruin a person with Narcissistic Personality Disorder, as well as many other Narcissists inflict on family members, both child and adult, and on co-workers and employees. The reason their behaviour continues decade after decade and the public is so often complicit in the dismissal of this as a serious issue, is that focus is placed upon victims, who are seen to be weak, non-assertive, ineffective, or even wanting to continue being abused, and quite often seen as probably having in some way provoked and irritated the Narcissist, and partially responsible for their own abuse. If the victim is very shy, or socially inept, or troubled by other social and personal problems, and particularly if they have suffered from mental health problems, they have little chance of others taking their side. They are often seen as people who complain too much, have too thin a skin, are unable to take difficulties with others in stride and shrug off things that the narcissist says. I know that again and again I have seen these reactions. Again and again perpetrators of stalking and domestic violence are portrayed as odd but harmless neighbours and those in their communities coming out to say what a nice family they were, what a polite and quiet man he was, although maybe a bit unsociable or odd. If someone is bullying, harrassing, targeting, gaslighting, or otherwise committing any of the many horrible narcissistic actions toward someone else, and people know about it, keeping quiet sends a very clear message to the perpetrator that others are not the least bothered, will consider their behaviour acceptable, will look the other way, believe their lies, continue to support them in their role at work and in the community, and even hold the victim at least partially responsible when incidents come to light. It is dangerous and it is difficult to speak out and stand against a narcissist. We MUST find a way! Lives are being ruined. Working with others who also see what is going on— at the very least, giving support and encouragement to the victim, offering them some options or at least a listening ear, could save a life and someone’s sanity. But it will also likely get the whistle-blower placed squarely in the narcissist’s target crosshairs. And Narcissists have their flying monkeys to lie for them and act as an army in their nasty campaign to wreak havoc. I still think the best way to deal with a Narcissist is to be careful, keep your cards close to the vest, plan wisely how to deal with them and extricate yourself from their orbit, and seek trustworthy confidantes, but be very careful in trusting anyone. Often the Narcissist plays on the confidante’s sympathy and puts them in a supporting role like a double agent, and this often takes the form of getting dirt on the confidante to blackmail or intimidate them, cooking up ways to make them feel punished or abused if they support the victim, and setting up double bind situations where they have little choice. Still, if there is a group of strong individuals committed to seeing justice done, and these people approach things as a strong united front, it could work. When courts and law enforcement officials and politicians finally get a clear picture of how many people are doing these horrific things to others and getting away with it, one hopes they will put in place some very harsh and consistent ways of apprehending and charging and convicting anyone who seeks to control, abuse, and ruin the life of another. I have a lot of doubt that will happen anytime soon. At the very least, organisations should have good training programmes in place starting with senior members of boards and management and going on down the line to low level workers, to educate people in spotting Narcissistic abuse, making the right decisions and standing behind the victim. If they would place some safeguards, and make a clear and lasting commitment to fire Narcissistic employees who target others, if the companies trained and placed at various levels trained confidential policies with support people who will break up the ring of bullying, represent the victims, and employ ways to protect them from Narcissists within their organisation, it might work. If the consequence for Narcissistic abuse were losing one’s job and that being seen as a shameful and undesirable blot on their employment record, and that happened in every proven case, there would be change. This is the least they can and should do, and will be extremely beneficial in the long run, as Narcissists ruin worker morale, contribute to so much fraud and violations, employee burnout, mental health problems and turnover that affects the company’s bottom line. However the Narcissist knows that the company or other employer is mainly focused on profit, and they are often experts at producing that or pretending to produce good results in order to keep their jobs when senior officials learn of difficulties with workers. And on the domestic violence perpetrator’s horizon, if there were support networks to keep the spouse/partner/children in the home, cared for and protected, and the perpetrator lost their job, their status in the community, their opportunities to play the big winner and hot shot, or poor mistreated and misunderstood partner of an emotionally unstable spouse/child/partner, etc. If police clamped down early in the saga of incidents, and if the victim had a range of options instead of facing running away to a refuge or months or years of destitution and loss of career, possessions, and reputation…. well, we would all be better off. Who stays in their job, home, community, and friendships; and who runs away seeking shelter and some way forward for themselves and their children without any or substantial backing and financial means to get justice? Not the Narcissist or other abuser! This must change!

column1: How does losing a father affect a daughter?
column3: Losing a father can have profound and varied effects on a daughter, influencing her emotionally, psychologically, and socially. Here are some key impacts: Emotional EffectsGrief and Sadness: The immediate response is often intense grief, which can manifest as sadness, anger, or confusion.Fear and Anxiety: A daughter may experience heightened anxiety about her own safety and the stability of her family.Guilt: She might feel guilty about the loss, questioning if there was something she could have done to prevent it.Psychological EffectsIdentity Formation: The father-daughter relationship is crucial for identity development. Loss can disrupt this process, leading to feelings of incompleteness or confusion about self-worth.Trust Issues: Loss may affect her ability to trust others, especially in future relationships, leading to difficulties in forming close bonds.Resilience: Conversely, some daughters may develop resilience and coping skills as they navigate their grief.Social EffectsIsolation: She might feel isolated from peers who cannot relate to her experience, leading to feelings of loneliness.Changes in Relationships: Relationships with other family members may change, either strengthening or straining as everyone copes differently.Support Systems: The loss can lead to reliance on friends or other family members for support, which can be beneficial or detrimental depending on the dynamics.Long-Term EffectsMental Health: There may be an increased risk of mental health issues such as depression or anxiety in the long term.Future Relationships: The loss can shape her expectations and behaviors in future romantic relationships, influencing attachment styles.Life Choices: The experience may affect her life choices, career paths, and parenting styles in the future.Coping MechanismsTherapy and Counseling: Professional help can facilitate healthy grieving and coping strategies.Support Groups: Connecting with others who have experienced similar losses can provide comfort and understanding.Creative Outlets: Engaging in art, writing, or other forms of expression can help process emotions.Ultimately, the effects of losing a father vary widely based on individual circumstances, the nature of the father-daughter relationship, and the support systems available. Each daughter will navigate her grief in her own way, shaped by her personal experiences and resilience.

column1: Are anxiety disorders genetic and not psychological?
column3: Anxiety disorders are seen in some cases to “run in families” and for that reason they are deemed to be genetic. However the research has not shown anything convincing. It is far more likely that anxiety disorders run in families where there are some inhumane members that use underhanded foul game play to gain power and influence over others in relationship. If this is happening in a family then as the family grows and extends and either new inhumane people are born into the family or marry into the family or become friends of the family, so the younger members, as they interact with these inhumane people, can be affected. I don’t think that one can call anxiety psychological as in being a part of the person’s psychological make-up. But rather it is psychological in that it is in the psychology involved in the underhanded foul game play. Thus, while the person unwittingly reacts will they suffer. With knowledge of what they are up against they can get well again.
