column1: My sister wants me to take care of her kids while she’s in labor, but my husband and I both have full-time jobs and our own kids. How do I tell her I can help out but not the entire time?
column3: I guess it depends. I know not everyone can afford time off work and I know many jobs aren’t flexible. I lost count the number of times I worked an afternoon shift as a nurse and the night staff called in sick last minute and I had to work a double with no notice. it’s not the kind of job you can walk out of and leave the patients. Even though I wasn’t the manager or owner and it wasn’t my responsibility to staff the facility , I was still unable to leave the patients without care that would cost me my licence and job. I see both sides that it’s only a few days and you may need her help some day so make it work. But as a nanny and sitter ive done a lot of stays with kids while the mum was in labor - most times it’s a day or less but one time the mum had to have a c section and she and the baby were in hospital weeks. I was with the kids for the first week and then the father returned from overseas (in the army ) and I stayed on helping out the next week. I had to cancel other jobs and miss class (back in the days when I was a student ) and they did pay me after for my time and re Imburse me the money I spent on food etc - I remember going through the kids piggy banks to buy food before the week was over. I was quite young and she had no one else and while I was happy to do it and didn’t feel I had much choice / I do wish she had planned a bit better for any eventuality ! She wasn’t expecting to be away long of course but she left her kids with a 19 year old student with no money and not a lot of experience for a week with no help. Which isn’t ideal. other families I have done this for have said they do have parents and siblings but don’t want to impose on particular as each family member had children or health problems or jobs - and as they didn’t know the day or time the mum would go into labor they preferred to arrange a sitter. They paid me for being “on call” and I had numbers of relatives in case some unforeseen thing happened I wouldn’t get stranded again. each family is different and each relationship. For me I would do it for my sister. I would think she would do it for me. But at the same time if she couldn’t I would be fine with that. I’d only ask her I think as she loves to have time with the kids as does my mum - and they might be unhappy if I hired a sitter without Asking them if they wanted to do it. But it is a good idea to line up plans including someone who can step in if it’s longer than a day and money for that person to feed the kids - especially if the mother is a single parent and there isn’t a partner to help out. I don’t know your job or commitments or your children’s needs , or your relationship with your sister and how close you are (or want to be ) to her and her children. its a special time to be a part of helping out to welcome someone to the family. But everyone has limits and If you can’t take time off without dire consequences that affect you and your family then I would tell her I would love to help but we are in a rough spot. Who cares for your kids when you are at work ? As a nanny I’ve often had cousins come over etc so maybe you could arrange something and ask you sister to chip in for cost of someone to babysit or help out. Of it mentally of physically you can’t cope with the responsibility of it maybe offer to pay for her to hire a sitter? if my sister was totally uninterested in helping out to welcome a niece or nephew into the world it would cause a lot of damage. If she was sick or struggling mentally or legitimately could not take time off without a dire consequence that I would understand. I guess it depends would she do it for you ? Do you have the kind of relationship with her and her kids to help out ? My sisters kids are like me own to me, I would drop anything I could to care for them as I would my own children. she would too. But it seems like more of an annoyance to you so maybe you don’t have that kind of closeness with her or the kids. Maybe she doesn’t help out or be involved with your kids either. I guess it’s up to you how important she is and the kids are and how involved you can be without harming your job or income or means to care for your self and your children. But maybe she has taken advantage of you in the past and you really can’t get involved for some reason , it is hard to put things on hold especially as you can’t plan for when she goes in to labor , and many jobs like nursing for example you can’t say “my sister is going to have a baby in the next few weeks so can I have time off when she does to mind her Kids?” I can’t take time off last minute without there being someone to take over from me. which is one reason I don’t work that job anymore. even though you have your own children you and your husband still work in jobs where you can’t take time off easily , not even for your own children , so to be expected to do it for someoene else’s isn’t reasonable I can understand that. to answer the question if you really can’t do it be honest. If it’s because you’re in danger of losing a job tell her that. I’m sure she won’t want that either. Maybe help her find a sitter. If it’s because you don’t have time with your own children’s needs tell that too. If you just don’t think you can cope emotionally I would tell her honestly and explain you just can’t. If you just like your job and working that’s fine , explain to her you both work full time and can’t even be there for your own children at times let alone hers too. I do find it hard to understand not wanting to do it. But at the same time I know how hard some jobs can be and how a few hours can turn into weeks with a complication. Be honest that you can’t do it and will help her find a sitter and be someone the sitter can call in an emergency. Same way you would get a call from your own kids sitter in an emergency and have to leave work. But you can’t commit to taking them for the full time. Or just do it. It’s a day or two , with children who are part of your family at a special time another member is being born. It means something to be part of that and help out if you can do so. Same time I don’t see what the big deal would be for her to hire a sitter lots of people do.

column1: How do beauty standards affect health?
column3: Social media affecting teenager’s mental health is a controversial topic that has been around for quite a while. Many studies have been done to prove social media negatively impacts teens. The studies put social media in bad light, creating negative stigma towards it. Making majority believe social media causes teens to have issues such as depression, anxiety, self-harm, and narcissism. While it is easy to blame social media because research says to do so, I believe that our society is the main reason teens struggle with mental health issues. Society has set beauty standards in the beauty industry, making teens have a lower self-esteem, feel or become isolated if they do not look a certain way, and can even lead to physical health problems. Beauty standards have been impalement to our society from the very begging and has been something that has daunted teens to this day. The article Beauty Throughout History, written by Sharom Romm, talks about the history of how beauty standards were set. The author quoted Plato by saying, “the three wishes of every Greek to See BEAUTY, …to be healthy, to be beautiful and to become rich. Greek parents-to-be were so concerned about their offspring's beauty that they placed statues of Aphrodite or Apollo, the two deities of physical appearance, in their bedrooms to help them conceive beautiful children.” This shows how even in the past people would go through such great lengths just to make beautiful children. The ancient Greeks culture has contributed many ideas to our western civilization beauty standards being one of them. As we know, beauty standards are constantly changing, but that does not mean that the social pressure to fit in ever goes away. For example, in the 17th and 18th century, voluptuous women were considered to be very beautiful. This can be seen in many art pieces bigger curvy women were being painted since they were the ideal figure. Bigger woman were seen as beautiful because that meant they were very wealthy since they could afford to eat well. In today’s society, the beauty industry almost makes it their duty to reinforce what beauty is meant to look like. Although some major companies use bigger sized or even different colored models, they still modify the model’s images to make sure they look more “appealing” hiding all blemishes or imperfections such as stretch marks and cellulite. This still creates feelings of inadequacy amongst teens because even people who might look like them are still perfect affecting how they see their own body image. According to researchers at Bradley Hospital, Butler Hospital, and Brown Medical School, “Adolescents with negative body images are more likely to be depressed, anxious and suicidal than those without intense dissatisfaction over their appearance, even when compared to adolescents with other psychiatric illnesses.” The beauty industry takes advantage of social media since the majority of users are teens. They promote their brand, making influencers feel pressured to fit the image online. The article, “Like” it or not, Social Media’s Affecting Your Mental Health, is another of many articles that blames social media saying that teens suffer from mental health problems because they seek validation. The author states, “They’re searching for validation on the internet that serves as a replacement for meaningful connection they might otherwise make in real life.” Often times teens feel as if they might be judged harshly by the people around them in real life. When online, they can feel encouraged by their friends. If teens seek validation online, it might be due to the fact that many adults grew up with certain beauty standard as well, making then judge teens appearance. The set beauty standards make teens feel like outcasts if they do not fit the ideal image, causing them to isolate themselves. In the case of girls, most of their insecurities are brought out by mothers who have also been negatively affected by the beauty industry’s image of beauty. In the article, Teens feel pressure to be “perfect”, the author Madison Riehle says, “Low self-esteem issues frequently take root at home where mothers can not only pass on their own insecurities but take out their self-loathing on their daughters, according to family therapist Susan Badger.” When having both a family member and constant reminders from beauty industry advertisements of what beauty is supposed to be, there is a greater chance that the teen is going to feel that they are not beautiful because they look different. If teens do not feel beautiful because of their differences, they are most likely to feel isolated. They feel like they have to change but they cannot, so they just shut everyone out both mentally and physically. According Medical News today, “isolation has a significant impact on health, contributing to conditions such as depression, anxiety, and dementia.” The isolation caused by not fitting the perfect image leads to serious mental health issues that can often times lead to self-harm and even death. Not only has beauty standards affected teens mentally but also physically. For example, the well know Victoria Secret models have the very slim figure that can only be achieved by a strict diet and exercise. Those models have a great amount of influence towards teenage girls. Many might even look up to them so much that they look into their dietary habits. When a person switches from a regular diet to the extreme diets of the models the drastic change can affect the body negatively. A model eats roughly about 1,300 calories a day according to the Sun Magazine. The average number of calories a healthy teen should eat a day is 2,800 which is a bit more than half. Changing a diet drastically like that can lead to health issues. When going onto the google search engine and typing in “How to lose” the first things on the drop list are questions on fast ways to lose weight. Research says 27% of those searches are most common in teens. As seen down below. When looking at all the slimmer bodied models, it is almost inevitable to not compare or even question one’s psychical appearance, and it can even lead to eating disorders such as anorexia and bulimia. A study done by The University of Vermont Medical Center says that 0.9% of girls will struggle with anorexia in their lifetime, 1.5% of women will struggle with bulimia in their lifetime.” Instead of the beauty industry eventuating models best, they should normalize average or real people’s bodies. Many times, being skinny does not equal being healthy. Everyone deals with the pressure to match the set beauty standards differently and it may not be health for most teens since its always so easy to point out. Just because social media is a platform used by many teens who struggle with mental health problems it does not mean it is the culprit. Big beauty industries abuse the power of social media to sell their name at the cost of many teens mental and physical health. If it was for ancient Greek being so vain beauty standards wouldn’t have been set and nobody would have been affected, but they did, so all that’s left is to accept everyone for who they are. Unfortunately, all the beauty industries standards have done is negatively impact teens by lowering their self-esteem, causing them to feel depressed and cause more harm onto themselves, and even spread the negativity onto others. The beauty standards set by society causes isolation in teens if they don’t feel like they fit in, they tend to be more reserved and even search for validation online rather than in real life in hopes to be accepted. Teens are often affected by their parents as well because their own parents struggle with insecurities caused by the beauty standards set. The beauty industry’s beauty standards are also to blame for health issues teens are having. They look for any way fit the image at any cost, even if it means outing their health on the line, all because the standards have been set so high that if they are not met, it does not make a person beautiful. So next time you read an article about how social media might be affecting a teens mental health, you might want to rethink if it is social media or the people abusing the power of it.

column1: What are some patterns of an emotionally abusive person?
column3: Feeling insulted and wounded. Never measuring up. Walking on eggshells. If these statements describe your relationship, it is likely you are being emotionally abused. In general, a relationship is emotionally abusive when there is a consistent pattern of abusive words and bully behavior that wear down a person's self esteem and undermine their mental health. What's more, mental or emotional abuse, while most common in dating and married relationships, can occur in any relationship including among friends, family members, and coworkers.Emotional abuse is one of the hardest forms of abuse to recognize. It can be subtle and insidious or overt and manipulative. Either way, it chips away at the victim's self-esteem and they begin to doubt their perceptions and reality. The underlying goal in emotional abuse is to control the victim by discrediting, isolating, and silencing. In the end, the victim feels trapped. They are often too wounded to endure the relationship any longer, but also too afraid to leave. So the cycle just repeats itself until something is done. Impact of Emotional Abuse When emotional abuse is severe and ongoing, a victim may lose their entire sense of self, sometimes without a single mark or bruise. Instead, the wounds are invisible to others, hidden in the self-doubt, worthlessness and self-loathing the victim feels. In fact, many victims say that the scars from emotional abuse last far longer and are much deeper than those from psychical abuse. Over time, the accusations, verbal abuse, name calling, criticisms, and gaslighting erode a victim's sense of self so much that they can no longer see themselves realistically. Consequently, the victim begins to agree with the abuser and becomes internally critical. Once this happens, most victims become trapped in the abusive relationship believing that they will never be good enough for anyone else. Emotional abuse can even impact friendships because emotionally abused people often worry about how people truly see them and if they truly like them. Eventually, victims will pull back from friendships and isolate themselves, convinced that no one likes them. What's more, emotional abuse can cause a number of health problems including everything from depression and anxiety to stomach ulcers, heart palpitations, Eating disorders, and insomnia. How to Spot Emotional Abuse When examining your own relationship, remember that emotional abuse is often subtle. As a result, it can be very hard to detect. If you are having trouble discerning whether or not your relationship is abusive, stop and think about how the interactions with your partner, friend or family member make you feel. If you feel wounded, frustrated, confused, misunderstood, depressed, anxious or worthless any time you interact, chances are high that your relationship is emotionally abusive. Here are signs that you may be in an emotionally abusive relationship. Keep in mind, even if your partner only does a handful of these things, you are still in an emotionally abusive relationship. Do not fall into the trap of telling yourself "it's not that bad" and minimizing their behavior. Remember, everyone deserves to be treated with kindness and respect. Emotionally abusive people display unrealistic expectations. Some examples include:Making unreasonable demands of youExpecting you to put everything aside and meet their needsDemanding you spend all of your time togetherBeing dissatisfied no matter how hard you try or how much you giveCriticizing you for not completing tasks according to their standardsExpecting you to share their opinions (you are not permitted to have a different opinion)Demanding that you name exact dates and times when discussing things that upset you (when you cannot do this, they dismisses the event as if it never happened)​Emotionally abusive people invalidate you. Some examples include:Undermining, dismissing, or distorting your perceptions or your realityRefusing to accept your feelings by trying to define how you should feelRequiring you to explain and explain and explain how you feelAccusing you of being "too sensitive," "too emotional," or "crazy"Refusing to acknowledge or accept your opinions or ideas as validDismissing your requests, wants, and needs as ridiculous or unmeritedSuggesting that your perceptions are wrong or that you cannot be trusted by saying things like "you're blowing this out of proportion" or "you exaggerate"Accusing you of being selfish, needy or materialistic if you express your wants or needs (the expectation is that you should not have any wants or needs)​Emotionally abusive people create chaos. Some examples include:Starting arguments for the sake of arguingMaking confusing and contradictory statements (sometimes called "crazy-making")Having drastic mood changes or sudden emotional outburstsNitpicking at your clothes, your hair, your work, and moreBehaving so erratically and unpredictably that you feel like you are "walking on eggshells"​Emotionally abusive people use emotional blackmail. Some examples include:Manipulating and controlling you by making you feel guiltyHumiliating you in public or in privateUsing your fears, values, compassion or other hot buttons to control you or the situationExaggerating your flaws or pointing them out in order to deflect attention or to avoid taking responsibility for their poor choices or mistakesDenying that an event took place or lying about itPunishing you by withholding affectionEmotionally abusive people act superior and entitled. Some examples include:Treating you like you are inferiorBlaming you for their mistakes and shortcomingsDoubting everything you say and attempting to prove you wrongMaking jokes at your expenseTelling you that your opinions, ideas, values and thoughts are stupid, illogical or "do not make sense"Talking down to you or being condescendingUsing sarcasm when interacting with youActing like they are always right, knows what is best and is smarter​Emotionally abusive people attempt to isolate and control you. Some examples include:Controlling who you see or spend time with including time with friends and familyMonitoring your phone calls, text messages, social media, and emailAccusing you of cheating and being jealous of outside relationshipsTaking or hiding your car keysDemanding to know where you are at all times or using GPS to track your every moveTreating you like a possession or propertyCriticizing or making fun of your friends, family, and coworkersUsing jealousy and envy as a sign of love and to keep you from being with othersCoercing you into spending all of your time togetherControlling the financesThe first step in dealing with an emotionally abusive relationship is to recognize that it is happening. If you were able to identify any aspect of emotional abuse in your relationship, it is important to acknowledge that first and foremost. By being honest about what you are experiencing, you can begin to take control of your life again. Here are seven more strategies for reclaiming your life that you can put into practice today. Make your mental and physical health a priority. Stop worrying about pleasing the person abusing you. Take care of your needs. Do something that will help you think positive and affirm who you are. Also, be sure to get an appropriate amount of rest and eat healthy meals. These simple self-care steps can go a long way in helping you deal with the day-to-day stresses of emotional abuse. Establish boundaries with the abuser. Firmly tell the abusive person that they may no longer yell at you, call you names, insult you, be rude to you, and so on. Then, tell them what will happen if they choose to engage in this behavior. For instance, tell them that if they call you names or insult you, the conversation will be over and you will leave the room. The key is to follow through on your boundaries. Do not communicate boundaries that you have no intention of keeping. Stop blaming yourself. If you have been in an emotionally abusive relationship for any amount of time, you may believe that there is something severely wrong with you. Why else would someone who says they love you act like this, right? But you are not the problem. Abuse is a choice. So stop blaming yourself for something you have no control over. Realize that you cannot "fix" the abusive person. Despite your best efforts, you will never be able to change an emotionally abusive person by doing something different or by being different. An abusive person makes a choice to behave abusively. Remind yourself that you cannot control their actions and that you are not to blame for their choices. The only thing you can fix or control is your response. Do not engage with an abusive person. In other words, if an abuser tries to start an argument with you, begins insulting you, demands things from you or rages with jealousy, do not try to make explanations, soothe their feelings or make apologies for things you did not do. Simply walk away from the situation if you can. Engaging with an abuser only sets you up for more abuse and heartache. No matter how hard you try, you will not be able to make things right in their eyes. Build a support network. Stop being silent about the abuse you are experiencing. Talk to a trusted friend, family member or even a counselor about what you are experiencing. Take time away from the abusive person as much as possible and spend time with people who love and support you. This network of healthy friends and confidantes will help you feel less lonely and isolated. They also can speak truth into your life and help you put things into perspective. Work on an exit plan. If your partner, friend, or family member has no intention of changing or working on their poor choices, you will not be able to remain in the abusive relationship forever. It will eventually take a toll on you both mentally and physically. Depending on your situation, you may need to take steps to end the relationship. Each situation is different. So it is best to discuss your thoughts and ideas with a trusted friend, family member or counselor.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: My story: How I got my life back, one small move at a time I used to stand tall and survey the world around me with confidence. During the two tough years of my husband’s illness, I lost my balance. Every consideration in my life focused on his well-being. I never paused in my full-time role as a caregiver; in fact, I considered it a gift to accompany him as I always had in our marriage, this time (sadly) on the journey to the end of his life. He would have done exactly the same for me. In his acceptance of me as his caregiver, I felt his ultimate trust in me as his life's partner. I drew upon every ounce of my strength to be patient, loving, and physically strong, and to keep him oriented, safe, and calm. As his condition worsened, my efforts became futile; dangerous times began in earnest. When he tried to exit our moving vehicle on Route 128, the looming crisis I had hoped to delay finally made itself known, on this day, in this way. When my husband died in hospice in December 2013, I lost my bearings. My life-long career was in shambles. My husband’s beauty salon was shut down. My elderly mom was in a nursing home. I couldn't fall asleep before two in the morning but woke up at dawn nevertheless. My adult children needed me to recall memories of our family life together — buckets of tears always accompanied the telling. I attended loss of partner bereavement meetings where the participants bonded in shock and pain. I felt as if I had died too and had entered a world that made no sense. After some time, I looked for a reason to get up everyday. And if I got up, I wanted to stand firm on two feet, eat a decent breakfast, and walk out the door, even if I had to shovel the snow. But, where in the world to go? I had attended a weekly caregivers support group at the senior center in the next town over. During those two years, I sometimes peeked into the gym to watch the exercise class in progress — but caregivers have no time to spare. This time I walked in. I took a place in the back row and followed instructions robotically. My body moved, but my heart and mind were frozen. I told myself, “You don’t need to focus laser-like on the needs of another human being as you did for 703 days and nights. Just focus on ONE SIMPLE THING. Stay with it at all costs. Finish the class. Then you can leave, and cry at home some more. After a few weeks, I noticed voices of classmates directed at me: “Hi, how’s it going, do you like the class, you’re new here, welcome.” I responded politely, shared the morning experience, then ventured to ask others how they were doing in return. My flexibility and balance started to improve, once I paid attention more mindfully to the moves. Not counting the days or the weeks as the winter moved on, I realized to my surprise that I did not have to hold on to the back of the chair for dear life anymore. I figured out that balance meant so much more than just standing still and not falling. My balance was a force within me, and if it kept changing, I would change, and my life would change too. In the Spring of 2014, I visited my son and his family in Israel for a month. The years of caregiving and months of intense grief had left me profoundly exhausted. I slept in a single bed in a single room with a single window overlooking the side of a steep and stony hill. If ever I envisioned what a physical place of healing looked like, this would be it. When I returned home and to the exercise class, various people came up to me to ask, “Barrie, are you okay, where have you been, were you sick, we missed you, good to see you again.” These were people who did not know my husband or me, the suffering of his last two years, or the journey that was in store for me, grieving a husband in one year and fated to lose my mother the next year. The many sincere expressions of concern for me, a newcomer, from new people in my new life, felt like blessings washing over me, freely and generously. Like Blanche Dubois, I was open to admitting that “I have always depended on the kindness of strangers.” Moved to tears, I fled to the ladies’ room and wept, this time not for my husband, but for me.

column1: What are some effective ways for a person with BPD to self-soothe when overwhelmed by anxiety?
column3: Sometimes anxiety occurs because of emotional dysregulation / immune dysregulation (which is stress related) with BPD and causes an ‘ emotional loop’ so that it is impossible to think about what is causing it. Sometimes the emotional pain becomes so severe that you feel as if you can hardly breathe/you feel panic. This makes you vulnerable to reacting from your emotional self. Sometimes there may be critical voices in your head coming from yourself or someone else from the past. If you are aware of the pain, anxiety or critical voice, this is the time to do a BREATHING EXERCISE in order to calm your self down. The following exercise is from the NHS and best learned and remembered when you are feeling relaxed so that you are ready with it when needed. Begin it immediately while standing and then sit or lie down: Make yourself as comfortable as you can. If you can, loosen any clothes that restrict your breathing. If you're lying down, place your arms a little bit away from your sides, with the palms up. Let your legs be straight, or bend your knees so your feet are flat on the floor. If you're sitting, place your arms on the chair arms. If you're sitting or standing, place both feet flat on the ground. Whatever position you're in, place your feet roughly hip-width apart. • Let your breath flow as deep down into your belly as is comfortable, without forcing it. • Try breathing in through your nose and out through your mouth. • Breathe in gently and regularly. Some people find it helpful to count steadily from 1 to 5. You may not be able to reach 5 at first. • Then, without pausing or holding your breath, let it flow out gently, counting from 1 to 5 again, if you find this helpful. • Keep doing this for 3 to 5 minutes. Breathing exercise for stress Once you have overcome the worst of the anxiety attack become aware of yourself and your body. Take notice of your emotions/feelings and thoughts. If possible name them and ACCEPT ( validation) them and allow them to naturally subside. (Don’t try to suppress them or hold onto them). Allow your body to totally relax as you accept yourself just the way you are without any judgement. This is MINDFULNESS. Another helpful technique used for children but just as useful at any age is to use the senses : COPING SKILL SPOTLIGHT: 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 GROUNDING TECHNIQUE HOW TO DO IT: This technique will take you through your five senses to help remind you of the present. This is a calming technique that can help you get through tough or stressful situations. Take a deep belly breath to begin. 5 - LOOK: Look around for 5 things that you can see, and say them out loud. For example, you could say, I see the computer, I see the cup, I see the picture frame. 4 - FEEL: Pay attention to your body and think of 4 things that you can feel, and say them out loud. For example, you could say, I feel my feet warm in my socks, I feel the hair on the back of my neck, or I feel the pillow I am sitting on. 3 - LISTEN: Listen for 3 sounds. It could be the sound of traffic outside, the sound of typing or the sound of your tummy rumbling. Say the three things out loud. 2 - SMELL: Say two things you can smell. If you’re allowed to, it’s okay to move to another spot and sniff something. If you can’t smell anything at the moment or you can’t move, then name your 2 favorite smells. 1 - TASTE: Say one thing you can taste. It may be the toothpaste from brushing your teeth, or a mint from after lunch. If you can’t taste anything, then say your favorite thing to taste. Take another deep belly breath to end. Coping Skill Spotlight: 5 4 3 2 1 Grounding Technique — Coping Skills for Kids Medium or Long term things to consider: Was there some form of emotional abuse (with physical abuse and /or sexual abuse and/or neglect) ? Am I accepting that there was abuse in the past? Is it necessary to forgive what happened ? Is that still causing anger/ anxiety ? Were my parents abused? Do I want the generational nature of abuse to rest with me? Can I accept what happened and let it go? Have I been taught that it wasn’t ok to cry, to be angry or to show other appropriate emotions? Do I bottle emotions up and then eventually explode like a volcano? Has that caused issues with my relationships that are causing anxiety ? Was I taught to hide my feelings so as not to upset my parents/ caregivers ? Do I hide my feelings in fear of the reaction from others? Do I feel angry instead and turn this anger inwards towards myself ? Does this anger cause my anxiety? Did I hide my emotions as a child following a bereavement because I thought my family couldn’t handle them? Did I have to be the strong one? Did I become a parent for the remaining caregiver? Did I learn that expressing pain would only burden people and so I hid my emotions? Is that causing my anxiety? Do I think my parents /caregivers have received these same messages themselves from their parents? Did I have a sick parent/ caregiver ever since I can remember. Did I have to be strong for their sake? Did I have to be the parent? Did I have to take responsibility for them and in doing so repress my emotions, feelings, thoughts, my own needs? Am I blaming myself or others for the way I feel? Is that causing my anxiety? Am I telling myself to be something or to do something that someone else wants/ or wanted but it doesn't feel quite right? Is that causing anxiety? Am I really a bad person because I have expressed emotion in the past? Am I judging myself for events that have happened that I can not do anything about? What has caused my anxiety this time? How can I change my emotions, my feelings, my thoughts and my life so that these anxiety attacks stop happening? There are levels of VALIDATION : • Acknowledgement that ‘I feel anxious' • Allowing — It’s ok that I feel anxious ( that doesn’t mean you like it) • Understanding that it makes sense under the circumstances ( speak out what those circumstances are ) It may be helpful to prepare some validating statements that you can read/ say out loud to yourself over and over when you realise that you are invalidating your emotions. That way you can change your self talk to something positive and validating. You are teaching yourself to be kind to yourself. You are also teaching yourself SELF CARE, SELF LOVE and SELF PARENTING. Be PATIENT with yourself as well as this process may take a long time. Thinking about yourself and speaking out loud to yourself in this way is a method of understanding yourself better. Linking emotions with feelings and thoughts helps to change patterns that are no longer helpful. Is there a trigger to the latest anxiety attack that you can remember: • an external event such as an argument • a thought • an image • a memory Had that trigger lead to secondary emotions/thoughts, a chain of emotions/ thoughts? These are secondary emotions. e.g. you have an argument with a friend, the argument makes you feel bad, you then judge yourself increasing the amount of pain your are experiencing. It is helpful to self reflect and consider the situation and the chain of emotions, feelings and thoughts that caused the severe anxiety attack. Sometimes it isn’t possible to work it all out or it is difficult to name the emotions/feelings. Printing a DBT emotion wheel and a feeling word list may be helpful. About 10% people have ALEXITHYMIA which makes this process more difficult though still possible. Gradually you will learn how to identify the emotions you experience. Write the emotions/feelings down and then think about whether that chain was an old pattern and then change it into something positive. E.g. I had an argument with .....and was angry, it is healthy to have a disagreement and express anger sometimes. I wasn’t allowed to be angry as a child so this is progress. I can grow from this. Anxiety following disagreements is an old pattern. I will phone ..... and perhaps we can agree to disagree, or I will apologise if I think it was really my fault, then we can stay friends and move on. Whatever the situation, thought, memory or image comes to your mind replace it with positive words, memories or images and write them down/describe the image or draw a picture. If there was a situation write down a solution and then take action. Write down if your solution worked. Celebrate your progress. JOURNALING is a good idea because it enables progress to be seen with passing of days, weeks, months and years. It is important to be disciplined about doing this self reflection on a regular basis in order for the brain to learn new patterns ‘rewiring'. This is COGNITIVE BEHVIOURAL THERAPY ( CBT) Regular MINDFULNESS MEDITATION twice a day for 20 minutes is good practice that will calm the autonomic nervous system and bring it into balance. Headspace have some free meditations you can try – if you find the good then may want to invest in continuing with them. There will be others on the internet that you can try free of charge. Consider joining practical emotional guide on quora. If you find that you cannot concentrate on the meditation ACCEPT that and start listening again. If you fall asleep, ACCEPT that too. It may mean that you needed a nap. ACCEPT how you are without judgement. EXERCISE — If possible take mindful walks where you stay present noticing your surroundings, the trees, flowers, birds, buildings, the sounds, the colours etc. Walk for at least half an hour and make a decision to enjoy the walk and smile sometimes even if you don’t feel like it. If you haven’t been exercising build up these walks gradually increasing the pace but still being mindful. Walk for at least half an hour noticing how you feel as well. The walks should make you feel better. If they don’t your immune system is struggling then cut the pace back or walk less time or less often e.g. walk 15 minutes daily or walk every other day. Swimming is an alternative exercise. Over time you should find that you can gradually do more. These 2 exercises are probably the safest but you may choose to do other exercises with experienced supervision. DIET — If the emotional dysregulation has also caused some immune dysregulation you may find it helpful to think about your diet whether you realise or not that it is unhealthy. Say to yourself that you love your body and want to nourish it well. You may find it helpful to cut out refined sugar, alcohol and eat a ‘clean diet’ i.e. leave out processed food. Processed food is the ready made meal that often has numerous flavouring or preservatives. If you look at the ingredients on the packet you will see a long list of chemicals including added sugar. These types of meals are best left out. Eat plenty of salad and vegetables with protein. Try to eat some raw vegetables /salad every day. If you can afford it eat organic. You may find that this diet makes you feel better and that the feeling of anxiety (emotional dysregulation) will subside. Nutritional psychiatry: Your brain on food - Harvard Health Blog REGULAR SLEEP is also important 7-9 hours per night is considered normal. You may find you need more sleep if your anxiety/ dysregulation has not been controlled well. Allow the extra rest being kind and patient with yourself. As you heal you will find the emotional dysregulation will fade or be absent some days. Avoid people and circumstances that trigger you and make you feel unwell. This can be hard because the people that you need to avoid may be members of your own family or friends. If you want to still be in touch with them put BOUNDARIES in place and understand when to say NO. Hopefully they will respect your new boundaries and become used to them. Gradually make GENTLE CONNECTIONS with other people which may also help with other issues with BPD such as EMPTINESS and building an IDENTITY Building MEANINGFUL CONNECTIONS is important to avoid loneliness which can also be a cause of anxiety. There is a link between the different personality characteristics of BPD. Rachel Harris's answer to How can someone with borderline personality disorder cope with the horrible feeling of emptiness? The following article covers some additional helpful suggestions : Healthy Coping Skills for People With Borderline Personality Disorder It is important to have therapy — DIALECTICAL BEHAVIOUR THERAPY ( DBT ). You cannot heal totally on your own. ASK FOR HELP FROM YOUR MEDICAL PRACTITIONER. Some of the content above was taken from a book called ‘Calming the emotional Storm’ by Sheri Van Dijk. Thanks Amie for your A2A

column1: What is the impact of losing your mum at a young age?
column3: Losing a mother at a young age can have profound and lasting effects on a child. The impact varies based on individual circumstances, but some common emotional, psychological, and social consequences include: Emotional EffectsGrief and Sadness: Children may experience intense feelings of loss and sadness, which can persist for years.Anxiety and Fear: The loss can create a sense of insecurity, leading to anxiety about the future and fear of losing other loved ones.Anger and Guilt: Children might feel anger towards the situation, themselves, or others. They may also experience guilt, wondering if they could have done something to prevent the loss.Psychological EffectsDevelopmental Challenges: The loss can disrupt normal development, potentially leading to difficulties in emotional regulation and coping mechanisms.Mental Health Issues: There is an increased risk of depression, anxiety disorders, and other mental health issues in bereaved children.Identity Formation: The absence of a mother figure can complicate a child's sense of identity and belonging, affecting their self-esteem and self-worth.Social EffectsIsolation: Children may feel isolated in their grief, especially if their peers do not understand their experience or if they feel different.Changes in Relationships: The loss can alter family dynamics and relationships with siblings, caregivers, and friends. Some children may become closer to remaining family members, while others might withdraw.Struggles with Trust: Experiencing such a significant loss can lead to difficulties in forming trusting relationships later in life.Long-term ConsequencesCoping Strategies: The way a child learns to cope with grief can influence their future responses to loss and adversity.Resilience: Some children develop resilience and coping skills that help them navigate future challenges, while others may struggle with ongoing emotional issues.Impact on Parenting: Adults who lost a parent at a young age may have different parenting styles, influenced by their own experiences of loss.Support and Healing Support from family, friends, and mental health professionals can play a crucial role in helping children process their grief. Open communication, counseling, and support groups can provide valuable resources for healing. Ultimately, the impact of losing a mother at a young age is complex and varies widely based on the individual's personality, support systems, and circumstances surrounding the loss.

column1: What is the history behind shaving one's head after the death of a loved one in some Hindu traditions?
column3: Tonsure (the act of cutting the hair or shaving the head) after the death of an elder member of the family is a age-old Hindu custom. In Hinduism, the underlying concept is that hair is a symbolic offering to the gods, representing a real sacrifice of beauty, hence shaving your head shows your grief for the departed soul. Also, Hair on the head is treated as an adornment and as a symbol of vanity. On the death of an elderly person in a family, the Hindus consider the children of the family not to be egoistic in nature but be humble, devoted and submitted to nature. So they need them to give up their adornment and vanity in humiliation. Source: Wikipedia

column1: What are some Korean eating customs that seem strange to foreigners?
column3: The rice bowl is always to be kept flat on the table, not held in your (left) hand above the table. Yet one of many 양반/yangban-class artifacts of years gone by, in that holding the rice bowl closer to your face is a sign of poverty and/or extreme hunger. It’s food to your mouth, not bowl to your face.The average Korean individual’s avoidance of “solo eating out” can seem a bit odd: eating out alone carries a subtle air of shame or pity, although less than it used to a decade or two ago. Sure, since eating out together is a highly socialized ritual for us all that can be quite enjoyable (and preferred over eating out solo), but I have not seen many cultures in which eating in a restaurant alone is so avoided whenever possible by the average individual.If you brought food to a place where others are present and it’s either announced or obvious that you have stuff ready to be eaten, then you better have enough for everyone. The whole “Sorry, I had to rush here and brought my breakfast with me…don’t mind me eating” thing is greatly frowned upon. Go to another room or outside to eat in private before entering a group environment.Rice is always placed on your left, soup bowl on your right. Reverse it and it means that death is coming, whether you plan on it or not.As the eating table 밥상/ bapsang in the average household was small yet for used for all family members, the first to eat would finish up swiftly, making room for the younger members of the family. There is no “may I be excused” culture, and rather it’s normal for the one to finish up to clear his/her place without a word.The actual reason that rice is considered essential in each meal (beyond being the grain of choice) is that it plays the role of (1) flavor to accompany all other dishes, since even the tastiest of meat “…is nothing without rice to accompany it”, and (2) to offset savory tastes, keeping the meal from tasting overly salty.Eating soup from the same pot, double-dipping soup spoons and all. 찌개 / jjigae (stew in a hot-pot) is a family affair, and it's not ucommon for households and even restaurants to have one single pot, off the heat, to share from. Although having individual bowls for soup (국 / guk, an entirely different broth concept) is commonplace, bowls for personal use of 찌개 / jjigae are mostly found at resturants in the West.Continuing the 찌개 / jjigae theme, many people are surprised to find out that 된장찌개 (soybean paste stew) is the third most common regular dish/food/entrée found almost daily in every Korean household (after rice and kimchi), a relative unknown to many Korean-BBQ-only aficionados.In the average Korean household, children are raised to be well aware that talking during a meal is discouraged. Koreans tend to eat quickly and move on from the meal to do other things, because the eating table is simply a place for eating (also see #5). In modern society it’s no longer as serious an issue as it used to be and parents do have “How was your day, Sonny?” moments, but it’s still not a place for extended conversation.
column9: There’s another interesting point about Korean BBQ and rice, that many westerners may not realize. After having one’s fill of some delicious BBQ meat cooked at the table (갈비, 불고기, 삼겹살, 주물럭), you will then be asked if you now want to have a “meal” (shiksa 식사). Now? A meal? That means finishing up with rice and a common bowl of 된장찌개 (soybean paste stew). No matter how much BBQ you eat, it’s still not really a “meal” (shiksa 식사) until you have rice.

column1: What's the most disturbing story in history?
column3: Death Chairs of the Poor ClaresStone seats at the putridarium in Clarisse Cemetery, Castello Aragonese (Castello Aragonese d'Ischia) For some cultures, death is the beginning of a purification process that starts with decomposition and ends with skeletonization.[1] These people believe that when a loved one takes his or her final breath, it is the beginning of a journey to the land of the ancestors, and the corpse must completely decay before a soul is considered purified and can ascend to the afterlife. The Aragonese Castle of Ischia is already unique in itself, standing on a tidal volcanic island connected to the main island of Ischia only by a causeway.[2] But one of the many rooms inside the castle has a particular history worthy of a gothic novel or horror movie. Built by Hiero I of Syracuse in 474 BC, two towers were built to circumvent Etruscan fleets from attacking Cumaea, situated on the mainland opposite Ischia.[3] Nearby volcanic eruptions from Monte Epomeo forced Hiero's garrisons from the island, which remained partially populated for decades.[4] In 326 BC, the fortress was captured by Romans, and later by the Parthenopeans (the ancient inhabitants of Naples).[5] In the following centuries, the island was occupied by various peoples, including Byzantines, Arabs, Normans, and Angevins.The Aragonese Castle The castle as it stands today was constructed in 1441 by Alfonso V of Aragon, who connected the rock to the island with a stone causeway instead of the previous wood bridge.[6] Contractors fortified the walls in order to defend the almost 2,000 families that occupied the island during the 16th through 18th centuries against devastating raids of Greek and Turkish pirates[7]. It was not until the 16th century that the Castle's infamous death chairs in the castle came into existence. Between 1575 and 1810 (when the remaining 16 Claires left the island), the Aragonese Castle was home to a community of nuns belonging to the Order of Saint Clare (known also as the Poor Clares).[8] The nuns had a convent in the castle (which was called the ‘Convento delle Clarisse’) and practiced a rather unusual burial practice.St. Clare of Assisi - Feast Day August 11 The Poor Clares were founded by Clare of Assisi in the year 1212. Little is known of Clare's early life, although popular tradition hints that she came from a fairly well-to-do family in Assisi.[9] At the age of eighteen, inspired by the preaching of Francis in the Asisi Cathedral, Clare ran away from home to join his community of friars at the Portiuncula, on the outskirts of town.[10] Although, according to tradition, her family wanted to take her back by force, Clare's dedication to holiness and poverty inspired the friars to accept her resolution. She was given the habit of a nun and transferred to several Benedictine monasteries, first at Bastia and then at Sant' Angelo di Panzo, for her monastic training.[11] By 1216, Francis was able to offer Clare and her companions a monastery adjoining the chapel of San Damiano, where she became abbess.[12] Clare's mother, two of her sisters and some other wealthy women from Florence joined her Order. Clare dedicated her order to the strict principles of Francis, setting a rule of extreme poverty far more severe than that of any female order of the time.[13] Whenever a nun died, her corpse would be taken to the cemetery, the ‘Cimitero delle Monache Clarisse’, an underground, windowless crypt carved out of limestone and placed in a sitting position on a ‘death chair’.[14] The corpses were left on these stone chairs to decompose. Each death chair had a hole on its seat, under which was placed a special vessel.[15] These were meant to collect the fluids that were produced during the decomposition process.A closer look at an individual death chair. (https://www.worldatlas.com/webimage/countrys/europe/itischiatwo.htm) After a year or two, the corpses transformed into piles of bones. The living Clares or a surviving family member of the deceased nun collected and cleaned the bones, whose whiteness was considered a symbol of purity.[16] The bones were eventually stored in an ossuary. The ossuary became their final resting place, representing the soul out of purgatory at peace and releasing mourners from their duty to mourn.[17] In fact, the ossuary frequently was placed on display in a public part of the church or at least was visible through a grate, serving as a reminder of souls in heaven.[18] This practice was not unique to Aragonese Castle, other monks and nuns from as far north as Milan to Sicily in the south practiced the same ritual in the area which is known as a putridarium.[19] The practice was part of broader, older tradition, known as “double death” or “double burial” where the moment of death was merely a rest during a longer journey to salvation.[20]Crypt at Chiesa Madre in Fiumedinisi (Consider the Putridarium | The Order of the Good Death) Surviving nuns would visit their dead sisters on a daily basis, praying and meditating on death and the ephemeral earthly life.[21] The process was an allegory for death. The time the corpse spent in the putridarium was thought of as analogous to the time a soul spent in purgatory (a temporary Hell), before being allowed into heaven.[22] It was believed that while the soul of a family member was in Purgatory, the living could atone for the sins of the deceased to ensure safe travel to the afterlife. They also believed that if they took good care of the decomposing remains the dead would look favorably on the living and reciprocate those good deeds.[23] When the bones were removed, cleaned, and bleached their whiteness was considered proof of the soul’s newfound purity as the sinful nature of humanity had been burnt off in hellfire.[24]Putridarium at San Sebastianello Whilst this may have been a good form of spiritual exercise, it would almost certainly have been detrimental to their physical health. Spending several hours in such an unhealthy place, the nuns often contracted serious illnesses, which in some cases were deadly.[25] Putridaria started falling out of use in the later part of the 17th century until their extinction in the early 20th century. Mostly because people believed they were unsanitary and that corpses emitted deadly effluvia or miasma.[26]Aragonese castle. The Bourbon prison In 1809, the Aragonese Castle was shelled by the British, during the Napoleonic Wars.[27] The damaged buildings were abandoned, and the convent was presumably one of them, as the Poor Clares left the castle in the following year. In 1823 on the orders of king Ferdinand VI of Bourbon dynasty, the castle was appropriated as a prison until 1860.[28] Whilst the convent is no longer home to a community of nuns, the ‘death chairs’ are a grim reminder of their presence in the Aragonese Castle.Footnotes[1] Morbid Monday: Resurrection through Decomposition[2] Castello Aragonese d'Ischia[3] "Hiero I of Syracuse" on Revolvy.com[4] Global Volcanism Program - Wikipedia[5] A History of Ischia[6] The Aragonese Castle[7] Aragonese Castle[8] Poor Clares — Cloistered Life[9] St. Clare of Assisi - Saints & Angels - Catholic Online[10] Poor Clare Sisters[11] History of the Poor Clare Order in Britain[12] http://Bellucci, Gualtiero (2005). Assisi, Heart of the World. Assisi: Edizioni Porziuncola.[13] Inside the Cloister[14] Le suore non sepolte e la meditazione sulla morte[15] Consider the Putridarium | The Order of the Good Death[16] http://Antonio Fornaciari, Valentina Giuffra e Francesco Pezzini, Processi di tanatometamorfosi: pratiche di scolatura dei corpi e mummificazione nel Regno delle Due Sicilie, Borgo San Lorenzo, All'insegna del giglio, 2008[17] symbolism of ossuaries christianity[18] The Aragonese Castle and Porto Ischia[19] Consider the Putridarium | The Order of the Good Death[20] Double Death[21] The Aragonese Castle and Porto Ischia[22] Consider the Putridarium | The Order of the Good Death[23] Morbid Monday: Resurrection through Decomposition[24] Apocalyptic Midnight Death Cult[25] http://Monte Epomeo[26] https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=https://twitter.com/goingmedieval/status/1040590009290694657%3Flang%3Den&ved=2ahUKEwjR153ksoHoAhUJHs0KHfovCigQFjATegQIBRAB&usg=AOvVaw3p69CkjF0X8JP1i1aLuhE2&cshid=1583344782679[27] Death Chairs of Poor Clares Cemetery[28] Aragonese castle. column1: Have you ever experienced culture shock in your own country? If so, what was the event or custom that was different or new to you?
column3: Oh yes I did. No surprises there considering that I am from India where we have cultural differences every 250km. 🙄 Anyway… I'll talk about the biggest one so far. It's about washing one's hair. Now while I am totally aware of all those scientific papers that vouch against washing hair everyday, I am from a culture where a person who has not washed their hair is viewed as plain dirty. Most people in Kerala wash their hair everyday. And taking a bath twice in a day is very common here. This is irrespective of religion, sex, caste, whatever. It's a Malayali thing. Here, people ask ‘kulicho?’ (Did you take a bath?) in the same tone as asking ‘kazhicho?’ (Did you eat?)… apparently they are of equal importance. And body washes are not baths according to Malayalis. That's just freshening up. A bath without washing one's hair is not a bath.This makes sense because Kerala is a humid area and people are generally very hairy all over. So it is imperative that people need to wash themselves daily if they don't want to make others faint with their body odour. And having thick hair on our heads ensures the same stinky scalps if we don't wash it every single day. This is why most Malayali people apply oil everyday to their hair. Otherwise so much of washing hair would have made our hair coarse and brittle. But we all know how naturally beautiful Malayali hair is.Anyyyyyway… there I go veering away from the topic… So in many parts of India, washing hair is NOT ALLOWED on certain days of the week. On Mondays, women should not wash their hair as it will put a burden on their daughters. Even mopping the house or clearing cobwebs isn't permitted on Mondays. On Tuesdays, people who are afflicted with the bad effects of Mars (Mangal / Chovva dosham) are not supposed to wash their hair.On Wednesdays, mothers of one son should not wash their hair because it may affect the son's health in a bad way. Also, newly married women are asked to wash their hair on Wednesdays to beget a son. 🤦🏻‍♀️ If only things were that easy! Oh and women shouldn't generally wash their hair on Wednesdays because some ill luck will befall their brothers.On Thursdays, many women don't wash their hair thinking that they will forfeit the blessings of Brihaspati (Jupiter) and Goddess Lakshmi and that they will lose all their wealth if they do. Even washing clothes is discouraged on Thursdays. Also their husband's age is reduced it seems. 😐 Saturday hair washes are a strict no-no because it can upset Shani (Saturn) it seems. Some cultures don't allow their women to wash their hair during pregnancy. There is a ritual hair wash after childbirth and then again they will have to go without washing their hair for six weeks after the child is born. Imagine going for 7 or 8 months without washing your hair? 😳 Apparently this custom was in place from the time when women used to bathe in rivers. It was believed that too much bending was not good during gestation. The contaminated water of the river was also a concern for the wellbeing of the unborn child and later the newborn one. Though those are things of the past, the tradition still remains. Why? I don't know.There are some cultures that don't allow people to wash their hair on their birthdays. And on death anniversaries of a family member. The belief is that when one washes the hair, the dirty water will fall into the mouth of the ancestors. Umm… okay then. And then you have Kerala…😅 Images: Google images
column9: I have lived in different regions across the length and breadth of India… and I have never heard about any of these superstitions regarding Hair-wash… Perhaps, the only one I am aware of is… girls/women should mandatorily wash and cleanse their hair/head/scalp after their menses are over, every month (Perhaps, this is not applicable to the Malayali folks but to most others who was their Hairs only once, twice or thrice a week, not everyday)

column1: Is it wrong for an atheist to refuse to attend a baptism?
column3: It is neither right nor wrong. It may be rude, depending on how you do it. Almost all cultures have ceremonies to mark the big transitions of life - birth, marriage, and death. Those who have religious beliefs will do so with rituals defined by their religion. But that doesn’t make a baptism an inherently religious ceremony. It is the universal ceremony of welcoming a child, performed according to the traditions of the Christian church. Were you to attend the baptism, you would not be announcing your Christianity, you would be respecting the parents right to celebrate their child’s birth according to their own beliefs. I remember one atheist who not only went to the baptism but accepted the role of godfather. He said that he read up what he was promising to do, and the only bit he had any difficulty with was promising to “renounce the Devil and all his works”. However, he decided he could have a good try at that, and accordingly accepted the role, as an atheist.
column9: Sorry, but baptism is a purely religious ceremony. That being said, I probably would go if invited because it can also be a meaningful personal experience for the parents as well.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: Coping is a tedious process. Some people can spend their entire lifetime coping with the loss of a Dear one. It is always advised to undergo the grieving process - starting with Denial and Isolation to Acceptance. This is the Kubler-Ross's 5 Stages of Loss and Grief. The detailed process is given here: The 5 Stages of Loss and Grief Most cultures have an inbuilt mechanism in the form of tradition, social buffers etc to cope with loss. The Hindu tradition requires the eldest son, presumed to be the closest one to the deceased, to undergo a ritual for 11 days(duration can vary in different cultures). The ritual requires cutting off most contact from the outside world, no materialistic indulgence, no sins(Alcohol, smoking etc.), a veg non fried diet etc. This essentially is the time for reflection and allows the person to collect himself in order to take care of affairs. This takes care of all extraneous stress agents like work pressure, bad eating habits, stressful contact with other people. This is also akin to the first stage of Kubler-Ross's 1st stage of coping with Loss and Grief - Denial and Isolation. I have read that coping with loss works best when you find something that needs your complete indulgence such as a work of art or finding your passion, getting a pet etc. The important thing to understand is that Grief and Loss only end with Acceptance. Only once you accept that you have lost your phone, will you buy a new one.

column1: Why do people cover the mirrors in the home of a person who has recently died?
column3: As per the ancient Indian Architectural science of Vaastu Shaastra, mirrors are regarded as surfaces that absorb energy. Hence Mirrors are usually veiled with curtains in Indian houses. Personal observation will tell you, that if you are in a room with a large mirror, you inadvertently and indiscreetly tend to look at your reflection more often than you normally would. Indian faith says that this habit encourages self absorption. Remember that legendary image of Narcissus looking engagingly at his own reflection?It saps you of your positive energy which can be otherwise channeled towards more productive tasks. I am not aware of this tradition of covering mirror after incidence of death, and whether it is practised in India. However, considering that many religions consider the soul to leave our physical body in energy form, this ritual may have an underlying intent to protect energies of the soul to ensure its free liberation.
column9: How does inadvertent glancing at mirror corroborate that mirror saps you of your positive energy? There is absolutely no scientific backing to it, and there is no better term then pseudo-science for what this theory is!

column1: What are some peculiarities of Chinese culture?
column3: Death rituals: The color worn for mourning is white, as opposed to black in the West. At the entrance to the tomb of Mao Zedong in Tiananmen Square, they sell white carnations which people place in front of a statue of Mao before entering the chamber where his body (or what passes for his body) lies under glass. When a family member dies, the body is always cremated (by law-see comment below) and the ashes are placed in a small box and the box is installed in a glass-fronted shelf (example above) about two to three feet wide that is part of a wall of such drawers in a large mausoleum. The one I had the privilege to visit was reserved for "heroes" of the revolution. Inside each shelf, family members place small objects that have some meaning associated with that person: a photo of the person as a soldier, a photo of a couple on their wedding day, along with miniatures of things as odd as telephones, automobiles, furniture, and synthetic flowers or plants. In the attached photo (if viewable), it is difficult to tell if there is an ashes container. In some cases, the deceased was a soldier killed in Korea or during some other conflict and in this case the body may not have been recovered. (Photo by Foster Winans. All rights reserved. Taken in Taiyuan, Shanxi Province.) Periodically, the family will visit the tomb, remove the contents, dust everything off, and put it all back as part of a ritual of bowing, etc. I witnessed this when traveling with Ji Chaozhu when we visited the tomb of his father and mother. It was quite loving and moving.

column1: What are some of the most weird tribal cultures?
column3: Ma'nene ritual is a traditional ritual in Tana Toraja, Sulawesi island. Indonesia. This ritual is a ritual in which corpses that are tens or even hundreds of years ago are removed from the grave to be cleaned and replaced with clothes and cloth. This traditional ritual is included in the traditional ceremony of death. This ritual begins with the arrival of family members to the grave in the form of a house where the corpse is stored to retrieve the bodies of their deceased parents. Before opening the coffin and lifting the corpse, the tribal leader would read a prayer in the ancient Toraja language and ask permission from the ancestors so that the community would receive grace and blessings every planting season until harvest. Then the body is cleaned using a brush after being removed from the coffin and the clothes are replaced with new cloth or clothes. After the new clothes are put on, the body is put back into the grave. The Ma'nene series of events closed with the gathering of family members at the Tongkonan traditional house to worship together. Usually the Ma'nene ritual is carried out simultaneously in one family or even in one village, so this tradition lasts quite a long time. The timing of the Ma'nene implementation is based on an agreement with the family and tribal chiefs through the Village Deliberation. This tradition is held once every three to four years to strengthen the relationship so that families who are far from where they live can see their parents or ancestors. Ma'nene Ritual pictures

column1: What is the significance of the 13th day death ceremony ritual in Indian culture?
column3: Why Hindus have last ceremony on 13 Days? Scientific reason: In olden days if anyone dies the cause of death was unknown. Therefore, easier way to check whether it is infectious virus or not, was to isolate the family. If any infectious virus or bacteria existed it doesn’t infect others and village would be saved. During this period visitors were not eating at the deceased house. Twelve days were enough to determine this. If no more symptoms in the family, on 13th day, a special ceremony was performed and the family members would cook food for relatives and friends. It is so similar to the quarantine at present. Emotional reason: Death of anyone in the family is always a severe mental shock. To relieve the mind from stress, and bring peace, due to the departure of the dear ones, the daily rituals were created by the thoughtful elders, so that gradually the mental agony gets reduced. Friends and neighbors bring food to the family to help them during this period. Also, it gives time to remember the person who died and pray God to keep the soul in peace. Thirteen day rituals are estimated time for reaching normalcy. Safety reason: Travel is also prohibited during this period. This makes perfect sense as driving/travel is always risky with troubled mind. Practical reason: This time is also believed to be utilized to plan for future or how to proceed further in the absence of the deceased person. During this ceremony the responsibilities of the household are passed to the eldest son in front of all the friends and family.. Secondly, a 13 day gap between death and the last ceremony allows more people to attend the event ceremony and this would presumably bring more benefits for the dead person. This would have been an important point in the days before trains, cars and planes were available. Religious reason: It is believed that after death, the soul of the dead person hangs around for 13 days because it is unable to break the relationship with its physical boy, which it was associated with for so any years. (It does not make any sense to me as the body is cremated as soon as possible after the death of the person) It is said that it takes one God’s day for soul to reach His abode. Also, it is said that God’s one day is equal to our one year which means our twelve months. So the mourning period is designed to 12 days and the last ceremony is performed on the 13th day. Some Hindu’s do some ceremony every month to follow the God’s one year theory.

column1: Where did the aristocracy, that were not captured, flee to at the fall of the Byzantine Empire?
column3: Immediately before and after the fall of the Constantinople, several prominent nobles fled to Italy. By the 15th century, the Italian city-states of Genoa and Venice among others had displaced Byzantium as the primary trading powerhouses of the Mediterranean. The ascendancy of budding Italian mercantilism and enterprise ensured that wealthy seekers of fortune and power had to look West, not to their Eastern homes, to broaden their connections and influence. Therefore, many Byzantine noble families had some sort of connection to residents of Italian city-states, whether with bankers, fellow nobles, or diplomatic and political allies. After the fall of Constantinople, such connections came in handy for aristocratic refugees (Harris 2010). Consider, for instance, the flight of the prominent Byzantine family of Notaras to Italy. Its head, Loukas Notaras, was the megas doux (grand duke) of Byzantium before he was executed by sultan Mehmed II along with the members of many other prominent Byzantine families. Luckily for his surviving children, however, Notaras was the scion of a family that shared business connections with the Genoese and possessed Genoese (as well as Venetian) citizenship; he had inherited an immense fortune that was deposited in the Bank of St. George of Genoa as well. Thus, Genoese authorities were certainly well-disposed to pay a ransom for two of Notaras’ four surviving daughters, who were imprisoned and enslaved after the fall of Constantinople at the urging of Anna Notaras, another of Notaras’ daughters who actually escaped Constantinople before it fell. After their freedom, the daughters were able to stay in Genoa, although Anna for one later moved to Venice. As mentioned, the Italians of Venice, Genoa and Rome played an important part in aiding, rescuing, and sponsoring the aristocratic family members who did get captured and were put up for ransom. Those living in Italy connected with captured aristocrats could persuade local governmental and even church authorities to seek out the captured, whose ransoms would then be paid. It was a luxury only the aristocracy could afford. In addition, immediately before the fall of Constantinople, a few rescue ships sent from Venice and Genoa were able to carry a few refugees to Italy in safety. It was mostly notables, of course, who managed to squeeze onto those ships' rosters; it was on them that two of Notaras' four daughters were able to escape the fall of Constantinople.A view of the Scuola dei Greci, a cofraternity for Greeks established in Venice in 1498, to whose church the aforementioned Anna Notaras donated several of her Byzantine icons - where they still remain today. Italy was the natural destination for many Byzantine refugees - though most were not aristocrats and in fact had to beg for sponsorship - because it had begun hosting a large number of Greek émigrés since the Sack of Constantinople in 1204. By 1453, significant Greek communities were already established in major cities like Florence, Milan, Rome and Venice. The Greeks - numbering over 1,000 in Venice alone -, while not embraced by the Italians, certainly kept Byzantine Greek culture and traditions alive in Italy; they were relatively few in number but could be influential and vocal. Italian cities were thus particularly attractive to refugees in need of a new home, and in fact housed a large number of prominent Greek community leaders and scholars such as the aforementioned Anna Notaras, the Catholic cardinal Bessarion, and the scholar Demetrios Chalkonkodyles (brother of the historian Laonikos Chalkonkodyles).Engraving of Basileos Bessarion, the Latin Patriarch of Constantinople-in exile. Before the fall of Constantinople, he relocated to Rome, where he was influential in religious affairs, promoted Greek scholarship, and advocated for Byzantine exiles and refugees. What of the Byzantine ruling family of Palaiologos? Where did its members end up? Well, the Palaiologos family was in a decidedly scattered state after the fall of Constantinople. The brothers Thomas and Demetrios, brothers of the fallen last Byzantine emperor Constantine XI, ruled until 1460 as Despotes of the Morea (what is now called the Peloponnese region in Greece), the rump state of Byzantium. In 1460, Mehmed II conquered it and Thomas fled to Italy, where he was recognized as the heir to the Byzantine throne, while Demetrios, favored by Mehmed, was appointed to govern a town in Thrace until he fell out of favor and was sent into a harsh but paid exile in Hadrianople, the former Ottoman capital. The son of Thomas, Andreas, inherited his father's title but was crushed by debt; he traveled to Russia and around Europe looking for money to no avail, and was forced to sell his imperial title twice - first to king Charles VIII of France and then to that famous couple, Ferdinand and Isabella of Castile. Other members of the family fared better. Thomas' daughters certainly did, compared to their brother. One daughter, Helena Palaiologina, became the Despotess of Serbia in 1456, de-facto ruling Serbia after her husband died in 1457 until the Ottomans conquered it two years later. She then became a nun. Another daughter, Sophia (Zoe) Palaiologina, fled the fall of Constantinople to her father's domain of the Morea, was called to Rome after it fell, and finally married prince Ivan III of Moscow in 1472. In Moscow, Zoe promoted Byzantine court ritual, entertained the idea that Moscow was a successor to Rome, and eventually became the grandmother of Ivan the Terrible. Finally, two surviving nephews of Constantine XI actually were unable to escape Constantinople after its fall. They were taken into Mehmed II's court at Hadrianople, raised as Muslims, and indeed both became high ranking, favored courtiers; one nephew, Mesih, even became Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire.A fresco by Pintoriccio depicting Thomas Palaiologos, one of the two last Despotes of Morea and de jure Byzantine Emperor until his death in 1465. Some Byzantine aristocrats fled to other parts of Europe, as far as England and Russia, even. Some fled to other Christian kingdoms in the Balkans, like Serbia and Bulgaria. Many who did not want to travel far settled down on nearby islands with substantial Greek populations like Crete or the Morea. The vast majority of refugees, however, were not aristocrats with connections to other European states, and had little choice, if at all, in their living conditions after the the fall of Constantinople. The vast majority of aristocrats did not live to escape Constantinople before Mehmed II executed them. A large number of former Byzantines who did survive, particularly commoners, did not end up in Rome or Venice but in Hadrianople as prisoners and slaves, and died as prisoners and slaves. In the 1470s, Mehmed II reneged on his early policy of stamping out the traditional Byzantine aristocracy and instead hoped to install the former Byzantine Greek Christian nobility in his realm once more where they could be kept close under his watch. He invited the few remaining members of former Byzantine aristocratic families, such as those of Sphrantzes and Laskaris, back to Constantinople after promising them full protection. There, some of them became members of Mehmed’s court, while others went about their lives almost like they had never moved. Thus, a sizable Greek populace continued to be maintained in Constantinople, and many aristocrats who had initially fled to other places eventually returned there. Mehmed’s son and successor Bayezid II upheld Mehmed’s policy, encouraging Greeks who had fled Constantinople to return.
