column1: Why are Eastern European countries like Poland and Hungary so reluctant to allow immigrants from the Middle East into their territories?
column3: There are a number of reasons, not all of them related to the type of migrant. Firstly there is a wide perception that Merkels flinging open of the doors of Germany was a performative gesture to cleanse Germany of its past reputation. To this countries like Britain and France which have colonial history and sins of their own in relation to the middle east and third world enthusiastically join in because there is a level of social guilt that they look to abate through these actions. Countries like Poland often feel no obligation to take part in these performances, having been colonised themselves for roughly 200 years by three imperial powers, then Nazis, then Communists - give or take a decade or so in between. What it can feel like is that there is an accusation from the West that Poland is not being ‘civilised’ in not taking part in the same cleansing ritual, however Poland does not have the same history, or the same guilt, it has not reaped the benefits of imperial brutality, and being forced to partake in this ritual in the same way would be quite insulting. it is in some ways another form of colonisation; forcing another country to share in your historical guilt, and scapegoating them as ‘racist’ when they reject this burden. We see this also in another form with ‘Polish death camps’ written often in the media, then decrying Polish attempts to legislate against this as holocaust denial. Beyond this, Prussia and Nazi Germany were two of the colonising powers at different times during the disappearance of Poland from the map - both attempted to destroy the Polish nation and culture. Can you imagine what it then feels like to have the successor state then use soft power to step over your hard won national sovereignty? All in all this feels equivalent to someone performing a murder and rape of your family members then getting angry at you because you don’t want to help them clean up the blood and semen out of their carpet. Framing it as being only about race misses a massive piece of the cultural and historical context between Germany and Poland.

(Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose wanted ruthless dictatorship in India for 20 years - Times of India ►) Can you call him a villain? It was his way of nation-making and for him he was right. His perception of nation-building was different from others, that’s the thing. Now let’s talk about Godse... Nathuram Vinayakrao Godse was born into a Maharashtrian Chitpavan Brahmin family. Most of us know about Peshwa BajiRao who also belonged to the same community. It is said that Chitpavan brahmins are very protective of their culture, ritual, and motherland. Be that as it may, Godse dropped out of high school and became an activist with RSS and Hindu Mahasabha.He participated in protest marches including the protests of 1938–39 in Bhagyanagar against the Nizam of Hyderabad who was trying to turn Hyderabad into an Islamic state for which he was jailed for a short duration. In 1946, Godse left the RSS and Hindu Mahasabha over the issue of the partition of India. His relations with many members of the RSS soured, and he felt that the RSS was softening in its stance. Neither Godse nor any Hindu organization was with Gandhi. Why so?Let’s see some statements of Gandhi Ji “We should dispassionately think where we are drifting. Hindus should not harbor anger in their hearts against Muslims even if the latter wanted to destroy them. Even if the Muslims want to kill us all we should face death bravely. If they established their rule after killing Hindus we would be ushering in a new world by sacrificing our lives.” He advised to Sindh Hindus during partition “I said that you should suffer bravely, but non-violently unto death. But if you cannot do that and must make a disgraceful surrender of all including honor, your womenfolk, and religion, in that case, the only safe and proper course for you to take is migration, not singly, but of all the Hindus and other non-Muslims” There is no doubt that Gandhi had his own way of nation-building and he wanted everyone to follow it. Let me give an example: If you are going with an old man through a jungle and suddenly a lion attacks you. What will you do? You will defend yourself. Isn’t it? But if the old man with you says, ‘See, finally we all shall die one day. What’s wrong to help the animal and become it’s prey now?’’ Will you connect yourself to this idea of the old man? This is a good idea but only for that old man as he has no strength left to defend himself and he has already lived his life. But as a young man, you might not connect with this idea. In Bhagavad Gita Lord Krishna also says to Arjuna in chapter 2, shloka 33 “But If you will not fight this righteous war, then failing in your duty and losing your honor you will incur sin.” Hence we can say Gandhi was fighting in the way that he considers righteous. Bose was fighting in the way which he considered righteous or his Dharma ( righteousness). And Godse was fighting in the way that he considered righteous. You also can see in Mahabharata, how each individual was fighting for a cause which he considered to be Dharma. Karna had his ways, Duryodhana had his ways and others had also their ways. Gandhi Ji preached ‘Ahimsa Paramo Dharma’ which let us know the essence of non-violence. But on the other hand, Godse perhaps was following the opposite way which was right for him or his Dharma. Godse never supported Gandhi’s ideas and approached Gandhi on 30 January 1948 during the evening prayer at 17:17 on 30 January 1948. He first bowed down to Gandhi and shot him in the chest three times at point-blank range.Now Before Godse was hanged, he gave his final statements where he spoke from his heart about what he believed and the reason of Killing Gandhi Ji. ‘’Gandhi is being referred to as the Father of the Nation. But if that is so, he had failed his paternal duty inasmuch as he has acted very treacherously to the nation by his consenting to the partitioning of it. I stoutly maintain that Gandhi has failed in his duty. He has proved to be the Father of Pakistan. His inner-voice, his spiritual power and his doctrine of non-violence of which so much is made of, all crumbled before Jinnah’s iron will and proved to be powerless. Briefly speaking, I thought to myself and foresaw I shall be totally ruined, and the only thing I could expect from the people would be nothing but hatred and that I shall have lost all my honor, even more, valuable than my life, if I were to kill Gandhiji. But at the same time, I felt that the Indian politics in the absence of Gandhiji would surely be proved practical, able to retaliate, and would be powerful with armed forces. No doubt, my own future would be totally ruined, but the nation would be saved from the inroads of Pakistan. People may even call me and dub me as devoid of any sense or foolish, but the nation would be free to follow the course founded on the reason which I consider to be necessary for sound nation-building.” “I have to say with great regret that Prime Minister Nehru quite forgets that his preachings and deeds are at times at variances with each other when he talks about India as a secular state in season and out of season, because it is significant to note that Nehru has played a leading role in the establishment of the theocratic state of Pakistan, and his job was made easier by Gandhi’s persistent policy of appeasement towards the Muslims. I now stand before the court to accept the full share of my responsibility for what I have done and the judge would, of course, pass against me such orders of sentence as may be considered proper. But I would like to add that I do not desire any mercy to be shown to me, nor do I wish that anyone else should beg for mercy on my behalf. My confidence about the moral side of my action has not been shaken even by the criticism leveled against it on all sides. I have no doubt that honest writers of history will weigh my act and find the true value thereof some day in future.” All these things are in their places and the reader should use his own conscience before jumping into any conclusions. column1: How does Hinduism perceive filial piety and ancestor worship? How is it different from the Confucian perspective, both in nature and degree?
column3: Hinduism perceives filial piety and ancestor worship as very important. The Vedas, the authoritative texts of Hinduism, give mandatory rites due to the Gods (Deva Yagnya) and to the ancestors (Pitri Shraddha); these are the first two obligations that we Hindus have. The Veda tells us to treat our mother as a god, our father as a god, our Guru as a god, and our guest as a god. However, it also tells us to follow only their good deeds and not others; if our parents or ancestors have done bad deeds, we should not carry these forward into the future, but only their positive points. Almost every Hindu scripture states that good, virtuous people show respect, honor, and reverence to their parents and observe the Vaidik rituals of filial piety and ancestor worship. Growing up as a Hindu, going to the temple it was common for the priest to say “Bow to your parents” at a certain step in rituals. Often my mother was there in person and I would bow directly to her; otherwise it is done mentally. Hindu ancestor worship involves lots of rituals, often with food offerings, which are quite important in many Hindu homes. The basic ritual format of ancestor worship is as follows: when a family member dies, the family observes a mourning period generally lasting ten, eleven, or thirteen days, varying by community. The family member’s death date is fixed on the Hindu lunar calendar. On its first anniversary the family performs the Tarpana ritual, in which they prepare the departed person’s favorite food and offer it to them in remembrance and love. There are also certain days when the ancestral spirits, called the Pitris, are said to come in the form of birds, especially crows, to eat the offerings, and so families offer the departed person’s favorite food to crows on these days. Often this is extended to additional wild animals, especially birds, and some families do it every day. Many Hindu families offer the first cooked meal of the day to crows, considering this to be offering the first share of food to their ancestors, since whenever ancestral offerings are made, the ancestors must be fed before any of the living humans eat. Cows are also fed in this way. There is also the Shraddha feast, a small feast of very specific ritualistic preparations, which is offered to certain brahmins in honor of the ancestors.Many Hindus hang clay pots full of freshly cooked food from trees as offerings for the ancestors. Usually trees outside the village are selected for this, as it is considered dangerous to go near such a tree at night. Ashvattha (Pipal) trees are the most auspicious type of tree to use. Even in modern culture, ancestors play a central role in a typical Hindu family. Most Hindu families believe that the spirits of their ancestors watch over and protect them, and they maintain connections with them, even if they don’t perform all of the orthodox rituals. In modern cities, where many Hindus no longer live in the traditional household arrangement with a large extended family together in a home, ancestor worship is no longer as elaborately performed by many Hindus, especially those with busy modern jobs. Often it is being done in simplified and more minimal form. But many hundreds of millions of Hindus still live in rural villages, where they usually still perform the full ancient rites (and some do so even in modern cities, especially housewives or retirees). It is still not rare to find Hindus who regard ancestor offerings as equally important as the lives of their living family members.Certain days in the year are especially connected with the ancestors - the waning moon in general, the dark moon day (Amavasya) in particular, and a certain period of Shraddha days in autumn, as well as the lunar anniversary of specific family members’ deaths. Many Hindu families keep these days sacred and do not schedule other big events on them, but dedicate them to the ancestors.As a Hindu, I am no expert on Confucianism. I do know that Confucians worship ancestral tablets in their home. Many Hindus do keep and worship ancestral shrines in their home, such as a small table with a photo of the deceased, where a light is kept lit and offerings like incense are regularly made. I have not seen it like Confucian tablets with nine generations’ names written on it. I also know that a lot of Confucian ancestor worship focuses on graves. This is not shared in Hinduism, which generally does not make graves, but cremates the dead and disperses their ashes in rivers.

column1: How does the idea of "family honor" work in cultures that use the principle?
column3: Specific to historical China, “family honor” could mean the reputation owned by a family at a place. To understand how it works, one has to know the history and culture behind it. In historical China, rural areas were organized and managed by elite families. Emperors’ governance never reached to these areas. The government officials had to stay in cities and were forbidden to enter rural areas for any reason. For every village, there was a big family or several big families in charge of everything. They were responsible for children’s education, scheduled harvesting, conflicts resolution, birth and death rituals, public transportation, or even armed activities against hostile villages. These big families were elected by the villagers and certain qualifications should be met. For example, the quantity of family members, the wealth and power they could wield to protect public interests and the reputation their family members have all fall in the consideration. So where does the reputation comes from? For example, a family has a son who is a government official but another family hasn’t such a son. Although they may equal each other in other aspects, the former would gain more reputation than the latter. The former family would be more suitable for the position to run the village. Therefore, it becomes quite important for such families to possess and nurture “family honor” because that is where power and wealth come from. For thousands of years China has relied upon such societal systems to prosper and evolve, where “family honor” deserves more scrutinization.

column1: Why is the education system in the US very bad compared to other countries and how could other countries serve as a sort of model to the US with regard to improving? In other words how could the US learn from other countries?
column3: The problems of American education are overwhelmingly the problems of American culture, which right now look like this:Materialistic philosophy. This is by no means a uniquely American problem, but it’s on full display in the U.S. With social media and political tribalism, it’s one of the three main mental illnesses destroying American lives. I’m including universities in this, not just high schools, but I agree fully with Alain De Botton, who helped me with some of my own problems with low self-esteem re: the annoying American question “what do you do?” Schools don’t do enough to counter the sick fear of Americans that an ordinary life is humiliating and that we only have social value if we’re “extraordinary.” (I highly recommend two of his moving talks included here in a footnote.[1] [2] De Botton said some of the most important things that need to be said about Americans today, and he said it kindly, unlike many of our immature critics on Quora.)I have no direct experience of Germany’s educational system, but with the caveat that I do not know that system directly, I really like the idea that students can pursue technical trades in Germany’s version of high school and pursue perfectly honorable lives at “nuts-and-bolts” jobs. I may be romanticizing this: there must be classism and disdain in German society, too, but something in their approach to education at least tries to work against it. Americans have become disdainful toward people seen as “the help,” because we’re too prone to assign you value based on your worth and your resume. (Mileage may vary based on distance from New York, Silicon Valley and our extremely arrogant universities.)Another problem is the unwillingness of smart Americans to become teachers. I have several friends and family members who left teaching in their 30’s because of the annoying bureaucracy in schools and because they were losing authority over their students’ behavior. One of my cousins left teaching to become a pharmacy tech. Another cousin left to become a janitor. They’re happier now. The U.S. absolutely creates some smart people, but they frequently avoid going into teaching. Why? It’s not just the pay.More visiting speakers. Bring them as often as possible. Kids get tired of their teachers. (A lot of teachers aren’t very good.) But there’s a lot of interesting people who’ve lived interesting lives and have real-world experience. Invite them to talk at a school. Eva Kor, a well-known survivor of Auschwitz and a “Mengele twin,” lived in my hometown. She spoke at my high school once. Eva was obviously more interesting than the regular history teacher.iPhones. Ban them in schools. Even the U.S. Surgeon General came out recently with a scathing report directly blaming phones and social media for the enormous spike in suicidal ideation and nosediving self-esteem in young people. iPhones and social media caused the worst global mental health crisis in 100 years — and not just in youth, but they’re especially effected by it. Several school districts in the big, bad state of Florida have banned student use of iPhones during school hours, with enormous success. These students are now socializing, talking and looking less unhappy by the minute. To me, it’s far less important that American children know the capital of China than that they’re not committing suicide because “I’m not as pretty” as some vapid “babe” showing off her butt on TikTok. What are your priorities? Relative trivia? Or more critical human values?Math and hard sciences are overemphasized. But frankly, art and literature can be, too. Cooking should be introduced as a class. Cooking builds problem-solving skills, self-esteem (it’s hard and gives you a sense of real accomplishment when you master it), and teaches healthy eating habits. It promotes community and cooperation with other students because kitchens are often community spaces. It’s also fun. Children need to have fun at school. Math is rarely fun, I’m sorry. Eating and the rituals around it are unbelievably important.Introduce World Religion classes. It can be taught fairly. This matters. Humans are interested in these questions. They’re valid questions. Ignorance of other people’s beliefs creates bad citizens. Kids are also terrified of death: it is valid to listen to what other humans have had to say about death. Educating people about religion does not have to be indoctrination.There should be more animals in school. Veterinary classes. I’m not saying this to promote “safe spaces.” (I’m very skeptical of padded cry rooms.) I’m saying that animals are good because animals tend not to judge you — OK, cats judge you sometimes — and kids feel horribly judged today, mostly by each other. Teenagers are really, really interested in animals, even in the age of Zuckerberg when it seems like teenagers are interested in virtually nothing. I’m sure some scowling old Gradgrinds reading this will scoff at me and bark that “we need to make sure kids are successful for the job market!” (Rawr.) Why are you so cold and uncreative? I want kids who have warm hearts (correction: I want kids who keep the warm hearts they had when they were five.) I know schools can’t exactly have a horse farm outside, but take kids to one. Go on a lot of field trips. I’m not “Grizzly Man” here, but humans and animals are not meant to live on two ends of a sad divide. Animals certainly had a role to play in the first 99% of human history. We’ve created a world with fewer of them, and now we’re ridiculously lonely. That feeds our completely unnecessary and frankly stupid mental health crisis — in the United States and in many other “developed” countries.More gym class. Gym class is really, really good. Not just for the body. For the brain. “But there’s not enough time!” So after all our time-saving devices, there’s less time than ever? Got it.If anyone’s suggestion to improve American schools is just “more facts!” then honestly I don’t know where you’re coming from. What’s your goal? The creation of a data filing cabinet, or of a human being? One of the virtues of the United States is that we don’t have a national education system. We only have states and local school districts, all of which have some freedom to teach as they see fit. So if my projects seem too ambitious, they’re actually not. One school district could implement some of these changes and that would be helpful. Change doesn’t have to start at the national level.Footnotes[1] Materialism | Alain De Botton[2] We Desperately Need Peace of Mind in This Troubled World | Alain De Botton

column1: What are the most bizarre unsolved historical mysteries?
column3: Windeby I -originally dubbed the ‘Windeby Girl’. (Windeby Girl and Weerdinge Couple) In 1952, on the Windeby estate near Schleswig, Germany, two bodies were found in a small bog, beginning decades of speculation into the supposed tragic love affair of the two corpses.[1] The owners of the estate decided to harvest peat from a bog to be sold as fuel. Almost immediately, the peat cutters discovered the remains of a male (originally thought to be a 14-year-old female- Windeby Girl) now known as Windeby I.[2] Despite ceasing work immediately, the machinery used for the peat cutting had already severed one of the body’s legs, one of its feet, as well as one of its hands.[3] Shortly thereafter, a second body (a middle-aged man known as Windeby II) was found sixteen feet away. An examination revealed that he had been strangled with a hazel branch and then placed in the bog. Sharpened, forked branches had been jammed into the peat around him to ensure he did not rise from his watery tomb.[4] Small twigs of flowering heather were found on the woolen headband, indicating that burial occurred in late summer.[5] Professor P. V. Glob (who studied Windeby I after its discovery) believed the body to be a fourteen year old girl. Glob described the body's position in the peat:She lay on her back, her head twisted to one side, her left arm outstretched.... The right arm was bent in against the chest, as if defensively, while the legs were lightly drawn up, the left over the right. The head, with its delicate face, and the hands, were preserved best: the chest had completely disintegrated and the ribs were visible.... The hair, reddish from the effects of the bog acids but originally light blond, was of exceptional fineness but had been shaved off with a razor on the left side of the head.[6]Upper body of Windeby I. ( CC BY-SA 3.0 ) The exquisite preservation of these corpses comes courtesy of some peculiar bog chemistry. Bogs begin when moss dominates a low-lying patch of land, causing the soil to become waterlogged and acidic. Bacteria have a difficult time surviving in such conditions and thus can’t break down the dead moss and other vegetation, which instead simply pile up and become peat.[7] But most bogs cannot pile their peat layers very far above the surrounding land, because the bog plants depend on minerals from groundwater to survive. If the bog rises too high, the plants can’t reach the nutrients they need. Along the coast, however, the vegetation can get minerals in the spray that comes off the ocean, and thus the bogs can grow into raised domes a few yards high.[8] Cut off from groundwater, these bogs depend on rainfall, which they soak up like sponges. A corpse in such a place can stay moist for centuries, but it’s protected from bacteria by the harsh chemistry of the bog water. And the tannins produced by the moss turn a corpse’s skin to leather.[9] There were no grave goods found with the Windeby I bog body, apart from a woolen band covering the eyes and a collar around the neck.[10] The woolen strip was woven using the sprang technique[11] from brown, yellow, and red threads., possibly used to cover the corpse’s eyes after death, or to hold the hair back, in which case the band would have slipped down over the eyes due to the shrinkage of the body.[12] One German scholar suggested that Windeby I may have been blindfolded at burial "to protect the living from the gaze of the dead." [13] Based on the body’s slender build, it was initially assumed that it belonged to a female. In 1970, the body was reexamined, yet so little of it remained, scientists could not say with certainty that the body was female.[14] This misconception continued until 2007, when a re-assessment of the remains using DNA analysis suggested that it was more likely that the Windeby I body belonged to a male. Heather Gill-Robinson, a biological anthropologist in charge of the German Mummy Project in Mannheim, examined the skeleton, which had been removed from the Windeby bog body during conservation.[15]"My examination of the skull and the pelvis suggests that this person was a young male," says Gill-Robinson. "Although I'm not really sure that I was the first person to test the idea, I'm certainly the first to have explored it in the 21st century, using modern technology and perspectives." [16]Reconstruction process of the face of Windeby I (Other Bog Bodies: Windeby I) Interestingly, Windeby I's head was partly shaved.[17] This was not part of the ritual associated with his demise, but rather that one side of the head was more exposed to oxygen than the other, causing the hair on that side of the head to experience a greater rate of decomposition. Alternatively, the hair might have been accidentally damaged by the peat cutters or during excavation. Reconstructing what went on so long ago is more than usually difficult. The civilisations that produced the bog bodies left no written accounts of themselves; little is known about their customs and religions, and much of the evidence comes from outsiders who had their evidence at third hand, and saw the rites they wrote about as evidence of barbarism.[18] Increasingly sophisticated computer programs and use of medical technology such as CT scans, radiocarbon dating and 3-D imaging have resulted in additional and potentially more accurate answers to the mysteries of the peat bog mummies. Yet, archaeologists continue to turn to the Roman historian Tacitus in search for insight into the circumstances surrounding the death of the Windeby bog bodies. Tacitus in Germania, praised the tribes who lived beyond Rome’s north-eastern borders for the straightforward nature of their justice.[19] According to Tacitus (whose source was possibly the accounts of traders who had visited the north), members of the Germanic tribes could:“Launch an accusation before the Council or bring a capital charge. The punishment varies to suit the crime. The traitor and deserter are hanged on trees, the coward, the shirker and the unnaturally vicious are drowned in mirey swamps under a cover of wattled hurdles.” [20]The murdered bodies that emerged from bogs millennia later seemed to confirm Tacitus’ judgment. The majority of the bog people had not died of natural causes. Most had been hung--the ropes were still around their necks--hit over the head, or stabbed.[21] Some, like Grauballe Man, suffered particularly cruel treatment, with broken bones, slit throats, and crushed skulls.[22] A number of the women had had one side of their heads shaved, a sign of disgrace at least since medieval times, suggesting to some that they were being punished for infidelity.[23]Tollund Man (Were the Mysterious Bog People Human Sacrifices?) These people, archaeologists proposed, had clearly committed some terrible offense and this savage execution was their sentence. Tacitus seemed to support that view: basically, the Germanic tribes that lived beyond the Rhine had the custom of punishing wrong-doers by having their executed bodies staked in bogs.[24] Yet some bodies, like that of Tollund Man, were treated more gently by their handlers, who even dug them graves in the bogs rather than simply tossing them in.[25] Some researchers claimed that Tollund Man’s noble visage suggested he could not have been a criminal. Rather, he represented a chosen sacrifice to a bog deity.[26] One Danish archaeologist proposed that the bog bodies were sacrificed to an earth goddess called Nerthus.[27] This theory as well was based on the writings of Tacitus, who described a rite in which slaves were made to pull a wagon carrying Nerthus’ image through the fields.[28] Afterwards the car, the vestments, and the divinity herself are purified in a secret lake. Slaves perform the rite, who are instantly swallowed up by its waters. However, it is worth noting that Tacitus’s writings on the customs practiced by the Germanic tribes were based on second or even third hand accounts. In addition, Tacitus intended to shame his Roman readers for what he perceived as decadent behavior.[29] Therefore, the accuracy of this ancient source may be called into question. Another challenge to this interpretation is that the Windeby I bog body displayed no signs of trauma, as one would expect if the person were executed. Instead, the remains exhibit growth interruptions in the bones, indicating a sick young man who may have died from repeated bouts of illness or malnutrition, which finally resulted in death.[30] For decades after their discovery, similar confusion surrounded the Weerdinge Couple, two bog bodies found in 1904 in the Netherlands. The pelvis of one was preserved, making it easy to identify him as a man, while the other was identified as a woman because of its slightly smaller stature.[31] Their intimate pose—one body seems to be gently holding the other—touched people, and they were soon nicknamed Mr. and Mrs. Veenstra ("veen" is Dutch for bog), or Joan and Darby.[32]Weerdinge Couple (Windeby Girl and Weerdinge Couple) But the Weerdinge Couple is actually two men. Some wondered if this could be proof for the Roman historian Tacitus's claim that Germanic tribes punished homosexuals by executing them and throwing them into bogs.[33] But his supposed knowledge of this practice is at least 150 years removed from the time of the Weerdinge men's death.Perhaps the men were sacrificed together (one man's stomach was sliced open at the time of his death), were comrades who had fallen in battle, or were family members buried at the same time; for now, their relationship remains uncertain.[34] With Tacitus in hand, for a long time researchers believed that the two bog bodies belonged to an adulterous couple who were caught and punished.[35] Despite the publication of recent analyses, many continue to adhere to this misidentification.[36] Even the recent publication of the results from the radiocarbon dating of the two bodies from Windeby revealed that they are not contemporaneous, and that the so-called “male lover ” was in fact 300 years older than Windeby I.[37] Windeby I has been radiocarbon-dated to between 41 BCE and 118 CE.[38] From their earliest discoveries, bog bodies have generated fascination and speculation in equal parts. Northern Europe's answer to Egyptian and Peruvian mummies are typified as individuals who either willingly or unwillingly met a violent demise as part of an unknown ritual. When two bog bodies are recovered in close proximity, a romantic relationship in this world and the next is often implied.[39] Time after time, advancements in scientific analyses have illustrated how fallible those assumptions are. At the time of their discovery, the immediate classification of the Windeby bog bodies based on the assumption that the smaller corpse was female would not have been overly questioned. It was only a short leap to make the assumption that the close proximity of two bog bodies implied a male/female intimate relationship, and not one of genetically related family members. A similar scenario applies to the Weerdinge Couple. It would be decades before scientific advancements led to the reclassification of the two bodies as both being male, not female and male as initially stated. Chronologically, these couples are often separated from one another over hundreds of years, reflecting the continuation of long-standing communal rituals, practiced over time. It is perhaps the implied ritual aspect that scholars find most intriguing and mystifying. Based on first discoveries of bog bodies, it was believed that the individuals died under violent circumstances to appease angry gods. Scientific advancements in the last decade demonstrate the need to revisit, reanalyse and revise earlier perceptions. While many may have died in a ritualistic manner, some may have died of natural causes or simply fell into the bog and perished. Now that science has unlocked the secrets of bog body formation, it is time to turn our attention to reconstructing these individuals’ lives, identities and deaths without imposition of societal mores.Footnotes[1] https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&source=web&rct=j&url=http://mspace.lib.umanitoba.ca/bitstream/1993/20275/1/Gill-Robinson_The_iron.pdf&ved=2ahUKEwjniYXw2NzrAhUDCs0KHd53Aow4ChAWMAF6BAgJEAE&usg=AOvVaw0Tnh8AFCeYyvbk3eRSPmh1[2] Other Bog Bodies: Windeby I[3] Windeby girl[4] The Bog Bodies at the Schleswig-Holstein Landesmuseum[5] Expedition Magazine - Penn Museum[6] The Bog People[7] https://science.sciencemag.org/content/277/5334/1929.2[8] The Curious Case of the Bog Bodies - Issue 27: Dark Matter - Nautilus[9] Bog Bodies[10] Expedition Magazine - Penn Museum[11] A European Cultural Community[12] Windeby I, Bog Body from Germany[13] Bog Bodies of Europe: The Most Famous of the Peatland Mummies[14] Windeby Girl and Weerdinge Couple[15] North Dakota State University[16] Windeby Girl and Weerdinge Couple[17] 'Windeby Girl' Mummy's Secret - She Was A Boy[18] The People of the Bog[19] Tacitus on Germany[20] The bodies in the bogs[21] Who Were the Ancient Bog Mummies? column1: What are some superstitions which are really not superstitions?
column3: Superstition refers to any belief or practice which is explained by supernatural force, but actually these practices have a meaning behind it. 1.Using lemon and green chilies to avert buri nazar The nimbu totka which is one of the most visible 'superstitions' probably stems from a culture that encouraged their use because of the qualities of lemon and chili. Both are rich in different vitamins and thus our ancestors probably tried to propagate their usage through symbols during ceremonies which slowly turned into a totka.2.Don’t go near peepal tree at night Most of us know the reason behind this popular saying - trees release carbon dioxide during nighttime. So, there is no truth in the belief that peepal tree is inhabited by spirits and ghosts, they might scare you during that time.3.Eating curd and sugar before stepping out Eating curd and sugar before stepping out is considered to be good luck because the consumption of curd has a cooling effect on the stomach and the sugar which is added provides instant glucose. This combination is indispensable for Indians and its consumption slowly linked to good luck.4.Swallow Tulsi leaves, never chew Tulsi leaves should not be chewed it needs to be swallowed. The science behind this is that the Tulsi leaf is healthy and it contains a little amount of Arsenic. Thus chewing it directly can result in the degradation of enamel.5.Sweeping the floor during the evening brings bad luck The belief that sweeping the house after sunset brings bad luck, it is one of the superstitious beliefs that we have all encountered now and then. The reason behind is that our ancestors preferred to clean their house during day time because of the sunlight and to avoid sweeping away something precious. But this reason soon turned to a superstition.6.Don’t cut nails after sunset. Cutting of nails after sunset is not considered to be good at all. But the truth is something different as nail clipper blade might hurt you during the dark time or during the absence of the light.7.Lizard Falling On Human Is Bad Luck It is said to be bad luck if a Lizard falls on a human but the scientific reason behind is that the lizards are poisonous in nature which release poisonous chemicals from its body in order to protect them from their enemies and if these lizards fall on a human body or inside a food then it is bound to make it contaminated. So baths are often taken if a lizard falls on a person.8.Fallen Hair around the House Will brings Fight In Your Family It is often believed that fallen hair inside the house will bring fight in your family but the real reason was something different. If someone leaves the fallen hair inside the house it may enter inside the food due to wind so it may lead to fighting among the family members.9. Crush the head of a snake after killing it Superstition says that one should crush the head of a snake after killing it otherwise its kin might find animage in its eyes and seek revenge. In fact the reason is that a snake can bite or kill a person even with a detached head.And in order tocompletely neutralize it, it is necessary to crush its head.Also, beinga cold-blooded organism, even if some of its vital organs stop working it will stay alive for hours and die a slow and painful death. So it is recommended to crush its head to give it a painless death.10. Plastering floor with cow dung is auspicious Cow dung plaster is considered auspicious just like any other product of a cow. Hence, mostly all rituals dictate the usage of cow dung to plaster the floor. Our ancestors started this practice to guard against insects and reptiles which are repelled by the pungent smell of cow dung. They did not have the luxury to buy bottled commercial disinfectants like we do. But over time this practice became a ritual and we find ourselves following it in spite of it being redundant in the contemporary world.Image courtesy :Google Moreover these practices are actually seeking hygiene, calm mind and body.

column1: The Bible: In The Book of Job, chapter 2:12 "…and they rent their mantle, and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward heaven" I see it all throughout the Bible about "rending their mantles" what does this mean?
column3: Rending (rent is the past tense of rend, to tear something) one’s robe, tunic, or cloak/mantle, is a traditional sign of mourning or anguish in Semitic cultures, and preserved as a religious symbol in Judaism. So too is placing dust or ashes on the head. I believe to this day, as part of mourning the death of a family member, Orthodox Jews will tear a piece of their clothing. It’s been 50 years and more since I was a Catholic, so cannot be sure if the ritual marking on Ash Wednesday had its origin in the Judaic custom of sprinkling dust or ashes on the head in token of mourning.

column1: What reasons do Tamil people celebrate Diwali?
column3: Just like there are so many cultural concepts changing within different regions of India, Tamils also have their own set of beliefs and way of celebrating Deepawali festival. (Diwali is more of a urban term than an actual word of the festival)Deepawali is one of the 3 big festivals that all connected families and relatives meet and thus lot much is spent on the festival. The other two festivals where people buy new clothes and celebrate with family and relatives are Pongal and Oor Thiruvizha ( annual village festivals) We can say these as get together festivals as the above 3 ones is about people having feast and be happy. These 3 festivals arrive exactly when the harvest is done -October Harvest for Deepawali, Jan harvest for Pongal and also April-May harvest for Oor Thiruvizha. Rest other festivals are society or individual family based festivals or purely spiritual or religious festivals. So yes Deepawali is when people travel to meet their families and I am also travelling tomorrow to my native to celebrate with my relatives as everyone will be back. I will speak the reason of us celebrating and also about other variants in customs to my known knowledge. The main day of Deepawali festival here in Tamil Nadu is on Chota Diwali ( as in North) which is called as Naraka Chaturdashi in Sanskrit. Its said that Lord Krishna with the help of Satyabhama killed Narakasura on this day and he had asked Krishna that let people celebrate his death day as a festival by having a feast,exchnage sweets and oil bath and let them wear new clothes. Thus we don’t have any any particular god to worship on this day. We get up early as 4 in morning and our parents give us a oil bath after a massage and in hot water ( Its said that the water turns to Ganga in the morning 4 to 6 and also Goddess Lakshmi sits in the oil at this time only on this day). We start the day by bursting a cracker indicating that the festival has started. After this as per some family customs, some families offer sweets and new clothes to their ancestors, some worship their ancestral Gods and some worship Lakshmi and some families don’t worship any particular God and they do a simple pooja . In those days children has to touch the elders feet after the pooja and elders will give some money to the children. Post this , people prepare non veg dishes in mutton and chicken with Dosa and Idli ( Do you know before Idli and Dosas became famous, it was only a Deepawali food?) and families feast together as breakfast. After this sweets preparation starts to give to the relatives or family members who have come to the house. One important ritual that happens is inviting newly wed couples to the house of bride’s in laws called as Thala Deepawali( first Deepawali) . People also invite them to Thala Pongal or Oor Thiruvizha but Deepawali is very special. In those days , I heard and now also some very cultural families in rural side prepare sweets before this day only like Adhirasam, Murukku, Thattai, Kuzhal, etc. Tamil Brahmins prepare one more sweet called Deepawali Lehyam. Nowadays due to time constraint people prepare sweets on the day of festival itself and every person sits together to prepare these sweets thus we exchange words and laughter and helps to bond well. It will be evening by that time and thus it will be the time for bursting crackers and thus people will get together to burst the colorful ones. There is no pooja in the evening and thus we don’t light any Deepams.( Also its cause this time we have North East Monsoon rains here and its very windy) The next day of Deepawali is the Amawasya day which is main day of Deepawali in North. Now this day some communities celebrate as Nombu ( Also called as Kedara Gowri Nombu) which is dedicated to the worship of Lord Shiva and Parvathi. All Tamil communities don’t have Nombu and only some communities have it (mainly in Northern and western parts of Tamil Nadu) This day we ...

column1: Adult What are some ideas on how to make the death of a sister or brother easier to handle?
column3: The death of a family member is always hard, especially if they were close. WE each grieve in our own way and for different lengths of time. Remembering the loved one and memorializing that person can help. Writing in a journal your reminiscence of the individual can help. Remembering those annoying quirks can help. Each culture handles death in different ways too. That is why the Irish have a wake or in New Orleans they have a parade and party. In Mexico on the “Day of the Dead” they gather at the grave site and have a meal with the departed. In the US, we don’t really have a “ritual” that helps to alleviate our sadness but you can speak to other family members for solas, or clergy. If you have lost a sibling and the grief is over taking you. Write your loved one a letter expressing your sorrow at their passing. Put all of your love, anger, frustration and grief into the letter, pour your heart out. And tuck it away.

column1: What are some classic supernatural/mythical animals and creatures from your culture/country?
column3: I hope someone from Culture of Indonesia answers this question, as they have some amazing mythical creatures! Australia has the bunyip (devil or evil spirit), from Wikipedia: ‘…said to lurk in swamps, billabongs, creeks, riverbeds, and waterholes.’ No one really knows what they look like, there are scores of varying images, because to see it is to be so terrified, you cannot afterwards describe it. Here is a comical, coin-operated tourist representation at Murray Bridge (a town called after a bridge over the Murray River) about 45 minutes’ drive from my home. The pool is still, you insert your coin, the water starts roiling, this creature arises from it and makes roaring sounds:Min Min lights are another from aboriginal myths. Wikipedia: ‘…most commonly described as being fuzzy, disc-shaped lights that appear to hover just above the horizon.’ The lights appear in the far Outback or in the deserts closer to towns and cities. Anyone who chases and catches the lights is never seen again.Kadaitcha (many spellings) Man is a real person, sent by elders of a tribe to track down and punish someone who caused someone else’s death. He wears oval shoes made from feathers mixed with blood (you can’t hear him coming), and no one is allowed to look at him as he passes. A bit like ‘Watch the wall, my darling, as the Gentlemen go by.’ To have a Kadaitcha Man on the hunt for you is terrifying; he’s relentless. No pictures, because this is secret business. Illapurinja, from Wikipedia: ‘literally "the changed one", is a female Kurdaitcha who is secretly sent by her husband to avenge some wrong, most often the failure of a woman to cut herself as a mark of sorrow on the death of a family member. Believed to be entirely mythical, the fear of the Illapurinja would be enough to induce the following of the custom.’ Pointing the bone is another real one. From Bone Pointing ‘The ceremony of bone pointing is a common ritual for bringing sickness among the [Australian] Arunta. The pointing bone or pointing stick is usually about nine inches in length, pointed at one end, and tipped with a lump of resin at the other. The stick is endowed with magical power by being 'sung over,' that is, curses are muttered over it, such as 'may your heart be rent asunder' and 'may your head and throat be split open.' On the evening of the day on which the bone has been 'sung' the wizard creeps stealthily in the shadows until he can see the victim's face clearly by the firelight. He then points the bone in the victim's direction and utters in a low tone the curses with which the stick was endowed earlier in the day. The victim is supposed to sicken and die within a month at the most. Two men may cooperate in the pointing operation. Spears may also be endowed with magic by 'singing' over them. A person who knows that he has been injured, even slightly, with a spear thus prepared will be likely to waste away through fear unless counter magic can be brought to his aid. --from "Primitive Theories of Disease" by Spencer L. Rogers in Ciba Symposia (April 1942)’I want to add a true story to this. Around mid-training as a nurse in a male surgical ward, a physically magnificent pure-blood aboriginal man was in the adjoining neurology ward, admitted for persistent headache that grew worse. No tests could discover what was causing it. I was also nursing an aboriginal man in my ward, so I introduced them both on one of those sunny days we took patients outside or for a walk in the adjoining Botanic Gardens. I also asked him to visit the man in his ward as he faded away and became weak and bed-bound. He did visit, but was reluctant to go again. Next thing we heard the other man had died, cause of death still unknown. My patient said nothing when I told him, but as he was discharged, he said to me, ‘That man had the bone pointed at him.’ No wonder he didn’t want to visit someone ‘accursed’ again. But it shows the power of psychological belief.

column3: Some Significant Works from 21st Century :Dancer in the Dark , 2000 : An east European girl goes to America with her young son, expecting it to be like a Hollywood film.Yi Yi , 2000 : Each member of a middle class Taipei family seeks to reconcile past and present relationships within their daily lives.In the Mood for Love , 2000 : Two neighbors, a woman and a man, form a strong bond after both suspect extramarital activities of their spouses.Lost in Translation , 2003 : A faded movie star and a neglected young woman form an unlikely bond after crossing paths in Tokyo.Before Sunset , 2004 : Nine years after Jesse and Celine first met, they encounter each other again on the French leg of Jesse's book tour.There Will Be Blood , 2007 : A story of family, religion, hatred, oil and madness, focusing on a turn-of-the-century prospector in the early days of the business.The White Ribbon , 2009 : Strange events happen in a small village in the north of Germany during the years before World War I, which seem to be ritual punishment.White Material by C. Dennis , 2009 : Amidst turmoil and racial conflict in a Francophone African state, a white French woman fights for her coffee crop, her family and ultimately for her life.Tree of Life , 2011 : The story of a family in Waco, Texas in 1956. Dolan , 2016 : Louis , a terminally ill writer, returns home after a long absence to tell his family that he is dying.Frantz by F. column1: What is a proper way to reply to the question,"how are you" or "you ok?" when you are in deep emotional pain but do not feel that answering as such is appropriate for the time or place?
column3:
How are you?' or 'How are you going?' is a greeting rather than a question in most western cultures. It is simply an expansion of the 'Hello' greeting and requires nothing more than a fine, okay or a not too bad, thanks. How are you? in reply. Most people know, if they actually think about it, that when you say, 'Good thanks' in reply, there's a chance you're not really. But it's a ritual and both sides are observed without real thought. You will know when someone really wants to know how you are; a friend will ask you quietly in private when you are sharing a drink or a cup of tea and then they will wait for you speak. We have all been through difficult phases in our lives when saying 'I'm fine, thanks' to an acquaintance was technically a lie - but what is the alternative? Telling your customers that you just had a death in the family and you don't know how much longer you can hold it together? Yes, I am being a bit flip there - but this has happened to me; having to spend a day in retail saying Have a nice day every 5 minutes when a family member had killed themselves the night before. Ara Sedaka	Is it the worldwide norm (general practice) that Jewish parents deliberately show Holocaust literature and movies to their children?	Updated 10y	Ara Sedaka	Yes, it is. There is an actual holiday", or rather, a memorial day, specifically for the Holocaust, יום השואה (yom hashoah), which is observed by Jews worldwide, so it is a very explicit policy in Jewish culture, and most Jewish parents go farther and encourage their children to read books like Number the Stars, The Devil's Arithmetic, Night, Day, etc. etc. There are a lot of reasons behind this. One is basic Jewish culture. We remember our dead. In many ways, Judaism is somewhat agnostic on the subject of the afterlife. There is actual doctrine on what comes after death, but it's really not discussed by anyone who isn't a theologian. We don't have any regular holidays or rituals on getting a good afterlife or resurrection or any of that kind of thing. Rather, the living ritual on death is much more focused on being remembered—on having been such a good person while you were here that your very memory continues to be a blessing after you are gone. Because of this, a LOT of Jewish observance and ritual is about remembering the dead. We sit shiva, we say yahrzeit, and when a particularly grievous tragedy occurs, we create a holiday to remember it: these include Passover, Tzom Gedaliah, Hannukah, Purim, Asarah b'Tevet, Lag b'Omer, Tisha b'Av. Part of the tragedy of the Holocaust for Jews is that it is literally impossible to remember all who died. In far too many cases, anyone who would remember the dead was killed also. And so it has become a communal responsibility to remember those who were killed there, so many of whom do not have surviving family to say their yahrzeit. So that collectively as a people, we can continue to make their lives a blessing. Another is that few Jewish families were untouched by the Holocaust. I have rarely met a Jew with any European descent who could not name a specific family member who was killed. So, it's not only part of our cultural history, it's part of our personal history. My mother had to explain the Holocaust to me so that I would understand why I had so few relatives on my mother's side and, conversely, why we were so close to even distant relatives. And lastly, yes, as ‎Amir E. Aharoni (אמיר א׳ אהרוני)‎ said, the idea is to make this story so well known that such events never happen again on this Earth. Never again is a motto that, of course, we have already failed; but that does not change the importance of continuing the mission.

column1: According to Hinduism, if a person doesn't have a son or any enfants, then how can he/she get moksha? How can they get (pinda daan) without having any children?
column3: I think there is a misunderstanding here. The moksha you can get from pinda dana is merely liberation from the sad and dreadful condition of a ghost - not the actual liberation from all material conditioning that is the final purushartha. The four purusharthas (dharma, artha, kama and moksha) are personal attainments, and they cannot be acquired through the agency of children. Nobody else can make you evolve, it's something you need to do by yourself. And the only way to attain actual moksha is to overcome your material identifications and attachments, and realize your true Self. Regarding pinda dana: unevolved people who are strongly conditioned by their material identifications and attachments usually remain bound to the circumstances of their incarnation even after death, and they are unable to move on. This is the condition of ghosts. All non-evolved persons remain hovering in this condition for some time after death, depending on the strength of their attachments, and all cultures have some remedies to help them go through this difficult passage. See for example the various versions of a “Book of the dead” especially in Tibet and Egypt. The Vedic system or true Orthodox Hinduism offers some specific rituals in this category, such as pinda dana, shraddha, tarpana, etc. Qualified brahmanas are supposed to conduct these rituals (as ritviks), but these days it's extremely difficult to find any (if they exist at all). In any case, the karta of the rituals for the dead doesn't need to be a seminal child born from sexual intercourse. It could be an adopted son or daughter, a disciple, or any family member or friend. What is even more important, a seminal child could sometimes be the worst choice, especially if he is forced into engaging in the ritual, or has some grudges or negative feelings towards the deceased, doesn't believe in the value of the ritual, etc. In such cases, the results will be disastrous. So please stop the madness of fertility clinics.

column1: Aren’t Hindus meant to keep facial hair?
column3: Answer : No. It is because facial hair has NO specific purpose or meaning to Hindus that we want to keep them for prolong period of time. Furthermore, most of our male Gods are clean-shaven, except for a few which you can count with one hand.Lord Brahma is shown as bearded person, but there are also versions of Him being beardless and younger looking.Lord Narasimha is shown with a “beard” which is understandable considering His Avatar was that of a Man and a Lion and male lions have manes.Lord Parasurama (Rama with an Axe) is shown with a beard as He is also an Ascetic person. Which means He choose a life of Spiritual like the Rishis, constantly training His weapons, arts and Meditation.Also, sometimes Lord Shiva has a beard but that is not a common views among Hindus when depicting the image of Lord Shiva. Basically, facial hairs are sign of masculine traits among male humans. While a lot of Gods and Rishis has long hair (which could extend to their shoulders and further down like Lord Shiva does), facial hair are not considered as good-looks for a male Hindus, especially when mustaches and beards are (in some Indian culture) are considered manly traits (Pride of oneself). So Hindus attend to remove facial hairs occasionally and in some situation, as demanded by rituals (such as birth of a baby (who will be shaved for the first time in a temple), religious penance and as ritual involving death of a family member).

column1: What are common scams in India?
column3: My Bade papa died in the year 2020 By COVID. He was the sole earner of his family. An Ex-Army person and was just retired from his second Govt job after Army. Everyone was shocked! There was chaos, there was unrest in our family. We couldn’t believe that ‘he was gone. He has so many after retirement plans. He wanted to visit Rameswaram with his family for once. He wanted to purchase a farm house and do stuff, but he was goner. He had Two daughters and one son. My cousin brother is a Job aspirant and my two sisters are married. Anyhow, we all gathered the courage and gave a final bid-adieu to him. NOW THE SCAM STARTS!! So In our Culture there is a Prathah ( Tradition) that from Day 3rd to the 10th day of the death we have to do Some rituals for the deceased soul, so that The soul may go to heaven and Rest in peace. The Rituals goes like this. ·There will be a feast in the name of dead everyday from day 3rd to day 10th. And on 12th day there will be a grand feast.The family has to feed to ‘Brahmins’ and also to give them some ‘Donation’ every day. (3-10)All the Male direct family members will have to shave their heads on 10th day.They will take bath in ‘Ganga jal’ and have to wear new clothes. Etc.So, like everyone else we have started Following the tradition and gave feast and donation. Day-3 – The Menu was Poori, Matar paneer, Gulab jamun and salad for 50 people. There was 5 Brahmins that came and we donated Rs.500 to each. Day – 4 – Dal bada, Aloo dum, jalebi and Salad, papad for 50. There attended 7 Brahmins and we paid them Rs.500 each. Like that till the 9th day The number of Brahmins have increased and reached to 15. We couldn’t say No and had to pay Rs.500 each. On the 10th day i..e on ‘Dasah kriya’ – The Head Brahmin of the 15 started demanding Rs.1000 each and Rs.5000 for Him along with 50kg of Rice with vegetables and Dhoti, Chaddar. This time as a educated person myself, I couldn’t hold my anger and started arguing with the Head brahmin. I said “you are looting people in the name of tradition” and you do not pose the quality of a Pandit. He started playing his old game that ‘The deceased soul will not get peace’. ‘Brahmin is like God, and you are disrespecting your god’ Blah blah. And to add to that he started doing all this loudly Infront of my window Aunt. Guess what happened next? He wins. My Father took control of the things and have settled all their demands. Total cost of the DEATH. 1. Total Hospital bill – 2.5Lakhs 2. Total donation – Around 50-70K 3. Total for food - 1lakh. (Including grand fest) 4. Total on clothes – 10-20k 5. Total mental trauma – Unlimited!! ………………………………………………………………… So how it is scam? Imagine, when a not so wealthy person dies. What will happen to his family? Can they spend 2Lakh for all the rituals? If They can’t spend that much will ‘The deceased soul’ won’t get peace? Is this our real tradition? What if, someone takes Loan for fulfilling all these rituals? Should donation be demanded?

column1: Do young Aboriginals still do traditional "Walkabout" in modern Australia (as seen in the 1971 film "Walkabout" with Jenny Agutter)?
column3: I am not an Aboriginal person, so I give the following explanation as an interim answer, until an Aboriginal person can provide a better, more accurate answer. The term "walkabout" is an English word for aboriginal people disappearing for a period from the workplace. They prioritise their responsibilities within their culture, over obligations imposed by white people. Not only was there no understanding of Aboriginal culture, there was also no recognition of that culture in Australian employment law and custom. To understand it, perhaps imagine that a family member has died, but your boss tells you that you must work on the day of your father's funeral. Or on Thanksgiving. Or your daughter's wedding. Or your son's Congressional Award ceremony at the Whitehouse. We take it for granted that your cultural obligation to attend these events trumps any work obligation. And you are right. Anyone I know would go anyway, and stick the finger up to the boss, even if it meant getting fired. This doesn't happen often, because Christmas, Easter, funerals etc are written into workplace law - law written by and for Christian white people. Aboriginal people have many more cultural obligations, and these are felt just as keenly. They prioritise their obligations even if ordered to attend work. They are often fired for doing so. As a community, they carry a reputation for being unreliable, when they search for work, because of their insistence on attending to culture. And still, in 2020, there is still no recognition in workplace agreements, legislation etc that allows for and protects a worker who has these obligations, although Some workplaces are now informally making room for other cultures' events, like Eid, Passover, and Aboriginal Sorry business ( after a death in the family). There are many stories of Aboriginal people ending up in gaol for driving whilst disqualified, when they were obliged to facilitate (by driving) relatives attending "sorry business" or some other cultural obligation. The courts, police, prisons, legislature, all need to start to negotiate with Aboriginal people about their needs so that this doesn't happen. Nobody wins from a young person in gaol. For very traditional Aboriginal people, there will be times when they are obliged to "go bush" with elders to go through education, rituals and initiations appropriate for his or her age. Once again, these are not negotiable, and can lead to similar problems. It is better to talk about "Cultural Obligations" rather than "going walkabout".

column1: Why do Tamil people burn fire crackers when a person is dead? What is the reason behind it?
column3: Well, Not all do….. Tamil people follow traditions that are combination of both Dravidian and Vedic Hindu rituals in almost everything and as such even in death too. We don’t celebrate deaths all the time. As you know, most of the time, the elders in our family die and that is common as of old age and as such you can see people bursting crackers, women singing songs related to the deeds of the dead person ,drums on one side and some men dancing to the beats of drum. Funeral ceremony for that matter among Tamils are not so silent unlike in rest in India. As per the Dravidian customs, its said that , if a person dies of old age or dies due to a long caused illness, he gets free from the shakles of life and they are free of these human problems and if such a death happens in a family its called as -Kalyana Saavu or marriage death wherein all the rituals are done in grand manner equal to a marriage. At this point of time,the members of the family are ofcourse sad but still because its the death of that person its celebrated as like a marriage from singing songs to dancing and busting crackers and on the Anthim Sanskar day or Kariyam in Tamil, a big non veg feast is served to relatives and friends but this is not followed if anyone dies young below 50 years as he/she still has the responsibilty of family and in such case , the death is seen as a big lose for the family and only veg feast is served to the relatives and friends.( We have many more rituals that are to be followed). As per Dravidian concept, they become spirits or Gods of the family and protect the family and ofcourse it should be celebrated and there was no concept of rebirth in Dravidian culture . This can also be seen as such most Tamils in past buried their dead and either plant a tree or place a stone ( Nadukal or heroic stones) over the dead.Later after the vedic customs started,Tamils started to burn their first borns while the rest were buried by placing a a plant in their own land( similar concept is seen among Malyalees also and other south Indian communities) thus merging both the old dravidian and vedic customs. Now also among our relatives, we bury our dead in our own lands instead of going to burial grounds or cremation grounds and we place a plant over the ground which later grows into a tree and also important things are placed along with the( But Muslims and Chistians construct a tomb and use a coffin but no such thing or concept was followed in ancient times among Tamils).
