column1: What are some less known facts about Indian festivals?
column3: Chhath Puja is an ancient Hindu festival dedicated to sun god ,Surya .This festival is performed to thank the sun god for sustaining life on earth and to fulfill their wishes .According to Hindu Mythology Sun worship is believed to cure a variety of diseases including leprosy . The rituals of this festival are very rigorous involving holy bath , absataining from drinking water for more than 36 hrs , offering prashad and arghya to setting and rising sun .All these rituals are observed over a period of four days . What does word "Chhath" means ?? It is a compound of two words : "Chah" means "six stages " and "Hath" means "science of Hath yog" .The word refers to process of obtaining solar energy through six stages involving Hath Yog . When is it celebrated ?? It is performed on Kartik Shukala Shashti ie on 6th day of month of Kartik(month of Lunar Calendar) , exactly 6 days after Diwali. What is the history associated with Chhath ?? According to epic sanskrit poem Mahabharata , Draupadi and the Pnadavas observed this festival on the advice of sage Dhaumya . As a result Draupadi was able to solve her recent problems and also later Pandavas regained their lost kingdom .It is also belived that this festival was started by Karna (Surya putra Karna and king of Anga Desh ... present day Bhagalpur in Bihar) . Our ancient rishis used this method to remain without any external intake of food as they were able to get energy from suns rays . What about the Prashad? Prashad includes sweet and friut offerings in bamboo winnows .Food is strictly vegetarian and is cooked without salt onion or garlics . How is Chhath celebrated ?? Four days of Chhath : Day 1: Nahay Khay (bath and eat) devotees or Paravaitin take dip in holy river Ganges (however this is not possible nowadays due to migration of people ) and carrying it home to prepare the offerings . This day only a single meal is taken by the devotee . Day 2 : Kharna Fast is observed for the whole day which ends a little after sunset . After the worship of earth offerings of Kheer , puri and banana are distributed among family and friends . From this day for 36 hours the devotee abstains from drinking water . Day 3 : Chhath Sanjhya Arghya Throughout day prasad is prepared . On evening all the family members accompany paravaitin to a river bank , pond or a water body to make offering (arghya) to setting sun . Prayers are offered to setting sun . The scenaro near the water body can be compared to carnival with all the family members and friends accompanying the devotee to the bank , ritual rendition of folk songs , carried on through oral transmission from mothers and mothers-in-law to daughters and daughters -in-law are sung on this occasion . Folk songs sung on this occasion reflect the culture mythology and history of Bihar and UP . But now days bollywood songs (parody remixes) have taken prominence . On the night colorful event of Kosi is held .Lighted earthen lamps are kept under a canopy of five sugarcane sticks . The 5 sticks signify human body made of Panchtattav .Lighted lamps signify the solar energy sustaining human being . Day 4 : Parana This is the final day of chhath Puja .Early mornings all the devotees along with their family members and friends reach the river bank before sun rise to perform morning arghya . The festival ends with breaking of fast by the Paravaitin .and distributing of prashad to friends . In which part of India is Chhath celebrated ? It is mainly celebrated in Jharkahnd , Bihar and UP .But since people has migrated from these areas to other parts this festival . Why is evening arghya offered before morning arghya ?? It represents that circle of life starts with circle of death and sun is the main source of energy responsible for life on this planet . P.S. Text copied from my blog mJ_Blog: Chhath ...

column1: What were ancient Slavic societies like?
column3: I will focus on the earliest Slavic tribes. I will talk about the period when they officially enter history, which is around 5th century which is when they were first noticed by the Romans. I will touch on the hypothetical stuff of what they were like before that time period, and a bit on the later times until 10th century, before Christianization. Disclaimer : There’s a bunch of disclaimers in this answer. I written this answer a few years back, so this should be the most important disclaimer of all - please bear with my typing mistakes and general lack of writing skills, and obviously any factual mistakes that I make, which i hope people will correct me on. I promise I’ll get around to fixing up this answer and cleaning it up a bit one day :D Also I want to say that I am no scholar,i study history in collage. But I am no scholar, which means this is not a scientific work/article. I am simply a person with a partuicular interest in ancient slavic history and I have spent some time learning and reading about the subject. In this answer I will try to picture the ancient Slavs, and bring them closer to the common person that is interested in a answer to this question.The information is drawn from many places off the internet and some works of actual scholars, and know that I am trying to have the information displayed to be as objective as I can. Before we start, i would just like to mention that you should definetly take a look at the comments from this answer, because there’s more information from knowledgeable people, about other things that I also failed to mention, because it’s of course, impossible to grasp all information in a answer like this, and the answer is really long as it is, and to those people i would like to especially give thanks. This is bound to be a long read. So I hope you have some time and plenty of coffee.I’ll probably keep editing this answer and adding stuff in as I want this answer to be good, detailed as much as I can make it detailed and not boring to read.. Ancient Slavic societies were a group of non-unified tribes, and this is important, not unified under a single king or banner.They lived close together, but rarely (to our written knowledge) banded together against a common enemy. So for example, maybe you would have a certain tribe that would run away from marauding Huns,and their neighbors possibly staying because they are in good relations with the Huns. They originate from the Przeworsk Zarubinsky culture, from the area of modern day Ukraine - Belarus border. This is new : The people in 1–2 century AD that were their ancestors, and by that the ancestors of Antes and Sclaveni, were Sporoi (translation: scatter grain) and Veneti (translation: friendly). Jordanes himself wrote in his work Getica: Although they derive from one nation, now they are known under three names, the Veneti, Antes and Sclaveni The Sclaveni and the Antae actually had a single name in the remote past; for they were both called Sporoi in olden times Now I have to adress this part, some people connected the Sporoi to the Serboi, and then to modern day Serbs. However, I don’t really understand how was this connection made, as the names are not similar at all. Experts like the Ukrainian historian Mykhailo Hrushevskyi mentioned how the whole linking to the Serboi is wrong, as Serboi inhabited lands too far away from the Sporoi, or Spali / Spalaei. Moreover many arguments have been made how many Slavic tribes had same names as time went on, hence, it is still not concluded, and it is still a open topic. But I agree with Mykhailo Hrushevskyi, and not because I am a Croat (for all you big patriots) but because I really do not see the relation between two people. In any case, Spalaei/Spali/Sporoi might very well be the same as Palaei, and if that is true, then the whole name is from a royal Eastern Scythian family of a Scythian king Palus..Early Slavic Tribes, with their earliest homeland somewhere in modern day Belarus, with the early Slavic tribes, Veneti (Wenedi) shown here (along with the rest of the Proto Slavs), and later on Antes and Sclaveni. Later development of Slavic tribes, after the final migration to the south. As you can see it is a rather delicate and tideous matter to figure out the origins of Slavs, or anything else..So let’s talk about something a little more colorful and interesting. A bit about Religion, mythology and beliefs that stayed after the introduction of Christianity The ancient religion of the Slavs was of the Indo European “stock”,very classic Indo European pantheon,you have your thunder deity,sun deity,your spirits,etc.The early slavs had this ancestral worship concept in their religion,honor of the kin,rod,and their worship of a deity was very regional,so a tribe that lived close to the sea would worship the deity of wind,Stribog,notice that they didn’t really have a early deity of the Sea,like..Greeks for example,because early Slavs didn’t live close to the sea,really,so they had no god of the sea.The war bands would worship a god of war,Perun for example.StribogSvetovid, Svantovit,Sventovid,god of war. Their whole religion and mythology was a classic Indo-European mix,but with a very forest,swampy click to it-sort of like the Balts,but with a slight Iranic click to it with the solar elements for example.The places of worship were usually hilltops,holy groves,and the home itself,where you would find maybe be a idol of a god.Also there was the tradtion of inscribing the symbol of the thunder god,on the pillars of the home,so a thunder doesn’t strike the home and burn it down ( this tradition still is alive in Poland, check the comments to this answer by Bartosz Dziuba ) ,the six-petaled rose was the symbol present in slavic embroidery,and other objects.I’ll show you a picture of the symbol and some examples of the symbol in real life. This is thought to be the the symbols of Perun,the god of thunder and war,which were apparently still inscribed on roofs in Russia in early 19th century. (Note:Possible revival of a tradition because of rise of Panslavism and Nationalism in the period)A picture of a stone cross on a grave from the 1800s that i took myself.Notice the rose symbol on the top beam of the cross and also the right beam which is preserved.Notice the symbols.I have also seen this same exact symbol on a wall or stone ( I forgot where was it ) somewhere in Turkey,so unfortunately it may not be a symbol unique to the Slavs.. Some other actual Slavic symbols found of pottery finds in towns,remember that pottery was traded,so there can be a pot from Frankia or Denmark,that got to the city where the pots were found.A nice illustration of a place of worship,as a hilltop.Archeological Slavic pagan worship site locations across Eastern EuropeA picture of a “worship ritual” - St.John’s day / Summer Solstice / KUPALA night celebration on 22nd of June (still celebrated among slavs,in some places,but it’s also a tradition in other european peoples,pointing again-to the Indo European connection,even though people like Finns celebrate this as well,even though they - Linguistically are not of the Indo-European group) Mythology Rusalka - drowned beautiful women,that will drown a young naive man who gets tricked by them,similar to mermaids. Vila, Samovila, Samodiva and so on are creatures rather similar, or in some cases same as the Rusalka in the more eastern Slavic mythological sphere. A specific thing that the Vila ( or whatever you want to call it, depending where you are from ) does, is that it weaves the horse’s hair in the stables during the night. My grandfather told me that his father saw one of these in the field one night, but as he got older, he realized it was just a story to scare children with…Or maybe his father really thought he saw something? :) First picture is the Rusalka, and the second one is the Vila. Lesnik/Lešij/Leshy - a forest spirit in the form of a old man,or even a man/demon made out of tree branches and wood,that may trick you or kill you.He is also described to have a wife and kids,and usually portrayed as neutral then a hostile being,his actions would be the answer to how you act in his forest.He is usually accompanied by packs of wolves or bears.My favorite: Baba Jega,later after christianization - Baba Roga in southern slavic ( Grandma - Baba ,Roga - Horns,Horned) is described as a rather ugly looking old woman,a grandma who flies around in in a cooking pot,cleaning her trail with her silver broom,often known to kidnap children who stray too far from the house or do not listen to their parents,but also known to help at rare times.Later on,after the introduction of Christ to the Slavs,Baba Jega remains,as Baba Roga,in the southern slavic lands,as the same grandma who now lives in the wells,and if you bend over to look too far,to look into the well,she will grab/snatch you,pull you down into the water,and drown you.This may point on how the ‘horned’ grandma first of became >Horned< as a reference to Satan,and a reference to degenerate paganism,as a heathen belief,and also that she now lives in a well,as a shelter,as in - she managed to hide away from Christ.I myself have grown up with this same fear as a kid,therefore you can be sure i stayed the hell away from the damned wells,so the fear had it’s use,as you can see.Domovoi,Domovik, Djeduška, Starik, Khoromozitel - A house spirit in eastern slavic mythology which may help you around with your house chores if he is happy,or hurt you and disturb if he is not and many others.The word for ‘Home’ came from it - ‘Dom’.He is described as a grandfather,a master of the house,and he lived in the attic of the house,can be heard at night,as he silently weeps,and has a wife Domovika who lives in the basement of the home..It was considered great misfortune to actually see the Domovoi,as it meant that he foretells the death of a family member.Domovoi also has a wife, a female version of himself which lives in the basement of the house, while he lives in the attic.Many more slavic legends and stories hold more of these creatures,these are just a few that i mentioned,that I either know a bit about or can remember at the moment,but as you can see there is a way to seperate and group them together.There is the ones in the field,home,forest and water,and the ones who weave destiny,ones that bring luck or misfortune etc etc.Because the slavs believed the world was filled with these spirits,and they believed that the gods came in the form of the animals that they saw,so in a way a sighting of a bear may mean that Veles has visited you.That is how they may have interpreted a sighting of a animal,like wolf,owl,bear,fox.. I would also like to add a bit about later slavic mythology, because Slavs, especially in the Balkans it seems, have long believed in mythological creatures. I am telling you, old people believed in them until the 2000’s because i remember as a child, there was a article in the news papers about a “Drekavac” in a forest in Bosnia. Yes, I know what it sounds like, and I am telling you, it’s true. My grandfather told me about a mythological being that he was told as a child about… The night hunter it’s a hunter that walks with his hounds during the night, God cursed him to hunt during the night because he didn’t go to church, and so after his death, he was cursed to roam the forests and fields during the nights and full moons especially. My grandfather told me about a story, that his father told him, when his father was walking during the night, he saw something run across the nearby field, trough the grass, and he believed it was the night hunter’s hound chasing a rabbit, then my grandfather added that it was most likely a two birds flying low, just above the grass. Other stories include the graveyard, and the things people heard when they traveled at night near the graveyards and so on. One more creature i should mention is the Vampire which originates from the Balkans, there’s even Ottoman writings in 1700’s that mention them, or mention that people talked about them. A bit about the theory of the writing system I should mention that there is a theory that Slavs actually had a writing system,before they adopted the Glagoljica,Hlaholika,Cyrillic etc. that was given to them from the Church,by Cyril and Methodius.The writing system mentioned consisted of incisions,called rezi,which is mentioned by a Blugarian monk : Before, the Slavs did not have their own books, but read and divined by means of strokes and incisions, being pagan. (Strategikon) "but lay down a certain period after which they can decide for themselves if they want to return to their former homelands after paying a ransom, or to stay amongst the Slavs as free men and friends". Later,Gardizi,mentions the same law: If someone makes fornication, he or she would be killed, without accepting any apologies. MILITARY Romans said that they don't wear armor, which may be a thing for a certain tribe,but I would say it's unlikely,as that is probably just a another bit of roman propaganda,or a isolated case,as armor was worn by anybody who could afford it,or loot it off the battlefield. Sure,not wearing armor may be still true as Slavs prefered gurella tactics and ambushes,so armor would be less desireable because you need speed and mobility if you are using such a tactic of warfare.But if it was a open field battle armor,if available,was indeed worn,no doubt about it. They prefer to fight on foot, advancing on the enemy; in their hands they carry small shields and spears, but they never wear body armour. They are armed with short spears; each man carries two, one of them with a large shield.Also Romans mention,that they prefer to employ guerrilla tactics,and often spring out and surprise attack from the flanks. Perhaps my favorite similar/related word from Sanskrit and slavic languages is the word “YABHITI”(Sanskrit) to the Slavic “Jebati” which means “to have sex” ,but my fellow Slavs very well know what that means and in what context it’s used ;) The religious Iranic aspect of dualism of deities is also present in the Slavic mythology,with Perun and Veles,Belobog and Chernobog,essentially the evil god and the good god and vice versa.Although it is sometimes not clear when a god perceived as all evil and malevolent,for example Veles is usually perceived as a evil god,but he is also a god of the harvest,cattle etc,so people also worshiped him as well. The Baltic relation consists of a mix of some linguistic similarities and some religious similarities.For example, linguistically,there are words that are similar,random example; the word for Fog,in a Baltic language (I think it's Lithuanian) its Miglas,and in many Slavic languages its Magla. The similarities in religion is the whole atmosphere,the whole feeling of religion,the forest-swamp feeling is also very present in the Baltic pagan religions.Also,the name for a deity in the Slavic pantheon is essentially the same as the one in Baltic,Perun (slavic thunder deity) and Perkunas (Baltic) also, curiously,there is a similar thunder deity in the Finnish pantheon,Perkele (which is a slur word today, after the Christianization,means something like : God dammit).There are more similarities with the Baltic people,stuff like the whole marriage aspect is rather strongly present in both the Slavic and Baltic mythology and pagan religions,also the horses and chariots which is a very clear Indo European aspect of religion.Perun rides his steed. Conclusion and a bit of history on Pan Slavism and Pan Illyrianism In conclusion,I think Slavs as a people are a interesting topic,as I myself have been actively doing research,for about 2 years now,since the minor rise of Pan-Slavism,reading about and listening about the topic.I have noticed that there is too much of the Panslavist propaganda getting inside,romanticizing the history of Slavs,deteriorating it,and having people believe it,which had people like Goran Šarić,Jovan Deretić,and probably many others to use the opportunity that is the pure ignorance of the people,for their own gain,selling their sh*t books filled with completely insane statements,like in the case of my (not,thank god) friend Jovan Deretić - The Virgin Mary is a Serbian woman,etc.Other thing that Panslavism has ruined is the infamous genetic argument,that some people may have noticed I hate.((( WHICH SLAVIC COUNTRY HAS THE MOST R1A1 HAPLOTYPE THEREFORE MAKING IT THE MOST SLAVIC???))) or (((ARE SERBS/CROATS/ALBANIANS ACTUALLY THE DIRECT DESCENDANTS OF ILLYRIANS BECAUSE THEY HAVE THE I2 HAPLOTYPE??))) We,Slavs,know about ourselves the least,our history books don’t tell us about ourselves,but rather have a half of the page about our ancestors,portrayed as filthy culture-less barbarians,which i think,from what I have written above,is a blatant and disgusting lie,paired with modern Slavs mostly hating their neighbor Slavic people,because modern politics is just that,and sadly we cannot run away from it.. column1: I want to die at age 45. I don't want to become a senior citizen. What about you?
column3: Most people don't want to die any earlier than they have to. But there is definitely a certain logic to it. There is a particularly good Star Trek TNG episode (S4E22) about a culture that has set an age limit of 60 for all of its members. When they turn 60, they undergo a suicide ritual called the Resolution: a big celebration, at the end of which the person ends their life. The guest star of this episode is a scientist from this planet who is about to turn 60. For a time he considers the idea of seeking asylum on board the Enterprise in order to continue his work. But in the end, he changes his mind and goes back home in time for his Resolution. This episode, more so than most, does a good job of presenting this as a moral grey area, making numerous interesting points on both sides. The central issue, I think, is the idea of death with dignity. These people prefer to leave the world while still being vigorous, in control of their faculties, and not imposing a medical burden on their family and the rest of society. This point is hard to ignore. One thing most people don’t realize is that suicide rates are highest among the elderly (65+). There are often legitimate medical reasons why someone would want to end their life, yet modern society does not even give us this option. Instead, suicide is criminalized and people are granted no agency or dignity over the manner in which they leave the world. Would it not make more sense to have something akin to a Resolution, where you throw a celebration of your life, then say goodbye? Would that not be better than slowly slipping away in a hospital bed over a period of months or years, either totally unconscious or suffering and in pain? Or worse yet, the scenario where a family member or a police officer discovers your body decomposing in your house, forgotten and alone? Why is it that we prefer to humanely euthanize our pets to prevent their suffering, yet assisted suicide is forbidden for humans? That one is a real head-scratcher, for me. The closest thing we have in most of the US is the is the DNR (do not resuscitate) agreement, but you’re still required to exist through it all the way to the end, to the point where your body actually fails. I’m not advocating an age limit like in that Star Trek episode — and 45 or 60 certainly seems way too early — but for a society that supposedly values personal freedom so highly, it feels like we could do a much better job at honoring people’s wishes regarding the end of their lives. If you have a right to life, don't you also have a right to death?

column3: Indian culture and rituals has been shown so good in movies and serials, and also assumed by people but reality is different. For example Dowry is a lifelong continuous process not a one time gifting event. Dowry starts when two family agrees for the wedding. On this approval of wedding from both sides between two families, bride family gives some money to groom family. I am calling it dowry because there is no proper description given for these, those rituals just shows you system of patriarchy that runs in society, there is no proper address of such issues in the society.Lagan(Dowry) Then on two days before wedding, bride family gives groom family a huge amount of money, jewellery, furniture, appliances, clothes etc. Transportation of stuff also manages by girl’s family. This is considered as real dowry in our society. Because highest amount of money and stuff exchange happens on this day. Also this is very visible kind of exchange. Also called as lagan in Haryana (India). Len-Den (Take-Give). Then on the wedding day, girl’s family gives clothes with money to most of the relatives of boy’s family. This ritual is called Len-Den in the society. But I feel this is only Den(Give) not Len(take). Wedding day Brides family arranges feast party for every relatives with priority given to groom family and relatives. Lots of money being spent on food, tent, decoration, lights, Len-den(Take-Give), ritual, DJ, drones, flowers etc. Weddings these days becoming more and more big and fatty, called Big fat wedding due to societal norms and show off. All these leads to extreme pressure on mainly father and brother of bride, mostly they sell their properties and takes loans for such wedding. Sometimes ends up in suicide due to debts. All these drama in a wedding doesn’t give any surity that this marriage relationship will go perfectly. Sometimes divorce happens very soon even if the divorce not happens, this is waste of money and resources. Then next day of wedding, male only relatives of boy comes to girl’s home and enjoy a heavy expensive feast and formal hospitality. Also recieves money. God bharayi This is ritual where girls when become pregnant, they are given blessings, but these blessings are in form of money and stuff. Girl’s parents gives money with clothes to girl’s relatives because they meet during this ritual, and as I told you earlier, every time the girl’s family member meet with boy’s family member, girl’s family member always gives some money and/or clothes to boy’s family member. Pregnancy in mayka During the pregnancy, girls will be sent to parents house called mayka, so that girl’s parents will take care of her pregnancy and all expenditure on it. Girls are being send to parents house because during pregnancy, they are not capable of working, and need extra care, and when girls (Bahu) is not working, they are useless burden on in-laws family. Who will care? In-laws! Child Delivery by girl’s parents Mostly delivery of child is supported by girl’s parents. They are expected to pay hospital bills, transportation etc. Kua poojan In haryana, this is a ceremony of celebrating the birth of child. Mostly it’s done for boy baby born, but these days girl baby kua poojan is also seen. The reason behind this was money given by government to support girls, reduce female foeticide, and improving sex ratio. Due to these continuous support, some parents started celebrating girl’s kua poojan on their own wish, which is a good sign. Sometimes coins or eatable given equal to the weight of child. Bhat In this ritual , when girl’s children getting married, girl’s parents side people including parents brother or any relative, they give a gift to girl’s child in their wedding, this gift contains cash, jewelry etc. Same as dowry. Death At the time of death of girl, girl’s side people goes to girl’s in-laws home and do some ritual and give some clothes and money to girls’ in-laws. Teej This is a festival in India, comes on 3rd day of starting day of Shrawan(rainy) season. In this festival, people from girl’s family side most probably brother or father, they give some sweets, eatable to girl’s in-laws family, that can be readymade or home made or mixed. Also they gives fruits, and cash to girl’s in-laws. Makar Sakranti This Ritual is same as Teej but only difference is, it’s celebrated on 14 January. These rituals are definite, but there are uncertain rituals like birthday celebration of any family members in girl’s in-laws, then girl’s parents gives money, any function in girl’s in laws house. Girls parents goes and give money. In simple words Once a knot tied, girl’s family becomes giver and boy’s family becomes taker, even the generation passed away, but rituals goes on till eternity. column1: How was the divorce and widowhood system seen in the Sambandam concept of marriage in Kerala?
column3: Thanks Mayur Bangar for the question How was the divorce and widowhood system seen in the Sambandam concept of marriage in Kerala? I have made a detailed answer on the concept of Sambandham culture that prevailed among erstwhile upper castes of Hindu society of Kerala traditionally before it ended by 1940s-50s era completely. You can read my original answer on the concept of Sambandham as I don’t need to explain the system again here Arun Mohan (അരുൺ മോഹൻ)'s answer to What is Sambandham in Kerala? The basic tenant of Sambandham concept is consensus Live-in relationship. The basic concept of Marriage and husband-wife relationship or father-mother-children concept of family was not allowed among most of upper Hindu castes. So the basic purpose of sexual relationships were to produce offsprings and beyond which there is no sanctity to the relationship. So technically there was no marriage culture as such, rather it worked fully on live-in relationship style. The basic advantage of this system is commencement and termination of relationship at will and instantly. There were no huge rituals or process for start of this sort of relationship as well as end of this relationship as the society were both Polyandrous (women entering into sexual relationship as many as men as she likes) as well as Polygamous (men entering into sexual relationship with as many as women he likes). In a way, Sambandham system was much more sexually open system with no baggage of one-man/woman life time commitment etc. Due to this, many of traditional Hindu codes of chastity (Pavithratha) or marital vows or marriage concepts donot apply in Kerala context.As I said, Sambandham can be started quickly. In those days, Nair or Nampoothiri or Kshyatriya men in their trips around would identify ladies of higher castes/communities, normally in temples or any public places. When they like her, they may approach her uncle or mother at her family house. In some cases, they do directly approach to lady’s house out of intention to form an alliance with the family. Sambandham works only if lady’s uncle and senior members of family agree to it. If they agree, he will visit in evening soon after Sandyavandanam (lighting lamps for evening prayers) and offer a piece of cloth (Mundu/Dhoti) to the lady with whom he wish to enter into a sexual relationship. When the lady accepts the Mundu, the Sambandham has officially been commenced. The acceptance of Mundu from a man is called Pudamuri (Pudava means marital cloth and Muri means acceptance) and thats the official indication of start of sambandham. The lady is supposed to keep the Mundu with her untill termination of Sambandham. The existence of Mundu signifies the ongoing Sambandham relationship. General rule was that, at a time, only one Sambandham can be done, but in Travancore side, it wasn’t that strict, so a lady can have multiple Sambandhams at a time. The only condition is that, she should remember, who gave which Mundu to her. One thing to note- Sambandham happens at woman’s own house. There was no legal marriage, so the lady will never leave her house. Rather the man who will be known as Sambandhakaran (or consort as in British English terminology records) lives in wife’s house as long as Sambandham goes on. Thats why the rule of One Sambandham at a time existed. If the love was much stronger, the Sambandham shall go forever and the man will live in wife’s house forever. However officially he will be an outsider in wife’s house and can’t own or manage wife’s properties. He can simply stay there and live there as long as the wife pleases OR till her natural death. In all ways, the so-called consort or man’s status in this relationship is always inferior to the status of woman. He was an outsider and never enjoyed any privilege or status in woman’s perspective.An old pic of Queen Sethu Parvathy Bai who sits in a throne like chair with her consort- Rama Varma Koyil Thampuran sitting on a stool to signify his lower positionNow to the question How divorce works in Sambandham? Its the most easiest process. Divorce is called Ozhimuri in Malayalam and under Sambandham, Ozhimuri, its very instant and quick. The lady has full right to decide whether she wants to continue the Sambandham or not as the relationship works under lady’s pleasure. The Sambandhakaran has no much say on this. If he doesn’t want to continue, he can cease visiting the lady’s house as he has no personal responsibility to the lady. But he can’t cancel Sambandham by himself. Whereas the lady can. For lady to cancel Sambandham, she has to simply return back the Mundu which was given during the start of Sambandham. The Ozhimuri customs is simple. The lady summons the Sambandhakaran, but won’t allow to enter into the house. Rather make him stand at the forecourt (Thirumuttum). Then either she or her maid will come out, give the mundu to Sambandharakan and shuts the main door in front of him. That signifies termination of Sambandham with that man and he must leave the house. He will have no more visiting rights to the lady’s house. Ozhimuri customs vary from region to region, though returning of Mundu is more common across Kerala. In Malabar side, 10 threads from Mundu is taken and its twisted in front of the Sambandhakaran and broken into two and thrown opposite sides. That means the relationship is broken forever. This custom is locally known as Noolacharam (Nool- Thread, Acharam- Ritual) In Kochi and Central Kerala side, Mundu is returned in hand and door is shut to signify Ozhimuri In Southern Kerala side, instead of Mundu, the betal leaf box of Sambandhakaran will be kept at the Padipura door (main gate door) by the maid when he makes a visit to the lady’s home. The act of keeping Betal Leaf box at the gate door signifies, he is no more welcome to the home and Sambandham has officially ceased. His personal effects will be also kept outside, which he can collect and leave. A scene from Malayalam movie- Ozhimuri when the martriach of the family decided to terminate her relationship with her Sambandakaran by placing betal leaf box outside the house that symbolizes end of relationship and he has to leave the house In all cases, Ozhimuri was arbitrary and fully decided on will of the lady. In case, both lady and Sambandhakaran continues the relationship forever and if the lady dies first, then an automatic Ozhimuri happens. In such case, the man loses his right to live in that house and must leave after completion of Pela period (16 days from date of death)How Widowhood system worked Well, there is no concept of widowhood among upper Hindu castes of Kerala in past(barring Tamil Brahmins and Nampoothiri ladies who follows Patriarchal rules) There was no marriage at first place, so how there will be widowhood in event of death of husband. Infact there was no husband itself. The man was called Sambandhakaran which means Consensual Mate or just a consort… Death of Sambandhakaran effects nothing to the lady and her children born to him as he was an outsider. Even the traditional mourning rules (Pela) will not apply over them as he was no one for them. He was just a consensual sexual partner only This was one key reason, Kerala never had any concept of widowhood or its related issues See, in traditional Hindu marriage codes, a Marriage means setting relationship for 7 lives, not just this life. Once a man and woman enters into a marriage relationship, it means both man and woman will serve each other for 7 lives. If husband dies first, she has to sacrifice all pleasures of life and fast till end of her life, to get back the same husband in next birth. That’s why widowhood was a big deal and created lot of tortures or hardships for widows in reality as they were supposed to fast to get back the same man as husband in next birth. Its for this reason, at the time of marriage, 7 steps/rounds are made around the sacred fire to signify the commitment made for 7 lives (Saath Janam ke Rishte as said in Hindi). This never worked in Kerala. Even today, Malayalee Hindus never do 7 rounds around Fire (barring some communities like Nampoothiris or Tamil Brahmins etc) as we never enter into any marital vows of 7 lives. As a result, in Kerala Hindu culture (for all communities barring Nampoothiris), marriages are more of social contract prevailing between 2 individuals in this life time. Its never a matter of 7 lives. We never perform marriage in front of sacred fire (Agni) or invoke Agni thro’ a homam. In many traditional Indian marriages, the rational behind invoking Agni thro’ a Homam or a Havan etc is to have Agnideva (God of Fire who is also the divine messenger of gods) solemnizes marriages on earth on behalf of Gods. So only Agni can break a marital relationship (in form of cremation when Agni takes the body). Thats why widowhood concept do exist incase husband dies and wife stays back. But as Kerala never had sanctity for marriages, we never invoke Holy fire for Kerala marriages even today. As a result, none of the marriages are solemnized by Agni, hence no widowhood concept even today. Since 1940s, many North Indian concepts crept into Kerala system thro’ renaissance movement. So widowhood concept also came, but not severe or hard as one sees in North India, other than avoiding wearing Kumkum on forehead or bright color sarees (that too now reduced). In Sambandham times, there was no Widowhood concept among those who observes.Saying so, this wasn’t applied to Nampoothiri community who followed typical patriarchal rules as seen in North India. So Namboothiri women seriously suffered horrors of widow hood and never had liberty of easy divorce at will.

column1: What is the significance of Shraddha Pitru Paksha in Hindu tradition?
column3: History and culture have always played a predominant role in the Sanatana Dharma. In Hindu tradition, about a fortnight is usually earmarked every year for paying homage to our ancestors. This 16-day period is known as Pitru Paksha, or shradh . It is believed that the soul wanders in various worlds after a person dies. To ensure it finds peace and tranquillity and blesses those who are alive, people perform ‘Shradh’ rituals and repay their debts to the dead ancestors. Pitru Paksha begins after Purnima Tithi (full moon day) in Ashwin month, Krishna Paksha. This year, the Pitru Paksha begins on 11th of September, 2022 and ends with Mahalaya Amavasya falling on the 25th of September, 2022. Pitru Paksha marks the start of the waning phase of the lunar cycle. During this period, various rituals are carried out to pay respects to the dead. As mentioned earlier, it is believed that those who don't find peace in death, their soul wanders around the Earth to check on their family members. To ensure that they attain Moksha (salvation, getting free from the cycle of life and death), people perform pind daan (offering food to the soul). According to astrology, people who suffer from pitru dosha (curse of the ancestors) perform shradh rituals and offer food to the crows, cows, animals, alms to the indigent. Every Religion has its rituals in their own way and the nomenclature and observance may slightly vary. For example, in Islam too, there is an identical procedure which is being observed during Ramlan month. In Christianity, they visit the cemeteries and offer prayers to the deceased.Every month, Amavasya day is considered auspicious for the worship of forefathers and poojas are made. The dark fortnight of Ashwin month (September-October), also known as Ashwin Amavasya or Pitru Paksha (Mahalaya), is especially sacred for offering oblations to departed ancestors. The Mahalaya Amavasya is the day that marks the culmination of the Pitru Paksha period and the beginning of the Devi Paksha. The tarpan rites and offering pind daan for an ancestor should be done on the Tithi on which the person died. One should feed the Brahmins and also offer clothes to them. If the tithi of death is unknown then tarpan and pind daan should be done on the Amavasya of Shraddha Paksha. What is “Pitru Dosha”? If one does not perform the rituals prescribed in the Shastras like performance of annual Shraddha ceremony, observance of Mashalaya Paksha and performance of rituals for the ancestors, etc. then, “Pitru Dosha” or the curse of the ancestors is supposed to be hovering around that family. For example, there might be frequent skirmishes in the family or the members may be afflicted with chronic ailments, the agony of not having any children or those born are suffering from mental instability, etc. There may be consistent economic crisis in the family and failure to achieve success in work. While performing Pitr Pooja no meat should be taken or the offering of the same to the ancestors is forbidden. Elderly people should be respected. For those who observe the performance of rituals with dedication will be showered with blessings for prosperity, longevity and happiness. Complete celibacy should be observed during this fortnight and if a bird or animal comes to your house, it should be offered food or eatables as it is believed that ancestors do visit in their garb. Shaving should be avoided during this period or the cutting of nails too. The shopping of articles should also be avoided.On the thithi of the dead, Shradda ceremony is performed. Tarpan should also be performed for those ancestors. Every person born on this Planet owes three debts viz., Debts owed (a) to Devas (b) Rishis and (c) Pitrus. The first debt could be cleared through the performance of daily worship through Agni (Agnihotram), Five Mahayagnas. The second debt owed to Rishis should be overcome through the thorough learning of Vedic scriptures by adherence to celibacy. The Pitr Ruṇa (रुण) can be siphoned off by marrying a girl from the same Varnasrama with a good family background and begetting progeny. The children should be brought up by being debonair. The Pitru Paksha period of fortnight is considered to be their duration for visiting their family and children and after the expiry, they return back to their world. The Pitru Tarpan shall bring forth wealth, fame, longevity and finally after demise takes to Heaven. The following Sloka briefs in essence the above:- “Dhanyam, Yashashyam, Aayushyam, Swargyam, Shatruvinashanam, Kulachantharakam Cheti, Sraaddhamahur Maneeshinah: He, indeed, is a Brahmana in whom the status of Brahma exists,—that condition which is bereft of attributes and which has no stain attached to it. The boon-giving Brahma, while he created all creatures, himself said that the distribution of human beings into the four orders dependent on birth is only for purposes of classification. It would be apt to recollect Thirukkural in this regard: அந்தணர் என்போர் அறவோர்மற் றெவ்வுயிர்க்கும் செந்தண்மை பூண்டொழுக லான். அந்தணர் அறம் செய்யச்சொல்லும் வேதம் ஓதுவர். பிறருக்கு நன்மை செய்வர் The Brahmana is a great field in this world,—a field equipped with feet for it moves from place to place. He who plants seeds in that field,. That Brahmana who wishes to achieve his own good should always live upon the remains of the food that may be there in his house after gratifying the needs of all others. He should always adhere to the path of righteousness. Indeed, he should tread along the path that belongs to Brahma. He should live engaged in the study of the Samhitas and remaining at home he should discharge all the duties of a householder. He should always be devoted to the study of the Vedas, but he should never derive the means of subsistence from such study. That Brahmana who always conducts himself thus, adhering to the path of righteousness, worshipping his sacred fire, and engaged in the study of the Vedas, comes to be regarded as Brahma. The status of a Brahmana once gained, it should always be protected with care, THERE ARE MANY THINGS IN THIS WORLD WHICH CANNOT BE FATHOMED THROUGH THE YARDSTICKS OF SCIENCE

column1: What is the difference between Native American tribes that have two spirit individuals and other indigenous peoples, such as Australian Aboriginals or Maori New Zealanders?
column3: I Googled “Christian soul definition” before answering about Māori, remembering our ideas have been influenced by 200 years of Christianity. What I found was often vague and the word “unknowable” came up a lot. I know very little about Native American beliefs so I don’t know how ours compare. With no written scriptures the meaning Māori give to our word wairua (spirit) is mostly agreed by consensus. To us today it’s “disembodied individuality” that’s immortal and invulnerable, came from an ancestral homeland called Rangiatea (and stays connected) and after death returns to another called Hawaiki along a spirit path that includes ritual visits to ancestral sacred mountains with genealogical connection, finally departing from the pohutukawa tree halfway down the cliff at Te Rerenga Wairua (Cape Reinga that Pākehā incorrectly call Reeanga) then underwater to Three Kings Islands before flying across the waves. However they also seem to be “here” when needed as a marae karanga powhiri (the ceremonial start of a welcoming ceremony) summons them to assemble in the space reserved in front of the carved house to take part in the occasion, and many Māori believe they are also watching over us and guiding us in our daily lives. Being abstract they can of course be in two places at once. How much of that detail is due to missionary influence is anyone’s guess, but I suspect not a great deal as many Māori very easily adopted Christianity, although it was common practice for members of a family to join different denominations in case the beliefs of that particular missionary turned out to be false! Māori do have two other abstract spiritual attributes. One is mana which roughly translates as personal well-being, protection and power. We talk about restoring the mana of people who have suffered misfortune or fallen by the wayside, and leaders are said to possess a lot of mana. The other is mauri which is usually translated as “vital essence” and is possessed by both living and inanimate things. For instance some stones possess mauri, and often a mauri stone will be buried under the corner of a house to protect it and its occupants. The biennial cultural festival Te Matatini has its own mauri stone that is ceremonially handed over to the hosts for the next one (in 2025 Te Kahui Maunga, in their dialect it’s mouri) at the conclusion of each festival[1] to empower them to organise and run it.Footnotes[1] Te Matatini 2025: Journey begins as Te Kāhui Maunga receives mouri stone

column1: What were the reforms made by Mao Zedong?
column3: A lot. Mao inherited a country poorer then current Somalia. A rotten corpse totally devastated after decades of war, invasions, massacres and looting armies. Chiang Kai Shek removed all the gold and Stalin removed all industrial equipment in Manchuria. There was nothing standing but rotten staunch. And that rotten corpse was under total embargo from US-led West for more then two decades after he did take power in 1949 and removed all western influence. Making his task to uplift the country a hellish nightmare. No one wanted to have any connection with China at this time. The dirty kid in the school block. Only USSR and Pakistan did lend a hand. That should not be forgotten. In the last decade, China has collaborated much more expansively with Pakistan. Examples since 2010 include A-100 rocket launchers, HQ-16 air defence missile systems and VT-4 tanks, which are reportedly now being tested in Pakistan.[1] For Pakistan’s defence planners, the collaboration with China on defence technology is not only about equipping their own armed services. They are also hoping they can become arms exporter and, in doing so, help to boost the country’s low foreign currency reserves.Mao Zedong is one of the greatest leaders in Chinese history. His major achievement, in short, is to transform the weak, scattered, socially unequal, culturally setback, economically backward & colonized, war-tortured China into an independent and militarily secured country. The premise and perspective of my review: Mao is well known across the world, people either admire him as a hero, or distaste him as an evil dictator. Many of these biased points of view are very often based on untrue stories or ideological stereotypes, and debates and controversies are never absent on this subject. The first problem with the lack of a thorough, unbiased, comprehensive review of this man is the missing of verified biographical details. Many accounts and incidents that truly happened in history are still under seal. The western academia and media, however, tended to cite other sources into discussion, sometimes unverified personal accounts, sometimes rumors, sometimes even made-up stories. Apart from insufficient materials on Mao’s biographical dimension, another problem in reviewing this man’s historical influences and impacts, both domestically and globally, is the enormous scale and continuing development of which. Take the Cultural Revolution as an example, the impact and result of this massive turmoil is still emerging. It could be interpreted as a disastrous event that halted China’s development for a decade (as many people would have thought), or it could be a cornerstone of China’s super-fast modernization afterwards. It is just too early to label such a drastic and influential event into a final conclusion, which is indiscreet and illogical. Therefore, the following review of Chinese former leader Mao Zedong would be based on publicly accessible and verified materials, mostly the man’s political, military, economic and cultural achievements. And all conclusions would be drawn upon confirmed historical records. Duly notice that I’m not intending to make a comprehensive and final review on him, I’ll focus on achievements we can be sure of. Three dimensions of my review:Politics and MilitaryEconomicsCulture1. Achievements on Politics and Military: The Stood Up Chinese People. At the time when Chinese Communist Party was founded by a couple of reforming activists including Mao Zedong, China was a “semi-colonial & semi-feudal” society. The majority of Chinese people lived in unimaginably inhuman oppression and exploitation under landlords, warlords, capitalists and colonists. The class contradiction in China was so severe that those oppressed people: the workers, the average farmers, the women were treated like livestock, or pure-dehumanized-animals, by the ruling class. It was one of the darkest era in modern history, the entire China was like a gigantic Auschwitz and people were suffering like hell. There is no language bad enough to describe those atrocities. The superficial government of ROC was consisted of mostly KMT members, but the real power belonged to warlords. The warlords formed alliance with local capitalists, landlords and colonists to maintain absolute control on their territories, making China a de-facto scattered country. The warlords’ military ambition was never to fight for the Chinese people, they fought wars with other warlords to expand their own power and they were subsidized by different colonial empires. War ripped China again and again. The famous chairman of KMT, Chiang Kai-shek, was a constant winner of those warlord wars and became the most powerful person in China. It was heart-bleeding to review that period of China’s history, just simply death and oppression. The armies of ROC were supposed to protect Chinese people from invasions and colonization; instead, they pointed their ruthless guns to the people. When the Imperial Japanese army engineered the Mukden Incident, or “September 18th Incident’’ to invade Manchuria (North-Eastern provinces of China), Chiang Kai-shek was too busy extinguishing Chinese population (soviet regimes in southern China) and refused to fight against the Japanese invaders. He notoriously claimed: “Internal pacification before external resistance”. I. Mao Zedong, alongside with other Communists, built the “People’s Army”. Discipline and political education were implemented thoroughly in Mao's army, the soldiers were disciplined and self-disciplined against what other armies constantly did: bully, hurt, abuse, cheat, discriminate, rape, rob, arrest, interrogate, kill ordinary people. Mao Zedong was particularly concerned about the disciplines and political awareness of the army. He proposed that the party branch should be built on company level so that the soldiers would be loyal to the party rather than to commanders, and soldiers' personal goal would be transformed from pursuit on personal benefits to pursuit on a collective benefit of all Chinese people, which at Mao’s time was the belief of CCP. Later, his thoughts on the construction of the army were published as “Three Rules of Discipline and Eight Points of Attention”:The three rules enjoinedprompt obedience to orders,no confiscation of peasant property, andprompt delivery directly to authorities of all items confiscated from landlords.The eight points were: 1. Be polite when speaking 2. Be honest when buying and selling 3. Return all borrowed articles 4. Pay compensation for everything damaged 5. Do not hit or swear at others 6. Do not damage crops 7. Do not harass females 8. Do not mistreat prisonersThe army built under Mao’s thoughts was drastically different from KMT ones. Mao’s army was able to bring military victory to Chinese people while Chiang's couldn't. During the Sino-Japanese war, the ROC’s army, led by Chiang Kai-shek, lost China’s capital city and more than a third of China’s land to Japanese invaders, and it was incapable of evicting Japanese invaders out of China. Mao’s army was a modern army that fought for the people, of the people, by the people. Unlike KMT’s warlord coalition system, Mao’s army didn’t swear loyalty to any person (not even Mao himself), they swore to protect the Chinese people and uphold their communist faith. It was the first army that Chinese people truly put their trust on, truly relied on when in need, and wholeheartedly adored. II. Mao’s political achievements were also critical to a modernizing China we see today, on government level: a. Establishment of a real-functioning central government that was able to govern entire China. Chiang Kai-shek and his ROC government was never able to completely govern this big country, and repeatedly faced fiscal crises (e.g. acute depreciation of currency) that turned the government into complete disability. On the contrary, Mao established a government that was efficient, centralized, effective and fiscally stable. Decisions from the central government would be implemented at local levels, and currency was valued and stabilized. The weakness and incapability commonly seen in the previous ROC government were not seen in Mao’s PRC government. This is still benefiting China till this day, the high efficiency and strong implementation of policies we see today has been existing since Mao’s era. b. Mao’s political shrewdness made China stand independently in the bi-polar international politics in the Cold War era. China once was a “little buddy” of the “big brother” USSR at the start of Cold War era and stood against the US both politically and militarily. At the 70s, Mao sensed the potential threat coming from the USSR and boldly detached China from the Communism community and restored diplomatic relations with the US and other western nations. Backed up by the nuclear weaponry (which again was a result of Mao’s insistent will), China was able to stand independently between the two powers and regained the permanent seat in the UN Security Council. His decision was a foundation of China’s international influence and economic globalization that we see today. So, Mao’s political and military achievement can be concluded that, he founded a modern Chinese nation-state and relieved the Chinese people from unimaginable oppression.2. Achievements on Economic Development: Industrial Revolution. Although China began industrialization since late 19th century, China failed evolve into an industrial economy and remained a predominantely agricultural economy until the late 20th century. The hindrance of China’s industrial revolution was namely repeating wars, colonized market, poorly educated labor force, corrupted and incapable government etc. The ROC government wasn’t able to absorb the majority of population into industrial production, and thus when they left mainland for Taiwan, China was still pathetically poor. Thus, Mao did something incredibly laudable: to industrialize China. Mao’s utilitarian approach to the USSR and the PRC government’s huge mobilization capability enabled China to quickly attain an industrial foundation. “First Five-year Plan of China (1953-1957)” was a massive plan for industrialization assisted by USSR. There were 156 projects on infrastructure, heavy industry, national defense industry, energy industry etc. Those were precious foundations of industrial power that later on enabled China to build nuclear weaponry, satellites, vaccinations, combustion engines, chemical fertilizers etc. that were critical and indispensable to the country’s further developments. There wouldn’t be any massive industrialization and urbanization in the past thirty years without the Mao’s industrial foundation. And of course, there wouldn’t have been an independent diplomatic status during the Cold War if China hadn’t have a nuclear weaponry. Mao’s foresight on China’s economic development were poignant since he laid out all the crucial foundations upon which China develops today.3. Achievements on Culture Aspects: Controversial Yet Progressive: The most controversial part to review was Mao’s influence on China’s culture, so I would stick to proven achievements. Other unmentioned “feats”, such as breaking traditional cultural heritages during the Cultural Revolution, are still influencing China today and thus we need more time to tell the consequences. I. Education: In 1949, the year PRC was established, illiteracy rate in China was 80%, and only 20% of eligible children were receiving education. That was pathetic. Chinese people, like their ancestors, were mostly uneducated, illiterate, alienated to modern science. A well-educated labor force is the core of a country’s economic development and technological breakthrough. But China didn’t have it. In 1949, Chinese people were still believing that ghost would come to take children’s souls away when children were sleeping, and that sickness was caused by spirits and ghosts. Superstition was prevalent in the minds of Chinese people. People feared cameras because they thought taking a photography is taking away a person’s soul. Mao, feeling a strong urge to bring knowledge and enlightenment to Chinese people, urged relentlessly on education and literacy. He initiated four literacy campaigns briefly after the establishment of PRC, these campaigns successfully transformed more than 100 million illiterate population into literacy and made them valuable workers of industrial economy. Besides literacy campaigns, the PRC government in Mao’s era built a comprehensive education system ranging from primary school, middle school, high school, vocational school, colleges and graduate school. The socialist education system gave the majority of Chinese children a chance to learn knowledge and skills for the first time in history. II. Gender Equality. Before establishment of the PRC, women in China had the lowest social status. They were regarded as property of the family, thus they were sold or traded to different men for different purposes. Women were not human in the old agricultural Chinese society. The traditional social dogma objectified women by the idiom “an unaccomplished woman is a virtuous women”, and trained women to live a “three obedience and four virtues” life. The “Three Obedience and Four Virtues” were: obey your father before marriage, obey your husband after marriage, obey your son after death of the husband; virtue of women morality (utter loyalty to the husband), virtue of proper speech (free expression banned), virtue of modest manner (obey every male in daily life), and virtue of diligent work (do all the hard chores without complaint). Before Mao, women lived as reproductive tools and slaves. Perhaps the most famous traditional Chinese ritual that oppressed women was the binded feet.(Warning! Graphic content!) Female, as young as three or four years old, were required to bind her feet to constraint of growing. Male dominated traditional Chinese society viewed this kind of inhuman women feet attractive and ethical because it had a symbol of obedience and modesty. The bones in her feet were distorted and cannot sustain a woman to walk too long, thus minimizing the possibility of her running away from the family. This shit had been prevalent in rural China till 1949. Mao, being a socialist leader, supported complete liberation of women. He constantly wrote about gender equality in his articles, he lectured, and he encouraged women to participate in the Chinese Communist revolution and to join the party. He wrote “Women hold up half the sky”, that until this day it was still remembered worldwide.(Above: A propaganda poster of gender equality. Below: a banner of a protest in the US with the famous quote.)The new women in Mao’s era:This is a statue depicting women soldiers in the Red Army. They walked as normal people, they fought in wars with real guns, they did everything a male can possibly do. Reading about these young, energetic, educated, persistent women in historical materials always make me tremendously happy and touched.Look at her! A fine, independent young female soldier! First time in thousand years of history that a woman would do exactly what a man would without being criticized or harassed. Not limited within the party and army, Mao incorporated gender equality into the very basics of the PRC: The Constitution. After the establishment of PRC, gender equality was stressed out as an important mission of the CCP. Mao’s socialist system provided equal rights to women, banned inequality in employment and education, and campaigned to renew the old stereotypes. Equal rights in economy and marriage were legislated, women organizations were encouraged. The result was a huge improvement of women’s status in China. (Complete gender equality is still developing up till this day, but Mao laid out its foundation by destroying the traditional oppression to women. This is definitely a huge achievement, given the stubbornness of traditional values.)To this point, I think it’s safe to say that Mao Zedong is a savior of Chinese civilization in 20th century. He turned a failing country into a politically independent, economically developing and socially progressing nation. Without him, there is a high probability that China would still be a scattered civilization consisted of hundreds of thousands of nobility and hundreds of millions of pathetic, dehumanized poor people. Bravo, Chairman MaoFootnotes[1] VT-4 - Wikipedia

column1: I had a cat for 18 years. I felt more emotion and sadness upon losing him than I did when even my father died. Is this wrong?
column3: It is perfectly normal. Losing a parent can be very difficult, an unusual type of loss that is different from losing another family member or friend. Both good and dysfunctional relationships need processing, so whether your dad was your best friend or an abusive jerk will affect your experience. His death may force you to evaluate unresolved childhood issues or consider your genetic links to mortality. Yet this is an expected life experience, one of the big ones on the journey to growing up: one’s parents simply do not live forever. There is tremendous cultural support and spiritual ritual around such loss, which help with coping and processing. Everyone is sympathetic: your boss, your teachers, your friends. You were a kitty parent. For many people, losing a furbaby is absolutely as traumatic as losing a child. Losing a human child is unexpected — we hope and plan to outlive them. Yet the tragedy of loving a cat is knowing their life spans are short and their eventual deaths can be devastating. My cat Giles loves me intensely and unconditionally, even when I am sad, stressed, sick, have screwed up, or am a useless lump who needs a shower. He forgives me when I give him meds, take him to the vet, or accidentally step on his tail. He loves other people, too, but daily demonstrates I am his clear favourite, the centre of his world. The loss of a beloved pet is made worse because culturally we do not have the same support mechanisms to process grief over animals. Some people will grok your pain and offer real support and understanding. Others will be astonishingly cruel and insensitive (‘It was just a cat. You spent how much to save it?’) Expect only meagre sympathy from others who might care but underestimate the impact. Most workplaces do not validate sick or bereavement time for the death of an animal. Grief is complicated. It is normal to experience a wide range of deep and complex emotions, including guilt, shame, sorrow, fear, relief, gratitude, and even moments of joy. Let yourself feel what you feel. And may you be comforted by many happy memories during your time of sorrow. What is remembered, lives. ❤️

column1: Adult What is the whole process of a funeral procession in Tamil Nadu?
column3: Thanks for A2A. I guess, I can't give a generalized answer, because, people from different community have different process of funeral processions. Even,same community people has different way of funeral processions because of their different geographical locations, like North Tamil Nadu people from same community, has different way compared to South Tamil Nadu people of same community. I only know about the Hindu funeral processions, hence, I will steer clear, of other religious based processes. Sorry, this will be a very looooonnngggg answer ; I will try to highlight only the things which are similar to almost all the hindu communities. Once, a person is dead, first, the room or the place where the body is to be kept for the display is cleaned.The body is covered with white cotton cloth(in the case of men, and a saree in the case of women) and made sure that eyes are closed and in order to stop the body from inflated due to the oxygen getting into their lungs, the nostrils, ears are covered using cotton plugs. Body is kept either on the floor or the cot or nowadays, a refrigerated glass display box, by having the head placed towards the South direction, which is considered as the direction where the lord of death "Yaman" or "Yamraj" lives(Similar to grim reaper of western culture). A traditional oil lamp called as "Vilaku" is lit adjacent to the side where the head was placed. A one rupee coin will be placed on the forehead, which is meant to be the fees for the person who cremates him on the crematorium. There are other rituals, which changes according to the sex of the dead person, women and men. Again, some differences, if the women was dead as a sumangali(dead, while her husband is still living) and a women dead as a widow. I am not quite sure of all the rituals. I will try concentrate on rituals followed for men. Then, the people, mostly saivaites(people following saivism or followers of Lord Shiva) start to recite Thevaram and Thiruvasagam verses(Religious literature verses written by nayanmars or the great saints of Saivism). Then comes the OPPARI or LAMENTING. Women, gather around with open hair, start to sing their sorrows due to the person's death, singing the feeling, of how they miss that person, stating some of the greatness and achievements of the dead person, etc. They say those things in a musical tone. In Tamil culture, or even I would say, most of the Indian culture embraces music on their every occasion and treat it like part of their life. From the first day of the birth to the last day of the life. Thalatu(lullaby) to the last Oppari(lament). every aspects of life of Indians are filled with music. In some community, the person who is about to perform all the final funeral rites, will be made to shave their hairs on their head and also shave their beards and moustache and won't eat anything until the cremation is done. The music band like the traditional, thappaatam and a changu(Chank - a species belonging to sea shells) blower is called to perform together. The general reason behind it is said as, in olden days(like during pre-modern age), where the medical field were not proper, and can't entirely conclude that a person was dead or not, these music percussion instruments are banged to make sure that a person is dead and not having a very deep sleep ;). Then the persons are called for constructing a "Paadai"(A stretcher like structure) made of 2 bamboo stems, placed parallel to each other and "Thennai Olai"(Coconut tree leaves) are used to create an interlinked mesh like structure to support the body while carrying. Optionally, these paadai are created even more bigger, like a big structure made of bamboo and decorated with flowers as per the individual's choices.Image Source: Page on fotolibra.com In the recent times, Some thing like the above picture are made, but still the main paadai is same as the simple 2 bamboo sticks and the coconut leaves. While all these things are being done, simultaneously, the purohit, will start some rituals, where the dead person's eldest son is opted to do the final rituals or the person who the dead person choose themselves before dying, if, the dead person don't have a son for themselves. According to the beliefs, generally, the rituals are 2 types, one is making aware of the fact that a person is dead to both their current generation family and the ancestors of the family. They make them ready to take their ultimate journey towards THE ONE or called as "Parama Aatma" in Hindu culture. Saivaites, say, the dead people's souls reach Lord Shiva. The another part which the purohitars do, is the rituals for making sure that the soul starts the journey towards the swargam(Heaven) and try to release the soul from the death-rebirth cycle(Reincarnation) and get moksha(Salvation). Once, all the religious rites done at the place where the body was kept in the house, the body is taken towards the crematorium, on the built paadai, by only men, because, women are not allowed to go to the crematorium, I really don't know the reason, behind, it, IMO, I guess, it is said, because the women being more emotionally attached to the dead person, seeing lively, the body of their loved person getting cremated, they might get psychologically affected. The body was taken to the crematorium, either by taking the body through the streets by people carrying paadai on their shoulders or bullock carts, where the people play the thappaatam and dance throughout the way until they reach the crematorium. (The dance and the music is supposed to be taken as the metaphor, whatever you do or dance in your life, you can't take anything or do anything after you stopped breathing. there is a comedy dialog too like "Even though if a person is a great dance master, he can’t dance for his own funeral" ;) There, the purohitars will perform the rites, like putting the white rice on the mouth of the dead body(No idea, why they do that, sorry :( ), then the relatives get a sandalwood, if they can afford for it, to put it on the logs which will be used to cremate the body, there, the body is kept on the logs and the dried cow dung, which are used to cremate. The, person who is performing the final rites, will first initiate the fire. Now, in recent times, the modern crematorium shelters are used, where they use closed and supervised crematorium chambers. Once, the cremation is over, the people will go back to home, take a bath and complete few rituals and have food. They will wait for the next day. The second day, the person who did the final rites, will go to the crematorium, to collect the ashes or even some bones remained after the body burnt, they put it on a jar filled with milk, to separate the bone from a wooden chunk,(Bones will be drowned and wooden chunks will be floating), then they take the ashes in a sealed jar. People decide the place, where they can mix the ashes, some chooses, the sea, some chooses the holy place like Kashi or Rameshwaram and carry the sealed jar to those places and mix the ashes on the Ganges in Kashi or the sea at Rameshwaram. Others, opt the local rivers as the place for mixing the ashes. These are pretty much similar proceedings of a Hindu community's final funeral rites. I have only mentioned few highlights or the drop of the processions, from the actual processions, which are like an ocean. Hope this helped you to get a little bit of an idea about the subject. Edit 1: Iam adding additional points shared by Mr.Seshadri Nagarajulu sir Wonderful answer. I will add few which comes to my mind.The rituals are done by the eldest son of the dead woman. (Since bearing the eldest son proved that she is fertile.(the first issue could be a girl too. But this is what I read))If the dead happens to be a man, the rituals are done by his youngest son.If the dead don't have sons of their own, their nephews do it.As per our tradition, from the moment a person a dies none of the family members will eat anything. Only after cremation/burial they will eat. But this is not followed much now a days.The corpse is given a head bath. They rub traditional perfumes on the corpse.A new white cloth is spread on the corpse (for men) and a saree (for women)If the dead is a married and the spouse is alive, garland exchanges takes place. ( as done during the marriage)If the dead is a man, the woman gets a new set of dress from her parents/ siblings. She wears it after the corpse is given the bath ( just like we do in marriage. During marriage too we wear new cloths).Then the corpse is away for burial/ crematorion.The head of the corpse is facing the home till a certain distance.At a usual place the body is performed a pooja and now the head faces the cremetorium.All the way till the corpse reaches the burial/crematorium, flowers are thrown on the road. There may be late comers. If the funeral procession has passed a particular road the latecomer may not know the exact way to the burial ground/cremetorium. They can identify the route by just looking at the road.On reaching the burial/ cremation ground, first the son performs a pooja.Then he gives/ throws rice & milk. This is just giving food to the departed soul.If its burial the body is lowered into the pit and the pit is closed.Then a mud pot with water is placed on the shoulder of the son.He will go round the body (if its funeral)/ fresh mud cementry .For each round a hole is made in the pot.On the third round the pot us slipped and he throws a lighted wood on the cemetery/body. And he goes back to home.Before lighting up the body is fully covered with dry wood/cow dung cakes, camphour & kerosene.The rituals mentioned is almost correct. Still every caste, region has its own variation. If some thing is wrong, its my mistake only. Explaination point 18: The pot symbolises the life /body we got during birth. It was filled with soul (water here). As the man goes on his life journey he gets old ( a hole is made and water seeps out). Finally he dies, the soul goes to the God (the pot is broken, the remaining water reaches the ground). This act is done to make others (those who are around during the ceremony) realise that death is inevitable and ensure that they live a meaningful life. No one has told me the last explaination but this is what I reasoned. I am open for corrections Disclaimer: The things I have mentioned here are my own interpretations of the funeral processions of people belonging to the Hindu community from North Tamil Nadu only, please feel free to comment here if there are any errors in my answer, I am all ears and happy to correct it.
