column1: Are there many gun owners who, erstwhile opposed to stricter background checks, now take the position that they are sadly necessary because the expression of one's Second Amendment rights are too often intruding upon other rights?
column3: I'm sure the anti-gun zealots like to pretend to themselves that their proposals are so “common sense”, and the problem so critical that there are a good number of gun rights supporters who have begun to soften their resolve. But nothing of the sort is happening - because these proposals are “common sense” only to those who are fundamentally ignorant about guns, and to anyone with any familiarity with the gun culture, they're f'ing nuts. Ran across an interesting article that tried to explain just why gun owners tell pollsters they support the idea off background checks, then so universally reject the proposals that are actually made: Game theory and guns: why universal background checks are a debate - and how to solve itIf universal background checks have 90% support, why haven’t they already become law? This is the simplest of the three, and it comes down to a difference between support for the general concept and support for how it works in real life. The thing that polls in the 80-90% range is this exact wording (with minor variations in different polls): “Would you favor or oppose background checks on all potential gun buyers?” Background checks have been mandatory under federal law for all gun store purchases since 1993. That requirement doesn’t apply to sales between private individuals, because forcing background checks for all sales (e.g. sales between friends) was politically unpopular and didn’t have the votes in Congress. So private sales were offered as a compromise to get the law passed. “Universal background checks” is the term for now revoking that compromise and expanding the law to cover all firearm transfers, whether the seller/transferor is a gun shop or just a private individual. But an actual law has to go into more detail than: Run background checks on all potential gun buyers. Thanks. – Congress What kinds of detail? I’m going to set a timer for 60 seconds and start thinking of edge cases a universal background check law would have to account for. Ok, here goes:Loaning guns on a ranchLoaning guns to a hunting buddyInheritancesGifting to family membersGifting to a friendLoaning to friends or familyRepairSafe keeping for travThat last word should be “travel”, but I stopped typing when the 60 seconds were up. If you don’t live in a high-gun-ownership area, I know these edge cases seem silly. “What, you’re going to give your teenager a rifle for Christmas?” The answer, believe it or not, is “Actually, yes.” In much of the country, gun ownership is swirled into foundational cultural rituals like it’s Neapolitan soft serve. Giving your kid a rifle for Christmas isn’t just utterly normal, it’s a time-honored rite of passage. Telling a ranch hand to grab the rifle out of your truck before he leaves to guard some livestock for a few days isn’t just a convenience, it’s how you keep the ranch running. Loaning your new pistol to a friend so he can try it out isn’t just a favor, it’s a way to deepen that friendship just like loaning him a book or going out to dinner. (For more on edge cases, see David Kopel’s detailed breakdown of the universal background check bill from earlier this year.) (And while I’m writing parentheticals, suicidal ideation is an edge case I didn’t think of in the 60-second sprint above. But it’s a big one. Two-thirds of shooting deaths are suicides. We should all want it to be incredibly, trivially easy for someone to say to a friend or family member, “I’m going through a deep depression. Could you hang onto my guns for a while?” Universal background checks make that illegal. People with severe depression aren’t going to drag a friend to a gun store, involve the gun shop owner in their private mental health issues, and pay a transfer fee for each gun. BJ Campbell wrote a piece specifically about this non-obvious suicide risk of UBCs.) Again, this will all seem easy to dismiss if you live in a place where these things aren’t normal. But that’s the point — there are a lot of places where these things are normal. People aren’t going to drive an hour to the gun store with their friend or family member, pay a fee, do a background check, loan the gun, and then do the whole thing over again when the person gives the gun back. They’re just not. And not only are they not going to do it, they’re going to resent whoever tried to make them. That’s all purely descriptive — whether a UBC law is good, bad, or indifferent, as an empirical matter people will break it pretty much universally. Cam Edwards described this with a different cultural touchstone that could help bring the problem closer to home: “Trying to enforce a law requiring background checks on gun owners selling one of their firearms to another individual would be like trying to enforce a law requiring you to show ID before you can get a beer from your buddy’s cooler at the neighborhood BBQ.” So the answer to this section’s question — “If universal background checks have 90% support, why haven’t they already become law?” — is coming into focus. The vaguely-worded question of whether buying a gun should require a background check is what gets 90% support. And yes, you’d expect 90% of people to “sure, why not” that general idea in a quick phone survey. But once people see what the details of a UBC law look like in real life, things change. Rephrase the question to capture those details — “Should it be a felony to lend your hunting buddy a gun if his gun breaks?” or “How much jail time should you get for giving your cousin a gun for his birthday?” — and people sour on it quickly. That’s descriptive, not speculative. Empirically, these laws are a lot more contentious than the 90% talking point suggests. David Kopel summed up how UBCs fare in state-level referendums: “Actual election polls tell a different story. Defeated in Maine, passed by less than 1% in Nevada. Passed with 59% in Washington. Once voters learn how miswritten these bills are, including HR8 in Congress, support plunges.” UBCs only got 59% of the popular vote in Washington, a state that hasn’t elected a Republican senator since 1994 or a Republican governor since 1980. UBCs were rejected by Congress in the 1993 Brady Bill, specifically as a compromise to get the bill to pass — and the early ’90s were a high-water mark for support for gun control. Shortly thereafter, the public began a 25+ year trend of steadily declining support for gun control across nearly every demographic, and that trend continues through the present. In terms of long-term trends, statistically gun control has never been less popular than it is today. Taking all this together, it’s just not plausible that UBCs actually have popular support. Once people see the details, they read it as an attack on their lifestyle. These laws have gotten traction in places where that lifestyle has been extinguished (or never existed) as a significant cultural bloc. Everywhere else, UBCs simply do not have support outside of phone surveys.

column1: Can you explain the concept of a meaningful life in Hinduism and if it is present in Hindu philosophy?
column3: A meaningful life in the Hinduism is one that is dedicated to the fulfilment of the five debts - RUṆA - with which each of us is born. The framework of this discharge of the five debts is called Pañca Mahā Yajñas the function of which is to create and maintain harmony in three spheres of our lives (tri hita karaṇa). 1. Harmony between humans, families, communities, nationalities etc. 2. Harmony between humans and the environment and all other sentient beings that share the environment with us. 3. Harmony between humans and the deities. The debt incurred is called RUṆA and the means of discharging the debt is called YAJÑA.Pitru ruṇa — debt to the parents and the ancestors.Pitru Yajña — The fact of our birth, and the loving care, protection and nurturing of our parents obligates us to them and to our grandparents and all the other members of our family. This debt is discharged by — 1. honouring our parents and paying them respect. 2. Seeking their advice and guidance knowing that they are our greatest well-wishers. 3. by marrying and procreating to continue the line. 4. After marriage in householder stage it is our duty to take care of them and support them in their old age. 5. Upon their death we need to perform their funeral rites appropriately. 6. Thereafter the performance of the śrāddha ceremonies to honour their memory. 2. Rishi Runa — debt to the sages Brahma Yajña — Our sages (Rishis) have dedicated themselves to the path of enlightenment for the welfare of all beings. These magnanimous sages have performed intense austerities to realize the truth and have passed down their wisdom through their disciples in order that we too may spiritually develop, unfold and progress towards enlightenment. The debt that we owe them is called “brahma’ which means ‘immense’. It is discharged by:— 1. Taking the trouble to study their teachings daily, to spend some time every day reading spiritual books such as Gita, Upanishads, Ramayana etc. 2. By researching, investigating and studying our cultural heritage or at the very least making the attempt at being culturally informed about the basics. 3. Teaching this knowledge to our children, passing on our spiritual and cultural heritage. 3. Deva Ruṇa — debt to the gods Deva Yajña — The Devas are the cosmic forces which administer and govern the universe under the direction of the Supreme Lord. All these forces of nature and cosmic principles are rewarded by making daily offerings to them to show our gratitude and to help us cultivate an awareness of the underlying cosmic consciousness behind all phenomenal appearances. 1. We should keep an altar at home and make daily offerings of flowers, water and incense. 2. Whenever possible we should go to the temple to make some offerings and attend festivals. 3. On festivals and special occasions we should conduct a puja or havan ceremony at home. In the Gīta Kṛṣṇa says that the one who enjoys the bounty of the gods without offering them anything in return is verily a thief!इष्टान्भोगानिह वो देवा दास्यन्ते यज्ञा-भाविताः । तैर्दत्तान् अप्रदायैभ्यो यो भुङ्क्ते स्तेन एव सः॥ iṣṭān-bhogān-iha vo devā dāsyante yajñā-bhāvitāḥ | tair-dattān apradāyaibhyo yo bhuṅkte stena eva saḥ || 3:124. Manuṣya Runa — debt to society Manuṣya yajña — We are by nature social animals and cannot live in isolation. Everything that we enjoy comes to us through the agency of other people. We are therefore indebted to the society in which we live. Traditionally this debt was discharged by daily offering hospitality to strangers in the village. An orthodox Hindu would try to feed a stranger every day. There are three minimal requirements which must be offered to a guest; a seat, water to drink, and kind words. Nowadays we can discharge this debt by:— 1. By welcoming and offering hospitality to strangers whenever and however possible. 2. By caring for the poor and the needy whenever the occasion arises. 3. By contributing to social causes such as disaster appeals. 4. By even paying taxes, abiding by the laws of the country and by fulfilling our civic duties in everyway possible we are contributing to the welfare of the society. 5. To protect others in the society and to ensure we cause no harm in anyway or obstruct the legitimate pursuits of other communities. 5. Bhūta Runa — debts to the elements Bhūta yajña — And lastly we are part of an environment which is made up of the five elements and consists of plant and animal life (bhūtas = elementals). This ecosystem is vital to our survival and thus it is our duty to continually protect it. This is done through:— 1. Joining tree planting programs and minimization of habitat destruction. 2. Supporting sustainable farming methods and protection of wildlife. Try to buy ethically produced foods avoiding factory farming 3. Decreasing our consumption of valuable resources. In our homes we can take the effort to limit the amount of water, gas and electricity consumed. 4. By becoming proactive in recycling and avoiding the unnecessary generation of harmful waste — such as the use of plastic bags and all unnecessary packaging etc. These five sacrifices form the basis of Hindu practice. It’s the discharging of these debts that form the core of our ritual and social duties. These yajñas unite all Hindus in common practice whereas theological and philosophical beliefs and convictions may differ widely and serve to divide one group from another.

column1: Are there family members you've chosen to not talk to anymore?
column3: I have not spoken to my identical twin sister for 13 years now. We were 36 years old then. Why? The ultimate end was her doing - she was living with me, my husband and our two young kids. We were caring for her 4 yo son so she could go back to shift work. She wasn’t paying her way, would sleep all the time, and basically was taking us for a ride. The three kids were treated the same and were like brothers. She came home early one day while I was cooking dinner and hid in the dining room. I’d been at work all day, and at this time I had three kids under 4 in the kitchen. I was grumpy because she had not cleaned the stove after spilling stuff on it, so I had to do this before I could get the kid’s dinner. She overheard me basically grumping one line about that she should have cleaned the stove. She burst into the room and screamed at me like a banshee. Anyway, she took off and disappeared for about a week with her son. Next thing I know there is a removalist truck at the house and she was packing up and leaving. I was home studying for exams. She said she’d be back to clean - I told her not to bother. Just go. That was all good and well, but then I was called into the children’s creche office and was told that she’d been taken in by good Samaritans and was telling everyone that we had abused her and her son. They initially believed her, but then smelled a rat. The creche director did not believe her - knew me and my husband… and her. So, she did not put in a ‘mandatory’ report to the government which could have seen us lose our kids and my husband his teaching job. This of course was not an isolated incident. My twin sister had a long history (since early childhood) of very difficult behaviour and had been very negative, and caused me lots of grief throughout school, university and beyond. She was seeing psychiatrists by 15 and blaming everyone for everything. She was a massive drain on my psychological resources with regular threats of suicide, self-harming etc etc. She was diagnosed with Borderline Personality Disorder. She would have everyone believe that we were seriously abused as children (we grew up in a strict environment, but we were not abused). All my life I had put up with her drama, abuse and lies. At 36 she’d throw tantrums and write me 20 page hate-mail letters claiming I was mean to her in a fight when we were 4… stuff that was ridiculous. The accusations, negativity… claims of abuse… vitriol… Ugh!! I tried setting my boundaries - including that I’d not discuss historical incidents, nor read her hate mail. She started sending it to my work. She started sending some to my husband too. She also wanted to ‘share’ my husband… that is another story. Anyway, after she ‘disowned’ me I’ve gone on to NOT miss her drama at all. It isn’t the way I’d have preferred things to be, but it is the necessary way for things to be. Since she disowned us… she’s gone on to turn on our father, my brother, my (now late) mother… and disowned them all too and has stopped any of us from seeing her son (who is about to turn 18). They were all accused of ‘abuse’ in one form or another too. She speaks only to our younger sister who lives overseas - and our younger sister pays dearly for that privilege with being manipulated and hit up for money by my twin. I am quite happy to remain estranged from my twin sister. People think this is strange and unnatural of me. I really don’t want or need to invite the drama back into my life. I know through friends that my twin’s behaviour has not changed - she’d now disowned her new husband (of 5 years) family too… Our mother died unexpectedly in September of this year. She had not seen her grandson or daughter in 13 years. This caused her great pain - not so much about my sister, but not seeing her grandson. Mum did not want anything more to do with my sister either. There had been attempts at reconciliation in the early days - but, my sister remained nasty and wouldn’t reconcile unless Mum just accepted everything she demanded (lies and all). Mum had written my sister out of her will. She knows this now and we are expecting her to challenge the Will. She’s already pretended to be grief stricken and is claiming that I am trying to rip her off because her name wasn’t on Mum’s death certificate. I had nothing to do with the death certificate! Here we go again…. I hope not!
column9: Thank you for your response - and, yes our stories are similar. I find that most people cannot fathom identical twins not being ‘very close’, or estranged as in our cases. I spent the first 36 years of my life dealing with her accusations, lies, and poor behaviour. By 36 I had a husband, a toddler, and a baby. I just didn’t have the energy for her crap any more, and I had to put my family first. Up until this point she’d only directed her behaviour at me. My family thought my complaints about her behaviour (when I asked them for support) were just trivial twin spats. However, without me as a punching bag, my twin went through the family rather quickly. They have all had a massive eye-opener about what she is really like. She’s now alienated her husband’s family (I know this through friends). I have surprised myself in that I do not miss her at all. I thought it would be emotionally very difficult to stay estranged, but the reverse is true. I think I cried once - but, that was from sheer exhaustion as much as anything. My life is considerably less stressful and has considerably less drama in it now. Had she not been my twin, there is no way I’d have maintained a friendship with her (she churns through friends too). Even as twins, we are entitled to enforce our personal boundaries and keep trouble at arms length (or further).

column1: (Endgame spoiler) What is bittersweet about Tony Stark’s death?
column3: Let’s do a partial character study on Tony Stark!“At age four, he built his first circuit board. At age six, his first engine. And at 17, he graduated summa cum laude from MIT.” Seems great, right? I mean he’s a genius. His father was the Howard Stark. So, he was set to inherit billions of dollars. His life seems great! Only it wasn’t exactly perfect — or all that great. Howard Stark wasn’t exactly father of the year. “He was cold, he was calculating. He never told me he loved me. He never even told me he liked me, so it’s a little tough for me to digest when you’re telling me he said the whole future was riding on me and he’s passing it down. I don’t get that. You’re talking about a guy who’s happiest day was when he shipped me off to boarding school.”And you might be inclined to argue in Howard Stark’s favor that he left that “sweet” message for his son in Iron Man 2 (2010). “Tony. You’re too young to understand this right now, so I thought I would put it on film for you. I built this for you. And someday you’ll realize that it represents a whole lot more than just people’s inventions. It represents my life’s work. This is the key to the future. I’m limited by the technology of my time, but one day you’ll figure this out. And when you do, you will change the world. What is and always will be my greatest creation is you.” When I first watched Iron Man 2 (2010), something about this message always rub me the wrong way. Despite Tony obviously being very affected by this, it didn’t sit right with me. I mean after the way that Tony described this father? Howard leaving a heartfelt message for Tony didn’t seem right. But then I realized why it rubbed me the wrong way… This message wasn’t meant to praise Tony or extend fatherly support. Nope. This is Howard Stark’s way to continue to live on when he is gone through his son. I mean calling Tony his creation is like calling Tony just another one of his “accomplishments” — something that he can take credit for. It means that anything Tony achieves is essentially then a product of Howard. Howard only cared about Tony’s mind — and Howard wanted to take all the credit for that. I mean even when Tony was young and building things, probably trying to impress his father, Howard only cared about publicizing and putting him on the cover of magazines. And even then, it wasn’t enough for Howard because to him nothing Tony did would ever compare to Captain America. “That’s the guy my dad never shut up about?” — Tony Stark, Avengers (2012)Steve Rogers: You know, I'm glad Howard got married. I only knew him when he was young and single. Tony Stark: Oh, really? You two knew each other? He never mentioned that. Maybe only a thousand times. God, I hated you.If you need any indication on what his childhood was like growing up with Howard Stark and living in Captain America’s shadow, just look at this scene:The look on his face as he stares at the prototype shield, the symbol of his father’s affections, with a furrowed brow. You can see it briefly on his face, a look of disdain. Tony then proceeds to say, “It’s exactly what I need to make this [the coil] work.” And uses the prototype shield as merely a stabilizer for his creation — what will soon be used to create an entirely new element!As he tells Peter Parker in Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017): “My dad never really gave me a lot of support…” Imagine having a father who doesn’t really support you, compares you constantly to a legend from the ’40s, and never even tells you he loves you. (Howard is also abusive, but we won’t get into that) Which is why Tony Stark developed his arrogant persona and his various other external “armors.” As seen in this flashback scene from Captain America: Civil War (2016):Young Tony Stark: At the Pentagon. Right? Don't worry, you're gonna love the holiday menu at the commissary. Howard Stark: You know, they say sarcasm is a metric for potential. If that's true, you'll be a great man some day. I'll get the bags.(Let’s ignore the fact that his parents are leaving him for the holidays.) (check out my answer for a more detailed analysis into Tony’s “narcissism”.) Of course, this would be the last time that Tony ever sees his parents alive again. It would be that day, December 16, 1991, that Tony lost his parents, who despite all their flaws were the only family that he had. Sure, Tony had Rhodey already but Rhodey during this period was presumably in the military. So, really at this point, Tony Stark was alone.Yinsen: And you, Stark? [referring to if he had a family] Tony Stark: No. Yinsen: No? So you're a man who has everything and nothing.He had to face the death of his parents — which he believed was an accident (most likely he blamed Howard). Which he admits he didn’t handle too well. “It doesn't change the fact that they never made it to the airport… or all the things I did to avoid processing my grief, but…” All the things he did included augmenting the armored, arrogant persona. He pushed people away. He became more abrasive and shut people out because he didn’t want to deal with any more loss. It was much easier for people to leave you if you believe they never cared about you. But of course, that didn’t stop Tony from caring about them — despite that he acted like he didn’t. Examples:*Names his AI after his childhood butler, Jarvis. *Keeps all of his old robots (e.g., Dum-E) around even if they are outdated. Iron Man 3 (2013)Happy Hogan: Badge...badge...badge. Badge, guys. I put a memo in the toilet, come on.(Later) Tony Stark: Sunday night's PBS 'Downtown Abbey'. That's his show, he thinks it's elegant. [he pauses for a moment] One more thing...make sure everyone wears their badges. He's a stickler for that sort of thing, plus my guys won't let anyone in without them.Harley Keener: She's six! Anyway, it's [little sister’s plastic Dora watch] limited edition.(Later) Tony Stark to his captors: Careful, there. It’s a limited edition… [captor breaks the watch] Okay, that wasn’t mine to give away. That belongs to my friend’s sister. And that’s why I’m gonna kill you first.*Tony later replaces the watch with a new one* Avengers (2012)Pepper Potts to Phil Coulson as they leave: Fantastic. Ooh, I want to hear about the ah- cellist, is that still a thing?(Later) Tony Stark to Phil Coulson: I’m saying, take a weekend; I’ll fly you to Portland. Keep love alive.(later) Tony Stark to Steve Rogers: No. There was a uh- cellist, I think.So, as the shirt Tony wears in the flashback scene suggest: Tony Stark is a softee. Tony Stark has always wanted a family. He was still missing that love and support that a family gives from his biological family, so he was always looking to create a surrogate one. Despite not acting as he cared about people or relationships, he always did care. This theme was introduced in Iron Man (2008) when Yinsen asked Tony if he had a family. Tony’s soft, detached “no,” which was later contrasted with Tony’s admission to Pepper, “I don't have anyone but you.” And Tony’s embrace to Rhodey after being rescued:This theme only continues forward: Iron Man 2 (2010)Tony to Pepper: “And then I realized it’s you. It’s always been you.”This scene where Rhodey worries about Tony:Interaction between Tony and Rhodey that reminds me of my little brother and me:Tony: You have a big gun. You are not the big gun. Rhodey: Tony, don’t be jealous. Tony: No. It’s subtle all the bells and whistles. Rhodey: Yeah. It’s called being a badass. Tony: Fine. All right. You go up to. I’ll draw them in. Rhodey: Don’t stay down here. This is the worst place to be. Tony: Okay, you got a spot. Where’s mine? Rhodey: It’s the kill box, Tony. Okay, This is where you go to die.And then in Avengers (2012), He only knew these people for… a day or two tops? And at the end of the shabang, he was already making plans for them to move into his tower?! Can this dude be any more obvious on how much he wants a family… a place where he belongs? He was trying so hard to make the Avengers his family.He knew Banner for a few hours and invites him over. “You know, you should come by STARK TOWERS sometime. Top ten floors, all R&D. You'd love it; it's candy land.” (Which he later does give him a lab for himself in Stark Towers as seen in Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015)) In Iron Man 3 (2013)Tony to Pepper: But threat is imminent, and I have to protect the one thing that I can't live without. That's you.Rhodey and Tony casually talking and then when Tony begins to have a panic attack Rhodey quietly tries to calm him down:Colonel James Rhodes: Take it easy. Tony...Look at his family at the end, worried and watching over him as he gets surgery:In Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015)Tony has designed a lot of the Avengers tech, given them a home, and built suits for them (see my post here for more details). Bruce Banner has his own lab in Stark Towers. “Hey Banner, Dr. Cho's on her way in from Seoul, is it okay if she sets up in your lab?” After Iron Man 3 (2013) Tony fully intended on leaving the suits, after all, he had promised Pepper. He wanted to settle down with her and live a “normal” life. Only he couldn’t because he was still dealing with his anxiety and PTSD over the threat from space… so he couldn’t quit. Tony Stark cannot quit being Iron Man as long as the alien threat from Avengers (2012) continued to haunt him, and as long as he could be doing more to protect the ones he loves (For a more detailed answer on Tony’s PTSD check out my answer here and also this one). Which is why he responds like this to Helen Cho:Helen Cho: This is the next thing, Tony. Your clunky metal suits are going to be left in the dust. Tony Stark: Well, that is exactly the plan.Tony Stark still craves that normal life, one where he can just be around the people he loves. Which is why at the end of Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) he tells Steve Rogers, “Yeah? Well, it's time for me to tap out. Maybe I should take a page out of Barton's book and build Pepper a farm, hope nobody blows it up.” Then Captain America: Civil War (2016):One of the main reasons why Tony advocates for the signing of the Accords is because he wants the Avengers to stay together. Most of his actions were born out of the fear of losing the Avengers. If you want more insight into what I mean, check out these answers on the film for more details (here, here, here). Interesting to note that Steve Rogers actually refers to the Avengers as Tony’s family in his apology letter at the end of the film. “Tony, I'm glad you're back at the compound. I don't like the idea of you rattling around a mansion by yourself. We all need family. The Avengers are yours, maybe more so than mine.” Then Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017),Tony sees himself in Peter Parker. He also sees a chance to be better than his father by offering support to Peter. He also sees Peter as the kid who will be better than him. I wrote a detailed answer on why Tony feels so emotionally attached to Peter and why he sees Peter as a son-figure. You can check that out here. At this point, you see more of how Tony seeks out surrogate family members in others.I want to digress for a moment to talk about how the theme of family for Tony is also paralleled with the theme of legacy. Iron Man (2008):Voiceover: “With the keys to the kingdom, Tony ushers in a new era for his father's legacy” Yinsen: “Look, what you just saw, that is your legacy, Stark.” [referring to the weapons] Tony: “Obie, I just don't want a body count to be our only legacy.” Obediah: “This is your legacy.” [Referring to the arc reactor]Iron Man 2 (2010):Tony: “It’s not about you. It’s not even about us. It’s about legacy.” Justin Hammer to Whiplash: “But if I might make a suggestion, you know, you don’t just go and try to kill the guy. I think, if I may, you go after his legacy. That’s what you kill.”Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015):Tony to Nick Fury: “I wasn't tricked, I was shown. It wasn't a nightmare, it was my legacy. The end of the path I started us on.” [Referring to the Avengers and the world dead]Ever since Yinsen opened Tony’s eyes to what his legacy was, Tony has been working on changing it. He wanted to be different. He wanted desperately to make amends for what he’s done and change his ways. More on this later…Back to family… In Avengers: Infinity War (2018), the first scene with Tony Stark is him discussing family. He wants to have a kid, so much so that he dreams about it. They opened with this. They opened with Tony Stark’s desire to have a family. He even excitedly asks Pepper to confirm, “Yes?” and then mutter a small plea, “please.”“Apropos of that, last night, I dreamt, we had a kid. So real.” Of course Tony later loses a part of his family. He loses Peter Parker in his arms.Tony only ever wanted a family. He believed he found that with the Avengers, but then the Accords happened. He believed he found that with Peter, but then Thanos happened. At the end of Infinity War, Tony wasn’t sure if he even had Pepper or Rhodey (the only constant family in his life). And thus the dream in Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015) came true. Tony Stark watched as the people around him, his friends and family, dusted away. Remember the worst part of his dream was that everyone else died and he didn’t. And look at this moment,Tony is staring at his hand, waiting for himself to turn to dust too… only he doesn’t. And his worst nightmare comes true. Everyone around him dies, and he survives.And finally, Avengers: Endgame (2019).The threat from space, the source of Tony’s PTSD had won. Everything Tony did to prepare wasn’t enough, and he couldn’t protect everyone he loved. The first thing he tells Steve when he lands after being stranded in space for 22 days is, “I lost the kid.” As the Avengers were sitting in the conference room looking at the pictures of the fallen, Tony’s sunken face as he sees Peter Parker among them is absolutely crushing. He was too malnourished, exhausted, and defeated to join the Avengers on their first revenge plot, but I’m assuming once they returned and told Tony that there was nothing they could do because Thanos had turned the stones to atoms, that was the final defeat Tony needed. At the end of the day, Tony Stark is a realist. He tries to find solutions and obsesses over things when there’s a possibility. When there’s nothing he could do, he tries to focus on what he has left. The threat from space came and went. He lost. But there was nothing he could do. So he started to rebuild his life with what he had left. And he did…He had the kid that he mentioned at the beginning of Avengers: Infinity War (2018). He built Pepper that farm he was talking about in Avengers: Age of Ultron (2015). He retired, and he had a family. When Morgan interrupted his work, he didn’t get angry as his dad did. Instead, he averted all of his attention to her. He left his work (which was extraordinary since he just discovered time travel) and went with his daughter to get juice pops. He had everything he always wanted — or at least everything he thought he could have.A single picture of Peter Parker. That’s what it took to remind him of everything he had lost — what the world had lost. Time travel was a crazy idea. But he figured it out, and now he had an actual possibility of bringing everyone back. However, it was still very risky, which is why this exchange between Pepper and Tony happens.TONY STARK: “I sometimes feel I should put it in a locked box and drop it at the bottom of a lake... go to bed.” PEPPER POTTS: “But would you be able to rest?”Pepper asks Tony whether he’d be able to rest. Pepper knows more than anyone that Tony cannot rest as long as there is a chance that he could be doing more. Remember, the reason he couldn’t retire all those years ago was because he wasn’t able to rest knowing that the threat from space was out there. Tony Stark is incapable of sitting back, knowing that there is a chance to bring everyone back and fix things. But Tony Stark had everything he wanted. He had Pepper, Rhodey, Happy, a nice quiet farm… he had a kid. He finally got the family he wanted; he was finally able to retire. That’s the heartbreaking “bitter” part. Tony Stark had only ever wanted family, kids, a life. But he couldn’t have that knowing that Peter Parker and half of the universe couldn’t. So he makes the sacrifice for Peter, for Morgan, for Pepper, for his family, for the universe.And as Tony is dying, not able to utter a single word as he stares at his loved ones for the last few moments, Pepper manages to hold it together for him. She smiles through tears and assures Tony, “We're gonna be okay. You can rest now.” He defeated the threat that gave him years of PTSD and anxiety. Everyone was back — including Peter Parker. His family would be taken care of. This was Pepper telling him that the world didn’t need Iron Man anymore... he didn’t need to worry about that. They would be okay… and he can finally rest. Tony getting the peace he deserves was the “sweet” part. And finally, this is the legacy that Tony Stark has left.One that the next generation of superheroes will need to protect. No one will replace (or become) “Iron Man” but what they can do is carry on his legacy of being Earth’s — the Universe’s Best Defender. “Legacy. What is a legacy? It’s planting seeds in a garden you never get to see.” — HamiltonAll credit to quotes and photos used belong to Marvel Studios. Gifs belong to their original creators.

column1: How can someone deal with the demise of a loved one?
column3: I loss my father last year at the age of 77 on Memorial Day last year. I don’t care how strong you are, your mind has a “mind of it’s own” and will remind you to slow down . For men, grief is very different than how woman experience it. Woman are more prone to crying it out right away, but for me, it was more of a shock. The first month the reality hits you in the form of “shock”. I would work double the hours I normally would, there was an odd surge of adrenaline in me. I threw myself into work right away and my mentality to push forward was in overdrive. Then the holidays came around the corner and a mild depression hit me like a brick wall. The holidays did it for me, it made me reflect on the time’s I had with my father from childhood to his last breath. That’s when the realization hit me hard. I had stopped all of my work, flat-lined. I spent weeks feeling a giant void. There were days I would only go as far as to do grocery shopping around the corner from my house, but beyond that, nada. Friends would call to check in, wanted me to hang out… nada. One insight that’s valuable is this:Listen to your body and mind. Whatever you do, don’t force yourself to hard. If you feel like laying on a couch for hours, do it.If you feel like calling out of work, do so. Take all the time you need off. This country doesn’t give people enough time off for mental health and that sucks. If they don’t understand, give them the boot. You don’t want to work for someone who treats you like a number.Taking the time to process everything is important and essential, I can’t stress it enough. Mental health is much more important than anything else.Don’t hold back either. If you feel like letting everything out, do so. This will help you heal faster.You’ll go through periods where you feel like dwelling and doing nothing. That’s totally normal.You may get angry at really stupid things. That’s normal.Grieving takes time.Don’t compare the length of your grieving time to someone else. Everyone is different in this process.Remember you’re not alone in this journey. Everyone from animals to humans experience loss.After 3 months, I finally passed all of those phases and I felt feeling like myself again. I began to pick up my flow of working, visiting friends, etc. Hobbies helped dramatically. Purpose fulfills you. One never forgets these hard times, but you definitely can overcome it. To whomever you lost, remember that’s what they’d want you to do as well - move forward and do great. The show must go on. If we do not allow ourselves to grieve, we will stunt our ability to attach. We will cheat ourselves of the joy of deeply connecting with another person. We will have difficulty remembering the joy if we hold onto the pain. If we do not grieve effectively, we stunt our own growth and will find it difficult to attach again. And we may find it difficult to remember the joy thereby tarnishing the memory of our loved one.

column1: My dog died and I can't get over it. This has traumatized me and I can't find reason to go on. What is wrong with me?
column3: I lost my childhood dog, Olive, four months ago on September 7, 2021. I had her from ages 5–18, basically my entire life. I cry at least once a week, though some weeks I spend multiple nights weeping. I often feel like something is wrong with me - how can it hurt so much? How long will the pain go on? Her death is the only thing that has ever made me want to die. Not to kill myself - just for the pain to stop, for death to be no more, for her to come back. I wonder how many years I’ll cry like this for her. I try not to believe the lie that there is something wrong with me or that I’m emotionally unstable for experiencing this depth of sorrow. Because the truth is, when you form a bond and attachment to something that only ever pours into your life, and you do the same for it - and then you lose it - a profound amount of suffering and grief is to be expected. Olive slept by my side nearly every night of my life for almost 14 years. I was homeschooled all the way until my graduation, so nearly every day we spent together as well. When she was sick I cleaned up after her and comforted her. I protected her from harm, gave her probably at least a million kisses in her entire lifetime, and said “I love you” even more times than that. She went blind towards the end and became sick often too. The only thing that kept her happy was being held and talked to - the rest of my family members knew she was nearing the end so they started to distance themselves emotionally, but I refused to. In that last year of her life I loved her more deeply and intently than ever before. I took her for walks every day. I talked to her every day as she sat next to me while I did school. I held her at night until she fell asleep. When she was sick I woke up at 4 am every morning for weeks cleaning up her accidents. I led her when she couldn’t see anymore. Then, when we finally had to put her down, I went with her to be with her as she died. My mom said I shouldn’t because I would be too traumatized, but I had to. My baby wasn’t going to die alone. And so I held her as she took her last breath. I’ve never cried so hard in my life. And I can’t stop crying now. But that’s okay. She was the love of my life. It’s only right to weep. There should be no shame in your sorrow. I know it hurts and I’m so sorry. Just make sure you choose to love again. Yes, it’ll hurt like nothing else when you lose another dog, but our lives were meant to have animals in them. I don’t think there’s any other way to live. I just got two new puppies for Christmas and though it feels now that I won’t ever be able to love them like I loved Olive, I know I will and I know it will be worth it. Just keep swimming, just keep loving ❤️

column1: How does one comfort a friend who just lost a loved one?
column3: First, send a sympathy card with a handwritten note. Speak about their loved one and let them know you are available to talk anytime if they want to. Or, if they need something else, just ask! Nothing is more comforting than the cards as they can be reread and are so lovely to put up around the house. Most people in this culture are conversation avoidant about death, but people grieving want to talk about the person and their feelings. Grief is physical and takes time to process. Some days you don't want to get out of bed. Trying to shortcut the process won't work, only delay the pain. My little sister took her own life last year and six months later I am better, but it still comes over me like a tidal wave. One of my friends came over with his daughter the day she died and took us all out to dinner. I will never forget that generosity and understanding. It was so comforting to be surrounded by love.My friends and the letters got me through. I answered all of them and that too was healing. My little sister is the one on the right in the red checked dress. Her friends around her all wrote to me and told me funny stories about their childhood as I was older and they had their own world apart from the older siblings! The girl standing in the back is still a strong individualist and I was her babysitter. We communicate regularly now after many years apart. Hope this is helpful.

column1: What are the behavioral changes that could happen to somebody post-narcissistic abuse?
column3: I’m going to answer this as the target of my husband’s abuse. Consider that the behavioural changes started long before the target was aware that anything was changing within them. These changes were subtle and took time to develop, beginning when the relationship began. In my case, that was nearly 29 years ago. They target us because we already had substantial vulnerabilities… deficiencies in our boundaries, self-esteem, confidence, and self-worth. These deficiencies may have not been perceptible to us, but they were to our narcissist. We had considerable positive qualities as well. Perhaps it was beauty, or success, wealth, connections to opportunities, security, etc. Any combination of positive qualities and traits combined with our deficiencies made us a perfect target for them. Simply put, they manipulate our deficiencies to access and benefit from our qualities. Because of our deficiencies, their manipulations aren’t spotted as red flags, so we become quickly and easily ensnared, enraptured, and it is at this point that their work truly begins. This is when our behavioural changes start to manifest. The narcissist alternates between loving us and pointing out flaws — flaws in ourselves, or with our families, or friends, our occupations, our hobbies, our children — everything. Without realizing it, we begin to “adjust” ourselves, taking on their likes, their hobbies, accommodating their desires, etc., all the while abandoning little parts and pieces of who we are. It is subtle, and the process of devolving into their projections of who we should be is so imperceptible, that it feels like we are “waking up” to things we never knew about ourselves. We truly believe that these changes reflect who “we” really are. Eventually their friends become our friends, their hobbies become our hobbies, our finances become joint finances, our careers accommodate them, and maybe they even decide to career change into what we’re doing, and we give them opportunities! These lists of changes go on and on, and we don’t even notice it happening. If they’ve charmed our families and closest friends, these people will reinforce the changes in us by telling us how “lucky we are to have someone like (the narcissist)” because we “seem so happy”. One day, we become not so special to the narcissist anymore. We don’t realize this of course, and they’re not completely done with us yet either, so they certainly don’t tell us. They do, however, start to behave in “over the top” ways with sporadic, odd episodes of sweetness or helpfulness that strikes us as “odd”. They do this as they start to look for our replacement, and any signs we perceive of infidelity they will deflect and gaslight until we feel bad for even thinking such things. At the same time as this is happening, (known as the “devaluation stage”), they also begin to distance themselves from us, where once we were inseparable. We also find ourselves enjoying those shared hobbies and pastimes they projected by ourselves, and they no longer have any desire to join us or spend time with us at all. Their friends, whom we thought were also our friends, also start treating us differently. There is an aloof quality in them that seems off, and it makes us uneasy. Our family also starts to pick up on these false characteristics in the narcissist, and they also begin to suspect something is not quite right. Some of them may even tell us of their suspicions or speculations, and this adds to our building anxiety. Some may even accuse us of not working hard enough in our marriage, and make us feel like what is happening is our fault! We begin to see a hint of insincerity in the narcissist’s kindness towards us, and it leaves us with a sense of dread and confusion. We begin to behave uncharacteristicly around the narcissist, taking great care to not anger them, and trying to find ways to reconnect with them. After all, and as we may have been told, marriage takes work, and we are partly to blame for our failing relationship… right? The divide grows between the narcissist and ourselves. We grow more and more depressed and perhaps even a bit anxious, but we aren’t sure why. Some of us may find our health begins to suffer, or we grow very tired and don’t have enough energy to get through the day, or evening routines. We stop enjoying things we once loved, and we find ourselves working hard on our relationships where once they seemed so effortless. Nothing we try seems to make our partners happy. They aren’t happy with with us, nor do they seem to be happy about anything. In fact, they’ve grown irritable about just about everything, and on top of being argumentative they may even show physical demonstrations of rage by ripping doors off of their hinges, or whipping electronics across the room and shattering them against walls. We also find that we are taking on more and more responsibility with everything from general housekeeping, to raising the kids, and we may even find ourselves the only one bringing in an income as they move from job to job, claiming they were victimized by getting laid off or fired by some toxic boss or colleague who didn’t like them. We make excuses for our partners, blaming their despondency towards us, our family, our homes, and their careers on external stressors, and fully believe that as long as they can just get past this, or that, then everything will be OK. Then one day the bomb drops. It could be the discovery of an affair, or perhaps they just simply decide to up and leave one day. Maybe it’s both. Maybe it’s more. Whatever the turning point is, it is sudden, it’s traumatic, and we aren’t prepared for it. In the aftermath of being discarded by someone we placed the trust of our lives and our hearts in, we struggle with our self-identity. Their friends whom we thought were our friends, and their families, have all borne witness to their smear campaigns against us. We learn that they have been talking about “us” with those friends, their families, and even perfect strangers to substantiate their claim that they were the victim, trapped in a loveless marriage, and had no choice but to turn outwards to find love and acceptance in others, and ultimately leave their wife and family behind. These people wholly believe their smear campaigns against us, and suddenly those people whom we thought were our friends and family aren’t as close to us as we thought they were, and it is immediately and eerily perceptible. We are summarily discarded by them too, which adds to our grief and cognitive dissonance. We are humiliated and filled with shame, defenceless against accusations we never knew were launched against us. We find ourselves estranged from many of our own authentic friends, because those people were not friends of the narcissist. If our narcissist has turned us away from our families, we find ourselves without support here either, or in a position where we have considerable rebuilding to do of our own despite the traumatic situation we are currently in. In essence, everything that we shared with the narcissist is gone, especially if they’ve been thorough with their smear campaign against us. If you’re lucky, you caught them off guard and they couldn’t complete the job, or you have friends and family they either didn’t have access to, or were able to see through their crap all along. The journey of healing after narcissistic abuse begins with their discard of us, or in other cases where the target wakes up and runs. This is the pivotal moment when we are stripped of all that was false, and we must begin to see the fantasy and accept the reality. Some of us may have lost some very trusted friends, or valuable members of our family because of the way the narcissist treated them or made us believe were false. Some of us may have even lost our means to be self-reliant or self-sufficient, because they made us believe we didn’t need employment or weren’t very good at what we did. Most of us probably feel terrified because we were told by the narcissist that nobody else cared about us as much as they did, and now they’ve left us and we’re utterly alone, unlovable, and not worth more than dogshit on the bottom of a shoe. We may be in danger of losing our children because their smear campaigns have targeted our parenting abilities, or they’ve been turning our children against us. The behavioural changes we experience are associated with the trauma of discovery that much of what we knew was based on fantasy, and everything we trusted most dearly resulted in betrayal on such a massive scale that it is impossible to describe. The cognitive dissonance of trying to reconcile facts is unbelievably disarming, and is combined with grief more severe than losing a loved one because there is no plausible cause for their sudden and violent departure from our lives. It is extremely difficult to describe and worse, the authorities and the law have absolutely no justice to provide to us, or protect us from it. Most who haven’t been touched by this simply cannot understand it, because it is so inhumane that it is impossible for most healthy people to even imagine a fraction of what it is truly like. In the year following my discovery of what my husband truly was immediately after witnessing his grotesque sexual betrayal, after which he walked out on us and behaved as if I had never existed and didn’t matter at all, I have experienced the following:Unspeakable despair, and episodes of wailing until there was nothing left, for months.Uncharacteristic rage, I would scream at myself in my car on the way to work, and on my way home, for months.Terrifying numbness. I felt robotic, as if I were going through the motions of life in a dreamlike state, for months.Extreme hypervigilance. I felt I could trust almost nobody that had known my husband, except my immediate family (and at times I didn’t even trust them). I felt that everyone was his spy, and I knew he was out to get me (on one occasion he told me if we had stayed together he either would have killed himself, or snapped my neck).Fear. Fear unlike anything I’ve ever felt before. Fear of losing more than I already had lost… of losing everything. Fear of losing my home, my son, my job, my financial security, friends, family, everything.Physical health consequences that most noticeably included extreme weight loss and hair loss. I lost nearly 70 pounds and 1/3 of my hair within 11 months of discovery and discard. I can only hope I haven’t suffered more than this, but only time will tell.Depression, anxiety, and insomnia that needed to be treated with medication.Obsession for information about Cluster B personality disorders (he has been officially diagnosed with one personality disorder, but my therapists suspect he has several other comorbidities, including ASPD and NPD, based on accounts of his behaviours).Obsession with trying to figure out “what is wrong with me”, going as far back as my childhood.Endless intrusive thoughts and rumination about the abuse. To this day I continue reliving experiences I would rather forget completely. These are completely involuntary and unwanted thought processes.I am triggered easily into having very uncomfortable emotional responses and rumination whenever I find myself in a situation that is strongly connected with my narcissist or involves him in any way. For example, despite “no contact”, just hearing about his requests from our intermediate go-between person for access and visitation exchanges triggers tremendous anxiety and fear.While the process includes a whole lot more detail than what I describe above, those are among the most notable. Naturally my behaviour has probably looked a bit weird to people who don’t know me well personally, and those that do (close family and friends), I’m sure my behaviour has been at times quite frustrating and maybe even a bit scary. I can certainly say I wasn’t myself for almost a year, and I still think I have things to work on. The people who are in my ex husband’s close circle, namely certain members of his family and friends who have clearly revealed themselves to be “flying monkeys”, they probably think I’m batshit insane because there were a few occasions where I had a very hard time bridling my rage during exchanges with them, and I told them exactly what I thought of them as human beings for supporting someone who could enact such heinous devastation against his wife and child. Trust me, I didn’t hold back! There have been a lot of positive changes too. My home is more peaceful than it has ever been since involving myself with the narcissist, and I have repaired the damage he caused (fixed doors and walls he demolished, etc.). I have recovered financially, having discovered the depth of plundering he had been doing while we were together and marvelling at how easy it was to balance my accounts and have a surplus when he lost access to them, even without his added income, (and believe me, I get next to nothing from him by way of child support). My son is also showing signs of improvement in areas where he had always struggled, and severely plummeted directly after his father left. I am rediscovering the things I once enjoyed, and am reconnecting with old friends I had lost touch with. I have mended fences with members of my family the narcissist had convinced me were “toxic”. I have always been very lucky to have a wonderful job filled with supportive people, and an amazing boss. I never took advantage of this fact, and I am extremely grateful to have the security of being self-sufficient. Today, I see that the only thing I lost, was an idealistic portrayal of a fantasy that I always wanted for myself and our family. The narcissist mirrored this fantasy back to me for a while, but I now know it was never real. That was probably the hardest loss to accept and grieve, because the fantasy was exactly what I wanted, and he was so damned good at painting that picture that it actually seemed real, for a while.
column9: I am moved by your recount. My story is so similar. The only variation is that I left him (my husband of 35 years) before I learned the depth of his cheating. I overlooked it for many years, but my the suspicious whispers from my gut became louder and louder. As soon as I had any evidence at all, I walked out the door and never went back. I still don’t know what all happened and it does not matter that much anymore. He ruined one of our two children. It feels like I don’t even know her anymore. I wailed, I rolled around on the floor, I shook as I tried to do ordinary tasks. I tried to tell people who did not and would not listen. A year and a half I am still healing, but I am far better than before.

column1: What is the evolutionary advantage of feeling depressed after the loss of a loved one? Isn’t such crippling depression a disadvantage?
column3: I don’t think grief has an evolutionary advantage, rather it is the payment for close relationships. Depression after losing something insinuates deep connection to it; connection in a social or familial sense means a close-nit, functional unit that supports itself and gives it strength, increasing the adaptive fitness of all members. Humans especially suffer from loss because of our extended childhoods and long lives, because years upon years of exposure to an individual builds neurological circuitry so intertwined with everything else that they literally become a part of you. This relationship may grow and flourish, providing advantages to both individuals for decades, improving survival chances. Once that individual passes, depression will ensue, but typically only lasting 6 months, or the amount of time it takes to rewire the brain. If the trade off for decades of increased survivalability is 6 months of depression, the pain is worth it in a Darwinian sense.

column1: How do you handle someone close to you, such as a sibling, continuing to maintain a close relationship with your abusers?
column3: This is one of the more difficult issues to have to deal with as an adult survivor of severe familial abuse, and it requires clear communication and setting of boundaries to reduce any pain or conflict to the greatest degree possible. It is not unusual for adult survivors of severe familial abuse to go no contact with their familial abusers, at some point, for the sake of their own sanity, safety, and stability once free of their family of origin’s control and influence. When it comes to siblings, and other extended family members, there is often an internal battle for each of them concerning where to place their “loyalty” - between the abuser and the abused. Quite often, the abused ends up on the losing end, for multiple reasons beyond the scope of this question. We are able to accept the fact that not every family member experienced the monstrous side of our abusers, and that those who were not abused often are unable to fit the reality of abuse into their minds. No one wants to believe it is true, and if they do believe it was true, they do not want to believe how horrifying it was or how unforgivable it was. It is not something that stays in their mind, they have no clue of the details, and they can easily brush it away into the forgotten and “forgiven” past. At this point, we have had to go no contact with our entire family, other than one sibling. This sibling knows the abuse occurred, fully accepts and supports our decision for no contact, and does not give us any grief about it. If family comes up in conversation between my sibling and other individuals, I generally leave the room quietly. We do not have the right to make others go no contact with people who abused us, but did not abuse them; we do, however, have the right to protect ourselves from exposure to any familial discussion we do not wish to hear about. As hard and painful as it is for us to go no contact with those we loved at some point in childhood - due to trauma they perpetrated that we cannot simply pretend did not happen, and the fact that those “loved” ones who abused us never took responsibility, faced justice, apologized, or changed - we would not ask our sibling to go no contact with our abusers when they did not experience that abuse themselves. That is not to say there is no internal pain or cognitive dissonance involved in the situation. Our sibling protected their own children from our abuser(s), never leaving their children alone with our abusers, for which we are very thankful. Of course, there are members of my system who wish that our siblings would “choose us over the abusers”, but those system members understand the complexity, and have their own personal “splits” between loving and hating the abusers. That is, after all, how we survived our childhood to begin with.Not for reproduction.
