column1: How did you react when you found out Bob Saget passed away?
column3: Thank you, my friend, for this sorrowful question. Born with a multitude of congenital birth defects, I have endured many more than my fair share of corrective surgeries. The pain from surgery can last for days, weeks, even months. Yet, the sharp sting of grief cuts far deeper than any surgeon’s scalpel, and leaves scars on the heart that will never fade or heal. Having spent a large part of my childhood in hospital, I am well acquainted with the pangs of loneliness, the awful homesickness that invades the soul day and night. Yet, all of these emotions are swept away by the joy of coming home to family and friends. But, when we lose a loved one to death, a friend, neighbor, or colleague that heartache lasts forever. We will miss them, for the rest of our lives. Our lives were enriched by their presence. At their passing, a gaping hole is left in the heart…only they could fill. This is how I felt upon learning of the death of Bob Saget. My stomach sank to my knees. “Not again”, I whispered. “Not Bob, too.” My heart literally ached. I bowed my head and closed my eyes, but I was unable to stop the silent tears. Death of loved ones is the curse of growing old. One would think, after experiencing the deaths of so very many family members…friends…neighbors, it might get easier with all the practice. It does not. Just as every surgery rekindles pain afresh, so does the sharp sting of grief’s scalpel cut just as deeply, as at our first experience at losing a loved one. Of my friend, I can only say this. Bob Saget was a good and decent man. I can think of no higher compliment As with so very many others I have known, loved, and admired, I am going to miss Bob. Maybe the Angels in Heaven are laughing, now. But at his passing, many of us on Earth are left in tears. Forgive me. For me, far too many have died…too damned many. I feel very old.
column9: Thank you for taking the time to respond. Will you please remove my name from your answer?

column1: What do you do when your elderly parent refuses to move?
column3: You kiss your family, your friends, your time, your health and your sanity goodbye, because life as you know it is well and truly over. My father recently passed away, my mother is in assisted living 3 miles from my brother and his family and even though this sounds like a typical scenario it came about at the far end of the single most hellish time of my entire life. If you are about to take the same dark and terrible journey you have my sympathies, because there is no suffering known to Man that can prepare you for the waking nightmare you are about to face. My dad was a proud and obstinate man, and for most of his life these traits were equal parts endearing and annoying. When he reached his 80s and found himself in the grips of ill health and dementia, however, said traits multiplied to create a horror show for him and his as well as those well-meaners who tried to help our family. There is no stubborn like Senior Stubborn, and that goes double for someone who was bullheaded to begin with. It all started in 2000 when he retired for the third time, came to my home in Utah and bought a new car. He and my mom got in and drove from town to town looking for a place to put down roots after I begged him to just buy a house here and settle down near his family. They drove South, stopped in Vegas (which gave my wife and me a moment of hope) and then drove on to Tucson AZ, which is 880 miles from my home and 2200 miles from my brother’s. All was well with them for the next few years, although my dad hated snow so much that he refused to come up for Christmas for most of our daughter’s childhood. In 2009, he told me that he and my mom were getting too tired to go on any more vacations, and that was when the fun began. Over the next decade, my dad dug his heels in ever deeper as I desperately tried to get them to move close to either my brother or me. I begged. I pleaded. I reasoned. I bargained. I argued. I screamed. I cried. I prayed. Nothing penetrated, and overtures to my mom were rebuffed because she “didn’t want to upset him.” I told my dad literally hundreds of times that a storm was coming and that fail to plan, plan to fail was a real thing, and each and every time he simply changed the subject. As my parents’ ages advanced and their horizons narrowed, he refused to budge an inch and even when they reached the point where they couldn’t see, hear, walk or drive he still clung like grim death to the bizarre and irrational fantasy that they were living independently. Visiting or in-home professional help? “I don’t want strangers in my house.” Meals on Wheels? “We’re fine.” Calls of concern? “I’m getting tired of you calling all the time. Stop worrying about us!” Video chats via computer? Not really possible for two longtime sufferers of SITS (Senior Internet Technology Syndrome). Assisted living? Hateful glares, gritted teeth and slammed doors indicating that the subject was closed. Worst and most maddening of all were the standard responses to the oft-asked “So if you don’t want to do things our way what are you doing about this?” which were “We’re going to wait and see what happens” from my dad and “Pray for us” from my mom. My scattered family members as well as my wife and I took turns putting our lives on hold and rotating in and out of Tucson in a collective attempt to keep them alive and in so doing we only continued to enable their behavior. Many and expensive were the hours-long sojourns to the grocery store to pack the refrigerator with food that froze solid and had to be thrown out on the next trip and many were the arguments I had with my dad over what the State of Arizona was going to do with them should the authorities get wind of their situation. They both fell repeatedly and my mom finally broke her arm, which necessitated her hospitalization, her transfer to rehab and her forced acceptance of the hard truth that she was never going home again. This left my dad alone in their house and at the mercy of friends and neighbors who by now were growing as weary of the situation as I. As I said, I live nearly 900 miles away, and it fell to me as the eldest son and Power of Attorney to drive down and take the bullet. The crisis I had long been dreading had arrived full force, and it turned out to be far worse than I ever could have imagined. In October of 2018 my dad started losing weight and we all told him that he needed to find out why immediately. He of course resisted until five months later, when his regularly scheduled physical revealed that he had Stage 4 Renal Cell Carcinoma. One of his kidneys came out 3 days later, he stopped eating because people told him he needed to eat, as a hypertensive diabetic as well as an octogenarian major surgery survivor the results were predictable, and sixty lost pounds and several seizures later he was ruined. By the time my mom had her final fall my dad had reached the point where the next 911 call to his address was going to result in his removal from his home by Arizona Adult Protective Services, and since he was now alone my wife and I began the mad scramble to fix everything I had tried so hard to prevent. We succeeded in getting both of my parents into an assisted living facility but my dad fought us tooth and nail, both verbally and physically, every inch of the way. Having refused to make the hard choices when he could, those choices were finally made for him, and to say that he didn’t take it well is the understatement of the century. We acquired a small army of professionals along the way who gave the process their all and even with their help and dedication the project nearly fell apart 3 separate times due to the nonstop resistance of one hardheaded old man. When he passed, I was so overwhelmed and frantic that while his friends and my family were grieving I was trying to figure out who I needed to call next as he had done nothing to resolve his or my mom’s personal affairs despite-and the irony here is just staggering-having spent his last working years counseling retirees about making survivor preparations beforehand. I felt nothing at his funeral and still feel nothing at his loss because I didn’t and still don’t have the time. Where many parents leave behind a legacy of warm thoughts, happy memories and for the lucky few a Golden Goodbye, his swan song was a surreal symphony of suffering, sadness, confusion, chaos and stress. It is now a month and a half since my dad died, and the nightmare continues. We spent as much time as we could in Tucson and then we had to go home, which means that I am rolling the boulder for my mom long distance. As everything involving assisted living costs an obscene amount of money I have been fighting with three separate banks to gain full access to their funds, which has been its own special brand of misery. Trust me when I say that Big Finance is not your friend, especially when it comes to giving back what they have been permitted to hold (I now understand why people used to bury their money in mason jars). Fun fact: when you have finally succeeded in dragging your elderly parent to the bank to free up some of their money they can be very adept at making the cashiers wonder if you are trying to take advantage of the frail and innocent Senior they see before them. Ditto taking them to a legal office to verify your PoA. It seems that nobody on the outside can process the true nature of the situation when your loved ones dig themselves into a hole and then leave you holding the shovel. I didn’t know I could do dagger eyes until that particular trip but my wife told me afterward that I was pretty good at it. My parents’ house, which is barely 20 years old, is a wreck inside (think Hoarders on TLC). When we were there we burned up three shredders and filled countless garbage bags and there is still more paper and junk everywhere you look. It is absolutely astonishing to see just how big a mess two people can leave behind. As to the stuff that’s too big to fit in the garbage cans, they have two broken down cars and a garage full of bulging cardboard boxes that they never unpacked when they moved in and we are relying on their neighbors to clean everything out in exchange for rights to anything they want out of it all. Their bills and their endless piles of junk mail are coming to me now and I really do get the metaphor about trying to empty the ocean with a spoon. Legal and financial documents continue to arrive daily and no matter how many of them we fill out and how many details we include there are always more letters from the same places asking for still more information. Lather, rinse, repeat. My blood pressure, which was barely controlled before, spent nearly a year at the red end of the scale and based on some recently discovered mental and physical deficits I strongly suspect that I have had a small stroke. My wife and I are suffering from exhaustion and severe caregiver burnout and we were so stressed at one point that our marriage teetered on the edge of the very next word. For those of you who are in this bottomless pit and those who are about to jump in, I am sorry for your ordeal and I pray that your love for your parent or parents sees you through. For those of you in my parents’ age group who see yourselves taking their side, please stop telling your children that you love them. You don’t. Edit: My Dad’s funeral was on March 10th and the following day, which was the same day the WHO formally declared the world was in a pandemic, my brother and I moved my Mom 2200 miles to live 3 miles from him in Arlington VA. The plan was for her to live near him and his family so that she would not be lonely or isolated as she had no other relatives in Tucson. I had changed my Dad’s burial site from Marana Military Cemetery to Arlington National Cemetery and had an appointment for him to be interred in June with my Mom in attendance. 2 days after her arrival, the Great American Lockdown began, her ALF jumped on the bandwagon despite CDC exceptions for EOL visits and by the time my brother was allowed to actually see the loved one whose care we were paying for she had lost her English and didn’t know him. 3 days after that she was dead. She and my Dad were interred together in Arlington this month. My wife and I are still trying to clean up their mess more than a year after this all began and as for their precious house, I took a bath on it by selling it to a flipper who lived in their neighborhood. I traded any potential profit for not having to suffer the headaches involved in renovating and marketing a property at the bottom end of another state and also because I just couldn’t deal with One. More. Thing. Edit #2: On the 4th of October 2021, one year and two days after my parents’ burial, one year and four days after retiring from 36 years in civil service and three months shy of our 36th wedding anniversary my bright, brilliant, sunny, funny and fabulous 57 year old wife collapsed in our hallway and died in my arms. I lost my partner, my only daughter lost her mother and my mother-in-law lost her only daughter. The jury is still out on what took her from us but I have to believe that a year and a half of unremitting, soul crushing stress had something to do with it. My dad didn’t care who he had to kill as long as he could spend another week in his home, and the body count is now three and hopefully holding. Being patient and deferential toward my elderly and reality impaired parents was the single biggest mistake of my adult life and no other actions of mine have cost me so dearly. Senior Stubborn truly is the gift that keeps on giving.For those of you who are showing this article to your pre-Armageddon loved ones, this is the face of consequences. I miss you, Terri. Edit #3: Seven months after my wife’s death I met a wonderful woman whose spouse also died in a similar manner, and we were married this Valentine’s Day (insert cliche here). Like me, she has experienced a particularly harrowing form of grief and by virtue of her former job as an ALF Activities Director she has also seen my parents’ self-induced catastrophe play out dozens of times. She and I are very happy and we are actively looking for a smaller, less maintenance intensive home that is closer to both our daughters. Our shared goal is to make life easier for them, not us, and we believe that minimizing our end of life burdens on others is the best legacy we can leave. Onward and upward. Edit #4: I am very thankful for all the kind words-there were so many that I have had to resort to this insufficient but heartfelt message of blanket gratitude. I had no idea when I wrote this that it would resonate the way it has. For those of you who have gone through or are going through what I survived, you have my prayers and my utmost respect. Thank you again for making me realize that I was not alone in my struggles!
column9: Oh my friend, please write a book. You literally covered exactly the challenges, torment and pain of caring for older parents. Brilliantly written!!. I am now going through similar. The stress of caring for my father is effecting me emotionally, mentally and physically. NOTHING is good enough for him. I am the only child, so feel I should see it through. But I want out, its killing me.

column1: What was the most messed up punishment(s) you received as a child?
column3: I had a stepmonster. I'm still recovering from the effects of the emotional, psychological, and physical torture she inflicted on me during the 6 years (between the ages of 10 and 16) we shared a household, beginning in 1972. A few months after entering 5th grade, I foolishly insulted a bigger, stronger girl during class, starting a fight. I ended up being punished 3 times for this. My father, who was furious about having to miss a day's work, scared me out of my wits, pinning my arms behind me with one hand and trying to connect with my behind with the other. Until that point, he'd never raised his voice to me, let alone his hand, so I was terrified. This led to his making a fateful decision: I was to be “disciplined” by my stepmonster. After she demand I select a belt from the closet, she told me to lie face-down on their bed and beat me across the shoulders with it. I then went to school, where my father watched as the principal flipped up the back of my dress and attacked me with a thick wooden paddle that had holes drilled through it to decrease drag. But the worst was yet to come. I was a tall, strong girl. My stepmonster was irked that I'd lost the fight. She neither knew nor cared who started it or why. She was about 5′4″ and had to have weighed at least 250 lb., which was intimidating to me. To my disbelief, she beckoned towards her midsection and encouraged me to hit her as hard as i could. To her surprise, I rocked her back on her heels. She then told me two things that made my blood run cold: if I lost another fight, she'd beat me again; and if I ever hit her again, she'd break my arm. So not only couldn't I try to negotiate my way out of a fight, but she apparently could forsee my having a reason to want to attack her - and she was both willing and able to break a limb if I did. Before long, she developed what I must call an obsession with my bowel movements. She was sure I was constipated, though she neither explained what this was nor asked me to let her see my feces before I flushed. She was certain that she could tell if I was by smelling my breath (a medical impossibility). This led to her slapping me in the face for not telling her I was constipated with such regularity that I soon began to flinch if I was within range and her hand moved. She would then get so angry that I flinched that she'd slap me for flinching. One memorable night I awoke to hear her punishing the younger of her two daughters, who was three years my senior, screaming at and whipping her. I began to cry, and she heard me. She called me into her and my father's bedroom, where the beating was taking place. and demanded to know why I was crying. I made the grave mistake of being truthful: I told her that I was crying because what she was doing was wrong. She then made my stepsister watch her beat me for both feeling compassion and daring to believe that her beating her daughter bloody in the middle of the night was messed up. Her brutality extended to reacting to my efforts to communicate with her by accusing me of talking back, which was punishable by a slap to the mouth hard enough to cause a busted lip. This made it impossible for me to participate in band (I played a flute she'd demanded my impoverished mother buy), but the band director said NOTHING about my sitting out class with my cased instrument on my lap. I eventually became all but mute at home. After both stepsisters married and one moved far away, my stepmonster left me with the other one and her husband when she went to visit the one who'd moved. The stepsister with whom I stayed was an insecure young wife who, unbeknownst to her mother, had been pregnant when she married; the baby died in utero during the second trimester, so no one was the wiser but them, their pastor, and me. Her husband couldn't have been more loving and kind. He also decided to give me a driving lesson one day when he and I were alone in their truck. Inexplicably, she called her mother in tears, certain that I was throwing myself at him. Neither he nor I knew about that call. A few months later the stepmonster took me with her to visit the other daughter. During the long drive home there was an undercurrent of tension for no apparent reason that grew as the trip progressed. Then suddenly, without warning, she bashed me in the mouth hard enough to kill the nerve in one of my front teeth and, without taking her eyes off the road as she drove one-handed, hitting me in the face, she told me that she'd been waiting for me to confess to making a pass at my brother-in-law and was disgusted with me for failing to do so. Yes, I sustained a damaged tooth because I hadn't confessed to something I hadn't done! After a memorable beating a few months later, I went to the nurse's office to get a note excusing me from participating in tumbling in P.E.; I just told her that my back hurt. After lunch, my one trusted friend and I went back to her office to apply alcohol to my back, which was criss-crossed with bleeding welts. We heard the exam room door open behind us and the nurse's audible gasp of horror. My friend was excused, and the nurse invited me to show my back to my guidance counselor. I was 16 by then, and so brainwashed that I tried to explain why I'd deserved the punishment. The counselor's reaction was unforgettable. She looked me in the eye and said, “There is NOTHING you could have done to deserve this!” Soon afterwards, having responded to being confronted by the nurse and the guidance counselor by asking them if they'd die for me and informing them that because she would, they had no business criticizing her (wait… WHAT?!? How warped was THAT?), she announced that although she would ALWAYS love me, she didn't like me, and since she didn't spend time with people she didn't like, she wasn't going to. For a few months afterwards she'd come home after work to clean up, change clothes, and fix dinner, then leave after dinner and not return until after my bedtime. By that time my father had left her without warning, not so much as leaving a note, and remarried into a family where there was no room for me. For the first few weeks afterwards, she'd collapsed onto her bed when she got home from work and weep. Even though she was just grieving the end of a relationship (thanks to her regularly browbeating my father) that had lasted maybe 7 years, while I was coming to terms with losing the parent with whom I had primarily bonded, I held my grief in check and comforted her…until she noticed that I'd begun to let the housework slip. She angrily accused me of taking advantage of her being distraught, beat me up, and went back to being her old self again. After a few months of being virtually alone, I arranged to fly four states away to live with my mother again (despite my stepmonster having turned me against her before I turned 12; after he left, she'd turned me against my father, too). Six months after reuniting with my mother, I had a mania-driven psychotic breakdown - the first of many. I'm grateful to be a member of a faith community, a church family, if you will, that loves me and is helping me to heal (I'm a member of The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints; ironically, it's the same church I joined after joining my stepfamily, and while I was relieved of my Church membership at 18, I rejoined it in my 30’s on my own terms). I'm thankful for the 20 years I shared my life with a kind, gentle, older man who wept tears of joy on our wedding day (he passed away on Veterans Day, 2015 - a good day for a Vietnam veteran to die; he was only 67, but multiple health issues made nursing home care necessary for his last 18 months). I'm particularly glad that one of my former stepsisters (the one whose punishment I'd protested) went on to break the cycle of abuse with her five children; when I learned about that, I decided that my suffering was worth it. As the saying goes, hurt people hurt people; this was certainly true in my stepmother's case. Thanks to what I learned about her terrible childhood and miserable youth, I reached a point where it was possible for me to begin to forgive her (it's a process). I even had a civil conversation with her a year or so before her death during which I not only didn't attempt to induce her to apologize, but didn't feel it necessary to tell her what an emotional and spiritual struggle forgiveness has been, let alone for what I'm continuing to work on forgiving her. According to her widower, to whom she was married for over 30 years, never once did he see her angry. She received the highest honor awarded by the American Red Cross, and her obituary urged those who mourned her to make donations to their local SPCA. She made the most of her life, as I'm now making the most of mine.
column9: I am so happy you have gone on to lead a good life. I know how hard it is. I too suffered an abusive childhood, not the same in the details, but not at all dissimilar in the results.

column1: What was the greediest thing you’ve seen someone do?
column3: The names in my story have been changed for privacy. My mom’s fiancé (who was a beautiful and very loving man) passed away unexpectedly. To say my mom was devastated is an enormous understatement. There wasn’t a man she loved more, except her dad. My grandpa, 6 months later, also passed away unexpectedly. Had I not been full term in my pregnancy with my first child, to which my mom was the nanny so I could return to work, I don’t think she would have pulled through psychologically or physically. She was so devastated. She was also very vulnerable. Getting a $125,000 inheritance helped. Well, I thought it was great that she would have that to help her through her later years. She wouldn’t need for anything. She bought a little brick house for $60,000. I agreed that it was good that she had her home now. She still had money to fall back on. She was still deep in grief. She was a second generation antiques dealer so that house and her little business kept her going when she wasn’t watching my baby. Little did I know that one of my sisters, my oldest sister Carol, was plotting how she was going to take it all for herself. My sister was undeniably bipolar with an instant furious temper at someone saying the wrong word or committing a minor infraction. We had a PCP in the family that tried to treat her long distance with shipments of boxes of antidepressants. She never got officially diagnosed because she didn’t have health insurance. My sister was also extremely intelligent and had a high IQ getting her into MENSA. She was into real estate and was what I called a slum lord because that was the kind of houses she bought. She rented them out through HUD. Many times they wouldn’t pass inspection. She amassed about 30+ units. We all knew that she was very controlling, manipulative and greedy, but my mom and I didn’t know to what great extent. The time came for my mom to write up a will. She made me the executor of her estate. My sister Carol was furious! She really ripped my mom apart. She said that it was her birthright to be the executor because she was the oldest (actually my brother that passed away was the oldest, she was second). She continued to rip me apart calling me everything demeaning you can think of (that wasn’t a surprise, her and my sister treated me like that since early childhood). We all knew that she was resentful towards everyone in the family. She blamed all of us for her unhappiness. She made poor decisions but wouldn’t take responsibility for her life choices. She resented me because my mom agreed to be my nanny. Carol had a baby 9 years prior but my mom was not at a point in her life that allowed her to be Carol’s nanny for her son. My sister didn’t want to work anyway and wanted to stay at home with her baby, so I didn’t see what the big deal was. They could afford it. Everything died down about the will. Carol didn’t say anything to me about it. Then, I hear that Carol is trying to talk my mom into buying a small Victorian house in a tiny dying town not too far away. She said she could put her antiques in there instead of paying for storage units every month. She could even set it up as a shop because it was immediately next to the shops in town. The house was $20,000. Looking at how much Mom was paying for storages, it seemed to make sense. So Mom paid cash for it. We trusted Carol. Little did we know that it was part of my sister’s plan. A few months later, I hear from my mom that Carol is trying to talk my mom into buying another much bigger old house that is a foreclosure. I couldn’t understand how my mom was explaining it to me so I talked to my sister. I should have known she was up to something when she was talking to me so kindly and respectfully. She said, “I wanted to talk to you about this, being that you are moms POA and everything. There is this really big and beautiful house. It has four big bedrooms and a big living room and dining room and kitchen. It even has a big attic and basement. It’s being sold by the bank as a foreclosure and it’s listed at $15,000. I would buy this house for the $15,000 and easily sell it for $30,000. So I don’t lose money, I’ll step aside and let Mom buy it for that $15,000 and then she can give me $15,000. So that way she’ll be buying it for what it’s worth and I won’t be losing out on my profit. I can even go to the closing and act as mom’s proxy, but only for this one transaction. I will only be signing moms name as if it were mom sitting there. I won’t sign anything else. It will only be in moms name. That way she doesn’t have to take a day off of being your nanny and you don’t have to take a day off of work.” I said, “Omg! I cannot believe you would make Mom pay you $15,000! You don’t even own the house! You can’t say how much money it would sell for! You are just trying to get your hands on Mom’s money! No way does she need 3 houses!” At this point, Mom had her second house full of beautiful antiques. This made her happy and it was at the beginning of the antiques craze. She had collected a little fortune in popular high end and primitive antiques. My sister responded, “I could have just bought the house myself and not said anything! But Mom’s house is full and she is going to get another storage unit. She can live in it and put her nicest things in the big house I want her to buy, and still use the one she is using for storage now. She can rent out the tiny one she is living in to make extra money. And this way, there will be 3 houses, one for you, me, and we will give Vicky the crappy little one. She doesn’t need any more money (her husband was an accountant with a very profitable practice), she has more money than she knows what to do with.” I said, “Carol, I am going to auction everything and divide it all evenly. If there’s something that Mom wants you to have, she will put it in her will. If there’s something that you want that she doesn’t leave to someone, then you can bid on it at the auction and it will be taken out of your share. That way everyone gets an equal amount. I’m not doing that to Vicky. It will be done fairly. There are laws, too, you know! She said, “Why? What does she do for you?” I repeated myself and said, “It will be done fairly.” Carol said, “Well, anyway, Mom buying this house will be investing her money instead of spending it. And me and George (her husband) will use the money she gives us to fix up her house because it needs work done. Nothing major (just the electric and a lot of other things which were never done). So my mom agreed to buy this house. She signed a proxy paper for my sister to sign my mom’s name only on the deed and gave her the $30,000 in two $15,000 checks, one for her and one for the bank. The agreement explained to me and my mom by Carol was that only my mom’s name would be on the deed. We thought that was what happened. We both trusted my sister. I did not know that my sister never gave my mom a copy of her deed. She put her off for almost 10 years. I didn’t know this until the house burnt. But that’s not the end of it. A little over 9 years later, and another baby for me, my husband and I separated. Due to various things my sisters had done in the way of being domineering and butting in, not to mention constantly putting me down to everyone and doing what they could to make me feel left out (I have come to the realization that they are malignant narcissists and always used me as their fuel) and beneath them, I never told them of the emotional and psychological abuse going on in my marriage. When I finally told Carol that after 7 years of problems, I couldn’t take it anymore and I wanted a divorce from my husband, she sounded more joyful than I had ever heard her before. She sounded like she just hit the lottery. Then she went on to rip apart my husband (who had always hated her). I didn’t have time to tell my other sister Vicky because I was on my way to work. Before the day was over, both of my sisters had turned on me and sided with my husband. My husband’s physical intimidation for several years turned into violence and landed me in the ER that day. No doubt he felt like he could hurt me being that he had the support of my sisters. During that day, Carol barricaded my children in her home, tried to have me arrested, and told the police I was on drugs (all after my husband attacked me). I received the most horrible, hateful, abusive text messages from Vicki-who hadn’t even talked to me to hear my side. She told me that I didn’t deserve to have my children. My husband, along with my sister and friends they lied to about me, called my PCP and reported false information to him, prompting him to order a 302 arrest-to have the police arrest me and take me to the ER against my will for a psych evaluation where they held me for 7 hours only to let me go when they finally believed me. The police arrested me outside the Magistrate’s office at 9am when I was going to file assault charges. They wouldn’t let me file charges. During those hours in the ER, my sister rode my husband around to our banks to have him withdraw every cent from every account, even my children’s savings accounts. My sister took the witness stand in court and lied horribly about me, while looking at me with the most smug smile on her face. She even tried to have her kids lie on the witness stand, but that was very obvious. The judge didn’t believe them. For several months, both sisters tried to get my professional license revoked and get me fired. No one that knew me believed anything. My close friends stayed close. When it all happened, my mom didn’t believe a word they were spreading and came to spend the week with me. It was when I was filing for a PFA against my husband so I could get my children back. There are no words to describe what I went through. He was so psychotic I was afraid that he would hurt the kids or take them to the other side of the country where his family lived. My mom confronted my sister Carol about her lies. Carol told my mom that if she didn’t believe what she was saying about me, then she should never step foot on her property again or she would be arrested. Carol then tried to destroy my mom’s business and spread vicious rumors about her, too. We could not understand why my sisters, especially Carol, would do such horrible things to me. To say I was hurt was an understatement, but I wasn’t surprised. After several weeks, my sister Vicki tried to make up to me. I kept catching her in lies. I kept communicating with her because I knew she was two-faced and fake. I could use that to my advantage. They figured that if they both weren’t talking to me then they couldn’t keep track of Mom’s estate. Seven months later, there was a fire at the big house. It started in the electric panel in the basement and followed the wires into the attic, burning some of the attic and bedroom. We were able to save about 90% of her antiques, thanks to friends, and friends of friends, and my boyfriend (now husband) and his family. Of course, Vicki had to rush into town to keep an eye on where my mom’s estate was going and what was happening so she could report back to my sister and husband. We caught her several times trying to steal carloads of the nicest antiques. She thought I was so dumb, that I couldn’t possibly figure her out. When we were gone, but friends were there helping empty the house for demolition, Carol showed up. Guess what she was shoving into everyone’s faces-a fraudulent deed to my mom’s house with her and her husband’s name on it as co-owners. She was ordering everyone off of the property, saying that it was her house and her belongings, and she would have them arrested. The mystery was revealed. My sister wanted my mom’s estate to herself. She told Vicki just about the same backstabbing plan she tried to get me to agree to-to screw the other sister out of her inheritance. Only I wouldn’t do it. But Vicki agreed. They would pressure my mom to buy 3 houses and fill the biggest one with all of the expensive, high end, beautiful antiques. They conned her into signing the proxy papers under false pretenses. They attached Carol and George’s names to the deed. So on the day my mom would pass away, they would padlock the most expensive home with the bulk of the valuables in it and say to me, “We own this house and everything in it. Our names are on the deed. You are the executor of the broken down houses with all of the junk. Divide that 3 ways and you can get your pittance of the estate.” Nice thing to do to your sister on the day your mom dies, isn’t it? Only thing is, I have a very strong feeling that Carol wouldn’t have given Vicki a thing. My mom had no idea that Carol and George’s names were on it. I threatened to file charges against Carol. Vicki said she had an attorney friend and she would talk to him. I didn’t know at the time that what they did was a felony. Vicki said her attorney friend advised that Carol and George sign a quit claim deed to remove their names from the deed. So that is what they did. Unfortunately, my attorney was a lousy attorney and told me nothing. I still wanted to press charges but my poor mom just couldn’t take anymore heartbreak from Carol and George. My mom has been through so much hurt in her life so I dropped it. I have never spoken to Carol or George again. I kept trying to not see the lies and manipulation of Vicki, but her histrionic narcissism targeting me became unbearable. I cut her out of my life, along with her family and Carol’s family. My and my mom’s lives are happy and peaceful. My mom no longer has a relationship of any kind with Carol, George, or their four children. It’s a very painful shame that our family was so torn apart by pure, blinding greed. It has just been recently that I have learned about the Narcissistic personality disorder. Even though they have never been diagnosed, their actions are outlined in the description of the disorder. No contact with them is the only answer. The other insanely greedy thing I can say happened to my now new husband just before I met him. He was in an almost fatal motorcycle accident. He was in a coma for six weeks. As he was coming out of it in periods of partial consciousness, his daughter sat at his bedside saying, “Daddy, what is the PIN number to your bank card?” He trusted her so he told her. He woke up penniless. His daughter, 3 sisters and mother cleaned his $7,000.00 out of his account. When he had the accident, he had almost $800.00 in his pocket from selling some of his things to a friend. The ER staff put it in their safe. His family saw the receipt for it and bullied a nurse into signing it so they could get that, too. After he came home, they were all there and he was pissed. He asked who all took his money. Not one of his sisters, daughter, or mom said a word. All of these “self proclaimed Christians” sat in silence. They all think that if they don’t answer then they aren’t lying. They scratched out “lies of omission” in their Bibles. His very sweet, mildly mentally retarded niece said that she got $100 of it to pay her traffic ticket and that she would pay him back. She was the only one honest enough to tell the truth. No one else admitted to robbing him of almost $8000. How greedy do you have to be to rob your brother, father, or son when he is fighting for his life? Yes, I went from the frying pan into the fire when it comes to abusive, bullying, lying, thieving family members. Me and my husband’s family life parallel each other. We are no contact with a lot of his family, too. I could go on about the stealing his family has done to both of us. But I guess that will be for another answer. I need to go sage, pray, and meditate now. Quara is so cathartic! I was notified that my answer was collapsed because it violated the rule of being nice and respectful. Could someone please let me know what part of this is being disrespectful or not nice? It is an answer telling about family/people being cruel and disrespectful to my husband and me. I don’t understand who I was not nice to or disrespectful to. Thank you. Just to clarify: Apparently someone thinks that the way I used “mentally retarded” violates the rule of being nice and respectful and needs to be edited. My husband’s niece-my niece- has the medical diagnosis “mentally retarded”. She was diagnosed in childhood. I was not being disrespectful or demeaning. They refer to it as “MR”, just as someone who has multiple sclerosis refers to it as “MS”. Hers is very mild. She is the sweetest, most gentle and honest person. She is one of the very few people I know that say they are a Christian and actually live like it. Which is why she was the only one that said she got some of the money her mother, cousin, aunts, grandmother took from my husband’s account. She was the only one to pay him back. If someone thinks that the way I used this term is mean or disrespectful, I suggest they examine their own feelings towards this diagnosis. Which btw, is still stated as such on her records, and she has no problem or feelings of shame about it. That is, unless someone were to make her feel like she should be ashamed of her diagnosis. Cynthia T. Smouset
column9: Cynthia. I’m so sorry you have lived and are living this. I am happy to hear, however, you have finally seen the light enough to go no contact with them. Having 5 malignant narcs in my family, I certainly can relate with regard to the greed in the will. (The only problem is my NM is one of the narcs.) So I now have my husband and my cat as family. Do I miss having family? I miss having the idea of it. But nothing is worth going back to living in that kind of toxic filth. I’m so sorry for your experience. I’m so glad you’re out.

column1: Is it okay that my school is forcing me to go back to school a week after my dad died, 6 days after he was buried? They are forcing me to go back and I dont have a choice. I know people who got more time off to be able to process everything. I dont.
column3: Dear Blue, My deepest sympathy on the loss of your father. It’s very hard to lose a parent at any age, but especially heartbreaking when it happens during childhood or teen years. Be aware that grief takes time and that you are in the very earliest stage right now. Things will eventually get better, even as you continue to carry your Dad’s spirit with you throughout life. As some others have mentioned, everyone grieves differently. Since you feel you need more time to process this initial stage of grief, and are not feeling ready to return to school, you may wish to see a doctor or therapist in order to get a note excusing you for another week. In the meantime, are you getting emotional support from your Mom or other relatives? If your Mom is still with you, she may be temporarily emotionally unavailable right now, even though she loves you, because she is also mourning for your Dad. Professionally led grief groups can be very helpful at a time like this. Look online and see if there is one for teens in your community. (In Phoenix, AZ, the agency is called “New Song.”) If you are back in school, talk with your school counselor or school nurse. Find healthy ways to comfort yourself and see if there is a friend or family member that you can share your feelings with. Listen to music, take walks, write about your grief, plant a garden, or just take a bit of time to rest in your room with your memories, whatever activity helps you to feel better. Let yourself cry. There is no one way to mourn a loved one. Each person has to find the way that works for him or her. Grief is a journey that no one wants to take but that is inevitable for us all at some point in our lives. There is a good book on grief that has lovely pictures, and is not just for kids. As an adult, I found it spoke to me. It’s called “Tear Soup” by Pat Schwiebert and Chuck DeKlyen. My heart goes out to you during this difficult time. May your Dad’s memory be a blessing. Warmly, Bunny
