And the person he needs to learn to give it to is himself. We are humans, and all humans make mistakes in life. Yours are not any bigger than mine. I am still worthy. And so are you.

column1: What is your pet art?
column3: From My Modern Met: ‘Pet Artist Erica Eriksdotter Quit Her PR Job to Start a Successful Business Painting Deceased Pets’. Below you will find images of Her works embedded within an article that I am pasting for you word for word. If you too have loved and later lost fur babies you will understand why I have chosen this artist to highlight. Enjoy 💜‘Artist Erica Eriksdotter‘s life has been full of evolution. Born and raised in Sweden, she moved to the United States in her 20s to continue her studies. An avid painter from childhood, her love of watercolors transformed into the use of thin layers of acrylic paint. It was this breakthrough, that occurred while she was working full-time in public relations, that caused her to step away from one career and move toward another. Now a full-time artist, she specializes in commissioned paintings—particularly pet portraits to immortalize the love between owners and their furry friends. This knack for capturing the spirit of cats and dogs is informed by Eriksdotter's own experiences with her beloved animals. Now, she has a long waiting list of clients who seek out her talent in memorializing a lost pet or immortalizing their four-legged family member. Eriksdotter's journey from a career in PR to full-time freelance artist—all while juggling a family—is a courageous one. Her ability to follow her instincts and hone her craft speak to her tenacious spirit, which has paid off with a successful and satisfying career in the arts. We had the chance to speak with Eriksdotter about her love for painting, what she enjoys loves about creating pet portraits, and how she knew the time was right to make the leap to freelancing. Read on for My Modern Met’s exclusive interview.When did your love affair with art begin and was it a constant through your life? There was never really a starting point with my art, there just was. Painting has always been an essential way of being for me, whether it was finishing watercolor pieces while on the phone with girlfriends in my teens, or working on large acrylic statement pieces to exhibit in National Juried Art shows on the East Coast in my 20s and 30s. While the love affair with art has been constant, there have been times when it felt more of a resistance when painting. I knew what my heart wanted to put on the canvas, but it just didn’t flow for me. It was when I revisited acrylics again after years of working solely with watercolors that it just clicked for me. I played around and blended the paint heavily with water, and suddenly it was like a mix of watercolor and acrylic. It matched me. Finally, the bubbling creative feeling from within matched what came out on the canvas. Over 100 commissions later, I still use the same technique.You were working in public relations. How did you balance this and your art? I basically had two full-time jobs for over a decade. I’d come home after a long day in PR and sit in the studio finishing custom paintings or statement pieces for an upcoming art show. I spent 20 to 30 hours every week honing my skills with one painting after another. For several years my husband and I also traveled up and down the East Coast participating in National Juried Art shows on the weekends. I knew I needed to push myself to make it work. For me, there was no other choice—I had to paint. It was in my mid-twenties that people started commissioning me to paint statement pieces to add culture and meaning to their homes. That’s when I thought to myself… maybe this could work one day.Leaving behind one career for another is tough. When did you know it was time to make the leap into full-time art and how did you prepare yourself for it? It wasn’t easy to make a life-changing decision that impacted not only myself but also my husband and my—at the time—one-year-old child. After giving birth, my time became even more precious to me. Not only what I spent my time doing, but also how and with whom. I noticed how even more nurturing and fulfilling my time in the studio became, and how rewarding time as a mom was. While it wasn’t an easy decision, it was a natural step for our family to give it a try. One of my favorite expressions as an entrepreneur is “eff it, it’ll work out” in regards to taking chances and braving all sorts of situations. I had spent more than 30 years of my life painting and, for several of those years, with a waitlist. That didn't mean it would work, but it meant I knew myself, my work, and already a list of wonderful customers who would help me spread the word about my art.What was your first pet portrait and what drew you to painting animals? Our stray cat Lola has been instrumental in my decision to try my hands at painting animals. I never dared painting animals as a young painter because I knew how important those eyes are. They’re the window to the soul and if you can’t get those right, the animal has no spirit on canvas. She came to our patio as a stray in 2009, and she often lies in my lap while I paint, biting my paintbrush or getting wet paint on her fluffy tail. She knows when I’m sad or wake up from a bad dream in the middle of the night. Before I had children, she and I would cuddle all night. It was her soulful eyes that made me dare to ask my customers for photos of their pets to let me practice on. Before Lola, I grew up with a Yorkie who was always by my side. I think that’s why I understand my customers so well—20 years later and I can still break down and sob over losing him. He was my everything. To me, it was too emotional to practice on him so I asked my customers if they could share some of their photos of their beloved pets instead. They loved the results and people started commissioning pet portraits.Can you take us through your creative process in capturing the spirit of a dog or cat you are commissioned to paint? I ask my customers to provide me with photos of their animal, which often includes long emotional emails filled with tales of love and loss. I love those emails. I review the photos and “tap into” their furry friend’s likeness and personality. I let the pet’s character come to me. I loosely sketch out the pet and then it’s time for the first paint layer. I choose the paint tubes, mix the colors, fill the painting water, and pick my brushes. I start with the eyes. Once I’m happy with where the eyes are, I start on the rest of the face and gradually work my way out. I may apply several layers to one area, like an ear, before moving on to another area, like the neck.(continued) Every pet painting comes alive through many, many thin layers of watered down acrylic paint. After many, many hours on a pet, my favorite part arrives—the details! Each layer includes more and more details with smaller and smaller brushes, some no wider than two millimeters. I spend a long time applying details and painting thin hairs and I love every moment I get with these amazing animals. Once I’m pretty far along with the animal, I brainstorm the background color with the customer before applying it and continuing to fine-tune the portrait. I enjoy documenting the process via Instagram where people can see snapshots from the studio and watch me paint.What's the most challenging part, as an artist, about being commissioned to capture the likeness of a beloved pet? The most challenging part isn’t that people come to me with the big task of having me paint what may be the one thing they’ve loved the most in their life. It isn’t the emotional emails the customer and I exchange about their beloved animal. Nor is it to say goodbye to every pet portrait that I’ve spent 40 to 80 hours with in the studio once it’s finished. The most challenging part with a commission is that blank canvas that is staring back at me at the beginning of every painting waiting for me to make the first move.Is there one particular commission that stands out to you? It’s the stories of how much these pets meant—or mean—to their parents that stay with me. Those long emails that we exchange about how they may have rescued their dog and spent the next 10 years doing everything together, or how the cat that lived for 23 years slept on her parents' pillow every night. I truly feel so honored to do this work, especially after they’ve seen the portrait in real life, or they’ve surprised a loved one and seen them open their meaningful gift. I hold my breath reading countless love notes I receive of how healing the portrait is to them and how much meaning it brings to their home.What's the most satisfying part of your work? Many customers have lost their pets, and this experience becomes a place of healing for them. From start to finish, it’s a journey through grief as they see their darling sweetheart come alive on canvas through photos, videos, and even live painting on my Instagram. Many cry when they see the finished portrait for the first time—it’s a deeply moving and healing experience. To know that I have a part in bringing healing to their heartache is the most satisfying part, and that’s how I chose to serve.What's the most challenging part of your work as a freelancer? I’m also a professional juggler of a 3-year-old and a 4-month-old, as well as a freelancer which makes life quite interesting. Without childcare, it’s a bit tricky sometimes to make the schedule work, but it’s also my favorite thing (as long as it does eventually work out!). Luckily, my mother has helped me out immensely. Without her, this wouldn’t have worked.What do you hope that people take away from your story? I truly love what I do, and doing what I love makes me whole. An Instagram follower recently said on a post of mine: “Your compassion for others runs deep.” I consider it an honor to bring joy and healing to others through color and thrive on collaborating with them as they move through grief because it nurtures and fulfills me too. I’m grateful to serve in this way, and I think customers recognize that these portraits are a place of healing, full of love and joy, and don’t mind waiting more than a year to have one. Looking back at my life, I can see the stepping stones that got me here: my supportive family, losing Lucas—my darling dog as a teenager— and soon thereafter my father, moving to a different continent, daring to exhibit and later doing many art shows, saying yes to commissions, trying new things, etc. but the main stone, the big rock that got me here is that I kept showing up for myself. No matter the ups and downs and the things that felt like failures at the time, I consistently pushed myself and kept honing my craft every day. Every painting I finish in the studio today is a culmination of all those 30 years.’Studio Eriksdotter: Website | Instagram My Modern Met granted permission to feature photos by Erica Eriksdotter. column1: Will Meghan Markle ever be viewed the same way as Princess Diana was?
column3: I believe that, within a couple of years, Meghan Markle will be viewed as extremely unpopular as she will be exposed as the person she is. In my opinion, Meghan Markle is suffering from a very severe narcissistic personality disorder. All the proof for this belief is in her past and present behaviour. Okay - so maybe her half brother and sister do have personality issues of their own, but then, why wouldn’t Meghan? I don’t necessarily approve of the way that Samantha Markle has gone about getting publicity, but I do agree with what she says. She wants Meghan to get in touch with her ailing father. Diana was a troubled woman, but she was not a narcissistic one. She had a heart of pure gold, and her compassion for other people was endless and totally genuine. If this were not the case, there would not have been the level of grief that occurred as a result of her death. When she married Prince Charles. Diana was not on good terms with her own mother and one of her sisters. She had spoken of her step-mother as the major source of pain in her childhood. However, as an aristocratic young woman, who understood the importance of protocol, Diana would never have left any of these family members off her wedding list. It is absolutely morally repugnant and disgraceful that Meghan Markle is now living a seriously wealthy life, and has not done anything to help her father. He has made a few mistakes; the first of which involved staging a series of photographs for the papers. However, he did apologise to Harry and Meghan about this, and explained that he was attempting to create a better image of himself than the one the press had created - that of an old man living as a hermit in Mexico, eating fast food and drinking bear. Nevertheless, while Mr. Markle was once a successful, Emmy award winning lighting designer, it is obvious that he is now struggling to get by and living in less than acceptable living quarters. Princess Diana would be appalled by the sheer lack of care that Meghan has shown to her father. Yes - he has embarrassed her by doing further interviews, but he is desperate to communicate with his beloved daughter. He can no longer contact her by phone (the numbers he was given, no longer connect) and cannot get messages to her via the Palace. So, he is behaving as any distraught, desperate parent might - by reaching out to communicate via the only means he now has at his disposal. Meghan’s apparent excuse is that she cannot communicate with her father because she can’t “trust” him. That is a feeble and ridiculous excuse. If she has information about her life that she feels she cannot trust him with, then she doesn’t have to talk to him about it. She can communicate with him and talk about the weather! But the main thing she should be doing for him, is helping him financially and making sure that his health is okay. There are rumours that he invented his heart problems, but they come from a source that stated that the hospital had no record of him being a patient. It is most likely that the hospital stated that they could not reveal any information about whether he was a patient there or not. Hospitals are governed by very strict privacy laws and would not be informing the press of Thomas Markle’s admittance, or otherwise. And even if he did invent his heart problems - that merely goes to show that he has bigger problems; he is a desperate man trying to reach out to his youngest daugther. He hasn’t murdered anyone. He has not committed a crime. There has never been any suggestion that he abused Meghan as a child in any way, so what is wrong with Meghan Markle? I cannot see two women as more opposite than Princess Diana and Meghan Markle. Because Meghan does not come from any kind of noble background, she is a social climber. She doesn’t want her family around (other than her mother) because they might reveal the kind of family she is really from. When her half brother wrote and asked her for help with the press intrusion he was experiencing, her response was “these are distant relatives and have nothing to do with me”. Sorry Meghan - a half brother is never a distant relative, regardless of when you last saw him, and regardless of what he may, or may not have done in his life that might shame you. Where were Meghan’s black relatives at her wedding? They appear in her childhood photo albums. She obviously didn’t want them there either, because they did not match the image she wants to project of herself. And who writes “I have always cared for my father ….”. That was her response when he stated that he could not come to the wedding for health reasons. In the absence of an abusive father (which he certainly never was to Meghan), one would at least expect a daugther to write “I have always loved my father …” Meghan will never come to be viewed as anything remotely close to Princess Diana, because these two women are the polar opposite of one another. Diana grew up as an aristocrat and was naturally very regal. She was not a snob, like Meghan Markle obviously is. Diana had no need to surround herself with celebrities and deny her family, because she grew up as the daughter of an Earl, and her family mixed with the royals. Diana never had any need to prove her status, and she was therefore not embarrassed by anyone else that might be linked to her. Diana met Charles (as his girlfriend) when she was 19 years old. She was barely 20 when she married him. She can therefore be forgiven for believing in fairy tales, and not understanding the fact that she was chosen because she was an aristocratic virgin, which was the only acceptable kind of woman that Charles could marry. Times have changed. The Queen has had no option but to allow changes in terms of who can and cannot marry into the royal family. By the time William married Kate, there were probably wasn’t a single aristocratic or royal virgin left in the world! But at least Kate is English and comes from a family who are so rich, that she would never have to marry anyone for money. Having attended an elite British school, Kate is also familiar with the history of the United Kingdom and the relevance of the royal family. She understands the place that the royals hold in many Britons’ hearts. Meghan doesn’t understand this. How could she?? People defend Meghan and say “But she was a millionaire when she married Harry”. Her estimated worth was $5 million US. That makes someone very comfortable, but it does not make them very rich! Given that the median price for a house anywhere decent in Britain (and I imagine in the USA) is now over $1 million US, Meghan’s money would not have lasted very long her - especially given her expensive taste in clothing. Meghan was not a Hollywood movie star. Yes, she was a successful TV actress and I commend her for that. However, as an actress, she would have known full well that she might have ended up out of work once “SUITS” ended. That’s the life of an actor. Many a successful TV actor finds themselves out of work for years when a series ends. It’s only A grade movie stars who can relax when it comes to making money out of acting. Meghan has shown no compassion for her father; she has spent an inordinate amount of money on clothes since joining the royal family; her humanitarian efforts are to draw attention to herself; she would not have looked twice at Harry if he wasn’t a prince. For God’s sake, Harry’s already starting to lose his hair! Do you honestly think Meghan would have been interested in him if he were a postman? She is infatuated with him, but the infatuation comes from the fact that he is a Prince. When that infatuation dies down (as it does in all relationships), Meghan will not develop a deep and lasting love for Harry. She will go back to the USA - to Hollywood, where she knows she will be a sought after actress- all due to her past with the royals. Meghan will never come to be viewed in the way that Diana is viewed. When you look at photographs of the gorgeous Diana, you see a face that changes from picture to picture. Sometimes she is happy, at other times you see her sadness, and everything in between. When you look at photos of Meghan, all you see is the exact same smile, because she does not experience emotions in the way that normal people do. No one naturally has the same expression all the time. Her face is almost always one that conveys a fixed, and entirely false smile. She is purely concerned about herself, and making sure that she gets maximum exposure. Diana married Charles because she did love him and genuinely wanted a family. She did not have to marry a royal to feel good about her status, because she already had the status of an aristocrat. In many ways, Diana’s background is more regal than that of the royals themselves. Certainly in terms of the way the English view such matters, Diana is the quintessential English rose. She has a long line of English blood that is far purer than the royal family’s. That is not to say that I have a problem with Meghan being bi-racial. I would be very happy if Harry had married a loving, pure black girl with the same qualities as Diana. But Meghan and Diana are the direct opposite of each other, and it will not be very long that the world works this out. The Queen already knows that Meghan is a snake in the grass. The Queen is also smart enough to know that it is best to keep the enemy close!

column1: Why is Itachi so glorified by Naruto’s narrative?
column3: The narrative glorifies Itachi becaus the series is usually filtered through the perspective of the characters in Naruto, so Itachi’s story is glorified because of the characters’ biases, and the series in general has a penchant for victimizing it’s villains, which makes them harder to hate, judge, and oppose than villains usually are and it makes the bad guys fairly easy to sympathize with, at least on some level. Naruto is heavily perspective oriented show, as much of the information is conveyed through the biases, feelings, and emotions of each character rather than given as hard, clear facts. This is, in my opinion, what makes Naruto’s writing so ingenious and detailed; it makes for an excellent story and makes nearly all the characters relatable. It’s easy to relate to Naruto’s loneliness and desire to be acknowledged caused by being ostracized by the villagers, Rock Lee’s frustration as he wonders if he’ll ever be able to be as strong as those with special genetic abilities even though he trains far harder, Neji’s bitterness at being forced to serve the head family, Sasuke’s inability to cope with the trauma of his past, Kakashi’s struggle to cope with the loss of his team, Obito’s desire to bring about a better world, Nagato’s ambition to create a shinobi system that is fair, etc. It’s really easy to relate to Naruto’s characters on some level because the series explores each of the character’s backstory and emotions well and in-depth. The characters that don’t get a thorough explanation or a direct, detailed analysis of their feelings tend to be more disliked among the fanbase. Because of this, it can become almost easy at some points to dismiss certain villains’ actions as justified or acceptable because it’s easy to see where they’re coming from, even though they’re obviously horrendous acts of violence or cruelty and should be treated as such. For example, with Obito, Madara, Nagato, and Sasuke, they all wanted to bring about worldwide peace and were motivated to do so because of the trauma of their past. I suppose some might argue (though thankfully I haven’t seen many fans do this) that they are “good guys” because ultimately all they wanted was world peace. However, in truth Obito, Madara, Nagato, and Sasuke were villains and their actions were wrong because they were willing to murder people in mass droves for their goals. They didn’t care about cutting down people who were in their way, so long as it furthered their goals, which is the mark of a villain. Funnily enough, most of the fanbase will agree that Obito, Madara, Nagato, and Sasuke were all villains (although there is some justifying of their actions in the fanbase), yet I don’t see people calling these characters pacifists (like I see happen with Itachi) despite the fact that all four of them wanted world peace. And the fanbase will typically (though certainly not always) defend, justify, and excuse Itachi’s actions far more than any other villain in the series. The two biggest things that contribute to why the narrative glorifies Itachi is (1) Sasuke’s bias towards Itachi and (2) Obito’s biased recount of Itachi’s story. Let me start with Obito’s retelling of Itachi’s story, a tale skewered to paint Itachi in the light of a victim. This story is explicitly designed to victimize Itachi and make him look like a saint who had absolutely no other choice but to either (1) commit genocide or (2) perish with the rest of the clan, even though he had a whole lot of other options available, and life is never simple enough to be sorted into only two options for every big decision. Sasuke lapped up Obito’s story without taking much time to really think about the events and how bad or ill-thought-out or faulty Itachi’s decisions were, and how Itachi was largely at fault for his choices. Before diving into Sasuke’s biases, let’s step back and consider the story Naruto from Obito’s perspective. Obito recognized that Sasuke was a valuable asset, but also a potential threat to his goals if Sasuke should choose to oppose him and the Akatsuki. Obito was losing Akatsuki members at the time, and the more pawns he had in his game, the better. Obito wanted Sasuke on his side, or at the very least against the shinobi villages. Obito’s goal in telling the story of Itachi to Sasuke was to pursue his own goals. Obito wasn’t concerned with relaying facts; he cared about eliciting a certain emotional response from Sasuke. If Obito could have made up any kind of story to get Sasuke to side with him, he would have. But victimizing Itachi was an already available story that Obito used to manipulate Sasuke’s feelings and to turn him against Konoha, and it worked like a charm.We already know that Obito lied at points during his story, and he really skewered facts to highlight Itachi’s suffering. We see that because of how Obito’s story is one-sided, and because of how he exaggerates certain points to further his agenda. For example, he talks about how horrible it was that Itachi had to kill his lover – a rather strong term for a girl who had a one-sided crush on Itachi but Itachi himself was rather indifferent to. They were friends at most, and nothing more. Or how Tobi talked about how murdering his own parents was so hard for Itachi, and while true, it brokers no mention of how much Itachi resented his father (I’m of the opinion that Itachi’s decision to murder the entire clan was furthered in large part because of how much he hated his father and the suffering Fugaku caused Itachi) or how Itachi completely ignored his mother for most of her life (he didn’t even consider her opinion on the whole coup d’état at all until about a minute before he slaughtered her, while really implies that they’re not all that close). And having to kill his friends…what friends? Itachi’s only friend seemed to be Shisui, who was already dead. Otherwise it’s implied that Itachi was standoffish and had a lot of trouble getting along with people. Obito also made it sound like everything that Itachi did was for Sasuke…but if Itachi really had wanted to help Sasuke, he could have easily remained in Konoha and raised and trained Sasuke himself. All he had to do was pin the blame for the Uchiha massacre on Obito instead (a lie everyone in Konoha would have believed since none of them had witnessed the massacre) and then focus Sasuke’s hatred on Obito. Much of what Itachi did to Sasuke was selfish. If Itachi was as selfless as Obito says, Itachi would have never tortured Sasuke with the Tsukuyomi, or told Sasuke to kill his best friend, or egged his little brother on towards a path of hatred, etc. Itachi’s treatment of Sasuke is frankly abusive. Yet Obito makes him sound like a saintly brother: And if this isn’t victimizing Itachi, I don’t know what is:Obito makes even Itachi’s lies to Sasuke sound altruistic:Personally, I don’t see anything good about lying to a family member and letting them live their life based on falsehoods and lies, but Obito sure makes it sound really caring. Also, there’s no mention of how Itachi didn’t bring Shisui’s killer to justice but was content with upholding a corrupt system that murdered soldiers doing everything they could to maintain their peace. No mention of how many alternatives Itachi had available to him to stop his clan’s coup d’état that he could have tried but didn’t. Obito treats Itachi’s decision to slaughter his clan as an “either/or” choice forcibly imposed on him by Danzo, when in reality Itachi had several choices available to him. No mention of how much unnecessary suffering Itachi put Sasuke through, or how Itachi did nothing to stop Sasuke from being hunted by Orochimaru or becoming a rogue ninja. None of this stuff is mentioned because it doesn’t fit Obito’s narrative of victimizing Itachi. Obito’s narrative also happens to the be same one where the audience first learns of Itachi’s backstory. Because Obito’s story is skewered to victimize Itachi, viewers can’t help but feel sorry for Itachi. To be fair, Itachi is a victim of the system as much as Madara, Sasuke, Obito, and Nagato were; although it still doesn’t absolve them of their crimes. Because the first time we viewers hear about Itachi’s past is through a really biased telling of the story, it makes it difficult to sort through facts and formulate and a more “objective” opinion because the telling of the story and the lens we’re hearing the story through (Sasuke’s) is personally and emotionally biased. The first time I heard the truth behind Itachi’s actions, I was uncertain of how to feel about it (mostly because not enough information is presented by Obito to actually form an informed opinion, imo). Thankfully the anime explores the politics behind the incident further in the anime and the novels, which is why I much prefer to base the facts of the event off the other anime backstory arcs and the novel rather than Obito’s blatantly biased and somewhat inaccurate version of it.Now for the other big factor as to why the series glorifies Itachi so much: Sasuke’s bias. When it comes to his big brother, Sasuke is delusional, to be blunt. Sasuke extols his brother and holds him in high regards, to the point where Sasuke even once commented that Itachi was “perfect”. From comments like this and their interaction at other points in the series, we see that young Sasuke idolized Itachi and really looked up to his big brother. Originally, Itachi was the person that Sasuke was closest too and the person that Sasuke held most dear. Sasuke would have done just about anything for Itachi. Even later on, we see Sasuke throw away his life and future, whether in the pursuit of Itachi or to avenge his brother’s death and ensure that his brother’s legacy and sacrifices are not meaningless, so he was basically always following in his brother’s footsteps one way or another. Sasuke desperately didn’t want to believe that his own brother could be a horrible psychopath who murdered people – especially their own kin – on a whim. When Sasuke first found Itachi in his parents’ home the night of the massacre, he didn’t suspect Itachi, even though Itachi is the only one present in the room. There are a few other moments that cue viewers into how much Sasuke wanted to reject the reality that his brother was the Uchiha clan’s killer. First, when Itachi confronts Sasuke after Sasuke fled from their house, Sasuke says that “this isn’t like you, brother”, and it’s clear that Sasuke is having trouble processing the horrible truth that his beloved brother murdered everyone in the clan. Sasuke’s loses conscious soon after his conversation with Itachi on that night, and when he awakens in the hospital, the first thing he assumes is that it was all a dream. In other words, young Sasuke had trouble coming to terms with this reality, because what he saw his older brother do was too horrible and too uncharacteristic of Itachi to be true – at least that’s how Sasuke saw it from his limited perspective. And during Itachi and Sasuke’s fight, Sasuke admitted that he had trouble with accepting the evil Itachi who never cared anything about his younger brother, as he says, “I wanted to believe it was all just a horrible genjutsu, but no. I was trapped in reality.” I bring attention to these moments because they are important and provide a lot of insight into Sasuke’s character, particularly with his struggle to accept the cruel reality that he was thrust into the night of the massacre. Sasuke wanted to believe that his brother was a good person. He didn’t want Itachi to be the cold-hearted monster who murdered all the Uchiha; he wanted his brother to be the kind and caring person he remembered from his childhood. Which is why if there was any chance, even a small chance, that Itachi was still a good person and that Itachi truly did love Sasuke, Sasuke would seize upon that hope. Obito was the one who offered that hope, so unsurprisingly Sasuke snatched up that hope and held on to it, because Sasuke needed to believe that his brother still loved him and that Itachi had a reason for killing the entire clan (even if it was a reason that Sasuke didn’t agree with) and that his brother was not just a psychopath deranged killer who slaughtered people for fun. Since we experience the truth of Itachi from Sasuke’s viewpoint, it’s particularly easy to victimize Itachi since that is exactly what Sasuke does. Itachi chose to murder the Uchiha of his own volition, but Sasuke conveniently ignores that part. Sasuke wants to imagine his brother as the perfect idol he was frozen in Sasuke’s childhood memories, and he wants to imagine his brother as better than he actually is, so Sasuke uses Konoha as a scapegoat. Rather than accept that Itachi was a bad person who made a lot of evil choices, Sasuke refuses to acknowledge that Itachi is to blame for his choices, and somewhat absolves Itachi of his actions (though not entirely, as Sasuke does directly criticize Itachi for his abuse and neglect of Sasuke and Sasuke disagreed with Itachi’s choices and decisions). Instead of holding Itachi responsible, he holds Konoha responsible. Rather than acknowledging that Itachi was capable of making his own choices, Sasuke pins the blame on Konoha and believes that Konoha corrupted his brother and turned him into a psycho killer, whereas before the Leaf government got their claws on Itachi, his brother had been kind and, in Sasuke’s words, “perfect”. We see this from when Sasuke tells Danzo: “You made him do it!” There’s not acknowledgement that it was Itachi’s own choice to murder his entire clan. In Sasuke’s mind, Itachi is just another of Konoha’s victims who was manipulated into committing acts of evil, and for that, Konoha must be punished. As a side note, Sasuke isn’t completely wrong. Itachi was a child who was forced to deal with things that he should have never had to deal with. Because of the adults’ lack of responsibility, Itachi had to deal with a politically intense situation that he had neither the maturity nor the intelligence to deal with properly. Because of Konoha’s terrible, apathetic government, a lot of people were murdered and Itachi ruined and destroyed his and his brother’s life. That is the Leaf’s fault. But Itachi did choose to kill all those people, so he is not blameless. So Itachi is “glorified” because he is overly victimized by the secondary main character and Sasuke’s preference to hold Konoha accountable for Itachi’s actions instead of holding Itachi accountable for Itachi’s actions.That ties into Naruto’s treatment of Itachi as well, because Naruto is personally biased towards Itachi because of his relationship to Sasuke. Some may think that Naruto really admired Itachi, using the fact that he quoted him before the second Valley of the End fight. This might seem like another moment when the narrative is glorifying Itachi. Personally, I don’t think that Naruto admired Itachi much. Naruto is nice to most villain-turned-heroes, or a villains-who-pretend-to-be-heroes-and-once-or-twice-even-are like Itachi. But from Naruto’s perspective, I never saw him show much regard for Itachi in particular for matters that didn’t specifically relate to Sasuke. Itachi was only important to Naruto because he was important to Sasuke. Naruto vehemently opposed Itachi’s choices (since Itachi is almost like the anti-Naruto, in a way, as nearly everything Itachi stands for goes against Naruto’s philosophy). But the reason that Naruto takes Itachi seriously is because Sasuke does. Naruto knows that Sasuke has a very special relationship with his older brother, and he knows that Sasuke and Itachi have a shared past, and that isn’t meaningless. The reason that Naruto brings up Itachi before the Valley of the End doesn’t have to do with Naruto respecting Itachi the most. The reason that Naruto brings up Itachi is because he thinks that understanding Itachi’s feelings will be the most probable way to change Sasuke’s mind. Sasuke has been following his brother’s footsteps in one way or another for a long time, and Naruto knows that Sasuke respects Itachi, so Naruto pleas with Sasuke by using Itachi’s philosophy in the hopes of bringing Sasuke back to protecting Konoha. Also, Naruto says something to Itachi, like, “you’ve done enough for the village”, which again could be taken as praise for Itachi’s character. Although the exact interpretation for the meaning behind Naruto’s words is quite subjective. I personally feel like Naruto is saying that more as a way of stopping Itachi from causing any more damage than he’s already caused. After all, Itachi’s actions ultimately did a lot more harm than good, as Itachi did a lot to mess up Naruto’s life because of what Itachi did to Sasuke between manipulating him and murdering everyone that Sasuke had once cared about, especially since Naruto never says to anyone else that they have done enough for the village, even though other characters have done far more to protect Konoha in ways more in line with Naruto’s philosophy. So when Naruto says this, it’s with damage control in mind, although obviously that’s open to the individual’s interpretation, and some viewers might interpret the narrative as saying that Naruto is praising Itachi. Sasuke and Naruto’s viewpoints paint Itachi in a rosy light because they understand that Itachi was in a rough position. Naruto is extremely forgiving and does not condemn Itachi, and Sasuke can be as equally forgiving in the instances when he chooses to be, and we definitely see a high level of forgiveness from Sasuke towards Itachi. Sasuke and Naruto don’t directly say a statement like, “Itachi was wrong and his actions were evil” either, so while it is heavily indirectly shown that Naruto and Sasuke both vehemently disagree with Itachi’s choices, actions, decisions, and his philosophy, they don’t exactly directly verbally reject it, which could make it confusing for some viewers as to how Naruto and Sasuke feel about the Uchiha massacre, because it is more open to interpretation than it would be if they had directly denounced Itachi’s choices. Although really it’s clear from how Sasuke actively rejects his brother’s path and how Naruto is essentially the opposite of Itachi’s philosophy that they don’t agree with or support Itachi’s choices about the Uchiha massacre at all. Then other characters in the story make comments glorifying Itachi such as this:Itachi is an amazing shinobi from Hashirama’s perspective. That doesn’t mean that Itachi is a good shinobi, only that Hashirama thinks he is. Hashirama’s philosophy was that he would be willing to kill anyone, even his own family members, if it meant protecting the village. It’s a rather fanatical philosophy and we see that kind of mindset later leads to justifying atrocities like genocide and the murder of children, but that is what Hashirama believes. So if you agree with Hashirama’s perspective of what a good shinobi is, than Itachi is a good shinobi. But if not, than Itachi is not necessarily a good shinobi. But Hashirama’s statement isn’t a fact; it’s an opinion. It is also helpful to remember that when Hashirama says this, he was talking to an emotional teenager who was distraught over the death of his brother and threatening to destroy Konoha if the Hokage’s answers weren’t to his liking, so Hashirama had to tread carefully.Or in this instance when Fugaku called Itachi “kind/gentle” (I’ve seen it translated both ways), when there is absolutely nothing kind about Itachi in this moment. There’s nothing kind about destroying an entire clan and murdering innocents (including children) and murdering the very people who gave life to you and raised you. There is nothing kind about Itachi. But in context, while some readers might take this away from this as glorifying Itachi, it’s actually a statement that reflects Fugaku’s character, not Itachi’s. Fugaku and Mikoto fundamentally disagree with Itachi’s philosophy and decisions. However, Fugaku raised Itachi to stand up for what he believed in, and in the scene before they are killed, Itachi’s parents are concerned about their son’s suffering far more than their own. Fugaku warned Itachi that his suffering would last longer if he continued down his road, and the only thing that Itachi’s parents could do to ease their son’s suffering was by not making his cruel choice to slaughter them any harder than it already was by acting serene in the face of their imminent deaths and offering him kind words. This moment is a reflection of Fugaku and Mikoto’s selfless, kind nature, whereas Itachi only showed cruelty and lack of mercy mixed with his personal grief. It is Itachi’s parents, not Itachi, who are the kind ones in this moment.Hiruzen complimented Itachi as having a reasoning like a Hokage’s. But again, this is another one of those lines coming from a limited perspective. This doesn’t mean that Itachi had the mindset of a Hokage, it meant that Hiruzen believed that Itachi had the reasoning of a Hokage. But considering that Hiruzen was a trash Hokage who didn’t even deserve the title, Hiruzen’s opinion on what a Hokage should act or think like means very little, since he was an apathetic leader who idly stood by and refused to save his citizens from genocide and failed to deal effectively or decisively with other issues such as Danzo.There is that moment when Tobi calls Itachi a pacifist…that’s probably one of the most laughably inaccurate lines in the series, since Itachi is clearly not a pacifist. There isn’t a shinobi in the Naruto-verse who is a pacifist, and Itachi is one of the least-pacifist ninja of his day. Anyone willing to resort to mass-murder and genocide to resolve problems is not a pacifist by any stretch of imagination. In short, Naruto is a story conveyed in not just words but in deeds, and one must pay close attention to both to winnow out what is true and what is biased, subjective viewpoints from the characters. For people who don’t like to think about the story or the perspectives that it is being delivered through, they might take this narrative at face value and assume if a character says something, it is fact. But that is not true in Naruto any more than it is in the real world.
