column1: When did you realize your parents are terrible people?
column3: For so many years they had me convinced that i was the bad person. I was told practically on a daily basis that I was selfish, hateful, mean, unloveable, and had many more negative character traits and I believed every word they said. It wasn’t until, after seeking the help of many therapists, that I finally found one that was able to help me understand that I was exhibiting the symptoms of someone who had been living in abusive relationships and with abusers all of my life. Because when seeing other therapists I was so intent on finding out what was wrong with me, what I could change about myself so that I might be loved, that when one would tell me (which they all eventually did) that I was not the one with the problem, I would just find another therapist. You see, I thought that I had to do something to myself to even be loved by the people that raised me and when my therapist would tell me that nothing was wrong with me, that he/she had no advice for me or that the advice they had was to stay away from my family they never went on to explain about narcissistic personality disorder. About 5 years ago I found a therapist that explained to me how my behavior and my reactions to my everyday life were like someone who had been in a war. Rather than just tell me that nothing was wrong with me she would use my own actions and reactions as an example and compare them to the actions and reactions of someone who was well adjusted. Then together we would break apart the different situations in my life helping me to understand how the things that happened and the way I was treated in childhood contributed to the behavior I exhibited as an adult. She helped me to understand that I wasn’t born to be reactive. I wasn’t born to be anti-social and I wasn’t crazy and absent minded or forgetful. She helped me to understand and see how I’d been gaslighted for years and years. She helped me to see how I’d been lied to over and over again only to be labeled a liar myself. I realized that the difficulty I have getting along with my brother is due to years of triangulation set in place by our parents. She helped me to realize that I don’t have to respect people who don’t act in a respectful manner. I don’t have to love people that don’t act in a loving way toward me. I wanted more than anything for so many years to be a loved member of my own family and she helped me to realize that there was nothing I could do to realize that dream because it wasn’t me that was keeping it from happening, it was them. They wanted me to remain beat down and ineffective as a person. 5 years ago she helped me to understand that I would only ever be what they wanted me to be as long as I remained within their reach. Even today when a memory comes to mind it usually does so with some kind of revelation accompanying it. I’m still seeing a therapist, although not the same one (for reasons that have only to do with who Medicare will pay) and this therapist is still helping me to go through all the processes that go along with the grief of losing loved ones, the grief of realizing that I didn’t have a childhood, the practically constant shock of finally knowing why this or that happened, and finally accepting that for all those years I was told “I love you” and I loved people that were planning my own demise, my failures, my defeats and blaming me for all of theirs. Look at my life and it plays out like a text book on narcissistic personality disorder and the effects it has on the child being raised by one. I finally understand and believe that there really is nothing wrong with me, at least nothing I was born with, nothing that can’t be reversed with time. I can finally stop blaming myself. It’s been so hard, facing the truth about people that should have always loved me and realizing that they’re sick and trying to forgive them for things I’m not even aware of that they did yet. And it doesn’t even matter to them if I forgive them or not because their convinced that they’ve never done anything wrong and if they think they did they wouldn’t admit it anyway. There won’t be any closure, ay reconciliation, any apologies, or any understanding. There will be no validation for me other than that that I can give to myself and that’s just going to have to do. The short answer would have been just to write “5 years ago when I began to learn about npd and mothers who have it and the ways they torment their daughters” but I always do have trouble giving the short answer. Thanks for letting me get all that out. Good question.
column9: Me too! Same story! I was absolutely convinced I was fat, ugly, stupid, and ill-tempered. It took YEARS of therapy and some reading about toxic parenting to realize it was them, not me. Both parents are now dead and they never did realize how awful they were. They thought they were the BEST. Today I tell other people if their parents are addicts or vicious people, just walk away.

column1: Is it normal to want to seek closure or understanding from my ex narc as to why she treated me that way out of nowhere?
column3: It’s perfectly normal. What you’re feeling has a name: it’s called grief.My first love was a young sociopath. He died in a narcissistic collapse by suicide at 15 years old. When I’d experienced death before, it was my grandmother from cancer. While her death was painful, we knew she was sick: we had a chance to tell her we loved her and say goodbye. We had closure. When I experienced it suddenly as a teenager, I was thrust into a long, and seemingly bottomless, well of pain.The grieving lasted over a year. I can and do still cry for him sometimes, a quarter of a century later: I dream of him often. The grieving included a range of emotions: denial, anger, bargaining with God, depression, acceptance, and, much later, meaning. But more than anything, I wanted closure. I wanted a chance to understand why the suicide; why I wasn’t good enough to keep him alive; why he didn’t love me enough to stay; why he hurt me and his friends and family so brutally… AND I WANTED TO TELL HIM HOW MUCH I LOVED HIM.I’d pray to see his ghost. If he had to be gone, I at least wanted to say goodbye. I wanted closure.As I got older and trauma bonded to narcissists exclusively due to my family dynamics (I was the scapegoat child of two NPD parents, so I have BPD), I’d experience this again. And again. And again. EXCEPT THESE PEOPLE WERE STILL LIVING. And yet, it was just like the death I experienced in my childhood: it was sudden, shocking, unexpected, and there was no closure. AND THE HEALING PROCESS TOOK A LONG TIME.I thought something was wrong with me. Because narcissists move on very fast. They don’t emotionally attach to anyone and can’t survive without supply, and they don’t grieve. They only cycle through two stages of grief: denial and anger. They’ll stay in anger at you and smear you or rage on you even when you didn’t do anything to them. They’ll blame you for everything they did. And they’ll care nothing for your grief. They’ll even gaslight you for it or mock you; they may even enjoy it. They’ll say you are irrationally crazy for it.So while my narcissist partners or friends moved on fast and looked happy, I’d go back into a long grieving process that took a toll on my mental and physical health. I thought I was crazy, obsessed maybe.NO, I WAS GRIEVING. Due to having empathy and the ability to emotionally attach, I cannot project my pain via abuse to rid myself of it, I must process it. A lot of what is called “emotional dysregulation” or “emotional instability” for pwBPD is, in reality, regular grief. And for narcissists, who do not grieve, we seem to not move on fast enough. The grieving process takes time for those who cannot project their pain onto others, and the depression stage is dangerous, as it comes with suicidal feelings. Add to that the pressure to return to normalcy and sustain a living through work, and it explains why so many narcissist abuse victims end in suicide. The greater the love is, the longer and more difficult the grieving process.For a narcissist, you will know how great the love they repressed for you was via the extent of their rage and cruelty. The greater their repressed love, the greater their abuse and betrayal: this is because their grief manifests only as anger. It seems counterintuitive, but it’s really how they work. They can never resolve their grief—only deny and project it—it’s why they are always unhappy. And they don’t even consciously recognize they love you when they rage. It’s all suppressed and denied in favor of hatred and rage in order for them to cope with rejection or the shame of abusing and losing you; they’re projecting their self loathing onto you. However much they hate you is how much they hate themselves for not being able to love you. Hatred is love in the anger stage of grief.At the root, what grief means is that you are harboring feelings for someone who you can no longer express them to, because they are no longer there. With death, they aren’t there physically. But with a narcissist, they aren’t there spiritually. Even worse, the person you thought you loved was an illusion. Their mask falls and you realize that the person you trusted could betray you, could abandon you suddenly, and had no empathy for you or guilt for doing so. As you deal with this “death,” however, you are further tormented because they are still alive.That closure you’re desiring is the BARGAINING phase of grief. Because you’re thinking, “Maybe I can resolve this…If they can explain themselves,if I can express my pain,if they can apologize,if I can apologize or find out why I wasn’t good enough.Maybe we can even salvage some of the relationship and be friends, be civil…”But, here is the difficult truth: that is never coming. Only people with empathy separate by giving closure and compassion.pwNPD can’t confront or process shame. They can’t experience empathy for you. They never did. More than likely, they blame you for everything. They genuinely believe you deserve everything they did and they are perfect and superior to everyone. They have to believe that to survive the things they do to others.A year and a half ago, I was stalked, drugged, and sexually assaulted for several weeks by my apartment maintenance man. I knew he was a narcissist: it’s why I got attacked, because he heard my therapy on the microphone he installed on me, and my unmasking and rejection collapsed him and caused him to rage. When I tell this story, people expect that my only feelings would be rage and revenge. NOT. EVEN. CLOSE. I grieved.In fact, I’m still grieving. Anger was a part of it, but not nearly all of it. He wasn’t my lover or boyfriend. In fact, when I learned his shames, it turned out they repulsed me. However, even though he had NPD/ASPD, that’s not something that would make me hate a person. It’s only something that makes me not enmesh. I have narcissist students and family members. Narcissists have been deep loves in my life. And though I knew to steer clear of him because I thought he wanted to cheat on his wife, I’d thought of him as a friend. We’d both shared traumas with each other. I genuinely cared about him and felt for his pain: he had childhood trauma very similar to my own. To experience the attacks, while severely impaired due to being drugged, was such severe cognitive dissonance that I thought I was permanently brain damaged. My brain felt pulsing and swollen. I felt hunted by someone I’d cared about and confided in. It was a nightmare.To put together the stalking, find the microphone, and then for him to nearly kill me, continue gang stalking me, and gloat about the assaults after I fled still hurts my heart. Because I was kind to him. I was kind to him even while I was getting attacked, whenever I was conscious and we interacted. And you know what I still wish for more than anything else, aside from peace, safety, and healing? I WISH I COULD TALK TO HIM. I wish he’d reach out and tell me he’s sorry. I wish he’d thank me for my mercy in not putting him in prison. I wish he’d say I didn’t deserve it. I even wish I could tell him I don’t judge his mental health and I forgive him. I wish he could understand I cared for him as a human being. But, I think what I don’t like to admit is that what I really wish is that… …he would recognize that I’M a human being.But he will not. I have to grieve until I accept that.But I did get something that was almost that. And with other narcissists I’ve gotten clarity and meaning many years later. On the one year anniversary of the attacks, I Googled him to see if he was arrested or dead. My PTSD was bad. It suddenly popped up that he had a Facebook. He’d never had social media. His social media was full of warnings about toxic people. And since everything a narcissist accuses is confession, even their social media can be read that way. It was also full of my interests, which was unsettling. It had poetry, spirituality, pictures of the moon, space, even posts about Borderline Personality Disorder. It was like he was still mirroring me…and posting as if he knew I was watching. But it was peppered with a ton of misogynistic posts about why women were so weak and terrible. Yet the toxic people posts described him perfectly. They even confessed many of the things he did to me, like knowing the worst thing that has ever happened to a person and doing that thing to them. The post said those people are “trash.” He knew I’d been SA’d before, and he did that to me. Then one post said, “What’s behind a toxic person’s rage is that they love you and that scares them because they can’t control it.” Another said, “Whatever they did to you, you didn’t deserve it.”That REALLY STRUCK ME. It’s what I’d wanted to hear him say…but it was still unsatisfying. I wanted him to be brave, to say it to me personally, and allow me to reply. I WANTED REAL CLOSURE. Because several weeks of assault is a really strangely intimate trauma to experience with someone that I’ll never be able to adequately explain. It’s a toxic enmeshment that causes Stockholm Syndrome. I could’ve never imagined a pain like this mixed with such a profoundly agonizing empathy before it happened. I felt that a part of me died in the experience and I had to resurrect myself and relearn how to walk in the world all alone. After all I endured, after all his rage and tears and assaults and lies and even shameful truths confided in me, I felt I deserved closure. I sometimes can’t believe he wouldn’t want closure too. But, at the same time, I recognize that this whole idea is about as dumb and dangerous as hugging an Anaconda.BUT THAT’S THE TORMENT: GRIEF ISN’T LOGICAL. IT’S EMOTIONAL. On the anniversary of when I escaped, his profile disappeared again. But before it did, he posted artwork of a girl on a grave under the moon with pink hair, and that was my hair color when he assaulted me. (Taken one day before my attacks). It took me a while to make sense of this post of his, but I finally did. Sociopaths and narcissists are both prone to coded messages for truths they can’t admit. I realized the girl is me, the grave is him, and the person I’m grieving is his inner child, who I got to see glimpses of and hear about the pain… ….but his innocent, loving, feeling inner child was murdered in childhood, and it only operates in this world as a ghost. His inner child who I felt affection and friendship for was real, but it was no different than a haunting. The trauma he shared was real too: it’s what killed his inner child. And what a child ghost wants is what all the living dead want: to be alive. The jealousy of those whose inner child is still living will cause them to terrorize in anger as they wander this realm aimlessly in confusion, trapped in a purgatory—alive in body, but dead in spirit.So, I’m never going to get the closure I desire. When a child dies, there is no closure. And their ghost can never feel guilt or feel your grief: they’re too consumed with their own. But I’ve gotten some meaning, peace, growth, and understanding as I grieved. I understand evil in a way I never thought I would: evil is just the absence of love. And it visits us because of the spiritual death of a child. There’s a reason why a demon is defined as a “fallen angel.”May you find your meaning and healing too. Be patient with your heart as it grieves. The heart is an infantile thing: it cries without cause, it wants what it wants, it often doesn’t know what it needs. And it must be held gently and nurtured by a trustworthy adult who won’t abuse it. Make sure that adult is YOU.

column1: Can anyone give me examples of their narcissistic mother's actions? I know I grew up around a very toxic mom and had lots of childhood trauma, but I'm trying to understand things to a greater depth so I can heal and cope from it.
column3: Here is one of my most painful examples… The painting incident, as I like to call it, was the first time I saw red thru my own vision. I always thought that this was a figure of speech. It is very real, and the rage that exploded uncontrollably out of me was something I had no control over. This incident with my parents was on an evening with my husband gone for the night working, and them “helping” me with the girls. My second was still an infant. They bought over the predictable pizza and bottles of wine. They were drunker than skunks as usual, but still seeming functional. Helpful, no. Driving themselves, of course. Judgmental, you know it. I was just used to this misery, not realizing I could live a life without them. In our home we had a gigantic wall holding the only thing I got when my grandfather died (my mothers’ father). He was a sweet man who I had a strong bond with. He was my favorite blood grandparent. When I was in middle school and high school, I would spend days over at his house with him and my step-grandmother who I also loved. We would garden in his greenhouse, do yardwork, tinker with tools in his garage while listening to the country station. He never sexualized me like my dad, he didn’t drink himself into oblivion daily. He would talk to me like an equal and I have nothing but fond memories of him. My heart still aches for this man, and as I think about him writing I weep. I don’t know what he was like when he raised my mom and aunt. Absent and disconnected from the vile human my grandmother was is my guess, all the while neglecting his daughters. My mom never complained about him, only her mother. However, she hated when I would come home and tell her what a good day, I had with him. The confusion and jealousy that consumed her was noticeable, and I could feel her wrath under her skin. He died my sophomore year of college on New Year’s Eve. It was the worst loss I had suffered up until that point. His funeral was going to be held on the day I was supposed to return out of state for second semester. I wanted to stay for the service, and simply miss the first day of school. My parents would not hear of it. I was instructed and forced back to school. I missed my grandfather’s service. I was not wanted there. I was told, “it’s not that important,” “he knew you loved him,” “you said goodbye already,” “just go back to school, that is much more important.” So, I did, it’s not like I had a choice. I then gained about 20 pounds of grief weight and struggled to get thru the days. Fast forward about 4 years, I purchased my first home for my first horrible husband and me. I was given (or so I thought) a painting of an old mining town in my home state that hung in my grandfather’s office for his career as a banker. It was specially painted for him, and had his name written on one of the dilapidated buildings signs. It was the most cherished thing I had in my home. I looked at it with love everyday feeling the presence of my grandfather who I loved and missed so very much. When I sold the house that my first husband and I occupied the painting eventually found its place in my new home with my new husband and girls. It was my favorite thing. Move forward about 5 years from the painting being on my wall in my current home. I have now had the painting in my possession for 10 years. This night with my parents eating pizza and watching them get drunker and drunker, I was holding my infant, and my mom was sitting next to me gulping her white wine. She looked up at the painting and said with a familiar slur to her words, “I am just so excited to finally give the painting to your brother now that he bought a home!” That was the first time since my childhood that I felt the same feelings of confusion and mistreatment by my parents when it came to how different they treated the two of us. I felt the same betrayal in my mid-30’s as I did when I was a teen. It was amplified to level I had yet to feel. “What!” I yelled? “Oh honey, you remember, that painting was always meant for your brother, you were just holding it for him.” At that point I shot off the couch, and my drunk, useless, horrific father figure was standing over my kitchen island eating pizza and downing another glass of red wine. I walked up to him, stupidly thinking that he would have my back on this one and said “Dad, do you know about this, this cannot be right, you guys never told me this?” He looked at me with such disgust, annoyance, and disdain and said with booming authority, “Oh you know this, you must have forgotten, we told you when we gave you the painting that it was always your brothers.” I don’t know what was really said after that. This is when my internal world went red. I was screaming so loud at them I am surprised the cops were not called by concerned neighbors. I remember telling them how I am so sick of being second pick to my bother and being treated like a pile of garbage and lied to and made to feel crazy. They brushed me off and told me I was out of line. I kicked them out of my house screaming at them even as they drove away down the street. I literally ran them out of my house. I have never had emotional rage and anger engulf my body and mind like this incident. It was surprising to myself how furious, sad, and frankly confused and shocked I was. My mom called me the next day like nothing happened. I let her talk her standard bullshit of her life’s events and then I let her know I did not want to see them again. She threw a fit and pulled (up to that point) an academy award winning textbook gaslighting, guilt tripping, sob story, victim card of her life. Then she pulled out her biggest gun and questioned me about “how could I not let my grandchildren have their grandparents in their life. It’s not fair to them, what kind of mother would keep her kids from their own grandparents, and we won’t be alive much longer, and we love you guys more than anything, you must have just forgotten about the painting.” She then told me that dad remembers telling my ex-husband and he should have told me. Pawning their lies off on my ex-husband. Someone they know could not be called upon for a confirmation. Wow, just wow. I knew they were full of shit, but they had me in their grasp even still. After this conversation I was still sticking to my guns. I even called my brother and tried to talk to him about it and see what he was told, and if he could let me keep it because it meant so much to me. He simply hung up on me, annoyed that I called. He told me it was always his. Shut out by all three of my family members. I was out of line in all three of their eyes again, made to feel I was wrong in every way possible, that I am the asshole, as always. A week later I got this very extravagant seemingly caring card from mom in the mail. Let me be clear, it was not an apology. It was a gaslighting letter of pretend love and manipulation formatted to trick me into thinking that yet again, my feelings and memory are not correct. In this letter they also offered me up a painting that they claimed to have in storage that meant just as much to the family. All BS. I never saw the painting to replace the one I was losing. I ignored them for about a month. This is when they started reaching out to my wonderful husband and talking shit about my bad memory (triangulation) and enlisted his help to get the paining off the wall. My husband did it, trying to keep everyone happy and the family together. They came and picked it up and rented a U-haul and drove two states away to place on my brother’s wall. They never mentioned it again. It then took me another 6 years of being lied to and manipulated to finally tell them to permanently piss off.
column9: Good on you for moving on.Just reading your story made my blood boil.Long story but similar incident. I am 52 and it took me up until 1 1/2 year ago to walk away. I feel free finally.

column1: How did you change yourself after meeting a tragic death of a family member?
column3: Bear with me, this will likely be long, because it wasn’t one death, it was several, over a long time, culminating in 2020 with the death of my mother. To keep people’s grief private I won’t name folks or get too descriptive but when I was ten I lost a family member to cancer and then just a few months later that family member’s spouse committed suicide. I didn’t realize it at the time but that event basically ended my childhood. After that I was suddenly aware of illness and weariness and just the dark corners of the world. I had other relatives die, but they were very elderly, in their 90s and their deaths were sad but not tragic. We mourned them but could also be comforted that they had lived good, full lives. But then, in my 20s I had another close relative die in an accident, who was also in their 20s. Then a friend died in a car accident a few years after that and another friend from health issues and another from drugs. Later on another relative died in a car accident. In my young adult life I felt like I was tripping over funerals and grief. Every time I turned around someone was dying unexpectedly. The signposts of my life were turning into gravestones. Larger and larger parts of my life were remembered as before or after such and such person had passed. My focus changed from living life with death being a part of it to a string of deaths with maybe some semblance of life in between. I lost two babies before they were born. Almost lost the one I did have from birth complications. More elderly relatives dying. Work colleagues dying. It began to feel, in my 30s and 40s like all I was doing everyday was sitting around holding my breath waiting for the next one, because there was always a next one. You know that old experiment where they put rats in a cage with an electrified floor and give them a shock randomly every now and then? The rats lose hair, stop eating and become neurotic and eventually die. This is how anxiety and phobias are born. That kind of anxiety feeds into things like depression and OCD, even drugs. When you feel out of control and you don’t know when the next shock will come, life is just one held breath. You’re not living, you’re living in fear of the next moment because there is always going to be that next shock moment and it’s stifling and traumatic. And then, as it always does, the next moment came. My mum was diagnosed with a terminal illness. She went from a healthy 50-something to basically a shell of herself in less then ten years. My whole family had to watch her die, slowly, little bit by little bit, over just about a decade. Loss of mobility. Loss of bodily functions. Loss of teeth. Loss of job and independence. She sold her car. Loss of memory and mind. Meds making her ill. Infections. Blood tests. Black, blue, and purple arms. Watching little bits of her disappear over time, we slowly learned we couldn’t really think too far into the future. Will she be here next Christmas? For the grandkid’s birthday? Next week for her hair appointment? ER visits and hospital stays were growing closer together. The horizon, we realized, was approaching for her and it was getting to be a tangible sense of it coming, not just the ‘someday’ that we all live with. So, how did it change me? After being beaten around by the deaths of so many loved ones through the years, my mum’s experience helped me realize I could either live with a sense of impending doom or learn to enjoy today. Or just this moment when she is here, and laughing, or well enough to go out to eat, or just get out of bed. If I could sit and eat a piece of toast with her or a bowl of noodles and laugh at what the cat was doing, then it was a good moment to be enjoyed. If we could walk out to the barn and see the baby goats, it was a lovely time. We all dealt with her illness but didn’t dwell because dwelling would have tarnished the time we DID have. Her liver was affected and so she would swell up with fluids like a balloon and I would drive her into the city, at the end it was weekly, to have her drained. Sitting there for hours on end while it dripped out of her and while she received blood (thank you, blood donors, keep up the good work, bless you) were actually some of the best times when they could have easily been the worst. Attitude is everything in illness. Let me just say that liver disease is an evil nobody should have to suffer. But her sense of humor was fantastic, (bent a little sideways sometimes), and we had some legitimately fun times in that awful situation. The hospital hours-long conversations were legendary. Made the best of it. We made memories and they are some of the fondest I have, honestly. When she finally passed away, after one last stint in the hospital, I cried, but I found that it was out of joy for her not having to suffer anymore with that awful situation. I was relieved and joyful. We didn’t get to have a funeral because right then everything shut down for Covid so I had a lot of time right away to process my feelings about it. My husband told me weeks later that after she passed away it looked like a huge weight had been lifted from my soul. I have to say he was right. I didn’t want her to keep suffering and suffering and she wasn’t going to get better. I just wanted peace for her and she finally had it and I was happy for her. I realized that I never felt the need to grieve for myself and that was a first for me. Now, a year and a half later I think I have a much better view on death. You can never know what tomorrow will bring, so make the most of today, this moment. And, death is not some taboo thing to shove in the back of your closet, pretending it doesn’t exist, it’s part of life and having a healthy acceptance and view of it goes a long way toward the quality of your life while you are still here. This is not new or astonishing news or a revelation, it’s just maybe something that can’t be understood easily just from being told, people have to learn for themselves. But, maybe my story will help someone reach this realization sooner in their own life, so that’s why I decided to tell it. I feel like my relationship with death is a whole lot healthier now. Before, it felt like some kind of evil thief stealing loved ones away if I even blinked or let my guard down for a second, but with my mum it was pure mercy. My mum’s death allowed me to balance out my view of death and the weight really is lifted a great deal. In that way, her tragic death brought us both peace. As a kind of post script, as an example of her sense of humor, was this little gem. She had, a few years back, read about a hospital who had very kindly made Halloween cookies for its patients in order to spread some seasonal cheer. Some were pumpkins, some were skeletons, some were ghosts, etc. But the thing she found uproariously funny was that some were little tombstones with ‘RIP’ written on them. She said, “Imagine giving out ‘RIP’ cookies to patients in hospital beds and them looking at you like ‘are you trying to tell me something??”, she couldn’t get over how short sightedly, embarrassingly (for the hospital) hilarious that was. I asked her what she would do if someone gave her an RIP cookie in the hospital and she said she’d laugh her butt off because if you’re offended by a cookie you have much bigger problems than whatever you’re in the hospital for. And then she′d eat it because a free cookie is a free cookie! RIP, mum.

column1: What is the emotional impact of being estranged from one's child? Is it possible to overcome feelings of shame and loss? How do individuals repair their relationship with their child after committing a serious wrongdoing?
column3: I’m a mother who has been estranged by my oldest daughter for 2 years. It has been painful beyond words, a heavy weight in my chest that hurts with every breath. I’m starting to overcome the shame and guilt as I learn more about Estrangement, but the SENSE OF LOSS is like the death of a beloved young family member—only worse in the sense that, instead of bringing a family together in shared love and grief like the death of a child does. Estrangement tears a family apart in the cruelest kind of way, bringing out and cultivating the worst side of people. The virtues of love, kindness, acceptance, compassion, forgiveness and tolerance are replaced with selfishness, blame-placing, anger-venting, mean-spiritedness, isolating the estranged parent from others—and encouraging one’s other family members to do the same, thus cultivating the darkest side of them as well. If children learn by example, then grandchildren are learning that there is no emotional safety within the family—that love, if given, can be taken away in a heartbeat by a wrong word spoken or an innocent mistake made. How do individuals—parents—repair their relationship with their child after “committing a serious wrongdoing?” you ask? You can’t REPAIR IT. It’s not even ABOUT repairing a relationship after a “serious wrongdoing”—that would be easy! **Estrangement is about NEVER repairing a relationship. It is, in fact, about destroying a relationship and JUSTIFYING doing it and then ‘making sure’ that nothing can be done to fix it. The last thing an estranger wants to do is to “repair” the relationship The estranger will blame, lie, and manipulate to make sure that reconciliation never happens. IF MY daughter who estranged herself from me ever reached out to me to repair our relationship? I would welcome her with open arms! I would thank the Lord! I would cry 1,000 tears for the joy of being able to hold her lovingly again like I did when she was a baby! But will that ever happen? I’m learning to accept that it won’t. I don’t think my daughter has it in her to be compassionate and giving from the heart—she seems to enjoy being mean and venting her anger on me and turning other family members against me to prove to herself that ‘she’s right’ about me. And dig the knife in deeper about how bad I am. Let me mention first that by most peoples’ standards I’m a pretty ordinary, average mother and grandmother. I make friends fairly easily, am polite and courteous. I sometimes make mistakes but none serious enough to justify friends or family cutting me off. MY Story: My oldest daughter, now 46, had problems with friendships in school. I’ve always found her hard to talk to. She always wanted to dominate the conversation. I’d bring up something on my mind and she’d say, “Get over it!”, cutting me off, and start talking about herself. Then 2 years ago her father and I moved to a new house and our 3 children (and spouses) were helping us. The move wasn’t going well, it was frantic. I was still in pain from back surgery. Then in an I’ll-NEVER-let-it-happen-again moment—we found ourselves alone together (with no one else present to serve as witness to her outburst)—she started screaming at me saying, “You ruined my life! You were emotionally absent when I was growing up, I’ll never be happy. Ever, because of you. You’re a narcissist! It’s always all about YOU!” [Not true—my friends know I’m a good person] —And she’s never spoken ONE single word to me in the 2 years since. She texted her father saying that I had to see a psychotherapist for my Narcissism. I saw a therapist for 18 months just to appease her. And she emailed me non-negotiable terms—that I could only see my beloved grandchildren 4X/YEAR. [And the grandchildren loved coming to our house—they ask if they can come over when we’re on Zoom together (my daughter, thankfully, does let us Zoom with the children occasionally) And Now during the rare times that we ARE in the same home, my daughter scowls ‘don’t-come-near-me’ warnings at me and always stays at least 6′ away. She’s 46 YEARS OLD, for Goodness’ sakes! We parents paid for her college (out of state, no less)! We bought her her first car! We paid for her wedding (which for 17 years she’s angrily accused me of ‘ruining,’ by the way)! We’ve given her $1,000s every Christmas and birthday for years! We took in her 105 pound dog for 14 MONTHS during Covid when her family of 5 was trapped inside their center city house for months! We paid for all the dogs food, took him to the vet’s, and have cared for him whenever they go on vacation. And we have ALWAYS LOVED her. But she seems to have forgotten all of that. Maybe she thinks we ‘owed’ it to her. Maybe she thinks the money would be ‘hers’ through inheritance anyway. Maybe she thinks we were ‘throwing money’ at her (except for the 105 pound dog). NOW she twists truths and tells lies about me to other family members, including her 2 siblings. I can’t believe that a child that I gave birth to and raised could end up behaving like this! I grew up in an honest family, NObody in my family ever lied about anything, let alone told lies intended to hurt people! I found a helpful book entitled “Estrangement of Parents by their Adult Chidren” that describes my daughter almost to a Tee. First, the author explains, estrangement comes totally out of the blue from nowhere. [Her father and I can’t think of anything in her growing-up years that might have led to this—she left for college at age 18, never lived at home with us again—where did this come from suddenly at age 44?] —The parent is : 1. declared toxic and mentally ill. 2. Given a ‘label’ [Narcissistic in my case] 3. Child wants parent to apologize but won’t accept apology—rather than a path to repairing the relationship, demanding an apology is a way to manipulate and control the parent; 4. Child encourages other family members to estrange parent as well (her siblings); 5. Parent becomes isolated, unable to share their version of events 6; Child ‘gaslights’—-ie.,fabricates or misrepresents events, denies ever saying something, lies—which undermines parent’s credibility; 7; accuses the parent of having been emotionally ABSENT; 8. Blames the parent for the child’s own mindset of UNHAPPINESS and misery9. Child determines that only solution is to “walk away” 10; Child won’t AGREE TO NEGOTIATIONS because it isn’t reconciliation the child seeks, it’s JUSTIFICATION for the estrangement. 11. Child will only relate her abused-in-childhood history with family members and friends who aren’t likely to question their version of the story—by doing this they re-create family memory, determine relationships, and as a result control some or all of the family, not just the parent; 12. Parent’s trust in child is irrevocably damaged [and I fear this is true—I can’t trust her emotionally, there is no emotional safety with her 13; Child distances by declaring physical territory [only seeing grandchildren 4x/year]. There’s more. But who gets hurt by this? EVERYBODY. Grandchildren and grandparents are cut off from each other, grandchildren start to lose trust in parents and in relationships, feel perpetual disappointment when ask to see grandparents but repeatedly denied; they sense things aren’t right, the house doesn’t feel happy. Estrangement has been described as emotional death. Some say it is worse than an actual death because of the lack of resolution. I BELIEVE THAT because as a child my family suffered the loss of my 19-month-old sister and the loss of my 13 year old brother. Yes, those losses were agonizing beyond words and one never gets over them, but there’s a feeling of overwhelming love and gentle peace that comes with the deep sorrow of losing them and the loving warmth that comes with their memory. I DO LOVE MY DAUGHTER but the glow I used to feel for her is gone. The trust and emotional safety are gone. My heart doesn’t leap out to her with warmth when she comes into the room like it does to my other daughter, because there’s no emotional safety with my older daughter, no sharing of happiness with her. There is only anxiety, fear and hurt. I FEEL SAD for my older daughter because I don’t think she is ever going to know the feeling of trust and warmth that come in a truly loving give-and-take relationship. …and as her mother I can’t help but wonder what I did wrong that my daughter would end up being like this instead of a warm, loving person.

column1: What were the last words you said to your loved one before they died (i.e. parent, spouse, sibling, friend)?
column3: Use the time left wisely. Fill your days with laughter and love. Cross off a few items on your bucket list and tie up loose ends. Let go of regrets or fears for those left behind. Everyone has loved you with all themselves. From most, it was accepted, others not so much. Your soul mate will join you in time, continuing an epic love story that withstood the challenges of life, betrayals, heartbreak, laughter, insanity and the loss of child who you both loved but felt was never a true member of the family. It was always a family of 3, with one on the fringe or sitting on a stool so their head wouldn't be cut off in family portraits. I have loved as fully as I can- but it in some instances it was flawed due to poor decisions and trying to fit into a mold or relationships that I mistakenly thought were part of gaining acceptance. No one else is responsible for the choices and actions I made- they are mine alone to carry. Understanding the causes and ramifications, does not mitigate the actions and words that brought a family to its knees ( or so I was once told). Several times, I began a catastrophic series of choices and actions that ended in heartbreak, anger, disappointment, destruction, betrayal for all. Myself, I picked up what was left, faced the consequences, disappointments, anger and tried to figure it out again. For everyone else, they closed ranks, turned inward, shielding their hearts against future heartbreak and disappointment. That was/is never me. Hiding from the world, hurt, and danger was never me. Somehow, I always end up in the midst of it all. When you are told “we dont know you, and we cannot love someone we don't know, it is clear that I will never be allowed or encouraged to continue changing or make amends for past failures or hurts. I'm finally in a place where when I look in the mirror, I see what everyone else sees. I return smiles and nods from strangers without wondering if they mean me harm or if they are inwardly mocking me. I'm at peace with myself and OK with being me- faults and all. I'm stronger than I ever imagined for myself and those.around me. I no longer see doing the right thing as a negative, even though it often ends up as a trainwreck. I'm open with my emotions and feelings, even though those around me insist I care too much. My numbness is gone and I've become a serial hugger. Incredible from the child and young woman who flinched if loved one and friends invaded my personal space. I know that I will never be OK with being expected to choose between loved ones, friends and family members for one reason or another. It's cruel and a lesson I will never ever embrace or model for my son and your grandson- the one you rejected because he came from me- damaged goods. The one you refused to acknowledge and bond with, because you despised his mother. The one who symbolized that hope was dead- that I would never get it together and do what was expected of me in return for sacrifices that were made to ensure a profit down the road. I am fully conscious that failure to cut off or distance myself from those on the familial bad list is not permissible. We love who we love for reasons known only to ourselves. In this family, love is unconditional, but that doesn't mean you have to embrace their character faults or harmful behaviors. It doesn't mean your anger and hurt are not present and acknowledged. It means walking away is not option. For that to work, the others have to meet you halfway. You have to understand that you may find yourself standing alone, unable to force, bully or reason others to accept what they cannot. The only choice is to continue moving forward, carrying the love that always existed on your own. While the love remains undiminished, it does not mean that down the road, if your paths should cross again, those connections, memories and love will allow you to pick up where you left off. Sometimes, the adventures and inner changes you experienced ensure reconciliation is not an option. If that is where you are, it's OK and doesn't make you a horrible person. It makes you a realistic one. I owe you a debt of gratitude for finally forcing me to open my eyes and acknowledge in secret corners of my heart something I knew all along. I never believed I had the resiliency to face the fact, that I was nothing more than a “ gift with purchase”, raised and educated to ensure a sizeable profit for your eventual retirement- $100,000 to be exact. You always joked that “ you were spending our inheritance on luxuries, cruises, houses, cars etc”. But it wasn't a joke, it was a hard truth that you didn't need a 401K or savings for the later years, because I would do what I had been bred for- ensuring that there would be no interruption in lifestyle despite a lack of funds. Reading those words and the itemized payment plan you presented shattered my heart and soul. The one thing that terrorized me a child had come true- I was nothing more than a bank account. A child tolerated for an eventual pay day. I cried for days unable to tell those around me the truth. And then came a moment that changed everything. What was that moment? It was knowing that I would never allow my son to witness the demoralization and abuse of his mother. It was also the moment, when I realized that my inner reflection, expressed in terms of sadness, disappointment and grief was not rooted in the rejection and loss of my family, but because I simply no longer gave a damn. I could not come to terms with the fact that I didn't love my parents. I no longer cared if you were happy and healthy or how you spent your days. Family memorabilia and Christmas ornaments no longer caused tears or heartache. They became beautiful ornaments displayed openly for all to enjoy or representative of funny moments shared with laughter. Weeks, even months would pass, without a single thought of my fractured family. That in turn caused deep concern that there was something fundamentally wrong with me, as my parents had expressed. I thought it was a given, that despite their faults and abuse, a child adored and loved their parents, it was coded in their DNA. What was wrong with me? It took time and much reflection, to accept, that how I felt was legit, normal and not reflective of a broken soul. That sometimes, despite the love and memories, the only option is to go separate ways. Sometimes it just happens that way through no one's fault. Those last texts and emails, set me on a path- one leading in the opposite direction from those I loved and feared. It freed me to accept who I am- faults, trainwrecks, quirks etc, that in turn allowed me to be a better, and more honest and present mother, wife, friend and colleague. Trying to fit into the box others created and demanded, caused me to lose sight of myself and what made me me, not what others wanted me to be. It also freed me from the self destructive behavior that lead me time and time again, to put myself and my heart in harms way thinking this time will be different. It never is and it results in a hurt and devastation exponentially more traumatic than its predecessors. The fracturing of our family was not thoe result of one individual’s shortcomings. Each of us bears the blame and responsibility. No one is innocent. But unless all involved acknowledge their roles, we will remain at a stalemate- one that becomes more unsurpassable as each day passes. I wish things had played out differently. That Jarrett had had the joy of having grandparents who adored him and shared special moments like those stored in his mother's memories. That he was treasured and carried the best of all of us into the future. But that was never part of the plan. Instead he was greeted by a couple who were quite clear, no dropping in, no babysitting, no baby emergencies due to work requirements. You wanted nothing more than to be the cool grandparents who visited only on holidays, arms full of gifts. Someday I will have to explain why, when his grandparents lived a mile and a half away, he saw them at Christmas, for a few hours after his first birthday and at his kindergarten graduation. I hope this final irony doesnt escape you- your legacy, dreams, memories will live on in the hearts and minds of those you erased. Despite decades of physical and emotional abuse and neglect, there remains a part of me that smiles when retelling childhood stories and the adventures that opened up my world. Jarrett knows that struggles existed, the physical scars are plain for all to see. But I wanted him to form his own relationships with you without the darkness of my childhood. Turns out, I didn't need to worry, you made that decision for him. I'm sorry that you never had the opportunity to know him, to hear how he giggled the moment he heard Daddy's truck pull up to the house after being on the road. His voice is deep and there are times I think it is you, but we both know we will never hear each other's voices again. He is kind and compassionate, even with those he dislikes. He still comes home at the end of the day, lays across the bottom of my bed and shares his day and gossip. He still runs downstairs to share a new trivia fact he thinks will make day. I never let on that I know already and promise to include it in an upcoming class discussion or essay. When he smiles- the world and those around him shine in brilliant color. Watching him and his Lily, friend and girlfriend, laugh, play boardgames, draw is a miracle. He is so respectful and without knowing, displays all the quirks, behavior and kindnesses, that my Dan has done from our first date. These two saved my life and returned color, laughter, love and brilliance to my world. We are crazy, pranking one another, tossing sarcastic witicisms and yes have the occasional fight. But rather than retreated to nurse a wounded heart and soul, we muddle through it. Why, because that is how love should be, walking away is simply not an option. I have worked on this goodbye for months. It is perhaps the only time I can remember not saying “ Remember how much we love you, see you later”. I will always hold onto the laughter with the tears. One can only love deeply having experienced pain and heartbreak as I have. I believe you did the best you could, but I deserved better. Hopefully, I have shared with Jarrett, what you wouldn't or couldn't share with me . Despite it all, I would go through it all again and again just to be where I am today. I'm good, whole, no longer a damaged soul. Perhaps once you have transitioned you will take the chance to watch from above as Jarrett and I continue on our joint and separate adventures. To finally acknowledge that despite your best efforts, your daughter and grandson never stopped being your daughter and grandson. That despite it all, they loved you as only they could.

column1: What percentage of people with Down syndrome have children?
column3: I am unaware of percentages, but an extremely low percentage of people with down syndrome procreate, if that is what you mean when you ask “have children?”. i.e. against adopting children, which again, is likely never to occur. This Question begs the answer to the practical requirements regards “who will care for, and raise, the child to maturity born to individual with down syndrome T21, themselves with considerable special needs, who procreates?”. I later provide a genuine real life account of what occurs when a couple with down syndrome conceived, had a son, with down syndrome, via articles which report the statements of the mother of the female, who is also grandmother to her daughter’s son. We are fortunate to have such a reliable real life witness to inform of the practicalities, and events, which unfold. Generally males with down syndrome of the Trisomy 21 version, the most usual form of DS, are unable to procreate. Males with Trisomy 21 are generally viewed as not being capable of procreation due to many factors, including their very low testosterone levels. It is likely nature’s way of preventing procreation among people born with the genetic atypical condition, down syndrome T21, because, generally speaking, those with Trisomy 21 Down do not have the capacity to be active, responsible, parents. Having said that, nature can be unusual in that, in some cases a person with Down Syndrome, usually the Mosaic type but also Trisomy 21, male or female, can procreate and may have the (limited) ability, with support, more or less according to the individual’s need, to parent and care. There are reports a couple of males with down syndrome worldwide who procreated. That is a very tiny amount considering the long historical view over centuries. Before antibiotics were developed most infants with down syndrome did not survive their childhood nor reach maturity. These reports, of males with down procreating, are from obscure people, in relatively obscure parts in non-western nations so it is difficult to determine the truth, or not, of the claims except for the belief a male in USA, subsequently deceased, is the father of a son, Nic, with down syndrome born to mother, Lisa, with Down, over twenty years ago. Both have down syndrome. I will discuss this exceptionally rare example more fully later in my answer. It must be accepted it is possible, for males with down syndrome T21, that they, along with females, with down syndrome T21 may procreate BUT if they are similar to Lisa, they will not only have issues with their pregnancy but also great need of support for themselves and with the rearing of their infant to maturity. Then there is the future to contemplate. Both parent, and offspring, with down syndrome T21 beyond maturity will require assistance of various sorts -that outcome is known and accepted. The Question asked raises many issues and complexities which are not fully known. In my life experience with people with down syndrome, Trisomy 21 in the nation where I reside, I personally know of no-one, male or female who has procreated. Nor am I aware from my reading, of decades, of any individuals with down syndrome T21 who successfully procreated (birthed children) in my nation. There is a young man, Nic, living with down syndrome resident in California who attends what appears to be a live-in college course which attempts to provide their students, with down syndrome T21 and others with various developmental disabilities, basic living, and employment, skills. This now young man, Nic, is the outcome, of a sexual relationship between a female, Lisa, living with down syndrome, at a time when she lived independent of her mother, likely in an assisted living arrangement, and her former boyfriend- partner a young man also with down syndrome, who unfortunately now deceased. He died when Nic was a young child, leaving Lisa, Nic’s mother, desolate and in grief. I read fairly widely about this couple, and their son, all with down syndrome, T21. My reading informs the majority of the care for the baby, child, teen to adult years was provided by Lisa’s mother Patti. I will share some of these articles’ statements from my reading which I provide indented with a grey vertical line, to acknowledge the commentary is Patti’s, not mine. Here is what Patti has to say about the circumstances she found herself faced with not once, but twice.“It’s a big deal.(having a baby with down syndrome to raise especially when it is your grandchild, born of your daughter with down syndrome) If people think I’m going to give them permission to go out and do this, they don’t know”, says Patti as she discusses how her story may inspire other parents. “It wasn’t a fairy tale, it could have been a nightmare but it turned out pretty good. We wanted Nic to know his mum. It’s been a sacrifice but we can’t go back and I wouldn’t want to go back. I have no regrets.”Now later I present more full excerpts from two articles which arise from this poignant set of circumstances regards Patti, the mother and grandmother and involved intimately and personally with three people with down syndrome, her daughter, her former boyfriend and their baby with down syndrome Nic. I will leave you to discern for yourself, and to come to your own conclusions about the outcome of people with down syndrome if they procreate. i.e. They may, in some circumstances, be able to procreate, “have children” but can they “have children” and care for them all by themselves providing all that a child needs? The realistic answer is “No”. If one reads widely about this particular family resident in California then the answer is quite obviously “No” and arises from their experience. Therefore it becomes fairly obvious why there are not terribly many instances where people with down syndrome procreate, or “have children” as they do not have the innate ability to independently raise a child from infancy to adult years, not to mention the support care beyond for all the individuals lives. Nature wisely limits procreation within those who live with the condition, down syndrome, T21. I copy links to the articles, and photos in footnotes which provide full content, and context, to read if you wish. These are interesting articles which should adequality answer the question posed above. Naturally there will likely be contradictions to my viewpoint, and that of Patti, the mother and Grand Mum, which one may read about, but reading about claims to the contrary, is another matter to actually witnessing outcomes oneself which Patti does, and faced herself as the “person responsible” and has done so very well, and resolutely. Patti self-sacrificed, that is her own statement. Sacrificed her life to her daughter and her daughter’s offspring’s needs. The subject, and voice, mainly responsible in the articles, is Mother and Grand Mum, Patti White, to two individuals with down syndrome. She does not hold back her truth. She recounts her entire complex experiences, no holds barred except regards particular aspects pertaining to her privacy. Patti is a strong, and capable, woman that is obvious. She surpasses most Grand Mum’s ability to similarly tread BUT seems to receive State provided support systems, as does our family member now with advent of NDIS. Patti’s daughter moved to be independent of her, residing in some form of supported/assisted living, at age 18 - information one can read in the article link I copy below. Many parents, nor our peers, could choose that option for our sons, and daughters, at age18, in our nation, a state which remains the same many decades beyond. Such options, of assisted living - group home living, were not offered to parents unless we relinquished our sons, and daughters, with down syndrome to the State, to provide. It was, and likely remains, a very complex arrangement we have not investigated. Apart from that, what parent, except those forced by various severely adverse circumstances and extra tragedy, will consign their offspring to become basically a ward of the state? Such was, and is not, an option we could accept, nor was it an option for most of our peers. Patti seems to have enjoyed more than 12 years without full caring responsibilities for her daughter, when Lisa, who then was likely resident in some form of assisted care living, when living “independent” of Patti, her mother. Patti appears to have needed to resume more support when Lisa became pregnant which extended to Nic. Lisa’s son with down syndrome too, after he was born. This circumstance is understandable for those who are aware of the abilities, and the inabilities, inherent in people with down syndrome T21. Lisa herself had a very difficult time during her pregnancy particularly towards the end, and I read, in these articles, Lisa herself never wished to be placed in the same (pregnant) situation again. My reading of the “Voice” article conveys that Patti took on the support, and care, of her grandson Nic. Patti thus was again called to support Lisa, and simultaneously, to help her maintain her self-esteem by including her in the required activities, and in the raising of Nic, her grandson also with down syndrome. It reads that Lisa was basically another appendage to all this mothering, and training, her mother Patti undertook for Nic, to ensure he was not taken by state services. Perhaps California offers good, and reliable, support systems, and opportunities for people with down syndrome T21 and their parents, who find themselves in the circumstances Patti found herself facing twice. Patti was again greatly stretched and if she needed to do much alone, more stretched again. Please read the Down Syndrome Association “Voice” article and the other article copied to acquaint yourself better with Patti’s own account, and to better comprehend Patti’s, her daughter Lisa’s and grandson’s Nic’s lives yourselves. (see footnotes for article links). Most parents with offspring with down syndrome, five, and even three decades, ago at the time when our sons and daughters reached their majority, could not receive similar paid, out of parental home support for our intellectually disabled offspring. Those options then were not on offer in our nation, unless one relinquished their offspring with down syndrome to state care. To do that, relinquish one’s loved person to state services is not an option for most parents of those born with down syndrome. It was the case that unless we had the personal means to pay considerable amounts for private services in our homes, parents needs went unmet, while we strived to meet our people’s with down syndrome’s needs. With the NDIS now aging parents are provided more services. Can you imagine how a parent, either mother or father, who birthed a baby, with down syndrome, or not, would manage if they, their children, could “have” babies/children -i.e. Pro-recreate? It does not appear likely an easy proposition in my opinion. Personally I would not tolerate it, every parent I know feels exactly the same. I would certainly actively discourage any thought of such an outcome, though our family member and their male peers have absolutely no interest in being a parent. Yes, they enjoy being Uncles to their nieces and nephews who they shower with love and affection but are unable to care for these youngsters without supervision. Thus at 18, our family member, and their peers, with down syndrome could not live “independent” of us, with support, like Lisa embarked on her life, independent of her mother Patti, even if we wished unless we completely surrendered them to the state, so how would they fare if they could procreate? Similar outcomes to Lisa and Patti’s experience I suggest with the grandparents taking responsibility for their grandchild with down syndrome and continuing to support their adult son or daughter with down syndrome. And to arrange that outcome was not easy either for Patti, so then imagine attempting to care for offspring also? Almost impossible except for Patti’s journey reveals it is possible with her ultimate “sacrifice” of her own life. There was, and remains, no automatic passage to “group home” living or any living “independent” of parents living then, and not likely now in our Nation. Though with aging parents there are likely some more opportunities. There is a huge rigmarole, and a very long wait list and queue for what many accept as “dubious care and support” - entry generally goes to those most in need. So we must remain realistic to the possibilities, and outcomes, for rearing and caring for the infant to maturity, if in the rare instances a person with down syndrome T21 “has children” or in my term, is capable of “procreating”. Grand Mum Patti’s voice predominates in the article: “An Unexpected Motherhood” written by Leticia Keighley “A family story of how a young woman and a young man, both with Down syndrome, had a son…with Down syndrome” . Leticia's article briefly recounts Grand Mum’s Patti’s experience of raising her own daughter with down syndrome previously, then subsequently becomes the “person responsible” /surrogate mother, for her grandson, Nic, also with down syndrome. It seems likely along with the support of some state provided services, but these support services are certainly evident presently with Nic with down syndrome, resident in a purpose developed “college” course which teaches “independent living” and “employment” skills in a parallel fashion, alongside, but not with typical university students, at a University Campus in California. I read, selected, and copied below excerpts from the Voice article in March 2016 from The Journal of Down Syndrome Australia. I use inverted commas to denote all content I copy to use in my answer. Before one becomes overly enthusiastic about the concept of people with Down procreating, please inform yourself thoroughly by reading the article in full links provided in footnotes. Patti, Grand Mum of the now young man Nic with down syndrome informs she mostly raised her grandson with down syndrome herself along with schooling, and perhaps with other “user pays” services except for staff hourly rates, as occurs in our nation now with NDIS - Patti does not share all the private details of their journey, and supports used, so my understanding is an attempt - a “guestimate” of the finer private points. At the time of the writing of the “Voice” article, Patti says she needs to organise the input of volunteer, or paid (I don’t know which is the case, or perhaps there is a mix of both), “Circles of Support” for Nic her grandson. Patti is obviously attempting to provide for Nic and “hand on” her caring and support responsibilities to others as she is aging. Grandparents, who become surrogate parents do not last forever. Patti’s daughter Lisa, also with down syndromes, appears to receive State provided services in supported, or assisted, accommodation, as she previously did in those 12 years previous to the birth of Nic. I am unaware of the provision of accommodation needs for the developmentally disabled in California or USA. One would need to discuss with the local Down Syndrome Associations nearby in USA. Lisa likely already enjoys her own “Circles of Support” while also continuing to be supported somewhat by her own mother, Patti. It is difficult for me to confidently write of Patti, Lisa and Nic’s lives’ events without more information which may become available when Patti White’s book she says she is presently writing becomes available. I look forward to reading Patti's account of her life with her two intimate family members with down syndrome AND so should anyone asking the naïve question above.“Lisa (Patti’s then pregnant daughter with down syndrome) moved closer to Patti and Norm, (her step dad), when she was six months pregnant. After Nic was born, he (the baby) would stay three nights a week with Lisa and a support person stayed with her overnight to help with tasks Lisa could not undertake alone. It was very important for Patti to keep Lisa's self-esteem as a mother up so Lisa was involved in all the aspects of raising Nic including his therapy classes when he was young. Patti repeatedly told Lisa that she was the best mother she could be but the reality was that Patti and Norm (grandparents) had to raise Nic themselves in their own home. Nic (grandson with down syndrome) who has just turned 20 is a very handsome, accomplished young man with a wicked sense of humour. Talking to him was a riot. Nic swims every day and competes at a high level. He loves singing, and dancing, as well as playing football. (Don’t they all…those with down syndrome, enjoy dancing, singing and sports, our son and all his peers do). He has had a girlfriend for the past year, Hannah, who is a few years younger than him. Patti describes what it was like for Nic growing up. “For Nic, it was easy. It’s just normal for him because he doesn’t know anything else. He knows Lisa is his mum but he calls me mum too.” I asked Nic about his mother: “She’s fine and she’s loving… and I do love her as my mum and my mum always trying to teach me how to speak. I was learning to crawl and I was learning to walk.” “I have two mums. My mum Lisa is my greatest future in my life. She give me life and she give me love and she give me birth and she give me special needs and she is always wonderful and she is beautiful””Lisa and her boyfriend. And Nic as a baby with his parents over 20 years ago.Challenges: “The challenge is now on to help support Nic in his adult life by establishing a new Circle of Support for him(Lisa has her own circle of support which includes her mother Patti and Patti’s husband, Norm) and Hannah(girlfriend) to model what good relationships look like and help the couple make good choices for the future. While talking to the family I am struck by how happy, loving and contented they all are but Patti explains that this life has come with some great sacrifices too. Lisa was living a very independent life (likely supported by state paid disability support systems in assisted living) before she became pregnant, but afterwards she was unable to work (supported work most likely in a Goodwill store), her social life changed dramatically and she needed to remain much closer to her parents. She also lost a lot of female friends as their parents were afraid association with Lisa would influence their daughters to want babies too. For Patti (Mother and Grand Mum), the sacrifice has been enormous. At times she has held some resentment towards Lisa.” Some of the sobering facts - statements by Patti: “The word independence is a wonderful word and Lisa often uses it….we are all dependent to a certain degree. Their (people with down syndrome) dependence is different than ours; it never goes away. They cannot survive without parents or agencies. “i.e. paid and voluntary supports.Lisa with Nic when a child. Patti provides sobering accurate information to inform the realities involved when facing those born with down syndrome, and the realities for those who love, and assist, them life-long. All these necessities are involved without bringing into the equation the ability for the individual with Down to “have children” i.e. procreate and bring another child likely with special needs into the world. AND to respect the needs the outcome such procreation means, i.e. raising the individual from infancy to maturity and providing life-long support of various kinds according to the individual/s and their needs.Furthermore: “It’s a big deal. If people think I’m going to give them permission to go out and do this, they don’t know”, says Patti as she discusses how her story may inspire other parents. “It wasn’t a fairy tale, it could have been a nightmare but it turned out pretty good. We wanted Nic to know his mum. It’s been a sacrifice but we can’t go back and I wouldn’t want to go back. I have no regrets.” AS the original Voice article author, Leticia Keighley, outlines: “While Patti’s story is a cautionary tale in a lot of ways, it is also quite incredible. The Catch 22 that Patti had between respecting the personal autonomy of her daughter and handling the consequences of those decisions is really striking. It means parents have to think very clearly about the possibility of their child’s desire for a family of their own one day. It blows the discussion wide open to consider the kinds of supports someone with a disability may need to do this, and the kind of planning someone may need to prevent it depending on their wishes. Patti and her family didn’t choose this path but have made it work through a lot of hard work. Knowledge is power. Patti's story helps us rethink another assumption about people with Down syndrome and provides valuable information for others to help make their own decisions. Patti is in the process of writing a book of their life which will be a must read for a lot of families.”Above are excerpts only from the Down Syndrome Australia, Voice, article, written by Leticia Keighley and composed mostly with Grand Mum Patti’s voice. To read the complete article consult the links in footnotes. Lisa as a baby below.Above is a photo of Lisa as Patti’s infant child with down syndrome. The following is from a supplementary article’s commentary I include along with the photos in the article.“THE BEGINNING” “Twenty-five days after turning 18, Patti White gave birth to a baby girl with Down Syndrome, Lisa. While her little girl was in the incubator, the doctors came and told her how difficult it would be for her to raise her daughter. They suggested she abandon her child by giving it to the state. The young mother heard what they said but silently disagreed. White wasn't ready to give her daughter away, despite knowing raising a child with Down syndrome wouldn't be easy. She recalled: "I silently resolved that I would never abandon my child." “Lisa - Global Down Syndrome Fashion Show Lisa Newtop Model from 2016 Later Lisa as a young adult:“A NEW RELATIONSHIP” “While living independently in her apartment for 11 years, Lisa gained confidence. She felt comfortable in her skin and was never ashamed of her Down syndrome. Lisa worked at a local Goodwill store which helped her choose a career path that best suited her. When Lisa was 29, she met a 24-year-old man with Down syndrome at work and developed feelings for him. They started dating and often visited each other's houses, making (Patti) White worry about her daughter. White recalls: "I am a little concerned about the boyfriend. I'm not sure. But I am pretty sure they are being very intimate."”The outcome:“AN UNEXPECTED ANNOUNCEMENT” “The worried mother discussed her concerns with a knowledgeable friend who assured her that men with Down syndrome were sterile. Others also told (Patti) White not to worry because they were sure Lisa wouldn't get pregnant. Things took a different turn when Lisa surprised White with an unexpected announcement. When White returned to her desk after having lunch at work, she checked her phone and heard a message from Lisa saying: "Hi mom, I just wanted you to know you are going to be a GRANDMOTHER!"The situation develops: “As much as (Patti) White was shocked after discovering Lisa was pregnant, she feared her daughter would lose the baby to Child Protection Services. White explained that hospitals viewed disabled mothers as "detrimental" to their babies, so Child Protection Services often intervened in such cases. White recalled: "She [Lisa] said to me, 'If I have a baby with Down syndrome, he will be like me, and I'll be so proud of him.'" After dealing with a high-risk pregnancy, Lisa gave birth to her son, Nicolas, four weeks earlier than the expected date. His father was also there in the hospital room, but he and Lisa soon parted ways.” Sobering events continue: “SIGNIFICANT LIFE CHANGES” “When Nicolas turned five, his father passed away, leaving Lisa depressed. Soon, she had to undergo heart surgery, so (Patti) White and her second husband, Norm had to look after Nicolas. (Patti) White felt Lisa's life changed significantly after giving birth to a baby with Down syndrome because she needed assistance raising him. She had stopped going to work and mostly stayed with (her mother Patti) White and Norm. Moreover, her social life had also deteriorated because her friends' parents didn't want their girls with Down syndrome to hang out with Lisa, fearing they might start wanting to have babies.”A more recent photo of Lisa and Nic.Mother Lisa with son Nic both with Down Syndrome above. Both are likely models for an agency which uses their services. The second Article used for excerpts is written by Salwa Nadeem in 2022 and contains many of these photos copied below.Nic swam Varsity this year - above- (I presume 2022 as that is the second article’s provided date). This is Nic with his mom Lisa (above).2018 Aug1 Patti White (above) drives and delivers Nic her grandson with down syndrome to Wayfinders Fresno State ……………………………………………………………………………………………………………………………… One never knows what one is capable of until they are presented with the situation and circumstances I have found. Sometimes there is no choice, but to roll up sleeves and get on with it. But not aged nearly mid seventy as I am now. Full credit to Patti White, for being a super involved Mum and Grand Mum to her daughter and grandson with special needs.
