column1: What was the most painful day in your life?
column3: I have been avoiding writing about this for some time, but I think it’s time I just get it off my chest and move on. It’s about my first cat, Mimi. When I was about 9 or 10 years old, one of my childhood friends at the time came over to my apartment and knocked on the door. “Come with me!” He said. We both ran out of the apartment into the apartment garden area out front. Times were different then and we spent a lot of time outdoors. He showed me a box of kittens, all brown tabbies, striped black and white. After some begging, my parents let me keep one and I named her Mimi (this is actually, like, what all cats are called in Vietnam). One day, Mimi’s eyes opened up a little more and I remember my mom using cotton swabs to gently clean her eyes for her. Mimi must have been really young! I was an only child so Mimi and I spent a lot of time together. We would play all day with string and she would go crazy catching it. I would throw balled up socks against the wall and she would run to catch it, put it in her mouth, and bring it back like a dog. I would turn on cassettes of my dad’s karaoke singing (this was the ‘90s) and rock Mimi to sleep. She actually fell asleep in my arms. When Mimi was about 8 years old, my dad said he had found an injured cat at work. I asked him to bring her home and we named her Titi. Titi was only a few years old, super hyper and playful. Mimi was now older, calmer, and absolutely hated Titi. We had to deal with Titi bothering Mimi all day long and Mimi fighting Titi. Mimi was also very grumpy and looking back, I realize I had played with her way too much. I think she was overstimulated so was not as nice as cats can be. Anyway, there was more chaos in our one-bedroom apartment as we dealt with the two fighting cats. However, I didn’t want to get rid of Titi. Unfortunately, I didn’t know about how to introduce cats to each other or anything about how to properly have cats as pets back then as I do now. So I had a lot of cat scratches growing up. Soon, it was time for me to go to college. I attended school close by so was able to visit over the weekends. My mom continued to take care of the cats as she had been for 9 years. She took the cats to the vets, scooped their poop, fed them, and I now remember that when I was younger, she often complained of all the extra work. I realize now she had too much responsibility over my cats and I had none. One weekend, I heard bad news from the family. My dad’s mother, who raised him and loved him after his biological mother gave him up, had passed. My dad is a very quiet man who lets very few people close to him. His mother was one of the few that he would do anything for so this was a big tragedy for him. I faintly remember something else happened with my mom and her family. I don’t remember exactly what, but I remember talking to my family and just feeling the tension and stress looming over the household. Anyway, I came home to visit one weekend and something felt quiet and off. I looked around. “Where’s Mimi? Where’s Titi?” I asked. I don’t remember what my mother said but I remember just falling to the floor and crying. My parents had taken both my cats to the animal shelter. I was so lost and confused and didn’t know what to do. Oh, but maybe it wasn’t too late. Maybe they were still at the shelter? I called the shelter my parents dropped them off at. They told me that my cats were not used to being cages and were wild (I don’t remember what word she used specifically). They had to put them both down. Mimi was 9 and Titi was 5. Titi had so many more years to live and they had put her down too? I remember just sobbing and feeling so broken (as I cry now because the pain has never gone away). I felt that I had betrayed them. I cried as I imagined how scared they were as they were stuffed into cardboard boxes and hauled off to a strange and scary place. I imagined Mimi and Titi both being put to sleep, alone, cold, without me. I imagined their bodies tossed aside like any other stray animal that had no one to love or care for them. At night, I dreamed that they were alive and that it never really happened. I remember one painful dream in which I was playing with Mimi and she was alive and well. I was so happy! I threw her up in the air to catch her but when I looked up, nothing but ashes fell down on me. I realized then in my dream that I was only dreaming. I couldn’t escape this reality that my pet of 9 years was gone and I would never see her again. I never really forgave my mom and dad for what they did. I know they didn’t do it intentionally to hurt me. I know a lot of things were going on at home and they were stressed and having the extra responsibility of the cats was too much. If my parents ever bring up Mimi or Titi in a conversation, I close up and refuse to talk. I’m still bitter. No, I don’t want to talk to my parents about it. I’d rather not think about it after this post. And please—no comments about how horrible my parents are—they’re not horrible people at all. It’s been about 10 years since that day I found out the news but it still hurts. I now have my cat, Lilly, who actually turns 10 years old today. Today’s her birthday! I shower her with love and vow to never let anything happen to her. I also have Leo and Jasper, who are my boyfriend’s cats. Today, my dad loves Lilly and looks to cuddle and hold her when he comes to visit. He calls her his grandchild and she happily drools on his shoulder. I wonder to myself sometimes if my dad regrets what happened years ago and is today trying to make up for it. I just think that if Mimi were here today, I would have the money and time to take care of her and my mother wouldn’t have the burden of that responsibility. But you can’t go back in time and what happened happened. I just hope they didn’t suffer or weren’t alone for too long before they died. I console myself now with the thought that I have Lilly completely under my control and that I wouldn’t let anything happen to her. She’s totally obsessed with me and I give her the best life that I can. I also try to remember that the most painful day of my life so far pales in comparison to what others have had to go through. At least it was “only” a pet cat and not a best friend or family member, right? Right. Yet, it still stings. Despite it all, I had a really good childhood and if this is the worst thing that’s happened to me so far, I’ve had a really good life as well. I’m not looking to top this at all. I’ll get over it one day. Hopefully. I can’t stand the thought of seeing a picture of Mimi or Titi or I’ll lose it again, so here are pictures of my Lovebug, Lilly.Lilly sleeping peacefully.Lilly being weird.Warm and cozy.Her favorite way to lay on me. Oh, and this is when I shaved her, lol.
column9: Oh, you poor sweet girl! I'm SO sorry! I can imagine how devastated you must have been losing your babies/”siblings”. : ( They were not “just cats” and it doesn't matter that people have had far worse “worst days”! This is your story and you have every right to feel heartbroken. It sounds like you've forgiven your parents. I hope you can forgive yourself now and feel reassured by the fact that your kitties are in a better place with no cold, loneliness, or pain. I'm sure they know how much you love(d) them! I'm so sorry this happened to you. Our cats are part of our families and I understand how awful that day must have been for you. I'm glad you have some new fluffy little loves in your life!

column1: How was your life like after the person you loved most left you?
column3: It was very heartbreaking of course. It felt like a family member died and a part of me died along with him. But somewhere within that confusion and heartbreak there was some sign of relief as well. That he is no longer my problem and I felt lucky. But that is probably my defense mechanism kicking in to help me cope with the profound sadness. I was with my ex for 9.5 years, we were childhood sweethearts and that has been my narrative over the years. It became part of my identity. Who am I without him? I lived for him. We didn’t have a simple relationship. It was marred with plenty of drama that was fueled by addiction (he was a gambler and pothead) and deceit. We broke up and got back together many times over the course of our relationship. It’s just that the last time was final because he found an exit, he is done and that is that. I have my flaws too, I was unfaithful and we constantly hurt each other. It was a very dramatic relationship. In restrospect, it is for the best but at the time I couldn’t see it. As I was codependent, I did not want to leave him. I felt that I needed him and he needed me. No one will love him as much as I love him. Anyway, when we finally broke up for good, I thought we were getting back together. I didn’t believe it. I was in denial. Like after the anger dissipated, I thought he would come around and beg me to come back. But he didn’t. He was out gallivanting with his new chick. That was when I knew it was really over, over. I couldn’t show how devastated I was. But I think I lived with dignity. I only backslided once when I drunk dialed him after losing my phone in a club. It was embarrassing and weak on my part. But after that I never showed him all the under bellies. I swore that I will never allow myself to be that vulnerable and worthless again ever in my life. I continued to work. I did my own thing, I focused on healing. I focused on myself. I removed him from all forms of contact- number fb insta nothing. He is dead to me. That mindset works wonders in helping me move on. I kept in touch with his mom and his sister. They are really nice people. There will be an interim period where things get a bit awkward and there are gray areas where you don’t really know where you stand or how to act. But if in doubt, just be courteous. To me, no one owed me anything or is at fault, except him. But his family was really nice to me, so I owe them a lot too. But it’s like dealing with your ex’s family there is some form of protocol. Anyway, it was a harrowing experience but through that shithole, I’ve developed tremendous growth personally and I feel that if I can get over my ex, I can get over anything. So far what really helped me to cope depending on my mood at the time was divided into the parts when I felt: RAGE: the rage would suddenly come rushing suddenly, feeling abandoned, indignant, full of pride, full of HOW DARE HE???! Followed by violent thoughts of watching him die. I would have clips of scenarios where I watched him get run over by a truck, like I would get a real kick out of watching the car tyres run over his legs and he is stuck or pinned down and I just watch him scream in pain. Another scenario is he got kidnapped by thugs cos he owed the money lender money and they beat the shit out of him and leave him to die on the streets and I happen to watch all of this go down. I would be smiling and satisfied. SADNESS: this is marked by crying spells, like the tears just wouldn’t stop. I could be in the car on the way to work, I could be just making tea, going about my day and then the tears would come. It is usually accompanied by a familiar scent or memory of him and I realize just how pathetic I am and I couldn’t help myself. I usually cried myself to sleep and wake up crying. It happened often but not always. When I’m in this state, I allow the feelings to come, I completely embrace the feelings, it’s like the purge. Then I know I’m moving forward. I need to mourn the passing of my relationship. These were the predominant feelings I had. There were other feelings as well but most of the time I’m numb. I quickly started dating again, I needed good distractions and pick me up. He needs to be replaced. At least whatever needs that he has been fixing me, I need them fixed ASAP. Then I realize, wait a minute, this douche honestly didn’t really do much for me. LOL. I was basically in the relationship by myself most of the time. His participation was quite minimal and it’s really not difficult to replace him. But of course there’s love and attachment, so that but he was always in my heart and mind. I needed to expel him, I felt. But I think if I continue to struggle and force him out, it wouldn’t do me any good. So I started accepting, accepting that okay, I love him but it’s okay that it didn’t work out, you don’t need to be with people that you love. It doesn’t matter, it’s not the end of the world. It really isn’t. The world went by barely noticing the difference. It took years for me to really be over him. I’m not really sure if I’m really over him because we didn’t have closure. I don’t think we broke up properly but I figured not everyone gets that kind of privilege and looking back it’s not necessary to get closure. It’s just excuse to soothe your little ego and maybe catch a glimpse of “the love of your life”. i think I’m proud to say that, I didn’t die and he wasn’t the best thing to happen to me. But he was a pivotal character in my youth. So I cannot diminish his importance in shaping who I am. But I cannot let him continue to have any kind of influence in my life from the day that he chose to leave me onwards. So that’s what I’ve been working towards and that leaves me motivated. I realize there is no conflict, that I can continue to love him but I don’t need to express that love to him anymore. Somehow that knowledge is liberating and I’m no longer held in my own limitations of what I must be or how I must feel or what I must do. For him to leave me, it gave me back control over my life, my emotions, my affections, my needs, my thoughts. I no longer needed him to validate my existence. In retrospect, I’m glad that he left me because I didn’t have the balls to walk away from a destructive relationship just because “I love him”. How many of us are stuck in that loop for the same reason? For our same weaknesses? we have broken up for more than 7 years now and I still do think of him but I have no desire to be with him. I can truly recognize and own my mistakes now. I’m okay with it and I know this wouldn’t matter in the next decade or so, but I didn’t know that when I first broke up. I think we shouldn’t discount the heartbreak and just grief accordingly. Everyone is attached and respond to separation differently. So we should just be gentle to ourselves. Just keep going in the road to recovery.

column1: What helped you the most in establishing a sense of security?
column3: RECOGNIZING THAT THE VERY CONCEPT OF SECURITY WAS ALWAYS A DELUSION.We never have any security: we simply deny that we live in a world full of things that could kill us so that we can survive.Last year, the unthinkable happened to me: I became a victim of stalking. I had been stalked by narcissist exes before and I have the restraining orders to prove it, but I never really considered that real stalking. I considered it my fault for being intimate with abusers and not recognizing they were abusers until my heart was shattered. BUT THIS WAS DIFFERENT. This was not my lover, not my partner, not a family member, not even my friend. He was my maintenance man at my apartment complex. At best, he was a casual acquaintance. On the day he met me after I needed a new fuse in my apartment, he installed a faulty water heater that broke every day for weeks. It had a heating rod bent at a 90 degree angle covered in calcite: it should’ve exploded. But in that time, my maintenance man was there every day, asking me tons of personal questions, being as charming and kind as anyone I’d ever met in my life.After the water heater, other things began to break, and he became so familiar that he’d walk into my apartment as casually and comfortably as if he was my husband. I really liked him. I hoped we could be friends. He was married and I was six years celibate from sexual trauma, so I knew I would not pursue anything romantic. But I found him very attractive: too attractive for me, I thought. The idea that anyone would ever develop an obsession with me was unthinkable. I see myself as boring, middle aged, fat, ugly, and generally unlovable to men. I have had many lovers: I was very promiscuous in my youth, and I exclusively was trauma bonding to narcissists. What they taught me, like what my parents taught me, is that no matter what I do, people hate me. But the truth was opposite to my sense of reality. He was breaking my appliances to spend time with me. He was coming into my home when I wasn’t there and reading my journals. I found places he wrote in them and crossed out things he didn’t like later, such as that I sensed he was lonely or that I thought friendship was better than sex. He installed a microphone in my apartment. He heard everything from my bowel movements to my therapy sessions. And he heard me say that I suspected he was a covert narcissist and I should avoid him. Then he came into my apartment and put GHB in my Brita water filter. When I was in a coma, he took a crowbar to my screen door and came in and raped me. He drugged me and raped me for three weeks.While I was drugged, he went into my phone and shared my settings to his. So, when I finally was able to figure out what was happening, find the microphone, escape, report him, and flee, he had my GPS. He knew exactly where I was. The Apple Store confirmed that my phone was being shared to another device and I fled again to another city. I was homeless for weeks and went into thousands in debt to move. I couldn’t finish my teaching semester. When I finally settled in a new place, he sent gang stalkers as I was speaking to lawyers. I have no idea how he found my new location. Then he contacted an ex who raped me in 2005, someone I only dated for a month and never think about, but since he had access to my memoir I was working on, he knew exactly who hurt me the most and how, so he knew who hated me enough to join his terror campaign against me. My ex traveled over 1000 miles just to show up at my new apartment and threaten me for my stalker. I was so traumatized and the extent of the abuse was so unpredictable and the lengths he went to so drastic that it felt like my brain was swollen.I dropped my summer classes I was teaching, despite desperately needing money, got weapons and cameras, and I didn’t leave the house for three months. I still only leave the house for absolutely essential reasons, and I usually vomit before doing so. Every morning before work, the first thing I do is go straight to the sink and vomit. I just cannot stand to be around people. I can’t trust anyone anymore. This level of stalking changes a person fundamentally.The central questions of my existence became: HOW DO I FEEL SAFE AGAIN? WHO CAN I TRUST?Because one thing you learn in an experience like this is that very few people will believe you and have empathy for what you’re enduring. The apartment management admitted he beat his wife and physically attacked his boss and had an “ego problem,” and a prison record for deadly intent, but they said, “Rape is a big word, and he said you were obsessed with him and breaking your own appliances.” He’d already done the smear campaign on me before raping me: he accused me of his own behavior. Police said things like, “Are you sure you didn’t date him? Are you sure you didn’t lead him on? What do you wear to bed at night?” Women’s shelters were full. Some of my bosses and coworkers revealed themselves to be narcissists who had raped before as they victim blamed me and began treating me with disdain. Some of my very best friends vanished into thin air. When I showed up to hotels, crying and frazzled with two cats and a huge knife in my purse, they asked what was wrong, and I told them I was being stalked and raped, and they barely flinched and said that would be $200 please, plus fees for my cats. NEVER HAD THE WORLD FELT MORE COLD.It is a miracle, literally, that I didn’t kill myself. Because it seemed the only escape, and I felt so unloved. What I would’ve given for someone to hug me and say they’d help, but I had just moved to that state for a new job and I had no friends there. Only the maintenance man. And he wanted me dead.When you wake up every day knowing that someone is hunting you and wants to terrorize you and murder you, you enter a new dimension of the human experience. You enter the jaws of the darkest, most disorienting, bottomless despair. Life becomes Hell on Earth. Eventually, I had to return to work, but it was excruciating. How could I act normal when there was a man as dangerous as Jeffrey Dahmer walking freely? How was I supposed to function when I was constantly waiting to be murdered? I’ll tell you how: I FINALLY REALIZED I HAD NEVER BEEN SAFE TO BEGIN WITH. Safety was always an illusion.The police don’t keep people safe or prevent crime; they respond after the fact. They would only be proactive if I was a corpse. Many people have NPD and lack empathy, especially those in power, so my jobs have never been safe. I walk amongst rapists every day. Some of my students are rapists. Many of my best friends left me at my darkest hour and exposed themselves as narcissists, including my SISTER. The people I loved and sacrificed for did not keep me safe, and they didn’t even love me back. I wasn’t safe in my own bed. I wasn’t safe in my body.I was never safe to begin with. I just lived in a delusion that I was.The truth is I wasn’t safe even going back to my childhood. Both my parents are narcissist antisocials, and I was the scapegoat child. I experienced severe child abuse, and my parents also killed my pets. My father is a pedophile who raped black male children. They always let me know that they brought me into the world and they had the right to take me out. Sometimes, while being choked, beaten, or thrown into scalding hot water, I believed they would. Yet, I needed them to survive. And I wanted their love.So, I denied they were abusers and I blamed myself for not being good enough as a child. This is how I survived. I developed BPD as a trauma response. My first suicide attempt was at 8 years old. To survive the world after them, I told myself they were rare, that most people were good. I found myself with narcissist after narcissist. Sociopaths attracted to me like I was crack. I was surviving in fantasy, delusion, denial. I had to. I had to believe it was possible people could love me, if only I was perfect, if only I was good enough. When they didn’t, I told myself I must not be good enough yet. That if I got my degree in psychology and lots of therapy and fixed myself, I could leave this life of trauma. But even being able to recognize a narcissist, even being celibate, didn’t keep me safe.A few years ago, I woke in the middle of the night to a sharp knock: “Police!” I jumped out of bed and ran to my door to see ICE at my neighbors’ apartment. They were Mexican. My neighbor tried to run. BOOM. BOOM. BOOM. Three shots from a gun. Next thing I knew, it was four hours later, and I found myself shivering in my closet with my cat on my lap. I had no idea what happened to me in those four hours. I blacked out from PTSD. I was bereft. I couldn’t trust my own mind. Did that shooting really happen? It did. And my own tax dollars paid to traumatize me and my neighbors. That’s how “safe” this world is.Being an agoraphobic writer, all I do is read. It finally dawned on me: what have I learned reading about trauma from people all over the world, all throughout history?YOU HAVE NEVER BEEN SAFE. Everything can change on a dime. I’d spent every waking moment waiting for my stalker to kill me, when it was just as likely that anything else could kill me. I could get in a car accident tomorrow. I could lose my job and all financial security. I could end up in a mental institution. I could be framed for a crime and end up in prison. I could get a cancer diagnosis. I could get killed by a lover, parent, or friend. I could get Covid and die suddenly. Our economy could collapse. Our police could kill us. We could experience war. A poisonous snake could bite me. And in America, there is a significantly higher chance that you’d go to prison for killing your rapist before your rapist would ever go to prison for raping you. 99.5% of rape cases never result in any conviction, even with an abundance of evidence. I finally let that reality sink in: YOU HAVE NEVER BEEN SAFE IN THIS WORLD. You just needed to believe you could be so that you could survive. This is not a safe world. And given that we don’t mandate mental health care for children and adults, it gets progressively worse and less safe. I can get all the cameras, locks, and weapons I can find, and I could still drop dead from a heart attack tomorrow. And none of us are ever escaping death. So, what now? Where to turn? I turned to God.And I let go of my illusions. I have never been religious but I always adored religion, because the stories of religions around the world are full of magic. My home is adorned in ancient iconography of gods and goddesses as well as Christian, Buddhist, Islamic, Hindu, and Jewish iconography. I see all faiths as an interpretation of the same energy. And the mythologies have much overlap and many lessons. I recognized that I needed to have real faith: if I was alive, there must be a reason. And so I would walk through the valley of the shadow of death, and I would fear no evil, for God is with me. I CANNOT EXPRESS HOW MUCH THAT LIBERATED ME. I had no idea how afraid I’d been all my life until I let that illusion go, and it was as if an elephant had been sitting on my chest and finally released me. I could breath again. And with that first breath without fear, it was as if I was resurrected.I started enjoying my life much more. I recognized every moment I was alive as a blessing. I started to see my life in abundance rather than lack and fear. I became absurdly grateful for the smallest things. Just a moment ago, I noticed the sun was rising and the sky was a beautiful orange and pink. I set down my phone and took my coffee outside to watch it and I felt overwhelmed by God. What a gift to witness another sunrise 🌅. I thank God for everything from my hot water to a quiet moment reading. This doesn’t mean my life is void of grief. It is full of grief. But there’s something else I was missing all along: when I surrendered to my true powerlessness before God, I found the power within me.Violence, I realized, is not strength. Violence is ALWAYS FEAR. If someone feels they must be violent towards you, if they need to recruit others to attack you, it means you have an extraordinary power. It means they are terrified of you. What in the world makes me so terrifying to others? My love. MY EMPATHY. My intelligence. My talent. My creativity. My authenticity. My kindness. My excellence. Why else did they crucify Jesus, except for the knowledge that HIS LOVE WAS RADICAL, HIS LOVE WAS POWERFUL? It is a truly tragic world that those things are considered threats by those who lack them rather than balms that could heal them. It is a reflection of how broken we are as a species, how far removed from God we’ve become. And what’s more tragic is that I couldn’t see that in myself. I let these people convince me I was worthless and make me feel fear of their power, when we are all powerless before God. I let them rip me from the source that created us all: the divine essence of unconditional love. And when I found unconditional love, even for my stalker, I found the kind of love that will make you weep. The love of God in which you feel impossibly unworthy. God’s love always comes like a flaming sword through the heart.Today, I no longer fear my stalker, though he’s contacted me via my phone, gloated over raping me. I write about him and my experiences with sociopaths in the hopes that his pain and my own can be transmuted to light and meaning. I’ve mined his traumas as thoroughly as he mined my own. What I find as I pull back the layers of what happened were twofold:I realized that given my childhood trauma as a scapegoat and his as a golden child, I was going to be raped from the minute I opened my door to him: my fate was sealed.Nothing in this world could’ve prevented it. It was the result of the trauma that made us both.Inside, he is a deeply wounded and terrified child.I have cried for him more than I have cried for myself. And today, I believe wholeheartedly that he taught me some of the greatest lessons in my life by showing me his pain. In my heart, I forgave him fully. I don’t need him to be sorry to forgive him. I don’t need him to change. I only need to stop operating in delusion and embrace the unconditional love of God. I only need to see my empathy differently. I used to see it as something that I used to show others that I was worthy of love. But I no longer need to convince anyone that I’m a human being worthy of love. Instead, I use my empathy to show people the divine mercy of God.I no longer wish for abusers to recognize my humanity; I wish for them to recognize their own. I believe that no one in this world knows my stalker as well as I do, not even his narcissist wife he lives with. I know his darkest secrets. I know the weight of the traumas he’s projecting because I carry them. And while no one in this world has known me as well as he did, and hated me with the force that he did… …NO ONE IN THIS WORLD WILL UNDERSTAND HIS PAINS AND LOVE HIM MORE UNCONDITIONALLY THAN I DO. Except for God. Because I had to do the work of healing what he couldn’t heal within himself. May your chains be lifted, your illusions dissolved, and may love fill your heart. “Forgive them, Father, for they know not what they have done.” Luke 23:34

column1: Is it common for people to become distant from others after the loss of their mother and/or father, particularly if they did not have children of their own?
column3: Grief is a long and complicated process for every person. There is no right way or wrong way to grieve. There's also no time limit on how long grieving takes. Unfortunately, you will run into far too many people in this world who will tell a grieving person to “Get over it and move on.” The reason why people are so cruel and insensitive is because they don't want to listen to someone talk about anything that involves death (or something difficult that's going on in that person's life.) Lack of compassion, lack of empathy, selfishness is too common in this world. Grieving is INEVITABLE. At sometime during each person's life we will lose somebody who matters to us. Then, we are forced to struggle through lots of tumultuous emotions that are difficult to process and accept. If someone has a positive, loving relationship with their mother or their father they are going to grieve very deeply when they have lost a supportive, caring parent. If the child who is grieving the loss of their parents did not give their parents grandchildren before one or both parents died, that could intensify their grief. (Especially if the parents had mentioned how much they were looking forward to having grandchildren in their lives.) What The Grieving Child needs to realize is: it was never your responsibility to give your parents grandchildren at any stage in your life. The ONLY responsibility you have as a human being is to live your life in ways that make YOU happy— at any stage in your development. Please don't focus on What Might Have Been. Fixating on a reality that does NOT exist can keep you stuck for DECADES feeling guilty about something that was beyond your ability to control. Fate NEVER lets us know what kind of a curveball it's going to throw us next. We find that out when the curveball hits us in the head and knocks us upside-down. THEN we have to deal with the Fallout of whatever turmoil Fate just put into our lives. Grieving the loss of a family member ranks very high on the list of what anybody would call turmoil. If a child had a loving relationship with their parents, then they are going to miss that parent. They will miss the parent’s love, affection, and guidance. If the child relied on their parents to give them support, encouragement, and good suggestions about how to navigate Life's Challenges, then that child is going to feel as if they are ship bobbing around in the ocean after they lost their moorings. It is very easy for a child who is grieving the loss of a parent to feel as if they're floundering— because they don't know what to do next. Uncertainty and Fear torments all of us at one time or another. Sometimes Fear and Uncertainty torment us on a daily basis. The best thing to do is remember all the good times you had with the parent that you lost. It might even help you to think: “what would Mom or Dad have done if they were faced with this problem that's affecting me right now?” You knew your parents very well. If your parents made good decisions, then let their good decisions provide examples for you to make good decisions in your life. One of the blessings of this modern era is that the internet exists. No matter what kind of an environment we grew up in, we can use the internet to find all kinds of resources that will help us learn about any subject imaginable. If you choose your sources of information wisely, and you just keep reading until you find an answer that makes sense to you, then you can navigate lots of Life Challenges— whether you have anybody in your life you can rely on to guide you or not. I grew up with two very selfish, narcissistic, abusive parents who had multiple substance abuse disorders. This made my parents very violent, very unreliable, and created nothing but constant turmoil, upheaval, fear and dread for myself and my siblings as we grew up. Our father was a dictatorial, violent, tyrant. Our mother was a judgmental, withholding, abusive person also. They were both so mired in their alcoholism, and ruining their health with smoking, illegal drug use, gambling, sexual infidelities, and other things—that they couldn't provide a good role model for anyone, especially their own children Even if you happen to be grieving the loss of a parent who was destructive to you in every possible way, you are still going to be suffering (and even more confused about how to cope with all of the Relentless, Toxic, Memories and Fallout that your abusive family has caused to ruin your life—when you were a child, as a teenager, and now as an adult.) Childhood abuse, neglect, and traumas cause a lot of difficult psychological problems for the children who were forced to endure and survive that vicious environment. You could be dealing with PTSD; you could be dealing with chronic severe depression; you will DEFINITELY be dealing with chronic anxiety disorders; and you could be dealing with borderline personality disorders—and lots of other things— that will make it MORE arduous for you to figure out: “how amI going to navigate through all of this relentless toxic Fallout?” Start using the internet right now to read as much as you can on different Quora blogs and other psychology blogs to help you figure out how to cope with your grief (and any other issue that you are having in your life.) You don't need to get stuck— or feel as if you have to find somebody SPECIFIC to become a mentor to guide you. The internet is full of hundreds and thousands of articles that you can read from the perspectives of potentially millions of people. In the midst of all that information, you are going to find plenty of helpful suggestions which will help you create a happier life for yourself. Yes, you have to do all of that hard work yourself. Truthfully, doing hard work to create the type of life that you want for yourself has ALWAYS been MOSTLY your responsibility. It's when people allow themselves to depend on other people too much that they actually cripple themselves. Because they do not know how to be independent people who are autonomous and free to make their own decisions without having to consult anyone for approval or validation. Too many people live their lives craving the approval and validation of others who SELDOM or NEVER give them any kind of supportive, encouraging, or compassionate feedback. Don't lock yourself into that prison desperately waiting for the smallest crumb of attention or affection from a withholding or abusive person. Because you will waste your entire life waiting for something that will never happen You can escape from that prison ANYTIME you want to—by learning how to approve and validate YOURSELF. When it comes to grief, the most important thing is: NEVER allow anybody to minimize your suffering or invalidate your grieving process. You do whatever is necessary for YOU to HEAL. You know yourself better than anyone else ever will. . Nobody else knows what you feel—even if you can put it into words articulately. Nobody can accurately describe the sensations of the emotions that you are feeling. Nobody else can understand the depth, the scope, or the intensity of any emotion that somebody else is feeling. Honor your feelings. Trust your instincts. Concentrate on loving yourself. Be kind and gentle to yourself. Figure out ways to encourage yourself on the days when everything feels like you are trying to roll a boulder up a mountain (and gravity is conspiring to hold you back from reaching your destination or achieving your goals.) YOU WILL GET THROUGH THIS. Just keep trying. Remember these two quotes from a man I greatly admire: Winston Churchill: I read these two quotes everyday (because my life is always relentlessly arduous.) They help keep me focused on SURVIVAL. Churchill said, “Fear is a reaction. Courage is a decision.” Churchill also said, “If you're going through Hell, keep going.” I like Churchill's blunt realism and logic. I found those two quotes to be absolutely correct in many different situations. Sometimes our lives are Hell on Earth. But if we give up, then Hell and all of our enemies win. If you keep going, eventually you're going to find the tunnel that will allow you to emerge from that particular Hell. Churchill's wisdom reminded me of many famous legends I have read in Greek mythology, and legends from many different cultures all over the world. There's always some sort of a Hero's Journey to read about where they descend into the depths of Hell, go through an ordeal, and then emerge and they are back on the surface of the Earth. During that ordeal, the hero learns how resilient and determined they are to survive. Griief will not defeat you. In ways that are difficult to understand right now— grief will make you stronger. Grief will also make you more compassionate to others. Grief makes you stronger because you survived something that seemed like it was going to break you. But it didn't break you. That's when you realize that you're stronger than you thought you were. Grief also makes you more compassionate to others who are going through their struggles in life. Grieving means that you've lost something— or someone—who was important to you. Grief can feel very overwhelming. It's only when we are overwhelmed that we can truly understand what suffering, fear, dread, and confusion is actually about. So take the opportunity to share what you've learned as you have processed your grief. Because something that you share with someone else may help them cope with their grieving in ways that will help them heal too. You'll find such advice the more you keep reading online about how to cope with grief. I think it is very natural for people to pull away from others when they're grieving. I've done it myself. I've seen people pull away from others constantly when they're grieving. Grieving is a very personal experience. It's difficult to discuss. It's difficult to cope with. Every person on this planet means something different to everybody that they meet. One person's grief will be more intense— because dead person meant so much to them. Whereas another person, who barely knew the dead person, won't have much of a grieving reaction at all. And once you have that inevitable experience where some cruel person tells you that “You're overreacting; you just need to forget about your grief and get on with your life”— then you don't really want to trust anyone else by making yourself vulnerable. Because cruel people will take advantage of your trust and vulnerability— to say and do things to make you feel WORSE. (Then the mean person gloats about it—because they enjoy harming people.) You can see the their sadistic satisfaction in the smirk on their face. Grieving can make you feel very alone and very isolated. If you're concerned about somebody who seems to be retreating into themselves, and staying away from others, try to approach them very gently, with a great deal of compassion and understanding. Listen to what they have to say— and DON'T be judgmental about what they tell you. Don't try to tell them how to grieve—or how to live. Say things that are helpful, supportive, kind, encouraging, and compassionate and you will have done a very good deed for somebody who is in despair.

column1: How can we influence Saturn?
column3: Saturn and previous lives Karmas. Your previous lives Karmas are the basis of allotment and placement of planets in the horoscope of this life. Lord Bharma has meticulously penned your horoscope which usually tends to follow the same path as in the previous births with a difference of the free will that you have. This free will helps you to Karma correct yourself by positively influencing the planets. But Alas! We forget that it must be done by us and not by the almighty. Before I tell you the correct way to appease and influence Saturn, let us, first of all, understand what Saturn is all about. Let us understand what Saturn is: Saturn is like the setting Sun – the lackluster appearance of the sun at the time of setting is described as symbolic of leprosy contracted by Surya on the birth of Saturn. Sometimes Saturn is described as death, fate, grief, malefic and inauspicious. It is a grim reaper and considers it symbolic of death and other malaise occurrences. The placement of Saturn in the horoscope tells tales about our positive and negative encounter in life, it becomes our prime duty to negate the negativity and increase the positivity. A blessing, if Saturn is well placed in a horoscope: The person is a thinker, who speaks infrequently. His behavior is logical and well planned. He is hard working and speaks on any subject only after much thought. His dealings are transparent especially when it comes to money matters, and his life is spent comfortably and happily. He is gainfully employed and known to be a diligent worker. He is accommodating in all aspects of life and enjoys the reputation of being a tolerant person. Let us through our free will tend to increase this. Let us also know what Saturn does when ill-placed in a horoscope: The person tends to make enemies of people. He is crafty, cunning, greedy; he is neither trusting nor trustworthy, a coward, anxious and restless. He always pretends to be facing some problem or the other to shy away from his responsibilities, he is a miser and always puts on a facade. He is lazy, scornful in his behavior towards women, a liar and always discontented. This person always pretends to be distressed, and he is inevitably known for his evil ways. He is manipulative and attempts to convince people that he is right. He always looks out for his welfare only and is uninterested in matters of religion. He is openly abusive in his speech and quarrelsome at the best of times.
