column1: Have you gotten so mad at your therapist that you almost quit?
column3: I think my last therapist and I came to a mutual unspoken understanding that we didn't like each other, and thus decided to call it quits. I had seen several therapists at a university clinic - they were all students, so I got a new one each semester. Unlike her predecessors, the last one had a very cold personality, almost sullen. The moment I first saw her, she gave me bad vibes. She also gave me bad advice - well, advice that went against my personal code of conduct, such as encouraging me to pick fights with family members over inconsequential things. If I didn’t report back to her on how I showed “assertiveness” that week (aka picking fights and getting offended over little things), she would become irritated with me. But the thing that offended me the most was when she told me that I was nothing like a fictional character that I had always emphasized with. Now this might seem like a petty thing to be offended about, but I have never read about a character whose situation was so like mine. Like me, this fictional woman was a caregiver for a sick, elderly relative, and had to watch helplessly as her relative's health declined year after year. (I take care of my mother, who has has a rare neurological disease and many other serious health conditions.) She was intensely loyal to family, and sacrificed her dreams to help her loved ones. (I have tried to keep my dreams to a minimum, because at an early age I resolved to dedicate my life to taking care of my mother.) She did not have many close friends outside of her family, and because of her isolation made the mistake of trusting a false friend, who manipulated her for his own evil purposes. (Been there, done that, still have trust issues.) She was grieving for her brother and her parents, who had all died tragic deaths. (My life, too, has been deeply touched by the deaths of three relatives who were very close to me, and I'm still grieving their loses to this day.) She suffered from severe depression and suicidal idealization, and sought to end her life when she felt that all hope was lost. (I have depressive episodes, and suicidal thoughts were the reason why I decided to seek therapy.) When her life improved, her depression did not immediately go away, as she had experienced too much pain and grief in her life, but she resolved to help others by going into a medical profession. (I have always wanted to make the world a happier place for others.) Much to my shock, my therapist told me I was nothing like this character. She didn’t really give a reason why she had this opinion, but I think she implied that I lacked the courage that she believed my favorite character possessed. Many people associate this character with bravery and heroism, but if you really analyze her, you will see that this character was written as a deeply troubled woman who only accidentally became a hero. So I decided to show this therapist just how brave and assertive I could be. After all, I have been fighting inner demons since childhood, so I must have some degree of courage. I quit therapy, telling her that I no longer needed her services because my mental state had suddenly improved. I think she knew I was lying. I don’t think she cared. I was just happy to be rid of her, and she was probably happy to be rid of me.

column1: Have you ever witnessed something you believed was paranormal activity?
column3: When I was in third grade there was a girl who sat directly in front of me in our classroom. She had long red hair, fine up in pigtails, lots of freckles and was super smart. We didn’t talk too much, I was a bit stand off ish , mostly because like every other girl except for my mother she had cooties, had to keep my distance. She was the smartest kid in our class and although I was a fairly good student I could always count on an unobstructed view of all the correct answers to any test by just peering over her shoulder. She tended to be absent a lot, I figured she didn’t need as much school as the rest of us because she was so smart. For Valentine’s Day we all exchanged Valentines. You know those cheap little paper ones you get in drug stores. Every one was required to have one for every member of the opposite gender, no hurt feelings that way. When it came time for her and I to swap Valentines I gave her my generic drug store 2 cent special with my name not so neatly scribbled on it. She gave me a beautiful, hand made card , white lace ribbon glued to it , hand drawn flowers and lots of red hearts with a personalized sentence “ I love you very much Joe” I felt embarrassed as my card was so inadequate by comparison but also because the rest of the cards she handed out were of the generic dime store variety. The inevitable Joe and Mary sitting in a tree song started up from the peanut gallery. She didn’t seem to mind and just smiled at me. I thanked her profusely and told her how beautiful the card was . I was fond of her as much as any third grade boy is. That’s not much but at least my parents taught me civility and to consider peoples feelings and I did thank her very much for all the time and thought she had spent. We became friendlier to one another after that. I knew deep down that cooties was only a made up thing and we usually had a bit of conversation before class started at the beginning of the day . She was absent a lot though, I never thought to ask her why. It was one of the final days of school when the principal and the school nurse came in the room and my teacher told us the principal had a special announcement to make to us. He told us Mary had died. He went on to tell us that she died of a disease called leukemia. He told us a bit about her, things I already knew, that she was smart and kind . He told us about her family then asked us if we had any questions. There were a couple of questions but after that they left and the school day resumed. We were all left to navigate our feelings on the subject of death to ourselves. No grief counselors in the 1960’s. It was a very warm day, no air conditioning in our room but a door open to the outside was propped open and the door to the hallway was closed to contain the noise I suppose. There was one large oscillating fan in the front corner and we would wait for it’s brief pass while suffering through a seeming endless school day. When the principal left the door to the hallway did not quite latch and it slowly creaked open and closed to whatever wind current there was. It was a while after he left that a large gust of wind blew the door wide open and then a sudden shift of the wind slammed it shut . It startled most of us wide awake and the classroom wise guy did not skip a beat and said . “ maybe it was Mary” kids are cruel . We were well behaved enough that most did not laugh.For my part I just stared at the empty seat in front of me and felt sad. That’s not the paranormal part. Fast forward 9 years . High school graduation. After graduation I went to a graduation party on the other side of town . I had a little motorcycle and a learners permit which allowed me to ride it up to midnight. I was a well behaved kid, responsible, but that night I made many mistakes. I was drinking beer , too many and somehow had found a girl who enjoyed French kissing which was not my usual experience with girls at that stage of my life . Under age drinking. I totally lost track of time as I experienced the thrill of kissing and struggling to achieve 2nd base. I looked at my watch 1 am. I was in a world of trouble. My father was very strict , my eldest brother had come home ten minutes late from a party and the resulting punishment was a long and loud tirade, a confiscation of his stereo and a boot in his butt. I was too young and stupid to realize I was also kind of drunk. I needed to get home, things would only get worse the later it became. This was the seventies, no cell phones . My father trusted my judgment enough to allow me to buy a motorcycle, this was a huge breach of trust and I just knew my motorcycle would be confiscated and I would need to endure a loud and long scolding and a swift kick in the butt for good measure. I decided to take the backroads home as my chances of encountering a police officer were much less that way. I was speeding home, half drunk on curvy back roads. I knew these roads well but it was pitch black and no streetlights on these back roads. There was a steep s turn coming up. I slowed to 40 though the sign said 25. Suddenly to my left a woman in a long white gown stood by the edge of the road . The sight startled me and I slowed way down just as a dog came bounding out of a driveway. I put my foot out instinctively and it caught the dog sending it yipping away in pain. This all happened in a couple of seconds. I slowed to a stop looked back in my rear view mirror , the lady just stood there. I turned my head back , the lady had long red hair, freckles. She smiled, turned and left walking in to the thick woods which swallowed her from my vision in a few seconds. It was her. Mary. All grown up, beautiful, in a flowing white gown. If I had not been startled by her sudden appearance at the side of the road I would have taken that curve at 40, the dog would have caused me to lose control and a real good chance I would have died that night. I slowed down the rest of the ride, turned the engine off and coasted up our driveway, quiet as a mouse. Didn’t put the bike in the garage as it appeared all was quiet and I was hoping dad had fallen asleep. He had. He never realized I came in late . I am 100 % certain it was Mary, her face, long red hair, freckles. I was full of goosebumps. Years later, visiting my parents grave I meandered around the small town cemetery. Different names from my youth came to me as I found their final resting spots. Neighbors, teachers, a few of my peers, my childhood Dr. I sat on a bench beneath a large tree contemplating life, the hour glass of our lives constantly draining away. Someday I would be here , perhaps my children too but hopefully not before me . I got up from the bench and realized only then that it had been erected in Mary’s honor, her parents gravestone overlooked it. So sad to die so young but I truly believe she was, is my guardian angel keeping me safe .
column9: What a beautiful story. RIP Mary.

column1: What did Harry Patch do in WWI?
column3: INTRODUCTION Harry Patch was a man from Combe Down in the county of Somerset as well as the last verifiable man living anywhere on earth to have had firsthand experience of fighting in the trenches of the First World War. Born in 1898, Harry Patch was the youngest of three brothers, who were named George and William respectively. Harry Patch was born as Henry John, and he did not adopt the name for which he is now most well known until later in his life. The area that Harry lived in had a lot of Welsh heritage, and the name Combe Down is a rough translation of valley hill in that language. Unlike most people who fought in the war, Harry was conscripted, and he had no intention of ever setting foot in a trench until he was forced to leave his schooling behind. Prior to being enlisted into the army, Harry had been occupied with trying to become a plumber. His father and grandfather had both worked within the carpentry and house building industry, and as a way to keep up with tradition, all three brothers took a different trade related to housing.According to Harry, his great grandfather — whom he never met — was a coffin maker known for making daring and wild pranks on the towns people for his own amusement. For that, Harry remarked in an interview shortly before his death that not living to know his great grandfather as he was reputed to be was one of his “biggest regrets.” Nonetheless, little doubt can be cast regarding the biggest regret in Harry’s life, and it was not one which he had wanted to do. Being drafted into the First World War, Harry would lose most of his friends — from peacetime and wartime alike — alongside several of his family members; including his cousin Fred, who lived just down the street from his old house. It is therefore not surprising that rather than referring to the war as one of “duty” as many soldiers had done: Harry Patch would, until the end of his days, insist that war in general is nothing more than legal murder.EARLY LIFE Harry Patch was born on June 17, 1898 in Combe Down where he would spend his entire childhood as well as his immediate years after the war. At the time that Harry was growing up, the area he had been residing in was fairly rural, and he remembers that one of his most common forms of travel — other than walking — was by taking the canoe and paddling down the nearby river with his friends. One of his favourite hobbies as a child was to try and sneak into his parents’ vegetable garden and snatch some vegetables and even some nearby fruit as some sort of Spartan-like challenge. His reward being that if he was able to do so uncaught, he would be able to eat them. If not, he knew his father would come quickly and give him a “good kicking” for what he considered a punishment for getting caught. When he was asked in an interview what he thought about the sinking of the Titanic when it first happened, Harry admitted that he does not recall where he was or how he initially reacted. He was also forthcoming in acknowledging that in Somerset, boys such as himself were far more interested in trains than ships. Harry’s property was also apparently the site of a major wasp infestation — and many of the local swine were stung by them during the course of the summer of 1908 — and his parents had tasked him with disposing of them. He obliged, and a nearby shop owner gave him a cube of cyanide and instructed him on how to use it.Needless to say, Harry did not wear any protective gear when doing this, as he was never told about the dangers of using cyanide chemicals at close range. However, Harry did state very clearly that despite being in a field full of wasp and spraying away, he was never once stung by any of them. The wasp — according to his own words — would literally react in pain and drop in midair from being gassed. Harry admitted that he was fascinated and even intrigued by how quickly this could be done. A few years later, with the outbreak of the First World War, Harry would find himself becoming the wasp as he and many of his comrades were exposed to gas attacks; many of whom were blinded for life or killed.THE WAR YEARS Harry had always maintained until his dying day that the idea of the whole country going “mad” at the outbreak of the war is a myth. According to him, few people he knew personally had even thought about signing up during the early months of the war. One of those he did know, however, was his older brother, George, who was rejected from serving due to being considered physically unfit. As a result, Harry’s older brother would never see service during the war, though he and his brother, as well as his cousin Fred — who was killed in the war and his body never recovered — would find themselves fighting in various roles throughout, with Harry’s unit being specialised to do something that Harry never thought he could do: kill. He also stated that he had never even heard of the concept of the White Feather until after the war. Harry never felt pressured to go to war from anybody he knew personally, and he was satisfied with staying home to apprentice in becoming a plumber.In 1916, however, this all changed when Harry was called up for service during the midst of Britain’s Conscription Crisis. By May of 1917, Harry was in France, having been brought over by ship, where he and his mates slept on deck; a combination of overcrowding as well as the fear of torpedo attacks being factors that played on their minds.Above: Harry Patch Interviewed At Home Harry arrived in the trenches in late June of 1917 with sixteen other conscripted men and three officers. Before his arrival in France, Harry had been promoted to lance corporal, only to lose that rank when he allegedly confronted and fought a thief over his boots and never regained his rank. When justifying his confrontation with the alleged thief, Harry said that he could have done two things: walk away, or fight. And since he had been specifically conscripted to fight for his country, Harry chose the latter. The 7th Battalion of the Duke of Cornwall’s Light Infantry — the battalion had been assigned to — had sustained so many casualties during his time on the front that by July, nearly two hundred new recruits had been attached to the battalion in order to replenish the ranks.He had never wanted to be in this battalion, as he felt that he would have been more at home being from a battalion based in Somerset. Being a conscript and not a volunteer, Harry said that he lost out on such perks and was therefore not given a choice as to where he would end up. Prior to being sent to the front, Harry was assigned as a member of the Lewis Gun team and given an LG symbol on his uniform after Harry mentioned to an officer that he had some experience with assembling and using a machine gun.TEAM OF FOUR A member of the team that Harry was being sent to had recently been killed and a new replacement was needed. Harry would be chosen for it, and he was regarded by the other three men — of whom Bob Haynes was the leader — as the “new guy” and thus Harry had to prove himself to them. Believing that they would all perish at some point, Harry and his friends used to tell each other secrets about themselves that they wouldn’t even reveal to their closest family members. Harry’s squad consisted of himself and three other men, and one of the “codes” that his team adopted was that they were not to kill anyone except under circumstances where it could not reasonably be avoided. Whenever a battle was ongoing, they agreed to aim for the arms or legs as opposed to the torso or head. That way they could somewhat live with themselves afterwards with the thought that they did not sought out to kill anyone in particular.Above: Scene From The 1930 Movie All Quiet On The Western Front Depicting A German Machine Gun Team Mowing Down British And French Soldiers On one occasion, Harry was challenged with this code when his squad happened to be camped out in No Man’s Land, and a daring German soldier decided to play a gutsy move by charging at them with his bayonet. The machine gun had jammed, and it is likely that a violent melee would have ensued if not for Harry’s quick thinking. Taking out his Mosley pistol which had been assigned to him upon joining the Lewis Gun team, Harry fired his clip at the legs of the oncoming German and injured him. Cusses and threats flowed out of the mouth of the German soldier as he laid injured and crippled before Harry and his team. Even after stretcher bearers came to take him away, Harry could hear the German yelling words at him that Harry — unsurprisingly — could not understand. For this, Harry felt somewhat betrayed, as he thought that — if anything — the German should have been grateful for “giving him life.” He never found out who the German was that he shot, and in his twilight years he admitted to being glad that this incident had occurred earlier in the war when Harry’s “rage” had not yet peaked; otherwise, he believes he would have shot and killed the German in a heartbeat.AUGUST 16, 1917 This day was no doubt Harry’s second most memorable day of the war. It was also one of the bloodiest in his time on the front, when his battalion alone suffered hundreds of casualties in a span of only a few hours. As expected, Harry’s team were the main instrument in covering advances and retreats as their machine gun sprayed hundreds of bullets across the field every minute. Despite being the least experienced on his team, Harry was sometimes assigned to pull the trigger because of his claimed ability of being a “natural” when it came to aiming.Fortunately for Harry, he and his mates were able to survive the fighting, and they were relieved from trench duty for a month so that they could recuperate their losses. Nearly half their battalion had been killed or wounded in a single day, and Harry was fortunate — or unfortunate, as fate would have it — to be one of those who survived the battle relatively unscathed. Most machine gunners fought to the death, because they knew their chances of being taken prisoner was very unlikely. Lewis Gun teams were hated by the Germans as much as German machine gun teams were by the British. Harry was quoted in an interview as saying: “If you were captured, they would line you up, and shoot you with your own gun.”HARRY’S LOSSES Harry lost nearly all of his childhood friends in the war. He even recalled one canoe trip he had had in the summer of 1914 when he went canoeing with several of his friends where they played pranks with one another. He later pointed out that all of those people on the canoe trip died during the war, except for one other person who had survived, only to succumb a year later to disease while being posted in India before he could be returned home. Some of those on the Menin Gate and Thiepval Memorial include Harry’s cousin Fred; his childhood friends — Harold Chivers and Lionel Morris amongst them; the husband of his future sister in law; the former fiancee of his first wife — Ada Billington; and his entire squad team of five men — except for Bob Haynes — who were believed to have been killed by a shell at 10:30 PM on September 22, 1917, even though the war diaries suggest that the real date could have been September 23rd.When the shell that killed his three friends ignited, Harry was knocked out cold and later said he barely remembered the incident itself. He was brought to a military hospital where a two inch piece of metal was surgically removed from his leg. The surgeon offered to give it to Harry as a souvenir, but Harry declined, stating that he “already had it long enough.” Harry’s wound would continue to ache on and off for the rest of his life. Decades later, another doctor who was examining Harry told him that had the metal gone a quarter of an inch deeper, he would have bled to death before help arrived.MEETING NEW FRIENDS Shortly after Harry was taken to a field hospital, he met an Australian whom he knew most as ‘Digger.’ Harry reported that Digger was a horseman who was also known to enjoy playing pranks on others for his own amusement. One night, they were watching a silent film called The Grey Ghost and Digger had brought in a hammer. As soon as the image on the screen struck an object, Digger whacked the hammer so hard that it made a booming noise and everyone in the audience freaked out, with several of them ducking in reaction. Harry never got to see the end of the film, as both he and Digger were removed from the audience after this stunt. However, Harry later joked that he still found it worth it to be “hearing the first sound on film, ever.”Above: 1927 Film The Jazz Singer Was The First Film With Synchronized Dialogue Digger had tried to press Harry to come with him to Australia so that they could start their own farming business together. However, Harry felt too attached to his native Somerset, so he politely declined the offer, telling Digger that “I am a plumber, not a horseman.” Eventually, Digger was sent back to Australia after he was deemed “well enough” by a nurse, after he had tried to play a prank on one who kept waking him up, due to Digger suffering from what was likely bruxism.One night, Digger tied a rope around his finger with an object hanging over the ceiling with the intention that he would let it fall on the nurse and scare her. He intentionally made some grinding noises in anticipation that she would come barging in again. Rather than getting the nurse, however, he got the Head Lady of the Hospital who just happened to be coming in to check on him. After Digger was sent back to Australia, Harry and Digger corresponded for some years by letter. Much to Harry’s regret, however, they never met physically met up with each other ever again, and no photograph of the two was ever taken.NIGHT AT THE MOVIES Harry also met two other friends whom he claims had a mindset similar to Digger in playing pranks. On one particular occasion, one of them told Harry and his other friend that someone must have stolen one of their tickets, as there were only two of them left. He declared that all three of them would need to pull straws to see who would get shorted. As it turns out, the second friend was given the short straw, and he was told he would have to jump inside the suitcase that they had with them. His friend told the other guy he was “small enough” to fit in, and that they would get him inside that way. Once they got to the ticket booth, however, the friend with the tickets showed the employee three tickets and unzipped the bag to show his hiding friend. The other friend explained that he was “shellshocked” and therefore a little shy of being around other people.Soon after, a local military officer found out about the incident and questioned them on them being there in the first place. The officer refused to believe that they were recuperating from their wounds and therefore being given sick leave. As a result, the officer kicked them out of the theatre and ordered them back to their unit to be sent back to the front. While leaving the theatre, Harry accidentally bumped into a woman who was going out with a friend of hers. It turned out that they were heading for the same bus stop, so they walked there together. The woman would turn out to be Harry’s first wife, Ada Billington.Before Harry had departed to the Isle of Wight in preparation for his second tour on the front, he asked her to marry him. Ada declined. He later found out that it was because in 1914, Ada had been engaged to another man named Harold Thomas, who had been killed in action shortly afterwards. Ada’s sister had also been married and impregnated to a man who was also killed in action, and his body never found. Furthermore, her brother Bill had lost a leg during the war and moved to Chicago upon being discharged. Silently, her condition was set: she would only marry Harry after the war when she knew that he wouldn’t be killed.ARMISTICE DAY AND ITS AFTERMATH Harry had been in training on the Isle of Wight on November 11, 1918 when rumours circulated that an armistice was now imminent. If a flare went up, it would mean that the armistice had been signed and that the war was now over. Shortly after 11 AM, the flare did go up, and the men celebrated. An officer ordered them to fire their bullets “out to sea” so that they wouldn’t have to walk back to camp with them. One soldier standing beside Harry had a very different plan. Rather than shooting the bullets into the sea, he pointed his rifle across Harry’s rifle and began shooting away. Harry then yelled “what the hell are you shooting at?”He instantly got his answer, as the soldier was emptying his bullets into the nearby cabin where a whole bunch of officers and drill sergeants were stationed. Everyone in that cabin was forced to duck and cover in confusion as bullets shattered the windows and peppered the floor around them with gunpowder. Needless to say, Harry thought that he would finally be able to leave the army and return back to civilian life and resume his career as a plumber. Instead, he found himself still in the military for several months being forced to do saluting and parade marches from an officer who was almost universally hated by everyone. The officer in question was allegedly known to take out his pistol and place a lock on the safety and begin clicking with the threat that he would shoot them all for insubordination.One day, Harry was working in the kitchen when the officer did this again to a more bad tempered man in the unit. He walked to his tent and told several others what had happened. They all returned with rifles to the officer’s tent, and upon opening it, they pointed the rifle at his face and told the officer to “try his luck again.” Harry was informed as to what was happening, and he decided to join the protest by bringing his own rifle and imitating the other men who had their rifles drawn at the head of their officer. A nearby brigadier general was told what had happened, and Harry’s unit was placed into their barracks until the brigadier could arrive and find out what had happened. The officer was questioned first in private with the brigadier, before the men — Harry included — could be placed behind a screen and be given anonymity while expressing their grief against the officer in charge of the unit. The brigadier accepted the situation, and he had the officer transferred to a new unit and declined to reprimand Harry and his men any further.CIVILIAN LIFE Before Harry got his discharge, one of his senior officers tried to persuade Harry by reenlisting in the military, due to his ability to dismantle, build and aim a machine gun with such efficiency. When Harry made it clear he had no intention of remaining in the military, the officer remarked by saying that “it was a shame.” One of Harry’s most memorable days working as a plumber was when he was sent to the residence of a wealthy woman — that Harry described as being “like Queen Victoria” — who had him come before her in a majestic room full of decorations, surrounded by her butler, dogs and paintings. She told Harry that a thousand gallons of water had gone missing without explanation, and that she wanted him to figure out the cause behind it.The butler brought him to the water tower with the implication that there must be a leak, but Harry knew that this couldn’t be the cause, because otherwise the room “would be flooded and noticeable.” Eventually, the butler confessed that the real cause was that one of the maids had accidentally left the tub running because she was late for a date, and the butler had decided to cover it up by convincing the lady that it must have been a leak. Harry still decided to charge the lady for the bill for coming over, but he also agreed to not let her know what the real reason behind it was, as requested from the butler.BUILDING OF WILLS MEMORIAL TOWER Harry was one of thousands of men selected during the post-war years to help in the completion of the Wills Memorial Tower, which had been under construction since 1915. Being an expert in plumbing, Harry’s main job was to help in ensuring that the pipes were functioning and to look for any errors made by the carpenters in ensuring that they did not cause any leaks. One of their employers was apparently very cheap and he used to cut corners and even threaten to deduct Harry and his employers of their salaries if they did not agree to work overtime. As a way to keep that employer on his toes, some of the men used to intentionally let the ropes go loose while the employer was coming up the shaft on the side of the tower and let it fall for several storeys with the employer clinging for life before grabbing hold again as a warning.Upon completion of the tower in 1925, Harry and one of his coworkers whom he had befriended decided to place a penny in one of the cornerstones before sealing it off. Harry maintained that the penny was still there, though he admitted that their initials that they had used to mark their pennies were “probably long gone.”On June 9, 1925, Harry was selected to attend the opening ceremony with King George V present to give a speech for the unveiling of the memorial. In later years, Harry would admit that the ceremony did not “interest” him, as he barely had any firsthand memories of actually being there, despite being only a matter of feet away from the monarch.HARRY’S FAMILY Harry had two sons: Dennis and Roy. Both of them would serve and survive the Second World War. However, one of his nephews, Bob, who was the son of his older brother George, was killed in an aviation accident. At the funeral, George’s wife Lillian became so distraught at seeing her son in a coffin that she had a heart attack and died soon afterwards. Bob’s friend Hughes, whom he had encountered in Canada while training to become a pilot, had died in a similar accident only five months earlier. Hughes had been engaged to Harry’s niece May, who would not marry until she was fifty-eight and never had any offspring of her own.FROM PLUMBER TO FIREMAN Quite ironically, Harry’s career path changed in the war from one where he fought water to one where he fought fire with water. Due to being a plumber, he knew where all the quarries and pumps throughout the City of Bath were located, as well as the different water pressured that would be seen as regarded as an asset to the fire services. Even Harry’s father, who was now over eighty years of age had decided to rejoin the forces as a fire watchman to help Harry’s unit know where the fires were located.After the British had bombed the German cities of Rostock and Lubeck to the ground, Hitler had vowed to avenge their destruction by targeting British cities in retaliation. At first, major cities such as London were the main targets, but that was quickly halted once it became apparent that London was far better fortified against air attacks than it had been two years earlier during Operation Sealion.Instead, Bath — where Harry was stationed — became the main focus of the German raids of April 1942 because it was one of the biggest cities in England that was also not adequately prepared for a full Luftwaffe attack. On one particular night, Harry’s fireman unit was targeted by a German bomber that was also flying down towards them repeatedly for hours on end, spraying bullets in their direction. Some of them landed so close that Harry felt the debris flying in his face. Later on, Harry would state that he wished he still had his Lewis Gun with him, because he claimed that the bomber was flying so low over their heads that he was confident that he could have personally shot the plane down himself if he had one in his possession.Even though Harry’s main job during the war years was to work as a fireman — for which he said that during one raid, Woodsworth Street was levelled and he had to help in picking up the bodies and remnants of dozens of victims — he was still assigned to work as a plumber when no fires or threats of German air raids were reported. He was one of the few men who knew about PLUTO, which was a pipe that was attached to the ocean in order to give citizens and the military alike an endless supply of water in the event that the ordinary pipes were knocked out by a subsequent air raid.HARRY ON THE ARRIVING AMERICANS Harry claimed he was puzzled at the idea of seeing American soldiers — whites and blacks — being so segregated from one another to the point where most of them would not even converse with one another. He also later remarked that he thought that Black GIs were much more pleasant to get along with, as he considered black American soldiers to be better behaved than the white ones. On one occasion, Harry was invited to a wedding of an American soldier who had invited several black American soldiers to attend. Some of the white Americans became disenchanted about this and resorted to rioting in front of the congregation.A nearby police officer, who happened to be a boxer in civilian life but had joined the police forces upon declaration of war — came into the room and confronted the rioting American soldiers. Harry said that at that point, the gang of soldiers attacked him, and the officer was able to put an end to this by “knocking six of them out and forcing the rest to sit down.” Being in the police forces was a job that Harry had mildly considered when he was initially turned down for plumbing, but was rejected from the police forces for being too short. He had tried to stand on his toes when getting his height checked, and the doctor saw through this and forced Harry to lean backwards so that he would not be able to deceive him.D-DAY On the night of June 5, 1944, Harry had a day off and he was going out of Bath to take a break. German air raids had more or less subsided, and he figured that he deserved to take the evening off. He had befriended many Canadian, British and American soldiers, as he was one of the men who had to fix the utilities in the camps. When Harry arrived back to one of the camps early on June 6, 1944, he was stunned at what he had seen. NOTHING! The camp — which he claimed had once been so filled with men that many of them had to sleep in regular nearby houses — was now completed deserted with not even a man in sight, other than himself.When he entered the mass halls, he saw some unfinished breakfasts from some of the soldiers who had been unable to complete their meals before departing for France. A few hours later, Harry found himself with a group of older men who were assigned to clean up the camps and start setting up some barbed wires for the anticipated German prisoners who would be arriving shortly. By sunset, the first batch of German prisoners had arrived in the camp, and more of them flooded in during the following days and weeks until the camps became so full that some of them were located to nearby farms and workshops to work in civilian jobs. Harry admitted that he never tried to befriend any of the German prisoners there, but he maintained that he still followed the policy of treating them the way he would want to be treated.END OF HOSTILITIES Just days before the Second World War came to end, Harry had resigned from the fire department, as he did not expect that his services would be needed any longer. He once again returned to his life as a plumber, though it was not long before Harry would suffer another set of losses to his life. His father died that Christmas at the age of eighty-two while his sons — particularly Dennis — became damaged from the war and became a drunkard. During his later years, when Ada died in 1976, Harry moved in with his older son. However, he soon realised that Dennis had become so increasingly violent and bad tempered with drinking rages, that his son even resorted to selling all of Harry’s belongings — including the medals Harry had received during the First World War — just so that he could continue going to the bar and drinking with his friends. Eventually, Harry remarried a woman named Jean and moved out of Dennis’s home. Harry claimed to have loved Jean, but also admitted that his main reason for agreeing to marry her was so that he could flee from his older son, who had become increasingly crippled — physically and mentally.Shortly afterwards, his son Dennis came to Harry’s residence to reveal a swollen leg. Harry had his son committed to a hospital, where the doctor told Harry he had sclerosis of the liver and that he would not live longer than two weeks. Ultimately, his son lived for only eight days after finding out, and his younger son Roy, disowned his father, because he believed that he was responsible for his brother’s death. Harry never saw his younger son again, who died of cancer in 2002. Additionally, most Harry’s remaining family also severed connections with him until 2003 when he was now 105 years old and it was revealed that he was now one of the few remaining veterans of the Great War. One of his nieces, who had ceased talking to Harry nearly thirty years earlier, decided to resume contact with Harry upon seeing his name on television and in the newspapers.TWILIGHT YEARS Harry reportedly remained active right into his later years in fighting for everything from confronting several prime ministers about pardoning the men shot at dawn, to petitioning the mayor to give pedestrians safer places to cross the street. He had also been a lifelong pipe smoker until he was sixty years old when he gave up smoking. He also gave up drinking alcohol at around this time, because he realised that alcohol had a negative impact on the outcome of his two sons — particularly Dennis — who effectively drank himself to death. As a result, whenever people donated him money to “have a drink for them” Harry would refuse and instead he would donate the money to charity or to the legion.Above: Harry Patch Funeral Before he died, Harry also told the story about how he and his older brother George spent many summers trying to find the location of a smuggler’s tunnel based on the novel written by Meades Falkner Moonfleet. Harry, being a plumber, as well as a self-described history and geology buff, was able to help his brother in trying to find the location, but to no avail. One day, however, his brother wrote to him and told him to come see him on the weekend. His brother brought Harry over to a cemetery situated on a hill and pointed out the different colour patch in the grass. They dug their way through there, and sure enough, there was a tunnel that was four feet deep and more than three feet wide, which Harry and his brother concluded amongst themselves was indeed the tunnel that Meades Falkner had talked about.HARRY BECOMES A SYMBOL OF THE WAR By January 1, 2000, Harry was one of 350 people listed as being a verified living First World War to have served in the British Army. This number continued to drop until January 1, 2005, when Harry found out that he was among only nine living British veterans that could still claim to have fought in the trenches. The other eight men were: Cecil Withers, Smiler Marshall, Alfred Anderson, Harold Lawton, William Elder, Alfred Finnigan, Charles Lloyd and George Rice. By the year’s end, however, Harry found himself ALONE, as all eight men mentioned above died that year, leaving Harry Patch the only known combat veteran of the Western Front to still be alive by 2006. During the late 1990’s, Harry had helped the University of Bath in locating some old underground quarries he had discovered some seventy years later as part of the university’s research and construction projects.This became the first time that Harry made the newspapers, and the title was OLD MAN LEADS THE WAY! In 1998, with the eightieth anniversary of the war coming to an end, Harry also celebrated his 100th birthday with some friends and a few family members still in touch with him. It was also then that more news reporters took an interest in his First World War status, and it was also then that Harry began to talk more about the war than he ever did previously. Harry claimed he never once spoke about the war to his first wife Ada, despite being married for more than fifty-seven years before her death in 1976. When Harry’s second wife Jean died, he eventually found himself being cared for by some neighbours: Fred and Betty Isaacs. Fred died at the age of ninety-three, but he made a half-joke to Harry, asking if he would take care of his wife in the event he outlived him.Above: Harry Patch And Tony Blair Harry agreed, though he also admitted that he did not anticipate living as long as he did.
