column1: Do you feel sorry for Azula in The last Airbender?
column3: I just finished my second rewatch of the show, and I’ve read the comics. So spoiler alert, if anyone reading this cares. And this answer will be long, because while I understand that the question has a one word answer, I think the debate surrounding it is a testament to what a well-written show it is in the first place. If you hate long answers, skip this one. One of the central themes in Avatar is how every person is capable of great good and great evil. Aang says these words to Toph in “The Avatar and the Firelord”: Roku was just as much Fire Nation as Sozin was, right? If anything, their story proves anyone's capable of great good and great evil. Everyone, even the Firelord and the Fire Nation, has to be treated like they're worth giving a chance.The show goes out of its way to prove this. We see firsthand the negative impacts war has on everyone involved. The kid that Zuko helps in “Zuko Alone” loves Zuko, telling him that he reminds him of his older brother who left to fight in the war. When Zuko reveals his identity after saving the kid and his family, in a split second the child is repulsed. The kid is a part of a wider “machine”, and reacts based on how he has been conditioned. In that moment, what the war has done to this kid and his family, what the Fire Nation symbolizes for the entire world, what his experiences and upbringing have taught him — that determines his response. We see young Roku and young Sozin as kids goofing off on the royal palace grounds. Then we see how the Fire Nation’s once innocuous prosperity and prowess corrupts Sozin’s mind, causing him to toe the line between vitality and destruction, much like the element of fire itself. Culminating in him leaving his own former best friend to die, and for him to give in to this power trip, commit genocide, and start a reign of terror.Fast forward 100 years. We see innocent Fire Nation kids at school, not knowing what dancing is but reciting a pledge of allegiance to the Fire Lord by heart. We see Ty Lee, a bubby “villain” who could easily be one of the heroes. We see Fire Nation prison workers laughing and joking during break, making the most of their lives. Humanizing the enemy is one of the things that makes the show, and brings its central conflict to a level that we can empathize with despite it being a fictional universe. Because our identities are shaped by our environment, our upbringing, and the ideologies we are surrounded by. In real life, though we love to blame our problems on one human, that is almost never the case. Things are always more deeply rooted than that. And the show’s deliberate, rare inclusions of the “big bad”, Ozai, served to paint him as a living representation of his ancestors’ legacy and the bloodthirstiness which came with it, rather than a random evil guy who just wanted to kill everyone. Just like in real life, problems are never completely solved fighting “an evil big bad guy.” Humans are a product of nature and nurture and at its very core, the conflicts between the expectations the world places on us and our personal values is what drives the show. We see this in Katara, whose life and environment from childhood caused a deep, deep dislike of the Fire Nation. She saw her own mother’s life taken, in her stead, by a Fire Nation soldier. She takes a chance and trusts Zuko in the Season 2 finale, about to even heal his scar using the Spirit water, and is betrayed again. She has immense hate in The Southern Raiders, going all out with her bloodbending, about to kill the man who killed her mother. And she doesn’t. It’s a central conflict she is facing, between her personal emotions of hatred and understanding that Yon Rha, the soldier, is just a cog in the machine. That killing him, an individual, does no good, not her for her, not for anyone involved. We then have Zuko, who fought his nature vs. nurture battle over the course of three seasons. He is an angry, naive teen who believes in the Fire Nation’s inherent superiority because of how he has been brought up and conditioned. He barges into the Southern Water Tribe and burns down Kyoshi Island. He relentlessly pursues the Avatar, because his environment has taught him that his honor lies in his father’s opinion and estimation of him. His father, of course, has always looked down upon him because he doesn’t fit his role in this machine, that of the future Fire Lord, quite right. He isn’t naturally talented, or cunning, or authoritative, or powerful.His mother takes extra efforts to shower him with kindness because of this. Ursa, too, understands the machine and on some level, sees through it. She was forced into an abusive marriage because it was her role — what else could she do? She is innately kindhearted, but is rendered powerless in her situation in an abusive marriage to a power-hungry man. And when she finally breaks free of it once and for all, in an attempt to protect her son, she is banished. Leaving Zuko and Azula with no one else who doesn’t subscribe to the toxic mentality of the war. Zuko grows up with an abusive father, always feeling that he “isn’t enough” Despite this, Season 1 Zuko still feels he deserves respect, and commands it from those around him, because of his royal status. The side of him which values kindness, in his nature, is not important because he needs to play his part. He is forced into the machine, even though he doesn’t quite fit — and his uncle sees it. Zuko is banished, and his time away from the totalitarian, toxic regime is what finally opens his eyes to what a cog in the machine he has been this entire time. How what he has been trained to value and be is antithetical to his personal beliefs, antithetical to his mother’s beliefs, antithetical to his uncle’s beliefs. And finally coming to terms with this, understanding that true strength lies in turning away from what has been prescribed for you if it goes against your core beliefs, is what ultimately pushes him to become a hero.Even Iroh, who was once a celebrated general who laid seige to the walled city of Ba Sing Se for 600 days, was not always the peaceful, tea-loving man we all know. Iroh was forced to come to terms with what he really valued by the death of his son. This loss puts him on the path to understanding what a cog in the machine he has been this whole time. He was accomplished, celebrated — and he played his part perfectly. And this was his downfall. And this is what causes him to re- evaluate what makes a person strong, and shift his priorities. He returned, to his father dead and his sister-in-law banished. He took his nephew, the only one he had a chance to change, under his wing. Hell, the show even makes a point to paint Ozai, an abuser, as a human being — just a deeply repulsive, jealous, and angry one. And we see a baby picture of the man who caused immense direct trauma to every member of his immediate family. Why go so far, especially in a kid’s show? Because the central trauma of it lies in how we, as humans, are just wheels in this machine. That we are born with a clean slate, and can become corrupted over time by listening to what we think the universe has prescribed to us without following our own inner conscience. And for Iroh, Zuko, Ozai, Ursa, Azula . . . this machine was a war, started 100 years ago by a man who didn’t even know of their existence. And because of one bad decision made by a flawed human, generations of people suffered. Now is where we get to Azula. She is the second child, a female, born into a patriarchal royal family. But apart from that, she fits the bill for an heir — perfectly. As a child, she is not shown to be blatantly “bad”. She is shown to be astute, calculating, and dominating. These traits are the seeds for her downfall. She is the child that Ozai wanted in Zuko, powerful, intelligent, and cunning. She is a perfect cog in the machine, and all her potentially harmful personality traits only make her an even better fit. So all there is left for her father to do is to fine tune her until she fits the machine perfectly. Her dominating personality? Encourage it and teach her that fear-mongering is the way to go. Her intelligence and ruthlessness? Hone it and use it in service of her nation. And why would she ever think otherwise? Why would she ever have a reason to question this destiny prescribed to her? She wouldn’t. Because as we see, people — children especially— are cogs in a machine. They believe what they are taught to believe. Unless there is a blatantly good reason for believing otherwise. The Fire Nation is the greatest civilization in the world. Your worth as a human being lies in how useful you are in your nation. Your worth in your father’s eyes lies in your firebending talent and your ruthlessness. Your father’s approval is what ultimately matters over all else. Both Zuko and Azula, as children, clearly buy into this mentality and believe in it. And because Azula has these qualities already, she fits right into the role prescribed for her, and has no reason to turn to her mother, her uncle, for guidance and support. Not to mention that even without explicit indoctrination by her father, Azula firsthand sees what weakness can do to a person, in the form of her parents’ abusive relationship and power dynamic.This is what Ozai is like, abusive (physically and emotionally) even before his children are born. And thus Ursa is forced into her new life. She has two kids, and makes the most of the situation by loving them both.Growing up, it’s clear that Azula is never close to their mother like Zuko is, but still craves parental affection. However, she never lets it bother her too much (on the outside) because she has the “love” of her father, who approves of her violent acts while her mother scolds her. She is conditioned to believe that to be loved is to be weak, and so she doesn’t need parental love. Although just like any child, she still craves it deep down. We can see that there’s a dangerous lack of coparenting in the way Zuko and Azula are raised by Ozai and Ursa. Each of their parents bring mixed messages to the table. For very young children, who aren’t exposed to morality beyond the teachings of their parents and immediate surroundings, this is a confusing environment. Kids gravitate towards the parent who provides them positive feedback, and naturally adopt that parent’s worldviews. It’s also worth mentioning that royal kids like Azula and Zuko are probably more “distanced” from other kids and influences due to their status. Pretty much everyone around them is “inferior” to them (in terms of class), and their opinions and worldviews on morality don’t hold as much weight. We see how this sequestered upbringing impacts Azula and Zuko’s social skills in the Beach — they aren’t able to interact with normal kids without their royal status, since they’re not used to dealing with “equals”, in an environment where they don’t automatically get whatever they ask for. So basically all the lessons on right and wrong, proper behavior, and values are left to Ozai and Ursa’s parenting. Azula’s ruthlessness, naturally dominating personality, and prodigious skill make it so her father takes interest in her from (though we didn’t see it on screen) a very early age. He trains her himself, and is clearly more involved with raising her than he is with Zuko. Because Ozai is the one in power of the family, having her father as the parent who prefers her benefits Azula. Having Ursa, who is the “weaker” parent in the family, benefits Zuko in the long run, but in childhood and adolescence he still feels the need to fit in with this dominant “machine”, represented by his father. To a child, having one parent who scolds you and one who approves of you is often enough to draw the conclusion of favoritism. Kids think in largely black-and-white terms, and do not naturally consider the reasoning behind behaviors unfavorable to them. This means that Azula probably intuits that her mother truly does love her (and that the reasoning behind the scolding is genuine love) but it is not something she consciously realizes until she is at her breaking point years later. As a child, she simply sees her father’s conditional approval as love, and uses that to fill the void of parental love. But what about Azula’s other traits? The ones that make her human; the ones that aren’t quite as useful to her being a cog in this machine? Her jealousy of her brother, firstborn male, who gets a cool dagger while she gets a weird doll? Capitalize on it, and teach her that anyone who values her weak brother is a weak fool and a traitor, and that this behavior is to be avoided at all costs. Her jealousy of her brother, who receives love from her mother while she gets a scolding? Teach her that her mother’s values and opinions don’t matter in a household where your worth in the machine is defined by your power and competence. Her need for parental affection and approval? Give it to her — when she performs her duties. As a result, whether she realizes it or not, she is emotionally neglected. Her father’s constant praise builds up a false narrative that she is defined by power and perfection, and as long as she has these, nothing else matters. This makes it harder for her mother to connect with her emotionally, so she is not able to form healthy relationships with anyone who truly loves her. Her self-image is constantly reinforced by a steady pole — her superiority over her brother. Her father plays to her ego while simultaneously degrading his son, a cruel move, but one which also directly reflects Sozin’s legacy.See how messed up this statement is for both of them. For Zuko it’s clearly heartbreaking — who says that to a child? And for Azula it insinuates that she “never needed that kind of luck” — meaning intervention from her mother. It insinuates that her mother is weak and that her love is something given to the weak. It’s no wonder that she’s taught to suppress her needs for true parental love. And being better than Zuko is what her father uses as her fuel. It eclipses any potential regret she could have about being a cruel child, about manipulating others, about being “unloved” by her mother. Because the only opinion that matters is her father’s, exemplified by his status as Fire Lord, years of abuse of those weaker than him, and propaganda. And it works perfectly, because she goes from being this little girl:to this. In the span of about three years.It gets to the point where she becomes so war-hardened, sitting in this sea of military men, watching her brother get burned, watching the scene with glee. She has now completely assimilated into the machine. She thrives. The seeds were sown a long, long time ago. When her father used her need for parental approval, her jealousy of the natural heir, her ruthlessness, her competitiveness, to teach her that weakness is the absolute worst thing a human can have. And that when someone is weak, they pay the price. We see how exactly the main characters’ environments have shaped them from childhood through adolescence. For Zuko, he internalizes the treatment of his father, accepts it as his fault, and works to gain Ozai’s approval because that’s what he’s taught to value and nothing has pointed him to believe otherwise until he is banished. For Toph, she harbors deep resentment against rules, support, and norms because of how sheltered her upbringing was, and nothing points her to believe otherwise until she realizes how she needs Team Avatar’s help and there is strength in numbers. For Sokka, he internalizes the gender norms of the water tribe, being the only male left who is deferred to for major decisions. This, combined with his insecurity about what makes him a man and living in the shadow of his father, instills in him chauvinistic, sexist beliefs — until he embarks on a journey where he is forced to see how truly strong women can be in the form of Suki, Toph, Azula, and even his own sister. For Azula, her environment from childhood through adolescence has turned her from a kid who plays around and teases her friends and brother into a war-hardened young woman. Her royal, sequestered status, propoganda, her father’s abuse of his family and Sozin’s culture of looking down on weakness shapes her mindset into something toxic and twisted. And nothing points her otherwise. Her mother’s fate, her brother’s fate, her uncle’s fate — this is what happens when you are disloyal. This is what happens when you think your personal values are more important than playing your part. Her mother is gone. Her brother and uncle are gone. For three years, she is isolated with her father above her, everyone else below her, with no true equals and no positive role models. Because the qualities that made them positive role models were what earned her father’s wrath in the first place. Her friends are certainly loyal to her and love her to an extent, but she holds them in a dangerous position constantly, with her manipulative nature and what she can do with her power left unsaid in their every interaction. Now there are zero distractions. She lives a one-track life, perfecting herself as a cog in this machine. One hair out of place is enough to send her down the same fate as her weak brother. So she becomes a ruthless perfectionist. She performs her role in the machine perfectly, suppressing emotions, in a way using her perfectionism to compensate for love, which she never understood. Learning to hone the innocuous duplicitousness she had as a child into manipulation.She is never forced to look beyond the machine. Because she always fit perfectly. She has her father’s love. Intelligence, charisma, perfection, talent, and power. There was never a moment where she had to take a step back, like her mother did, like her brother and uncle did, because the machine served her perfectly. And the moments where she faltered? Where she thought maybe, just maybe, things might be wrong?We see Azula in the Beach, faced with the reality that outside of fulfilling her role as the cog in the machine, she has complete inadeptness in social situations. We see what happened to a child growing up isolated, in the royal family of a genocidal tyrant, only receiving positive feedback when she displays power and domination. She cannot socially function otherwise. She even admits to feeling hurt that her mother didn’t love her as much as Zuko. But does this matter in the end? No. Because though she knows she is a monster, she plays her role perfectly. She is better than Zuko, because the metric their father uses to define “better” is the most important in the world. She has witnessed this from childhood, living in an abusive household and seeing the impacts that weakness has on a person. Banishment, disfigurement, dishonor.Finally, she is betrayed by her two closest friends. And for Zuko, the one who held up her fragile self-image all these years, the example of weakness and failure. Zuko, the example of who she would become if she failed to meet her father’s expectations. He starts to gain friends. Starts to gain the loyalty of her former allies. Forges his own path in life, and goes from being dishonored to becoming redeemed. So what? Friends, trust, and loyalty are for fools anyways. It’s not like these things help her perform her role in the machine. Fear is the only reliable way. The fuel that kept her going, the feeling of superiority nurtured by jealousy and hatred, and the false premise she has constructed around herself, is called into question. Somewhere deep down, because she is very much still an impressionable child — her friends’ betrayal hurts her. So much so that she latches on to the only thing she has left for sure — her father. Her father, who provided her positive words when her mother scolded her. Her father, who told her she was born lucky. Her father, who gave her everything she wanted. And he discards her. “You can’t treat me like this! You can’t treat me like Zuko!” She recoils when he turns, afraid of facing his wrath, like Zuko and her mother did, for speaking out. In this moment, it’s not the prodigious, cool, collected firebender. It’s not the 14-year-old princess who conquered Ba Sing Se, doing what none of her ancestors could do, in a bloodless coup. It’s not the ruthless fighter who killed the Avatar. It’s a petulant cry, from a teenage girl who needs her father’s approval when all else fails. He tosses her a consolation prize to shut her up, and announces that he will become Supreme Ruler of the World. And leaves. Everything fueling her to perform her role, as a cog in the machine, screeches to a halt. Is she really better than her brother? Is the whole premise her father fed her to turn her into this monster even true? Was being this monster worth it, even if it meant losing all her friends? She is vulnerable.And the final straw, her most unresolved wound, surfaces.The one person to whom, being a perfect cog in the machine was not enough. “What are you doing here? You think I’m a monster.” “I think you’re confused. Your whole life, you’ve used fear to control people.” Everything her mother represented never mattered. Because she performed her role perfectly. Her father, the one in power, was pleased with her. Her mother thinking she was monster was an unfortunate side effect, a pill she had to swallow . . . or was it? As an audience, we know it’s not Ursa saying these things. It’s Azula herself. Azula knows she uses fear to control people. She knows her mother loved her. She knows she is a monster — and she chooses to hold on to this monstrousness, afraid that there’s nothing else underneath it. Nothing else to define who she is when for so long, the machine decided for her.Losing everything and everyone in her life is what starts to stop the gears slowly. She is forced to step back. Forced to re-evaluate what makes Azula herself. This hallucination of “Ursa” shows that there is some part of Azula, deep down, who knows who she has become, and resents herself for falling so deeply into the machine. But she clings onto this monstruous image of herself. She desperately clings on to believing her mother thought she was a monster and that she loved Zuko more. Because this is an easier pill to swallow than the truth: that her mother saw through her. And that her attempts to discipline her came from unconditional love. That love is a better predictor and motivator than fear. That she is not better than Zuko. That she is just a cog in her father’s machine. And it wrecks her. Faced with no support system. No friends. No parents. No brother. No equal. By being the cog in the machine, by letting her father control her and manipulate her jealousy and prop up her self-image, she alienated everyone who could have cared about her. She has no one to share this grief with, and is forced to continue spinning, like a broken cog, because what else could she do? Get banished? Get disfigured?The most disturbing thing is that this is a child wearing armor, half sane. She’s breaking, fighting like a marionette caught between the last shred of her sanity and her father’s thirst for power. Because she is a part of the machine. And when faced with her brother, who has finally broken free of it, it’s yet another reminder. She’s desperately holding on to everything she has left of her fragile self-image. Mom’s gone. Dad’s gone. Friends gone. But what she does have left — her superiority over Zuzu. Maybe she can salvage that. So, fueled by anger and spite, she impulsively fights. And she seeks to kill. To destroy. All her life, she’s been taught that her worth is in her power, her skill, her perfection, and her ruthlessness. That friendship, trust, and love, are useless. But suddenly, these very things which didn’t matter anyways are ruining her life. Taking her friends. Making her weak. The show goes out of its way to show what a tragedy this fight is. The music is somber and the focus is on Zuko and Azula; their expressions, their movements, their visceral reactions.It shows Zuko’s steely resolve. The manic confusion, fear, and pain Azula experiences when her whole falsely constructed worldview is swept out from beneath her.And when she’s finally defeated, by someone who represents not only her inferior, weak brother, Zuko, but someone she’s taught to look down upon, someone whose trust was gained by her brother — she’s left in shambles. Everything she has been taught to value, everything she has worked so hard to avoid — the weakness of her mother, her brother, her uncle — comes back to bite her as she loses, pitifully sobbing.Some people say she’s crying just because she lost and can’t handle it. True, but why would someone cry so hard at losing? Because to her, she is now nothing. Saying that she was a sociopath, an evil monster, or born evil is disingenuous not only to the writing of her character, but to the message of the whole show. One of the major themes is finding your own destiny. All the main players in the show were able to do this by seeing past their prescribed roles as cogs in the machine, struggling, and ultimately emerging from the ashes. The problem with Azula is that she never had a reason to do this. She never had to struggle. She fit the machine perfectly. She never valued friends, a social life, a healthy relationship with those who loved her unconditionally. Because of years of abuse and manipulation, living in a toxic, war-hardened regime, and witnessing what weakness can do to a person. Her upbringing and environment taught her that what mattered more than following your inner conscience was being a perfect cog in the machine. And it ultimately broke her.
column9: This is an extremely well-written and eloquent explanation of Azula. Though as a person who had a disturbed, abusive sibling, I do see a little more of her early behavior as less naturally childhood lack of empathy and more an indication that she does have deep-seated psychological issues naturally. Which certainly doesn’t preclude her living a healthy and productive life, or being happy. The idea that she was born with a higher than average lack of empathy (since empathy is both an innate and a learned behavior) does not make her a bad person. Even with in-born mental illnesses, children who show traits of being disturbed can benefit very much from consistent intervention, which Azula definitely didn’t have access to. To me, she helps model the social aspect of disability: her lack of empathy, sadism, manipulativeness, bursts of anger, and obsessive perfectionism suggest that she has a personality disorder of some sort, but in the environment where she is raised, this disorder is celebrated. Therefore, no disability. When things change towards being more human rights-based, suddenly she is treated as completely disabled - she is locked up and heavily restrained as a danger to others and possibly herself. She is exactly the same person as she was before, just with an added traumatic experience that counseling should have been able to help her with. It’s really too bad that therapists don’t seem to exist in the Avatar Universe. A lot of characters could really use them.

column1: How does it feel when all of your family members die at once in an accident?
column3: I am writing about this for the first time on social media as I am going through a lot of revelations about how I navigate life lately . At work , Abd in my personal life , especially when it comes to matters of the heart . I came on here to connect and relate , and find answers . my entire family ( parents and two younger siblings ) and I were in a deadly car crash when I was 10 . I survived , my dad and siblings were killed instantly, my mom in a coma for 2 years and then passed away as well ( I was not allowed to see her during that time even though it was my biggest wish ) . After that I was raised by my dads sister ( married with a child my age ) who , considering her own personality, own childhood trauma and her difficulty dealing with her own grief for my dad , really added to my struggle and put me through hell in a lot of ways . Nothing physical but mostly emotional abuse . I now realize she probably was just doing the best of her capacity, but it really affected my self-esteem, the way I relate to others, how of a people pleaser I became, how my attachment style turned to become anxious , how I have guilt, feelings of not being good enough, needing constant reassuring feeling I’m being punished , being worried I ll get rejected if I’m not what people expect from me , that I need to suffer ti feel alive , that in a burden … etc….. now as an self-sufficient adult that besides all this still has a enormous amount of love for life , I always find myself in reoccurring situations because of the trauma of loss, shock, unpredictability, the connection of - I need to please in order to be loved / accepted . when I woke up in the hospital stranded and immobilized on my bed ( several fractures, smashed organs etc ) and I was told everyone was gone …. The worse feeling of helplessness, powerlessness, deep pain in my soul that my family would never come back took over me. As an adult I really struggle with loss . It used to be so bad that even when I was just loosing something material, I’d feel it through my core because I would be taken back from that first trauma. Same thing in romantic relationships… also at this age of 10, even though I had had a loving childhood so far with loving parents , I really struggle now with my sense of identity . And because I felt guilty and punished by the all thing , everything I thought I knew and was , I questioned . I have been on a survival mode all these years ( in 49) even though I put my heart and soul fully in everything I do . I live and love deeply . Extremely sensitive to our world and everything around . Extremely empathetic. I attract wounded souls , narcissistic personalities ( especially work related ) but also beautiful humans and I am so grateful . It is just really hard to stand up for myself when ppl see through me and take advantage. Abd in the matter of the heart , I’m still trying to rebuild the family I lost , regain that sense of belonging but my fears of loss, abandonment and rejection, and not feeling in control really affect how I bond with people Abd who I fell for and it’s a constant struggle. As soon as I get attached, the wounded child wants to take over , cling for something that could make me feel safe . And I start abandoning myself in the process Abd worry I am going to loose what I have with a person . I’m trying to really go inward lately and recognize my patterns, my belief system and shift my perspective on everything . But I know for me it is a long life process and my pain will never go away , it’s all about living with it, making peace and self love at this point . And know that I am here for myself, and my family survives through me and my life journey . Love to all of you ! Don’t give up , life is a gift no matter how tough it is .

column1: How long can childhood trauma affect someone if not resolved? How do you resolve it?
column3: Childhood trauma can affect a person’s entire life if it is not dealt with. It would be more helpful if I knew what kind of trauma you are asking about. There are many forms of trauma and one answer does not answer or resolve all. I will address the trauma of losing a loved one as a child. In Feb. 1967 my maternal Grandma was sick. My Mom couldn’t stay with her because one of my brothers was in the hospital and she needed to be with him. An aunt was going to arrive on the midnight train but someone had to be there so I was elected. I didn’t mind, in fact I was happy about it. Spending time with Grandma any time was great. And I got the day off from school! She dosed for short spells on and off through the day. I brought her toast, hot tea and orange slices because that sounded good to her. I drug old photo albums into her room and sat on the floor beside her bed looking at pictures of people that I mostly didn’t recognize. When she was awake I’d ask her about the ones I had set aside and she told me about them. She talked about her growing up years in Missouri and becoming a school teacher when she was still in her teens. I had no idea she was sick enough to die. In November. she been sick with the flu and spent 3 weeks in the hospital. I was shocked seeing her when she finally got to come home. She’d lost at least 40 pounds and the contrast was devastating to me. My pleasingly plump, rosy cheeked Grandma was thin and her complexion was pale with an in oat of gray. But 3 months later she was looking much better. Our time together that day has always seemed extra sweet to me. My aunt arrived about 12:30 a.m. and quickly suggested I go to bed because I’d had a long day. I kissed Grandma goodnight, she said “I love you honey,” and I went to lie down. But I couldn’t sleep. I could hear the soft murmur of their voices for about 30 minutes and then I heard alarm in my aunt’s once and she came running down the hall to call my Mom. She was frantic. She couldn’t remember my home phone number or how to get hold of an ambulance. I took the phone and dialed my Mom. My aunt reported that Grandma had fainted and she wanted my Mom to call for medical assistance. Then she went back to mr grandma’s room but wouldn’t let me in I was crying. I didn’t know what was going on. My Mom must have broke all speed limits between our house and Grandma’s. She arrived before the ambulance. And she told my aunt I could enter the room. I watched as the paramedics worked on my Grandma. But she didn’t come too. Eventually she was loaded into an ambulance and we were off to the hospital. We sat in a green waiting room for what seemed an eternity before we were summoned to another area. A room without soothing colors. A room full of stainless steel tables on wheels and frightening looking equipment. My Grandma was lying on one of those tables, still dressed the in long pink flannel nightgown I’d given her for Christmas. My Mom and I approached the Doctor standing on the far side of the table. I instinctively touched her arm with my hand and felt the assuring warmness on my fingers. I thought Grandma was sleeping until I heard the doctor say she had died despite his efforts to save her. My world had just changed forever. The coldness of the room seeped into my bones and I cried inconsolably. When we left the hospital a short time later my Mom and I just silently cried all the way home. The next 3 weeks were a whirl of activity. My Mom and Aunts spent days at Grandma’s house sorting things. I was never again back in my Grandma’s house. I don’t know why. I know many of my cousins were there, but not me. I was in school. I couldn’t concentrate. It took effort to breathe. I didn’t talk or laugh. I was dying inside. I remember looking at the other students and thinking, ‘my heart and life has broken into a million pieces and no one even notices.’ And that included my family as well. With an adult perspective, I understand, but my childish perspective did not. The only happy thing was that exactly 2 weeks after Grandma’s death my little sister was born. That excited me! I was the oldest, and after 4 brothers in a row, I had given up hope of ever getting a sister. That was a nice change. But another change was just around the corner. As soon as school got out, we moved to Seattle. I knew there were fun things to do there, and I had cousins there, but I hated the weather. As time passed I found that we did less talking about Grandma. I missed her terribly but all my words and feelings were trapped inside me. Fast forward 50 years. At the age of 63 I discovered I had never really worked through my grief over her death. I went to therapy for it. You asked how the trauma gets resolved - by talking about it with someone who knows that grief will always have its day. Grief is patient, but it will demand attention at some point. So I spent almost a year identifying my feelings, talking about my feelings of being overlooked by my family even on the day of her funeral. After the church service we had a graveside service. I got separated from my family in the crowd of people, and the gray rainy day. I was standing on a small rise looking at the covered seating area where all the extended family had gathered. I could not get to them. No one missed me. No one was looking for me. If was as if I didn’t exist or matter. I stood under a huge tree that leaked on my coat, my hatless head, and I shivered; and I thought, ‘if Grandma were here, she’d notice I’m it there, physically and mentally.’ My grandmother and I had an amazing relationship. We bonded in a special way. I spent more time with her than any other grandchildren. I never heard a cross word from her. I learned so much from her. We loved working in the garden together, playing table games, watching The Twilight Zone and getting scared and giggling together! Nobody loved me like she did. And I felt guilty for many years because I knew I loved her more than I even loved my parents. I still love and miss my Grandma, but the deep sorrow is gone. It’s been resolved. It’s amazing to me how much those first 13 years of my life with her in it has affected all the remaining years. I am truly blessed! Whatever the source of your trauma, an accident, a crime, abuse, a major loss of any kind, these things traumatize us. There is no shame in needing to talk it out. It doesn’t have to be a therapist, if you have a really caring friend or loved one who will not judge you or just tell you to “get over it.” If that’s not the case I suggest a therapist or even a member of the clergy.

column1: What are some typical characteristics of a psychopaths mask?
column3: Psychopaths wear ‘masks’ or false personas in order to hide among normal people. Psychopaths are actors. Their masks include the pretense of having normal emotions, the pretense of having empathy and the pretense of having a conscience. Some psychopaths hide in plain sight behind a popular, outgoing mask, whilst other psychopaths hide in the background as someone who is completely nondescript. If normal people knew what they were really like then psychopaths would either be pushed to the margins of society, completely excluded, or harmed. Because they have to stay hidden psychopaths are usually extremely subtle in their manipulations, and when manipulating others often try to ensure that they have a level of ‘plausible deniability’ in whatever they say and do. Since childhood psychopaths have observed how normal people behave, though such behavior seems very strange to them, and they have learnt how to create appropriate masks. Until they get plenty of experience under their belts they can make many momentary mistakes or ‘mask slips’. Mask slips can include the wrong verbal or non-verbal reactions to others, a delayed reaction, unexpectedly revealing their true nature, or behaving in bizarre or inappropriate ways. Many mask slips occur when a psychopath is tired or bored, some occur when they’re under the influence of drink or drugs, and a few are deliberate – they can used to deliberately confuse or intimidate others, or to give the psychopath a thrill. To cover up potential mask-slips psychopaths may have a variety of stock responses for emergencies. Psychopaths find wearing their masks tiring and frustrating. Those who have most contact with them are most likely to see their masks slip (e.g. work colleagues), whilst those that are no longer useful to them are most likely to see their masks come fully off (e.g. partners). A psychopath without a mask on is typically either cold and indifferent, or cold and destructively manipulative. You should ALWAYS try to get an accurate idea of someone’s private life before entering into any deep relationship with that person, and ALWAYS try to assess the private life of any politician or other individual aspiring to high office. As part of their mask psychopaths will rewrite, distort or hide their personal histories, sometimes with the active help of others (e.g. naïve, duped or disordered family members). Psychopaths in positions of political power can be expected to persuade school friends to ‘forget’ what they know, journalists to back off, former partners to stay silent or sweet (e.g. by being bought off), and bureaucrats to ‘lose’ documents. Most people don't realize that psychopaths exist. However, psychopaths have known since childhood that they were different from the people around them. They view normal people as strange and even comical since normal people have emotions, a conscience, empathy and guilt, none of which psychopaths really understand. Psychopaths see normal people as different, weak and to be taken advantage of. Psychopaths watch normal people from behind their masks, but normal people don't see them. Psychopaths can have a variety of general-purpose masks for different situations, different places and different people. Some masks can require minimal effort (e.g. the disinterested loner with limited social skills) whilst others can require a lot of effort (e.g. the popular life and soul of the party who’s concerned for everyone else’s well-being). Psychopath’s don’t need to be liked, but being popular gives them access to a network of people’s lives and gossip which gives them a wide variety of opportunities to use people – in other words, predation and parasitism. Psychopaths can slightly adapt existing masks (e.g. for different people within an organization) or create completely new masks (e.g. in different places). Skilled psychopaths can switch fluidly and instantly between masks (e.g. a professional mask immediately followed by a baby-loving mask) or instantly switch on a mask (e.g. after emotionally abusing a partner a psychopath might seamlessly charm visitors). Their masks can include their role or job, their charity work, their clothing, their car, their hobbies, and the people they’re seen with (including ‘friends’, religious figures, partners and their own children). Their masks can also contain different mannerisms, gestures, body language, speech patterns, vocabulary, jokes, voice volumes and tones of voice that they’ve practiced, observed and collected over the years. Observations can come from the people around them or from T.V., movies, magazines, novels, the radio etc. Psychopaths often create the mask of someone who’s trustworthy, intelligent, considerate, honest, nice, fun, humorous, optimistic and VERY easy to like. It’s easier to catch flies with honey rather than with vinegar, and easier to blend in and manipulate people with a friendly face rather than a threatening or frightening one. Being seemingly likeable and beyond reproach also ensures that targets are rarely believed when they describe what’s happened to them. column1: Can two cluster b personalities be happy in a relationship?
column3: I have a nuanced answer to this question. I have BPD; since childhood, I have trauma bonded to borderlines, histrionics, narcissists, and antisocials due to my family dynamics. Those with cluster b disorders come from cluster b families in which all members have a disorder based on their position to the narcissist in the family. So bonding to these cluster b’s began with my sibling and my cousins and it happened throughout school too. Romantically, I attracted only narcissists, and more often sociopaths, as both my parents are sociopaths.I always attracted to the most traumatized children. People with cluster b disorders practice codependent enmeshment. We have what’s called “Favorite People” relationships. I always had more than one favorite person, so I just thought of them as my close friends, until I got therapy and eventually diagnosed with BPD and I could see the trauma bonding patterns and why these relationships weren’t normal. For one, I talked to these people all day, morning, noon, and night. We had no boundaries. The phone could ring at 4am. And if there was a crisis, everything stopped for them because they were…you got it!…like my family.Secondly, my favorite people who were narcissists did not like my other friends. In fact, when around them, they could be downright rude to them. I never questioned it, thinking some personalities just don’t mesh, but now I recognize they were jealous and seeking to isolate me. But I always defended my other friends because I loved them. And third, the friendships with narcissists would end in some shocking betrayals or sudden discards that triggered my abandonment issues and harmed my mental health.So I eventually realized that all my family, all my closest friends, and all my romantic lovers were cluster b trauma bonds. I do know many people outside of the cluster b spectrum, but they are more casual acquaintances, not friends I confided in. I should preface this my saying I’m seven years celibate from my narcissist sex addiction and 1 1/2 years without any favorite person enmeshment. And quitting the second one was the hardest one. Because, with no enmeshment, no one to talk about my day to, to vent my frustrations, to laugh with, to travel with…I started to feel like I don’t exist. Don’t get me wrong. I have friends. Many lovely ones and some are cluster b’s. But I’m trying to do the healthier thing, where you talk on the phone once a month, or shoot an email update, or send a funny meme now and again, rather than a codependent enmeshment. It was the losing of the enmeshment specifically that was, and sometimes still is, excruciating.So, the big question: 🥁 Can we be happy in a relationship? 🥁 If we are speaking in the terms of “happily ever after,” I think that’s a fantasy. I’ve yet to see any perfect relationship that didn’t have struggles, cluster b or not. So I think we should let go of this idea of a love that’s perfect and all good, all happy. Love is as messy as humans are.Let’s look at some of the combinations:A BORDERLINE AND A NARCISSIST OR SOCIOPATHHELL NO. RUN. Borderlines are born scapegoat children and narcissists are born golden children. After the initial lovebomb and idealization wears off in about two days, the narcissist will begin devaluing the borderline. The borderline will stay stuck in idealization, and keep internalizing abuses as their fault until they can’t take it anymore, until their lives feel at risk. They’ll nurture the chaotic emotions of the narcissist like a mother and be thanked with constant temper tantrums, just like their role was for the narcissist parents in childhood. If the borderline leaves, the narcissist will be triggered to their core wounds and rage on the borderline. Their life will be in literal danger. It’s extreme. Then the narcissist will blame all of it on the borderline and smear them and project onto them, hating them more than any other supply. The borderline becomes the scapegoat for shame.And thus these two repeat the patterns of their childhood trauma. I never cheated on a partner or did anything like what narcissists did to me, but I had toxic responses when I’d discover cheating or betrayals or lies, and just leaving a narcissist for abuse or discovering secrets always collapsed them, which took them to the point of mental collapse, thinking about suicide. And when they abused or raged on me, it gave me lifelong trauma and included domestic violence, theft of money, and sexual assault—that pushed me to the brink of suicide as well. So I think this combo is as toxic as it gets and should be avoided like the Black Death.I had a much better time with them as favorite people. They discarded me suddenly, especially when I was low, and it did take me to thoughts of suicide and severely break my heart, but they never raged on me. One didn’t even smear me. His partner asked him what happened to our friendship and he didn’t say a thing, so his partner asked me to tell him what he did. So, it goes to show that they can show restraint….and that might even be their version of love. Or shame. Or both.A BORDERLINE AND A BORDERLINE I’ve never seen a borderline date another borderline: I’ve only seen borderlines trauma bond exclusively to narcissists. But as friends, we absolutely do bond, and THANK EFFING GOD.I find myself so so happy with borderlines. They are the only people who understand the weight of my pain, and have such a way helping me carry it, as I try to carry theirs too. When we talk, we go deep, and we cry and cry. Today, a borderline student came to my office who I had in past years. She’s been going through some trauma at the hands of a narcissist she just unmasked through severe betrayal. The difficult thing with borderlines is that we were raised to think we were burdens, so we can be very afraid that our grief burdens people. It’s always been clear that many people don’t care or seek to make it worse. So, she walked in, sat down, burst into tears, and then started apologizing and saying she felt she should have asked if I had the emotional space for her pain or if she was violating my boundaries. That’s one of the toughest things about us: we are empaths so we absorb a lot of people’s feelings and it’s exhausting, so we constantly worry we will burden each other. We were burdened very young to have to absorb all the shames and mood swings of our parents, so we don’t want to overwhelm people because we were very emotionally overwhelmed children, with no one listening to our feelings. But when someone I love comes to me in pain like that, especially a borderline, they aren’t a burden to me ever. I actually think it’s a real honor to be trusted with someone’s pain, and I always hope I can help. But I act just like her with my borderline friends—always asking permission, always worried I’m an overload. This makes our relationships together far less clingy than other cluster b’s. And I trust borderlines with my life. They’ve never betrayed me and are genuinely as compassionate as me. Borderlines have kept me alive and also marched alongside me for human rights protests, always fighting to stand up for the scapegoats: because we know what it means to be scapegoated. BPDs are the nicest in my comments and DMs too. They have been very nurturing over some of the worst traumas I’ve shared, and their kindness helped a lot through my healing after my sexual assaults. As for romance, I can’t even imagine it so I can’t say how that would go. But I’m very happy in non-romantic relationships with Borderlines.HISTRIONIC AND A NARCISSIST OR SOCIOPATHThis combo is the most successful for narcissist marriages. They last the longest. Narcissists get away with the most with them. Though narcissists mostly ignore histrionics through the whole relationship. The reason it works is because the histrionic will not break their idealization of the narcissist for ALL THE MONEY IN THE WORLD. Don’t get me wrong, these relationships implode all the time. There’s cheating and discarding. BUT THE DENIAL OF THE HISTRIONIC IS JUST LIKE EVERYTHING ELSE WITH THE HISTRIONIC: EPIC.(Famous histrionic) This starts in childhood too. Histrionics were invisible children, so they were severely neglected. The ones I knew talked about being left at home alone at 3 or 4, helpless and terrified their parents were not returning. They entered a fantasy world in which they’d always be seen or obsessed over. They become obsessed with fame and sex….and narcissists, like their parents. But a narcissist could cheat while the histrionic was home and the histrionic would just CTRL-ALT-DEL the event to return to their Prince Charming: I mean that literally.Several of Jerry Sandusky’s victims who were molested as children by him said that his wife was upstairs and they were screaming and that she must have heard it, but she just went on her merry way. This is common in stories of pedophilia: a spouse that just…acted like nothing was happening, but they absolutely knew. The histrionic is wildly romantic, and nothing short of the narcissist walking out on them is going to change the movie version of their narcissist in their head. They can get a breadcrumb and think they hit the lotto. They will ride or die for narcissists, and they’ll think each one of them is Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing.And that illusion is only ending once the whole house is ash around their ankles and the narcissist is in prison. And even then…they’ll probably stay with them in prison. 🤷‍♀️A HISTRIONIC AND A HISTRIONICThese two go together like when magnets repel each other. It’s your JLo and Mariah. Your Kim Kardashian and Paris Hilton. They can be friends for a time, but they compete for stardom and attention, and they end up jealous of each other and claws come out. My histrionic friends tended to get kind of obsessively angry about other histrionics, and when I pointed out their similarities, they said they were aware of them, and it disturbed them.A HISTRIONIC AND A BORDERLINEI’ve only seen histrionics date narcissists. I cannot imagine the histrionic and borderline dating romantically. The histrionic usually requires a grandiose partner because their own fantasy world of fame is so wild. Histrionics also love romantic drama, so a borderline would not stimulate them for long. However, as friends, I’ve had very successful and happy relationships with histrionics. I am still friends with several of them, though not enmeshed, and I’m very grateful they are in my life story. They are a lot of fun. My grandfather was a histrionic and a pilot and I just adored his dreamy, daredevil world as a kid. Unlike narcissists, who have grandiose fantasies but are miserable, the histrionic has grandiose fantasies and is euphoric.(Famous Borderline and Histrionic). The histrionic’s baseline is that life is an adventure—their lives are a movie waiting to happen; and everything is beautiful. They are in touch with their inner children around middle school age, which makes them hilarious and also rebellious. They’re also very seductive. I had one FP Histrionic that lasted 16 years enmeshed. I was very happy with her the whole time. We were Thelma and Louise.We traveled the world, we wrote a book together, we did comedy shows that drew full houses telling funny stories about dating narcissists, we talked about books and feminism and men. We really lived to the fullest. And she inspired me. We had our issues and triggers, but we generally communicated well. But many of her friends said that when they were sick, she ghosted on them. I couldn’t imagine her doing that to me. But lo and behold, I got C-diff for several months, and she ended our friendship suddenly. I felt I lost a limb, and I got sicker. I think that it was because her dad died of an illness, and she can’t handle reality: when it gets sad or uncomfortable, she flees. Histrionics want to be happy and in dream land all the time. I had another histrionic who stopped responding to texts when I told him I’d been raped, but he came back months later like it was nothing. They just can’t cope with things that are not joyful. CTRL-ALT-DEL. Due to their emotional intelligence being middle school age, they also suffer from SEVERE jealousy.When my writing had any accomplishments, they totally shut down, never were happy for me. It was cruel. But it’s because they can’t handle a reality in which they aren’t the star of the movie. If you’re their co-star, they’ll treat you great—not nearly the same abuses as a narc—you’ll be laughing nonstop, but you’ll need to stay in your place and do not grow. There can be only one star.A NARCISSIST AND A NARCISSISTThis is a very common pairing. Narcissists attract to each other because it reminds them of their very first love: the narcissist parent who golden childed them and then abused them. Having a narcissist partner fulfills the fantasy of control and revenge that they didn’t have in childhood. The toxicity feels familiar, and they love to fight for hours and hours and hours. They love to cheat, triangulate, and project on each other. Often, when a narcissist leaves an empath, they’ll run straight to a more toxic relationship. Because a narcissist they can project onto and their projections are true, not delusion. They can abuse and get abused back and then justify their victimhood. Their hatred and unhappiness feels warranted with another narcissist. They can use them as a live in scapegoat. And narcissists need supply, so they’re more likely to stay through the worst abuses, having little capabilities of independence. They also both agree about their innate superiority and they agree that child abuse is the best way to raise kids.As far as happiness goes, I’ve experienced it with all cluster b’s, just in different ways. I wouldn’t trade the life I’ve had for one without them, and some are still in my life. One histrionic friend can always be counted on to send me the funniest animal memes while I’m crying. With narcissists, I’ve had wild passion and dark pain—a full human experience of extremes—and some of them are still very dear to me, like my sister or former friends, though they hurt me badly. We had a lot of happy memories. But romantically and platonically, narcissists and sociopaths were very abusive and dishonest. So, can two cluster b’s be happy? Yeah, euphoric. Our wounded inner children frolic together. Can it all go painfully wrong due to unresolved childhood trauma? YEAH. 💣 It likely will if both haven’t worked hard on themselves and have self awareness. Is there real love between us? LOADS OF IT. As if we are family….It’s not all good or all bad. It may not be healed enough to last forever though. In my mind, the good outweighs the bad and the love remains in my heart, even for many (not all) narcissists. And I’m thankful for them. But that’s a borderline type of perspective. Narcissists won’t be able to remember the love, processing it as hatred when the relationship ends, because they lack emotional memory and object permanence, but borderlines and histrionics remember the love. We talk about our past loves and favorite memories together all the time, even of narcissist partners who hurt us. We can be hurt and still remember the love before the blindside of abuse. We are deeply nostalgic and ruminating people in general. This is also from our neglected childhood: we always miss those who felt like our parents— just as we missed our parents’ love as kids.
