column1: What are your thoughts on life after death?
column3: I like this approach to the ‘life after death’ question. Personal. Not ‘what happens’ but ‘what are your thoughts’. Because it is personal. People report near death experiences (NDEs) or communications with or from the dead, then others rationalise and criticise. However, (without meaning to be rude) if you weren’t there having that experience, all your rationalising is meaningless. These events are life-changing, utterly compelling - but they cannot be communicated. Actually this goes for all spiritual and mystical experience. In fact, thinking about it, it goes too for all intense human experience: conducting a double-slit experiment, winning a race, falling in love, writing a poem: there’s something ineffable about it. If you weren’t there you won’t get it. There’s only an abstract story gutted of meaning. Anyway, some thoughts of a personal nature; then, maybe, a personal experience.Existence is a mystery. Totally. Utterly. This is often obscured by all those ‘experts’ who try to convince us they know the Truth. And I don’t just mean members of religious organisations promoting their beliefs as facts. Atheism and science are also belief systems (and I’d just love an atheist to challenge me on this), except that scientists and atheists only admit to having ‘assumptions’ not beliefs. But a belief is an emotionally charged assumption, and it is clear that scientists are emotionally committed to assumptions upon which their careers, reputations and, indeed, lives are based. How could they not be? They fight for their ‘assumptions’ with the same fear and fervour that a person fights for their religious beliefs. The most obvious manifestations of reality in our neck of the woods are matter and consciousness. No one knows what matter is. No one knows what consciousness is. Existence is a mystery.So all we have are beliefs. Or we can embrace the mystery of existence, loving the freedom of this, the sense of anything is possible, and the way it makes life so very much more mysterious, magical, rich with potential, and just plain interesting, than when we’re stuck in the box of an imposed belief coffined within spurious definitions.Google ‘invisible gorilla experiment’. It tells us that our brains have filters, both communal and personal. Due to the various conditionings and consequent blinkerings of our lives we simply can’t see what’s really going on around us. Our perception of reality is an illusion, a fantasy, mostly communal, partly personal. Scientific fact.Death is such a mystery that every belief and theory about it, no matter how extreme, is equally plausible. Some of you will struggle with what I’m about to write, and that’s good, because you need to be prepared to struggle if you want glimpses behind the veil. When certain men believe that if they die a certain way they will awake in a beautiful garden beneath which sweet waters flow with 17 or 72 (opinions differ) virgins to cater to their every desire, we have every right to loathe this belief, we can say it is socially problematic, but we cannot say that it is not true. We cannot even say that it is less plausible than the belief that when we die we merely cease to exist. We have nothing on which to base estimations of plausibility. In fact belief in personal extinction is equally problematic since it renders personal life ultimately meaningless; afflicts us with foreboding; encourages self-centred hedonism as the only rational response since there’s no point in self-denial and hard work; and discourages personal morality, which depends on the idea that the quality of our life after death may be determined by what we do in life. Well, we can attempt to base our morality on love of humanity, but the human race is often unloveable and ever more dominated by the unhuman mechanisms of commerce and bureaucracy that relegate our individual humanity to economic units, so it’s not easy. Maybe we can use family or community as a basis for morality, but then the authority of these is fraying before the onslaught of the 21st century. You might as well invent your own belief about what happens after death: no one can contradict you and if it gets you through the night, helps you do the right thing, and doesn’t hurt anyone it’s got to be good.Since time governs only matter, if you survive the death of your material body you’ll no longer be governed by time. This may explain why people feel compelled to erect monuments to themselves that people will ponder over for centuries to come, or why we place flowers on graves every Christmas for decades and look at old photograph albums and reminisce about the long-dead: we are sending energy to the deceased that they receive at the point of death, which may help them through the transition. It would also suggest that when people who report having had an NDE say they saw their great aunt Agatha, dead these 50 years, waiting to greet them, it doesn’t mean she’s been hanging around for 50 years wishing they’d hurry up and die so she could get on with her death: for her it’s the same moment in which she died.This is all just speculation, you understand. I don’t know either. But ‘speculate’ comes from the Latin ‘specula’: watchtower. It enables us to see more. What I’m doing here is challenging assumptions. Because whatever we believe about death it’s certain to be wrong. I suspect that if we do retain our consciousness of self after death our first reaction may be one of surprise.One of life’s little ironies is that many people who wish they could have ‘supernatural’ experiences probably have had them, but they’ve forgotten. I think such experiences are common, especially in childhood, but we are educated out of them, and our materialistic (in the philosophical sense) conditioning means that our brains don’t know what to do with these experiences and dismiss them either by forgetting them or rationalising them into something else. Also, they tend to be fleeting.Are NDEs universal? Why aren’t those who experience one able to verify it by saying they saw that picture secretly stuck on top of an ECG monitor that they should have seen had they really been floating up near the ceiling? Well, think about it. In the material world, there’s you, and there’s reality, and between you there is this solid wall with five tiny apertures in it, labeled sight, hearing, smell, touch and taste. Then you die, and suddenly that wall is no longer there, you’re immersed in reality, engulfed by it, no filters. Can you imagine what that would be like? Then you’re yanked back to your body. How can your material brain compute the memory of that? Perhaps it will dismiss it, forgetting it so that you say, “No, I didn’t have any NDE experience.” Or perhaps it will edit out everything but for one thing, something ‘seen’, a symbol basically, a freeze frame from a multi-dimensional movie.I had a friend whose mother had to go in for a serious operation. She was a farmer’s wife, a down to earth soul with no spiritual inclination and no interest in anything unconnected with farming and finance, who’d likely never heard of NDEs. Well, that common story happened: she was put under anaesthetic and awoke to find herself floating against the ceiling looking down on her body being operated on. Then she fell asleep again and awoke in bed. The surgeon visited and she told him what she had seen and he was able to confirm that she had witnessed the moment when the surgical team had been working frantically to resuscitate her. The punchline? She had been blind for many years. This was ages ago, but apparently, NDEs are so well documented now that there is a sub-file of accounts from blind people.Okay, now for my personal experience of communication from the dead. Be warned: you may find it disappointing. No Stephen King melodrama here. Just a tiny wee thing. But that’s why I think I should tell it, because most such experiences are like this. Context is everything, so some preamble: My dad was a farmer. Practical. Materialistic. He only ever thought deeply about farming. He was proud of the money he’d made. He bought a new Jaguar every two or so years. My mum was killed by a drunken driver when I was 21 and my dad remarried. I had no other immediate family until I married. But because my dad and I were so different, and because my stepmother took over the running of his life and was very much like him, we were never close. We had an amicable relationship and the pair of them showed kindness to me at times, but it was emotionally detached. Polite. No hugs. I couldn’t really say I loved him, but in terms of blood he was all I had and I respected that, as did he. One day when he was 77 he told me, apropos of nothing, that his father and eldest brother had both died when they were 78. I thought, “So what, I know that,” but then I looked at him. He was gazing at me intently and I saw fear in his eyes. It suddenly struck me that he had never really confronted the fact that he was going to die one day, and this arithmetical coincidence (farmers work a lot with numbers) had finally brought it home. It was only a year or so later that the dementia was diagnosed. There are, of course, multiple causes of dementia (a nurse in the dementia ward, when we were discussing mental functionality, told me, “Use it or lose it.”), but I can’t help wondering that a fearful appreciation of his ever-abbreviating, dead-end future caused him to retreat, first backward, then inward. His body died at age 87. By then he had been dead to me for years. I felt no grief. My wife asked me a week after the funeral, “How have things changed for you?” and I think I shocked her a bit when I said they hadn’t. The thing with dementia is that you don’t get the full experience of grief. When my mum was killed in an untimely, sudden and unexpected way, the full force of grief fell on me like a wall. But that some potentiality for grief I had for my dad was stretched out over eight years, attenuated, felt in small extractions, so that when his heart finally stopped, there was nothing left in my tank. With his departure I discovered that my step-mother harboured a long-suppressed bitterness towards me (the only person my dad ever loved was my mum) and she made it clear at the funeral that she wanted nothing more to do with me and my family. He was cremated and she kept the ashes at home for a few months. Then one day she phoned and said I could visit and pick them up. We had a brief, polite conversation at her door as she handed them over. I had vaguely expected something like an urn and was surprised to receive this little styrofoam (or something) box. There was a label on it printed in 12-point Times New Roman. I plonked it on the driver’s seat of my car and headed for home. I was driving along an open road with this innocuous little box sitting beside me. It felt strange that it contained all that was left in this world of my dad. I wondered if there was anything left of his consciousness somewhere that could perceive and appreciate this moment. This started me thinking about what happens to us when we die. My emotional state was detached. I came to terms with my own mortality when I was in my teens, when I went through a phase of being fascinated by the fact that I was bound to die. I decided back then that I would cease to exist when it happened. Over the succeeding four decades I have become accustomed to this idea, though my certainty of extinction has lessened. I have no beliefs about it, but if you threatened me with an imminent, violent and unpleasant means of discovering the truth for myself, I might admit to the speculation that an essential part of us that involves our consciousness does survive the death of our physical body, but we lose our sense of self, all those memories of physical events that we believe define us. But, really, I don’t know. What I do know is that while dying can be unpleasant, death is nothing to fear. I know this to such an extent that I actually find it hard to relate to people’s fear. My relaxed attitude about the business is such that the sense of tragedy we are supposed to feel in those movies and novels that end with the hero’s death leaves me largely untouched, unless it is done really well. So I was in this philosophical frame of mind when, suddenly, an emotion shot into me. It was a feeling of joy with an afterglow of relief, and it brought the words, “There’s nothing to be afraid of.” And that was it. There and gone in a flash. Warned you it was disappointing. My initial thought was, “Where did that come from?” Some time later – I’m talking minutes – it occurred to me to wonder if it was my dad’s last communication with me. Of course it might have been just a stray feeling manufactured in my brain. I know that. No one is more sceptical than me. I once tried out the Sceptics Society and dismissed them for being too credulous. True. Sceptical only of some things; unquestioning believers of others. But this feeling I had taking my dad’s ashes home (to his home, that is: the farm where I grew up with my mum and dad, long-since gone from our physical lives but held still in our hearts, which my urbanite step-mother had no interest in, and where I scattered his ashes across the land that he had loved) this feeling and accompanying words were such a non sequitur, so out of the blue, that they exerted an authority I cannot dismiss. Did the dead communicate? I don’t know. But if I had to put a figure on it, I’d settle for an 80 percent probability. Written here in case it helps.

column1: How do I get my old self back after depression?
column3: As I sit here, I am trying to do the same for myself. I moved across the country with my partner in 2020, we got to the new state two days before everything shut down for the pandemic. I came over here with high spirits, ready to find a new job over here and thrive without having my parents around me 24/7. Unfortunately, with the pandemic being bigger than we had anticipated, I was out of work for 4–6 months. Those months were not so easy on me. It was hard to meet new people and have a new social life because everyone was so paranoid about this crazy pandemic that we found ourselves in. Flash forward to when I finally got my first job over here, it was an amazing place of work until it wasn’t. My grandmother who was the glue to the family had ever so suddenly passed away, I was a wreck. I was across the country, and didn’t get to say goodbye to her. She was my best friend and that was the hardest pill I had to swallow. I did not know how to handle grief because I have never experienced it. Even now, in 2023, I am still healing from her loss. When it came to the new job, my coworkers were also reat, until they were not. I worked closely with another girl who had the same position as I did, except she was a tedious one. She always left work early, causing me to work a full schedule on my own and then shut down a whole office on my own. When she decided it was time for her to quit, that is when I mentally, physically, and emotionally began to feel the burn out. Due to this burn out, my relationship is still to this day still healing from my actions. I have never realized how intense depression really can be. I lost over 50 lbs within just that one year alone. I had to learn in a hard way that I am not good with my finances at all. I have issues with childhood abuse that had come to the surface because after years and years of pushing feelings and emotions so deeply inside me, they decided to come out. I am now in the biggest hole of my life. I put myself into so much debt, lied to my partner out of embarrassment because of this debt, and lost every single friend and family member I have had. My parents no longer speak to me because I decided to live with my partner once again when they knew that I was only digging myself a much deeper hole. So, what can I do to get myself out of this depression? I have created a vision board that is sitting on the wall in my room. The vision board is short term goals that I can look at every single day when I wake up and get ready for the day. Those goals include, getting in shape, fixing the relationship, going debt free, finding myself a hobby/passion because I have absolutely none, and so on. I have been getting back into fitness again, and it has been extremely impactful so far even though it’s been a short amount of time. I know I still have a lot of work to do, but this healthy lifestyle has really been a positive in my not so positive brain. I physically feel better and my energy feels like it’s running exactly the way it should have been. I have been reading a lot more. Reading is extremely good for a mind that is already burnt out. I have very bad ADHD, so when I read, I make sure to take my time doing so. If I lose focus, then I just reread it again. Treat yourself fairly, you really only get one life. I was on the brink of suicide, and now I can’t even think about that. That was not me during that time, I was just insanely so unhappy. Slowly though, I am building myself back up. You can do this too. I apologize if this response is every where, my ADHD does that a lot.

column1: Why did I stop feeling anything when grieving for my lost one when crying?
column3: Crying is a stress releiver, and the hormones it releases, or indeed triggered it, is the way the brain stops you from “going over the edge” yourself. Whether is be just sobs, or running tears and sobs, that is a good thing, and the reason you stop feeling anything. Actually you are, it is just that the hormones (endorphines) in the brain, through the crying over-ride the other emotion, particularly grieving, albeit temporarily, but in all seriousness will save you sanity. So you stop feeling anything is because the endorphines temporarily shut down that area of the brain, which means you stay alert. Grief is almost always assoicated with death, but it can mainfest iteself in the break up of a friendship which was very close and you discover you have drifted apart, but the person who is still emotionally involved with the relationship, but not realised that the other party has actually moved on, it is just that you have not realised. This happened to me many years ago, with a girl I truly loved, but becasue I worked with her didn’t want my emotions to intergere with the job. Indeed I left the company (not because of the emootional side, but the job I transferred to, I didn’t like and with a coupld of “head ons” with the branch manager decided to leave. I was only 19, so didn’t use the lines of recourse which I discovered I had when I had changed jobs completely and started in the area of accountancy I do now (Credit Management and legal enforcement). My kowledge of law over the following 20 years means that I no longer take any nonsense form employers and if there are issues and they are not prepared to negotiate the situation and try to fire me, I will take the legal recourses available to me. Although it has never saved my job (the employers will always make your life as difficult as possible after you have won a case) even so they have to pay the Costs of the Action the fiscal compensation awarded by the Tribunal; more to the point, the Adjudication, like a County Court Action for say the recovery of a debt, or even Family Division recourses are recorded public and can be applied for by “Discovery of documents” or by application to inspect the register. If incorrect then you can apply to Court for and Order to have them ammended to show the correct postion. I still had very strong feelings for P. and we did write to eachother, but I didn’ want to push things to fast in case I scared her off. In the meantime I had a series of promotions at work, but it meant I was spending more time at work. Although P & I did meet up for the odd dinner out, and indeed went to eachother’s for Sunday lunches (a bit awkward as she still lived with her parents at the time so a very emotional interaction was not really on the cards -:) ). In the meant time I had started buying my flat and that resulted in the ability to invite P. over to mine on a one to one basis. Regrettably I was living on the edge of my means, and working long hours to keep the coffers going. As a result of these long hours, and not having a telephone (to save on outgoings) meant that our only real means of contact was in writing. The mistake I made was that I never disclosed my feelings for her, and rather stupidly never used the phrase “ I love you” even when we met it was a cuddle not a kiss, again in part because I didn’t want to frighter her off. Crunch time came when I had written to her to inivte her away for a horse show and I had won free accommodation in a hotel for that weekend so this was a great opportunity to meet up and have her company on an extended basis. Now I was aware that she had a close relationship with her sister, and P. not being very confident on her own (by her own admission “didn’t like her own company) used to go away on holiday with her older sister, and also an old school friend, However what had naively never crossed my mind, was that she may be going out with other boys/men on a friendship basis as we had. She responded to my invitation to say that she was going away that weekend with a friend of hers, which I assumed was this old school friend. A couple of weeks later she wrote me a very cheerful letter to say that she had a great week end with “G.” and in fact he had proposed to her. Indeed it had never crossed my mind that she had been involved in other male friendships, let alone sleeping with them. Now I am not suggesting for a second that she was “cheating on me” as clearly this was a question of me reading too deeply in to the relationship, combined with allowing myself to get over involved with my job, and albeit unintentionally not spending more time with her side by side so to speak. Having read her letter telling me she was getting married to this man, I will be perfectly honest that I did burst in to tears. The reason I go in to so much detail is because what I am indicating here is that it does not have to be the death of someone you are emotionally close to, but that person may well be surving but in the case of P. misread my desires (in the strict sense of the word) but the loss to me in the sense that I could no longer even write to her (I am not going to get in a three way tug of war, particularly as she was now about to get married and it is not for me to intervene in a marriage, indeed in English Law it is a Civil Offence to do so and P. or her husband could apply for a Restraining Order against me. ( I have read Family Law, so am more aware than most of legal recourses available) and that would have caused possilby the break up of her marriage. Again not for me to do. The point here is that the fact I needed to cry was actually very important since although P. was clearly alive, it was not a physical loss but an emotional one, and in my mind she may well have died since I was mourning her loss in the context I would never see her again, even though 25 years on there is rarely a day where her name doesn’t cross my mind and wonder whether the marriage did work and indeed whether she decided to have children and if so what they would look like. Yes, I still have feelings for her, but they do not show themselves as strongly as they did and have faded away, albeit slowly over time. You /I stop feeling anything as that is the point of crying and emotional grieving as that it is the way the brain tries to help the concious side of not so much forgetting the events but “bundling them up” and putting them in to long term storage. So there is a certain empty feeling although I still love her and indeed still have the photographs of her when we went on these equine days out, along with most of the letters we shared between us. So the need to mourn a loss of a friend is very real and no different to losing a member of your immediate family. The crying is a way of the body and brain to releive the mental stress of your loss and in the process divert your mind to the fact you are crying with tears running down your face, and even want to cuddle a pillow or large teddy bear. All of that is part of the greiving process, and the fact you think your are not grievng whilst you are crying is becasue you mind has been distracted by the emotion of the loss in terms of crying and tears. The same goes for adults who lose their partner/husband/ wife ; and indeed I had to deal with my father who took the loss of mum very badly, and I stayed with him for a while, Of course you have this issue of “Big boys don’t cry” drummed in to males from a very early age, and there is still a certain amount of stigma surrounding men who do cry at the loss of a person they are emotioanlly very close to. As I said to my father, “if you need to cry, then cry, If you are worried about doing it front of me, then I will buzz of down the pub for half an hour, but don’t do anythingh stupid”. When I came back he was “cried out”; and the fact that he did thta mean the emptiness was no there and it created a “clean break”. He may have cried again later, I don’t know, but certainly he ws not “clingy” as some people (of either sex) who grieve but appear to show no outward emotion. So your reactions is no different in its presentation to others it is just because you have probably only ever come across people who greive openly, complete with sobs and tears. but similarl to yourslef “greive to themselves”, and that reduces the emotional tension in the same way, and yes the strength of your emotions will fade over time It took me in reality about 15 years (yes, years) for me to get over P. and indeed I have never been emotionally involved with anyone since and still single. Ironically in part because I have buried my head in my job and in the last 20 years re-developed my childhood epilepsy which has caused issues emotionally and mentally; ironcially more linked to my work as there are a number of things I can’t do, along with the obssession by employer about people being able to learn their computing suites on demand, which if you do not have a powerful short-term, rapid recall memory (as I don’t) and therefore cannot learn fast, that means many employers seem me as a write off or at best incomptent becuase I don’t know their computing suite or only shown once. Indeed I recall one girl (obviously younge than me) who was my would be supervisor (although I was actaully doing a serious debt reduction project and there was a lot of additional research over and above making phone calls and punching or retreiving information from the blasted computing suite. Indeed the fact I had to ask her to show me a couple of procedures a number of times, she snapped at me: “ Are you thick, don’t you have a brain or a memory ? “ I just replied: No, I don’t have a short term memory, but do indeed have a brain, and for the record I can draft legal papers to a level that you would not understand at first presentation due to the different way a summons and Particulars of Claim have to be drafed and worded. I then showed her a draft Partucular of Claim, which I was drafting to recover the debt (actually quite significant) and the Claim quite complex needing Exhibits to the Summons ( additional evidence that cannot be included directly in the Particularls of Claim. To conclude, what you are experiencing is nothing sinister or you should not feel blank and (in your view) have ceased greiving, but clearly it is temporary. However you have been distracted from it. Often that is why with girls in particular it is a positive thing to have a close friend with you, even stay with you a couple of nights in case you empotions suddenly surge and you need a cuddle or someone to talk to. With very best wishes. Regards Chris R- London

column1: You have a friendly neighbor that you've known since childhood. You recently learned that he served in the Waffen-SS during WW2. How do you react?
column3: For me, this is more than a hypothetical question: coming from a German-American family, I’ve been there. I spent, on and off, about half of my childhood in Germany (in Northern Bavaria), plus all of my college time (in Munich). During high school (“Gymnasium”) the Nazi era was covered extensively in history class and we were encouraged to go out and talk to the people who had lived through it. At that time, in the mid-70’s, the war had been over for about 30 years. So, every adult 35 years or older had consciously lived through the Nazi era. And just about any male 50 years or older had fought in the war. The most interesting thing was that you met people manifesting all levels of the trauma/grief spectrum (the traumatic experience of course being the defeat). There were“deniers” (“it never was that bad!”; “you are only hearing the bad things”; “history is written by the victors”; “we’ve heard enough about these things, it’s time to move on”);“anger”/”defenders” (“did you see what these savages did to our cities / our women / our country?; “the other side was just as bad”; “we only defended Germany”; “we couldn’t let The Russian overrun Germany”)“bargainers”/“negotiators” (“we did bad things, but which choice did we have?”; “there were also good things that happened, you have to look at the balance”)“depressed” (“this was horrible, we have to be ashamed”; “how can we ever look the French / the Russians / the Jews in the eyes again”)“acceptors” (“this was horrible, we may never deny, but we have to move on”)I didn’t run this as a scientific experiment (although others did), but I’d say where somebody fell on that spectrum primarily depended on two factors: the age they were during the first six years of the Nazi time (the pre-war period), and how “brown” their family was (“brown” being the adopted color of the Nazi movement, just like you’d consider the communists to be “reds”; not a scientific measure of course). No surprise: practically every adult male at that time (45+ years of age) had been a veteran of the war (pretty much every capable male was drafted for mandatory service). While I remember several individuals who were SS veterans, I only had meaningful contact with two of them. Nevertheless, I can recollect three different situations that I think are useful for this answer:“Deny”: I remember talking to a widow, firmly in the “deny” camp. Her husband had perished early on in the poison gas battles of WW1 in France. Following her recollection, their eldest son grew up with a mixture of extreme patriotism (“my father has given his life for this country”) and, I guess, an always present sense of wanting to take revenge. During the inter-war years they were a farming family without an adult (male) farmer. Many people helped them survive throughout the years out of solidarity and charity, and they were very grateful for that. The son volunteered for military service in 1939, hoping to fight against France. Given his excellent athletic skills and demonstrated patriotism, he was drafted into the Waffen SS. She never said it, but I read between the lines that he regarded this as an honor. In 1944 he perished battling the Soviets in Romania. His mom, who had now lost both her husband and her oldest son to wars, was firmly convinced that their “sacrifice” was for a good cause. This was the narrative she held til the day she died at age 96. Having said this, I never heard her giving any opinion about Hitler, the Nazis, the Holocaust, the repression of the German people during the Nazi rule, etc. The only thing that mattered to her was the personal pain she experienced for losing those two men. In denial, she had become completely apolitical. How did I deal with this? You listen, you let people talk, you don’t probe too much when it obviously causes pain; in the end, you are privileged to learn so much about their personal (and their family’s) history.“Anger”: I remember one individual who was the mayor of a neighboring town. As a high-school student I was covering the region for the regional newspaper and had gotten to know this gentleman somewhat. Very engaged in local politics, of course (he was an elected official) he worked extremely hard for his hometown. As a lawyer, he could have made many times more money than as a mayor, so he was clearly doing service to his community. I never got to know him well enough to ask him about “the past”. But his past caught up with him. Sege Karlsfeld, a well known French Nazi-hunter, outed him as one of the organizers of the death trains to Auschwitz from occupied France. Turns out, this gentleman had been, as an SS NCO, one of the administrators of the effort to put the “final solution” into action in the occupied territory (in this case France). In absentia this man had been convicted and sentenced to death by a French court (by that time, the EU had already stopped the death penalty, so he was in no danger of being executed; however, it was clear that his was a very, very, capital case). The mayor initially declared that this must be a mistake. A confusion of someone else with the same last name; “not me”, he declared himself totally innocent. His constituents spectacuarly supported him (he got re-elected with 85% of the vote). Being proven a liar on that, he then tried every trick in the book (“I didn’t know what would happen to those jews”; “only following orders”; “was only drafted as a soldier, didn’t volunteer for the SS”). None of that worked, the case was iron-clad and the evidence was watertight. Eventually, he was sentenced (by a German court) to a remarkably light prison sentence and served only part of it before being released for “good conduct”. Up to this day you will find people in the city he used to be mayor in who will claim that Klarsfeld got “the wrong guy”. You will even find some people who use Klarsfeld as an argument for maintaining their anti-semitic views (“can’t those jews leave us in peace?”). To be clear, I was not close to this individual on a personal level (although I did know him). And equally clear, this man did some excellent work for his home town. But the combination of deceit and denial from a person I thought I knew almost made me throw up at the time.I remember a second individual, back then in his mid fourties, a very gentle and highly intelligent man. He was the only SS veteran I really got close to on a personal level. He was drafted into the war in 1944 at age 16. Initially drafted for an army (Wehrmacht) unit, he was however assigned to an SS division that had been almost totally wiped out on the Eastern front. Being devout Catholics, his family had not been “very brown”. In fact, his mother had gotten into trouble stating that the Führer will lead us into ruin. He himself told me that he considered the SS people he had previously known as “thugs”. The family, like most of the Germans back then, I guess, considered the Western allies as “bandits” who destroy our cities (through aerial bombing). However, according to his recollection, it was either join this SS unit or be shot on the spot. Needless to say, he joined. He talked of two battles that he fought in, one in Hungary, one in Vienna. He got severely wounded during the last battle and got put on a hospital train bound first for Würzburg, then for Munich. He was told that even with excellent medical care, his chances of survival were slim - and in the destroyed Germany, there was little medical care to be had. He reported that on this train he spent more time with a priest than with a doctor. That train never reached its destination. It was instead captured by the advancing US Army. He was certain that he (and his fellow SS soldiers) would be shot on the spot. Instead, with huge effort, American military doctors brought him back to life and he made an almost full recovery. During the de-nazification trials he was classified as “minor” and was released from captivity when he left the hospital. Post-war he studied medicine and became quite an accomplished internist. He studied both the Hungarian and the English language, trying to make contact with the people he encountered during his military time (with limited success). Post-war, he had become a very outspoken anti-Nazi (and anti-communist), speaking out against totaliatarinism and abuse of power many times. He was insistent that “back then” he was “simply a soldier” and never participated in any war crimes. Although he fully admitted that his division had been culpable in quite a few. While he clearly knew of the concentration camps, he states, he was not aware at the time that they were, in fact, death camps. Given his young age at the time and his religious devotion, I was inclined to believe him (he died in the early 2000s).So, those are my three most distinct interactions with SS veterans, or their direct family. What have I learned from this?People strive for meaning, they want to put together a narrative that is logical and (if possible) untainted. They do that not necessarily in order to lie, but mostly in order to preserve their own sanity when confronted with a traumaGuilt, culpability, etc. are deeply personal and highly individual concepts. Somebody who puts together trains for the gas chambers has a very different level of guilt than somebody who gets forced into the fight as a child soldier (essentially as cannon fodder), even if both were SS membersMany of these people are looking for a way to redeem themselves. Working very hard as an elected mayor (which is not a highly paid position) or as a medical doctor are both ways to “help people”. In their own respective ways, both of these men had successfully turned their lives around 30 years after the warWhat is missing from this perspective is, almost always, the point of view of the victims. The mayor tried for years simply to deny they existed. The MD tried to make contacts, without admitting any personal guilt (maybe even rightfully so, I am not in a position to judge). But either way, those crimes against humanity have been committed, and they have been committed by those SS units. No way to deny this. For the mayor it was a “what goes around, comes around” situation. Even though he lost his elected job and (some) of his reputation, he still got off very easily. Justice was probably not served in his case.How did I react? These people are, first and foremost, human beings. I do not know enough of their personal history to pass judgement on them. Some of them have done terrible things; all of them have done some good things, too. I can listen to their stories and try to match them with historical evidence. This will never be 100% accurate, and my view can never be objective. And eventually, I know only 2 cases out of what must have been several 100,000. However, even so I probably know more cases personally, and have talked to them myself, than most people active on Quora today. While guilt is a personal thing, the war crimes really did happen.

column1: Does Arya Stark have a dark side?
column3: Arya Stark most definitely has a dark side. The more malevolent aspect of Arya’s personality is made apparent throughout both the television series (GOT) and the books (ASOIAF) as she ages. However, Arya’s dark side is nowhere near as vile or twisted as Joffrey Lannister and Ramsay Bolton. Arya’s propensity for cruelty is dwarfed by both bastards as hers is not inherent. Arya was not born evil. On the other hand, Joffrey Baratheon and Ramsay Bolton displayed sadistic tendencies since early childhood. Joffrey tormented his brother and mutilated a pregnant cat, and Ramsay was so violent and uncouth she begged Roose Bolton for help. These tendencies then blossomed into horrendous crimes like torture, murder and rape. Prior to the events of A Game of Thrones Arya has only been desired as shown to be a jovial girl with great compassion, if not a level of insecurity. This uncertainty in herself manifested for a few reasons:Arya was the only one of her full siblings who did not bear the Tully appearanceArya had little patience or talent for traditional lady-like pursuits/behavior, which meant that she was fundamentally contradicting the patriarchal and misogynistic society she lived inCatelyn showered Sansa with praise due to her aptitude in the feminine and artistic endeavors like singing or sewing. Arya never received such attention.Arya then developed an inferiority to Sansa to an extent.Arya felt an inexplicable kinship with Jon due to their similar looks and she empathized with his “black sheep” mentality.Arya was constantly made fun of by her elder sister Sansa, Jeyne Poole, and Beth Cassel who at some times even called her “Horse face” which is a terrible thing to say to a young girlSepta Mordane was quick to chastise Arya for her wild behavior or her difficulty in their lessons. She was not above comparing the two sisters (if I am not mistaken) with Sansa being the ideal girl, and Arya the incorrect kind.But all in all, Arya was friendly with everyone, slow to judge and quick to jump at the chance of adventure. She knew who she wanted to be and was determined to achieve it. She was on fantastic terms with all of her brothers and enjoyed playing with them, and had the adoration of her father and love of her mother. Arya never had any fear in challenging the status quo and was not scared to speak her mind. She was known to be very fierce and rash in some scenarios, and this passion was described as “wolfs-blood”. The girl’s temper could potentially evolve into a taste for violence but this is mere speculation. And eventually, King’s Landing would prove the birth of Arya’s combat abilities and sincere pride in herself. Here are a few quotes that explore her character before she is befallen with tragedy and confronted with how vindictive and feral the world is. Courtesy of Arya Stark “Ah, Arya. You have a wildness in you, child. The 'wolf blood,' my father used to call it. Lyanna had a touch of it, and my brother Brandon more than a touch. It brought them both to an early grave. Lyanna might have carried a sword, if my lord father had allowed it. You remind me of her sometimes. You even look like her.” [2] —Eddard Stark to Arya “Arya had always been harder to tame.” [70] —thoughts of Catelyn Stark “And Arya, well... Ned's visitors would oft mistake her for a stableboy if they rode into the yard unannounced. Arya was a trial, it must be said. Half a boy, half a wolf pup. Forbid her anything and it became her heart's desire. She had Ned's long face, and brown hair that always looked as though a bird had been nesting in it. I despaired of ever making a lady of her. She collected scabs as other girls collected dolls, and would say anything that came into her head.” [71] —thoughts of Catelyn Stark Once Arya witnessed her father’s execution, all bets were off as to when she would be forced to and willing to kill. Arya initially resorted to violence only in self-defense, her first death being the stablehand’s son in King’s Landing. However, Arya’s mentality became increasingly darker and more vicious to the point that she fixated constantly on those she would murder in revenge for the injustices they caused her on her List. First I will create a list of events that will have darkened Arya’s spirit and mind.Moving away from WinterfellWatching Joffrey threaten and hurt MycahSansa lying about the incident by the riverLosing NymeriaFinding out about Mychah’s deathSyrio Ferel’s death by Meryn TrantForced to live in the streets of King’s Landing surviving only on pigeons she stabbed with her sword and no permanent shelter.Being present at her father’s executionBeing forced to pretend that she is a boy conscripted to the Night’s WatchThreatened by Lommy and Hot PieLosing YorenNeedle being stolenWatching the prisoners at Harrenhal be tortured and murdered by The TicklerJaqen H’ghar’s offer of taking three lives for herBeing separated from GendryWitnessing the outside events of the Red Wedding, the death of Grey Wind and seeing Robb’s corpse with the direwolf’s head sewn on instead of his headLearning of her aunt, Lysa Arryn’s deathSubjected to Sandor’s fatalistic and cruel point of viewIndoctrinating herself into an order that wipes away individuality and worships the God of DeathRegularly beaten by the WaifSight stolen and cast out from the House of Black and WhiteGrievously stabbed by the WaifThe list of Arya’s darker behavior is pretty consistent through both the show and the novels so I will make list covering both:Oftentimes volatile/reactionary (Attacks Sansa physically for lying about Joffrey and Mycah (Season 1 and GOT)Empathic link with Nymeria further demonstrates her ferocity (Season 1 and GOT)Begins to reject the natural human emotion of fear due to Syrio’s teachings “Fear cuts deeper than swords”. Now, this is good advice to deal with times of crises but it is human to be afraid. (GOT through ADWD)Threatens to kill Hot Pie and Lommy when they demand her sword (Season 1 and GOT)Physically attacks Lommy and Hot Pie (GOT)Kills soldier(s) of Ser Armory (ACOK)Provides Jaqen with the name of people to assassinate (Both Season 2 and ACOK) with variations in targetsThe Tickler (TV Show), Chiswyck(ACOK)Ser Armory (TV Show), Weese (ACOKThreatens Jaqen with his own name to force him to kill more than one person, eventually many guards (TV Show), Several guards detaining Robb’s allies and she participates in the killing (ACOK)Takes pleasure in causing the deaths at Harrenhal information provided above: “Swift as a deer. Quiet as a shadow. Fear cuts deeper than swords. Quick as a snake. Calm as still water. Fear cuts deeper than swords. Strong as a bear. Fierce as a wolverine. Fear cuts deeper than swords. The man who fears losing has already lost. Fear cuts deeper than swords. Fear cuts deeper than swords. Fear cuts deeper than swords.” [69] —thoughts of Arya “I'm the ghost in Harrenhal, she thought. And that night, there was one less name to hate.” [15] —Arya after the killing of Chiswyck “Yes, it's you who ought to run, you and Lord Tywin and the Mountain and Ser Addam and Ser Amory and stupid Ser Lyonel whoever he is, all of you better run or my brother will kill you, he’s a Stark, he’s more wolf than man, and so am I.” [67] —thoughts of Arya “Ser Gregor. Dunsen, Raff the Sweetling, Ser Ilyn, Ser Meryn, Queen Cersei. Valar morghulis, valar morghulis, valar morghulis. [24] —Arya to herself Now all of these moments can be argued as justified or moral. These actions are only my opinion of her darker side. And I believe that Arya is still a good person at heart, but her cavalier attitude towards murder and her obsession with vengeance has diminished her integrity. I hope this helped.

column1: What should everyone know about relationships?
column3: “Experience'' is like a comb that nature gives us when we are bald.Warning: Long Answer ahead. But if you continue to read till the end, it may take you from mundane to a spritual journey. A.Everyone should Learn and Cultivate skills to manage relationships. And for this following may help 1.Reading the first chapter of “How to Win Friends and Influence People” by Dale Carnegie named “If You Want to Gather Honey,Don’t Kick Over the Beehive”. Lesson to be learnt:Don’t criticize, condemn, abuse others even if it is their fault. Because when we condemn others, they become defensive and they try to justify themselves. This would fail the very purpose for which we might have started to criticize or abuse the person. Your abuse will only create communication gap. Your acceptance and right approach can only create a WIN-WIN situation for all and establish peaceful environment consequently. Remember Change starts with YOU and we have no control over others but definitely have over ourselves. 2.Men and Women are different but in certain matters they can be considered very distant that one can be thought to be from Mars and another to be from Venus. There is a beautiful book named “Men are From Mars and Women are From Venus” that throws light on this gender specific aspects and is must read for those who want to build and maintain a healthy relationship with opposite genders. An excerpt from this book is quoted belowWhen a man is distant, rather than assuming he is not interested in her or imagining that he is mad at her, a woman can instead realize that he is just recuperating from a stressful day. With this insight she is free from worry and knows to give him space to be in his “cave” and eventually he will come out. Or when a woman is talking about the problems of her day, rather than assuming she is looking for solutions and giving solutions, a man can instead recognize that she is just needing to talk about her day and as a result she will feel better. With this insight, he is free to relax and listen without trying to interrupt with solutions. As in both of these examples, when we know what is really happening and what is required, relationships become so much easier.3. Reading “The 5 Love languages” by Gary Chapman. According to the Author there are only five ways people express love and want that to be reciprocated i. Words of Affirmation, ii. Quality Time, iii. Receiving Gifts, iv. Acts of Service, v. Physical Touch Following is an excerpt from this bookYour emotional love language and the language of your spouse may be as different as Chinese from English. No matter how hard you try to express love in English, if your spouse understands only Chinese, you will never understand how to love each other. My friend on the plane was speaking the language of “Affirming Words” to his third wife when he said, “I told her how beautiful she was. I told her I loved her. I told her how proud I was to be her husband.” He was speaking love, and he was sincere, but she did not understand his language. Perhaps she was looking for love in his behavior and didn’t see it. Being sincere is not enough. We must be willing to learn our spouse’s primary love language if we are to be effective communicators of love4. Learning to accept the other person involved in relationship as it is and not in the way we want them to be. This acceptance comes when we understand that we are all different having different experiences, different phobias,traumas,different karmic baggages and different destiny. Alone we came into this word, alone we shall leave it. There is no point in creating negative karmic repercussions by unnecessary fights. An excerpt from “How to Win Friends and Influence people” is relevant to be stated hereI often went fishing up in maine during the summer. Personally I am very fond of strawberries and cream, but I have found that for some strange reason, fish prefer worms. So when I went fishing, I didn’t think about what I wanted. I thought about what they wanted. I didn’t bait the hook with strawberries and cream. Rather, I dangled a worm or a grasshopper in front of the fish and said: “Wouldn’t you like to have that?”5. Learning to avoid fights. It is hard to practice as fights evolve out of expectations and we have most expectations on the persons we love. If we try to understand the pain of others that causes them to trigger fight against us, we can easily adopt this behaviour. Doesn't our loved ones deserve our empathy/compassion? Remember charity begins at home- if we fail to show compassion at home how can we be expected to show it on others. Other persons involved will definitely note our care if it is sincere and would reciprocate eventually. Or atleast for the shake of your children, you should learn not to fight. Children when in their formative years find their parents to fight for silly matters, have a tendency to find it hard to create loving relationship in their youth. They may suffer from insecurity and psychological issues that you won't like to invite.Very few are able to break the shackles of their childhood conditioning. Let your child have a healthy environment. 6. Learning some basics of human behaviour. From my childhood I had a strong feeling that I was a good human being. It took me many years(Precisely in the first year of my Engineering) to realise that everyone else is also having the same feelings about themselves. Then naturally question arises why there is so many problems in this world if everyone is good. Answer is obvious-IGNORANCE. But when this realization came something profound happened to me-I found myself forgetting all the misdeeds done by other people very fast, the judgement that people can be bad fall apart- I attributed it to my forgetful memory initially but later discovered that I do not forget their good deeds anyway. But by this I do not mean there is no bad people, there are indeed bad peoples and we should be careful about them, what I mean our near and dear ones are not that bad- there is a reason why we are in a family and what really differentiates a good and bad person is Right Knowledge and Karmic Momentum. (Later I discovered Arjuna expressed similar doubts to lord Krishna in Chapter 3 Verse 36. Rest of the verses of this chapter and in the 4th Chapter Lord Krishna explained the reason and the solutions. Please follow any standard text to learn that but let me quote one of the verses hereधूमेनाव्रियते वह्निर्यथादर्शो मलेन च | यथोल्बेनावृतो गर्भस्तथा तेनेदमावृतम् ||3-38|| Just as a fire is covered by smoke, a mirror is masked by dust, and an embryo is concealed by the womb, similarly one’s knowledge gets shrouded by desire.)And people values the most what they lack or faced scarcity of that in life. For example, for someone who had seen poverty, money is the most important means through which problems of the world can be solved. Person who didn't find their parents in their childhood, Care and Love is the most important means. People's behaviour is nothing but a result of their past experiences. When we understand that behaviour is temporary/changeable but peoples are permanent- peoples are more important than their behaviour, we make a shift in our approach and that helps to improve our relationships. 7. But two good people can come up to create a bad or toxic relationship that is harmful for both or one of them. Jyotisha(Astrology) is a great tool that can solve this riddle of life. But unfortunately finding good astrologer is not easy and learning astrology is very time consuming affair. There is something called Rinannubandh that is the reason for all our relationships-people come to complete their karmik rina(debt) and once that is over they leave apart. Let me tell you a story that I once learned from a Youtube Video.There was a gangster who did all illegal activities like murder, rape etc. One day while running from the police, this ganstar jumped into a flowing river and police couldn't locate him after that. As a twist of destiny, this man reached a holy place while flowing downstream and eventually rescued by monks from water and treated to become normal again but fortunately/unfortunately this gangster lost his memory. With good association, he became a good person and started to think himself as one of the them-as one of the monks and started to live a beautiful life. But one fine morning police was on the door. They recognized him, catched him and put him on the jail. Now this monk is pleading that please understand, I am not a gangster, there is a mistake,I am a monk. This is what happens with every soul who is born on this earth. Everybody thinks that they have done nothing wrong to deserve all this and everybody is a monk,everybody is a Sadhu.People change in their personal attributes many times in a single lifetime. So it is not quite unnatural to think a good person who is somehow suffering did something bad in past lives to invite such sufferings and when the astrological chart confirms that no doubt can remain thereafter. 8. We should not ignore the physical(Food, Sleep, Sex) or emotional needs (Love, Respect, Support, Care, Appreciation etc) of the other person involved to avoid disaster in relationship. Remember greatest desire of human being is to be appreciated. Although Money can not buy happiness but absence of it is a gurantee of misery and unhappiness- so do not ignore the pain of the earning member of the family-for some money is half the battle of life, for some it is full battle of life and few are lucky enough to find it easily. Right communication can prevent any disaster. Understanding other people's expectations and letting them know ours is all required but in a healthy and graceful manner. Uncommunicative expectations are very dangerous for any relationship as that expectations finds its expression in some bad conductSome people keep bottling their emotions only to outbrust in an inappropriate time and inappropriate manner and problem with bottling is that other person might be clueless what is going on inside and would eventually add up to more negative poison in the bottle. Let proper communication end this bottling habits to ensure a healthy and win-win situation in life. 9.Spoken Words are very very powerful. It can damage any relationship beyond recovery. Don't let it flow according to your mood. Your mood can become normal again but spoken words cannot be.And we should resist the temptations to start giving advice because most people can't take advice due to their ego or karmic momentum. And No amount of advice works when people are in mental turmoil. When we advise someone,we expect them to follow and this expectation may create unnecessary tension as we may lack practical experience(how it feels for other person) in implementation of that advice. Helping hands are much better than the helping mouth. 10. Do not break trust under any/most circumstances. Trust is like a glass, once broken can not be restored to its original form. When we do something wrong, most of the cases, acceptance is the easy solution that ends the topic then and there. But if we hide the truth when asked for, it can do double damage as truth can not be kept hidden for a long duration. Half truth can sometime become more dangerous than false statement, it keeps curiosity of the other person alive and doesn't let the topic to end. Every good human being knows “To Err is human” and No one is perfect. Some people even lie for apparently silly matters and eventually end up being in a toxic relationship. 11. Internet, Social media and Entertainment industry are polluting the minds of all by glorifying adultery, extra martial affairs, illicit relationships etc. But before you let the beast inside you overpower your good self, ponder over the following verse of Bhagbat Gitaकर्मणो ह्यपि बोद्धव्यं बोद्धव्यं च विकर्मण: | अकर्मणश्च बोद्धव्यं गहना कर्मणो गति: ||4-17|| You must understand the nature of all three—1.Recommended action(Karma: Fruitive Activities within the boundary of moral and ethical guidelines that binds the soul to the three Gunas and birth and death), 2.Wrong/Inauspicious action(Vikarma: Fruitive Activities against ethics and moral values which binds the soul with IGNORANCE and leads to rebirth in the lower species in future), and 3. Inaction(Akarma: Where Fruits of Action are renounced or offered to God which liberates the soul from karmic bondages). Profound(Gahana) is the manner(Gati) of Action(Karmana).Adultery is a crime even if it is allowed in penal code. When we cheat on somebody, that person may suffer identity crisis as he/she would lose a sense of belonging, trust, confidence, motivation etc and emotional pain consequently. So many broken relationships, broken marriages, and unhappy families can be attributed to this adultery. Remember we can escape the law but not our Karma. So before getting into a relationship,it is wise to understand the moral responsibilities. The pain we inflict on others would eventually return to us-may be in this life itself or may be in next life where we would be wondering why such things happen to us despite being a saintly person.
