column1: What is a BPD person to do when they have lost the only person that gave them attention and validation?
column3: First things first: if you are not currently working with a qualified mental health professional, seek one out. Validation needs to come from within and a qualified mental health professional can help give you the tools you need to start improving that aspect of your life. Other than that - it's hard to deal with the loss of a critical member of your support network. Devastating, even. Use the resources available from either a local support group for bpd, your qualified mental health professional, your family, friends, or online communities (such as Online Support Groups for your Health Challenges ) to help fill the gaps in your support network in the interim.

column1: What is a story you would like to share about something bad that happened in your life, from which something good came?
column3: Unlike the excellent anonymous answer Someone anonymous's answer to What is a story you would like to share about something bad that happened in your life, from which something good came? I’ve not experienced the loss of a child. However, I have lost family members and every loss is a tragedy. Rather than diminish the seriousness of each loss, they each come with consolations. Losing my nana when I was a very young left an emptiness that was hard to resolve, particularly as I was only a very small child too young to understand fully or attend the funeral. However, dealing with that loss made things a little easier when my own mother passed away, particularly since I had to give a eulogy. Although the loss of every family member is sad and comes with a desperately wrenching sensation, the funeral and time with family reminds me of how wonderful they each were and what a blessing they’ve been to my life. I certainly wouldn’t wish to have not experienced their life, even if the separation and sense of loss after they died saddens me. I wouldn’t be sad if knowing them hadn’t been so wonderful. Not necessarily something good in itself, but something that reminds me that bad things are the other side of good ones. After the death of my mother, my father ran a cancer support group for many years. The experience of his loss encouraged him to reach out to others in need and enable them share their resources to aid and comfort one another. Unless you’ve gone through this experience yourself, you don’t know what it is like. Sometimes it’s good to get together with other who know what you are going through. A word with someone who’s gone through it before or who is also going through this can be enough to give courage.
column9: Thank you for sharing Greg. What a great example of the suffering we may endure, and the positive that can come from it. I lost my father to cancer along with several other family members and a good friend.

column1: How can victims of crypto scams effectively document their losses to aid in the recovery process?
column3: The ensuing emotional devastation of a crypto scam experience becomes a massive challenge for victims to handle. Victims frequently must deal with financial troubles together with a mix of confusion and betrayal. Being exposed to a crypto scam puts you in the company of other victims while appropriate recovery actions will support your path to recovery. The primary step in recovering from financial loss requires that you create proper documentation. You can collect the required information through these following steps that will help your research:Begin by gathering every written document that pertains to the scam activities. Every message you exchanged with the scammer should be gathered including text messages and written emails and online direct messages. The smallest casual conversations with scammers offer important facts and details about their actions. Maintain comprehensive transaction documentation which combines a time-stamped list of all transactions with their financial details as well as the cryptocurrency usage. Keep all information about your wallet and your exchange platform ready for retrieval along with wallet and exchange details. Creating a definite sequence of events becomes possible through this process. Screen captures act as highly effective visual proof in situations like this. Screen capture each aspect related to the investment scam starting from the website through advertisements and every social media platform that initiated your investment. The fraudulent evidence can be verified through documentation. Maintain a written log to record all that has occurred. Record the complete scam progression as well as its emotional and financial consequences on you. The written documentation will help you clarify your thinking process and it remains valuable evidence if you need to take legal steps. Engaging with support groups enables you to access both support along with critical information regarding how individuals documented their losses. Local support groups together with online forums serve as outstanding resources for information. If you wish to report scams or seek professional help you should consult qualified experts who will determine what kinds of documentation you need.A structured system for storing all essential materials simplifies the challenging circumstances. A digital folder or physical binder containing organized documentation will prove valuable during case presentation situations. As an important step your loss documentation process needs completion yet you must prioritize supporting your mental health throughout this challenge. Supportive friends together with family members should be your chosen companions and you should never hold back from seeking professional help if the stress becomes too much to manage. As you travel through recovery you can reach healing through taking each step separately which may lead to a positive conclusion..

column1: How do I overcome the death of my girlfriend?
column3: Find a support group for family members dealing with death you can lean on. Google Grief Support Groups in your area. Find a grief therapist to talk to - even if it’s just a few times, they will have tools to help you.

column1: Why does my boyfriend ignore me since his father died?
column3: The loss of a parent is a lot worse than one would ever expect depending on how close you are or how sudden the death is. Everyone deals with death differently, the lost of a parent can be a milestone in life whether the person has not lived up to his or her expectations or their parents expectations yet. No one knows how they are going to react to the death of a parent until it happens. I am sure your boyfriend is depressed and angry and does not know nor want to express his emotions. I am sure his lack of attention doesn't have to deal with you or your behavior. I lost my father a few years ago and I was angry and felt no one new what I was going through. The one thing I suggest and helps with me and is necessary to heal is to go through the seven stages of grieving. I am sure you can get a copy by googling the phrase and many churches have pamphlets or support groups. Hopefully the opportunity arises where you or a close friend or family member can mention this to him. He needs to go through the pain and not around it or healing and not cover up the pain or it will linger and could get worse. Stay positive and don’t over impose but show you are there for him.

column1: Why is it taking me so long to move on from an abusive relationship with someone who has BPD/NPD?
column3: Relationships with psychopaths take an unusually long time to recover from. Survivors often find themselves frustrated because they haven't healed as fast as they'd like. They also end up dealing with friends & therapists who give them judgmental advice about how it's "time to move on". Whether you were in a long-term marriage or a quick summer fling, the recovery process will be the same when it comes to a psychopathic encounter. It takes 12-24 months to get your heart back in a good place, and even after that, you might have tough days. I certainly do! The important thing here is to stop blaming yourself. Stop wishing it would go faster. Stop thinking that the psychopath somehow "wins" if you're still hurting. They are out of the picture now. This journey is about you. If you come to peace with the extended timeline, you'll find this experience a lot more pleasant. You can settle in, make some friends, and get cozy with this whole recovery thing. So why is it taking so long? You were in love Yes, it was manufactured love. Yes, your personality was mirrored and your dreams manipulated. But you were in love. It's the strongest human emotion & bond in the world, and you felt it with all your heart. It is always painful to lose someone you loved - someone you planned to be with for the rest of your life. The human spirit must heal from these love losses. Regardless of your abuser's intentions, your love was still very real. It will take a great deal of time and hope to pull yourself out of the standard post-breakup depression. You were in desperate love Here's where we branch off from regular breakups. Psychopaths manufacture desperation & desire. You probably worked harder for this relationship than any other, right? You put more time, energy, and thought into it than ever before. And in turn, you were rewarded with the nastiest, most painful experience of your life. In the idealization phase, they showered you with attention, gifts, letters, and compliments. Unlike most honeymoon phases, they actually pretended to be exactly like you in every way. Everything you did was perfect to them. This put you on Cloud 9, preparing you for the identity erosion. You began to pick up on all sorts of hints that you might be replaced at any time. This encouraged your racing thoughts, ensuring that this person was on your mind every second of the day. This unhinged, unpredictable lifestyle is what psychopaths hope to create with their lies, gas-lighting, and triangulation. By keeping them on your mind at all times, you fall into a state of desperate love. This is unhealthy, and not a sign that the person you feel so strongly about is actually worthy of your love. Your mind convinces you that if you feel so powerfully, then they must be the only person who will ever make you feel that way. And when you lose that person, your world completely falls apart. You enter a state of panic & devastation. The Chemical Reaction Psychopaths have an intense emotional & sexual bond over their victims. This is due to their sexual magnetism, and the way they train your mind to become reliant upon their approval. By first adoring you in every way, you let down your guard and began to place your self worth in this person. Your happiness started to rely on this person's opinion on you. Happiness is a chemical reaction going off in your brain - dopamine and receptors firing off to make you feel good. Like a drug, the psychopath offers you this feeling in full force to begin with. But once you become reliant on it, they begin to pull back. Slowly, you need more and more to feel that same high. You do everything you can to hang onto it, while they are doing everything in their power to keep you just barely starved. Triangulation There are thousands of support groups for survivors of infidelity. It leaves long-lasting insecurities and feelings of never being good enough. It leaves you constantly comparing yourself to others. That pain alone takes many people out there years to recover from. Now compare that to the psychopath's triangulation. Not only do they cheat on you - they happily wave it in your face. They brag about it, trying to prove how happy they are with your replacement. They carry none of the usual shame & guilt that comes with cheating. They are thrilled to be posting pictures and telling their friends how happy they are. I cannot even begin to explain how emotionally damaging this is after once being the target of their idealization. The triangulation alone will take so much time to heal from. You have encountered pure evil Everything you once understood about people did not apply to this person. During the relationship, you tried to be compassionate, easy-going, and forgiving. You never could have known that the person you loved was actively using these things against you. It just doesn't make any sense. No typical person is ready to expect that, and so we spend our time projecting a normal human conscience onto them, trying to explain away their inexplicable behavior. But once we discover psychopathy, sociopathy, or narcissism, that's when everything starts to change. We begin to feel disgusted - horrified that we let this darkness into our lives. Everything clicks and falls into place. All of the "accidental" or "insensitive" behavior finally makes sense. You try to explain this to friends and family members - no one really seems to get it. This is why validation matters. When you come together with others who have experienced the same thing as you, you discover you were not crazy. You were not alone in this inhuman experience. It takes a great deal of time to come to terms with this personality disorder. You end up having to let go of your past understanding of human nature, and building it back up from scratch. You realize that people are not always inherently good. You begin to feel paranoid, hyper-vigialant, and anxious. The healing process is about learning to balance this new state of awareness with your once trusting spirit. Your spirit is deeply wounded After the eventual abandonment, most survivors end up feeling a kind of emptiness that cannot even be described as depression. It's like your spirit has completely gone away. You feel numb to everything and everyone around you. The things that once made you happy now make you feel absolutely nothing at all. You worry that your encounter with this monster has destroyed your ability to empathize, feel and care. I believe this is what takes the longest time to recover from. It feels hopeless at first, but your spirit is always with you. Damaged, for sure, but never gone. As you begin to discover self-respect & boundaries, it slowly starts to find its voice again. It feels safe opening up, peeking out randomly to say hello. You will find yourself grateful to be crying again, happy that your emotions seem to be returning. This is great, and it will start to become more and more consistent. Ultimately, you will leave this experience with an unexpected wisdom about the people around you. Your spirit will return stronger than ever before, refusing to be treated that way again. You may encounter toxic people throughout your life, but you won't let them stay for very long. You don't have time for mind games & manipulation. You seek out kind, honest, and compassionate individuals. You know you deserve nothing less. This new found strength is the greatest gift of the psychopathic experience. And it is worth every second of the recovery process, because it will serve you for the rest of your life. If you're worried that your recovery process is taking too long, please stop worrying. You've been through hell and back - there is no quick fix for that. And what's more, when all is said and done, these few years will be some of the most important years of your life.
column9: What an amazing and beautifully thought out answer. This what I’ve needed to hear! The struggle is unbearable at times especially when surrounded by people who don’t have nor want to understand the feelings that happen as a result of abuse. Thank you!

column1: My dog is dying, how can I live without him?
column3: I have a ten year old dog, going on eleven this January. I don't think she has much longer. I got my dog at five weeks of age when I was just starting a career in veterinary medicine. For a long time she was the only family and friend that I had. She was diagnosed with hip dysplasia at 6 months old. I was told she would need surgery when she was full grown. At two years, she was active and showed no pain, surgery was not necessary. Two years ago, she struggled to get around in the cold months. I thought it would be her time to go. I had xrays taken of her hips and the veterinarian who was also my coworker told me that he wasn't sure how she was walking. Her hip joints were completely deteriorated. But she had a healthy amount of lean muscle that kept her going. She was still eating and drinking and still had good days. That night she chased six dear several blocks into the creek with my husband in tow struggling to keep up. This past October she tore her ACL. She's had complications with anesthesia during dental cleanings so surgical repair is out of the question. I scheduled the appointment to have her put to sleep and when I took her to the vet, an old friend of mine, my dog started jumping on everyone and playing with the other dogs. She came home with me and though she's not the same dog she was years ago, I know she's not ready to give up. It's hard to watch her age and at a faster rate than me. But I've grown to, I'm now married and have a five year old son and I am 3 months pregnant. Only you will know when your dog is ready to go. Some dogs will die on there own at home and not suffer. There are vets that will do in home euthanasia. Some pet owners prefer to be with their pet when they pass on, others prefer to keep the memory of their pet alive and breathing. No choice is wrong. You are losing a family member, someone that has always been there, that you see usually more often than other people in your life. There are support groups for dealing with the loss of a pet. Don't be ashamed to grieve. You are not alone.
column9: I just received a notification on this. My girl I spoke of passed away earlier this month. She kept going, kept pulling on her leash until her last day. She ate a bunch of treats, she has just had a bath 2 days prior to passing along with a brand new bed. My husband came home went to walk her and she took her last breathe. I was in the bathroom when my husband called me. She looked so peaceful. I've cried, I've smiled while remembering her funny moments with friends and coworkers and I've cried again. I'll be getting her paw print tattooed on my wrist and and eventually her portrait on my thigh. I will hold onto her memory and remember everyday she was there for me. She gave me a reason to live and left me with a beautiful family of my own that I didn't have when she first came into my life. I tried to take my life for the first time at 12 when I was teased in school. My breaking point was losing a dog then. I'm 36 now, and I have the strength I need right now. She gave me 15 great years. I couldn't be more thankful.

column1: What are the most difficult and useful things people have to learn in their 20s?
column3: In your twenties.... 1) Your parents or close relatives begin to hit their forties or fifties or sixties, and begin to get sick. And they begin to become unwell, or the family finances begin to get stretched (parents nearing retirement, three kids in college and having to pay fees etc) and things begin to happen. You're not a child anymore so you are included in adult conversations about money, health and the care of relatives. Your family members may expect you to contribute to the discussion and possibly also contribute in other ways (financially, if you've got a job etc). Previously when you were a child you were always the first person people thought of when bad things happened, and the first priority was usually for support to be offered to you because you were 'too young to handle it'. When you hit your twenties, the shields are lifted and you'll have to be privy to the difficulties and problems hitting your family circle and instead of being the supported, you become the supporter. You may be the only person capable of driving your grandmother to hospital for appointments, etc. You may be the only person your parents will talk to about their financial troubles. And people expect you to be able to handle it. You're old enough now. Some of your family members may pass away during this time. Some of your friends may pass away. I've had both happen. You'll have to deal with it, and sometimes be the one who takes charge when others are distraught. You'll have to not only learn how to deal emotionally as well as practically with death and loss, but also how to do this without the support that you would have had when you were a child. 2) You have to change the way you view relationships with your girlfriend/boyfriend, friends as well as your family. Often this is a time when you start working, buying a house on your own, or a car, starting a family and so on. When you were 18, not wanting commitment was fine. When you're 28, your girlfriend may leave you if you're not forthcoming with the ring because she wants to settle down and find some stability and you're not offering it. When you were 18, spending entire weekends smoking pot with your friends was great. When you're 28 with student loans to pay and a job that you could lose if you show up high, hanging out with people who insist you do the things you don't want to do is just asking for it. You may have to leave a group of friends. The weed example is more drastic than others, but often the friends who drag you down do it subtly, without even realising it themselves. Every time you want to go and apply for a new job, or take a new course, they might laugh at you, or say 'but that will leave you less time to spend with us'. And eventually you'll look back a bit late and realise that you should have taken those opportunities because now you've been passed over for a promotion because you're not qualified enough etc. When you were 18, your parents were a massive drag and you couldn't wait to get out of the house. When you're 28, your dad may know how to fix the boiler without you having to fork out money to get someone else to do it. Your mom may be able to babysit your kids. Both of them will now have great experiences that you can gain from them - they can be something like walking quoras. Of course this may not apply to everyone, but certainly since I hit my twenties I realised how much my family's support means to me. 3) When bad things happen, they hit you harder, and you bounce back less well. When we were kids, if we ran out into the playground and fell down and grazed our knees, everyone flocked over to take care of us, and the wound would heal in a few days and it would all be forgotten, and we would be out and running again before the day was out. Now that you're older, the worst case scenario is much more grim than when you were a kid. If you get fired from your job, you could stand to be unable to pay your rent and end up in debt. And say you do lose your job, and you have to start from scratch and do everything again to get back to where you were before, you don't forget what happened. Some people don't get to bounce back from the bottom of the pit as easily as others, and end up unhappy and negative for months or years, sometimes for the rest of their lives. The secret to getting through it is to keep looking forward and trying hard. If you're not used to this then it will be an added challenge for you to keep convincing yourself there is a point to waking up in the morning. It's the ultimate challenge, and one that is almost prerequisite in order for you to actually become an adult. How old you are doesn't measure maturity as well as how many times bad things have happened and how you've dealt with these things each time. Of course the question asked means I've had to talk about fairly depressing things, but i think it's important to remember that it's a time of experiment, joy and new experiences, so enjoy what you can, when you can!

column3: I am very sorry for your loss. We lost our family doggie, Cyndi, 2 1/2 months ago. Kidney & Pancreas Failure. She was with us 14 yrs too. Our Fur-Babies r not just “ a dog.” They r family-members. We have cried & cried too. Believe me, Time is a big healer. Flow with your grief. Give in to your grief. column1: Adult How can you deal with the sudden death of a friend?
column3: Gather together with others with whom you shared the friendship of the dead person and share your loss as a group. Find ways to honor the persons memory that remind you all of happier times. Give yourself permission to grieve, do not feel you have to be the strong one who supports all the others. Find someway to make something good happen as a result of your friend's death. If the friend was living far from home and it will not be possible for you and your local co-friends of the person to attend the funeral you might consider having a simple memorial event were you are. Write letters to your friends family telling them about the qualities of your friend that were important to you, and share with them your sense of loss and the pride you have in having known their family member. Create a scrapbook together with all your friends who knew the person who died. Each person can contribute what pictures they have then have copies made for everyone so you each have more then you could have created on your own.

column1: Would you use a pet loss coach to help you work through grief over loss of your beloved pet?
column3: If you feel you need it and can afford it, sure. There are also online resources for coping with loss -- look at A PetLoss Grief Support Community. Loss of a pet is serious loss -- most of us spend more time with our pets than we do with anyone other than our spouse. And, if you don't have children, it's very common to bond with the pet as a surrogate child. Of course you feel devastated when you lose them. It's normal and natural to grieve. As a long-time pet owner, and as a foster of at risk cats, I can usually come to terms with the loss on my own. But, part of that is by recognizing that it is a real and significant loss. I'm surrounded by pet lovers, so I have a stronger support group than most -- for example, a friend's cat got a bad diagnosis on Saturday and we all spent Sunday with her to help her consider her options. If you don't have friends who understand, pet loss is even harder -- you know you've lost a family member, but society views it as a minor loss. (Although, you may find that if you reach out to friends who do have pets, they will rally around you.) I also had one loss that was very very hard to deal with. Long story, but boils down to a friend who was petsitting gave insulin to the wrong cat. And she died. It was horrible for us, for him, for the cat, and I had a really hard time accepting it. It didn't occur to me to go to a pet loss coach, but I can see where having someone to talk to might have helped. I hope you find the support you need and find solace in the memories of the good times you had together.

column1: How do you heal from having your mom pass away?
column3: Well, it’s definitely hard to lose a parent. And I don’t think any of us can imagine fully how we’ll deal with it until we’re actually facing the situation. But, as difficult as grieving the loss of a loved one is, it’s not impossible to get through it. I believe what’s important is letting yourself experience the range of emotions you’re bound to feel during a time like this (not bottling them up). And sometimes it can help if you look intogrief support groups. For instance, there’s an organization called GriefShare that hosts groups all over the country. Also, many people find therapy helpful as well. So, if you’re ever struggling to move past a loss of this nature, consider talking to a counselor. Lastly, surround yourself with the love of other family members and friends. Don’t be afraid to seek and accept their help. That can make a huge difference in your recovery…

column1: Adult How do I deal with family feuds at a funeral? I have no relationship with my family and I have anxiety about going to the funeral.
column3: I would bring a supportive friend, who could help me deal with any problems that arise. I would stay low-key, show up right before the service starts, and if I felt things were going badly, I would leave as soon as it ended. In my experience, emotions may be running high, so it is not a good time to rehash old issues, or try and mend fences. If there are some family members that you still have a relationship with, try to speak to them privately, instead of in a group. Sorry for your loss, and good luck.

column1: How do you help yourself and family members deal with ambiguous grief?
column3: Not sure what you mean by ambiguous grief. There's complicated grief, which is when you may be grieving more than one loss or have other issues in amongst the grief. But I'll take a stab at it anyway. Grief in general has its own timeline, and everyone grieves differently. Some may cry a lot and want to talk about it, and others may not. meet each family member where she is in the process. grief groups may help, hospices have them as do many churches. you may find different books helpful. there are loads, and many are specific to the type of grief; spouse, parents, child, etc. the relationship between the family member and the deceased is important too; closer family members will take it harder. cause of death makes a difference too; if someone committed suicide or was murdered, that brings in a whole set of different issues. generally be supportive, and don't forget to take care of yourself. You're grieving too.

column1: How do I recover from losing family?
column3: When you lose a family member, you learn to accept that grief comes in waves. It knocks you down and you pick yourself up. There are several good online grief support groups that can help you.

column1: What role does community support play in helping individuals cope with loss and grief?
column3: I speak from experience with the opposite. In January and February 2023 I was anticipating the loss of my mother. My sole family member and sole loved one. Losing the most important person is hard. It was very hard and a dark place to be in. I had no support from anyone. I was alone when waiting endless hours. It was a shock that I had no one to turn to. Former “friends” have let us down so badly. On the night of losing her, I called people who'd told me they would be there for me. They weren't there for me. I had to return to an empty house all by myself, knowing I had no loved ones to live for. I had searched for support groups. I had even requested (grief and social) support from 5 oncology-related social workers at the hospital! The day following my mothers death, I actively began seeking support groups to offer my help, to no avail! I am a Master of Laws, I have worked in medical care when I was still in high school, there is much that I can offer. But the social cohesion in our neoliberal country (The Netherlands) is at its lowest point. If you cannot see for yourself when dealing with bereavement, they leave you to rot.

column1: My husband was a TCS employee. He passed away a few months back. Does anyone know about death benefits?
column3: I'm truly sorry to hear about your loss. Coping with the passing of a loved one is undoubtedly challenging, and understanding the practical aspects like death benefits can add to the stress. In the case of a TCS (Tata Consultancy Services) employee's demise, there are certain benefits that the family may be entitled to.Gratuity: TCS typically provides gratuity, which is a lump sum payment made to the nominee or legal heir of the deceased employee. The amount is calculated based on the years of service and last drawn salary.Provident Fund (PF): The employee's PF accumulations can be claimed by the nominee or legal heir. This includes the employee's contribution along with the employer's contribution and interest accrued.Life Insurance: Many companies, including TCS, offer life insurance coverage to their employees. If your husband had a life insurance policy through TCS, the nominee or beneficiary can claim the death benefit.Employee Compensation Policies: TCS may have additional employee compensation policies in place. It's crucial to review your husband's employment contract, as it may contain information about any additional benefits payable in the event of death.Pension Benefits: If your husband was entitled to a pension, you may be eligible for pension benefits. TCS may provide a pension to the spouse or dependent children, depending on the company's policy.To navigate the process smoothly, consider taking the following steps:Contact TCS HR Department: Reach out to TCS's Human Resources department to inform them about your husband's demise. They will guide you through the necessary procedures and paperwork.Nomination Forms: If your husband had filled out nomination forms for the company's benefits, those forms will be crucial in determining the beneficiaries.Legal Assistance: If needed, seek legal advice to ensure all procedures are followed correctly and to understand your rights and entitlements.In case of death of employee-1) Group Life Insurance: Its 10 times of your annual salary package or Rs. 1 crore, whichever is less. Below is for Employee and his family- (You have to nominate the family members for the health insurance for the financial year.Only those family members will receive below benefits. Your spouse will be covered by default) 2) Group Health Insurance:Hospitalisation(cashless/Reimbursement)-> Up to 90k for each of the family members insured.Up to 7 lacs floating cover for family (Utilised in case your individual cover of 90k is fully utilised), Domiciliary->5K per insured (for domiciliary expenses). Grieving is a personal journey, and it's essential to take the time you need. While dealing with the practical aspects of death benefits, don't hesitate to lean on your support network or seek professional assistance to make this process more manageable.

column1: Adult My father recently passed away after fighting Cancer for 18 months. How can I best help others going through the same situation?
column3: I’m sorry about your loss. It’s wonderful that one of your reactions is to think about helping others. Let me ask you: what are your ideas of how you’d like to help? Are you wanting to help people experiencing cancer themselves, others going through having a family member with cancer, or people who have experienced the loss of a family member (through cancer, or otherwise)? Do you feel a call to work in a particular way to help others with similar experiences to yours? I can think of a number of things you could do, and only you can decide what feels right for you, with your talents, free time, opportunities, and interests. You could volunteer for a cancer support organization, or a hospice, or a hospital, helping either people with cancer, or their families, or both. You could help give respite care to families, or be a speaker for a program on grief & loss. You could organize fundraising events for cancer research (in general, or for a particular kind of cancer) or to help a particular family, or perhaps for prevention or early detection efforts. You can join already existing groups. Or on a different level, you could blog about your experiences and be an online support for others. Or inquire at your own church or in other social groups to see if there are individuals or families dealing with life-threatening illness who might benefit from a listening ear or a errand-runner or a driver to appointments or a cook or someone who could clean the house. If you found a lot of need, you could organize a support group for a particular family, or start a group that provides support & help to anyone in the area who has a certain diagnosis. So, I hope this is helpful for you in thinking about how you can be helpful to others!

column1: What is a family?
column3: Definitions Because "love" and "family" can have many different meanings, it's important to know how they're being used in the phrase "family love." What Is Family? A family is a group of people that function as a unit. The most common definition of family is a group that's made up of parents and their children living together. This is the definition we're talking about most often when we speak of family love. Family can also mean all the descendants of a common ancestor. Some people consider their friends like family. However, when we speak of family love, the love you have with your friends might or might not fit, depending on what type of relationship you have. What Is Love? Love is a word that's been used in so many ways it's nearly lost its meaning. We may say we love ice cream or skiing when what we mean is that we enjoy it. Love is properly used as romantic or sexual feelings and behaviors. In the context of family love, love refers to bonds characterized by deep affection, respect, loyalty, and healthy attachment. How Is Family Love Unique? Family love is what it is because family relationships are different from other types of bonds. The following characteristics of family love set it apart from other types of love relationships. You Can't Always Choose Your Family You typically choose the person you want to start a family with when you're an adult. You might choose children to adopt or bring into your family. If children are born into the family, your only choices are to love them or abdicate your responsibilities.But, most children have no choice about who is in the family group. You usually don't get to choose your siblings, and you certainly don't get to choose your parents. Yet, despite these limitations, family love still happens more often than not. It isn't always healthy love, but it is a deep connection nonetheless. You Face The Challenges Of Living Together Living in a family unit usually means sharing a living space. Privacy is limited because of your proximity. You have to share certain belongings, such as dishes, appliances, and furniture. You compete for the other family members' attention. What's more, to keep that space peaceful, each family member needs to respect the rights of the others to whatever degree is possible. For example, an infant is a member of the family, but they aren't capable of understanding how to respect other family members. The more mature that person gets, though, the more they need to be mindful of how their behavior affects the others. What Strongly Affects One Family Member Affects The Others When one member of a family experiences a profound loss, the other members of the family who live with them are usually affected by that person's distress. The family member who has lost their job or a friend typically expresses their emotion in some way, whether they intend to or not. Their behavior might change, and they may have less capacity to manage daily living. The other family members feel the effects directly or indirectly. You Have Family Traditions Nearly every family has some family traditions together. Family traditions may relate to holidays, but they can also be associated with other special days, situations, or rites of passage. As long as all the family members follow the traditions of the family, everyone knows what to expect. However, when something disrupts a family tradition, family members may feel disappointed or even distressed. You Share Family History Families of parents and their biological children share a family history that goes back for generations. Even if a child is adopted, they share the history of what has happened in the family since they became a part of it. The history of the family influences the current relationships between family members, so it's important that everyone resolves old hurts and misunderstandings to have a healthy family love. What Healthy Family Love Looks Like Families can be quite different from each other and still be built on family love. Healthy families are similar in certain aspects of family love, though. It's Unconditional Love Healthy family love is unconditional. No matter what the other family members say, do, or feel, you still love them for who they are. You might have completely different opinions and political views. You might strongly disapprove of something another family member does. You might even have to remove yourself from the family situation. In a sense, they are still your family and always will be.You Show Respect For Each Other When you healthily love your family members, you show your respect through your words and actions. You show family love by honoring the other family members rights, even when you don't agree with their choices. You Work Together To Achieve Family Goals Just as each person can have their own goals, families also have group goals they work together to achieve. For example, a family might decide together to go on a camping vacation. Each member may need to help by arranging their schedules, packing up what they need for the trip, and being present and ready to go at the agreed-on time. You Communicate With Each Other Effective communication is vital for healthy family love. Unless each person communicates their needs, the other family members aren't likely to help them satisfy anything beyond basic survival needs. Family members use words and gestures to express both their concerns and their approval. You Enjoy Activities Together Families that enjoy activities as a group build a stronger family love. Whether you're going on an outing or spending the evening playing board games, the interactions between you bring you closer together. You Help Each Other Your family can provide a strong support system for you. If you have healthy family love, you contribute by helping other families meet their needs and satisfy their desires. Unless you're the parent of a child, you don't take on responsibility for them; you offer your assistance because you want to make their life easier. Building Family Love Healthy family love is a choice that starts with the parents. It isn't something that happens without thought and dedication. There are several ways to build healthy family love throughout the lifespan of the family. Form Healthy Attachments As parents, you have a unique opportunity to teach your children how to have a healthy, secure attachment. By being a responsive caregiver, you can start the secure attachment that research has shown leads to higher social functioning later in life. Along with better mental and physical health, a secure attachment gives your child a greater capacity to form healthy attachments with others.Take Responsibility For What's Yours To Do Each person in a well-functioning family takes responsibility for what is theirs to do. The parents need to make sure everyone's physical and emotional needs are met until the children assume responsibility or become an adult. Sometimes it can be hard to figure out what you need to take responsibility for and what you need to leave for another family member to do. Talking to other parents, you admire or attending a parenting support group can help you sort out who needs to be responsible for what. If you're still confused about it, a therapist can help you sort it out. Encourage Healthy Development And Independence As your child gets older, they develop new skills and abilities. They have more opportunities to explore their world as they develop the independence needed to choose their activities outside the home. As a parent, you need to encourage their development into an emotionally strong, healthy adult. Give them the tools they need to learn. Give them support as they find their own identity. Allow them to move away from you emotionally at times while being there as a safe base when they need you. Be Prepared For Changes In families with growing children, family love changes as they mature. For example, during adolescence, children and parents renegotiate their bond so the children can move toward independence without completely disconnecting from their parents. Value Each Family Member No family member is more important than any other in a healthy family. Each family member is valued as a person in general, and as the unique person, they are. Show each family member that you appreciate them every day. You don't always have to say the words, but it's helpful to state the sentiment verbally at least occasionally. You can also show it through gestures, facial expressions, and touch. Be Kind Kindness is a quality that's sometimes undervalued. Kindness, though, is a hallmark of healthy family love. Not hurting others unnecessarily has to be balanced with self-esteem for authentic kindness. Be kind as a family member. If you're an adult, encourage your family members to be kind to each other. Make Time For Each Other A family that lives under the same roof but spends no time together doesn't have the opportunity to develop and maintain healthy family bonds. If the parents are so busy with their adult lives that they ignore their children, the family can't be healthy, and the children always suffer. Give your family members enough of your time to feel a strong connection with them. Practice Forgiveness When you don't forgive someone outside your family, it's easy to let that person drift out of your life. However, when a family member has wronged you, it's much more difficult to give up that relationship. You need to forgive your family members to reestablish healthy bonds after the conflict has been resolved.Develop Healthy Communication Skills Conflict resolution is a major challenge for most families. Healthy families increase family love and understanding by learning communication skills. As a parent, you need to teach your children how to communicate effectively without disrespecting others. When families communicate well, there are fewer conflicts, and the conflicts that happen can be resolved. Building family love is a full-time and often stressful job. If you find that you can't manage family relationships in a healthy way, it might help you to talk to a therapist for additional help. A therapist can help you by teaching you communications skills, helping you deal with unhealthy prior attachments, and building healthy self-esteem for yourself and among your family members. If you need this type of help, you can talk to a licensed counselor for online family therapy. Family love isn't a myth. You can have the kind of family love that makes life more bearable and ultimately satisfying. When you do, everyone in the family can benefit.

column1: Is Brexit going to make the UK more powerful?
column3: Is Brexit going to make the UK more powerful? Well let’s see how the US works with you, you know with all “Special relationship” and all. Just take a look at the recent problem with Bombardier in Northern Ireland. The US announced tariffs of 280% after Boeing complained about them getting a huge contract from Delta (despite the fact that Delta said that they wanted new planes not the second hand ones that Boeing were offering that weren’t even up to spec). When Bombardier appealed they were hit with an additional 20% taking the import tariff to 300%. So how did the the UK Government deal with that? They didn’t, they couldn’t. What were/are they going to do. Stop export to the US? Really, with a president that is all about “putting America First”. Now, how did the EU deal with it. Well they didn’t have to. Why, because of Brexit, they don’t have to deal with it. After all the UK is leaving the EU, and these things take time to resolve and by the time they resolve it, the UK will be out of the EU, so why bother. However the EU did do something different. (Spoiler Alert - Sarcasm incoming) Oh yes, Brexit is going to make Britain more powerful, it’s going to be so powerful, people will be amazed, it’s going to be yuge, it’s going to be a beautiful thing. EDIT: I wasn’t careful enough when I posted the above, concerning Bombardier, as was pointed out by a couple of readers. He.they are correct, Airbus bought into Bombardier. My mistake was to just assume, (I know , I know, never assume) that like quite a few, possibly many Europeans, when I/we hear the Company name Airbus, we automatically assume EU, because there would have not been any Airbus if it wasn’t for the EU. It is a company that is a joint venture, started by the various European companies in the industry: “Today's company is the product of international consolidation in the European aerospace industry tracing back to the formation of the Airbus Industrie GIE consortium in 1970. In 2000 the European Aeronautic Defence and Space Company (EADS) NV was established. In addition to other subsidiaries pertaining to security and space activities, EADS owned 100% of the pre-existing Eurocopter SA, established in 1992, as well as 80% of Airbus Industrie GIE. In 2001, Airbus Industrie GIE was reorganised as Airbus SAS, a simplified joint-stock company. In 2006, EADS acquired BAE Systems's remaining 20% of Airbus. EADS NV was renamed Airbus Group NV and SE in 2014 and 2015, respectively. Due to the dominance of the Airbus SAS division within Airbus Group SE, these parent and subsidiary companies were merged in January 2017, keeping the name of the parent company. The company was given its present name in April 2017.” The above was taken from the following Wikipedia page: Airbus - Wikipedia So in that aspect I was wrong, I was just too quick off the mark, and will endeavour not to make that mistake again. My main point however, remains. Airbus bought into Bombardier, to be more specific, they bought a 50% stake in the Bombardier C-Series aircraft. One reason, is because, as mentioned above, Bombardier has a plant in Northern Ireland and the loss of 4000 jobs there, would harm Republic of Ireland, which is of course a member of the EU. column1: How do you deal with elder family members suffering from dementia and symptoms of narcissistic personality disorder (NPD)?
column3: I do not want to seem callous, but the combo of NPD and dementia is a nightmare for both the patient and their family members. Plain and simple. A nightmare! People with dementia are very difficult to “deal” with. I prefer to say interact with. They live in an ever changing world of the present, the past, the delusional. All are real to them. Most are frightening and confusing. They may express their feelings in anger. They may express their feeling in not communicating. They may infantilize you. They may become obstinate and non cooperative. They may be the same manipulative NPD they always were. And there is no way we know “where” they are each time we speak to them. Hopefully you are not responsible for caring for a family member with dementia in your own. You really need a team of trained professionals throughout the day providing help to you. Your elderly family member has a behavioral condition that they have used as a survival strategy since childhood. They also have a neurological condition that involves the destruction of brain cells by plaque proteins strangling new and existing cells. Both conditions are not curable. It takes a very long time for family members to completely accept what may be happening. After a lifetime of being exposed to the npd’s abuse and manipulation, it is difficult to know whether the family member is jerking you around or actually has no clue what is going on around them. Please seek assistance from the neurological team treating your relative. Always communicate with the patient’s neurologist if there are new symptoms or if medications are not working or are producing adverse reactions.There are support services at many major hospitals for both the patients experiencing memory loss and their families. Social workers, and support groups for caregivers. This is not a diy project. Good luck

column1: Are the yakuza harmful to tourists?
column3: I had some experience with the Yakuza while living in Osaka. For about one year, I worked in construction with a small outfit. We mostly did wood deck construction in the mountains near Ikoma. However, my boss took a job in Aboshi (just west of Himeji) in the summer to reform/remodel what I can only describe as a ‘shack’. The client wanted to make this abandoned building his real estate office. No Yakuza involved at this point. The problem was, my boss bid the project at 1,000,000 yen in one month. He wasn’t the brightest guy (warm heart, but no business sense). I was warned by some others in my neighborhood when I started working with him that he was a bit conniving. After the month was up, my boss went to the client and asked for more money. An argument ensued, and the client refused to increase the funds and demanded that he (and his team) finish the job per contract. So my boss made a decision. He stole the clients van, removed all his tools from the site, and left. I was left at the site with one other expat (from Seattle - a master carpenter), no boss, and no forthcoming income to finish the project. I negotiated with the client and he agreed to pay each of us 10,000 yen per day to complete the project. For me (as an apprentice carpenter) that was fine, but my mate was a professional - those wages were a joke. So we left. Now the issue arose that our boss had fled with our income. My mate was owed about 400,000 yen. I was owed around 100,000. Thus ensued utilizing the connections in the Yakuza that my mate had. We met at a sushi bar (had my first raw/seared chicken there!) and talked to a gentleman named Tanaka. He only had one arm due to a car accident and was heavily involved in the RC airplane community. He was a member of one of the Yakuza families (I do not recall which - in fact, I’m not sure I was ever told). His first suggestion: kidnap our boss’ 14-year old daughter until he pays. He was completely serious. Over about 500,000 yen. After I helped my mate understand what was going on (my Japanese was a bit better than his), we politely declined to pursue this option. It didn’t end there. Mr. Tanaka, my mate and I visited my boss’ mother’s house near where I was living in Osaka. We sat down in her living room and had a ‘meeting’ with her. Tanaka was incredibly diplomatic and businesslike. He explained the situation to our boss’ mother, essentially shaming her family. It was all very polite. However, the family was quite poor, so there was no easy way to recover our monetary loss. I felt bad for the mother. She was a good woman. Her son was the problem, but had fled. In the end, we did nothing, realizing that there really was no way to obtain our pay and, of course, that kidnapping a child was definitely a bad idea. The thing is, Tanaka (and, of course, he would have had backing from the family had he needed it) conducted a business meeting, not a series of scare tactics. He evaluated the situation and understood (for himself and for us) that creating a ‘situation’ was not worth it. The Yakuza, when dealing with people outside of the family, are interested in harmony, just like the Japanese population at large. While they may employ more confrontational techniques (violence included) from time to time, my understanding is that these methods are employed more in inter-group levels than with the general Japanese public, let alone tourists. True, they extort and take somewhat shady measures to obtain wealth or status. But they are not ‘thugs’ as others have put it in their answers. This was simply my experience. I lost contact with Mr. Tanaka shortly after these events, but often consider this experience one of my most unique while living in Japan (I was there 16 years). I would never worry about dealing with the Yakuza as a tourist. The chances of an encounter are incredibly slim to begin with and their main interest is in protecting the family and supporting their businesses.
column9: Great. Fucking. Story. I lack your direct experience (although a Yakuza boss once ordered his car mates to help me push my car out of a rice paddy I drunkenly entered). There is a Netflix show called Tokyo Diner that paints a similar view of conflict resolution.

column1: Where can I find anxiety and depression chat rooms or support forums?
column3: What you should know about depression: The first thing you should know about depression is that it is a mood disorder in which it is very necessary for the person to be accompanied by mental health professionals to take care of their well-being and make sure that they receive appropriate help, being careful about the comments or thoughts they might have about the person and especially to keep confidentiality. A big part of psychological treatment used to deal with depression is based on social accompaniment, that’s why talking about it is positive, and it is a way in which the person can receive comfort and support. When someone who is feeling sad, or lonely, with no motivation gets to know that he is not the only one dealing with these feelings and that there is a lot that he could do, they perceive instant relief. If you need to talk about depression because you consider that you are experiencing some of the symptoms that accompany it, or because you have the need to discuss situations that occur to a family member, it is appropriate that you have someone to communicate with. Depression is a kind of mental disorder that is described as having intense sadness and loss of pleasure for activities that a person used to love before having the disorder. You could read more about depression symptoms here. Confidentiality is a key in mental health treatment, and you could ask for it. Depression Chat Rooms: Even though depressed people might feel alone, there are a lot of people going through the same struggle than you, that’s why sharing your thoughts about sadness, loneliness, or other bad feelings could be helpful. Sometimes you could think that people are going to judge you, so in order to feel comfortable about explaining your ideas, Depression Chat Rooms are a good idea because you will be able to talk with people that have gone through the same experiences. These organizations provide moderated chat rooms, which means a volunteer is present in the rooms to help make sure that all users are following site rules and treating each other respectfully. These rooms are not a substitute for professional treatment for depression, but you may find the community to be supportive.Depression and Bipolar Support Alliance (DBSA) offers peer-led online support groups and forums to give people living with depression and bipolar disorder a place to share experiences and coping skills and gain hope.Depression Chat Rooms from depression-chat-rooms.org aims to connect people who have issues regarding depression and anxiety. They also welcome people with similar or related health issues such as bipolar disorder and eating disorders. The website is independent, nonprofit, and free. Note that chat rooms on the site are moderated, while forums are not.Depression Forums has more than 70,000 members and offers forums on topics ranging from depression and anxiety to recovery and coping to medication and therapy that are moderated by volunteers.Depression Sanctuary is a nonprofit organization created to provide a safe, moderated platform for people with depression to seek support from other like-minded people. Membership is required to participate in the Depression Sanctuary chat rooms, but it's completely free to join. They offer hosted chats at specific times. Be aware that to keep the support group a safe and comfortable place for all members, certain rules must be followed while in the chat rooms. Depression Sanctuary is staffed by volunteers who also live with depression. Be kind and treat them with the same respect and care that you'd want for yourself.Depression Understood offers a depression chat room that is always open. They aim to have a relaxed, supportive, and informal atmosphere.HealthUnlocked runs in partnership with the Anxiety and Depression Association of America (ADAA) and offers a safe space for anxiety and depression support.Is necessary to explain that if you are having suicidal thoughts, your better option is to go with a psychiatrist or with a psychotherapist, in order to be supported and have the right treatment. column1: What is it like to tell a patient that he/she has dementia?
column3: I have had a lot of opportunities to do this in the last year during my Geriatrics fellowship at Stanford and the VA hospital, and it is an emotional experience for all parties involved. Dementia does not only affect the individual who has the condition. Often family and close friends note changes in behavior and are the ones who urge the individual to come in to be evaluated. Of course there is no one consistent response, but if I had to generalize about those diagnosed relatively early in the course of their disease (I’ll address the other group later), I’d say that the patient often does not respond with the breadth of emotion one might anticipate. Many times my patients have been nearly silent and saddened appearing when I tell them the diagnosis. I suspect because they have likely been frustrated by the deterioration in their own abilities for some time and already fear the diagnosis. They experience depression, fear, and a sense of loss. I find that far and above fears of memory loss, most patients worry most about being a burden on their family as their dementia progresses. They also often worry about having their driver’s license taken away (loss of independence), needing help toileting and bathing, and being placed in a nursing home. I have noted that I often do not see the anger and shock I often see with other diagnoses like cancer, because in the majority of cases of dementia, changes have been happening over a longer time course of months to years (some non-Alzheimer’s dementias can progress rapidly). Many times the loved ones in the room often have even more emotional responses to a diagnosis of dementia in a patient. I think often a diagnosis of dementia is not really a surprise to family members and close friends, because they have witnessed their loved one declining over time, and deep down know what is happening. However, it is hard not to become overwhelmed with emotion when a doctor confirms a negative suspicion. I find that family members, often children, usually think about the same things that I mentioned above that patients worry about, along with how they will juggle their own complex lives around taking care of their loved one. I have noticed that many times all parties involved react differently when they have witnessed a loved one go through a slow decline with dementia in the past. They often react right away with a desire to plan for the future: they have tangible questions about driving assessments, sometimes want to change their code status (resuscitation status), etc. Some patients I have seen also respond with denial, especially if they were evaluated at the urging of their family. Many highly functional older adults feel that doctors are mistaken, since they can still perform many complex tasks as they used to do. As a physician, I tell the patient and family that they are not alone and that I will continue to be the patient’s doctor, and continue treating them for all their medical problems. I urge them to take things one at a time and offer resources available (social workers are amazing!). The most important steps are always home safety, so I make sure they have the support system in place to ensure the patient is safe and can get food and shelter, medication etc. I encourage them to continue socializing and participating in all the activities that they enjoy. Many patients start asking about treatment options and course right away, and I answer these questions as appropriate for the situation. A few times during my medical training, I encountered people in the hospital or nursing home who truly appeared to have more advanced dementia, but had never been diagnosed. I suspect that, in these cases, the lack of a diagnosis may be due to the fact that not all primary care practices are equipped with support staff and resources to deal with these often complex patients. Perhaps surprisingly, when I diagnose patients like these with dementia, the family is often relieved to finally have an explanation for their family member’s severe decline. This is a general answer about providing a diagnosis of dementia to an early stage patient. Of course, people have been referred to me to be diagnosed at various stages of severity, and this is not often the same discussion. A person’s awareness of their situation and limitations, agitation triggers, etc. would be taken into account when having this discussion.

I read your answer & thought how fortunate your patients must be to have such a compassionate and knowledgable advoacate. It is a difficult path & it takes a diagnosis in many cases to get some things done- like convince an angry person to stop driving, to take over $ issues, to get help in place...it can be a nightmare! column1: Is my family member grieving or angry at me?
column3: Absolutely, and it is a sign of depression. More men than women manifest anger as an outward sign of depression, but some women will go that way too. Has your aunt gone for any therapy or counseling since the loss of your grandma? There is a well done grief support group called Griefshare; it is done through various churches and it is free. What if you suggested to your aunt that both of you joined one of those groups? The process of sharing your feelings in a safe, accepting atmosphere, when it comes to the grief of loss, is that both of you will be able to unload some of the heavier things there. Paradoxically, your aunt is probably trying to "protect" you from her sadness or heavier feelings, but by bottling it up, she isn't dealing with it and it's coming out in anger. You can google Griefshare for a group meeting near you. It's free. I think the workbooks cost like $20. The meetings are at churches but their not at all exclusive and they don't really hardly talk about God at all. They're good groups. Hope this helps!

column1: What is it like to grow up in a Native American reservation?
column3: I've watched this question for a couple of months, and so, I will attempt to share what it's like. My experience was growing up in the 50s, 60s, and 70s on a small, poor reservation in the upper Midwest. My family was poor, everyone we knew on the reservation and in the greater community was poor. The Bad Poverty. The poverty level on my home reservation is awful. The location, in a rural part of a rural state, far from any big cities, doesn't lend itself to a steady supply of jobs, much less ones that will afford any sort of financial security or benefits. What money people on the reservation could come by was often of an illegal variety. Growing up, I did not know anyone who didn't know of or have a drug dealer or user in their family. Everyone had ample alcoholics in their families. Nearly everyone had someone (or more) in their family who had been to or was in jail.Substance abuse. Like I mentioned, substance abuse ran rampant. Although I never used anything, I would have been hard pressed to count more than a dozen others who hadn't. IHC - there are many issues with the IHC system, especially the clinics on rural, poor reservations. For one thing, native doctors are like white buffalo - so rare that when they do occur, they don't hide out on reservations, but they're showcased and advocates on a wider stage. For another, being a doctor on a poor reservation is a quick-burnout setup. To be frank, a lot of patients are going to be substance abusers, many will be drug seekers. You'll see a lot of abuse of all sorts. You'll have to treat a wide variety of illnesses and serious injuries without adequate support or state-of-the-art technology. You will probably deal with some suspicion and distrust because you're likely not going to be native, or at least, not of any noticeable amount. Of course there will be many members of the community who will value you and respect you and be thankful that you chose to devote at least some of your career to caring for them and the community, but you'll also deal with a lot of the ugly side, too, and it might get lonely. You may be the victim of theft over and over, because you'll be viewed as wealthy. All these things add up, and so it's even harder to get a doctor, keep a doctor, or not have the doctor become so burnt out and jaded that care becomes subpar. There is almost always a long wait in a crowded waiting room. Appointments and paperwork can be tough to sort through and can take a good amount of time to get what you need (surgeries, glasses, referrals to specialists, etc). Lack of opportunities and role models. Most of my friends, brothers, and relatives growing up ended up dropping out of school as early as possible. What school they did attend, they did without care or study. They just didn't see a point. Everyone we had ever known was on the reservation; those who had left it often ended up coming home, more broken, more lost, and less self-assured than whey they had left it. There were no career jobs available to us; there didn't appear to be any reason for them to succeed. They had no one to look at and say, hey, I want to be like her or him. We had no one who had become a doctor or who had attended college - most of us didn't even finish high school. I was one of the only native women left to graduate high school at all, much less with enough success to be accepted into a college. I was an outlier on the reservation, someone who was hellbent on succeeding and getting out of there. I wanted a real life, one that was safer, was more comfortable, and that would afford me opportunities to travel, to experience other cultures, and mostly, to be safe, and have a life and a family far from the downsides of the reservation.The discrimination. When I attended school off the rez, whether it was at a Catholic school as a charity student or the local public schools, there was a stigma about being Native. Other children were mean to us and looked down on us, for the color of our skin, the condition of our clothes, etc, but even worse, the teachers, whether they were lay people or nuns, also treated us poorly as well. The corruption + discrimination. One time, growing up, I was a young teen and had a very scary, threatening situation happen to me at home, where I was in danger of assault and in fear of my life. I called the police, and when they found I was on the rez, they told me to hang up and call tribal police. When I called tribal police, no one ever came. The situation ended when a family member arrived home, and I remained unhurt, though traumatized, but even to this day, I have issues with trust and the police, because my experiences with them were never good. Even knowing this is the darker side, not the norm, I still sometimes struggle with it, and I was never personally on the "wrong side" of the law, just the wrong skin color. The Good Community. Despite the many bad and horrible things that can happen on a reservation, there are some positives as well. Community is strong. In times of need, of sorrow, and of tragedy, the community will pull together. Families that may otherwise have the modern equivalent of a blood feud with yours will still come comfort you in times of loss. They'll offer you love and support, food and company, and share in your hurt and offer you memories of your lost ones. Although everyone is poor, rarely are children starving, because friends or relatives (even relatives so distant that only in small communities like these are the ties acknowledged or known of) will feed them. Kids can troop over to just about anyone's home and be fed. It may not be the best of food, but children are rarely turned away. When you're in times of need, whether it's from losing a job or having blown all your money on your next hit, you can almost always count on a relative to help you, whether it's with some spare change, a hot meal, or a couch to sleep on.Celebration of life. Native funerals and the ensuing celebrations and gatherings are like none other I've ever experienced. The community draws together, the funeral is a celebration of life, an expressing of mutual grief and loss, and then a coming together of friends, of family, of acquaintances, for support and solace. The traditions are strong, the ceremonies themselves, when they use traditional elements like singing, drum song, dancing, burning sage and tobacco, etc, are beautiful. They're wrought with feeling, with history, and with a striking resonance of meaning. You can be of any faith - or none at all - and still feel the strength and energy of these times. Call it what you will, the Spirit is strong.IHC. Although, as I mentioned earlier, there are many challenges and opportunities for improvement, the beautiful thing about IHC is that it's available for all members of the tribes. No tribe member (enrolled) is without care, even if it is sometimes not the top of the line care.Respect. Though diminishing over the years, like many cultures, I still see more respect for elders and for tradition on the reservations than I see in day to day life in the big city we now live in (California). Elders are still mostly treated with respect and love, and they are given honor and tribute at gatherings.Powwows. Culture and tradition are still strong, even on my home reservation, which, as I mentioned, is a small and poor one. There is still an annual powwow each year, and the traditions are passed along to the next generations. It is beautiful to watch the newly walking one and two year olds dancing along beside the eighty plus year old traditional dancers. The drumbeat is alive and strong in our youth. Listening to the young adolescent drum group is akin to listening to the choirboys of days past; it's beautiful, it's haunting, and it's wrought with emotion.
column9: Fast forward to today--I'm guessing you're native american. Do you visit your family on the reservation? Have you inspired anyoen else to get out?

column1: Why do I become so lazy and always procrastinate after my mom's loss? I live alone.
column3: I’m so sorry you lost your mom! This is a very deep and profound loss, and it can take a significant length of time to heal from it. Obviously, I don’t know what your relationship was with her, but the deaths of our mothers cause deep wounds, no matter how difficult or troubled the relationships were. As a psychotherapist, my guess is that you’re not “lazy”, but rather, depressed. Depression causes all kinds of real bio-chemical changes in us, which result in decreases in physical and mental energy. Consequently, we often become apathetic and lethargic. It can not only be very hard to make oneself get anything done, but also hard to make oneself CARE whether anything gets done! That you live alone is not great, under the circumstances, because you don’t have another person around to distract you, or kind of pull you out of your own head. I would suggest that you seek therapy, sooner rather than later, because the longer depression goes on, the longer it takes to work oneself out of it. A good therapist can be a tremendous help in addressing what you’re going through in a way which allows you to get control over this process, and change it. Anti-depressants, taken in the short-term, can also be helpful during times such as these. That would be something for you and your therapist potentially to discuss. Please don’t try to deal with this alone! If you’re not comfortable going to a therapist, at the very least, find someone you can talk with regularly: that is, a friend; a family member; or a neighbor you feel close to. You might also inquire, from the social work departments of your local hospitals, whether there are any support groups in your town or city for people who’ve lost their parents. If it turns out that there is a group—go to it. Even if it makes you feel anxious—go. It’s better for you than being alone at home. I hope this helps a little bit. Good luck!

column1: How do I help them through this? My children just lost their Papa to “pulmonary fibrosis.” He was like a father to them. My daughter shows her emotions, while my son acts like nothing happened. My son’s grades are slipping. He won't talk to me.
