column1: From the perspective of a stillbirth mother or a close family member, what does it feel like to give birth to or participate in the birth of a stillborn child?
column3: My baby Gabriel died in my womb at 32 weeks. He would have been 12 this spring. He had a few problems we were monitoring throughout the pregnancy -- mainly a heart block issue and an abnormal growth rate. Gabe was closing in on 10 pounds and had at least a month to go, according to the doctors. One Saturday night I felt very sick and then his movement had stopped but I figured it was because he had little room inside me. Then my boss commented on Monday that I had "dropped." On Wednesday, at my routine checkup, we discovered he had died. I was so horrified, I opted to go immediately to the hospital to deliver him. No one really impressed on me that I might want to take time and make arrangements with my family and friends. In retrospect, I wish I had done this, but I just had an overbearing need to see him. It was decided to have him delivered vaginally although I don't know how this decision was made. It was my first delivery and as I said he was quite heavy and literally dead weight. Labor was induced around 4:00 pm and I finally delivered at about 7:30 am the next day. They had to give me a 4th-degree episiotomy to get him out, and two nurses were pushing on my belly while two doctors worked on me and the father and another nurse were at my feet, trying to help me push. I was passing out and my blood pressure was tanking. I had been pushing so hard that I pinched a nerve in my left leg and was lame for a couple of months afterward. The reason why I pushed so hard was I had given in to the pain at the last moment and gotten an epidural, so I couldn't feel what I was doing. After they pulled him out, they cleaned him up and asked me if I wanted to hold him. Of course I did! They had swaddled him in a blanket. His skin had peeled way from one of his fat cheeks, but it wasn't horrible looking. His lips were very red and he had a lot of dark hair on his head. He was still my beautiful baby. I unwrapped him to see what happened to him. He looked fully developed, with all his parts in place, and at that moment I felt like I had been subject to the rip-off of the century. It was a cruel, horrible joke. My future had been stolen from me. I couldn't hold him for very long because I was so exhausted and torn up physically and emotionally. It took them half an hour to sew me up. The mixture of emotions that beat you up after this tragedy is crazy-making. You try to find something to focus your anger and guilt on. You try to make sense of it. It tests your faith in anything. When a young nursing assistant asked me if I wanted to speak to a pastor, I told her God and I weren't on speaking terms. The indignities keep on coming, too. The body doesn't know the baby is dead, and the breasts fill with milk that baby won't drink. The hot ache of full breasts, the tenderness needed with urinating and evacuating, being crippled, and then the thoughtless comments just made me never want to be out in the world again. I needed medication to get me to sleep at night. Of course, I did "get back out there," but I am not the same person I was before I lost Gabe. Gabe's father and I didn't make it through the ordeal. He didn't want to talk about it. I was 41, so I decided not to try again. The physicality of the ordeal was too much for me and I knew that I would never get over the trauma of having lost him. So we felt that the reason we had decided to stay together was no longer binding. The only redeeming point of the ordeal was that we discovered it was the result of a genetic problem I carry, and not anything I did or didn't do while I was pregnant. He had Simpson-Golabi-Behmel syndrome, electrical problems with his heart, and three lung lobes, so Gabe's life would have been difficult and short. As for how one might help a friend who has been through something like this, don't talk to your friend about trying again unless she brings it up. If your friend has any other children, do not say anything like "At least you have so-and-so." That was the baby she and her partner were dreaming of. Just be present with her while she processes what happened to her. Everyone is different in how they grieve. Let her take the lead. Also, the father needs help dealing with his emotions. Everyone focuses on the mother, but the father is going under a great deal of emotional stress, too. He may feel especially alone and bereft. If you are concerned about such a thing happening to you, there are several practical things you can do to get through it that I wish I had known about and taken advantage of. Having a baby really is a physical challenge, so it's important to be as healthy as possible, and to know if there are any genetic issues you might encounter and do your best to emotionally prepare yourself. Still, you never know what life will bring. Pregnancy loss groups exist and it is a good idea to organize a memorial service for the baby so friends and family can show their support and acknowledge what has happened. Miscarriage is more common than people know and expecting couples need to be better prepared for the possibility. I think we don't talk enough about the ordeals women go through to bring children into the world. We hear all the beautiful stories of birth, but hardly about the tragedies. It felt like being inducted into a secret society the day I became the mother of a stillborn child. Obviously I continue to have sore spots inside me from this experience. Another sad result of this was that my girl friends were afraid to share their pregnancy news with me. Don't do that to your friend. Survivors of fetal death don't want to be left out of others' lives. One of my relatives, "my crazy Aunt Pam," always sends me a Mother's Day card, which I find comforting. Most people forget. For those short months that Gabe was inside me, I was a mother. I still am.
column9: Thank you for sharing something so personal and painful. It's very brave. In so sorry for the loss of your son.

column1: Has another parent ever gotten mad at you for saying 'no' to their child?
column3: OMG! Yes! We were visiting another country for my grandmother’s 90th birthday celebration. Over 200 family members from four generations were in town. We were crowded into the few homes of the people living there. My sons were playing with a large group of cousins as the jet-lagged parents napped. He came up to me with a 3 year old literally attached to his finger. She was biting him and would not let go! Calm as I could, I said, “No bite!!” much like I would say to a rambunctious puppy. She let go and ran off as I checked the wound (just dents, no blood). My son said he had no idea how to get this little kid to let him go and he didn’t want to hurt her by shoving her off (he was about 10) so he had wisely brought her to me. After being assured that he did the right thing, he went back to playing with the group of kids. About 15 minutes later my mother comes into the room and asks, “What happened?! You need to apologize!” It took me a minute to realize what she was talking about. I explained the situation, expecting her to be supportive. After all this is her eldest grandson who was being bitten by a feral tot! I was wrong. Apparently, the little girl had gone downstairs where her parents and her grandfather were sleeping. According to them, she was cowering under a table as if I had beat her to within an inch of her life! They were threatening to leave the country and go home to the states. I tried reasoning with my mother but she explained that a similar situation had happened with her and they had not spoken to her for nearly 20 years! They had only just started speaking to her and she really did not want it to happen again! The justice part of me wanted to refuse any apology. After all, their child had been biting my child! They said that I should’ve woken them up to get them to deal with the situation instead of disciplining their daughter/granddaughter. According to them, I should never have disciplined their child, no matter what was happening! I thought they were completely crazy. No one even apologized to my son for the girl biting him. This was so stupid! By the time I even figured out WHO this biting kid’s parents were, my son could have been injured. (Remember, there were a lot of people and many different families there. I had never before met most of them and had not seen any that I might have met since they were teens!) After about 30 minutes of arguing with my mother and feeling like she and I might never speak again, I decided to give in. These were people I rarely saw and hardly even knew but who my mother loved dearly and wanted to have a better relationship with. Because I was her daughter, they would continue not to speak with her as well! As ridiculous as the whole situation seemed, I decided to apologize. Throughout the week of the family reunion I watched as this little brat hit and kicked and pinched people and broke things. My children gave the little biter a wide berth when we were forced to be near her and never again allowed her close enough to get bitten. ( it was more than a little funny watching these three boys dodge away from the girl. To avoid more drama, we had not spoken to anyone else about the situation so no one knew what was going on. ) Although I was glad my mother and her brother would be on speaking terms again, I really had no desire to associate with the child. It would not have been a big loss if they never spoke to me again!
column9: Disgusting. If it had been my three year old, I would have made her apologise to you and your son as well as your mother. I would have too.

column1: What's the best way to help a family member who's bipolar and paranoid schizophrenic and refuses to take medication?
column3: I have bipolar II; while not as serious a condition as your brother, it took me 10 years to become stabilised on my medication. I take lithium and a few other 'heavy hitters' and remain well. The medications do not give me side effects, except I did gain some weight -- which I have been losing. I was determined to get well and medication was obviously going to be an essential part of this (which I think is true for all people with serious mental illness). I think gradually introducing meds one by one and allowing his body to adjust to it would help him to feel more in control and for the doctors and him to understand how it is affecting his well being. To dump a bunch of new meds on someone quickly creates a quagmire of frustration and side effects; poor monitoring results because everything is interacting with everything else. Which ones are doing the job? Who knows. (I'm talking about spacing the introduction of new drugs out at 8 week intervals -- or thereabouts). Recovery is a long steady process. Psychotherapy is as important as drugs, because psychiatrists just simply are not trained for deep emotional support of their patients -- they are there to dispense drugs. An ally who is not family is a core support--there is a great deal of shame and loss with mental illness. I think the money issue is tricky. They aren't good managers of money so where does your help stop and end? I think a strategy of how you will help needs to be drawn out on paper, agreed, and adhered to. The problem is, stress is the absolute trigger for making someone ill again and again. Why are they putting themselves into this situation? Maybe they need couples counseling to find a better way to run their personal lives to bring the stress down. You are in a tough place. You must not allow their dependency on you for money but you must also try to keep your brother safe, knowing there is the risk of suicide if stability is not found. Non profits run support groups for family members and this might be of use to you in making this decision.
column9: Note: Bipolar II is just as serious as Bipolar I. The suicide rates may even be higher for those of us with a Bipolar II diagnosis. Also drugs are not an "essential part" of getting well for everyone. For many of us the drugs are not effective and we often recover better than those who do find drugs effective. This is NOT to suggest you should discontinue your drugs if you find them effective.

column1: How does a student realise that he/she is suffering from depression? If you've suffered, how did you overcome it?
column3: Teen depression is a serious mental health problem that causes a persistent feeling of sadness and loss of interest in activities. It affects how a teenager thinks, feels and behaves, and it can cause emotional, functional and physical problems.Signs and symptoms that a student might be experiencing depression include:Feelings of sadness, tearfulness, emptiness or hopelessnessIrritability, frustration and even angry outbursts, out of proportion to the situationLoss of interest or pleasure in most or all normal activities, such as hobbies or sportsSleep disturbances, including insomnia or sleeping too muchTiredness and lack of energy, so even small tasks take extra effortChanges in appetite — often reduced appetite and weight loss, but increased cravings for food and weight gain in some peopleNegative changes in academic performanceUnexplained physical problems, such as back pain or headachesAnxiety, agitation or restlessnessFeelings of worthlessness or guilt, fixating on past failures, or blaming yourself for things that aren't your responsibilityTrouble thinking, concentrating, making decisions and remembering thingsFrequent or recurrent thoughts of death, suicidal thoughts, suicide attempts, or suicideIf you think your child is suicidal, encourage him or her to call the National Suicide Prevention Hotline at 800-273-TALK (8255). The hotline operates 24 hours a day, every day. Loved ones can call to learn how to help. Here is something you can do to overcome depression:- If you think your child might be dealing with depression, talk to him or her about what's going on and listen. Encourage your child to share his or her feelings with you or someone else trusted. Ask your child to make an appointment with a doctor as soon as possible. Encourage your child to spend time with supportive family members and friends or seek out student support groups.
column9: I love how you used the word doctor instead of psychologist, to show that psychological disorders are equivalent to health disorders and shouldn't be taken lightly, really well articulated 👍

column1: How do I cope with my cat's very sudden and unexpected death?
column3: We lost a young cat to FIP after about a year with her. She’s been gone longer than we ever had her (longer than she was ever alive, even), and typing this is still a little difficult. It was hard. All loss is. I found our situation to be particularly difficult since she was so young. While the loss of a pet is not generally thought of as nearly as difficult as the loss of a family member, I found that to not be the case. My partner and I had each other, and that helped a lot. There are many different support groups, either on the internet, and depending on where you live, possibly in your area, that would help you get through anything you are unable to deal with on your own or with your family or friends. Beyond that, all I can suggest is to honor your cat’s memory in the best way you know how. Think of the happy times you had, when it’s not to hard. And let yourself grieve when it is. We found that donating money to FIP research helped us feel better as well. There may be some similar unconventional activities (volunteering, donations, etc) you can undertake to help with the grieving process. We got another kitten, probably a bit sooner than we would have wanted to, but our other cat was clearly lonely and we didn’t want him to continue to suffer without a playmate. We love our new cat, and we know she is not a replacement for the kitten we lost. But when we first got her there were a lot of emotions, including guilt, that I found I had to process when I was expecting to be happy. Everyone is different, but I found that getting a new pet right away may not be a good decision. These days, I try to remember to savor the times that my cats are snuggled close, or playing with me, or even driving me nuts. I miss our little girl dearly, and that will probably always be true. I won’t offer any of the normal platitudes, but as someone who has been there, please know that I understand, and am deeply sorry for your loss.
column9: Hello Rachel, I am the grieving owner who asked the question above- Quora had merged my original question with another grieving owner’s. Thank you so much for sharing your feelings of loss and I am very sorry to hear about your beloved kitty. You must have loved him so very very much. It must be really difficult when she suddenly passed away. I appreciate your understanding and kindness. Your story resonates with me deeply. Jack my cat also lost his life to FIP two days ago under very sudden and traumatic circumstances. There were no symptoms at all and he was gone just like that. We were completely in a loss. I had to bury my beloved cat in the garden where he loved to play so much. I hugged him and cried to his ear that I will miss him. Jack had been also suffering from a broken pelvic fracture and recently had gum surgery too, we had been caregivers for him for two weeks and he seemed to be progressing well and gaining weight. He suddenly took a turn for the worse three days ago, we rushed him to the vet, got the shock ing FIP diagnosis, and the same afternoon his FIP took over and he left us. Our family broke down in tears and we are still in shock. I didn’t know how much pain one can feel after losing a pet you love. Grief waves come and come and I still look for him in his empty cage. I still cannot believe Jack is gone. I remember carrying him last weekend when he was sick, and telling him I loved him. I’ve been doubled up in pain crying. Currently I am doing up an online public memorial for Jack to help me find some closure but the deep pain still remains. We live in a developing country and no support groups are available in my city. Kind wishes, Ernhwee.

column1: What are some effective coping mechanisms to get over a traumatic experience?
column3: I learned that I was going through the grieving process. I share with you below what I learned and experienced while grieving a divorce from a narcissist after 25 years of marriage. Disclaimer: I didn't come up with the stages of grief from a relationship with a narcissist however, I do share my experience with each of the stages in hopes you will be able to understand and identify where you are in your process and what to expect as you grieve. Everyone grieves differently so your experience will be different from mine. For comparison:The traditional 5 stages of grief are: Denial, Anger, Bargaining, Depression, Acceptance.There are 8 stages of grief I experienced from a relationship with a narcissist: Total Devastion, Denial, Education and Self Doubt, Understanding the Narcissist, Rage, Depression, Healing and Self-DiscoveryI found leaving a narcissist is not like losing a friend or a family member. And it's not like losing a loving partner from a healthy relationship. It is a unique experience that can only be understood by someone who has been through it. Stage 1 Total Devastation - Not long after I divorced I started to experienced this total all-consuming devastation. I was in shock and disbelief. For the past 25 years I knew nothing but being a wife and a mother. I started having feelings of emptiness, thoughts of suicide and difficulty performing trivial tasks. I had this belief that I deserved this. I felt worthless. I thought I was nobody without him. I was jealous, crazy, needy, clingy, and felt everything was my fault. He sucked every ounce of self from within me. Self esteem, self confidence, self respect and self worth. I lost my ability to cope. I was unable to feel anything. Stage 2 Denial - The denial stage began when the my ex started waving his “happy” life in my face. To the world his life appeared flawless. I felt like I needed to prove that I was okay and everything was just fine with me too because then maybe he’ll want me back. I couldn't believe at that time I actually thought I wanted him back! I was very confused! I was in total denial of the reality of the situation. I learned denial is a normal reaction to rationalize overwhelming emotions. It is a defense mechanism that buffers the immediate shock of the loss. We block out the words and hide from the facts. This is a temporary response that carries us through the first wave of pain. Stage 3 Education and Self Doubt - With my confusion came this overwhelming desire to understand what happened. I began educating myself about Narcissist Personality Disorder. Not only to understand but in fear my sons could end up like my ex. Even with knowledge I still could not grasp the idea that someone can only love themselves. That he never had the capacity to love me the way I loved him. Doubt caused me to continue to blame myself and wonder if I was labeling him a Narcissist because I couldn't handle the "truth" (his truth of course) of how I ruined the relationship. I swung back and forth between my ex the idealizer and my ex who constantly devalued me. How could someone who claimed to be so in love with me also despise me? How could he go from obsession to contempt in the blink of an eye? It isn't possible. There's no way I married a narcissist. I must be wrong. He loved me. Right? Stage 4 Understanding the Narcissist - I learned this stage doesn't exist with the normal stages of grief but it was one of the most important in my recovery process. This stage took the longest and was the hardest to come to terms with. Educating myself only got me so far. To understand I needed to feel what he felt. I didn't know how. It was beyond my concept that a person could not be capable of loving no one else but themselves, unable to feel empathy or compassion for others. I came to realize for the first time in my life I was not able to empathize. I was consumed with my quest to understand how the Narcissist thinks, spending hours on Google and various websites and discussion forums. Finally one day I was able to match up his behaviors to the perspective of a narcissist and that is when everything clicked. It all began to make sense. From gas lighting, to mirroring, to love-bombing to the delayed criticism and the eventual devalue and discard. I was totally disgusted. I finally realized he never truly loved me. I was also able to see how his deliberate premeditated tactics used were meant to control me. The person I trusted was actively working against me. Betrayal was his strong suit. Stage 5 Rage - Once I understood the Narcissist completely self-doubt slowly turned into anger. I was able to clearly see how I was used, manipulated, and brainwashed. I wanted revenge. I wanted him to feel the pain I felt. I wanted to contact everyone in his life and tell them what he did. I obsessively talked about him with my friends and family, I had this overwhelming need to tell my story. I had been shut up and minimized (I shutter as I typed that word) for so long, my voice was finally free to speak the truth! I started to feel all of the things I wasn't allowed to feel in the relationship. Whenever I accused him of something he would turn it around and blame it on me so I would feel bad instead of getting mad. I found out cognitive dissonance caused a huge misplacement of my anger. Cognitive dissonance is the reason why I stayed in the relationship even knowing the truth. I started to feel delayed emotions. I was beyond anger. I am so grateful fear kept me from acting on it. Besides, I knew it would only help prove his point that I was the crazy one. I don't know how but I managed to remain calm and composed. Stage 6 Depression - I found out depression is anger turned inward. Not only was I angry with him I was angry with myself for not leaving the marriage sooner. I went back and forth between depression and rage for a while. One day, I would think I have reached the point where I could move on -- the next, I would wake up angry. I didn't want to be mad, I didn't like feeling mad nor did I deserve to be mad. All I did was fall in love. I spent most of my time isolating in my apartment surrounding myself with people who understood me on the various discussion forums I would join. At times I had obsessive, racing thoughts that left me feeling restless, irritable and discontented. My patience level was very low that sometimes the tiniest things would set me off. I was finally beginning to learn how to set boundaries and couldn't believe I let myself sink so low. I realized how much I lost. And I am not talking just friends, money, life experience, etc, but also my innocence. My perspective of the world had been shattered. I was no longer that “naive country girl from North Carolina” as he used to tell me. Instead of giving people the benefit of the doubt, I was starting to have trouble trusting. At times I would experience feelings of dread. Not sure why. Stage 7 Healing - this is the point where I started asking questions. I wanted to know why! How did this happen? What are my vulnerabilities? I have come to realize my vulnerabilities weren't my fault, but I knew I needed to understand how my ex so easily took advantage of me so it wouldn't happen again. I found a support group and started spending time with others who went through similar experiences as mine. Realizing I wasn't alone and that others were able to move past the abuse and live happy lives gave me the hope I needed. I got the validation I needed though sometimes talking about my experiences would trigger feelings of anger or sadness but I was able to more quickly acknowledge and process my feelings and move past them. Everything was starting to fall into place. Stage 8 Self-Discovery - This is where I began to discover my strengths and weaknesses. I worked through this with my sponsor in my support group. This allowed me to work on any weaknesses that could cause me to end up in another similar type of relationship and to practice how to use my strengths. I learned how to define what I wanted from a healthy relationship and I learned how to set boundaries. I learned how to speak my truth and express how I feel. I learned to love myself which was so important for me! How can I give away something I don't have? Plus learning to love myself allowed me get rid of some of my codependent behaviors I learned during my marriage. I am no longer a people pleaser who wants everyone to like me. No is a complete sentence with a period at the end. No explanation needed! I have learned to not care what others think about me. I was able to regain my self-respect, self confidence, self esteem and self worth but at a whole different level. Today I am a strong independent woman who does not need anyone in my life to validate my worth. It wasn't easy getting here but so worth it!! Acceptance and perseverance were critical. Through honesty with self, open mindedness, willingness I learned to change me and my entire perspective on life. I know now that I cannot change anyone or anything in life except me, my attitudes and how I choose to react to life. I started practicing Spirituality which is a beautiful place in my head and heart to be. Through prayer and meditation I have learned to appreciate life and to be grateful for what I have. I have a relationship with a God of my understanding. Acceptance has also allowed me to make peace with my past, knowing that I wouldn't be the woman I am right now at this very moment if not for the journey I was on. It is what it is I can't change it but I can change my tomorrows as long as I keep myself spiritually fit. I also learned to forgive myself and my ex. Not for him but for me. I remind myself he is sick, he has a mental illness. It doesn't excuse his behavior, discount my feelings or what I experienced in any way. It allows me to see him in a different perspective, one of compassion instead of bitterness. Love and tolerance, doesn't mean I have to like him. The point is that through forgiveness I healed and learned to let go of the past which has provided me such peace and serenity! Each morning I wake up I remind myself how grateful I am to be alive, for having my 3 beautiful sons in my life, for my amazing boyfriend who has shown me how to love unconditionally and for all the beautiful women in my life whom God has allowed me to to be of service to. I worked on my codependent behaviors learning to say no and to stop the people pleasing. I finally was able to forgive myself, accept myself and love myself. With that came such a freedom as I have never thought possible. I no longer cared about what others thought about me. I am comfortable in my own skin. And I learned strong, independent and confident women attract the right kind of man. I don't dare dwell upon the past or what could have been or what was lost. I can't change it so what is the point. I keep in the moment. Right here right now! I have no idea what the next minute, the next hour or the next day will bring and learned to not worry about it. That's Gods plan. I have let go of control and handed it over to God. I just sit back and enjoy life the way life is meant to be enjoyed, happy and content! Each day I look for ways I can be of maximum service to God and others! As a result, today I am not a victim, I am a survivor!
column9: As I've said before, Patricia, you are my inspiration x

column1: Why did none of the other Avengers get fat in Avengers: Endgame?
column3: Thor got fat due to deep depression. He lost his father, mother, brother, long lost sister best friends ,the warriors three and Heimdall plus half of the remaining Asgardians since becoming king. Picture that for a second. Your whole family gone. Then losing your friends. And everyone you cared about. Remember Asgardians are long lived people. Their Average life span is 5000 years. Royals like Thor is much longer. Plus death isn't the same for an Asgardians as it is for us humans. They can travel to the borders of Valhalla, Asgardians heaven. And visit the honorable dead. Now that Asgard is no more traveling to Valhalla is no longer possible. So Thor has never known real death before. The idea that someone is gone for good is a foreign concept. Thor is 1000 years old and never grieved before. The pain he feels is soul crushing. Then there is the guilt of failing to stop Thanos. Newly appointed King and 50% of his people gone. Not counting those he loss to Thanos aboard his ship. How do you face people that love and adore you? when you've loss their loved ones. Mothers, Fathers, Sisters and Brothers. Who like you find true death new concept. Thor couldn't bare to face them. To see their grief stricken eyes. To him they all blame him for their pain. Thor was wrong to feel this way. None blamed him. Yet, Thor sequesters himself in a small cabin and drowns his pain in mead and food. Plays video games to kill time. Thus he gets fat. Meanwhile, other Avengers deal with their pain in constructive ways. Hulk finds a way to a new better life. Captain America helps others with support groups. Iron Man starts a family. Black Widow organizes the New Avengers: Captain Marvel, Rocket, War Machine and Okoye. The difference between them and Thor is they have known death before. Be it a family member or friend. Be Hawkeye doesn't want to feel this pain so he converts it into hate and outrage. How can criminals, drug dealers and murders live while his family doesn't? He abandons non lethal trick arrows he normally uses for humans. Takes up a katana and becomes Ronin and leads a path of blood in his wake.

column1: What are the various support groups available in India to address different concerns?
column3: The various support group:- 1.Group analysis aims to achieve a healthier integration of the individual in his or her network of relationships. The focus is on the relationship between the individual and the group, thus placing emphasis on the essentially social nature of human experience. 2. An online weekly support group open to anyone who is experiencing Anxiety, Worry, Panic, OCD, GAD, Phobia, for adults ages 18+, led by a mental health professional. You’ll have a chance to talk with others who “get” anxiety and also learn self-help skills. 3.Most of us experience symptoms of depression at some point during our lives. Find support for individuals living with mood disorders like depression and bipolar disorder. We work together to learn how to break out of the downward spiral that often accompanies depression. Join this supporting, non-judgmental safe space to meet and share experiences of low mood, loss of interest, an inability to feel pleasure (anhedonia), loss of energy (anergia), and learn how to overcome the blues. while it’s perfectly normal to feel angry when you’ve been mistreated or wronged, anger becomes a problem when you express it in a way that harms yourself or others. Find support from each other to learn to manage your anger with the anger management support group. 5.Everyone experiences stress. Sometimes it can help you focus and get the task at hand done. But when stress is frequent and intense, it can strain your body and make it impossible to function. Finding effective ways to deal with stress is crucial to living well. Find support with this stress management support group to learn to better manage stress. 6.Grief and bereavement support group facilitated for family and friends who have experienced death of a loved one. Emotionally safe space for grieving and re-constructing meaning through grief and mourning. Meet others who are going through a similar experience share their stories. 7.A group setting offers a safe, supportive environment where you can share your thoughts and ideas, and learn from others experiencing similar challenges. During the group sessions, you’ll have a chance to connect with others who have had similar experiences and challenges you go through as a woman, to talk through your issues and to consider positive choices and strategies for the future. 8.LGBTQIA+ individuals experience greater risk for mental health conditions and suicidality. LGB youth are more than twice as likely to report experiencing persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness than their heterosexual peers. Join this Queer Affirmative Counseling Practice informed and Sex Positive support group to meet and share the difficulties that you face and listen to stories of others going through similar experiences as yours. 9.Seniors can share fears and frustrations, receive support without judgment and be reassured that others share similar problems. This provides support group members with an outlet for feelings that friends and family who aren’t in the same situation may not fully understand. 10.There is a social stigma that men should not be open about their emotional suffering. This causes men to be less likely to seek help. They may feel the need to appear strong to those around them. However, this will only exacerbate mental health issues. Joining a Men’s support group can help men work through their feelings. Talking to a group of people in a safe environment gives them a chance to speak openly about what they’re experiencing. A safe space for fathers, boys and men of all ages to discuss whatever difficulties or hardships they are experiencing. Issues might include family break-up, loss of a loved one, employment challenges, or absolutely any other experiences you wish to share.

column1: Why do my mom and siblings gossip all my personal stuff to relatives and friends? I realized that they are toxic for my direct family, but I am still in contact with them. They talk bad about my wife and blame her if I keep a distance from them.
column3: They are assholes! Why are they assholes no one can tell you. I don’t know why people think it’s ok to be an asshole these days. In your case it sounds like you have narcissistic people in your family. That is a mental disease that has no cure or nothing to help because those people will never believe they have a mental issue in the first place. It sucks but they are incapable feeling anything for anyone else but themselves like sociopaths. They are usually teaching one member of the family to follow in their footsteps (the golden child) and then the kid who can’t do a thing right even though they are doing everything right so it’s very confusing for the scapegoat child. Sounds like you are the scapegoat and your siblings are the golden children… probably because they have the same mental disease. It’s one of the worst things for the human race because all other diseases you can try and manage but what do you do for someone who doesn’t think there is anything wrong with them? It’s really the people around them need coping skills in order to deal with them. At least we can lock up phycopaths and sociopaths when they do something horrible, but the abuse from a narcissist is the worst because you can’t stop it or prove it as they can wiggle their way and lie through their teeth so well. It’s part of the disease. Look it up and see if it applies in your situation. Then you find a support group with others that also have to put up with their narc family member. Good luck and I’m sorry you shouldn’t have to live like that. They are toxic just let them go and have peace. You know who you are so get them out of your life completely. Your children don’t need to know them and get abused too. Just cut your losses and get far away from these people! Doesn’t matter that they are your family. They are lost causes and they will never ever get help for themselves. Stop the cycle with your family!

column1: My brother died a year ago and my parents have completely changed personality. They are less loving, more angry/aggressive, and I feel like I have no parents. What do I do?
column3: Im sorry for your loss… Its not easy to lose a close family member especially a child. I lost my daughter 13 years ago, she was 19. This is the worst pain your parents can feel. Its like there is a piece of their heart that is missing. It doesn’t matter how he passed… its the fact that he did. Have your parents reached out to any support groups? Talked with a therapist? When my daughter passed I went to therapy to help get through the pain. It helped, but it was still difficult to deal with. My friends were there and listened to me… And I say listened to me, because I needed to talk about it. Listening is the best thing you can do for a grieving parent. Your parents are trying to wrap their head around this and it takes time. Anger is one of the stages of grief. I could say time will make it better, but that isn’t necessarily so… every person grieves differently. My daughter has been gone for 13 years and I still have bad days. Birthdays, Holidays and the anniversary of her death are still difficult.. Also, when I hear any Little Mermaid song, I lose it… It was her favorite movie when she was little. Im sure your parents are going through all of these emotions as well. Please don’t take it personally that they aren’t the same… I know it hurts and you feel alone… it sounds like they are still angry with losing their son. This is why they should talk to a professional, and it might be a good idea for you to talk to someone as well. Get your feelings out! Cry when you need too.. laugh when you want too… its ok.. I wish you the best honey… Hugs

column1: What is the best way to deal with my 94-year-old mother who is extremely difficult to handle and gets agitated quite easily?
column3: Gently. Remind yourself frequently that she handled you for years and years through toddler stages, teen stages, and both of those stages came with you probably being easily agitated and difficult to handle. Put yourself in her position as well, she was probably very independent and able bodied, with full mental capacity. Now she is most likely losing bits of all of those things; and to her this will most likely feel like a loss. What has she lost so far? Probably the ability to drive, a spouse or siblings, her parents, many of her friends, perhaps her home, bodily functionality, memory issues, fixed or limited income. That is a lot to have to give up, and then on top of everything have your children have to care for you and possibly feel like a burden, but also aware that they are dependent as well. Caring for any older person is hard work, double that when it is your own family. There are many support groups open to people who are the caregivers of family members, try it out. You might be surprised at how similar you are to them, or can empathize with what they are going through as well. There are also countless books available for caregivers as well that can help. Sometimes we all just need a safe space to vent our frustrations at the situations, or look at things from a different perspective. And PLEASE make sure you are taking care of yourself and your needs too. Caring for our family members can be a 24/7/365 day a year job on top of any children and/or outside profession you may have. It is not selfish to make some time for just you. So o n to the practical advice on how to deal with her during difficult moments:Know the triggers. Try to find out if it seems to happen at certain times of the day. With Dementia in particular dawn and dusk tend to be times that can be challenging. Just knowing that the time of day can be a trigger will help time different tasks or conversations better. Or if she has no dementia, maybe it is pain or stiffness related. Is she more crabby upon waking after being in bed all night? She might be in pain. How is she sleeping? Does she need more rest or a trip to the doctor to see about a sleeping aid? Not getting enough sleep can definitely effect moods.Give her as much choice and autonomy as is safe. Give her options and choices that can give her the freedom of choosing her clothes, what she eats, when she eats or showers etc.You can always try redirection. If she is clearly frustrated with a task or conversation redirect the behavior. “Mom, I see that your having a hard time doing …(Difficult task or topic). , what if we come back to that later and do…(preferable activity). now instead” or “I hear what you are saying …(repeat the point of the disagreement). that would be very frustrating, what can we do together to make…(Difficult task or topic). easier?”Hope this helps.

column1: What do you do if you're depressed for days after finding your brother dead? My brother was my world.
column3: I can’t really think of anything more traumatic than finding a loved one dead. You should immediately find a grief counsellor in your area. It is only expected that you would be experiencing a torrent of anguish and depression. I would also keep in mind making an appointment with a psychiatrist or physician for medical help in dealing with your brother’s passing. There may be support groups in your area that could assist you in coming to terms with your trauma. Please keep your surviving family members in mind; they will also need help and support. I am terribly sorry for your loss. Good luck.

column1: How would the National Guard deal with the Project at Eden's Gate from Far Cry 5 at their full numbers and strength?
column3: I wrote a concept idea for it actually! I hope it sheds some light. Following the loss of contact with the Hope County Sheriff and a Federal Agent from the US Marshal Service, the Montana State Governor declares martial law and a state of emergency for Hope County. The Montana Adjutant General calls up the National Guard. The Project Eden’s Gate is declared a Domestic Terrorist Organization. Joseph Seed is placed at the FBI’s number 1 most wanted list as are the rest of the Seed “Family.” All members of said “family” are declared Domestic Terrorist Leaders, and all members of PEG are declared Domestic Terrorists. In addition, the Hope County Sheriff’s Department is deemed unreliable and no longer trusted by the Department of Homeland Security. Montana Highway Patrol shuts down all roads leading into and out of Hope County, and their presence over these roads are massively increased to patrol for PEG members as well as those fleeing the county. This is done in conjunction with fellow Local and County Law Enforcement Agencies. The Montana National Guard is activated and mobilized. Coordination is made with the South Dakota Air National Guard’s 114th Fighter Wing (operating F-16s) following reports of armed enemy aircraft in the county. 1st Battalion of the 163rd Infantry Regiment, 1st Battalion (General Support) of the 189th Aviation Regiment, the 143rd Military Police Company, 484th Military Police Company, and 190th Chemical Reconnaissance Detachment of the Montana Army National Guard are mobilized for immediate deployment. Special Forces Soldiers of the 20th SFG are deployed and inserted via HALO into the county. Their orders were to conduct unconventional warfare and Internal Defense, as well as either capture or eliminate each family member. A Fireteam is sent to track down and eliminate each family member while the other Green Berets are to assist in combat duties. All troops are equipped with MOPP Gear due to reports of chemical weapons. Once all forces are ready, the 163rd leads the way, entering the county from the South West. USAF F-16s fly in to intercept and destroy any and all PEG Aircraft. Several groups of soldiers of the 163rd enter via Chinook and Blackhawk. They assault several captured air fields operated by PEG. Most aircraft of PEG don’t even have the opportunity to take off as soldiers swarm the airfields and capture them. Those that manage to take off are quickly downed either by F-16s, Helicopters, or by MANPADs. Within the first day of entering the county, air superiority is gained. Equipped with Stryker APCs and M113 vehicles, the Army begins to push forward. More troops enter from the north and south east regions and begin to push towards the center. Towns and other population centers retaken by the Army are policed by the Military Police. Counterintelligence Agents in conjunction with CID Special Agents are integrated into these towns to prevent enemy spies. Military Police also process POWs as well as the County Jail, used both as a base and detention center. Special Forces Soldiers help train the various Militias in the region and hunt down enemy combatants. Special Forces Soldiers meanwhile tracks down the family members. Jacob Seed is promptly killed by Sniper fire. Faith Seed and John Seed are killed following raids approximately 5 days after the initial invasion. Jospeh Seed is captured as he surrenders after his bodyguards are killed in a sudden ambush and his compound surrounded by Special Forces Operatives. They eliminated all major leaders within 5 days. Joseph Seed is taken away out of the region and to an undisclosed location for transport by US Marshals in conjunction with US Army Criminal Investigation Division Special Agents. The location is kept Top Secret, Need to Know to prevent any possible attacks. PEG rapidly begins to fall apart due to loss of leadership. Within the week, all population centers are retaken by the National Guard, and PEG, while still a threat, is deemed no longer significant. Most forces pull out, however Military Police and Special Forces remain to police the region alongside Montana Highway Patrol as a new County Sheriff’s Department is created, while Special Forces continue to hunt down the remaining PEG forces, whom are now in-fighting and without leadership. CID and CI hunt down spies and infiltrators. 2 weeks following the campaign, PEG, besides a few straggler groups, is destroyed. Martial Law ends as remaining forces pull out. Until a new County Sheriff’s Department is raised, Highway Patrol serves as the police force. State and Federal SWAT Teams raid remaining compounds. 3 weeks following the campaign, the last remaining compound is raided and captured by the FBI Hostage Rescue Team. Only stragglers remain. PEG is declared defeated. Stragglers remain an issue for several weeks. Most of these stragglers are those of The Chosen. US Marshals and FBI hunt down these members. 5 weeks following the campaign, it had been over a week since the last attack. PEG is declared to be completely defunct and destroyed. Joseph Seed is tried by the Supreme Court and pleads guilty to domestic terrorism, kidnapping with intention to harm, torture, several murders in the first degree, and countless other crimes. He is given the death penalty. He did not wish to he represented in court, doing so himself, nor did he battle. The court was adjourned in less than 30 minutes. He is killed by lethal injection. Such occurs to countless other PEG members, but many more also receive prison time, mostly life sentences. Some, specifically conscripts, are pardoned. By the end of the campaign, military forces suffered only 23 casualties which include wounded and KIA, most of whom were injured, while several thousand PEG members are killed.
column9: The tactics are definitely realistic but it’s hard to believe the military would only suffer 23 casualties… this is the Montana National Guard, most they’ve seen are natural disasters, never any guerilla warfare or domestic terrorism, they’d definitely have at least something around 450 deaths, since the more trusted PEG members (the ones who have AR-C’s or higher) are near-equally trained by Jacob Seed, who is a veteran. Not to mention the fact they have RPGLs and .50 Cals, those would be able to hit thru APC’s without much problem. Anyways, pretty cool theory!

column1: Are there suggestions on how to make "no contact" easier for victims of narcissistic abuse and who may suffer from trauma bonds?
column3: Assuming you're ready, you know what you are dealing with now and you have your own best interest in mind. Like most answers said, “no contact” is still very difficult. Personally, I believe there’re 2 parts of this challenge 1. Truama bond is something strong and your brain was re-wired by the narcissist. You're unfortunately, an “addict” now. 2. Breakups are difficult to get over. That's just a fact. The difference is, a failed healthy relationship isn’t necessarily damaging to oneself. So the “no contact” is extra important here. I'm no expert, but I’ll share sth that helped me in my journey to recovery. It's an on-going journey for me, but as long I love myself, I’m feeling better each day.Acknowledge there's no quick fix. Face the harsh truth that this will take time and a lot of work. Then keep in mind to pace yourself, get over one hurdle at a time. Don't read too much into your urge to contact. Simply try your best to pull through, like fighting an addiction. Don't put more stress on yourself by giving any meaning to that urge.Remind yourself of the true happiness you want and remember that the narcissist have never and will never give you that. They will ruin all your chances at anything good, big or small. So you're not just fighting to break free, you're also fighting for your future.Tell yourself “I love you” everyday. Remind yourself of all the good things in your heart and cute things on the outside. Do you tear up when watching Lion King? That's so cute! Love yourself for that. Little by little, you’ll start to be able to tell real, genuine love from the toxic, fake lovebombing. Then that “drug” will gradually lose its power over you.I started to write my mental health journal. I named it “Keeping myself healthy and happy”. I ONLY write about ME, and I make sure to end each entry with sth positive. For example, if I thought about sth in the relationship that I miss and it made me want to contact. I’d acknowledge that it happened without going into any details about the relationship or him. I focus on writing about how I feel at the moment and how I know what’s best for me. Then end it with either how much better I feel after pulling through, or sth positive I learned about myself in the process. I write about my random thoughts and realization too. Writing helps me to organize my thoughts and clear my head. I find it really helpful because I’m not stuck with one idea in my head going round and round in circles (which drives me crazy and gives me headaches). Also, when I read my journal later. These are all good reminders and advises coming from me, the person who knows me the best.Create distractions for yourself. A relationship with a narcissist is an immense task. Your time/energy/emotions were all fully occupied by that person. Part of the “withdrawal” symptoms is actually the sudden loss of tasks/goals/direction. So create new tasks for yourself. Time to make “you” your new project. Workout, sign up for a class you might be interested in, watch shows you like, hang out with friends, pick up a hobby, write a journal if you want to try. And when you feel exhausted from stress or pain, sleep for 12hrs straight. Yes, sleeping is also a distraction. It still won't be easy. I broke down in public twice because the urge to contact hit me strong and unexpected. But I never stopped trying things that I think I might like. After a while, I started to really remember about what I enjoy. This strong grasp of “who I am” made it clearer to me how my life was paralyzed by that heartless person and his toxic energy. Which made “no contact” seems better and better in my eyes.No questions asked, just don't. Writing journal or doing activities are good, but impossible when you’re experiencing a real intense episode of “withdrawal” . When the urge to contact becomes too strong, my logic and reasoning are gone. So I stop trying to talk any sense into me all together. I look in the mirror and tell myself, there's no reason, you just don't call. No questions asked, you're doing “no contact”, so you just do it! I practice this, then cry until I’m too tired to go on. Then I’m calm again.Get all the support you can get. Is there any friends or family members that you would trust with sharing what happened to you? Talk to them, ask for their support. Get a therapist. Join a support group if you can find one. Look up your local crisis hotline. I have called my city’s crisis line twice already and they were very helpful. I’ll make sure to make a donation around Christmas time. Do all of the above and more. There's no shame in asking for help.Face the hard lesson, but be gentle and loving to yourself. Let's get one thing straight first, never blame the victim, never blame yourself. That being said, this is still an opportunity to examine and understand myself better. I always know that there’re sth underlying in my personality or sth happened in my past that made me chose/stay with that toxic person. I didn't go into that immediately. But one day, when I found myself thinking about what led me to ignore the first sign of trouble, I didn't force myself to stop. Instead, I tried to be very encouraging and nurturing with myself. I had a conversation with me about all of my fear, trauma, vanities, stubbornness and self-destructive side. I did not criticize myself at all. I admit that I wish I can be better, but I also fully understand that I did the best I could given what I had. And I am absolutely capable with growing and doing better in the future. In the end, I gave myself a hug and told myself “I’ve faced my issues and flaws. Now I know, my love for me is true.”There’re people out there who care about you. Friends, family and even strangers on Quora. We all wish you the best. Please remember that.It will get better. Never lose sight of that.

column1: Can you explain the concept of vicarious trauma?
column3: Yes, it something I deal with all the time. As a cancer survivor (7 years today from my surgery that removed my voice box and the cancer that infected it) and the President of a Laryngectomee support group. When a patient is faced with this extensive surgery (5–12 hours depending on circumstances) it is very traumatic. The effect on close family members is just as traumatic, not knowing if their loved one will survive or cope with the loss of voice and any other complications. The trauma of family can be worse than the actual trauma of the patient.

column1: As a lawyer, what’s the most heartbreaking case you’ve seen in court?
column3: As a trial attorney whose practice primarily focused child abuse, I’ve seen some really bad, bad things. Murdered babies, child and baby rape cases, true torture cases, I tell my friends that nothing fazes me or surprises me anymore. However, saying those words is like a curse, because every time I say that, along comes a new case. Sometimes death isn’t the worst thing that can happen to a child. All the names of the people here are changed, to protect their privacy. I represented a set of three siblings who were removed from their parents’ custody for general negligence. As could be expected, tragically, the boys were placed in separate homes, pretty far away from each other. Two of the boys were doing OK, and I mean “just OK” as in just getting by. The oldest boy, Jamie, age 10, was sent to live in a group home instead of with a foster family. There wasn’t anything wrong with him, there just weren’t enough foster homes available. The school called me because they said he was goofing off and playing all the time. My first thought was “boys will be boys.” Yet, when I spoke to the owner of the group home, I found her really harsh, and harsh is putting it politely. Maybe about a couple weeks later, I got a call again from the group home saying they were giving a seven-day notice that Jamie was to be out of their home. I panicked because I knew there was a desperate shortage of foster homes, especially for African American male children. I knew I had to salvage the placement if possible. My first question to the owner was why she wanted Jamie removed. She told me Jamie was screwing around, his teacher at the on-grounds school said he was calling attention to himself by falling out of his desk, and walking into people and walls, falling to the ground for no good reason, and they were tired of it. He often tried to laugh it off, but they didn’t think it was funny. I demanded that we have a full staffing to talk about this in person. I visited Jamie and told him about the complaints, but I wasn’t angry at him. I just wanted to hear his side of the story and wanted to know what he wanted me to do on his behalf. He became tearful and said he did crash into the walls and other things, but that it was an accident. He said he felt funny, but couldn’t describe how, and fell out of his desk. Same as when he fell to the floor those times. He said wasn’t trying to make a scene but these things were just happening. I asked him when was the last time he had a physical, and he said he didn’t know. That raised huge questions in my mind. I asked him what he wanted to see happen, and if he wanted to stay at the home, and he said he’d rather stay there than have to move. I gave him a hug, thanked him for sharing his thoughts with me and told him I’d do my best for him, and he could call me any time. I went forward with the full staffing a few days later, and the first thing I was told is that Jamie thinks he’s a clown. He continues to trip and fall all the time for attention and earlier that day, he was playing tag with some boys st lunch, and ran full speed into a palm tree on purpose. I asked if he was hurt, and they said he has a big bump on his head, but that’s what he gets. I became furious when I heard that. This group home charged the Department of Children and Family Services (DCFS) $10k a month[1] for Jamie’s room and board, and when a child is injured, under state licensing law, they needed to take him to the emergency room for an exam to make sure he’s OK. If any group home where any of my kids were placed didn’t do that, I’d call community care licensing and request a full investigation of their home, citing negligence, and I’d have no issue trying to get them shut down. Jamie’s social worker was as shocked as I was, as she had never heard about this incident as they never reported this to her. Ella demanded that Jamie be brought into the meeting immediately. When Jamie came in, he literally looked like he had been hit by a car. He had bumps and bruises everywhere, and the biggest knot I had ever seen on the upper left hand side of his forehead. He had lots of scrapes on him, and many scabs. My mouth dropped open when I saw him. I greeted him, got up, walked to him and he gave me a hug, slowly articulating, “This is Jojo my attorney,” to the group. Jamie’s social worker looked distressed and I know I looked furious. Ella, the social worker announced, “This meeting will stop, and I’m taking Jamie to the ER right now.” I asked Ella to call me and let me know what happened. As soon as I got back to my office, I called Community Care Licensing and made a referral about what we had just seen. Ella called me later that day telling me that Jamie’s brain had some odd markings on it that looked like port wine stains, and his brain was seriously swollen from head trauma. It turned out that Jamie has a condition called Sturge-Weber Syndrome. [2] He was taken in to emergency surgery so the neurosurgeon could drill holes in Jamie’s skull so his brain would have room to swell and then heal. A part of his skull may be removed and stored in his abdominal area so it would stay alive until it could be put back in place. Regardless of whether he’d have part of his skull removed, she said he would be fitted with a halo with screws put into his skull while he healed. I began to tremble, I was so sad and angry for Jamie and what he was put through, and felt overwhelmed that despite the thorough physical he was supposed to have had, and an interview with his mother, that this condition hadn’t been diagnosed in his history. After being released from the hospital, Jamie was taken to a different group home that provided service for children with acute medical issues. He called me, very upset one day, reporting to me that the other kids there had teased him, and told him they were going to get a screwdriver to tighten the screws that went from his halo into his skull into his brain. Some of the bigger boys actually chased him with a screwdriver, terrifying Jamie. I told him to sit tight, I was going to call Ella and get him out of there ASAP. Ella managed to get him out of the group home within days and into a medically registered and certified foster mother who was really good. I was so relieved for Jamie. Days later, Jamie called me, saying he was worried because he could hardly see anything, and he felt as if he was looking through a gray piece of fabric. My heart literally dropped into the pit of my stomach. I called Ella to ask her to get Jamie in to the doctor to see what was going on with his vision. She said she already did, and he was scheduled to have a piece of his skull removed to reduce the pressure in his skull . That was scheduled to occur within days, and Jamie was losing his vision due to complications of his Sturge-Weber Syndrome as well as pressure on his brain, and the vision loss may be permanent. [3] Meanwhile, Jamie’s spirits were up, and he was “relieved” to be set to have the halo and screws removed from his head, and eager to be normal again. I recall sitting at my desk after talking to Jamie on the phone with my eyes closed and tears flowing down my face thinking about what he was about to endure. It’s hard to say how, but sometimes you just know things. I called the Court Appointed Special Advocate’s office (CASA) [4] to tell them I needed an advocate for Jamie, explaining that he was about to undergo brain and skull surgery, was most likely going to be permanently, totally blind, and he has no parent or family members for support. The director of the CASA’s office agreed to find a good advocate for Jamie and would call me back. Within a day or two, the fastest time ever to get a CASA, I was called by Joe, who was highly versed in medical issues, as well as law and children’s issues, and would be appointed as Jamie’s Court Appointed Special Advocate. I was so thankful and relieved. On surgery day, Joe was there with Jamie beforehand, and waited in the surgical waiting room just in case something went wrong, and be there for Jamie when he awoke from surgery. Joe is a true godsend for this child. I went to the hospital right after my last case was heard. Jamie was awake, out of surgery and seemed a little nervous, but gave me a big smile when he heard my voice. He immediately piped up, “Hi, Jojo, they fixed my skull.” I told him, “I see that. How are you feeling? You look like you’re wearing a turban,” and did my best to smile at him. He grinned and said in his slow drawl, “Well, I’m OK.” Joe asked if he could talk to me in the hall, and I said “yes.” Once outside the room, Joe told me that Jamie was 100% permanently blind, but he doesn’t know if he’s in pitch black blindness or if he is legally blind but could detect shapes. He was waiting for Jamie’s therapist to let the therapist talk Jamie about the current situation. Joe wanted the therapist there, to help Jamie process the news, and he or she would identify the best way to deliver this devastating news. I was in full agreement. Meanwhile, Jamie’s social worker, Ella, was livid with Joe, because Jamie had asked for a few baseball caps to cover his head while he was bandaged up. Jamie didn’t want anyone to know what he was going through, but could handle himself just fine if he were asked questions from strangers. Baseball caps would camouflage the marks. I was disgusted. After all Jamie went through, she was twisted out of shape about a baseball cap? The social worker yelled at me too for not stopping Joe from buying the caps. She was also angry because Joe didn’t seek the surgeon’s approval before buying them, and she said the doctor would be angry because germs would be exposed to Jamie’s head too soon after surgery by wearing a cap. (Through the bandages and everything. Go figure …) I told her I will ask Joe to ask the doctor to make sure it’s OK for Jamie to wear the caps thinking it might defuse the situation. If it’s appropriate, give Jamie the caps and if it’s not, tell Jamie he could wear his caps when his head healed and the neurosurgeon gave an OK, so then he can look foreword to being able to wear them. The social worker was satisfied with that response — it gave her “power” in the situation and she could let Jamie know when he could wear his caps. The surgeon was such a doll, said Joe was very easy to interact with, and was thankful he was there. The surgeon said that after the staples and sutures came out, it would be fine for Jamie to wear caps as long as it didn’t rub or irritate any of the wounded tissue. By that time, Jamie’s mother’s parental rights were terminated, as she just couldn’t remain clean, sober and attend all her programs within the statutory time frame. This termination of her parental rights left all three children as legal orphans, which I was highly displeased about. I continued to get complaints from Jamie’s social worker that he wasn’t trying hard enough to learn the Brailler, he was crying all the time, he didn’t want to go to school, he’s lazy, he doesn’t care, etc. One day after I got another complaint call from Ella, I flipping lost my cool and blew up at her. I screamed, and I mean screamed into the phone so loud that the other attorneys in my office all crowded around my door to see what I was yelling about. “You ignorant self-centered BITCH!” I screamed. “It’s not Jamie’s job to make your life easier, it’s your job to make sure his young life is more bearable, and YOU FAILED! Yes! YOU FAILED!! You tell me how YOU would feel if you were taken away from you mom, your siblings, your school, were accused of screwing around when all the while you were having seizures and going blind but didn’t know why? Then, as if things weren’t bad enough, you got your head literally sawed open, got bullied at school and humiliated by the other kids, and then found out your mother is no longer your mother. And to ice the cake, you find out you are PERMANENTLY BLIND, and you have NO IDEA what’s going to happen to you!!! ANSWER ME!” I was shaking I was so angry, and so heartbroken for Jamie. My colleagues did nothing to calm me down, they let me scream at that social worker, and tell her that I didn’t care what county counsel (the social workers’ attorney) would say about my screaming, and I hope she tells them, and I hope she writes to the court about how loud I am, too. I told her that I know that our judge would just LOVE to hear about this, especially about how she was dismissing Jamie as being attention seeking when he suddenly started to fall out of chairs, or run into things. I dared her to go for it. When the call ended, I sat down at my desk, as I had been standing up and screaming down at the phone, I put my head in my hands and started hyperventilating and continued to tremble while I wiped my tears of anger off my face. “Good on you, Jo! You told her off and she had it coming. I would be pissed, too!” my colleagues told me, trying to be supportive. My supervisor entered my office and closed the door. She asked what was going on, aside from what she just heard. I gave her the low down, her jaw dropped, and she said I needed to walk this on to the court to let the judge know what was going on. I completed the walk-on paperwork, filed it with the court, wrote up my report, asked Joe to write up a brief report, served the parties, and got a hearing set for the end of the week. Jamie was transported to the hearing by his foster mother, and he arrived with a red tipped cane, was wearing a beanie and dark glasses. As he walked, he swayed from side to side. I gasped when I saw him, but held my composure, went up behind him, tapped him on the shoulder and said, “Boo!” as he spun around. “Hello, Jojo…” he said. I brightly said, “How’d you know it was me!?!?!” and started laughing. He said, “I’d always know you!” The hearing began, and our judge entered and took her seat. I reminded Jamie he was in the courtroom, so he has to remove his beanie. He said “Oh, yeah, I forgot,” as he pulled his hat off. I was not prepared for what I saw; I could see the exact shape of the piece of skull that had been removed from his head, and there was deep scarring along the lines of where it was replaced. Where the screws from the halo were, there were deep divets, with keloid tissue building up around it. The judge looked at Jamie, looked at me and ordered us all into her chambers and read the riot act. Ella, Jamie’s CSW, sheepishly stated that she’s also having difficulties with Jamie’s younger brother, John, because it was determined that he also suffers from Sturge-Weber Syndrome, and ever since learning this, he doesn’t “want” to behave. He uses it as an excuse to act up. Instead of cross-talking with the CSW, I told the judge that I’ve been in contact with John (age 8) and he’s terrified that he’s going to have the same thing happen to him as what happened to Jamie, so it’s totally understandable. I had already applied for a CASA for him as well. We went back out to the courtroom, the judge admitted my report, Joe, the CASA’s report into evidence, then ordered a full-scale investigation into the handling of this matter, and a 30-day progress return. She had words of encouragement for Jamie, and I asked for a full psychological screening for him with all appropriate mental health treatment, especially to deal with loss, occupational therapy and physical therapy to follow. I also asked for an IEP (Individualized Education Plan) as well as a Regional Center assessment because of the seizures. The court agreed, and made the orders. Jamie’s foster mother eventually adopted him, and he continues to thrive in her care. Jamie remains blind, 100% sightless, his scarring profound. After he settled into his blindness, and received lots of therapy, he learned Braille and how to use the Brailler (a special typewriter that types in Braille). And, I’m crying like a baby as I write this story, all my frustration, sadness, and pain are stirring up again. That group home Jamie was in no longer exists, but I don’t know and don’t care about why it’s closed. No child deserves to undergo such medical and emotional neglect. If his condition were properly diagnosed instead of blown off and reported as the child goofing off, something different might have happened. Jamie might not have had to endure all this suffering — I’m not a doctor, so I can’t say for sure. But, I’m confident it would have been handled differently. I’ve handled many, many abuse cases, but Jamie’s absolutely destroys me. Jamie was just 10 years old when this happened. I still believe it didn’t have to happen.Footnotes[1] http://www.cdss.ca.gov/Portals/9/FCARB/Lists/GHList.pdf[2] Sturge-Weber syndrome[3] Sturge-Weber Syndrome[4] CASA of Los Angeles
