column1: What does it feel like to have a family member with schizophrenia?
column3: I wish the system would recognize psychosis to schizophrenia in the same way they recognize blind people don’t see, deaf people don’t hear, the mute don’t talk, the color blind don’t see colors. Then we would have less family dealing with the stress of trying to reason with someone that has complete loss of touch with reality as seen in schizophrenia. I live in a state where we have couple hundred thousand homeless people mainly due to untreated schizophrenia or mental illness. Their family or supports tried to help them with medications, therapies, social security disability, government benefits; a room or their own rent controlled apt for the blind/disabled, but again our society does not teach a schizophrenic how to cope with psychosis the way it teaches the blind to read brail or the deaf to learn sign language or read lips or a mute person to learn to use handwriting to communicate. Instead, the lack of insight in the person with schizophrenia means they will refuse to get help. If a schizophrenic believes a piece of wood tells them paranoid things all day, it does not matter how much anyone reasons with them, they don’t see it that way, just like a blind person does not see. It seems an extremely sad crisis as people with schizophrenia did not have to end up on living on the street or railroading family into enabling the disease and denial. If you want to know what it feels like to have family with schizophrenia go visit a homeless encampment and try to reason with a schizophrenic to get off the streets. They won’t do it as they have lost contact with reality and many refuse to accept the disease. If you find yourself involved with someone with this devastating disease my suggestion, go to a NAMI support group for the family of mentally ill at a hospital where the ill family member just got put on a psychiatric crisis hold. The family support group will help you figure out the difference between empowering, enabling and ultimately saving yourself as so many with schizophrenia will refuse to accept this disease and learn to function with it.

column1: For those with dementia and close loved ones of those with dementia: What was the moment you knew something was really wrong?
column3: My mother has dementia, and was quite an independent woman. She was a widow for about eight years when memory problems became apparent. But when she got lost coming home from a trip to the doctor’s office - where she had gone for about 40 years - it was apparent something was amiss. She was diagnosed with vascular dementia, likely had a tiny TIA (transient ischemic attack) but imaging didn’t show anything. But from there things slowly deteriorated. She began hoarding and shutting people out from coming into her home. She became more suspicious of people and when something was lost, like a bill, insisted someone was going through her mail. Irritability increased as her frustration at the progressive loss of control occurred. Getting her to a medical appointment meant getting her out of the house. So I learned to tell her we were going to a restaurant for breakfast or lunch, and then on the way tell her we were dropping by the doctor’s first. If I said that at her home, she would refuse to leave the house, snapping “There’s nothing wrong with me! I don’t need to see a doctor!” By the way, she had a wonderful geriatrician who was a lifesaver in a lot of ways. This is the hardest part of dementia for family members, I think - the person is obviously becoming more impaired and lost, but also becoming more closed and self-protective. Anger often emerges and then is forgotten and then bursts out as you try to assist. Trying to make sure her house was safe was met with resistance, not wanting anything moved or touched. The question of when to more aggressively intervene is not necessarily very clear. I know I want my independence as long as I can have it! But eventually, with the help of her doctor, this was able to occur. Last word for anyone dealing with this: contact your local Alzheimer Association. They have support groups and a wealth of information that can be helpful for the primary caregivers as well as other family members. It really takes a community to give dignity to a person suffering from dementia - and to keep the caregiver sane. Because you are grieving the loss of the person you knew, but they are still there right in front of you, and it’s not going to improve. It’s so important to have support who won’t get burned out hearing about the latest escapades. A little humor with the right people can go a long ways.

column1: Why does thinking of people who have left my life make me cry uncontrollably? How can I stop this?
column3: Talk to your doctor, or counselor, or social worker, or a trusted friend. Someone can steer you to a grief support group. Everyone deals with grief in a different way. When I read “left my life,” I thought you were speaking of death. Maybe it’s because I have lost so many family members through death. But, people can leave your life in ways other than death! I know what that feels like, too, although I’m not equating my losses with your experience. Healing from loss of a person can take much time for some people, especially if we are sensitive individuals. I urge you to have someone to talk to, someone who is a patient listener. They may not have solutions, but it means everything to have someone validate your pain. I have known many people who run from pain, avoiding any validation. That hurts, too. In dealing with some of my losses, I found it helpful to learn and write about their lives. In other cases, I kept a journal to follow my thoughts and feelings as they change over the days and nights. To express my anger at loss, I once grabbed the end of a pillow and banged it hard against a closet door. In the case of one loss, I joined a support group and read books by people who were in the same boat as me. A support group can make you feel you are not alone! I hope this helps. Loss can be very hard to deal with, but time can lessen some of the pain.

column1: How do you deal with the loss of a parent when you can't talk about it with your other parent?
column3: You really just have to talk to someone else I think. Do you have siblings? You might be able to talk to them. If not, what about an aunt or uncle? And if not a family member perhaps a therapist or a clergy person. I think the best thing might be to join a Grief Support group. You can support one another through the experience of loss. By the way, I'm really sorry that happened.

column1: How do you deal with family members that distance themselves from you when you have chronic illness plus anxiety and depression?
column3: Be pleasant. Be polite. Be informative—to the degree you feel comfortable—but maintain your boundaries. Be aware some people are terribly afraid of mental illness. They may believe the mentally ill are dangerous and will do god knows what. They may also believe it is something you can catch. My own father believed this. Some people may never accept you—even after you recover—their loss. Do not spend too much time trying to sell them on your value as a person—-spend your time instead on getting control of your depression and anxiety. Be aware that 1 out of 4 people are bothered by mental illness. Depression can have genetic roots. Your family members may one day find themselves struggling the very thing you are. At that point they may be ready to face the realities of mental illness. Be ready to help—-and be a much bigger person than they are. Find people who will support and value you. Are there support groups in your area?Hospitals often have them or mental health clinics. Sometimes, sadly, in some families, the mentally ill have to build their own family of people who love, support, and value them.

column1: How do I deal with old home memories? I missed that home too much.
column3: I lived on the same property for the first 26 years of my life and in the subsequent 35 years have moved eleven times across six states. Some were my choice, some were not, and some were technically my choice but not really, due to circumstances. When I have a dream about “home” it is always the place where I grew up. I have a deep sense of nostalgia for that place. But I also established other homes that I was heartbroken to leave, while other places were really just a place to live and I was glad to get out and go somewhere else. I’ve found that when missing anything feels like it’s “too much,” when grieving what WAS starts interfering with the enjoyment of what IS, it’s time to pay attention. “Home” has an added layer of meaning than “house,” and implies that when you moved, you lost more than just your place of residence. If you just moved in the last few weeks or months—well, it does take time for a new house to feel like home, especially if you were in your old home for many years. You might need to hang some familiar things on the walls, or something new that you love, and just spend time walking around and noticing things. Get to know your new house like you would get to know a friend. Develop a routine. But if it’s been longer than that, or if the feeling is so strong that it is really interfering with you life, chances are that it’s something deeper that you’re missing. Figuring out what that is can be key to moving forward. You didn’t say why you moved, or how far you are now from where you were. If the move disrupted relationships or was the result of a death or divorce, missing the home might mean missing being able to share your home with friends and/or family, which might not be easy or even possible where you are now. You might be projecting the grief over a different loss onto your new home. Just like it takes time to feel at home in a new residence, it also takes time to establish new relationships and deal with grief. If you’ve suffered a major loss, seek out a support group or counselor. As you take the time to find and build new relationships, consider adopting a pet or getting some houseplants. It sounds silly, but especially for those living alone, having another living being to care for makes a world of difference. If the move was forced for financial or health reasons, your old home may represent a more secure past and missing it “too much,” might be a manifestation of anxiety over what might be next. If you moved because of the needs of a family member, it’s possible that resentment over having to leave a home you loved to help someone else is making it harder to let go. That one can be very hard to acknowledge since you probably love the person and might feel like a cad for complaining about the way the move has disrupted your life. But it’s real and normal. Acknowledge it and realize that you always have choices, even if your preferred choice isn’t on the menu. Missing an old and much-loved home is normal. But if you’re experiencing it as “too much,” chances are there’s something beyond the old house that you’re missing. Dig deep to figure out what that is, and you’ll have a better idea of how to make your new house a home.

column1: Has Putin made the biggest mistake of his life by invading Ukraine?
column3: Yes and no. No—at the moment, the incredible damage that the war has caused has been inflicted almost entirely on Ukrainians and their communities. The vast majority of Russians (unless they have had family members sent to the conflict zone) have not experienced nearly the same level of suffering. Russians in St. Petersburg or Moscow or Samara are not having to live in bunkers or flee their destroyed homes. Their cities have not suffered from a breakdown in essential services (electricity, water, medical care) and so they are not undergoing what many Ukrainians are. This is why many Russians still support Putin and his narrative of the war—it hasn’t harmed them personally (yet). No—despite international sanctions, Russia has not suffered that much economically. Russia is regrettably earning a tremendous amount of money shipping energy to Western Europe. Indeed, many of its customers are trying to stockpile Russian gas in advance of winter. There is simply no alternative at the moment for much of Europe: although alternative energy sources are being pursued and other options (like LNG from the Middle East) are being considered, these are long-term transitions that cannot take place immediately. In the interim, many Eastern European countries are almost entirely dependent on Russian energy imports—which is why countries like Hungary fought to exempt energy imports from EU sanctions. No—much of the world refuses to get involved and/or treat Putin as a pariah. India, which buys a lot of military hardware from the Russians, is still merrily doing business. China is buying Russian energy at a discount. Many African countries view the Ukraine crisis as not their problem and refuse to allow it to “get in the way” of their dealings with Moscow. Yes—one of the stated goals of the conflict with Ukraine was Putin’s desire that NATO should never expand to include Ukraine and indeed that NATO’s previous enlargement should be rolled back. Instead, his invasion has so horrified the two neutrals next door—Sweden and Finland—that the public opinion changed to heavily favour NATO membership almost overnight. Instead of two of Russia’s largest European neighbours being military neutral, their military strength is soon going to be combined with that of the massive NATO alliance. Putin set off a chain of events that forced Sweden and Finland to see no alternative to joining NATO—which is the exact opposite of what he wanted. Yes—Ukraine has been a valuable proving ground for Western military technology. Instead of having to wargame how certain military hardware (such as the HIMARS system) would perform against the Russians in a theoretical conflict, countries such as the United States have been able to see it employed against Russian forces on the actual battlefield. This will no doubt contribute to further refinement and technological progress. Putin has essentially given Western countries supplying Ukraine the chance to test out technology against his troops. Yes—prior to the conflict there was some resentment in Western European and North American countries against their troop deployments in Eastern Europe—the Baltic nations in particular. Some critics suggested that this was merely poking Vladimir Putin in the eye and the deployments should be ended or reduced. There is no serious talk of doing that now, which means that a theoretical Russian smash-and-grab attempt to seize Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania (mooted in the past) is out of Putin’s reach unless he wants to start WWIII. His Ukraine invasion has led to the reinforcement of the Baltics, rather than a loss of Western interest in them. Yes—Russia has always insisted that it is still a Great Power, that it belongs at the top table with the leading nations of the world. Part of the rationale for inviting Russia to join the G8 group of major industralized countries (even though it didn’t qualify economically) was that Moscow was a major military power and it was important to flatter Putin and keep him “onside.” This was abandoned after 2014 when the true character of Putin’s revanchist regime was revealed following the seizure of Crimea. With his government’s behaviour in Ukraine, Russia will never again be perceived by major Western nations as a responsible international interlocutor. It will be treated for a long time as a rogue regime. So the international respect that Putin craved from major Western countries—being treated as their equal—is long gone.

column1: Is it true that ethnic Koreans account for a significant proportion of Yakuza members in Japan? If yes, what are the reasons for it?
column3: The vast majority of Yakuza understandably come from the Japanese underclass. Japanese society is fairly equal and pretty much everyone is middle class, which means someone who couldn't fit in are deviants in a significant way, such as being 1) burakumin, the designated underclass caste in feudal Japan who did jobs considered unclean (sewage, slaughter house, leather tanning) or undignified (historically, street peddlers or street entertainers like dancers); 2) Korean; 3) people with criminal records, significant history of juvenile crimes, etc. Unlike the commonly held belief that Koreans in Japan are descendants of conscripts from colonial time, the majority of Koreans in Japan are economic migrants and many of them were refugees from the time of the Korean war, as well as the significant proportion of them who are political refugees from Jeju. (Jeju uprising). They spoke little Japanese and gravitated toward typical ethnic business like BBQ restaurants, pachinko parlour, ramen shops, etc. They often adopted Japanese names to avoid discrimination. But even for those second generation Koreans with Japanese names who spoke fluent Japanese, employment in a respectable company was completely shut out, because these companies would ask for koseki (like birth certificate in West). For burakumin, it was the same, because HR in Japanese corporations (at least up to late 70s) kept encyclopedia lists of buraku villages, so anyone whose koseki was registered in one of the lists was out. (And until very recently, you could not change your ancestral origin in a koseki.) Now, there is a quasi-legitimate reason for corporations to avoid Koreans or burakumin as if they have criminal record. For one, more than half of the Korean population in Japan voluntarily aligned themselves with Chongryon. Now, this was understandable if one considers that the south was under a military dictatorship and the south was pretty quiet over the right of Koreans in Japan, while the communist north was a vocal supporter of those who were openly against capitalist Japan and the USA. Similarly, burakumin had strong associations with the Buraku Liberation League, a fairly notorious direct-action group, which often functioned like a corporate racketeering group. And this is circular, but, even if a Korean or a buraku applicant himself may not be supporter of North Korea or the Yakuza, it is assumed that he probably knows or has a family/relative who is Yakuza or Chongryon member or any dodgey political organisations. And due to the lifetime employment system, which makes firing notoriously hard, it was so much easier to simply rule out a candidate from that background who are less than 1 % of the population. My uncle, despite being a university graduate, could not get a job in top-tier corporation, because they routinely asked for the father of a new recruit to sign guarantees for any financial loss caused. My uncle's father (my grandfather) died in the war and the fact that his mother (my grandmother) owned a few hair saloons and was financially well off didn't count (because she was a woman or/and hair saloons weren't respectable enough). Still, he got a job elsewhere, though not as good as what he could have gotten if he had a salaryman or a civil servant as a father. Anyhow, this kind of system makes it likely that Koreans or burakumin would make living in a pachinko (gambling) parlour, loan finance, construction, or the entertainment district, where you can’t avoid dealing with the Yakuza.

column1: Adult What are some of the most effective ways to fight depression?
column3: FIRST OF ALL IDENTIFY WHETHER IT IS DEPRESSION, STRESS OR ANXIETYStress : Stress is an everyday part of our lives and a normal reaction to a situation where you feel under pressure (emotional or physical) like meeting work deadlines, coping with annoying co-workers, Public speaking or sitting exams. Anxiety : Anxiety is is still having those feelings of stress long after the actual offending event has passed like an intense fear of being criticized, embarrassed or humiliated, even in everyday situations, for a period of six months or more. Depression : Depression is something more serious medical condition. It is a feeling of hopelessness. Person suffering from depression losses interest in all previously interested activities and find it difficult to sleep or continue even his regular activities. 2. ONLINE SCALE/TEST FOR MEASURING DEPRESSION, STRESS AND ANXIETY:beyondblueThe Depression, Anxiety and Stress Test3. HOW TO TREAT DEPRESSION: Consider the fact that continuous stress causes anxiety which may lead to depression . Which treatment is suitable for curing depression depends upon the intensity and type of ailment. Also how the depression patient is likely ton respond to treatment techniques decides about which treatment is to be followed. In case of acute depression medication is essential. THERAPIST/PSYCHIATRIST: They are professionally trained people to identify and treat depression medically. They use combination of psychological methods and medications to treat depression patients in efficient manner. So one should immediately consult a professional therapist if identified with depression. Allopathy treatment is advisable in case of acute depression and for long term effect (slow therapy) consult to Ayurveda and Homeopathy combined with Yoga and Exercise. Caution: Don’t depend on antidepressants for long time and every time when identified with depression —————————OTHER WAYS TO TREAT DEPRESSION ————————— LOVE AND SUPPORT FROM FRIENDS AND FAMILY: Our society has negative thoughts for depression patients. Depression patients tend to isolate themselves from their family and friends.So foremost treatment for depression is love and support from our loved ones.You can help a depression patient in the following manner:Help them to identify whether they are suffering from DepressionGet them to Therapist or PhysicianLove them and keep them happyMake them realise about positive aspacts of their lifeTalk to them and keep them engage in various activitiesAccompany them in their regular activitiesEncourage them for doing exerciseCook healthy food for themInvolve them in Social activities.Involve them in fun activities like games, music, movies etc.Most important step is to encourage them for treatment of their ailment. Sometimes depression may lead to suicidal practices. So carefully deal with such patients. EXERCISE: Exercise is the most underutilized antidepressant. When you exercise, your body releases chemicals called endorphin. These endorphin interact with the receptors in your brain that reduce your perception of pain. Doing exercise with your friends, partner and family members gives you emotional comfort with benefit of Physical Activity. So joining group exercise class is more beneficial.Exercise may also include:Housework, especially sweeping, mopping, or vacuuming, Jogging at a moderate pace, Low-impact Aerobics, Playing tennis, Swimming, Walking etc.MEDITATION: Various researches show that Meditation is very helpful in treating depression. It helps in lessening negative thinking, rumination, and lack of focus in depression patients.Meditation for beginners : Sit straight in noise free open area with fresh air and proper sunlight and concentrate on constant point. HEALTHY DIET: Cook says there's evidence that foods with omega-3 fatty acids and folic acids could help ease depression. It includes foods like low fat dairy, walnuts, whole grains, dark chocolate, fresh fruits, green veggies like spinach, carrots etc.Balanced diet with required nutrients is very beneficial . Skipping food is not good for depression patients. So eat regularly. REGULAR-HEALTHY LIFESTYLE: Not only depression patients, but everyone should follow a regular and healthy lifestyle. In fact a person with regular lifestyle is less likely to prone to depression and other stress symptoms. But set a gentle life routine initially otherwise it will affect depression patients negatively. ADEQUATE SLEEP : Depression can make it hard to get enough shut-eye, and too little sleep can make depression worse. What can you do? Start by making some changes to your lifestyle. Go to bed and get up at the same time every day. Try not to nap. Take all the distractions out of your bedroom -- no computer and no TV. In time, you may find your sleep improves. Additionally joining hobby classes, dance or exercise groups may also help, cooking, painting, outing with friends etc is also helpful for depression patients. Depression is just like another health problems and it is completely treatable. But avoiding or postponing proper treatment worsens the depression. Also our society need to change their mindset towards depression patients. Thank You. Information Source: Personal experience and Google image source : Google

column1: I'm 46 and was a long-time caregiver to my father who just passed. I feel alone, directionless. Where do I begin?
column3: Hello friend- If it feels any better, I have been in your shoes. I took care of my mother until she passed, and it caused friction between me and my family members as well. I also can truly relate about the feelings of loss and lack of purpose after a loved one passes. It has been over six years now since my mother passed away. For me, I had to look to find new purpose, new interests, and I had to work on myself. Likely you need to discover who you are again. Like you I can relate to the feelings of guilt. I looked around after my mother passed and here was my life- pretty much in shambles. I lost myself, my own world. My friends had mostly moved on. My family was angry and adversarial toward me. There is a huge adjustment you will have to make in your life. Mostly it will be a road to self-discovery and a journey of growth. For me, I had to find a way to make sense of my life. I truly wasn’t the same person that I was before my caregiving journey, and I don’t think anyone is. I have just written a book and it will be posted on Amazon later this week. It’s called “The Advocate’s Heart.” Stay tuned- it will be there soon!! There is a whole chapter in it about dealing with the grief and loss of a loved one, and gives some solid tools on how to cope and heal. My advice is to seek out caregiver support groups. There are several online, and you might even have one inside of your church or community. If there isn’t- start one! Think about interests that you once enjoyed. Did you enjoy exercise? Music? How about sports? My advice to you is immerse yourself in various activities, even though it’s hard to get up in the morning. Just take it day by day, and force yourself to get out and find your life again! You WILL meet people who will start to fill the void in your life. I promise you, if you take the caregiving experience you had with your father as the blessing it was, your heart will be big enough to be blessed tenfold again. Many (((HUGS)))
column9: I still have a son with CP that we are dealing with issues over needed medical equipment, loans for dental procedures, etc. My father passed away about 10 years ago, but my mom is now 97 and we are dealing with many issues with her care. She has some dementia and fell last week. There are so many things that change with age, the passing of our parents, and the fact that some friends cannot deal with the changes you go through, are common to many. This is one reason I am a passionate speaker and author writing and doing radio shows to help those who are coming behind to see that our lives are different. We need to help educate others and share our experiences with those who are just now starting this journey. I am coaching other caregivers to help with the bumps and distresses that happen. I would recommend a gratitude journal to remember the things you loved about your mom and dad and what lessons they taught you. It is good to remember with joy the things that you shared. If you want to reach out again, I have a website Courage to Overcome and a club, too. Even my radio program is by that name and I love to interview people to see what lessons they learned while they had caregiving challenges. I agree that you will find the things you were interested in before at some point, but sharing your journey is so helpful for us and others. Best to you in your healing.

column1: Adult How do you deal with the fear after losing a parent?
column3: Such a loss requires having those in one’s life who you trust and can depend upon to help you through this trying period in your life. The loss of a parent can be very emotionally challenging, and trying to reach out, if people don’t come to you, may be better than bearing the pain in isolation. So if you family and friends, now is the time to be close to them (if you trust them, as not all family members or friends are good to be around). There are some very good books, or various media on mourning and grief. These sources may help you to identify and understand the sometimes complex feelings that can come up, and the various stages people go through when they mourn. Some feel less alone in their grief if see others’ have gone through the same process. There are also those who benefit from participating in a small grief support group, or seeing a grief counselor, if one feels more comfortable 1:1. If you have a faith, you can always consult with your religious leader. You need not go through this alone, and to fully mourn requires feeling safe enough to do so. Here I am speaking of psychological and emotional safety, so you can fully express to yourself all the parent has meant to you throughout your life, as well as what place you had in her/his life. This experience can bring up things which you’ve never considered before, and sorting it all out, and fully mourning requires others. Bruce Kugler

column1: How does Hamas maintain its military strength in Gaza?
column3: Several factors are allowing Hamas to maintain some military strength in Gaza. More disturbingly Hamas appears to be regrouping and rebuilding some capabilities since the end of large scale IDF offensive actions. The IDF’s Rafah operation was the last offensive against existing and intact Hamas formations. With that operation, according to the IDF, roughly 23 of 24 Hamas battalions had been “dismantled.” That doesn’t mean all or even most Hamas in any one battalion were killed/injured, but enough along with command/logistics to make them ineffective as battalion units. Before the October 7 attack the IDF estimated Hamas strength at 25–40,000 armed men, leaning towards the lower number. In addition there were several thousand Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and several thousand more from other splinter groups or clans. Fighting over the past year indicates that the higher Hamas number was probably more accurate. So total opposition strength in Gaza was probably about 50,000 armed men as of the start of IDF offensive operations in Gaza. Including approximately 1000 killed during the October 7 attack, the Israeli government estimates it’s killed 18,000 combatants with some perhaps similar number wounded. Not all of these are Hamas. At least several thousand are PIJ and other Palestinian/Jihadist groups, plus armed clan members. These losses are easily sufficient to back IDF claims as to “dismantled” Hamas battalions. Losses of 20–30% killed/seriously wounded, especially with loss of command/communications/resupply are generally enough to render a unit ineffective or force surrender. However, despite this it does appear that Hamas has retained fighting capability in some “dismantled” battalions and rebuilt others. These estimates indicate that in terms of raw numbers there are still plenty of armed men around. To counter this the IDF continues attritional operations. In north Gaza successful IDF operations are a good news/bad news proposition. Good news—IDF is still killing/capturing lots of Hamas combatants. Bad news—there still are lots of Hamas combatants, and they are persistently try to infiltrate back into previously abandoned positions. Largely overlooked in its significance, was a relatively major Hamas attack on IDF positions around Jabalia on about 12/30/24. The IDF claims 106 Hamas killed against no IDF losses in the fighting, a significant tactical victory. That’s the good news. The bad news is this was a well coordinated, if badly executed, battalion sized attack, involving forces cut off by IDF operations around Kaman Adwal Hospital trying to break out, and forces trying to relieve them. The IDF acknowledges that Hamas is rebuilding its battalions, often with young poorly trained recruits. The conduct and results of this recent attack appear to demonstrate that, both as to the rebuild and current low quality. That’s bad for Israel in the long term though. If things continue to drag on, Hamas’ training, quality and organization will improve. We’ve seen it’s a mistake to dismiss that. The question is, why is this happening despite Hamas’ clear military defeats over the past year? And the answer is, Israel has allowed it. Israel insists on attempting to negotiate a release of hostages, at the expense of concluding the military campaign, so the war drags on and Hamas is regaining strength. Israel has left Hamas a mostly unencumbered sanctuary in central Gaza, from which Hamas’ decimated but still extant leadership still exerts control. It seems something similar has happened in Gaza city, despite the fact the IDF did move through there at the outset of the campaign nearly a year ago now. Hamas has plenty of food, water and fuel thanks to generous aid pouring into Gaza daily, and is probably getting at least small arms and ammo smuggled in some shipments. Israel’s war goals have always been contradictory, i.e., defeating Hamas and negotiating a release of the remaining hostages. The IDF, the Israeli government and public choose to pretend this isn’t the case, that somehow they can do both. But the math says no, and Hamas understands this which is why it won’t deal except for a result that guarantees its survival in Gaza. The only way both might be accomplished is if the incoming Trump administration would support an aid cutoff/reduction to Gaza and full implementation of the so-called “generals’ plan” which would amount to a siege of Gaza (particularly north Gaza) to (hopefully) force a Hamas capitulation. The IDF thus far has just implemented aspects of the plan, cutting a corridor in north Gaza, and encouraging (rather than forcing) a full Palestinian evacuation, coupled with periodic raids. Whether Trump would sign off on such a plan is unknown (it’s not impossible.) However, it is not even clear that the Israeli government would support such a plan, and there would certainly be serious opposition from the Israeli left, the UN, “international community”, international courts, and the hostage families. The alternative though is a continued stalemate in which Hamas gradually continues to strengthen or an Israeli capitulation to Hamas demands in a hostage for terrorists exchange.
column9: The IDF (hopefully ) will resume operations after Israel gets whatever hostages can be recovered. But as long as Hamas know that taking hostages ensures their survival this will continue - the answer - though unpalatable, is to not negotiate for hostage release but to leave them - unfortunate for the hostage, obviously - but then it stops working and Hamas can be decimated - tho it won’t resolve the wider more long term differences - if they ever can be ….

column1: My 6-year-old son passed away from cancer last week and my husband won't stop crying himself to sleep over it. How do I make him get over this minor setback?
column3: First off this is NOT a minor setback this is a major life change for the family. Please understand that everyone grieves differently and he is actually expressing his grief unlike you. You and your husband need to seek counseling along with the other family members. You need counseling to learn how to deal with your grief and how to respond to your husband’s grief. Please let your husband know there are men support groups that loss their child as well he can rely on for support.

column1: Would the United States be doing better with Coronavirus if Obama were president? Or is the president's role overstated?
column3: At the beginning of the Stafford Act, is the following text:“The Congress hereby finds and declares that because disasters often cause loss of life, human suffering, loss of income, and property loss and damage; and because disasters often disrupt the normal functioning of governments and communities, and adversely affect individuals and families with great severity; special measures, designed to assist the efforts of the affected States in expediting the rendering of aid, assistance, and emergency services, and the reconstruction and rehabilitation of devastated areas, are necessary.”It then defines the term emergency as:“Emergency means any occasion or instance for which, in the determination of the President, Federal assistance is needed to supplement State and local efforts and capabilities to save lives and to protect property and public health and safety, or to lessen or avert the threat of a catastrophe in any part of the United States.”The Stafford Act then, over 181 pages, describes how the President can use the many resources available to the federal government to provide that assistance. It also includes a list of other federal laws that define the role of the federal government in disasters and emergencies. For example:42 U.S. Code § 5170b.Essential assistance (a) In general Federal agencies may on the direction of the President, provide assistance essential to meeting immediate threats to life and property resulting from a major disaster, as follows: (1) Federal resources, generally Utilizing, lending, or donating to State and local governments Federal equipment, supplies, facilities, personnel, and other resources, other than the extension of credit, for use or distribution by such governments in accordance with the purposes of this chapter. (2) Medicine, food, and other consumables Distributing or rendering through State and local governments, the American National Red Cross, the Salvation Army, the Mennonite Disaster Service, and other relief and disaster assistance organizations medicine durable medical equipment, food, and other consumable supplies, and other services and assistance to disaster victims.There is, without doubt, a role for the federal government in assisting with emergencies and disasters and the law clearly states that the President is responsible for leading that effort. As head of the Executive Branch, the President is responsible for the operations of bodies like FEMA (The Federal Emergency Management Agency), Homeland Security, and the Department of Health and Human Services, which includes agencies such as the CDC (Center for Disease Control). There is a reason the country is called the United States of America and not just the States of America. There is a reason there is a federal government and not just 50 state governments. There are challenges and problems that are too large for any state to handle by themselves and there are things that are much better accomplished when the efforts are coordinated instead of individually handled by the states. Supply Coordination We have seen many examples of that in 2020. We saw states competing against each other for Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), medical equipment such as ventilators, and medical supplies such as testing kits. This competition allowed businesses and individuals to hoard equipment and engage in price gouging that resulted in suffering across the states. It is senseless that what was clearly a national need wasn’t coordinated at the national level. The Stafford Act explicitly says that the President can use agencies like FEMA and the State Department (for negotiating with international suppliers) to coordinate and facilitate supplies needed to attend to the disaster. What did this President do? He went to Jared(TM). Messaging Any leader of an organization will tell you that consistent messaging is key to accomplishing an objective. Our news is national. We cannot achieve consistent messaging when 50 different states are individually providing that message. We cannot achieve consistency messaging when different federal agencies are communicating different messages. We cannot achieve consistent messaging when the President contradicts his own cabinet members and agency heads. We cannot achieve consistent messaging when the President contradicts the medical and scientific experts. We cannot achieve consistent messaging when the President repeatedly contradicts his own messaging. The President is the “Communicator in Chief”. There is a reason the office holder is called “the president”. It is because it is their job to preside. The person who presides is responsible for keeping the group on task, for keeping their eyes on the objectives, for ensuring communication is open and unfettered. The person who presides is responsible for speaking for the group. America needed one voice to tell the people what was happening, what the plan was to deal with it, and what the people needed to do to support that objective. Possibly the most ridiculous thing in the history of the world is that the wearing of masks to reduce infection became a political thing. Wearing masks to reduce infection is basic medical science. We have known about it for more than a century. It has been successfully used in previous pandemics. It is used by medical professionals every single day. And yet the President managed to fuck up something so simple. Preparation It is a leader’s responsibility to be watching the horizon, to foresee approaching challenges and to prepare the group to meet those challenges. On March 25th, 2020, President Trump said:“Nobody would ever believe a thing like that’s possible. Nobody could have ever seen something like this coming, but now we know, and we know it can happen and happen again. - Donald J. Trump”It’s the leader’s job to see “something like this coming” and former Presidents did indeed see something like this as someday coming. In 2005, President Bush said:“If we wait for a pandemic to appear, it will be too late to prepare. And one day many lives could be needlessly lost because we failed to act today."President Bush had just read a book about the 1918 influenza pandemic and recognizing the seriousness of such an event he unveiled a plan at the National Institute of Health that called for early detection, international cooperation, stockpiling of vaccines and medical equipment, and public education about pandemic prevention. In 2014, President Obama gave a speech in which he said:“There may, and likely will, come a time in which we have both an airborne disease that is deadly. And, in order for us to deal with that effectively, we have to put in place an infrastructure, not just here at home but globally, that allows us to see it quickly, isolate it quickly, respond to it quickly. So that if and when a new strain of flue like the Spanish flu crops up, five years from now, or a decade from now, we’ve made the investment, and we’re further along to be able to catch it."The Obama administration put together a 40 page plan for dealing with pandemics. You can read the document, here, it was titled Playbook for Early Response to High-Consequence Emerging Infectious Disease Threats and Biological Incidents. The Trump administration ignored that document. The purpose of the document, as it said in its introduction, was:“to assist US Government experts and leaders in coordinating a complex US Government response to a high-consequence emerging disease threat anywhere in the world with the potential to cause an epidemic, pandemic, or other significant public health event, by providing a decision-making tool that identifies 1) questions to ask; 2) agency counterparts to consult for answers to each; and 3) key decisions which may require deliberation through the Presidential Policy Directive (PPD)-1 process or its successor NSC process.”Wow. We sure could have used such a tool in 2020. The idea that “nobody could have ever seen something like this coming” is stunningly ignorant. Hell, in 1994, I knew that something like this was coming, after I read Pulitzer Prize winning investigative journalist Laurie Garrett’s book The Coming Plague.

column1: Why did Trump lose the 2020 election?
column3: I propose these reasons:His behavior. Trump was one of the meanest, crass, dishonest, incompetent, bone ignorant Presidents ever, if not the meanest, crass, dishonest, incompetent, bone ignorant President ever. He was embarrassing and infuriating to have to listen to, and the lying and the grade school insults were just unprofessional as well as childish, and at times, sickening. He acted like a low level Mafia thug when talking about perceived enemies who had the audacity to disagree with or challenge him. He never showed any real interest in learning the job or taking the business of leading the free world seriously. His own staff called him a moron and a threat to America’s security. People did not like their President acting like an abusive toddler and fighting with everyone, even our allies while embracing/kowtowing to some of the world’s worst dictators and traditional enemies of America to the point where national security professionals were leery of him. Trump clearly never grew either as a leader or a human being in the office—he was the same classless, arrogant, ignorant, repugnant oaf coming out as he was going in.His criminal/morally suspect behavior. Trump has been caught in many scandals, some of them with the potential of being criminal, and it seemed every day brought out more and more criminality. People close to him were being indicted and jailed, and were just at best, morally suspect. He was impeached over various and sundry behavior as President, with hundreds of former AGs stating that if he weren’t President, he would have been indicted based on the findings in the Mueller report. Reports as well as testimony from former associates revealed a pattern of criminal behavior as a businessman as well as thuggish behavior to keep people in line. Most people not steeped in right wing media could see with all that smoke, there was probably a fire in the Oval, and it is looking as though he will spend the rest of his life fighting off jail sentences.His divisiveness. Everyone but white men were in Trump’s crosshairs during the last four years. His divisiveness motivated women, minorities, young people of all racial groups who supported the protests, and LGBTQ to turn out in record numbers. Some of these groups, such as young people, did not vote in significant numbers in the past, but this time they were fired up enough to get to the polls in droves. Trump lost a lot of conservative women as well who were tired of the childish, thuggish, macho man misogynistic behavior from him. Minorities in particular, especially black and brown people, genuinely feared another four years of Trump and Barr/DOJ, given their words and behavior during the protests, the tone deaf denials of systemic racism in law enforcement, the treatment of immigrant families by ripping kids from their parents with the prospect of many of those kids never finding their parents again, the stacking of the Supreme Court, and the support/weak disavowal of militias and other white supremacists. With the encouragement/work on the ground by people like Stacey Abrams, professional athletes, and other celebrities to turn out the vote and educating voters on how to make sure their vote would count, minorities and young people registered and voted in record numbers.But, even with the above factors, the odds were pretty decent that Trump might have been able to slither into a second term thanks to uneducated white men, seniors, and some white women, just like last time. He lost some people in those groups but not all of them—there were still enough of them in the right geographical locations to put him back in the Oval on the strength of the electoral college (remember in 2016, he lost the popular vote, and won the EC by the narrowest of margins in key districts). But Trump was definitely hurting even with the EC advantage. Biden still had a chance to peel off some of them—the polls were always fairly tight between the two of them. But what really finished Trump off was:COVID. Reality caught up with Trump. People measured the Trump inaction, lies, lack of empathy, and rhetoric up against what was actually happening on the ground: mass death, illness, filled up ICUs, economic hardship due to job loss and a busted up economy. Unfortunately for Trump, this was one issue all the lies in the world couldn’t make go away; the virus punctured a hole in the fantasy Trump had been existing in. They saw an out of touch, lazy, ignorant President who pushed quack treatments, was willing to let people sicken and die without trying to do even small things like wearing a mask and laying off those indoor packed rallies, refusing to negotiate with Congress to provide economic relief to people pushed out of work and were facing eviction, ignored/stifled the medical professionals and meddled in CDC policy, lied to the public about the lethality of the virus, and who couldn’t even keep himself, his family, and the Oval Office staff safe. And of course, eight months after the ‘rona hit our shores, we are still having to wear masks everywhere, social events are curtailed, America is heading into the holidays having to forget about family gatherings and having to deal with the memory of family members who will no longer be able to celebrate Thanksgiving and Christmas. People are sick of this virus, but it is threatening to worsen over the next few months. The worst part is that other nations have managed to control the virus while we are still watching it get worse with no end in sight. People, in particular seniors who made up the bulk of the illnesses and deaths, looked at that and didn’t like what they saw.COVID killed him off. It exposed Trump as a person who didn’t deal in reality, who was just a crazy dangerous old man in over his head, who didn’t care that almost a quarter of a million American citizens he swore to protect and defend had died while he gave crazy press conferences full of lies and bullshit, and was willing to stand by and let the virus go wild and sicken and kill more people (even his own family) without coming up with any kind of plan of action to get America back to normal life. Seniors, a huge voting block for Trump, were scared for themselves and wondering if they would ever be able to see their kids and grandkids ever again and turned against him. All of the above, along with unusually high turnout among all voting groups that sat out 2016 who were motivated to actually get up off their butts this time and vote because they were alarmed by Trump’s behavior over the last few years, combined to knock out Trump.

Four more of that, please!” And showed up at the polls to vote for him. And they didn’t disappear, so…Houston, we have a problem. A big one.

column1: Do nurses and doctors ever feel uncomfortable or unsafe treating a patient? How do they handle this kind of situation?
column3: The night they brought an already dead gangster to the ER we knew there could be some major disturbances accompanying the body. Gang violence tends to promote more gang violence. Every culture has its way of dealing with death and as far as I’m concerned, that’s all right with me as long as further violence is not a part of the equation, especially as it relates directly to me or my staff. Of those staff members who may be likely candidates for spillover personal violence, the social worker is the only person who has the job of working directly with the family when there is the likelihood of death. Every one else can disappear when their part of patient care is over but the social worker on duty has to stay until the survivors are past the worst part of grieving and beginning to return to their previous level of functioning, or at least be willing to go home. That may take a lot of energy and a lot of time in the danger zone and the person on duty who has to be in that situation is a prime candidate for abuse of some kind. That’s been me on several occasions and because of it, I had bad feelings about tonight’s death- real bad. Usually, when someone is in the process of dying, I have an opportunity to shuttle back and forth between the family and the medical staff giving increasingly sad information about the probable outcome. During that time, even as the news is getting worse, I can get to know the family and friends and let them get to know me a little. I’m not some robot messenger who can do this kind of work without feeling any of their grief and I want them to realize we are all humans too and that death, even for someone we may not like, effects us. Whatever happened before the dying guy got to the emergency department doesn’t matter now; only the family’s crisis is of concern to me and I try to make that clear. Usually I can do OK with the task and I can form alliances and bonds with the key people in the group. But when I don’t, it gets scary and for me there’s nothing scarier than being in a room full of gangsters I haven’t had a chance to form a relationship with, whom I don’t know at least one of from a previous death scene, who don’t care a damn about me, the staff or the hospital. I hate to be in a room full of guys so angry they would burn down the place that may have to save their lives some time, maybe even that same night. I hate to be the one to have to tell that group of guys that someone they loved couldn’t be saved. He’s dead. How I hate that word. The word that brings an end to hope- even false hope. The word that signals a change in everyone’s life from that moment on. The word that spins off the end of this event and onto another one that may have a rival gang in the same room hearing the same news, maybe on the same night and if I’m really unlucky, on my shift. The natural reluctance to say the “D” word is shared by my colleagues and it’s common to have hospital security or even the real police, with guns, stand by to prevent problems when the “D” word is coming. Nobody wants to be at the vortex of the negative energy that emanates from the finality of “He couldn’t be saved. He died.” For a violent death, the aftermath turned out to be relatively peaceful: the parents were sad and tearful but not surprised. The other family members were supportive, and, crying together, they went to view the body. After paying their last respects the family left, then the detectives left and I went into my office, put my feet up on the desk and closed my eyes. I took the deep breaths I had learned from one of the rehab social workers that were supposed to bring calm and relaxation. It was just starting to work when my beeper went off. I called the number flashing on the little screen and heard the words I knew were coming. “The guy who died has some friends out here. Lots of them. They don’t know he’s dead yet.” It was late and things had become quiet in the ER. “Is there anyone else in the waiting room?” I was afraid to bring them into the conference room where I usually broke bad news to big groups. With this big group I didn’t want to be in a closed space telling twenty gangster guys their friend was dead. “No. Just them.” “Tell them I’ll be right out.” A couple of cops I knew came in through the ambulance entrance to take a report on a traffic accident. Because I knew them, I could ask for help on something that wasn’t related to why they were there, so I did. “Could you guys sort of take a cruise through the waiting room? You don’t have to do anything. I just want those guys to know there are real cops here. Real cops with real guns.” “No problem.” They came back a couple minutes later and I thanked them. “Don’t thank us Bob. If something happens we won’t be much help just because we’re cops with guns. Half of them probably have guns too.” I looked past them, through the bulletproof glass partition, into the waiting room. If somebody told me the dead guy had come to town with a professional football team and all the other players were now in the waiting room it would have been believable. Big guys. Angry guys. When I opened the door, the last clear thought I had was that this had never come up in graduate school. I could die during this test of my social work skills and nobody had ever trained me for this situation. But then again, I guess they did. I was taught to treat everyone with dignity and I was taught to hold the ethics of my profession in high esteem. I was taught to do the right thing, even if it seemed like the wrong crowd. Fearlessly, (well not fearlessly, bravely might be a better word- brave because I was terrified but did it anyway) I walked into the center of the crowd and asked, “Are all of you friends with Mr. J.?” They nodded. They came closer. They surrounded me. “I’m sorry to tell you but we couldn’t save Mr. J. We did everything we could but he was too injured. I’m sorry, he died.” As the “D” word slipped from my lips I felt my knees get weak. My heart was racing. I was getting an adrenaline headache. “I was there when he died. I know he wasn’t in any pain. It was a peaceful passing.” They yelled. They cursed. They threatened retaliation. They spoke deeply about the injustices of life. Some walked outside, some hit the wall and kicked chairs, and some got glassy eyed and just stood there. I did too. Nobody had done anything to me yet and after a minute or so I didn’t think they were going to and then I wasn’t scared any more. Whatever these guys had done before this moment, and I’m sure there was plenty, didn’t matter now. What did matter was that I was in the middle of a group of people who had just lost a friend and they needed to grieve the same as anybody else and I was the guy that was there to help them. I brought them into the dead guy’s room, two at time, and they said their good-byes. Some cried openly and some talked about him. Some talked to him and some kissed him. Some hugged each other and promised to do better in life. Nobody scared me. Nobody called me names except for a couple of guys who called me “Sir”. Everybody was orderly and kind and sad and for some reason they seemed to get smaller as the night went on. I never did figure out who had the guns. Grief, expressed as grief, is a profound experience. I am always caught up in it when it happens around me, even with total strangers. Their pain of loss affects me deeply- it reminds me of the pain of my own losses and scares me about my future losses by reminding me how transient life is. Tonight that transience was glaringly obvious in the room full of gangsters. I was relieved they were up for the true grief experience, because if they weren’t, someone would suffer. Maybe them. Maybe me. Maybe the guy who brought all this on by shooting Mr. J.
column9: So beautifully written and you captured the feelings of these gangbangers so well. It gave me a perspective on them as people with feelings for each other. I have had a few experiences with angry gangbangers in my ICU regarding a critically ill patient. My coworkers wanted to get security to throw them out. But I treated them like any other family member, and explained what was going in with the patient, what we were trying to do for them. At first they were screaming at me, not listening. But I said, you aren't giving me a chance to explain or answer your questions. They calmed down, listened and ended up thanking me for being kind to the patient and to them..I was amazed because I was scared at first but I tried to call up within me every ounce of compassion I could. I asked God to help me see them as persons, not gangsters. And to remember my job is to heal, to care, not to judge or be scared. It was one of the most fulfilling experiences of my 31 year career as a critical care nurse. One I will never forget. Mary Helen Barletti RN,CCRN (Emeritus),AAS,BA,BSN,MA,MSN

column1: How can I heal from my childhood trauma?
column3: One doesn’t overcome it without discovering what it was. Not to move on, but in to what happened to you as a child.(Come prepared or not at all. I just love this picture of a strong child. I meditate and replace my own image with this pose to heal.)My parents both had drug and alcohol addictions.My cousins sexually abused me as a child.I was emotionally abused by my family.I was neglected.I was trained to please and accommodate others.The counter-training was:That’s what happened to me. I had to learn how to not rely on drugs to take care of my pain like my parents did. I had to learn how to engage alcohol with control and moderation and enjoy it without overdoing it.I had to learn how to separate sex, abuse and sexuality. I had to learn that though my cousins raped me, they are rapists. They would rape anyone that they had the opportunity. It happened to me BUT it was not personal. They would rape anyone that they had the opportunity to.I had to learn to accept the dissonance of the actions at me and that it was not personal to me.It happened to me, not because I am me.I then had to learn too, that the initiation into sex was not correct and that I had to re-form what was the difference between abuse and my choices.I then had to discern that my sexuality was different than my experience of sex though the physicality may’ve been similar in gender, sex, sexuality, positioning, interest, passion.I had to learn that my family was wrong.About themselves.About me.About their worldview.Even in love of my family I had to point to them as the wrong way to do things. It meant that I had to critically examine everything that they were presenting, had presented, thought of whatever I was or am doing.I had to understand that their wrongness meant that I would have to seek love, mentorship, guidance from other venues.It meant that I was alone in my life after basic care.It meant that I had to learn to fit in the pieces that my family didn’t know and acknowledge that spottiness.That meant that finances, real estate, business, entrepreneurship, education, higher education, etiquette, social class hidden rules, sexuality, sex, manhood, dignity, professionalism, computers, nature, love, etc.. had to be learned on my own or cleaned up from their lessons.They neglected me because of the distraction of their own dysfunction.They did not recognize when I needed attention, love, adoration, support.None of my family have read any of my books. Nor been to any of my classes or workshops. Yes, I’ve thanked them, dedicated work to members and have pictures of them with my work but no one I am blood related to has made any time or attention for my work.And that’s okay.Their lack of attention and inability to understand my value is not the definition of me nor my work. But whether I see it in compassion or with analysis, my Art cannot be seen because so many of them did not learn or have opportunity to create Art themselves.There were some that did and were able to assist and propel me in example, if not in direction and support.I had to learn boundaries because it was to my family’s advantage, to my abusers benefit, that I not know or have boundaries. I had to learn that again they were wrong and that I had to learn those boundary making skills both internally and externally.To learn and change and accept the above based upon what happened, it meant that I had to actively seek out ambrosia and pipe it directly to what happened, not to answer just feeling better. The difference that meant was:Two years of Incest Anonymous groups every week at The Center in NYC, as a teenager, just sitting silently in the back row, listening to what sexual abuse, sex, sexuality, manipulation, pain, confusion sounded like and what resonated and new strategies.In college, I participated in a yearlong peer group on sexual abuse and then with the group’s help, constructed a magazine cover story that I wrote and went out all over the city.Further in college, I did an all ages group around dysfunction and abuse.I took self defense and martial arts classes and began to exercise and control my relationship to food better because this is my body. I needn’t hide nor cower with it. I can protect and care for it. I must.In my early teens, my mother and I went to therapy to deal with the catastrophic divorce of her and my father and learning how to deal with trauma.In my 20s, I did a year of therapy about boundaries, relationships, sexuality, with a private therapist.Spiritually, I acknowledge the brief weeks I went to jail over a small violation as stripping me of every one and thing in my life and casting me into a pit with real wolves. And I used every trick, guile, threat and weapon in the impressive and well stocked arsenal of Kyle so that I walked out without a loss of dignity and no one put their hands on me. I can protect myself even in the unimaginable.In my 30s, I did a year of therapy about my life choices and planning/goals, with a private therapist. (I do a singular year every decade of my life. As a tune up/maintenance check.)It meant acknowledging my relationships that were warped by my upbringing and not blaming those people but changing and sometimes eliminating those relationships. It meant that i have had to take 100% responsibility for my life and my choices, actions and thoughts.I have had to move from a time where I was without choice, therefore a victim, to an adult who had trauma from my childhood that had to be healed, changed, examined by me in order to grow up. My family did not get a say so in my healing nor did I get to live my life past the second I recognized their brokenness as a victim, without taking 100% responsibility for my existence from then.It happened to me, I was a target, victim-hood is an agreed upon result.I do not agree to being a resulting victim. Big shift in consciousness. (It may have something to do with why I didn’t talk much at 19 in those IA meetings—-there was a lot of victim-identity confusion going on.)No matter who or what was done to me, my responsibility was to heal it. Forgiveness, apologies, repayment, none of that is in the package of my taking 100% responsibility for my self, my existence, my pain, my trauma, my life.I often tell workshops on trauma the story of going to my terminal mother’s rehab/hospital where family had gathered for Christmas/her birthday party and one of my rapists, David, a cousin, effusively greeting me at the party room door, hugging me, chattering on exhaustively from across the room, peppering me with questions. (Years before when I revealed to my mother that I was going to the IA meetings, she confronted my cousins’ parents, my aunts, and that particular cousin she was intending to give a large sum of money to for his help in a civil case. I felt compelled to reveal the truth and it changed the amount she gave him by two zeroes, he got singular thousands rather than her intended tens of thousands.) Fast forward to the party and he’s doing all this performance, my stepfather knew he would be there and my mother is in a wheelchair from mild strokes, heart surgery, leg amputation, and there are all these strangers and half strangers and unknown extended family—-it’s a lot of emotional manipulation, drama, good intentions, terminal illness, sadness, going on. And I felt nothing for my cousin the rapist, not rage or anger or let me give him a piece of my mind—-I hadn’t seen him in almost 20 years—-I simply felt nothing. So I’m sitting there examining this space and I realized: “Oh, he’s popping off all this guilt because he is not healed from the kind of person he was/is and he thinks I’m going to go apeshit on him. He does not possess the healing of how he was traumatized so that would facilitate him traumatizing others so that he would not even attempt to apologize (the second cousin apologized to my mother once but not to me. “And that was their narcissistic handshaking that did nothing for or to me, who’d experienced the trauma. I had to learn that abusers and parents who were narcissists would steal even your apologies. “Years later she got money from him, Eric, the second abuser over his guilt about me for herself. Her unhealed trauma acting out. I watched them all with pity and when she was terminal pointed it out to her, the cruelty she’d waged at me with it. But I told her I didn’t have to forgive her—-she was obese, dying, diabetic, bald, no teeth, an amputated leg. What had she profited?) “But I’m not going apeshit on him. Why? I am not his victim. He did things to me that I investigated but can’t legally prosecute him over, he has no connection really to my life other than another cousin, his brother, being close to my mother and therefore him here. I’m here for an entirely other person/reason. My stepfather had shown a “tell”, a little psychological and physical “thing”, earlier that day, that he knew my cousin David would be there and in fact wanted it to “do” something to me. (Because of my stepfather’s issues of competition with me that my mother had purposefully exacerbated, his inadequacy issues and his underlying trauma of my mother dying, much as his had as a child. Trauma begets trauma begets trauma begets manipulation begets lashing out begets trauma.) And it isn’t doing anything to me. I am not reacting as anyone is expecting of me. Look at my cousin. He’s poor, he looks like a meth addict, he has no job, he’s in his late forties, he has no real relationships nor children, he has no discernible future. Not a good look for a Black man. He is for intents and purposes, dead. I’ve got degrees, a hell-ah resume, a TV show in NY, multiple books published, teach at Columbia University, friends, colleagues, respected work, a dollar extra in my pocket—-I have used my lifetime to amass things that matter to me and bring me joy in multiple spheres and I've got 50 more years to do even more! Ahhh, abusers like my cousin (and stepfather) need to tear at that because they do not know how to create it for themselves. And I am no longer available for them to tear at in large, overt ways because that space of trauma, I have made assiduous effort to heal what happened. Therefore they can no longer touch “me”. I don’t wish him dead because they don’t “exist” to me. They are not real, incarnated into my reality, of positive or negative value. Some things in life move from negative to neutral. Indifference is worse than hate because it has no emotional investment, no interest in the target.” You do not overcome it. You detail what happened. As much as you know and can remember and then you organize systems to deal with each branch of the trauma tree and you infuse the whole tree, branch by branch, issue by issue until you have yet another kind of tree in your Garden of Life that you can proudly take 100% responsibility for and visit, talk to others about, teach others with, use to discern others with. The trauma was part of the spiritual and soul’s intention within your life, it cannot be exorcised. It must be acknowledged and nurtured to evolve.(Me rocking plaid for the first and last time! That’s the healed formerly traumatized but indefatigable child inside, getting back to that blossoming, bright spirit tree.) #KylePhoenix #TheKylePhoenixShow
column9: This is the most brilliant response I have ever read about healing yourself out of what happened to you. Blessings to you!
