column1: What is the rudest/meanest thing a family member has said to you?
column3: My best friend of 18 years died on Feb 14, 2004. Her son Alec, my Godson, was 11 at the time. My kids were 2 and 6 weeks, and my step kids were 11 and 15. I had always been involved in his life, and he started spending weekends at my house, and we talked every day. That tapered off over the years,. He and his dad had lots of anger issues, especially through the teen years. I helped as much as I could. In August of 2017, Alec (25 years old) asked if he could come over. When he got to my house, it was obvious he was very ill. It took all day to convince him to go to the hospital. He finally consented, and I stayed there all night with him. I even called his dad to come to the hospital, which he did not want me to do. Alec ended up admitted to the hospital for 8 days, and he told us he was having liver problems, but didn’t know why. (He made us leave the room anytime staff came in to give updates). He was released with prescriptions, which I filled. He came to stay with us for two weeks, while he recovered. He got better, and went back to his apartment. On Dec. 16, he came back to my house again, and his symptoms had returned. I tried all weekend to convince him to go back to the hospital, and he refused. The afternoon of Dec. 18, he died in my son’s bed. We called an ambulance, but he was already gone. We found out that he was in the final stages of liver cirrhosis, and had been an alcoholic for years. We’d had my sister and step daughter over for dinner, and they were here when we found him. His dad got here after the police, coroner, and detectives did. They told us that there was nothing we could have done to save him in those last two days. My sister then decided that Alec’s death was my fault. She thought I should have somehow known that he was an alcoholic, recognized the symptoms of cirrhosis, and forced him to go to the hospital in those last two days. I sent her web pages of proof that cirrhosis, in the final stages, is not curable. I sent her the police report, coroner’s report, and toxicology report, that clearly showed the effects of long-term alcoholism, that I did not cause. The day Alec died, his dad moved in with us, and has lived here for a year now. My sister decided she doesn’t like him, and that I should throw him out. He has no money, no family, and nowhere to go. When I refused, she said I should have thrown Alec out of my house for refusing to go to the hospital. I told her I don’t throw people out for refusing to do what I demand they do. I don’t control other adults’ life choices, and can’t force people to do what I want. It’s been a year now. My sister still barely talks to me, and refuses to see me or come over for the holidays. She has managed to make our grief even more difficult, for her own selfish reasons. She barely even knew my Godson, and certainly doesn’t care that he’s gone. She’s just using his death as an excuse to be even more horrible to me than she was before.
column9: You are a warm and caring individual, and the kind of friend we’d all like to have in a crisis. Your sister? Well, I was raised to try to be polite. But as you say, you don’t control others’ behavior and demand that they do what you think they should. As long as you can distinguish between someone you are helping because you chose to do so, and someone who is taking ruthless advantage of you and having a toxic impact on your life, what difference does it make to anyone else? Now, if your sister had said: look, X is stealing from you, dividing you from your friends, making it hard for you to get to work, etc. — that’s a different kettle of fish.

column1: I have an employee who went out on a 3-month FMLA to care for an ill mother. Said mother died within the first week of the FMLA. When is it legal to require her to return to work?
column3: FMLA is a catch all 22, so to speak. Even though the mother passed early on during the leave, it is possible she is using the time to take care of the estate or she is suffering from depression or going through the stages of grief. All of which are absolutely normal and returning to work, may not be the first thing on her mind to do at this time. I wish more employers were understanding that when a close family member passes that some time maybe needed to figure out what to do with matters of the estate and give them time to grieve and such.

column1: When a family member died because of cancer and exhaust, should I have had moved them to a hospital to save their life or just accept that they died?
column3: First of all, my condolences with the loss of your relative, but what are you really asking about? You (should) know that even with the best possible treatment, by and large ≈50% of people having cancer eventually will die because of the cancer. You can’t just move a relative to a hospital because (s)he’s dying, at that stage it’s usually far too late to do anything useful for her/him, so totally useless, dying at home is infinitely better than dying at a hospital, so “have them moved to a hospital to save their life” usually isn’t a reality, they were already dying, but more wishful thinking, or you feeling guilty - like all people grieving at some stage of their grief do - unless it was in an early treatable stage of the disease, but then (s)he wouldn’t have died. For some people the very small benefits (often prolonging life by no more than 2 months) of treating incurable cancer isn’t worth going through all the sometimes very horrendous side effects, under such circumstances people very rationally could chose to forego any palliative chemotherapy, operation etc., just opt for true palliative treatment, which according to me is treating pain, anxiety, shortness of breath, depression, and all other treatable discomforts, aiming at making the rest of one’s life as “good” as possible, not aiming at prolongation of life at the cost of often terrible side effects, to me that isn’t “life” but “suffering”. Do take some time to read about the process of grieving you’re in the middle of, please read The 5 Stages of Grief & Loss | Psych Central Wishing you all the strength you need, and all the best!

column1: How do you tell a family that they need to clean their house better?
column3: My beloved husband died after a sudden illness. He was in Intensive Care for three weeks, in the coldest part of the winter here in Ottawa His two brothers came for part of the time but could not stay all the time. I spent all day with him at the hospital and came home to as many as 10 phone messages from his grief stricken family scattered around the world. As well as feeding his brothers and managing the house. This was in 1995 - pre e mail. My own family was minimally supportive. When he died I had a group over at my house after the funeral, my husband’s 2 brothers were also staying with me. They had to fly in from the US I managed funeral arrangements and all the sad details of death by myself. My van was stolen out of my driveway at night and the pipes froze and burst in a vacant rental property owned by my husband during this 3 week period. I was so exhausted and overwhelmed that I could hardly think straight. I wrote down everything I had to do and crossed off my list that which was done My brother and his wife drove from Toronto for the funeral and stayed at a hotel The following summer I was so lonely. I asked for family to visit. My sister in law said she would not come to stay because when she had come for the funeral my basement had been untidy and she thought she could smell mold. This was the end of February in Ottawa. I told my brother that if he had really cared they would have been helping me clean during this awful time, not looking for opportunities to score points That was when I realized that I could never expect any understanding ot support from my family EVER I have never asked for anything from them since. I am a very different person now because of this experience I wrote this several years ago, but it keeps coming up and has so many comments. So it’s time for a sequel.. I kept contact with my family, expecting nothing from them, and did not make a fuss about the situation described above. I pulled my life together, myself, made a career, adopted a child, renovated my home, travelled. Lots of things have happened - My brother had a disabling brain bleed about 10 years ago and had to retire; my mother died I kept working until 4 years ago, while raising my little girl. Life progressed. I kept visiting them on a regular basis even through the pandemic They have not visited me. Last spring, my sister in law died. She had been complaining about a bad back, - turned out it was 4th stage bowel cancer. So I went to visit my brother who is living on his own, even though he now has mobility issues and needs a wheelchair to manage. It turns out that my sister in law had been totally controlling of him, resisting socializing and telling everyone he was too disabled to function in the world. She had the entire basement stuffed with stuff. I mean STUFFED. She was a hoarder. There was like an alleyway between floor to ceiling rows of stuff in the large family room down there. She was a crafter and literally had a room full of wool and fabric and all kinds of things. My brother had one small room which he fitted up as a library with his books, computer and tv, and where he spent the majority of his time. They were barely speaking to each other, and then not in a civil fashion, by the end of the pandemic. The family is still trying to get rid of all her stuff, and my brother is much happier and more friendly now. He is functioning like a different person. They lived together hating each other for so many years —- I am so glad that I sucked it up and carried on, and did not give in to bitterness and revenge. Think of these people wasting so much precious life in trying to prove who was —- whatever, and forgetting to live. And there is so much irony in her complaints about my home, while she was hoarding stuff in her own.
column9: I’m sorry for your loss. When my brother in law was ill and eventually died, my sister in law had spent a lot of time at the hospital with him, so my husband and I stuck around to clean her house for her, so it would be in good shape for when his family came after the funeral. That’s what family is supposed to do, not criticize.

column1: If you had a family member that passed away, what were their last words to you?
column3: It is likely their lack of words is more common, and this happens all too often. Many people don’t get the privilege of talking to their loved one before they die even if they desperately want some form of conversation between them. If the person is old, or very ill, they are likely to die without communicating at all to the person who sits valiantly by their bedside for days on end. They may not even recognize them. A sick person is sometimes in too much pain to talk, or they may be so sedated that words do not come to them. Then, of course, some people die when they are unconscious and words are not spoken at all then. Old people can live, or rather exist, for quite a while as if they are in another world before they die. It is often hard to take this in, but many observers say the person talked about loved ones gone before them as if they were in the same room. People on their deathbed sometimes say the departed have come to take them to the next stage of their journey. It is hard to fathom what is going on in a person’s mind at the time of death. Of course, death comes to us all eventually. It is an inevitable part of life. As a nurse, I witnessed many deaths and one of the strangest things is that people quite often draw their last breath when their relatives are out of the room. Their visitors may only go to the canteen for something to eat, but it seems that this is the very time the person chooses to let go. We can never know why this is. We cannot read a person’s mind. But it often seems unreasonable to the relative or friend who is left behind. I would say, the words a dying person says to you are not as important as the words you say to them. It is an opportunity to mention what the person has meant to you, and to tell them how much you love them. Let them die with that knowledge and you will feel there is more closure to a difficult phase of grief that is to come.
column9: Absolutely correct for some reason they want to be alone when they die.

column1: Can cutting off toxic family members and starting over in a new location bring peace? Is it possible to find a way out of a toxic family situation?
column3: In many respects, yes. Cutting off toxic family members and beginning anew brings a great deal of peace. In other respects it does not, but even in those cases it beats the havoc that those toxic members create. My recommendation is to escape toxic family and start anew. Together with my wife and three kids, I left my hometown and home state of 45 years and moved to a different state and city. The impetus was because my covert abusive mother died suddenly leaving my malignant NPD father behind. As much as my mother was an enabler for my father's abuse, which angered me constantly, she did provide some kind buffer between myself and my father's targeted abuse. When she passed, I told myself I needed to get as far away as possible. My wife agreed — she was fed up with how he and my Golden Child older sister treated me, herself, and our three kids. The struggle to move was real. I spent $31K on moving costs, went into significant debt with my wife to carry a new 30-year mortgage at 45 years old, plus I shouldered more debt for financing renovations to a house built in 1915. I'm sure many readers by now will think I could have escaped for much less, but when you have three kids who you love and want to protect and give them good housing the costs become quite high. So what was the trade? For 🕊️ peace, I traded:New financial debts that I will now work as hard as I can to hopefully, one day, pay back in full. Probably to the end of my days.New uncertainties about how I will be able to afford an education for my children as they grow.Becoming a stranger in a strange land so-to-speak. I knew virtually nobody in the city we could afford to live in.Having to answer each and every person I meet in this new neighborhood their question of "what brought you and your family here?" Probably the hardest question I have ever had to answer on the spot so that I don't come off like a weirdo. Obviously, I cannot divulge details of the true, underlying reason, for my move.Jabs from my mother and father's flying monkey family friends. One of them said: "enjoy your new life!" as if I was doing something terribly wrong by “abandoning” my widowed father. Another shook their head and said "you gotta do what you gotta do"Moving through the many stages of grief for having lost pretty much my entire family of origin in a matter of a year.My children wishing they could go back to their hometown to see their old friends. Seeing their wistful faces when they think of their hometown breaks my heart to pieces.So, I ask you: do you think this list of trades brings peace? One would think not. But let me tell you that all of the hardships the escape brought is worth every penny, every tear, every sob, and every new stressor. I've been physically away for about two years now and I've made some friends, and found good company through various community organizations. My kids have made friends, have been invited to sleep overs and parties. My son joined the cross-country running team at his high school and plays pickup basketball with kids in the neighborhood. My girls hang out with their new friends. My wife founded a meet up for professionals in her field. I am growing my business without being constantly blind sided by my toxic family's demands and devaluing of who I am. I'm now teaching as an adjunct at a local university with incredibly intelligent and creative students. Life is better, but true peace has not yet come for me, but it's 💯 percent more peaceful than if I had stayed enmeshed in the toxicity of my family of origin. I know of the challenge of moving on from toxic family. It's damn near impossible. Like you're caught in quick sand. But you can do it! Keep trying to break away. G-d is on the side of all scapegoats because they shine the most light here on Earth. Leave before your candle dims — the world needs to hear from you and your story. G-d bless you and yours. 🕊️✌🏼
column9: I’m glad you, your wife and your kids got away from the toxic environment. I mean the toxic household. Shame on your parents for treating you horribly. So is your narcissistic sister. They’re sick and twisted people. It’s great that you’re doing well.👍🏽👍🏽👍🏽

column1: Why do family members sit at home for 13 days when someone dies in India?
column3: Well in the Puranas, it has been said that a soul stays on Earth for 13 days after the body dies and then is taken to an unknown destination. Hinduism is an astonishingly flexible “religion”, it openly claims that no man on Earth can ever guarantee the true nature of what happens after death, whether it is rebirth or heaven/hell or merely the return to nothingness. It puts forward multiple theories, those which seem more practical are followed, such as this. I’m unsure of the actual reason for the exact “13” days but it could have a few normal reasons iePrivacy- When a close family member dies, only you and those as close to the deceased as you were can understand the pain. No cousin, friend or outsider can empathise with you. Don’t get me wrong, they may be feeling an incredible amount of pain- however each individual’s experience and level of sadness is unique, incomparable and unmeasurable. Hypocritical? Maybe, but it puts forward a simple reasoning. Isolate, mourn, go through the stages of grief, then go back to your normal life. The weight of their death may never go away but it slowly transitions from the painful memory of their loss to a happy memory to reminisce their presence.Disruption in day to day life- You see, when a family member dies, especially someone who you lived with, your daily routine changes after their death. You need to adjust accordingly. Who will wash the dishes now? Who is in charge of calculating the household taxes? Where will i sleep? EtcComplete attention to other requirements like your employment, projects etc cannot be given- Rather than putting it at the back of your mind for a long time, being distracted by worldly matters, take 13 days, fully realise and reflect on it and then slowly return to your normal life.

column1: What are the typical stages of healing after cutting ties with toxic family members?
column3: 1.) Grief 2). Disbelief 3.) More grief 4). Overwhelming sadness 5.) Losing hope.. 6.) Eventually, I stopped crying as much. It was similar to my entire family dying all at once, so it took a long while for my tears to stop. 7). And, then I got really mad. I felt so disappointed that no one bothered to love me back and that I had been Scapegoated my entire life! 8). After I got mad, I had an epiphany that I was grieving over a bunch of ASSHOLES! And, why should I!? These people were never kind to me. They never cared about me! So, why was I feeling so sorry for missing them?! And, that's when I was really able to let go of them (assholes). And, that's when I really started to heal and a lot of things made sense to me. 9.) Me. Me. Me. I got to focus on ME! I wasn't that nasty ugly person they made me feel I was. That was all PROJECTION! In fact, there wasn't anything wrong with me. That hate filled veil was finally being lifted and I could see things a lot clearer. 10.) SELF LOVE. It is a wonderful thing but you can't achieve it unless you cut toxic people out of your life and leave them there. Good luck to you!
column9: “It was similar to my entire family dying all at once” That is exactly how I felt, and I felt very sorry for myself for it too. Your list is a great outline of the journey. It does eventually get better if you stay the course, and stay no contact. I had to cut ties, block texts, and emails, put away photo albums,and quit opening holiday cards. Resisting any and all flying monkeys and hoovering. Eventually it worked.

column1: Adult What is the acceptance stage of grief?

column1: What are some ways to cope with grief during the first year?
column3: For me, I guess I took the long way home when it comes to grief. The first four years after my husband died of stage four lung cancer, I refused to go through grief. I did everything I possibly could to suppress it and push it way deep down inside of me. Of course, there was occasions of meltdowns in uncontrollable emotions but I just rolled the wave of grief for a minute and then just carry-on. I work three jobs at the time and didn’t have much for anything else. Then I went down to two jobs and took in my mother to live with me so I could care for her, that alone took me away from having to deal with my own grief. Then when I decided to start dating again, it was only with the idea of companionship, and the idea was really from my family members and close friends telling me that I need to go back out there again. So I did, and I met someone who I fell in love with, and we were going to get married and everything was fine until the second year of our relationship. Everything got bad, then went to worse. Experience was so hard and I found my heart breaking, and I seen myself Going down a path that I knew I would not make it out. But by the grace of God I did and I moved on. Only to be greeted by another loss in my life. My mother passed away from dementia and I think at that point in my life, I had no choice to deal with grief. Losing my husband and getting my heart broke right after that and then I lost my mom. That’s when I knew everything was going to come to a head and that I would have no other choice but to deal with the grief and try to get it over with. and so the question you asked is how do we cope with grief in the first year and for me it was almost 9 years later, that I am at a place of peace and acceptance still with occasional meltdowns and fears that I once had but threw it all how I got through it and how I deal with it now it’s only because God love me enough to save me And I feel in my spirit that my purpose here on earth is not completed yet. As for the memories of my husband and my mom and my dad, I live with fit every day and I thank God for allowing me to have had them in my life. Don’t put off grief because I would hate to see anyone wait until many many years later to do so because one way or another you will have to deal with it.
column9: I will tell you what not to do, don’t stuff it. Don’t be stoic. OMG! be messy, yell, scream, throw things. The person you lost meant something to you, right? So act like it mattered, because it does matter. Don’t hide in bed forever, get out and be a part of life, but also grant yourself time to cry. If others don’t like it, oh well, fuck them, they don’t know because the one you mourn was special TO YOU. When they lose someone special to them, maybe then they’ll understand. When my husband died after a long illness, his family were all a bunch of selfish pricks, so I had that to deal with. But a few months later, when I asked his mom if we could all get together, share stories, talk about him, she sneered at me, ‘you’ll NEVER get us together for that!” Damn it, I wanted to share stories, to laugh, maybe cry, but I had to hear these things…and to be told no, like he meant nothing to no one? Stay away form toxic people…grieve, but then, I hope you dance, as the song goes. When? You’ll know.

column1: What gift do you get for someone who is terminally ill and lives a considerable distance away from you?
column3: My best advice about what to get for someone with a terminal illness is that it be something they would be able to enjoy during the time they had left. This is obviously influenced by their functional status and how much time they probably have - don't give a sky diving lesson to someone who's already bed ridden - or a stamp collecting kit to someone with a month to live. Get them something they would like if they weren't going to die, but restrict the potential items to those they can actually use in their current state of health - and enjoy during the time that they have. Something personal would be best - something that shows the love you have for them - something that one of their friends or a family member might want to keep after they're gone. A framed picture of you with them - or with both of you and other friends enjoying a memorable event in your lives. An electronic picture frame with a collection of those types of pictures might be even better. People spend a lot of time reflecting on the memorable events of their lives while they're in the process of dying, so anything that facilitates that process will be something they'll appreciate. It's too bad your friend/relative lives so far away. I think the best gift you can give someone who is terminally ill is the gift of your presence. Death is an emotionally (and frequently physically) painful process and there are a lot of people who are just too uncomfortable with it to want to spend much time with someone who is dying. True friends will spend time with them - and be a comfort as they travel the lonely road to the end. If you have the opportunity, go and visit them. My own experience is pretty specific, since it involved my daughter, Katrina, who died at age 21 from a very rare form of cancer. We wanted her to have everything she might want in life, knowing that it had to be compressed into roughly a year - the time from when we knew she was terminal until her death. We took out a home equity loan so we could treat her to whatever she wanted - we could always pay back the loan over time, but we would only have her with us for a while. We wanted her to have every experience she desired. My wife's and my philosophy about raising our (five) children was that since they would face adversity in their lives, we wanted them to figure out solutions to the problems they encountered without our rescuing them - and suffer the natural consequences of their choices. This would best prepare them for life in the real world (after they left the nest). Since Katrina was not going to have a "life in the real world", however, we decided she should enjoy as many experiences as possible in the time she had left - and skip the smaller growth experiences like paying charges for over-drawing her checking account, having privileges revoked for not maintaining an adequate GPA, etc. (She did, of course, have opportunities for emotional growth by facing her own mortality, reflecting on her life's experiences, going through the stages of grief, and ultimately coming to the acceptance of her death, so taking away her driving privileges for getting a speeding ticket didn't seem worthwhile). She turned twenty one during that year and we had a birthday party for her in the city where she was attending college and where she was active in her sorority. We then flew her and eighteen of her sorority sisters to Las Vegas for a special birthday party. We spent a few weeks in Europe with Katrina, a girlfriend of hers and her boyfriend - which included a cruise around the Adriatic Sea on a luxury cruise line. Her car was totaled when a dump truck ran a red light and broad-sided her (she was literally "hit by a Mac Truck") so we let her pick out whatever car she wanted (within a realistic price range). She was only able to drive it for a couple of months due to the physical limitations imposed by her disease - nevertheless, she was chauffeured around in it by her boyfriend for some time after that. (Three years later, I still drive that car. Soon after I started driving it, some of my (very superficial) physician colleagues asked (in a half joking manner) if my financial status had been impacted by some bad investments since I was no longer driving a car "worthy" of the doctors parking lot. I simply told them that it was the car we had gotten my daughter before she died, and I felt a sentimental attachment to it. They looked at the floor and were obviously sorry they asked such an shallow question.) If anyone wants to hear more of Katrina's story, see Gary Larson's answer to What is it like to lose a child?If you are interested in “No Nonsense” answers to serious medical questions, please follow me. (>200 answers on cancer, medicine and human behavior.)
column9: What a lovely post. Thank you for sharing. Several years ago, I had a friend dying of colon cancer. She didn’t have much money so I bought her an expensive lotion to help with her drying skin. She loved it because it was something she couldn’t afford. Then one day, she asked me about what she should be buried in. We discussed it and then I told her about a dress I had bought and never worn. It was an expensive dress and one I was saving for a special occasion. I decided to bring it for her to see the next day. She loved the dress and told me how wonderful it would look on me. So I swallowed my memory of the price and offered it to her to be buried in. She started to cry and was so grateful, I knew I had made the right decision. After she died, I really knew it was the right decision. She looked absolutely beautiful in that dress. I’ve never forgotten how beautiful she was and it’s been almost 20 years ago. Another friend thought I had lost my mind, but I have the comfort of knowing that beautiful white dress is gracing her in her grave.

column1: Why can't I show the emotion I should at, like when a family member dies?
column3: Who says you aren’t showing adequate emotion? The only one who can determine this…is you. No one else lives in your body. No one can hear your thoughts and none knows when or how you pray. Everyone handles grief differently. Processing grief can take a life time. The intensity of your grief is matched by your love. As such, there is no parameters when it comes to grief.. For some…we may grieve in private. You do what is right for you. Not anyone else. I’m attaching the stages of grief. This isn’t all inclusive…but is a guide for you in processing all stages of grief. This is the model by Dr. Kubler-Ross.Five stages of grief - WikipediaConcept in psychology According to the model of the five stages of grief , or the Kübler-Ross model , those experiencing sudden grief following an abrupt realization (shock) go through five emotions: denial , anger , bargaining , depression , and acceptance . Critics of the model have warned against using it too literally. [ 1 ] Introduced as "The Five Stages of Death" by Swiss-American psychiatrist Elisabeth Kübler-Ross in 1969, [ 2 ] this model has been known by various names, including "The Five Stages of Loss", [ 3 ] "The Kübler-Ross Model", [ 4 ] the "Kübler-Ross Grief Cycle", [ 5 ] the "Grief Cycle", [ 6 ] "The Seven Stages of Grief", [ 7 ] and the "Kübler-Ross Change Curve". [ 8 ] [ 9 ] The model was introduced by Kübler-Ross in her 1969 book On Death and Dying , [ 10 ] and was inspired by her work with terminally ill patients. [ 11 ] Motivated by the lack of instruction in medical schools on the subject of death and dying, Kübler-Ross examined death and those faced with it at the University of Chicago 's medical school . Kübler-Ross's project evolved into a series of seminars which, along with patient interviews and previous research, became the foundation for her book. [ 12 ] Although Kübler-Ross is commonly credited with creating stage models, earlier bereavement theorists and clinicians such as Erich Lindemann , Collin Murray Parkes , and John Bowlby used similar models of stages or phases as early as the 1940s. [ 13 ] In the foreword to the first 1970 English edition of On Death and Dying , Colin Murray Parkes wrote, 'This book describes how some American individuals have coped with death.' [ 14 ] In her book, Kübler-Ross states that the medical advancements of the time were the mark of change for the way people perceive and experience death. [ 10 ] Due to this, pediatricians have been seeing fewer life-threatening ailments for their patients compared to one-hundred years ago. [ 10 ] In her 1974 book Questions and Answers on Death and Dying , Kübler-Ross had by then observed that the stages are not experienced in a strictly linear progression. She noted, 'Most of my patients have exhibited two or three stages simultaneously, and these do not always occur in the same order.' [ 15 ] She later regretted writing them in a way that was misunderstood. [ 16 ] "Kübler-Ross originally saw these stages as reflecting how people cope with illness and dying," observed grief researcher Kenneth J. Doka, "not as reflections of how people grieve." [ 17 ] In the 1980s, the Five Stages of Grief evolved into the Kübler-Ross Change Curve, which is now widely utilized by companies to navigate and manage organizational change and loss. [ 18 ] [ 19 ] [ 20 ] As of 2019, On Death and Dying has been translated into forty-one languages, with the 50th anniversary edition published by Simon & Schuster. column1: Can you describe a moment you almost “lost it” in the military?
column3: Echoing the other responses I did lose it. Big time. It was Friday August, 31 2001. We were back in the barracks on weekend liberty preparing for a normal night out on the town drinking heavily. We never made it to town. My platoon sergeant showed up which put everyone on alert because the NCOs were never in our barracks except for surprise inspections. He didn't look like he was on ther warpath though; he looked sullen like his dog had just been run over. I was fast friends with our new platoon sergeant or at least as friendly as a subordinate could be. Despite him being higher rank we were the same age and from the same hometown. A few of us were cautiously now waiting in the common area. Oh shit he’s walking right at me. He puts his head down and I'm wondering which family member died. He said “I'm sorry to have to tell you this but your waiver didn't go through. The CO…” I didn't hear another word that he said. He was telling me that I was being separated from the Marine Corps. I could feel my blood begin to turn to lava. My mind is racing. I was told my waiver was a formality. I was already back to light duty. I was going to be cleared in two weeks. How could I have let this happen! What am I going to tell my parents? What will I do for the rest of my life. Why me!!! I didn't say anything. I maintained military bearing and said “Aye sergeant". Most of the rest of the night is a blur. Thanks to copious amounts of alcohol I went through all of the stages of grief in one night, though I went straight to anger. Red hot anger. At first I was mad at everyone else. All the shitbags that complained all the time about being-in. I wanted to be in and they're kicking me out?!?! There was a lot of alcohol fueled screaming at the top of my lungs from the balcony at anyone and everyone that got to stay but didn't want to. Looking back I wonder how we weren't busted that night. We weren't allowed to drink in those barracks. Even if someone did it was sneaking a six pack into their room and drinking quietly. We had contraband hard alcohol bottles flying around the common area and there was nothing subtle about our soiree. Maybe duty was too lazy to climb to our barracks at the top of the hill. Maybe they came by and I don't remember. Later, once the vodka moved me into the acceptance stage the party livened up. I hit up my wall locker to put on a show for everyone. What outfit would you guys call this? I model my new uniform which is comprised of my dress blue jacket, cammie trousers, and necktie. How about my alpha jacket with dress blue trousers in boots? At some point during my amateur modeling career everything goes dark. I wake up the next day with my face sideways against the floor but the rest of my body jackknifed across the bed still in one of my Frankenstein uniform concoctions. There was vomit forming a trail from the bed to my face that had turned to gel. When I rolled over a perfect silhouette remained in what looked like a viscous pool of fruity pebbles. A mild hangover was the least concerns. That was the first morning that I stopped feeling like a Marine. I hate that feeling. I wish for one moment I could get back the feeling of putting on freshly starched and pressed cammies with tight arm rolls and my name embroidered on the front. One last chance to lace up my boots, run through the door as a don my cover rushing late to formation as a proud Marine. I never will. I let everyone down. I let my family down. I let down all my new brothers and sisters. I let down everyone that pushed me to make me a better Marine. I was not the best Marine by any stretch of the imagination but I loved it. I loved waking up a Marine, brushing my teeth a Marine, getting a shitty barracks cut a Marine, having the worst boots at a spit shine party a Marine, even getting my ass chewed by gunny a Marine. No matter how stupid what we were being forced to do I was at least doing it as a Marine. And no matter how bad we were getting fucked with, no matter how ridonkulous some new edict from command was, no matter how many times my dickhead squad leader made me redo my room inspection I never complained. It all came with the job I loved. The Marine Corps that I loved. Practically everyone complains. Not me. Not on Friday at 1700 when we're at a all-hands townhall about suicide prevention after some blue falcon went across the bridge not down the river. Not at 0530 when I'm being rousted for remedial PT and I'm too drunk to walk let alone run. Not even as I have to wave goodbye to my newest brothers to board an airplane home with tears and blood dripping down my face (I celebrated my newfound freedom by piercing my own ears in the car ride to ther airport). No complaints. At least not about my beloved Marine Corps.

column1: Will I ever feel "normal" again after the death of my brother?
column3: I know that feeling. My only brother, the youngest of my parents' three children, died in a single car accident on December 12, 1987. He was 24 years old, and left behind a grieving mother, father, two sisters (I'm the oldest), a girlfriend, a daughter and literally hundreds of friends. I was devastated when I saw him in the hospital. I remember hearing a very loud, agonizing scream, and when several nurses gathered around me, I realized that I was the one screaming. I kept trying to get to his bed, but the nurses and other people led me away. I can't remember too much after that. I thought that by the time we got to be senior citizens, he would be pushing me around in a wheelchair, laughing as I scream hysterically because he would lift the chair up into a wheelie and scare me. Our grandchildren would run after us, laughing and yelling, "Do it again! Do it again!" We had that kind of high spirited, laughter filled relationship that had a lot room for pranks and jokes, even after we became adults. And suddenly, he was gone. There is an permanent ache, an emptiness inside of me that I feel everyday. Sure, I have moved on, somewhat. I've accomplished a lot since his death, because I often think about how he was like my pep squad. If I started moving into one of my depressions, he would come into my room, sit on the foot of my bed and tell me a hilariously animated story about something that happened to him. It was like he knew that I was feeling down without me ever saying a word. He believed in me, even when I didn't believe in myself. And I was his "Big Sis"; his protector when he was a little kid, and his corrector when he became a girl and party crazy teenager. It took years of therapy and tears before I realized that he was still cheering me on, wanting me to go out and have a good life. I miss him so much, but I also know he would never agree to me sitting around being depressed over him. That's not how he would want the memory of him to be honored. And I accept that. It's difficult; there's no doubt about that. But I urge you to get grief counseling and don't turn down offers of help from friends and family members. You will need their help during the acute grieving stage. My mother, father, sister and I walked around like zombies for the first year after my brother died. My now adult children says our family has never really recovered from losing him. That's true. However, we have made peace with the fact that he is physically gone, but he's still very much with us in spirit. Please take care of yourself this time of grief, and in the years to come. I believe that our loved ones who have moved on to the next stage of life would want that for us.
