column1: I don't cry or feel anything, when someone close to me dies. Am I normal or stone hearted?
column3: I wouldn't say it's normal not to feel grief when someone close to you dies, much less that you're stone-hearted, in fact, I would say far from it; you have to understand that not every person grieves the same way when he/she loses a family member or friend. Some people are stone-faced and don't feel much, if anything, in the way of grief when someone close to them dies; there are others that may only experience one of the stages of grief, others multiple stages. Then there are others, such as myself, who, at times, go through *every* stage (bargaining, denial, anger, grief, and finally acceptance), but again, it all depends on the person and how he/she is able to handle the death of a relative, friend, or even a beloved pet. Personally, as I mentioned up front, I go through every stage of grief, though there are some instances where I was never truly able to accept that a deceased person that I had any ties with (relative or friend) had, in fact, died, much less be able to move on; others, I was able to accept that fact and move on, though slowly but surely. The one I have never truly been able to forget and move on from, however, came in June of 2001, when, one afternoon (June 27, specifically), I got home from running errands and about 15-20 minutes after I got settled, the phone rang with the news that I had hoped never to hear: Stevie Nestor, a one-time friend of mine from my former school (whom I, sadly, had lost touch with some 12, maybe 18 months prior) had, on June 25, suffered fatal injuries in an accident returning home from a rodeo in Greeley, Colorado. The worst part of all is that Stevie was *not* wearing her seatbelt at the time of her fatal accident and was subsequently ejected through the windshield after the car crashed into a guardrail; Stevie was pronounced dead at the hospital shortly after 2:00 the next morning (June 26). She was just 16 years old. While on the phone, my initial reaction was shock, as I obviously didn't see it coming, followed by anger asking "Are you (Bleep)ing serious?", to which the caller replied "Yes, Eric, it's true; Stevie's dead, and with emotion in her voice, she said, "I'm sorry". After I hung up from Stevie's mom (the person who called me with the news), I was on my knees sobbing from not only grief, but also out of anger, knowing that I hadn't had an opportunity to say goodbye to Stevie before I had left to go back to my old school, then move back to my home town about six months later, much less talk to her one more time before she died. The rest of that day, and again the next two days after that, I was an emotional mess; at times, all I could do was cry, and absolutely nothing, or almost nothing, nor any person, could provide much comfort or solace, if any at all. At times, I also tried very hard not to think about the phone call I had received telling me that this had happened, and also tried any and every way possible that I could think of to distract myself, E.G. continuing an essentially fruitless job search that I had started about a month prior to this, as well as spending time with my grandmother (this was the day before the funeral) and telling her what had happened and asking her what she would have done if it had been her losing a friend from school, E.G. what she would have done to distract herself (if distracting herself in such a case was possible at all), and also, asking her what Bible passages I could reference, including Psalm 23. The day of the funeral (June 29), I managed to stumble out of bed around 7:00 am, thinking that I would be okay; physically, I was fine, but emotionally, as mentioned in the last paragraph, and as my mother and sister could tell over the last two days, I was a mess. At times, I had either been crying or had been attempting to stifle tears, proving unsuccessful at times. I got up (again, around 7-7:15 am), showered, brushed my teeth, got dressed, and ate breakfast (though my appetite was somewhat wrecked over the last two days), then took off for the cemetery around 9:30-9:45 am (this is where the service would be held). One of my former schoolmates pulled out of the funeral procession long enough to offer me a ride (which I accepted), and we got back in line and proceeded to Stevie's gravesite from that point. From the time the service started (around 10:30 am), I was an emotional mess, as was everyone else. I managed to keep myself composed for about the first 10 minutes or so, during which time I belted out a very moving rendition of the song "Angels Among Us". However, when the song got to the bridge which went "They wear so many faces; show up in the strangest places; they grace us with their mercies in our time of need", my voice began to quiver, though I did manage to keep my composure until shortly after I had finished. By that time, I, along with everyone (or almost everyone else) at the service, was either crying or on the verge of crying. My singing had never, and I do mean never before, nor since, moved anyone to tears. There were times during the service aside from this, however, where I tried to bite my lip and unsuccessfully stifle tears when my chin trembled, but during those times, Stevie's warm and angelic voice spoke to me from inside my heart saying "Eric, I know you feel sad about me being gone and also angry that you didn't get to say goodbye to me before you left to go back to your old school and before I flew away to Heaven, but just know that I will always be inside of your heart until the day you come to Heaven yourself. In the meantime, if you feel the need to cry, just cry; don't hold it back. If it was the other way around, and you flew away before me, I know you would feel the same way and you wouldn't want me to hold back my tears, but instead, you would want me to cry just like you need to cry now. It's okay to be sad about it." After the service was over, I managed to catch a ride home from the same girl who gave me a ride to the cemetery, but we were both so weak from crying that we had to pull over at least once before continuing to my apartment. So, yes, speaking from experience, there are times where people either (A) don't show much, if any, emotion when it comes to mourning a person's death, (B) the only emotion they feel is shock or denial, or at times, they don't know what they feel, or (C) they experience every stage of grief (shock, anger, denial, grief, and acceptance). Either way, there is absolutely zero shame in showing no, little or much emotion when someone close to you passes on.
column9: He’s asking why he/she can’t cry and not your life story

column1: How does one move past the stages of grief without affecting their family's welfare?
column3: Don’t be afraid of grieving and don’t expect that you can ever move past the stages of grief without affecting your family. Everyone feels grief in different ways but nobody should be alone in their grief. Find a healing project for yourself and encourage your family members to find their healing project. When my 13-year old son, Jared, died by suicide, the entire family went through many stages of grief and felt that grief at different times, days, months and sometimes years after he died. We did not grieve alone and one of the first things we did when Jared died was to get counseling, each of us individually and together as a family. I promise you that if you grieve together as a family, talking about your loved one, how you are feeling, how you are missing him/her, you will grow closer together as a family. Get out the photographs and remember the good, and maybe some of the crazy things you did with your loved one. If your loved one died in a traumatic way, try to get past that as quickly as possible. Remember that death is only a moment in time and the life of that person was of much more value than remembering how they died.

column1: What was it like to be in the Soviet Union just after it collapsed?
column3: The USSR disappeared legally in December, 1991, but it was dying for quite some time before and after that date. Not quite as long as Rome did, but it was not an overnight event either. I think we started to feel it soon after Gorbachev introduced his "reforms". We did not know about the country's dependency on oil. Neither did we know that oil prices had dropped. That's why Gorbachev's actions marked for us the timeline first. The shock from published revelations about behind the scenes dealings came next. Then came the take over attempt in August 1991, followed by Communist Party ban, USSR legal disappearance, inflation (I lived in the Ukraine then and saw it rocketing up to 3000% a year - all life savings have gone) and finally criminal elements taking over "legally" - that was the end of the USSR. How was it? Shock, disbelief, utter desperation, sense of betrayal, denial, anger, depression - all stages of grief and loss, except bargaining (with whom? nobody even listens to you) and acceptance (that would mean dying, at least for me). People committed suicide - physical and spiritual. There were many neurosis. One member of my family, shocked by the change, barely could walk for a year and does not remember that year at all. Even today, when I write it, my fists tend to clench, my heart rate goes up and my eyes become moist. Our life, as we knew it, was robbed from us. We were thrown away like a garbage, casually, without a moment of a thought or hesitation, without even a glimpse of attention - the most insulting way. Those, who had called us to sacrifice for the most noble cause during Soviet times, were the first to turn coats and to take advantage of us, ordinary people, who toiled all their lives. The people who took the biggest hit had not taken advantage of the Soviet system, did not steal, did not cheat, who worked hard for the benefits of the others first, then for the family second. Imagine during the war an army takes losses and pushes into enemies trenches, you are wounded, but continue fighting, helping your friends, and suddenly your commander starts shaking hands with the enemy brasses and orders you to lay down your weapon and strip naked, so they could sell your weapon and your uniform for their - join with former enemy - advantage. You ask, "What about me?" But they do not bother to answer. They even do not try to listen. They don't care, preoccupied with their own insatiable desire to acquire more stuff, grabbing everything in sight, pulling the peg leg from a beggar in the street, if they thought they could sell it too (the medals for his war heroism or peace time achievements this beggar had sold and drank away already, darn it!). You are shoved away casually like a nuisance, unless there is something else they can take from you, of course. Are you dying? Good! We can sell your corpse for parts. There are many buyers abroad. That's how it was to live in the Soviet Union just after it had collapsed. EDIT (added after the USA President elections 2016): From what I read, those people who voted for Trump felt similarly. I commiserate and hope that the new administration will stand by the promises given to them during the election campaign.
column9: It wasnt the soviets who betrayed you though. It was the neoliberals - yeltsin and his 'reformist' ilk. Though, truly, what was done to you were done to many other countries. Like mine. But it didnt happen in the fast, lighting-like fashion with the immediately visible disasters you experienced. It was a slow process or neoliberal rape.

column1: My dog has died and I'm so depressed. People are saying "It's just an animal." but I can't get over it. How can I feel better?
column3: Dogs can become family members. Like with humans it can be love at first sight or they can grow on you, but fact of the matter is that it is love none the less. On top of that dogs don’t judge, don’t hold grudges and they will allways be there when you need them. They are very sensitive to your emotional state and will often try and assist you with whatever it is that you are going through. Therefore it is very easy to get emotionally invested with them. And therefore the grief is similiar to losing a human loved one. People that never experienced this deep emotional connection cannot and will not understand this. They are missing out ofcourse. But they also have less to lose. You have experienced it. And are now experiencing a great loss. And you have every right to go through your stages of mourning. And noone can put a deadline on that grief. That is tip number 1: It takes however long is needed. Give yourself that time. Having said that, grief is painfull. And holding on to pain for too long is not healthy. I have loved and lost dogs. And I did not totally overcome it. But the pain isnt sharp and stinging anymore. It is now bittersweet. And bittersweet I can handle. Tip 2: Don’t push away the pain and the tears but allow them to come and go through it. Pushing them away will only increase your pain and sorrow. If you need to cry, do so. If you need to scream and shout or throw plates against te wall… Just do it. Let the negative stuff flow out of you. Tip 3: Take the walks you used to do together. Watch as many pictures as you can. Remember each precious moment together and think about how blessed you have been, to have had those moments together. Maybe write the most precious memories in a journal, decorate it with pictures. And go over them time after time. In the beginning this may hurt, but don’t be affraid of that. Over time the sharp edges will fade and you will read that journal with a smile on your face. Tip 4: Make a shrine. Take a picture of your late dog and put it in a nice frame. Find a place in your home where you like, somewhere you can see it well. Put a candle next to it, maybe a well liked toy or a treat, other momentums to remind you of the good moments. Keep the candle lit, whenever you are around. Take care of the flame like it was your dog. Try and take the time, each time you pass the shrine with the lit candle to remember something nice about your lost friend. Again this may hurt, but don’t be affraid of that. Over time the sharp edges will fade and you will pass the shrine with a smile on your face. Tip 5: Don’t substitute your lost friend. Do not take in another dog untill you are truly ready. But when you are, embrace a new canine friend. He will contribute to your healing. But only if the sharp edges allready have faded a bit. Tip 6: Play with other dogs. (dogs of family, friends, etc.) They may feel your grief and comfort you. These tips may seem totally idiotic to people that do not understand this bond between you and your late canine companion. But don’t let that stop you! There are so many people that CAN relate! Keep that in mind as you find your way to bittersweet memories <3 I wish you all the best, trying to work through this <3 Hope these tips help.
column9: Many people say ‘Oh, I could never love another dog after this one goes…I could never replace him.” I thought the same thing…but after my dog Henry died unexpectedly, I was in a deep hole of depression. There was such an empty place in our home that he filled. My husband decided we needed another dog sooner rather than later…that was his coping method. We adopted our Lab, Rookie. Before long, I felt like the clouds of depression were lifted away. Henry was still very much in my heart and always will be. But the good boy that he was would never want his mama to be sad…and he probably would have welcomed a friend to play with, too. I still feel Henry is here watching over Rookie (and us) until we meet up at the Rainbow Bridge.

column1: How did your marriage end?
column3: Badly, but I suppose they all do. I met my future wife while in my last year at university (22 and 19 respectively) and we soon moved in together. For the most part, what followed was 13 mostly happy years together, but we we were only actually married for the last four years. We did a lot together, moving cities and states, completing degrees, building careers, going on holidays, and going out and having fun in our 20s. That’s not to say there weren’t issues. She was always fairly high-maintenance, impulsive, a tad impractical and quite selfish, but more social, outgoing and fun loving than me, and my parents were ‘difficult’ with her, but they also were with me (and still are!). But for the most part, I would have thought highly compatible. I’d always intended not to have children young, but by the time I approached my early 30s, was looking to settle and start a family. We’d ticked off buying the house and dog and that last long o/s holiday (where she had been quite difficult, so the cracks were starting to show), but it was clear that things had changed and she was thinking differently about the future. Unlike my parents who were and still are happily married, her parents had some difficulties in an on-again/off-again marriage, and I think the prospect of a loveless marriage weighed heavily on her, especially with children.Our marriage progressively worsened over the final year: she was spending long hours at work, drinking too much and doing her best to avoid me. We were fighting over everything. I was really hurting from coming home to a dark house on a Friday night and the unanswered or turned off mobile phone, and she just stopped doing things for me. I would tearfully ask why she was hurting me, to which she would reply in a rather impersonal third-person sort of way that she didn’t mean to hurt anyone. I begged her to talk, read relationship help books and started to work on myself as a person and what I could do to first ‘fix’ myself and then hopefully us. I pulled out all stops and did everything I could to try to make her happy. About 2 mths before it ended, I broke down with my father and he asked whether she was having an affair. I honestly trusted her and replied no. But gradually clues started to build up. The phone calls at home with no answer (which she blamed on an aged great aunt), the texts, her joining the workplace gym, the ‘forgotten’ wedding rings on the dresser, the strange pair of sunglasses found in the car, the prescription for the Pill which she has supposed to have stopped taking, stopped talking and planning for the future. Some of the lies she told me were in hindsight frankly ridiculous, but trust in someone you love can be a hard thing to break. When I was offered a job o/s, she even said I should decide for myself, which sounded strange to me at the time, but became abundantly clear soon enough. Ultimately, she had an email a/c with a very straightforward security question for someone who knows someone well, my desperation turned to shameful curiosity, and I accessed her emails to the third party. Reading them made me sick to my stomach. I confronted her, but she lied about how serious it was, but by the next day she’d obviously decided it was time. I think she’d resigned herself to the marriage ending months before, but wasn’t brave enough to take the next step. Things went very quickly from then, she just wanted out, especially money. I begged her to think it over as I didn’t even know how I felt, even with the betrayal, but she was adamant and said she couldn’t because of ‘unresolved feelings’ for the other party, now living o/s. Over the next few weeks we lived together but separately (that was incredibly difficult) going about the routine of work like robots and I went to my lawyer and we agreed on an amiable split of assets (it could’ve gone worse for me, so I was grateful). I also went to a doctor for antidepressants and sleeping pills as I was really at a low point. I told her in the car just before we signed the property settlement that there’d be no turning back as far as I was concerned if she signed and she nodded approval. We had hardly spoken many words for weeks and then went home to each of our own parents for Christmas.I returned home first after the New Year, and when she also did, told me she’d bought an o/s flight on impulse, but I knew exactly what was going on. We lived in the house for the next few days (I had bought out her share, but no exchange of monies yet) and was quite cold with her when she left. She was gone for a month and during that time rang many times, which I didn’t answer or return. Members of her family also rang, who I did talk to, and they said she’d lost her way and was very upset and whether there was any chance of a reconciliation. Who knows whether this was them, her talking through them or whether she was just concerned for me as a person, but my pride and self-respect meant I wasn’t going to reconsider. As much as it hurt, I’d made the psychological break that day in the car and I wasn’t going to cry for her any more. My family and friends told me that without trust there’d never be a future in any marriage. When she returned, she moved out immediately and I never contacted her again in any way and dealt with all legal matters through my lawyer, who eventually played hardball with signing the divorce papers, etc. I did all this as I just wanted it over. She rang and sent emails, but I only talked to her once on the phone, once when she unexpectedly dropped in, and two times when we exchanged photos to copy and made small talk (and she apologized and said sorry, to which I said nothing) in a car-park over the next 4 years. I’d met someone new about 4 mths after the split, but my feeling is that she now very much regretted what had happened and angered that I had moved on. At one point she said “They’re right, you don’t know what you’ve got until it’s gone” and in my mind I agreed, but for the exact opposite reason. I went through all the stages of grief, with repeated playing of Linkin Park’s “In The End” in the anger stage! Even with a new love the next few years were difficult as had lost many shared friends and couldn’t help being drawn into a dark place from time to time. It takes a long time to heal. I eventually moved interstate (but have since returned) and have never contacted her or even read the two emails she sent me in the past 13 years. Frustratingly, she popped up as a suggested contact on LinkedIn, so I know she now works interstate and I believe hasn’t remarried or had a family, but as I no longer keep contact with her family or friends, am not entirely sure. It’s unlikely we’ll ever unexpectedly meet again, but I would probably just wave her off as she has long ceased to be anything to me. I know some will think I’m being vengeful and that being on friendly terms would help heal me as well as her, but I’m honestly comfortable with the choices I’ve made. I was not interested in revisiting past excuses or reasons or regrets and just wanted to move on and build a new life. We make the choices that suit each of us and our circumstances best and who’s to say what’s wrong or right other than ourselves. I now have a wonderful caring and giving wife (who I have spent more years with now than my first wife) and two gorgeous children who all have made me happy beyond belief. My only regret is that I had to go through so much misery to get to somewhere wonderful, but it’s all part of the journey and I’m a much better person for it.
column9: There's someone on Youtube I follow who had almost the same thing happen to her. It was very sudden. One month he was making future plans, talking about moving or taking a vacation with the family. Then about two months later he told her he wanted a divorce, no explanation. When she asked him if they could go to marriage counseling and try to fix things he said he didn't want to fix it, he just wanted to split. She felt completely blindsided and thought he had been happy and they had been fine. He claimed he'd been unhappy lately and just wanted to end things. She was upset because she hadn’t told her what was wrong or given her indication he felt that way. She never had the chance she to try. So she documented her journey and recovery after a long marriage just fell apart. I was really surprised that a decades long, primarily happy marriage could just fall apart so suddenly when one person almost inexplicably snaps and doesn’t want to be married anymore. But I found more stories like hers after that and now yours. I'm sorry that happened to you but I'm glad that you have found happiness and a loving spouse.

column1: Do you regret your marriage, and why?
column3: YES, I married a NRI, who was educated abroad right after high school and was living there since ten years. His family too, was educated, comprising of engineers, architects and professors. We met socially in an arranged set up by both families. Few meetings more and we liked each other and got engaged. (very common in India). Things were normal and neutral till then…regular calls at night and good morning texts…Slowly mother in law started criticising my way of talking and answering. Gradually I kept distance from her, I talked to her but in limits. Among all these, we got married. Things were fine between me and him(my ex husband) till the news of my father’s last stage cancer broke ( just after 4 months of marriage). We were living in Singapore, while his family and my family lived in same hometown. Doctor had diagnosed my father with last stage cancer and predicted 2–3 months of life span. My husband and my in laws knew this very well, as the doctor was my father in law’s friend, still not letting me come down to India for next 15 days!! REASON : I am married woman, my first responsibility is my husband and his family. ( my terminally ill father was not a big issue as per them ) My mother in law kept saying that I should go there once Chemo therapy gets over…Imagine is already knowing Chemo therapy has no meaning at this stage. My husband said “ My mom is saying right”. Somehow I fought with my husband and MIL and came to India. My father was very happy and also very emotional when he saw me in hospital where he was admitted. Last I saw him at airport, when we were leaving for Singapore after marriage. Next I saw him in ICU bed, in cancer unit. Here is when everything started and got to see true colors of my husband and his family. They started torturing me saying “How can I leave my husband and stay with my parents ?? I suppose to balance both. I am suppose to take care of house. I am suppose to take care of in laws. thats our culture!!”. Staying with dying father, supporting mother and being there for younger sister thats not in our culture. You see the hypocrisy and heights of inhumanity. my father in law even called my ailing father several times to scold him saying “when are you sending your daughter back to our son. our son is alone there”. (how can a person behave like this to a person who is already on his death bed, just few weeks away from death???) His son, being very healthy ( 100+ kgs) is more important than my dying father. This ordeal continued for 2 months and 10 days (till my father died). So many threats for divorce, threats of setting me “ablaze” continued. I saw my father dying a little every day, and also I tolerated my husband’s and my in law’s threats for whole period of 3 months. My father passed away and they asked my family on very next day that “either send her back to us or we will divorce her”. I had enough, I decided I want divorce from such emotionless robot who can do nothing else other than following his parents commands. The day after my father expired, we had some rituals where family members donate money and few useful things to needy people and perform some worship. my husband called my mother saying “ MY Daddy told its not required to go in this ceremony so I am not coming”. My mother, lost husband aged 53; We are two sisters, no brother. At least he should have come just for the sake of coming to the ceremony because, to my mother he was equivalent to son. I wonder why do such man marries at first place??? such kids should never go out from their daddy’s lap !!! But my family convinced me to give him one more chance, though I had lost all the love and respect for him and his family because they did not let my father die peacefully. How can one be so inhuman to fight with a person who is already on the death bed. still I went back to him. but things between us continued to deteriorate. Whenever my mom called me because of feeling alone or upset, my husband started fighting, threatening me for divorce and banging doors !! He always behaved that he and his family did me a huge favour by “allowing me and letting me” stay with my father for “looong 2.5 months”. I utter a single word, I would get divorce threat from him and his parents !! One day, all limits were crossed, I finally decided to move out from such marriage. Thats it, 11 months of marriage and I put an end to it. In the span of one year, I got married, saw my father dying, cremated him, received almost 10 threats of divorce and finally divorced him !!! I regret my marriage because I really loved him. I never imagined a person could be so heartless and so selfish. He was no more than a ROBOT who was controlled by parents. We never had honeymoon, because his parents wanted him to save all the annual leaves and spend those leaves staying with them in their hometown!! and look at the irony, When my father was serious, almost before some 15 -20 days before his death, My husband fought with me because he wanted me to leave my father in such condition, go back to him and plan a FAMILY!! WHY MY FATHER IS OF NO IMPORTANCE ??? WHY HIS DEATH WAS NOT THE MATTER OF GRIEF??? WHY THEY HATED WHEN I CRIED FOR MY FATHER?? WHY THEY EXPECTED ME TO LEAVE MY DYING FATHER ALONE AND BE WITH MY HUSBAND TO COOK FOR HIM ??? I am not pseudo feminist here…but what would have happened if his father suffered cancer and died instead of mine!! He would have left every thing in singapore and would have left to his hometown same day!! His father, of course he is much much much more valuable than mine !! now i am cynical towards love, since i have seen such heights of inhumanity and selfishness, i dont trust love anymore. after all love doesnt mean candle light dinners and movie dates. the person i loved was the one who never stood by me when I needed his support the most. I hate myself too, because we dated for 9 months before marrying, there were few red flags but still i thought they could be solved with understanding. I didnt imagine him to be such spineless and selfish. I hate myself for loving such a person !! Staying alone whole life is much better than Spending life with such mean, emotionless inhumans!! Edit 1: When I got married, my father was normal. Cancer was detected after 4 month of marriage. it was detected by father in law’s friend who was surgeon. So they knew very well that my father is going to die soon in 2 -3 months. they knew how aggressive the tumour was!!! what still kills my heart is, when my father went unconscious and serious, my husband behaved so insensitively with me and my family. few of his words are …“ When are you coming back?? What are your priorities ?? Why dont you pay attention to me? why dont ask whether i had lunch or not??? What about our family planning??” (we were married for just 6 months then, my father is on the verge of death) My husband lived there alone for 10 years. then he could not keep patience for just 3 months?? I was not on world tour with my friends….I was with my father and my mother( to her, her whole world crumbled down) and with my sister who just stepped out from teenage and this news broke !! Why didnt he had any tenderness for me ?? I liked him thats why i married him and not because he was NRI. My meaning was despite living in such developed nation like Singapore for 10 years, He was so orthodox or god knows what!! Someone has commented that i didnt love my husband because of obesity. Let me clear, I married him because I loved him, and I didnt mind his obesity. i mentioned he was 100+ because my father has lost 40–50 kgs of weight by then, he had severe hallucinations and severe internal bleeding. my mom has lost 15 kgs due to stress. I too had lost much weight due to stress. EDIT 2: Thank you all for your supporting words and love :) Tanaya Dave : There were many red flags in 9 months of dating. Very first one was he insisted on informing everything to his parents first. for example, if I want to invite him yo my house for dinner, I had to inform his parents first. If i want to go on a half day trek with my friends, I need to inform his parents (this was before engagement). Second red flag was on the day of engagement: his mother did not let my mother come on to the stage. yes MY MOTHER WAS DENIED ENTRY ON THE STAGE. next day when i informed him about this, he said it was the their “tradition” . When i argued about it that there is no such tradition where girl’s parents cannot come near the stage…he got angry and said “I can not admit that my parents made a mistake. What do you want me to do?? Do you want me to shout on them or put them behind the bars?” This was insane behaviour. third was when he simply denied any sort of honeymoon. because his daddy got very upset by the name of honeymoon. His daddy wanted him to save all the annual leaves and spend with them. How can a person totally deny his son’s honeymoon to save leaves and spend time with them?? I agree, spending time with parents is important but spending those beautiful days with wife and get to know each other is also important. his parents already were coming to Singapore the next month to stay with us for 15 days. Basically all signs were clearly stating that his family is the center of our relation, marriage and everything. Priyanka Snell You are right sister, there were red flags which we thought can be sought out with understanding and affection we develop once we start staying together. But everything happened was so fast and so out of imagination. Here we talk about girls reaching moon and even farther, In that era, we never imagined people could be so orthodox and consider wife/daughter in law a bonded slave. TOO ALL THE GIRLS WHO ARE YET TO BE MARRIED : Clearly mention to the prospectus groom before finalising marriage that, “Like your parents, my parents will be equally important for me. and I will have to help them and support them whenever they really need.”
column9: I am just so glad that you spent the last few months with your father and did not buckle under the demands of your in laws. There are many women who are conditioned to believe that listening to their in laws is their utmost duty and while reading your answer I kept hoping that you are not one of those. You went to your father against all odds, kudos to you for being so strong. Really proud of how you dealt with it. Sending you lots of strength and love.

column1: What words of encouragement/empathy/consolation would you say to a person who just lost a friend/spouse/family member? [I keep in mind, that Covid19 got me by surprise]
column3: I couldn’t be sure from your question whether or not you meant that this person had Covid - 19. Either way, death is death. No matter the circumstances it is always traumatic for the survivors. What can you say to encourage/empathize/console this person? Most people are in this position at some point in their lives. We cannot find the words. We cannot put ourselves in another person’s shoes no matter our good intentions. The funny thing is that a person in grief is going through certain emotions - it is a continuum - so no matter what we say it will hardly ever be remembered or even heard at the time of mourning. When somebody dies the relatives and friends immediately go into shock and denial. They are not yet ready for the depression that usually follows a death. They are certainly not at the stage of acceptance. So bear in mind that your presence is far more important than your words. Sitting quietly with the person, a hand in theirs or an arm around their shoulder is enough. Don’t worry about the words, ‘Sorry for your loss’ is good enough for most people. Just let them do the talking if they want to. The fact that you care enough to want to help shows that you are a kind person. I am sure they will be grateful.
column9: Amen 😇🙏 … Thank you very much Ms Sally

column1: Is it true that oncologists refuse to be treated for terminal cancer?
column3: Some refuse. It depends on the type of cancer, the prognosis, f they have a child graduating from high school or some other milestone they’d like to be around to see etc. They’ve seen it all. They’ve seen the suffering only to get to the next stage and suffer some more. Lay people see what happens on TV, where people are awake and speaking comfortably and then close their eyes and dye. This is not what happens in the real world. Or they may now someone who had cancer. If these lay people weren’t intimately involved in the cancer patient’s care up until the end they do not know. They know only what they are told because they probably didn’t go visit their dying friend or relative because it was too hard for THEM! I digress. The oncologist sees what the patient goes through, what their family goes through and what the medical profession goes through just to keep the patient alive for another 6 months or maybe a year. When several doctors have said there is no hope and I’ve had to help my family members make these decisions, my question to them is always, “To what end?”. If you got 3–6 months extra what would that time be like? In those 3–6 months your family members could be through the first stages of grief and you would not have to suffer and worse watch them see the anxiety and fear in your eyes. For me, I’ll never get over the fear in my brother’s eyes. I can only imaging what he was feeling. Again, it’s all about the prognosis, the odds and if you are a betting man.
column9: While all this is true, I’m not sure the anxiety, fear, pain and suffering go away just because someone decided against treatment. Cancer causing your body to shut down is often not going to be easy or peaceful whether you’ve had chemo or not.

column1: If my ex cheated on me, why do I still love him and think that he will come back and change?
column3: The ex relationship comes with grief as if a family member had died. And it is even a struggle because the ex is still alive making trigger emotions likely. One stage of grief is denial: The person will come back to me. I have changed. He just needs time to get over it These are some denial thoughts. But trying to restore an ex relationship is like trying to warm up burnt coffee. It's difficult to do and doesn't taste good once warmed up. The stages of grief are because you are a lover. And when love is lost lovers feel the pain. Let your sadness remind you that you are a lover. Time to move on.

column1: What are examples of times superheroes have "snapped"?
column3: There have been several, although most of them happen in alternate realities. Green Lantern and Scarlet Witch snapped in continuity. And it wasn't about “losing it" against their enemies. They killed their friends.When Mongul and Cyborg Superman destroyed Coast City, Hal Jordan tried to recreate it using his Green Lantern ring. The Guardians of the Universe objected. Pesky little gnomes. They informed Jordan via projection that he was using his ring for personal gain and would not be permitted to charge it. So he drained the energy from their projection and flew straight towards Oa. The other Green Lanterns tried to stop him. He destroyed them. Not “he knocked them around and left". He killed them and took their rings. Even those who weren't dead after the fights suffocated in space because Hal took their rings. Kilowog tried to stop him. Jordan burned Kilowog to a skeleton. Desperate, the Guardians released a prisoner from the central battery to stop Jordan. They released Sinestro.I love that line. You know… you probably should ha- Jordan then drained the central battery and left. He later appeared, calling himself Parallax, and tried to rewrite all of existence in order to save Coast City. It should be noted that Jordan's break was later ascribed to Parallax, the yellow entity of Fear. But at the time, it was all Hal. Now, let's talk about Avengers Disassembled. The Avengers were doing pretty well. The mansion (they used to have a mansion) was fine. Members were respected. Tony Stark was the freaking Secretary of Defense. Until, one sunny day, the Jack of Hearts came to the door of the mansion. When Scott Lang opened the door, Jack said “I’m sorry”, then he exploded. Half of the mansion went with him. So did Scott Lang.Meanwhile, Tony started stumbling on stage in front of the nation. He looked drunk. He acted drunk. He felt drunk. But he had not touched alcohol in years. Before the Avengers could regroup, the tragedies kept coming. Vision flew a quinjet into the rest of the mansion, leveling it completely. He then apologized and released five copies of Ultron (who immediately attacked). She-Hulk went into a Hulk-like rage and nearly killed Cap and Wasp. It culminated with an attack on the mansion. Kree. Out of nowhere. After rallying the Avengers (and SHIELD) for a counterattack, a gravely injured Hawkeye died bringing down one of their ships.Not long afterwards, the remaining Kree simply left. As the Avengers were trying to help their wounded and regroup, Dr Strange appeared in astral form. He had detected chaotic magic at dangerous levels. Cap started to put the pieces together.Wanda Maximoff had lost her damned mind. You might not know that Wanda had two children, twin boys, with her husband.Here's a family picture. The children were conceived in their love by her powers. They weren't real. And they vanished. Wanda had been lost in grief. Working with Agatha Harkness, the Avengers had Wanda’s memories of the children suppressed. One supposes they went to great pains to hide all indications that the Scarlet Witch had two children with the Vision, which had to have been a pretty big story at some point. Anyway, Janet (the Wasp) accidentally reminded her. Wanda caught one slip that Janet made and began to investigate. Wanda was destroying the Avengers from every direction. Cap, of course, was convinced that he could “get through” to Wanda by talking to her. Sometimes I’m not sure if that man is naive or just arrogant.Wanda was holding her own against the Avengers, pulling enemies and old friends from, well, somewhere to fight them. Dr Strange took advantage of Wanda’s distraction to confront her with the Eye of Agamotto , forcing her to see the truth. Wanda collapsed, catatonic. Her father came for her. Magneto knows how it feels to do terrible things out of grief, and he wanted to help his daughter. But it gets worse. Magneto took Wanda to Genosha. Charles Xavier tried for months to counsel her. She later took over both of their minds and used Xavier's power, plus her own, to create a world where every mutant and hero got their deepest wish. The House of M was a world ruled by Magneto. Where Gwen Stacy never died. Where Wolverine had all of his memories. All of his memories. Including what she had done. Wolverine worked with Luke Cage and Layla Miller, a young mutant, to restore the memories of members of the X-Men and New Avengers that they could find. Except Steve Rogers, an elderly WWII veteran living in Brooklyn. The, um, assembled team of heroes traveled to Genosha to confront Wanda in the palace with Magneto, Pietro, and Lorna. When Hawkeye confronted Wanda first and asked, with tears in his eyes, why she had killed him, we learned that Wanda had not forgotten like the others. She knew exactly what she was doing and was more than willing to protect it. She killed Hawkeye again, this time in person. The team of heroes faced Magneto and his defenders with little success. But when young Layla was able to show Magneto the truth, he did not react as Wanda would have expected. Ruling the world meant little to him at this cost to those he cared about, especially Wanda. Wanda’s grief, anger, and frustration gave way to an eerie calm. She gave up on this dream (and, once again, her recreated children) with three words.…No more mutants.All but 198 of Earth's mutants lost their powers but not the effects of those powers. Wanda’s tearful statement most likely would have stripped all of Earth’s mutants of their power, but Dr Strange managed to erect a hasty defense. Many of the former mutants died. More found themselves in untenable situations, like the suddenly normal-sized Blob who still had all of his original skin (which was tough enough to defy cutting). Others found themselves targeted by anti-mutant groups who became aware of their sudden vulnerability. And since no new mutants were being born, their enemies detected a possible change to render them extinct, once and for all. The remaining 198 gathered at the Xavier mansion, which was fenced and guarded by government troops. They were persecuted more than ever. To this day, the mutant population has not recovered. The Marvel Universe is still feeling the effects of that one.
column9: Wow…I actually got chills reading this answer. First time that’s happened on a Quora this year. I never came across this House of M storyline and really goes to show that Scarlet Witch could be the most powerful being in the Universe unassisted by gadgets, asteroids, enchantments, gauntlets, or anything else. That’s insane…Magneto should have more kids. Bookmarked and upvoted.

column1: How does one comfort a friend who just lost a loved one?
column3: I lost my father in 2005. Completely sudden. My mother fell apart. She did not seek out therapy. She continued working as normal. She was starting to unravel... Then she passed four years later from cancer. I lost both of my parents before the age of 27. Do NOT tell a grieving person to be 'strong', or 'chin up', or 'move on'. Anyone who says that is not a friend. Anyone who says that has not lost a parent or anyone else deeply close. Do NOT give out platitudes like 'I'm here for you. Whatever you need'. That means NOTHING. It may sound nice, but ultimately, a grieving person is in shock, denial, and overwhelmed. In fact, talk LESS. Listen MORE. Don't say shit unless you MEAN IT. And don't say anything you wouldn't do. Offer to cook and/or clean. Do menial things around the house that need doing. If that grieving person is able to, they ought to take a LOA from work. This is dependent on who has passed, ultimately. But if it is a spouse or parent, absolutely. I was a complete and total basket case after my mother passed. I was her primary caregiver and I was beyond broken. Thankfully, I found a counsellor with a degree in Thanatology. This is the study of death, dying and bereavement. I learned more about grieving and how we view death and grief in this screwed up society than I ever thought possible. There are no 'stages' in grief. This is a serious misnomer. Grief is a roller coaster. You may feel fine for a few minutes, a couple of hours, days, weeks, months. And then BAM! Suddenly, you are hit with a memory, a flashback, and you are sobbing uncontrollably in your car driving home from work. You may be in that spin for a few minutes, hours, or days. Then you'll come out of it again. Only to rinse and repeat down the line. Time heals nothing. I find as I get older, and now that I have started a family, I miss my parents even more. Grief never, ever leaves you. You only learn how to cope with it in a more tolerant fashion. Be completely and totally kind to yourself in your moments of utter pain and sorrow. You don't have to like it. But do not bury it, shove it away, or pretend it isn't there. You will pay dearly for your misplaced pain. Cry, scream, walk, run, sob, sleep. Do whatever it takes. But be good to yourself. That includes removing people from your life who do not wish to understand your pain or help you by simply being there and listening. Those who talk too much, do not do.

column1: Why is my life pointless without my cat?
column3: Many people become very strongly attached to their pets. This is not unusual, most especially for people who are alone. Our pets are family members, and when a pet dies, we grieve just as we do for a human we care about. It is normal and healthy. Unless you are having suicidal thoughts, feeling numb, or that life is pointless for awhile, is often a fairly normal stage of grief. If you ARE having suicidal thoughts, please call the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline at 988 or 800–273–8255. If you are alone in the world, your pet is truly your best friend. THIS IS A HUGE LOSS. Allow yourself time to grieve. Loss of a pet makes loneliness feel worse than ever before. It’s not easy just to “go out and meet people,” and a lot of people don’t understand that. Try talking to a counselor to help you get through the hardest part of this time of grief, and after some time passes, go to the animal shelter and give another cat a loving home. The best way to honor the memory of a deceased and beloved pet is to save the life of another one. You will never replace your best furry friend — every animal is a unique individual — but you certainly can have another furry friend in your life. Or are there other circumstances? Sometimes, a person may be in horrible living situation with other people, and when their beloved companion animal dies, they have no friend or comfort in a difficult situation such as an abusive relationship, and they feel all alone. If you are in an abusive relationship, please seek the help you need to get out. If you are a minor, and your parents are abusive, confide in a school counselor for help.

column1: What is some of the best advice you have received about handling grief?
column3: Sigh… this is so hard to deal with… I completely understand. My sister, whom I considered my only family member died 3 years ago this upcoming July from stage 4 neuro-pancreatic cancer that was also producing tumors in her liver. It’s incredibly tough. There are so many stages of grief and losing a loved one who was so close to you can take a good bit of time to heal and move through. I truly don’t believe that we can ever truly “get over” the loss of our loved ones, but we CAN heal and move through the stages of grief and begin to breathe again, take small baby steps of daily living where every moment isn’t consumed with thinking and mourning them. For me, it took the first 6 months, truly, of lots and lots of tears, which are liquid healing that God gave us for intense emotions when words fall short. If you feel them coming, let them fall, they are there to help to heal you and help to begin to close the wounding in your heart where they once occupied. I’ve found great help and healing in writing in a journal. One thing that I desperately missed was being able to text, call and communicate whenever I wanted or needed to. We lived 3,000 miles away from each other, so this type of communication was daily. I visited her every 3–6 months for about 2–4 weeks to take her to oncology appointments, take care of her house and growing boys. Some of the best advice I’ve received was to journal and write your loved one letters, keeping them apprised of your daily life, it helps to “park” your words, feelings and emotions. It’s good that you are on here with others who have gone through similar things. But perhaps finding an in-person grief counselor or grief counseling group where you can meet up regularly or when you feel up for it can really help too. I believe that we really can help to heal each other by sharing our similar experiences and any tools we might have used to help along the journey. It really is a journey to adopt a new normal, it’s not easy and there are no short cuts to grieving. Just try really hard not to get stuck in any one stage as that can cause a prolonged grieving process. It really will be okay, I know it doesn’t feel like it right now, but each day will be a little bit easier to cope and move forward. You are stronger than you know.

column1: How can someone help a friend, partner or family member that has lost someone?
column3: One of the things that happens is very often loneliness. The loved one dies and everyone is around dropping off food and making cups of tea and generally being helpful. The funeral takes place and suddenly the house is empty. Even if there are people living there the missing hole is just huge. That is often when the bereaved need support. As has been said in other posts offer it on their terms. The seven stages of grief are real so help them go through it.

column1: Should I reach out to my wedding guests that RSVP’d and no-showed? I still had to pay for their plate. No apologies yet either.
column3: One of my daughters was married during the COVID-19 pandemic. Guests (including family) were asked to take a rapid test on the day of the wedding, and stay home if they were sick Even though COVID is officially no longer at the pandemic stage, I would still want people who were sick with any communicable illness to stay home, rather than putting all of the attendees at risk. Think about it this way: There are probably going to be some family members there who are medically vulnerable. Who would ever want their memories of their wedding day to include grandma or grandpa catching something and having to be hospitalized, or even dying from it?!? No thanks! I'd rather have the sick person stay home and send their regrets for having to miss it. And there are plenty of other valid excuses — like when the invited guest or someone they take care of has a medical crisis, whether from an accident or illness (or an early delivery, for someone who is pregnant). Or they were flying to the wedding, and their flights were cancelled or they missed a connection, and they couldn't rebook in time to get there. In my religion, someone who lost a family member is supposed to avoid weddings or other public celebrations for a month, for most family members — and for a whole year if they lost a parent. I wouldn't expect someone to violate their religious beliefs for my sake. If the death occurred after they responded, ideally they would cancel their response, but in their moment of grief they might not remember. Simply put, there are lots of valid reasons why someone would RSVP “yes", and then find themselves unable to attend. When possible, it would be courteous to inform the host(s), but it's often too late to change the catering numbers.
column9: I've never bailed out on an event I rsvp’d to. But, I think what you said is pretty standard. Always give a reason if they have to.

column1: What happens when a borderline personality disorder meets a sociopath? Is there any chance for this kind of relationship or both are incompatible in every way possible?
column3: When a borderline meets a sociopath, an atomic bomb of childhood trauma goes off. There is a good chance there will be some kind of relationship, and it will end like Hiroshima. You’ll be astounded at the pile of wreckage two souls can leave in their wake. They are incompatible in every way, and they are also Ying and Yang.Borderlines and sociopaths are born of the same root: narcissistic families and abuse. In my experiences trauma bonding to narcissists, the less violent narcissists came from a family with only one narcissist parent. However, the sociopaths I’ve known, those with NPD/ASPD, came from a family like my own: both parents were not only narcissists, but they were both sociopaths. This means we came from households with extreme violence, extreme emotional and physical neglect, with parents engaged in criminal activity and mired in addiction. We were exposed to pedophilia, rape, incest, animal abuse, racism, sexism, homophobia, and every other flavor of hatred. Our parents, however, told us they were God, they were perfect, and every bad thing they did was justified. We were regularly told that we are worthless. This similar childhood trauma makes borderlines and sociopaths feel familiar to each other upon meeting.To understand how they differ, you have to go back to their childhood trauma. Sociopaths only think in three terms when it comes to people, and this includes their children: golden, scapegoat, or invisible. They put their children in these categories on sight, as they do with all people. For the golden child, the next generation narcissist/sociopath, one or both parents names the child after who they think is the best person in the world: THEMSELVES. The sociopath will be a Jr., will have a name that rhymes with their parents or mirrors it closely, or will have their first name as a middle name or the same middle names. Some famous examples: John Wayne Gacy, serial killer Father: John Stanley Gacy Theodore Bundy, serial killer Mother: Eleanor Bundy Jeffrey Lionel Dahmer, serial killer and cannibal Father: Lionel Dahmer Casey Marie Anthony, murderer of her golden child daughter, Caylee Marie Anthony Mother: Cindy Marie Anthony.The list goes on and on… The golden child is deemed perfect at birth, and taught to parrot the identity of their parents exactly to attain love, which comes to them in the form of spoiling. However, the minute they are not perfect to the sociopath parent, they are then introduced to the cycle of abuse: SHAME. Like everyone is destined to with a narcissist, they eventually split their golden child to ALL BAD, and the golden then gets the same treatment that the scapegoats to the narcissist always receive: EXTREME, RELENTLESS ABUSE AND HATRED. This usually happens in early childhood; however, they will use the tactics of spoiling to periodically lovebomb and manipulate the golden child, or to triangulate them with siblings throughout their life.When the golden child is cast off from their pedestal, they have their very first mental collapses: the narcissistic collapse. My sister started having them at 2: she would headbang for hours, peel the skin off her fingers, hit herself. She would scream like an animal being tortured. She’d shiver in my arms for hours when it finally ended. In those moments, the golden child becomes suicidal. They feel they have been cast off from love, cast off from God. In those moments, the sociopath child is born.Love becomes THE MOST DANGEROUS THING IN THE WORLD TO THEM. It makes them VULNERABLE. Vulnerable to a collapse in which THEY MIGHT DIE. So, they REPRESS LOVE AND TRUST. Everyone in the world becomes a potential predator. And they bury their shame, trauma and grief. Forever. Under the fantasy self, the mask.But shame must go somewhere—and they don’t have the ability to process shame yet. They are too young. Their brains are not developed. Therefore, they must PROJECT THE SHAME. They must give it to someone else. It is the same thing as a puppy raised by the fist: they become a biter and a fighter. For the narcissist child who was beaten, they will beat their spouses. For the narcissist child who was raped by an adult, they will rape children. Every trauma that was done to them is what they will be projecting. For life. Because they never could process the grief. They have complex PTSD, yet they can only cycle through denial and anger. They are like ghosts reliving the pains that killed them over and over: THEY DIED IN THOSE EARLY MENTAL COLLAPSES. Their ability to love died. Their potential to develop empathy died. Their humanity died. The monster was birthed young. These are personality disorders because they root young and are lifelong. They know nothing of God or the Devil. They don’t know why they are doing what they’re doing. They operate on instinct. Like vampires, they’re eternally young because their brains are stunted emotionally to toddler age from the brain damage of their child abuse. Like vampires, they only know they need blood, and they don’t feel bad about it, though they know they must hide in the shadows.And like vampires, they will mostly mate with other vampires. That’s the easiest and most familiar. Nearly all the sociopaths I’ve known married other sociopaths, and sometimes had long relationships in which they resented each other, much like the way vampires stuck together in Anne Rice’s Interview with the Vampire. (Rice, btw, was named after her father—her real name was actually Howard; her husband was a Jr.) But every now and then, a vampire falls for a special kind of human, one who is opposite of them in every way, and yet the same in many ways too, more enigmatic and alluring than other people are to them. It never ends well.For every genuine Borderline I’ve known (as opposed to covert narcissists who say they are borderlines, which is a common mask they wear), we have a couple things in common:We were named after someone who died tragically, or a former “friend” of the narcissist parent, or a family member the narcissist parent hates, like their sibling.WE ALL ALMOST DIED AT BIRTH.The second one is the most mysterious. This is usually a question I ask when I suspect someone is a borderline, because most borderlines are unaware of what they are, just like narcissists. Borderlines without diagnosis will sometimes identify themselves as “empaths.” I’ll ask, “Where did you get your name?” and then “Did you almost die at birth?” They always respond the same way, YES! HOW DID YOU KNOW? We all have stories of umbilical cords around our necks, of being born premature and living on machines for months, of our mothers nearly miscarrying us and being on bedrest, of horrific complications. My mom always told the story of my birth as a story in which I nearly killed her, born blue and dead. And she always told me the same thing about it: I wish you had died. This is how the scapegoat child enters the world: our very birth is a battle to survive with a parent who hates us. Then they hate us with every fiber of their being and punish us for the rest of our lives. To survive a life with no love, WE REPRESS AND DENY IT. We think we must’ve deserved it, and we work very hard to try to earn love from the people we need to survive. We become self harmers and people pleasers and perfectionists. We cannot hate those who hate us. We repressed our hate and anger just as narcissists repressed their love. We love our abusers, and we work very hard to get our love returned to us. It always feels SO CLOSE TO POSSIBLE. We can’t quite figure out WHY we aren’t lovable. Love becomes endless agony. So we sink into despair, suicidal ideation, self harm, addiction, mental collapse.The Borderline and the Sociopath are, therefore, the embodiment of THE LIVING DEAD.One thing we tend to have in common when we meet is we love horror and have a kind of courage and impulsivity that makes no sense. As if WE CAN’T DIE. As if WE KNOW WE ARE ALREADY DEAD. We know the truth: there are more ways to die than just the body. The Borderline died at infancy. Fallen angels, we repress everything but the energy of love. The Sociopath died in early toddler years. Fallen angels, they repress everything but the energy of hatred.The energy of hatred is the same thing as death and destruction. The energy of love is the same thing as life and creation. Together, we are the whole energy of the universe, conscious and in human form.Every sociopath I knew, at some point, called me their personal angel. Every sociopath I knew, at some point, became my personal demon.If the sociopath is the energy of death and the borderline is the energy of love, the reason these two attract to each other is because… DEEP DOWN, WHAT THE ENERGY OF LOVE YEARNS FOR IS DEATH. DEEP DOWN, WHAT THE ENERGY OF DEATH YEARNS FOR IS LOVE. Both feel like an erasure of agony, an erasure of self, the end of pain. The end of existence. The end. Finally.In Interview with the Vampire, when a troop of vampires parades a naked woman on stage and prepares to devour her, one says to the terrified woman, “Do you know what it means when death knows you by name?” She whispers, “It means no pain.”To love a world full of brokenness is agony. To hate a world full of beauty is agony. We want the pain to end.Aside from my parents, I’ve had several relationships or friendships with sociopaths. I didn’t know then I was a borderline, or that they were anything other than normal human beings. It took me degrees in psychology, much trauma, and much therapy to awaken. The first sociopath was my first love at 15. It ended in his suicide. The others always ended in rapes, violence, stalking, restraining orders, and stunning betrayals and secrets. The sociopath to awaken me and impact me most was not someone I was in a relationship with, but my apartment maintenance man. He stalked me, installed a microphone in my apartment, drugged me, and broke in and raped me for several weeks. He continued to stalk me and terrorize me after I escaped. When he raped me, IT WAS AS IF HE DIED INSIDE OF ME. I have spent this whole year thinking about his childhood trauma and his pain. I feel like I have been carrying a child’s corpse in me and crying for it, praying to resurrect it, to exorcize its demons, to heal it. I wake up every day and revisit this trauma, just like a ghost. What he projected into me was AGONY, DESPAIR, and DEATH. I keep replaying conversations with him in my head, because of all the sociopaths I’ve known, I felt a very strange intimacy and honesty between us. Even as he raped me, I had deep conversations with him in those weeks. He didn’t reveal his full truths, but he revealed more shames to me than he would to most people. It felt as if he wanted my love. I sometimes fantasize he’ll reach out and apologize, even though I’ve already forgiven him and I don’t need his apology to know I didn’t deserve what he did. And I know remorse is not a feeling he experiences. Why do I have this ridiculous fantasy? Because I want death to come back to me and make the pain go away. Or I want the power of my love to be able to heal his death, resurrect him from misery, which I know every sociopath experiences, because I’m an empath: I can feel it. It is what makes love so painful for me. But hate and love repel each other…or they eclipse each other. They don’t heal each other.But what happens to a sociopath when all the love they have repressed to survive is unearthed? I’ve seen it again and again: it is the agony I carry with me daily. They experience this only for brief moments, and this is also something that Interview with the Vampire details symbolically and vividly: After the death of Claudia, a child vampire that Louis and Lestat had as a companion, Louis goes into his coffin and “gives himself over to grief.”He feels as if the grief is bottomless, and he will NEVER STOP CRYING. This is something I’ve heard from my parents, my sister, my favorite people, and lovers who were sociopaths when in a collapse: THEY DO NOT THINK THEY CAN EVER STOP CRYING. The weight of their despair is like nothing you’ve ever seen. As a borderline, I always cried WITH THEM, and it was always THE MOST TERRIFYING PAIN. Sociopaths on Quora have even written me and detailed this feeling: they have brief moments of being able to feel they love someone, and then they are so overcome with HORROR and SHAME and GUILT over the terrible things they’ve done to those they love and over how worthless and unworthy they feel of love, that they must shut it down just to survive it. Louis cried for a day…and then HE GOT REVENGE. Narcissistic Rage and Projection of Pain. Later, he experiences it again, as he sees Lestat, his maker and former companion, who is also overcome with loneliness and misery, begging for him to return and be his companion again. He says he feels the weight of grief that overcame him with Claudia, but it was more than that: it was the weight of everyone he’d ever loved and everything he’d ever lost and every evil he’d ever done. A single tear escaped his eye, and he shut it down and left Lestat.He realized that to survive as a vampire, there’s a coldness that needs to be cultivated and protected. He says he felt a pain so terrible, his mind veered away from it and said, “no, don’t take me back there,” and his mind receded from it. That pain was LOVE. As he discusses this with Armand, his vampire companion, he says, “We looked for love and goodness in a life which is living death. When you do evil and seek love, you only have desperate confusion and longing and the chasing of phantom goodness in human form.” He says he always knew that the answer to his quest for happiness and love was always “his own death.” But he is a living thing, and his instinct is to live, not to die. He looked for others like him, for God, for the devil, and no matter what, love brought him to the same truth: he was evil. Therefore, his life was that of the living damned. “Damned in his own mind and soul.” After Louis finishes his life story, the interviewer is outraged. “All this power and this is how it ends?! Despair?!” Louis says calmly, “It couldn’t have ended any other way.”A relationship with a borderline and a sociopath will always end in some form of DEATH. It may be a physical death, a metaphorical death, or a spiritual death. The deaths will be mutual. If they survive physically, the lesson will go back to the same one of their childhood: HOW TO ENDURE A BROKEN HEART ALONE. HOW TO WALK THROUGH THIS LIFE AS THE LIVING DEAD.With my maintenance man who raped me, I saw several moments where he looked at me with that brief look of despair and love. As an empath, I could feel the weight of it and those expressions are burned in my brain. I believe he felt love for me, and that his desire for love was why he stalked me to begin with. He could feel love in my energy. The sociopath and the borderline are the ghosts of orphans. And that love he felt was such a threat to his very existence that he had to attack it, because nothing made him more vulnerable, brought him closer to his own death, to suicide. To death, love is a predator. After he’d look at me with those expressions of grief and love, he’d rape me with the most extreme anger, or even grief. One memory I have while drugged is of him crying and calling me mama as he raped me.After this event in my life, the person I had been completely died. After the first rape, I was very drugged when I woke up, and I questioned, for weeks, if I was alive or in the afterlife. Only my pain seemed proof of my life. After I escaped, I spent months questioning if I’m dead, how long I’ve been dead, or what being alive even means. I think there are more ways to die than we realize. How many times have I died and continued to walk? And when will my body finally follow my soul in death?But with the energy of destruction always comes the energy of creation. Borderlines who survive sociopaths tend to alchemize their deaths into new life. After my rapes, I wrote a memoir, a book of poetry, and hundreds of essays on Quora about my pain. I felt impregnated by pain. I turned my death into art, I rebirthed it into a new life. Such is the mysterious energy of the universe.There’s a reason why sociopaths and empaths are magnets in trauma and tragedy. We play out the same story that many have played out before. Like Ying and Yang, The empath teaches the sociopath that there is love inside of them. The sociopath teaches the empath that there is hate inside of them. Both of us find these feelings unbearable, torturous, unsurvivable. Thus, we both confront our own worst fears: the mirror.When a vampire loves a human, only three things can happen: —The vampire feeds on the human until death —The vampire turns the human vampire and the human resents them —The human discovers the vampire is a monster and flees in horror There is no happy ending. But both will be haunted by this love. They will walk through the rest of their days wondering, Am I a ghost? Am I a curse? Or am I a prophecy?“To write his truth, I must acknowledge my own. In the honest story, I have to tell you why he came for me. Why he returned again and again: I was an orchard of forgiveness. An orchestra of yes and yes and yes. I unfurled my fists. Softened every softness. Invented new words for mercy.” -Jeanann Verlee, “The Sociopath’s Wife Knows Endurance”
column9: What an unbelievably heartbreaking and hauntingly beautiful read..

column1: What are some of the best things and life lessons you have learned from an animal?
column3: This is Greenie. I met him in 2006 in a park in Toronto. Greenie was part of a tightly knit family of four ducks at the park who could not fly. They were not original to the park; they had probably been dumped there years ago after being purchased as Easter presents, and for some reason, they survived and thrived. Flightless, they thrived. Amidst dogs and foxes and the taunting of the other ducks who could fly, the little family thrived. And then they started to get old. Three members of the family died in quick succession, and Greenie was left on his own. He had never been on his own, and he was beside himself with grief. That first winter, when he had nobody left to call his own, he curled up into a ball and just drifted on the cold water of the pond. It was as though he wanted to die, too. But when spring came, Greenie made an effort. He tried swimming with small bands of other male ducks. Though he was different: bigger, different colours, flightless, he tried to make friends. He tried to fit in. It was a struggle at first. The other ducks tolerated his presence but didn't warm to him. Greenie kept trying. He didn't get discouraged. For a whole summer Greenie kept making an effort; every day approaching new ducks, trying to find a duck that would warm to him and be his friend. And he finally did meet one friend, and then another, and he was happy again. Not that he didn't miss his family every single day, but he learned how to cope and go on, because that is what we all must do, animal or human. I know all this because I visited Greenie nearly every day for seven years and watched his transformation out of grief, into coping, and into enjoying his life once again. I am a shy and introverted person. Greenie taught me that shyness has no value in the real world. If you want companionship you have to make an effort. You have to seek friendship, and accept the awkwardness that this seeking will inevitably bring. When you're looking to make friends you can't be ashamed to let it be known that you might not have any, just at the moment. I am currently trying to be as brave as Greenie was in reinventing his life. I'm in the awkward stage, but I saw Greenie go through it and get past it, and I hope I'm as successful in making that transition.

column1: Does the difference in reactions to grief mean that some people are less saddened by their loss or are suppressing their feelings?
column3: Different people handle their grief differently. VERY differently. Their expressions of grief many times originate in their family—some families are very stoic around death rituals of loved ones. They express their grief openly when they are alone, or at some future time—in a private setting. Sometimes the grief is delayed. My family was that way—their was a solemn calm during the visitation and funeral, but later family members might break down and weep. Often not in front of the kids. A real Germanic/Christian way of dealing with death. The dead person is with God—no reason to mourn. Is not the dead one in Heaven? But we do mourn, either publicly or privately because there is doubt about the afterlife, and then there is the fact that we miss that person so much. You can call it suppressing of feelings, but what is important is that grief is somehow dealt with over time and the griever can come to a sense of peace. If you do not grieve for one death, you will probably grieve for two people at the next death. Your body and mind will help you express your sorrow. There are 5 stages of grief (maybe more) and people work through those in their own manner. Much of that can be very private. Cultures that encourage open and public expression of grief may be helping people work through their grief in a more direct way. Western culture tends to suppress much of the open expression—though that may change over the decades to come. Ultimately, most people do move through the stages of grief in their own way. In the end, grief does have to be experienced in a person’s personal level and manner, whether public grief is the norm or not. Grief not attended to can cause even greater grief later on in life, when other loved ones die and the sorrow builds to a breaking point.
