column1: What is the best advice for a young, first-time startup CEO?
column3: I think the biggest single piece of advice I can offer is to manage your own psychology. This, more than anything else, is fundamental for success, in my experience. It's also one of the things that gets discussed the least. We talk a lot about motivation, how execution is more important than the big idea, measuring the right things, working hard, establishing a great culture, etc.. But none of this matters if you've not got a grip on your own psychology. Do everything you can to try and stay level headed. Every difficult thing that can happen, will happen at some stage. You'll have to fire people. You'll realise you're on track to bankruptcy in X months. You'll have to stop working with that small, under-performing supplier whose business will probably go bankrupt when you leave. You can't make the tough calls without a handle on your head.Speak to other (ex-)CEO's - they will be the only ones who can relate to the problems you're having (because you'll quickly find few others will, and while empathetic family & friends will be supportive, it's just not the same as hearing things from someone else who's been there). See a Professional Therapist - on a regular basis, or at the very least when you're facing challenging times, it'll be worth every penny (believe it or not, they're not just for people in times of grief or experiencing mental health issues, and it's not a sign of weakness). Learn how to identify the assumptions you're making - about yourself, your company, your team, your customers, your partners, your suppliers... We all make hundreds every day, and many CEO's are completely unaware of it. We have a tendency to put ourselves at the centre of a problem when we don't know the answer, and it's rarely the case.Compartmentalise - find an escape from the business, even if it's just a few hours each week. It doesn't matter whether you meditate, run, climb (my favourite), play guitar, paint or get lost in a video game. All that's important is that you can regularly completely immerse yourself in something that isn't business. Address personal problems - whether you admit it or not, you bring your personal problems to work. Whether that's because your next door neighbour's barking dog means you're not sleeping, or a close family member died. These things all impact our minds, and if you run away from your personal problems, rather than tackling them head-on, you won't perform as well as you can.It's not easy, and you'll never be perfect. Your psychology will always occasionally get the better of you, so don't beat yourself up about it. But don't ignore it. Keep learning, and finding ways to get better. Over the last few years as an entrepreneur, I've experienced some of my lowest, and highest moments. 3am simultaneous hardware failures that lead to us losing hundreds of thousands of people's files, when I was running my online storage company. Successfully navigating that same company's acquisition a couple of years later. Having to tell Pint Drop's angel investors that we'd lost their money, and were closing down the company. Making our first non-founding hire, at Cobloom. Make sure that the highs don't blind you to problems, and the lows don't leave you unable to get out of bed in the morning. It's a rollercoaster ride. It takes a lot of resilience to lead a company, and the more time you spend off your "psychological best", the more mistakes you'll make, and the faster you'll burn out.

column1: How can I help my mildly intellectually disabled sister cope with the upcoming losses of our elderly pets?
column3: I have always viewed pets, especially such animals as dogs with a shorter lifespan usually, as God’s way of helping children learn to cope with death. Usually, when a family first experiences death after having children it is with the family pet. In many cases a strong attachment has been made and the pet is, to quote others, “a member of the family.” When that member dies, the young child often experiences his or her first loss. During that time a child learns to grieve, remember, and celebrate the life of the pet. All the usual stages of grief are experienced in most families. Family members will even gather in many cases, have a funeral or ceremony to remember the pet and allow young children to even see and participate in a burial. In essence the child often faces his or her first loss with a pet. Later, when family members such as grandparents and others pass, the child has the basic coping skills in place. As I stated, I believe this is one of God’s avenues to help prepare young children to face death later in life. As such, the death of a pet for a person with Intellectual Disabilities (ID) is no different. The core to remember is that ID does not mean the person can not understand or will not understand, it simply means the person may understand differently or accept it more slowly than others. The greatest mistake I have seen in my work and in my opinion through My QIDP is for parents or friends to try to “hide” or “avoid” the death. It is better to confront it, discuss it, and use the moment for teaching. Remember, just as the child will eventually experience death of family members beyond the family pet, the person will ID will have those same moments later in life. By allowing and encouraging the person with ID to deal with death now in a family pet, you will be preparing the person for the future. Ultimately, how your sister will depend on your sister’s individual needs. It’s easy to establish that she will have to deal with death either now with a pet, or later with a human person, but it is harder to say how you should do that. I do not know your sister or anything about her so giving recommendations on dealing with the death of a pet can only be general. I can not, for example, get into how you might pray together since I do not know if you pray, or how to have a funeral, since I do not know you and your sister’s specific beliefs and/or views. What I can say, is that regardless of specific beliefs, we all deal with death. Perhaps a general way to deal with a pet is to talk first with your sister and remind her that all things die. You might compare this to someone else's’ pet that has died or a family member. She needs to know that it’s okay to be sad, to feel bad and to cry. She needs to know that her pet will always be her pet, but that he or she has simply had to move on due to old age, an accident, or something else. It also helps to remind her that she was good to her pets, she was their friend, and that although the pet’s life was short compared to the life your sister will live, for those few short years or time that the pet was here, it was happy because the pet’s best friend was your sister. Remind your sister that she gave the pet the best life he or she could have had and that you know the pet is always thankful for having your sister as a friend. If you have a strong religious background, then incorporate that into your teaching. I once saw a cartoon of a man arriving in heaven. He was pretty old looking and had just arrived at the gates of heaven. In the background you can see a dog running at full speed from the other side toward the man. The man has an astonished look on his face as the angel says, “Oh, we know all about you! He’s been bragging about you for fifty years now!” My first pet was a German Shepherd named Archie. I had him from the time I was a small kid, maybe four or so, until he passed away when I was sixteen. I arrived home and we found him sick. I sat beside him until he died. After he died, my dad and I drove him for two hours to the family farm and buried him. This was a huge deal since my dad got in from work, took us both on the drive and then had to get up the next morning for work. He was extremely supportive of my desire to bury Archie on the family farm. To this day, Archie’s grave is still on that farm, but I know in my heart that when I die, I’ll meet him and many other pets again. I look forward to the day I can tell Archie how my life went after sixteen - your sister can do the same thing - she needs to know to live her life to the fullest, so that some day she can tell her pets all about her life and what she saw after they went ahead of her to get everything ready.

column1: How do families handle Christmas when a loved one has just died?
column3: This question is ambiguous. It might mean, “What differences are there in the celebrations people arrange at Christmas if someone they love has just died?” Or it might mean, “How do people cope emotionally at Christmas if someone they love has just died?” On the first point, there can be two basic answers. One is, that different societies, traditions and denominations may have specific rules for what you do at Christmas if it occurs within a specific period after the death. If that is what you want an answer on, all I can say is that you have to ask someone within your own community. Even within a single denomination, you may find there are local variations, or variations depending on how closely related you were to the person who died. In my own denomination, there are no specified rituals or practices. You need to do what seems most appropriate to yourself and others similarly affected. The other is that, even when there are no fixed rules, your celebrations need to do some or all of the following, at least: (1) Recognise that grief is different for different people in different circumstances. My wife died three years ago, and my grief is considerably different from that of my children. I had been aware that she might die well before me for 25 or 30 years, but for children, even adult children, your parents are immortal. (2) Give opportunities for people to talk about the person they miss — if they want to — and to share their memories (3) Understand if some might want to skip celebrations this year (4) If someone wants to stay away, be alert to the possibility that that person’s children or other family members might not want to be away, and perhaps make arrangements that both requirements be met. (5) Some might need to go off quietly and cry. Make sure there is a space for that to happen, if possible — and get a supply of tissues in! (6) In some households or similar groups, it might be appropriate to share a prayer of thanksgiving to God for the loan of that person’s life and the gift of each moment shared with her/him. If the question is about coping at Christmas when a loved one has recently died, some of that is covered above. but a few clues are:Don’t pretend that the loss doesn’t really matter, or that you are not feeling the lossTake things at your own pace — but make it your goal to eventually be able to participate in all kinds of celebrations and activities without that personYou might easily become irritated with others who are celebrating without your own depth of feeling. Remember that each of us has our own feelings, and you can only be responsible for your own. If you are irritated, you can always say, calmly and truthfully, “I am grieving, and just now I feel very raw. I know you might feel differently, but I can’t cope with how we are all at different stages of grief and handling it in different ways. I hope you will excuse me if I take time out/go home now” etc.I hope this helps in what, I suppose, is a difficult time.

column1: About the grief that I'm still facing, why does it seem like my other family member doesn't suffer any pain of losing our mom? Why does it seem like it's just me who’s dying in this pain of grief? My sister just said that I’m being so sensitive.
column3: Every single person grieves in their own way. There is no set way to grieve. There are stages of grief but not everyone experiences them in the same order or stays in them for the same amount of time. I lost my only child to suicide when he was 15 in 2015. I will grieve every single day for the rest of my life. Some days are gut wrenching and others are do-able. I've been told that I should have moved on, gotten over it and then others have asked how do I get up in the morning. Here's the thing, grieve in your own way as your sister is grieving in hers. You are two different people and neither way is wrong. I am truly sorry for the loss of your mom.
column9: I agree with Rhys about the cycle, or maybe better described as a rollercoaster, of grief. I, too, lost my 15 yo son to suicide in 2017. We were so close and it happened so suddenly (impulsively over a bad dream in the early am.) But Richard Martini, a frequent Quora writer, suggests moving from grief to nostalgia. Because our loved one does not want us to suffer, and they are still very much in our lives though we can not see. My son has come as a beam of light at my bedside, a katydid crawling inside his window, tapped me on the head on the anniversary of his death, sent a text related to a conversation with my daughter the night before, photo bombed my daughter in a wedding picture, and showed up as an orb moving across the floor when I was trying to recreate the photo bombed picture. Just be aware of potential signs from your loved one that they are still connected to you.

column1: One of my family members is dying. First I was shocked and cried a lot but now it's just normal and sometimes I don't feel bad at all for him. Why?
column3: Thanks for A2A. I am so sorry that you are losing a family member. It is difficult at any age and you must be puzzled about what you are feeling now. I have taken a Hospice course and we discussed the different stages of grief. Some people believe there are only 4, others 5, and the Modified Kubler-Ross Model indicates that there are 7. A grieving person may experience all of these emotions or in your case only a few. They are: 1. Shock 2. Denial 3. Anger 4. Bargaining 5. Depression 6. Testing 7. Acceptance. In your case you were shocked which is the initial paralysis of hearing the bad news and then you experienced anger and an outpouring of emotion when you cried. Your final stage was acceptance which means you have come to terms with the death and are ready to go forward. I hope this explains why you are able to return to normalcy. In my case I went through a number of these stages when my dad died. I thought that I had accepted his death after a long period of grieving. But months and even years later I would see something that reminded me of him and I cried again. I don't think we ever forget but we can manage to go on in many cases. Losing someone you love is one of the most difficult aspects of life. If we can't find some sort of acceptance then we can't move on. Also there is no limit on grieving. For some it takes a long time; for others it may be a short period. Please ignore any requests that you should get over it. I believe people are trying to help because they do not want you to be sad. I will ask that you take as much time as you need, Youssef.

column1: How come my husband’s family doesn’t talk to me after his death? Why would they say they would be there for me and they aren’t?
column3: I’m sorry your late husband’s family isn’t stepping up as they claimed. That is an awful feeling. Without knowing a lot of details I will simply outline a little of what I walked through when my brother died 13 years ago. My brother was 39 and took his own life. I had no idea he was suicidal, but many of my family members did. I was in shock from the moment I heard the news. As we rallied to help prepare for services and close down his business lots of well intentioned promises were made. The adrenaline was flowing at this point to simply get through this first stage of the process. It was hard. But not as hard as the day I walked into my home and had to face the reality and finality of his passing. In the months after the funeral all those well intentioned promises got pushed to the back burner while I learned to breathe again. She lost her husband, the love of her life, I don’t fathom to know the depth of her pain. But, I was desperately trying to figure out how to go on missing a piece of who I had always been. It’s the strangest feeling in the world I have felt yet. When I resurfaced from my own grief it had been a year. I took stock of what had been going on that year and realized I was not the only one who had retreated within themselves. I imagine my sister in law felt abandoned by us. Not only were we overcome with grief, but now we had to redefine the relationship with my sister in law. The man who brought us together was gone. Does she want us around? Does she want us involved? What will happen when she finds new love again? Will my brother’s child want anything to do with us? It’s not as simple as it sounds, to be there for someone. My best advice is to reach out and say, ”I really miss you all, please come around.” Perhaps plan a family meal and help them in seeing you still want them there. After the first year, I finally said to my mom, ”We need to do our normal family Christmas. It’s your turn to host.” and we invited my brother’s widow. She didn’t attend that first year. But, we did the same thing at the next holiday and sure enough, she came and was able to bring my nephew. (He is severely autistic and doesn't travel well.) It took time. It took intentionally reaching out, going both ways. But, we are at a point where we flow like a family again. And we spend time together. When she finds new love, we will welcome him with open arms as one of our own. Right now, everyone is hurting and grief is so tricky to navigate. Be patient and be open when the timing is right I bet you all will find your flow again. May you find peace and comfort as you move forward in this life and may the coming years bring joy and abundance.

column1: How does it feel to pay child support for a child you rarely see?
column3: First, I will confirm that I am paying a pretty decent amount of child support for my kids. $800/mo is no small amount, and it definitely puts a dent in the wallet at about 40% of my take home pay. So it sucks, but if I knew the money was going to their benefit, I’d have no problem with it. The sticking point lies with the second part of your question, “for a child (or children) that you rarely (or in my case, never) see”. For that, I will refer you to a entry from my blog: “To Envy Those Who Grieve” I went to a funeral a short time ago. While nearly all funerals are sad, this one was particularly heartbreaking, as the deceased had passed away, suddenly, unexpectedly, and at a relatively young age. A mother, still in the prime of middle age, was taken without warning. A large and loving family had gathered from all over the United States to grieve the passing of a woman that they all had fond memories of. Although I didn’t know the woman at all, it was obvious that she would be missed by a great many people. While I sat and watched the family pour out their grief during the funeral, and then later the burial, a strange emotion came over me. It was an emotion I would have never expected to feel at a funeral, and it took me some time to identify it. It was envy. I felt envious of the family that had gathered to mourn the loss of someone they loved so much. I felt ashamed of this emotion at first, and I tried to bury it. I was there to support someone who had lost a close family member, this was not the time to be focused on myself. But later on, once I was alone, I began to reflect on what I had felt, and more importantly, why. I obviously didn’t envy the family for losing a loved one. I have many people in my life whom I love dearly, and I would not want to lose any of them. I have had loved ones die, and I certainly did not want that to happen to again. What I envied was not their grief, but rather that they were able to express it. My sons are gone. Not dead, but just… gone. They are gone from my life, and the lives of my family. When my wife filed false allegations against me, and took my children from me, it was terrible, but it didn’t feel like they had died. It was a terrible feeling, a great loss, and it was very painful, but it didn’t feel like death, with its shock and finality and hopelessness. At least, it didn’t at first. Unlike with death, there were moments of brief hope. For five long years, every occurrence was a chance at getting my sons back into my life. Every time I went to court, I believed the judge would hear me out, and award me time with my children. When my wife hit me with her car, I thought for sure she would be charged, and I would be able to see my kids. When my wife intentionally burned down her own house and tried to frame me, and the arson report concluded that she had done it, I thought surely something would change. When my daughter was taken from my wife, and I spent nearly a year EARNING her back from foster care, I believed that the authorities would force my wife to reunite us with the boys. But each time I was disappointed. And slowly, creeping up more and more each day, the feeling that they were dead formed like a malignant tumor, growing inside my heart. It feels like my sons are dead. I know that they are not, but they have been removed from my life as surely as if they were placed in wooden boxes and lowered into the ground. No voices, no pictures, no word of what they doing has come my way. I don’t even know what they look like today. I know from letters that were sent to the judge, and from what my daughter tells me, that they hate me. They think I am a terrible person, and that they want nothing to do with me. This is all so different from the relationship we had before. I was once their hero, their confidant, their champion – I was their father. The last time I saw Aiden he was sick, but he insisted on spending time with me, even though he felt awful. The last time I saw Seth, I held him while he cried in my arms, as I tried to console his fears about his parents splitting up. Now, in their minds, I am dangerous, a cancer, someone to avoid at all costs. Such has my wife poisoned their minds and hearts against me. Everything I knew about my sons is gone. Our relationship no longer exists. The children they once were no longer exist. It has been five years now – they are both approaching 15 years of age, well into their teens. To me, they are still nine years old, frozen in my mind at the age I last saw them. But the children I knew have grown up, and every connection I had with them has been severed. Even if we were reunited tomorrow, nothing that we once had has been preserved – we would have to start our relationship from scratch. I have lost my sons. Throughout history, our society has developed ways of dealing with grief. We have a funeral for the deceased. We tell stories of fond memories with them. We look at photographs of the ones we’ve lost, and we remember the joy they brought to our lives. We pour out our grief, and those around us acknowledge the loss, and they comfort us. Then, as the final gesture, we lower a casket into the ground, or present an urn of ashes to the family. The survivors go through the stages of denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and finally acceptance. And often there is a stone at the final resting place, a marker of the one who has been removed from our lives. I will see none of that. I will not get to hear others laugh telling stories of my sons, or cry over how much they will be missed. I will not be able to gather my family together in mourning, and watch a collage of photographs showing their lives. I will not see a casket lowered into the ground, or hold an urn, as a tangible reminder that my sons are gone. I will never allow myself to fully reach acceptance, because no matter how distant and dim hope becomes, it is always there, taunting me, just out of my grasp. There is no demarcation line, etched in stone, no marker to indicate the day my sons were taken from me. My sons are gone, and I must envy those who grieve. Blog here: Walter Singleton
column9: That is heartbreaking. I’m so sorry. Unfortunately I’ve witnessed the other side of the equation too. I help out with my son’s Cub Scout pack that has a lot of boys without active fathers in their lives, too many of them lost to drugs, mental and emotional issues, or just unable to step up and be the kind of daddies their boys need. I’ve also got a grandson (from an adult daughter) whose daddy isn’t a part of his life because he loves himself and his drugs more than his son. Despite that I would never badmouth him in front of my grandson because I don’t want to eliminate the possibility, however remote, that he may change and become an active part of his son’s life someday. In my book there are few sins worse than to alienate a child from a parent just because the adults can’t get along. I am so thankful to this day that my parents never did this to us when they divorced, and that to this day all sides of the family can get together without acrimony. I hope sincerely that your sons will grow to see the truth someday and decide to be a part of your life again.

column1: Are there different stages in the grief of a relative dying? My mum has not stopped crying and I feel like a sociopath as I haven't cried once yet all the rest of my family are getting emotional.
column3: Yes, there are different stages of grief, and for some, grief is delayed so the first thing those people may feel is nothing or numbness. This numb stage enables people to take care of various things that need to be done and then the emotional feelings come later when there is less to attend to. Feelings of grief may show themselves as anger, rather than sadness, even misplaced anger against other family members. This is one reason there end up being so many nasty fights in families after a loved one has died. So do not be hard on yourself about this issue. Each one grieves in their own time and in their own way. But if you begin to see family members attacking others, don´t judge those people too hard. Many people feel much anger and don´t even realize it is coming out of grief. People also can get extremely egocentric while grieving. So if you see a usually generous family member who suddenly wants everything for themself, this does not mean that is actually their real personality finally coming out. People need to set kind limits on these kinds of nasty behaviors that often creep up in families after important deaths, but by calling them by their true name of grieving. For example, somebody could say, “We are not really fighting about possessions right now. People feel angry out of grief. So maybe we need some outside help such as a grief counselor to help us do this right now.” (to save horrible family fights that may take years to heal between some individuals.) May life be gentle to you and your loved ones while you are adjusting to your recent loss.

column1: Should I continue to sleep with my dead dog? I can't let him go. I am devastated.
column3: I am sorry to read that you lost your dog. I’ve had to hurt too, so many times. For mine, in order to help me let go and remember them fondly, I’ve buried them on my farm and planted a red bud above their heads. Each spring that tree bursts out in purple flowers that pollinators LOVE, shortly after the flowers do their thing, the heart shaped leaves erupt. Those hearts remind me of all the love I shared with those pets. I don’t want to sell the farm to move back to my hometown, I don’t want someone cutting down those trees, so I understand your difficulties in letting go. As a veterinarian, there are a few things about handling a deceased pet I need to share with you. First as a pet’s lifeless body lies there, it will decrease in temperature. This temperature drop with tell the fleas and ticks that it is time to find a new host. Their buffet boat is sinking and they need a new one. If you are near by, you will be the next host. Next, the smooth muscles controlling sphincter tone will lose their ability to contract. Your pet’s body will leak urine, feces & ingestia. Much of that material will be full of bacteria, enzymes and material In various stages of digestion and decay. After a period of time the bacteria Inside the pet’s deceased body will begin to produce gas, fermenting and expanding your pet’s alimentary system, it’s intestines will eventually rupture internally and those bacteria will continue to destroy tissue. This is very natural way to return a lifeless body back to the circle of life, creating nutrients for other smaller beings that clean up the earth & thus create nutrients that are used by plants & fungi, feeding larger animals and keeping this living cycle of all earth’s organisms going. It’s natural, but it doesn’t smell good and it will make your pet not look it’s best. It will also expose you to very dangerous bacteria like E. coli, salmonella and many others. As far as your options that allow you to let go of your pet’s physical body & cling to only the love, memories and companionship you shared, you have many. Cremation with ashes returned in an urn or box of your choosing, a clay foot-print, a locket of hair, keeping its collar on a toy animal that somewhat looks like your pet, you can bury and plant a special plant over it, writing a thank you / friendship letter to your pet, reading it to your friend as you let it go, either keeping the letter or placing it with the pet or it’s bedding that you bury/take to cremation with it. You can do so many things, but keeping its lifeless body isn’t a good idea. We all feel the pain and heart ache of loss, you NEVER stop loving them, they just don’t get lives as long as ours, saying goodbye is difficult. Their life essence is gone, their body is an empty vessel, their spirit has moved on. I believe in my heart that if the pets knew we’d be SO SAD when they were gone, they’d choose to avoid us to prevent us from hurting. I also believe that when your pet passes on, there is another very desperate animal that could really use your love and attention, one needing a good home. But you have to open your heart and home to a new pet and that means letting go of the one you’ve already loved for so long. Grief is rough on us all. THERE ARE PLACES TO CALL for free grief counseling, hospice/ hospera/ hosperus, these places help with grief counseling, they know who can help you deal or cope. Call a friend, a family member, your regular veterinarian, the local shelter. They may be able to help. Be aware that the shelter or the veterinarian may have an animal in their care that needs a temporary home, it may be sad for losing its own Owner or just need help getting through a rough spot too. Sometimes taking in an animal that needs help is therapeutic. It never replaces the pet you lost, but it helps you both have a heart to hold next to yours while you mourn, grieve, heal and move forward. If you are concerned that there is a deeper issue as to why you cannot let go, please reach out to a qualified therapist or counselor. The loss of a pet is a REAL, PAINFUL, EMOTIONAL, HEART BREAKING & GUT WRENCHING, MISERABLE, NO FUN, horrible event. It’s going to happen if we own pets. Parrots and tortoise outlive humans, but cats and dogs have shorter life spans. As a veterinarian, I KNOW that no matter how long you know a pet that you love, you NEVER stop loving it. I cry to this day about my dog Benji that died when I was 4, Freckles, Hairy, Maddie, Addison, Maggie, Othello, Lexi, Bugsy, Allie, Gator, Will, Tucky, Cleopatra, Pandora, Kafka, Cisco, Ebert, Nettie, Penny, Laverne, Mirage, Pigpen, Yellow Dog, Bitty… and unfortunately, the list goes on and on… cows, horses, ferrets, goats, sheep… dogs & cats, even fish and snakes…. yep. I loved and still them. I’ve had animals all my 50 years… it NEVER gets easier losing them, but the chance to love them makes it all worth while. Honor your pet by thanking it for being your best friend, confidant, companion, thank it for the love it CHOSE to give you, remember how much joy you felt… take your time to grieve, but seriously think about helping teach another animal how to love when it feels all is lost. Unfortunately, the COVID-19 pandemic has made it where many of us veterinarians have taken in the pets of older clients we lost. It’s been devastating. But the animals need homes to take them in instead of going to a scary shelter when all they’ve known is the love of their owner. One thing is for certain, you must let the physical body of your beloved friend go. It will become a health risk if you hang onto it for more than a few hours. There ARE people that can help if you need help. I know that you have internet access, you may readily search groups/organizations in your area that can help. All you have to do is reach out. Best wishes, good luck and sorry again about your loss. It’s not any fun at all. I’ve been there more times than I wish to recall. It’s traumatic each time. Please allow someone to help you with your options. Give your friend one last thank you from me, for being there for you. I’m positive your friend would want you to find a new friend to help out or maybe even adopt as a full time pet! Hope that information helps you heal. The hardest part of loving them is letting them go. Unfortunately, it’s what we have to do on occasion. It’s part of the circle of life and pets make our lives better. I’m sure some other pet need your help when you’re ready to help them. Until then, please contact a grief counselor, your veterinarian or a therapist to help you get through. Best wishes.
column9: A very kind compassionate answer. I agree that letting go is very hard, but I’d add that the longer we delay burying our beloved pet means the longer our lasting memory is of the dead dog, rather than the living one. Once your pet’s spirit has left its body, the remains are no longer the dog, just the body it occupied while it was alive. Beloved as that body is, it isn’t your dog any more. Hold onto the happy memories, rather than the empty shell of your dog, and let him go. He’s with you in your heart and will stay safely there so long as you live.

column1: Does a person with no belief in God reach for God when in desperate need?
column3: No. Heart attack in 2013, barely survived the night. 24 hours later I'm walking in a ward full of men who look like they're never going to wake up again surrounded by crying families and all I could think of was how lucky I was. And to be thankful that I was in the right place at the right time to survive what happened. But my thankfulness was not directed at anything. 3 weeks ago I was told that I have metastatic, malignant lung cancer, stage 4 it appeared as pneumonia and they drain 3 l of what look like beer out of my plural cavity. A week later the diagnosis came in and the fluid had switched to black. That was February 11th. 3 days ago they drained another 3 l and it has blood in it. I've seen this before, I've watched people go through this and I know the next part is going to see chunks of meat coming out of those. Because of the nature of the cancer as an Ros one mutation they might be able to halt it for a while and give me more time than if it was run of the mill cancer. I have no desire to embrace religion, only my children. And in fact I do not wish to embrace a belief that makes my demise okay. I'm not going to rage against the dying of the light but I'm going to Revel in the time I got left because once it's gone it's gone. You can follow me for as long as I can post and see if I give in. It isn't pride, it isn't refusal to believe it's just whatever compels you to be religious is something that I have never understood or felt. There will be no bargaining, no pleading, because life is not fair, grief does not have to be distributed according to some plan. And that belief that somehow there was a plan to this I believe is where the anger and the pleading and the resentment comes from. But I have never thought that life was fair, and why is this happening to me after losing all six of my family members to cancer? Why not? S*** happens
column9: I admire your attitude and resolve. I was a believer, then a doubter, now an atheist. I honestly felt true relief when I realized I really did not believe in an afterlife. All religion ever did for me was make me anxious, no comfort whatsoever. There is a peace in accepting reality that I think believers do not understand. You have my respect, sympathy, and best wishes - may your journey be as painless as possible.

column1: How do you help a child who has lost a parent?
column3: When a child loses a parent, he or she goes through the same stages of grief that an adult goes through: shock and numbness, grief and depression, an emotional distancing from the loss and finally adapting to the loss. Although the stages are the same in children as in adults, children often display their feelings differently. Children may react with denial, anger toward the deceased parent, or guilt. Kids under age three don't understand the finality of death but they do feel the loss. Toddlers may actually be more affected by changes in routine than by the loss of the parent. When a parent dies, children need reassurance and lots of attention and affection. They may fear the loss of other family members. Sticking to their routines and schedules as much as possible will help them feel secure. So will enforcing rules. Sometimes adults make the mistake of being lax with rules when children are in a difficult situation, but this is actually unsettling for them. Keep an eye out for depression in children who have lost a parent. Signs may include the development of minor illnesses like intestinal upsets or colds, playing less, or becoming clingy and dependent. These children need to feel secure and to feel they have a safe place to go to talk about their fears with someone who is open to discussing this subject with them.

column1: How did you deal with the death of your parents?
column3: Know that you are not alone. I know how you feel. I have already lost both parents by my 30s and miss them dearly. Nothing can prepare anyone for the loss of a parent, and each person’s journey with grief is unique. However, I talk publicly about grief and have some advice based on my own experience that I hope can help.What To Do If You’ve Lost a Parent: First Days Aid:Allow yourself to feel whatever you feel. Be it sadness, relief, guilt, or regret. Whatever. You have permission to feel. Embrace it. Let the emotions come rolling in. Roll with it. Don’t feel guilty if you don’t feel sadness yet. Shock and numbness are common first reactions. When my dad took his last breath, I was numb. Robotic. Empty. I could not process what had just happened.Let yourself cry when the reality hits. It will feel like a bad dream. When you wake up, allow yourself to feel the sorrow. The night I lost my mom to cancer, I was scared to go to sleep and wake up to a new reality without her. But I had to. The tears came like waterfalls the next morning.Notify your closest circle of loved ones. They will become your support system. Your care team. However, don’t make any social plans if you don’t feel like it. You’ll need a few days to process what just happened and be with your family and a select few.Take turns being strong for each other in the family. Now more than ever you need each other. Be there to comfort your widowed parent. They might seem to be doing ok, but underneath the facade they may be crumbling. My mom revealed to us years later after my dad passed that she suffered from depression. We had no idea. I wish I had known. Your siblings need your support too. And you need them. My brother became my rock during our time of grief and I would text him at all hours of the night. Like clockwork, he would be there to comfort me.Divide urgent tasks amongst family members. This includes calling the funeral home and notifying relatives. It can be too much for one person to handle physically, mentally or emotionally so share tasks.First Week Aid:Treat yourself. Do some of your favorite things. Eat. Go for a hike. Your mom or dad would’ve wanted you to be happy. Don’t let one thing wash over everything. This means that you are allowed to have happy moments even amongst the sad ones. Don’t feel guilty abut indulging. Let your friends cheer you up! Within the first week that my dad passed, a bunch of my closest friends came over with large bags of Flaming Hot Cheetos. My favorite snack — yummm! I couldn’t stop eating them.Prepare for the funeral. Yes, it will be sad and difficult. But it’s also a time to remember the life of an amazing human. Write down what you might say at the funeral and gather photos to share. It might even bring your family joy as you look through old photo albums and tell stories. Also if your family wants to incorporate something non-traditional at the funeral, — DO IT. Forget about the norms. Do it their way. We played a video of my mom’s last opera performance at the funeral. Italian opera at the mortuary — Mama would’ve approved.Let your wider social circle know. Maybe this means you or a close friend sends an email out. Or maybe you want to post on social media about your loss. Different people have different styles, so do what is comfortable for you. I found it incredibly therapeutic to post on social media about my loss. The support was overwhelming and people who I hadn’t heard from in years reached out to share their personal experience or heartfelt empathy. Some told me they felt they knew my mom through my posts and cried with me when she died.Remind yourself that they live on in you. You are their legacy. They may have left this earth but they live on in your genes. They live on in the way they raised you. They will continue to see the world through your eyes. It’s a beautiful realization to know that they are still very much with you and within you. After we lost our mom, my brother and I trekked the Annapurna Circuit in Nepal in her honor. When we finally reached the highest mountain pass, we knew that she was right there with us, seeing the majesty of the Himalayas through our eyes.First Month Aid:Accept that life has a new normal now. You will desperately want the power to go backwards in time. You can’t. You will think about “the way things used to be” when they were alive. You just lost a central pillar in your life. It’s natural. Adjusting will take much longer. However, now’s the time to recalibrate and accept a new normal. I coped by telling myself that I had to start a new chapter. I see life as a book. My parents were in many chapters but there’s still much left in the book. They will continue to remain in my heart as I turn the page.Know that it’s normal to self-isolate or feel bitter. You might just want to be by yourself. Grief can be a lonely experience as each individual’s pain is unique. As an extrovert, it felt weird for me to not want to talk to people, but hey that was my new normal at the time. I felt sometimes like I was on an island of my own, as no one could possibly understand how I felt (I thought). Other people’s social media posts became too much for me. How could someone post on Facebook about Kim Kardashian’s outfit?! Didn’t they know that I just lost the most important person in my life?!!! Who caaaares about celebrities? Lalala…island of my own.Do NOT compare the death of your parent to another death. This is a futile exercise. Death does not choose. There is no one “fairer” death than another. My mom died at the age of 68 which is so young, yet my grandma at 93. When it’s time to go it’s time to go. Also, some of us got the chance to say goodbye to our parent with terminal illness and some of us didn’t in a sudden accident. Each loss is different. Don’t compare them.Understand that grief is non-linear. You may have heard of the Five Stages of Grief. Some days you will feel totally fine, happy even. You might be out on a bright sunny day laughing with friends and then BAM! It hits you and knocks you to the floor. Sit with it for a moment. Breathe. Know that the sudden force of grief will pass. But know that it will also come back, maybe when a familiar scent fills the room so be ready for it. Triggers are everywhere but that means treasured memories are too.Find routine again. Do whatever you have to do to find a sense of normalcy again. If work makes you feel good, then work. It can give you a sense of purpose and a healthy distraction. After I lost my mom, I went back to my client work the next week. I wrote an email to my colleagues at a biotech company and reminded them that the work that we did mattered. We made cancer medicines. Medicine that could’ve saved my mom and so many others.Honor your parent’s life. Think of it as the celebration of a life rather than the mourning of a loss. Since we had a private funeral reserved for family only, my brother and I wanted to do something for my mom’s friends and our friends too. A month after my mom’s passing, we honored her life by renting out an entire gallery to exhibit her art. Over 100 people came to celebrate her extraordinary life. You can view our exhibition “Extraordinary Human” here.Read about the grief of others. You will know that you are not alone. My book recommendations are: “Option B” by Sheryl Sandberg & Adam Grant (which has a very active online community), “Wild” by Cheryl Strayed (or her articles online about grief), and “The Year of Magical Thinking” by Joan Didion.Big hugs and condolences. <3 Be kind to yourself and know that it just takes time. The above was taken from an article I had written to help others with grief. You can read the full article here: First Aid For Someone Who Has Lost a Parent – Jenn M Choi – Medium.

I was fearful of confiding in them for fear of up setting my grandfather. All could do was imagine my father would come home one day. They found his grave 74 years after my birth. The emotion that spilled out as i stood by his grave was like a tidal wave. Thank you.

column1: Is it normal for a child to have no reaction to death? My son is five years old, and when someone passes away (like a pet or family), he doesn’t have a reaction to the information. He just says "oh okay" and moves on.
column3: OP here with a little more information My parents died when he was a little over two. We have lost at least a dozen family members since then (most in the same year). He is no stranger to death and seems to understand that someone dying means they aren't here anymore. When we had to put down one of our dogs a couple of years ago, he cried and mourned. He said “Missy is dead like your parents". Recently my brother in law's cat, whom my son has known since he was a baby, died suddenly from health complications. My son had no response to this. I told him what happened and he said “oh okay" like it didn't bother him and moved onto the next topic of the day. I know children handle grief and death differently because they do not know what is going on. I'm just a little confused by his lack of reaction to the concept of people or pets dying. I don't know if he skips right to the acceptance stage of grief because he's so used to it, or if it might be something more?
column9: It sounds from that though as if he understood it when it was the dog being put down and was upset. I imagine that the dog meant more to him than the cat. When your parents died he likely didn’t understand what it meant, and by the time he did understand it, he may have had insufficient memory of them for it to be greatly upsetting. He may not really know who most of the rest of the dozen were. You also don’t see what’s going on inside his head. My favourite great aunt (who lived nearby) died when I was four and I really missed her, but that likely wasn’t visible from the outside - for some reason it didn’t trigger any real upset in me: just sadness and disappointment. She was old and was a smoker, so it didn’t come as a great shock as it was too predictable. It was similar when my grandmother died, and I knew she was terminally ill - I likely showed no sign of upset again at home, but it did hit me out of the blue at school the next day, which is the very place you don’t want to burst into tears. You aren’t necessarily going to see a child’s biggest response to something of that kind even if there is grief there - it would be easy enough to miss it.

column1: What kind of support can someone who has lost their mother expect from a therapist?
column3: This is going to depend on the needs of this client. Anyone at any age or stage of life can lose their mother. When a parent dies, grief is normal but so much depends on the type of relationship this parent and child had, their personal resources, prior losses in the person’s life, other family members, social factors and so many other individual possibilities!
column9: My mother raised me respectfully, she made my roots happy, when I left home at 16, we became detached and were never the same again, when she died, I failed to grieve and still haven’t.

column1: Is global warming skepticism in its death throes?
column3: “The 5 stages of grief and loss are: 1. Denial and isolation; 2. Anger; 3. Bargaining; 4. Depression; 5. Acceptance. People who are grieving do not necessarily go through the stages in the same order or experience all of them.” from The 5 Stages of Grief & Loss “Acceptance” in this model is a short-hand for dealing with the new reality you live in, for doing the grieving and moving forward … for doing the grieving rather than avoiding the grieving, so you can move on. This is how humans generally deal with a loss, sometimes with a religious leader or therapist guiding us forward through the steps. When a family member dies, “denial” is often the first step … not because we don’t believe they died, but because we are in psychological denial. The scientific debate has been absurd for a while. I think with global warming we have many, many millions of dollars going into anti-therapy trying to keep us stuck on a step. On Quora, I’ve been seeing a lot of people jumping to “depression.” Scientists — those people so few people actually listen to, despite summary reports being on the same web you’re reading now — have not quite been saying the world is going to end. Massive extinctions, a few generations where hunger might come back, where many extra famines like the ones that led to catastrophe and refugees in Syria and Central America are very likely, wars that otherwise wouldn’t happen. That’s not the end of the world — that sounds a lot like adding all the problems of the twentieth century to the 21st just because we couldn’t cut back a bit on pollution, but it doesn’t mean that people with time to kill on Quora will definitely all die, no one responsible is saying that, but there’s a spasm of depression going around Quora that wasn’t there before. There’s also a lot of “bargaining” happening as people grasp at ways to bring carbon out of the atmosphere or geo-engineer — there are some ideas for this that are serious, over the long term, and a lot of work, but given how bad climate change is going to be they may be helpful anyway … that’s not what I mean. I mean a lot of people who haven’t reached the “acceptance” stage of opening a magazine written by scientists to see what is actually going on are jumping at any crazy idea about geo-engineering, without really looking. As we face the early smaller impacts of climate change, I expect we will be all over the map on stages of grief. Denial will likely move often to isolation (not wanting to deal, rather than arguing with something right in front of our faces), anger (I have some of that), bargaining, depression (I expect as we see the future we’ve made for ourselves, unless we change — next time there is a famine that causes a crisis that causes refugees like Syria or Central America, do we let them in? — if we keep putting climate refugees in cages on our border we will face a darkness) → and there are people already getting to work if you want to join them, have been for a while.

column1: How can I overcome the fact that one of my beloved young family members is no more?
column3: My father killed himself when he was just 27 years old. At the time of his death I was 4 years old, but this year I will be turning 27. As a four-year-old it is difficult to see your father as a young man or to grieve a life not yet fully lived, but every year since I turned twenty I have felt time creeping up on me more quickly. What seemed at four-years-old to be a long life, now seems shockingly brief. I don’t believe there is one answer or solution for overcoming the death of a loved one at any age, but from my experience as someone who has both spent time grieving such a loss and also someone who works with the bereaved I can offer you a few small things that I have found to be helpful.Name the loss. If the grief you are experiencing is due to death, say that rather than using euphemisms. Using the word “loss” or others like it can be trivializing or confusing to your brain. When speaking to children, using the words “death” and “died” is especially important due to the concrete nature of their developmental stage.Grieve now. Often people try and push away their feelings of grief to deal with at a later date when it might be easier. Grief is not easy and waiting does not make the process faster or easier. Allow yourself to feel and accept that sadness is not the only feeling that may come up. It is not uncommon for the bereaved to experience anger, confusion, anxiety, or any number of other feelings.Ask for support. Death is universal! There are so many resources out there to support the bereaved. While there are many different ways to experience and cope with grief, there are also many different organizations set up in many different ways to help. If at first you don’t succeed, look again! It is likely that there is support out there that will work for you.One of the most important ways to support yourself in moving through the death of a loved one, is allowing yourself time. There is no right or wrong way to grieve and the process is not linear. Please know that while the hurt may never fully go away, the feelings will change over time and with some work, you can develop the skills to cope with them.

column1: What should I do if my boyfriend's grandfather just died, and he won't let me comfort him?
column3: Unfortunately I have far too much experience with death, funerals and grieve but that means I might be able to offer you some advice. Although everyone does go through the 5 stages of grief, we all go through those stages differently and we can go through one or more of those stages more than one time. If your boyfriend won’t let you comfort him, then for right now do not comfort him. The next time you talk to him, say to him something like “I am not going to bring this up again after today because I know you don’t want to talk about it right now. I just want you to know that if there comes a time you want to talk I am here for you. If you want to scream I will scream with you or just stand back and let you go, if you want to cry I will cry with you or just hold you while you cry, if you want to tell me everything you have ever done with him I am here to listen and if you want to just sit in a dark room in silence I will sit with you. I know there is nothing I can say that will make this better and everyone works through their grief in their own way and I just want you to know that I am here and I care (or I love you) and I will continue to be here with you and for you in any way you need. Then give him a few, literally a very few, seconds to take that all in and if he says “ok” or “thank you” or even says nothing at all that is alright. Because you already told him you aren’t going to talk about this anymore so you aren’t. What you are going to do next is this: Ask him if he wants to play a video game, go play pool, go do anything you know HE is interested in. Be the person who listens to what ever he says and be the one he can be with and not focus on his grandfather. Right now every family member, friend and acquaintance is telling him, when ever they see him, how sorry they are, asking how he is doing, how his parents are doing etc etc? Be the one person in his life that does not make him think his entire world revolves around the death of his grandfather. If you want to support your boyfriend through this very difficult time in his life, you have to listen to what his wants and needs are right now. Let him grieve the way he needs to and just be there for him any way he wants you to. If there comes a time he wants to talk to you about this, he will start the conversation with you and not you with him. Just remember that time may not come, but that too is ok and has nothing to do with you at all.

column1: I don't feel sad when a close family member, let's say my grandmother, dies. I do care but I cannot cry or feel sad. How do I pretend to grieve and cry to not look heartless to my family?
column3: Grief is a very confusing emotion. It isn't the same thing as sadness or depression and it isn't the same thing as anger or longing. It is a very unique experience. There is no need to pretend to feel something. Some people cry at funerals, some people do not. However you feel is completely fine. I do not often feel sad at funerals even if it's someone very close. But down the line I start to feel the different stages of grief in my own way. No one is expecting you to behave in a certain way, other than not to be socially disruptive with crass jokes or screaming, or anything down those lines, needless to say. Just be respectful and your genuine self. The feelings and emotions may or may not come later. That's totally normal.

column1: How do you personally deal with grief?
column3: I went through a very long, hard grief. And I'm dealing with another type of grief today. When my sister was killed 17 years ago, less than two months after my wedding where she was Maid of Honor, I nearly died myself. It took me days for it to really sink in. That first year was hell. I don't wish that on anyone. Nightmares. Anger. Stress. Deep depression. I quit taking care of myself and seemed to live in a daze. I despised anyone who's siblings were still alive and they could hangout with them, call them, feel their embrace, and hear their laughter. About two years after her passing, I reached out to a nonprofit that works with people like me. For another year. l attended vigils, listened to others speak about their loss, made fiends with those who's siblings we're killed too. I started speaking, volunteering, talking to members of the community and government to get help changing laws to help prevent what happened to her, our family, ever again. Today, I work for that nonprofit. I've spoken to over 120,000 people. Got two laws passed, Now, I'm on the board to create education material to be used for kids, so they don't feel alone if it happens to them. Is my grief gone? No. Have I forgotten abouther, what happened to her? Absolutely not. I give myself grace when I have a bad day. I reach out to my trusted friends or make an appointment with my counselor if I need to. I've learned to live life without her. Somedays are easy. Other days I feel like I'm walking through quicksand. Right now, I'm going through another type of grief. Grief that 10's of thousands deal with everyday. My partner told me over the summer they no longer love me. They don't want to be married to me anymore. Wait, they “love" me, they're just no longer " in love” with me. To say I was blind sided is not even close to how I feel. Months later, I've gone through all the steps of grief. But just like with the loss of my sister, going through the stages of grief isn't linear. It's a good day, moving forward. Followed by going back with a leap. I will never "get over it". But, I will do what I can, no matter how much it sucks, to live with it. Try my damnedest to be happy, focus on me and my kids, and continue moving forward.

column1: My cat recently went to the vet to get her eye inoculated. While doing so they shaved her whiskers. Is it bad that I am mad at the vet for doing this?
column3: You’ve probably heard the saying that feelings are neither bad nor good, it’s how you deal with them that matters. You and your cat have gone through a trauma. This will cause feelings of loss, possibly feelings of guilt on your part for being the one to have had to take kitty to get this done even though it had to be done, and maybe other feelings. That’s okay. Our pets are like family, so when big things happen to them, we grieve about it the same way we would grieve if it happened to a human family member. (Some people get angry at the doctor who diagnosed the cancer. That sort of thing.) Is it possible your anger is just a stage of grief? Or a deflection of other uncomfortable emotions surrounding the event which you aren’t ready to look at yet? When my kitty was dying from kidney failure and I knew I needed to let her go, I thought I was ready. She was ready. But the day I took her in to the vet, I got angry at the vet and made insulting comments about her to her staff on my way out. Later I recognized it for what it was. I wasn’t ready to start the tears. I loved that cat so much. So let yourself work through the feelings, recognizing that the procedure was necessary, the vet did the best job possible to help your kitty, you did what could be done to help your kitty, and you are going to be a loving cat parent who will help kitty heal and recover. And those whiskers will grow back♥

column1: For Buddhists, how does the concept of "attachment" apply to the closest people in your life?
column3: Buddhists try to move through to the end stage of grief, which is acceptance, and not get hung up in the middle more than necessary. Arguing with or resistance to external or internal reality is unskillful. As Katherine Rand said "be with it". Frequently the event is over quickly and the echos in our being are what really need examination and observation. Which isn't to say it get's easy. Kübler-Ross model The stages, popularly known by the acronym DABDA, include:[2] Denial — "I feel fine."; "This can't be happening, not to me." Denial is usually only a temporary defense for the individual. This feeling is generally replaced with heightened awareness of possessions and individuals that will be left behind after death. Denial can be conscious or unconscious refusal to accept facts, information, or the reality of the situation. Denial is a defense mechanism and some people can become locked in this stage. Kubler Ross recommends that family members and health professionals not prolong denial by distorting the truth about the person's condition. [3]Anger — "Why me? It's not fair!"; "How can this happen to me?"; '"Who is to blame?" Once in the second stage, the individual recognizes that denial cannot continue. Because of anger, the person is very difficult to care for due to misplaced feelings of rage and envy. Anger can manifest itself in different ways. People can be angry with themselves, or with others, and especially those who are close to them. It is important to remain detached and nonjudgmental when dealing with a person experiencing anger from grief.Bargaining — "I'll do anything for a few more years."; "I will give my life savings if..." column1: Adult Do the five stages of grief always hold true?
column3: GoI am not sure this helps, but I will try. I lost my husband of 5 yrs. When he was only 23 and we had 3 very young children. Our daughter was only 5 months old. 0ur youngest son was 3 and our oldest was about 4 1/2. I was beyond devastated, but I had 3 children that needed me as much as I needed them. I was young, my husband was young; however my children and I had so much love and support from our family members it took an extraordinary amount of effort for me to get out there and get going again to do what I had to do. I didn't really get the underlying idea of grief during that first year. Then another tragedy struck, beyond my wildest fears. My daughter at 11 months old was severely anemic and had to be hospitalized for shots everyday in her belly. She pulled herself up in her crib and the side came down, she fell out. She got a subdural hematoma on the right side of her brain. The doctors said it would dissolve itself and go away as it was only under the first layer of skin. After a few days as scheduled and her shots were done, she seemed ok so they discharged her and sent her home. The put her on phenobarbital to take in cause she had any small tremors from the fall. That Saturday as I had laid her down on the couch to dress her after she'd had breakfast she had a grandmal seizure that actually thew her little body off the couch. I ran next door to my neighbor who was a paramedic and fire man. I knew he was home that morning. He put his emergency light on top of the car and got Becky and my self in.His wife had my boys with her.When we got to the hospital he ran back in to the ER with her. I tried to go to but they kept stopping me. It was long when they came out and they told me she died. I don't know how I managed to continue on other than for my boys. I covered up myself, my feeling, my everything! My parents were overwrought losing her. They couldn't even attend her funeral. I barely remember it. And for that I am thankful. That was in 1975. My dad was my rock and besides that I was a daddy's girl. He passed away in 1984 but we knew he was dying and him and I were okay we had talked about it all. Yes I grieved, but I wasn't destroyed by it. Then in 1995 I was living in Florida and my oldest son was too, along with his baby daughter and his wife. My first born grand daughter, Savanah. We had been there for a few years by now and we loved it there. My son worked at the Space Center and he wife worked at the famous Dixie Crossed Roads. Everything was Great! My youngest son Rodney lived in Ohio and he stayed with my mother after my father had passed. He didn't care for Florida. He had come to Florida several times and had even gotten a very good job on one of his visits. Eventually he just decided that it wasn't where he wanted to be, so he went back home. Christmas wasn't far away my oldest Roger was going home to visit to see everyone. Early on the morning of 12-13-95 the phone rang I knew then it wasn't good news but not the news I got. It was my brother calling to tell me he had let me sleep as long as he could and that my son had died late last night or in the early morning hours in a car accident less than a mile from home. This was where we had grown up at out in the country on a back road. He was only 23. HIS DEATH CHANGED MY LIFE FOREVER! I will never be the same and neither will my surviving son. A person can only survive so much without it changing them. Grief and sorrow comes in all shapes and sizes. It comes upon you in waves the loneliness, the remembrance, the anger, the why. My husband's death is an ache in me that will never go away! Losing my beautiful children WHY? I know people say don't ask that question well to hell with those people because I still do!! 23 years this Christmas since my son died and I still can't celebrate the holiday. It was his favorite. I use to make it a point right after he passed that I had to come back home every year at XMAS to visit all the graves and decorate. Suddenly after several years. I just completely stopped. I ended up losing an entire year of my life. I lost all conscience memory and didn't even know how old I was. I was in a psychiatric hospital for awhile, but I had to be. So I wish you the very best and I will pray for you in all you do. Let go and let God.

column1: What 3 films do you think best portray the experience of grieving?
column3: Three big ones come to mind right away:Terms of Endearment - Probably one of the best because it covers the grieving from several family members and friends when the character played by Debra Winger dies of cancer.The Lovely Bones - The premise for this movie is all about loss, grieving, and frustration from start to finish. The killer of Susie Salmon gets his just desserts in the end, but no one in the family ever finds out the truth, which is the most difficult part of the story for audiences.UP - Believe it or not, this Pixar-animated movie isn’t really about a kid and an old man who go ballooning for a rare bird. It is about the loss of a wife the old man loved for decades, and how he eventually finds a way to cope with his loss. This is a main fixture of the film, and the movie itself is a tear jerker in parts.Honorable Mention:Love Story - This one with Ryan O’Neal and Ali MacGraw started the whole ‘my husband/wife is dying’ genre. It does a reasonably good job of portraying grieving, but it was a first effort, after all. After Love Story, the genre got better.Rabbit Hole - How do parents deal with the loss of a child? Nicole Kidman and Aaron Eckhart show the stages of grief very well in this one after they lose their four-year-old son to a car accident. The down side is that the movie was made on a modest budget of three million dollars and barely reached five million at the box office. It was probably TOO much grief for moviegoers.Ordinary People - Although it is a bit dated these days, this one about grief and relationships didn’t win all those Oscars for nothing. (Six nominations, four wins.) Directed by Robert Redford, maybe it SHOULD be in the top three.
column9: Wonderful answers that cover well the spectrum of grief. Thank you.

column1: Adult Which of the seven stages of grief do people get stuck on the longest?
column3: One of the biggest and most painful mistakes about grieving is actually believing that there are five or seven stages of grief. The five stages of grief, as created by Elizabeth Kubler-Ross, were not to help people going through the process of grieving the loss of a loved one. It was actually created to help people with the dying process itself. The detrimental aspect of using the five stages of grief as a yardstick is because it can create the belief that we're somehow doing grief wrong. We aren't!! Yes, one could argue that they could apply to grieving and one could equally argue that we bounce back and forth between different stages. Personally, I think it's harmful and painful to assign names to the different stages of grieving because it equally implies that a scale like that can accurately define what we're going through at the moment. Believe me, I get it. After my husband died by suicide 7 years ago, I clung to anything to help me understand what it was I was going through and, equally, how to get myself out of it. The reality of loss is that it's painful and affects us on so many levels that we just never expected. If it does give you comfort to use the stages, then by all means do whatever brings you comfort!! But never, never believe that you're grieving wrong by using a somewhat arbitrary list. Pain is pain. And it will be painful until it's not. Time is the great equalizer. I believe that I had one of the worst experiences following my husband's death because not only did I come home to find him hanging in our garage, but it didn't take very long before every member of his family turned on me. I was asked not to attend his cremation service because I wasn't “close family". They were brutal and cruel. Aside from dealing with his sudden and violent death, I was also dealing with the betrayal of his entire family. I still can't believe that people could be so vicious. I can tell you based on my own experience that the first year is the worst. Don't make the mistake that I did and believe that when the clock strikes midnight on the end of year one, and the beginning of year two, that everything would be better. It wasn't. But as time passed, and I gradually began to see that the life I had before he died was gone and never to return, I began to settle in to my new life. It may seem like like a completely foreign idea, but nature is kind, meaning that the wisdom of our body actually does protect us during times of unbearable stress and pain in the form of brain fog, to name one. You may feel like your brain is trying to slog through mud but it's actually a way to prevent all the pain and grief from completely overtaking you. Gradually, the shock and grief will begin to subside, and the new you will emerge, kind of like a snake shedding its skin. Hang in there, dear one. You can do this. I made it through intact and actually became a far better human because of it. I became a deeper, more self-aware, kinder person. My husband's death changed me so radically and entirely for the better. I wouldn't wish what I went through on my worst enemy, but in the end, it turned out to be the greatest gift I could ever be given.
