column1: If you were part of a family and you were someone diagnosed with Alzheimer's, what is the correct thing to do?
column3: I don’t think there is one “correct” thing to do, but based on experience with my older relatives, this would be my plan. Actually, I think it is best to activate parts 2–6 of this plan before a diagnosis, maybe by the age of 70 if not before:Tell the family about the diagnosis. Talk about my financial resources.Talk with them about where I will live. I would want to stay at home if it is safe for me to do so, but I would acknowledge that I might not understand when it is no longer safe, and that I trust them to make the next decision. People often say they would want to take in a family member with dementia, but it is an extraordinarily difficult commitment, especially if the person lives into the advanced stages of the illness. I would give them permission NOT to take me in, or to call it quits if it isn’t working. I would encourage consideration of memory care options, maybe even visit a couple of places and describe what I liked about them (while being aware that options may change in the future), and let them know I trust them to do what seems right at the necessary time. Give them permission to put me in a nursing home if/when needed. Legally, they may not need my permission if things are bad enough, but families have a hard time with this decision, so telling them in advance that it is ok will prevent some of the associated grief and pain.Try to find a family member who is willing and able to be my durable power of attorney and medical POA to make decisions and handle financial matters for me when needed. I might be able to have one person fulfill both roles, but if not, the two should be able to work together well.Get my legal and financial affairs in order. See an attorney ASAP, as I would be unable to execute a will if the Alzheimer’s is very advanced. Make sure family knows where my financial accounts are, where I have information regarding life and health insurance, and where my will and other legal documents are kept. (Make sure that any family helping with my care - POA, etc. - is named in the will. Even if my resources end up being exhausted before I die, they will know I wanted to show my appreciation.)For the person who will be the POA, go over my bills and other legal documents on a regular basis so that they will be better prepared to take over when needed.For all of the family, but especially the person who will be my health care POA, make sure to talk with them about medical preferences. For me, those decisions would depend in large part on how advanced the dementia is when the medical problem arises. I would choose not to have extraordinary measures used to keep me alive. Cancer surgery or radiation/chemo might be something I would want in the early stages of dementia if it would alleviate pain, but would not want otherwise (keep in mind that people with advanced dementia often have great difficulty in cooperating with medical procedures - medications or other forms of pain management would be my choice at that point). If I live long enough, Alzheimers can actually be considered a terminal illness, and I would support the use of hospice care at that point.

column1: Do you feel that keeping text messages and voicemails from family members and friends who have passed away is beneficial for mental well-being? If the answer is yes, at what point does it become unhealthy?
column3: Grief is the last stage of love. Love is not supposed to die when the loved one dies. I’m not sure if it’s beneficial, but it’s definitely okay to hang on to those things - or physical objects - for as long as they comfort you.

column1: What is something I can do to help cope with losing a pet? Is there something in memory for my pet? It’s been a year now and I think about him everyday.
column3: Friend, this is completely normal. You lost a loved member of your family. I wish I could say something to help you feel better. You know when we lost Colleen our Irish Setter, I received some important advice from the vet: he said: “John, your extended family and friends will be sympathetic, they understand how much she meant to you. But there's one thing I want you to be ready for. John, you just lost a loving member of your family. You are going to feel it like you would if it was a human family member. That's normal and appropriate. Here's the thing though, your extended family and friends, despite their love and good intentions, can't help but consider this the loss of a pet, don't expect their sympathy to last anywhere near as long as if it was your sister or brother who died.” Yes, this was true, I didn't hold it against any of them, but knowing about it made it much easier for me to deal with. Sometimes it helps folks to learn about the 5 stages of grief that we all go through with terrible losses like this. I suppose it helped me because I felt like knowing whats going on and what to expect was comforting. If you choose, you can just Google it. Here's a few things they typically don't tell you, but might help: All of us go through these stages in the same order, but there is no “proper" timeline. You'll take as long as you need to get through each stage. Yes, its normal for there to be overlap between sequential stages, don't sweat it. You'll get there. I'm sorry for your terrible loss. Wish I could do more.
column9: I think only time will heal I still miss Champ although he departed 26 months ago. If you are young and healthy the love of another pet too will help relieve your pain. However, bare in mind every being has their own personality. All have love to give in return for your love.

column1: I’m a 26 year old man going to be 27 in July and my mom died last November of stage 4 liver cancer, I was very close with her and am still not over this and am very sad about this even 5 months after it happened. How do I cope with this?
column3: Sigh… this is so hard to deal with… I completely understand. My sister, whom I considered my only family member died 3 years ago this upcoming July from stage 4 neuro-pancreatic cancer that was also producing tumors in her liver. It’s incredibly tough. Five months is still a very short period of time since her passing. There are so many stages of grief and losing your Mom who was so close to you while still being relatively young yourself can take a good bit of time to heal and move through. I truly don’t believe that we can ever truly “get over” the loss of our loved ones, but we CAN heal and move through the stages of grief and begin to breathe again, take small baby steps of daily living where every moment isn’t consumed with thinking and mourning them. For me, it took the first 6 months, truly, of lots and lots of tears, which are liquid healing that God gave us for intense emotions when words fall short. If you feel them coming, let them fall, they are there to help to heal you and help to begin to close the wounding in your heart where they once occupied. I’ve found great help and healing in writing in a journal. One thing that I desperately missed was being able to text, call and communicate whenever I wanted or needed to. We lived 3,000 miles away from each other, so this type of communication was daily. I visited her every 3–6 months for about 2–4 weeks to take her to oncology appointments, take care of her house and growing boys. Journal and write your Mom letters, keep her apprised of your daily life, it helps to “park” your words, feelings and emotions. It’s good that you are on here with others who have gone through similar things. But perhaps finding an in person grief counselor or grief counseling group where you can meet up regularly or when you feel up for it can really help too. I believe that we really can help to heal each other by sharing our similar experiences and any tools we might have used to help along the journey. It really is a journey to adopt a new normal, it’s not easy and there are no short cuts to grieving. Just try really hard not to get stuck in any one stage as that can cause a prolonged grieving process. You are so blessed to have had her for as long as you did and her impact upon your life is forever imbedded into your DNA and life as you move forward. Honor her by carrying on and putting one foot in front of the other. Honor her by teaching your eventual wife/partner about her and any future children you may have. They will love on her through your eyes. It really will be okay, I know it doesn’t feel like it right now, but each day will be a little bit easier to cope and move forward. You are stronger than you know.

column1: How do I make my husband forget about his mother who died recently and make him focus on me and work?
column3: Once you have experienced death of a vitally close family member or loved one, you will better understand. There is no timeframe for mourning and grief. To sink oneself into a person or activity to numb the pain is said to “stuff emotions.” This leads to eating disorders, depression, and many other mental health issues. Allow your husband all the time he needs. Ask him to go to grief therapy with or without you. Search Quora for, “what does it feel like when someone you love dies?” Also look for “stages of grief.” I hope this information can help you understand your husbands feelings better. Please know, that there is no timeframe for grieving and the sadness will never go away completely. There is no replacement for a mother or father and losing a parent is one of the hardest losses a person will ever experience in their lifetime.

column1: Adult How does society view grief and mourning, and how does it impact those who are grieving?
column3: I believe grieving has changed significantly in the past fifty years. I have served as a church organist, and fewer families are choosing to have viewings of their loved ones and church services to commemorate their lives. At one time there was a traditional mourning period which was respected by the families and members of the community and those who did not observe it were open to public criticism. I think we have a better understanding of the stages of grief thanks to Elizabeth Kubler-Ross. While she did not speak for the entire population or every individual, her work helped us to be more understanding of ourselves and our attitudes. In general we tend to be more tolerant of people who have lost a younger loved one and respect their choices. When a nursing home resident dies more often the public response was that it was time, or a blessing. We sometimes fail to acknowledge that close family members still feel the loss acutely even though the passing may have been expected and the family may have begun grieving some time ago.

column1: How would you develop Neji's character unlike Kishimoto and make him a top tier Akatsuki level shinobi which he deserves to be?
column3: First of all. Neji shouldnt have died in the war. And most importantly, its disrespectful to have him die the way he did. Neji's character and significance to the whole franchise goes deep. He is the original alpha hyuuga introduced in the series. He was the genius of Team Gai. Neji was a representative of a clan with a dojutsu (byakugan) equally feared as the sharingan.. Not only that, he belonged to a bloodline tracing its roots to otsutsukis. All these elements alone puts him in the higher ranks of his class.Plus. Neji was the first to use the 64 palms, a secret taijutsu of the main hyuga branch, thats passed down from generations to generations. He learned this forbidden taijutsu all by himself, defiant of the clan rules imposed upon him. Whats fascinating about nejis character is his background. As much as everyone thought hyuuga was an honorable family equally feared and respected because of their byakugan and their status as one of the strongest clans all over the shinobi world, neji despised being in that family.. This surprised the audience that the first main opponent for naruto wasnt an arrogant heir from a powerful family, but a disgraced outcast like himself, tied in a clan with a dirty open secret.Neji, unlike naruto, wasnt writing his own destiny. He was trying to escape this destiny forced upon him, albeit subconsciously. He was about to release all that hate upon hinata --the person who directly benefits from his slave status.. The polar opposites of neji and hinata gave a paradox, a black and white that separates two significant order of things.. At this point, everyone now realized that chuunin exams wasnt just a test to know who passes and who fails. There was more meaning to it. And genins are put in a situation where they can kill or be killed. The genins are pawns representing generations of conflict.As much as neji being the first true test for naruto's character development and moral standing, he was also the first opponent to challenge naruto's belief in himself over destiny..After getting defeated by naruto, neji actually gained more from that fight.. Instead of considering himself a loser, he became a believer of naruto's philosophy, that one dictates his own destiny. He found a new direction for himself… he was now a master of his own fate.. (To me, its a pity to have all these elements be disproved in the end, when we realize naruto was truly a child of the prophecy all along, and that he was a reincarnated demigod).If i was to change the whole story of neji, i would change it at the 4th great ninja war. I wouldnt let neji die. Instead, i would have kiba die for naruto. Kiba talked naruto down a lot. They both shared the goal of being hokage too. And it would have been a great redemption for his annoying character to do something positive for naruto at the end of his life. It would also deliver the same heartache if he tells naruto in his dying words “hey buddy, i guess im leaving you the hokage position after all. Please take care of akamaru”I would continue the story from there. Neji would have survived the war, and have Hinata's father sacrifice his life for neji in time of danger. This would have been a good healing for their family feud. It would also be a symbolic end to the tradition of having a branch family member sacrifice their life for the main branch. It would also have been a great time to pass the clan leadership to neji as the new head of the hyuuga.Then if i will add. This moment would have been when nejis forehead mark will be released, ending his slave status… and have hinatas father repay the sacrifices of nejis father, and redeem the discrimination forced upon the side branch for generations. then perhaps the grief of the situation may have neji awaken a new dojutsu evolving from byakugan. (I think its a pity that the byakugan was only seen evolving straight to tenseigan, when it never had a middle stage like the mangekyo sharingan and eternal mangekyo sharingan) fast forward to toneri arc. I wouldve loved to have neji fight toneri being the new clan leader. He and toneri were both branch family members, and having a conversation between them would be great.In the movie, Hamura gave his chakra to hinata. Which is a shame given that hinata is not the fighting type…it would have been great if hamura just gave neji his entire chakra and let neji awaken the Tenseigan himself. And have a tenseigan vs tenseigan battle between toneri and neji. At this point neji would be equal (if not stronger than) naruto and sasuke. I have reasons why i dont like boruto as a character so id rather have himawari be neji's pupil.. And also because she has a byakugan. It would be nice to see himawari be developed by neji as an elite ninja. If himawari learns 64 palms, in conjuction with shadow clone jutsu, she can multiply the palm strikes to how many clones she has. If himawari does 64 palms with 3 clones, she would be the first to ever do a 192 palms…. Or if she does 10 clones, himawari would be the first to do 640 palms! Imagine how savage himawari would be! Or what if 100 shadow clones? Overkill. I would also love to see neji train himawari to be a battlefield ninja. If she summons 100 shadow clones, while simultaneously using byakugan to surveilance an entire battlefield, himawari would be the best tracker of all.. And if she learns flying raijin, she basically becomes the battlefield god. I would also love to see neji fight s-class shinobis with dojutsu and taijutsu. It wouldve been nice to see sasuke vs neji, and rock lee vs neji during chunin exams.. Or neji fight akatsuki members.. Sadly weve been deprived of those moments. The sad part about nejis character was that he was right all along. And that he had been trapped and chained in something he couldnt overcome. And that in time when destiny calls upon you, you present yourself by embracing death with open arms, happily serving your purpose as a slave. The only choice you are given is how you choose to accept or feel that moment.
column9: I totally agree with you. Neji didn’t deserve to die, he had so so much potential and his character development would’ve been awesome too see.

column1: I moved on from the guy I loved, and now we're very good friends. I am also dating someone else. But now he's about to get married. I am happy for him, but also really sad. Why is this?
column3: People we have been very close to or intimate with are very much like members of your family or a best friend. They are not easy to forget, as you're learning now. Many former spouses and partners are surprised when an old flame comes to them in a dream. Or they may think someone who resembles a partner on the street resembles the person they haven't given much thought to for ages. Because we split up doesn't mean a wit to the unconscious mind, that just whips these images out when we least expect it. "But I don't love him anymore" won't spare anyone. If one of the spouses still loves the absent partner, There is a greater likelihood of sustained mourning, or denial, or any of the stages of grief described by Elizabeth Kubla Ross, in," On Death and and Dying * If grief is extended more than a few weeks or is causing a deficit in work habits, taking care of routines, or has negatively affected social life, its a good idea to see a psychotherapist or social worker well trained and competent to get the individual through the grief and back to the joy of living. Allowing depression to continue for more than a short while may cause long term depression, which is more persistent, morbid, and difficult to treat. Therefore, to be avoided. See what Web-MD has to say about the subject: Grief and depression Grief is the natural response to the death of someone close to you, causing feelings of sadness. If the grieving process takes over your life causing feelings of hopelessness, helplessness and worthlessness, seek medical advice about grief and depression. As well as being caused by a death, grief can also be due to: Being separated from a loved oneLosing a job, position or incomeA pet dying or being lostChildren leaving homeMajor life changes, such as divorce, moving home, becoming an "empty nester" or retiringRoss, Elizabeth Kubla," On Death and Dying" 8/29/2008, Taylor and Francis, LTD. column1: Adult My 35-year old wife has recently passed away. What do I say to my 3-year old son? Should I continue to let him see the photos in our phones and tabs?
column3: I'm sorry for the loss of your wife. The pain and trauma of such loss can be unimaginable so it's important that you mourn. The disappearance of your son's mother can be traumatic and uneasy for him for years to come which is important that you tell your son that his mother is not returning. Although he may not comprehend, you have to explain the beginning and ending of ones life. He might not understand it now but may wonder why you never told him before when he can comprehend. I have met plenty of kids who have lost a parent at young age. I notice that some feel that their parent left them by choice which can be traumatic and leave one feeling isolated. These are the kids who were told “Mommy isn't coming back” without further explanation when they were young. Some of these kids develop mental disorders in their teenage years and the psychologist will always say that the loss of a close one is a major factor in the development of mental problems. You need to explain to your son that his mom has passed away. That she is now watching him from the stars and if he misses her, he should just look for a star at (sun included) because as long as there is a star out, his mom is thinking of him and missing him back. You need to tell your son to pick out a favorite picture of his mom that reminds him of happy thoughts to keep with him. Your son may not take any of it lightly and might need your support. You need to give him something of hers that reminds him of it. This will all aid in his mourning process. He may or may not experience the many stages of grief. Regardless of how hard it may be for the first week, your son will eventually forgive his mom. He will grow up like a normal kid. He may try to find himself a mother figure in a family member or even a teacher. The important thing is for your son to know his mom DIED and won't be coming back although she would want to if she could. I know many people are advising you to abstain from telling him but he will feel as sad as you would if your mom suddenly disappeared without explanation. Your son is a little man. He can take it.

column1: Since Jan 2022 I’ve lost 3 family members, all grandparents. 2 taken too early by cancer, one whose death has been prepared for 18 months. How can I deal with this mass sadness and grief?
column3: I am an older lady, annd am in that stage of ife where all of my friends start suddenly dropping dead. A bunch dropped dead over the last 5 years of sudden cardiac events or cancer. My mom and my sister died. Then COVID hit, and a bunch more left this world in another bunch. I lost most of my Aunts and my Uncle too, There is no one alive now who knew me as a child. None. I have lost 2 spouses, and two newborn children… and this is what I have found out: It is best to consider that they are not suffering. They don’t miss you. They are not stressed out about their chores or their debts. They may not be able to share joy or give you support or advice in real time anymore, but THEY will suffer no more pain or struggle. They have had their run. Done their time. YOU are suffering. You are suffering because you miss all that they added to your life! It IS terrible… but they are not really gone! You carry them with you wherever you go. You have been shaped by their grace, wisdom, companionship, and love. They are still here in your heart - but without all the trials of living. All around you, other people are also grieving. YOU are not done yet. You must carry on, paying forward all that they have given you. They would want you to be ALIVE. When you enjoy something they would have enjoyed, enjoy it for them too. Almost everyone has lost people close to them - more lately, true. Seize the love and joy in your life, and try to bear the suffering patiently. Even this suffering will fade in time.

column1: Are the stages of grief described by Elisabeth Kubler-Ross still (ever were) accepted professionally as a viable workable model for therapists?
column3: I studied Kubler-Ross in college. She even came to campus to speak. I understood her stages to be the emotional phases one goes through when dying. They were at some point reframed as the 5 Stages of Grief and became part of our understanding of how grief works. Okay. I guess they knew what they’re doing. Then my son was killed and I was the one grieving. A couple things happened. I did, in fact, experience anger, denial, depression, bargaining, and acceptance, but something was wrong. I was confused by my response. According to the model, I wasn’t grieving normally, and neither were other grieving family members I interacted with. I didn’t experience the stages in that order, sometimes I looped back to what I believed were stages that should have been over and done. Some lasted so briefly they didn’t even apply. And I didn’t even get a chance to bargain. In reading other materials written for grieving parents I found some models with only three “stages” and one model with over a dozen. Finally, over 20 years later, some still come back to visit, perhaps haunt, me from time to time, mostly on significant days. It just didn’t make sense. It wasn’t clean and neat the way that researchers love to have their laundry lists. It was too messy. What was a grieving father to do? As I worked through processing all this for my own book, What to Do When the Police Leave: A Guide to the First Days of Traumatic Loss, I realized that you sometimes have to ignore all the things people say and just feel what you feel. You have to ask yourself, what’is real at this time and in this moment? Sometimes emotions that defy cognitive processing are the only thing to latch onto, so you hold on for dear life. Not comprehending, only feeling as your brain goes through massive changes to accommodate the loss. This is the messy grief of neural adaptation as you take it one day at a time, one minute at a time, if need be as you struggle to regain your footing on an ever changing emotional landscape. These stages may very well be applicable when dying. I don’t know. I haven’t been through that, yet. They also appear to be rather suitable when facing a slowly evolving catastrophic event or tragedy. Perhaps they can be used to understand a reality, but they can not be used prescriptively to define or create a reality. Frankly, they are not likely to even be of much use in acute tragic events when one comes out the other side alive. They’re just not. And for the grief-stricken who must go on living, they are confounding and, in my opinion, best not used except as exemplars along with other models. The grieving do not need Kubler-Ross’ death model. Instead, they need a life model. One that acknowledges the reality and significance of their loss and grief, while giving them hope for post-traumatic growth and continued purposeful life post-trauma. They need more than a laundry list wrapped up in a neat little package and tied with a black bow, because at the end of Kubler-Ross’ model lies death, and we have had enough of that. It’s time to move to a life model, a hope model, and an honest model that we can use as a road map out of the forest and on the path on our way to our new normal. I hope this helps.

column1: Adult How can you deal with the sudden death of a friend?
column3: One goes through all of the stages of grief that were listed by Kubler-Ross. That can take many years in and of itself. 7 STAGES OF GRIEF But in addition, as a sibling, you may well find yourself in the throes of anxiety and depression related to having survived when your sibling did not. That's come to be known as Survivor's Guilt, and it's not just for soldiers and cancer survivors. Anyone who has had a close friend or family member taken unexpectedly or in a chaotic and horrific way can feel as if they were the ones who should have gone first. I'd consider that an additional stage of grief that didn't make the cut in the list of the original 7. The Moral Logic of Survivor Guilt Read about the stages of grief and survivor guilt, recognize that whatever you're feeling is normal and typical in this situation, and allow yourself time to learn how to be yourself without that other person. Particularly with a close sibling, that can be very difficult. The new normal that does not include regular contact with and reliance on that other person can be difficult to sort out at first. Get help with that if you need to. There's no shame in grieving a loss, though here in the US in this point in time we tend to shame each other for such "weakness". It is not weak. It's transitional. See it as such and work through the effort it takes to restructure your way of being.

column1: What should you expect if you refuse cancer treatment?
column3: This is what happened to my father-in-law Jim 6 years ago. He was 72, a kind, caring and generous man who treated me like a son, since I was literally the son he never had, his having raised two daughters, one of whom couldn’t keep a husband. Of all my wife’s numerous family members, he and his sister Betsy were my favorite in-laws of all time. Jim had an aggressive form of bone cancer which was eating him up. At the time he was living in Florida and the hospitals in his area were, shall we say, not the best. He was tired, very sore, losing weight, difficulty walking, lack of appetite. He opted against chemo for a few reasons. He felt the cancer was so aggressive that chemo would only prolong his misery, and it ultimately wouldn’t save him. As a Catholic, he also reasoned that when he passed away he would go to heaven and see his parents and deceased family members/friends again. I had a beer with him in Florida, the last time I ever saw him alive. He was stoic and calm about his impending fate. I won’t say “he faced it like a man” because plenty of women are as strong or stronger. He faced it with resolute steel, is all I will say. That last outing was the one and only time I ever called him “Dad.” It was always “Jim.” Jim entered hospice not much later. He died at home shortly thereafter. It was less than 6 months after his diagnosis. He had been a hale and hearty tall man with a bit of a belly and a fleshy face due to his love of Manhattans and Italian food. I attended his funeral which was open-casket. I didn’t recognize him even after seeing him alive just a couple of months before. He looked like a thin, emaciated waxwork, a poorly made facsimile of his former self. I’m so sorry this happened to him, we miss him all the time, and my wife Susan will never get over the loss of her Dad at only 72. Rest in peace, Dad. I love you. And I hope I see you again somehow.

column1: What is your view on the central government rejecting foreign donations for the Kerala floods?
column3: A village has about 200 families. As usual, some of these families are rich, while some others are poor and middle class. The number of people in each family also varies greatly. Due to this, there are 2-3 families which may still be middle-class even though if you consider the total income of such families then they may be among the top ones in the villages. The total income of the family “A” is the 5th highest in the village, but it is still a middle-class family due to the fact that it is a large family, thereby meaning that the income per person may be comparatively less. Its total annual income is ₹ 26,11,012. Unfortunately, one day, there is some accident in this family which causes a temporary distress to one of the family members. Other family members try to help the distressed family member. Now, there is another family “B” which has the 30th rank in the village from the point of view of total family income. Its total income, though, is only about ₹ 3,77,435 per annum. Family “B” offers some free financial help to the distressed member of family “A”. This distressed member of family “A” wants to accept this free help. But, the head of the family “A” steadfastly refuses to accept this free help. Though the head of the family “A” does not want to use impolite words to someone offering free help to one of its members, what it wants to convey is that “we are not beggars”. It hurts the head of the family “A” that it has the 5th highest income in the village, and yet it should accept free help or free alms from some other family (especially from a family which has 30th rank in the village from the income point of view). For that matter, the family “A” does not want to accept alms or free help even from the richest family in the village. It is a question of its self-esteem. In any case, the financial distress caused to one of its family members is not such huge that it cannot be taken care of. Now, consider that the said village is the “world”. Substitute India for family “A” and UAE for family “B”. The above numbers (of income) represent their GDPs in million dollar terms, and the ranks mentioned above represent their GDP ranks in the world (India is expected to have already become the 5th largest economy in the world, though a formal announcement may take some time since statistics gets changed after some time-gap).[1] For last about 15-20 years, it has been the consistent policy of the Indian Government to decline foreign aid. We don’t want to present India to be a country that receives alms from other countries or as a country that cannot take care of itself. Tomorrow, if there is a natural calamity in China or Japan, and if India wants to offer some ₹ 1000 crore as free aid, will they accept it? Look at how media in other countries uses sarcastic language about aid being given to India. For example, Daily and Sunday Express of UK has this headline: “Foreign aid FARCE: Now 'wealthy' India sent £279MILLION a year of YOUR cash”. It says that:[2]“Ministers have repeatedly been criticised for giving taxpayers’ cash to India given that the country has a space programme and nuclear weapons as well has having one of the fastest-growing economies in the world in recent years.”Or, see another news report, as per which a then British Minister (called “Secretary” in UK) is reportedly saying that too much of Britain’s foreign aid budget is being “stolen or wasted on inappropriate projects”; she was “infuriated” by the apparent squandering of taxpayers’ money that is meant to be spent on helping the world’s poorest people; India is shown as the 10th highest recipient of the British bilateral aid in this news report.[3] So, being a nuclear-state and having sent space vehicles to Mars and Moon, and having become 5th largest economy in the world, do we still want to accept alms or free aid from other countries for a natural calamity? Does it help our reputation as an important nation in the comity of nations? Look at how people in other countries scoff at us for squandering their tax-payers’ money. Do we want this insult at this stage of our civilisation? Do we not want to develop any self-respect? Kerala floods are, no doubt, one of the biggest natural tragedies. The economic loss has been put at about ₹ 21,000 crore to the nation. But, do you know that the Jat agitation in Haryana in early 2016 resulted in loss of ₹ 34,000 crore to the nation?[4] A large number of people were affected adversely then too. Huge economic losses have been caused during agitations of Gurjars, Patidars, Marathas, SC & ST Bharat Bandh, etc., too. Please pardon me for saying all this – my intention is not to underestimate the gravity of situation on ground or to hurt the feelings of anyone. The purpose of this comparison is not to compare the two types of tragedies, but just to highlight that we as a nation are capable of taking care of economic losses. But, did we take any foreign aid to recover from those situations? In fact, no such aid was even offered from outside. Even during the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami, which was a much bigger disaster with thousands of people having died, the then Prime Minister Manmohan Singh had politely refused to take any foreign financial aid. Likewise, after the 2013 Uttarakhand floods, in which thousands of people had died, India did not take any foreign aid. After the 2014 Kashmir floods also, no foreign aid was accepted by India. Therefore, for last 15-20 years, it has been a consistent policy that India has itself done the rebuilding and rehabilitation work after various disasters. How do you expect India to suddenly reverse its policy on accepting foreign aid to take care of natural calamities? Is India not capable of handling the situation? Fortunately, governments in India and people in India have come to help their Kerala brothers and sisters in the hour of need. True, there are many political parties and people with vested interests, who will create unnecessary controversies on the amount of aid given or not given. But, the fact remains that India stands united in relief and rehabilitation work in Kerala. So, I don’t see anything wrong in the Government of India politely refusing to accept any foreign aid for taking care of Kerala floods. Kerala flood is India’s problem. And, we the Indians, can deal with it unitedly. And, I genuinely hope what the Centre has given is only the interim relief, and not the final one.Update (23 August 2018): I don’t belong to any political party. However, I don’t think I am estopped from putting the statistics of central help given at the time of various grave natural calamities in past several years, including for the recent Kerala floods, to put the things in correct perspective, leaving the rest to the esteemed readers to form their opinion (for source, see footnote[5] ):Footnotes[1] List of countries by GDP (nominal) - Wikipedia[2] Foreign aid FARCE: Now 'wealthy' India sent £279MILLION a year of YOUR cash [3] These Are The 10 Countries That Receive The Most UK Foreign Aid[4] Jat stir: North India may face Rs 34,000 crore loss, price rise[5] What India has given disaster-hit states since rejecting foreign aid

column1: What terrifies you most about human psychology, including mental illness?
column3: Pick's disease. Pick's disease is a type of fronto-temporal dementia which mainly targets the prefrontal cortex. It turns an otherwise healthy brain into this:Notice how only the frontal lobes, specifically the prefrontal cortex, is affected. Interestingly, patients with pick's disease don't really have salient symptoms. They retain their memory unlike other dementias, their intelligence is normal, they have no problem with motor control, and everything seems fine. Apart from the fact that they turn into jerks. Many of you would've heard of the story of Phineas Gage. If you haven't, he's the dude that was messing with gunpowder with a tamper rod, and it exploded, resulting in this:He proceeded to make a full recovery, but his personality was changed permanently. Since his ventromedial prefrontal cortex was practically obliterated, he lost the functions of emotional control, and became extremely abusive, violent, profane and impulsive, which he was not prior to his injury. Pick's disease affects exactly that, and some other areas of the brain. Pick's disease also atrophies the polar prefrontal cortex, the dorsolateral and medial prefrontal cortex, and parts of the anterior cingulate gyrus, resulting in the following impairments:Cognitive control: They will fail to exhibit goal-directed behaviour, which means that they will often lack motivation to even do the most mundane of things, despite recognising the need to. A patient might lose the motivation to work, talk to people, clean after themselves and other things.Emotional control: À la Phineas GageTheory of mind: The failure to understand that other people also have their hopes, desires and subjective feelings. A total loss of empathetic concern for anything.Self-control: Extreme impulsivity, reckless behaviour, failure to delay gratification. Often leads to inappropriate acts, such as sexual harassment, violence amongst others.And other less salient ones. So imagine that a loved one comes home one day, and they're acting up a bit. They seem rather ticked off, and they get annoyed at trivial matters. Most people would justifiably attribute that to a bad day, perhaps because of work or whatnot. This persists, and eventually worsens. At that point, most would assume that they're going through a “phase”. Frankly, it's not until cognitive control is severely hampered when such patients get diagnosed of the disease by neurologists. My professor recalled one patient that acknowledged that human waste matter was foul and disgusting, despite sitting there in his urine-soaked pants because he “didn't bother”. And that's only the start of a nightmare for their family. Such patients require extensive care because of the loss of cognitive control, and most elderly homes cannot deal with them because they're great “troublemakers”. Thus, the burden falls onto family members, who have to tend to a patient who's constantly denigrating them, harassing them and can be increasingly violent, verbally or physically. Not surprisingly, it is extremely demoralising for the caregivers, even if they are aware of the disease and its implications. It's practically like being stuck at the bottom of an abyss, until the dementia eventually takes the patient's life. Absolutely depressing. That's what terrifies me. A disease which strips one's executive functions of control, which is extremely hard to detect until late stages, and has sweeping negative consequences for all those around them. Thank goodness it's a rare disease. Edit: I certainly didn't expect this from a post about an obscure neurodegenerative disease, but thanks for the 2600+ upvotes.
column9: The great Bengali poet Kazi Nazrul Islam suffered from Pick's disease. He spent many years in mental hospitals. The great poet lived for a long time without being able to produce anything of value owing to this terrible disease.

column1: What are some quick coping skills one can use when dealing with depression around the holidays?
column3: Managing depression at the holidays requires more than just a few quick coping skills, but If I had to give someone three things to do, it would be these: Get More Light The holidays come (for many) at the time of the year when there is the least amount of available daily sunlight. The shorter, darker days impact many who struggle with symptoms of depression…increasing fatigue, decreasing mood, and affecting appetite and sleep patterns. For anyone whose depression worsens with the loss of sunlight, I recommend taking a short walk at lunchtime outside to get some sun exposure. Getting outside during the day (if you don’t get the opportunity to do this where you work or live) helps to break up the day, so your experience of arriving at work and departing in the dark isn’t all you experience of your environment. Also, keep your interior rooms bright with several lamps until about an hour before bedtime. Just Say No to Drama Everyone has increased demands placed on them during the holidays and co-workers, friends, neighbors, and family members (not to mention you!) may show the strain. People are eating unhealthy food more often, drinking alcohol more, sleeping less, trying to get more done in less time, and worrying about additional problems unique to holiday finances or family issues. Sometimes that creates the opportunity for “drama” to unfold. Whether that occurs in the workplace, in the checkout line, or at family get togethers…the holidays are rarely the time to attempt to manage conflict successfully. Table any heated discussions or simply refuse to participate. When the holidays are over, you can revisit any issue that is unresolved when heads are cooler and everyone is less stressed. Plan Your Pitstops The weeks between Thanksgiving and New Year’s can feel like running a marathon for anyone with depression. So, like a good marathoner, plan your pitstops, where you’re going to stop, refresh, refuel, and relaunch. Schedule in downtime, time with that friend who always helps you keep perspective, a session with your therapist, a massage, a nap, a run, or just time to chill alone. Write these into your planner, just as you would important commitments. Because they are. Calculate how low your personal energy battery charge will be after events you are saying “yes” to, and schedule your recharge time accordingly. If you plan your pitstops, you’re less likely to run out of emotional fuel. ———————————————————————————————- I wrote a more general answer related to self-care at the holidays here: Anita Sanz's answer to How can we take care of ourselves when faced with holiday demands?

column1: When a demented or otherwise legally impaired person is placed in a long term care facility, isn't it their obligation to see that their patients eat, take their medicine, and bathe?
column3: Residents cannot be forced to eat, take medications, or take a bath. The refusal of patients to participate in these Adls is enforced by the Resident’s Bill of Rights. These refusals to participate must be thoroughly documented by nursing. The physician and the responsible party of the patient must be informed of ongoing refusals. Adequate nutritional intake is addressed after the patient has lost several pounds via a Residents at Risk team. This weekly meeting involves the Director of Nurses, Dietician, Director of Therapy, Assistant Director of Nurses, and Nursing MDS coordinator. For weight loss issues, the patient is examined for reasons due to lack of appetite. The appropriateness and safety of appetite stimulants are reviewed and prescribed as deemed by the patient’s physician. A weekly weight is kept of the patient to determine if the medication is indeed effective. Nutrient dense snacks should be made available according to the patients diet. Therapy is often asked to step in to observe the patient and determine if the patient has a self feeding difficulty. If so, therapy will evaluate and treat the patient only with the Md’s consent. Therapy may observe factors such as: Does the patient have tremors, pocket food in their cheeks, or have dentures that are inappropriately fitted? Is he confused as how to use the utensils to consume his food? Does he have the proper utensils to consume his food successfully? Does he prefer to eat most foods with his fingers? Is the patient’s attention to task impaired? Does he have swallowing issues? Does the patient need a diet texture change to enable him to consume his food safely? Sometimes, the patient responds well to a friend or family member visiting at one or more meals to encourage the patient to eat. The responsible party may assist his loved one as needed. The patient may even consume more food if the responsible party eats with the patient in a traditional family style. We humans often prefer to eat with those we know and love. The patient may be seated at a feeder table for one on one assistance from nursing staff to assist the patient in safe and adequate nutritional intake. The patient is on the Resident at Risk list for at least a month, or longer if weight is not increasing. As for for refusing to take medications, the physician must be made aware of this refusal as well as the responsible party. Appropriate referrals are made by the physician for OT and ST per swallowing, cognitive, or memory issues. Compensatory measures are used to assist the patient in swallowing or to redirect the patient as needed to take his medications. Nursing may offer the medications via liquid or crushed form as appropriate or in a food (often jelly or pudding) which the patient desires. Results of successful or unsuccessful medication intake are reported to the physician as soon as possible. Accurate and thorough documentation is essential to correctly depict the pt’s response to intervention. If a patient is refusing a bath, sometimes he or she will allow a family member to visit and assist with this process as feasible. A different nursing assistant may be successful in encouraging the patient to bathe with decreased anxiety and fear. The patient may be approached at a different time of the day for a bath. Dementia patients often respond to the morning or early afternoon better than later in the evening. Dementia progresses with the Sundowning Syndrome. Occupational therapists may receive a referral from the doctor to step in and analyze the bath/shower to determine how to reduce the anxiety and fear associated with this routine as well as to increase safety. Caregiver and family instruction should be rendered. The physician may prescribe a mild anti-anxiety medication to assist the patient in tolerating this process with reduced stress. Remember to ask questions to determine the best treatment possible for your family member. Responsible parties, please attend quarterly care plan meetings as feasible to voice concerns to the attending staff members. This attendance helps us to provide better care to your relative. Best wishes for quality healthcare to your loved one. Your input truly counts!

column1: Does everyone in a family require a life insurance?
column3: Life insurance policy is an arrangement between an insured and an insurer, where the insurer promises to make good the losses of the insured in case of an uncertain event i.e. in our case, death of the individual. The insured pays a premium to mitigate this risk. Basically, it is an instrument to cover the contingency of an uncertain event. The one and the most important benefit of having a life insurance policy is to have a secured financial future and maintain the same level of lifestyle even after a human loss. Life insurance is certainly important to mitigate the risk of unwarranted death. However, it is important to understand whether everyone in the family requires a life insurance cover. So, does everyone in your family require life insurance policy? Primarily, anyone who has dependents and is an income earner needs Life Insurance. Homemakers also offer tremendous economic value to a household. Therefore it is highly recommended that they are covered with a life insurance policy too. Therefore one can purchase life insurance policies for: 1) Family members earning an income and supporting other financial dependents in the family 2) Home makers - in whose absence one might have to arrange for care takers. If you have dependents in your family (such as parents, spouse or children who are financially dependent on you), then in all such cases a Life Insurance Policy will financially support your family in case of your death. Here are some of the important points to consider to evaluate the amount of insurance cover: 1. Number of dependents 2. The kind of lifestyle 3. Cost of children’s education 4. Investment requirements 5. Affordability and current level of income Another point to ponder about is - what if you don’t have financial dependents? In that case, you may not wish to purchase a life insurance policy or purchase policies for others in your family. However, if you have plans of settling down in the future, you might wish to purchase a life insurance policy for yourself - as the premium amount would increase as you become older. Once you get settled, you can always include your dependents as nominees. Liked this answer? Check out a few more questions answered by us: Why is term insurance crucial if you are self-employed? Why we should take insurance?

column1: Each day I sleep with the guilt of not making my day productive but the next day I waste it again. I am getting depressed now. What should I do?
column3: I swear! I didn't ask this question. But I had the same question when ruthless UPSC shackled my confidence and buried it in Mariana Trench. Believe me! I was in the same vicious cycle where you are.In those days, Generally, I woke up at 9–10 A.M. There was no enthusiasm to leave my bed meanwhile a heap of ‘The-Hindu’ newspaper was staring at me to finish it ASAP. Heap? because I didn’t read a newspaper since 10–12 days. In normal days, reading a newspaper is the first thing in my daily life. Aaah! Cellphone worked as The Bermuda Triangle for me, You lost when you unlock it. Simple. Unnecessarily scrolling of meaningless social media platforms, You can find me watching movies and Tv-series on Amazon Prime and Netflix as someone is paying me to watch it. I didn’t care about rating or quality, I needed an escape from reality, and my dearest smartphone was doing its job perfectly. Afterall I am a human. Obviously, I got bored watching these things. There is a mall in nearby, So I went there without any purpose. Here I was lost in my numb thoughts but surrounded by happy faces in that mall. Their every smile was mocking me for living a pathetic life. I used to return from that mall with a bullshit thought— Today is the last wasted day, I will work my ass off from very next day. After having dinner, I tried my best to make a schedule of the century. After drafting a schedule, There was motivational videos, songs, movies where I used to waste my next 3–4 hours. Eventually, I slept with guilt after successfully wasted a day. Unfortunately, the same cycle repeated the very next day.After 10–12 days, I was tired of this vicious cycle. And after each passing day, I started hating myself. My smile was the second thing I lost after my self-confidence. I was not interested in making a conversation with my family members. Whenever anyone called me, I was ready with an excuse to end that ongoing conversation. Gradually, This bizarre life was eating me alive. No pledge, motivational videos, etc was working on me. And, I was losing a part of me with each passing days.One fortunate day, My father called me for a random thing but I was lost in my shitty thoughts. Papa: Subhash! Everything good? Should I lie or should I tell him about my current life? I don’t know what happened to me. I explained him my vicious life-cycle in one go. Papa was at loss for words for a while. But I know he has always a solution for my every problem.Papa: Take it, easy lad! Don’t provide surplus foods to your devil brain. Because overthinking is the first step to a miserable life. Don’t waste your energy in drafting a perfect schedule of the millennium.“Then what should I do to terminate this self-harming lifestyle”— I asked.Papa: Start working, Just act rather than make a plan for next decade. No planning, no self-pity letters to yourself. Treat your present day as a battle, when you start winning your day then every misplaced piece will fall at the right place.That night, I didn’t make any time-table, No motivational videos. Nothing. Honestly speaking! The very next day was not a perfect day but I did fairly well. Gradually, I terminate that vicious cycle.Each day I sleep with the guilt of not making my day productive but the next day I waste it again. I am getting depressed now. What should I do?I know how it feels. But no one will come to rescue you from this shithole. This is your battle, you have to fight it till your last breath. Now, I don’t know I will ever achieve my goal or not. But I was not even in the race when I was sleeping with guilt after wasting my days. Sleeping with the guilt or wounded after a battle? Choose wisely.
