column1: How did people of Pakistan in 1971 feel and react after their military surrendered to India in Bangladesh?
column3: Edit: Thanks for the all of the views and upvotes guys, I'm glad y'all found my story touching. I just wanted to clearify a few things that some of y'all have asked me about. First, my Paternal Grandfather was in politics and he was affiliated with the (Convention Muslim Leauge) in fact, we have a picture of my grandfather shaking Ayub Khan’s hand. Second, I'm not an ultra-proud Bihari, I love my ethnicity and people but I'm not so proud of the bad things Bihari people and politicians do. Some people have bashed me for being proud to be a Bihari like it's a bad thing, Biharis have a long way to improve in terms of their public figure. Third, I am NOT an Indian faking as a Pakistani; I don't even know why people even think of this stuff. Also, I'm not here asking for apologies from Bangladeshis a lot of you guys have said sorry and it's okay, I should be saying sorry to you guys lol. Finally many of you have asked if I still preserve the Bihari culture at home, the answer is yes of course. We speak Maithili and Bhojpuri in addition to Urdu, celebrate the 3 main Bihari festivals and we still eat our yummy Bihari food. Many of you guys are interested in the life of non-Urdu Speaking Migrants in Karachi (Biharis, Gujaratis etc.), please watch the HUM TV Telefilm “Bihar Colony” and you'll get a good feel of our cultural preservation.This question relates a lot to my family background, I apologize if I get too personal but the entire story is necessary. My maternal and paternal grandparents were born and raised in beautiful Bihar (I’m proud to be a Bihari), they got married around the time of the partition and decided it was best to move to Dhaka (then East Pakistan). We come from a huge family on my mothers side so only my grandparents and 2 other smaller families came to Dhaka (My maternal grandmother and Grandfather are related by 9 generations apart) beacuse of educational opportunities. Both my grandfathers went to Dhaka University and got their degrees, by maternal grandfather was a high paid government officer (he was some sort of Engineer) and my paternal grandfather had many sugarcane plantations and entered politics as well. All of my aunts and uncles and my parents were born in Dhaka. Over time both sides became wealthier and lived pretty good lives, in a Bengali society they were a minority being Biharis. The 1971 war was about to start, and my paternal side knew of the upcoming crisis, they gave their house up to a member of their extended family and left to Islamabad; they left an empty house, taking every piece of furniture, clothing and jewelry with them. My mother’s side on the other hand wasn't so lucky, they had a feeling that things were going to take a turn so they tried buying tickets for Karachi which was impossible since my uncle was a newborn baby and he couldn't receive a ticket. December 16th rolled around, the day when the Bengalis celebrated their victory, angry Bengalis who hated he Urdu-Speakers and Pakistanis went around taking up the male heads of Urdu Speaking and Pakistani families ( Keep in mind we spoke Bhojpuri Bihari in the house and we were not Urdu-Speakers, in addition our family was apolitical). The Bangladeshis came into our house and took my maternal grandfather and my oldest uncle; only my oldest aunt knows how my grandmother felt as she was old enough to understand what was happening. Immediately they had to leave all of that wealth behind and flee Dhaka, originally my grandmother took a bundle of cash but found out that people were getting killed for having money and so she threw it into the river. My grandmother went alone with 7 children ranging from ages (1–16) camp to camp until she reached India and then to here hometown Sasaram, Bihar. News that my oldest uncle was alive and with the Pak Army made my grandmother leave her parents and siblings in Bihar for Kathmandu, Nepal where she waited one year to get a flight to Karachi. Upon arriving in Karachi she went to the house of one of the 3 families that also fled Dhaka to Karachi, she lived their for a while until she managed to get her own house. Now the 2 other families that we were related to came with everything, when introducing my grandmother to others they would say “Ye he hain jo Dhaka se lut put kar aayein hain” or “This is her, who was looted in a Dhaka and came here”. Such insensitive remarks hurt a woman with 7 kids looking for her 8th child and who was suffering from the loss of a husband. My oldest uncle came to Karachi 3 years later and found his way to my grandmother, he has never told anyone where he was or what happened to him and no one is allowed to ask him what happened. My maternal grandmother built her self up, her kids were educated and left for abroad and we became a wealthier family after many years of a struggle. In 1971, the feeling of a Pakistani who didn't experience any of that was ignorant to the losses on both sides, many were upset over the loss of territory. In 1971, the feeling of my family who were considered Pakistanis, was of betrayal by the government who failed to protect its people after the war. The loss of an innocent life in my family made my maternal grandmother wear a white saari for the rest of her life. It stripped the luxory and wealth that we had for nothing. My mother and her siblings grew up without a father, once a distant family member found a picture of my grandfather and gave it to us, at least my mother and her siblings knew how their father looked. In 1971 Pakistanis that were impacted by the war felt cheated as the new Bangladesh government came and took their Bengalis living in Karachi but the Pakistani government left us Biharis to die. There are still Biharis in Bangladesh living in poverty and are called Straded Pakistanis. In 1971 my grandmother wanted to forget the partition and return to her India where her entire family lived. As per the military who surrendered by grandmother always said that had the Pakistan army not been so cruel to the Bengalis maybe our grandfather would have been alive. I respect the Bangladeshis and I am glad that they got their own nation, Pakistan is a deadly poison that lives in the subcontinent. I found out all of this a few years ago, I am a U.S born citizen to Pakistani parents and upon questioning them I learned all of this information. So in overall, I'm glad that that the Pakistan Army surrendered so Bangladesh became a nation; but I'm also sad that the army and government could care less about their people living in Dhaka who were not Bengali.
column9: Sad your family had to go through such a traumatic ordeal. Bangladeshi angst should have been with the Pakistan army instead of common people.

column1: I lost my job. When I told my therapist, she emailed to ask if I was okay. I responded not really. How do I recover from the end of my career and the loss of a therapist I thought cared? I'm devastated.
column3: I am so sorry you lost your job. I have been down that road several times in my life before I became a therapist. It IS devastating. What support do you have? Family, friends, partner/spouse? You will be caught between crisis management and grieving. Your question seems to be about the loss of your therapist and like others, I am also not sure about loss of your therapist. If you did not part on bad terms, then tell her/him about your feelings of loss. Why DO you feel she didn't care? Small steps. Weep, cry, be angry, allow all the emotions to come through. Journal, write letters to your job, yes, weird as it may seem, write to your job tell it how much it meant and why the loss is so bad. The internet is filled with suggestions on what to do after a job loss, so read the articles, but first, self-care. Don't make hasty decisions, talk to a trusted friend, family member, spiritual adviser. If you want to continue therapy, ask your therapist for a discount or even if s/he will consider a few pro-bono sessions. Look out for credit/financial counselling places that can help you to re-organise your finances. Take tiny, tiny steps. Watch motivational videos on You Tube. I still watch them when I am down. My go to guy is Les Brown, an oldie but goodie. You watch whatever who ever you are drawn to. Keep away from negative, violent, dark, sad stuff, it may take down a darker hole. Good wishes to you. Thank you for reaching out to us out in the web. You are not alone.

column1: How is the British healthcare system unique?
column3: So Carol knows ‘firsthand’? Carol, that means you’ve experienced that *yourself* and from your Quora answers, you are very much American and in America. Now, as an American who has lived in Great Britain since 1998 and has actually experienced both systems for long periods and with a variety of medical needs first hand, let me be honest, Carol has an agenda that is not based in reality. Firstly, the UK healthcare scheme (English is only England and it’s the same in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, hence ‘UK’) is not unique. I’ve also experienced health care in France and it’s much the same. My friends in the Netherlands, Italy, Germany, Norway, Czech Republic, Denmark and Belgium all experience much the same as we do. Now, to deal with Carol, on cancer, since she brought it up. From 1990 I had yearly pap smears because my result was not normal. They would alternate, one year okay, one year abnormal, they just kept doing yearly paps, no follow-up. I was on Medicaid so really, where was the incentive to keep a young mother of 3 alive, after all, she clearly had no money. So nothing was done, nothing was done at all. I came to the UK in 1998, married a local guy and in 2003 had a baby. At the postpartum check they did not like the appearance of my cervix and scheduled me to have a pap smear done. As a young mum with a newborn I did zero follow up and was in no rush to comply so it was the system pushing things forward with no help from me. After the pap they immediately referred me for a colposcopy to check out the abnormal result. In August I was having my first colposcopy with Leep diathermy to remove cancerous lesions. I continued to have colposcopies every 6 months, receiving more treatment to remove the lesions when necessary, for 3 years. During this time I was also, due to my age, referred to the Cancer genetics unit at the top UK cancer hospital as an outpatient. A full workup of my American family cancer history was done and on the basis of that I was put on yearly mammograms and give BRCA 1 & 2 genetic testing for breast cancer genes. This went on from 2005 until this past November when I was finally released as an outpatient and put on ‘community screening.’ My first mammogram with them is this Thursday. That baby is 16 years old and the NHS kept me alive to mother her, give birth to her two younger sisters, helped my cousins in the US with their genetic investigation and kept me feeling safe and supported while dealing with this issue. I returned to the US when my father was dying of cancer. He had a cough that he sought help with from his GP and though he was a lifelong smoker in his 70s with a persistent cough, the US system *gave him a prescription for cough syrup*. From the UK I insisted he go back and demand some testing, which he was reluctant to do on his pensioners income. When they finally got off their ass and tested him, it was quick, that much is true, they put him in every machine they had in rapid succession but the lack of self-motivation in the system meant that all they could tell him is Stage 4 lung. My mother called me and said ‘what does that mean’ and I was so disgusted all I could manage was ‘it means 6 months, 18 if you’re very, very, very lucky’. He was not that lucky and was dead in 6 months and to maximise our time together I rented a house and stayed in South Carolina for that year. I called to schedule my yearly mammogram but being uninsured, was of no interest to anyone. I was told, and this is rich considering SC’s general hatred of it, to call Planned Parenthood. Instead I said sod this and came home to the UK where the system I pay into actually acts like it cares about me. I could go on, I’ve had 3 children in the US and 3 in the UK, one of my children had asthma, one had pancreatitis, 2 had impacted wisdom teeth, 1 had temporary hearing loss from infection, 1 is on the autistic spectrum, I had allergy diagnosis and treatment, etc. etc. We’re a big family, plenty of anecdotal evidence. What I will say is this: the minute I could return to the UK, I did. I have never seen a medical expenses begging box here, never had a friend or family member die or have their condition worsened by medical delays here, and never minded paying 32% tax to a system that educates my children better (all of my kids are very average students here but while we were back in America, all of them were bumped up a grade on the basis of their admittance testing), keeps me living in a safe place and cares for my family’s health needs. The UK may seem ‘unique’ to Americans because it is humane and not profit driven. Y’all need to get out more.
column9: Wow! Sometimes it takes someone from the outside looking in to tell us how lucky we are.

column1: What does a 'functional family' look like (vs. dysfunctional) and how can we get there?
column3: I think all families probably have at least a little dysfunction. After all, nobody’s perfect. And we all came from families that had some dysfunction in them too, to some degree, and we tend to unconsciously emulate what we learned from them. That said, there are qualities I think healthy families practice, or at least strive for. This is what healthy families do: They give unconditional love to their kids. If the kids misbehave or get in trouble, the parents make it clear that it’s the behavior they disapprove of and not the kid. No matter what happens, they make sure their kids know they are loved and valued. They provide the kids with a safe, protected environment to grow up in. They provide for the kids’ basic needs in terms of food, clothing, shelter, medical care, educational needs and overall stability. They are emotionally supportive, loving, caring, nurturing, and encouraging. They provide wisdom and guidance. They set clear rules and boundaries, so the kids know what is expected of them. They teach their kids social skills, manners, morals, cooperation, how to solve problems, and how to negotiate their way through the complexities of life. They treat each other and their kids with respect. They consistently model kindness, consideration, and appropriate behavior in all situations. They do not favor one child over another. They treat everyone fairly. They make time for laughter and play. They do fun things together as a family. They encourage each kid to develop a sense of humor, and show them how to use humor to diffuse difficult situations, or help get them through tough times. They take time to listen to their kids and answer their questions. They acknowledge and validate their kids’ feelings. They help them to deal with difficult emotions like fears, hurt, anxieties, anger, grief, loss, rejection, etc. They notice and encourage each child’s individual talents and skills. They help steer their kids into activities in which their talents and skills can grow and flourish. They recognize the importance of nurturing their kids’ self-esteem, and encouraging their individual uniqueness. They admit when they are wrong, and model how to apologize and make amends for wrongdoing. They also demonstrate the need and importance of forgiveness. They make their home a refuge from the outside world. No matter what harsh things family members may have to deal with in the outside world, they can always come home to comfort and acceptance and love and safety. They are welcoming towards friends, neighbors, relatives, and others, and model how to treat guests graciously and kindly. Their home is a welcome place for their kids’ friends. They demonstrate their values and beliefs through the way they live and conduct themselves. They discuss current events with their kids, and have conversations about the TV shows they watch, and ask questions or make comments to help develop their kids’ critical thinking skills. They model social responsibility through activism or volunteering or donating to charities. They teach their kids about responsibility by assigning them regular chores. If they have a pet, they demonstrate responsible pet care and teach the kids how to treat their pets. The parents stand up for their kids and advocate for them whenever necessary. If someone accuses their kid of something, they listen to their kid’s side of the story and make sure the kid knows that as long as they are telling the truth, the parents will back them up 100%. If there is a crisis of some kind, the parents demonstrate good judgment in dealing with it. They demonstrate the ability to remain calm and focused in finding a solution and doing what has to be done. They train their kids to become as independent and self-sufficient as they can be for their age and level of maturity. The kids are rewarded with additional privileges as they demonstrate that they are able to follow rules and behave responsibly. Open and honest communication is expected and encouraged. Kids are encouraged to express their opinions and ask questions. Parents teach tolerance of different opinions, but also model how to work together and make compromises in order to problem-solve. The parents are responsible and dependable. They can be counted on to do what they say they will do, and follow through on promises. Consequences for misbehavior or breaking the rules are consistently enforced. Individual weaknesses, flaws, and disabilities are accepted and worked-around. Areas that can be improved are encouraged. There is no belittling or demeaning someone for their faults. The family accepts that everyone has different strengths and weaknesses. Individual preferences are taken into consideration. Everyone doesn’t have to be the same or like the same things. Family members take turns choosing activities or meals or other things so that everyone has a chance to have what they want. There is a spirit of unity, harmony and cooperation. Maybe not 100% of the time, but most of the time. Family members help each other. Family members want what’s best for each other. Family members celebrate each others’ successes and achievements. They comfort each other when they experience hurt or loss. They show up for important events of other family members. They “get” each other, and are there for each other.
column9: This is a very insightful answer. It's easy to look at the negatives but we need perspective to look at the positives. I wish there was a book for building a functional family.

column1: If a psychopath loses family members such as a father, a mother, a spouse or their children, how would they feel?
column3: Just found out my father is on death's door a couple of days ago. Honestly, I was quite happy - don't get all excited though and think ‘ahhh, nasty psychopath’ etc. I was ‘happy’, as in pleased with my natural reaction, because from the instant I heard and from then on, I felt absolutely NOTHING. Why?? Well, I'd had an honest relationship with my father, and perhaps because it was an honest relationship it also wasn't always an easy one. I suppose one can never be quite certain one has said all one needs to communicate to another human being, but ever since I was a very young child I basically decided that with those ‘close’ to me, either by necessity, or by choice, I would ALWAYS speak my own truth (with consideration for them to whatever degree I found appropriate in each circumstance). Hence: nothing had been left unsaid to my father, and I already know there is simply no way I'll feel ANYTHING when he dies. I mean, seriously, WHY WOULD I?? No grief, no pleasure, no anything - he was alive, then he's changed into something which is alive in a different way - not being religious here, simply that he'll transform into food for the soil etc. My mother died, she was just gone. It was weird, I preferred it when she was around - but she was gone - that's it (and I was very close to her). A spouse, well, we'll see… that may be more interesting. Still, I would expect at most a numb sense of his absence, I like him a lot - but dead is dead. Update:Ok, got news my father died today. Sequence of events:I had a business meeting to go to, and got the news I suppose 20 minutes before I was supposed to leave for the meeting. I couldn't get my sister on the phone, so texted to let her know.Attended the meeting which went extremely well.Hadn't told the person I was meeting with about my father's death, as honestly, I'd forgotten - I entirely focused on the strategic meeting. Speaking afterwards with his PA I had to give family information for some paperwork and mentioned my father had just died. When the PA clicked he'd died VERY recently she was blown away I'd come to the meeting (I wasn't surprised in the least, my father dying didn't change the need for the meeting, nor it's nature).I decided to drive for a while and see if that changed. It didn't…I'll observe how things progress and update here. Who knows? It's an interesting time to watch myself and see what happens…A few weeks later, no change. Life carrying on after my father's death, exactly as it had before. No sudden surprise emotional ‘anything's’ on my side. My SO got a bit emotional about me NOT getting emotional, but he's like that from time to time. He’s neurotypical, and sometimes he just doesn't get it I suppose… in this case it was particularly irritating to be told that I should be grieving, upset, inconsolable - yet was ‘cold’. I pointed out that I wasn't even cold, I was precisely as I'd been prior to my father's death, and that he'd liked me then - so the issue wasn't with me, but HIS idea of what I ‘should’ ‘feel’ like. Being inner circle and fully aware of the nature of psychopathy I would've imagined he'd know better… These emotions can seem to just move into a neurotypical mind like uninvited guests! A few apologies from him later after he'd regained self control and he's moved on to other things. So, in short, that's about it for a relative's death as experienced by (my personal) psychopathy. Additional: Lexa Thorne’s comment (below) spurred the following response from me: ‘When my mother died quite young in 2004 -things were actually somewhat different. I've been trying to pin it down, and it's far from simple to discern. I'm uncertain if this is a psychopathy related issue, but I very strongly suspect it is. The issue, for me anyway, is that I find it to be difficult to ‘compare’ myself to other people, any other people. It's not like I am unaware of them, it's simply that I can't seem to compare myself TO THEM. This fact interests me, particularly as in other ways I'm very good at making complex evaluations and comparisons. With people, and myself being one of those used in the comparison - I'm somewhat at a loss, as I am what and who I am. It's that rock solid core self confidence psychopathy confers - which isn't egotistical in the least, it's just precisely what it is (comparisons to others simply aren't required - which concisely also removes jealousy/envy etc as they simply can't exist). So, to my mother and my experience of her death. Firstly, we were very close (well, probably not close by neurotypical standards there was no ‘emotional bond’ as I understand most people experience - however, it was as close as I can be with another human) - only my SO gets near that level of ‘close’, and even then only by slow, hard earned, increments. Importantly, though my mother definitely wasn't psychopathic, she did know how to best ‘manage’ me. We had what I would describe as an easy, almost ‘adult’, relationship from as young as I can recall. To put this into its proper perspective, and to blow apart one of the common pre-suppositions about psychopathy - my loyalty (?) kicked in with regard to my mother's very long dreadful years of illness - and, if I could have given MY LIFE to my mother in exchange for hers, the ‘no fear’ aspect of psychopathy would've kicked in and overruled the self interest aspect. It's a loyalty thing taken to the extreme I suppose, and looking back even now I know if we could have exchanged my healthy mind and body, my life, for her hell on earth and upcoming death - I would've done so. So, to death and grieving. In my mother's case, when she passed there was a gap, a void. The void annoyed me, and that niggling annoyance ‘disturbed’ my equilibrium (although everyday life continued unabated). I was quite surprised that the ‘disturbing annoyance’ continued for a fairly long time. With regard to some other aspects you've mentioned: ‘I would expect a psychopath to experience indifference when a parent dies (unless that parent is giving them money, and that stops when they die).’ My life has been filled with ups and downs, gains and losses of fortune. I will always be self sufficient though, and as I pointed out to my SO the day we got together and he let me know he had nothing - (and I have a lot) - “money isn't my currency”. Strangely, it seems it's never crossed his mind to ask ‘Then WHAT IS your currency??’ - that's the question I would've asked if the roles were reversed. ;)’
column9: I would expect a psychopath to experience indifference when a parent dies (unless that parent is giving them money, and that stops when they die). If you are a curious psychopath, the rest may be of interest to you. You are correct about the “uninvited guests” aspect of emotions sometimes moving into our minds. Most of us (NTs) like our ability to feel emotions, but not when grief and loss moves into our heart. Grief and loss are normative and appropriate for us given the loss of a loved one, BUT grief does linger far too long (like uninvited guests). That emotion is not pleasant to experience. It feels agonizing to us, and you can relate to emotion on that level. TIP: The more empathic the NT is, the longer and more profoundly they will feel that grief and loss. So, if you’re the kind of psychopath that prefers a highly empathic partner (because they’re very trustworthy people), be forewarned. Their software is preloaded to feel the loss of a loved one more deeply and for a protracted period. This correlation is direct. As an NT, when I try to comprehend how a psychopath feels when someone dies, I just remember how I feel when I’m walking at night and step on a snail. I stop for a moment, switch the light app on my cell phone so I can see where I’m walking, and I get on with the business of the evening. I do cringe the moment I feel the snail being crushed, but by then it’s dead, it didn’t suffer, and I go on my way and complete my tasks with no sense of loss. With a loved one, NTs cannot “reason” our way out of grief, but logic and reason can help us with acceptance. Even if we are relieved our loved one is no longer suffering (i.e. cancer, Alzheimers, life support), we still feel their loss, and it can take a long time to heal. That is the way our brain functions. Trust me on this topic; genuine grief and loss is NOT pleasant for us, however, for the way NT brains works, it is entirely normative, as are the stages of grief that NTs experience. As a psychopath, once you understand that the stages of grief are normative for the NT brain, it would be illogical for you to expect NTs to feel differently, just as it is unreasonable for NTs to expect you to feel things that you cannot. Psychopaths are going to get annoyed by NT emotions. NTs are going to get annoyed by psychopath’s lack of certain emotions. Acceptance of those two facts is what each has to work on, and until each accepts the logic and reason behind the facts, each will reveal their weakness: a lack of knowledge or a lack of acceptance of the facts.

column1: With the understanding of narcissistic abuse, along with having healed your core wounds, what, if anything, stands out about the whole experience of having been with a Narcissist?
column3: I think that the stand out experiences of having relationship with narcissists, is how skewed my sense off reality became. Deep down I always sensed I didn't know my own full history. It turns out I was right. What I didn't understand, actually couldn't understand, was the degree to which I lived with gaslighting and cognitive dissonance. Once I finally started trying to understand what was missing, I stumbled upon websites and utube videos discussing narcissism. What continues to blow me away is how long I identified my now dead father as an undiagnosed malignant narcissist. I've accepted that as truth for almost 30 years. Yet I had no curiosity about what that meant. My ignorance about how his disorder impacted my whole family. I knew his treatment of me was far more extreme than my siblings. I didn't understand how my identity as the scapegoat would continue long after his death. I also wasn't able to correctly identify how some of my family members followed suit and have become folks that I believe are somewhere on the Cluster B spectrum. I'd bought the story that everything wrong about my family was my fault. In doing so, I discounted my own reality of doing my very best to try and keep my mother alive and our family intact. The damage I've sustained and internalized was tremendous. I'm not sure I'll ever be able to engage in any real life relationships with anyone, let alone a romantic one. The coming holidays has amped up my inner pain and loss. I'd been ok with that, trying to continue self care, especially mindfulness, despite my roller coaster emotions. It's been exacerbated today as one of my family members, who I went no contact with 6 months ago, reached out asking if I wanted to chat as I've been on her mind and Christmas is coming. Ugh. I don't know what I want to do going forward. I have a much more clear understanding of my family dynamics after this 6 month period of research and acceptance of my new normal. Yet I still struggle with knowing what is best for me in relation to my family of origin. The most impactful of growing up with folks with narcissistic adaptations is that I don't have a consistent belief in my reality when dealing with my family of origin. I allowed others to define me in ways that were never true, e.g. I am a stupid liar when truth is extremely important to me and I am not, in any way, stupid. There are lifetime consequences when someone has been systematically gaslighted all of their life. At some point the person gaslighted can lose the ability to even question the nonsense put forward as reality. ❤️ Nora
column9: You are stronger than you think given what you’ve undergone with your family of origin. I have disengaged with some family members who I believe are on the cluster b spectrum. When in doubt I don't engage. One of the lessons for me has been to listen to my gut feeling. I wasn't paying attention to my gut feeling for most of my life. Best wishes. My discard date is Dec 17 -2 years ago. I am very thankful for my freedom.

column1: What is the history of Japanese jacket wrestlers (judoka) beating up founding family members of Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (the Gracie family)?
column3: To understand this, one must know the history of Brazilian Jiu Jitsu (BJJ). BJJ is a direct “son” of the original Judo. And Judo is a “son” of the original Japanese JuJutsu, an old martial art used by the samurais in real wars, that was banned with the end of the Feudal Japan. Kano’s strategy was to send his students on world tours, challenging other martial artists, in order to show how efficient Judo was, and to pursue his dream of making Judo a Olympic sport. The Gracies learned Judo from one of these students, the Judoka Mitsuyio Maeda, in the beginning of the XX century. Originally, Judo was called Kano JuJutsu, and that’s how it was taught to the Gracies. Since nobody wrote JuJutsu in the Latin Alphabet, JuJutsu became Jiu Jitsu. The Gracies then started teaching this new martial art in Brazil, focusing on self-defense. They called it Gracie Jiu Jitsu. However, Judo took a different approach. In the pursuit for the Olympic nommination, Judo became more and more sport-focused, trying to make the fights more appealing to the general public. Several moves were banned, a point-system was designed, and the International Judo Federation was created, in order to organize and establish the rules of the sport. When the Gracies moved to Rio de Janeiro, the capital of Brazil at the time, they saw the opportunity to spread their martial art, using the same strategy Kano used. They started challenging other martial artists to fights, being extremelly sucessful.Helio demonstrating Jiu Jitsu to the Brazilian Army. In the beginning of the 1950’s, Gracie Jiu Jitsu was already a respected and feared martial art in Brazil. Helio Gracie hadn’t had any losses, even though he was a 5´8″ (1,75m) 132lb (60kg), fighting much bigger opponents.3 Japanese Judokas, Toshio Yamagushi, Jukio Kato e Masahiko Kimura, were visiting Brazil at the time, for Judo demonstrations. They proposed a fight between Jukio Kato and Helio Gracie, since Kato and Helio were about the same size. Helio, then, asked to fight Kimura, who was a lot heavier than him, weighting 176 lbs (80kg). Kimura declined the offer, stating that “If I beat Helio, people will say it was due to the weight difference. I’m confident Kato will beat him, so this will be the fight”.Kimura Jukio Kato and Helio Gracie fought on September 6th 1951, at the Maracana Stadium, resulting on a draw. A second fight was schedulled for September 29th, in Sao Paulo, on the Pacaembu Stadium. This time, Helio won the fight, leaving Kato unconscious. Kimura then accepted to fight Helio. The fight was schedulled to happen at the Maracana stadium, on October 23rd.Kimura, confident that he would win quickly, declared that if the fight lasted more than three minutes, Hélio Gracie could be considered the winner. Hélio replied that "a fighter never runs away from the arena. Kimura can break my bones, but he won't break my morale. A good sportsman doesn't care about winning or losing, but fighting."On the schedulled date, 40 thousand people, including the vice-president of Brazil, attended the stadium to watch the duel.Eager to fulfill his promise to defeat Hélio Gracie in less than three minutes, Kimura started the fight by going for the Brazilian. Being on top, Kimura tried to finish the fight in every way, but Hélio dodged and used his famous guard to prevent the Japanese from threatening him.After the three minutes predicted by Kimura, the Japanese crowd no longer smiled so much, and the fighter himself showed more and more determination to win the fight as soon as possible. Even passing Hélio's guard and mounting the Brazilian, Kimura didn't get the submission in ten minutes of the first round. The first round then ended with Kimura throwing Hélio four times with osoto gari, ouchi gari, uchi mata and harai goshi. Kimura also inflicted painful and suffocating grappling techniques on Hélio, such as, kuzure-kamishiho-gatame, kesa gatame and sankaku jime. On the way to their corners, Hélio's smile contrasted with the Japanese's lack of expression. Kimura started the second round by taking Hélio down, and repeated the takedown five minutes into the fight. The violence of the fall made Hélio lose consciousness, not recovering it in time to defend the Japanese's indefensible armbar – which would later be named after him. Even without any possibility of extricating himself, Hélio refused to tap. Realizing that his brother would have a fractured arm, and knowing his fiber, which prevented him from giving up the fight, Carlos Gracie invaded the platform and tapped the ground three times, ending the fight.In an interview after the fight, published in the book "Carlos Gracie - the creator of a dynasty", by Reila Gracie, Hélio explained the reason for facing Kimura: “It didn't matter to me, as a Brazilian, before 40,000 brothers, to be defeated by a true giant - giant in size, energy and technique. A giant who wouldn't even give me the slightest chance. It meant a lot to my conviction, to my cartel and, why not say it, to my personal vanity. Despite being clearly defeated in the ring, I was comforted by the press and the public, because everyone had understood my intention, my desire to prove, with my possible massacre, the importance of fighting without hope of victory.” Kimura, throughout his life, gave numerous testimonies of praise to his rival, always calling him "the man who never gives up".
column9: You forgot to mention that they had their match on much thicker and softer mats than the regular mats. The Gracies knew if they fought on regular mats, Helio would lose quickly. Kimura was famous for having such a powerful o soto gari, it would KO his opponents. At first Helio said he was already unconscious when Kimura applied the udi garami, or what is now known in jiu jitsu as a kimura, and came to after his bone snapped. Later when marketing GJJ to the world, they came up with the ridiculous story how Kimura was 100 pounds heavier than Helio, and him sacrificing his arm out of pride. There's a reason the Gracies refuse to give out the entire video of their match, but the few clips there are show that Kimura outclassed Helio in every way. Props to Helio for his accomplishments, Gracie Jiu Jitsu is indeed a powerful system, but a lot of what they say is BS.

column1: As an ER nurse, have you ever taken care of someone who was alert, and responsive, but their lab work or imaging told a far different story as to how seriously ill they really were?
column3: I know this question asked for an ER nurse, which I am not, but I do have an answer to this. I used to work in a home for the elderly and those with dementia, while many spend many years at the home the truth is it was a waiting room for the final curtain call, some would die in the hospital but the majority of the residents were able to know their time was soon and would die in their beds at the home as comfortable as possible. One woman said she ‘was just under the weather’ but then she was feeling better, when actually she’d taken a bad fall in the night after deciding to walk around without her zimmer, she was found quickly but had suffered bleeds and other problems, it was a chain reaction and one thing after another was just getting worse one after the other but she claimed “everyone’s just fussing, I feel better, what’s the bother?” She had dementia but was still able to hold a strong conversation and take in information even if she told you the same story again soon, she was witty and very cheeky and she seemed like her good old self, when actually everything was showing she was getting worse, the nurse said “in other patients they can barely talk in her condition, never mind cracking jokes and knitting”. Then we thought she was showing signs of the end, she got slower, sleepier, more mumbles until she was basically just making hums and groans and this went on for a whole week and a half. In her final few days she suffered from bad circulation and we had her on as much support and things to make her comfortable while her family and professionals kept her company. I worked in activities so I rarely saw residents during their end of life care but she had a grandson around whom I watched when the family would get emotional or the grandmother was in a particularly hard to watch state so I was more involved in this case, especially as carers would ask me to assist in small things like notes and messages, just normal things like collecting towels, fluids etc. Due to the poor circulation and her condition she was extremely pale, almost grey, but her fingers, toes and even her mouth were practically black in colour, her eyes didn't focus on anyone, she twitched and didn't talk in conversation and was very weak and we knew she could go at any moment. That’s when I got the fright of my life, me, two of the family members, a nurse and a carer were in the room, talking to the family to keep their minds off things when all of a sudden the dying woman sat upright, threw the covers off of herself and looked at us with total focus and mid conversation, voice a bit wobbly but words clear as day and quick. Everyone, including the nurse were at a loss for words, because the woman wasn't trying to stand we didn't need to intervene but it was a shock, she was still grey and black around the lips and fingers, frail and considering she’d been on the decline for weeks only able to make simple noises it should have been impossible. But there she was, mid conversation with us on the topic we’d been having and she had been listening in great detail, she was her usual cheeky self even asking the male carer for a smooch then elbowing her daughter *nudge, nudge*. Her daughter got teary eyed and she was the comforting mum, even wiping her daughter’s tears with a black thumb, she became very self aware and looking at herself, claiming she hadn't ‘looked like this since [she] was 6 and playing in soot’ and laughing, she asked to see her grandson and after a little hesitation I went to get him, I explained outside the room what she looked like and that she was still very sick but she would love a gentle hug from her handsome grandson. He did and they had a weirdly nice day, nobody entirely sure what to make of it, then as I’m aware around 8am the next day she woke up from a sleep to the company of her daughter and son-in-law who had returned from home to sleep just before 7am and messaged for a carer, she said “are there no boys available?” very cheekily to the female carer and she said “not till this afternoon, I’m afraid” “oh, I’ll go back to sleep then, I was hoping a handsome man might dress me, you can go” and shooed her out with her hand and then rolled back as if to sleep (visible appearance and near death health stats exactly as it had been the day before.) Literally half an hour later she passed away.
column9: As a Hospice Nurse, we would sometimes call this the “the Last Goodbye.” It's somewhat common as a patient is actively dying and typically happens about a day before their death. I would explain to families ahead of time about the possibility of it happening so they wouldn't be surprised. One of my patients was very near death and had been unresponsive for days when he suddenly woke up, sat up and asked his family for a steak dinner. His family later told me how they had sat around his bed then…eating, laughing and sharing memories. After about an hour he layed back down, went to sleep and never woke back up. His family, like most friends and families, were grateful for that last special time together. Occasionally, I've seen “the Last Goodbye” turn out to be a disturbing event for the patient and/or family; I have no clue as to why it's sometimes a bad experience, unless it's the patient expressing his fear of dying.

column1: Why do I cry almost every day?
column3: How long has your crying been going on? If it's been more than a week, medical advice is typically to check in with your health care provider. (I'm not a medical professional.) Crying easily and feeling miserable are typically signs of depression. When you cry because you feel hurt (emotionally) and you "normally" would not be that emotional about it, that also suggests depression. When you cry "for no reason," you actually are crying for a reason; you're just not conscious of what it is. If you're anything like me, even happy things can make you cry when you're depressed-- thinking of something kind someone has done for you, for example. Some people feel miserable and cry easily due to high anxiety. But often, that degree of anxiety is manifested (in part) by depression. Meanwhile (until you can see a health professional), here are a few practices that might help. Or maybe not; everyone is different.Listen to uplifting music-- music that is not nostalgic for you, music that is not sad or angry in its lyrics.Be sure you are getting 7-8 hours/night of deep sleep. (Try home remedies first, like a cup of camomile tea or a small bowl of milk and low-sugar cereal before bed.)Let the tears out but attempt to bring yourself back to a quieter mental state afterward. Tears release hormones that can be quite helpful in dissipating the underlying tension you feel. But it's important to do what you can after "a good cry" to calm yourself down.Close your eyes and take a few deep, slow breaths at least every 2 hours. Be careful not to do too many of these breaths as they can cause hyperventilation.Jot down what "losses" you have had in the past 3-6 months: Have you lost a friend? A family member? A pet? A job? Has someone you care about deeply disappointed you (another kind of loss)? Have you lost something else that meant a lot to you? Have you disappointed yourself in some major way (another kind of loss)? Writing this list might bring tears, which is just fine. Knowing what's at the root of your emotional state will be really helpful in recovering from it. Do not self-medicate. No alcohol (which is a depressant) or over-the-counter drugs that you think might help. These substances can worsen your symptoms considerably!I'm sorry that you are feeling miserable and crying frequently. Get help.
column9: You people always sit there and say get help, yet you don't even understand that the help that is offered just makes eveeyrhing worse and more hopeless. column1: Why would a man lead you on?
column3: PREFACE If you’re looking for answers on Quora, you’ve probably been hurt by a man who was irresponsible with your feelings. There’s shock, embarrassment, and loss. You’re looking for answers, a place to process, and reassurances. I’m here for you! I disagree with some of the responses to this question, which echo the (sexist) popular wisdom: you didn’t keep your guard up. Your boundaries were weak. You didn’t follow the “rules,” and carry yourself as “a woman of value.” You didn’t make the man “earn it.” You were naive and didn’t see the signs. I’m here to empathize with you and tell you that this was not your fault. I’m an intelligent, professional woman who works in public relations. My currency is relationships and getting to the bottom of peoples’ intentions. And yet, I found myself in your shoes. So before we dig into the “why,” I ask that you show yourself some compassion. WHY: EMOTIONAL LABOR Men still aren’t doing their own emotional labor. If they’re immature, they’ll lead a woman on for a plethora of reasons that fulfills any or all of their needs. Though I’m hopeful for the “woke” generation, a great deal of men are unable or unwilling to rely on their inner resources as they experience normal, everyday struggles. Coddled by family members and outdated social structures, misleaders can live a long time without learning emotional regulation. So it’s not surprising that some take no responsibility for their own behaviors and feelings. This can show up in subtle ways, like apologizing to a man to spare his ego. It can be as egregious as excusing his abuse. None of us want to be used. Rest assured that it takes a lot of manipulation, enabled by generations of male privilege, in order to commit love fraud. Thus the maxim: “Women fake orgasms (to spare egos). Men fake relationships (to feed egos).” PROFILES OF MISLEADERS Misleaders devalue women, believing they’re entitled to a woman’s attention and care. Vulnerable misleaders look for women they perceive to be easy targets. They prefer high empathy women. They’ll lead with interest and win your sympathy. At the beginning, the care will be mutual and reciprocal. Just as you develop intimacy and shared vulnerability, a precursor to healthy love, he discards you and says you misread his signs. He intended to use you as an emotional cushion for as long as possible, so his withdrawal will feel sudden and cruel. Misleaders also do it for entertainment and sport. These types seek out the assertive and confident among us, because they’re in it for the challenge and ego stroke that comes from a woman’s resistance and capitulation. Typically, these are men prone to novelty-seeking. They may hide their history of commitment issues, which were present long before you entered the picture, because they see healthy relationships as dull and unexciting. They’re also persistent as fuck. Some will carry on for years until they gain your trust. Once you give in, the excitement of pursuit is gone. He vanishes and says you misunderstood him. Because of their novelty-seeking drives, these misleaders are often covert emotional cheaters. Don’t be surprised if you learn that they’ve been engaged with several women at once. The worst of the lot are those who mislead their female friends. They’re the laziest and most exploitative of the fakers (demisexuals, beware). It’s less work to manipulate you if you already trust them. Because most women won’t risk losing a friendship unless it’s serious, it can take overt signals, or outright lies, to get you to relax a boundary. Once you’re into him, the connection intensifies due to familiarity. You’ll feel like you’re falling for your best friend, and falling hard. But as it turns out, you just imagined those feelings. You’ll feel embarrassed and exposed. He’ll expect your grace and forgiveness, as he “lets you down gently,” and assumes you’ll just go back to being “friends.” Finally, there’s the try-before-you-buy misleader. He’s not in touch with his wants, needs and feelings. Instead of going to therapy or doing the inner work needed to know himself better, he uses women to “find” and understand himself. From the beginning, this man is completely unsure about you, but he’ll behave as if he’s all in. He starts to imagine himself in a “test” relationship with you, until he learns you’re not what he wants. This is the misleader most likely to ghost you or deal with confrontation by using the silent treatment. He’s a total coward. IT WAS INTENTIONAL “But it wasn’t intentional!” You’ll hear this excuse from most of the men who misled you. It’s bullshit. Don’t let yourself be gaslit nor tolerate accusations of “crazy.” In the vast majority of cases, misleaders are reading the emotional subtext quite well. The question is whether they acknowledge it and do something about it, or ignore it and let you get hurt through passive neglect. Both are unacceptable. Instead of communicating with you and letting you go, misleaders reap the benefits of your affection while they furtively pull away. Case in point: I read about one woman who was dumped unexpectedly at the end of what she was told would be a romantic holiday. While the man accepted blowjobs and orgasms from her all weekend, he already knew he didn’t care for her. He’d never been “serious,” and it was her fault for misconstruing what was “just casual and fun.” WHAT NOW Because you’re healthy and, unlike the other party, don’t use people for emotional labor, you already know that healing will be done on your own. This can make a connection with a misleader especially painful. There’s deception and loss, without the acknowledgment of a relationship. Some of your friends will be unhelpful, because it’s easy to minimize what isn’t formal. Though you’ll probably find that there are sympathetic women who have been in your shoes before. In most cases, I suggest complete withdrawal (no contact) as a preferred response. It signals that this person utterly fucked up. They’re not worth an iota of your time. Misleaders don’t feel guilty about what they did. But if they’re going to develop a conscience and feel the urge to apologize, it will only happen after they experience the loss of you. Save your valuable energy, and be wary of that they may come back to try and pick at the carcass of this “relationship.” There won’t be a second opportunity to earn your trust. But you will cooly accept their apologies if they offer them. If you feel the need to tell the person off, accept that confrontation puts you at a bit of a disadvantage. It makes you even more emotionally unattractive and shows that they’ve managed to get under your skin. One time, a misleader laughed at me when he explained I was imagining his overtures — he had mused about having a baby with me — and that fucking set me off. If it’s cleansing and helpful to get angry, then do it. Just know that this will be your final and only interaction if you lose your cool with a misleader. Subsequent attempts at contact, if only for closure, can be twisted and misconstrued. Since the misleader is claiming that you imagined his interest, these efforts only make you look crazy and “obsessed with him.” Delete the misleader’s contact and block him on social media. If you need to vent call a friend or reach out to kind strangers on the internet. There are plenty of forums out there for broken hearts. IF HE WAS A FRIEND If your misleader was a friend, getting over this is not going to be easy. You’ll need to accept reality, manage your image, and decide whether he was your “friend” at all. Relationships are complex and only you have the context needed to make decisions. That means that you’ll have to use your intuition to navigate yourself through nuance and uncertainty. Because your misleader was a trusted friend, not just some fuckboy, you’ll be improvising and reevaluating things as you work through your feelings. The betrayal will cut differently, so you’re going to want to react and argue. Especially with a friend with whom you’d normally be candid. My advice is to ask for space and take your time. Don’t make hasty decisions that allow a dysfunctional person to quickly reenter your life without consequences. And don’t throw away a friendship if you deem it worthy of forgiveness and preservation. It usually takes two weeks to accept a sudden romantic loss (and much longer to grieve it). It takes at least another two weeks to parse the romantic feelings from the friendship, so you can then start looking at it objectively. Only you can look at the big picture and decide what comes next. You’ll want to reflect on the length of the friendship, your shared history, and the misleader’s overall pattern of behavior. You might consider other circumstances where you were granted forgiveness by him and decide you would extend it in return — so long as there’s concern and remorse. If you decide to be magnanimous, the relationship will have to start from zero. Boundaries are clarified and trust rebuilt little by little. If there’s any violation of that, you immediately pull away. Perhaps indefinitely. If you’re connected to the misleader through with school, work or overlapping friends, you’ll need to deal with this with even more nuance. If you don’t want the friendship, you’ll need a strategy for civility. Take the high road and let it go, but be smart by keeping your distance in social situations. Be formal and polite and cool. Manage your image by not talking about with the misleader with those who might gossip — again, your friends on the internet are here for you! LOVE YOURSELF Misleaders are cowards skilled at manipulation. They’ve mastered the art of the mindfuck. You’re going to feel pretty raw and rejected, so it’s important to love and care for yourself. Try to make healthy choices and stick to positive routines. Start off by giving yourself one week to do whatever you want — mope around, be reclusive, cry, feel sorry for yourself. Then focus on self-care and healing. There are countless strategies for taking care of yourself. Some might include venting, writing down your feelings (and not sending those impulsive texts!), and paying attention to emotional pain you might be storing in your body. A bath goes a long way in relaxing tension, and studies have shown that acetaminophen can help you recover from heartbreak more quickly. Take care of yourself and remember that none of this was your fault. You did nothing to deserve being mislead. You trusted a person in good faith, which is necessary to build healthy relationships of all kinds. Because of this, it’s likely you have a community of good people around you. We’re here for you in this difficult time.

column1: How do you recognize signs of psychological trauma in a person?
column3: If it’s hard for the person that suffers from psychological trauma to recognize it, it’s even harder to notice it in someone, especially if you didn’t know the person before the traumatization, and even more difficult if the psychological trauma is complex. Psychological trauma causes a series of changes in mood, sleeping, tolerance, physiology, etc., but these changes can be clear and distinguishable just after a traumatic event, or subtle and imperceptible if the traumatization happened through a long period of time. For example, a person can become reactive if you criticize them, but you can’t know whether the reaction is a trauma response or if simply a bad mood one. The person may be anxious but it may be really difficult to know if the anxiety is a habit or a symptom of trauma. With a trained eye, you may be able to recognize psychological trauma symptoms by how the autonomic nervous system reacts to stimuli, by how easily the person becomes overwhelmed when experiencing emotions or remembering, by how they are driven by fear, by how the person feels defeated or hopeless, and by how much a person dissociates and in what circumstances. But you need to observe the person very carefully and attentively besides asking many questions and understanding their experiences. In general, I advise not to diagnosticate people if you are not a mental health professional. Labels affect self-esteem and influence behavior. If you are just curious, you can always read the diagnosis criteria on the DSM or the ICD to learn more about how many different symptoms need to be present for someone to really meet criteria. It’s almost impossible to be monitoring people around and have a mental count of how many symptoms they have, right? But here are the 2 different ways to see if someone meets criteria to be diagnosed: The ICD-10 criteria say:The patient must have been exposed to a stressful event or situation (either brief or long-lasting) of exceptionally threatening or catastrophic nature, which would be likely to cause pervasive distress in almost anyone.There must be persistent remembering or “reliving” of the stressor in intrusive “flashbacks,” vivid memories, or recurring dreams, or in experiencing distress when exposed to circumstances resembling or associated with the stressor.The patient must exhibit an actual or preferred avoidance of circumstances resembling or associated with the stressor, which was not present before exposure to the stressor.Either of the following must be present: Inability to recall, either partially or completely, some important aspects of the period of exposure to the stressor. Persistent symptoms of increased psychological sensitivity and arousal (not present before exposure to the stressor), shown by any two of the following: Difficulty in falling or staying asleep.Irritability or outbursts of anger.Difficulty in concentrating.Exaggerated startle response.Criteria B, C, and D must all be met within 6 months of the stressful event or at the end of a period of stress. (For some purposes, onset delayed more than 6 months can be included, but this should be clearly specified.)The DSM-5 says:Exposure to actual or threatened death, serious injury, or sexual violence in one (or more) of the following ways: Directly experiencing the traumatic event(s). Witnessing, in person, the event(s) as it occurred to others. Learning that the traumatic event(s) occurred to a close family member or close friend. In cases of actual or threatened death of a family member or friend, the event(s) must have been violent or accidental. Experiencing repeated or extreme exposure to aversive details of the traumatic event(s) (e.g., first responders collecting human remains; police officers repeatedly exposed to details of child abuse). Note: Criterion A4 does not apply to exposure through electronic media, television, movies, or pictures, unless this exposure is work related.Presence of one (or more) of the following intrusion symptoms associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning after the traumatic event(s) occurred: Recurrent, involuntary, and intrusive distressing memories of the traumatic event(s). Note: In children older than 6 years, repetitive play may occur in which themes or aspects of the traumatic event(s) are expressed.Recurrent distressing dreams in which the content and/or affect of the dream are related to the traumatic event(s). Note: In children, there may be frightening dreams without recognizable content.Dissociative reactions (e.g., flashbacks) in which the individual feels or acts as if the traumatic event(s) were recurring. (Such reactions may occur on a continuum, with the most extreme expression being a complete loss of awareness of present surroundings.) Note: In children, trauma-specific reenactment may occur in play.Intense or prolonged psychological distress at exposure to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event(s).Marked physiological reactions to internal or external cues that symbolize or resemble an aspect of the traumatic event(s).Persistent avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by one or both of the following: Avoidance of or efforts to avoid distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event(s).Avoidance of or efforts to avoid external reminders (people, places, conversations, activities, objects, situations) that arouse distressing memories, thoughts, or feelings about or closely associated with the traumatic event(s).Negative alterations in cognitions and mood associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by two (or more) of the following: Inability to remember an important aspect of the traumatic event(s) (typically due to dissociative amnesia, and not to other factors such as head injury, alcohol, or drugs). Persistent and exaggerated negative beliefs or expectations about oneself, others, or the world (e.g., “I am bad,” “No one can be trusted,” “The world is completely dangerous,” “My whole nervous system is permanently ruined”).Persistent, distorted cognitions about the cause or consequences of the traumatic event(s) that lead the individual to blame himself/herself or others.Persistent negative emotional state (e.g., fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame). Markedly diminished interest or participation in significant activities. Feelings of detachment or estrangement from others.Persistent inability to experience positive emotions (e.g., inability to experience happiness, satisfaction, or loving feelings).Marked alterations in arousal and reactivity associated with the traumatic event(s), beginning or worsening after the traumatic event(s) occurred, as evidenced by two (or more) of the following: Irritable behavior and angry outbursts (with little or no provocation), typically expressed as verbal or physical aggression toward people or objects.Reckless or self-destructive behavior.Hypervigilance.Exaggerated startle response.Problems with concentration.Sleep disturbance (e.g., difficulty falling or staying asleep or restless sleep).Duration of the disturbance (Criteria B, C, D and E) is more than 1 month.

column1: During the day I feel really tired. What can I do to get Instant energy?
column3: Finding that last breath of strength beyond what you thought was possible Tapping into hidden strength can be summoned when you least expect it. As a young person, I have always thought of myself as shy, weak and easily lead. Admiration would wash over me every time I saw someone outspoken and stood up for what they believed in. I was petrified of even having an opinion - let alone expressing it. Becoming an outcast and demanding other people's attention was not my intention, so I stayed quiet and out of the way. Life has a funny way of nudging you out of your quiet space - or more so, pushing you over the water's edge and forcing you to learn how to swim. My first attempt at building strength began in the gym. After that, I went from being a weaker link to someone that grew to be strong and confident. As you start to build upon your self-belief - knowing you can and will lift the weight you want - eventually, that mindset begins to affect your life in more ways than one. As you start to quash all of your negative self-beliefs in strength capabilities, then the outside world becomes a lot easier to conquer. Some of the most trying times in life are those in which you have to find that last drop of inner strength when there isn't anything left to take. I know that feeling all too well now. When my mum was first diagnosed with pancreatic cancer, every month that progressed saw me exhausted, drained and unable to find the energy or stamina for even the simplest things. Cooking my meals, let alone being here for my family, was a stretch. So was working long hours to meet all my deadlines whilst sitting in a hospital room with three other terminally ill people - it was tough. The most heartbreaking thing you could ever watch is your parent slowly become weaker and weaker. As I look through old photos of mum and how she used to look - I can see just how much cancer has already taken away from her. Although it's tough to find inner strength when you are tired, I have discovered a few strategies that have helped me deal with the emotional pain of my current situation. Although it's not a foolproof cure, the steps are achievable for anyone who wants to keep pushing through emotional and mental anguish daily. Most of us in situations where we must deal with a terminally ill family member - there is no choice in the matter. We have to find ways to help us cope better and lead a semi-normal life as best as possible. Step one: Schedule some self-care time every day. If this is only realistic for one hour or 10 minutes - make the most of it. You spent that precious time unwinding in any way that resonates with your inner wellbeing. It could be going for a stroll in the sun, calling up a friend for a chat, drinking a nice, warm cup of tea, taking a warm bath or a go for a swim in the ocean. But, this one thing your soul calls out for you to do is revitalising and will initiate more strength inside of you. During this time, if emotions or particular self-talk comes up - acknowledge and accept that for what it is. Don't try to suffocate it with denial. Instead, let it come out in whatever way it needs to - be it crying, sadness or an emotional outburst. Now is the time to have it out with your emotions, and in due time, they will pass. Step two: Exercise is essential to maintain. I prefer lifting weights and power walking. Some people love yoga or running. Whatever it is, do it more often. Schedule that time for your health. Think of it as an investment in your mental health and wellbeing. Sure, it will take a bit of time - but you are worth it. That time is well spent on you - the most beautiful person in the world. Step Three: make the time to nourish yourself properly. As easy as it is to divert towards junk, or fast foods for that matter - this strategy will leave you feeling tired, drained and moody. Instead, pick live foods which will nourish your soul and increase energy levels. Think of green smoothies, fresh salads, high protein sources like eggs, chicken and seafood. If you are vegan, beans, lentils, and nuts will be your best accompaniments. Energy is required to gain strength in physical and mental clarity. So keep feeding yourself well, and you will have an abundance of both. Step Four: Talk to someone you trust. I love to check in with colleagues, friends and family members when I can. It's pretty easy to isolate yourself when things are tough. But, in my case, bothering other people with my problems and challenges is a stretch. You aren't bothering people at all (something I need to realise too). The ones who love and care for you are worried - checking in to see if they can help without sounding nosy and suffocating. Help them out a bit by touching base with them first and starting a conversation. We all need someone to turn to - even god or whoever you believe in. Speak with someone, and you may find clarity or have an insight. When we are in the moment, we can get lost in confusion. The people who love us can help steer us back to where we need to be. Step Five: Take a short break to refresh. Maybe you need a day or two off work, perhaps a day just for you. Once you separate yourself from something draining or challenging, you come back refreshed and revitalised, ready to get back into the trenches again. If you can't have a full day, why not half? That's still enough to do some unwinding or catch up with another person. Although it can be challenging to do some more than others, I encourage you to make an effort in putting the most important one as your daily habit. If we show self-care and love towards ourselves, we build and regenerate what’s missing within. Keeping a part of ourselves nourished allows us to tap into unknown strength for challenges, and it’s within those challenges that we become resilient. We must always fill the well with goodness to keep taking out of it. You can't get much from a dried-up well. Remember that. column1: What are some "rules for living" you have developed since starting recovery from narcissistic abuse?
column3: Rules for Living after Narcissistic Abuse;Develop a relationship with yourself first and foremost; in order to fully recover from any abusive situation, give time yourself time and space to heal. After an abusive relationship, you are in trauma so healing is your first priority, and necessary to understand your behavioural patterns. Remember that you are suffering from Complex PTSD so take your mental health seriously.Seek professional help; you will need all the help you can find to understand abusive relationships and why you didn’t see the red flags. I know now that the counsellor doesn’t need to use the N word in order to help you recover, although it would be nice to find someone who truly understands. Advice on how to heal from an abusive relationship is a good start.Buy Pete Walkers book ‘From Surviving to Thriving’ because it’s a comprehensive guide to recovery from C-PTSD. I have found that reading it one chapter at a time helped me and I worked on myself taking baby steps.Take the time to re-evaluate your values and erect strong boundaries; it’s time to understand what is important to you so that anyone who tests your values will set alarm bells ringing. Adopt the motto ‘to thy own self be true’ because anyone who professes to even like you, let alone love you, will never walk over your values.Be careful in whom you place your trust; you now know that even family members can’t be trusted let alone so called ‘experts’, so you have to trust yourself to weed out the good from the bad.Grieve the loss of who you once were; it’s hard to come to terms with the reality that you had a narcissist in your life since you were born. It doesn’t necessarily have to be a parent but a caregiver of some sort. You were a child so that injured child still resides inside you. Ask yourself what you’d do if an abused child came to seek comfort from you and then realise that you need to nurture your own inner child.Remember that you are a survivor; you are stronger than you’ll ever know so please be very kind to yourself and stop putting everyone else before you.Begin to thrive; there is an enormous difference between surviving an abusive relationship with a narcissist and going into the future as somebody who has healed. This is not an overnight process but it involves retraining your whole thought process and examining your behavioural patterns.Anger is a natural reaction but don’t stay in this emotion; being angry all the time is just using up your valuable time that you need to devote to your recovery. Don’t give Narcissists the satisfaction of destroying the good qualities that are part of you.The above will take some time post break-up so, if you manage to do all of the above, you’ll be ready to live a life free from abuse. It’s in your hands now and you must take the responsibility for the adult person you now want to be.
