column1: Can your therapist get fatigued of you? Can they stop caring as much as they used to?
column3: Can your therapist get fatigued of you? Can they stop caring as much as they used to? There are so many layers to that set of questions. First, of course, anyone can encounter empathy fatigue or burnout, resulting in less ability to care than they used to have. The most compassionate parent or child in the world, might run out of steam caring for their ill family member if it goes on a long time, and there is no end in sight. If they’re smart, they get some help, take a break, and come back to it refreshed. Some don’t get help, and it’s bad for all concerned. As therapists are human, they can have this happen to them. The major differences are two: 1. The therapist is supposed to be trained to care for themselves and learn to recognize the symptoms to remind them they need to do more self-care, and to DO more self-care, so they don’t reduce their efficacy as a therapist, or worse, completely burn out and have to leave the profession. 2. The therapist is working with clients who are not the loved ones of their own life. The problems of their clients may be tremendously sad, but they are not the problems of the therapist. Proper training helps therapists learn to keep those boundaries, exactly so they can be strong when their clients are in deep pain. The clients count on that strength. Generally, if a therapist is having compassion fatigue or worse, burnout, it is not over a single, specific client. It is usually a general thing. If a therapist is having a specific problem with a specific client, it is time for the therapist to consult with a colleague or supervisor to help them figure out what it is about that client that is getting to them. As therapists, the job is to meet with people who are having problems, some of whom may not be able or willing to engage in their own treatment in a way that they must, in order to improve their situation. But they came to therapy, so they are on the right path, and therapists know part of their job is to help clients engage in the process. There may be situations where a client is paying the therapist just to placate the courts or a family member, and is not actually interested in engaging in the process, so they are taking the spot from someone who needs and wants the spot, and will benefit from it. In such a situation, it seems possible for a therapist to get tired of that client. But that situation is so rare—personally, I have never encountered it. Most clients who “refuse” to engage in treatment, but continue to come back, really do want to engage but they are not ready to. Then it is the therapist’s job to work with them to bring them to the place where they are ready to engage. Unfortunately, I have colleagues who have told me of clients who have been in this pre-engagement stage of therapy for years, and the therapists have tried everything they can think of, but the client doesn’t budge. In this case, it does sometimes happen that the therapist finds they tire of that particular client. Perhaps it is a reflection of a mismatch between therapist and client, even a lack of ability on the part of the therapist to manage this specific kind of client. The therapist might feel the client would be better off with a different therapist. The client might feel they are happy to keep going to therapy, have someone pay attention to all their complaints, and not have to change a thing. The client may not be at all interested in working with a therapist who pushes them. The client may want to just keep things as they are. But therapists, like everyone else with a career, do need some amount of seeing that their work accomplishes something worthwhile. Helping a client feel comfortable with being unwilling to change anything, may not suit a therapist, and they could get tired of that kind of client. If a therapist is properly trained and well-suited to the job, they should not be prone to getting “tired of” their clients. If a therapist is properly trained and well-suited to the job, but is getting tired of their clients, that therapist needs help. The nature of therapy is that clients will have accomplishments and setbacks, will do better, and then do worse. The more clients uncover issues and have successes working on them, the deeper into the issues they get. People only are able to deal with more distressing issues when they learn to deal with the less challenging ones. (Eventually, the worst ones can be found and handled—it doesn’t only go down, but in the middle it can sure feel like therapy just keeps digging up more trouble.) This means that in therapy, most clients will get better for a while as they improve in the first challenge, but then as they improve, they will feel safer and more capable, which leads to them bringing up harder, more painful, or more challenging issues. It’s like being able to lift heavier weights after training. The more you train, the heavier the weights you can lift. Often, the clients themselves do not realize this will happen, and what comes up later surprises the clients more than the therapists, who are used to this pattern. (I always explain this to my clients in advance, but some things just don’t really make sense until you experience them first-hand.) Personally, I tend to care more about my clients the longer I work with them, just because I know more about them, and they have become part of my life for longer. That said, there are times, say a particular session, where I might feel frustrated. Maybe that session seemed to not go so well, and I can’t figure out what I could have done better. I might have a flash of aiming that frustration at my client, but that passes. It’s not my clients’ job to make me happy!! If I got frustrated with my client, that is a giant red flag for me, that I need to work on myself. I have had a few clients who did not continue to work with me because they did not really want to work on their lives, they really only wanted sympathy, and generally to have a professional tell them they were a victim and everyone should pity them. Very few like that! But it happens. If their goal is to accept their situation, that’s a reasonable goal. For example, working on handling the feelings and returning to functional after the death of a loved one, is an excellent goal in therapy. Getting the therapist to agree with you that your life is permanently ruined, and everyone should take care of you forever, because you are destroyed by your loved one’s death, is not a good goal of therapy. When I try to help a client be more comfortable in their own skin, and manage to find a way to live a decent life even if terrible things happened in their lives, I am not denying that terrible things happened. I am asserting the positive option of focusing on what is good or possible in whatever life they may have. I had a client who was dying. She wanted to discuss some things she didn’t want to burden her family with, before she died. I was able to help her find a way of engaging her family such that they felt good about being her support in the end, and without her feeling like her revelations were too much for her family. I helped her and her family live the end of her life better, even though there wasn’t much life left. She died with less stress, and her family was happy to have contributed to the important process of the end of life. She still died, and the family still was sad at the loss. But we worked together to improve the parts that could be improved. Clients who feel I am too unwilling to accept defeat, choose to look for someone else. And I’ll admit, there have been two or three clients over decades of my career, who I found irksome. I considered them challenges, and I worked as hard as I could with them. Each chose to stop working with me, and I’ll admit I was relieved. Luckily, they were outliers (which is saying something, since I only work with outliers—these were outliers of outliers). And I still think about them, and wonder how I could have done things better. But I forgive myself, and allow that some people really are not ready to work on themselves, no matter who the therapist is. Or maybe I was just not the right one for them. I’m no superhero, and it is unrealistic to imagine I could help every single person who comes to me, even if their issues are within my areas of experience. Bottom line, if a client feels their therapist is getting tired of them—speak up! If one of my clients is under the impression that I’m tired of them, I absolutely want to know. I cannot work toward fixing the situation, if I don’t know the situation exists. What if one of those clients who did not want to actually improve anything, had told me they felt like I was tired of them? I would have explained my frustration. I would have been entirely honest, and explained that given the issues in their lives, either their problems were improvable, or they were not. And either we should work on improving the issues, or work on accepting them. But persistently being told the problems could not be fixed, and accepting them was not possible, was leaving me confused. I would ask them what they wanted to accomplish in therapy, what their goal or goals were. It would surely not be an easy conversation, but with those conflicts on the table, then we could work with reality. Reality is always an improvement over fantasy. Not that fantasy doesn’t have its place, but in therapy, reality is crucial. If your therapist really is fatigued of you, if your therapist really has lost their ability to care about you, and you are sure of this and you have discussed it with your therapist, then it might be time to either take a break, or try for a new therapist. But it isn’t always clear that the therapist is actually tired of the client. Many years ago, in a group therapy session where I was one of the clients, I had a problem with my contact lens. It got dry, or there was a speck of dust, I don’t know. But my focus on the group evaporated, as my focus on my irritated eyeball grew. Suddenly, one of the group members accused me of rolling my eyes at what she had said. I had no idea what she had said, heck, I didn’t even know what the topic of conversation was at that point. I explained that I had something going on with my contact lens. They didn’t believe me! At that point, my eye was in so much distress, I had to excuse myself to the bathroom to wash my eye with water, and try to fix the problem. I did manage to clear out whatever it was, and returned to the room, only to face being accused of lying to the group, and pretending to fix my contact lens as an excuse to leave the room. Nothing I could say would convince them. Not even my one bloodshot eye! I share this story to point out, I realize if you have a conversation with your therapist, and tell them what they did that lead you to feel they were tired of you, they may tell you a story about what really happened. They had a stomach ache, or they were unfortunately distracted by what an earlier client had said, and maybe their excuse was simply the honest truth. And maybe it was a lie to try to stop you from feeling bad. Here’s my advice: believe them. Because, if they are telling the truth, that’s a good reason to believe them. And if they are telling a lie, their discomfort with you will come up again and again—it will show up in new ways, and you can point it out then. Many clients come into therapy because of traumatic histories, especially in how they interacted with family members. And these clients often feel like people don’t really care about them, because someone important to them, like their parent or spouse, told them they cared, but they really didn’t. This lead to them not being able to tell when someone was telling them the truth regarding the meaning behind their behaviors. And that can lead to not believing one’s therapist when they tell you they had a real reason for behaving a certain way, and it was not because they were tired of you. A good therapist will recognize such a pattern, and discuss it with the client. They will tell you they understand why you would feel that way, and open up the conversation to allowing you to work through those feelings and beliefs. A therapist who is not good at the job, or who is lying, might get angry with you for not believing them, and if you keep trying to talk about it, will block engagement on that subject. This is why it is always the best approach to tell the therapist if you feel like they are tired of you. If they’re good, that gives them an opportunity to help you. If they’re not good, it gives you an opportunity to see them get defensive, and disallow you to continue to talk about your feelings. Then you’ll have a clearer sense of what’s going on, and how to proceed. One time, in my 20’s, a therapist told me I was “too much” for her, and recommended I see someone else. I was devastated! I was angry. I was a lot of negative things. But—I was also better off seeing someone else. And she—she was probably overdue for better training, a sabbatical, or a career change. Clients all come with issues, that is the nature of seeking therapy! If a therapist has trouble with that, it’s a problem. But many clients come to therapy with difficulties recognizing proper treatment. Clients can over- and under-react to how they are treated. They may put up with things that are terrible, or they may react to a contact lens problem as if it were proof of emotional abuse. It’s always a careful dance between therapist and client, to keep things real. And it is so worth it.

column1: How do hospice workers avoid burnout?
column3: Hospice workers are subject to burnout or its variants compassion fatigue and moral distress just as many other healthcare workers are. I think there are several factors that can prevent burnout for hospice workers -- specifically clinical staff: 1. Temperament and being well suited to the job. The fastest path to burnout in hospice is NOT being temperamentally suited to the job. To be successful in hospice, you have to not only know and accept but positively embrace the fact that nearly (not all!) your patients will die, and many of them quickly without saying a word or opening their eyes. Your job, as a nurse or social worker or chaplain or nurse's aide or physician, is to do everything in your power to ensure that your patient will have a comfortable and dignified death and his or her family members are supported through the process. If you can do that, know you did that, and go home smiling, you are well suited to the job. If you are distressed or saddened or feel that you have failed no matter how "good" the person's death is, you probably need to be in a different setting. This "strategy" for avoiding burnout is mostly innate rather than learned. It's why many hospice workers refer to their work as a "calling" rather than a job or even profession. Still, it is possible to learn how to "reframe" goals and the meaning of success and strengthen your hospice heart. An excellent guide for individuals and organizations in doing this is Brenda Clarkson and Myra Lovvorn's The Heart of Hospice: Core Competencies for Reclaiming the Mystery. 2. Abundant and frequent self-care!! Successful hospice workers learn (and this can/must be learned) how to leave their patients behind when the hospice workers go home. Setting firm boundaries between your work and home life is crucial, as is finding some source of joy, recreation, healthy distraction. Healthy is the key word -- exercise, good sleep, personal pampering, stress management, good diet, and no substance abuse are matters of survival. Hospice care addresses the physical, emotional, psychological, and spiritual needs of patients and families; hospice workers must look after their own just as aggressively. Many find great relief and refreshment in activities that are really different from hospice work -- caring for children or rock climbing, for instance -- or highly creative, regenerative activities like art, music, writing, and so on. It's also important to learn techniques for instant self-care. It's all very well (and important) to be able to turn off work and find your joy when you go home at the end of the day or night, but you also need to "find your happy place" in the midst of it. When patients are suffering no matter what you do, when families are fighting or in distress, when colleagues make mistakes that you have to fix, when ten different people want a piece of you right now. 3. Support from your colleagues, supervisors, and friends/family. Friends and family need to be sources of solace, people to whom you can safely vent without fear of judgement or rejection, and constructive distraction. There's nothing so healing as being greeted at the door with a hug or a "come see what I did today!" They need to listen when you want to talk and be able to talk about something else when you don't want to share. Colleagues and supervisors should be automatic sources of support because, after all, they know exactly what you are having to deal with. Sadly, hospice agencies are not automatically any better at dealing with their workers' stress or distress than any other organization. When hospice staff have experienced significant loss themselves or been stricken with disease or suffered breakdowns from burnout, I've seen some agencies respond with exquisite care and support. I've seen others be total boneheads (or worse) about it. Good support from your colleagues means having good team and interpersonal training and regular refreshers, a "safe" place and time to express yourself, a mechanism (such as an ethics committee) to hear about and address moral dilemmas or ethical conflicts, personnel policies that respond to extraordinary needs for time off or flexible schedules, and a real commitment to internal caregiving and compassion. Hospice is hard work, but it is also -- for those who can cope and even thrive within it -- extremely rewarding and life affirming. When it isn't, for too long, it's time to take a break or even move into another field. You can always come back!

column1: How do you get through the Dark Night of the Soul? How long does it usually last?
column3: To know how to get through a dark night of the soul requires you to realize the purpose of it. To make it simple, the purpose of a DNOTS is always and without exception to experience and be guided towards a spiritual awakening and to stop identifying with your ego. How long it lasts entirely depends on how much there is to get rid off. For some, it may last a few months but for others, it can last many years. Because your deep-rooted identification with ego (your ego is your conceptual self. The self that only exists as thought patterns in your mind and is therefore formless. It has no real presence in the external) is what causes a DNOTS in the first place. It is what keeps true self-actualization and the truth away from you. Think of a dark night of the soul as an ego death. Your ego dies so you can become who you truly are. Here is how you can handle a DNOTS:View it as an opportunity for a spiritual awakening.A spiritual awakening is not some kind of woo-woo bullshit. It is another term for becoming self-aware. Aware of your true self and your true nature that is free from social conditioning and ego. Your true self is the presence that experiences everything, the consciousness itself. It is not your beliefs, emotions or thoughts. It is also not your wealth, your car, your clothes or the titles, successes and achievements in your life.Endure the pain.A DNOTS is always very painful because it brings with it the realization that what we believed to be true was a lie. This period of your life may be caused by the unexpected loss of a family member which reminds you of your mortality, a breakup or divorce, the end of a career or any other devastating setback. Know that the pain you feel arises from the ego, your conceptual self. It is in pain because it can no longer sustain itself, since what it believed to be true was not true at all.Renew yourself.Use this DNOTS to make a new beginning in your life and hit the restart button.Meditate.Educate yourself about meditation and spirituality. Meditate daily for 15–30 minutes.Take massive action.Leave the toxic environment you are in and get into one in which you can grow, where you are loved, respect and cared for. Also do the changes you need to make. If you need therapy, take therapy. If you need to lose or gain weight, workout and eat healthier. If you have been very needy, narcissistic, toxic or bitter and resentful, heal yourself. Do what you have to do in order to heal, to transcend neediness, to become less narcissistic and less toxic and find joy in life. This is how you can let go of the past.Experience the freedom and bliss of a spiritual awakening.As I said before, every DNOTS ends with a spiritual awakening. This is basically a state of joy, freedom and new-found enthusiasm for life. But don't just wait for this awakening to come. Keep taking action. You will know when you reached a spiritual awakening. It may not come after months or years but you will 100% experience it at some point.
column9: I just read about the dark night of the soul in your book. Your words couldn’t have come at a better time for me. Everything you said is true. I came out the other side much better for it. Thank you Daniel.

column1: In your opinion, did George W. Bush do more harm or good during his time as president?
column3: In his defense, he had an incredibly bad start stemming from the hanging chads in Florida. Moreover, any nominee, irrespective of party, would have fought tooth and nail to prevail under those conditions, especially after his opponent had conceded by phone. Any conduct short of that would have been regarded as highly self-defeating from a political standpoint and would have seriously undermined his and other family members’ future political aspirations, as the term “wimp,” somewhat unjustly applied to his father, would have acquired even deeper meaning and lasting significance for the entire family. Moreover, one should bear in that any presidential nominee, irrespective of party, not only is heading but also carrying the rest of the ticket, so any admission, display of weakness or outright concession has implications for other nominees. Also, Republican nominees, certainly a generation ago when “W” entered office, are invariably bled and weakened by a thousand cuts over the course of the campaign - their intellect and command of language invariably questioned and, with the context of mainstream entertainment, ridiculed. W’s intellect was subject to especially severe scrutiny by the media, some commentators regarding it as a potential national security concern. Moreover, W’s entire life before his presidency essentially was characterized by some as inconsequential, given the fact that he was the son of an Ivy League-educated former president who wielded enormous power and influence long before his presidency. To be sure, that has been the nature of politics certainly since the New Deal era when managerial liberalism extended its influence not only into the federal bureaucracy but also into the major academic, political and cultural institutions to the point where it has become virtually culturally hegemonic as well as the default political ideology among political and cultural elites To repeat: Bush faced some major obstacles upon assuming power - arguably more than his immediate predecessors, significantly because of the protracted electoral impasse in Florida. Yet, any incoming Republican president has to take special care not to hand a sword to his political nemeses, which W did, even playing into his media stereotyping. The “WMD” debacle - the claim that Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein possessed chemical weapons though none we found despite invasion and regime change that cost billions of dollars and hundreds of lives - proved to be the worst mistake of his presidency, placing the the GOP in Watergate territory, serving the narrative of a party operating at the behest of corporate interests. In the weeks following Saddam's overthrow, this was exacerbated by the “Mission Accomplished” banner conspicuously displayed above the deck of the carrier onto which Bush flew, in Top Gun style, to receive the accolades of a grateful nation, even though U.S. occupation forces faced a protracted insurgency that lasted months and that only perpetuated the media narrative and the view that the 41st president's privileged son indeed was a bit of a ne'er do well, a recovering alcoholic who, after, finding religion, had embarked on a self-help regimen which alas, included serving a gig in the White House. Moreover, as things worked out, “Bush 43” arguably was the president who sank the rather rickety fusionist ship that had paved Ronald Reagan's path to power and sustained a what was perceived as a reasonable sucessful two-term presidency. Fusionism, as the term implies, involved the forging of two elements deeply rooted in the American experience and culture: a devotion to a relatively unhampered market and religious sentiment, broadly expessed as religious values. Yet, the fusion ship had begun to take in water and list during the administration of “Bush 41,” who never seemed as devoted to this modus vivendi in quite the same way as his predecessor. As it turns out, both of these presidents were equally disposed to free trade agreements that, despite the hundreds of billions of dollars that accrued to the U.S. and, for that matter, the global economy, resulted in the unemployment of millions of Americans and in the economic decline of cities and towns across the United States. This sense of displacement had begun to set in during the W presidential era. Yet, W, despite what he regarded as his impeccable evangelical credentials and his crafting of a new, humane form of Republicanism dubbed “compassionate conservatism,” never managed to gain much traction with what soon would become the heartland, populist right. Many on the right regarded his re-packaged conservatism and his domestic programs with ambivalence, if not suspicion. And after what amounted to the loss of the post-Cold War peace dividend following the impasse in Iraq and the disastrous 2008 economic crash, Bush ended up falling between two stools, failing to build a bridge to moderates and demographic groups at least somewhat receptive to elements of Republican messaging, even while alienating much of his own base. He is presidency likely will be remembered as a transitional one, certainly the one that ended the quarter century of conservation fusionism when Republicans could extol simultaneously market capitalism and traditionalism. In a very real sense, W failed conspicuously and arguably destroyed the elements that kept this tenuous balance in place.
column9: An interesting and fair analysis. While W seems to be a relatively decent human being, especially compared to former President Trump, he seems to have been largely out of his depth for the challenges of his presidency. The invasion of Iraq is possibly the greatest foreign policy mistake of any US president in my lifetime (up there with opening the US economy to Chinese imports).

column1: How do you find out if you have C-PTSD?
column3: To really find out whether —or in which ways— you were hurt by having been exposed to toxic stress for a prolonged period of your life is a difficult task. The first step is to understand the story. There are circumstances that increase the possibility of having developed C-PTSD. Everything that qualifies as a scary environment besides the obvious (like neglect, sexual or physical abuse, etc.):unstable family members (alcoholic relative, incarceration, aggression, mental illness, physical illness, sudden or painful losses, etc.)emotionally abusive relationships (relatives, leaders, spouses, job environment, oppressive/racist systems, etc)the use of weapons in the house or neighborhood (living in a dangerous building, war zones, shelters, political instability and abuse, military, etc.)living under difficult and challenging circumstances (undocumented, political asylum, racism, poverty, religious intolerance, divorce, prolonged chronic illness, foster care, etc)experiencing constant rejection, bullying, criticism, shaming, unpredictability, surgeries, frequent or prolonged separation from caregivers, instability, frequent relocation, etc.The story and circumstances tell you how often and how severe the system may have felt threatened. The more threatening and the longer the situation was endured, the higher the probability of having negative consequences that affect the way your nervous system operates. Assess emotional stability After learning about the possible situation that destabilized the system, it’s important to learn what type of strategies the person’s system “chose” for survival. Living in a threatening environment continuously activates survival strategies until it reaches the point where the system can’t handle any more small changes and make the changes permanent, becoming traumatized. After that, the system operates differently than before with the goal to stay afloat. This means that during the threat and after developing C-PTSD, the body suffers alterations trying to “adjust” to the circumstances. These adjustments could be seen as strategies for survival. They become automatic reactions that modify personality, behavior, and the sense of who the person is. To assess emotional stability is necessary to understand what type of strategies developed due to the circumstances, and which ones are healthy and which ones are unhealthy, and how much control the person can exercise over them. An emotionally stable person can withstand difficult situations, handle adversity, and remain productive and capable throughout. If the person is not emotionally stable, that will reflect on the way they react, and the way they feel out of control. Executive functions Executive functions are altered by trauma. Having an assessment of them can also be an indication of whether trauma developed or not. People that suffer from C-PTSD will lack many of them. The list is extensive but it’s worth checking them. The more executive functions missing, the higher the probability of suffering from C-PTSD. That means that the prefrontal cortex (PFC) may have not developed appropriately, or that became inactive, slow, or imbalanced. A good list of them could be found here What are the signs of poor executive functioning? Symptoms The list of symptoms is even longer than of all the functions of the prefrontal cortex. Here I included a very long list Antonieta Contreras's answer to What are some unusual signs of C-PTSD? Checking for symptoms is obviously necessary to evaluate the presence of C-PTSD. The more symptoms, the higher the probability of suffering complex trauma. Some of the most important symptoms are those similar to PTSD plus:feelings of shame or guiltdifficulty controlling emotionsperiods of losing attention and concentration (dissociation)physical symptoms, such as headaches, dizziness, chest pains and stomach achesself-cutting and self-destructive behaviorisolating from friends and familyrelationship difficultiesimpulsivitymood swingsextreme anxiety and irritability; uncontrollable anger and rageparanoia and being suspicious of other peoplefeeling empty, hopeless, and worthless.Emotional/Traumatic Reactions Recognizing the way the system reacts and in what circumstances it reacts is a life long pursuit, but also necessary to evaluate whether complex trauma is present. We all have emotions and therefore, emotional reactions, but complex trauma reactions are out of the ordinary. Their characteristic is that most people won’t understand them, while they are extremely evident for the sufferer. The sufferer would consider evident why they react the way they do, and spend log time trying to explain it or justifying themselves for it, while others may consider it inappropriate, extreme, illogical, and will may call it drama. That creates confusion and further activation since the reason for the reaction and the reaction itself get invalidated. The sufferer believes s[h]e knows the reason but in reality, most people with C-PTSD won’t be aware of the connection with trauma, and therefore, don’t know the real reason for their reactions. They will attribute it to the event, or the actions of others when it’s really a reaction based on trauma. The traumatized person can’t let go easily the feelings of hurt, and the emotional dysregulation. Perception Once the nervous system gets altered on a semi-permanent basis, the perception of time, safety, and meaning get distorted.TimeTime gets distorted and the past feels current, and the present may feel absent. People carry believes that were developed during the time of extreme stress, making them pervasive throughout their lives. For instance, If someone made fun of them and made them feel inadequate, they will feel inadequate in many circumstances even when they have proof that they are not. A series of events will make them feel inadequate even when it’s only them that perceive it that way. The way they felt during the development of the complex trauma will remain and will feel real years after the stressful/traumatizing situation is over.SafetyPeople with complex trauma feel unsafe in general. They lack trust in others and in themselves. What for someone could be a comment, for someone that got traumatized due to criticism will sound like an attack. Something that seems mildly dangerous would be extremely scary for them.MeaningSince the person lives in survival mode, situations that seem “normal” to others could seem extreme (unfair, threatening, hurtful, infuriating, etc.) to someone with C-PTSD. They feel like victims or accept a martyr stance feeling less than others. They suffer from self-doubt constantly, and/or dissociate from the sense of who they are, and what the actions of others mean. They may lack a sense of style, or an understanding of social norms. Very often they find their own meaning of things trying to make sense of life. Recognize triggers Triggers are a good indication that the nervous system got altered and therefore there is trauma. Triggers have to do with the type of events, circumstances, or any other element that can cause distress either in an exaggerated way, or in an incomprehensible way. For example, people can get activated and start getting angry, feisty, ruminating, etc., because of someone throwing the garbage on the floor. For a person with no traumatic responses, the event will pass inadvertent or will fade away in minutes, while to someone with C-PTSD the distress could last hours or even days. They may seem illogical or extreme, but they have an effect on the person that feels absolutely real. Even when it’s very hard to identify triggers right away, noticing that there are certain things that could create more distress that what could be considered normal is a good indication of dysregulation and possible traumatization. Inexplicable medical issues Most people that suffer from C-PTSD complain about medical issues that are hard to explain for medical professionals. They can also present chronic illnesses that are not congruent with their age or with their family medical histories. They could be allergies, digestive problems, pain, insomnia, and even rheumatoid arthritis. The more of these indicators you have, the higher the probability of suffering from complex trauma.

column1: Why don't physicians inform patients about the realities of life sustaining treatment?
column3: In general because of Time. Life sustaining treatments are done for the purpose of sustaining life in that moment. Explaining the realities of all the possible or probable sequela from initiating and continuing life sustaining treatments would take too much time. Time the patient would not have in order for such treatments to be effective and time the doctor does not have to give. I had an anaphylaxis occur in 2002, very bad, 6 months after getting married at an orthopedic dinner at an upscale restaurant. My wife, an anesthesiologist, almost had to perform a tracheotomy, but the paramedics arrived in time to intubate me. The reality is that without intubation and an airway, I would be dead. Attempting the airw → well the realities stem from me going home the next day (which I did), to me remaining intubated for airway swelling for days, to me requiring a real tracheotomy which would then heal over weeks to months, to me having brain damage, kidney failure, multi-organ failure and then eventual and/or prolonged time at a nursing home before death. There is no time to ask, “Hey, do you want this guy intubated, because here is the reality…” I use the airway example because it is an easy one to understand. Oxygen is good for life, no oxygen is bad for life and lethal after a few minutes. But, there are many life sustaining treatments that are not so easy to think about. Many cardiac problems are salvageable in the moment (thus preventing death), only to leave the patient a cardiac-cripple… unable to be off oxygen and unable to do much of anything for the remainder of their life. Removing a lung to save someone from lung cancer works to stop the cancer from killing them within months but often leaves a patient with air hunger for the remainder of their days, sometimes years of agony. Placing a patient on dialysis to ‘get them through’ a period of kidney dysfunction is great if the kidneys begin working again, but sucks if they are now dependent on dialysis 3 times a week for the rest of their life. I could go on and on… so many things in medicine we perform in the moment for the expectation of the best outcome possible. Once a patient is stable, the effects of life sustaining treatments can be explained to the patient and/or the family members. These ‘reality’ conversations can be very difficult especially as it becomes obvious the ‘best outcome’ will not be happening to a loved one or yourself. Doctors do not have a crystal ball. However, we can, on average guess very well as to probable outcomes, given large populations - 100’s of patients, all suffering the same injury. For example - Age greater than 90 years, compound femur fracture. Given 100 patients like this: With NO treatment - 99/100 will die within 8 weeks, WITH surgical stabilization, 90/100 of them will die before 8 weeks, of the 10 remaining 9/10 will die between 8 weeks and 8 months, 1/100 will live longer than 8 months. Or, my self-example of a 31 year old otherwise healthy athletic male anaphalyxsis from peanuts: With NO treatment - 100/100 will die within 8 minutes (3 minutes for brain damage, 5 minutes for brain death, 8 minutes for cardiac death due to lack of oxygen, WITH intubation/tracheotomy stabilization, 100/100 of them will live for the next 8 minutes, of the 100 remaining 99.99/100 will live between 8 minutes and 8 days, 99.98/100 will live longer than 8 weeks. That’s right, 1/10,000 31 y/o males with that particular severe anaphylactic reaction would die secondarily ‘to the treatments’ or in the ICU between 8 minutes and 8 days.. and one more will die in a nursing facility secondary to brain damage/multiple systems organ failures. Right before the family/patient and the doctors make the decision to proceed with surgery/treatment or not proceed with surgery/treatment… there is no way to know with any certainty what outcome for a single individual will occur. At the TIME of the decision, there is no way of knowing. Furthermore, the discussion of whether to proceed or not needs to be made in a matter of hours… normally not enough TIME to thoroughly go through the probabilities for a single patient. Worse, we doctors, generally do not speak in terms of specific patients, we speak in terms of populations of similar patients in order to convey to probabilities of a treatment working or not working. Trauma patient comes in, they had a severed artery in a car wreck. Pulled from the wreckage they had lost almost 80% of their blood. Without treatment, they would die. Other than this deep cut, they had no broken bones, no head trauma, no other life-threatening injuries. Surgical repair proceeded without incident. They required transfusion for their organs to be perfused. A transfusion reaction two hours after surgery in the ICU caused a code-blue. They were resuscitated only to eventually find out they had brain and organ damage secondary to the blood transfusion reaction and resuscitative efforts. They died about 18 months later in a nursing home from long-term care complications. While this case did happen and is a possibility with every large-blood loss trauma… do you discuss that with the patient or their family before giving them blood or doing the surgery to fix the laceration? I’ve been involved with many trauma and cardiac operative cases. I have experienced near-perfect cases on very good candidate patients where the outcomes should have been awesome… die 48 hours later. I have had patients brought into the ORs dead, literally, with CPR being done to them and then, miraculously, they were eating breakfast 48 hours later in the ICU. I have experienced things that science cannot fully explain and that I have no real capacity to explain to myself, the patient or family members. How is one supposed to have a discussion about THIS patient THIS time for THIS family member and compassionately explain the realities (probabilities) for the patient and the life sustaining treatments when often minutes count? There is no TIME to do this in a way that would do justice to the enormity of the discussion. Which leaves us (doctors and patients or family members) having the discussion AFTER the realities of life sustaining treatments become obvious. I think that may be what you are asking with your query… the reason is HOPE. The one thing that you do not want to take away from a patient with life threatening illness or injury is Hope. Sometimes there is no hope. Sometimes you have to tell a patient they are going to die soon. Those are rare that you know, with absolute certainty, that a patient is going to die. For everyone else, there is a possibility, and there is hope. That is why we doctors do not inform patients about ALL the realities of life sustaining treatments… there is no TIME to do so and doctors have to hold on to HOPE for their patients and, honestly, for themselves as doctors doing their jobs day after day after day. A doctor who has lost hope is no good for anyone. I hope this helped you understand a little better - you asked a very hard question in a general manner. ~Chris Dr. Christopher Yerington Columbus, Ohio Bio: Retired from clinical anesthesiology by a disability in 2010, Dr. Yerington has turned his love of teaching and service to others to his family, medical colleagues and community. He speaks, writes and educates medical groups and residency programs about the importance of great disability and life insurance, basic physician-financial literacy and work-life balance. Chris also consoles and counsels young doctors on stress, burnout and physician-suicide. Having attended law and business schools, Chris is a perpetual student of human life, a scientist and an optimistic futurist in his heart.

column1: How does one recover from narcissistic abuse?
column3: I can only speak from my experience, but the single most effective remedy for me in overcoming narcissistic abuse has been to build up my own sense of self-worth, value, and self-respect. This is a process that requires work and diligence to daily maintenance, but gets easier, like second nature as time goes on. The biggest step for me in figuring out where I needed to grow and change was in identifying my values and being honest with myself about when and how and why my actions weren’t in line with my values, and taking steps to align them. When my actions are in line with my values my self-respect, value of myself, and my core sense of self-worth grow. As my self-respect grows and I value myself more I am less willing to give that up for someone else’s value system that doesn’t line up with my own. The longer I do this, the more positive I feel about myself, the more confident I become and the more effective I am in life. The more true love I have for myself the more self-respecting my behaviors are, the more I become aware of what I could lose and how much I would like to hang onto the self-love and material life that I have gained. It’s an uphill spiral, opposite the downhill spiral of low-self worth. It was very difficult for me to see and accept that my sense of self-worth and self-love needed work. I was “nice” to everyone. I was helpful and I valued that. I cared about people deeply. I thought I was a good person and I didn’t think that I had any lack of self-love. I could always find a reason that I felt angry or negative, depressed, unsure, or insecure and down on myself because there were a lot of obvious reasons. I was sure that the only reason I was a victim of abuse was because I was too nice, because I cared so much for people and was a selfless person. I didn’t see my selflessness as a detriment. In fact, I had been convinced that it was a positive trait that would take me where I wanted to be in life, and would be gratifying and fulfilling. However, this was not the case. That only works with a healthy amount of selflessness and mine was to a fault and became toxic to the point of secretly hoping people I loved would do for me things that I could do for myself because I spent all my energy doing for them what they could and should do for themselves. My sense of where I stopped and they began got distorted through enmeshment with a lot of other toxic people. But when the chaos of other toxic people in my life was eliminated through cutting contact and developing friendships with healthier people, I was still unhappy. I lived alone with my child and I was essentially stable for a few years and then found myself in yet ANOTHER relationship with ANOTHER very abusive person, who I truly thought was the kindest, most caring man, and that I was lucky to have him. When it became abusive and I lost a lot again, I knew I had more work to do. In desperation I returned to an exercise I had done in the past, and extended it. The first part of the exercise (numbers 1 and 2) was suggested by a previous mentor. I found that recognition of these things was not enough to maintain recovery from abusive relationships and subsequent destruction. I had to address my self-worth and love myself though my actions, and be accountable to myself each day about it. The exercise is this:make a list of everything you value (from morals to material things and everything in between.make a note of what kinds of actions would imply that this was actively something I make a priority (to solidify the definition of the value and how it is expressed in action). A simple example is my income: I can express that I value my income by budgeting my paychecks in a way that aligns with my other value. I can also express that by putting effort into my work and showing up on time to do my job. Another is my friendships: I can express that I value my friendships by making efforts to maintain them (calling my fiends to check up on them, listening to them or helping them when they need it AND using appropriate boundaries to keep toxicity out of those friendships.Daily, take an inventory of my values against my actions. Did any of my actions go against each value? How did I honor this value today? How did I feel when this happened? How do I physically ad emotionally and mentally feel about betraying my own values? Do I owe anyone an amends for my actions including myself? Did I show self-love in my actions? What could I have done differently and why didn’t I do it that way in the first place?watch for patterns. What values do I continually betray? Is it for the same reasons? Do I truly value those things? Am I ok with not listing that as a value and if so, what would a more appropriate value be if any? If I am not ok with it, but keep doing it, what is the core belief that keeps me coming back to a behavior that I am not ok with doing? What core beliefs keep showing up in the betrayal of multiple values?Then core beliefs begin to appear as patterns in my behavior. This gives me the opportunity to decide if the core beliefs are serving me well or not. What are the pros and cons? If they once served me for protection and are no longer needed I can safely say goodbye to them. If they continue to have negative consequences through my actions and my feelings about my actions they contribute to shame and diminished self-worth - what role does negative self-worth play in my life and serve me? If I am experiencing internal or external consequences that I do not want to let go of for some kind of protection, then something in my life needs to change so that I am safe, or something in my perception needs to change so that I feel safe. Some of my core beliefs are not about safety, but belonging. For instance, I grew up with a lot of men in my family who are at least a bit sexist and some of my core beliefs had to do with roles of males and females in a family, marriage and society. If I act in keeping with their projected beliefs then I stay “in with the boys” in the family and I feel a false sense of protection from the family unit, even if they are not there and do not protect me. If I go against their ideals I feel more alone = rejected= unlovable = unworthy and my sense of self needs an adjustment in perspective to feel worthy and lovable without their approval. Keep in mind that this all happens without me informing them of my feelings or actions, it’s something that has been ingrained in me over time. It’s no longer about them. I have to fix it in myself. So I adjusted my beliefs according to what I am comfortable with, and without ever telling any of them, because it’s not about them, I feel more self-assured and confident in my own beliefs and strengths. When the topics did arise in interactions with my family members, I simply acted according to my own beliefs quitetly and with confidence and no need to explain. I can be respectful of their beliefs and my own at the same time. If it comes up in conversation and I value the person and feel comfortable with them, I explain myself and why it is important to act according to my own needs and way of doing things and then I don’t put any stock in any potential judgment, because my worth no longer depends on their acceptance of me in any way. My worth begins to come from my own adherence to my own values and the positive results I gain from practicing actions that align with my values every day.assertiveness. If I have something I need to address with someone whether it be a boundary or asking for help, or stating a preference I ask for it or say it politely without apologies or any unnecessary explanations knowing that my needs and values are imperative to my self-worth, and my effectiveness in life, my survival, and my success. I am considerate of others but I no longer compromise my own needs for the wants of others. Assertiveness has become very easy when it once took great courage and risk of vulnerability to muster. My core and my life are now built on a much stronger foundation, so if someone doesn’t agree with my need and is not happy to oblige, I can kindly find another solution that doesn’t require them to change their beliefs but doesn’t compromise mine. I rarely feel angry or bitter or afraid or resentful, insecure, or in need of anything I am not able to obtain through legitimate means because of this way of rewiring my thinking and acting accordingly.diligence. I work hard for what I have as well as to maintain it. I am accountable to myself. If I do not maintain what I have gained I lose it. I have shown myself that more than once. This includes emotional, mental, financial and spiritual wellness, and material possessions as well as relationships and jobs. When I begin to counter my own beliefs I lower my standards for how others should treat me because I don’t feel good about myself and my guilt tirms to shame, and shame opens the door to letting toxic people into my life and once again losing what I’ve worked for.if I get an uneasy feeling in my gut I can usually tell if I am appeasing someone else’s wants, values and beliefs instead of my own, and I can assertively adjust my actions so that they are more in line with what I know to be my own value system now that I have become much more self-aware and accountable.I can let go of toxic relationships and environments more easily without guilt or shame, knowing that I am doing it in self-love, not making decisions based on fears or low self-worth. I know what boundaries I am comfortable with and am practiced at maintaining them, and I know how to forgive myself when I mess up without feeling like a worthless idiot (because I’ve messed up a lot and learned, and still learning from it).I become a person who no new narcissist or other abusive person I meet wants to mess with and some actually begin to show respect for from a distance. I enjoy my hobbies and my healthy relationships and the gratitude I have for everything that I get to do and have in my life compared to when I am not loving myself with respect and honoring my own values.this becomes habit and a new way of living free of abuse and inner torment and betrayal. However, it still needs to be maintained. If I do not actively check in with myself intentionally I can begin to build poor habits again, and revert to less healthy ways of living, and the spiral can go back down.Again, this is just something that I came up with for myself with the influence of many different things in my life, and the original suggestion from a mentor in a recovery program for codependency. It works well for me if I am diligent and it infiltrates my entire life and being, as does the codependency and do the abusive relationships if I indulge. I still care deeply for others and do help others, but with boundaries. Rather than just sacrificing for others I now sacrifice for myself as well, and I know that it trickles into my relationships with my kids and family and my friendships, as well as my abilities as a parent, and in my work/career life. My answer sounds a bit like I am fully recovered and this was a process I realized one day and kept at it and got “all better”. It’s not. I still have PTSD after numerous forms of therapy and numerous therapists, support groups and meetings over the years (my sumltoms and behaviors are much improved however). My self-esteem and self-worth are much improved. But this process began about 13 years ago and I have lapsed into the downward spiral a few times and entered into 2, yes 2 marriages since then that became abusive with men who were very narcissistic, one was diagnosed with NPD during the course of our marriage and one is currently in an evaluation process and we are still married but separated. The fact is that I came into the world with a parent with NPD and grew up with a twin sister who I believe has it, and a lot of alcoholism and codependency in my family, and carried the torch into my own personal relationships with friends and potential life partners. Therefore, I cannot expect my recovery to be any more simple than the complexity of what I am recovering from, and it’s a lot. It’s not that I like the abuse, I don’t. I like the warm fuzzy happy feeling I get when I meet someone who feels so familiar at a time that I have let down my due diligence, and gotten lonely. This loneliness comes from slacking in my daily maintenance…. When I have gotten into another such relationship it is when I have been “too busy”, “too happy”, “too stressed” to keep up with my self-care and accountability to myself and others about my recovery. When I slack, I lack. When I lack I get lonely, because I am not maintaining my friendships and hobbies and regular sleeping, eating, habits and maintaining a balanced and fulfilling life. This loneliness and the subsequent fuzzy feeling with the new love breeds denial, and the person who is trying to fool me succeeds. I don’t mean to discount their part in fooling me and abusing me. It’s not to be discounted. However, it not easy to do when I am on top of my own game. Once I realize it, I panic “oh my god I’ve done it again! How could I have let this happen?” But once I can see past the pain I know how it happened…. And I can only try to learn from it, keep moving forward, and become my own best friend again. The current husband I met 3 years after the last. I didn’t handle the time in between well. I had been badly conned and abused and choked in my sleep by some I trusted and loved, someone I knew from my childhood and married after meeting again in adulthood. It was such as shock…. I thought I had “recovered” and was “healed” from previous abuse and was impervious to it, but didn’t recognize when I let my gaurd down enough to let in a wolf in sheep’s clothing…. A third time. I was blinded by the idea of the kid I once knew and I didn’t see the red flags for what they were. I believe that getting involved with my next husband was a direct result of not having done the maintenance and self-care I needed to maintain self-love and self-respect in the 3 years following my divorce. I was ashamed and riddled with guilt and trauma, and couldn’t overcome the nightmares enough to sleep well. On top of it, this experience along with some other factors instigated a long bout of PTSD symptoms from trauma from my first seriously abusive relationship with my child’s father, which I had thought was resolved because I had done a lot of therapy and personal growth work. I went to therapy again, and some of it was helpful. But when I was still suffering from sleep deprivation a year into it I opted to drink wine as a solution to my sleep problems and it worked so well that I didn’t feel the need to go to therapy anymore. I focused on my material growth, reclaiming my financial stability after being taken from again, and I actually took a different approach to love and dating for a few years. I dated but didn’t get close it serious with anyone and I began to shut down. When I met my current husband I was doing well from the outside, but I knew I had to do something more productive than drink wine to go to sleep at night and stave off the nightmares. I wanted a quicker fix and I knew that alcohol wasn’t a good long term solution. I know the problems that can come with drinking excessively. I met my next husband who presented himself as a peer specialist and mentor for people recovering from PTSD when in search of support and friendships. I was no longer drinking wine every night and I was very depressed. I met him online (the first time I had done that), and he seemed to be a great person to talk to, and was quite helpful at first. We were friends and then began dating and it moved quickly from there. However, nearly everything he told me was a twisted version of the truth or a flat out lie, and I was pregnant and engaged before I began to figure it out. This was another huge embarrassment for me…. But this time I didn’t feel shame. Shame is a useless and counterproductive emotion that I indulged in when I was so shocked over what happened with the previous husband. When the second marriage was going the same way and it was my 4th major relationship in my adult life with a similar pattern, I couldn’t afford to indulge in shame. I knew how it happened and I knew my part and I chose to grow. I was having a baby and I didn’t want to put my child or the baby on the way through anything more, and I didn’t want to lose myself. I feared that if I didn’t grow I would not come back from this one, and my kids needed me, and I needed me. So I went back to my old faithful daily maintenance and slowly I’m getting my life back, my mind back, and feeling like myself again. I can’t really say I’ve ever lost the love I’ve grown for myself, but I have lost self-respect and had to earn it back. At times my emotions are in full force and at times I can step back and observe them, being mindful. The mindfulness is taking over again day by day, which I am extremely grateful for. I’ve been separated from my husband for about a year and a half and the more emotional distance I have from him and his circumstances the better my mindset is. The better my mindset is, the better I handle each situation. I do have to say though, I did have better boundaries in this relationship and the previous one than in my first two, and that’s definitely helped me a lot! I think my self-view is a lot more realistic than it used to be, and my awareness of others including my partners is stronger, and my assertiveness has probably saved me in both marriages, as it brings out the narcissistic traits in them and brings to light what I am in denial of. He is in his own form of recovery program now but his is his and mine is mine. What I do, think, and feel is not dependent on what he does, thinks or feels. If we don’t get back together that’s ok. If we do, that is great as long as it is a healthier version this time. I don’t long for him or anyone anymore and I maintain my friendships and my own self-care and recovery program again. It’s been a long road to get to the place where I am not completely broken anymore and nothing can completely break me anymore, and I am grateful for the experiences I’ve had…. And the next level of growth that each low, each relationship, each loss brings me back up to. I sometimes wish it were easier, and then I remember that most people never have the reason or opportunity to delve into themselves and really learn what self-love is all about, and I am pleased and content with myself and my progress. I know this is more of a answer than you were looking for. Thank you for reading, and thank you for the question to answer.

column1: How do children benefit from taking care of pet animals?
column3: Everyone has heard that a dog is “man’s best friend,” but the truth is, they’re so much more than that. Children love dogs because they’re cute, cuddly, and oh-so-friendly. But did you know that growing up with a dog can actually benefit a child’s physical and psychological development? There’s a lot parents can do to teach kids responsibility at a young age. It’s common to have children clean up their room, take out the trash, and do other chores around the house. Most parents underestimate the lessons kids learn from caring after family pets.”Children in dog owning families have more traditional values, better academic achievement, and greater respect for their parents,” said Elizabeth Omerod, companion animal veterinary surgeon, and member of the Pet Health Council in London. Here are 9 main reasons why every kid needs a dog growing up. Teaching Responsibility When children ask for pets, parents often object that dogs are a big responsibility. Most don’t see the opportunity of teaching responsibility and only predict the financial loss. Kids quickly realize that dogs have their needs. Pets require daily feeding, exercise, and affection, not to mention grooming and potty time. While most parents force their children to clean their room, there is no real-life consequence for not doing so. Adopting a dog teaches kids how to establish a routine and prioritize important tasks before they invest energy on free time. The goal is to eventually have your kids on autopilot, feeding and playing with the dog themselves. Keep in mind that adult supervision is essential! Tasks Your Kids Can Do:Food and Water: Having your kids feed the dog twice per day establishes a routine and emphasizes the importance of discipline. Furthermore, they will check on the dogs water supply, ensuring they learn that small tasks are important.Clean Up: Have the kids clean up the dogs toys before bed time. Older children can start picking up poop, teaching the importance of dirty work.Brushing: This teaches the importance of caring for something with care. Its imperative that kids are gentle and learn to read their dogs.Daily Training: Have your children assist you with training basic commands like sit, down, and stay. This introduces leadership early on and show that dogs must also follow the rules of the home.Physical Activity Today, about one in three American kids and teens is overweight or obese. The prevalence of obesity in children more than tripled from 1971 to 2011. With good reason, childhood is now the number one health concern among parents in the United States, topping drug abuse and smoking! Adopting a dog forces our kids to get physical without feeling like a chore. High blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and elevated blood cholesterol levels can easily be avoided by long walks or playing chase around the yard. Most dog owners take their pets out 3-4 times per day and walk 2+ miles. Tagging kids along is a golden opportunity to bond and get their butts of the couch. Older kids should be able to walk the dog on their own further drilling the importance of responsibility. Staying in shape lessens bullying and builds self-esteem. Engaging Physical Activities For Kids:Soccer: Believe it or not, some dogs love soccer, especially herding breeds like Border Collies and Australian Shepherds. I find myself playing soccer with Sasha, my German Shepherd, every morning while brewing coffee. This can be challenging because of the dogs quick reactions and will get your lungs going.Tug of War: Great exercise to get your pet tired and your kids to engage in strength training. Tug of war engages the back and bicep muscles. Kids love to run around the house having the dog chase them for the rope.Tag! You’re It!: Play tag with your dog. Take turns who is it. With my dog, he’s never it and I always have to chase him but that’s okay because we are both sweating after about 15 minutes!Boost Self-Esteem and Prevent Depression We all have dark memories from our childhood. Low self-esteem can greatly alter how kids think of themselves and negatively affect their decision making as an adult. When kids feel good about themselves, it sets them up for success in everything from school to friendships. If they think others won’t accept them, they may not participate as often. They may allow themselves to be treated poorly and have a hard time standing up for themselves. While we can’t control what happens at school, the family dog will always accept your child no matter what. Caring after pets gives a child a sense of accomplishment and helps him/her feel independent and competent. Recent study at Pacific Lutheran University in Tacoma, found that children who helped care for a puppy in preschool were more popular and better able to understand other students feelings. Dogs can curb depression is both kids and adults. How Dogs Make Kids Smile:Long Day: Kids get the same feeling of love when they arrive back from school. No matter the difficulties they may have encountered in school or fights they may have had with parents, the family dog will always greet them.That Special Friend: Give them a four-legged creature to love who loves them right back, and a friend to talk to and play with when no one else is around.Leader: Trained dogs that listen to every command gives kids a sense of power and boost in self-esteem. If they assist in training this show that deep inside lays a leader further adding the feeling of importance.Understanding The Cycle of Life Life and death is a tough lesson for all of us. Learning about them via the lives of animals can be an easier way for both parties to learn about these basics of life. While experiencing the death of a pet can be difficult and painful, it can also be an important learning experience. The way in which their parents and others near to them deal with the situation will have an influence on how children cope with death in general throughout their lives. This introduces the meaning and value of life early on and breeds compassionate adults. It inspires our children to help those in need. Samantha, young girl, lost her dog when she was 8. She saw a hungry dog that was beat up and was looking at his last days. Samantha remembered the pain of losing her pet and inspired her mom to adapt the dog and save its life. This compassion goes beyond pets and opens an understanding mind to human feelings. Bring The Family Closer Due to technology and age, my family rarely communicated. We all have jobs and only acknowledge each others existence. When we adopted Sasha, our German Shepherd, the family was talking and spending time together, playing with the dog. Arguments were drastically reduced and began weekly hiking trips that further bonded us. Its incredible how a dog can solve so many issues. During an argument Sasha would start jumping on us and resolve the situation. Dogs can feel the tension and will do anything to comfort us. Beginning some 10,000 years ago, humans and canines formed a unique pact that benefited both species. Back then they helped us hunt and today they keep us together. How Dogs Benefit The Family:We All Love The Dog: Angry or not, everyone in the household wants to pet and play with the dog. This brings family members together and eventually irons out any beef.Trips: Dog owners tend to go on trips more often to get their fluffy friends excited. This could be hiking, going to the beach, or simply walking in the park. Long trips with the family means more time together with the common goal of showing the dog a good time.Working Together: Family members must take turns feeding and walking the dog. This forces everybody to sacrifice their time and often take other shifts if needed. This builds trust between family members and creates good karma.The Social Ice Breaker Technology makes is making it increasingly difficult to socialize with other human beings. Facebook, Twitter, text messaging, and other electronic nonsense breeds insecurity and anti-social tendencies, making life in the real world impossible. People that love dogs provide a golden opportunity to engage in small talk and build social skills. I find myself talking to strangers that ask questions about my dogs age, breed, and way of life. Regularly talking to strangers develops the ability to read people and develops the skill of asking difficult questions. A University of Missouri study found that pets may also help children with autism to develop social skills such as sharing, introducing themselves, and asking for information. Other Social Benefits:The Talk: If you want to engage in a serious conversation with your kids, do it on a long walk with the dog. This gives you an easy hour of chat without the technological distractions such as computers or televisions.Dog Parks: Regular trips to the dog park allows teenagers to meet new people and develop relationships as they meet on regular basis. They wont have time to construct ideas on answering questions like on their texting devices.

column1: Is it true that a lot of Americans will put their parents in nursing homes when their parents get older?
column3: Yes-ish. Many older people don't want to live with their children and actually look forward to a time and place where their day to day needs are taken care of without being a burden to their children, where they can be close to their families and yet where they can live among their peers. Some of them can't afford it, though, and need their children's financial assistance to be able to manage. I wish I could have had my mom stay with me at the end of her life but she couldn't; it would've made me certifiably insane to worry about her physical safety and well-being everyday while I was at work, and to deal with the lack of privacy and independence, including freedom to travel, to parent without her judgment, and to have a social and personal life. Further, I could never have taken care of her and addressed her medical issues with a clear head; I appreciated having someone else responsible for delivering medications and some basic healthcare which I could not provide, either with respect to time or emotional comittment. There are few things that are more difficult and challenging with respect to dignity and self-worth than taking physical care of a previously fiercely independent and self-sustaining parent. I worked in a nursing home when I was 16 and know first-hand the specific requirements of the aging. Although I knew I could deliver that care, I also knew that my own relationship and biases with respect to my mom would color my diagnosis and observation of her behavior; and not serve her as well as I might be able to if I did not have 24-7 responsibility for her physical care and well-being. Fortunately, she had no more than a limited passing desire to live with me, and we were fortunate enough to be able to afford the expense associated with her late-in-life care. It was absolutely the best possible thing we could do and it provided her with the respect and ease of life she deserved, and assuaged some of her inevitable loneliness because she could be with other people in her peer group, and not spend all day alone because her daughter had a full-time job and a family that she also had to care for. We were very lucky; many families are not that lucky, and it's incredibly difficult for them. More than 30% of family caretakers in the US are said to suffer from depression - situational - primarily as a result of the stress and pressure, financial and emotional, that being a caretaker of an elderly parent places on them and their family relationships. Keep in mind that there are many different kinds of "nursing homes", too in the US; there are senior centers and living apartments, which are basically smaller (downsized) places where seniors live, where some meals might be provided, and where some basic services are available; a cross between a college dorm and a hotel for older adults. There are assisted living centers, for people who need more care with dressing and bathing or who may need oxygen or need walkers or wheelchairs to navigate without fatigue; and skilled nursing facilities, for people who are in poorer health and need daily nursing care. There are also facilities that specialize in Alzheimer's care, for instance, that are set up with various protective security features and specially trained staff to make sure that those living there are safe and don't wander into the world, confused and lost. Many Americans might wish to put their parents in "nursing homes" when they get older and many older parents might want to be able to be there to retain their independence and dignity; but they might not be able to afford it, or fear that their independence will be even more compromised than it already is when their health begins to deteriorate. Moving to a nursing home actually helps them to retain their independence in light of their failing health and not to be so dependent on family members, who in turn may become increasingly anxious or resent the energy and financial commitment required to physically and personally care for an aging parent. The close relationship between the caregiver and the impaired person — a relationship involving shared emotions, experiences and memories — may particularly place caregivers at risk for psychological and physical illness. More than 60 percent of Alzheimer's and dementia caregivers rate the emotional stress of caregiving as high or very high; one-third report symptoms of depression. The 24/7/365 aspect of caregiving can be daunting as most people survive an average of four to eight years after an Alzheimer's diagnosis, but some live as long as 20 years with the disease. (The impact of Alzheimer's disease on caregivers and families ) However, not all families and not all older parents are the same. Many might prefer to be with their children, or need to live with them due to financial reasons, and have children who either feel obligated or desire to have their parents live with them. Some older people are in excellent health with only minor health issues (like failing hearing, or vision loss); but many are not. Every situation is different. So, yes-ish. "A lot" of Americans will put their parents in nursing homes when they get older, either with the parents' full consent or at their urging; and many Americans will wish they could but can't afford it. And many Americans simply age, without anyone to help or care for them, one way or another. According to the latest figures, one in three seniors in America dies with Alzheimers or another form of dementia; over 5.2 million Americans have Alzheimers right now, and 70% of them live at home. (45 million or more are said to suffer from Alzheimer's world-wide) Alzheimer's Association 800,000 of those suffering from Alzheimers in the US live alone. As someone who's witnessed the tragic deterioration in capacity that is dementia in both my own family and in people that I cared for and have known at various stages in my life, I think that's terrifying.
