column1: I am a medical student and my dad died during my second year of med school. I feel powerless and I don't believe in medicine anymore. How can I deal with this?
column3: So sorry to hear about you loss. Although his passing was not unexpected, experiencing the way this terrible debilitating eventually fatal disease affected your formerly again healthy father, reducing him to a very ill person loosing all muscular control and eventually succumbing to it, must have been terrible to see. At present, you are in mourning after this devastating loss, as you know after at first a phase of denial the second phase involves guilt, anger, usually aimed at oneself. While these emotions are part of the normal grieving process, you need to come to term with them first before you can accept the fact. The fact that non medical people have asked you why you couldn't save your father just shows that lay people mistakenly think docs can cure any patient, as a part of the denial of eventual death in western society. Don't let this make you feel guilty or sad, you know it's stupid. Let me tell you what I experienced as a dad myself: when a lot younger, 30 years ago, our then 6 weeks old baby daughter got Pneumococcal meningitis (through blood poisoning from a middle ear infection). I diagnosed the meningitis myself, took her to our pediatrician friend who after one night at our hospital transferred her out to a nearby academic child's intensive care unit, although there was no delay, we lost her after two intensely grueling weeks. At that time I was our hospital's intensive care physician. So much for having a doctor in the family to take care of the medical woes of the family. It didn't affect my confidence as a doctor, though. My (also medical specialist) dad passed at 67 yo just two months before I graduated as a MD. He very much would have liked to be present at the graduation ceremony. Unfortunately a year before he had developed pancreatic cancer, incurable most of the times, even nowadays. We knew of the grim prognosis, but it never crossed my mind why I wasn't able to cure him. It just wasn't on the cards, so we accepted it. Having grown up in a medical family, and by that time having done two years of rotating internships, I already knew that sometimes we win, sometimes we lose, and accepted it as part of (medical) life. We can't promise to cure all our patients, just that we will do our utmost best for our patients, which in some instances would mean either watchful waiting, or deciding to forgo aggressive therapies just concentrating on the patient's comfort and well being. I don't know what made you decide to do med school in the first place, but since at present you're not your normal self, being in such a deep mourning, don't do anything rash, look for counseling (from student counselors at your med school?). When you feel better, if still in doubt make a list of for and against arguments as you see it, and what alternatives you have, and talk it over with someone with a good judgement you trust, be it a friend, family member, counselor or student-colleague. Btw, familial ALS only occurs in 10% of ALS patients see Genetic Testing for ALS I fervently hope you can come to a good decision on what to do with your life next. Wishing you all the best! PS: After so many decades I think these adverse medical experiences in my family have made me empathize better with patients and their families, maybe making me a better doc....

Second option may bring fights between me and my husband or my inlaws. I don't want to have a rift with him because of these people. So, I learnt to handle it in my own way without hurting any one and at the same time making them realise mine and their boundaries. Without spoiling my peace'of mind and harmony in the house. It needs patience as well as intelligence. You don't get results in a single attempt always. It doesn't happen overnight. 2. House hold work. I treat work as work. There is no great work or small work. It's importance depends on the situation. Either become an expert to improve the quality of our life or leave it and keep expecting some miracle would happen. Getting help from my husband thrice or four times in an year, no way helps me!! So, I realised learning anyskill will help me to grow in life. Lessens my dependecy on others. Then quickly I started learning household works. I didn't fall in any ‘ism' or any agitation of equality. Because simply it doesn't work out with our life styles. He does help when he is free but that's not enough. I have to take the in-charge role of a home manager. 3. I know what it is and how anyone feels if they are not financially independent. I know all the possibile situations in which a wife may feel insecure, has to depend on her husband for her needs. Future scares sometimes. Loss of husband, husband's loss of job, sudden expenditure, health issues, so I concentrated on systematic savings and investments , health insurances etc. Calculated for likely old age needs. Rationalised my house hold chores and made time for earning in my own way in a small and medium level. Once you start getting little earnings,the other kind of problems would start. Suddenly your near and dear feel financial ungencies. Expect you should help them. Again you have to master the art of smartness. 4. A house wife!! Many feel she doesn't do any work. Wear a nightie and watch TV morning to mid night. So, she is expected to take care of all genuine, not so genuine necessaries, emergencies of her both side families. Again you should be firm while not being rude to tell them you have your own life to live. Some occassional or genuine help is different. You are ready to do anything for them but at the same time you can't go running to them whenever they whistle for help at each silly and sundry problems of theirs. You can't run to them leaving your family and your life. 5. Cooking, cleaning. Again I planned a lot before receiving any guest. Whenever I get time, I cut and keep the vegetables, make tamarind pulp and other necessary items in fridge. Ready to use items. So, I need not spend much time in cooking. One way it has become as a disadvantage also. Relatives and friends started saying, '’you can go to Rama's house anytime. She can make a tasty food within minutes.!!’’ I used to grind my teeth while trying to smile. 6. I never felt humiliation as a house wife, though I have some jealous, mean people around me. I learnt to keep them in their limits. 7. Few stupid people mocked me. ‘We can't sit at home like you!!! I too replied ‘I can't leave my house like you'. I know this argument takes us no where. Every life, it's needs, the society she lives is different. What I faced in my life you may not face. You may think my problems are trivial. I may think you are wearing a mask of exaggeration! There are many things a person faces after her or his marriage. Whether they are problems, changes, differences or challenges depends on your life and how you take it. Not only a wife, a husband also faces them. Money problems, house hold chores, relatives, inlaws, children, educational expenses, health issues, what not! How they affect you? The way you let them. If you think those are problems, they appear like problems. If you think they are challenges, they appear as challenges. If you have a spouse who can understand and respect your contribution to his life and family. Nothing can challenge you. If you have a spouse who takes you for granted and think you are a parasite on him, life appears as a problem and challenges you at every minute.
column9: A fact of Indian wife. My wife also fits well here. As a husband I take care to make sure she has all she has to deserve. She makes sure I stay fit to face outside challenges. Her in-laws or my in laws don't matter. They are taken care of equally. Before going to bed we spend some time every day to discuss all trivial issues and the plans what we should do, plan our daily life, some small arguments ocassionally and little things to challging situations. We sleep happily until she wakes me up the next morning with a sizzling hot cup of green tea. Not everyone we know are happy as they seldom see us gruffly any time. But sometimes we are, but nobody can notice. It's been 32 years for us like this.

column1: If you woke up to find 99.99% of the population disappeared overnight, what would you do?
column3: I think most people in our world have imagined this scenario in an introverted manner. Likely when they are laying in bed at night and the mind relaxes and starts to think about things like this. Admittedly, it is cruel and probably thought of as sick. However, you would be quite surprised at how likely the majority of human’s (being honest) would say that this kind of scenario wouldn’t necessarily be a bad thing in their eyes. 99.99% of our population suddenly gone is unfathomable. However, considering that one of the most basic realities of the nature of humans is to gain more space, gain more material, and gain more of anything and everything for yourself. For the most part, our intentions aren’t to hurt our neighbors in the process, however it is human nature to want more. This being said; out of the 7.4 billion +/- world population - All the sudden, 740000 people would inherit the earth for themselves. We are talking pre 10000BC era numbers. So what would I do? I think any normal person would probably spend their first day in this new world in utter shock. They would likely wonder around trying to digest the fact that the modern world has come to a screeching halt. Crashed car graveyards on the freeways and roads. Houses could be on fire from stoves that never got turned off, cars that crashed into buildings. I know I would be frantically calling and rushing around to check on the status of my wife and immediate local family members only to find that they have all likely disappeared or not answering their phone. A normal human would start to realize pretty quickly that they are alone and vulnerable. Although you want to take time to weep and digest the possibilities of your family being gone, especially the longer distance ones that you can’t confirm, a person starts to think of self-preservation. Assuming all these people just vanished and everything else was untouched as is. In most places in the world, the essential life utilities would still be available for some limited time. Water would still run through faucets, gas would flow, and power would still run for some time until unmaintained facilities gave away or shut down. Internet would still run for the most part for a while. I would have to prepare myself for the eventual loss of these amenities. In the short term, I have to think about self-preservation until I adjust to this new world, I would need to make sure I have all the resources available. I am located in a pretty low populated area within the United States. If the suggested 99.99% disappearance was proportionately even to the population in locations in the world, then there might only be about 140 people left in my entire state. So here is what I would do within the first 3 days. - Go down to the car lot. Get access to a Hummer, a truck or a full sized SUV - Find me a motorbike and load it up on an attached trailer. - Find me a good sheltered home with a fire place just outside the city. - Take a motorbike back to the city. - Find me a large semi truck, or moving vehicle. Load the bike up and then head to the local Grocery to stock up on water and as much food as I can. - Drive it to my new property outside the city. - Take the bike back to the city and get another semi or moving truck. - Head to the local outdoorsman store (sportsmans, or cabelas) and load up on guns, power generators, survival gear, warm clothing and blankets. - Take it back to my property and head back to the city once again. This time I would ride around until I found a semi hauling a fuel trailer. There are always at least a few gas stations around town that are getting their tanks refilled by a large gasoline truck. Drive it back to my property. - Next it is on to the Hospital. Load up on antibiotics, life support systems, and critical care supplies. Basically for the first few days I would stock up on items that would help me survive, transport myself, protect myself, and care for myself in a world where I don’t know who is out there that can help me. Once I have gotten over the initial shock of this major event and established an environment where I know I can survive with all my supplies and ability to mobilize myself; I would start thinking about my longer distance family and if they are alive or not. By this time I have already confirmed if my local family is around or if they are gone. I could never have closure though unless I gave them an honorable burial memorial of the sort. As hard as it would be, I would do that for my local family. Then I would have to rationalize and plan a trip that is to come where I can confirm the fait of family outside of my state. I would also have to figure if staying where I am at is best for my future, or if finding another place in the world would be better. For me, I am a pretty independent person. I am an avid outdoorsman. I grew up on a farm knowing the value of hard work and the simple standards in life that truly make a person like me happy. Some people in a post event world like this would search out for a 7000 square foot home, put on a tuxedo, go down to a car lot to grab the highest end luxury car and then drive around in this free world sipping wine. Although I wouldn’t deny doing something like that on a bored day, I think for me I would decide to stay on the move and travel somewhere warm. Eventually power, gas, and even water would cease. Survival in a cold climate is harder considering the effort it would take to stay warm or get around in snow covered roads that won’t be maintenance through the winter. After a few weeks of morning and coming to conclusion that my family is gone. I would probably start realizing the potential I have in this world. I no longer need to worry about a job in order to get what I want. I no longer need to schedule vacation or save up money for a flight to get where I want to go. My first goals though are going to be to put closure to my longer distance family members. But I need to prepare for dangerous travel. Who knows what is out there waiting to take advantage of me. I would probably go down to our local military base and find access to a militarized Hummer. I would find me a fairly good sized travel trailer and start stocking up with food, water, medical supplies, power generators, cooking and shelter supplies, weapons, ammo, and enough barrels of gasoline to get me around for weeks or months. It is time to make an 8 hour drive to Portland, Oregon to confirm the fait of family there before making the long trek across the country to Georgia to confirm fait of the family there. I won’t talk about the possibilities of encountering other people or groups. This isn’t the walking dead and how I will interact, friend, or fight other groups. I am just discussing what I would do in this world.After I have closure and have confirmed if I am the only survivor of my family. I would probably head south. I would probably spend several years travelling between Texas, Southern California and Central America. During the Hurricane seasons I would probably make my way north or west to the south pacific around San Diego. The rest of the year I would probably spend exploring and enjoying the beaches and coast from Cancun all the way to Ecuador. After a year or two, I will likely have fully digested and healed from the loss of family and accepted the world that I now live in. If I haven’t been robbed and killed by other survivors, I may have found friends or a beautiful woman to start enjoying my time with. With such reduced population, maybe the aquatic life would be making a come back. Fishing would be much better. I would start training myself on the ways of navigation. I would learn how to run a fairly large boat or small charter. I always wanted to see the Galapagos Islands. After 5-10 years I may get confident enough with sea travel that I would make my way up the coast along the states and Canada. I would eventually cut across the island chain of the bearing sea to Japan.Once in the east, I would make my way down Japan to Okinawa. The birthplace of Karate. Since I studied Okinawa Kenpo for 20 years, I would love to visit. I would probably spend a year or two exploring and seeing places in China, Taiwan, and maybe southeast Asia. Then I would make my way to Australia before departing for a settlement period in my life. If my navigation doesn’t get me lost at sea, by this time I would be a bit older hitting late 40’s and early 50’s and I would set out for either Fiji or Tahiti. What better place to live out a more relaxed time of your life than Fiji or Tahiti. I would find me a nice simple hut on the water. Sail around collecting food and supplies from surrounding islands, and try to relax and enjoy life for a while.I think when I hit my mid to late 60’s. If my health permits, I would make my final travel plans. It is time to make the trek back home to where my family and friends are all buried. Even though I got to travel to some absolutely gorgeous places in this world, I would want my final resting place to be where I grew up, where my roots are, and where my family lays at rest. Traveling back around Asia, across the Bering sea and back down the Canadian coast, I would land at Astoria Oregon. I would take a few days to collect and gather supplies and transportation capabilities and then swing by Portland Oregon once again to say my final goodbyes to some of my family at rest. Then I would travel 8 hours back to Boise, Idaho where I would live out the rest of my days hopefully in peace before I kick the bucket.

column1: What are the pension problems for central government employees retiress?
column3: There are certain avoidable problems in pension matters for retirees from central government departments. A decade after my retirement, I am still doing my best when some retirees approach me with their genuine problems related to pension. They fail to pay due attention before their pension documents were progressed towards checking for correctness of dates of birth of self , spouse and dependent family members. If these pensioners have unmarried/ widowed daughters or disabled children these facts should have been furnished to their offices while in service to get the concerned dependent family members continued health cover (in service these employees might have been covered by CGHS health cover) after retirement . Some retirees believe that the health insurance provider for their employed children will take care of parents requirements also. This attitude is patently wrong. No health insurance provider in our country takes care of regular health issues, except for hospital admission and surgery if any. Last pay drawn of employee at the time of retirement is not properly verified when pension papers are progressed. This lapse leads to protracted correspondence. When PPO (Pension Payment Order) is issued the retirees need to get sufficient copies attested and they should keep in a place accessible to spouse and children. Otherwise family members would be running in circles searching for these vital documents.These retirees should ensure that their pension SB account is jointly held by Pensioner and the spouse. In addition, Pension Disbursing Authorities including Banks have not covered themselves with glory when family pension is to be disbursed in the unfortunate event of a pensioner passing away. These pension Disbursing authorities take a minimum of three months to convert regular pension into family pension, though central government has been prodding them to release family pension at the earliest in a time bound manner. Since retirees failed to brief their spouses and children how to progress papers for converting regular pension into family pension, after their lifetime, family members in addition to suffering emotional loss on account of passing away of the Pensioner, family members are pushed to financial distress. With a little advance planning and paying attention minutely by retirees,, many of these hassles can be smoothly ironed out.

column1: Has loyalty ever caused you great harm, or loss?
column3: I have a cousin that I grew up with. A nice enough kid, but then when we hit puberty, her insecurities grew much faster than her body. She was on the tall side and skinny as a rail. No figure. I, on the other hand, also on the tall side, started getting boobs and hips when I was in 6th grade. I was also very smart and self-confident even at a young age. Maybe because I was the oldest kid in our family & had a Mom that stressed education; whereas, my cousin was the 3rd girl with a doted on younger brother. Her mother, my aunt was all about being pretty and popular — because she had not been either, while my Mom, her sister, was popular, pretty, and smart. My aunt was very jealous of my Mom. For my cousin, looks and popularity were her end game. She worked hard at being both….you know, a cheer leader, prom princess kind of girl, with lots of girly drama. I was more into getting good grades and reading and hung out with fun girls also into doing well in school. I loved my cousin (she was family), but I also felt sorry for her. Looking hot and flirting with boys were her main preoccupations even at 15-16. Getting an education was mine. Still, despite our differences we were fairly close until high school graduation. I went on to college. She got knocked up & married the abusive jerk, only to divorce him. This totally affected her financially, of course. While I was also poor, I made it through college and eventually got my BA, and started a good career. My cousin ended up in low paying jobs looking for a man to adore and support her. She married another jerk and divorced him. She dated a lot. One man was supposedly embezzling money from his job, which she knew about as I recall. He was also married, which he had hidden from her. When she found out, she took a bunch of his money and bought herself some fine boobs. And she dumped him by visiting his wife with photos. It was a dramatic mess and she loved it. But those new boobs? Oh, they opened up a new world for her! She really turned heads now and she loved it! She eventually married a man attracted to her looks and destined to make more money than most of the men she had dated — but he was a tightwad. At age 33, we both became pregnant and had girls. At this point, a specific pattern of behavior reared its head. From our 30s into our mid-60s, my cousin would unexpectedly pop into my life and at some point, she would just as mysteriously disappear for years at a time. She tended to pop in when she “needed”me. I called these times On Seasons & Off Seasons. She never gave me any explanations, but by our 30s it was clear to me that she had become a shallow, superficial, and flakey person. She was also funny and often endearing, and I loved her, although I often felt sorry for her. She was pretty on the outside, but after years of focusing solely on her looks, she had failed so far to develop a strong character and never learned critical thinking skills. In other words, she wasn't too smart in some ways. Lets face it, looks fade. Being smart and/or educated is always better. I, too, was considered beautiful, but I always cared more about learning and growing into a whole person. During our last On Season, which lasted 4 years into our mid-60s, most of it was spent dealing with her personal drama. She'd leave her husband and then move back. It was always about her life. She'd have problems with friends and family. Not much time for my life. And at that point in our lives, I was dealing with advanced breast cancer while she was dealing with squeezing as much spending money out of her Hubby as possible. At first, I was sympathetic to her marital drama. She really laid it on thick about him. In time, I realized she was the real problem, not just him. Unlike all the other Disappearances, our final one hit me like a ton of bricks. As in it occurred at the same time as my Mom's health crashed. So while my Mom and I had been supportive, loving, and loyal for those 4 years, even while her mother became ill & died, my cousin was a no-show in my life. This was the first time I truly needed her and she blew me off. I was devastated! I had stuck by her through so much in so many ways, and she had nothing for me or my Mom. I needed her! My Mom needed her. I was a mess for months. For those 4 years of being so close (I thought), I was totally unprepared for this new Off Season. I had thought that by our age that she had matured and that life's lessons had taught her how to be a better, wiser person. She was a vital and important part of my life. She regularly said I was important to her, more like a beloved and cherished sister (she was no longer speaking to her 2 sisters). Oh how wrong I was about her. She had not evolved or learned squat about life despite various experiences. She had not learned any Life Lessons. Instead, she lied to and manipulated me as horribly as she had other family members and friends. I was not spared her bad behavior. The stories I could tell! And I should have been wary, but I was not, unfortunately for me. In the end, I realized that my love and loyalty meant nothing to her. I was disposable. Looking back, I came to realize that she needed a constant parade of adoring people in her life to make her feel good about herself. When she grew tired of one person, she'd move on the next. Our being family and growing up with each other simply had little value despite her initial interest and fake devotion. Loyalty and family are important to me. Because of loyalty to her, my Mom and I alienated other family members that had already experienced my cousin's endless need for attention and drama. i never cared what her reasons for disappearing were. What I cared about this final time was the When and How she disappeared. The When: She disappeared just as my Mom's life fell apart and became a 2 year hell filled with agony. The How: She disappeared like the weak coward she is and like a thief in the dead of night, leaving no trail after stealing her victim blind. I don't plan on forgiving her. I am good with that, and at peace. Sometimes I miss the cousin I thought she was. I don't miss the cousin she really is. If she is true to form, eventually I will here from her. This next time, however, the door will be closed. I finally learned that painful lesson.
column9: Thanks for sharing, I learnt so much from your account. How tragic that it started in childhood, was a train set on its course & she had no awareness or drive to stop it. Never learnt to validate herself & build her independence, to know her abilities within herself. It must have been hard to let go of who you knew she could be at her best; & realise that your relationship wasn’t truely mutual

column1: I have no friends, no partner, and almost no family. How do I cope?
column3: (Before you read this, don’t worry you will be okay <3) Without furtherado, here is my excessively long anwser~ Whatever the particular reason may be for you feeling lonely, know that there are healthy ways to cope when you feel like you don't have any family or friends. Better understanding the reasons as to why you are feeling lonely can be immensely helpful as you work through this process.Whatever the particular reason may be for you feeling lonely, know that there are healthy ways to cope when you feel like you don't have any family or friends. Better understanding the reasons as to why you are feeling lonely can be immensely helpful as you work through this process. No Family No Friends Linking back to the primal brain, social connectedness is an aspect of the human drive for survival, with social rejection being innately discouraged as the brain experiences pain equivalent to a physical injury when these incidents occur. With the tendency to move away from this type of pain, socialization is further encouraged on an automatic level, making it an important aspect of the basic human needs, along with food, shelter, and warmth. The absence of feeling connected can lead to stress, mental health issues, and physical health issues. If you are feeling lonely, there are proactive steps you can take. Processing Negative Core Beliefs If you are feeling lonely, you may experience some negative beliefs about yourself which may leave you feeling even more disconnected and subsequently isolating yourself more as this pervasive cycle continues. Perseverating over having no friends or family members to connect with can bring up thoughts of feeling not good enough, being unlovable, and feeling rejected. To identify your negative belief(s) regarding feeling alone or lonely:Begin with a neutral statement about your social situation (for example, "I don't have any friends or family members").Next, ask yourself what this means about you (for example, "I'm alone").Continue to ask yourself what your previous statement means about you (for example, "Being alone means that no one wants to connect with me").When you finally get down to one statement and feel as if there is nothing beneath it, this is your core negative belief (for example, "I'm unlovable").Identifying negative core beliefs can be draining work, so take your time and be patient with yourself. Negative core beliefs often arise out of childhood or early memories and can be very difficult to challenge as they operate on a largely unconscious level. Reframe Your Negative Core Beliefs Work on reframing your negative core belief regarding loneliness. Doing so can help you understand the why behind your social disconnection in some circumstances. For example: Instead of, "I have no family or friends", the healthier statement could be, "I'm beginning to examine my difficulties with socializing and am working towards building healthy relationships." Whenever the negative thoughts about loneliness start to take over, remind yourself of your healthier statement until it becomes a more habitual thought. Practicing Self-Care On an unconscious level, people tend to attract others with similar levels of mental wellbeing. Practicing healthy self-care is not only good for your own health and wellness, but it may also draw other emotionally healthy individuals to you versus others who may end up being unreliable and/or hurtful as friends or partners. Take some time to get to know your own self-care needs until you come up with a solid routine. Explore Your Socializing Needs Everyone will have their own unique socialization needs. This means that what may feel like solid connection to one person may not be fulfilling for another. While some people feel connected texting, chatting in online forums, or writing blog posts, others may need in-person interaction to feel connected. To better understand your socializing needs, ask yourself:Do you feel connected after chatting with someone via social media?Do you prefer phone calls or texting?How long does a fulfilling conversation last, at minimum?Do you feel connected to others after posting your work or thoughts online?Do you feel connected after posting something anonymously?How do you typically feel after an in-person conversation?Setting Personal Socialization Goals Once you've figured out your social needs, set a few attainable goals for yourself and once completed, continue to build upon them. Some goals may be:Joining an online forum of interestPosting in an online forum once a weekRe-connecting with a former friend who you lost touch withJoining an online or in person group or clubParticipating in an academic or creative classJoining a book clubConnecting with one new person a weekUnderstanding Your Roadblocks While there may be reasons outside of your control that can influence your social life, you may also have some personal difficulties that feel challenging to overcome. Some may include:Mental health diagnosis or symptoms- can make connecting with others feel incredibly difficult and at times impossible depending on the specific diagnosis and symptomsIntroverted nature- you may find that too much socialization feels exhausting but are having a hard time finding others who really get youUnhealthy family system- you may have experienced unhealthy attachment patterns growing up and struggle to connect with trustworthy individuals who you can rely onLoss of friends and family- your friends and family members may have passed away, leaving you feeling as if you're starting from scratch when it comes to meeting new peopleSeeking Help If you are estranged, disconnected, and/or have friends and family members who have passed away, it can lead to some very painful feelings. If you have identified your own roadblocks but are having a hard time working through difficult feelings or meeting emotionally healthy individuals, you may consider finding a therapist who can assist you in processing what you're experiencing. If you are having thoughts of self harm, or thoughts of harming others, reach out for help right away. Getting yourself to an emotionally healthy place is the first step in making healthy connections with others. How to Be Happy When You Have No Family or Friends Happiness is an emotion that is unique to each individual. It may take time for you to figure out what makes you happy in terms of your social life. To begin the process of exploring what makes you happy:Take time to grieve the loss of your relationships or the relationships you wish you had. Processing your feelings can help you move forward while taking the time to acknowledge your emotional process.Understand how often and in what way you'd like to connect with others to feel socially satisfied. Understanding your needs is a great start in cultivating relationships.Explore activities and opportunities that you feel drawn to.Take time to get to know yourself and what your needs are.Is It Normal to Have No Friends? About 30% of Millennials report feeling always or almost always lonely, while Generation X comes in at 20% and Baby Boomers at 15%. While the majority of human beings crave social connectedness, there are some that don't find it fulfilling for one reason or another. Everyone is different and will have their own unique social needs when it comes to friendships. While there is no "normal", it's important that you explore what feels best for you when it comes to relationships. What Happens When You Have No Family? Whether you have lost your family as a child or adult, there are ways to cope with not having any remaining family members. This may mean that they passed away or you're estranged from them. Whatever your unique reason or experience is, not having a family can feel incredibly difficult, isolating, and painful for some individuals. If you don't have a family, know that you can create your own by surrounding yourself with healthy and supportive individuals who care about you. Give yourself permission to define what family means to you. Loneliness Versus Being Alone Loneliness is wanting to connect but being unable to for some reason. Being alone means that for reasons outside of your control, you are without the connection to others. Being alone can also mean that you do have some connection to others but internally feel alone, even in the presence of others. If you are lonely, you may want to take a more proactive approach when it comes to connecting with others, while those who feel alone may want to do some internal reflection and processing. What to Do When You Have No Family or Friends Feeling lonely can come with unique challenges depending on the circumstances. Better understanding why you are feeling lonely can help you work towards processing your given situation. (Thank you for reading, p.s follow me for more, this took forever <3)

column1: How did you retire young and what did you do after you retired?
column3: I retired from my career, but not because I was financially secure. In fact, it was quite the opposite. I have PTSD from a career as a helping professional. I became an anti-social social worker with depression and anxiety so severe that I can no longer work in my field. I have to work, even though doctors agree that I am mentally disabled. I just can’t put a mask on and play a role as The Professional anymore. So, because of that and other reasons, I work at ____-mart by day and read tarot cards by night. Life goes on and I am far from retired. Everyday, I am getting better and better!Social Worker Burnout: Signs, Causes & 15 Tips to Manage Self-care Social workers have one of the highest risk jobs for chronic stress and burnout among healthcare professionals, especially when workloads are high and they don’t feel valued. Signs of burnout in social work include mental, physical, and emotional exhaustion, a loss of meaning and purpose, increased negativity and cynicism, and decreased productivity. What Is Social Worker Burnout? Burnout is a state of chronic stress and exhaustion that social workers may experience due to the demanding nature of their job. Social workers are at risk for burnout because they are exposed to the effects of trauma, poverty, and social and racial inequality on a daily basis. They spend a lot of time and energy thinking about, attuning to, and caring for their clients’ needs. When social workers are not able to turn this off, take a break, and care for themselves, stress becomes chronic resulting in burnout. Social workers may also experience a decrease in productivity and begin to dread or avoid their work. Compassion Fatigue Social Work Compassion fatigue occurs when social workers internalize their concern for their clients to the point that they feel helpless and ineffective, ultimately losing their ability to feel compassion and empathy. Social workers may feel distant, detached, even indifferent to their clients’ struggles. This disconnection is one of the hallmark signs of burnout. Strong emotional boundaries and self-care can help decrease the risk of compassion fatigue. Social Worker Burnout Symptoms A social worker experiencing burnout may notice that they have lost their energy and passion. They may start dreading work, feeling more cynical, negative, or detached, canceling client appointments or chronically running late. They may feel exhausted or helpless to change the situation, be less effective in their work or start daydreaming about leaving the field. Some signs and symptoms of social work burnout include:Physical and emotional exhaustion or burnoutFeeling ineffective as a social workerLack of patience and focusLoss of enthusiasm about the workHeightened irritabilityFeeling emotionally drainedSleep issues/fatigueLoss of inspirationFeeling distracted or unable to focusIncreased cynicism or negativityCauses of Social Worker Burnout High caseloads, high client acuity, and low pay are well-known causes of social worker burnout, and this has become even more significant during the pandemic. A recent study found that following the start of COVID-19, 26.21% of social workers met the diagnostic criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), 16.22% reported severe grief, 63.71% reported burnout, and 49.59% reported secondary trauma. Potential causes of social worker burnout include:Increased client needsHigh caseloadsLow wagesLimited resourcesOrganizational structures and stressorsEthical dilemmasWorkplace conflictFunding concernsUnsafe situationsInability to detach from clients’ issues or taking on their problemsSecondary traumaExposure to abuse, poverty, and social and racial inequitieshttps://www.choosingtherapy.com/financial-stress/Funding requirementsDeadlinesEthical imperative to respond to social justice concerns Culture of overworkHow to Prevent Social Worker Burnout: 15 Self Care Tips Fortunately, there are ways to prevent or manage this type of stress, including caring for one’s mental and physical health, setting limits and boundaries, and seeking out professional support and consultation. Social workers can reduce their burnout and deal with feeling overwhelmed by prioritizing self-care, support, and stress management in their personal lives. Ways to prevent social worker burnout include: 1. Practice Physical & Emotional Self-Care Social workers have all heard the saying, “You can’t pour from an empty cup” but this is more than a cliche. It is critical to recharge (or refill) physically and emotionally in order to be able to stay healthy and continue to help others. 2. Leave Work at Work It can help social workers to have rituals when they transition from work time to personal time. This can be especially important when working from home. For example, social workers can get to a stopping point with current tasks and write down a list of all of the things that need to be taken care of the next morning. If commuting, it might help to identify a boundary like a river or highway, and think about leaving work on the other side once that boundary is crossed. 3. Take Advantage of Resources Provided by Your Employer Employers may have several resources available including supervision, EAP counselors, coaching, and other support services. Social workers are encouraged to find out about and take advantage of these resources. 4. Keep an Open Dialogue With Your Boss Oftentimes, employers will say that they are blindsided when they find out an employee was struggling with burnout, and they had no idea. It is a good idea for social workers to talk to their employers about their concerns before burnout becomes more serious. 5. Ask For What You Need Social workers tend to put their own needs last. To avoid burnout, social workers need to be able to identify their own needs, and communicate them clearly and directly. 6. Eat Healthy Physical and mental health are directly related. Eating healthy food will give social workers more energy and vitality to face the challenges of the day. Since social workers are often booked up or on the run, it’s a good idea to pack healthy nutritious snacks and lunches. 7. Set Realistic Goals Social workers can burn themselves out by setting too many goals at once, seeking perfection or simply being unrealistic about what can be accomplished in a day. There may be times when social workers need to lighten their to-do list and set reasonable goals and expectations. 8. Take a Vacation Nothing beats a true vacation for unplugging, recharging, and leaving stressors behind. It’s helpful for social workers to have a trusted colleague cover their phone and emails so they can leave the office with confidence. Everyone needs to be able to unplug sometimes, and social workers are no exception (though plan wisely to avoid the post-vacation blues). 9. Build Self-Care Into Your Day Social workers can build self-care micro-strategies into their busy day so they don’t have to wait for their next day off or vacation to take care of themselves. Ideas to get started include keeping a full water bottle handy all day, starting the day with a 2-minute meditation, standing up to stretch or move between clients, or listening to music. 10. Connect With Family & Friends & Tap Into Their Support Like everyone else, social workers need support from people who care about them. Since they are often the ones doing the helping, it can be a struggle to ask for support. Try scheduling a regular date with a friend or family member to help you stay connected. 11. Observe How You React to Client’s Traumas & Make Changes as Needed Social workers are at risk for secondary trauma due regular exposure to their clients’ traumatic experiences, pain, and struggles. Signs of secondary trauma including intrusive thoughts or images, increased startle response, and avoidance of places or people that remind them of the patients’ traumatic events. 12. Meditate Meditation helps many people feel more calm, grounded, and present. Formal meditation is setting a time and sitting for a specified period of time, and informal meditation is noticing the present moment through the senses. Both types have excellent mental and emotional benefits and are good additions to the daily routine. 13. Exercise The link between exercise, improved mood, and reduced workplace stress is supported in research. 30-60 minutes per day, five days per week is generally regarded as a great place to start.6 14. Laugh Finding ways to laugh, be silly,and have fun is a great way to de-stress. Laughter releases endorphins, the feel-good chemical that helps people feel happy and content. 15. Seek Out Peer Support & Consultation Social work can be isolating because it is hard for those not in the field to understand the struggles. Confidentiality restrictions also prevent social workers from talking about their work. Peer and consultation groups can be a great way to process work stress with others who understand and still protect confidentiality. When to Seek Professional Help Social worker burnout can require additional help to overcome. Telltale signs of this are insomnia or sleeping too much, changes to appetite or weight, severe anxiety, and thoughts of death or suicide. Other signs that a social worker should seek professional help are being easily startled, having intrusive thoughts/memories/dreams, and avoidance of triggers. There are many modalities of therapy that can help with stress and burnout management, including cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), internal family systems therapy (IFS), and mindfulness. Eye movement desensitization reprocessing therapy (EMDR) is also helpful for vicarious trauma. For help finding a therapist, start your search through a free online online therapist directory. Final Thoughts On Social Work Burnout Social workers tend to put the needs of others before their own, taking on their clients’ stress and putting them at risk for burnout. It’s critical to practice self care in social work so that you can more effectively provide great care for others, as well as enjoy your own work and personal life. With self-care in place, social work can be an incredibly rewarding, purpose-driven and fun job![1]Yep. That was me over ten years ago. I am a recovering social worker now. ; )Footnotes[1] Social Worker Burnout: Signs, Causes & 15 Tips to Manage Self-care

column1: How do I get over an extremely painful separation?
column3: Source: Google A Seperation can be one of the most stressful and emotional experiences in life. Whatever the reason for the split—and whether you wanted it or not—the breakup of a relationship can turn your whole world upside down and trigger all sorts of painful and unsettling emotions. Even when a relationship is no longer good, a seperation can be extremely painful because it represents the loss, not just of the partnership, but also of the dreams and commitments you shared. Romantic relationships begin on a high note of excitement and hopes for the future. When a relationship fails, we experience profound disappointment, stress, and grief. A seperation launches you into uncharted territory. Everything is disrupted: your routine and responsibilities, your home, your relationships with extended family and friends, and even your identity. A breakup also brings uncertainty about the future.What will life be like without your partner? Will you find someone else? Will you end up alone?These unknowns can often seem worse than being in an unhappy relationship. Handling Pre-Separation Phase-Recognize that it’s OK to have different feelings. It’s normal to feel sad, angry, exhausted, frustrated, and confused—and these feelings can be intense. You may also feel anxious about the future. Accept that reactions like these will lessen over time. Even if the relationship was unhealthy, venturing into the unknown is frightening.Give yourself a break. Give yourself permission to feel and to function at a less than optimal level for a period of time. You may not be able to be quite as productive on the job or care for others in exactly the way you’re accustomed to for a little while. (No one is superman or superwoman; take time to heal, regroup, and re-energize.)Don’t go through this alone. Sharing your feelings with friends and family can help you get through this period. Consider joining a support group where you can talk to others in similar situations. Isolating yourself can raise your stress levels, reduce your concentration, and get in the way of your work, other relationships, and overall health. Don’t be afraid to get outside help if you need it.Allow yourself to grieve the loss of the relationship - Allowing yourself to feel the pain of these losses may be scary. You may fear that your emotions will be too intense to bear, or that you’ll be stuck in a dark place forever. Just remember that grieving is essential to the healing process.Loss of companionship and shared experiences (which may or may not have been consistently pleasurable)Loss of support, be it financial, intellectual, social, or emotionalLoss of hopes, plans, and dreams (which can be even more painful than practical losses)The pain of grief is precisely what helps you let go of the old relationship and move on. And no matter how strong your grief, it won’t last forever. Grieving Phase -Don’t fight your feelingsTalk about how you’re feelingRemember that moving on is the end goalRemind yourself that you still have a futureKnow the difference between a normal reaction to a breakup and depressionReach out to others for supportConnect face-to-face with trusted friends and family members.Spend time with people who support, value, and energize you.Get outside help if you need itCultivate new friendshipsPost-Seperation Phase - Treat yourself like you’re getting over the flu. Get plenty of rest, minimize other sources of stress in your life, and reduce your workload if possible. Learning to take care of yourself can be one of the most valuable lessons you learn following a breakup. As you feel the emotions of your loss and begin learning from your experience, you can resolve to take better care of yourself and make positive choices going forward. Some really useful Self-care tips:Make time each day to nurture yourself. Help yourself heal by scheduling daily time for activities you find calming and soothing. Spend time with good friends, go for a walk in nature, listen to music, enjoy a hot bath, get a massage, read a favorite book, take a yoga class, or savor a warm cup of tea.Pay attention to what you need in any given moment and speak up to express your needs. Honor what you believe to be right and best for you even though it may be different from what your ex or others want. Say “no” without guilt or angst as a way of honoring what is right for you.Stick to a routine. A seperation can disrupt almost every area of your life, amplifying feelings of stress, uncertainty, and chaos. Getting back to a regular routine can provide a comforting sense of structure and normalcy.Take a time out. Try not to make any major decisions in the first few months after a separation or divorce, such as starting a new job or moving to a new city. If you can, wait until you’re feeling less emotional so that you can make decisions with a clearer head.Avoid using alcohol, drugs, or food to cope. When you’re in the middle of a breakup, you may be tempted to do anything to relieve your feelings of pain and loneliness. But using alcohol, drugs, or food as an escape is unhealthy and destructive in the long run. It’s essential to find healthier ways of coping with painful feelings.Explore new interests. A seperation is a beginning as well as an end. Take the opportunity to explore new interests and activities. Pursuing fun, new activities gives you a chance to enjoy life in the here-and-now, rather than dwelling on the past.Making healthy choices: Eat well, sleep well, and exercise. When you’re going through the stress of a divorce or breakup, healthy habits easily fall by the wayside. You might find yourself not eating at all or overeating your favorite junk foods. Exercise might be harder to fit in because of the added pressures at home and sleep might be elusive. But all of the work you are doing to move forward in a positive way will be pointless if you don’t make long-term healthy lifestyle choices.Learning important lessons from your seperation It can be difficult to see it when you’re going through a painful seperation, but in times of emotional crisis, there are opportunities to grow and learn. You may be feeling nothing but emptiness and sadness in your life right now, but that doesn’t mean that things will never change. Try to consider this period in your life a time-out, a time for sowing the seeds for new growth. You can emerge from this experience knowing yourself better and feeling stronger and wiser. In order to fully accept a seperation move on, you need to understand what happened and acknowledge the part you played. The more you understand how the choices you made affected the relationship, the better you’ll be able to learn from your mistakes—and avoid repeating them in the future. column1: How does it feel to get fired from your job suddenly?
column3: Watch how people treat you when you are felled by a loss like this. Hardship doesn't build character or improve empathy... It only ever exposes what was in the person's core all along. I lost two careers suddenly and permanently because of an auto accident. I had a brain injury, and in the time I was rehabilitating, one of my former employers claimed I had voluntarily quit the job prior to the accident. By the time I had enough cognition to understand what had happened, my home, entire metalsmithing studio, and bank account, had all be cleaned out in increments by my former boyfriend and even a pair of my family members. Many of these thefts were within a few feet of me while I nearly died again from a fever and sepsis caused by neglect of proper care of my scalp wounds. I owe my life many times over to a best friend, who sacrificed much he'd never be able to regain in his self-imposed duty to help me get proper medical care, rehabilitation, and who successfully investigated and prevented further thefts. Other long-standing friends also rallied around me, and each did what they could to help me. The most some could do was try to find ways for me to access help, or, to just simply be supportive, humorous, and optimistic company. All this helped far more than words will ever be able to encompass. I am grateful for kindness that proved I had earned better than what the bad people in my life had done to me. That means everything in recovering from a devastating blow to one's independence and self-worth, and it makes a huge difference. It's been seven years now, and I'm still clawing my way out of poverty. I am making a determined effort to reequip my metalsmithing studio, but it's slow going because I want to own it, not owe it to someone else, because I already have a ton of student loans to pay off for a career I can no longer be employed in. I've not been able to do much more than rehabilitate until the last two years, but I am very proud of how far I've come. I never would have made it to this day if I didn't invest in getting and keeping good people in my life. They are not rich, but they love and care for me as much as I love and care for them in turn. Ironically, the people who stole from me are wealthy, and they justified their thefts by asserting I didn't deserve what I had. I had earned everything they took, and if they felt that what they took was more valuable than my well-being, then that tells me what they are worth. Life will never stop beaning you with screwballs, so prepare for that fact.

column1: What can Rahul Gandhi learn from his father Rajiv Gandhi?
column3: Oh, yes definitely. One can learn from anybody. I would like to tell two stories here. Let me tell a million-dollar lesson I learned from a small businessman in Champa in the Janjgir-Champa district state of Chhattisgarh. Kosa Silk of Champa is famous for its purity and is made by people belonging to Dewangan Caste. Kosa is also exported to other countries from here. I do not remember his name, it's a story from 2012. The story goes like this - I was sitting with him over a cup of tea. The gentleman runs a small shop of mixed consumer durable goods. He is not much educated only a class VIII pass but with solid business knowledge. I was dumbstruck. These small-town people are very simple and honest. He told me his stories, that he has achieved everything all by himself. There was a time everybody told him to wind up his business as he was making losses and there was no way to sustain these losses. But he did exactly the opposite. He sold all his wife's ornaments and put all his stake in the business. Do you know why he did it? He told me that “when things are not going well, increase your stake so that that there is no point of return. You can not go back. I have put everything at gamble, including my beloved wife’s ornament. Do you think I will let it go? No. That was my turning point” Trust me I had tears in my eyes, I stood up and hugged him. Possibly no management school could teach you what he said that day. Increase your stake in things you love to do that all the doors to back off get closed Rahul has been written off by most political Pundits. But he has not given up. He has started the “Bharat Jodo Yatra” which nobody has taken up in decades. He is increasing his stakes, he is putting everything at stake. My next story is MP. It's about a lady who created a financial model. I especially went to meet her. I don’t remember the name of her village. Her name is Reva Devi, an Adivasi woman, uneducated. In dire need of money, she went to the nearest bank branch with her pair of buffaloe to get a loan. She offered her buffaloes as a mortgage and asked for a loan. Just imagine the scene of two buffaloes inside a bank. The branch manager didn’t know how to react. But somehow managed to make her understand that banks can not take buffaloes as mortgages and sent her back. But this indomitable tribal lady was not going to sit tight. She started her movement of creating self-help groups for financial assistance, initially in her village, then in all the nearby villages. Soon she became a role model in the entire state. She was also honored by the union government for her tremendous contribution to the society.New roads are to be built when all the doors are closed. Life always teaches you some lessons. But there are people who wouldn’t take no for an answer no matter how much difficulty they face in life. They challenge back life. Rahul has made a new beginning by starting the “Bharat Jodo Yatra” This is a great beginning. He asked for votes from the public, but the public refused to give him mandate and refused to listen to him. So he has gone to the public to listen to them. One needs to change the way to look at life when one sees a roadblock. Ordinary men stop and return when facing a roadblock. But an extraordinary person looks for alternatives or even removes the roadblock. People have reservations about Rahul. So he has to go and find out what are those reservations and resolve them. Coming back to your question - What can Rahul Gandhi learn from his father Rajiv Gandhi? Two of the Gandhi family member died for neglecting security concerns. Indira Gandhi was advised to remove the Sikh security guards from her duty. But she refused to do so and lost her life. Rajiv was repeatedly warned by PLO leader Yasser Arafat to cancel his election campaign in TN, particularly at Sriperumbudur. Yasser Arafat was Chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization (PLO) from 1969 to 2004 and President of the Palestinian National Authority (PNA) from 1994 to 2004. He was a very good friend of Rajiv. Arafat was aware of the conspiracy to assassinate Rajiv and was constantly warning Rajiv to be careful. Like Fidel Castro, Arafat himself had an invincible security arrangement and had an extensive intelligence network to thwart innumerable attempts by Mossad to assassinate him. Unfortunately, Rajiv didn’t heed to his friend’s advice and was assassinated at Sriperumbudur. The irony is that it Rajiv Gandhi government created the SPG for VVIP security. But VP Singh removed his Z plus security and provided just two constables of Delhi police for his security. So the first lesson Rahul should take is to never undermine the security concerns. Secondly not to trust anyone, particularly the leaders who are highly ambitious and have aspirations for the PM’s chair. Rajiv was betrayed by two of his closest party colleagues - PVN Rao and V P Singh. Both became PMs. He needs to keep a close watch on all his key officials and team member. Thirdly Rahul needs to study all the political decisions of his father good and as well bad, more so the decisions which led to his failure. Those could be the biggest learning in Rahul’s political journey. Fourth - Rajiv Gandhi had a team of advisors to guide me on various matters. Though he got them in place after becoming PM. However, Rahul has to do it in advance. He needs a few groups of advisers - Political, Economical, Grooming, a strong IT cell, a team to design his speech after making threadbare analysis, and a team of strategists for image building, and publicity campaigns.

column1: What steps should I take to ensure successful psychological recovery after a traumatic event?
column3: First I’m sorry to hear you have suffered such an event. You will need to be gentle with yourself. Yes, do see a good trauma therapist but in terms of self care know that your whole system will have gone into shock and will need calming day by day. I’d suggest having a friend or family member, who knows something traumatic has happened to you, check in every day at the same time. Perhaps you can arrange to have a short walk with them. Perhaps you have a dog, or can offer an extra walk for a neighbour’s dog every day. The rhythm of getting up, washing, dressing and going out may seem simplistic but it is exactly this connection to every day sensory experience that gets disrupted in traumatic stress disorders. The same applies to preparing and eating simple healthy food you like. Think about good food as your “medicine” as it is easy to skip meals or comfort eat when anxious or depressed, both of which are frequent responses to trauma. If you find yourself spacing out and loosing time know that this will pass. It’s called dissociation and you can gather yourself by returning to your breathing for a few minutes. Put one hand on your heart and another on your belly and sit or stand with your feet firmly on the ground. You can say something like “ I’m here now, I’m safe,” or “it’s Tuesday” or anything to orient yourself. You can also follow this up by quietly naming five things you can hear, five things you can see and five things your body is touching or you could move slightly to touch. Maybe you could also write these things down. What these little exercises do is return your nervous system from a hyper vigilant flight/ fright /freeze state to normal resting alertness. You may have to do this again and again over then next few months. When you are ready playing an instrument, singing in a choir, art making,( even colouring,) gardening, cooking mindfully or the practise of a familiar martial art will also help. What all these activities have in common is a bringing of your physical body into an harmonious connection with your feelings and thoughts, and in some cases into connection with others, all of which is disrupted through trauma. Your therapist should help you with traumatic memories, any intrustive thoughts or images or overwhelming emotions. Often such feelings will connect you with other losses from your past. Just know that these feelings will come up and that they will pass. In time you will contain the images or sounds and be able to witness them and tolerate the feelings they bring. Your therapist should be a witness in this and you may also find a support group or a particular friend helpful. Friends do not always have to hear details again and again, or even at all, but can help simply with their presence. Don’t isolate yourself but ask those who offer to just come over occasionally and keep you company. If you belong to a church or mediation group ask for support. There is always a grief process of some sort after a traumatic incident and recovery can take some time. There are lots of good books and websites: Drs. Peter Levine, Bruce Perry, Bessel van der Kolk, Gabor Mate all write about trauma, neuroscience and recovery helpfully and so does Judith Herman, however a lot of reading may itself be stressful, so dip in by all means, but overall be guided by your therapist and good self care. Best

column1: Adult How different has life become for an average citizen of Azerbaijan and Armania since the war began?
column3: An Azerbaijani here. Many things have changed.The greatest change is that Azerbaijanis have recovered a significant part of their self-esteem after decades. The Karabakh war of the 90s which resulted in a defeat for Azerbaijan, brought on territorial losses, displacement of over half a million Azerbaijanis only from the occupied territories (Nagorno-Karabakh and 7 adjacent district), brutal series of war crimes against hundreds of civilians, had significantly hurt the national pride of Azerbaijanis. Last several days did a great job in helping Azerbaijanis recover that pride. Azerbaijanis always had their full trust in the army but seeing it in action made everyone proud. For the first time in 27 years, Azerbaijanis heard the announcement of the liberation of civilian settlements and with tearful eyes rejoiced at the news of at least some of their compatriots decades later losing the title of “Internally Displaced Persons” and getting a chance to go back their homes. Indeed, these are historic times for Azerbaijanis.Azerbaijanis got again reminded that they and their plights are at best either ignored or they face immense enmity from many in the international community. Global media outlets i.e. Reuters, BBC didn’t shed any light on the Azerbaijani side of the conflict, didn’t care to mention about over half a million Azerbaijani IDPs waiting to go back their homes, which have been reduced to complete, uninhabited ruins over the last three decades, and instead focused solely on unfounded stories from tabloids on Syrian mercenaries. Russian media unleashed a full terror on Azerbaijan and Azerbaijanis, completely ignoring them and their side of the story. Russia provided arms to Armenia. Iran did its best to allow the smoothest delivery of them to Armenia. Only Turkey and Pakistan clearly stood on Azerbaijan’s side. So, all these strengthened the feeling among Azerbaijanis that they are alone in this fight and will be, and they should push only ahead taking everything in their hands as the international community is only there to make empty calls for ceasefire with no substance and then doing nothing to follow up.Azerbaijanis are terrorized. Our second largest city Ganja with half a million population was shelled. Many of my friends from Ganja, who live abroad, share how much they fear for the lives of their family, friends in the city as they can wake up any day to the news of their home having been shelled and their family members gone. Many other Azerbaijani cities have been shelled, and so far over 30 civilians have died as a result of civilian objects hit by missiles fired by the Armenian army. Mingachevir (4th largest city) hosting the largest hydro-power station was targeted as well.Ganja, Azerbaijan after being hit by Armenian missiles. column1: Why do we hear phrases like "youthful idealism"? What happens when people get older?
column3: Youthful idealism is the cheapest, least difficult form of idealism. All it takes is hope, and it's easy to have hope when you haven't encountered any adversity. Many young people have been successful at everything they have tried, because school is an artificial environment where all problems have solutions. Changing the world turns out to be long, hard work. And it is chancy work -- success is not guaranteed. You might spend ten years going down one path, only to find that it was the wrong path. Or the problem you chose might turn out to be incredibly difficult, beyond the capability of humanity in your lifetime. There is no force limiting the difficulty of problems, as there is in school. Some people, when they encounter these difficulties, give up their idealism. They are just not willing to put in the long hours. Or they just don't have the resources. Once out of school, they have to work all day just to pay the rent, or to help family members. Or, they can't deal emotionally with the possibility of failure. The uncertainty bothers them so much that they would rather not try. Some people fall victim to confusion. In the beginning, they saw only one viewpoint, their own. As they gain experience, they learn to see other people's viewpoints, and they discover that some of those viewpoints are completely different from their own. They are shaken to find that what seems like a big problem to them, might actually seem like a near-ideal state of affairs to some other people -- and that they can learn to see the other point of view! They fail to synthesize all of the ambiguity and complexity of the world into their worldview, and lose their bearings. Some people become terribly embarrassed by their idealism, and want to put it behind them. It's normal for our views to mature and get more complex as we get older. That can make our earlier views seem simplistic and foolish. Some people really hate feeling foolish, so they disavow their younger self, and from that point on, they try to adopt only "safe" opinions that could never make them feel foolish later. Some people fail to find a place to productively apply their skills. They literally don't know where to start. If you look at any really successful project (idealistic or not), you will find some serendipity -- people who just happened to be in the right place at the right time, with the right connections and skills. Some people never have that serendipitous moment, and eventually conclude that they just aren't needed right now, as if they went in for jury duty and their number wasn't called. Some people just become more selfish. After years of self-sacrifice at a nonprofit or in a political entity, they feel like they have paid their dues. They are still living like college students, while their friends who are less talented now have nice houses and cars, healthy food to eat, and the freedom to go on awesome vacations all over the world, even though these friends haven't worked as hard. They decide that they deserve the same things -- if anything, they believe they deserve more, because of the virtuous nonprofit work they did. Once all these people have dropped out, what emerges at the other end of this process are the veterans, the grizzled campaigners. They haven't accomplished everything they set out to accomplish, but they've accomplished some of it. There have been losses and compromises, but the flame still burns within them. Now: they have become tactical communicators. They don't always say what they're thinking -- they tailor their words to the people around them. They know that most people aren't motivated by idealism most of the time, and might actually be intimidated or turned off by it. Many people feel sad about the loss of their youthful idealism, or they feel guilty that they have abandoned it. Or, if they gave it up as impossible, they get invested in that impossibility and feel threatened if other people show that it might not be so impossible. They want to shut those people down to justify their own life choices. All of these types of people use the phrase "youthful idealism" to dismiss attitudes that trouble them. So, the veterans of idealism will choose their words carefully. Instead of talking about their idealism, they talk about what they are most proud of, their results. As for your second question: Having kids is part of saving the world. Where do you think the world comes from? :)

column1: How do I get detachment in life?
column3: Before pondering on how to get detached from this worldly life let me make you understand about some facts. There are three terms in this context: Attachment, Detachment and Non-attachment. Here is an examples to get proper understanding of these aspects:A patient goes to a doctor to seek diagnosis for his illness. Here the patient has attachment with himself. Because he has to take care of himself. But the patient has Detachment with the doctor. Since he has to get well by the treatment of Doctor so he wants that his doctor be ok at least till the time he get cured from his illness. Because if anything wrong happens with doctor the patient will be affected (may be a little bit) since that doctor is treating him. But the doctor has Non-attachment with the patient. The state of his feelings for the patient falls under the category of Non-attachment. Although he is treating the patient and he is willing that his patient get well soon with his treatments but still he doesn't have any attachment with that patient.Attachment is the biggest strength and biggest weakness as well. though it gives you the power to love someone more than yourself, It becomes difficult to live when you loose something you are attached to.You can have a state of Detachment with your self realization / self awakening power, but it is difficult to be in the state of Non-attachment. It is highest state you can be in. You can be detached from this worldly life without leaving all the worldly thing. But for this you have to change the way of thinking, you have to change the way you are taking these worldly things seriously, you have to change the mindset and make yourself understand that these worldly things are only available for you till you are breathing, till you are alive. All of your family members, relatives, worldly stuffs, luxuries etc has a connection with you till you are alive on this earth. The fact is you are mortal and every other worldly living / Non-living thing is mortal. So, why to be so much attached to these things which may be detached to you forcefully by the act of nature.I am not suggesting to let everything go from your hold. I am not suggesting to live your life like a celibate, but you should practice to be surrounded with all these worldly things with a feeling of detachment. The day you will have developed this state of divine, you will definitely be able to live a life without having worries. In this wicked world people quarrel on such silly things that are really nonsense and worthless only because of ultimate attachment with their stuffs (for example quarrel on getting scratch on their car in result of hitting by another's car). Develop the state of divine by awaken your true self, by self realization. Ask few questions from yourself :Was it really worth, being so much worried, sad and frustrated on your past losses (your losses of physical stuffs etc)?What is the ultimate goal of your life? Only living with pleasure of mortal things or something else?Where you will go after this life? What is the reality of afterlife? What will happen with your soul after your life? What will happen after your 60-70-80... Years?When you will search the answer of these questions you will learn many things which would ultimately help you to live this journey fruitful and meaningful. Your family deserves you. You deserve your hard earned worldly stuffs. Be attached to your are beloved ones. But beware of serious attachment with anyone. It will give you much pain if you loose any of the worldly thing. So, it's better to have a state of Detachment while being attached to all of these worldly things.Have a meaningful and worries free life ahead !!(photos source: Google)

column1: What is typical guilty pleasure of Pakistanis?
column3: Representing the unique guilty pleasures of a population of 210 million is indeed a challenging task.. when people come from different regions, races and economic classes.. Yet here is a half baked attempt! First let’s talk about our vices:-From smoking to smoking up, naswar (chewing tobacco), gutka (betel nut) to having paan… all Pakistanis are addicted to their specific choice of poison..So what do we do for fun - oh we find ways to keep ourselves entertained… whether that is playing Ludo (board game), Billiard, Street Cricket or Foozball on the streets..Other fun things that happen in your car (other than the dancing car)The long drives - either alone or travel trips with your friendsThe street food that you rush to on your car, cycle, motorbikeThe headbanging to music especially to QawalisThe bumper stickers (Translation: Heart for sale, priced at one smile only. Falling in love is injurious to health: Ministry of Love)But are you Pakistanis really free to do whatever you feel like you ask..? Oh we would do anything for free..First thing on your mind when you go to a friend’s/new location : Tera net ka password kya hai ( Translation: What’s your Wifi password)A friend’s small achievement can be used to blackmail them into giving a treatYou get invited to a party and don’t have to pay for the booze.. ??? Pinch me, or am I in heaven already…Weddings bring their own set of pleasure/joy to PakistanisFree Wedding Food - Consider it like the Buffet of Life.. where people loosen their belt and their standards.Dholkis/Tappas - where the family members are singing together as there is competition between the boys and the girls sideDance Practices and the Final You Think You Can Dance.. from both parties representing the bride’s side and groom’s side..The Aunties/Family member who find it extremely self-pleasing to comment on everyone/everything under the sun while simultaneously scouting talent (read future bride/groom) for their progeny.The Uncles who want to know what are you doing with your life and rub their kids achievement in your face….How could I forget eating the Bidh at the weddingsThe weird and inappropriate jokes at the Joota Chupai Rasam (Shoe Hiding Tradition) while the Bride’s family tries to extract money from the groom for returning the shoe.Also aerial firing at weddings…Public LifeSpeaking of aerial firing of another kindSomething that happens seasonally Summers - Taking a dip in your nearest water source is a public affairWinters - walking around wrapped in a quilt..(End of Part 1) 1) Charpai in the Sun - Eating kinnow (Winters)2) Juggatbaazi - While most of the older ones grew to know this through stage dramas.. the quick wit is definitely ingrained within our society.. which can be a good thing (meme material) and a bad thing (troll, hate, online abuse)3) juggad (innovation)..
