[ https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Nice1．False: The vocational education and training centers in Xinjiang are "concentration camps" detaining over one million Uyghurs. Fact check: ◆The vocational education and training centers, established in accordance with law in Xinjiang, are no different in nature from the community corrections in the US, the Desistance and Disengagement Programme (DDP) in the UK, and the deradicalization centers in France. All of them are useful measures and positive explorations for preventive counter-terrorism and deradicalization, and are in line with the principles and spirit of the UN Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy and other counter-terrorism resolutions. ◆The education and training work in Xinjiang is guided by the spirit of the rule of law as well as international principles on counter-terrorism and deradicalization. It has solid legal basis and follows well-defined legal procedures, and is done in a way that makes no linkage to any specific region, ethnic group or religion. There is no such thing as "suppression on ethnic minorities" or "persecution of Muslims". ◆The claim that "nearly one million Uyghurs are detained", an outright rumor, is based on two highly dubious "studies". The first "study" was done by the US government-backed Network of Chinese Human Rights Defenders (CHRD) with interviews of only eight people. The CHRD applied the estimated ratio shown in this absurdly small sample to the whole of Xinjiang, drawing a crude conclusion that one million people were detained in the "re-education detention camps" and two million were "forced to attend day/evening re-education sessions". The second "study" was done by a far-right fundamentalist Christian Adrian Zenz, a.k.a. Zheng Guoen. According to The Grayzone, a US-based independent news website, Zenz is a senior fellow in China studies at the far-right Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation established by the US government in 1983, and a senior member in a research group set up with the masterminding of the US intelligence community to study Xinjiang's vocational education and training centers. He believes he is "led by God" on a "mission" against China. In September 2018, Zenz wrote an article published in the Central Asian Survey journal, concluding that "Xinjiang's total re-education internment figure may be estimated at just over one million." According to The Grayzone, Zenz based this conclusion on a single report by Istiqlal TV, a Uyghur exile media organization based in Turkey. Far from a journalistic organization, Istiqlal TV advances separatism while playing host to an assortment of extremist figures. One such character who often appears on Istiqlal TV is Abduqadir Yaqupjan, a leader of the East Turkestan Islamic Movement (ETIM). Maybe it was because the reference he cited was too absurd even to himself, that Zenz admitted that "there is no certainty" to his estimate. But Zenz "bumped up" his estimate again in November 2019, claiming China was detaining 1.8 million people. 2. False: The vocational education and training centers in Xinjiang carried out "political indoctrination and intimidation" over the Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities. Fact check: ◆The vocational education and training centers in Xinjiang provided courses on standard spoken and written Chinese language, legal knowledge, professional skills and deradicalization, to address the inadequate language proficiency, lack of legal literacy and job skills, as well as the varying degrees of religious extremism influence among their trainees. The purpose of the centers is to tackle terrorism and religious extremism at the root, not so-called "political indoctrination and intimidation" by any means. ◆Through all-round learning, the trainees have freed themselves from the influence of terrorism and religious extremism. Their overall capacity has been improved, as evidenced by a markedly increased understanding of the law, the ability to speak and write in standard Chinese, acquisition of practical skills and the general improvement in employability. Most of them have found jobs that give them a stable income, and notably improved their families' living standards. 3. False: The vocational education and training centers are poorly conditioned and lack medical facilities. The trainees are subjected to forced political indoctrination and torture, and are deprived of their rights to exercise religious customs, use local ethnic languages among others. Fact check: ◆The vocational education and training centers strictly follow the basic principle of respecting and protecting human rights enshrined in China's Constitution and other laws. The trainees' basic rights and personal dignity are well protected, and insults or abuse against the trainees in any manner are prohibited. The centers fully guarantee the personal freedom of trainees. The centers are managed as boarding schools where trainees may go home on a regular basis and ask for leave to attend to personal matters, and enjoy the freedom of correspondence. ◆Trainees' freedom of religious belief is fully respected and protected at the centers. Those with a religious belief can decide on their own whether to take part in legal religious activities when they are at home. ◆The centers fully respect and protect the customs of all ethnic groups and provide a rich variety of nutritious halal food free of charge. ◆The trainees' right to use the spoken and written languages of their own ethnicity is fully protected at the centers. All regulations, curricula and canteen menus at the centers are written in both standard Chinese and local ethnic languages. ◆The centers have well-equipped facilities. Dorms are furnished with radio, television, and air conditioning or electric fans. Medical facilities are set up to provide free health counseling services and treatment for trainees. There are also venues for basketball, volleyball, table tennis and other sports, cultural venues such as reading rooms, computer rooms and cinemas, as well as venues for performances like auditoriums and open-air stages. Singing and dancing performances of different ethnic groups, sports games and other extra-curricular activities are often held to meet trainees' learning, living and entertainment needs to the greatest extent possible. ◆Legal counseling rooms are set up in the centers to help address trainees' law-related difficulties and questions promptly. There are psychotherapy rooms to provide psychological counseling services and care for trainees' mental health. All trainees are covered by old-age, medical and other social insurances and free medical check-ups. 4. False: Detainees in the mass internment camps in Xinjiang include permanent residents of the US and Australia. Fact check: ◆The vocational education and training centers in Xinjiang have never received trainees who are not Chinese nationals. 5. False: Xinjiang's special operations against violent terrorist activities aim to suppress ethnic minorities under the pretext of fighting terrorism. Fact check: ◆Xinjiang had suffered long and deep from terrorism and extremism. Statistics show that from 1990 to 2016, ethnic separatists, religious extremists and violent terrorists plotted and conducted several thousand violent terrorist cases and incidents, killing a large number of innocent civilians and several hundred police officers, and causing immeasurable property losses. These incidents inflicted untold sufferings on the people of various ethnic groups in Xinjiang. ◆In the face of a grave and complicated counter-terrorism situation and the urgent demand from people of all ethnic groups for suppressing violence and terrorist crimes and protecting life and property safety, China's Xinjiang region has taken a series of active measures. Responding to the United Nations Global Counter-Terrorism Strategy and other counter-terrorism resolutions, Xinjiang has upheld the principle of not linking terrorism with any particular region, ethnic group or religion, and acted in accordance with the law to crack down on violence and terrorist activities that violate human rights, endanger public security, undermine ethnic unity and aim at separating the country. Since 2014, a total of 1,588 violent and terrorist groups have been taken out, 12,995 violent terrorists arrested and 2,052 explosive devices seized. Such operations have effectively curbed the rising trend of frequent terrorist activities and protected people's right to life, right to health, right to development and other basic rights to the maximum extent. These measures have received full support from people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang. ◆Through law-based counter-terrorism, deradicalization and vocational education and training, Xinjiang has not seen a single violent terrorist case in the past three-odd years. Extremist infiltration has been effectively curbed, public security significantly improved and people's sense of fulfillment, happiness and security markedly enhanced. ◆In October 2019, more than 60 countries spoke in support of China's Xinjiang policy at the United Nations General Assembly. Among them, over 30 are Islamic countries. In contrast, none of the few countries criticizing China's Xinjiang policy are Islamic countries. ◆Since late December 2018, more than 1,000 people from over 90 countries visited Xinjiang in 70-plus groups. They include UN officials, foreign envoys to China, representatives of relevant countries to Geneva, journalists and members of religious groups. After their visits, they expressed the view that Xinjiang's counter-terrorism and deradicalization efforts are in line with the purposes and principles of the UN in fighting terrorism and upholding basic human rights and that these efforts deserve to be fully recognized and emulated by others. 6. False: China restricts the freedom of communication and movement of Uyghurs in Xinjiang in the name of counter-terrorism and deradicalization. Fact check: ◆Xinjiang has never restricted the freedom of movement of Uyghurs or people of any other ethnic group. In Xinjiang, anyone from any ethnic group, except those prohibited from leaving the country for suspected crimes, can exit and enter China freely. Several hundred thousand people from Xinjiang are now overseas. ◆Xinjiang has never restricted Uyghurs or people of other ethnic groups from contacting their overseas relatives. They can do so not only through international phone calls, but also through voice and video chats on instant messaging apps such as WeChat and QQ. They can also do business and trade with people in other countries through various communication means. 7. False: Xinjiang conducts large-scale surveillance on local ethnic minorities. Fact check: ◆It is an international common practice to harness modern technology and big data in improving social governance. For example, there were 4.2 million surveillance cameras installed in the UK as early as 2010, the highest number in the world then. Today the country has about six million cameras, one for every ten people. In the United States, facial recognition is conducted in the top 20 airports against passengers. The city surveillance system built by New York police has devices covering every neighborhood of the city watching people and vehicles on the street and tracking and screening information on people's mobile phones. What Xinjiang has done in this respect pales significantly in comparison with these two countries. ◆The cameras in urban and rural public places, main roads and transport hubs in Xinjiang are installed in accordance with the law for the purpose of improving social governance and forestalling and combating crimes. These measures make people feel safer and are widely supported by people of all ethnic groups. The measure does not target any specific ethnicity, not to mention that cameras by themselves identify or target no specific ethnicity. They are there to deter bad guys and protect good people. 8. False: Mass forced labor against ethnic minorities is taking place in Xinjiang. Fact check: ◆According to a US news website the Greyzone, the forced labor stories were in fact a PR blitz orchestrated by anti-China forces from the US and Australia. ◆The stories were cooked up by the Australian Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI) which has long been funded by the US government and American arms dealers. To serve the interests of its sponsors, the institute blatantly spread disinformation to vilify and demonize China, particularly on Xinjiang-related issues. Together with anti-China forces in the US, the ASPI made up baseless and biased stories to smear and attack Xinjiang's counter-terrorism and deradicalization efforts. The institute has no credibility whatsoever. Former Australian Ambassador to China Geoff Raby sees the ASPI as "the architect of the China threat theory in Australia". Former Qantas Airways CEO John Menadue said the institute "lacks integrity and brings shame to Australia". ◆Ethnic minority workers from Xinjiang are part and parcel of the country's labor force. They have the rights to be employed, sign labor contracts, obtain labor remunerations, take rest and vacations, acquire labor safety and health protection, and enjoy social insurance and welfare as prescribed by law. They have the freedom to choose their occupation. Their personal freedom has never been restricted. ◆There are only limited job opportunities in the four southern Xinjiang prefectures (Hotan, Aksu and Kashi prefectures, and Kizilsu Kirgiz autonomous prefecture) as industrialization and urbanization there are underdeveloped. The government of the Xinjiang Autonomous Region has taken measures based on the wishes of local people to help them find jobs in their hometowns, nearby cities or other areas of Xinjiang, or in the provinces and cities that have pair-up assistance programs with Xinjiang, thus ensuring peoples' right to work to the maximum extent. Since 2018, Xinjiang has helped 151,000 surplus rural workers from poor families in the southern prefectures to find employment elsewhere. With an average annual income of over 45,000 yuan, these workers have all been lifted out of poverty. ◆China has been improving its legal system and its State Council has established an inter-agency mechanism to crack down on crimes such as human trafficking and forced labor. Such efforts have proven effective. China earnestly fulfills its international obligations and has ratified 26 international conventions on human rights. China will continue to strengthen exchanges with all parties and fight forced labor and other crimes together. 9. False: Xinjiang has demolished a large number of mosques. Fact check: ◆Xinjiang has seen sound development of the religion of Islam. The number of mosques in Xinjiang has grown from some 2,000 at the beginning of reform and opening-up in the late 1970s to 24,400 today, more than 10 times that in the United States. In Xinjiang, there is a mosque for every 530 Muslims on average. ◆Xinjiang takes the preservation and maintenance of mosques very seriously. Some cramped and dilapidated mosques, those with poor layout designs and those inconvenient for religious activities have been rebuilt, relocated or expanded in light of the needs and wishes of local Muslim communities. Such adjustments have been welcomed by religious leaders and believers. 10. False: Graveyards of ethnic minorities are demolished in parts of Xinjiang. Fact check: ◆Under the regulations of the local authorities, the government does not promote cremation for ethnic minorities observing traditional ways of interment. On the contrary, it takes concrete measures to help preserve the tradition, by designating burial ground and building dedicated cemeteries. Besides, there is no restriction on other ethnic customs followed in weddings, funerals, and name-giving ceremonies. 11. False: The "Pair Up and Become Family" program is designed to monitor ethnic minorities in Xinjiang. Fact check: ◆Since 2016, an extensive ethnic unity campaign has been conducted among government officials and people of different ethnicities in Xinjiang. Some 1.1 million officials have paired up and made friends with 1.6 million local people, treating each other like family members. They have respected and helped each other, and forged deep bonds through close interactions. The officials leveraged their expertise to help local people explore ways to shake off poverty and address difficulties in their lives, such as access to medical services, job opportunities and education. The campaign, with its real, substantial benefits to the public, has been well received by the people of all ethnic groups. 12. False: The local government sends Uyghur children to boarding schools and separates them from their parents. Fact check: ◆The boarding school system is an effective means to improve education in China's remote areas and ease the burden on students and their families. In Xinjiang, students of all ethnicities attend schools closest to their homes. Those living near the campus can be commuter students. For those living further away, schools provide them with free accommodation, plus free meals for those from rural families. It is up to the students and their parents to decide whether to live on or off campus. 13. False: The Chinese government forces sterilization, abortion and birth control on Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in Xinjiang. Fact check: ◆The Chinese government protects the lawful rights and interests of all Chinese without distinction of ethnicity. Over the years, the Uyghur people and other ethnic minorities have enjoyed a preferential population policy. In the four decades between 1978 and 2018, the Uyghur population in Xinjiang increased from 5.55 million to 11.68 million, accounting for 46.8% of the total population of the autonomous region. ◆To put things into perspective, let's look at the situation in the United States. Racial and ethnic minorities in the US have long been the targets of bullying, exclusion, and widespread and systemic discrimination in the political, economic, cultural and social aspects of their lives. Take Native Americans as an example. For quite a long period of time, the US government had been enforcing a policy of genocide, segregation and assimilation against Native Americans. For nearly a century after its founding, the US was uprooting and killing American Indians in its Westward Movement. The Native American population plunged from 5 million in 1492 to 0.25 million in the early 20th century. It now accounts for a mere 2 percent of the US population. Another example, African Americans. African Americans have a COVID-19 infection rate five times that of white Americans, and a much higher mortality rate as well. This highlights the racial inequality in the US. The recent death of an African American George Floyd and the massive protests that followed once again shows that the systemic racial discrimination in the US has reached a point where racial and ethnic minorities "can't breathe". It calls for an urgent solution. 14. False: The Chinese government's brutal crackdown on Muslims is a human rights violation not seen since World War II. Fact check: ◆One of China's five ethnic minority autonomous regions, the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region is home to 25 million people of different ethnic groups who live and work in harmony. Among them, ten ethnic groups, including Uyghur and Hui, consist mainly of Muslims. The Muslim population has been growing steadily, accounting for nearly 60% of the total local population. ◆Under a system of ethnic regional autonomy, China treats all ethnic groups equally and pursues prosperity and development for people of all ethnicities. It ensures that ethnic autonomous areas exercise the power to self-govern in accordance with law, and protects the legitimate rights and interests of ethnic minorities. In Xinjiang, every chairperson of the People's Congress, the autonomous regional government, and the CPPCC regional committee is from ethnic minority groups. Ethnic minorities take 64.2% of the seats in the 13th Xinjiang People's Congress, and 46.7% of the seats in the 13th CPPCC Regional Committee of Xinjiang. ◆Xinjiang fully implements the policy of freedom of religious belief. The freedom of religious belief of all people, regardless of their ethnicity, is fully protected in accordance with law. Believers and non-believers enjoy the same political rights and economic, social and cultural rights. ◆On 25 May, George Floyd, an African-American, was killed in Minneapolis in a brutal assault by a white police officer. His death triggered massive demonstrations and protests across the country, throwing into sharp relief the public outcry and anger over the systemic racism long in existence in the country. The UN Human Rights Council held an urgent debate and adopted a resolution voicing strong condemnation and urging concrete measures from the US to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms of Africans and of people of African descent. 15. False: The Chinese government uses COVID-19 to "wipe out" Muslims. Fact check: ◆Thanks to the joint efforts of the people of all ethnic groups in Xinjiang, COVID-19 has been effectively contained in the region. As of 29 June, a total of 76 confirmed cases had been reported in Xinjiang, including 73 cured cases and three deaths. With no new confirmed cases for over 130 days, Xinjiang has resumed full normalcy in economic and social activity early on and is back on track for economic and social development. ◆On 9 December 2019, Shohrat Zakir, Chairman of the Government of Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, announced that all the trainees at the vocational education and training centers had completed their studies. There is no risk of cluster infections at these centers. 16. False: In media reports or social media posts about "missing persons", overseas Uyghurs tell stories about their "families" and "friends" in Xinjiang who have "lost contact" or "gone missing". Fact check: ◆Xinjiang has never curtailed the freedom of travel of Uyghur people or people of any other ethnic groups. Nor is there any restriction on communication with relatives abroad. ◆It has been verified by the relevant authorities that the so-called "missing persons" mentioned by overseas East Turkistan elements are either living a normal life or simply non-existent. column1: Is it ever a good idea to share the "emotional neglect" aspect of our diagnosis with our parents… Or should we simply embrace "what was" and move on with that acceptance and/or resignation in striving for our CURE?
column3: When I was going through my own authentic recovery from emotional disorder, experiencing epiphany after epiphany related to my underlying misperceptions about the nature of feelings, self, and life (which is the root cause of all emotional disorders), my next major revelation was that these misperceptions that I had always lived with could only have come from my emotional teachers - my parents. Consider for a second that a teacher cannot teach you things that he or she does not know. If your parents are emotionally unhealthy, it is impossible that they will teach you emotionally healthy perceptions and attitudes. So whatever attitudes your parents truly live with, this is what you observe and learn from as a child.Too many people will ignorantly tell you that the origin of things like Borderline Personality Disorder is ‘trauma’. This is a lie. It is a lie that completely overlooks the most relevant aspect of the development of emotional disorders. Borderline Personality Disorder is not a ‘mental illness’, and it is not a ‘mental health’ issue. It is an emotional disorder, which simply refers to the emotional frustration and confusion that results from the natural disharmony in one’s approach to life, and this disharmonious approach to life is the result of being taught inaccurate perceptions about the nature of feelings, self, and life. How were you ‘taught’ this? By observing your own parents’ consistent attitudes towards these things. So why is the cause of emotional disorders not ‘trauma’? Because not everybody who has an emotional disorder was locked in a basement as a child and burned with cigarettes. But every single person who has an emotional disorder was exposed to unhealthy, underlying attitudes on the part of their parents. And by the way, it is not the ‘trauma’ of being chained in the basement that does real harm, anyway. Rather, it is how this behavior reflects the true attitudes that the parents who do such things live with in regard to the nature of feelings, self, and life. Remember what I said: Children observe their parents’ attitudes, and use this to form their own concrete understanding about the nature of feelings, self, and life, themselves. So being chained in the basement clearly reflects a twisted, unhealthy attitude towards feelings, self, and life. After all, if feelings mattered, if children mattered, if you mattered, then your parents wouldn’t be chaining you up in the basement. But does something as dramatic as this have to be in your past history in order for you to have received the same messages, or to have been exposed to the same unhealthy attitudes? No. If your parents laugh when you’re afraid, because they think you shouldn’t be afraid, the effect on a child is exactly the same, because the messages in the attitudes are the same.How about when your parents tell you to stop crying? What attitude is reflected there? The unhealthy, erroneous attitude that you are feeling the ‘wrong’ thing, that you can choose what you feel, that your feelings are bothersome. Is there such a thing as human-beings feeling the ‘wrong’ thing? Or of being able to choose what we feel? Of course not. Feelings are never good or bad, right or wrong. Whatever you feel about anything is just what you feel. Feeling is something we experience, not something we do. You can see from the example how, although there is no obvious, dramatic ‘trauma’ going on (that ol’ favorite lie of misdirection pushed by the inept professional community as a group), the child is still being exposed to a profoundly harmful attitude. The abuse is in the false education one is receiving about the nature of their feelings. A person given this bullshit education will go on to use this template to understand everything in their lives for the rest of their lives. (Unless they do the work to identify and fix these unbelievably-powerful distortions, such as I did.) Now what do you suppose went through my mind as I had these revelations for myself in my own authentic recovery? I felt great excitement. One of the first things I couldn’t wait to do was to meet with my parents and to share all of these great epiphanies with them. For me, these insights were earth-shattering and enormous. I could see how my fundamental misperceptions about the nature of things like feelings, self, and life had negatively and powerfully affected my entire life. Not only that, but I could see how it had negatively and powerfully affected my parents’ entire lives, and how they were directly responsible. (Children are not responsible for their own physical, mental, and emotional care because they are not fully developed physically, mentally, and emotionally as human-beings. So the inherent responsibility belongs to parents, who are indeed enjoying full development as human-beings. So it is not a matter of if the parents are able to properly live up to their inherent responsibility, it is instead a matter of if they are capable. I am not able to play the piano, but I am capable - meaning that at any time, if I want to learn to play the piano, I can. It is a possibility that exists within me. All adults are capable of parenting healthfully, even if they are unable, due to ignorance, or disinterest, etc. It is their capacities [capabilities] that is relevant for these discussions, not their abilities.) I naively believed that my parents would be just as excited and amazed as I was by these new things that I was learning. But here is the interesting thing about escaping emotional disorders: Information is only as good as the receptiveness of the person hearing it. Do you know what denial is? It is an overwhelmingly powerful phenomenon that we as people are prone to. Denial is any time our feelings rebel against a reality.Denial is so powerful that it can literally blind you to what is right there in front of your nose, and it can reinterpret reality so that you can look a thing right in the face, but see it as something entirely different than what it is. Both of my parents went straight into denial. They refused to even consider that they had any role whatsoever in the very real, painful, destructive issues that I was dealing with. They got bitter, they got mean. They taunted these ideas as being ridiculous. When backed into a corner, they got heated and defensive and dismissive. It was the exact opposite reception that I was expecting. Later, talking to a wise psychologist about these things and trying to make sense of my parents’ blatant refusal to see what is so obvious as to be undeniable, I was told, “To accept these things, they probably would not be able to live with themselves.” Denial: When our feelings are so opposed to a thing that our feelings outright rebel against the reality of it. At this early stage in my authentic recovery, this experience was indescribably discouraging. I am going to be frank with you and share that this one experience with my parents - their failure to care about any of these things, or to accept any responsibility whatsoever - set me back at least a year, and maybe longer. (The full process of my authentic recovery from Borderline Personality Disorder lasted approximately seven years, unnecessarily.) So today, when I am counseling others on whether or not to confront parents, my advice is to not do it. Here is the reason why: Your recovery does not depend on anybody else - including your parents or other family members - understanding and accepting the things you are learning, or the changes in perception that you are making. Their understanding is completely irrelevant to the nature of what it is you are really trying to do. You often hear the term ‘closure’, yes? And when you hear this term, it is often used in the context of somebody else having to do a thing, or some external thing having to happen, before one can experience it. But this is just another lie. True closure is simply acceptance. Acceptance is the healthy opposite of denial. It is the ability to look at at thing and simply see it for what it is. Note that acceptance does not mean agreeing with a thing, nor does it mean liking a thing. It is also not an intellectual achievement, but rather an emotional achievement. (Mourning is an example of denial. It is one’s emotions rebelling against the reality that a loved one has died. What happens when a person emerges from mourning? Acceptance. One’s feelings cease rebelling against the reality of the loss.) Since confronting your parents is most likely to end in crushing disappointment, and their understanding is completely irrelevant to your authentic recovery from emotional disorder anyway, there is really no practical reason to do it. My strong recommendation therefore, is to put your urges for involving your parents aside and to focus on yourself and your recovery. The more you learn, the more insights you will gain along the way, and the more you will see all of these things in context. This means that every day you will be gaining a better understanding about the greatest ways to view, and approach these situations. So it is reasonable, at the very least, to put off conversations like this with family members until you are far, far along in your authentic recovery. By the time you have advanced to a certain point, you will probably have identified for yourself things that you once thought was pressing or necessary that were never necessary or constructive at all.My name is Brian Barnett, with The Last Symptom, LLC (thelastsymptom.com). I lived with Borderline Personality Disorder for the first 35 years of my life, completely unaware. After a crisis which ruined my life at the time, I was forced to recognize that I lived with an emotional disorder, and over the course of roughly 7 years, I managed to authentically rid myself of Borderline Personality Disorder once and for all. I now help others do the same. If you would like more insights on the topic of authentic recovery from emotional disorders such as Borderline Personality Disorder, I encourage you to read my articles here on Quora, as well as at thelastsymptom.com, and to take advantage of my free, weekly podcast The Last Symptom (available on every major podcast platform of your preference), where I address these things in great detail.

column1: What are some good ways of keeping from losing it after a bad break-up?
column3: Build on yourself. And I don't mean weight loss or fake weepy hyping yourself up that the next relationship will be “the one". Do something for you that's not going to make you gain weight or lose alot of money. It helps to regain control by doing simple things for yourself. After the chores and cleaning is done, because it can distract you and help keep you sane, do a glow up with skincare and self care. Start a small hobby. I started making soaps and then made a small underground business in high school plus gifts to family members for supporting me. You can even declutter other “trash" from your life. Donate or upcycle. Start an herb garden and breathe in fresh air. Read in a park with sunshine and people watch with a beverage. Also, walk around your home with something cozy or sexy depending on your mood. Do whatever makes you feel comfortable and wonderful. Because you are worthy, all by yourself and the next person will know that.

column1: Is it possible to become a full time private investor?
column3: Yes, this is how my family lives now. I retired from cubicle life in my late 30s. I started at 21 with no school, mortgage, car, or consumer debt and about 8k in savings. I am very frugal as consistent with my upbringing. I've never owned a fancy European car or worked in any finance role. I invest in higher payout C and S corporations, Partnerships and REITs. All of my expenses are covered. I do basic financial health checking of investments, but all of my trade timing, entry prices and loss exits are technical analysis based. Yes it is possible. It takes time to train yourself to understand a method entirely, believe you can do it, and actually do it. And I mean 800% entirely. Not just reading a book once or twice, memorizing answers for a school exam. You have to be able to trust yourself to make big money trading decisions and act consistently. If that means reading 200 books and a few of them 11 times over then that's what it takes. Forget investment banking. That's for sales and employee personalities. They are not investors or traders despite their titles. A bank prop trader is an order taker and book loss mitigator, not a profit seeker through speculative risk. Certainly not with his own money. You stated you wanted to be an investor which is a completely different set of skills. You need to learn how to function in a market environment that is without structure and has no regard for your well being. This is different from anything else you have experienced. Even in prison the warden is legally obligated to care for your health. Noone will correct, punish, help, praise, or chastise you. You are on your own in a market and must develop deep personal responsibility. For me it begins with how I lived before I came to the markets. Living with very low expenses and no liabilities is very key. Again, I see it as part of the training process. I don't just think I can live a simple life without a high salary job. I actually lived this way for years at a real functional level. I know it because I lived it and can rely on it. I saved and invested over 60% of my net salary for over a decade. I'm the only one I know that has done this and the only one I've met that has transitioned from employee to investor / trader. I am hoping you can also. Every one of my friends and family that bought a house, drove new foreign cars, ate at fancy restaurants, upgraded granite counter tops, had extravagant weddings, etc. is still working and will be until 90. Keeping up with the neighbors will keep you on a treadmill. It's cliche at this point, but still true. I personally believe I was able to break free because my parent's thrifty values instilled beliefs of low material vanity. While I have vanity over my physical fitness, I never give a first thought to how my car or house is perceived. Even decades later, my wife still notifies me when it's awkward that I don't give praise to someone's car or house that they were expecting. I just don't care how fancy something is. Never enters my mind. Show me how many pullups you can do, charts of your best trades, or a machine you built in the garage and I'm seriously impressed. Live frugally, learn to cook and shop, repair things and manage your own finances. These are the skills needed for the modern world we live in. If you're constantly bleeding big expenses every year for a luxury lifestyle or goods, or professional repair services, you'll never get there. As an example, I traded a family member's account from 80k up to 7 figures in capital value completely for free. Then invested it into yielding over 90k per year and less than 12% in taxes. They told me I was no longer needed. They still work, have trouble meeting monthly expenses, spending money frivolously. How is that possible with 2 jobs and a portfolio cash income? They are now cannibalizing the portfolio and spending the cash. They also blame me for their financial problems and complain about the taxes. I could give them a multi-million dollar income and they'd still blow through it and blame me for not making it a billion per year. Is this a problem with income or expenses? Being thankful or having a bad attitude? No one ever believes me when they ask what the secret is. Everyone I know believes that my secret is being smart, or just lucky. Yes, I am lucky and thankful to be born a free American citizen, but most everything else as an adult was earned day by day. I've had Ivy league educated friends say, "Yeah he's rich but he's also really smart and doesn't spend it." They refuse to see that I have been learning to fix houses, computers, cars, relationships, cook, shop, trade, and invest for decades. I have no need or compulsion to “blow it on an Italian sports car.” The concepts are completely beyond their box of thinking. I don’t need a new $100K kitchen - I’ll build cabinets and make counter tops myself. I don’t need a fancy new German car to validate me - I have a beautiful wife and don’t work so I have no need to impress any women, neighbors, clients or people at the office. Life isn’t a constant competition or sales pitch for me so I’m not worried about “making a decent salary” just to keep up with the Jonses. Living a frugal lifestyle with low expenses has nothing to do with being smart. Anyone thinking this is stuck in a limited belief system. And I didn’t go to an Ivy League or fancy Graduate school for letters after my name, so why am I retired and they’ll be working until they’re in a coffin? I can say with 100% authority from personal experience that having a high IQ has 0% correlation with making money consistently as an investor / trader. Friends and family want to believe that there’s some magic silver academic bullet. Like Harry getting a wand, Luke getting a light saber, or Bilbo finding a ring. If they just got the silver bullet higher paying job, their lives would magically resolve. If they just took the right classes or got the right degree, they’d could finally get that promotion or start a new career. That dysfunctional belief couldn’t be further from reality for so many reasons. Yet I’ll bet it’s a belief that 99 of 100 adults have about getting ahead and fixing their lives. What about the jumbo mortgage, 3 car payments, kids in private school, alimony, child support, huge restaurant bills, trips to Hawaii? Will those magically disappear or keep bleeding them dry? What about water cooler complaining to the same cube dwellers every day and watching other people do great stuff on YouTube? Will that build self confidence on the road to financial independence? The first thing to do is get expenses under control. The next thing is to start learning and doing many things for themselves in order to build belief and confidence and save money for investment. They never even start step 1 and step 2 takes time. They start from a shaky foundation with their lives in chaos and can never build the next level. No one becomes Warren Buffet over night - even Warren Buffet. It's a belief combination of everything in life. A set of attitudes developed over time that I can do almost anything I need or just choose to do without. Self training. Trial and error. A continual process. Doing more of what works and eliminating what doesn't. Especially with trading and investing as money amplifies everything. I am serious when I say that it has 100% to do with how you think about and improve yourself. How you see and treat yourself in your own head. As for "breaking in" to finance. Consider that you have always been living a world that requires savings, frugality, expenses, money management, and investment at a personal finance level. You were dropped in it on your birthday. The train was moving on day one. This is what I mean by writing that it's "how you think". You already broke into finance when you were born. Think of all things from better leveraged angles, always assume you are never seeing the entire story. In looking to make a “decent salary”, consider that your language limits you to a small box. Salary is Salarium in Latin, which means to be paid for a service with salt (sodium chloride crystals). You want salt? You’ll get a canister of Mortons. In trading and investing you are a hunter keeping what you kill. You are not providing any service to a master. There is no salary, there is profit or loss. You are engaging with the real world of Capitalism and trade. Your assets are at risk and you are winning or losing. You are taxed differently and exposed to different financial and psychological risks. It starts with thinking differently about cash and income, not being paid a salary from a master. Your experiences and memories combine with words which are symbols to create distinctions about how you perceive the world. Choose the words you use in your head wisely.

column1: An Indian octagenarian said, ritual by many Indians of not offering flowers, bangles or kumkum dot on forehead of widows is because they expect it. Why are educated perpetuating archaic "tradition"? Do they know its hurtful, outdated & emotional?
column3: Why are you bothered about this ritual? If you really are concerned about widows, I will give you a true example of my mom's friend. When she lost her husband in 1990s, she was offered a small job in her late husband's office. My dad somehow convinced her to take it up, she had a son who is now in engineering. The lady had assumed that her family members would keep taking care of her like earlier days, so at first she was not ready to do a job outside her home. Later on after years, she was the sole earning member: her husband's brother, his wife and her FIL stay in the same house earning nothing! Whenever she met my parents, she has been thankful to my Dad for his guidance, that job helped her in her son's education and livlihood. She says that after her FIL (he is sick now) dies, she will move out to the govt provided house, her son is also grown up to protect her in case her BIL( brother in law) creates issues. Now after so many years, she would be able to get rid of him! That BIL and his wife are now worried- they have enjoyed life till now claiming that they are taking care of their widowed SIL and his son. That's exploitation disguised as care for a poor widow! This is the reality of widows who are even earning, so can you imagine the situation when she has no income!? Instead of bothering about rituals like gifting flowers or kumkum, we have a much serious issue to actually look into. Last weekend I was discussing about widows’ situation in India with a retired uncle of mine. Reason: Post retirement, he was planning to operate a small snack making business for 3 ladies who had lost their husbands and are in mid-age in his village. “You city kids have no idea what sort of miseries these women have to go in the villages. I hope I do my part towards the society by giving them a respectable income earning source” he remarked. I finally understood what he meant as I went to the Puri Jagannath temple in the auspicious month of Kartik last week, lots of old ladies in white were busy worshipping God for their late husbands, mostly in ragged clothes. We city born kids don't understand what challenges these women might be facing since we have not been involved too much into these society rules. Well my sister actually insisted that my Grandmother (we lost Grandpa few years ago, she is the ruling authority of my family now!) has to attend her wedding breaking this old tradition of widows not attending wedding ceremonies. My grandmother is a village woman but she happily attended it guiding the whole ceremony. And her sister (she lost her husband a few years ago) is the village head now. So for me, I thought that widows have no problem in being accepted in the society since my family has been doing so since long. However when I discussed with my uncle, the harsh reality suddenly showed up with Dad sharing the first story I wrote about. Women especially in middle age with kids suffer the most when it comes to being widows without any income. Remarriages are possible only when they don't have kids- thankfully it is acceptable in our side of the country. They are not made to wear white, they can wear colored clothes. However they don't use kumkum (which is a symbol of a married woman). Some use bindis if they want, wear gold bangles too in rural areas. So it's not that society isn't changing when it comes to what to wear etc. The tradition that is asked in the question is about offering “flowers, bangles, kumkum dot” is one followed in South India. It is called Haldi Kumkum. It's not a tradition in other parts like North or East India. This ritual was especially done for married women, the items gifted are symbols of a married woman. Calling someone who has lost her husband also isn't done by progressive folks since she would get reminded of the loss of her loved one in such occasions. It's hard to cope with the loss, reminders aren't a great thing… However personally speaking: yes when a woman who is totally dependent on her husband becomes a widow, it's a really hard challenge for her to cope up with the change especially in small town and villages. People should support her, but it rarely happens, many would try to dominate and take away her share of property etc. Instead of bothering about this so called social stuff like kumkum etc, we should be more concerned about them having a decent life. In that way, I would rather support my uncle in helping these ladies get some money via hardwork rather than bothering about functions or traditions. My way to challenge the society rules is not about questioning these old traditions, it's about helping the women be self dependent and live life on their own terms.

column1: Why are Filipinos so fond of taking selfies?
column3: There are myriad reasons why Filipinos are so fond of taking selfies. Some Filipinos may live self-absorbed lives and imagine themselves to be the main character of a movie in their own minds. But not all Filipinos take selfies for shallow or frivolous reasons. Some reasons and motivations may be rooted in cultural or social realities: The Philippines is ranked second in social media engagement in the world. According to an article by the Philippine Daily Inquirer, Filipinos spend an average of 10 hours on social media daily while the average usage worldwide was at 7 hours. With this high engagement in social media, Filipinos must take a lot of selfies to post on social media or else there would be little to talk about or comment on. Social media, internet craze keep PH on top 2 of world list The Pilipino diaspora and the need to tend family ties. I t is common knowledge that about 10% of the Philippines' adult population migrates internationally for work annually. This means that around 1 in 10 Filipinos living in the Philippines will have a close family member living in another country where they work as contract workers. The fastest way close family members can keep in touch with each others’ lives is by posting selfies on social media. Selfies as a means to keep in touch It is not uncommon for Filipinos to have a parent or two parents working abroad at the same time in the same or different countries while their children stay in the Philippines under the care of close relatives. It has been documented in studies that half of all Filipino OFWs working abroad are women.Philippine Statistics Authority. Studies suggest that some female OFWs may be wives who opt to work abroad to escape abusive marital relationships. This is because divorce is not available in the Philippines. Posting selfies of themselves communicates that they are alive and well, happy and free from domestic abuse. If they have children, posting selfies of the children will show that they are not being neglected or abused. Studies have shown that some female OFWs are panganay or eldest siblings, and they work abroad to support their immediate family members. Their parents may be sick and need financial aid for ongoing medical treatment or their siblings may need financial assistance to finish schooling. Selfies of the siblings or parents they support may communicate the need for more support to be sent or that the support being sent is sufficient and is being used efficiently and wisely as intended. Studies also suggest that some female OFWs are mothers who use information and communication technology, especially messaging applications and social media to “mother" their children. They call or message their children to inquire if they've had their breakfast or dinner, if they've done their homework or if they did well on their tests. From this, we can infer that Filipinos' use of social media might be related to ensuring the continuation of close family relationships despite the physical distance. In other words, Filipinos are engaging in long distance relationships with the help of social media and posting selfies is one way by which they cultivate family ties. Selfies and social media are the latest way to communicate In the 1970s, 1980s, and 1990s, before the internet and social media exploded on to the world stage, Filipino OFWs kept in touch be sending cassette tapes of conversations or ruminations, or they took a lot of photos, which they then had to develop and mail to their family member abroad. When video cameras became popular, Filipino families videotaped all family events and sent the video tapes to their family member abroad. Selfies as proofs of life These means of communicating were precious reminders of live and affection. They are also proof of health and life. For an OFW abroad who keeps sending money to their family in the Philippines, the pictures and videos motivate them to keep working so that their family can be well provided for. They may also be visual representations of goals: to send their kid or sibling, nephew or niece through kindergarten, elementary, high school, and college, and then, they can retire. Often, Filipino OFWs work abroad with the goal of buying property and building a family home. The relatives in the Philippines will then take photos of the building process to show how the construction is progressing. It is said that OFW families celebrate every holiday and birthday and they take pictures of those celebrations to assure the toiling OFW family member that they are thriving and happy and not despairing because of their family member's absence from their lives. Every celebration must be remembered with a photo, a selfie. It assures family members in the Philippines as well as abroad that despite the absence from each other, love and familial feelings are still present. Selfies maintain extended family networks for social support Because Filipino society has only recently evolved from agricultural and collectivist ways of living, extended family relationships are still important. Filipinos count as “family" even their first and second cousins. They even count as family those people with whom they have merely fictive family relationships such as ninongs, ninangs, and inaanak (godfather, godmother, and godchildren). And these are relationships that are actually maintained by updating each other on family news (who died, who was sick, who got married, who was single again after separating from a domestic partner (kinakasama) or romantic partner (boyfriend or girlfriend). With parents leaving to work abroad, often, extended family members take on the responsibility of being the legal guardian of the OFWs' children. For mutual protection and support, often, the OFWs in the family pool their resources to support all their children and nephews and nieces who all live with a grandparent or a spinster aunt or a bachelor uncle. The maintenance of these relationships is important because there is very little social support available from the government. The extended family is the source of a referral to a pediatrician, a dentist, an obstetrician, or surgeon and even a lawyer. The extended family may also be a source of funding or loans in cases of emergency. So, to maintain these relationships, one has to post selfies updating extended family abroad of their health status. Zoom funerals and weddings during Covid-19 Meeting applications such as Zoom has been a godsend for relatives to “attend" family events such as funerals or weddings and christenings, graduations or celebrations for passing a board or bar exam and the oath-taking ceremonies. Families are enabled through Zoom to consult with each other and reach a consensus as to issues such as whether an elderly relative's life support should be ended or maintained, whether surgery should be undertaken. For these reasons, it is not bizarre to see photos of a relative lying on a hospital bed, or pictures of a corpse inside a casket, or an urn with the deceased's ashes inside them. To Filipinos with family members in different continents, these photos are not inappropriate. They are not breaches of privacy. They are important family news. Seeing pictures such as these enable them to deal with feelings of isolation, grief, anxiety, and still feel that they are part of the family they had left in the Philippines and because of the lockdown, they cannot go home to see and be with. I would say taking and posting selfies were a coping mechanism, a proactive way of living life despite the limitations imposed by the pandemic. Filipino culture is also collectivist and selfies cement social relationships In the last century, in the provinces, families were large and there were as many as five to ten children per family. The big number of children was necessary to share and divide labor on a family farm. Now, Filipino families are still big when compared to Western societies. In the urban areas, families can have as many as 3 children and in the rural areas, families can have as many as 4 children. Decisions such as where children should go to school or where they should go to university is usually a family decision. When Filipinos migrate from the provinces to the cities to attend university or to work. They may keep in touch with their family in the provinces but when they need social support in a city where they have no family, having a barkada or a close-knit group of friends often stands in place of family. It is not only teenagers who have “barkadas," a person can have a neighborhood barkada comprising kids from their neighborhood or kids they used to play with; they may even have a school barkada (kids they went to school with), a church barkada (kids they sang in the choir together with or attended the same Sunday School classes with), and a work barkada or officemates. Filipinos often maintain these barkada relationships because they may be a source of connections necessary to find other or better work, to start a business, to enter government service, to find work abroad, or even to find a romantic partner or spouse. Maintenance of these social relationships include being friends on social media and updating friends on personal news such as getting a new job, or a boyfriend, marrying said boyfriend/girlfriend or separating from said boyfriend/girlfriend. Even sickness or a death in the family may be shared on social media (complete with pictures) so that friends in the Philippines or abroad can commiserate and even send financial contributions to help defray expenses. This happened during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and 2021. I know of people who were financially hard up and they had turned to Facebook to raise funds for hospitalisation during Covid. Some people who had access to medications or medical services were able to send help to people who needed them because of social media. These could not have been done without posting selfies. If a member of one's barkada has migrated for work in Canada or the US, for instance, that person may be a source of information if a friend wants to migrate for employment as well. That person can even be a roommate or flatmate when the other succeeds and they are both working abroad. Filipinos tend to rely on family or friends instead of relying on government aid. During the early days of the pandemic, the Office of the Vice President of the Philippines used social media to send home quarantine kits to people who needed them because they were experiencing Covid symptoms. The appeal for aid or assistance was done by posting selfies and sending the selfies to the messaging app associates with the Office of the Vice President. In times of natural calamity such as during a flood or a volcano eruption, selfies are a way by which people assured their friends and family that they are safe or they are in danger. The family members can then alert public officials to rescue their distressed family members. In memoriam I have posted selfies with people in my life who have died as a way of remembering them on special days like their birthdays or their death anniversaries. I have posted selfies (throwback pictures) of me with my brother before my brother died. Those selfies are usually accompanied by long posts about missing my brother and why I miss him so much. I now see it as a way by which I make sense of the loss. It is my way of keeping my brother's memory vibrant for me and my other siblings. It is a way for me to inform my children of our family history. I post pictures of myself with my departed mother-in-law for the same reason. Those people I have lost are still very much a part of my existence and I celebrate their contribution to my develoent as a person. Posting selfies of myself with them is a way by which I show that I am ever mindful of their physical absence but emotional presence in my life. Pics or it didn't happen Increasingly, because people own mobile phones with cameras, they tend to document anything from traffic conditions or road accidents they encounter while en route to or from work or school. They can record uncommon weather events such as a rain of hail or a tornado. If they happen to have witnessed a car accident or a crime committed on the street, they also post it and these have been used as evidence in prosecutions. If they meet a well-known celebrity or politician or public figure, Filipinos will take a selfie of themselves with the celebrity or public figure. In fact, these types of selfies were used by a lot of supporters of candidates in the last election. People posted selfies of themselves wearing their candidate's colours or of themselves while attending a rally. This helped a lot of candidates reach more people than purchasing spot ads on prime time television. I have seen people post selfies of themselves while standing in line to get vaccinated. They posted several selfies documenting how long it took to finally get their shot. I am sure there are more personal reasons why Filipinos take and post selfies on social media. This answer just scratched the surface.

column1: Why do we humans cry when we lose our lovely ones while we don't actually know where they are going?
column3: We cry because we’ve known them, loved them and have become emotionally attached to them. We’ve hugged them. Talked with them, snuggled with them, cared for many of them, helped many of them, cried with them, laughed with them and we’ve shared so many precious moments with them. This includes humans and non humans. I experienced loss of loved ones from a very young age. Just as I was beginning to ‘bloom’ (becoming more self confident, more cute, a tad popular), at 16 yrs old, my dad passed. So suddenly. So traumatic. So surreal, to me. I’m an ‘only child’ and my mom truly ‘fell apart’. She became almost suicidal at times. I went to school, worked 2/3 days a week after school) and came home to care for my mom. I didn’t want to cause my mom to be more stressed and depressed, so I cried alone when she wasn’t with me……..or sometimes when I was with a close friend ….. and my mom never ever knew how many tears I shed back then. The most difficult thing, for me….still…after almost 77 yrs… is loving with detachment. I’m much better than I used to be, but as an empath I feel heartache and sorrow deeply when a family member, close friend and/or the non humans (cats, dogs, birds, rabbits, hamsters, opossums, raccoons, all the feral cats I loved/am still loving) who were/are in my life isn’t ’physically there’ any more. All arises, changes and passes? This is life. Grief is the price we pay for loving and/or caring for others. But oh, how wonderful is that emotion called ‘love’? I envision ‘love’ as being a warm glowing light deep within us. I feel that this ‘pure love’ we’ve felt/given (while living) is infinite. This is just my opinion.
column9: So true mom!!❤️

column1: Why have you decided to not speak to your family anymore?
column3: Going anonymous so I can talk about my family without them being identifiable. It wasn’t an easy decision, and every so often I try to give them another chance. With my father, there’s no bad blood and I haven’t cut him off so to speak. He’s got problems though. Part of it makes it extremely hard for him to maintain his part of the relationship. He wants to, and he loves me, but the onus is on me to keep that relationship going 100%. That’s tough, especially being in the place I am today emotionally. There is more to the story, but I don’t want to talk about it here. Suffice it to say he’s a good guy and he means well, it’s just really hard keeping a relationship going. It makes us both sad this is the case. On my father’s side of the family, a lot of people have unfortunately passed on. Sorry, I can’t go into more detail here. My mother and that whole side of the family is different. There’s quite a bit of abuse on that side of the family, and my mother put enormous amounts of pressure on me to keep up relationships with other family members that were abusive. She is emotionally abusive as well. It took me a long time to really see what was going on, and then to have the will to do something. When it’s hammered in that you do your duty to your family regardless of the consequences to your own self, it’s hard to truly extract yourself. My mom also has a rather chaotic life. It’s hard dealing with that at times. I’ve got my own struggles, and it can be a burden that’s extremely harmful at times to deal with the fact that she does have so many problems. It’s hard too because it comes out of the blue. She’ll be fine for years sometimes, then things will go off the rails. She also had unreasonable expectations for the amount of contact we were to have. We live in different towns, and I have a busy life. Less so now, but at the time I had one day of the week free. The rest was jam packed. I was expected to spend at least 4 hours of my free day on the phone with her. It always had to be when she had time. When her free time changed, I was expected to adapt. It didn’t register that I worked when she wanted to talk and this work schedule couldn’t be changed. Since it was work I love doing, I think she saw it as frivilous and thus not a valid excuse. Which, ugh. I slaved for years to get to the point I could get that job, and I work my ass off at that job. Yes, it’s my dream job and no I don’t make a fortune (and it will never be my full time job), but I fucking earned it and I’m not giving it up until I have to or am ready to retire. I put up with a lot of this, and it took a long time for it to finally be enough. I remember the exact day it happened. I was living in a foreign country. I quietly but actively planning suicide, and while most people didn’t know that, it was obvious I was majorly and profoundly depressed. I was working a lot, and that work required a lot of speaking and a lot of playing a wind instrument. One day I woke up with a horrific pain in my mouth, and found out I had a cavity in one of my wisdom teeth. While my wisdom teeth all grew in straight, they caused lots of problems. The ones on my right were already gone, and it was an easy extraction. I opted for an extraction of the problematic wisdom tooth and the one remaining tooth. Should have been easy, they looked exactly like the ones that had been removed with great success. It wasn’t. The extraction was awful, I required stitches. I did this on a Friday afternoon even though I couldn’t take off from work on Saturday. It wasn’t supposed to be bad, though. I was only supposed to work two hours without a lot of speaking, but it ended up being six with nothing but speaking and playing. I had to deal with feeling my stitches tug and rip, and I had to keep at it. After work, I had a wedding I really had to attend (long story, but not mine to share and not really relevant to the story), and so I soldiered on. My mom called when I was on my way back from the wedding. She wanted to continue crying about her ongoing drama that she herself caused. This was a situation I had next to no sympathy for her in because, no matter how you stared at it, she didn’t just do this to herself, she was the bad guy. I listened to her and talked on my way home, but when I got home I tried wrapping it up. I’d told her several times what kind of day I was having, but she just brushed it off. She then told me she was going to call back on her other phone so we could talk even longer. I’d had enough, I told her in no uncertain terms that I cannot do this today. Of course, things are all or nothing with her, so this meant started a huge row. It ended with her deciding I’d decided to cut off all contact from here on out. I was too much in pain and too exhausted to care at that moment, but I figured I’d care quite a bit when I was feeling better. Then a strange thing happened. I got better and didn’t feel horrible about it. I felt relief. After I got some distance, I saw just how dysfunctional things were. It wasn’t until about six months had passed that I started mourning the loss of the relationship. I haven’t maintained complete radio silence, but I’ve been a lot more cautious in how I interact with her. It’s not easy, but it’s not easy cutting someone off completely either. At this point, we’re again into a long period of not talking. I think she thinks she’s punishing me right now, but honestly, I try to just get on with my life. She’s still manipulative, she still gets herself into insane situations. Besides that, she still doesn’t understand how my life is. My physical and mental health are both pretty terrible right now. She doesn’t seem to understand exactly how much serious health and mental problems take their toll. She’ll claim she does, then she’ll go back to complaining that it’s not like the old days where we talked for four hours a day. With my brother it’s been harder. I love him so much, and he is a really great guy. Part of the struggle with maintaining contact with him has been his work schedule. He works as much as me, but seems to work the exact opposite hours almost. The other problem is our mother seems to now be 100% his problem. After that fight I mentioned above, he contacted me asking if I could help with the burden of dealing with her. I was honest and told him I was planning on killing myself, that intellectually I knew that was a bad idea, but it’s hard to battle against those thoughts when “not killing yourself” is an abstract idea almost. He said he understood and just asked that I got better. I told him I was trying. He’s started distancing himself from her too, which is really great. But she still manipulates him in an attempt to manipulate me. It’s hard to know that keeping contact with him causes him problems. He also needs to do his part and keep in contact with me as well. I can’t be expected to be the only one who reaches out.
column9: I was with you until the last sentence. The irony in the fact that after everything it seems that you have picked up your mothers traits unbeknownst to you. I do hope you see the irony in your last sentence and are self aware enough to change the trajectory to not fall into becoming like those we try to strongly to avoid. Just food for thought. I do hope you have found a balance in your life I’m the years this was posted and everything have fallen into place where you are in a stable confident place in your life. All the Best!

column1: Why does no one want a bipolar diagnosis?
column3: I don’t think anyone wants a diagnosis of any illness, because who wants to be sick? Also, a diagnosis of bipolar disorder is distressing because it is not curable. [1] It can be managed with excellent results however. But, with mental illnesses, there is unfortunately still a strong stigma that exists in our society towards mental health disorders. Also, most people, unless they have been through having a mental illness or are very close to someone who has, do not understand what its like. They may have fears and prejudices towards the mentally ill, or just become very uncomfortable with the thought of having to deal with someone who has a mental illness. Thanks to the way those with bipolar disorder (and every other mental disorder) are viewed by many people in this society, they can feel embarrassed and even ashamed to admit they suffer from such an illness. Approximately 2.6 percent of American adults suffer from bipolar disorder. [2] What causes bipolar disorder?There is no single cause for bipolar disorder. Indeed, like all psychological disorders, bipolar disorder is a complex condition with multiple contributing factors, including:Genetic: Bipolar disorder tends to run in families, so researchers believe there is a genetic predisposition for the disorder. Scientists also are exploring the presence of abnormalities on specific genes.Biological: Researchers believe that some neurotransmitters, including serotonin and dopamine, don’t function properly in individuals with bipolar disorder.Environmental: Outside factors, such as stress or a major life event, may trigger a genetic predisposition or potential biological reaction. For instance, if bipolar disorder was entirely genetic, both identical twins would have the disorder. But research reveals that one twin can have bipolar, while the other does not, implicating the environment as a potential contributing cause.What are the different types of bipolar disorder?Bipolar I is considered the classic type of bipolar disorder. Individuals experience both manic and depressive episodes of varying lengths.Bipolar II involves less severe manic episodes than bipolar I; however, their depressive episodes are the same.Cyclothymia is a chronic but milder form of bipolar disorder, characterized by episodes of hypomania and depression that lasts for at least two years.Mixed episodes are ones in which mania and depression occur simultaneously. Individuals might feel hopeless and depressed yet energetic and motivated to engage in risky behaviors.Rapid-cycling bipolar individuals experience four or more episodes of mania, depression, or both within one year.What are the risk factors for bipolar disorder?Cyclothymia (see definition above). About half of individuals with cyclothymia will experience a manic episode.Any other psychological disorderA family history of bipolar or other psychological disordersAlcohol and substance abuseMedication interactions. For instance, antidepressants may trigger mania.Major life changesSevere stressThere are four possible bipolar states that someone with the disorder can manifest.ManiaHypomaniaDepressionA mixture of mania and depression (called a “mixed episode”).What are the symptoms of mania?Feelings of euphoria and elation or irritability and angerImpulsive, high-risk behavior, including grand shopping sprees, drug and alcohol abuse, and sexual promiscuityAggressive behaviorIncreased energy and rapid speechFleeting, often grandiose ideasDecreased sleep (typically the individual doesn’t feel tired after as few as three hours of sleep)Decreased appetiteDifficulty concentrating; disorganized thoughtsInflated self-esteemDelusions and hallucinations (in severe cases)How is hypomania different?Hypomania is less severe than a full-blown manic episode. Hypomanic individuals can seem pleasant, friendly, energetic and productive. Though it doesn’t sound problematic, increasing hypomania can lead to risky behaviors and full mania.What are some symptoms of depression?Feelings of hopelessness and sadnessInability to sleep or sleeping too muchLoss of interest in formerly enjoyable activities; loss of energy (sometimes to the point of inability to get out of bed)Changes in appetite and weightFeelings of worthlessness and inappropriate guiltInability to concentrate or make a decisionThoughts of death and suicideWhat is a mixed episode like?Mixed episodes involve simultaneous symptoms of mania and depression, including irritability, depressed mood, extreme energy, thoughts of suicide, and changes in sleep and appetite.What type of medications are used to treat bipolar disorder?Mood stabilizers. These medications are prescribed to help stabilize manic symptoms, prevent future episodes, and reduce suicide risk and are the most commonly prescribed medications for bipolar disorder. The most well-known of these is lithium, which seems to be effective for most people who experience manic and hypomanic episodes. Other commonly prescribed medications for bipolar disorder include anticonvulsant (or anti-seizure) medications (because they also have mood stabilizing effects). These medications include: valproate (Depakote), carbamazepine (Tegretol), lamotrigine (Lamictal), gabapentin (Neurontin), and topiramate (Topamax). Every medication has its own set of potentially serious side effects. For instance, Lamictal can cause Stevens-Johnson syndrome, a potentially fatal skin disease, though this is rare and is entirely avoidable by careful, slow dose titration.Atypical antipsychotics. The newest medications, atypical antipsychotics, were originally developed to treat psychosis (a symptom of schizophrenia). Like the mood stabilizers above, atypical antipsychotics help to control mood swings. These seven medications are commonly prescribed for bipolar: aripiprazole (Abilify), risperidone (Risperdal), olanzapine (Zyprexa), quetiapine (Seroquel), ziprasidone (Geodon), clozapine (Clozaril), and olanzapine/fluoxetine (Symbyax). Contrary to popular belief, these medications aren’t without significant side effects, including rapid weight gain, high cholesterol and risk for diabetes, which occurs most commonly with olanzapine and clozapine. In some cases, atypical antipsychotics have been associated with a life-threatening condition known as diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA). In June 2004, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requested that all companies who manufacture atypical antipsychotics include a warning about the elevated risk for hyperglycemia and diabetes (see here ). In addition, several organizations, including the American Diabetes Association and American Psychiatric Association, have published recommendations for doctors on how to treat patients taking these medications. For more information, read the press releases at the American Diabetes Association website.Calcium-channel blockers. Used to treat angina and high blood pressure, these medications — including verapamil (Calan, Isoptin, Verelan), and nimodipine (Nimotop) — also have mood stabilizing effects. They have fewer side effects than other bipolar drugs but aren’t as effective.Combination therapy. When one medication isn’t working, a doctor might prescribe two mood stabilizers or a mood stabilizer along with an adjunctive medication to treat symptoms such as anxiety, hyperactivity, insomnia, and psychosis. For example, Xanax (alprazolam), a fast-acting benzodiazepine, typically is taken for two weeks before mood-stabilizing medication starts to work. Antidepressants might be prescribed for patients who are in a depressive phase, but research suggests they aren’t effective. They can trigger mania and exacerbate episodes long term.What types of psychotherapy are helpful for bipolar disorder?Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) helps individuals develop strategies to cope with their symptoms, change negative thinking and behavior, monitor their moods, and predict their mood to try to prevent a relapse.Interpersonal and social rhythm therapy is a combination of interpersonal therapy and CBT. This newer treatment focuses on circadian rhythms to help clients establish and maintain routines and build healthier relationships.Psychoeducation teaches individuals about their disorder and treatment and gives them the tools to manage it and anticipate mood swings. Psychoeducation also is valuable for family members.Thanks for the request!Footnotes[1] Is bipolar curable? Treatment and long-term management[2] Bipolar Disorder Fact Sheet | Psych Central
