column1: I’m in my thirties now and didn’t accomplish many of my 20s goals. What should my goals be in my 30s? What should anyone in his 30s focus on so that he will not regret later in his 40s?
column3: Thanks for asking. Forget about losses and nonaccomplishment of 20s. Feel determined to take bigger strides during 30s so that you regain your momentum and lost advantage. Jot down your interests. Make a priority list. Pick up the best three or four items. Narrow down as future goals. Work out requirements for fulfilling these. Use SWOT analysis. See your strengths. Note down your weaknesses. Keep window open for opportunities. Be wary of threats. Leave room for steady improvement. Add quality, refinement and beauty to your outputs. Devise suitable plans in a way that you do not feel bored. Whatever you do is a thing of beauty and is joy for the remaining decades 40s, 50s and so on. Keep in mind that you are likely to touch triple figures. Thus, be focused on maintaining good health, physical as well as mental. Your goals can be:career-related, so go after required education,earning, saving and financial stability,clarity in pursuit of objectives (with passage of time),family-related; good interactions with others too,comfortable last decades of life should be in mind as well.Although it is good to perpetuate self-care, it has to expand in effective resource distribution so that others are also benefited. At the same time, involvement in unnecessary issues has to be avoided so that your time is not wasted. You can guide family members accordingly. Hope this answer is helpful. Thanks for reading.

column1: What did you assume was exaggerated until you experienced it?
column3: Overweight people encounter significantly different social interactions/treatments compare to their thinner counterpart.Of course, I always knew that overweight and obese people were treated differently. They are usually the “silent ones” or the person who is ignored around the office/classroom. But it never occurred to me just how different these treatments can be. Growing up in Texas, a large number of my friends and people who I interacted with were either overweight or clinically obese, so I never held any strong discriminatory attitude toward “fat” people in general. In fact, I think I have a significant positive bias toward overweight people. (I am going to use overweight and fat interchangeably, I am aware that a person can be significantly overweight according to their BMI but has a low body fat, and I fully acknowledge that BMI is not a scientific metric.) So I didn’t get the sense that fat people carried significantly more burdens of discrimination compare to their thinner counterpart. That is, until I intentionally gained weight to experience weight-related discrimination first-hand (I was inspired by brave souls like the author of “Black Like Me - Wikipedia” and some other people who did self-experimentation Michel Foucault - Wikipedia). In about two years, I went from 170 lbs. to 240 lbs. All I did was eating three to four meals a day. I was overweight and this was visible through outward appearance (I am not tall) and at this time I lived in a more liberal part of the country where (on average) people were thin. Here are the things I found that were different compared to when I was thin:You are more likely to be ignored completely in any social situation, even when the topic of conversation is your own subject of expertise. Apparently to a lot of people, your outward appearance strongly correlates with your personality, intelligence and ability. Their level of patience correlates negatively with your weight.You are more likely to be ignored or not be taken seriously by the opposite sex.People no longer laugh with you, they laugh at you. You need to do things to draw attention as attention will no longer be given to you. So you are constantly living between the extremes of being ignored and being the court jester. Your entire existence is reduced to stereotypes. You are now Kevin James, Seth Rogen, Jonah Hill or nobody.People assumed that I have always been overweight. I felt that people would not understand why I would try to intentionally gain weight, in other words, most people simply assumed that being overweight is something innate or psychological to a person - lack of self-control, greed, laziness, you name it.Other overweight people ignore you and are even less willing to make friends with you compared to thinner people. This lack of camaraderie is the most curious aspect of carrying a marginalized identity and very counter-intuitive to me (any marginalized identity, such as being black, Asian, gay, trans, etc.). I feel that there is significant shame amongst people who are overweight or obese, and they attribute their happiness and self-esteem based on their weight instead of individual accomplishments or capabilities.People assumed that I was either in a position of power/authority or in poverty depending on how I dressed on that particular day. In other words, I was treated in binary terms, whereas thinner people enjoyed a wider range of perception.Close friends (even those who are obese) would look at you in a different light and insert topics such as exercising or dieting in casual conversations. It felt that people assumed that I was oblivious to my weight, even though I weighed myself constantly to track progress. There is this myth that overweight people do not care about their weight.Your family member will go into “hyper mode” over any weight-related issues. I get the feeling that they are linking my weight to my state of mental health rather than my physical well-being. It felt to me that our conversations ultimately boiled down to the question: are you trying to kill yourself / why do you want to die early? This is because they were constantly bringing up death when they talked about health consequences of being overweight or obese. How would you like to be reminded that you are going to die soon on a daily basis?I faced harassment from completely random strangers. This is when I got to know micro-aggression for the first time. People in the elevator would “suddenly” switch to topic on weight loss and obesity related concerns whenever I walk in and I can see them peering at me. Random strangers would hurl insult at me on the street, with one person telling me that I “should stop eating donuts” while I was crossing the road.So what have I concluded? People are judgmental and possess strong prejudice even though they overwhelmingly deny any overt feeling of bias. Silence, apathy, and even a lack of open hostility do not imply a lack of discrimination. There is a strong subconscious fear of death that seems to motivate people to stay “in shape”, but on a conscious level, most people simply attempt to stay thin so not be associated with negative stereotypes associated with fatness. I am aware that as an overweight man, I face significantly less prejudice compared to that against overweight women, and I believe that latter can be attributed to this idea that sex with overweight people is somehow deviant. I have not thought deeply about the combined effect of my race and my weight on other people, I assume that people see me as less threatening and there are research evidence to support this claim (The Babyfaced Black CEO Phenomenon). Would I encourage anyone else to try this experiment? Well, it is up to you. But there are legitimate health consequences for doing any weight-related experiments in ways you cannot anticipate. For example, I developed a strange cough at my highest weight that persisted for over a year. You can get random rash on your body that are difficult to explain or treat and they can leave a scar. You cannot control your fat distribution, and you also cannot control how you appear after weight loss - you may not look the same afterwards - certain places will appear to be “sunken” but not to a worrying degree. Finally, you will sweat non-stop with any physical activity such as picking up stuff around the room. So it would be correct to attribute a lack of physical activity among people who are overweight to avoidance of excessive perspiration instead of “laziness”.

column1: After going no contact with toxic family members, how long until they're not in your thoughts every day?
column3: When I realized that the situation was totally hopeless and that the only solution was no contact, I found that what happened next was the same grief as if she had died. All children love their parents, no matter how mean they are, and they all long for the parent to acknowledge, respect, and love them. To make the step of going no contact with someone who is incurable requires wisdom, self-discipline, and bravery like that required to remove your own toxic appendix. It saves our lives but the decision is still painful. I thought that decades of pain and effort had prepared me for it. But no. I found that I still had to grieve not only over the loss of the fragments of good in our relationship but I had also to face the grief of knowing that no contact meant that I would never be acknowledged, respected, or loved. In my experience, how long it takes until they are not in our thoughts every day is the same as one would expect with any other grievous loss, from one to two years, except that narcissists have had such a strong influence in our lives that the imprint is more intense. I didn’t feel fully released until she died. Even now, three years after her death, I have almost nightly (but not necessarily painful) dreams about her. I think these dreams are probably part of the work of healing. It seems reasonable to me that the “daily” aspect of thoughts is normal and natural for any serious loss so my advice is, to be patient. It helped me to realize that, karmically speaking, this is our work, to work our way through the grip of it into the best wholeness that we can produce. I think we should feel self-respect for having been smart enough to make the decision and endure the consequences in order to save ourselves. I am still sad over the loss of what could have been, but it has taught me to tend to others’ hearts with tender care. I have worked through my anger and resentment to reach forgiveness and even tenderness toward her, that child who was so wounded in her own life that she had to build such deep walls to protect herself that it cut off her humanity. That is why people become narcissists, and I don’t think we are fully released until we can forgive.
