column1: What was John F. Kennedy's personality like?
column3: JFK came across as open, confident and self-deprecating. People who met him were generally awed and remembered him for the smile, the tan and how he seemed to connect with nearly all he met. An extremely complicated man, he was not an extrovert nor did he have deep relationships with women or men. He preferred to engage one on one or with a small group of people he trusted and respected. Just prior to the end of his life this began to change (with Jackie) when their son Patrick died two days after his birth August 7, 1963. Those close to Kennedy said they had never seen him break down or openly display emotion. This change was the reason Jackie travelled with him to Dallas 105 days later. John Kennedy could have lived a life of privilege, avoided serving in the Pacific arena during WWII and focused on taking care of his family and his health. Because his elder brother Joe Kennedy Jr died on a bombing flight from England to Germany, JFK volunteered as a lieutenant in the Navy, had his PT boat rammed by a Japanese destroyer. Kennedy barely escaped death while getting all but two of his men to safety. It was the competitiveness that ultimately cost him his life. The strongest part of Kennedy’s personality was his willingness to listen to others from military to economics to civil rights. He valued political courage highly and in his day it was an abundant quality without respect to party affiliation. From experience he learned and when proven wrong, was willing to accept the counsel of others and act upon it, always giving credit where due. He displayed supreme self confidence which was characteristic of the personality that caused him to stand out in the universe of military and political giants of his time. But those who knew JFK say that he shared only small bits of himself with any single person. Even his best friend outside of family, Paul “Red” Fay, asserted that nobody knew Kennedy completely aside from his younger brother Robert. His ability to compartmentalize (or inability to be completely open) created the reality and the myth of Kennedy. Much is attributed, even more forever unknown with certainty. Fifty-six years ago today America was on the brink of armeggedon over the Soviet buildup of nuclear missiles in Cuba. After early misjudgments and the failed Bay of Pigs invasion, senior members of government questioned whether the young president was up to the job of navigating the danger. Many in his inner circle of advisors urged bombing Cuba but Kennedy chose a delicate path around the confrontation with Soviet Premiere Khrushchev, allowing the Soviet leader to save face with hardliners in the Kremlin. One can only imagine how the Missile Crisis would have been handled by today’s leaders. Kennedy did not threaten, gloat or mock. He opened a direct line with the Kremlin to try and avoid future conflicts that threatened a world war. Those near him praised his composure and willingness to consider opposing views. In the end, he added 1,036 days to the time since a nuclear weapon was fired in anger. I suspect this would have been his proudest achievement. We can only identify John Kennedy the man through his actions in office and through the words of friends like Fay. For me personally as a 65 year old man the assassination of JFK ushered in the “post heroic” era in America and set us on the path to division and a tearing at the fabric of our democracy. It accelerated by ratcheting up the Vietnam war, Watergate and ultimately taking us back to an ugly time in American history. As Robert Kennedy warned, “We can’t wait for a savior.” A wise man recently repeated that warning. Unlike JFK, we as a society seem unable or unwilling to learn and alter course. Diplomacy is discounted, allies devalued. Ironically, the technology born from the space program Kennedy proposed in 1961 is enabling and accelerating the fractures in society that place America in jeopardy of drifting toward the sort of autocratic regime posed by the Soviets after World War II. We have moved toward Middle Eastern and Asian dictatorships and away from the allies who stood beside us in the victory over Nazism and other 20th Century conflicts. We don’t need to return to the distant past to “make America great again”. The revival of racism, bigotry and isolationism coupled with an alarming loss of tolerance and civility run contrary to the ideology of Lincoln, the Roosevelts, Kennedy and Reagan. Time is running out on the best of America and we cannot wait for a savior. Sadly, there are no personalities like John Kennedy ready and willing to step into that void for the good of the country. The motives now seem to be greed and self aggrandizement. >>>>>Thank you for taking the time to read this message. It is NOT meant to be partisan and I hope it isn’t taken as such. Since the late 1980s there has been a concerted effort to diminish the role JFK played on the world stage. Whether it’s about marital infidelity (true) or revisionist history about his plans for the US role in Vietnam (he planned to pull out the advisors after the 1964 election) or civil rights. <<<<<<
column9: Nice summary of the life and character of JFK; however, it is incorrect to state that JFK's competitiveness with his older brother, Joseph P. Kennedy, Jr., resulted in the incident of his PT boat being sunk by the Japanese during WWII. It was the other way around. Joseph sought out the dangerous WWII mission that cost him his life as a highly competitive response to the praise his younger brother, JFK, received for his courage after the sinking of PT Boat 109.

column1: If a covert narc cannot feel, how do they know they are hurting you?
column3: They know because they carefully study you for as long as it takes in order to select the perfect way to torture and harm you and only you in a way that is so personal and devious that it will break you. The plan is to do something to you that others will never believe, yet it will take you years to recover and even then you will be a shell of your former self. The more you hurt, the better they feel. It is an absurd version of projection that allows them to mask their own pain and insecurity while they draw strenghth through their toxic grip on your spirit. They transfer their own suffering to you without you even realizing it. Then they draw your positive life force out and steal it for their own. It sounds crazy and I would never believed it could happen until it happened to me. The narc who did these things to me described her feelings in a public blog once, under an assumed name. She said something like (I must paraphrase here but trust me, this is the nice version)… “I feel like I am standing on the edge of a black hole, a giant abyss of nothingness. I move my feet all the way to the edge and I am not afraid. I dare to look down into that giant, ugly, black pit of evil and hate and I feel nothing. I am on that ledge. I am about to fall in…” Yes, that is quite a lovely concept, isn’t it? I believe that is a very clear picture of how that person felt at that time. But here is the best part… do you wonder what could have been so terrible that could have happened to elicit such a feeling? Do you almost feel sorry for that person or think they need to be rescued or loved? There was a time when I probably would have felt that way. But horror is a better way to describe my rection that day when I read her words. I knew exactly what triggered it.. I had just told my family and close friends that my husband and I were expecting our first child. The narc was caught off guard and did not know how to control the situation or prevent me from getting positive attention in my life. It was all about her, after all, so my pregnancy was somehow an attack against her. Anyone who feels such great loss and deep, almost suicidal sounding sadness, over news that an innocent, harmless baby will be born into a loving family… well that is pretty disturbing. But that is not even the point of my story becausd you might think that proves the narc had feelings. But, you would be wrong. And this is how messed up they are…. The narc wrote that blog because she knew how much it would hurt me to believe that my unborn child could bring her to such an evil and vile place in her mind. She did not care if i was having a baby. She hated kids. But, what she did want was to turn others’ happiness for my family into sympathy and attention for her. She wanted others to think twice before expressing their happiness about my unborn child because they would not want to be insensitive to her and her suddenly invented story about being unable to have children of her own. And if I behaved in a manner that indicated I was happy about being pregnant or did not believe her story about being unable to conceive, which was a complete lie, I would be seen as evil. It was a perfect plan and went far beyond what I even have time to describe here. But, trust me, they know what they are doing. Just like a zoologist can understand some of the communication the apes have with one another, without actually being an ape, a narcissist can understand what hurt looks like and how to inflict it. They get a rush off of it like you might get after you drink too much coffee. But just like a caffine buzz, their rush does not sustain them. If you continue to keep them in your life, you will suffer until they decide you are no longer any fun to mess with. Your reputation will be shot, and you will wonder where all your friends went. And when they believe you are at your lowest of low points, they will discard you and move on. Or they will shift their loathing to another one of your family members, maybe even your newborn baby, and the fun will start all over again. So, if you suspect you have a narc in your life, get as far away as you can as soon as you can.
column9: This resonates so much, Cheryl - all joy or expressed joy, taken out of expecting your baby! At one time I thought I couldn’t have children, but I didn’t dramatise like this when others had children. Then I conceived, and my narcissistic mother’s reaction to the news was not joy but ‘I’ll worry.’ My first child was born 9 weeks prematurely, she didn’t come near him for weeks, and I looked with envy at other new mums in NICU whose mothers had flown from interstate or overseas. She promised to be there for the next child’s birth, changed her mind and passed our home on her way home, didn’t meet that child for 5 months. For exactly the reason you’ve articulated - loss of attention to her. And that was typical of her and my narcissistic sister: anyone getting attention in the family - for life-threatening illness, a wedding, a death, a new baby, another death, whatever - was kerosene to the fire of screaming need for attention and for crises to be created, invented, whatever. My sister admitted herself to the same hospital where my husband was close to dying, for a trivial procedure and demanded all the attention from me. She and her family cold-shouldered me because I didn’t give ‘enough.’ ‘Call so and so, and so and so, tell them how ill I am, have you washed my nightgowns, why do you have to leave me and visit your husband?’ (!!) She was in the same hospital as an uncle who died, and barely mentioned his name. When I travelled overseas, she invented a marital breakdown. In the middle of the grief over our father’s death, she made an incredible fuss about having one stitch out of a wound. For 30 years I’ve been No Contact (and with mother, who died many years later) and it is bliss not to have the phone tied up for hours and hours with her need for attention.

column1: During the Matsya Battle, Arjuna was able to defeat the Kaurava army within a few hours without any support from an army. Why wasn't he able to do the same thing during the Mahabharata War?
column3: A doctor is never allowed to conduct surgery on his family members. He may have conducted multiple surgeries with complete finesse and success. However, when it comes to operating his own blood or family, his hands would shake. As per the ethical guidelines, when a doctor operates on his own family member or a blood relation it can dwindle his professional judgement as well as his emotional state can influence his decision making process. It can be difficult to maintain a professional and detached state of mind. We can learn about Arjuna’s situation taking the above analogy. He was not fighting against any other kingdom, but his own family. More importantly, his own kith and kin; his great grandfather who loved him immensely, his preceptor who taught him all the skills to be a warrior and his cousins (whose downfall will end the entire Kuru clan). Arjuna was an greatly skilled warrior but also an empathetic individual who cared for his people too much. He would willingly give everything for his people. However, seeing himself to be the cause of their death will surely leave him out of sync with his rational self. That is where Shri Krishna comes into picture. From a metaphorically perspective, Shri Krishna plays the role of the prefrontal cortex of a human brain that helps one think rationally and not let the limbic take over your system. Shri Krishna who held the reins of his mind, took the mind into right trajectory by bringing in back to his senses, making him act rationally than on an emotional level. Does that make him any less doctor or levy people to question his skills? How is Arjun able to fight in Virata battle without support? Virat battle didn't require Arjuna to kill anyone. It was more towards save the cows that were taken away by Kauravas. The Kauravas had stolen the cattle of Virata on the pretext of making Pandavas come out of disguise. The motto was to identify the Pandavas and send them again on 12 years of exile in addition to a year incognito. The Pandavas were indebted to Matsya kingdom for giving them shelter during their Agyaatvaas. They found it morally necessary to help king Virata in saving his kingdom and get back his cattle, now that their commander-in-chief Keechak had also passed away. There was no bloodshed required of his kith and kin. Arjuna was fighting on behalf of Matsya kingdom. The goal was freeing the cattle and protecting the kingdom from any attack. What was different about Mahabharat battle? On the other hand, Mahabharat war was a more personal one. Here victory meant the downfall of his own clan. Killing his family, his great grandfather, teacher, cousins, making their sisters in law widow and in short being the reason for the destruction of his family. Additionally, the battle of Kurukshetra was going to be a major devastating one. Bloodshed was confirmed. It was a do or die situation. When you are pitted against those you love and hold dearly and have to be the cause of their downfall, how will you feel? Will property, money, fame or anything deemed important to you. You would rather want to forsake everything so that your loved ones don't have to bear any trouble. Besides, to be reasoned as the cause of your loved one's downfall is a big blame to carry for a lifetime. Thus, Arjun felt despondent and lost and Shri Krishna had to recite to him the Gita. The below reference clearly highlights Arjuna lamenting about killing his family, his cousins all for kingdom. He finds it futile to destroy an entire clan for kingdom and prefers to better die in the battle himself than see his clan getting destroyed.Hrishikesha placed that magnificent chariot between the two armies, in front of Bhishma, Drona and all the other rulers of the earth and said, ‘O Partha! Look at those of the Kuru clan who are assembled here.’ There, Partha saw fathers and grandfathers, teachers and maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons and friends, fathers-in-law and well-wishers in those two assembled armies. ‘“Seeing them, all the friends and relatives assembled there, the son of Kunti was overcome with great pity. And in sadness, uttered the following words. ‘O Krishna! Having seen these relatives here, assembled with a desire to fight, my body is going numb and my mouth is going dry. My body is quivering and my body hair is standing up. My skin is burning and the Gandiva is slipping from my hands. O Keshava! I cannot stand and my mind is in a whirl. The omens that I see are ill ones. I don’t see any good that can come from killing one’s relatives in a war. O Krishna! I don’t want victory. Nor do I want the kingdom or happiness. O Govinda! What will we do with the kingdom or with pleasures or with life itself? Those for whose sake we want the kingdom and pleasures and happiness, they are gathered here in war, ready to give up their lives and their riches—preceptors, fathers, sons and grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law and other relatives. O Madhusudana! I don’t want to kill them, even if they kill me. Forget this earth, even for the kingdoms of the three worlds. O Janardana! What pleasure will we derive from killing the sons of Dhritarashtra? Although they are assassins, sin alone will be our lot if we kill them. Therefore, we cannot kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, with their friends. O Madhava! How can we be happy after killing our relatives? Although their minds are befuddled with greed and they do not see the sin that comes from opposing friends or from destroying the family line. O Janardana! We can see the sin that comes from destroying the family line. Why should we not have the knowledge to refrain from committing this sin? When the lineage is destroyed, the traditional family dharma is also destroyed. When dharma is destroyed, evil overwhelms the entire lineage. O Krishna! When evil arises, the women of the family become corrupted. O descendant of the Vrishnis! When the women are corrupted, hybrid castes are born. Hybrid castes ensure that the lineage, and those who destroyed the lineage, both go to hell. Because their ancestors fall and are deprived of offerings of funereal cakes and drink. From those sins of those who destroy the lineage and from hybrid castes being generated, the ancient dharma of the castes and the dharma of the family are both destroyed. O Janardana! If the family dharma is destroyed, those men are doomed to spend an eternity in hell. So we have heard. Alas! Because of our greed for the kingdom and for happiness, we have got ready to kill our relatives.Chapter 883 (23), Bhagavad Gita Parva, Section 63, Mahabharat This is the reason, Shri Krishna had to use different tactics like sometimes praising him for his valour to boast his confidence, other times to lift the weapon himself or sometimes praise the opponent so that he doesn't get too carried away by emotions and fight with equal might and balance of mind. In short, the Mahabharat battle was a personal one. Victory also meant loss of the family and near ones and more importantly, being the one who will take away their life for kingdom. This is what made him get a support - which was more of an emotional and mental one than support in using weapons. Shri Krishna was the perfect friend, mentor, guide and a support who ensured Arjuna's mental and emotional balance is maintained. It is very easy to fight a battle when there is no personal stakes involved. It is equally challenging when the battle is on a personal level involving our close ones.
column9: Defeating and killing are also two different things. At Matsya Arjuna defeated everyone but killed nobody. In the war, he killed many and it took time.

column1: What did you think after reading C.S. Lewis?
column3: I answered a similar question a while back[1]. Since then, I have had the opportunity of going through one of Lewis’s lesser known works — A Grief Observed. It is a very short book, written in the aftermath of his wife’s death (due to metastatic breast cancer), and is a poignant account of his struggle with indecision and self-doubt. In my previous answer, I made an (entirely unoriginal) observation about Lewis with regards to his non-fiction works:In these books, Lewis plays the role of neither the writer, nor the theologian. He is a rhetorician at his best, which is not surprising considering that much of the content of Mere Christianity first appeared as a radio broadcast, and The Screwtape Letters was written to warn the readers against temptation. […] All in all, I think Lewis was an interesting figure and an engaging theologian. It is just that his religious rhetoric is not persuasive enough for me.It is difficult to judge A Grief Observed with any degree of objectivity, and perhaps, it is not the right way in any case. I can not say with absolute certainty that I understand what Lewis was going through. I have lost family members. I have grieved for friends. I deal with death on a regular basis. But I am not married, and have never lost a romantic partner, thankfully. To use my previous answer as a springboard, in this book, Lewis is neither a theologian, nor a rhetorician. He is an ordinary man — angry and confused, trying to come to terms with an experience, which is overwhelming, frightening, and painful. His opening sentences are:No one ever told me that grief felt so like fear. I am not afraid, but the sensation is like being afraid. The same fluttering in the stomach, the same restlessness, the yawning. I keep on swallowing. At other times it feels like being mildly drunk, or concussed. There is a sort of invisible blanket between the world and me. I find it hard to take in what anyone says. Or perhaps, hard to want to take it in. It is so uninteresting. Yet I want the others to be about me. I dread the moments when the house is empty. If only they would talk to one another and not to me. There are moments, most unexpectedly, when something inside me tries to assure me that I don’t really mind so much, not so very much, after all. Love is not the whole of a man’s life. I was happy before I ever met H. I’ve plenty of what are called “resources”. People get over these things. Come, I shan’t do so badly. One is ashamed to listen to this voice but it seems for a little to be making out a good case. Then comes a sudden jab of red-hot memory and all this “common sense” vanishes like an ant in the mouth of a furnace.It is a feeling of being entangled in a web of unidentifiable emotions. A feeling of disorientation, which I too often see — though not necessarily comprehend — in people who have lost their loved ones. It is said that rationalism was the bedrock of 18th century Enlightenment. It was (and I guess it still is) hoped that it would subsequently supplant faith, heralding an era where reason would be the ultimate, and only, arbiter of the fate of humankind. Yet, what is rationalism if not another kind of faith: Faith in human reason, faith in the method, faith in empirical assessment of efficacy of the said method. And what do you do when tragedy strikes at the foundations of that faith. For some, the tragedy has to be some sort of world-shattering event — Reign of Terror, Holocaust, etc. But for most of us, it is the ordinary, everyday misfortunes — which leave no trace in the grand scheme of things — that stun us, and make us question the very reason of our existence in an incomprehensible world. This is exactly what Lewis does in A Grief Observed. He questions his faith. He questions the senselessness of the natural laws. He even questions his love for his deceased wife, when he remembers her suffering, and realizes that his grief would fade with time.What sort of a lover am I to think so much about my affliction and so much less about hers? Even the insane call, “Come back” is all for my own sake. I never even raised the question whether such a return, if it were possible, would be good for her. I want her back as an ingredient in the restoration of my past. Could I have wished her anything worse? Having got once through death, to come back and then, at some later date, have all her dying to do over again?The text is interspersed with Lewis’s theological musings as he attempts to reconcile his loss with his faith, though I am not sure if believers would be much comforted by his conclusions. Even if we are made in the image of God, we are but a handful of dust to begin with, and to dust we shall return in the end.Lewis married Helen Joy Davidman in 1956 — who was 19 years his junior, an American Jew, a divorcee, and a mother of two boys from her previous marriage. Lewis (along with his friend and fellow Inkling, J.R.R. Tolkien) was a celebrated Christian apologist, and the British Christian community was, to put it mildly, dismayed. Davidman was an accomplished writer in her own right, and couldn’t care less. On the issue of divorce, Lewis had once remarked that:A great many people seem to think that if you are a Christian yourself you should try to make divorce difficult for every one. [..] There ought to be two distinct kinds of marriage: one governed by the State with rules enforced on all citizens, the other governed by the church with rules enforced by her on her own members. The distinction ought to be quite sharp, so that a man knows which couples are married in a Christian sense and which are not. (This excerpt was later published in The Screwtape Letters.)His views drew a sharp criticism from the more religious British Christians. Tolkien, in fact, penned a letter in response, but had the good sense not to send it to Lewis. The following passage gives a glimpse of his conservative, and frankly myopic, views regarding marriage and divorce:Toleration of divorce – if a Christian does tolerate it – is toleration of a human abuse, which it requires special local and temporary circumstances to justify (as does the toleration of usury) – if indeed either divorce or genuine usury should be tolerated at all, as a matter of expedient policy.In his younger days, Lewis had often struggled with his faith. He finally converted to Christianity at the age of 33 (under the influence of Tolkien, no less). He was as firm a convert as any. And yet, I can not help but wonder how he endured these attacks from his fellow Christians, which were, in effect, directed towards his faith. I suppose it is impossible, even for a believer such as C.S. Lewis, to remain entirely unaffected by the opinions of those he held in high esteem. No man is an island, after all.I guess I digressed. I am wont to do that. Apologies. To answer this question, I will repeat verbatim what I said in my previous answer:All in all, I think Lewis was an interesting figure and an engaging theologian. It is just that his religious rhetoric is not persuasive enough for me.And add that:He was a human, with all the strengths and weaknesses which adorn our kind.Footnotes[1] Himanshu Mishra's answer to As an atheist, what did you think after reading C.S. Lewis?
column9: There’s actually an historic novel coming out next month about the Lewis/Davidman relationship. Becoming Mrs. Lewis: The Improbable Love Story of Joy Davidman and C. S. Lewis: Patti Callahan: 9780785224501: Amazon.com: Books

column1: Did Anne Frank deserve what she got?
column3: On March 28th, 1944 the Minister of the Dutch Government in exile, Gerrit Bolkestein, gave a speech. He called upon the people of the Netherlands to keep journals, diaries, and correspondences so that the atrocities and oppression of the Third Reich could be made public. Listening to that speech was a teenage German-Jewish girl named Anne Frank who had been keeping a diary for almost 2 years. Resolved and inspired she went through and began to make edits to publish what she wrote after the war ended. Though she never saw her diary published, it would become one of the most powerful pieces of literature ever to exist.Annelies Marie "Anne" Frank was born in Frankfurt in June 1929. The 2nd daughter of Otto and Edith Frank she grew up in relative comfort and ease with her older sister Margot. On June 12, 1942, for her 13th birthday, she was gifted a diary by her parents. Red and white with a checkered pattern the diary became a part of her life as she mused on friendship, family, and life as a teenage girl.By 1942 the Frank family had moved from Germany to the Netherlands to escape Hitler (they had moved there years earlier in the 1930s). They were safe there for years and Anne learned Dutch. Then the Nazis conquered the Netherlands and suddenly there was no escape for the Frank family. In mid-1942 the Nazis began rounding up Jews in the Netherlands. The Frank family planned to go into hiding on the 16th of July, 1 month and 4 days after Anne received the diary. Then on July 6th bad news struck as Anne’s older sister Margot received a “call up” letter from the Zentralstelle für jüdische Auswanderung (Central Office for Jewish Emigration- controlled by the SS). Now realizing they were on the radar, the Franks immediately went into hiding. They departed for the “Achterhuis” or “annex” where they could wait out Hitler for years if need be.The space itself was relatively large and not the tiny attic many imagine. Well concealed it was the perfect hiding place for the family. Trusted confidants such as Miep Gies, Victor Kugler, Johannes Kleiman, and Bep Voskuijl kept the family supplied with essentials while they set about living their lives confined to this 3-floor apartment/home/hiding place. They were soon joined by the Van Pels family. made up of Hermann Van Pel and his wife Auguste with their 16-year-old son Peter. Then finally the last member of the group was Fritz Pfeffer, a German-Jewish dentist also fleeing the NazisIn the annex, Anne did most of her writing. In one of the first entries from Sunday, June 14, 1942- about 3 weeks before the family went into hiding- Anne wrote in part about her friends.“Afterwards (her Birthday at school) they all danced and sang around me. When I got home Sanna was already there. Hannah came home with me after gym class…. Hannah and Sanna used to be my best friends. They used to say there goes Hanna Anne and Sanna”.Hannah Pick-Goslar was a very close friend of Anne’s at school.What makes Anne Frank so special is the connection it creates. It chronicles the horror Jews in Europe faced but through the lens of a real, relatable person. Anne’s choice to write as though it is a conversation, speaking to the reader, makes it even more powerful. It feels as though Anne is writing to you making the emotional impact hit all the harder. Anne expresses the misery of living in hiding, the evil actions taken against the Jewish people of Europe, the loss of her friends, and the constant terror of being discovered. Additionally, she writes about conflicts with her mother, her deep love for her father, her jealousy of her older sister, a desire to be her true self, and even her first kiss with Peter Van Pels. She even wonders about the nature of her love for Peter. Is it real or due to her lack of options in the annex? It is powerful, beautiful, and authentic. I love an academic overview of the Third Reich as much as the next historian but the “realness” of Anne’s writings makes it something that humanizes the victims of the Holocaust in a very real way.On Saturday July 15th, 1944 Anne Wrote“It's really a wonder that I haven't dropped all my ideals, because they seem so absurd and impossible to carry out. Yet I keep them, because in spite of everything I still believe that people are really good at heart. I simply can't build up my hopes on a foundation consisting of confusion, misery, and death. I see the world gradually being turned into a wilderness, I hear the ever approaching thunder, which will destroy us too, I can feel the sufferings of millions and yet, if I look up into the heavens, I think that it will all come right, that this cruelty too will end, and that peace and tranquillity will return again.On August 4th, 1944, a mere 3 weeks after this was written the annex was raided by SS-Oberscharführer Karl Silberbauer and a team of police. All 8 members of the annex were captured and after being questioned and detained, were deported to Auschwitz. Upon arrival, the men were separated from the women and so Otto was separated from his 2 daughters and wife. Of the 1,019 Jews who arrived at Auschwitz that day, 549 were sent to the gas chambers.Anne was stripped naked, disinfected, had her head shaved, and was tattooed. Once in the camp, Edith (her mother), Margot (her sister), and Anne were told about the selection process and gassing. Knowing that her father was older Anne believed he had been killed already and mourned as best she could. While at Auschwitz the now 15-year-old Anne did manual labor for 12–16 hours per day while being fed next to nothing. She developed scabies and eventually both Margot and Anne were quarantined into the “infirmary” where sick people were left to die. Edith Frank stopped eating entirely and would give her meager ration of food to her daughters through a hole in the wall of the infirmary. Anne recovered and Margot recovered enough not to be murdered and returned to manual labor. In October the 3 Frank women were scheduled to be transported to Bergen-Belsen as the Red Army advanced towards Auschwitz. Edith, having not eaten for weeks so that her daughters would survive, was too weak to travel and was left behind as Anne and Margot were forced onto another train. Edith would die a few days later of starvation and exhaustion.At Bergen-Belsen, Anne saw Hannah Pick-Goslar- the Hannah that was her “best friend” in that early entry. This happened sometime in January or the start of February 1945. Hannah and another friend of Anne’s also Bergen were shocked at the sight of Anne. The vibrant girl they knew had a shaved head, shivered uncontrollably, and was emaciated. Margot was bedridden and near death, being cared for by the Van Pels who had made it to Bergen also. In the short conversation they had with Anne they learned that Anne knew her parents were dead and no longer had a desire to survive.Anne would contract Typhus sometime in February of 1945- about a month before Bergen was freed. She was crammed into the infirmary with other sick patients where they were left to die. Her sister Margot, now deathly ill, fell out of bed and died from the shock of the impact. Alone in the world, emaciated, depressed, and sick, Anne died there in that dark miserable place.Unknown to Anne during her ordeal Otto had not been sent to the gas chambers and survived. He returned to the Netherlands and was informed that his wife and 2 daughters had died. Additionally, the Van Pels had all died along with Fritz Pfeffer making Otto the sole survivor. Miep Gies, one of those who had helped hide and support the family, had found the diary of Anne Frank after the annex was raided. She decided to keep it and when she was reunited with Otto she handed him the red and white checkered diary explaining that this is Anne’s legacy. Indeed it was to be her legacy. The diary would go on to be translated into 70 languages and sell 30 million copies- that was the first version. Anne Frank became one of the most well-known victims of the Holocaust. An innocent teenage girl, a kind loving person, who died alone and sick in a dingy room at only 15. So that answers the question. The direct answer is that “no” Anne Frank did not “deserve” her fate. It fills me with rage that such a question could be asked. That’s why I chose to write about Anne and her legacy rather than try to argue that a kind teenage girl deserved life. Did Anne deserve to become an internationally known figure for her writing? Absolutely. In the immortal words of Anne Frank,"Whoever is happy will make others happy too"Never forget.
column9: Deniers exist and since the publication of this work, they have challenged it. So let’s tackle that here and nowLIE: “Anne Frank’s diary was written in a ballpoint pen which did not exist in WW2” This is false- the entire work was written in a fountain pen. 2 scarps of paper and page numbering in the diary were written in a ballpoint pen but in a different hand writing-likely added by Otto Frank as he compiled the diary for publicationLIE “Otto Frank wrote the entire thing for money” The diary has been extensively studied by forensic analysts, handwriting experts, and historians and is 100% authentic. Anne attended school in Germany and the Netherlands where we have mountains of stuff she wrote while in school. The handwriting is a 100% match. The studies on this are EXTREME and complete.LIE “If the Holocaust was real how did Anne end up in a hospital” Anne ended up in a dingy overcrowded room with no doctors or medicine- basically left to die in quarantine by the Nazis. The bigger question is why was a 15-year-old girl in a concentration camp at all?LIE “Anne died because the Allied bombing cut off supplies to the camp” This is a common attempt to blame the Allies for what happened and is total BS. If it was the Allied bombing that caused a lack of medication then why did so many thousands die before bombing raids even kicked off? How did those in Auschwitz die in 1942 when the area hadn’t been touched by a bombing raid?LIE “It was edited to make the Nazis look bad and lie” This is one of those lies mixed with some truth. When Otto decided to publish the diary he excluded certain things- in particular musings on sex, details of Anne’s rather innocent relations with Peter, and negative things said about Anne’s mother Edith as the two were fighting at the time.Version “A” is the unedited original diary Anne wrote that was meant to be personalVersion “B” was edited by Anne herself after hearing that speech and deciding to publish it. She took out some things she thought were not interesting and added more detailsVersion “C” is the version Otto edited, excluding parts that were inappropriate for the diary of the 13-year-old girl at the time- mostly stuff related to sex and Edith Frank.In 1980 Otto willed the diary to the Netherlands State Institute for War Documentation. There- an extensive investigation was proven to be genuine.Thus we get to the “definitive edition” which includes versions A, B, and C as well as background on the situation of the family and the historical context.In 1998 5 previously unknown pages were found- which were added to the definitive addition.

column1: What is some advice for someone having to be a caregiver to their aging father?
column3: Dear Heather, what is most important in the care of your father, is setting appropriate boundaries of self-care. I explain this more in my book “The Soul of Caregiving, A Caregiver’s Guide to Healing and Transformation” soon to be released on Amazon next week. By setting appropriate boundaries of self-care, I mean to seek appropriate help, you don’t have to do it all by yourself, a common cultural myth, and that you recognize what you can and cannot do. Check with social and church agencies for help. Ask members of your family to assist. Take days off, get your hair and nails done, visit with friends, join a support group. I am attaching a story I include in the book of a person called Annabelle. Let me know if this is helpful. Annabelle was drawn to woundedness in unexpected ways in becoming the caregiver of her father suffering from Alzheimer’s. Miz Annabelle, as she likes to be called, found that as a caregiver to her father, she discovered something about herself that was hidden for years. True to her southern heritage, Annabelle excelled in gracious hospitality, manners, and service. Lordy, she would not have it any other way, as there was a tradition and a family name to uphold. Something we all experience keeping up with the Jones. Raised in Savannah, her mother taught her the fine delicate societal norms of being a Southern Belle, after all her name was Annabelle! To say she loved this role is an understatement. She flaunted it anytime she could, often amusing her father, whom she adored. When her mother died two years earlier, Annabelle assumed the primary caregiver duties. In the beginning, the obligation to help out became an act of loving service. She had fond memories of their having meaningful conversations. As weeks and months grew into a year and more, her resolve grew thin. “At first,” she said, “the obligation led to spending many hours with my dad.” This drew her to experience a deeper understanding of compassion, while at the same time, she noticed that her relationship had changed. She was no longer her father’s caregiver, but his caretaker. Notice the shift in tone, the shift from two adults communicating equally with each other to one of a parent-child relationship with Annabelle being the parent. Slowly, Annabelle realized that her father was slipping more and more away from her, present in the body, but no longer present mentally, emotionally, or spiritually. Annabelle was experiencing the first symptoms of anticipatory grief, when one begins to realize something has changed, like the person you love and have known somehow left the room, yet, is still physically present before you. Then one day when asked by her pastor how she was feeling, Annabelle sighed trying to sort out the emotion she felt, like unraveling a string from the ball of yarn she felt buried inside her. “I feel numb,” she responded. Yes numb, because she had been burning full throttle on all of her cylinders not realizing she was just worn out using up her reserve energy. Numbness implies a loss of energy, a loss of distinguishing one feeling from another because for so long, she had to stuff her feelings in deference to her father’s needs. She was beginning to experience the first signs of burnout. One feeling that did emerge was she often felt guilty. Was she doing enough? With her pastor’s help, Annabelle started questioning, “Am I selfish, if I consider my own needs?” No easy answer as being overwhelmed clouded her judgment. She was consumed in meeting the needs of her father. If she only tried a little harder, spent more time, tried more remedies, would that give her more time with him? Unconsciously, she was trying to fill in a hole that had no bottom, preventing her from experiencing the eventual loss of her father. We caregivers sometimes fail to recognize, as the ancients did before us, we are not gods. Being addicted to perfectionism only becomes self-defeating. The walls of her Southern façade couldn’t protect her. Annabelle pondered. And then she began to question, where does selfishness come from? “Why would I blame myself or feel guilty about meeting my own needs?” she asked. Consider what she discovered in exploring the definition of selfish: inconsiderate, thoughtless, ungenerous, self-indulgent, uncharitable, and self-aggrandizing to name a few. Clearly, this was not the case. If anything, she was selfless, disregarding herself and her own interests. Selfless to such a point, that she silenced the inner promptings of her Soul to care for herself. Important to note that it was only in this place of questioning that Annabelle had come to this juncture. The illness of her father and Annabelle’s experience of her own lack of self-care were now her teachers. Annabelle learned earlier in life that wearing the mask of a Southern Belle, implied that self-care was something softies did. A familiar trap most caregivers fall into. While the relationship changed between Annabelle and her father, he still became the catalyst that brought Annabelle’s walls of perfectionism, like the walls of Jericho, come crumbling down. She no longer had to be a steel magnolia, as she was experiencing what a wounded healer is, that gave her permission, now for the first time in her life, to recognize her own vulnerability, her fears, and her limitations and at the same time discover the hidden strengths she had for personal growth and transformation.

column1: Why can't my kids play by themselves in our neighborhood the way I did when I was a kid?
column3: Jane Chin and Webb Smith both have good info. To add to that, I'll reinforce that the media has really pushed the idea of possibilities out there, but the sensationalism of strangers vs. family members makes for a lopsided coverage. Almost all the family abuse, sexual or physical, I have dealt with over the years never made the news. So Jane is very correct when she says it is more family members than strangers. I remember when the big scare went out in the late 70's and all of a sudden there were all these kids tied to their parents with straps and dog leashes. Our mothers used to tell us to just go outside and it was our responsibility to entertain ourselves. We created everything for the most part out of what was available. During "Sand lot" baseball, football, basket ball, two captains picked teams one at a time so you had a chance to be on a winning teem 50% of the time. Even if you were crap as a player. The idea was to play. Now as Jane Chin says, It is all about winning. And almost all the toys are for indoors. The game boxes and movies allow for nothing but isolation. TV of anything to entertain them on demand. Thing is, notice the kids get very tight when they play video games. That is because they are losing 10-20 times more than winning. Sometimes a lot more. And as soon as they do win, it is to another level where they start losing again. For my self as a hypnotist, it is a set up. What has more familiarity on the emotional front? That's who you're becoming. A person who is full of emotional losses will feel they need to win at any cost. There also is the access to friends as never before. Texting, Facebook, twitter, phoning. All this is easier than going over there. I can get my social needs done with out leaving the comforts of home. There is music available at any time to distract me from my thoughts and that music is pumping ideas into me with a beat that most are not even aware of. I have had some girls who could sing the lyrics to popular songs, get them written down, have them read them, and then they were appalled. Somehow the real meanings don't register when listened to in the trance of the music. We also have a society that fell into the belief; you should avoid being bothered, instead of heeding the old slogan;" No Pain no Gain." We then developed a group of over-indulged kids who truly believes the world should just give them what they demand. It has been their experience so far. There were no real penalties to pay. It also is interesting, in a paradoxical way, that the outdoor sports for a lot of kids is now extreme. They are doing things to get dangerously hurt, whatever the conveyance. And they film it I helped out a kid whose mother always ran interference for him when ever he got in trouble in school or out. His brother was always the one in trouble and she didn't like him. So when the good kid was a senior, he got in trouble for drugs. He did juvenile detention and she bailed him ASAP. A year after that, she died. He got into more drugs and trouble then went to prison. I took a video of his dads funeral because he couldn't attend. By now he has spent more time locked up than free. And you know, in some ways it is like he grew up, because all the real stuff is taken care of for him. He's dependent. Webb's statements about a similar numbers of sociopaths I take issue with. Having dealt with criminals most my adult life. I have seen a shift in society that is reflected in a number of arenas. I started hitch-hiking cross-country when I was 16. I used to pick up hitch-hikers. Won't do either any more. Too dangerous. Not that it wasn't then, just more so now. The child porn was at an all time low by the early 80's. When the internet got popular, it started climbing and now is at such an unbelievable level, it has certainly increased the perversion. Notice the law typically doesn't find a dozen pictures on hard drives, it's more is like 10,000. The deviance on every front has expanded and the more it is suppressed the way it is, The more it lures. A quick example was about a decade ago when they were working on new internet tags for addresses. Dot SEX was proposed. The conservatives voted it down as it would be obvious people were going for sex stuff. It would have let filters and people that wanted it, to deal with stuff straight. Much like the constable who set up the red light districts in London years ago. But it was too blatant and they believe you can control behavior by just outlawing it. War on sex, war on poverty, war on drugs, war on immigrants. Yah, those are working. A friend of mine had her dad sneak across for the seventh time at 86 with a walker. How? A coyote helped him. By just the ratio of more humans, socio-pathology has increased, but I also see more deviance because of the hypocrisy that permeates society so much now. So, why can't kids play like they used to? Media.Thinking strangers are most likely to abduct or abuse the kids.Loss of neighbored playing and insistence on adult supervised win-lose games.Decline of outside toys except for extreme sports.Proliferation of Movies at home and TV on demand.Proliferation of gaming systems.Facebook, Twitter, texting and phone time.Computer time with expanded internet capability.Music is always available.Over protected, Over indulged.More sociopaths.
column9: Awesome answer, Mike, I didn't think about the fact that more toys are made for "indoor" play than outdoors these days, I'll pay attention to this next time in the store, I bet you're right! Actually even outdoor play is "organized" play now... observe the proliferation of franchises like "My Gym". I understand the importance of structure for young children, but we're going overboard with structure, I think. No more exploratory play!

column1: How can I get over a break up?
column3: Getting over a breakup can be a challenging process, but there are steps you can take to heal and move forward. Here are some strategies that may help:Allow yourself to grieve: It's natural to feel a range of emotions after a breakup, including sadness, anger, and confusion. Allow yourself to experience these emotions without judgment and give yourself time to grieve the loss of the relationship.Reach out for support: Don't hesitate to lean on friends and family members for support during this difficult time. Talking to trusted loved ones can provide comfort, perspective, and encouragement as you navigate the healing process.Take care of yourself: Focus on self-care and prioritize your physical, emotional, and mental well-being. Make sure you're getting enough rest, eating healthily, exercising regularly, and engaging in activities that bring you joy and relaxation.Limit contact with your ex: While it may be tempting to maintain contact with your ex, especially if you're hoping to reconcile or remain friends, it's often best to give yourself some space and distance to heal. Consider setting boundaries and limiting communication until you've had time to process your feelings.Focus on personal growth: Use this time as an opportunity for self-reflection and personal growth. Consider exploring new hobbies, setting goals for yourself, or pursuing activities that you're passionate about. Invest in your own growth and development as an individual.Practice forgiveness: Forgiveness can be a powerful tool for healing and letting go of resentment. This doesn't necessarily mean reconciling with your ex or condoning their behavior, but rather, letting go of negative emotions and finding peace within yourself.Seek professional help if needed: If you're struggling to cope with the breakup or experiencing intense emotions that are impacting your daily life, consider seeking support from a therapist or counselor. A mental health professional can provide guidance, support, and coping strategies to help you navigate this challenging time.Remember that healing from a breakup takes time, and it's okay to seek support and take things one day at a time. Be patient and kind to yourself as you work through the process of moving on.

column1: What was the first thing you did after a break-up? I am most likely to be single again, and am looking for answers that can help me do the ‘first right thing’.
column3: First of all, I am really sorry to hear this. Breakups of any kind, are never a pleasant experience and I speak this from a first hand experience. There will be a myriad of things going through your mind in this phase and it is important to stay calm, collected, sane and in the company of people whom you trust and who love you. I was lucky to have immense support from my colleagues, my boss, my parents and my close friends. I thank all of them till date for being with me when I desperately needed a support system. I will share with you an email that my Dad had sent me after my breakup. It made me cry but it also made me strong and look forward to life beyond and after the relationship. I hope it will help you too. Here goes: It’s never easy when significant relationship ends. Whatever the reason for the split – and whether or not you wanted it – the breakup of a long-term, committed relationship can turn your whole world upside down and trigger all sorts of painful and unsettling feelings. But there are things you can do to get through this difficult time. Even in the midst of the sadness and stress of breakup, you have an opportunity to learn from the experience and grow into a stronger, wiser person. Healing after breakup Why do breakups hurt so much, even when the relationship is no longer good? A breakup is painful because it represents the loss, not just of the relationship, but also of shared dreams and commitments. Romantic relationships begin on a high note of excitement and hope for the future. When these relationships fail, we experience profound disappointment, stress, and grief. A breakup launches us into uncharted territory. Everything is disrupted: your routine and responsibilities, your home, your relationships with extended family and friends, and even your identity. A breakup brings uncertainty about the future. What will life be like without your partner? Will you find someone else? Will you end up alone? These unknowns often seem worse than an unhappy relationship. Recovering from a breakup is difficult. However, it’s important to know (and to keep reminding yourself) that you can and will move on. But healing takes time, so be patient with yourself. Coping with Breakup Recognize that it’s OK to have different feelings. It’s normal to feel sad, angry, exhausted, frustrated, and confused—and these feelings can be intense. You also may feel anxious about the future. Accept that reactions like these will lessen over time. Even if the relationship was unhealthy, venturing into the unknown is frightening. Give yourself a break. Give yourself permission to feel and to function at a less than optimal level for a period of time. You may not be able to be quite as productive on the job or care for others in exactly the way you’re accustomed to for a little while. No one is superman or superwoman; take time to heal, regroup, and re-energize. Don’t go through this alone. Sharing your feelings with friends and family can help you get through this period. Consider joining a support group where you can talk to others in similar situations. Isolating yourself can raise your stress levels, reduce your concentration, and get in the way of your work, relationships, and overall health. Don’t be afraid to get outside help if you need it. Allow yourself to grieve the loss of the relationshipGrief is a natural reaction to loss, and the breakup of a love relationship involves multiple losses:Loss of companionship and shared experiences (which may or may not have been consistently pleasurable)Loss of support, be it financial, intellectual, social, or emotionalLoss of hopes, plans, and dreams (can be even more painful than practical losses)Allowing yourself to feel the pain of these losses may be scary. You may fear that your emotions will be too intense to bear, or that you’ll be stuck in a dark place forever. Just remember that grieving is essential to the healing process. The pain of grief is precisely what helps you let go of the old relationship and move on. And no matter how strong your grief, it won’t last forever.Tips for grieving after a breakup: Don’t fight your feelings – It’s normal to have lots of ups and downs, and feel many conflicting emotions, including anger, resentment, sadness, relief, fear, and confusion. It’s important to identify and acknowledge these feelings. While these emotions will often be painful, trying to suppress or ignore them will only prolong the grieving process. Talk about how you’re feeling – Even if it is difficult for you to talk about your feelings with other people, it is very important to find a way to do so when you are grieving. Knowing that others are aware of your feelings will make you feel less alone with your pain and will help you heal. Journaling can also be a helpful outlet for your feelings. Remember that moving on is the end goal – Expressing your feelings will liberate you in a way, but it is important not to dwell on the negative feelings or to over-analyze the situation. Getting stuck in hurtful feelings like blame, anger, and resentment will rob you of valuable energy and prevent you from healing and moving forward. Remind yourself that you still have a future – When you commit to another person, you create many hopes and dreams. It’s hard to let these dreams go. As you grieve the loss of the future you once envisioned, be encouraged by the fact that new hopes and dreams will eventually replace your old ones. Know the difference between a normal reaction to a breakup and depression - Grief can be paralyzing after a breakup, but after a while, the sadness begins to lift. Day by day, and little by little, you start moving on. However, if you don’t feel any forward momentum, you may be suffering from depression. Reach out to others for support through the grieving process Support from others is critical to healing after a breakup. You might feel like being alone, but isolating yourself will only make this time more difficult. Don’t try to get through this on your own. Reach out to trusted friends and family members. People who have been through painful breakups can be especially helpful. They know what it is like and they can assure you that there is hope for healing and new relationships. Spend time with people who support, value, and energize you. As you consider who to reach out to, choose wisely. Surround yourself with people who are positive and who truly listen to you. It’s important that you feel free to be honest about what you’re going through, without worrying about being judged, criticized, or told what to do. Get outside help if you need it. If reaching out to others doesn’t come naturally, consider seeing a counselor or joining a support group. The most important thing is that you have at least one place where you feel comfortable opening up. Cultivate new friendships. If you feel like you have lost your social network along with the breakup, make an effort to meet new people. Join a networking group or special interest club, take a class, get involved in community activities, or volunteer at a school, place of worship, or other community organization. Taking care of yourself after relationship breakup A relationship breakup is a highly stressful, life-changing event. When you’re going through the emotional wringer and dealing with major life changes, it’s more important than ever to take care of yourself. The strain and upset of a major breakup can leave you psychologically and physically vulnerable. Treat yourself like you’re getting over the flu. Get plenty of rest, minimize other sources of stress in your life, and reduce your workload if possible. Learning to take care of yourself can be one of the most valuable lessons you learn following breakup. As you feel the emotions of your loss and begin learning from your experience, you can resolve to take better care of yourself and make positive choices going forward. Self-care tips: Make time each day to nurture yourself. Help yourself heal by scheduling daily time for activities you find calming and soothing. Go for a walk in nature, listen to music, enjoy a hot bath, get a massage, read a favorite book, take a yoga class, or savor a warm cup of tea. Pay attention to what you need in any given moment and speak up to express your needs. Honor what you believe to be right and best for you even though it may be different from what your ex or others want. Say "no" without guilt or angst as a way of honoring what is right for you. Stick to a routine. A relationship breakup can disrupt almost every area of your life, amplifying feelings of stress, uncertainty, and chaos. Getting back to a regular routine can provide a comforting sense of structure and normalcy. Take a time out. Try not to make any major decisions in the first few months after a breakup, like starting a new job or moving to a new city (in our case it is joining to a family, so job changing is actually family joining but new job demands proving your capability). If you can, wait until you’re feeling less emotional so that you can make better decisions. Avoid using alcohol, drugs, or food to cope. When you’re in the middle of a breakup, you may be tempted to do anything to relieve your feelings of pain and loneliness. But using alcohol, drugs, or food as an escape is unhealthy and destructive in the long run. It’s essential to find healthier ways of coping with painful feelings. Explore new interests. A breakup is a beginning as well as an end. Take the opportunity to explore new interests and activities. Pursuing fun, new activities gives you a chance to enjoy life in the here-and-now, rather than dwelling on the past. Making healthy choices: Eat well, sleep well, and exercise When you’re going through the stress of a breakup, healthy habits easily fall by the wayside. You might find yourself not eating at all or overeating your favorite junk foods. Exercise might be harder to fit in because of the added pressures at home and sleep might be elusive. But all of the work you are doing to move forward in a positive way will be pointless if you don’t make long-term healthy lifestyle choices. Learning important lessons from a breakup In times of emotional crisis, there is an opportunity to grow and learn. Just because you are feeling emptiness in your life right now, doesn’t mean that nothing is happening or that things will never change. Consider this period a time-out, a time for sowing the seeds for new growth. You can emerge from this experience knowing yourself better and feeling stronger. In order to fully accept a breakup and move on, you need to understand what happened and acknowledging the part you played. It’s important to understand how the choices you made affected the relationship. Learning from your mistakes is the key to not repeating them. Some questions to ask yourself:Step back and look at the big picture. How did you contribute to the problems of the relationship?Do you tend to repeat the same mistakes or choose the wrong person in relationship after relationship?Think about how you react stress and deal with conflict and insecurities. Could you act in a more constructive way?Consider whether or not you accept other people the way they are, not the way they could or “should” be.Examine your negative feelings as a starting point for change. Are you in control of your feelings, or are they in control of you?You’ll need to be honest with yourself during this part of the healing process. Try not to dwell on who is to blame or beat yourself up over your mistakes. As you look back on the relationship, you have an opportunity to learn more about yourself, how you relate to others, and the problems you need to work on. If you are able to objectively examine your own choices and behavior, including the reasons why you chose your former partner, you’ll be able to see where you went wrong and make better choices next time. Breaking up a relationship is extremely hard on both the person who is initiating the break-up as well as the person who is at the receiving end. Whatever the circumstances, when a break up occurs, it breaks your heart. The abrupt breakup usually carries a lot of emotional baggage. Let's find out how you can do further to deal with this situation. Accept the end - Once the break up happens, you need to put it behind you and cope with the negative feelings that well inside you. The most important thing is to accept it. Do not cling onto the hope that a miracle would happen and things would go back to normal. Do not hope that the break-up would be reversed by some magic and you would be back together as if nothing happened. This would make things unbearable for you. Rather, you should accept it. Accept that your relationship is over. Accept that the other person would not be there for you any more. You cannot hope to erase the pain unless you face it head on. The best starting point to getting over a breakup is to first accept fully and completely that the relationship has come to an end permanently and that there is no looking back from here on. If there is even the slightest denial in your mind or heart there is little hope for a complete recovery. Through denial you are only going to prolong your suffering. Respect yourself - Never blame yourself for a break-up. Be kind to yourself and your feelings. Do not punish yourself and do not entertain thoughts of ending your life or anything as drastic. There is life after a break up and chances are that the right person is there out looking for you just at this very moment. Don't you want to meet that special person that God has created only for you? Respect yourself enough to give yourself another chance to be happy. Pamper yourself for a while - It hurts when you live through a break up. You need to replace the negative feelings created in your heart (and which influences every part of the body) with positive feelings. The easiest way to create positive feelings is to indulge in yourself. Do something you love - go to the movies; go for a world tour or a great tourist destination for a great vacation; treat yourself for a special body massage or beauty treatment; start a new hobby; binge of some food you love; buy some excellent jewelry; etc. Center all your attention on your pleasure for a while. Wash away your hurt by indulging yourself. Forget the revenge mode - Falling in and falling out of love happens. It is sad - but it happens. Accept this as a fact and do not seek revenge for being set aside for another person. Break up are usually emotionally shattering because they are interpreted as rejection. However, it is not rejection. It is a way to say that "I am not getting what I want from you." This is fine - nothing personal. Everybody is entitled to their opinion and happiness. Respect this choice and forget revenge. When you hate or plot for revenge, you can never let go of the past. Remember, "Revenge is the confirmation of pain." It also ties you up with the past - never allowing you to really move ahead. Do you really want that? Forgive – There is so much power in true forgiveness that it has the capacity to heal the deepest of wounds. Hate, resentment, anger and spite would be the normal emotions you will feel towards your ex after the breakup. But ask yourself if you are willing to pollute your life with these negative feelings. You can never recover from these feelings fully unless you forgive your ex and yourself for everything that happened. Time is the best healer - Understand that it takes time for you to stop feeling the hurt n your heart. Give yourself the time to heal. Do not hurry the process along as if you do, the clogged emotions would erupt one day in a harmful way. Realize that the hurt would leave you gradually just as a wound would gradually heal. Move on - Aim ahead. Do all that you find possible to move on as normally as possible. Keep yourself surrounded by well-meaning friends and family with whom you could openly converse regarding your feelings. The more you are able to vocalize these feelings, the better you will be able to deal with a breakup. Everything happens for the good - Understand that everything happens for the good. Use this event as a learning measure for self growth. This is just a step in your journey towards finding the true love of your life. After the initial burst of emotions, there is bound to be some calm. This is the time for some clear introspection so that you don’t have to go through this suffering again. Question your suffering –Here are the questions you should ask yourself, it helps to write down the answers instead of just mulling it over in the mind. Can I be really sure that this break up is a bad thing for me? Can find out at least 5 good reasons why this breakup is a good thing. You will be amazed at sense of relief and peace you will feel if you work through the above questions with an open heart. Be sure to write out 5 reasons even if you find it difficult to come up with even one initially. Self inquiry is the best way to get over a breakup because it eats through all our misplaced thoughts that cause suffering. Let the tears flow – Whatever be your gender, sorrow will lead to tears. Suppressing the urge to cry can lead to harmful side effects. Crying allows the body to expend the suppressed pain and release the negative energy. You will notice a feeling of lightness once you cry through a painful experience. Getting over a breakup can be emotionally draining and it’s important to be gentle on yourself by letting go of the need to control your emotions. I wish you all the strength and support to overcome this phase and start the next chapter of your life with renewed enthusiasm, liveliness and optimism. God Bless, Stay Khush!
column9: Yep “God Bless, Stay Khush!”, I like this last line you included the most vital element of the answer. Of course the other parts of the answer was petty good to read. Krishna (God) bless you too sir. Hare Krishna

column1: Can an elderly parent refuse to go to a nursing facility, and if so, what would be the next options?
column3: Yes. Possibly no options l. Let's start with definitions. In California, for example, "elderly" is defined as age 59 and older. These days many people work to age 70 or older. Gee, we also just elected two elderly men in a row as US president. There is only one way you can legally force someone into care:Court ordered Conservatorship that the person is deemed incompetent to make their own decisions.OR - a hospital or doctor releases a patient direct to care facility because he/she cannot take care of him/ herself anymore, such as dressing, bathing, restroom, etc.in #1, there are three ways all requiring two doctors with one being a psychiatrist to support Conservatorship if it is a mental health issue. If someone is in a coma then doctors will suffice. Person has to be at risk of hurting others, themselves or lastly can't take care of themselves any longer. The last is rarely used and that is why many people who can't care for themselves live in vehicles or on the street. So - Why would someone not want to go into adult residential care.Fear of facing they likely won't come out again, that they will die there or in hospital.Fear of loss of contact with family. Approximately 75% of residents never were visited by family even before COVID. Zoom is helping change this by providing more contact.Fear of losing control of assets or their things that move with them. Theft is assumed as normal in many adult residential care facilities. Do not send valuable things there, including furniture. I even went through this - lent a computer desk to my boyfriend's dad. Within two weeks the facility changed his room and his cool desk went missing! It was a loner and gee, what a surprise the facility couldn't explain its disappearance even though staff moved him.Fear of change - Giving up what has been home for a long timeFear of losing ability to leave an inheritance. Adult residential care is $3800–4200/ mo average for assisted living and $5000–7000/ mo for memory care. Most of the time a parent's home is signed over to the care facility. Then if person is bumped out or dies in 5–7 years, rarely are their refunds to an estate.Feeling out of control because he/she is losing memory and having problems focusingDementia patients may fear losing access to going outside to walk.WHAT ARE THE OPTIONS if the elderly person is diagnosed with Dementia or Alzheimer's and is wandering, leaving on water or turning in stove burners then walking away or going to sleep, this is potential self harm or harm to others. Then it is time to take away car keys and get a court ordered Conservatorship. It is a lot of paperwork… California it was well over 100 pages I have compiled a multitude of forms and evidence. It is a full time "job" for weeks staying focused. And after judge rules for a Conservatorship, you celebrate maybe for a day - because now on top of finding a adult residential new home for your person ( if you are the conservator, otherwise the court appoints and pays for a lawyer), you have less than 364 days to prepare for the next time you must be back in court. Most states or provinces require the Conservator / Committee to be monitored monthly and the decision reviewed yearly. FOR THE ELDERLY OR SENIOR If you are being pressured by a family member to go to a care facility and you want protection, talk to your doctor. He/she cab help you and you also want to hire an eldercare lawyer to protect your rights. The lawyer and doctor can be your best assets to protect you if you are quite capable of living alone. FUTURE On the other side of COVID risk, I think more entrepreneurs and aging independents will embrace adult assisted living as an awesome way of life. I have traveled and done hotel living. Loved it. Keep working and order room service. Sweet! Housekeeping, utilities, cable snd Internet built in to one bill. Talk about a stress free life! FAMILY MEMBERS OF ELDERLY Social Security / SSI accepting facilities can be scary places with low ratings. Contact your licensing agency and review fines against facilities for free. You need to know whether they are fined for paperwork being a few days late, or, were they fined for dangerous situations.
column9: Wait, 59? Elderly? Wow. My mom is 81 and still works part time. I'm not there yet but, I thought maybe 70, 90 for sure is elder status, but, it really depends. Use it or lose it has been my motto since I hit 55. So I continue to use everything. Interesting post. Thank you

column1: What is something you saw while on an airplane that you couldn't believe?
column3: There was a domestic flight our family along with the extended members took to go up north for a vacation many years ago. My children and nieces, five of them, were aged between seven and eleven and obviously we had to pay attention to them and needless to say they needed to sit with an adult [family member] who could look after them while the plane was in flight. Straightforward and easy thing to do you would say and I would agree. Kids loved to stick together and unaware of safety regulations, we parents made sure we did the right thing by following the procedure. I made a point to my wife that our boy and his nephew, both aged nine, had to be separated and either me or she took that seat. To my mild astonishment, she seemed reluctant and said I shouldn't be too worried. I reminded her of the procedure and she took no heed to it. At that point, I made a move to intervene and would ask the niece to move so had to ask their apparently clueless parents to take care of their boy. His father, who spent two years as steward with United Airlines insisted it was ok and they boys could sit side by side on their own. Other family members overheard the conversation and chose not to swap seats, dismissing it as petty issue. I looked at him and said you were a steward and you said this is ok. He was upset but kept to his decision that if they wanted to be together so we should let them. Well, you know an idiot when you see one and this is it. My wife knew I was not one who puts up with ignorance or carelessness so she sensed I would take his brother to task so she urged me rather cluelessly to take it easy. I gave her the look of “are you losing your mind?” Raising my voice, I said I expected the kids to be taken care of properly by us who were their carers. We could comply with the procedure first and foremost. Their safety was of paramount concern to me though it might not be the case for them. He was clearly upset but his thinking clouded more by him losing face not reasons. I was seething myself, bewildered and upset by a poor judgement. I was thinking I would take better care of his son had he travelled with us. Shortly a flight attendant came and advised us to move one of them and I then moved to sit with my son. They swap seats and took their son without protesting that it would be ok to keep them there. Me as myself, I looked him in the eyes and said, “you're such an idiot”. And that idiot almost jumped at me. Yes, I could sit idly throughout and waited and saw it sorted out properly. The one thing that prevented it was a brainless response of his — an educated person who frequently flew as passenger and for a few years was professionally hired and tasked with taking care of thousands of passengers on an airplane. It’s a known fact that many Thai people are careless when it comes to safety regulations, traffic law and so on, incurring huge human and financial losses. This gross ignorance took place.even with a well-trained individual who simply did the job well to get paid and not because he was aware of the safety risks. Once he left the position, he became his own self again. United’s frequent fliers who perhaps flew with this guys across the Pacific should consider yourself lucky. It was a great move by United, also due to mounting losses, which decided to let him go.
column9: Sorry Komson, it seems to me that you made a very big fuss about not very much.
